# Patrologia Latina, Vol. 110

## Complete Course of Patrology

Or, a complete, uniform, comprehensive, convenient, economical universal library of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III: a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that existed during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with certain manuscript codices, corrected with the greatest care; continually elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the preceding three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating its subject matter; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also by works possessing some authority and influence with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which everything that each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is immediately apparent to the reader which Fathers commented on the individual texts of the books of Scripture, and in which places of their works they did so.

An edition incomparably accurate and easily preferable to all others when one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reissued works, the very convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and especially this collection itself: a single, systematic, and chronological gathering of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but for the first time assembled in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

## Second Series

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III, prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the universal library of the clergy, or of complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

The Patrology is printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. Two hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; three hundred volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for eight hundred francs. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

## From the Year 826 to the Year 844

# Homilies (C)*

## I. Homilies on the Principal Feasts, and Also on the Virtues

### Preface to Haistulf, Archbishop

[Cols. 0009–0010A]

To the holy and venerable Father Haistulf, archbishop, Rabanus, a lowly servant of the servants of God.

Obeying your commands, most blessed Father, I have composed a sermon for preaching to the people concerning everything that I believed necessary for them. First, I have treated what observance they ought to maintain on the principal feasts that occur throughout the year: namely, that, while free from worldly work, they should not become empty of the divine word, but, recognizing God’s will, should strive to fulfill it in their actions.

Next, I wove for them a discourse on various kinds of virtues: faith, hope, and charity; chastity, continence, and the other kinds of virtue—how, by desiring and preserving them, they might please God and receive eternal life in heaven with the holy angels.

Afterward I added another sermon concerning the various errors and enticements of vices by which the ancient enemy deceives and cheats the human race: namely, the evils of pride and vainglory, anger, envy, deceit, avarice, gluttony, and fornication, together with their like, so that Christ’s sheep might know how to escape the bites of the fiercest wolves and the most savage dragon, and how to avoid dangers once foreseen.

But because, owing to various intervening occupations, I was unable to publish these together, I sent them to you separately at different times, written on separate sheets as opportunity dictated. I ask you, therefore, to order them all to be gathered into a single volume and to have this letter placed before them, so that readers may know that, if they find anything useful in them, it is not the diligence of my own effort but the obedience owed to your command.

I earnestly beg you also, Father, as a kind of reward, to grant this favor to my smallness: whenever you entrust this little work for reading or preaching to any of those subject to you, whether your subjects or devout persons, command them to assist my frailty with their prayers before the most just Judge, so that by his grace I may continue longer in the course of the present life and may deserve to reach future blessedness happily.

May the divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ deign always to preserve your blessedness unharmed, holy Father. Remember us.

# First Homily: Before the Nativity of Our Lord Jesus Christ

[Cols. 0010A–0012A]

As the most sacred solemnity is now approaching on which our Savior mercifully wished to be born among human beings, dearest brothers, consider attentively how we ought to prepare ourselves for the coming of such great power, so that we may deserve to receive our King and Lord joyfully and gladly, with glory and praises, and to exult with rejoicing in his presence among the blessed assemblies of the saints, rather than, rejected by him because of our foulness, deserve eternal shame among sinners.

Therefore I ask and admonish you to labor, as far as we are able, with God’s help, so that on that day we may approach the Lord’s altar with a sincere and pure conscience, a clean heart, and a chaste body, and receive his body and blood not for judgment but for the healing of our soul.

For our life consists in the body of Christ. The Lord himself said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6). Let the person who wishes to have life therefore change his life. For if he does not change his sinful life so as to live justly, he will receive the true life—which is the body of Christ—for judgment, and will be corrupted by it rather than sanctified, killed rather than given life.

Thus the Apostle said: “Whoever eats the body of the Lord and drinks his blood unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Corinthians 11).

Although it is fitting that we should at all times be adorned and resplendent with good works, especially on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, as he himself said in the Gospel (Matthew 5), our good works ought to shine before people, so that God may be glorified in everything.

Consider, brothers: if an earthly king, or any powerful householder, invited you to his birthday celebration, in what sort of garments would you take care to appear adorned—how new, how clean, how splendid—so that neither their age nor their cheapness nor any foulness might offend the eyes of the one inviting you.

With such zeal, therefore, insofar as you are able and with Christ’s help, strive to have your souls arranged with various ornaments of virtue and adorned with the jewels of simplicity and the flowers of sobriety, so that with a secure conscience they may proceed to the solemnity of the eternal feast, that is, the Nativity of the Lord and Savior: shining with chastity, resplendent with charity, white with almsgiving, radiant with justice and humility, and bright above all with love of God.

For if Christ the Lord knows that you are thus prepared to celebrate his Nativity, he himself will deign to come—not merely to visit your souls, but also to rest in them and dwell in them forever, as it is written: “For behold, I shall come and dwell and walk among them, and they shall be my people, and I shall be their God, says the Lord God” (2 Corinthians 6; Isaiah 52).

Oh, how blessed is the soul that by good works deserves to receive Christ as guest and inhabitant—always joyful, always cheerful, always glad, and estranged from every horror of vice. Conversely, how unhappy is that conscience which has bloodied itself with such evil works that Christ cannot rest in it, but the devil begins to rule there.

If the medicine of repentance does not quickly come to such a soul’s aid, it is abandoned by the light and seized by darkness; it is emptied of sweetness and filled with bitterness; death attacks it, and it is separated from life.

Yet let no one who is such despair of the Lord’s compassion or be broken by deadly desperation. Rather, let him hasten to repentance; and while the wounds of his sins are still fresh and burning, let him apply to himself the healing medicine of tears. For our physician is almighty, and he is accustomed to heal our wounds in such a way that he does not allow even traces of scars to remain.

Let us only have faith in him, devote ourselves always to good works as far as we are able, and never despair of his mercy.

Thinking constantly on these matters, dearest brothers, let those who are good strive, with God’s grace, to persevere in good works. For “it is not the one who begins, but the one who perseveres to the end who will be saved” (Matthew 10).

Those who recognize that they are slow to give alms, quick to anger, and headlong in the practice of lust should, with the Lord’s help, hasten to rescue themselves from evil, so that they may deserve to accomplish what is good; so that, when the day of judgment arrives, they may not be punished with the ungodly and sinners, but may deserve to reach eternal rewards with the just and merciful.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# Homily II: Also Before the Nativity of the Lord

[Cols. 0012A–0013B]

Whenever, dearest brothers, you desire to celebrate one of the feasts of the saints that are observed throughout the year, determine with all zeal and care to prepare yourselves with the adornment of sacred virtues, so that you may be made worthy of the heavenly banquet and of the fellowship of the saints, with whom you desire to rejoice.

At the divine table, therefore, human food is not found; rather, the bread of angels is set forth, as it is written: “He gave them bread from heaven; human beings ate the bread of angels” (Psalm 77).

Let a person, according to the Apostle, test himself, and thus eat of that bread and drink from the cup (1 Corinthians 11).

For although Christ our Lord rose after his passion and ascended into heaven, nevertheless, as we believe, he observes and carefully considers how each of his servants strives to prepare and arrange himself—without avarice, anger, pride, or lust—for the celebration of the solemnities of his saints, and especially for his Nativity. According to how he sees each person adorned with good works, so he distributes to that person the grace of his mercy.

If he sees someone approaching his table clothed in the light of charity, adorned with the pearls of justice or mercy, chaste, humble, kind, merciful, gentle, and sober, he will distribute his body and blood to him through the ministry of his priests, not for judgment but for healing.

But if he sees someone adulterous, drunken, greedy, proud, envious, deceitful, avaricious, slanderous, and abusive, I fear that what he himself foretold in the Gospel may be said to him: “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” (Matthew 22). And, God avert it, may what follows come to pass: “Bind his hands and feet and throw him into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (ibid.).

Behold what sentence the person will meet on the day of judgment who, without the remedy of repentance, approaches the Lord’s feast stained by the filth of vices.

Therefore, brothers, whenever the day of the Lord’s Nativity or the other feasts arrive, abstain for several days beforehand not only from the unhappy intercourse of concubines but also from your own wives. Keep hatred toward no one in your heart. Let what gluttony used to squander begin, through mercy, to be distributed by justice to the poor.

For there are some who think drunkenness either no vice or only a small one, and do not remember that the Lord said to his apostles: “Take heed to yourselves, lest perhaps your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and the cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly; for like a snare it will come upon all who sit upon the face of the whole earth” (Luke 21).

And the Apostle says: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which is debauchery.” And again: “Do you not know that the unrighteous will not possess the kingdom of God? Do not err: neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who have intercourse with males, nor thieves, nor the avaricious, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God.”

And the prophet says: “Woe to those who rise early to pursue drunkenness and drink until evening, so that they burn with wine” (Isaiah 5). And again: “Woe to you,” he says, “who are mighty at drinking wine and strong men at mixing drunkenness” (ibid.).

Therefore whoever is inclined to drunkenness, and wishes to urge or compel others to it, will be guilty both for himself and for them on the day of judgment, and will render an account to the Lord.

But because the Lord’s Nativity is now near, brothers, cleanse yourselves from every filth of vice and prepare yourselves with greater zeal through good works. Preserve chastity with your own wives. Do not covet anyone’s property or wife. Take nothing from anyone by force or fraud. Invite the poor more frequently to your little banquets. Assemble earlier for the sacred vigils. In church, standing, either pray or sing psalms. Neither utter idle or clownish words there yourselves, nor fail to correct those who wish to utter them. Be at peace with everyone, and restore to harmony those whom you recognize to be at odds.

If, with Christ’s help, you faithfully wish to fulfill these things, then in this world you will be able to approach the Lord’s altar with a secure conscience, and in the future to reach eternal blessedness happily.

# Homily III: On the Fast of the Tenth Month

[Cols. 0013C–0014C]

> **Note:** [Col. 0013D] In various places, from a sermon of Leo the Great on the fast of the tenth month.

The majesty of God’s grace, beloved, works this every day in Christian hearts: that all our desire may be transferred from earthly things to heavenly ones.

Yet the present life also is carried on by the Creator’s aid and sustained by his providence, because the one who grants temporal things is the same one who promises eternal things.

Whatever the fields, vineyards, and olive groves produce for human use—all of it has flowed from the divine goodness. This goodness, varying the qualities of the elements, mercifully assisted the uncertain labors of farmers, so that winds and rains, cold and heat, days and nights might serve our needs.

Human reason would not be sufficient by itself for the results of its labors unless God supplied growth to the customary plantings and irrigations.

Therefore it is full of piety and justice that we too should assist others with the things that our heavenly Father has mercifully bestowed upon us.

For [there are] many who possess no share in the fields, none in the vineyards, none in the olive groves. Their poverty must be provided for from the abundance that the Lord has given, so that they too may bless God with us for the fertility of the earth and rejoice that what was given to its possessors has also been made common to the poor and to travelers.

For this reason the justice of God has permitted them to labor under various hardships, so that he might crown the wretched for their patience and the merciful for their goodwill.

Although every season is suitable for this work, beloved, the present time is especially appropriate and fitting. Our holy fathers, instructed by the law and inspired by God, established the fast of the tenth month, so that, when the gathering of all the fruits had been completed, a reasonable abstinence might be dedicated to God, and each person might remember to use abundance in such a way that he would be more restrained toward himself and more generous toward the poor.

For almsgiving and fasting are an exceedingly effective plea for sins; prayer raised with such supports swiftly ascends to the divine ears; and nothing belongs so truly to each person as what he spends on his neighbor.

That portion of bodily possessions which is supplied to the needy passes into eternal riches.

Therefore, brothers, as we are about to celebrate the Lord’s Nativity, let us cleanse ourselves from every filth of sin. Let us fill his treasuries with gifts of various offerings, so that on the holy day there may be something from which travelers may receive, widows may be refreshed, and the poor may be clothed; so that many may give thanks to God on our behalf, and our offering may be sanctified in the Holy Spirit.

Let us therefore fast on Wednesday and Friday of the present week. On Saturday, having worthily completed the fasts, let us celebrate together the most sacred solemnities at the relics of the saints who are venerated in this holy place—and especially at the memorial of the holy apostle Peter, at whose most sacred body the Roman Church performs the office of this day.

This most holy apostle, therefore, with the other saints of God—as we experience and believe—unceasingly keeps watch in pastoral care over the sheep entrusted to him by the Lord, entreating through his prayers that the Church of God, established through his preaching, may be free from every error and remain firmly established in right faith and good works.

# Homily IV: On the Nativity of Our Lord Jesus Christ

[Cols. 0014C–0016A]

I ask you, dearest brothers, to receive with willing hearts the sermons that the Lord will grant on this most sweet day—a day on which even unbelievers and sinners are moved to compunction; on which the ungodly is touched by mercy, the penitent hopes for pardon, the captive does not despair of return, and the wounded desires healing; a day on which the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world is born (John 1).

Christ our Savior, in whose nativity the one who has a secure conscience rejoices more sweetly, the one who has a troubled conscience fears more attentively, the good person prays more affectionately, and the sinner begs more devoutly—this is a sweet day, truly sweet, bringing pardon to all who repent.

I promise you, little children, and I am certain that on this day, if anyone repents from the heart and does not return to his vomit of sin, whatever he asks will be given him—provided only that he does not doubt in faith and does not return to his former pleasure.

Today the sin of the whole world is taken away, and does the sinner despair? But consider what repentance must be like. Many continually call themselves sinners, yet they are still pleased to sin. That is a confession, not a correction; the soul is accused, not healed.

No one makes true repentance except through hatred of sin and love of God: when a person turns in such a way that he does not return; when he repents in such a way that he does not repeat the sin.

As the Lord is born today, dearest brothers, let us promise vows to our Redeemer and fulfill them, as it is written: “Vow and pay your vows to the Lord your God” (Psalm 75).

Let us make our vows sweetly and confidently; he will grant the ability to fulfill them. Whatever we promise him, let us nevertheless hope to receive from him.

But in this promise let no one think that I am referring to perishable and earthly things. Rather, let each of us offer what our Savior has redeemed in us—namely, our own soul.

And if you ask me how I am to offer my soul, which he himself holds in his power, I shall tell you: through holy conduct, chaste thoughts, fruitful works; by turning away from evil and turning toward good; by condemning vice and loving God; by loving one’s neighbor; by showing mercy to the wretched, since we too were wretched before we were redeemed; by forgiving those who sin against us, since we were all under sin; by trampling down pride, since the first human being was deceived through pride; by casting away envy, since through envy the devil deceived the human race.

If anyone has hitherto been lustful, let him henceforth promise chastity. If anyone has harbored envy against a brother, let him cast it away and exchange it for goodwill. If anyone has committed murder, let him promise today and now produce worthy fruits of repentance, and let him presume in no way to receive communion before complete repentance, lest he condemn himself as doubly wretched by receiving the Lord’s body unworthily.

If anyone has had a slanderous or cursing tongue, let him make it pray more and resound with God’s praises. If anyone has been devoted to excessive drinking, let him henceforth vow sobriety. If anyone has been prone to anger, let him learn gentleness. If anyone has seized another’s property by force or fraud, let him distribute his own possessions to the poor. If anyone has often lied, let him henceforth speak the truth. If anyone feels himself to be cruel, let him stir up mercy in his heart. If anyone was proud and disobedient, let him promise before God and human beings that he will practice humility and obedience.

When you have done these things, beloved, you offer God a pleasing vow. The angels who guard your lives present such an offering before the sight of the divine majesty. After this, blessing and enduring salvation will come to you, and, as Solomon said, “Your memorial shall not be forgotten” (Wisdom 16).

It will be said of you: “Behold my people, whom I acquired with my blood; they have satisfied me with vows and filled me with fragrances. I shall be to them as Lord, and they shall be my people; and captivity and desolation shall no longer be among them, says the Lord God.”

Holding this promise, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, bringing sanctification to completion in the fear of God. Let us strive to celebrate this present feast in such a way that we may deserve to enjoy forever the heavenly joy of the saints.

May this be granted by the author of this solemnity, our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# Homily V: Also on the Nativity of the Lord

[Cols. 0016A–0017A]

Let us exult in the Lord, beloved, and rejoice with spiritual gladness, because the day of our redemption, our new restoration, and eternal happiness has dawned. On it we ought, with hearts raised upward, to adore the divine mystery, so that what is accomplished through God’s great gift may be celebrated with the Church’s great joys.

The Son of God therefore enters the lowest regions of this world, descending from his heavenly seat but not departing from the Father’s glory. He is generated in a new order: in a new order because, invisible in what belonged to him, he became visible in what belongs to us; incomprehensible, he wished to be comprehended; existing before the ages, he began to exist in time; Lord of the universe, he assumed the form of a servant, veiling the dignity of his majesty; God incapable of suffering did not disdain to become a suffering human being; and the immortal one submitted to the laws of death.

Therefore, whoever piously and faithfully glories in the Christian name, weigh this grace of the divine dispensation with a just judgment.

You had once been cast away because of transgression; you had been expelled from the dwelling of paradise; you were dying through long exile; you had been dissolved into ash and dust; you had no hope of living. Yet through the incarnation of the Word you were given power to return from afar to your Creator, to recognize your Father, to be made free from slavery, and to be advanced from a stranger into a son.

You who were born from corruptible flesh may be reborn from the Spirit of God, and by grace obtain what you do not possess by nature.

Therefore, beloved, since we possess the confidence of so great a hope, remain steadfast in the faith on which you have been founded. Show by worthy works what you are called: you bear the distinguished name of your Lord and are called Christian from Christ. This truly takes place only if you keep Christ’s commandments and do the will of the heavenly Father.

Do not despise your least brothers, with whom you share the fellowship of Christ’s name. Rather, according to the Lord’s command, invite them frequently to your banquets.

It is not right that, in a holy solemnity, within a Christian people belonging to one Lord, some should be drunk while others are tortured by the danger of hunger.

We and the whole Christian people are servants of one Lord, redeemed at one price. We entered this world under the same condition, and we shall depart from it by a similar exit; and, if we act well, we shall likewise come to one blessedness.

Why, then, should the poor person not receive food with you, when he is to receive the kingdom with you? Why should the poor not receive at least an old tunic, when he is to receive with you the robe of immortality? Why should the poor not deserve to receive your bread, when he has deserved to receive with you the sacrament of baptism? Why is he unworthy to receive even the scraps of your food, when he is to come with you to the banquet of angels?

Consider these things more attentively, brothers; hasten to fulfill them without delay, so that when the day of judgment comes we may not hear, together with those who now despise the poor: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire” (Matthew 25).

Rather, may we deserve to hear with the just and merciful: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom, because I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink” (ibid.).

May our Redeemer, who was born today, grant that we may hear this most desirable voice—he who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# Homily VI: On the Octave of the Lord

[Cols. 0017A–0018B]

You have just heard from the Gospel reading, dearest brothers, the reason for this most sacred feast. As the holy evangelist Luke wrote: “When the eight days were completed for the child to be circumcised, his name was called Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb” (Luke 2).

This was that child who in the beginning was the Word with the Father, and the Word was God: “He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1).

But what does it mean that the child was circumcised on the eighth day, except that, although he was true God and had always been with the Father, he was likewise true man for our sake and assumed true flesh for our salvation?

Thus Christ the Lord was one person in two substances: in the substance of God and in the substance of a human being, without sin. And so it is true what the Gospel subsequently testifies concerning him: “The Word,” it says, “became flesh and dwelt among us.”

Because our Redeemer wished to be born into the world for this purpose—that he might save the human race according to his name—he suitably adapted himself to every order.

He wished to be circumcised according to the law in order to redeem those who were under the law.

The Lord of the temple did not refuse that sacrifices be offered for him, so that he might appear as the Redeemer of those who, from the beginning of the world until the time when circumcision was given, or after circumcision had been given, pleased God among the other nations; those who, by offerings of sacrifices or certainly by the mere power of faith, commending their own souls and those of their own people to the Creator, took care to be released from the bonds of the first guilt.

Finally, that is, when he was already about thirty years of age, he was baptized by John, to demonstrate that he is the author of our cleansing and that he himself is the Lamb who takes away the sins of the whole world (John 1).

He also received the name Jesus on the same day as his circumcision, following the example of the ancient observance. Abraham, who first received circumcision, deserved on the very day of his circumcision, because of his great faith, to be called Abraham—that is, “father of many nations” (Genesis 17). Previously he had been called “exalted father.” Likewise, in the law, those who were under the law, once circumcised, immediately received names.

In the same way Christians now, following this example, customarily give names to those baptized at the time of baptism, so that the practice may conform to authority, since religion commends it.

But what does this legal circumcision signify? The prophet shows us when he says: “Circumcise your hearts, and not your bodies.”

The Apostle commends this circumcision of the heart to us: “Put off,” he says, “the old human being with his deeds, who is being corrupted according to the desires of error, and put on the new human being, who is renewed day by day according to the image of the one who created him” (Ephesians 4).

The deeds of the old human being—that is, the sinner—are: vainglory, avarice, fornication, impurities, debauchery, service of idols, sorceries, enmities, quarrels, jealousies, anger, strife, dissensions, factions, envy, murders, thefts, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. “I warn you that those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God” (Galatians 5).

The works of the new human being—that is, the righteous person—are: charity, joy, peace, patience, goodness, kindness, faith, modesty, endurance, continence, humility, sobriety, and things like these. Whoever serves in these things pleases God and is approved by human beings.

By this circumcision, brothers, I ask you to circumcise yourselves, so that you may deserve to become members of the one who today wished to be circumcised for our sake and to receive the name that the angelic oracles had previously proclaimed concerning him: Jesus Christ, our Savior.

He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages without end. Amen.

# Homily VII: On the Epiphany of the Lord

[The supplied source ends here, at the heading of Homily VII.]

We recently celebrated, dearest brothers, that solemnity on which God clothed himself with human weakness; and shortly afterward, the occasion on which he willed to be circumcised according to the Law. Now, however, we honor and venerate with divine praises that event by which God revealed himself in a human being through his powers. This festival too is called by the Greek term *Epiphany* [Col. 0018C], which we may interpret as “manifestation,” because on this day the rising of the star from heaven provided a divine announcement and led the Magi, who were diligently searching, to the cradle; or because in the waters of the Jordan the Savior consecrated the nature of water by his baptism for the restoration of the human race, and through the coming of the Holy Spirit and the proclamation of the Father’s voice the true God was made known; or because at Cana of Galilee, at a wedding feast, he changed water into wine and, as the Gospel testifies, “revealed his glory” at the beginning of his signs, and his disciples believed in him; or because he satisfied five thousand people with five loaves, and was proclaimed by the declaration of the crowd: “This is truly the prophet who is to come into the world” (John VI).

After hearing, then, of all these mysteries [Col. 0018D], as the holy Fathers have handed them down to us, this present day has become venerable because on this day God—Christ—was manifested in a human being through such signs. Certainly all these events contain venerable mysteries, but at present they do nothing else for us than commend the catholic faith to us, namely, that faith which works through love, and teach us to live in such a way that we may please our Creator in all things.

But I would like, brothers, to say something to you about those three gifts which the Magi offered to our Redeemer on this day. They offered him, as you have just heard when the Gospel was read, gold, frankincense, and myrrh. These three gifts contain a threefold meaning: in the frankincense they offered Christ the honor due to God; in the gold, royal dignity; in the myrrh, the burial of his body.

Let us therefore also offer sincere and holy gifts to our God—that is, faith, hope, and charity. Let us offer the gold of wisdom, the frankincense of devoted prayer, and myrrh in the mortification of the flesh. Let us offer devotion in the flesh, uprightness in speech, and integrity in action. Let us offer purity of mind, chastity of body, and the guardianship of humility. Let us offer compassion, patience, and self-restraint. Let us offer kindness, sobriety, and mercy.

For these are gifts pleasing to God, these are acceptable offerings: they are indeed offered to him, but they benefit those who offer them. He needs nothing, no gift whatsoever; rather, this is the best gift for him—that he should have grounds for rewarding. He demands nothing more from us, asks nothing more, except our salvation. For he considers everything to have been provided by us if we act in such a way that everything may be provided for us by him.

But from him we must ask for the power to accomplish this, so that his mercy may go before us and his mercy may follow us all the days of our life, so that we may dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days. May he himself deign to grant this, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY VIII. ON THE HYPAPANTE, OR THE PRESENTATION OF THE LORD IN THE TEMPLE

The sacred and most celebrated solemnity of today’s feast, dearest brothers, by which we duly venerate the fortieth day of the Lord’s Nativity, [Col. 0019C] is shown by the sacred reading of the Gospel that has just been read to be dedicated to the greatest humility of that same Lord our Savior and also of his undefiled Mother. It explains that those who owed nothing to the Law nevertheless submitted themselves in every respect to the decrees of the Law in order to fulfill them; and for this reason it recalls that they observed at that time the period of purification prescribed by the Law of Moses.

For the Law commanded (Leviticus XII) that a woman who had conceived and given birth to a son should be unclean for seven days, and that on the eighth day she should circumcise the infant and give him his name. Then for another thirty-three days she was to abstain from entering the temple and from the bed of her husband, until on the fortieth day after the birth she should bring her son with offerings to the temple of the Lord.

It also commanded that every firstborn male should be called holy to the Lord, and therefore that clean animals should be offered to God, while unclean animals should be exchanged for clean ones or killed; that the firstborn of a human being should be redeemed for five shekels of silver; and other matters which the book of Leviticus enumerates sufficiently.

Since the Law says that a woman who had conceived and given birth should be declared unclean and, after a long period, should be purified together with the child she had borne by offering victims to God, it is clearly evident that it does not describe as unclean the virgin who gave birth without receiving male seed, together with the son who was born to her, nor teach that she was to be purified through offerings.

But just as our Lord and Savior, who divinely gave the Law, when he appeared in human form willed to become subject to the Law in order to redeem those who were under the Law, so that we might receive adoption as children, [Col. 0020A] so also his blessed Mother, to display an example of humility, did not refuse to submit to the ordinances of the Law.

“And to offer,” he says, “a sacrifice according to what was said in the Law of the Lord: a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.” This was the offering of the poor. The Lord commanded in the Law that those who were able should offer a lamb for a son or daughter, together with a turtledove or pigeon; but those who were unable to do this should offer two turtledoves or two young pigeons.

Our Redeemer, therefore, mindful in every respect of our salvation, willed not only to become human, although he was God, but also, although he was rich, to become poor for us, so that he might make us rich by his poverty and adopt us as children of God by his humanity.

But because today we celebrate with solemn rites the arrival of the Savior with his Mother at the temple, let us imitate those persons who came there to meet him, as we have just heard from the Gospel: holy Simeon, led into the temple by the Holy Spirit, took the child into his arms and blessed the Lord; and Anna, a devout woman and widow, arriving at that same hour, gave thanks to God and spoke about him to all who were awaiting the redemption of Israel.

Let us also go to meet Jesus, and receive him joyfully in the arms of good works. Let us confess his great name, proclaim his mercy, and declare his wonders, which he has performed for us, to all who await the redemption of Jerusalem and the consolation of Israel.

Foreseeing this consolation in the Spirit, the Psalmist says: “O Lord, you will make us glad with joy in your countenance; delights are at your right hand unto the end” [Col. 0020C].

Let us offer him simplicity of mind, which the dove signifies; let us offer chastity of body, which the turtledove represents; let us offer him, together with sobriety of conduct, the compunction of the heart, which is signified by the song of both birds. For Scripture says: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (Psalm L).

These are the gifts, these are the sacrifices in which Christ delights and rejoices. “The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new.” Thus we ourselves shall be an offering pleasing to God if we wash away our former sins with tears and works of mercy; and if, pierced by the desire for heavenly blessedness, we live well and say to God daily in prayer: “My soul thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Psalm XLI.)

May he bring our desire to fulfillment—he who for our sake was made incarnate and handed himself over in order to redeem us by his blood, Christ our Savior, who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY IX. ON THE FIRST SUNDAY OF LENT  
*On the Lord’s fasting and the rationale of the Lenten fast, and on chastity and continence with one’s own wives.*

*(Gospel of Matthew, chapter IV.)*

The reading of the holy Gospel that you have just heard, dearest brothers, reveals the beginning of this most sacred observance, when it explains to us the mystery of the Lord’s fasting. For the holy evangelist Matthew relates that after his baptism and after the descent of the Holy Spirit upon him, our Savior was led by that same Spirit into the desert to be tempted by the devil; and after he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he afterward became hungry, and the tempter approached him and tempted him. But, overcome by the true words of the divine Law and repelled by the Lord’s command, he departed; and after the devil’s departure, holy angels came and ministered to our Redeemer as the true Lord and Creator.

In all these events, therefore, our Redeemer gave us an example, beloved brothers: he fasted for us, fought against the tempter for us, and conquered for us. Christ’s victory is our glory. Thus, by mortifying our flesh through abstinence, we must prepare our souls for temptation and, gaining victory through prayer and the word of God, hope for eternal blessedness in heaven with the holy angels.

But because the reading is appropriate to these days—for we have heard of the forty-day abstinence of our Redeemer, and we are beginning the season of Lent—we must examine why this abstinence is observed for the number of forty days.

Moses fasted for forty days in order to receive the Law a second time (Exodus XXIV); Elijah abstained in the desert for forty days (3 Kings XIX). The author of humanity himself, coming among human beings, took no food at all for forty days. We too, insofar as we can, strive during the yearly season of Lent to afflict our flesh through abstinence.

Why, then, do we observe the number forty in abstinence, unless because we have acted against the Lord’s commandments either through bodily pleasure or through the inclinations of the soul? In this mortal body we subsist from four elements—that is, earth, water, fire, and air—and we are moved by four inclinations of the soul: fear, desire, sadness, and joy. The Lord’s commandments, however, were given through the Decalogue. Since, then, through the desires of the flesh and the inclinations of the soul we have despised the commands of the Decalogue, it is fitting that through fasting and the grief of repentance we should afflict that same flesh forty times.

There is also another interpretation that may be understood concerning this season of Lent. From the present day until the joys of the paschal solemnity there are six weeks, [Col. 0021D] which amount to forty-two days. When the six Sundays of abstinence are subtracted from these, only thirty-six days remain in abstinence.

Since the year consists of three hundred and sixty-five days, while we afflict ourselves for thirty-six days, we give God, as it were, the tithe of our year through temperance, justice, prudence, and fortitude. We who have lived for ourselves in our desires throughout the year should mortify our flesh through abstinence in the tithes owed to our Creator.

During this most sacred season no one should presume to eat a midday meal, except on Sundays, unless perhaps someone is prevented by illness from fasting. On other occasions fasting may be a remedy or a reward; but in Lent, for one who can fast, not fasting is a sin. At another time the person who fasts will receive pardon; in Lent, the person who can fast but does not will experience punishment.

Even the person who is unable to fast should prepare privately for himself alone—or, if another sick person is with him, for that person in the house—whatever he is to eat. He should not invite those who are able to fast to a meal, lest he increase his own sin through another person’s gluttony.

Maintain chastity, brothers, with your own wives; attend the churches; rise earlier for the nocturnal vigils; if possible, gather daily for the sacred solemnities of the Mass; devote yourselves frequently to prayer; ask continually for the forgiveness of your sins; extinguish the flames of sins through generous almsgiving; strive to be reconciled with your Creator through good works; [Col. 0022B] keep peace with everyone.

Thus, while awaiting holy Easter, may you be able to find grace in the sight of our Redeemer, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY X. ON THE SECOND SUNDAY OF LENT  
*On repentance to be made from the heart and generosity in almsgiving.*  
*(Gospel of Matthew XV.)*

We are now observing the season of Lent, as you know, dearest brothers. It was ordained by the Lord’s own teaching and commended by the apostles and apostolic men, and the Catholic Church venerates it throughout the whole world. The Fathers rightly and fittingly decreed that it should be observed near the commemoration of the Lord’s Passion, so that, according to the Apostle, by sharing in Christ’s sufferings we might deserve to become sharers in his resurrection.

This is rightly done if, repenting from the heart, we strive during these holy days to wash away all the stains of our former life through fasting, daily prayers, and tears, just as the Lord also teaches us through the prophet, saying: “Return to me,” he says, “with all your heart, in fasting and weeping and mourning; and tear your hearts and not your garments, and return to the Lord your God, for he is gracious and merciful, patient and rich in mercy, and ready to relent concerning evil” (Joel II).

And again: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezekiel XXXIII).

But perhaps someone says in his heart: “I would indeed like to fast, but I cannot; I would like to abstain from meat and wine, but illness does not permit me.” To this I give the following advice: If you cannot fast, give alms; and the weaker you are in one respect, the more generous you should be in the other.

It is good to fast, brothers, but it is better to give alms. If someone can do both, that is best; but if he cannot, it is better to give alms, because fasting without almsgiving is like a lamp without oil. Just as a lamp lit without oil can smoke but cannot give light, so fasting without almsgiving torments the flesh but does not illumine the soul with the light of charity. Hence it is written: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke XI).

But perhaps, hearing this, someone thinks to himself: “I would like to give alms, but I have absolutely nothing to give.” For those who have nothing with which to give, good will is sufficient, according to what is written: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II).

But who can excuse himself when the Lord has even promised that he will repay a cup of cold water? (Matthew X.) Why did he say “cold”? So that no poor person might excuse himself on the grounds that he lacked firewood, or claim that he had no vessel in which to heat the water.

Finally, through the prophet the Lord exhorts us and instructs us to give alms in such a way that scarcely anyone can find an excuse for being poor. For he says: “This is the fast that I have chosen, says the Lord: Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless and destitute into your house” (Isaiah LVIII).

He did not say that one should give an entire loaf, since perhaps the poor person had no other; rather, he says, “Break it,” as though he were saying: If you are so poor that you have only one loaf, break off a portion even from it and give it to the poor.

“And bring the homeless and destitute into your house,” as though he were saying: If you complain that you are so poor that you have nothing from which to give food to a poor person, at least prepare a bed for a stranger in one corner of your house.

“If you see someone naked,” he says, “cover him with clothing.” He did not say, “Clothe him in purple or expensive garments,” but “Cover him”—that is, cover his nakedness with whatever clothing you have.

“And do not despise your own flesh,” he says—that is, every human being who shares your nature.

What shall we say to these things, brothers? What excuse shall we be able to offer, when we possess large and spacious houses and scarcely ever deign to receive a stranger, not knowing—or rather, not believing—that Christ is received in every stranger, just as he himself said: “I was a stranger and you welcomed me” (Matthew XXV); and: “As long as you did it for one of these least ones, you did it for me” (ibid.)?

We find it burdensome and distasteful to receive Christ in the poor in our own country. I fear that he may repay us in kind and not receive us into his blessedness. We despise him in this world; I fear that he may in turn despise us in heaven, according to what he himself said: “I was hungry and you did not give me food, and I was a stranger and you did not welcome me”; and: “As long as you did not do it for one of these least ones, you did not do it for me.”

May God, brothers, turn away from us what he will then say to such people as judge: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.” May he grant that we avoid this and instead hear what he will say to the blessed and to those who give alms: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

May he himself grant this—he who redeemed us by his blood, Christ, our Savior and Judge, who lives and reigns as God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY XI. ON THE THIRD SUNDAY OF LENT  
*On perseverance in prayer; on assembling in church; and on the prohibition against hunting or playing dice during the holy days.*

[Col. 0024A]

The Apostle Peter exhorts us, dearest brothers, to be vigilant and concerned for the salvation of our souls, lest, perhaps surrounded by the snares of the ancient enemy, we become entangled in the traps of sins and, bound by an enormous chain of crimes, be assigned to eternal destruction.

“Be vigilant,” he says, “and pray, that you may not enter into temptation, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour. Resist him, strong in faith” (1 Peter V).

Therefore at all times, but especially during these most sacred days, we must devote ourselves to vigils and prayer, so that through the grace of Christ we may escape the deceits and wickedness of the most cunning tempter and remain diligently in God’s service.

At every time, both day and night, without sleep or rest, the devil and his angels surround the Christian people and seek someone whom they may deceive by their poisonous arts. But they are especially hostile when they see the servants of God—that is, the Church of Christ—preparing for battle against them and wishing to fight with all their strength under Christ the King.

For that most wicked enemy is distressed when he sees that his former sheep wish to depart. He rages, becomes angry, and storms, and is stirred up against them with all his strength, believing that whatever is saved for Christ is lost to him.

Since, therefore, beloved brothers, we are preparing through a forty-day fast to receive the Lord’s sacrament, let us be attentive to prayer, to assembling in the holy churches, and to offering the Lord devout prayers and supplications there.

Let us fast for as many days for our sins as the Lord fasted for our crimes. After his baptism the devil tempted him; he did not know that he was the Son of God, and therefore dared to tempt him. But because he knows that we wish to become children of God, he strives to overcome us and, like a slippery serpent, to coil around our feet, lest we be able to ascend to heaven.

If, then, the deceitful and wicked one dared to tempt the Lord, how much more will he not fear to deceive us? If a ruined vessel fought against the Son of God and its own Maker, how much more boldly will it attack us, who are mere human beings?

But alas, what grief! There are some who during these holy days devote themselves more to earthly business, vain games of dice, hunting, or hearing lawsuits than to hearing the word of God or persevering in prayer.

Do you think that person is fasting, brothers, who at first light does not keep vigil for church and does not seek the holy places of the blessed martyrs, but rises, gathers his servants, arranges his nets, brings out his dogs, and searches through the woods? He drags his servants along with him, perhaps servants who are hurrying to church instead, and by his pleasures heaps up the sins of others, not knowing that he will be guilty both of his own offense and of the destruction of his servants.

He spends the entire day hunting, now raising an excessive shout, now secretly ordering silence; happy if he catches something, angry if he loses what he had not possessed before. He conducts himself with such zeal as though fasting had been imposed precisely so that he might hunt.

There are also many who, returning from hunting, care more for their dogs than for their servants. They make the dogs lie down or sleep beside them and provide their daily food in their presence, while they do not know whether one of their servants is dying of hunger. And what is worse, if food has not been carefully prepared for these dogs, the servant is beaten on the dog’s behalf or even killed.

In the homes of some people one may see sleek and fat dogs running about, while human beings walk pale and staggering. How, then, will such people ever have pity on poor strangers, when they show no pity at all to their own servants?

We must understand, brothers, that this fasting is acceptable to God not merely when we chastise our bodies through abstinence, but also when we clothe our souls with humility. Let us be gentle toward our servants, gracious toward strangers, and merciful toward the poor.

Rising at first light, let us hasten to church; let us give thanks to God; let us ask forgiveness for our sins, requesting pardon for past offenses and vigilance concerning future ones. Throughout the day, let either prayer or reading be constant for us. Whoever does not know letters should seek out a holy and learned man and nourish himself through conversation with him.

Let no worldly activity draw or hinder us from divine service. Let no board game distract the mind; let no pleasure in dogs lead the senses astray; let no profit from business pervert the soul through greed. Whatever you do in these vanities or in other foolish pursuits contrary to God’s command, although you may abstain from food, you are not fasting, because you are indulging your own pleasure rather than doing the Lord’s will.

For this is the saving fast: just as the body abstains from feasts, so the soul must be restrained from vices. Let us fast equally from food and from sin, so that our labor may, through God’s grace, bring forth for us an everlasting crown. Amen.

# HOMILY XII. ON THE FOURTH SUNDAY OF LENT  
*On mercy and the forgiveness of debts owed by those who offend us.*  
*(Gospel of Luke VI.)*

We read in the Gospel that our Savior commanded and said to his disciples: “Be merciful, because your heavenly Father is also merciful; forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you. In the measure with which you have measured, it will be measured back to you.”

Although it is necessary, dearest brothers, to observe this saying of the Lord at all times, it is especially necessary during these days, when we strive to merit the forgiveness of our sins and to reconcile the Lord’s mercy to ourselves, saying to God daily in prayer, instructed by heavenly teaching: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

Otherwise we may appear by this saying to accuse ourselves before the Lord rather than reconcile ourselves to him, if contrary to his commands we rise up hard and harsh against our neighbors.

We must all do penance, and we all need forgiveness, because we have all gone astray. For if, according to the testimony of Scripture, not even an infant of one day is free from sin, who would dare claim to be immune from sin and reject the remedies of repentance?

The blessed apostle John also says (1 John I): “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity.”

But what is greatly to be lamented is that some, consigning their sins to oblivion and growing proud through worldly boasting, not only fail to consider themselves guilty, but do not even take care to absolve themselves from their own offenses through mercy shown to others. Rather, forgetful of the divine commandments, they exercise the power of their domination over their servants and subordinates in such a way that during these days they do not hesitate to beat them with scourges, inflict punishments on them, and fetter them.

If a servant happens to be slow when the time comes to eat, his master immediately tears him with blows and wants to satisfy himself with the servant’s blood before satisfying himself with the pleasure of the meal.

What kind of fasting is theirs, brothers, when they fast not in order to call forth the mercy of God, but in order to elicit the groaning cry of a suffering household?

Whoever desires to merit mercy from God must himself be merciful first. For it is written: “Judgment without mercy awaits the one who has not shown mercy” (James II); and: “If you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins” (Matthew VI).

How absurd, then, that a Christian master should not spare a Christian servant during these days, paying no attention to the fact that although the servant is one by social condition, he is nevertheless a brother by grace. For he too has put on Christ and shares in the same sacraments; he has the same God as Father that you do. Why should he not be used by you as a brother?

Consider your origin, brothers. The entire human race was indeed begotten from one man, Adam; born mortal, we are mortal. We are born in the same way, we die in the same way, and we decay in the same way. Alone and naked we entered this world; alone and naked we shall leave it. Only the good or evil works that we have done here follow us when we depart, and each one of us will have to give an account for himself before the tribunal of Christ.

Therefore, brothers, let those among you who rule over others command them with charity; and let those who are subject serve those who rule over them in charity.

Let them hear, not me but the Apostle, commanding them in this way (Ephesians VI): “Servants,” he says, “obey your earthly masters with trembling and fear, in the simplicity of your hearts, as you would Christ—not serving merely for show, as people-pleasers, but as servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart; serving with good will, as the Lord and not human beings; knowing that whatever good each one does, he will receive this back from God, whether slave or free.”

To those who rule, the same Apostle says: “And you, masters, do the same toward them, refraining from threats, knowing that both their Lord and yours is in heaven, and there is no partiality with God: whether servants or free, we are one in Christ” (ibid.).

Admonished by such words of Christ’s Apostle, brothers, let us strive to preserve charity among ourselves and the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. Let no one find it burdensome to forgive small offenses committed against him by his neighbor when he desires to have great and enormous crimes dissolved before God.

Thus our fasting, prayer, and almsgiving will be acceptable to God if they are offered through charity, because “charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter IV); and: “God himself is charity, and whoever remains in charity remains in God, and God in him” (1 John IV).

May he himself grant that we possess this charity here in blessedness and through it come to eternal blessedness—he who redeemed us through it, Christ our Savior, who lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY XIII. ON THE SECOND SUNDAY OF LENT  
*On the truth of the catholic faith and the harmony of good works.*

[Col. 0027B]

It is altogether necessary, beloved brothers, that in this most sacred observance of Lent, just as we mortify our bodies through fasting, so we may enliven our souls through spiritual devotion and illumine them through the word of God, so that through the will of the inner person and the conduct of the outer person we may be able to please our Creator in all things. But before all else, right faith is necessary for us, because, according to the Apostle, it is impossible to please God without faith (Heb. 11). Therefore I ask you, brothers, that when we unfold the exposition of the Creed, you listen with particular attention, because the teaching of the Creed is the power of the sacrament, the illumination of the soul, and the fullness of belief: for what is taught and learned in it is both the unity of the Trinity and the Trinity distinguished in persons, the excellence of the Creator, and the mercy of the Redeemer. By this the bond of unbelief is loosed; by this the gate of life is opened; by this eternal glory is prepared. This, I beg you, brothers, quickly and firmly commit to your memories. And if you desire to have sons or daughters at the approaching baptism, if they are already of an age capable of understanding, make them know before baptism the faith which they must profess. But if that age is not yet suitable for this, you too must learn that faith which you wish to profess on their behalf, so that when they reach a fitting age you may recognize that you are obliged to teach it to them.

The Creed is as follows, which, commended by the apostles, the holy Church firmly holds:

[Col. 0027D]

I believe in God the Father almighty, Creator of heaven and earth; and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord: who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried; he descended to the dead; on the third day he rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty; from there he will come to judge the living and the dead. I believe in the Holy Spirit, the holy catholic Church, the communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and eternal life. Amen.

Beloved, the wording of this Creed must be repeated to you, so that we may implant more effectively in your understanding the things we say.

I believe in God the Father almighty, Creator of heaven

[Col. 0028A]

and earth.

First he says “I believe,” because our God does not command us to scrutinize divine judgments, but to believe; not to demand an explanation, but simply and immovably to offer faith.

“In God the Father”: therefore God did not first begin to exist and afterward become Father; rather, without any beginning, he is always both God and Father. Since he was always Father, he always had a Son, whose Father he is.

He says “almighty,” because he can do all things and nothing is impossible for him. He created heaven, earth, the sea, human beings, and all things that exist, live, perceive, and discern—not by some act of labor, but by the sole command of his word.

“And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord.” Observe that just as we must believe in the Father, so also we must believe in his only Son. And because, in majesty, the Lord is equal to the Father, we owe him as much honor and as much service

[Col. 0028B]

as to the Father.

“Jesus” is interpreted as “Savior,” while “Christ” is derived from chrism, or anointing, because just as ancient kings were anointed with sacred oil by priests, so our Lord Jesus Christ was filled through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit.

“Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary.” Therefore Christ’s flesh was formed in the Virgin’s womb not from human seed but through the work of the Holy Spirit. Thus she who gave birth to the Savior was a virgin in childbirth and remained a virgin after childbirth.

“Suffered under Pontius Pilate.” This Pilate was judge at that time, appointed by the emperor over Judaea. The Lord suffered under him, and his mention here serves only to indicate the time.

“Was crucified, died, and was buried.” The cross on which he was crucified in the body we carry figuratively on our foreheads, and by it we are defended from the enemy. And just as Christ was truly born, so also he truly died and was buried.

“On the third day he rose from the dead.” The delay of the three-day burial clearly shows that while the body lay in the tomb, that soul triumphed over the dead.

“He ascended into heaven.” Therefore he placed above the heavens, at the right hand of God—that is, in the honor of God the Father—the condition of our nature which he had assumed by being born from a human mother, so that he might exist as our propitiator.

“From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.” He will come to judgment in the very body in which he ascended into heaven. He will judge Christians and pagans, the righteous and sinners, the faithful and the impious.

“I believe in the Holy Spirit.” Observe that, just as we believe in the Father, so also we must believe

[Col. 0028D]

in the Son and in the Holy Spirit. For whoever does not believe in even one person of the Trinity will gain nothing by believing in the other two.

“The holy catholic Church.” It must be understood that we should believe that there is a Church, but not believe in the Church, because the Church is not God but the house of God.

He says “catholic,” that is, spread throughout the whole world. The churches of the various heretics are not called catholic because they are confined to particular places and their own provinces; but this Church is spread from the rising of the sun to its setting by the splendor of one faith.

“The communion of saints.” That is, we hope for fellowship in heaven with those who have died in this faith.

“The forgiveness of sins.” We hope that this is granted to us through the gift of the Redeemer: fully in baptism through faith, and for those things we commit after baptism, through confession, true repentance, and good works.

“The resurrection of the flesh.” Let us believe that the flesh which we bear in this life under mortal conditions will rise immortal and will give an account because of its partnership with the soul.

“Eternal life. Amen.”

You must also truly believe, brothers, in eternal life in heaven, which “Amen” signifies that you can receive with Christ and his saints, if you faithfully hold the faith we have explained to you and preserve it through good deeds. I beg you to commit it well to memory, strive to prove it by a worthy manner of life, and carry it through to the end of this life, so that by it, through Christ’s gift, you may be found worthy to attain eternal rewards. Amen.

## HOMILY XIV. FOR PALM SUNDAY

*(Gospel of Matthew 10.)*

It does not seem inappropriate, beloved brothers, to explain briefly to you amid these sacred celebrations of the Mass what the observance of today’s feast signifies. For some of you know the reason for this feast; others, although they see the rite of worship performed outwardly with the rest, do not inwardly understand it with the heart.

The holy Gospel indeed relates that, as the time of his passion approached, our Redeemer, going toward Jerusalem six days beforehand, commanded his disciples to bring him a young donkey. When it had been brought, the apostles placed their garments upon it and made Jesus sit upon it. The very great crowd spread its garments on the road; others, cutting branches from the trees, likewise spread them along the way, so that the donkey might proceed without stumbling.

Those who went before and those who followed cried out, saying: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel; hosanna in the highest.”

The Lord Jesus entered Jerusalem with such a triumph. We have celebrated these events today according to their historical sense in memory of our Redeemer, considering it fitting to make known to you what they signify spiritually.

This donkey on which the Lord sat signifies the gentile people from whom we come. The apostles, freeing us through the preaching of the Gospel from the bonds of the enemy—that is, the devil—brought us to Christ. Placing their garments upon it—that is, covering the nakedness of its sins with the Lord’s commandments and spiritual grace—they made the Lord sit upon it, that is, dwell and rule within it.

The very great crowd that spread its garments on the road signifies the martyrs, who handed their bodies over to death for Christ and gave us, who are the Lord’s beasts of burden, an example, so that for the faith of Christ we may patiently endure every adversity.

Those who, taking sacred testimonies from the branches of fruitful trees—that is, from the prophets—spread the road before us each day, order our way so that without the stumbling-blocks of sins, under the Lord our rider, we may be able to enter the holy city, that is, the heavenly Jerusalem.

That those who went before and those who followed cried, “Hosanna to the Son of David,” signifies that the saints who preceded the Lord’s coming in the flesh, and those who followed after his ascension, sounded his praises in harmony and truly proclaimed his majesty. For what the prophets and patriarchs foretold would happen concerning him, the apostles and evangelists narrated as already fulfilled.

Considering these things, beloved brothers, let us weigh the mercy of our Creator, who first created us good and immortal, and afterward, when we had become frail and mortal through transgression and the fall, freed us from the power of the devil and the bonds of sins through his Only-Begotten Son.

Let us humble ourselves beneath so great a rider, because his yoke is easy and his burden is light. Let us strive, as far as we can, that while carrying him we may avoid the stumbling-blocks of sins.

We have a prepared road, because every divinely inspired and dictated Scripture teaches and instructs us how to proceed by a straight course to our homeland and, through faith, hope, and charity, come to our Creator through good devotion.

The holy day of Easter is now approaching. This week, brothers, is fuller of heavenly mysteries than all the other weeks of the year. During this week the Savior taught daily in the temple until the time of his passion. In this week—that is, on the fifth day of this week—at the mystical supper he himself first gave his disciples the sacraments of his body and blood, when he also washed their feet. On the sixth day he completed the mysteries of his cross and passion; on Saturday he rested in the tomb.

Therefore, all of us who have labored well during this Lent up to now should strive to persevere in this until its end. And all of us who have been sluggish until now should at least during these seven days hasten to find mercy with our Redeemer through fasting, generous almsgiving, vigils, prayer, tears, and compunction of heart.

Then, on holy Easter, when we are about to approach the Lord’s sacred table, may his eyes find nothing offensive in any of us, lest he perhaps say to us: “Friend, for what purpose have you come? How did you enter here without a wedding garment?” May he himself grant that we avoid his anger and find his grace more fully—Christ our Redeemer and Savior, who

[Col. 0030D]

with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XV. ON THE LORD’S SUPPER

*(Gospel of John 13.)*

It must not be omitted, beloved brothers and those named sons of God, that we offer you some admonitory address concerning this holy and precious day of today’s celebration, which the whole Church of God, spread throughout the world, celebrates and honors. For just as the body cannot live without daily nourishment, so neither can the soul, whose condition is far more precious, live without the word of God.

For just as the flesh returns to the earth from which it took its origin, so the soul returns to heaven, if it is continually nourished and refreshed by divine speech, which is its food, because this surpasses every sweetness of honey, as the prophet David testifies, saying: “How sweet are your words to my throat, O Lord, sweeter than honey to my mouth” (Ps. 118).

Therefore let it be certain and known to every human being that just as he was born into this world, so he left the world, as the evangelist John testifies concerning the Son of God in this Gospel reading which you have just heard, saying: “Before the day of the Passover feast, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father.”

The Son of God, from whom all honor and power proceed, was dishonored in many ways for our sake: scourged with whips, struck with blows, spat upon in the face, bound by the hands, wearing a crown of thorns, sold, and finally receiving death through the passion of the cross. Rising from death, he ascended to his Father in heaven, from whom he had descended.

So we too must pass from this world to our Father, who is Christ himself: abandon wickedness and practice righteousness; give temporal goods for the sake of eternal ones; leave the devil and his evil works, and do and love the things that please God; love God with all our heart and all our mind; love our neighbor, who is every Christian, as ourselves; avoid lies, pride, murders, fornications, thefts, and the other things like them.

If, then, we do these good things and avoid the evils I have mentioned, we too imitate the Son of God, ascending in like manner to our Father who is in heaven, who rules and possesses all things together.

It follows: “Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.”

The Lord loved his own who were in this world so greatly that he even handed himself over to death for them, because no one has greater love than the one who gives his life for his friends (John 15).

Then the supper was prepared. As the disciples gathered with their teacher, the devil immediately put into Judas’s heart that he should betray his teacher and our Lord to the Jews. For just as the devil injects evil thoughts into the minds of the wicked and unjust, as Judas was, so the Holy Spirit implants holy and righteous thoughts in the good and just.

As he had always done for his disciples, sending them to kings and governors, he said: “When you stand before them, do not think beforehand about how or what you will speak, for what you should speak will be given to you in that hour” (Luke 25).

Judas, the betrayer and traitor of God, came to the banquet without faith. For if he had truly possessed faith, he would never have betrayed him to the impious Jews.

Jesus knew that God the Father had given all things into his power, including his own betrayer. He was conscious of what he ought to do for his friends and that he had come into this world from God the Father, yet he did not leave him in his divinity. He would return to him again and would never abandon us from his grace.

He rose from supper, laid aside his garments, and immediately began to wash the disciples’ feet, fulfilling the duty of a servant although he was the Creator of all things—of the heavenly, earthly, and infernal realms.

But he first came to Peter, because he was the highest and chief of the apostles. And rightly so, since he had granted him the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever he would loose on earth would be loosed in heaven.

Then the exceedingly holy Peter was greatly alarmed that the Son of God, the Creator of himself and of all things, should wash the feet of his servant, and he said: “Lord, are you never going to wash my feet?”—because you are Lord and I am a servant; you are God, I am human; you are Redeemer, I am a sinner.

Jesus answered him: “What I am doing, you do not know now, but afterward you will understand”—as though he had said: “You do not yet understand the mystery of this deed, but afterward you will understand it, because if I do not wash your feet, you will have no share with me.”

Again he refused, saying: “You shall never wash my feet.” But then, terrified by the Lord’s words—for he had said, “If I do not wash your feet, you will have no share with me”—he added: “Lord, not only my feet, but also my hands and head.” If you threaten that I will have no communion with you because my feet must be washed, then, so that I may have some share in your communion, I refuse no part of my body to be washed.

Jesus answered: “He who has been washed needs only to wash his feet, but is wholly clean.”

This signified the following: Whoever comes to holy baptism and is baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is immediately wholly clean, both in soul and in body, because in the bath of baptism human sins are forgiven and wiped away. Before he is baptized, he is called a son of the devil; afterward, however, he is called a son of God.

This is what the Lord signified when he said: “He who has been washed needs only to wash his feet, but is wholly clean.” For just as feet, which tread the earth, cannot be without some dirt, so no one in this world and in this mortal flesh can live without sin, as the apostle Saint John testifies: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1).

When a person, after baptism, is stained by some evil work, he must again be cleansed through the same grace of divine goodness: that is, through money, almsgiving, and prayer; by mourning the wrong he has done and seeking the good he lost by sinning.

Spiritually, the Lord washes our feet daily when he intercedes with God the Father for us. Likewise, we ourselves must wash our feet daily by confessing our sins in our hearts with the Lord’s Prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

When the Son of God had completed all these things I have enumerated by humbling himself, he said to them: “Do you know what I have done for you? If I, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet, so that just as I have done for you, you also may do.”

It was as though he had said: “If I, God and Lord, have forgiven your sins, how much more ought you to forgive one another’s sins.”

When the evangelist says that the Lord rose from supper, this means that the Son of God descended from the heavenly throne of the Father to earth by taking our flesh upon himself. In this he laid aside his garments, because he humbled himself and became obedient to God the Father unto death.

He girded himself with a linen cloth because he assumed the form of a servant. He poured water into a basin when he poured his blood upon the earth, so that he might cleanse the footsteps of those who believe in him, which had been stained by earthly sins.

Then he wiped the feet with the linen cloth when, by dying for us with his own bodily flesh, he cleansed the crimes of our sins. Thus he had washed the disciples’ feet when, through the shedding of his blood, he completed the cleansing of our redemption.

When he is said to have taken his garments, this means that on the third day he rose from the tomb with the same body with which he had died on the cross, clothed again and made immortal.

When the Gospel reading says that Jesus reclined again, it signifies that he again ascended into heaven to his Father, from whom he had descended, sitting at the right hand of God and in the majesty of the Father’s divinity. From there he will come again to judge the living and the dead.

At that judgment, may you be found worthy to discover that very God, together with the others who judge the world in righteousness, gentle and merciful, so that you may reign with him in eternal blessedness throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XVI. ON HOLY EASTER SATURDAY

*(Gospel of Matthew 28.)*

Behold, beloved brothers, the long-desired solemnity has arrived, in which our Savior, having bound the prince of darkness, shattered the gates of death, and taken away the captive souls as his spoil, rose in glory, triumphing over hell.

On this night, as we have just heard from the Gospel reading, when our Redeemer rose, a great earthquake occurred.
