The angel of the Lord descended from heaven and, approaching, rolled away the stone from the entrance of the tomb, and sat upon it. The Jews, because of their extreme faithlessness, had placed and sealed it and secured the tomb with guards.

The appearance of the angel was like lightning, and his clothing like snow. The guards were terrified before him and became like dead men.

The same angel said to the women, who, inflamed with love for the Savior, had come to the tomb: “Do not be afraid. I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. He is not here, for he has risen as he said. Come and see the place where the Lord was laid. And going quickly, tell his disciples that he has risen, and behold, he goes before you into Galilee; there you will see him. Behold, I have told you.”

Christ is born, suffers, and rises for us and on our behalf, so that through him we may be reborn into life. For all things were restored through him on this night.

On this night, as the firstfruits of those who sleep, Christ rose. On this night our captivity is loosed, and the life lost in Adam is restored. On this night the ancient first-formed human being, an exile, returned to the homeland of paradise, as Christ moved the cherub. From this night of the Lord’s resurrection paradise stands open: it is closed to no one except himself, and opened to no one except through Christ.

For the Lord rose today in order to show us the image of the future resurrection. Therefore today the people of God, rising through the life-giving bath, illumine our Church with the brightness of snowy whiteness, in the likeness of the resurrection.

We must give thanks to our God, beloved, because while we celebrate the solemnity of holy Easter, we already see in those reborn the likeness of the future resurrection.

This, then, is what I admonish you, beloved brothers: whenever the Easter solemnity comes, all men and women who have spiritually received sons from the sacred font should recognize that they have become sponsors for them before God. Therefore they must always show them the concern of true charity; admonish, discipline, and correct them, so that they may preserve chastity; keep virginity until marriage; restrain their tongues from curses and perjury; utter no shameful or lustful songs from their mouths; not be proud or envious; not retain anger or hatred in their hearts; not observe omens; never hang amulets or demonic signs upon themselves or their own; flee enchanters as ministers of the devil; hold the catholic faith; run frequently to church; and, setting aside idle talk, listen attentively with their ears to the divine readings.

They should receive strangers and, as established in the Scriptures, wash the feet of guests. They should themselves maintain peace and strive to restore those who are at odds to harmony. They should show priests and parents honor and the love of true charity.

It is fitting, then, that you admonish your sons and daughters concerning all these things and those like them, so that you may come happily with them to eternal blessedness.

Let no one deceive himself, beloved brothers. Let no human being live only for himself. Rather, as I have often urged, whoever has built up any number of people through the example of a holy life will receive the reward of blessed recompense together with and on behalf of all those people. And whoever has offered any number of people the example of an evil manner of life—even if they do not follow him—must know that he will render an account for all those people, because he gave them an occasion of death and prepared for them a cause of destruction.

Therefore, as I have already urged above, with the Lord’s help we must show our newly baptized an example of good conduct as far as we can, so that we may not receive punishment for their destruction but, through the Lord’s grant, may be found worthy to attain forgiveness of our sins and possess eternal joys through their edification. Amen.

## HOMILY XVII. ON EASTER SUNDAY

[Col. 0034D]

Our Passover, beloved, is the resurrection of Christ. For “Passover” is interpreted as “passing over”: from death to life, from suffering to glory, from hell to paradise.

In the fact that Christ died, our death was destroyed; and in the fact that he rose, he granted us the ability to rise, and made us pass from unbelief to the catholic faith, from idolatry to the worship of the one God, from sin to righteousness, from error to truth, from discord to peace, from useless servants enslaved to the service of the devil into the number of God’s children, from exile to our homeland, and from punishment to a crown.

Therefore, beloved, Christ’s Passover is the kingdom of heaven, the salvation of the world, the downfall of hell, the glory of those above, the life of believers, the resurrection of the dead, the testimony of divine compassion, and the price of human redemption. The destruction of death has been abolished. [Delete “abolished.”]

This feast, consecrated by God’s mystery, announces the power of the Lord’s resurrection through the angels, makes it manifest through the peoples, and multiplies good things through the hearts of believers.

This, then, is the day of which the Psalmist once sang beforehand, saying: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Ps. 117).

It is higher than all days and brighter than all others, for on it the Lord rose; on it he gathered for himself a new people through the spirit of regeneration, as you see here; on it he filled the minds of individuals with joy and exultation.

This day of Christ’s resurrection is life for the dead, forgiveness for sinners, and glory for the saints.

Therefore, just as the Virgin Mary, the Lord’s mother, holds primacy among all women, so this day is the head of all days on earth. And just as in the Scriptures we read of the Holy of Holies and the Song of Songs, so with good reason we call this the solemnity of solemnities.

Christ has now opened with the thief that fiery sword and the gate of paradise which no one had been able to break through. The gate of paradise, which was opened to no one before the Lord’s passion, has from the time when the Lord suffered until the present day been both closed and opened: closed to sinners and unbelievers, opened to the righteous and believers.

Through it Peter entered; through it Paul entered; through it all the holy martyrs entered; through it, each day, the souls of the righteous enter from the whole world.

There are two gates: the gate of paradise and the gate of the Church. Through the gate of the Church we first entered—that is, through faith and baptism—for if we persevere faithfully in doing good, after the end of this life we shall enter through the gate of paradise.

The holy Church is certainly the house of God, and we must live in such a way that we are not cast out of that house and, having been thrown outside, devoured by beasts—that is, by evil spirits—of whom the prophet says: “Do not hand over, O Lord, the souls confessing you to the beasts” (Ps. 37).

Let us therefore remain constantly in her who is the mother of us all, that is, the Church, so that we may be found worthy to reach the kingdom of the eternal Father, to whom she herself has begotten us as children by adoption.

Let us celebrate this most sacred solemnity in the manner taught us by the apostle Paul, who says: “Not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness” (1 Cor. 5)—that is, not in the bitterness of human malice, but in the sincerity of divine holiness, which consists in chastity, humility, goodness, mercy, kindness, righteousness, gentleness, patience, truth, peace, and benevolence.

This is the mass of Christian holiness, which the leaven of human malice corrupts—that is, lust, pride, envy, iniquity, greed, intemperance, falsehood, discord, hatred, vainglory, cruelty, and injustice. May the author and giver of all good things, the maker of this most sacred feast, Jesus Christ our Savior, make all these forms of corruption alien to us and preserve in us the sincerity of his truth. He lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XVIII. ON THE OCTAVE OF EASTER, OR ON THE OTHER SUNDAYS AFTER EASTER

[Col. 0036A]

These are the days, beloved brothers, which the catholic Church venerates throughout the whole world in honor of the Lord’s resurrection. For after his resurrection our Savior, as blessed Luke testifies (Acts 1), appeared to his disciples for forty days by many proofs and manifested to them the truth of his resurrection.

Therefore, according to the tradition of the holy fathers, we must all regard these days as festive and celebrate the glory of Christ’s resurrection with spiritual joy. We should not maintain the severity of fasting during them, although sobriety must be observed at all times.

The period of Lent, which we kept before Easter with fasting and affliction of our flesh, represents the type of the present age, in which, through the mortification of our bodies, we ought to share in Christ’s sufferings.

But this period which we observe after Easter until holy Pentecost presents, because of Christ’s resurrection, the image of the life to come. During it we sing praises to God with great joy. For “Alleluia,” which the holy Church frequently uses in the praises of God during these days, is a heavenly song, as the apostle John testifies in his Apocalypse (Rev. 19), and it foreshows for us the glory of the life to come, when, rising from the dead in imitation of our Redeemer, we shall sing praises without ceasing to our Creator forever in eternal blessedness with the holy angels.

But because, beloved brothers, we are now celebrating the Easter season, let us rejoice in hope in such a way that we may reach the reality; so that what has already gone before in our Head, we too may be found worthy to receive on the last day.

Let us relax our bodies in such a way that the purity of the mind is not darkened. Rather, abstaining from every game, drunkenness, wantonness, and shamefulness, let us devote ourselves to sober relaxation and holy sincerity, so that whatever we do not acquire now through bodily abstinence, we may seek through purity of mind and uprightness of conduct.

Hear me, brothers, all of you who stand in the Lord. I address you in the words of the Apostle: “Behold, the night has advanced, but the day has drawn near. Let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the weapons of light. Let us walk honorably as in the day, not in revelries and drunkenness, not in bedrooms and debauchery, not in strife and rivalry; but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13).

Thus may you put on both eternal life and the garment of immortality, to receive which you were reborn in baptism: “For all who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3), and you have become his members.

Since, therefore, you are members of Christ, I admonish you to pay attention to yourselves, lest you perhaps lose that dignity.

Great and immeasurable is the dignity of becoming children of God and brothers of Christ. But beware of human beings (Matt. 10)—I do not mean only pagans, Jews, or heretics, but also evil Catholics, who confess God with their mouths but deny him by their deeds (Titus 1).

Choose for yourselves, among the people of God, those whom you should imitate. For if you wish to imitate the crowd, I fear that you will deviate from the truth.

Among the few who walk the narrow way, choose those whom you should follow, because narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life, and few enter through it; broad and spacious is the way that leads to death, and many go along it (Matt. 7).

Abstain from robberies, frauds, and perjuries. Let the whirlpools of drunkenness be driven away from you. Flee fornications as you would death—not death which separates the soul from the body, but that in which the soul will burn forever with the body.

What benefit is it, brothers, that Satan says sins are slight when Christ shows that they are grave? The devil says that sins of the flesh are not serious: that it is permissible to eat and drink to satiety and to lie with a woman—and in this way he deceives.

He did the same against the first human being, to whom God had said: “On the day when you eat from it, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2). The enemy came and said: “You shall not die by death, but your eyes will be opened and you will be like gods” (ibid.).

God’s threat was dismissed, and the devil’s promise was heard. Did it help when the woman said, “The serpent deceived me”? Did the excuse defend her, and was condemnation not the result?

Do not accept the devil’s promise, for he is truly your enemy. Rather, listen to the command of Christ, who redeemed you and gave you an eternal kingdom.

Conduct these days of joy in such a way that you may reach true joy in heaven. Celebrate this temporary Passover in such a way that you may rejoice eternally with Christ and his holy angels, through the favor of our Redeemer himself, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XIX. ON THE LITANIES
It is necessary, dearest brothers, that you not be unaware of the reason for this assembly, for according to the ordinances established by our fathers of old, men and women, children and elders, you have all gathered together. This, then, is an appropriate time for us to seek to reconcile God’s mercy to us, so that through fasting and bodily discipline, through prayers and compunction of heart, we may deserve to find forgiveness for our sins and grace in his sight.

For we read in the prophets that when divinely decreed destruction threatened the city of Nineveh, and the time for its overthrow was approaching according to the Lord’s sentence (Jonah III), those dwelling there had no other defense than to set aside their lavish feasts, undertake continual fasting, and abandon the ambition of riches in order to clothe themselves in the humility of poverty. Thus they might receive a remedy from the very things through which ruin had come upon them: they might soften by abstaining the anger of the Divinity which they had provoked by their self-indulgence, and humility might mitigate the offense which pride had brought upon them.

For it is said that in that tribulation the king himself, having laid aside his imperial purple and removed his royal insignia, girded his limbs with sackcloth and rolled himself day and night in sackcloth and ashes; that human beings and animals alike fasted, and that they cried out mightily to God. The entire kingdom of the Ninevites would then have perished, had repentance not preserved it as its protector.

But why did infants and animals fast, whose sins are not accused? The child fasted so that the elder might escape; the innocent fasted so that sinners might not perish. All abstained together, so that the sins committed by some might be absolved by all.

So let us also, brothers, with consenting minds and united faith, cry out to the Lord our God:

“Let us adore and fall down before God; let us weep before the Lord who made us, for he is the Lord our God” (Psalm XCIV),

patient and abundantly merciful. Let us entreat him with tears and groaning, that he may turn and forgive, turn back from the fury of his anger, and that we may not perish.

[Col. 0037D]

Therefore, brothers, what is greatly to be lamented is that some of you not only fail to do these things during these holy days, but—what is worse—live more shamefully and act more wickedly than on other days. For when these days arrive, they prepare banquets for themselves and make ready their houses so that self-indulgence may be practiced in them with greater care. Men and women go out in public not in sackcloth or mournful dress, but groomed and adorned, as though these were days of rejoicing rather than of repentance.

When the holy crosses and the relics of the saints are carried out by the clergy with the litanies, they do not persist in prayer or follow the banner of the holy cross with praises. Instead, they leap upon their ornamented horses, race across the fields, break into laughter, strive to outrun one another, and raise a loud cry amid guffaws. By doing these things they not only make themselves useless, but also hinder others from giving themselves to prayer.

When they return home, they invite to a banquet not the poor, the blind, or the weak, according to the Lord’s command (Luke XIV), but their neighbors and companions who share the same desires and pursuits. They devote themselves to feasting and to draining cups; if they can, they acquire musical instruments—the drum, the cithara, the flute, and the lyre. Amid excessive drinking they sing songs composed by the art of demons, and thus consume the entire day and night.

What, then, are these things, brothers, other than the machinations of the ancient enemy and the mockeries of demons: separation from God and union with the devil, deprivation of life and consumption by death, exclusion from heaven and confinement in hell? For these people, according to the Apostle, serve not God but their own belly; not Christ but Belial.

I beseech you, brothers, avoid the behavior and companionship of such people; and if you can draw them away from such foolishness, make every effort to do so. If not, take care that you do not perish with them, for we are now celebrating days of compunction and repentance.

And although at all times, dearest brothers, we ought to seek God’s mercy with a chastened body and a contrite heart, and faithfully ask him for forgiveness of sins, nevertheless now, because of the due and most grievous drought threatening on account of our sins, the attacks of the pagans, and pestilence together with mortality, we ought with immense wailing and groaning, with constant prayers and more generous almsgiving, to implore God’s mercy. May he grant us the blessing of heavenly waters, deign to restore peace, grant forgiveness of sins, and in his goodness deign to bestow prosperity.

[Col. 0038A]

During these days especially, let us try to put an end to idle stories; as far as our strength permits, let us strive to pray and sing psalms, and live on sober nourishment. If we desire to receive peace in our times, let us not neglect to preserve peace with our neighbors. Let our anger rage against no one, and God’s indignation will quickly cease from us, according to the Savior’s promise:

“If you forgive their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins” (Matthew VI).

Let no one deliberately seek occupations by which he may withdraw himself from the assembly of the Church. Without doubt, the person who does not seek spiritual medicines during these three days by fasting, praying, and singing psalms loves the wounds of his sins.

For these days were appointed by our holy fathers in the spring season to be celebrated for this purpose: that, before the ripening of the new crops and before every activity of summer or autumn, we might anticipate the face of the Lord in confession and jubilate to him in psalms (Psalm XCIV), so that his mercy may follow us all the days of our life. Thus may he himself grant us the salvation of our souls, health of our bodies, fertility of our fields and vineyards, security from our enemies, and repel the plots of all adversaries; and throughout the whole year, by granting tranquil seasons and peace, may he deign to keep us in his holy service.

[Col. 0039A]

Let each of us run—let us all run—along the path of the Lord’s commandments, and let us not stand in the way of sinners. Against the snares of the devil let us arm ourselves with spiritual weapons. Let us take up the shield of faith, the breastplate of righteousness, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Ephesians VI).

Let us pray that we may not enter into temptation, that we may not be surrounded by Satan, that our life may not be endangered, that, because our sins demand it, we may not be handed over to the power of the adversary and cast into prison—namely, into eternal fire and outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth: pain without end and everlasting destruction, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels (Matthew VIII, XIII). May he himself, by his grace, grant that we may avoid this and attain eternal blessedness and heavenly glory—he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XX. ALSO ON THE LITANIES

### On the Lord’s Prayer (Gospel of Luke XI)

Just now, dearest brothers, when the Gospel was being read, we heard our Savior say and command us: “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; whoever seeks finds; and to the one who knocks it will be opened” (Luke XI).

And he not only commanded us to ask, but elsewhere also taught us how to ask:

“When you pray,” he said, “do not speak at excessive length, as the pagans do” (Matthew VI);

for they suppose that they will be heard because of their many words, since they devote themselves more to exercising their tongues than to cleansing their souls.

“For your Father,” he says, “knows what you need before you ask him.” And of him it is written: “Man looks at the face, but God looks into the heart” (1 Kings XVI); and again: “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are vain” (Psalm XCIII).

Our God and Lord, therefore, does not seek a multitude of words, as though he were ignorant of our will—he to whom all things are known before they happen, for all things are naked and open to his eyes (Hebrews IV). Rather, he seeks the inward and pure affection of our heart:

“Thus you shall pray: Our Father, who are in heaven.”

It is as though he had admonished us by saying: “You have begun to belong to a great family; do not cling to earthly things, since you have found a Father in heaven.” For he teaches all who wish to have one Father, God, to be brothers of one another.

Under this Father, master and servant, emperor and soldier, rich and poor are brothers. All Christian believers have different fathers on earth—some noble, some ignoble—but they invoke one Father, who is in heaven. And if our Father is there, our inheritance is prepared there for us.

Since, therefore, we have heard from whom we should ask, let us now know what we should ask, lest by asking wrongly we offend such a Father.

The first petition, then, is: “Hallowed be your name.” The name of God is always holy; why, then, do we ask that it be hallowed, unless so that we may be sanctified through it, and so that God’s sanctification may appear and remain in us?

Another petition follows: “Your kingdom come.” Whether we ask or do not ask, the kingdom of God will come. Why, then, do we ask this, unless that what will come to all the saints may also come to us, so that God may count us among his saints, to whom his kingdom will come?

In the third petition we say: “Your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.” What else do we ask here except that, just as the angels serve him in heaven, so we may serve him on earth? The angels and his saints obey him; they do not offend him or provoke him to anger, but carry out his commands by loving him. This, then, is what we pray: that we too may fulfill God’s commandment in love.

These words can also be understood in another way. Heaven in us is the soul; earth in us is the body. What, then, is “Your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth,” except that just as we have heard God’s commandments, so our flesh may also agree with us, lest, while flesh and spirit contend, we be less able to fulfill God’s commandments?

These three petitions, therefore, pertain to eternal life, because in them we ask for eternal things. For always and without end we ought to desire to be sanctified in the Lord’s name, for his kingdom to be established in us, and for his will to be fulfilled. The remaining four petitions concern the present life.

[Col. 0040A]

The Lord’s Prayer continues: “Give us this day our daily bread.” We may ask God the Father for what is necessary for the body, signifying by bread whatever we need; or we may understand the daily bread to be that which we are to receive from the altar. For why do we pray that he give it to us, except so that we may not commit anything evil by which we might be separated from such bread?

The word of God that is preached every day is also bread. Because it is not bread for the belly, it is not for that reason not bread for the mind.

When this life has passed, we shall no longer seek that bread for which hunger asks, nor shall we receive the sacrament of the altar, because there we shall be with Christ, whose body we now receive in the sacrament. Nor will those words then be spoken by us which we now speak to you. Nor will a book need to be read when we see him himself who is the Word of God, through whom all things were made, by whom the angels are nourished, by whom the archangels are illumined, and by whom all the powers of heaven become wise. They do not seek the fruitless words of speech, but drink the one Word; filled from him, they pour forth praises and do not grow weary in praising. For the psalm says:

“Blessed are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever they will praise you” (Psalm LXXXIII).

Therefore, in this life we ask for what follows: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” In baptism all debts—that is, all sins—are completely forgiven us. But because no one here can live without sin, even if without some grave offense by which one might be separated from that bread, no one can be without sins on this earth, and we cannot receive more than one baptism at once. In prayer, however, we receive that by which we may be washed daily, so that our sins may be forgiven us each day.

But this happens if we do what follows: “As we also forgive our debtors.” Therefore, my brothers, I admonish you—my children in God’s grace and my brothers under that Father—I admonish you that whenever someone offends you and sins against you, and then comes, confesses, and asks your forgiveness, you should forgive him and immediately release him from your heart, lest you prevent God’s forgiveness from coming to you. For if you do not forgive, neither will he forgive you.

This too, then, we ask in this life, because here sins can be forgiven, where they can be possessed; in that life they are not forgiven, because they are not possessed.

Then we ask, saying: “Do not lead us into temptation.” For God does not himself lead someone into temptation; rather, he permits the person whom he has deprived of his help and abandoned to be led into temptation, by a most hidden ordering, although often for evident reasons and according to evident merits.

To be led into temptation, however, is one thing; to be tempted is another. To be tempted is to be tested, as it is written: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous people” (Ecclesiasticus XXVII). To be led into temptation is to be overcome and corrupted by temptation.

“But deliver us from evil”—that is, from every sin, or also from the author of sin, namely, the devil, so that he may not seduce and deceive us by his temptations.

We must pray as long as we are in this present life, so that we may not only avoid being led into the evil from which we are free, but also be delivered from that into which we have already been led. When this has happened, nothing fearful will remain, because then our joy will be complete.

Let us all, therefore, dearest brothers, hold in memory this Lord’s Prayer, which was instituted by its very author and by the giver of all good things, and let us hasten to possess it with the understanding of our heart. Let us pronounce it with pure lips and a peaceful mind, and commend it by good works.

For he who commanded us to ask in this way knows what it is useful for him to grant us. Whatever we ask according to his will, he himself hears—namely, Jesus Christ our Lord, mediator between God and human beings, who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXI. ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

*(Gospel of Mark XVI)*

The sacred readings recited during these solemn rites of the Mass disclose the beginning of the most holy festival, dearest brothers, which we celebrate today. Forty days ago, therefore, we celebrated the time of the Lord’s resurrection on the Lord’s Pasch; today we venerate the solemnity of the Ascension of that same Redeemer of ours.

For after his resurrection our Savior appeared to his disciples for forty days and truly demonstrated by many proofs that he had risen. Finally, he appeared to the eleven while they were reclining and, as he was about to ascend into heaven, bestowed upon them words of preaching for their confirmation. He displayed the greatness of faith, foretold the signs that would follow those who believed through their preaching, and, blessing them, promised the coming of the Holy Spirit.

After this, while they watched, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their sight. He was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God. In the same humanity in which he ascended today, he will come at the end of the ages to judge the living and the dead.

As two angels foretold to the apostles while they gazed at him going into heaven:

“Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven.”

[Col. 0042C]

When you hear that the Lord has ascended into heaven, you are filled in your hearts with immense joy; you utter due praises with your mouths and show your gladness even in your faces, because in your minds you contemplate the majesty of Christ and the glory of the heavenly kingdom.

And truly, great and ineffable is the reason for rejoicing when we hear and consider with believing hearts that, in the sight of the holy multitude, the nature of the human race has ascended above the dignity of all heavenly creatures, passed beyond the angelic orders, been raised higher than all the ranks of powers, and been brought to the seat of God the Father.

Since, therefore, Christ’s ascension is our advancement, and where the glory of the head has gone before, there the hope of the body is directed, let us exult with worthy joy and rejoice with devout thanksgiving.

For today we have not only been made secure as possessors of paradise, but in Christ we shall also enter the heights of heaven, having obtained more through Christ’s ineffable grace than we had lost through the devil’s envy. For those whom the poisonous enemy cast down from the happiness of their first dwelling, the Son of God, having assumed a body, has placed at the right hand of the Father.

Let us ascend, beloved, with Christ for now in our hearts; when his promised day arrives, we shall follow him also in body.

[Col. 0043A]

Nevertheless, we must know, brothers, that pride did not ascend with Christ; greed did not ascend, lust did not ascend, envy did not ascend. None of our vices ascended with our physician. Therefore, if we desire to ascend after our physician, we must lay aside vices and sins. For these press upon us as though with fetters and strive to bind us in the nets of sins.

Therefore, with God’s help, according to what the Psalmist says, “Let us break their bonds” (Psalm II), so that we may safely say to the Lord: “You have broken my bonds; to you I will sacrifice an offering of praise” (Psalm CXV).

As we ascend, however, let us not exalt ourselves or presume upon our own merits as though they were our own possessions. We ought to have our hearts above—but toward the Lord. To raise one’s heart upward but not toward the Lord is called pride; to have one’s heart above toward the Lord is called refuge.

See, brothers, a great miracle: God is high. You raise yourself up, and he flees from you; you humble yourself, and he descends to you. Why is this? Because he is exalted and looks upon the humble, while he knows the proud from afar (Psalm CXXXIX). He looks upon the humble from near at hand, in order to raise them up; he knows the exalted—that is, the proud—from afar, in order to cast them down.

Christ rose again to give us hope that the human being who dies will rise, so that by dying we would not despair or think that our life ends in death, but might be concerned for the soul’s salvation and rest after death.

He ascended into heaven before the eyes of the apostles, sits at the right hand of God, and made us confident that he will place us at his right hand. Therefore, for now we must believe, so that afterward through faith we may deserve to behold God.

Let us cleanse by faith the eye of our heart, because only in this way can we see God, as Truth itself said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.”

Let us humble ourselves under the mighty hand of God, so that he may exalt us on the day of visitation (Matthew V). For he who now ascended peaceful and gentle will then come stern and manifest. Fire will burn before him, and a mighty storm will surround him (Psalm XLIX). He will sit on the seat of his majesty, and all nations will be gathered before him, so that each may receive according to what he has done, whether good or evil.

Those who have done good will go into eternal life; those who have done evil into eternal fire (John V).

He himself, therefore, is our way, and he himself is our homeland: according to his humanity, the way; according to his divinity, the homeland. If we run faithfully, we go through him; if we persevere in the race, we shall reach him.

May he himself grant this to us by his grace, he who today has ascended above all the heavens and given us the hope of eternal life, Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXII. ON THE DAY OF PENTECOST

The more we grasp the joys of today’s celebration, dearest brothers, the more we desire them; and the more eagerly we drink its sweetness, the more ardently we burn with thirst for it.

Today, therefore, we celebrate Pentecost—that is, the fiftieth day from the Lord’s resurrection—on which the Paraclete Spirit, from the Greek term *paraklētos*, interpreted as “comforter,” descended upon the apostles according to Christ’s promise. He kindled their hearts with the flame of his love and, illuminating them with the light of complete knowledge, made them overflow with heavenly joy while they stood amid the distress caused by their persecuting Jews.

First of all, it must be understood that this solemnity was consecrated not only by evangelical gifts but was also foreshadowed long ago by the mysteries of the Law and, at the Lord’s command, observed every year through sacred rites.

For, as we know, on this day, while the disciples were in the upper room, suddenly there came a sound from heaven, and the Holy Spirit, appearing in the vision of fire, gave them knowledge of all languages (Acts II). When this sound had occurred, devout men who had gathered at Jerusalem from various nations for the sake of the Paschal festival came together. They were astonished and marveled, because each one heard them speaking in his own language of the mighty works of God.

When the disciples explained that the Holy Spirit was the grace they were seeing—formerly promised by the voice of the prophets, but then sent as Christ’s gift—three thousand men among them believed, and, having been baptized, they too received the gift of the Holy Spirit.

This is the annual celebration of this day; this is the ever-gracious festival of heavenly grace. To impress its memory more deeply upon the hearts of the faithful, a most beautiful custom of the holy Church has arisen: every year the mysteries of baptism are celebrated on it. When believers have been washed in the saving font, a venerable temple is prepared for the Holy Spirit who comes upon them.

Thus, in it there is celebrated not only the remembrance of what happened long ago, but also a new coming of the Holy Spirit into the new sons of adoption.

Let your charity attend, then, to how the type and figure of the legal festival harmonizes with our celebration. After being freed from Egyptian slavery and after the sacrifice of the Paschal lamb, the children of Israel went out through the desert in order to come to the promised land. They reached Mount Sinai, and the Lord descended upon the mountain in fire, accompanied by the sound of the trumpet, thunder, and flashes of lightning. On the fiftieth day after the completion of Passover, he proclaimed the Decalogue of the Law to them in an audible voice (Exodus XIX). And in memory of the Law that had been given, he established that each year on that day a new sacrifice from the produce of the same year—namely, two loaves of the firstfruits—should be brought to him at the altar.

[Col. 0044D]

So also, after the sacrifice of the true Lamb, that is, Christ—for “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians V)—on the fiftieth day likewise, that is, today, the grace of the Holy Spirit was given to the disciples gathered in the upper room, that is, in the height of heavenly commandments.

When visible fire appeared outwardly, it invisibly irradiated their breasts with the light of knowledge and kindled them with the inextinguishable heat of love. Immediately after receiving the gift of the Holy Spirit, the apostles themselves offered a new sacrifice in two loaves—that is, in two peoples—when, by preaching to those who had gathered, they converted many to the faith. They offered these people—reborn in the baptismal font and sanctified by the grace of the Spirit, truly the firstfruits of the New Testament—for communion at the Lord’s altar.

Therefore, brothers, considering these things and reflecting upon them with a pure mind and simple faith, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of the flesh, so that we may deserve to receive the Holy Spirit.

If we leave this world, we shall receive a Paraclete like the apostles, that is, the Spirit of truth, whom the Father will send us, because there is no partiality with God the Father. The promises made to the apostles benefit us if we perform the works, desires, and actions that the apostles performed.

But if, by fulfilling his commandments, we complete the Lord’s Law, which is without blemish and converts souls, we commit ourselves through Christ’s grace as heirs of the Lord and coheirs of Christ to an everlasting inheritance and to dwelling with the angels.

Therefore I beseech you, dearest brothers, to believe with complete faith in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—one God in Trinity and Trinity in unity—lest the feet of your understanding limp, your eyes see what is perverse, or your hands become withered.

For everyone who does not rightly follow the Catholic faith has weak feet and is dried up by the withering of his hands. Do this, beloved; strive for this, lest some part of your limbs be diseased by such weakness. Let neither gluttony be abhorrent in you, nor greed displease, nor unbelief languish. Thus, thoroughly cleansed and purified, may you become God’s dwelling place, and may the Holy Spirit, who is read to have descended upon the apostles today, deign always to be in you.

This may our Lord Jesus Christ grant, he who promised that same Holy Spirit and reigns with the Father in the unity of that same Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXIII. ON THE FAST OF THE FOURTH MONTH

After those days of joy during which our Savior, following his resurrection, dwelt bodily on earth with his disciples, and after the Lord’s Ascension and the coming of the Holy Spirit—which it was worthy to venerate through solemn celebration—our holy fathers, admonished by the authority of the Law and instructed by evangelical truth, established, dearest brothers, that a fast should be celebrated. Through it we offer our Creator the gift of our devotion in the manner of the firstfruits which, according to the Law, were brought to the Lord around this time.

The Lord therefore commanded Moses, saying:

“Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: When you have entered the land which I will give you, and have reaped the grain of your land, you shall bring to the priest a sheaf of the first ears of your harvest. He shall lift up the sheaf before the Lord, so that it may be acceptable for you” (Leviticus XXIII).

A little later, speaking about the day on which the seventh week is completed, he says:

“You shall offer a new sacrifice to the Lord from all your habitations: two loaves of the firstfruits, made from two-tenths of fermented fine flour, which you shall bake as firstfruits for the Lord. And with the loaves you shall offer seven unblemished yearling lambs, one bull from the herd, and two rams. They shall be a burnt offering with their libations, a most pleasing fragrance to the Lord, and so forth” (ibid.).

All these things we too ought now to observe and perform spiritually in the holy Church.

We offer a sheaf of the firstfruits of our harvest to our priest when we offer to the supreme Priest the faith of the Lord’s Passion and resurrection—he who rose as the firstfruits of those who sleep. He will lift it up so that it may be acceptable before the Lord, because, as John says:

“We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, who now appears before the face of God for us, and he himself is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John II).

We offer a new sacrifice to the Lord from all our habitations when each of us, by his own will and according to the evangelical commandments of the New Testament, offers to God the mortification of his body.

For the Old Law commands: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Genesis II); and again: “If you are willing and obey me, you shall eat the good things of the land,” says the Lord God (Isaiah I).

But the New Testament commands as follows:

“Strive to enter through the narrow gate” (Luke XIII).

“The one who wishes,” says the Lord, “to come after me, must deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke IX).

And the Apostle says: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Galatians V).

We offer two loaves of the firstfruits to the Lord when, according to our measure and as far as we can, we fulfill the Law and the Gospel, which are truly the food of our souls. These loaves are made from two-tenths of fermented fine flour—that is, from the teaching which conveys the perfect divinity and humanity of Christ—and they cannot be baked except through such teaching.

With these loaves we also offer seven unblemished lambs when we present before God, in harmony with the Law and the Gospel, the innocence produced in us by the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit.

We offer one bull from the herd when we confess Christ, born according to the flesh from the lineage of the patriarchs and crucified for us.

We offer two rams when we strive to fulfill the more excellent commandments, which ought to be followed by the other virtues as by sheep. Such commandments include:

“If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have, and give to the poor,” and so forth (Matthew XIX);

and:

“Love your enemies and do good to those who hate you,” and the rest (Matthew V).

The sacrifices and libation of these things—namely, knowledge and practice—are a fragrance pleasing to the Lord. As the Apostle says, “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God.”

This offering also pertains to the feast of Pentecost, because it graciously bestows through the Paraclete Spirit the completion of all perfection.

Therefore, brothers, after the most celebrated festival of Pentecost had been completed, our holy fathers established this saving fast so that through abstinence and earnest supplications we might offer ourselves acceptably to God.

Some, instructed by evangelical authority, established it on the basis of the Savior’s answer when the Pharisees and the disciples of John asked why his disciples did not fast. He replied:

“The children of the bridegroom cannot mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them; but days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast” (Matthew IX).

For this reason they established that, after the Lord’s Ascension—he who is the true bridegroom of the mother Church—and immediately after Pentecost, they should begin the fast on the following day and extend it for forty days.

Whoever does not wish or is unable, because of bodily weakness, to do this should at least properly complete these three days of salutary abstinence.

The fast of the fourth month is indeed commended to us by the reading of the prophets, and no one is permitted to violate it. Therefore, you are to fast on the fourth day, the sixth day, and the Sabbath during this week, as the authority of the holy and apostolic Church of Rome has ordained from ancient times.

[Col. 0047A]

Now, then, come, beloved, during these holy days to the sacred solemnities of the Mass. Pour out your prayers there with tears before the Lord, asking his mercy, so that he who consoled you for a time in veneration of the Lord’s resurrection may deign to console you forever in the vision of his heavenly presence.

When the office of the Mass has been completed and you have gathered at home to dine, do not forget the poor. Give them their portion, as I have often reminded you, because it is unworthy that when you seek God’s mercy more earnestly, you should yourselves be found merciless toward your neighbors.

For it is written:

“Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke XI);

for just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin, while love covers a multitude of sins.

May he himself grant you an abundance of this, he who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood, Jesus Christ our Savior, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXIV. ON THE BIRTHDAY OF SAINT BONIFACE THE MARTYR
The joy of this present day, dearest brothers, as you listen, I consider it fitting to discuss with you in a peaceful discourse filled with love, and to recall to mind the memory of the blessed bishop and martyr of Christ, Boniface: how, having completed the course of his life in time, he reached everlasting blessedness. And it is fitting to think upon the memory of him whom eternal memory holds; for it is written in the Psalm: “The righteous man shall be in everlasting remembrance; he shall not fear evil report” (Psalm 111).

This verse, therefore, brothers, appropriately suits so holy a man, who not only loved justice in his mind [Col. 0047D], but also preserved it in his preaching and practiced it in his works. For this reason the soul of this righteous man now lives in rest with the saints, removed and secluded from all the punishments and darkness of the impious. At the end of the age, when he receives his body—not mortal but immortal, not natural but spiritual—for “what is sown in dishonor shall rise in glory”—he will be made equal to the angels of God, and in that very eternal memory the righteous man will be.

But from what evil report will he not be afraid? Hear this also, and act in such a way that you may not fear evil report. For our Lord Jesus Christ says that the one who deceives no one cannot himself be deceived. “When the Son of Man,” he says, “comes in his glory, all the nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them as a shepherd separates sheep from goats; he will place the sheep at his right hand [Col. 0048A], but the goats at his left” (Matthew 25). He recalls their good works and rebukes the evil deeds of the others. Not to prolong our discourse, he will say to those who are at his right hand: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” In this memory, indeed, the righteous man will be forever.

He will also say to those on the left: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.” He will not fear this evil report—and why, unless because, while placed here, he had previously obeyed his Creator with proper fear? I believe, brothers, that you are not unaware of the thoroughly tested contest and most celebrated victory of this most holy man. Following, according to the word of Truth, the eight precepts of blessedness, he attained true blessedness.

For the Lord says in the Gospel [Col. 0048B]: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5). See, brothers: was not this saint poor in spirit? Choosing voluntary poverty, abandoning his own possessions and inheritance, relatives and parents, he renounced this world perfectly, as one dead to it—living humbly, nobly enduring exile, and striving in his pilgrimage to gain Christ alone, so that he might possess the kingdom of heaven with him forever.

“Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.” He was indeed meek, because he harmed no one and brought accusation against no one; rather, he endured with the greatest patience the injuries inflicted upon him by others. When they cursed him, he did not curse them in return, but blessed them instead, and prayed for those who persecuted him. For this reason also he will possess the land of the living forever with the holy angels.

[Col. 0048C] “Blessed are those who mourn now, for they shall be comforted.” He too chose to have tribulation and hardship in this world with Christ’s poor rather than laugh for a time with the false joy of the rich of this age and afterward mourn forever. For when he had been ordained bishop by the apostolic see and sent as an apostolic legate to the Germanic people and to the Franks, he fulfilled in himself the testimony of the Psalmist, which was spoken concerning preachers of the holy Gospel:

“Going forth, they went and wept, sowing their seed; but coming, they shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves” (Psalm 125).

“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for justice, for they shall be satisfied.” This was always his desire; this was the hunger of his mind and the thirst of his soul: to keep within himself the ordinances of the Lord’s commandments [Col. 0048D] and to persuade others likewise to do so, so that he might say to the Lord with the Prophet: “But I shall appear in your presence with justice; I shall be satisfied when your glory is made manifest” (Psalm 16).

“Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.” And why did this outstanding preacher undertake so great a labor of exile, unless because, driven by the compassion of mercy, he grieved over the losses of others as though they were his own? Therefore, concerning the correction of many, he found everlasting mercy before the eyes of God.

“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” He was pure in heart, possessing so great a light of wisdom in his mind. Hence it is written elsewhere: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.” Whoever possesses true wisdom cannot in any way be deprived of the sight of God [Col. 0049A].

“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God.” This martyr first made peace within himself, when he subjected all the movements of his flesh to the command of the spirit; and thus he preached to others the word of reconciliation. Accordingly, after destroying the reign of sin, he acquired many children for God through baptism and the preaching of the Gospel.

“Blessed are those who suffer persecution for justice, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” He therefore suffered persecution for justice not only from pagans, but also from heretics and schismatics, as well as from false Christians. They assailed him with powerful hatred, tore him apart with insults and reproaches, and, laying ambushes, very often plotted to kill him. But the Lord protected him, so that the seedbed of the Gospel might spread more widely. Finally, while preaching the word of God [Col. 0049B] to the people of the Frisians, he departed to the Lord with the palm of martyrdom.

You have heard, dearest brothers, how this holy bishop and martyr of God advanced through each of the forms of blessedness and to what perfection he attained. Let us, who are his disciples, imitate his progress according to our own measure; let us follow his teachings, and thus, with God’s help, we shall reach his reward.

Let us praise his soul in the Lord, because it now rejoices with the holy angels in his presence. Let us also honor his body, because “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Psalm 115). Let us commemorate his passion, and thus, at the place of his relics, celebrate the glory of his triumph. For we do not set up an altar to Boniface as though he were God; rather, we have made Boniface an altar to the true God, because [Col. 0049C] his soul is indeed the dwelling place of God. May he who granted that we might reach this joy through the prayer of Boniface, who crowned him in triumph, grant it to us also—Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXV. ON THE BIRTHDAY OF SAINT ALBAN THE MARTYR

The holy solemnity of the most blessed martyr Alban, which has gathered us together, dearest brothers, in the name of the Lord, demands that something be said about the merits and glory of so great a martyr; yet nothing can be said worthily. Nevertheless, let us too praise him more through devotion than through ability—or rather, let us praise the Lord in him, the Lord through him, and him in the Lord.

For what would he be [Col. 0049] without the Lord? When the voice of the martyrs was read from the Psalm, it was heard to say: “Our help is in the name of the Lord” (Psalm 123). If the help of all of us is in the name of the Lord, how much more is this true of the martyrs? Where the struggle is greater, greater help is necessary.

It is easy, brothers, to celebrate the solemnities of martyrs, but difficult to imitate the sufferings of martyrs. Two things make the way of Christians narrow and constricted: contempt for pleasure and endurance of suffering. Whoever therefore fights in this manner should know that he is fighting against the whole world. For if he conquers these two things—that is, whatever flatters and whatever threatens—then he conquers the world in this way. The world’s pleasure is false and almost transitory [Col. 0050A], but the martyr’s crown becomes everlasting.

The blessed martyrs therefore lived for themselves and, when they died, left us an example: an example of living well, of upright conduct, and of courageously enduring suffering. For this reason the Lord willed that martyrs should suffer various punishments throughout the world: so that, as trustworthy witnesses, they might convict the present age through the example of their confession of faith, and so that human weakness—which scarcely believes the Lord’s preaching even after prolonged hearing—might at least believe in the presence of the testimony of martyrdom.

All martyrs must therefore be venerated with the greatest devotion, but those whose relics we possess must be especially honored by us. The others assist us through their prayers; these assist us also through their suffering. With them we have a kind of intimacy, for they are always with us: that is, while living with us in the body they protect us, and after departing from the body they receive us [Col. 0050B]—here, lest the stain of sins take hold of us; there, lest the terror of hell overwhelm us.

For this reason our forebears made provision that we should join our bodies to the bones of the saints, so that while Tartarus fears them, punishment might not touch us; while Christ illumines them, the darkness of shadows might flee from us. Resting, therefore, with the holy martyrs, we shall escape the darkness of hell—not through our own merits, if not, but at least through the truth of faith and the holiness of fellowship.

The martyrs are not possessed by the gate of hell, for the kingdom of paradise holds them. We see that they already reign here; we frequently behold them liberating people possessed by the most unclean demons; and we see our natural weakness relieved by them: the blind are given sight, hearing is granted to the deaf, movement to the lame, speech to the mute, and health to the weak. These and other miracles performed through the saints are known to all [Col. 0050C]. Therefore, brothers, let us venerate in this age those whom we desire to have as defenders in the age to come. And just as we are joined to them bodily through the bones of our parents, so let us also be joined to them through imitation of their faith.

Let us love what they loved, and hate what they hated; let us seek what they sought, and shun what they shunned. They loved God with all their heart, all their soul, and all their strength, and their neighbors as themselves. So let us place nothing before the love of God, and let us help our neighbors in every way we can. They hated vices and avoided sins; let us likewise detest vices and avoid sins.

They, fleeing the luxury of this life, sought eternal life through right faith and good works [Col. 0050D]. Let us likewise renounce the pleasures of the flesh and seek the blessed life and joys that will endure without end through the faith that works through love.

We shall clearly be unable to be separated from them in anything if we join ourselves to them both in religious devotion and bodily fellowship. May he grant this to us through the intercession and merits of that holy martyr whose sacred relics we stand beside—he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXVI. ON THE BIRTHDAY OF SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST

Now, with the Lord’s favor, dearest brothers, the much-desired feast has arrived. Therefore let all who [Col. 0051A], devoted to good works, had prepared themselves well for so great a celebration rejoice more confidently; but let those who have until now been more sluggish in doing this earnestly seek God’s mercy at least now, with tears and lamentation, so that they may not forever lack the perfect joy of the saints.

Today, brothers, we also celebrate the birthday of Saint John the Baptist—something which, as we read, has never been granted to any other saint. For throughout the entire world the birthday of the Lord alone and that of blessed John are celebrated and honored, and rightly so, because both births are full of mystery.

John was born of a barren woman; Christ was conceived by a Virgin. In Elizabeth barrenness is overcome; in blessed Mary the ordinary course of conception is changed. Elizabeth bore a son after knowing a man; Mary believed the angel and conceived a human being. Elizabeth conceived a human being, but only a human being; Mary, however, conceived God and man [Col. 0051B].

Great, therefore, is John, whose greatness the Savior himself also attests, saying: “Among those born of women there has not risen a greater than John the Baptist” (Matthew 11). For he surpasses all and everyone; he precedes the prophets and rises above the patriarchs. Whoever has been born of a woman is inferior to John; but he who was born of a Virgin is greater than him.

Hence John himself says: “He who comes after me was made before me, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to untie” (John 1); and: “From his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace” (ibid.). Because he saw himself and all human beings dealing with grace together, he excluded no one from this number as though anyone were without need. It is as if he were saying [Col. 0051C]:

“We all—prophets, patriarchs, apostles, all the saints who were sent beforehand before the Incarnation or sent by the Incarnate One—we have all received from his fullness. We are vessels; he is the fountain. He is the Creator; we are creatures. He is God; we are human beings.”

This, then, brothers, is the mystery in the birth of the Lord’s precursor and in the birth of our Redeemer: in the prophet’s birth our humility is signified, while in the Lord’s birth our exaltation is signified.

John was born as the day was diminishing, but Christ as it was increasing, because it was fitting that human fame should diminish and the glory of God be exalted. Feeling this also, John says: “I must decrease, but he must increase” (John 3).

The same was fulfilled in the sufferings of both: so that the human being might be diminished, John’s head was cut off; so that God might be exalted, Christ was hung upon the wood [Col. 0051D].

Why the Lord and our Savior called blessed John a lamp, and why he wished him to be sent beforehand, I shall briefly explain to your charity. John was sent beforehand like a voice before the Word, a lamp before the sun, a herald before the judge, a servant before the master, and a friend before the bridegroom.

Because the darkness of sins and the night of unbelief had oppressed the whole world, and people were unable to look upon the sun of justice, blessed John was sent beforehand like a lamp. Thus the eyes of the heart—which, oppressed by the disease of iniquity, could not see the great and true light—might first become accustomed to seeing a faint radiance in the light of the lamp; and, as the cloud of sins was gradually removed [Col. 0052A] and the moisture of unbelief dried up, they might, when Christ arrived, be gladdened rather than tormented by that heavenly light.

For just as you invite eyes afflicted with disease to see if you show them the faint glow of a lamp, but cause them greater pain if you thrust a great light upon them, so our Lord and Savior, who is the true light, could not have been endured by the whole world unless he had first sent blessed John before him like a lamp.

Since, then, we have recognized the blessed precursor of the Lord as a lamp who preceded the true light and bore witness to the light so that all might believe through him, let us run to him and hear what he proclaims.

He is indeed a voice, as the prophet Isaiah says: “A voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight. Every valley shall be filled [Col. 0052B], and every mountain and hill shall be brought low; the crooked places shall become straight, and the rough ways smooth; and all flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Isaiah 40).

Let us also prepare the way of the Lord who is to come to our hearts. Let us remove the obstacles of sins through confession and repentance. Let us make straight the paths of our conduct, which were previously crooked and winding. Let us pave the way of true faith with good works. Let worldly pride be cast down, and let fearful faintheartedness be raised up. Thus, when all things have been arranged, ordered, leveled, and brought together, we shall see the salvation of God as it is, because “his place has been made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion” (Psalm 75).

May he grant that we enjoy his perpetual vision, entreated by the prayers of his precursor—he who for this reason had descended from heaven and, triumphing over death, had ascended on high: Jesus Christ our Savior, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXVII. ON THE BIRTHDAY OF THE HOLY APOSTLES PETER AND PAUL

Today, dearest brothers, the birthday of the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul is renowned throughout the whole world. In what part of the world could such devotion remain hidden, when the greatness of their glory is proclaimed everywhere, with their virtues bearing witness? Indeed, the prophet David says of them: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18).

Throughout all the earth the power of Peter’s miracles is proclaimed; and to the ends of the world the Epistles of Paul [Col. 0052D] have penetrated. For who has not heard how blessed Peter the apostle once restored the strength of his feet to the lame man who sat at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, who had been weak from his mother’s womb (Acts 3), so that what nature had failed to provide, apostolic grace might restore?

Or what place is without Paul’s Epistles? Where are the words of the apostle Paul not read? And which of the faithful has not inscribed them in writing, retained them in the heart, and preserved them in conduct? Paul was named by the Lord a vessel of election: a good vessel in which the precious treasures of Christ’s commandments are stored; truly a good vessel, from whose fullness the substance of life is continually distributed to the peoples, and which is full.

Therefore, brothers, the Lord Christ rightly caused these two apostles to stand out among his saints [Col. 0053A], whom by his judgment he exalted to such great glory. For to Peter, as to a good steward, he gave the key of the kingdom of heaven; to Paul, as to a capable teacher, he entrusted the office of ecclesiastical instruction. This was so that those whom the one taught unto salvation the other might receive into rest, and that for those whose hearts Paul opened through the teaching of his words, Peter might open the kingdoms of heaven to their souls.

Thus blessed Peter and Paul stand out among all the apostles and surpass them by a particular distinction. Yet among the two it is uncertain which should be placed before the other. For I think they were equal in merits, since they were equal in suffering; and that they lived with a similar devotion to the faith, since we see them reach the glory of martyrdom together.

Let us not think that it happened without reason that, on one day, in one place, they endured the sentence of one tyrant. They suffered on one day so that they might reach Christ together; in one place, so that Rome might not be lacking to either; under one persecutor, so that equal cruelty might bind both. Thus the day was appointed according to merit, the place according to glory, and the persecutor according to virtue.

And in what place did they finally suffer martyrdom? In the city of Rome, which holds the primacy and headship of the nations. This was so that where the head of superstition had been, there the head of holiness might rest; and where the rulers of the pagans dwelt, there the rulers of the churches might remain.

From this we can understand what the merits of the most blessed Peter and Paul were: the Lord illumined the region of the East through his own passion; and, so that nothing might be lacking, he graciously illumined the West in his stead through the blood of the apostles [Col. 0053C]. Although his passion is sufficient for our salvation, the martyrdom of both has also been given to us as an example.

On this day, therefore, the blessed apostles shed their blood. But let us consider the reason why they suffered these things: namely, because, among their other miracles, they also struck down that famous magician Simon through their prayers, bringing him headlong from the empty air.

When that same Simon called himself Christ and claimed that, like a son ascending to his father, he could rise by flying, and when, puffed up, he suddenly began to fly through magical arts, Peter then knelt and prayed to the Lord. Through holy prayer he conquered magical levity. Prayer ascended to God before the flight; a righteous petition arrived before wicked presumption. Indeed, while Peter remained on earth, he obtained what he was asking before Simon reached the heavens toward which he was striving. Humility ascended higher than pride; love penetrated the inner heavens more powerfully than presumptuous wickedness [Col. 0053D].

Then, although the passion of each was different, it was nevertheless filled with the equal holiness of grace. Peter endured the death of the cross like the Savior; and, through the likeness of his devotion to the Lord, he was not deceived even by death, so that he whom he imitated in faith he might also imitate in suffering.

Paul, however, was beheaded, because he was shown to be the head of faith for the nations, and so that he might demonstrate to the faithful that, through the severing of his head, the true Head, which is Christ, cannot in any way be separated.

See, brothers, how many patrons we have [Col. 0054A], what leaders of our religion, what helpers of our joy. Therefore, whenever we celebrate the memory of the holy apostles or of Christ’s martyrs, let us set aside all worldly business and hasten together without any delay.

Let us render honor to those who won salvation for us through the shedding of their blood, who offered themselves to the Lord as a sacred offering for our propitiation—especially since almighty God says to his saints: “Whoever honors you honors me; and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10).

Let us honor the holy apostles and the martyrs of Christ with solemn worship; let us honor them with praises, honor them with devotion, and honor them also through imitation. Thus, through their prayer, we shall reach everlasting fellowship in their joy. May the Lord, the author and giver of all good things, grant this—namely Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXVIII. ON THE BIRTHDAY OF SAINT MARY

The desired day of blessed and ever-venerable Virgin Mary is present for us, beloved [Col. 0054B]. Therefore let our earth, illumined by the birth of so great a Virgin, rejoice with the greatest exultation; through whose childbirth the condition of those fashioned from the earth is changed, and through whom guilt is erased.

For in her the divine sentence of misery has been cut off [the source prints *praecisa*, with *praecisum* supplied as a correction], which says: “In sorrow you shall bear children,” because she bore the Lord in joy. Eve mourned; she exulted. Eve carried tears; Mary carried joy in her womb [Col. 0054C], because the one brought forth a sinner, while the other brought forth the innocent. She gave birth as a virgin and remained a virgin after childbirth.

Both are miracles, brothers: that she was pregnant without corruption and, in giving birth, remained a virgin.

“Hail,” the angel said to her, “full of grace; the Lord is with you”—the Lord with you in your heart, with you in your womb, with you in your body, with you in your help. Rejoice, blessed Virgin: Christ the King from heaven is in your womb. Therefore you shall be blessed among women, you who have brought forth life for men and women alike.

The mother of our race brought punishment upon the world; the mother of our Lord brought salvation to the age. The one struck; the other gave life. Through disobedience, obedience has been exchanged.

Thus Mary joyfully carries the infant; exulting, she embraces her son; she carries him by whom she was carried. Hear, therefore, the voice of her words [Col. 0054D], in which she said: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior, because he has regarded the lowliness of his handmaid. For behold, from this time all generations shall call me blessed, because he who is mighty has done great things for me” (Luke 1).

Finally, after that blessed prophecy, while the Virgin silently wrestled within herself in the alternation of her thoughts over what kind of greeting this might be, the heavenly messenger continued: “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found grace with God. Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus.”

But she said: “How shall this happen, since I do not know a man?” And the angel said to her: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you. Therefore the holy one who shall be born from you shall be called the Son of God.”

Without delay the messenger returned, and Christ entered the virginal bridal chamber.

Let us therefore rejoice also, brothers, on the day of so great a Virgin, who alone among all women was worthy to conceive in her virginal, chaste, and holy womb the King whom the heavens, earth, and sea cannot contain. May she herself, as a devout intercessor, stand for us before the Son—he who carried her with all glory to the palace of heaven, and who now lives and reigns with her forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXIX. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF SAINT MARY THE VIRGIN

Since the festivals of all the holy virgins who preserved purity of mind and body until the end of life, and through God’s mercy triumphed over this wicked age [Col. 0055B], are worthy of praise, consider, brothers, how worthy of veneration is that solemnity on which the Virgin of virgins departed from this temporal life into eternal rest.

We believe not only that she is memorable among us, but also that she has become exceedingly honorable among the holy angelic spirits. They rejoice there with solemn gladness when they behold the mother of the Lord and supreme Creator enjoying eternal blessedness with them: that mother who conceived offspring in her womb and remained chaste; bore a son and remained a virgin; the immaculate mother, incorrupt mother, untouched mother; the mother of the only-begotten Lord and King of all, the Fashioner and Creator of everything.

He is the one who is without a mother in the heights and without a father on earth; he who in heaven, according to his divinity, is in the bosom of the Father, and on earth, according to the assumption of the body, was in the bosom of his mother [Col. 0055C].

This Virgin Mary is therefore called the mother of God’s only-begotten Son: worthy of the Worthy, immaculate mother of the Holy One, one mother of the One, unique mother of the Unique. For no other only-begotten God came upon the earth, nor did another virgin give birth to the only-begotten one.

Therefore, marveling at her greatness with the silent words of our hearts, let us cry out in her praise, dearest brothers, and say:

“O truly blessed Virgin Mary, recognize your glory—the glory, namely, that the angel announced to you, or that John prophesied through the mouth of Elizabeth, while he was still in the secret of his mother’s womb [the source supplies *egressus*, ‘having emerged,’ as an editorial reading]: ‘Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb.’

“You were also worthy to receive the advent promised to the whole world [Col. 0055D] through so many ages past. You became the dwelling place of immeasurable majesty. The hope of the earth, the ornament of the ages, and the common joy of all—you alone possessed these for nine months as a singular gift. The Initiator of all things was initiated by you, and from your body he received the blood to be poured out for the life of the world. Through your one childbirth, the life of all ages was born. You were worthy to call the Father of angels your son.

“Behold, you have been exalted above the choirs of angels. Beside the King, your Son, you will reign as a blessed mother and queen forever. The one to whom you gave the hospitality of your womb gave you the kingdoms of heaven.”

Yet in saying these things, brothers, it seems to me that every praise falls short of her glory and every prayer is unequal to her honor [Col. 0056A]. Let the angels praise her; let the archangels proclaim her; let all the powers of heaven and all the assemblies of the saints exult in her praises. Even so, her dignity still seems to me to exceed the honor paid to her.

But as we consider these things, brothers, let us neither despair nor draw back. Rather, let us be stirred according to our ability to praise her, and let us exult in proclaiming her. For what is lacking in our ability, her goodness will complete.

Let us cleanse our conscience from dead works and prepare ourselves to confess so great a name. Let every person and every age strive to adorn themselves with good morals in order to celebrate so great a festival, and let each strive to remain in the calling to which he or she has been called.

Therefore, all men and women who have undertaken the purpose of virginity should strive to persevere in it, so that they may be holy in body and spirit [Col. 0056B]. Let them remember God’s discipline; let them hold justice together with religious devotion; let them be steadfast in faith, humble in fear, strong for every endurance, gentle in bearing injury, ready to show mercy, united and harmonious in fraternal peace, and most prompt for every good work.

Those who are devoted to marriage should nevertheless possess virginity in the right faith, in which the whole Church is called the bride of God. The Catholic Church, however, which consists of virgins and boys, married women and married men, is called a virgin by one name. Hear the Apostle saying: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11).

Let married people preserve conjugal purity; let them abstain from what is unlawful; let them do good works [Col. 0056C]; let them love hospitality, and let them not be sluggish in giving alms.

Those who appear to be rich in this world should not be proud in their thinking, nor place their hope in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who provides all things abundantly. Let them learn to do good, to become rich in good works, to give readily, to share with their neighbors, and to store up for themselves a good foundation, so that they may take hold of eternal life.

Those who are poor should not fail in faith, but should strive to become rich in virtues. For it is written: “God chose the poor of this world, rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom which God promised to those who love him” (James 2). And the Prophet says: “I was young and now I am old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring begging bread” (Psalm 36).

Whether they are noble or ignoble, servants or free, men or women, old or young, let us all alike hear the Apostle saying: “Stand firm in the faith; act manfully and be strengthened. Let all your things be done in love” (1 Corinthians 16) [Col. 0056D].

And if, by acting in this way, the holy Mother of God sees us present at her festival, she will easily obtain for us both timely consolation in the present and eternal life in the future. May our Lord Jesus Christ grant this, he who lives and reigns as God with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXX. ON THE FAST OF THE SEVENTH MONTH
## HOMILY XXX. ON THE SEVENTH MONTH

According to the ordinance of the divine law, dearly beloved brothers, the celebration now approaches which the ancients observed as the Day of Atonement and the feast of Tabernacles. It admonishes us to understand that, in the pilgrimage of this present life, cleansed from every stain of sins by the blood of our Mediator, we ought to seek our future homeland in heaven. For we have no lasting city here, but seek the one that is to come (Heb. 13). In order that these matters may be clearer, let me briefly recall to your charity the very words of the law.

For the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Speak to the children of Israel: In the seventh month, on the first day of the month, you shall have a sabbath, a memorial with trumpets sounding, and it shall be called holy. You shall do no servile work on it, and you shall offer a holocaust to the Lord” (Lev. 23).
