And a little later he says: “On the tenth day [Col. 0057B] of this seventh month shall be the most solemn Day of Atonement, and it shall be called holy. You shall afflict your souls on it and offer a holocaust to the Lord. You shall do no work on that day, because it is a day of propitiation, that the Lord your God may be propitious to you. Every soul that is not afflicted on that day shall perish from among its people,” and the rest (ibid.). And somewhat later: “In the seventh month,” he says, “you shall celebrate a feast and dwell in booths for seven days. Everyone of the race of Israel shall remain in tabernacles, that your descendants may learn that I made the children of Israel dwell in tabernacles when I brought them out of the land of Egypt: I am the Lord your God” (ibid.).

See, dearly beloved brothers, with what great authority the rite of this solemnity was first instituted by the Lord. It must by no means be violated; rather, it should fittingly be venerated with every honorable practice of virtue, as also of sobriety and chastity, fasting and holy prayers. Nor should it seem burdensome to your love if we explain a few words from the foregoing passages, for you will celebrate more sweetly that whose meaning you know well.

The number seven, then, first bears an evident figure of perfection and completion, whether specifically of each one of us or generally of all the elect. This is indeed denoted by the fact that God rested from his works on the seventh day, enabling us to infer from it our own rest, of which Paul says: “For he who has entered into that rest has himself rested from all his works, as God did from his” (Heb. 4). But the beginning of the completion of times is the coming [Col. 0057D] of the Lord, concerning which John the Evangelist says: “Little children, it is the last hour.” This is precisely what the time of the seventh month fittingly signifies: in it we shall begin to have rest—that is, to be free from evil works and released from the heavy burden of sins.

Therefore in this month the trumpet of apostolic preaching invites us to sanctification and forbids us to perform servile works. For it is no longer time to do servile works, since the time past suffices for doing the will of the Gentiles, in which those shameful things were done. And just as we have presented our members as weapons of iniquity for iniquity, so we must present our members as weapons of righteousness for sanctification (Rom. 6). This is the true holocaust of the Lord.

What we recalled above concerning the feast of Tabernacles signifies that we who have been delivered from intelligible Egypt—that is, from the darkness of unbelief—and from the slavery of the spiritual Pharaoh, who is according to the corruption of the bricks of this present age, ought to dwell as pilgrims in tabernacles throughout the whole time of this life, which revolves in the sevenfold course of days. We should say with the Psalmist: “I am a sojourner in the land and a pilgrim, like all my fathers” (Ps. 118); and: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (ibid.). Let us imitate our head, Truth itself, who said: “Foxes have dens and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Luke 9). Going before us to the heavenly homeland, he promised us: “I go to prepare a place for you, and I shall come again and take you to myself, that where I am, you also may be” [Col. 0058B] (John 14).

Receiving this most joyful promise of our Redeemer, dearly beloved brothers, let us turn all our desire toward his love. Let us not be covetous or puffed up, intent upon present prosperity; rather, let us hasten through the labor of this present life to attain everlasting rest. “For through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14). Let us be ready for almsgiving, generous in bestowing relief upon our needy neighbors. “Naked we entered this world, naked we shall depart from this world” (Job 1). Let us lay up treasures for ourselves in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not dig through [Col. 0058C] or steal (Matt. 6). Let us chastise our flesh with fastings and vigils; let us mortify bodily pleasure, so that the strength of the soul may flourish in us.

“For every soul that is not afflicted on that day shall perish from among its people.” This plainly means: Whoever lives luxuriously and sluggishly in the present life shall be excluded from the assembly of the saints when the just Judge renders eternal rewards to those who have contended well, but everlasting punishments to the idle and negligent. In this present week, brothers, according to the ordinance of the holy Fathers, we must fast on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday, so that on the days of propitiation, through fastings and almsgiving, prayers and supplications, we may deserve to find mercy in the sight of our Creator.

Let none of us withdraw on the aforesaid days from the gathering of the Church; rather, during the sacred solemnities of the Masses, let each strive there to commend himself to God in prayer with tears and compunction of heart, so that he may receive forgiveness of past sins and, helped by grace in the future, may be able better to keep himself from all sins: through the gift of our Redeemer Jesus Christ himself, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXI. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT MICHAEL THE ARCHANGEL

As we celebrate the solemnity of blessed Michael, dearly beloved brothers, we are pleased to say something to you concerning this feast, so that your mind may raise itself with greater strength to heavenly things in proportion as it recognizes that it venerates on earth the memory of those whose dwelling is always in heaven. Thus the holy Fathers wisely provided that, although throughout the year we have various celebrations of holy martyrs and confessors on their birthdays, when they triumphed over death and were reborn to eternal life, at least on one day we should solemnly venerate the memory of the holy archangels. Since we always need their help against the snares of the ancient enemy, we may together in the common assembly ask the Lord for their aid.

The Lord created the natures of angels and human beings to know himself; and, because he willed them to endure forever, he also undoubtedly created them in his own likeness. There are nine orders of angels, and man too was created as the tenth; yet he did not perish from his Creator even after his sin, because eternal Wisdom, shining with miracles in the flesh as though from the light of a vessel, restored him. For, as the sacred utterance testifies, we know angels, archangels, virtues, powers, principalities, dominions, thrones, cherubim, and seraphim, who stand ever devoted in the camp of the heavenly King and never cease from his praise.

Yet it must be understood that the word *angel* is a name of office, not of nature. Those holy beings of the heavenly homeland are always spirits, indeed, but they cannot always be called angels, because they are angels only when something is announced through them. Hence the Psalmist says: “He makes his angels spirits” (Ps. 103), as if to say plainly: He who always has them as spirits also makes them angels when he wills. Nevertheless, ecclesiastical usage has prevailed that the citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem should generally be called angels, because of the many meanings contained in the one name “spirit.” For in Greek *angeloi* are “messengers,” and *archangeloi*, “chief messengers.” Those who announce lesser things are called angels; those who announce the greatest things are called archangels. They are also designated by individual names, so that their power in operation may be signified even by their names.

For in that holy city, in which full knowledge is perfected by the vision of almighty God, they do not receive proper names because persons without names could not be known by name. Rather, when they come to us to perform some ministry, they also take names from their ministries among us. Michael means “Who is like God?”; Gabriel, “Strength of God”; Raphael, “Medicine of God.” Whenever some work of wondrous power is performed, Michael is said to be sent, so that both deed and name may make it understood that no one can do what God is able to do. Thus the ancient enemy, who proudly raised himself to God’s likeness, is said to be about to fight with the archangel Michael at the end of the world, so that, slain by Michael, he may learn that through pride no one rises to the likeness of God. Gabriel too is sent to Mary, because he is called the Strength of God: he came to announce him who deigned to appear in humility in order to overthrow the powers of the air. Raphael, who was sent to heal Tobit’s eyes, was fittingly called the Medicine of God.

We must know, then, that when these angelic spirits come to us, they so fulfill their ministry outwardly that inwardly they are never absent through contemplation. Thus they are sent and yet stand by, because they are present to God everywhere. They love, obey, and remain in humility; they enjoy an inestimable good and therefore rejoice with ineffable gladness. They have perpetual peace among themselves and desire to keep peace with us. They are devout, kind, merciful, and full of love; they count nothing dearer than God and wish to kindle us to this love. They do not fear an end to their joy, and they desire that we should have this security with them in heaven.

But while I say these things, brothers, turn inward to yourselves; examine the merits and thoughts of your secret places. See whether you already do any good thing inwardly with yourselves; see whether, among the number of these companies which we have briefly touched upon, you find the lot of your calling. Woe to the soul that recognizes none of these goods in itself; and a worse woe still threatens it if it understands itself to be deprived of gifts and yet does not grieve. Whoever is such, my brothers, deserves great grief because he does not grieve. Therefore let us ponder the gifts granted to the elect, and with such power as we can let us pant after love of so great a lot. Whoever does not recognize the grace of gifts in himself should grieve; but whoever recognizes a lesser gift in himself should not envy a greater gift in others. For those heavenly distinctions among blessed spirits are so constituted that some are set above others, yet all are united in one and the same love.

Let us love one another, dearly beloved brothers; let us also love those spirits of the heavenly homeland and, insofar as we can, imitate their heavenly manner of life in good conduct. Above all things and beyond all things, let us love our Creator, beseeching his mercy that he who willed from the beginning to enroll us among the companies of the holy angels may, moved by the prayers of his holy archangels, bring us into their fellowship—Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXII. ON THE REVELATION OF SAINT MICHAEL

The church established and consecrated throughout the world in honor of blessed Michael the archangel demonstrates by its very foundation and dedication that his memory is to be venerated. It is commended not by the splendor of metals but by the distinction of its signs; fashioned in a humble form, it is endowed with heavenly power, since the archangel, mindful of human frailty, came from heaven and deigned with his own hand to establish it, so that mortals might there obtain the grace of heavenly gifts.

Situated on the summit of a lofty mountain, it is shown to be hewn from the mountain’s own stone in the likeness of a cave. There is a place in the territory of Campania, between the Adriatic Gulf and Mount Garganus, where the city of Sipontus is situated. Two hundred and twelve miles from the city walls, at the mountain’s highest summit, this place bears the aforementioned church of the blessed archangel.

A little book kept in the church itself tells how it became known to mortals. In that city there was a certain very wealthy man named Garganus, from whose experience the mountain also received its name. While his cattle, of which he possessed an immeasurable multitude, were grazing here and there along the slopes of the mountain, it happened that a bull, disdaining the company of the herd and accustomed to walk alone, failed to return home when the cattle came back.

Its master gathered a crowd of servants and searched for it along every trackless path. At last he found it standing on the summit of the mountain before the entrance of a certain cave. Disturbed that it was wandering alone, he seized his bow and shot at it with a poisoned arrow. Twisted back as though by a gust of wind, the arrow immediately struck the man who had shot it.

The citizens were troubled and astonished at how this had happened, for they did not dare approach more closely. They consulted the bishop about what should be done. He ordered a three-day fast and advised them to seek the answer from God. When this had been completed, the holy archangel of the Lord addressed the bishop in a vision, saying:

“You have done well to seek from God the mystery that was hidden from men. Know that a man was struck by his own weapon, and that this occurred by my will. For I am Michael the archangel, who always stand in the presence of the Lord. Since I have determined to dwell in this place on earth and to keep it safe, I wished by this judgment to demonstrate that I am the inspector and guardian of everything that is done there and of the place itself.”

When the citizens had learned these things by the revelation, they made it their custom to pray to God there and to call upon the holy Michael for aid. They saw two doors there; the southern one, which was larger, could be approached by several steps descending toward the west. Yet they did not dare proceed farther into the precipitous cavern, and every day they devoted themselves to prayer before its entrance.

Meanwhile the Neapolitans, still wandering in pagan rites, attempted to attack the Sipontines and Beneventines in war; Beneventum lies fifty miles from Sipontus. Instructed by the counsels of their bishop, the Christians asked for a three-day truce, so that during a three-day fast they might implore the protection of Saint Michael as a faithful defense.

During this time the pagans invited the aid of false gods with obscene games. But on the very night before the day appointed for battle, Saint Michael appeared in a vision to the bishop. He said that the prayers had been heard, promised that victory would come, and warned them to meet the enemy at the fourth hour of the day.

The Christians therefore went out joyfully in the morning, confident of angelic victory, and met the pagans. At the first onset of battle, Mount Garganus was shaken by an immense tremor, frequent flashes of lightning flew through the air, and a dark mist covered the entire summit of the mountain.

The prophecy was fulfilled which, praising God, says: “He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire” (Psalm 103). The pagans fled, driven partly by the sword of the enemy and partly by fiery arrows. Pursued as far as Naples, while their adversaries yielded ground everywhere, they at last entered the walls of their city half-dead, insofar as any could escape the danger. For it had become clear that the angel of God had come to the Christians’ aid.

They saw that nearly six hundred of their men had been killed by lightning. Immediately submitting their necks to Christ, the King of kings, they put on the armor of faith.

When the Christians had returned home as victors and were bringing vows of thanksgiving to the Lord at the archangel’s church, they saw in the morning, beside the northern door mentioned above, small marks resembling the hindmost footprints of a man, deeply impressed in the marble. They recognized that blessed Michael had wished to display this sign of his presence. Later a roof was added and an altar installed there, and the church itself was named because of the signs of the footprints—*Oppidania*.

There was much uncertainty among the Sipontines about what should be done with the place, and whether they ought to enter it or dedicate a church there. After deliberation, they built and dedicated a church to the east of the site in the name of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles; in it they also established altars of the blessed ever-virgin Mary and of Saint John the Baptist.

At last, having found a salutary course of action, the bishop sent messengers to ask the Roman bishop what ought to be done. At that time he happened to be on Mount Saraptim, almost fifty miles from the city of Rome. The inhabitants call him Saint Sylvester because he had once hidden there in exile during a persecution for the faith. He sent back this instruction:

“If it is a human being who is to dedicate that basilica, it ought to be done especially on the day on which the victory was granted. But if the guardian of the place himself has decreed otherwise, then on that same day his will must above all be sought in this matter. Therefore, as that time approaches, let us both undertake a three-day fast with our citizens, asking the Holy Trinity to bring to its appointed completion the gifts that he has deigned to bestow through the ministry of his supreme see.”

It happened as the bishop had suggested. During the night appointed for the fast, the chief angel of the Lord, Saint Michael, appeared in a vision to the bishop of Sipontus and said:

“There is no need for you to dedicate this basilica, which I myself built. For the one who founded it has also dedicated it. You need only enter and, with me standing by as its patron, frequently visit the place in prayer. Tomorrow, while you celebrate Mass there, let the people receive Communion according to custom. It will be my task to show how I myself consecrated this place.”

In the morning they arrived with offerings and entered the southern door with great persistence in prayer. Behold, there was a long portico extending northward and reaching a small rear door, outside which were the marble footprints we have mentioned.

Before one reached this door, however, a very large basilica appeared to the east, approached by steps. Together with its portico, it seemed able to hold nearly five hundred people. A venerable altar, covered with a red cloth, stood near the middle of the wall facing south.

Around it was the angular structure of the building—not constructed with upright walls in the manner of human workmanship, but roughened like a cave with precipitous rocks jutting out in many places. Its roof also had differing heights: in one place it rose to the summit, while elsewhere it could scarcely be reached by hand.

I believe that, taught by the archangel of the Lord, we ought to seek and love not the adornment of stones but purity of heart.

On the outside, the summit of the mountain is partly covered by a forest of hornbeams and partly broadened into a green plain. When the celebration of Mass had been completed, all returned to their own places, astonished and filled with great joy.

The bishop, assigning the duties of ministers, singers, and priests and having lodgings constructed, ordered that the entire daily course of psalms and Masses be celebrated there in due order. No one dared enter during the night; after dawn had passed, they sang the morning hymns there.

From the very rock that covers the sacred building, north of the altar, a sweet and exceptionally clear water drips drop by drop. The inhabitants call it “the Drop.” A glass vessel prepared to receive it hangs suspended from a silver chain, and it is customary for the people to climb the steps to this little vessel and taste the heavenly Lord’s liquid. It is sweet to the taste and health-giving to the touch.

Finally, some people, after enduring the burning heat of prolonged fevers, drink this Drop and immediately receive the swift refreshment of healing. The sick are also frequently healed there in countless other ways, and many miracles are demonstrably performed by angelic power alone—especially on the day of his feast, when a crowd from the surrounding provinces gathers in greater numbers than usual and the presence of angelic power is somehow believed to be greater through the multitude.

Thus what the apostles said spiritually seems to be enacted bodily: that angels are ministering spirits sent for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation (Hebrews 1). In Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXIII. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT MARTIN, CONFESSOR AND BISHOP

By the gift of divine grace, dearly beloved brothers, you have gathered today to celebrate the feast of Saint Martin the bishop. Among the feasts and memorials of the other holy Fathers, his solemnity stands noble and eminent—and rightly so, because from the earliest beginnings of human life he was so prepared for divine grace that, during his childhood, when he was first called by God’s choosing, he immediately appeared perfect.

Indeed, before he had yet been reborn through the sacred water of baptism, but had merely been instructed in the word of faith and made a catechumen, an event occurred. He possessed nothing except his weapons and the simple dress of a soldier. In the middle of winter, which had grown harsher than usual, so that the force of the cold was killing many people, he encountered at the gate of the city of Amiens a naked poor man.

The man begged passers-by to pity him, but everyone passed the wretched man by. The man of God understood that, since the others were not showing him mercy, he had been reserved for him. Yet he did not know what he could do, since he had nothing except the cloak he was wearing; he had already spent the rest on a similar act.

Therefore, taking the sword with which he was girded, he cut the cloak in half and gave one part to the poor man, then put the remaining part around himself again. When those standing nearby mocked him because he appeared in a deformed and mutilated garment, he bore it without resentment and looked toward the reward that was to come.

On the following night, when he had given himself over to sleep, he saw Christ clothed in the portion of his cloak with which he had covered the poor man. He gazed intently at the Lord and was ordered to recognize the garment he had given away. Then, amid the multitude of angels standing around him, he heard Jesus say in a clear voice:

“Martin, still a catechumen, covered me with this garment.”

Consider, brothers, from how great a perfection this holy man began his way of life. From this you can infer toward what end the course of his life proceeded.

At the age of twenty, therefore, he received the sacrament of baptism. Not long afterward he abandoned military service and attached himself to the confessor Saint Hilary, becoming a monk. In this vocation he lived so nobly that the Lord also confirmed his devotion by signs and miracles.

Meanwhile he was ordained bishop of the church of Tours. In this rank he so balanced the practice of religion that in the monk one could recognize the primacy of a shepherd, and in the shepherd admire the practice of monastic rigor.

Why say more? In every respect he became a distinguished defender of evangelical teaching and, in the frequency of his miracles, equal to the apostles in grace. Concerning him, as Sulpicius Severus writes, there is an outstanding volume.

He drove legions of demons from crowds of possessed people; removing various illnesses from the sick, he restored them to their former health; by his word he healed the weak and lepers; and, through the grace of the Holy Spirit revealing it, he foretold many things future or present. In addition to these deeds, he is also proclaimed a magnificent raiser of three dead persons.

He was often visited by angelic ministrations and was consoled by the words of the holy apostles, and especially by those of the Mother of God.

O blessed and true Israelite, in whom there was no deceit! He judged no one rashly, condemned no one unjustly, repaid no one evil for evil, and showed the greatest patience toward every injury and slander of his adversaries. He often even wept for the sins of those who slandered him, who attacked that quiet and withdrawn man with poisonous tongues and viperous mouths.

Never was there anything in his mouth except Christ; never was there anything in his heart except devotion, peace, mercy, and love.

Behold, brothers, what a great and brilliant lamp Christ placed upon a lampstand in his Church, so that all who enter may see the light. Which of us could fail to find in his way of life light, in his teaching brilliance, and in his example radiance? But since no one is unable to find these things, take care that no one be unwilling to do so. We shall not easily escape punishment if we neglect so great a grace.

We all rejoice to celebrate Martin’s feast; let us take care to follow Martin’s examples, so that we may attain Martin’s reward.

Let us not, therefore, be proud, arrogant, boastful, empty-talking, deceitful, irascible, abusive, envious, blasphemous, slanderous, greedy, drunk, lustful, or lovers of worldly pleasures—for Martin was none of these things. Rather, let us be humble, obedient, truthful, gentle, patient, kind, merciful, peaceable, gracious in speech, generous, sober, self-controlled, long-suffering, and full of love for God and neighbor—for Martin was undoubtedly all these things.

In this way we shall also please Martin, and in this way we shall always be able to have Martin himself as our intercessor. May this be granted us by him who caused his confessor, happily serving him, to enter eternal joy and appointed him over all his possessions: Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXIV. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT ANDREW THE APOSTLE

*(Gospel of John 1)*

From the reading of the holy Gospel that has just been read, dearly beloved brothers, you can weigh—and by weighing understand—how far the weakness of our faint-heartedness, lying low, falls short of the solidity of apostolic perfection, and how greatly our obstinacy differs from the obedience of the Fathers who went before us.

You heard that, at the sound of a single command, Peter and Andrew left their nets and followed the Redeemer. They had not yet seen him perform any miracles, nor had they heard anything from him about the reward of eternal recompense. Yet at one command of the Lord they forgot what they seemed to possess.

How many of his miracles have we seen? By how many scourges are we afflicted? By how many harsh threats are we terrified? And yet we disdain to follow him who calls us.

He now sits in heaven, admonishing us to conversion; he has already subjected the necks of the nations to the yoke of faith; he has already overthrown the glory of the world; and, as its ruins multiply, he announces that the day of his strict judgment is drawing near. Yet our proud mind refuses willingly to abandon what it daily loses in this life.

What, then, dearly beloved brothers, shall we say at his judgment, when we are moved neither by commands nor corrected by blows to abandon our love of the present age?

Perhaps someone says silently to himself: “At the Lord’s voice, what or how much did these two fishermen leave behind, since they possessed almost nothing?”

But in this matter, dearly beloved brothers, we must consider their devotion rather than their wealth. He left much who retained nothing for himself; he left much who abandoned everything, however little it was.

Certainly we possess even what we have with love, and we seek in desire what we do not have at all. Peter and Andrew therefore left much when both abandoned even the desire to possess. You leave much behind, brothers, if you renounce your desires.

Our external possessions, however small they may be, are sufficient if the interior of the heart is offered in its entirety. For God weighs the heart, not the substance; he does not consider how much is offered in his sacrifice, but from how much it is offered.

The kingdom of God is worth as much as you have. It was worth half of Zacchaeus’s possessions, because he kept the other half in order to repay fourfold whatever he had unjustly taken. It was worth Peter and Andrew’s nets and boat; it was worth the widow’s two small coins; it was worth another person’s cup of cold water.

The kingdom of God, as we have said, is worth as much as you have. The hand is never empty of a gift if the treasury of the heart is filled with good will.

For this reason the Psalmist says: “My vows are upon me, O God; I will render praises to you” (Psalm 53). It is as though he plainly said: “Even if I have no external gifts to offer, nevertheless within myself I find something to place upon the altar of your praise.” Nothing richer is offered to God than good will.

Good will means fearing another’s adversity as our own; rejoicing in our neighbor’s prosperity as though it were our own advancement; considering another’s losses our own and counting another’s gains as our own; loving a friend not for the world’s sake but for God’s sake; enduring even an enemy; doing nothing to anyone that you do not wish to suffer yourself; denying no one what you rightly desire to be given to you; assisting your neighbor’s need according to your strength, while desiring to help even beyond your strength.

But this sacrifice of good will, brothers, is never fully offered unless desire for this world is completely abandoned. For whatever we covet in it, we undoubtedly begrudge our neighbors. And because envy is always opposed to good will, as soon as envy seizes the mind, good will departs.

Therefore the holy preachers, so that they might perfectly love their neighbors, strove to love nothing in this world, judging that nothing is richer than love, which makes those who possess it abound in every good.

Since, then, dearly beloved brothers, we are celebrating the feast of blessed Andrew, we must imitate what we honor. We also venerate this in the memorials of the holy apostles: that, when the Lord called them, they immediately and perfectly abandoned earthly things, so that they might pursue heavenly things more earnestly and, with Christ, possess the kingdoms above.

So let us also, at the Lord’s command, despise earthly things and, having abandoned temporal matters, obtain eternal things.

If we are not yet able to abandon our own possessions, at least let us not covet those of others. If our mind is not yet kindled by the fire of love, let it have the bridle of fear in its ambition. Thus, strengthened by its progress, while it is restrained from desiring what belongs to others, it may eventually be led to despise what belongs to itself.

Meanwhile, until that perfection comes to us by the Lord’s grace, let us not neglect, brothers, to give alms from our possessions, to love hospitality, and to share every good thing with our needy neighbors according to our means. In this way, by the Lord’s generosity, we shall be able to rise to greater things, because God is won over by sacrifices of this kind.

May he himself lead us to the vision of him who is our way, who is the truth, and who is the life, Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXV. ON THE FEAST OF THE APOSTLES
If the solemnity of all the holy martyrs ought to be pleasing to us, dearly beloved brothers, how much more pleasing that of those who followed the present prince of the martyrs; and if that of lambs, how much more that of rams. For all those who afterward confessed Christ even unto death became their sons, not by the generation of the flesh but by imitation of their virtue. The peoples of the nations offered these men, concerning whom the Psalmist sang beforehand, saying: “Bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Ps. 28).

To these, when he urged them to confess his name, the Lord promised not only that he would crown their victory, but also that he would aid them in the contest. In them he was also admonishing those who would come after them, since he left in writing for posterity what he was saying. Therefore he addressed them, exhorting them:

“When they bring you before rulers and authorities, do not consider what you should answer or what you should say. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10).

He forbade them to deliberate and commanded them to confess: for he preferred to remove human presumption and bestow divine grace, so that they might be timid in themselves but bold in God. Hence, in another psalm, the voice of the martyrs says to God, as though out of the human side of weakness and in fear: “Deliver me from my enemies, my God, and free me from those who rise up against me” (Ps. 17); and shortly afterward, trusting in divine help, it says: “I will guard my strength from you, Lord” (ibid.).

For wishing to show his apostles as eminent above the other throngs of the faithful, as well as above the ancient righteous and prophets, the Lord said to them:

“Blessed are the eyes that see what you see, and the ears that hear what you hear; for many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke 10).

And again elsewhere he said:

“I shall no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15).

Again, in another place, he said to them:

“Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven” (Matt. 18).

Again elsewhere (Matt. 19), when Peter asked what benefit he and his companions had gained by leaving everything and following the Redeemer, he answered:

“Amen I say to you, that you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

These are the light of the world (Matt. 5), because through them the Lord first bestowed upon this world the light of faith and true knowledge, and rescued nations and peoples from the darkness of errors and sins. These are the salt of the earth, because through them those born of the earth received the seasoning of the taste of eternal life, so that they might restrain the wantonness of the flesh and be preserved unharmed from the putrefaction and worms of sins and vices.

These are the twelve precious stones that John describes in his Apocalypse as placed in the foundation of the heavenly building (Apoc. 21), because their preaching laid the foundations of the Church. Hence Paul also says:

“You are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Eph. 2).

These are the twelve gates of the new Jerusalem, which descends from heaven, because through them we first entered by the gate of faith and were counted among the citizens of the saints.

Considering these things, therefore, dearly beloved brothers, let us recall what such great leaders of God’s people taught us. Let us strive to fulfill by our deeds what they commanded; let us learn from their example to despise the riches of the world, not to love the pleasure of the present age, and to desire the heavenly kingdom; to prefer nothing to Christ, but to obey his commands in all things; to love poverty in present possessions, to possess the riches of virtues, to seek the treasure of wisdom, and to desire spiritual delights; to envy no one, but to love all human beings—friends in God, and enemies for God’s sake—for this alone is true love. For carnal and vicious love drags one into ruin and is comparable to hatred. Hence it is written: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this age is made an enemy of God” (James 4).

These, then, our leaders, perfect in the love of God and filled with love of their neighbors, were able to overcome the assault of the world and subdue the bloodstained age because they loved nothing in all things except the will of God. So let us also, brothers, love to do God’s will in all things; let us love our Creator in himself, and the creature in its Creator. Thus we shall possess the most ordered love, because God is love, and whoever loves this love loves God. And if we love in this way, God himself will love us; the holy apostles, our judges, will also love us and will intercede for us, so that at Christ’s universal judgment we may be crowned with them forever.

May he himself grant this, our judge and Lord, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXVI. ON THE BIRTHDAY OF THE MARTYRS

Because today the day of the blessed martyr’s commemoration has dawned—the day that the Lord has willed us to celebrate with you, dearly beloved brothers—let us, with his gift, say something about the glory and endurance of the martyrs.

Worldly glory was despised by them, and therefore their endurance was proved. For their glory lay hidden in heaven, because their endurance was exercised on earth. Whoever does not shrink from their endurance will arrive at their glory. It is considered wretched to suffer hard and harsh things in the flesh, because it truly is burdensome; but unless it were burdensome to everyone, it would not be glorious for the martyrs.

Thus the holy martyrs seemed insane to many frivolous and greedy people when they suffered so much for Christ’s name and always confessed him truthfully, even though they were driven to deny him. Some were beaten for a very long time with rods and whips; others were struck with clubs and leaded scourges; others were torn limb from limb; others killed by the sword; others flayed and drenched with melted pitch and lead; others tortured by the heat of burning coals; others consumed by flames; others drowned in the sea; others assigned to wild beasts; others killed by the horror and hunger of prisons.

As many kinds of punishments and deaths as the enemy could devise, so many did he inflict upon the martyrs without any pity. Yet although they suffered horrors openly, secretly they were crowned ineffably.

Many sought earthly glory; many brave men considered that blood ought to be shed for their country and did not hesitate to shed it, so that they might possess glory among posterity even after death. But what is the glory of those men compared with that of the martyrs? What an emperor could discover, a fisherman was able to discover.

The tombs of emperors, consuls, and brave men who conquered and subjugated the world by arms are at Rome. An emperor deigned to enter the fisherman’s tomb; yet the fisherman received him as he prayed at his own tomb, having laid aside his diadem. Behold: if the martyrs had desired earthly glory, they were not deprived even of that, since they sought honor among the angels.

We see their glories on earth and marvel; what would we suffer if we saw them in heaven? How great an astonishment of admiration would seize us if we saw the martyrs glorifying among the angels, whose commemorations we see peoples celebrating?

But we wish to rejoice with the saints and do not wish to endure the world’s tribulation with them. For whoever does not wish, insofar as he is able, to imitate the holy martyrs will not be able to reach their blessedness.

Thus the Apostle also proclaims, saying (2 Cor. 1): “If we are companions in suffering, we shall also be companions in consolation.” And the Lord says in the Gospel: “If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you” (John 15). Whoever does not wish to endure hatred with the head refuses to belong to the body.

But someone may say: “Who is able to follow the footsteps of the blessed martyrs?” To him I answer: with the Lord’s help, we can imitate not only the martyrs but also the Lord himself, if we wish.

Hear not me but the Lord himself, crying out to the human race and saying: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. 11). Hear also blessed Peter admonishing us: “Christ suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2).

Behold: Christ says, “Learn from me”; blessed Peter says, “So that you might follow his footsteps.” Likewise the Apostle Paul cries out: “Be imitators of God, as beloved children” (Eph. 5).

What shall we answer to these things, brothers, or what excuse shall we be able to offer? If someone tells you that you ought to imitate the virtues performed by the Lord, your excuse may reasonably be that it is not granted to everyone to perform virtues and miracles. But to live justly and chastely, and to preserve love toward all, is commanded to everyone with God’s help.

For the Lord himself did not say: “Learn from me to raise the dead or to walk with dry feet upon the waters.” He did not say this; but what did he say? “Because I am gentle and humble of heart.” And again: “Love your enemies and do good to those who hate you, just as your heavenly Father makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked” (Luke 6).

Although there are many other things in which we ought to imitate God and the blessed martyrs, these two are nevertheless primary: that we should be gentle and humble of heart, and that we should love our enemies with all our heart and all our strength.

Concerning loving enemies, dearly beloved brothers, no one will ever be able truthfully to excuse himself. Someone may say to me: “I cannot fast; I cannot give all my possessions to the poor and serve God in a monastery.” But can he say: “I cannot love”?

Someone may say: “My enemy has done so many evils to me that I cannot possibly love him by any means.” You consider what a human being has done to you, but you do not consider what you have done to God. If you examine and investigate your conscience carefully, you commit far greater sins against God, without any comparison, than a human being has committed against you. With what face do you wish God to deign to forgive you much when you are unwilling to forgive a little?

But you, brothers, because every day you say to God in prayer, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6), forgive, and it will be forgiven you. For the Truth himself cries out terribly and says: “If you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your heavenly Father forgive your sins.”

Let us therefore imitate the holy martyrs of Christ in faith, humility, gentleness, patience, long-suffering, and love. Thus we shall be able to have the martyrs themselves as intercessors before God, so that our sins may be blotted out and eternal rewards bestowed upon us.

This may our Lord Jesus Christ grant, who lives and reigns as God with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXVII. ON THE BIRTHDAY OF THE HOLY CONFESSORS

Today, dearly beloved brothers, we celebrate the day of our holy confessor, on which, leaving this laborious life, he was reborn into perpetual life; on which he finished the labor of the contest and received the reward of confession.

For just as the Church is accustomed to celebrate the triumphs of the holy martyrs, so also it celebrates those of the blessed confessors: the former because, completing the contest, they earned the palm of martyrdom; the latter because, persevering in the confession of the true faith, they received the crown of life.

And rightly both are honored in equal measure, because both proved to be true witnesses of Christ and true praisers of him. For *martyrs* in Greek means “witnesses,” while *confessors* in Latin signifies “praisers.”

Concerning these the Lord says: “Whoever confesses me before human beings, I also will confess him before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 10).

But this confession, brothers, must be maintained not only with the mouth but also with the heart and deed together. For the Truth himself says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 11).

This holy man pleased the Lord because inwardly, through faith, and outwardly, through preaching and the practice of a good example, he duly praised the Lord.

He belongs to the number of those servants who, according to the Lord’s parable, when their master came, returned the talents entrusted to them with profit and, being well rewarded, entered into the joy of their master.

Therefore the servant who returned the doubled talents is praised by his master and brought to eternal reward. To him the Lord’s voice says: “Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your master” (Matt. 25).

All the goods of the present life are little, however great they may appear. But then the faithful servant is set over much when, having conquered every affliction of corruption, he rejoices in eternal joys in that heavenly dwelling.

Then he is perfectly admitted into the joy of his master when, taken up into that eternal homeland and joined to the companies of angels, he inwardly rejoices in his gift, so that there is now nothing outwardly for him to suffer from corruption.

Thus this holy man kept good watch at the Lord’s command, and blessed is the servant because, when his Lord came, he found him watching. The one watches who keeps the eyes of his mind open to the sight of the true light; he watches who preserves in action what he believes; he watches who drives away from himself the darkness of sluggishness and negligence.

Hence Paul says: “Awake, you righteous, and do not sin” (1 Cor. 15).

For the Lord made him recline with his saints—that is, he granted him refreshment in eternal rest. “And passing by, he will minister to him,” because he satisfies him with the illumination of his light. For the Lord’s “passing by” means leading us into the contemplation of his brightness: we see after the judgment in divinity the one whom we behold in humanity at the judgment.

Therefore, my most beloved brothers, watch more attentively. Fix the eyes of your mind upon the condition of your mortality. Prepare yourselves for the judge who is coming through daily tears and lamentations. Since certain death awaits everyone, do not anxiously concern yourselves with the provision of temporal life. Let care for earthly things not weigh you down. For however many masses of gold and silver may surround the body, and however many precious garments may clothe it, what else is it than flesh?

Do not therefore consider what you have, but what you are. Do you wish to hear what you are? The prophet indicates it, saying: “Truly, the people are grass” (Isa. 40). For if the people are not grass, where are those who, together with you, celebrated the commemoration of this blessed confessor whom we honor today, when a year had passed?

Oh, how many and how great were the things they were planning concerning the provision of the present life! But when the moment of death stole upon them, they were suddenly found amid the things they did not wish to see, and at once they lost all the temporal things that, having handled them as though they were stable, they seemed to possess securely.

Since, then, the hours flee in their moments, act, dearly beloved brothers, so that they may be held fast in the reward of good work. Hear what the wise Solomon says: “Whatever your hand is able to do, perform diligently, because there is neither work nor reason nor wisdom in the underworld to which you are hastening” (Ecclus. 5).

Since we do not know the time of our coming death, and cannot work after death, it remains for us to seize the time granted before death and usefully labor at whatever we can. Thus, after the end of this life, Christ may grant us to rejoice in the heavenly kingdom with his confessors rather than to be punished with sinners in hell.

May he himself grant us to avoid his anger and obtain his grace—he who redeemed us, Christ our Savior, who lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXVIII. ON THE BIRTHDAY OF THE VIRGINS

The immaculate Lord consecrated to himself an immaculate household even in this body filled with the filth of human frailty, while throughout the whole world Mary’s virginal flower binds unfading crowns and preserves, with immaculate devotion, the scepter-bearing court of chastity.

Hence integrity persevered so far as to seize the trophy of sanctity among maidens and, following in the footsteps of the virgin mother, to reach the heavenly bridal chamber.

Virginity is indeed a holy thing; it is a perfect thing, the principal virtue, possessing a special crown in the kingdom of God. Virginity is not praiseworthy because it is also found in martyrs, but because it makes martyrs.

Who could comprehend it by human ingenuity, when not even nature can comprehend it within its own enclosed laws [Latin *inclusis*; perhaps *inclusam*]? Or who could encompass what lies beyond nature’s ordinary course with natural speech [printed *completus*; perhaps *complectitur*, “embraces”]?

It summoned from heaven what it was to imitate on earth. Nor did it seek the manner of life from heaven without reason, since it found its bridegroom in heaven. Crossing beyond the aerial clouds, the angels, and the stars, it found the Word of God in the very bosom of the Father and drank him in with its whole heart.

For who, having found so great a good, would abandon it? Therefore Scripture says of him: “Your name is an emptied-out perfume; therefore young women loved you and drew you onward” (Song 1).

This order already bears the image of the future resurrection. Hence it is written in the Gospel: “At the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but they will be like the angels of God in heaven” (Matt. 22).

Let no one, then, wonder if those who are joined to the Lord of angels are compared with angels. For this truly becomes the image of God, corresponding to the holiness of the Lord, the more radiant portion of Christ’s flock.

Through them and in them the glorious fruitfulness of Mother Church rejoices and blossoms abundantly. The more abundant virginity increases her number, the more the mother’s joy grows.

Most sacred virginity persevered in its rank even unto the shedding of blood, because Christ had watered it with his own blood. The spirit burns toward heavenly things; nothing earthly pleases. Whatever had pleased by its earthly appearance is seen as deformed, because only the radiance of the precious pearl shines in the mind.

Concerning love of it, Solomon rightly says: “Love is strong as death” (Song 8), because, just as death destroys, so the love of eternal life kills the love of bodily things. For whoever it has perfectly absorbed, it makes, outwardly, as though insensible to earthly desires.

This holy woman whose commemoration we celebrate today could not have died bodily for the Lord if she had not first died in mind to earthly desires. For more rightly did her spirit, at the summit of virtue, laugh at tortures and trample rewards, standing before armed kings and governors: stronger than the one striking her, higher than the one judging her.

What shall we, bearded and weak men, say in the face of this, when we see maidens going to the heavenly kingdoms through the sword—men whom anger overcomes, pride inflates, ambition disturbs, and lust defiles?

If we cannot attain the kingdom of heaven through the battles of persecution, let it at least be disgraceful for us to be unwilling to follow God through peace.

Behold, in our time God says to no one: “Die for me”; rather, he says: “Kill within yourself only unlawful desires.” Therefore, if we are unwilling in peace to subdue the desires of the flesh, how shall we give that very flesh for the Lord in war?

Let each one of you know this with certainty: whoever here does not wish to crucify and mortify within himself the desires of the flesh will certainly not reach eternal joys in the future.

But because present joys are followed by perpetual lamentation, flee here, dearly beloved brothers, vain joy, if you fear weeping there. For no one can rejoice here with the age and reign in the future with Christ.

Therefore restrain temporal joy, which passes away; tame the pleasures of the flesh. Whatever delights in the mind with childish cheerfulness, let the discipline of youthful seriousness restrain it. Thus, while you voluntarily flee temporal things, you may receive eternal joys without labor.

By the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXIX. ON THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH

With the divine favor of almighty God and with his clemency granting assent, you have gathered together well today, dearly beloved brothers, so that we might dedicate a house to God, at his own command and in accordance with his saying: “Make me a sanctuary, and I will dwell in your midst, says the Lord God” (Zech. 2).

But we do this worthily only if we strive to become God’s temple ourselves, and if we endeavor to correspond to the solemnity we celebrate. Just as we have diligently adorned the walls of this same church, kindled many lights, and raised various voices through litanies and prayers, readings and hymns, striving to offer praise to God, so also let us continually adorn the inner chambers of our hearts with the necessary ornaments of good works. Let the flame of divine and fraternal love continually increase within us; let the holy sweetness of the memory of heavenly commands and evangelical praise continually resound in the sanctuary of our breast.

These are the fruits of a good tree; this is the good treasure of the heart; these are the foundations of the wise architect, which today’s reading from the holy Gospel commends to us.

We must possess not merely the form but rather the power of piety. The mystical history of the Old Testament also carefully suggests this to us, when Moses built the tabernacle (Exod. 40), or Solomon built the temple for the Lord as a type of the holy Church (1 Kings 8).

Both houses are reported to have been firmly founded, and all the materials that were in them are described: precious stones, from which the temple was constructed; incorruptible wood, from which the entire tabernacle was made and the temple was adorned within and shone with a covering above; gold, with which the walls of the tabernacle were clothed inside and out, and with which not only the walls of the temple but also its ceilings, beams, doors, doorposts, and floors were covered.

The vessels and utensils of both houses were almost all golden and made of the purest gold. The fruits of trees offered in the Lord’s house were also commanded to be pure and choice—namely, those of the vine and olive, frankincense, myrrh, or liquid myrrh, and other things of this kind.

All these things, understood spiritually, proclaim the true sincerity of our faith and conduct, and mystically teach how we may become God’s house.

Let us therefore hear what our Redeemer himself says about the construction of his house, which is us, in the reading from the holy Gospel that has just been recited to us:

“There is no good tree that produces bad fruit, nor a bad tree producing good fruit” (Matt. 7).

Our king therefore seeks good trees and their good fruits for the construction or service of his temple. But what the end of the bad tree will be, he teaches elsewhere, saying:

“Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. 3).

By trees he means human beings, and by fruits, their works.

Do you wish to know what are the fruits of the good tree and of the bad? The Apostle teaches this:

“The works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, impurity, lust, the service of idols, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousies, anger, quarrels, dissensions, heresies, envy, murder, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these” (Gal. 5).

Do you wish to hear whether the trees that produce these fruits belong to the heavenly temple of the eternal king? The Apostle adds:

“I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God” (ibid.).

He subsequently enumerates the fruits of the good tree, saying:

“The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, goodness, kindness, faith, gentleness, self-control” (ibid.).

These fruits, together with the trees from which they proceed, truly belong here to the house of faith and there to the dwelling of heavenly blessedness.

Therefore let us pray, dearly beloved brothers, to God the almighty Father, author and giver of all good things, that by his virtue and wisdom he may make us good trees, render us fit for the building of his house, and deign to found and place us upon that rock of which the Apostle says: “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10).

May he protect us against the varied flood of persecutions by the breath of his Spirit, preserve us unharmed forever without the ruin of sin, and gather us into the heavenly Jerusalem, consecrating us as his perpetual dwelling—he who lives and reigns eternally and perpetually in perfect Trinity and unity, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XL. ON THE ANNUAL FESTIVAL OF THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH

*(The Gospel of John, chapter 10.)*

From the authority of the Gospel reading, dearly beloved brothers, we are taught to commemorate this feast, where it is read that the Feast of Dedication took place in Jerusalem and that Jesus was physically present there at that time (John 10).

These celebrations were called the *Encaenia*, the solemnities of the temple’s dedication, which the people of God, following the ancient tradition of the fathers, were accustomed to celebrate each year. Following their footsteps today according to the custom of the Christian world, we have striven to observe solemnly the annual day of the dedication of our church with divine praises and vigils.

We ought to celebrate this festival with the greater devotion because we have learned that it was especially pleasing to our Redeemer—so much so that on that occasion he himself deigned to enter the temple, speak to the people, and disclose the mysteries of his divinity.

“It was the Feast of Dedication in Jerusalem, and it was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple in Solomon’s portico.”

If, then, he wished to walk in the temple where the flesh and blood of irrational animals were offered, how much more gladly will he visit our house of prayer, where the mysteries of his own flesh and blood are celebrated?

If he did not disdain to walk through the portico in which a formerly mortal and earthly king, however powerful and wise, used to stand in prayer, how much more does he desire to visit and illuminate the inner chambers of our hearts—provided that he perceives them to be Solomon’s portico, that is, provided that he finds in them his fear, which is the beginning of wisdom.

For we must not think that only the house in which we gather for prayer or to celebrate the mysteries is the Lord’s temple. We ourselves, who gather in the Lord’s name, are called and are his temple much more fully, since the Apostle plainly says: “You are the temple of the living God” (1 Cor. 3), just as the Lord says: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” (2 Cor. 6).

If we are God’s temple, let us take diligent care and strive through good works that he himself may often deign both to come into his temple and to make his dwelling there.

Let us beware of the example of winter, lest, when the Lord comes, he find our hearts numb from the warmth of love, just as he found the hearts of the Jews hardened by unbelief, and therefore quickly turn away from and abandon them.

Rather, let us labor with all our strength and with his help so that our God may not find in his temple—that is, in us—anything that offends the eyes of his majesty. Let the dwelling of our heart be emptied of vices and filled with virtues; let it be closed to the devil and opened to Christ. Let us labor so that, by the keys of good works, we may be able to open for ourselves the door of the heavenly kingdom.

For just as evil works close the door of life to us, as though with bars and bolts, so without doubt it is opened by good works.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, let each one examine his conscience. When he recognizes that he has been wounded by some crime, let him first strive to cleanse his conscience through prayers, fasts, or almsgiving, and then presume to receive the Eucharist.

For if, recognizing his guilt, he himself withdraws from the divine altar, he will quickly attain the forgiveness of divine mercy. For just as the one who exalts himself will be humbled, so, conversely, the one who humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14).

Whoever, as I have said, recognizes his guilt and wishes humbly to remove himself from the church’s altar for the correction of his life need not fear being wholly excluded from that eternal and heavenly banquet.

I beg you, brothers, attend carefully. If no one presumes to approach the table of any powerful person in torn and soiled garments, how much more ought each person who has been struck by the poison of envy or hatred, filled with the poison of anger, wounded by the arrows of greed, polluted by the vice of drunkenness, or defiled by the filth of lust, to withdraw reverently and humbly from the banquet of the eternal King—that is, from the Lord’s altar—lest, because of presumption and obstinacy, he be separated from the eternal banquet of God and the fellowship of the saints, and be cast forever into the fire with hands and feet bound.

Rather, let him strive, made sober and clean through repentance and almsgiving, peace and self-control, to approach the Lord’s table here with confidence, and in the future to arrive rejoicing at the fellowship of the holy angels and apostles, prophets and martyrs, and all the other righteous.

May our Redeemer and Savior Jesus Christ grant this to us by his grace, he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XLI. ON SUNDAYS
It should be known, most beloved brothers, that our holy Fathers therefore ordained and commanded Christians to rest and abstain from earthly business on the feasts of the saints, and especially on Sundays, so that they might be readier and more prompt for divine worship, having no hindrance that could delay them from it, and might leave aside earthly care at the time when they could more readily attend to God’s will. Hence the Lord himself says through the Prophet: “Be still and know that I am God” (Psalm 45). But those who, entangled in various cares and [Col. 0076C] occupations, despise this command of God and refuse to devote themselves to divine contemplation—I fear that at the future judgment, when they knock at the Lord’s door and ask that it be opened to them (Matthew 25), the Lord will answer them: “Truly I say to you, I do not know you. Depart from me, all you who practice iniquity” (Matthew 7); and those who now neglect to seek God will then be rejected by him.

Therefore, my brothers, let it not be burdensome for you to devote yourselves to divine worship on Sundays and on the feast days of the saints. The apostles and apostolic men decreed that Sunday should consequently be observed with religious solemnity because on that day our Redeemer rose from the dead. It is called the Lord’s Day so that on it, abstaining from earthly works and the allurements of the world, we may serve divine worship alone, giving this day honor and reverence because of the hope of our resurrection that we possess in it. For just as the Lord Jesus Christ himself, our Savior, rose from the dead on the third day, so we too hope to rise on the last day.

It is evident also from the holy Scriptures that this day is solemn: it is the first day of the world; on it the elements of the world were formed; on it the angels were created; on it, too, Christ rose from the dead; on it the Holy Spirit descended from heaven upon the apostles; and on the same day manna was first given from heaven in the wilderness. Through these actual signs [Perhaps: “special deeds and signs”], therefore, Sunday stands out as distinguished. For this reason the holy teachers of the Church decreed that all the glory of the Jewish Sabbath should be transferred to it, so that what they celebrated in figure we might celebrate in truth. For our true rest will come when the resurrection has been accomplished and the reward has been perfected alike in soul and body.

Let us therefore observe Sunday, brothers, and sanctify it, just as the command concerning the Sabbath was given to the ancients, the lawgiver saying: “From evening to evening you shall celebrate your Sabbaths” (Leviticus 23). Let us see to it that our rest is not fruitless, but that from the evening of the Sabbath day until the evening of the Lord’s Day, withdrawn from rural labor and from every business, we devote ourselves to divine worship alone. Thus also we rightly sanctify the Lord’s Sabbath, the Lord saying: “You shall do no work on it.”

Let everyone who is able come to the evening and nocturnal celebration, and there pray to God in the assembly of the Church for his sins. Whoever cannot do this should at least pray in his own house and should not neglect to pay his vow to God and render the due measure of his service.

On that day no one should absent himself from the sacred celebration of the Mass, nor should anyone remain idle at home while the others go to church. Nor should he occupy himself with hunting and become enslaved to the devil’s service, roaming through fields and forests, raising shouts and laughter, and uttering no groan or words of prayer to God from the depths of his heart.

What is even more detestable is that some who come to church do not enter, do not attend to their prayers, and do not wait in silence for the holy celebration of the Mass. Instead, while the divine readings are being read inside, they remain outside either bringing lawsuits and striving to attack others with various accusations, or sweating over dice games or in useless places. Sometimes, what is worse, some are inflamed with excessive anger and quarrel most bitterly, so that they attack one another with weapons or clubs and often commit murder.

This is done especially by those who, filled with envy and hatred, go to the assembly of the Church under the devil’s leadership—not to help themselves, but to harm others. If such people perish there through homicide, or are suddenly carried off by death, where do they go except to eternal torments with the very one whose footsteps they have followed?

Do not do these things, my brothers; do not deceive yourselves; do not give the devil a place in your assembly (Ephesians 4), but rather prepare within yourselves a lodging for Christ. Devote yourselves not to conversations outside, but inside to psalmody and prayers. Do not chatter with one another in church, but remain quiet.

There are many people, especially certain women, who chatter and talk so much in church that they neither hear the divine readings themselves nor allow others to hear them. Surely, my brothers, is an assembly conducted in this fashion and with this disorder fit to take place in the house of God? Is it fitting to stand in such a manner in the presence of God and his holy angels?

There is still another matter, greatly deserving of sorrow, about which I wish to complain to you: there are some, especially the powerful of this world, who, when they come to church, are not devout in celebrating the praises of God. Instead, they compel the presbyter to shorten the Mass and to sing according to their pleasure. Because of their gluttony and greed, he is not permitted to follow the Church’s custom, so that one brief portion of the day may be assigned to the service of God, and the remaining hours of the day, together with the night, to their pleasures.

Do not do these things, my most beloved brothers, and do not consent to those who do them; for not only those who do such things perish, but also those who consent to their perpetrators.

Above all, therefore, do not bring or hear lawsuits on feast days, but do so at another time and with justice. And do not overturn just judgments by accepting gifts, because, according to the Lord’s sentence: “With whatever judgment you judge, you shall be judged” (Matthew 7).

Let none of you get drunk, because a drunkard is very much like a madman. Do not, by drinking [“in names,” as printed], erase your names from heaven. Indeed, there are many—what is worse—who not only make themselves drunk but also compel and urge others to drink more than is proper. From this quarrels and murders often arise among them.

Do you not consider, brothers, whose will they are following in this? “Drunkards,” the Apostle says, “and murderers shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6).

I beseech you, most beloved—fathers and mothers, brothers and sisters—by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and by his coming kingdom and judgment, withdraw yourselves from everyone who walks disorderly, and walk worthily of the calling to which you have been called. Do not neglect your dignity, but consider the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.

You have been called the sons of God, because the true Son of God has freed you. Strive to please so great a parent by good conduct, so that he may not hand you over, as utterly wicked slaves, to everlasting punishment, but may lead you, as his dearest children, to the heavenly homeland, so that you may be fellow heirs of his Son Jesus Christ, with whom God lives and reigns in the unity of the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XLII. AGAINST THOSE WHO WEARIED THEMSELVES WITH SHOUTS DURING AN ECLIPSE OF THE MOON

I rejoice greatly, most beloved brothers, that I see you loving the Christian name, frequenting the churches, desiring the baptism of Christ for your sons and daughters, and devoting yourselves to the worship of the true God. But I grieve greatly to see many of you wandering, bound by certain foolish practices, and mingling certain false things with the truths of the Christian religion—something that ought by no means to happen. For it is written: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (1 Corinthians 5).

When, a few days ago, I was remaining quietly at home and was considering with myself how I might increase your progress in the Lord for your benefit, suddenly, on that day around evening and the beginning of night, such a great shouting arose from the people that its irreligion seemed to penetrate even to heaven.

When I inquired what this shouting meant, they told me that your cries had assisted the suffering moon and helped its eclipse by your efforts. I laughed and marveled at such vanity: you were offering help to God as though he himself were weak and feeble and, unless assisted by our voices, could not defend the heavenly lights that he had created.

The next morning, I asked those who had gathered to visit us whether any of these things had become known to them. They admitted that they had experienced similar and even worse practices in the places where they themselves had stayed. One reported that he had heard the bellowing of horns, as though men were being summoned to war; another said that he had heard the grunting of pigs. Some related that they had seen certain people hurling weapons and arrows against the moon, while others scattered fires toward heaven. They declared that certain monsters—I do not know what kind—were tearing the moon apart, and that unless they themselves came to its aid, those monsters would utterly devour it.

Others, to satisfy the deception of demons, had cut apart their hedges with weapons and broken the vessels they kept at home, as though this would greatly help the moon.

What madness is this, brothers, and what insanity? Are you stronger than God, so that you attempt to fight on his behalf? Or are your pigs more powerful than his angels, so that they need their grunting? How will you give aid to heaven and the stars, when on earth you are not even strong enough to protect yourselves? “Why should ash and dust be proud?” (Ecclesiasticus 10).

For it is written: “A man’s way is not in his own power; his spirit will go forth, and he will return to the earth” (Psalm 145).

What shall I say to you, brothers? Shall I praise you? I do not praise you in this matter, because, deceived by the devil, you have in no small measure given yourselves over to pagan error. And where does this come from, if not from the pagans, whose company you love and whose customs you imitate? I have often forbidden you their company and their abominable feasts, but greed prevents you from obeying me.

You love money and do not fear Gehenna; you desire bodily pleasures and neglect the eternal salvation of the soul. Therefore you will be able to possess neither bodily nor spiritual health, because, as the Apostle Paul says: “That is why there are many sick and weak among you, and many are asleep” (1 Corinthians 11).

Do not go astray, brothers; do not be deceived by errors of this kind: “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it” (Psalm 23). “Blessed is he whose God is the God of Jacob, whose helper he is; his hope is in the Lord his God, who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them, who keeps truth forever” (Psalm 145).

The monsters which, as you say, tear the moon apart at the time of its eclipse are nothing. It is not right to believe that human beings can be changed into beasts. Rather, this invention of demons presents such things to brutish and foolish people through various phantasms, so that they may more easily incite them to idolatry.

But lest I leave you doubtful and anxious about the obscurity of the moon that recently occurred, this, brothers, is not some portent. It is the natural force that causes the sun and moon to suffer an eclipse—that is, a darkening—of this kind. Clear reasoning shows that, when the moon, because of its lower course, intervenes before the sun, the sun cannot pour its light upon our eyes; this occurs at the time of its new phase. Likewise, the moon, which is illuminated by the sun, is darkened by the shadow of the earth at the full moon—that is, on the fifteenth day of its cycle—when the sun is on one side of the sky and the moon shines from the other.

Therefore, brothers, when such a thing occurs, there is no need for you to weary yourselves with shouting. Leave the Creator to his creation, for he knows how to govern his work, since he was able to create it.

If, therefore, unusual signs appear in the sun, moon, or stars—for it is necessary that such signs occur before the great day of judgment, according to the word of Truth—do not then weary yourselves with such superstition. Instead, pray in your hearts for the Lord’s mercy, and sign yourselves with the sign of Christ’s cross, so that he who deigned to redeem you through the holy cross may, at the coming of his glory, graciously preserve you unharmed from every error under its protection: Jesus Christ our Lord and Savior, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit comes and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XLIII. AGAINST PAGAN ERRORS, WHICH SOME OF THE UNINSTRUCTED CHRISTIANS FOLLOW

[Col. 0080B]

We read in the Old Testament that the Lord commanded his people, whom he chose for himself as his inheritance, in this way (Leviticus 20): “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy. Do not walk according to the statutes of the nations whom I am going to drive out before you. For because of their crimes I detested them and separated you from the other peoples, so that you might be mine. When you enter the land that I will give you, destroy all the inhabitants of that land; break their inscribed pillars, shatter their statues, and devastate all their high places. You shall not permit sorcerers to live in your land. A man or woman in whom there is a spirit of a python or of divination shall surely die; stone them. But if you do not kill such people, those who remain will be like nails in your eyes and spears in your sides; they will oppose you in the land of your dwelling, and whatever I had thought of doing to them, I will do to you.”

You have heard, most beloved brothers, how terribly the divine voice threatens those who allow their adversaries to dwell with them. I fear that your fellow inhabitants will become a cause of scandal and ruin for you, since you imitate their most wicked customs.

How will those who associate with the devil and his ministers on earth reign with Christ and his angels in heaven? How will those who do not reject the abominable banquets of the pagans rejoice at the everlasting banquet of the saints? Or how can those who here present the devil with deadly games in idols sing praises to God with the angels in everlasting light?

The Apostle forbids us to maintain such associations and says (1 Corinthians 10): “Most beloved, flee from the worship of idols. I do not want you to become partners with demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons; you cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons.”

And again, in another place (2 Corinthians 6): “Do not be yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership is there between righteousness and iniquity? Or what fellowship between light and darkness? What agreement is there between Christ and Belial? Or what share does a believer have with an unbeliever? What agreement is there between the temple of God and idols? You are the temple of the living God; as God says: ‘I will dwell in them and walk among them; I will be their God, and they shall be my people.’”

Therefore, most beloved brothers, cleanse yourselves of such errors. Correct and remove your sons and dependents from this wickedness. Let none of you seek out charmers—*charagios*—or diviners or sorcerers; let no one question them about any matter or illness. Let no one employ enchanters, because whoever does this evil immediately loses the sacrament of baptism and straightaway becomes a sacrilegious person and a pagan. Unless great almsgiving and harsh, prolonged penance come to his aid, he will perish forever.

Likewise, do not observe omens. When you are on a journey, do not pay attention to birds singing, and do not presume to announce demonic divinations from their song. Let none of you observe on what day he leaves his house or on what day he returns, because God made all the days, as Scripture says: “And there was the first day, and the second day, and the third day” (Genesis 1), and likewise the fourth, fifth, sixth, and the Sabbath; and it says: “God made all things very good” (Genesis 2).

Do not observe or pay attention to those signs that are not only sacrilegious but also ridiculous—sneezes. Whenever necessity requires you to hurry anywhere, sign yourselves in the name of Christ, faithfully reciting the Apostles’ Creed or the Lord’s Prayer, and travel confidently in God’s help.
