And because, when you begin—through God’s inspiration—to despise and reject all the sacrileges mentioned above, I know that the devil will take this badly, seeing you withdraw from his friendship and company and despise the sacrileges by which he deceived you. He will cause you some trouble, send you some illness, or take away some animal of yours, either through disease or by causing it to stray. God permits this to happen in order to test you, so that he may know whether you have come to him faithfully, whether you despise all the devil’s schemes, and whether his love is worth more to you than the loss of any animal.

But if, once or twice, you despise with your whole heart and complete faith the troubles that the devil has brought upon you, God will thereafter deign to drive the devil so far from troubling you that he will never be able to deceive you by his cunning.

For Christ our God holds the devil and his ministers under his sole power. He cannot harm you or anything belonging to you in any way except insofar as God permits it.

God permits this for two reasons: either to test us, if we are good, or to chastise us, if we are sinners. Therefore fear him alone, serve him alone, preserve purity of mind and body, flee every kind of fornication as a plague or death, be temperate, humble, gentle, and patient, love frugality, and strive to persevere in right faith and good works to the end of life. Thus you will reach eternal life without delay, through our Redeemer Jesus Christ himself, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XLIV. ON THE GOOD CONDUCT OF CHRISTIANS AND, IN CONTRAST, ON THE CONDUCT OF THE WICKED

[Col. 0082A]

It is fitting for you, most beloved brothers, carefully and attentively to consider the Christian name, which we all rejoice to bear: what it signifies for us, what it promises, and what good it confers upon us—that is, what it signifies in religion, what it promises in hope, and what it confers in reward.

For we are called Christians from Christ, the only-begotten Son of God. Therefore, whoever says that he is a Christian ought to walk as he walked—that is, in justice, holiness, and truth. This is what the Christian name admonishes us to do.

And whoever follows Christ in these footsteps is journeying toward the heavenly homeland and will receive everlasting life in heaven.

It is not enough for us, brothers, that we have received the Christian name if we do not perform Christian works. The name “Christian” benefits the person who loves charity, flees drunkenness, detests pride, and rejects envy as the devil’s poison. A Christian is one who does not steal, who does not give false testimony, who neither lies nor swears falsely; who does not commit adultery; who comes frequently to church; who does not taste the fruits of his fields before first offering something from them to God; who gives the tithes to be distributed annually to the poor; who shows honor to his priests; who loves every person as himself; and who hates no one.

Indeed, he is not merely a Christian: Christ himself dwells in him, because he fears fraudulent scales and double measures as the devil’s sword.

A good Christian is one who, when he comes to church, presents an offering to be placed on the altar, and, according to his means, gives silver or food to the poor; who receives strangers into his home and washes the feet of his guests; who not only does not stir up disputes but also restores those who are at odds to harmony; who lives chastely himself and both admonishes by his words and teaches by his example his children or neighbors to live chastely and soberly.

A good Christian is one who, whenever the holy solemnities arrive, preserves chastity with his own wife for several days beforehand, so that he may communicate more securely and, with a free and secure conscience, approach the Lord’s altar with a chaste body and a pure heart; who knows the Apostles’ Creed and the Lord’s Prayer by heart and faithfully teaches his sons and daughters to know them as well.

Behold, brothers, you have heard what good Christians are like. Therefore, as far as we can, let us labor with God’s help so that the Christian name may not be false in us, nor the sacraments of Christ suffer injury in us, but so that we may always both consider Christian works in our hearts and fulfill them in our actions.

For what sort of Christian is the person who scarcely ever comes to church and, when he comes, does not remain in church to pray for his sins, but to bring lawsuits or stir up disputes and quarrels; and who, if he finds an opportunity, drinks until he vomits? After making himself drunk, he rises like a frenzied and madman and, in the devil’s manner, dances and leaps about, singing shameful, amorous, or lustful songs.

Such a person does not hesitate to steal, does not fear committing adultery, gives false testimony, curses, swears falsely, and is not afraid to commit any crime whatsoever.

Therefore, whether they are men or women, those who do such things receive the Christian name and the sacraments of baptism not for healing but for judgment; and unless they do penance, they will perish forever.

Behold, brothers, we have shown you what good Christians are like and what wicked Christians are like. Imitate those whom you see to be good. But those whom you recognize as wicked, correct always, rebuke them, and admonish them, so that you may receive a double reward both for your own progress and for their correction.

This is granted by our Lord Jesus Christ, judge of the living and the dead, who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XLV. ON FAITH, HOPE, AND CHARITY

Whoever bears the Christian name, and whoever has been instructed in the divine sacraments, most beloved brothers, must know the meaning of the Christian religion and recognize the charity of faith—that faith which, as the Apostle says (Galatians 5), works through love. In the present life it strengthens and confirms believers, and in the future it leads them to the contemplation of God.

For the blessed and outstanding teacher of the nations set before our soul three necessities, saying: “Now faith, hope, and charity remain—these three; but the greatest of these is charity” (1 Corinthians 13).

First, therefore, the Catholic faith is necessary for the Christian, because by it the sons of God are distinguished from the sons of the devil, and the sons of light from the sons of darkness. Through it we are reborn in baptism and obtain eternal salvation, as it is written: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark 16).

This is the gate of life; this is the doorway of the kingdom. Through it the knowledge of truth is learned and the knowledge of divinity is received. Through it we find the grace of God. Otherwise we cannot please God, because “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews 11).

Truly blessed is the person who both lives well by believing rightly and preserves right faith by living well. Therefore, just as faith without good works is fruitless, so good works accomplish nothing without right faith.

Hence the blessed Apostle James said: “What good will it do, my brothers, if someone says that he has faith but does not have works? Can faith save him? Faith without works is fruitless. For just as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead” (James 2).

Above all, brothers, strive to have faith that is right and undefiled. According to the rule of apostolic teaching, memorize the Creed established by the holy Fathers, and, living religiously, strive to observe it.

Flee the poisonous doctrines of heretics. Shudder at the deadly poisons of sorcerers and enchanters. Utterly reject the wicked traditions of diviners, sorcerers, and *charagios*, which have fellowship with demons. Let nothing be held in your mind, professed by your lips, or displayed in your conduct except what the Catholic faith praises, loves, and proclaims.

After this faith, learn to have firm hope. Hope draws our soul toward invisible things, implants our intention in heavenly and eternal realities, and binds it, as it were, with indissoluble bonds. It does not deceive but faithfully leads those who obey it to eternal blessedness.

Therefore, no one, however heavily burdened by the weight of sins, ought to despair of the goodness of divine mercy. Rather, with the hope of certain mercy, he should daily ask its forgiveness with tears. He may confidently hope for it if he ceases from committing evil deeds.

For this reason, we must neither sin persistently on account of hope for pardon nor despair of pardon because God justly punishes sins. Avoiding both dangers, let us turn away from evil and hope for forgiveness from God’s mercy.

Likewise, in every anguish of tribulation, we must hasten through hope to the consolations of heavenly mercy, because in him alone all hope and salvation undoubtedly consist, as the Prophet says: “In God is my salvation and my glory; God is my help, and my hope is in God” (Psalm 61).

When, brothers, we urge you to possess right faith and firm hope, we especially exhort you to strive in every way to have charity within you and to show it in your works. For through it and in it you will possess true blessedness, because without it no one will see God.

The Apostle declares it greater than faith and hope because, when the others depart, it alone will remain. Faith is followed by hope, and hope by blessedness; but charity undergoes no transformation—only perfection remains for it.

Charity is the art of all the virtues; it is the promise of the kingdom; it is the highest reward of the saints in heaven. In everlasting joy the saints have nothing more pleasing or sweeter than the perfect love of God. Because they see him as present, they love him more sweetly and enjoy that good more fully.

You ought to know, brothers, that charity holds primacy in all God’s commandments. Without its perfection, nothing can please God, as the Apostle Paul testifies (1 Corinthians 13). He shows that neither martyrdom, nor contempt for the world, nor the distribution of alms can accomplish anything without the duty of charity.

Hence the Lord himself answered: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind” (Luke 10). He added a second commandment like it: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments the whole Law and the Prophets depend.”

By the words “with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind”—that is, with your entire understanding, entire will, and complete memory—he teaches that God is to be loved.

Love of God consists wholly in observing his commandments, as he says elsewhere: “If anyone loves me, he keeps my words” (John 14).

Hence Truth itself says elsewhere: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13).

The Apostle likewise says: “The fullness of the law is love” (Romans 13).

The evangelist John likewise says: “We have this commandment from God: that whoever loves God should also love his neighbor” (1 John 4).

If anyone should ask who one’s neighbor is, let him know that every Christian is rightly called a neighbor, because in baptism we are all sanctified as children of God, so that we may be spiritually brothers in perfect charity.

Spiritual birth is nobler than bodily birth. Of this Truth itself says in the Gospel: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3).

Whoever understands his neighbor in this way and loves him will undoubtedly possess true charity within himself.

Consider these things carefully, therefore, brothers, and always work out your salvation with faith and love, having firm hope that whatever good you do in the present will be immeasurably rewarded by him in the future, because Jesus Christ our Lord is the author and protector of our salvation. He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XLVI. ON CHARITY
I am pleased, dearest brothers, to say something to your love in contemplation of charity. The more it inflames the heart, the more abundant a discourse it provides; and the more fully it extends itself in discussion, the more sweetly it refreshes you. For charity itself comprehends without error and preserves without labor the manifold abundance and most profound teaching of the divine Scriptures in the person whose heart is full of charity, as the Apostle says: “The fullness of the law is charity” (Rom. XIII); and in another place: “The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (I Tim. I).

What, then, is the end of the commandment except the fulfillment of the commandment? And what is the fulfillment of the commandment except the fullness of the law? Therefore, what we said there—“the fullness of the law is charity”—we have also said here: “the end of the commandment is charity.”

There can be no doubt that the temple of God is wherever charity dwells; for John says: “God is charity.” When the apostles said these things and commended the excellence of charity to us, they could surely only belch forth what they had eaten. For the Lord himself, feeding them with the food of salvation and with the word of charity—which is himself, the living bread that came down from heaven—said: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (John XIII). He who brought the newness of life against the oldness of death himself sets the new commandment against the old sin.

Therefore, whoever wishes to extinguish the old sin, extinguish desire by the new commandment and embrace charity. For just as “covetousness is the root of all evils” (II Tim. VI), so charity is the root of all good things.

Charity securely possesses the whole greatness and breadth of the divine utterances, by which we love God and our neighbor. For the one heavenly Teacher instructs us and says: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength, and you shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments the whole law and the prophets depend” (Matt. XII).

If, therefore, you do not have time to examine all the sacred pages, to unfold all the volumes of discourses, or to penetrate all the secrets of the Scriptures, hold fast to charity, on which everything depends. In this way you will hold fast what you have learned there, and you will also hold fast what you have not learned. For if you know charity, you know something on which even that which you perhaps do not know depends; and in what you understand in the Scriptures, charity is evident, while in what you do not understand, charity is hidden. Thus, the person who holds fast to charity in conduct holds both what is evident and what is hidden in the divine utterances.

Therefore, dearest brothers, pursue charity. It is indeed the sweet and healing bond of minds, without which the rich man is poor, and with which the poor man is rich. It endures in adversity; in prosperity it exercises restraint; amid harsh sufferings it is strong; in good works it is cheerful; in temptations it is most secure; in hospitality it is most generous; among true brothers it is most joyful; even among false brothers it is most patient.

In Abel it was pleasing through sacrifice; in Noah it was secure through the Flood; in Abraham’s pilgrimage it was most faithful; in Moses, amid quarrels, it was most gentle; in David, amid tribulations, it was most meek. In the three youths it looks innocently upon the gentle fire; in the Maccabees it bravely endures savage fires. It is chaste in Susanna toward her husband; in Anna after her husband; in Anna (sic), apart from her husband; free in Paul to rebuke; humble in Peter to obey; humane in Christians to confess; divine in Christ to forgive.

But what greater or more abundant thing can I say about charity than that the Lord himself, through the mouth of the Apostle, resounds its praises while showing the way that surpasses all others and saying:

“If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but do not have charity, I have become like sounding brass or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so that I move mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing. And if I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing.

“Charity is patient; it is kind; charity does not envy; it does not act wrongly; it is not puffed up; it is not ambitious; it does not seek its own interests; it is not provoked; it does not think evil; it does not rejoice over iniquity but rejoices with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Charity never fails” (I Cor. XIII).

How great is this soul of tongues, prophecy, power, the salvation of the sacraments, the foundation of knowledge, the fruit of faith, the wealth of the poor, the life of the dying! What is as magnanimous as dying for the ungodly? What is as kind as loving even enemies?

Charity alone is not weighed down by another’s happiness, because it does not envy; it alone is not lifted up by its own happiness, because it is not puffed up; it alone is not pierced by an evil conscience, because it does not act wrongly. Amid reproaches it is secure; amid hatreds it is beneficent; amid those who inflict injury it is peaceful; amid ambushes it is innocent; amid iniquities it groans, and in the truth it breathes freely.

What is stronger than charity—not to repay injuries, but to endure them? What is more faithful—not to vanity, but to eternity? For this reason it endures everything in the present life, because it believes everything concerning the future life; and it suffers everything imposed here, because it hopes for everything promised there. It will rightly never fall, because it remains without failing.

Therefore, brothers, pursue charity; and by thinking devoutly and living holily in it, produce the fruit of righteousness. Under its guidance, strive to reach the highest good. For once the highest good has been attained, you will possess eternal blessedness. May he himself grant that we reach it—Jesus Christ our Lord, who is blessed charity and beloved blessedness, reigning with the Father and the Holy Spirit as one sole and true God, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XLVII. ON CHASTITY AND PURITY

Chastity and purity hold a glorious and distinguished place among the other virtues, dearest brothers, because chastity alone enables human beings with pure minds to see God. Hence the Truth himself says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V); as though he were saying conversely: “Wretched, on the other hand, are those whose hearts are polluted by carnal desire, because they are plunged into eternal darkness.”

Chastity is an angelic way of life. Chastity together with humility merits the dwelling of the Holy Spirit, whom the uncleanness of lust drives away, as Scripture says: “The Holy Spirit will flee from a body subject to sins” (Wis. I).

Our members ought to be dedicated to God, not to fornication. Let a person set the flames of eternal torments against the desire of his flesh. Let a young man become accustomed to chastity, so that he may be worthy of God’s wisdom. Where there is bodily impurity, there dwells a diabolical spirit, which takes especial delight in the defilement of our flesh.

All impurities displease God, especially those that are unnatural. Holy Scripture therefore admonishes us, saying: “Do not follow your desires, and turn away from your will. If you grant your soul its desires, it will make you a joy to your enemies” (Ecclus. XVIII).

The most wise Solomon likewise uttered judgments concerning the avoidance of carnal impurity, saying (Prov. V): “For the lips of a prostitute drip like a honeycomb, and her throat is smoother than oil. But her end is bitter as wormwood and sharp as a two-edged sword. Her feet descend to death, and her steps penetrate to the underworld. They do not walk along the path of life; her steps wander and cannot be traced. Now therefore, my son, hear me, and do not depart from the words of my mouth. Keep your way far from her, and do not approach the doors of her house.”

He said this not only about the impurity of prostitutes, but also about every carnal desire that urges the soul to consent to its cravings. The mind’s reason, however, must restrain the impulses of the flesh and bridle its wicked pleasures.

Again, the one mentioned above, forbidding young men to live together with women, says (Prov. VI): “Can a man hide fire in his bosom without burning his garments? Or can he walk upon coals without scorching his feet? So is the one who goes in to his neighbor’s wife: he will not be clean when he touches her.”

Likewise blessed Paul admonishes us: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman” (I Cor. VII), as though danger arose immediately from touching. For the chastity of young people is beautiful, pleasing to God, and useful for every good thing.

Whoever has spiritual or carnal children should nurture them in chastity, for God, not in fornication, for the devil. What benefit is it for a man to have, nurture, and love a son if he nurtures him for eternal torments?

Those who live in chastity have an angelic way of life on earth. Chastity unites a person to heaven and makes him a fellow citizen with the angels. Whoever has a lawful wife should use her lawfully at appropriate times, so that, according to the Apostle, he may be free for prayer and may deserve to receive God’s blessing in children.

Let no one say that he cannot guard himself from fornication. “God is faithful,” the Apostle says (I Cor. X), “and he will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation he will also provide a way of escape.”

Such a temptation is given to every person, whether in the desire of the flesh, in worldly ambition, or in any other distress of temptation—a temptation which he may either overcome with praise or succumb to with shame.

Chastity is necessary for everyone, but especially for the ministers of Christ’s altar, whose life ought to be an instruction to others and a continual preaching of salvation. The Lord ought to have as his ministers people who are corrupted by no pollution of the flesh, but rather shine through the restraint of chastity and radiate examples of complete uprightness among the people. To them the Lord says through the lawgiver: “Be holy, because I am holy, the Lord your God” (Lev. XI). For God is light, and there is no darkness in him at all, nor can any filth be joined to him.

Therefore, dearest brothers—whether men or women, clergy or laity—according to the Apostle’s admonition (II Cor. VII), “let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God.”

Let us strive to please in every way him who has called us to his eternal glory, so that we may be able to reign happily with him forever, by the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XLVIII. ON THE PURSUIT OF WISDOM AND MEDITATION ON THE DIVINE LAW

You ought, dearest brothers, to love learning divine wisdom and desire to understand it with a pure heart and chaste body, because the knowledge of God is granted to those who seek him faithfully and meditate upon him earnestly. Nothing is better than the knowledge of God, because nothing is more blessed; indeed, it is true blessedness itself.

Hence the Savior says to the Father: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII).

Hear, therefore, brothers, how this knowledge of wisdom may be attained. First of all, a person must seek to know what true knowledge and true wisdom are, because “the wisdom of this world is folly with God” (I Cor. III).

True knowledge is to withdraw from the service of the devil, which consists in sins; and perfect wisdom is to worship God according to the truth of his commandments. For blessed life is acquired in these two things, as the Psalmist says: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXVI; I Pet. III).

It is not enough for anyone not to do evil unless he also does good; nor is it enough to do good unless he also leaves evil undone. Everyone who is wise in this way will unquestionably be blessed forever. For the knowledge of divinity is blessed life; the knowledge of divinity is the power of good works; and the power of good works is the fruit of eternal blessedness.

For this good we have the consolation of the divine reading of the Scriptures, because the reading of the sacred Scriptures is a significant foreknowledge of blessedness. In them, as in a kind of mirror, a person can consider himself—what he is and toward what he is tending.

Constant reading purifies everything; it inspires fear of Gehenna; it stirs the reader’s heart toward heavenly joys. Whoever wishes always to be with God ought frequently to pray and read. For when we pray, we speak with God; but when we read, God speaks with us.

The reading of the holy Scriptures provides a twofold benefit: because it educates the understanding of the mind and, drawing a person away from the vanities of the world, leads him to the love of God.

The labor of reading is honorable and greatly benefits the cleansing of the soul. Just as the flesh is nourished by bodily foods, so the inner person is nourished and fed by the divine utterances, as the Psalmist says: “How sweet are your utterances to my throat, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. CXVIII).

But that person is most blessed who, while reading the divine Scriptures, turns words into deeds. All the holy Scriptures were plainly written for our salvation, so that we might progress in them toward knowledge of the truth.

A blind person stumbles more often than one who sees; likewise, one who is ignorant of God’s law sins more often through ignorance than the person who knows it. Just as a blind person scarcely walks the right path without a guide, so a person scarcely walks it without a teacher.

Therefore, dearest brothers, whoever among you can read and understand the sacred writings should devote himself to them, so that he may frequently engage in meditation upon them. Those, however, who cannot grasp the meaning of sacred reading from the reading itself should listen more attentively to the interpreter, so that they may at least receive edification from it.

When, instructed by heavenly teaching, you learn, beloved, what ought to be done and what ought to be avoided, do not delay in doing what you inwardly recognize through understanding. For, as blessed James the Apostle says: “It is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law” (James I). The Truth himself also says: “The servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it will be beaten with many blows,” and so forth (Luke XII).

It is likewise written elsewhere: “For the one who knows how to do good and does not do it, for him it is sin” (James IV).

Therefore, strive with every diligence to know the will of God. Once you have learned his will, strive with all your strength to do it, fulfilling his commandments. Earnestly ask that, persevering in this, you may reach his promises.

May he himself deign to help you in this—the one who by his goodness called us and by his grace liberated us, and who promised the heavenly kingdom to those who fight well: Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit as God, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XLIX. ON FASTS, VIGILS, AND PRAYERS

When the Lord had been questioned by the apostles—those to whom he had given power over every force of the enemy, so that they might cure the sick and cast out demons—because they could not drive a demon out of a lunatic, he replied: “This kind of demon does not go out except through prayer and fasting” (Matt. XVII).

By this he clearly showed us how great is the power of abstinence together with pure prayer, since it can accomplish what apostolic power could not. We do not say this, brothers, as though we denied that the apostles, the leaders of the Church and guides of God’s people, practiced abstinence, or as though we claimed that Christ was unable to grant them complete devotion. Rather, the disciples were still inexperienced. While remaining with the bridegroom during the days of the wedding, they could neither fast nor read; they therefore had to be instructed in this way, by which the arrogance of the ancient enemy could be overcome most effectively. Thus the Church, which was to be taught through them, might learn how it ought to fight against the most wicked enemy and how it could conquer him.

We must therefore understand that the perfect fast is the one that crosses the heavens together with almsgiving and prayer, because it reaches the throne of the most high God. For then, when a person has become spiritual, he is joined to the angels and united more freely to God, if abstinence from the flesh is exalted by prayers.

Through fasts and prayers, the hidden mysteries of heavenly things are revealed and the secrets of the divine sacrament are disclosed, as is demonstrated by clear indications in the prophet Daniel and the Apostle Peter.

Thus, as long as Adam abstained, he remained in paradise; he ate, and he was expelled. Fasts are powerful weapons against the temptations of demons, for demons are quickly overcome through abstinence.

Hence our Lord and Savior also teaches us beforehand to overcome their attacks through fasts and prayers, and by his own example he wished to train us for this. He fasted and conquered the devil; he prayed and cast out the prince of this world. For unclean spirits will thrust themselves in with greater confidence where they see frequent feasting and drunkenness being practiced.

Abstinence emaciates the body but enriches the heart; it weakens the flesh but strengthens the soul.

It must also be noted that fasts are acceptable to God only when joined to good works. Those who abstain from food but act wickedly imitate the demons, who have no bodily food but always possess spiritual wickedness. For the person who truly abstains from food is the one who also fasts from acts of evil and from the ambitions of the world.

It is better to refresh the mind, which will live forever, with the feast of holy preaching than to fill the belly of death-bringing flesh with luxurious banquets.

The Savior himself taught us, brothers, to devote ourselves to vigils and to persist more frequently in prayers, saying: “Therefore keep watch at all times, praying that you may be considered worthy to escape all these things that are to come and to stand before the Son of Man” (Luke XXI).

The Apostle Peter likewise exhorts us in similar words: “Keep watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour. Resist him, strong in faith” (I Pet. V).

His fellow apostle Paul shows us what kind of vigilance ought to be practiced, saying: “Awake, you righteous, and do not sin” (I Cor. XV); and again: “Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the weapons of light. Let us walk honorably as in the day” (Rom. XIII).

That person keeps true watch who, while restraining his body from sleep, does not permit his heart to be weighed down by wicked desires, but keeps the eyes of his mind open to behold the true light. He keeps watch who preserves in his deeds what he believes; he keeps watch who drives away from himself the darkness of sluggishness and negligence.

To such a person the Lord promised a great and immeasurable reward when he said: “Blessed is that servant whom, when his master comes, he finds watching. Truly I say to you, he will set him over all his possessions” (Matt. XXIV).

Prayer offered to God ought to be pure and tested by the groaning of the heart, not overflowing in the noise of the voice, because “a person looks at the face, but God looks upon the heart” (I Kings XVI).

And how can someone offer prayers to God for him to hear when the one who utters them does not himself hear them? Alas! We often see certain people in churches bowing their bodies before the sacred altar in prayer, while their eyes wander here and there, and not only do they fail to wet their faces with tears, but they even break into laughter.

What madness is this, brothers? Such prayer does not appease God but provokes him; and from the very place where such people ought to obtain a remedy, they prepare torment for themselves.

Therefore, dearest brothers, when you come together for prayer in the house of the Lord, stand there reverently and with fear and trembling. Whatever you wish to obtain from God, ask him with humility and with a good intention of heart. Above all, ask for those things that pertain to eternal salvation.

As for present matters, ask only for what is necessary, not for those things that are needlessly increased through luxury for the sake of desire or bodily pleasure. God does not gladly accept such prayers, and he often does not grant the request of one who asks in this way.

Hence the Apostle James rebukes us, saying: “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, so that you may spend it on your desires” (James IV).

Learn from the Truth himself what prayers God gladly favors. For he says: “Ask, and you will receive, so that your joy may be full” (John XVI).

Full joy will not be in the present life but in the future life—that is, in the perfect knowledge of God, when there will be no weakness or distress.

As for present advantages, let us not be excessively anxious, but let us do what the Prophet exhorts: “Cast your care upon the Lord,” he says, “and he himself will nourish you” (Ps. LIV). And in the Gospel the Lord himself says: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. VI).

Think carefully about these things within yourselves, brothers; practice them outwardly in your deeds; strive to persevere in them until the end of your lives, and the Lord of peace will be with you. Amen.

## HOMILY L. ON SELF-CONTROL

Divine law admonishes and exhorts us, dearest brothers, to avoid the desire of this world and devote ourselves to the salutary practice of self-control, lest the allurements of pleasures lead us through various desires and, having ensnared us in the trap of death, hand us over to the precipice and abyss of hell.

Wisdom speaks to a person and says: “Do not follow your desires, and turn away from your will. If you grant your soul its desire, it will make you a joy to your enemies” (Ecclus. XVIII). For love of this world produces hostility toward God. Hence it is written: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this age is made an enemy of God” (James IV).

Knowing this, the Apostle John persuades us and says: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the charity of the Father is not in him, because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life” (I John II).

His fellow apostle Paul likewise warns us and says: “Let those who buy be as though they did not possess; and those who use this world, as though they did not use it, for the form of this world is passing away” (I Cor. VII).

The Savior himself also shows in his parable that the riches and pleasures of the world choke the word, so that it bears no fruit. Elsewhere he commands, saying: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. XVI); and again: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses,” he says, “cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV).

Considering these things, therefore, dearest brothers, weigh how necessary self-control is for us, through which you can become worthy disciples of Christ and enter with him into the everlasting kingdom.

Self-control and sobriety do not consist only in bodily integrity, but also in dress and adornment, in life and in conduct. Every self-controlled person ought to abstain from all illicit things; but he ought to use what is lawful with modesty and sobriety.

It is not fitting for a Christian, to whom the heavenly kingdom has been promised, to long for the profits of the world. Rather, he should live worthily for his Lord through self-control, so that he may rejoice with him forever.

He ought to love chastity and flee fornication; not devote himself to greed, but be content with food and clothing; not be proud or place hope in the uncertainty of riches, but think humbly and despise the pomp of the world.

He ought not to be talkative and arrogant, nor deceitful, abusive, or double-tongued; neither a whisperer nor a slanderer. Rather, he ought to speak truth from mouth and heart and restrain his tongue from excessive speech, because it is written: “In much speaking you will not escape sin” (Prov. X).

He should close his eyes against vanity; turn his hearing away from vulgarity and falsehood, indeed from every evil word; not love loud and unrestrained laughter; not eagerly offer his throat and nose to the enticement of sweet foods and pleasant odors, but rather seek the good and sweet fragrance of virtues.

He should carefully guard his hands, feet, and all the members of his body, so that they do not become weapons of iniquity for sin, but rather powerful weapons for God in destroying the spiritual enemy.

Above all, a soldier of Christ ought carefully to guard his heart, lest boasting lift it up, anger inflame it, envy pierce it, greed attack it, lust burn it, sadness weigh it down, sluggishness and idleness burden it, and—what is more serious than all these—heresy tear it apart through presumptions of novelty.

For whoever strives through self-control to keep the hidden things of the heart quiet within will certainly guard the members of the body more easily against wicked deeds outwardly. For it is written: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, because from it life proceeds” (Prov. IV). It is written elsewhere: “Death lies beside the entrance of pleasure.” And the Savior says in the Gospel: “The good person brings forth good from the good treasure of his heart, and the evil person brings forth evil from the evil treasure of his heart” (Luke VI). Again he says: “From the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, and the rest” (Matt. XV).

Since, therefore, fruits—whether good or evil—come forth from the root of the heart, it is necessary first to cleanse the heart, and then to discipline our flesh itself through fasts, vigils, and useful labor, lest the desire of the flesh defile the mind. For it is difficult for those who live in luxury to have a pure heart.

Hence the Apostle said (I Cor. IX): “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified.” And again (Gal. V): “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires.”

Let us live soberly and devoutly in this age, awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us, so that he might redeem us from all iniquity and cleanse for himself an acceptable people, zealous for good works (Tit. II).

When he comes in his majesty with thousands of holy angels, may he grant us the rewards of eternal life for our good labors and holy conduct, rather than repay us with everlasting torment for the desire and pleasure of the present life. For it is truly written concerning him that he repays each person according to his works—namely, Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LI. ON MERCY AND FORGIVENESS

[Col. 0093D]

Among all the things human life needs, mercy is especially necessary. For the more fragile and corrupt nature is, the greater its need for the provident gift of kindness. Therefore, brothers, since our life cannot subsist without mercy, let us learn how first to call forth divine clemency upon ourselves, so that, according to the multitude of his mercies, he may deign to assist our misery. In this way, during the course of the present life, we may avoid the loss of our salvation and, in the future, escape eternal destruction.

To obtain this, dearest brothers, as Holy Scripture shows us, the chief good is mercy. Concerning it the Savior himself says: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. V).

A sinner cannot hope for mercy from God if he does not show mercy to those who sin against him. Therefore, let a person forgive a temporal debt, so that he may deserve to receive an eternal good.

If we desire our souls to be cleansed of the filth of sins, let us not deny mercy to those who sin against us, so that on the day of retribution we may be helped by works of mercy to obtain the Lord’s mercy.

How can a person expect mercy from God if he is cruel to his fellow servants? If anyone wishes God to have mercy on him, let him likewise show mercy to his debtors. He may most certainly expect forgiveness, because he knows how to forgive others.

In the Gospel the Lord strengthened us excellently by his example for the work of mercy, saying: “Be merciful, as your heavenly Father is merciful, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Luke VI).

Every act of mercy will make room for each person according to the merit of his works. Whoever practices mercy offers to God a sacrifice that is very pleasing.

In a judge there ought to be both mercy and discipline, because either one without the other cannot function well. If there is mercy alone, it will give those subject to judgment confidence to sin. Again, if discipline is always present, the mind of the offender will turn to despair, and the judge will not deserve mercy from God.

But a person ought to begin this mercy with himself. How can someone be merciful toward others if he is cruel toward himself? He is cruel toward himself who prepares everlasting flames for himself through his sins.

The truly merciful person begins with himself and carefully guards himself, lest he be punished with the devil; and in this way he provides others with what he sees to be good for himself.

Through forgiveness the Lord taught us how we can obtain mercy from him, when he says in the Gospel: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke VI). Again: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins; but if you do not forgive people, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins” (Matt. VI; Luke XI).

This true statement also proclaims great mercy toward us to those who are able to understand it correctly. God judges us according to our own judgment. In a certain sense, it is in our power how we are to be judged by the judge.

If we judge mercifully those who offend against us, God judges mercifully concerning us when we sin against him.

Let us therefore look to his example, as the teacher of the nations admonishes us (Col. III): “Forgive one another; if anyone has a complaint against someone, just as God forgave you in Christ, so also do you”—that is, just as God in Christ forgave us our sins, so let us also forgive those who sin against us.

The same Apostle says elsewhere (Rom. XII): “Repaying no one evil for evil”; and in the same passage: “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.”

We must know with complete certainty that each person will receive from God the kind of forgiveness that he himself has granted to his neighbor. Then our prayer for our sins will quickly reach the ears of almighty God, if the prayers of those who have offended are acceptable in our ears.

Whoever knows how to forgive sinners mercifully will most certainly receive the clemency of divine compassion. Hence it is written: “Whoever is inclined toward mercy will be blessed by the Lord” (Prov. XXII).

We are forgiven in the same way that we have forgiven those who have harmed us by whatever wickedness.

There are many kinds of acts of compassion. When we perform them, we are helped so that our sins may be forgiven. But none is greater than the mercy by which we forgive from the heart whatever another person has done.

For not only does the person who gives food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the naked, lodging to the traveler, and other things of this kind give alms; the person who grants pardon to one who sins also gives alms.

And the person who corrects with a blow someone over whom he has been given authority, or restrains him through some discipline, while nevertheless forgiving from the heart the sin of the person by whom he has been harmed or offended, or praying that it may be forgiven him, gives alms—not only in what he forgives and prays for, but also in what he reproves and punishes with some corrective penalty—because he shows mercy.

Therefore, brothers, I beg you to devote yourselves above all to mercy and to help your neighbors in whatever ways you can. Be ready also to forgive your neighbors their offenses, so that for this you may be able to obtain forgiveness of your sins from the omnipotent Judge and may deserve to possess eternal life perpetually with all the saints in the heavenly kingdom.

By the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LII. ON PEACE AND UNITY
We read in the Gospel, dearly beloved brothers, that when our Savior and Lord was approaching his passion and was making known to his disciples his departure from this world to the Father, among the other words that he bestowed upon his beloved companions for them to remember, he especially commended the good of peace and unity to them as a special gift, saying: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14), as though he were saying, “I have left you in peace; in peace I shall find you.” In departing, he wished to give what he desired to find in all things upon his return; he gave this as an inheritance to his own, and promised all the gifts and rewards of his pledge in a life of peace [Col. 0095D]. Therefore, brothers, if we wish to be heirs of Christ, we must remain in his peace.

Christ gave us peace, as you have heard; he commanded us to be harmonious and united, and instructed us to preserve intact and inviolate the bonds of love and charity. He wonderfully displayed the adornments of this peace elsewhere, saying: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5). Behold: the one who has already begun to be a peacemaker begins to be called a son of God—not merely to be called a son. Whoever refused to embrace peace denies God the Father to himself; whoever scorns being a peacemaker denies himself as a son.

The sons of God, therefore, ought to be peacemakers: gentle in heart, simple in speech, harmonious in affection, and faithfully joined to one another by the bonds of unity. Yet this peace is to be preserved with the good and with those who keep God’s commandments, not with the wicked and criminal, who have peace among themselves in their sins. Christ’s peace advances toward everlasting salvation; the peace that exists in the devil reaches perpetual destruction. We must always have peace with the good and war against vices. The evil of impious people is indeed to be hated; but the people themselves, although they are evil, are to be loved, because they are God’s creatures. The peace that exists among the good, however, binds together the harmony of brothers and the charity of neighbors.

Peace especially wins the favor of the Spirit of God; peace is the mother of love; peace is the sign of holiness. Concerning it the Lord says through the prophet: “Love peace and truth” (Zechariah 8). Peace is the health of the people, the glory of the priest, the joy of the homeland, and the terror of enemies, whether visible or invisible. Peace must be guarded with all our strength, brothers, because whoever remains in holy peace always remains in the Lord and has fellowship with God’s saints.

It is the priest’s duty to admonish the people in peace concerning what they ought to do; it is the people’s duty to listen humbly to what the priest advises. Whatever is not permitted, it is the shepherd’s duty to forbid, so that it is not done; it is the people’s duty to listen, so that they do not do it. All—both those set over others and those subject to them—must preserve the bond of unity in faith and love in every respect, because without peace neither the priest’s prayer nor the people’s offering is accepted.

Therefore, if we wish to be heard quickly by God, and if we want our gifts to be received by him with favor, we must certainly live in peace. Concerning this, Truth itself deigned to instruct us: “If,” he says, “you are offering your gift before the altar, and there you remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled with your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5).

Since God desires our unity and harmony, the Savior himself shows this in the Gospel when he speaks to the Father: “Holy Father,” he says, “keep them in your name, whom you have given me, so that they may be one as we are” (John 17). Hence the Apostle also exhorts the faithful, saying: “I beseech you, brothers, that you think the same thing and all speak as one” (Philippians 2). And again: “Let there not be,” he says, “jealousy and strife among you. Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy be removed from you, together with every form of malice” (Ephesians 4). In the same place he says: “Bearing with one another in love, being eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace: one body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling” [Col. 0096D].

Such unanimity existed formerly among the Apostles. Thus the new people of believers, keeping the Lord’s commandments, held to their charity. Scripture proves this when it says: “The multitude of those who believed were of one heart and one soul” (Acts 3). And again: “They all persevered with one accord in prayer, with the women and Mary, the mother of Jesus, and his brothers” (Acts 1). Therefore they prayed with effective prayers; therefore they could confidently obtain whatever they asked from God’s mercy.

Among us, however, unanimity has diminished to such an extent that the generosity of our works has also been weakened. At that time they sold houses and estates and, storing up treasures for themselves in heaven [Col. 0097A], offered the proceeds to the Apostles for distribution to the needs of the poor. But now we do not even give tithes from our inheritance; and when the Lord commands us to sell, we instead buy and increase our possessions.

Just as the vigor of faith has withered in us, so the strength of believers has grown weak. Therefore, observing our times, the Lord says in his Gospel: “When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith on earth?” (Luke 18). We see fulfilled what he foretold: in the fear of God, in the law of justice, in love, and in works, there is no faith. No one considers the fear of what is to come, the day of the Lord and the anger of God, the punishments that await unbelievers, or the eternal torments appointed for the faithless. Our conscience would fear these things if it believed; because it does not believe, it does not fear at all. If it believed, it would take care; if it took care, it would escape.

Let us rouse ourselves as much as we can, dearly beloved brothers, and, having broken away from the sleep of our former idleness, let us remain watchful for observing and carrying out the Lord’s commandments. We know what kind of people he commanded us to be when he said: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands; and be like people waiting for their lord when he returns from the wedding, so that when he comes and knocks, they may open to him. Blessed are those servants whom the lord, when he comes, finds watching” (Luke 12).

We must be girded, lest when the day of departure comes he find us hindered and entangled. Let our light shine and gleam in good works, so that this very light may lead us from the night of this age to the light of eternal glory. There, with Christ, who is the author of true peace, and with his holy angels, may we enjoy eternal peace and everlasting happiness [Col. 0097C]. This is granted by our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LIII. ON KINDNESS, HUMANITY, AND ALMSGIVING

We have heard the Apostle, dearly beloved brothers, speaking gently to us and saying (Titus 3): “The kindness and humanity of our Savior God appeared, not because of works of justice that we had done, but according to his mercy he saved us, through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that, having been justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life.”

Therefore, if the kindness and humanity of our Savior, without any merits of ours preceding it, came freely to our aid, why do we, dearly beloved, if we wish to become heirs of his kingdom, not extend works of mercy to our neighbors? Truth itself says: “Give, and it will be given to you; with the measure with which you have measured, it will be measured back to you” (Luke 6). And again: “If,” he says, “you have not been faithful in unrighteous mammon, who will give you what is yours?” (ibid.).

For we must understand, brothers, that we need kindness and humanity, so that from those things which the heavenly Father has mercifully bestowed upon us, we too may help others, and not delay in offering whatever comforts we can to our needy neighbors. For “he who has mercy on the poor lends to the Lord, and he himself will repay him” (Proverbs 19) [Col. 0098A].

There are many who possess no share in the fields, none in vineyards, and none in the riches of this world. We ought to provide for their poverty from the abundance that the Lord has given us, so that they too may bless God with us for the fruitfulness of the earth, and rejoice that what has been granted to those who possess it has also been made common to the poor and to strangers.

Blessed is that granary, and worthy of the multiplication of every kind of fruit, from which the hunger of the needy, the weak, and strangers is satisfied. God has permitted these people to labor under various hardships so that he might crown the wretched for their patience and the merciful for their benevolence.

For the most effective supplication for sins is found in almsgiving and fasting, and prayer raised with such support quickly ascends to the divine ears, because, as it is written, “the merciful man does good to his own soul” (Proverbs 11). The portion of bodily resources that is supplied to the needy passes into eternal riches for the giver, so that through compassion for the poor and through almsgiving we may merit God’s mercy and the forgiveness of our sins.

For whoever does not turn his attention away from the poor person quickly turns the Lord’s hearing toward himself. The Lord says: “Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful” (Luke 6); and: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5).

What Truth has promised to return, humanity may confidently expend. Be constant, Christian giver: give so that you may receive; sow what you may reap; scatter what you may gather. Do not fear loss; do not sigh anxiously over an uncertain return. When your substance is well distributed, it increases. Your Rewarder wishes you to be generous; and the one who gives so that you may possess commands you to give, saying: “Give, and it will be given to you” (Luke 6).

O miser, if you love gold or the riches of this world, give so that you may not lose them. If you preserve them, you will undoubtedly lose them; if you distribute them, you will possess them eternally. Truth itself says: “Store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not break in and steal. For where your treasure is, there also is your heart” (Matthew 6; Luke 12). Certainly, by wisely distributing temporal things, you acquire eternal ones.

Do not be timid in giving, lest you be poor in the recompense, because “whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly” (2 Corinthians 9); but “whoever has mercy on the poor will be blessed” (Proverbs 14). Therefore, “a man’s riches are the redemption of his soul” (Proverbs 13). He honors God who has mercy on the poor.

“Hide almsgiving in the bosom of the poor,” Scripture says (Ecclesiasticus 29), “and it will pray for you.” As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin. “Do not despise the hungry soul, and do not provoke the poor in his distress” (Ecclesiasticus 4). Whoever turns his ear away from the cry of the poor will not have his prayer obtain God’s mercy.

While you live, do good to your soul by giving alms to the wretched, because after death you will have no power to do good. At your banquets, let the poor eat, and let Christ be present in them.

There are three kinds of almsgiving. One is bodily: to give the needy whatever you are able. The second is spiritual: to forgive the person by whom you have been injured. The third is to correct the offender and lead those who have gone astray back to the way of truth [Col. 0099A].

By all these forms God is appeased and eternal life is obtained, as Scripture agrees when it says: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11). And again: “Forgive,” he says, “and you will be forgiven.”

The Apostle James also says: “My brothers, if anyone among you should stray from the truth, and someone should bring him back, he should know that whoever brings a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins” (James 5).

But this is done well and in proper order if each person first begins this good work of mercy with himself, so that he may have mercy on himself and not be plunged into punishment beneath the burden of his sins. Hence it is written: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Ecclesiasticus 30), so that while he devotes himself to correcting others, he himself may be made free from vices [Col. 0099B].

Therefore, so that we may be fully able to do these things, we have a strong helper and merciful giver for this purpose—namely, the mediator between God and human beings, the Lord Jesus, who lives and reigns with God the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LIV. ON THE FEAR OF GOD AND TRUE HUMILITY

The prophet and psalmist David, who, as Scripture testifies, was chosen according to the heart of the Lord and did all his will, himself showed in a certain passage what our Creator seeks and loves in us, saying: “Who is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high and looks upon the humble in heaven and on earth?” (Psalm 112) [Col. 0099C].

If, therefore, the Most High Lord, whose excellence and greatness have no end, considers and approves humility in every creature of his—in what is established above and in what is established below, namely, in angels and human beings—how necessary it is for us always to strive for humility and preserve it in all things, so that we may thus please our Creator.

How great is the virtue of true humility is easily recognized from the Lord’s words. To condemn the pride of the Pharisees, he said: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14). By the steps of humility one ascends to the heights of heaven; the exalted God is reached not through pride but through humility (James 4). Of this it is said: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (1 Peter 5).

Hence it is also said in the Psalms: “The Lord is exalted, and he looks upon the humble, but he knows the proud from afar” (Psalm 137). He speaks of the proud as “exalted”; he looks upon the humble in order to raise them up. He knows the exalted—that is, the proud—in order to cast them down.

Let us learn humility, through which we shall be able to draw near to God, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11). Through pride the wonderful creature of the angels fell from heaven; through humility, the weakness of human nature ascended into heaven.

Humility is an honorable practice among human beings, as Solomon says: “Where there is pride, there will also be disgrace; but where there is humility, there is wisdom” (Proverbs 11). Another wise man likewise says: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God” (Ecclesiasticus 3) [Col. 0100A].

God also says through the prophet: “Upon whom shall I look, except upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66). Whoever is not humble and quiet cannot have the grace of the Holy Spirit dwell in him.

God became humble for the sake of our salvation; let proud human beings be ashamed. To the extent that the heart is bent downward in humility, it advances upward: for whoever is humble will be exalted in glory.

The first step of humility is to hear the word of truth humbly, retain it faithfully, and carry it out willingly. Truth flees the mind that it does not find humble. The humbler a person is regarding himself, the greater he will be in God’s sight. The prouder he appears among human beings, the more cast down he will be before God.

Whoever does good works without humility carries dust into the wind. Scripture also says: “Why are earth and ashes proud?” (Ecclesiasticus 10), while what he seems to gather through fasting or almsgiving is scattered by the wind of pride.

Do not glory, O human being, in your virtues, because you will have another judge, not yourself. Before that judge, strive in your heart to humble yourself, so that he may exalt you at the time of his recompense.

Descend in order to ascend; humble yourself in order to be exalted, lest, once exalted, you be humbled. Whoever seems contemptible to himself is beautiful before God; those who displease themselves please God.

Therefore be small in your own eyes, so that you may be great in God’s eyes. You will be more precious before God the more despised you have been in your own eyes. Let the greatest humility be your highest honor. The virtue of humility is the praise of honor.

But no one can possess this virtue of true humility without the fear of God, because neither can exist without the other. What does the fear of God accomplish? Listen, brothers: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm 110). It is a great safeguard against sin always to fear God’s presence. Whoever perfectly fears God carefully guards himself from sins.

It will be well with the person who fears God on the last day, and his reward will endure forever. If someone is ashamed to sin in the sight of a human being, how much more ought he to be ashamed to commit iniquity in the sight of God, who considers not only deeds but also hearts? Those who fear God with holy fear seek what pleases him [Col. 0100D].

There is one fear belonging to sons and another belonging to servants. Servants fear their masters because of punishment; sons fear because of love for their father. If we are sons of God, let us fear him because of the sweetness of charity, not because of the bitterness of fear.

A wise person fears God in all his works, knowing that he can never escape God’s presence, just as the Psalmist says to God: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence?” (Psalm 138). Likewise, neither from the east nor from the west—understand: nowhere—is there a place to flee from God.

Whoever fears God will receive his teaching; and those who watch over his commandments will find everlasting blessing. The soul of the one who fears God is blessed, and it remains safe from diabolical temptation.

“Blessed is the person who is always fearful” (Proverbs 28), and to whom it has been granted always to keep the fear of God before his eyes. Whoever fears the Lord turns away from the crooked path and directs his steps toward the road of the virtues.

The fear of God drives away sins and adds virtues. Fear makes a person cautious and attentive, so that he does not sin. But where the fear of God is absent, there is a disordered life.

Whoever does not fear God in prosperity should fear him at least in adversity; let him flee to the one who wounds and heals: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord, who greatly delights in his commandments” (Psalm 110).

The fear of God drives out the fear of Gehenna, because it makes a person avoid sin and practice works of justice. After this, he will arrive at that fear which is called holy and endures forever and ever, because it exists in love.

Therefore, brothers, let us fear God so that we may love him, because perfect love casts out servile fear (1 John 4). In this way we shall be able to possess an abundance of security and the fullness of every good.

Hence the Prophet also says: “Fear the Lord, all you his saints, for those who fear him lack nothing. The rich have become poor and hungry, but those who seek the Lord shall not lack any good” (Psalm 33).

Therefore I beseech you, dearly beloved, always to keep the fear of God before the eyes of your mind and to flee entirely from forgetfulness of God’s commandments. Diligently consider how those who fear God and obey his commandments go to eternal life, while those who despise him and scorn his commandments go into eternal punishment.

Also keep true humility within your heart, and express it sincerely in your conduct before your neighbors, so that they, instructed by your good examples, may glorify God and strive with you to receive eternal recompense in heaven [Col. 0101C]. This is granted by our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LV. ON CONFESSION, PENANCE, AND CONTRITION OF HEART

We ought to consider, dearly beloved brothers, what Holy Scripture teaches us to do, so that we may avoid the torment of Gehenna and reach heavenly joy, and so that through repentance we may recover the good that we lost through sinning. This can happen in no other way than through salutary contrition and true confession.

Contrition of heart is therefore born from the virtue of humility; from contrition comes confession of sins; from confession comes penance; and from true penance comes the forgiveness of offenses.

Contrition of heart is humility of mind, accompanied by tears, remembrance of sins, and fear of judgment. Tears usually flow from the twofold source of contrition: either when the mind carefully considers the evil of its deeds, or when it sighs with desire for eternal life.

Hence the Prophet says: “My soul thirsted for the living God. When shall I come and appear before the face of God? My tears have been my bread day and night” (Psalm 41). Again: “My soul longs and languishes for the courts of the Lord; my heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God” (Psalm 83).

There are four kinds of feeling by which the thought of a just person is pierced with salutary sorrow: remembrance of past crimes, recollection of future punishments, consideration of his pilgrimage in the misery of this life, and desire for the heavenly homeland, so that he may be able to reach it as quickly as possible.

When these things occur in a person’s heart, we should understand that God is then present to the human heart through grace. Hence it is said in the Psalm: “I have declared my life to you, O God; you have placed my tears in your sight, as in your promise” (Psalm 55). The promise of forgiveness that we have from God awakens tears of repentance in our heart [Col. 0102B].

The sweetness of contrition is a desirable treasure in the human heart. The human soul that is pierced with contrition in prayer gains greatly toward salvation. When contrition is poured out through prayer, there is no doubt that the presence of the Holy Spirit is in our hearts.

But contrition is salutary when it urges a person to confess his sins and to turn toward a better life. Holy Scripture therefore frequently urges us to flee to the remedy of confession—not because God needs our confession, since everything we think, say, or do is present to him, but because we cannot otherwise be saved unless, in repentance, we confess what we have wickedly and negligently done.

Whoever accuses himself of his sins does not leave the devil another opportunity to accuse him on the day of judgment—provided that he confesses in repentance, wipes away what he has done, and does not renew what he committed.

“Confess your sins to one another,” says the Apostle James, “and pray for one another, so that you may be saved” (James 5). The blessed Apostle Paul likewise says: “With the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10).

Solomon also speaks of confession of sins: “Whoever hides his crimes will not prosper; but whoever confesses and abandons them will obtain mercy” (Proverbs 28).

It is a great remedy of salvation, brothers, not to repeat the wicked things we have done, and not to reopen the earlier scar of our wounds. Hence the evangelist John says: “If we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity” (1 John 1).

The Psalmist likewise says: “I said, ‘I will confess my iniquity against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the wickedness of my sin” (Psalm 31).

While alive, let the sinner confess what he has done, because confession is not fruitful among the dead, nor does penance advance toward salvation there. Behold, now is the time of salvation; behold, now is the acceptable time before God.

Now is the time of forgiveness for the repentant; but after death there will be a time of vengeance for those who neglected to confess their crimes. All the impious have bitter repentance amid torments, but their repentance does not benefit them for forgiveness; rather, their conscience torments them and increases the punishments they suffer.

They could have guarded themselves against the enormity of their torments through confession, but they neglected to do so. Thus they are tormented outwardly by flames and inwardly by their own conscience [Col. 0103A].

How can a physician heal a wound that the sick person is ashamed to show? God desires our confession so that he may have a just reason for forgiving. Whoever conceals his sins and is ashamed to confess them profitably will have God, whom he has as a witness, again as his avenger.

A person judges himself most effectively in this life, so that he may not be judged by God with perpetual condemnation. Every sinner ought to have a twofold weeping in penance: either because through negligence he failed to do good, or because through audacity he committed evil.

Confession justifies; confession grants forgiveness of sins. All hope of pardon rests in confession. Confession is a work of mercy, the salvation of the sick, and the sole remedy of penance available to our strength.

The Savior himself displays its power in the Gospel, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is drawing near.” John the Baptist likewise says: “Produce fruits worthy of repentance.”

The worthy fruit of repentance is to mourn past sins and not to commit them again, as Scripture says: “Do not add sin upon sin, and say, ‘The mercy of God is great’; for mercy and wrath come from him.” The Lord says through the prophet Isaiah: “Wash yourselves; be clean.”

The person who mourns past sins and does not again admit what must be mourned is washed and clean. The person who mourns what he has done but does not abandon it, and after his tears repeats what he had lamented, is washed but not clean.

Concerning those who return to their former offenses after their tears, the blessed Peter says with terror: “The dog returns to its vomit.” “Son, you have sinned,” Holy Scripture says; “do not add to it again, but pray concerning your former sins that they may be forgiven you” [Col. 0103C].

True penance is not measured by the number of years but by the bitterness of the soul. Therefore the blessed Peter immediately received forgiveness from the Lord, because he wept most bitterly over the guilt of his threefold denial.

Penance that has been prescribed, [perhaps: however] though it be of however short a duration, if it is undertaken with the innermost bitterness of the heart, is not despised by God, the just judge, who considers the secrets of the heart. God does not require merely the length of time; he weighs the sincerity of the penitent’s feeling.

Whoever trusts in Christ with his whole mind lives forever through his faith, even if he dies burdened with many sins. As the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “I am the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live; and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die” [Col. 0103D]. He spoke of the death of the soul, which comes upon it because of the sickness of sins.

God is merciful by nature. He is ready to save through mercy those whom he cannot save through justice; he desires all human beings to be saved and none to perish. Through the prophet he says: “On whatever day the sinner turns, he shall live and shall not die.”

No matter how sinful and impious someone may be, if he turns to penance, he should not doubt that through God’s mercy he can attain salvation.

In this age God aids those who practice penance; in the age to come, penance is of no benefit, but we shall give an account of our deeds. Only in this life is freedom for penance available; after death there is no opportunity for correction.

Therefore, brothers, let us not waste the time granted to us. As much as we can, let us labor through God’s mercy, so that now, by tears and groans, washing away the former filth of our sins through worthy penance, we may deserve to be found clean in body and soul on the day of the Lord, by that judge of the living and the dead who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LVI. ON NOT DELAYING TO TURN FROM SINS TO GOD

We read the Apostle, dearly beloved brothers, saying: “Whatever things were written were written for our instruction, so that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope.”

Behold, in the writings inspired by God we find this written: “My son, do not delay to turn to the Lord, because you do not know what the coming day will bring; for whoever delays turning endangers his soul, because death does not delay. If death finds him delaying his conversion, it leads him to torments.”

To think about conversion tomorrow and neglect it today is, brothers, a loose and dangerous, paralyzing thought. Why do you, sinner, pretend not to turn, and do you not fear that sudden death may steal from you the day of conversion? Do people not die suddenly?

If it is good to abandon sins and turn to God, let it be done quickly. God promises you forgiveness if you turn from your sins; he has not promised you the security of living for a long time.

Therefore let each person turn to God more quickly, and when he has found him, let the wicked abandon his way and the unrighteous person his thoughts; and God will have mercy on him, for he is abundant in forgiveness.

If the final day suddenly arrives, delay perishes and condemnation remains. You do not wish to perish? Return to God and live. Do not despair of forgiveness of sins, nor put your confidence in a longer life.

Turn, therefore, and do penance. “Tomorrow,” you say, “I shall turn.” Why not today? You say: “What harm is there if I say it tomorrow?” I answer: What harm is there if you say it today?

Perhaps you say: “My life will be long.” I reply: If it is long, let it be good; if it is short, let it too be good. But who can endure a long evil? You do not want a long bad meal, yet you want a long bad life?

You buy an estate and desire it to be good; you wish to take a wife and seek a good one; you wish children to be born and hope they will be good. And, to speak now of the most trivial things, you buy shoes and do not want bad ones—yet you love a bad life?

What has your life done to offend you, that you alone wish it to be bad among all your good things? “Do not delay to turn to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day” (Ecclesiasticus 5).

These are God’s words, not mine. You have not heard them from me; I hear them with you from the Lord. Perhaps you answer: “Tomorrow, tomorrow.” O raven’s voice! The raven did not return to the ark; the dove did.

If you wish to do penance only when you are no longer able to sin, then your sins have abandoned you, not you them. He is sufficiently alien from faith who waits for old age before doing penance.

We must fear that, while he hopes for mercy, he may fall into judgment. For then he will not find forgiveness who has wasted the time suited to forgiveness. There he cannot merit from God what he asks, because here he did not wish to hear what God commanded.

Whoever neglects the time given for penance pours out prayers in vain before the tribunal of Christ. Each one of us, brothers, ought to hurry to turn to God while he can, lest, if he is unwilling while he can, then, when he wishes to enter, he be entirely unable.

Therefore we must always fear the final day, which we can never foresee. Behold, even this day on which we speak has been granted to us as an extension for conversion; and yet we refuse to mourn the evils we have committed.

We not only fail to mourn what we have done; we also increase the things that must be mourned. But if some illness seizes us, if signs of sickness announce approaching death, we seek an extension of life in order to mourn our sins [Col. 0105B]. We ask for such an extension with great intensity of desire, although we now regard the time granted to us as worthless.

Let us now, dearly beloved, consider the riches of our Creator. He saw us sinning and endured it. The one who forbade us to sin before our guilt does not cease, even after our guilt, to wait for us to receive forgiveness.

Behold, the very one whom we despised calls us. We have turned away from him, yet he does not turn away. Hence it is said through Isaiah: “Your eyes shall see your teacher, and your ears shall hear the voice of one admonishing behind you” (Isaiah 30).

A person is admonished as though face-to-face when, created for justice, he receives the commandments of righteousness. But when he despises these same commandments, he has, as it were, turned the back of his mind to his Creator’s face.
