Yet behold, the Creator still follows behind and admonishes him, because we have already despised him, and nevertheless he does not cease to call us. We have, as it were, turned our back to the face of the one whose words we despise and whose commandments we trample; but he stands behind us and calls us back when we have turned away. He sees that he is despised, yet he continues to cry out through his commandments and waits through patience [Col. 0105C].

Consider, therefore, dearly beloved brothers: if a servant of any one of you suddenly became proud while you were speaking to him and turned his back to your face, would not the master, being despised, strike his pride? Would he not inflict wounds of strict punishment?

Behold, by sinning we have turned our back to the face of our Creator, and yet we are tolerated. He kindly calls back those who have turned away in pride; and although he could strike us as we turn away, he promises gifts so that we may return.

May such great mercy from our Creator soften the hardness of our guilt, and may the person who could have experienced the evil he did by being struck at least grow ashamed at having been waited for.

Have confidence, therefore, my brothers, in the mercy of our Creator. Consider what you are doing; reconsider what you have done. Look upon the abundance of heavenly compassion, and while the merciful judge still waits, come to him with tears.

When you consider that he is just, do not neglect your sins; when you consider that he is gracious, do not despair. God the human being gives human beings confidence before God: he is a great hope for us who repent, because our advocate has become our judge [Col. 0105D]. He lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LVII. ON CONTEMPT FOR THE WORLD AND THE FUTURE REWARD

[Col. 0106A]

Blessed John the Apostle warns us, dearly beloved, and urges us to despise perishable things, saying: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world, because the world is passing away, and its desire. But whoever does the will of God remains forever” (1 John 2). Likewise blessed Paul the Apostle, writing to Timothy, instructs and teaches us: “Command the rich of this world,” he says, “not to be high-minded, nor to set their hope on the uncertainty of riches, but on the living God, who gives us all things abundantly for enjoyment. Let them be rich in good works, readily give, share with those who have nothing, and lay up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of the true life” (1 Tim. 6).

Pay close attention, brothers, and carefully weigh what is said. For when the rich are commanded to lay up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of the true life, there is no doubt that this present life is false. Above all, the rich must hear this—those whom the poor behold and then murmur, groan, envy the one who is praised, desire to be their equals, and grieve that they are not their peers. Amid their praise of the rich, they commonly say: “These alone exist; these alone live.” Therefore, because the poor flatter the rich with these words, saying that they live, let the rich not be puffed up by the flatterers’ words and suppose that they truly live. “Command,” he says, “the rich of this world not to be high-minded, nor to set their hope on the uncertainty of riches, but on the living God, who gives us all things abundantly for enjoyment” [Col. 0106B]. Let them be rich—but where? “In good works,” he says. Let them readily give, because they do not lose what they give; let them share with those who have nothing, and thereby lay up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of the true life, not agreeing with the flatterers who say that they live, and that they alone live.

This life is a sleep; these riches flow away like things seen in dreams. Hear the psalm, O most wretched rich man: “They have slept their sleep, and all the men of riches found nothing in their hands” (Ps. 75). Sometimes even a beggar lying on the ground, trembling with cold but nevertheless overcome by sleep, dreams of treasures, rejoices and exults in his dreams, and does not deign to recognize his ragged equal; and as long as he sleeps, he is rich. When he awakens, he discovers what he had falsely rejoiced in; when he wakes, he discovers what he must truly grieve over. Thus the rich man who is dying is like an awakened poor man who had seen treasures in a dream.

For there was a certain rich man—unnamed and not to be named—who clothed himself in purple and fine linen and despised the poor man lying before his gate. He clothed himself in purple and fine linen, as the Gospel testimony relates, and feasted splendidly every day. He died, was buried, awoke, and found himself in the flames. He therefore slept his sleep, and that man of riches found nothing in his hands, because he had done no good with his hands.

Riches are sought for the sake of life, not life for the sake of riches. How many have made agreements with their enemies that they should take everything but spare their lives; whatever they possessed, they paid as the price of life. If perishing life is bought at so great a price, at what price must eternal life be purchased? Give something to Christ so that you may live blessedly, if you give everything to your enemy so that you may live as a beggar. From your temporal life, which you redeem at such a cost, estimate the worth of eternal life, which you neglect.

You live for a few days, even if you are destined to reach old age; for all the days of a human being, from infancy to old age, are few. Even if Adam himself were to die today, he would have lived only a few days, because he would have completed them all. You redeem a few days—and troubled ones at that—in such poverty and amid so many temptations. You are willing to have nothing in order to possess yourself: today redeemed, perhaps dying tomorrow; released from one man, perhaps to be slaughtered by another.

O human being, fragile in body, changeable in time, dissolved by death, weighed down by burdens and wearied by anxieties, hear my advice: relieve yourself by giving to the poor what you have acquired through labor. Give to one who has nothing, because you too have nothing. You never possess eternal life; therefore give from what you have, so that you may receive what you do not have.

A beggar knocks at your door; you knock at the door of your Lord. God does with his beggar what you do with yours. Therefore give, and it will be given to you. If you are unwilling, you will see for yourself. The poor man cries out and says to you: “I ask for bread, and you do not give it; you ask for life, and you do not receive it. Let us see which of us suffers the greater loss: I, who am deprived of a morsel, or you, who are deprived of eternal life; I, who am punished in my stomach, or you, who are punished in your mind; finally, I, who burn with hunger, or you, who are destined to be burned by fire and handed over to living flames” [Col. 0107C]. I do not know whether the rich man’s pride will be able to answer these words.

“The Lord says: Give to everyone who asks you.” If to everyone, how much more to the needy and wretched, whose emaciation and pallor beg, whose tongue is silent, while squalor and groaning ask for alms. Hear me, therefore, O rich man, and let my counsel please you: redeem your sins with almsgiving; do not lean upon gold. Naked you came forth from your mother’s womb; naked you will return to the earth. And if you will return naked to the earth, for whom are you gathering things upon the earth? I believe that if you could carry anything with you, you would devour living men.

Behold, you will return naked. Why do you not distribute the money you have gathered, whether rightly or wrongly? Send ahead what you are going to, and transfer your perishable possessions, so that you may reach the kingdom of heaven. If you were to give ten solidi to someone who would afterward return a hundred to you, how greatly would you rejoice, with what happiness of spirit would you exult? If you rejoice in usury, then lend at interest to your Lord; give to your God from what is his. For when the interest has multiplied, he will repay you.

Do you wish to know how greatly he will repay you? For a morsel, for a coin, for a tunic, you receive eternal life, the kingdom of heaven, and endless blessedness. Compare eternal life and everlasting riches with your morsel: there is no comparison. You give earth and receive the one who made heaven and earth. He himself is our reward; without him the rich man begs, and with him the poor man is exceedingly rich.

For what does the rich man possess if he does not possess God? What does the poor man not possess if he possesses God?

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, if you desire to be rich, love true riches. If you seek the summit of true honor, strive toward the kingdom of heaven. If you love the glory of dignities, hasten to be enrolled in that heavenly assembly of angels. Retain in your minds the words of God that you receive with your ears, and strive to fulfill them in your deeds.

Behold, everything you do in this world is passing away, and every day, willingly or unwillingly, you hasten toward the final judgment, without any interruption of permanence. Why, then, is what must be left behind loved? Why is that toward which one proceeds neglected? Love heavenly things, reject earthly things; seek eternal things, neglect temporal things, so that with him you may possess the everlasting kingdom, who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY LVIII. ON JUDGING JUSTLY AND NOT ACCEPTING FALSE WITNESSES

[Col. 0108B]

We heard the Lord in the Gospel, dearly beloved brothers, commanding and saying: “Do not judge, and you will not be judged; do not condemn, and you will not be condemned. For with the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged” (Matt. 7). In this he did not prohibit the administration of judgment, but showed the proper manner of judging. He restrained obstinacy and taught justice. For elsewhere he himself says: “Judge with just judgment” (John 7). And in the Law: “Justly,” he says, “you shall carry out what is just.”

Everyone who judges rightly and justly carries a balance in his hand. In its two pans he bears justice and mercy: in accordance with justice he renders the sentence for sin; in accordance with mercy he moderates the punishment. Some matters, therefore, are to be corrected by a good judge through equity, while others are to be forgiven through mercy.

Judgments must be made without respect of persons. Nothing is more unjust than accepting gifts in judgment, because “gifts blind the hearts of the wise and subvert the words of the just” (Deut. 16). “With the judgment with which you judge,” says the Lord, “you will be judged.” Therefore let the judge fear God the Judge, lest, when God judges, he himself be condemned.

He who condemns the innocent or justifies the wicked for gifts, or bends his heart through love or hatred of any person, will not be able to preserve the truth of judgment. No ruler ought to appoint foolish or wicked judges. A foolish man, through negligence, does not know justice; a wicked man, through greed, subverts the very truth he has learned.

The poor are almost more grievously torn apart by wicked judges than by the bloodiest enemies. No robber is so greedy for what belongs to others as an unjust judge is for what belongs to his own people. Unjust judges are worse than enemies: enemies can often be avoided by flight, but judges cannot be escaped because of their power. They themselves strive to gather riches by oppressing their fellow citizens. They themselves strive to gather riches by oppressing their fellow citizens.

Sometimes good judges have rapacious ministers, and are stained by their crime if they do not restrain their rapacity. Such men perish through the sins of others, because, as the distinguished teacher of the world says (Rom. 1), not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to those who do wickedness, are made worthy of death [Col. 0109A].

Often wicked judges, for the sake of greed, delay or pervert judgments and do not bring cases to an end until their purse is filled. When they judge, they consider not the case but the gifts. Wicked judges, according to the prophet’s word, are like wolves that do not leave anything for the morning at evening; that is, they think only about the advantage of the present life and nothing about the future, snatching everything in the manner of wolves and scarcely leaving anything for the poor.

An angry judge cannot fully examine the matter before the court, because, blinded by the darkness of rage, he does not see the brightness of justice. In judgment, one must consider not the person but the case. For it is written: “You shall not show partiality in judgment.” Wicked judges err in their sentence concerning the truth when they attend to the rank of the person, and they often harm the just when they wickedly defend the impious.

The acceptance of gifts in judgment is a betrayal of truth. Those who fear God and judge justly will receive eternal rewards from God.

The judge must therefore take care not to be deceived by the trickery of false witnesses, lest he share with them in the punishment of their crime. “A false witness,” says Solomon, “will not go unpunished” (Prov. 19). “Whoever gives false testimony against his neighbor, his lamp will be extinguished on the last day” (Prov. 24). Elsewhere he likewise says: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1), because, through fear of some power, it conceals the truth and calls down God’s anger upon itself, since it fears a human being more than God.

A lying witness is liable to three persons: first, to God, whose presence he despises; next, to the judge, whom he deceives by lying; finally, to the innocent person whom he harms by false testimony.

It often happens that false witnesses, when separated, are soon discovered to be liars. No one should flatter himself if he hears false testimony spoken against someone and does not expose it on the grounds that he himself is not speaking falsely. Both are guilty: the one who conceals the truth and the one who speaks a lie, because the former is unwilling to help, while the latter desires to harm.

Blessed is the one whose testimony is found acceptable in the sight of God.

You ought to know, brothers, that justice is overturned in judgments in four ways: through fear, greed, hatred, and love. Through fear, when, because of dread of some authority, anyone is afraid to speak or judge the truth; through greed, when a judge is corrupted by the reward of some gift; through hatred, when, because of hostility toward someone, he desires to harm another; through love, when a powerful man defends friends or relatives against justice [Col. 0109D].

By these four means the equity of judgment is often overturned and innocence is harmed. Those who oppress the poor are more deserving of grief than those who suffer injustice. Those who are oppressed soon bring their temporal misery to an end; those who oppress them are assigned to eternal flames.

In this world, the good are often judged by the wicked; in the future life, the wicked will be judged by the good. Often, even here, the good are unhappy and wretched in the eyes of human beings, while the wicked are happy. In that eternal recompense, however, the good will always be blessed, and the wicked will always be wretched.

Those who fare well in this world should strive above all not to lose eternal blessings; those who suffer hardships should bear them bravely, so that they may be found worthy of eternal blessedness.

I earnestly exhort you, dearly beloved brothers, always to bear this in mind whenever you judge someone, defend someone, or consent to those who do such things: do not abandon truth and justice, but strive to observe them in everything. Thus may you deserve to receive from your true Judge—namely, Truth itself, which will judge the world in equity and justice—an unfading crown with the blessed in eternal blessedness, through him who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY LIX. ON AVOIDING PRIDE AND VAIN GLORY

[Col. 0110B]

You ought to know, dearly beloved brothers, that you are soldiers of the heavenly King and that you must fight against his enemies. For blessed Paul the Apostle says (Eph. 6): “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against rulers and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places.”

If, then, the enemies against whom we must fight are spiritual, we must fight with spiritual weapons. Our enemies are demons; their weapons, with which they fight invisibly against us, are vices. Against them, therefore, with Christ our leader and commander reigning over us, let us wage our battle with the sacred weapons of the virtues, and with the help of our King we shall easily obtain victory.

For, encouraging his followers in the battle line against the enemy, he himself says: “Do not be afraid; he who is in you is stronger than he who is in the world. Have confidence, because I have conquered the world” (John 16).

For pride is the first and source of the ancient enemy’s unknown missiles; wherever it has entered, it drags behind it the troops of all vices. Our Creator especially detests it; hence it is written concerning it: “Every arrogance is an abomination before God”; and again: “Pride is hateful before the Lord and human beings” (Sir. 10). And again: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Prov. 3).

The greatest and first sin of the devil was pride; and through it he deceived the first human beings. Hence it is written: “The beginning of pride caused human beings to apostatize from God, because their heart departed from him who made them. For pride is the beginning of every sin; whoever holds fast to it will be filled with curses, and it will overthrow them in the end. Therefore the Lord dishonored the assembly of the wicked and destroyed them to the end. God destroyed the seats of proud leaders and made the meek sit in their place. God dried up the roots of proud nations and planted the humble among those nations. The Lord overturned the lands of the nations and destroyed them to their foundations. He dried them up, scattered them, and caused their memory to cease from the earth. God destroyed the memory of the proud and left the memory of the humble in understanding” (Sir. 10).

Therefore pride is worse than every vice. It often arises even from good deeds, when a person takes pride in his good works, and afterward, through pride, loses what he had through love. It is also the last of all the vices. “He began to take pride in these things”—this sentence must be placed first—“and from on high he brings ruin.” Pride is likewise the beginning of every sin, as we have said, because when the soul despises the commands of the Creator, it immediately falls into the pit of some sin. For every proud person lies so much lower the higher he raises himself, and falls so much more deeply the more exalted he lifts himself.

Whoever is exalted through his own pride is condemned by God’s justice. Hence it is written: “Before a person’s ruin, his spirit is exalted” (Prov. 16).

Therefore, brothers, nothing must be avoided by a Christian more than pride, which provokes God’s anger. Pride made demons from angels, while humility made human beings like the holy angels. The proud desire to be praised for what they do not do; the humble shrink from having whatever good they do recognized.

Let no one, then, be lifted up by his own goodness or seek praise for himself, even if he does something good. Rather, let him desire that God be praised in his gifts, since he does no good except what God has given him to do. Therefore he ought to refer everything he does well to God, not to himself.

For the Lord says in the Gospel: “Take care not to practice your righteousness before human beings in order to be seen by them” (Matt. 6); that is, do not do good with the intention of receiving empty praise from human beings. Whatever good you do, do it for the love of God, for the salvation of your soul, and for fraternal love.

For this reason the Lord himself said of certain people who give alms, or prayers and fasts, in order to receive praise from human beings: “Truly I say to you, they have received their reward” (ibid.). Whoever does any good so as to be praised by human beings has received the reward he sought and should expect no recompense from God, because he did not act for God’s love but for the empty display of human praise, as hypocrites are accustomed to do.

The Lord Christ greatly detests this vice of seeking to please human beings through good works, and he repeatedly strikes the Pharisees, who were such people in Judea, with a terrible curse, saying: “Woe to you, hypocrites!” (Matt. 23).

But, according to the Apostle, “Whoever glories, let him glory in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1). Whoever does not seek praise is not disturbed by insult. Nor should a person consider himself good merely because someone else praises him, since others do not know what he is like within. Let him reflect that God is the examiner of the heart.

What does it profit an evil person to be proclaimed good? A person’s deed is truly good when he desires to please the one from whom he has whatever good he possesses or does, and performs what he seems to do well. Whoever through such deeds desires to please not God but human beings labors in vain and sows into the wind.

Let each person strive to be great in his works, but let him not seek human favor because of his greatness, lest he lose what he had and become small.

Blessed Paul the Apostle rebukes those who glory in their own accomplishments, saying: “What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4). Therefore whoever turns some gift of God that he has merited into his own praise undoubtedly transforms virtue into vice and the good he has done into sin.

For when a poor person is fed for the sake of boasting, even the work of mercy itself is turned into sin. Thus, whatever good a person does, he must seek praise for God, not for himself, as the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5).

Therefore, my most beloved and most longed-for brothers, beware of pride, which God resists; avoid boastfulness, which displeases God; abominate arrogance, which is an abomination before God. Always maintain humility in all your conduct, the guardian of the virtues. Keep it in your heart, show it in your speech, preserve it in your deeds. Whatever good you do in word or deed, do everything for the glory of God, saying with the Prophet: “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Ps. 137).

In this way you can escape the punishment of Gehenna, which the proud deserve, and reach the heavenly kingdom, which the humble deserve, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY LX. ON AVOIDING ANGER AND HOMICIDE

Our Lord and Savior, dearly beloved brothers, instructing us through his word and example in gentleness and patience, entirely rejected the obstinacy of anger and rage, so that what the commandment of the Law could not fully accomplish might be completed by the precept of the Gospel.

The Law prohibited homicide, but because it permitted anger—the seedbed of homicide—it did not completely remove the vice itself. Our Redeemer, therefore, who came not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, fulfilled by his command what was lacking in the Law, removing the occasion of anger. He commanded us not only not to become angry and not to kill, but also to endure most patiently the adversities inflicted upon us by others.

Anger is a certain passion of the mind which, if it is not governed by reason, turns into fury, so that a person becomes unable to control himself and does what is improper. If anger takes possession of the heart, it removes all foresight from a person. He can neither seek the judgment of sound discernment, nor possess the virtue of honorable contemplation, nor have mature counsel; instead, he seems to do everything in a kind of headlong rush.

From it arise swelling of mind, quarrels, insults, shouting, indignation, presumption, blasphemies, the shedding of blood, homicides, desire for vengeance, and remembrance of injuries. It is conquered by patience and long-suffering, by the intellectual reason that God has implanted in human minds, and by recalling the Lord’s Prayer, in which we say to God: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

Therefore, if we desire to attain that highest divine reward of which it is said, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God,” anger must not only be cut away from our actions but also uprooted from the inner depths of the soul.

It will not greatly profit us if the fury of anger is restrained in speech and never brought into action, if God—who is not unaware of the secrets of hearts—sees that anger is present in the hidden recesses of our breast.

It is as though all kinds of venomous serpents or wild beasts, while they remain in the wilderness and in their lairs, were harmless, and yet they cannot be declared harmless merely because they harm no one. This is not due to a disposition [affectus] of goodness but to the necessity of their solitude. When they find an opportunity to cause harm, they immediately pour forth and display the venom and savagery hidden within them.

The Gospel saying commands that the roots of vices be cut away rather than their fruits, which, once their sources have certainly been torn out, will no longer sprout. In this way the mind will be able to remain continually in all patience and holiness, when these things have been uprooted not from the surface of actions and deeds but from the innermost recesses of thoughts.

For this reason, so that homicide may not be committed, anger and hatred are cut away, without which the crime of homicide can in no way be admitted. “Whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matt. 5); “whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3)—namely, in that he desires in his heart that the person should perish, although he is known not to have shed that person’s blood among human beings with his own hand or weapon.

The Lord declares a person a murderer through the disposition of anger, because he repays each person with reward or punishment not only according to the outcome of the deed but also according to the desire of the will and intention.

The distinguished preacher to the world says: “Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy be removed from you” (Eph. 4). Nor can the anger of a man accomplish the justice of God. Anger without moderation is without reason. “A gentle answer calms anger, but a harsh word stirs up fury” (Prov. 15). “An angry man,” says Solomon, “provokes quarrels; the patient man calms those that have been aroused” (ibid.).

Who could endure a spirit that is easily angered? Anger has no mercy, and erupting fury knows no end to vengeance.

If anger, O man, has overtaken you, calm it. That anger is evil which disturbs the mind so that sound counsel is lost. Anger is just and necessary when a person becomes angry with his own sins and is indignant with himself while doing wrong. The Prophet says: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4). He permitted what belongs to nature and removed what belongs to guilt.

Let another person’s anger be softened by your patience. “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Rom. 12). Let another person’s sin be your reward. If another’s anger displeases you, let what displeases you in the other also displease you in yourself. Do not stain the tranquility of your mind through another person’s disturbance.

Do not make yourself equal to a fool, because “anger rests in the bosom of a fool.” If you become angry against him, there will be two evils: you and him. It would be better for you to be good, even though he is evil. Why should you become evil through another person’s wickedness?

But what is even more serious is that one person calls for the death of his enemy: the one whom he cannot pursue with a sword, he pursues with prayer. The person who is cursed still lives, and yet the one who curses is already held guilty of his death.

God commands that an enemy be loved, yet God is asked to kill an enemy. Whoever prays in this way fights against the Creator in his very prayers. Hence it is said under the name of Judas: “Let his prayer become sin” (Ps. 108). That prayer is sin which asks for what the one being invoked himself forbids.

Therefore Truth says: “When you stand to pray, forgive whatever you have in your hearts” (Mark 11).

But suppose our enemy has grievously sinned against us, inflicted losses, injured those who helped us, and persecuted those who loved us. These things would have to be retained if our own sins did not have to be forgiven. For our Advocate composed a prayer for us in our case, and the one who is our Advocate is himself the Judge of that case. He inserted a condition into the prayer he composed, saying: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

Since, therefore, the same Judge has come who was our Advocate, the one who made the prayer himself hears it. Either we do not do what we say when we say, “Forgive us our debts,” and the rest, and by saying this we bind ourselves even more; or perhaps we omit this condition from the prayer, and our Advocate does not recognize the prayer he composed, immediately saying to himself: “I know what I instructed them; this is not the prayer I made.”

What, then, must we do, brothers, except show true affection of love toward our brothers, so that just as our hands remain free from slaughter outwardly, our hearts may also remain unharmed by hatred within?

For murderers, as it is written, will not possess the kingdom of God (Gal. 5); and “whoever hates his brother is in darkness” (1 John 2). First cast hatred away from yourselves, and then, with God’s help, you can avoid homicide.

Thus you will not merely fail to enter the outer darkness with the author of homicide, that is, with the devil; rather, with the peacemakers you will possess the heavenly kingdom of the most sweet Son of the Father. May Jesus Christ our Lord, the author and restorer of our salvation, graciously grant this to you and to us with you—he who lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, in perfect unity and Trinity, God, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY LXI. AGAINST ENVY AND HATRED
[Col. 0114D] To be jealous of what you see to be good, and to envy those who are better, seems to some, dearest brothers, a light and insignificant offense. And since it is thought to be light and insignificant, it is not feared; since it is not feared, it is despised; and since it is despised, it is not easily avoided. Thus it becomes a blind and hidden destruction which, though less clearly perceived and able to be guarded against by the prudent, secretly afflicts unsuspecting minds.

I therefore think that nothing must be more carefully avoided by a Christian, and nothing more vigilantly guarded against, than that anyone should envy and be seized by resentment; lest someone, caught in the blind snares of a deceiving enemy, should, while a brother through envy is turned into hatred of his brother, unknowingly be slain by his own sword. That you may gather this more fully and perceive it more clearly, let us return to its beginning and origin. Let us see where jealousy began, and when and how it began; for this exceedingly destructive evil will more easily be avoided by us if its origin and magnitude are known.

From the beginning of the world, therefore, the devil both perished first and destroyed another. He who was supported by angelic majesty, he who was acceptable and dear to God, after he saw the human being made in the image of God, burst forth into jealousy through malicious envy. He did not first cast down another through the impulse of jealousy before he himself had been cast down on account of jealousy: taken captive before he took captive, destroyed before he destroyed. While, stirred by envy, he robbed the human being of the grace of the immortality that had been given, he himself also lost what he had previously been.

What a great evil, dearest brothers, is that by which an angel fell; by which so lofty and splendid a sublimity could be ensnared; by which he himself was deceived who deceives others! From that time envy rages throughout the earth, while the envious person obeys the teacher of destruction, destined to perish through envy, and imitates the devil. As it is written: “But through the devil’s envy death entered the world” (Wis. 2). Therefore those who belong to his side imitate him.

From this, then, the beginnings of brotherhood were violated; from this, unspeakable parricides began: when the unrighteous Cain hated the righteous Abel, when the evil man persecuted the good through envy and resentment. So powerful was the fury of rivalry in bringing the crime to completion that neither brotherly affection, nor the enormity of the crime, nor fear of God, nor the punishment for sin was considered.

Considering these things now, dearest brothers, let us vigilantly and courageously fortify hearts dedicated to God against so great a destruction of evil. May the death of others contribute to our salvation; may the punishments of the imprudent bring health to the prudent.

[Col. 0115C] No one should suppose that this evil is contained in only one form, or enclosed within brief limits and a narrow boundary. The manifold and fertile destruction of jealousy extends widely. It is the root of all evils, the source of slaughter, the nursery of sins, the material of faults. From it hatred arises; from it hostility proceeds.

Jealousy inflames avarice, when someone cannot be content with his own possessions because he sees another richer. Jealousy arouses ambition, when someone sees another greater in honors. When jealousy excites our senses and reduces the hidden things of the mind into its own power, the fear of God is despised, Christ’s teaching is neglected, and the day of judgment is not foreseen. Pride is inflated, savagery embittered, impatience shakes everything, discord rages, anger grows hot; and the person who has been made subject to another’s power can no longer restrain or govern himself.

From this the bond of the Lord’s peace is broken; from this brotherly love is violated; from this truth is adulterated, unity is torn apart, and people rush into heresies and schisms. When priests are slandered, when bishops are envied; when someone complains that he was not ordained instead, or disdains to bear another as his superior—then he rebels, then he resists, proud through jealousy, perverse through rivalry, an enemy not of the person but of the honor, through hostility and resentment.

What sort of soul is it, and what corruption of thought does it contain, what great rust of the heart, to be jealous of another’s virtue or happiness? That is, to hate in another either his own merits or God’s gifts; to turn another’s good into one’s own evil; to be tortured by the prosperity of the distinguished; to make another’s glory one’s own punishment.

[Col. 0116A] Other evils have an end, and whatever is committed is brought to completion by the consummation of the offense. In adultery, the crime ceases once the sexual violation has been perpetrated; in the bandit, the wickedness comes to rest once murder has been committed; possession of the booty sets a limit to the plunderer’s rapacity; and completed deceit imposes a limit upon the forger. Jealousy has no end: it is an evil that persists continually and a sin without limit. And the more the one who is envied advances through better success, the more the envious person burns in the greater fire of resentment.

Hence come a threatening face, a grim expression, pallor in the face, trembling lips, gnashing teeth, savage words and unrestrained insults, hands ready for the violence of slaughter—even if they are meanwhile empty of a sword, they are armed with hatred in the mind driven mad. The apostle John declares in his Epistle that whoever is jealous of and hates his brother is stained by the crime of murder, saying: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer. And you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him” (1 John 3). And again: “Whoever says that he is in the light and hates his brother is still in darkness, and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes” (1 John 2).

“He who hates his brother,” he says, “walks in darkness and does not know where he is going.” Thus, ignorant and blind, he is hurled into punishment, into Gehenna, withdrawing from the light of Christ, who warns and teaches: “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8).

He follows Christ who adheres to his commandments, who walks along the way of his teaching, who follows his footsteps and paths, who imitates what Christ both taught and did. Take care of yourself, O human being, and strive to be healed from the very source from which you were wounded. Love those whom you formerly hated; cherish those whom you envied through unjust slanders. Imitate the good, if you can follow them; if you cannot follow them, at least rejoice with and congratulate those who are better. Through united love, make yourself a participant with them; through the fellowship of charity and the bond of brotherhood, make yourself their co-heir.

[Col. 0116D] Your debts will be forgiven when you yourself have forgiven; your sacrifices will be accepted when you come to God as a peacemaker. Your thoughts and actions will be directed by God when you think about what is divine and just, as it is written: “The heart of a man thinks what is just, so that he may be directed by God” (Prov. 6).

You have many things to think about. Think of paradise, to which Cain did not return after he killed his brother through jealousy. Think of the heavenly kingdom, to which the Lord admits only those who are united and harmonious. Think that only those who are peacemakers can be called sons of God, who by divine birth and law correspond in unity to the likeness of God the Father and of Christ.

Think that you stand beneath the eyes of God, while he himself observes and judges the course of our conduct and life. Let us therefore believe that we can proceed and arrive at this point only so that we may one day be granted to see him, if by our actions we now please him who sees us; if we show ourselves worthy of his grace and forgiveness; if, intending always to please in the kingdom, we first please him in this world.

Without doubt we shall please him then if we are now free from all jealousy and the resentment of envy, and love our neighbors with true affection. For “the peacemakers are sons of God,” and “whoever loves his brother is born of God and will see God.” May he grant us to enjoy this perpetual vision, he who freed us from everlasting death, Christ our Savior, who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXII. AGAINST DECEIT AND AVARICE

[Col. 0117A] It is fitting for the Christian who is striving toward the heavenly kingdom and longs to receive the riches above to restrain himself from present things and flee, as deadly poison, the evil of love of money—*philargyria*—which especially enslaves the human race, lest he desire to obtain anything through deceit or retain with rapacious excess what he possesses. For every deceit displeases God, and avarice is compared by the Apostle with idolatry.

“But for the avaricious person,” Scripture says, “nothing is more wicked. Why should earth and ashes be proud? Nothing is more unjust than to love money. Such a person has sold his own soul” (Eccl. 10).

Avarice, which the Greeks call *philargyria*, is an excessive desire to acquire or retain riches. This plague is insatiable and resembles dropsy. For just as one suffering from dropsy thirsts more the more he drinks, so the avaricious person desires to possess more the greater the amount of money he acquires. And since he has no limit in possessing, he has no limit in desiring.

[Col. 0117C] From this arise envies, thefts, robberies, murders, lies, perjuries, plundering, violence, unrest, unjust judgments, contempt for truth, forgetfulness of future blessedness, and hardness of heart. It is opposed to mercy and almsgiving toward the poor and competes with every form of piety.

Our Lord, therefore, who urges us to be kind to the poor and wretched from our own possessions, himself forbids us every form of avarice and every unjust acquisition of money. He who says, “Give alms from your just labors,” himself exhorts us through his Apostle, saying: “Do not defraud one another” (1 Cor. 7).

[Col. 0117D] For whoever acquires something through any kind of deceit loses the equity of justice. Tell me, avaricious man; tell me, greedy man; tell me, criminal: what have you acquired? Perhaps you say, “I have acquired gold,” and you speak truly. Behold, you acquired gold through deceit, and through injustice you lost faith.

If you found faith for sale in the marketplace, if you were a good man, how would you have purchased it? Why are you not afraid to lose what God wanted you to have in your heart? You have gold or silver or some other precious thing in your chest, but loss in your conscience. You have lost riches better than all these: faith, justice, love of God, and love of neighbor.

You consider your profit but do not consider your loss? If you rejoice in this profit, why do you not mourn those things that have been lost? You have lost more than you acquired.

O rich man, through power you seize what you desire to have, and through injustice you lose what God wants you to have—that is, everlasting blessedness. If a thief or robber had lost an eye during a theft or robbery, perhaps afterward he would not have committed theft or robbery. Yet such a person does not know that in this kind of sin he has lost the light of the heart, which is better than every bodily light.

[Col. 0118A] Rather, avaricious man, give to the poor what you have than acquire through deceit what you do not have, so that you may find in heaven what you gave on earth. Why are you afraid of losing your money, but not afraid of perishing altogether? For the sake of acquiring money you give false testimony, lie, seize what belongs to others, swear and perjure yourself—things which the law forbids. When you do all these things, why are you not afraid that you will burn entirely for eternity?

Why, avaricious man, do you love gold more than your soul? For what will it profit you if you gain the whole world but suffer the loss of your soul? The Lord himself also says in the Gospel: “Beware of all avarice, because a person’s life does not consist in the abundance of the things he possesses.”

Do not the rich die in the same way as the poor? Riches cannot help on the day of vengeance, nor will they free those who misuse them from everlasting punishments.

Do you wish, brothers, to know how disastrously and harmfully this tinder, unless it is carefully cut out, bears fruit for the destruction of the one who has seized it, and how it prevails over every kind of branch of vice? Look at Judas, counted among the number of the apostles. Because he did not wish to crush the head of this serpent, consider how it killed him with its own poison and, entangled in the snares of desire, drove his crime toward such a sheer precipice that it persuaded him to sell the world’s Redeemer and the author of human salvation for thirty pieces of silver.

[Col. 0118C] He would never have fallen into so wicked a crime of betrayal if he had not been infected with the disease of love of money; nor would he have become guilty and sacrilegious in the Lord’s transaction if he had not first been accustomed to pilfer the purse entrusted to him.

Although many detest Judas’s crime, few nevertheless strive to avoid it. The one who sold the Lord is judged guilty by human beings; but the one who exchanges truth for falsehood is scarcely reproved by anyone.

Pay attention, brothers, to what I am saying: whoever, for love of money or earthly advantage, sells the truth betrays Christ and shares in Judas’s crime. For the Lord himself says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” Certainly, whoever sells truth for money abandons life; and therefore, through this wicked bargain, he earns not eternal life but is plunged into the punishment due to falsehood.

[Col. 0118D] Do not, brothers—do not—be bound by the chains of avarice. Do not be ensnared by love of things that pass away. Raise your hearts upward; desire eternal blessedness. For this world passes away, and its desire, but the word of the Lord remains forever.

The Apostle Paul therefore warns us and says: “The time is short. From now on, let those who have wives live as though they had none; and those who weep as though they were not weeping; and those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing; and those who buy as though they did not possess; and those who use this world as though they did not use it. For the form of this world is passing away” (1 Cor. 7).

[Col. 0119A] That person who has a wife lives as though he did not have one who strives to please his spouse while nevertheless not displeasing the Creator. He also weeps, but as though he did not weep, who is distressed by temporal losses in such a way that he nevertheless always consoles his spirit with eternal gains.

He rejoices, but as though he did not rejoice, who is cheerful over temporal goods in such a way that he nevertheless always considers everlasting torments; and while he lifts his mind with joy, continually presses it down with the weight of prudent fear.

He buys, but as though he did not possess, who prepares earthly things for use and nevertheless prudently foresees that he will soon leave them behind. He also uses the world, but as though he did not use it, who brings together all necessary external things for the service of his life, yet does not allow these same things to rule his mind, so that things subject to him serve outwardly and never break the purpose of the soul striving toward higher things.

[Col. 0119B] All such people therefore take up all earthly things not for desire but for use. They use necessary things, but desire to have nothing in common with sin. From the very things they possess they daily acquire rewards, and they rejoice more in good works than in good possessions.

Think about these things, then. Since you cannot abandon everything that belongs to the world, conduct external matters well in outward life, but inwardly hasten eagerly toward eternal things. Let nothing delay the desire of your mind; let the pleasure of no thing in this world entangle you.

If something good is loved, let the mind take delight in better goods—that is, in heavenly things. If evil is feared, let everlasting evils be set before the soul, so that when it sees that they are there and that there is more for it to fear, it may not cling to anything here.

[Col. 0119C] For accomplishing these things we have as our helper the mediator between God and human beings, through whom we shall obtain all things more quickly if we burn with true love for him, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXIII. AGAINST FEASTING, DRUNKENNESS, AND COARSE JESTING

[Col. 0119D] There are certain vices, dearest brothers, which, although serious, seem in our times so light to some people that they think their practice is either a very minor matter or no wrongdoing at all. Thus they now prevail in human perversity to such an extent that among the morally ruined they deserve not only not to be condemned as sins or crimes, but even to be praised as virtues.

Of such people it is rightly said through the prophet: “They proclaimed their sin like Sodom, and did not hide it” (Isa. 3). In a fitting recompense for their error, the Lord likewise says to them through the prophet: “Woe to you who call evil good and good evil, who put darkness for light and light for darkness, who put bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter” (Isa. 5).

Among these vices, feasting and drunkenness now reign especially with impunity, since not only common and low-born men but also the more noble and distinguished of the earth are entangled in these evils. Every sex and every age has turned the evil of gluttony into a habit. “The sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the one who does wicked things is blessed” (Ps. 9).

[Col. 0120A] This plague has grown so greatly that it has taken captive certain people from our own order—that is, from the number of priests—to such an extent that they not only failed to rebuke the drunken, but themselves became drunk.

What wickedness is this, brothers, that so bitter an evil tolerates no authority and no dignity remaining unharmed? Virtues are disparaged and vices exalted with praise; abstinence and sobriety are condemned, while gluttony and drunkenness are praised.

For they say: “They are truly generous, and only those who devote themselves to drunkenness and gluttony observe the laws of mercy and charity.” As though mercy and charity consisted in deceiving oneself and dragging others with oneself to destruction.

Did the Apostle Paul, brothers, preach charity in such a manner? He says: “Charity is patient, charity is kind; it does not envy, it does not act wrongly, it is not ambitious, it does not seek its own; it is not provoked, it does not think evil, it does not rejoice over iniquity but rejoices with the truth” (1 Cor. 13).

[Col. 0120B] As you have heard, then, charity is kind, yet it does not act wrongly. It is not ambitious, seeking what is its own and not what belongs to God. It is patient, yet it does not think evil or rejoice over iniquity.

Tell me, you who praise feasting and drunkenness: is it good or evil to blind the light of the mind through drunkenness, to lose reason, to disturb the sight of the eyes, to lose the power of speech, to be master of none of the limbs’ functions, and to become like one raging or possessed?

Did God create a human being like this? Is this the glory of the image of God, of which it is written: “God made the human being in his own image; in the likeness of God he created him” (Gen. 1)? Do you dare to call God raging in your likeness? Such blasphemy would be intolerable, because he is supremely good, alone blessed, and powerful, King of kings and Lord of lords.

[Col. 0120C] He saw all that he had made, and it was very good (ibid.). From this it is understood that drunkenness was not created by God, nor commended by him to human beings among the things he made, because it is not good but exceedingly evil—and not only evil in itself, but also the producer of other evils.

Believe me, brothers, for almost all evils arise from this. From it are stirred up anger, quarrels, dissensions, slanders, rivalries, factions, envy, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, robberies, blasphemies, and similar things. Of these the Apostle says: “Those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.”

[Col. 0120D] But in order to make clearer how detestable a thing drunkenness is, we think that the testimonies of the sacred Scriptures must be employed. For Truth itself says to its disciples in the Gospel: “Take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and the cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly; for it will come like a snare upon all who dwell on the face of the whole earth” (Luke 21).

It is as though he were saying openly: Beware of dissipation, drunkenness, and the ambition of the present age, lest the last day find you entangled in these vices and thrust you into eternal imprisonment to be punished with the lovers of the world.

Through the prophet Isaiah also, the Lord threatens drinkers in this way, saying: “Woe to you who rise early to pursue drunkenness and drink until evening, so that you may burn with wine. Harp and lyre, tambourine and flute, and wine are in your feasts, but you do not regard the work of the Lord, nor consider the works of his hands. Therefore my people have been led away captive, because they had no knowledge; and its nobles have perished from hunger, and its multitude has been parched with thirst. Therefore Sheol has enlarged its appetite and opened its mouth without measure; and its strong men and its people shall descend, with its high and glorious ones, into it” (Isa. 5).

[Col. 0121B] In the same prophet, shortly afterward, the divine rebuke continues, saying: “Woe to you who are mighty at drinking wine and strong men at mixing drunkenness, who acquit the wicked for gifts and take away the justice of the just from him. Therefore, as the tongue of fire devours stubble and the heat of the flame consumes it, so their root shall be like ashes and their shoot shall rise like dust. For they have rejected the law of the Lord of hosts and blasphemed the word of the Holy One of Israel. Therefore the anger of the Lord was kindled against his people, and he stretched out his hand over them and struck them. The mountains were shaken, and their corpses became like refuse in the middle of the streets. In all this his anger was not turned away, but his hand was still stretched out” (ibid.).

Through Solomon likewise, divine Wisdom detests drunkenness and forbids it, saying: “My son, do not be among the banquets of drinkers, nor among the feasts of those who bring together meat for eating; those who devote themselves to drinking and contribute their shares will be consumed” (Prov. 23).

[Col. 0121C] Shortly afterward, as though astonished at the condemnation of such people, it adds: “To whom is woe? Whose father is woe? For whom are quarrels? For whom are pits? For whom are wounds without cause? For whom are bloodshot eyes? Is it not for those who linger over wine and devote themselves to emptying cups? Do not look at wine when it glows, when its color shines in the glass. It enters smoothly, but in the end it will bite like a serpent and spread poison like a basilisk” (ibid.).

In the Law also, the Lord commanded Aaron, saying: “You and your sons shall not drink wine or anything that can cause intoxication when you enter the tabernacle of testimony, lest you die. It is an everlasting ordinance throughout your generations, so that you may have knowledge to distinguish between holy and profane, between polluted and clean, and so that you may teach the children of Israel all my statutes which the Lord has spoken to them through Moses” (Lev. 10).

[Col. 0121D] Behold, dearest brothers, you have now heard from the sayings of the sacred Scriptures how greatly feasting and drunkenness displease our Creator, and what condemnation they bring upon those who abuse them.

Please refrain from lingering over so great an evil, because it robs you of present prosperity and everlasting life. Let your banquets be sober; let just men be your table companions; let your glory be in the fear of God. Let the thought of God be in your understanding, and let all your speech concern the commandments of the Most High.

For a talkative person who is reckless in his speech is hateful, because, as it is written: “Whoever is inconsiderate in speaking will experience evils” (Prov. 13).

[Col. 0122A] Remember how the Lord earlier commanded his priests and ministers of his tabernacle to beware of drunkenness. For, as the Apostle Peter testifies, you are “a royal and priestly race, a holy nation, a people for possession” (1 Pet. 2), and you ought daily to serve God in his true tabernacle, which is the Church.

Cease, then, and abstain from feasting and drunkenness, from excessive talk, coarse jesting, and vanity. Always pursue what is good toward one another and toward all, so that you may deserve to become members of him who is the true priest and our true Lord, King of kings and Lord of lords, Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXIV. ON GOOD ZEAL AND THE DISCERNMENT THAT MUST ALWAYS BE MAINTAINED

Our Redeemer, then, who restrained the disputes of his disciples about precedence, showed what they ought to dispute about: “Strive,” he says, “to enter through the narrow gate” (Luke 13).

The narrow gate, therefore, and the constricted way lead to life, and few are those who enter by it. What else, then, did Truth itself wish to indicate to us through this statement, dearest brothers, except that through right intention and good zeal we might attain eternal life alone?

“The soldier who has competed lawfully will be crowned” (2 Tim. 2); but whoever turns back after undertaking a good contest is recognized as unfit for the kingdom of heaven.

Good zeal and good will certainly consist in wanting, through the observance of God’s commandments, to reach everlasting joy, so that whatever one does may be directed toward pleasing God, and so that through it one may not greedily seek anything transitory for oneself.

[Col. 0122C] A good work is rightly performed when it arises from the right intention of thought. Hence Truth says well in the Gospel: “The lamp of the body is the eye. If your eye is simple, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness” (Matt. 6).

What is expressed by the eye except the intention of the heart that precedes its work? Before it exercises itself in action, it already contemplates what it desires. And what is designated by the term “body” except each action, which follows its intention as though following an observing eye?

The eye, therefore, is the lamp of the body, because through the ray of a good intention the merits of an action are illumined. “If your eye is simple, your whole body will be full of light,” because if we intend rightly through simplicity of thought, a good work is produced even if it appears less good.

[Col. 0122D] “And if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness,” because when something right is done with a perverse intention and is seen to shine before human beings, it is darkened before the judgment of the inner Judge.

With vigilant care, therefore, our intention must be weighed in all our works, so that it seeks nothing temporal in what it does and fixes itself entirely in the solidity of eternity. Otherwise, if the structure of our action is placed outside its foundation, it will collapse when the earth gives way.

But in order that your work may reach a good end, discernment is extremely necessary for you, brothers, because discernment is the mother of all virtues. Often virtue is lost when it is held indiscriminately; when it is interrupted with discernment, it is preserved more fully.

Nor is it surprising that we understand this in bodily matters, since we see it taking place in incorporeal things as well. Through use, the bow is drawn back so that at the proper time it may be stretched with benefit. If it does not receive the relaxation of rest, it loses through the very practice of tension its power to strike.

[Col. 0123B] Thus at times virtue in its exercise is preserved when it is set aside through discernment, so that afterward it may strike vices with greater force, because for the time being it prudently ceases from attacking them.

The proper measure is accepted when the life of spiritual men is placed before the eyes for consideration, when the examples of preceding fathers are shown to each chosen soul as a rule for living. From their lives one may consider what to preserve in one’s own actions, so that, observing the path of a just boundary, one may neither fail by neglecting the least things nor extend oneself proudly beyond the greatest; neither attempt to accomplish less than is sufficient nor seize more than one has received. Otherwise one will either fail to reach the measure one ought to attain or, abandoning that same measure, fall outside the boundary.

[Col. 0123C] The gate that leads to life is narrow, and the person enters it who is carefully constrained for its sake in all that he does by the subtlety of discernment. For whoever expands himself with a secure mind according to his own desires closes off for himself access to the narrow gate.

In order that the measure of this earth may be preserved, a line is stretched over it from above. Through the sacred writings, the subtle life of the saints is spread out before us, so that our lesser works may advance and our greater ones be moderated; and through the discernment displayed in their lives it is determined what and how much we ought to do.

Therefore, dearest brothers, exercise yourselves in every pursuit of spiritual virtues, and do not neglect to preserve yourselves with discernment in all things. Do not grow accustomed to doing anything beyond measure or reason. For the person stretches his foot toward a precipice who does not attend to the limit of his measures.

[Col. 0123D] Often the person loses what he could have achieved who rashly hastens to seize things he cannot reach. Even the ministries of our limbs are useful to us only when we carefully preserve for each its proper function. We see light with our eyes, but hear a voice with our ears. If someone, reversing the order, were to apply his eyes to a voice and his ears to light, both would be open to no purpose.

If someone wished to distinguish odors with his mouth and taste flavors with his nose, he would destroy the function of both senses by perverting their proper use. For when these things are not adapted to their own uses, they abandon their proper functions and do not rise to foreign ones.

David therefore had well kept the foot of his heart within the measures granted by divine generosity when he said: “I have not walked in great things, nor in things too wonderful for me” (Ps. 130).

[Col. 0124A] He would walk beyond himself in wonderful things if he sought to appear great beyond what he could be. He is lifted above himself in wonderful things who strives to seem capable even in matters for which he is not sufficient.

Therefore, dearest brothers, diligently do whatever good you can, and meanwhile carefully and attentively preserve the measure of discernment in all things. Run in the race of this life in such a way that you may attain eternal life. Compete in the Christian contest in such a way that you may be crowned by Christ.

Above all, hold fast to true humility. Whatever good you do, attribute it to divine grace, not to yourselves, because “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1).

Commend your contest to the Lord in your prayers. Fix your hope in God, and above all desire to enjoy his perpetual vision. When you reach it, you will rejoice with unspeakable gladness, and, having obtained the highest good, you will rejoice forever with the holy angels, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

*(The homilies that follow were not entered in the index of homilies; nevertheless, they followed in the manuscript copy, and perhaps they are not by Rabanus. See Pamelius.)*

## HOMILY LXV. ON SUNDAYS, WHENEVER YOU WISH.

[Col. 0124C] It is fitting, dearly beloved brothers, that every Christian willingly listen to sacred Scripture, and listen even more willingly once he has heard it. For hearing the divine words benefits a person only when the preacher’s voice is fixed in the ear of the heart. For it is not merely hearers of the word who will be justified, but doers of it (Rom. II). Therefore, dearest ones, hear the word of the Lord, understand it, and carry out all the Lord’s commandments; turn back to the Lord and do penance, so that your sins may be blotted out. Fear the Lord and give him honor, for his judgment has come, and he himself will judge all nations.

Let us love God the almighty Father, who has power in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all that is in them; let us hasten toward that blessed [Col. 0124D] life where we hope always to remain. Let us despise this earthly life and desire that heavenly life. This life is wretched, deceptive, and full of desire, or filled with scandals: here we live in labor, and in sorrow we die; this life has an end, but the kingdom of God has no end.

Let us therefore examine ourselves, because we do not know the day or the hour when our Lord Jesus Christ will come to judgment. On that day the Lord will come from heaven with his angels and with all his saints to judge all nations, and he will repay each person according to his works. Therefore, my brothers, let us hold fast to those virtues that bring the greatest gains to our souls.

These are the virtues of souls: to love God and one’s neighbor, and to hate what God does not love; to pursue patience and avoid all impatience; to guard the chastity of body and soul; to despise empty glory and trample upon all perishable things; to possess humility and abhor the swelling of pride; to restrain anger and suppress fury; to avoid all folly and embrace divine wisdom, and to subject every desire of the flesh to the mind; to despise greed and give away one’s own possessions; to prefer heavenly things to earthly things; and to meditate more earnestly day and night upon the judgment of God. These are the virtues of the soul, from which every spiritual fruit will arise.

For God does not wish to be loved merely in words, but with a pure heart and righteous deeds. Whoever says, “I love God,” but does not keep his commandments, is a liar. God is not a hearer of words but an examiner of the heart, and he loves those who love him in simplicity of heart.

Alongside these virtues of the soul mentioned above, my brothers, there are certain opposing vices that proceed from the root of iniquity and plunge people into the pit of hell when they commit them and do not amend their ways. These are gluttony, fornication, greed, anger, empty glory, and pride. From these arise feasting, drunkenness, an indecent place [Note: perhaps “dishonorable profit”], foolish speech, lying, thefts, perjuries, the desire for shameful gain, false testimonies, inhumanity, rapacity, murders, enmities, quarrels, envy, impatience, indignation, contempt, disobedience, murmuring, and detraction.

Let us beware of these vices and of others as well, withdraw from them, and amend for the better what we have negligently done wrong, lest, suddenly overtaken by the day of death, we seek time for penance and be unable to find it. Let us continually meditate upon the virtues mentioned above by acting, confessing, doing penance, coming constantly to church, praying, keeping vigil, and giving alms.

For those who do these things there will be eternal life, and they will enter that kingdom where the King of kings and Lord of lords is; where there is light without darkness, life without death, joy without sorrow, and health without pain; where no one hungers or thirsts; where there are greater and better spiritual goods than the human tongue can recount, which God has prepared for those who love him—things which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and which have not entered the human heart (I Cor. IX). To this kingdom, with the help of our Lord and Savior, we shall attain, so that we may reign with him for everlasting ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXVI. ALSO ON THE FOREGOING SUBJECT

Listen, dearest brothers, to how great the danger is for the priests of Christ—that is, for bishops and presbyters—who do not announce to you what you ought to do and what you ought to avoid. For if we do not announce these things, so that you may correct yourselves from evil works, we shall have to render an account for you on the day of judgment. And if each person can scarcely escape punishment for his own sin, what will become of the priests? For we have been commanded to announce to you without ceasing:

“Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near. Let the wicked abandon his way, and the unjust man his worst thoughts” (Isa. LV).

For this life is like a person living in another’s house: he does not know on what day or at what hour he may be told, “Come outside, for the house in which you are is not yours.” Thus our end is unknown to us.

Therefore we warn you that there must be no negligence concerning what you promised in baptism before the sight of God and the angels; and if there has already been negligence, let penance come to your aid. You made two promises: first, that you would believe in God the almighty Father, and in Jesus Christ his Son, and in the Holy Spirit; second, you promised to renounce the devil and all his works.

Much is contained in these brief words. Whoever renounces the devil and his works is the one who flees criminal sins [Col. 0126B] that plunge people into eternal punishment: sacrilege, murder, adultery, false testimony, theft, robbery, pride, envy, greed, covetousness, anger, feasting, drunkenness, and the rest. For the holy Apostle does not lie when he says: “Nor will the drunkards possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI).

Therefore let no one deceive himself. Whoever is a drunkard, if he does not do penance for that drunkenness and remains in it until his death, will perish forever and burn in an everlasting flame without end. Likewise, an oath must be feared, because it is said through the Holy Spirit in sacred Scripture: “A man who swears much will be filled with iniquity” (Eccli. XXIII). For whoever commits an offense through an oath [Note: perhaps “perjury”], even though he lives in body, is nevertheless dead in soul.

And whoever recognizes that he has even one of these sins in himself cannot possess the kingdom of heaven unless penance comes to his aid. But if we wish to find true remission of our sins, let us make a true confession with our whole heart and with tears, because the tears of penitents are reckoned before the Lord in place of baptism, since no guilt is so grave that it cannot be erased through penance.

Therefore, dearest ones, redeem your souls from the punishment of hell while you live in this life, for after death no one will redeem you if you have died from this world without confession and penance. Let us do penance and distribute alms to the poor from earnings acquired by honest labor, because just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin (Eccli. III).

Let us love God with our whole heart, our whole soul, all our strength, and our whole mind; then let us love our neighbors as ourselves. This is the greatest and first commandment of Christ.

And observe the Lord’s day, so that you perform no servile work on it, because on that day God created the light; on that day he rained manna in the wilderness; on that day the Redeemer of the human race freely rose from the dead for our salvation; on that day he poured out the Holy Spirit upon the disciples. Such must be the observance that, apart from prayers, the solemnities of the Mass, and what pertains to eating, one should do nothing else. If there should be a necessity of sailing or traveling, permission is granted, provided only that on this account Masses and prayers are not omitted.

And whatever craft God has granted each person by which he can feed or clothe himself, from that portion let him give a tenth for the redemption of his soul to the church or to the poor.

And believe most certainly this: every person, however sinful and however criminal, who had previously committed evil deeds, if he gives alms and death finds him in a good disposition, will never descend into hell, but will be lifted by angels into heaven. Therefore we must hasten now to amend our sins, so that we may mourn what we previously did wrongly and cease to do it any longer. For God will not ask what sort of people we were at the beginning, but what sort he finds us to be near our end.

May he himself lead us to his kingdom, [Col. 0127B] to whom belong honor, glory, might, and power, for ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXVII. ALSO ON THE FOREGOING SUBJECT

Dearest ones, it is necessary to proclaim to you what we have learned through the sacred Scriptures. Yet you must first know and understand that you are to believe in God the almighty Father, in Jesus Christ his Son, and in the Holy Spirit. In these three persons and names let us believe in one God, the almighty Father, creator of heaven and earth and of all things visible and invisible. This is the Word of God that we preach.

For if we confess the Lord Jesus with our mouth and believe in our heart, we shall be saved. Therefore the merciful Lord also exhorts us through the prophet Joel [Col. 0127C] to turn from our sins, saying: “Turn to me with all your heart, with fasting, weeping, and mourning” (Joel II); “for I do not desire the death of sinners, but that they turn and live” (Ezek. XXXIII).

And again the Lord says through the prophet: “Do not delay turning from your sins, and do not put it off from day to day” (Eccli. V), because our end and our death do not delay.

These, then, are the capital sins from which we must turn: pride, envy, murders, manifold fornication, which it is unlawful to recount in full; thefts, robbery, false testimonies, perjury, detraction, covetousness, empty glory, unjust gains, drunkenness, feasting, and sacrilege—which is every worship of idols and demons—that is, auguries, and those who make offerings to stones, trees, or springs, or practice incantations or divinations, and the rest.

These are the works of Satan, which Christians renounce in baptism. The devil seeks these works in us on the day of our death. And if that ancient enemy finds us guilty and unamended concerning the works mentioned above on the day of our departure, then he drags us naked and weeping with him into hell and eternal punishments, where there is darkness without light, fire that will never be extinguished, and worms that never die; where ears hear nothing except mourning, groaning, and the gnashing of teeth; where those who here, through their greed, refused to give food and drink to the wretched who were hungry and thirsty will hunger and thirst forever; [Col. 0128A] where there is every evil and no good for those who refused to amend their ways.

Nevertheless, let no one despair of the Lord’s mercy, for the Lord himself says through the prophet Ezekiel: “On whatever day the sinner turns from his injustice, all his iniquities will be forgotten before me” (Ezek. XXXIII).

Therefore, dearest ones, let us hasten to abandon every evil, amend ourselves, and do the whole will of the Lord. First, let us hold right faith and love the Lord with our whole heart, our whole mind, and all our strength; then let us love our neighbors as ourselves.

Let us have within us fear of the Lord, humility, charity, peace with everyone, kindness, patience, modesty, justice, self-control, and mercy.

These are works of mercy: to give food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the naked; to visit the sick and those shut up in prison and minister to them; to receive traveling strangers and the poor; to praise justice and detest iniquity; to assist widows and orphans; to distribute alms to the poor; to aid the afflicted; to bury the dead; to pay tithes from all possessions; to pray always; to guard the chastity of body and soul; to love fasting; continually to make confession and do penance for sins; and for each person not to do to another what he does not wish done to himself.

For those who do these things, eternal kingdoms are prepared. And the Savior of the world, our Lord Jesus Christ, will say to them on the day of judgment: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV).

Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Matt. XXIII), where there is light without darkness, life without death, joy and gladness without end; where there is joyful youth without fear of old age, health without sickness, security without fear, an unchanging kingdom, spiritual knowledge, good will, and everlasting exultation; where there are greater and better goods than the human tongue can recount, which God has prepared for those who love him (I Cor. IX).

May the almighty God grant this to us, he who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXVIII. AT THE VIGILS OF THE DEAD

The blessed Apostle admonishes us (I Thess. IV) not to grieve over those who sleep—that is, over our dearly beloved dead—as do the others who have no hope, namely, the hope of resurrection and eternal incorruption. For this reason Scripture, which is utterly truthful, calls them “those who sleep,” so that when we hear that those who sleep will awaken, we may not despair at all.

Hence it is also sung in the psalm: “Will the one who sleeps not rise again?” (Ps. XL).

There is therefore a certain sadness over the dead whom we love, in a sense natural; for it is not opinion but nature that abhors death. Nor would death have approached human beings except because of the punishment preceded by guilt. Therefore, if animals, which were created so that they too would die at their appointed time, flee death and love life, how much more does the human being, who was created in such a way that, if he had wished to live without sin, he would have lived without end.

Hence it is necessary for us to be sad when those whom we love leave us by dying. For even though we know that they do not remain separated from us forever, but go ahead for a little while and will be followed by us, nevertheless death itself—which nature flees—when it overtakes a loved one, saddens within us the affection of love.

The Apostle therefore did not admonish us not to grieve, but not to grieve as do the others who have no hope. We grieve, then, at the deaths of our own because we are compelled to lose them, but with the hope of receiving them again. From one side we are distressed; from the other we are consoled. From one side weakness afflicts us; from the other faith restores us. From one side the human condition grieves; from the other the divine promise heals.

Accordingly, funeral pomp, costly processions of mourners, elaborate care in burial, and lavish construction of monuments [Col. 0129B] are whatever consolations of the living, not aids for the dead. But there is no doubt that the dead are helped by the prayers of the holy Church, by the saving sacrifice, and by almsgiving distributed for their spirits, so that the Lord may deal with them more mercifully than their sins deserved.
