The whole Church observes what has been handed down by the Fathers: when those who have died in communion with the body and blood of Christ are commemorated in their appointed place during the sacrifice itself, prayer is made for them, and it is commemorated that the sacrifice is also offered on their behalf.

When works of mercy are performed for the sake of commending them, who could doubt that they benefit those for whom prayers are not vainly offered to God? It must not be doubted at all that these things benefit the dead—but those who lived before death in such a way that these things could be useful to them after death.

For those who departed from their bodies without faith working through love and without its sacraments receive such acts of piety from their relatives in vain. While they were here, they lacked faith’s pledge, either by not receiving God’s grace or by receiving it without effect, and they stored up for themselves not mercy but wrath.

New merits are therefore not acquired for the dead when their own perform some good deed on their behalf; rather, these consequences are rendered according to their preceding merits.

[Note: [Col. 0129D] The passage is corrupt. See Saint Augustine, *On Faith, Hope, and Charity*, chapter 110.]

[The text is corrupt:] For it was not won except when they were living here, so that these things might help them when they had ceased to live here. And therefore, when each person brings this life to an end, he cannot have anything afterward except what he deserved in this life.

Let the devout hearts of relatives therefore be permitted to grieve over the deaths of their own with a grief that can be healed, and let them pour out consoling tears under the condition of mortality. May the joy of faith quickly restrain those tears, by which the faithful are believed, when they die, to depart from us for a little while and pass over to better things.

Let us also console them through fraternal services, whether those offered at funerals or those performed sorrowfully, lest there be a justified complaint from those who say: “I waited for someone who would grieve with me, and there was none; and for comforters, and I found none” (Ps. LXVIII).

Let there be, according to our means, care for burying and constructing graves, since these too are counted among good works in the holy Scriptures. Not only in the bodies of patriarchs and other saints, and in the human corpses of any who lie dead, but also in the body of the Lord himself, those who performed these acts are proclaimed and praised.

Let people perform these duties of the final service toward their own dead, and let them provide alleviation for their human grief. But those truly cleanse the spirits of the dead and offer oblations, prayers, and supplications for them with much greater devotion and abundance who love their own dead in the flesh but not in spirit, not merely carnally but spiritually. Amen.

## HOMILY LXIX. ON THE CELEBRATION OF THE DEAD AND THE RESURRECTION OF THE DEAD

When we celebrate the days of our dead brothers, we ought to keep in mind both what is to be hoped for and what is to be feared.

There is reason for hope because “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. CXV); but there is reason for fear because “the death of sinners is very evil” (Ps. XXXIII). Therefore, because of hope, “the righteous will be in everlasting remembrance”; because of fear, “he will not fear an evil report.” For there will be a report greater than any other when it is said to those on the left: “Go into the eternal fire” (Matt. XXV). From this evil report the righteous will not be afraid, for they will be on the right, among those to whom it will be said: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (ibid.).

In this life, by which we are led between the highest goods and the greatest evils, in the midst of intermediate goods and evils—that is, in neither of the two supreme realms—for whatever good a person may have here is nothing in comparison with eternal goods, and whatever evil he experiences in this life is not comparable with eternal fire—in this middle state of life, then, we must hold fast to what we have now heard from the Gospel:

“Whoever believes in me,” he says, “even though he dies, will live” (John XI).

What does “he dies, he lives” mean? Even though he dies in body, he lives in spirit. Then he adds: “And whoever lives and believes in me will never die” (ibid.).

Certainly, “even though he dies”: how, if he does not die? Rather, even though he dies for a time, he will not die forever. The question is resolved in this way, so that the words of Truth are not contrary to one another, but can instruct through the affection of piety.

Therefore, although we are destined to die in body, we live if we believe. Our faith is especially distinguished from every faith of the pagans by belief in the resurrection of the dead. They do not accept it at all, because they have no place where they could accept it. For the will of a human being is prepared by the Lord, so that it may be a receptacle of faith.

The Lord says to the Jews: “My word does not find room in you” (John VIII). Therefore, it finds room in those in whom it finds what can receive it. For the word that contains finds in them what it can contain—the word that God, by promising, does not deceive.

For he who seeks the lost sheep knows both which sheep he seeks, where he seeks it, and how to gather its scattered limbs, restore them to a single salvation, and establish it in such a way that he will not lose it again.

Let us therefore console one another in these sermons of ours. The human heart can fail to grieve for a dearly beloved dead person; yet it is better for the human heart to grieve with another and be healed than, by not grieving, to become inhuman.

Mary clung to the Lord and grieved for her dead brother. But why are you surprised that Mary grieved then, when the Lord himself was also weeping? It may move anyone to ask how he wept for the dead when he immediately commanded him to live. He did not weep for the dead man whom he himself raised, but for the death that human beings acquired for themselves by sinning. For if sin had not preceded, death would certainly not have followed.

Therefore bodily death followed too, preceded by the death of the soul. The death of the soul preceded it by withdrawing, and bodily death followed when the soul departed. The soul departed willingly, and was compelled unwillingly to leave. It was as though it were said to it: “You withdrew from the one whom you ought to have loved; withdraw from the one whom you loved.”

For who wishes to die? Absolutely no one—and so entirely no one that it was said to blessed Peter: “Another will gird you and carry you where you do not wish” (John XXI). If there were no bitterness of death, there would be no great courage among the martyrs.

So too the Apostle says: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve as the nations do, who have no hope.” He did not merely say, “so that you may not grieve,” but “so that you may not grieve in the same way as the nations, who have no hope.”

For it is necessary that you grieve—but where do you grieve? Where the body that lives from the soul becomes lifeless when the soul departs; where the one who walked now lies; the one who spoke is silent; the eyes no longer receive light; the ears open to no voice; all the functions of the limbs have fallen quiet. There is no one to move his feet for walking, his hands for working, or his senses for perceiving.

Is this not a house that some invisible inhabitant adorned? The one who cannot be seen has departed; what was seen with grief remains. This is the cause of sadness.

If this is the cause of sadness, what is the consolation for this sadness? The Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with a trumpet; and the dead in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive and remain will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord.

Let sorrow perish where there is such great consolation; let mourning be wiped from the soul; let faith drive out grief. In such great hope, it is not fitting for the temple of God to be sad. There dwells the good Comforter; there dwells the one who does not deceive in promising.

I know that we grieve for the dead for a long time, because death is bitter. The Lord himself passed through it. Let these few words suffice for your love. May he console you more abundantly who does not depart from your heart, but deigns to dwell there in such a way that he may also deign to invite us at the end. Amen.

## HOMILY LXX. ON THE RETURN OF THE HOLY AND MOST GLORIOUS CROSS OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST

At that time, after Constantine Augustus had gone to war against the tyrant Maxentius, a sign of the holy cross had been shown from heaven, and he himself had successfully gained the victory; after Helena, the mother of the aforesaid ruler, had found the holy cross, and it had been clearly declared by the healing of a sick person and the raising of a dead person as a sign of its power, the queen, having obtained what she had vowed, had the saving wood cut in half, so that she might carry one cross to her son at Constantinople and preserve the other, enclosed in silver cases, at Jerusalem. She used wise counsel in this arrangement, namely, that where the Lord’s limbs had been fitted to punishment, there the cross might be venerated by the people in glory.

After the passage of many years, when, because of the burden of human sins, the Lord permitted the Christian people to be scourged by the savagery of the pagans, a certain profane and impious man named Chosroes gained the kingdom of the Persians. He dared to erupt into such arrogance that he ordered himself to be worshiped as God by the inhabitants of neighboring nations whom he devastated in a barbarian assault and subjected to his wicked rule; he ordered himself to be called “king of kings” and “lord of lords.”

Nor was this alone enough to bring about his condemnation. After he had subjected Syria and Palestine, and Egypt as well, he brought under his most savage rule the kingdoms that lay beyond and below the frontier territories, gathered around in a circuit. He came to Jerusalem, overturned the churches of Christ, and devastated, burned, and plundered the entire neighboring region.

When he wished to approach the Lord’s sepulcher, he returned in terror; nevertheless, he carried away part of the saving wood that the devout queen had left there as a testimony to its power. For he had made himself a silver tower, within which, glittering with gems, he had constructed a golden throne. There he had placed an image of the sun’s chariot and of the light—or of the stars—and through concealed pipes he had brought channels of water, so that it might appear that rain was being poured down from above. When the structure of the tower was moved around by horses pulling it in a circle through an underground cavern, it seemed to imitate, as far as the craftsman’s skill allowed, a kind of thunderous roar.

In this place he had prepared a seat for himself, and beside it, as though he were God’s associate, he had placed the Lord’s cross. After entrusting the kingdom to his son, he himself sat in such a shrine.

At that time Gracchus held the imperial power, a man vigorous in arms, learned in speech, handsome in body, and although devoted to secular affairs, wholly Catholic in faith. He was therefore humble, kind, and devoted toward the worshipers of God.

Chosroes’ son, advancing against Gracchus, encamped his army beside the great river Danube. At last, through the inspiration of the Savior’s clemency, it pleased both rulers that they themselves should fight one another in the middle of a bridge over the river, and that whichever of them fortune granted victory should, without harm, assume command as victor over the army.

An agreement was also made under oath that if anyone from either people dared to come to the aid of his ruler, he would have his legs and arms cut off and be drowned in the river. When both peoples had approved this pact, they fought one another as stipulated and came together in the middle of the bridge.

At last, the Lord, moved by the tears of the Christians, granted his faithful Gracchus triumph over the enemy through the power of the holy cross, to which the ruler mentioned above had commended himself with particular devotion on that very day. Such a change of mind seized Chosroes’ army that they not only refused entirely to violate the pact mentioned above, but also voluntarily submitted themselves, with all their household and offspring, to Gracchus both in power and in faith.

He received them kindly and showed them this clemency: they all hastened to baptism. They unanimously promised that they would do so.

The most Christian ruler himself, traveling with only his army throughout the surrounding kingdoms that Chosroes had held, came to Chosroes’ seat. He went up to him with a few companions and found him sitting on a golden throne. No one from his army had brought him any report of the war’s destruction, because all hated him on account of his cruelty and pride—and not without reason, since he was openly opposed to God. How could he have been loved by God’s creature?

When Chosroes, trembling, offered words of greeting to Gracchus, the latter replied: “If you wish to have salvation: because, though unworthy, you treated the wood of the holy cross honorably according to your ability; if you are willing to believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, promise that you will be his servant—the one whose servant I am—and make this confession truthfully, I will give you the Persian kingdom alone with its patrimony, and your life, when you have given me hostages of peace. But if you do otherwise, you will immediately perish by my sword.”

When he would not agree at all, Gracchus drew his sword and cut off his head. Nevertheless, he ordered him to be buried, since he had been a king. He ordered his son to be baptized and himself received him from the sacred font; for the boy was ten years old.

He also produced under the son’s name descriptions of the Persian kingdom. He assigned all the silver of the tower as plunder for his army, but reserved the gold and gems, in vessels and utensils, for restoring the churches that the tyrant had destroyed.

Receiving the most glorious wood of the cross that the impious man had carried away, he brought it to Jerusalem. All the people went to meet it joyfully, with palm branches, candles, lamps, and various displays of glory, some proceeding ahead and others following behind, with hymns and songs.

When the emperor had descended from the Mount of Olives through the gate by which the Lord had entered when he came to his Passion, he wished to enter while seated and adorned with the royal diadem and imperial ornaments. Suddenly the stones of the gate descended and closed against one another, forming a single wall.

As they looked on in amazement, seized by great terror, they looked upward and saw the sign of the holy cross shining in heaven with fiery brilliance. For an angel of the Lord, looking upon it in his hands, stood above the gate and said:

“When the King of heaven, the Lord of the whole world, entered through this passage to accomplish the mystery of his Passion, he did not present himself clothed in purple or shining with a diadem, nor did he seek the vehicle of a powerful horse. Rather, seated upon the back of a humble donkey, he left his worshipers examples of humility.”

Then the emperor, rejoicing in the Lord at the angelic vision, laid aside the insignia of imperial power. Barefoot and girded only with a linen band, he immediately took up the Lord’s cross in his hands, his face drenched with tears. Raising his eyes toward heaven, he hurried forward and proceeded as far as the gate.

As soon as he approached it humbly, the hardness of the stones perceived the heavenly command, and the gate immediately raised itself and opened a free entrance to those entering.

At that same moment the most pleasant fragrance returned. A divinely borne breeze had carried it from the province of Persia over long distances of land to Jerusalem, at the very moment when the holy cross had gone forth from Chosroes’ shrine, borne by Gracchus. It gladly filled everyone’s breast. The natural fragrance of terebinth, balsam, and myrrh surpassed all spices.

Immediately, the acclaim of the people’s joy, raised on high, praised God’s power. Thus the glorious Augustus burst forth in praise:

“O cross, wondrous sign, on which our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, suspended, condemned the punishment of death [perhaps *portavit*, ‘bore’] for the burden of our crimes, and his blood, worthy of adoration, was poured out as the price of our salvation before thrones and angels, amid a shining multitude of virtues!”

“O cross, brighter than the stars, celebrated throughout the world, greatly beloved by human beings, holier than all! You alone were worthy to bear the burden of the world. Sweet wood, sweet nails, it bore a sweet burden.

“Save this present assembly, gathered today in your praises and marked with your standard.”

When he had said this, he restored to its place the most precious piece of the wood that he had brought with him.

Then, as the Lord renewed ancient miracles, on that same day one dead person received back his own life; four paralytics obtained the health they had lost; ten lepers received clean skin; fifteen blind people were restored to sight; many were also freed from demons, and many others were liberated from various illnesses.

Then the emperor, having completed his prayer and offered many gifts, had the churches repaired at his own expense, restored privileges issued by authority, returned captives to their own homes, and provided suitable assistance. He returned to Constantinople, relying upon divine perseverance.

In the sign of the holy cross there were many abundant increases of miracles, by the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and glory, with the almighty Father and the Holy Spirit, for all ages of ages. Amen.

## II. HOMILIES ON THE GOSPELS AND EPISTLES

[Col. 0135]

## PREFACE. TO LOTHAIR AUGUSTUS

[Col. 0135A]

Health, victory, and perpetual life to the most beloved emperor, Lothair Augustus.

Let your Clemency know, my lord, that just as you ordered me to write the first part of the homilies on the Gospel and apostolic readings—which I carried from the Nativity of the Lord through the vigils of Easter and, when it was completed, sent to you—so I have extended the second part from Easter to the fifteenth Sunday after Pentecost, so that you might have something to be read in your presence, at suitable hours, during the spring and summer, if it pleased you.

I intend and resolve, if God so wills, to carry the third part from the point noted above through the end of the year, and likewise to send it to you when it has been completed. Near the end of that work there are also sermons written on the feasts of the saints, as well as on other celebrations that the Fathers established for observance for various reasons.

Finally, the readings that are recited at the vigils of the dead have been placed here, according to your request. May the Lord’s will be done, so that this may be profitable both for you and for your people. I have done as much as I could; but I do not doubt that, through your sound judgment and good diligence, you will complete what my inability denied me.

I therefore trust that this will bring me no small consolation, and that for you an eternal reward for the completed work will be prepared in heaven by the giver of every good thing.

## HOMILY ONE. AT THE VIGIL OF EASTER, ON HOLY SATURDAY

Reading from the Epistle of the blessed Apostle Paul to the Colossians.

[Col. 0135C]

“Brothers, if you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on the things that are above, not on those upon the earth,” etc.

Let us faithfully venerate, dearest brothers, the honorable solemnity of our Lord Jesus Christ, with his gracious clemency favoring us, and let us admire his ineffable compassion. For he not only assumed human flesh for the sake of our redemption, but also deigned to undergo various kinds of punishment for our salvation, so that, although after the long sleep of our sluggishness and laziness [Col. 0135D] we have been awakened—not unwillingly but willingly—by the sweetness of holy and Christian religion, at the gathering for this most holy solemnity, we may gladly and devoutly rise again with all diligence, according to what the Apostle says in the present reading: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, [Col. 0136A] where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on the things that are above, not on those that are upon the earth.”

It is as though he were saying that we who were created in the image of the holy Trinity, baptized by a threefold immersion through invocation of that same holy Trinity, are renewed into that same image; and that we who fell most grievously into death through a threefold sin—that is, through wicked thought, through the delight of the flesh together with consent to evil deeds, and through consent to evil deeds—then, raised for the third time from the font and having received remission of all sins through Christ’s grace, should rise to life, just as he himself rose on the third day.

But if we wish to rise with Christ, let us first die to the world and to carnal desires, and let us lay aside the old person—that is, an evil will, or a depraved habit and most wicked pleasures. Let us clothe ourselves in kindness [Col. 0136B] so that we may do good to our neighbors with complete devotion, and after the love of God place nothing before love of neighbor, but love them as ourselves.

Then follows: “Set your minds on the things that are above, not on those that are upon the earth,” seeking only what is heavenly, not what is earthly: dying to the earth, but living for the Lord; pursuing heavenly wisdom, not earthly wisdom. For it is added:

“For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God,” because we are children of God. Hence it follows: “When Christ, your life, appears, then you too will appear with him in glory.” For it is not yet apparent what we shall be and what kind of people we shall be at the judgment; but when Christ appears to judge the living and the dead, then we too shall appear together with him, to be raised in glory [Col. 0136C].

For Christ is born, suffers, and has risen for us and on our behalf, so that through him we may be reborn to life amid tribulations and rise with him in virtues. For everything has been restored through him on this night. On this night he himself rose as the firstfruits, so that afterward we all might rise. On this night, therefore, our captivity is loosed; the life lost in Adam is restored. On this night Adam, the first-formed man, returns from exile to his homeland, paradise. On this night of the Lord’s resurrection, paradise stands open to all; it is closed to no one except by that person’s own act, and opened to no one except by Christ.

Therefore, with all diligence, let us beware lest, because of the works of the devil that drag us toward destruction, we ourselves close to ourselves the open path of the heavenly kingdom. Rather, through works [Col. 0136D] of justice and mercy, let us make the way to the kingdom of heaven level and accessible for ourselves.

Let us therefore recall in our humility the humility of our Lord undertaken for us; let us keep vigil humbly on this occasion, and humbly pray to him who has illumined this night for us with the glory of his name. To him we say: “My God, illumine our darkness” [Col. 0137A]. Let us ask him to give light to our hearts, so that, just as we see this splendor of lamps with rejoicing eyes, so may we behold with an illumined mind the splendid glory of this night. Let us pray to him who, having slept for our salvation, may hear us keeping vigil at his solemnity.

Let us therefore keep vigil and pray both outwardly and inwardly, and celebrate this vigil. God speaks to us in his readings; let us speak to the Lord in our prayers. If we obediently hear his words, he dwells within us, and we may pray to him, to whom belong honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY II. ALSO ON HOLY SATURDAY

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Matthew.

[Col. 0137B]

“At that time, in the evening of the Sabbath, as it dawned toward the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb,” etc.

We must ask why the evangelist, describing the night of the Lord’s resurrection, says: “In the evening of the Sabbath, as it dawned toward the first day of the week,” since the customary order of time has evening growing darker toward night rather than dawning toward day. But the evangelist, speaking mystically, sought to indicate how much dignity this most sacred night had received from the glory of death’s defeat. He did so by saying that its beginning—the time when the women devoted to Christ began to keep vigil in his service—was already dawning into the following day.

For the Lord, author and arranger of the seasons, who rose in the final part of this night, made the entire night festive and radiant with the light of resurrection [Col. 0137C]. From the beginning of the world’s creation until this point, the course of time had been ordered so that day preceded night, in accordance with the order of the first creation. But on this night, through the mystery of the Lord’s resurrection, the order of time was changed.

Because he rose from the dead at night, but on the following day showed his disciples the effect of that resurrection, and, sharing a meal with them, confirmed the truth of his power while they wondered and rejoiced together, that night was most fittingly joined to the light of the following day. Thus the order of time was established so that day follows night.

Indeed, it was once most fitting that night should follow day, because humanity, having fallen through sin from the light of paradise, descended into the darkness and afflictions of this age. Now it is most fitting that day follows night, when, through faith in the resurrection and by Christ’s gift, we are brought back from the darkness of sin and the shadow of death to the light of life.

Therefore, beloved brothers, since we have recognized that this special night has been illumined by the grace of the Lord’s resurrection, we too must diligently take care that no part of it grow dark in our hearts, but that the whole of it shine into day. Now, as we keep vigil with fitting devotion and praise, and when the vigils have been completed, let us celebrate the paschal festivals of the Lord’s day with a sober and pure conscience.

“He came,” it says, “Mary Magdalene and the other Mary, to see the tomb.” These two women, bearing one name and possessing the same love and devotion, who came to visit the Lord’s tomb, signify the two peoples of the faithful, namely the Jewish and the Gentile peoples. With one and undivided devotion, wherever his Church is spread throughout the world, they desire to celebrate the passion and resurrection of their Redeemer [Col. 0138A].

The great earthquake that occurred when the Lord rose from the tomb, just as a great earthquake also occurred when he died on the cross, signifies that earthly hearts, previously cast down and deprived of heavenly hope, must be shaken by faith in his passion and resurrection and moved by a saving fear toward repentance, so that they may be raised to everlasting life.

The angel came and fulfilled the service of his ministry that he owed the Lord. Because Christ is God and man, the angelic ministries always due to God are not lacking amid the necessities of the humanity he assumed; as the detailed account of the holy Gospel proves most abundantly [Col. 0138B].

He rolled away the stone, not to open the door for the Lord as he came out, but to provide human beings with evidence that his departure had already taken place. For he who, while still mortal, was able by being born to enter the world though the womb of a virgin remained closed, could now, without any doubt, having become immortal, rise and leave the world though the tomb remained closed.

Nor should we pass over why the angel, witness of the Lord’s resurrection, appeared seated, since the one who proclaimed the joy of his birth to the world is read to have stood beside the shepherds. To stand is the posture of one who fights, but to sit is the posture of one who reigns.

The angel who preached the Lord’s coming into the world rightly appeared standing, so that by standing he might also signify that the one whom he preached was coming to overthrow the ruler of the world. The herald of his resurrection is rightly remembered as having sat [Col. 0138C], so that by sitting he might also represent that, after conquering the author of death, he had already ascended the throne of an everlasting kingdom. Concerning this, appearing shortly afterward to his disciples, he himself said: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.” And the evangelist Mark says: “The Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Lord.”

He sat upon the stone that had been rolled away, by which the entrance of the tomb had been closed, to teach that by his power he had cast down and overcome the bolts of hell, so that all whom he found there belonging to him might be lifted up to the light and rest of paradise, in accordance with the prophetic word: “You too, by the blood of your covenant, have brought out your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water.”

“His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing like snow,” so that by his very appearance and countenance he might signify that the one whose glory of resurrection he announced would be both terrifying in condemning the rejected and kind and gentle in comforting the elect [Col. 0138D].

In lightning, the terror of fear is expressed; in snow, the soothing quality of brightness. To show this divine distinction, the angel himself appears in such a way: he terrifies the impious guards of the tomb with fear and casts them to the ground like dead men, while he refreshes the devout women visiting the same tomb with gentle consolation and strengthens them so that they will not be afraid.

Moreover, in familiar speech he first says that he knows they are seeking Jesus, and, because he has already risen, adds this; then, with an honorable and joyful commission, he orders them to proclaim the joy of his resurrection [Col. 0139A]. How blessed were the women who, taught by an angelic oracle, were found worthy to announce the triumph of the resurrection to the world and to proclaim to the dead the overthrow of the dominion that Eve had acquired through the serpent’s deceitful speech!

How much more blessed will be the souls of men and women—however many, on the day of judgment, when the rejected are struck with fear and worthy punishment, are aided by heavenly grace and found worthy to triumph over death and enter the joy of blessed resurrection!

As they were running to announce it to the disciples, Jesus met them and greeted them, showing that he comes to the aid of all who begin the way of virtue, so that they may be able to reach everlasting salvation.

“But they approached and took hold of his feet.” Let us see, brothers, in the Lord rising from the dead [Col. 0139B], the reality of our flesh; let us see the glory of the new incorruption. Earlier we read that he rose while the tomb was closed; now we read that the women took hold of his feet and worshiped him.

He rose through the closed entrance of the tomb and came out, thereby showing that the body which had been dead and enclosed in the tomb had already become immortal. He offered his feet to the women to hold, so that he might make clear that he truly possessed flesh which could be touched by mortals.

“Go,” he said, “tell my brothers to go to Galilee; there they will see me.” O wondrous compassion of the Savior, wondrous kindness! Before his passion he was accustomed to call his disciples, and sometimes even his servants; after the resurrection he calls them brothers, both to show by rising again that he had resumed the same humanity which he had possessed, and to raise them up to merit and behold in his flesh the crown of immortality in which he already excelled [Col. 0139C].

That he foretold that the disciples would see him in Galilee, and, as the continuation of the holy Gospel makes clear, presented himself there, also mystically indicates both the power of his resurrection and the progress of our spiritual life. For Galilee is interpreted as “made migration,” and rightly he is seen by the disciples in Galilee who had already migrated from death to life, from corruption to incorruption, and from punishment to glory. Thus he commended the victory of the resurrection not only by the display of his body and the exhortation of his speech, but also by the name of the place in which he appeared and spoke to them.

But we too can enjoy the joy of his resurrection only if we now strive to migrate from the corruption of vices to works of virtue [Col. 0139D]. Therefore, my brothers, we must take the greatest care that, since we have recognized the time of the resurrection of our Lord and Savior and are celebrating his solemnities, we may migrate through continual progress in good works to contemplate his majesty.

Because we do not know the time of our resurrection, although we have no doubt that it will come, let us keep vigils for its expectation at all times, and especially on this night. Let us beseech the mercy of him who humbly accepted death for us and soon thereafter sublimely conquered it, that at the time of our resurrection he may grant us to migrate from death to life.

Let us ask him who was sacrificed as our Passover, Christ, to grant that we may worthily carry out the solemnities of paschal joy that we have begun and, through them, reach everlasting joys; through the same Lord Jesus Christ, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY III. ON THE DAY OF HOLY EASTER

Reading from the Epistle of the Apostle Paul to the Corinthians.

“Brothers, purge out the old leaven, so that you may be a new dough, just as you are unleavened. For Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed.”

The resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, dearest brothers, strengthens our faith when it is believed as an event, and renews its memory when it is solemnly celebrated [Col. 0140B]. Since Christ rose many years ago, we rightly say that he rises today when this solemnity returns each year.

Today the Lord has risen. Therefore what is repeated every year we must perform with complete devotion, and what happened once we must hold by faith. That happened so that we might be redeemed; this has been instituted so that we might not forget.

For anyone who wishes to celebrate this day worthily must remember what the Apostle Paul says in the present reading: “Purge out the old leaven, so that you may be a new dough, just as you are unleavened.” Therefore all the leaven of sin must be removed from our hearts, so that with a pure mind and upright conscience we may become like unleavened bread and thus celebrate the Lord’s Passover rightly.

But if we retain the leaven of sin and [Col. 0140C] wickedness in our hearts, we do not deserve to celebrate the Lord’s Passover. Therefore the Apostle says: “Purge out the old leaven, so that you may be a new dough, just as you are unleavened.” We are unleavened if we are free from every entanglement in sin. For, as the Apostle says, a little leaven corrupts the whole mass. Therefore we must purge and cast away from ourselves all the leaven of sin, so that we may deserve to enjoy so great a solemnity of Passover.

Since the Lord has wished to make us participants in the holy Passover, let us pray that we may worthily receive its mysteries, so that we may rightly deserve to attain the Lord’s blessing.

This, dearest ones, is the day of the Lord’s resurrection and the beginning of our redemption. This is, I say, the day that the Lord has made. Let us rejoice in it; let us all celebrate it with one harmonious voice, a joyful spirit, and [Col. 0140D] a contrite heart. Let us express spiritual joy in psalms and hymns, in memory of Christ’s passion and resurrection and in hope of the life to come.

Behold, on this day, when we hear “Alleluia,” our spirit is somehow made joyful and wholly suffused with delight. For “Alleluia” means “praise to the Lord in the highest.” Since it is fitting for us to sing praise to the Lord in the highest with a devout mind at all times, but especially on this day, let us strive to rejoice in praise of our Lord not only with our mouths but also perfectly through our deeds, with voice and heart, so that through him we may deserve to rejoice in the heavenly life—he who with God and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, one God, through immortal ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY IV. ALSO ON THE DAY OF HOLY EASTER

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Mark.

[Col. 0141A]

“Mary Magdalene, Mary of James, and Salome bought spices so that they might come and anoint Jesus.”

You have heard, dearest brothers, that the holy women who had followed the Lord came to the tomb with spices, and that they rendered the service of their humanity to him whom they had loved while he was alive and who was now dead.

But the event signifies something that must be done in the holy Church. We must hear what happened in such a way that we also consider what we ought to do in imitation of it. Therefore, if we believe in him who died and seek the Lord filled with the fragrance of virtues and with the reputation of good works [Col. 0141B], we certainly come to his tomb with spices.

The women who came with spices saw angels, because those minds behold the citizens above who proceed toward the Lord with the fragrances of virtues and holy desires.

We should note what it means that the angel is seen sitting on the right side. What is signified by the left except the present life? And what by the right except everlasting life? Hence it is written: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me.”

Since our Redeemer had already passed beyond the corruption of the present life, the one who had come to announce his everlasting life sat on the right. He appeared covered with a white robe because he announced the joys of our festival; for the whiteness of the garment declares the brightness of our solemnity [Col. 0141C].

Shall we say “our,” or “his”? To speak more truly, let us say both “his” and “ours.” The resurrection of our Redeemer was our festival, because it restored us to immortality; and it was a festival of the angels, because, by recalling us to heavenly things, it filled up their number.

Thus, at his festival and ours, the angel appeared in white garments, because, while the Lord’s resurrection brings us back to things above, the losses of the heavenly homeland are repaired.

But let us hear what the angel says to the women who are coming.

“Do not be afraid.” It is as though he openly said: Let those who do not love the coming of the citizens above be afraid; let those tremble who, weighed down by carnal desires, despair of being able to attain fellowship with them [Col. 0141D]. But why are you afraid, when you see your fellow citizens?

Matthew, too, describing the angel’s appearance, says:

“His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing white as snow.” In lightning there is the terror of fear; in snow, the gentle brightness of whiteness. Since almighty God is both terrifying to sinners and gentle to the righteous, the angel, witness of his resurrection, is rightly shown both in the lightning of his face and in the whiteness of his appearance, so that by his very form he might terrify the rejected and soothe the devout.

Hence, too, it is rightly said that a pillar of fire went before the people traveling through the desert at night, and a pillar of cloud by day. In fire [Col. 0142A] there is terror; in the cloud, the gentle comfort of the vision.

Day is understood as the life of the righteous, and night as the life of the sinful. Therefore Paul says to sinners who have been converted: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.”

Thus the pillar was shown by a cloud during the day and by fire at night. Almighty God, gentle to the righteous and terrifying to the unjust, will appear in this way: when he comes in judgment, he will caress the former with the gentleness of mercy, but terrify the latter with the strictness of justice.

But let us now hear what the angel adds.

“You seek Jesus the Nazarene.” In Latin speech, Jesus is interpreted as “saving,” that is, “Savior.” At that time many could be called Jesus, though not substantially but only by designation. Therefore the place is added, so that it might be made clear of which Jesus he was speaking: “the Nazarene.” And [Col. 0142B] he immediately adds the cause: “crucified.” Then he adds:

“He has risen; he is not here.” “He is not here” is said with respect to the presence of his flesh, although he was nowhere absent with respect to the presence of his majesty.

“But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you into Galilee.” We must ask why Peter is designated by name among the disciples. If the angel had not expressly named him, the man who had denied his master would not have dared to come among the disciples. He is therefore called by name so that he would not despair because of his denial.

In this matter we must consider why almighty God permitted the man whom he had decided to place over the entire Church to fear the voice of a servant girl and deny himself. We recognize that this was done through a dispensation of great compassion [Col. 0142C], so that the one who was to be the shepherd of the Church might learn through his own fault how he ought to show mercy to others.

First, therefore, he displayed that man’s weakness to him, and then placed him over the others, so that from his own weakness he might learn how mercifully to tolerate the weaknesses of others.

It is rightly said of our Redeemer:

“He will go before you into Galilee; there you will see him, as he told you.” Galilee is interpreted as “made migration.” Our Redeemer had already migrated from passion to resurrection, from death to life, from punishment to glory, and from corruption to incorruption. He is first seen by the disciples after the resurrection in Galilee because we shall see the glory of his resurrection joyfully afterward, if we now migrate from vices to the height of virtues.

He who is announced in the tomb is shown in the place of migration, because he who is recognized in the mortification of the flesh is seen in the migration of the mind [Col. 0142D].

Let us migrate from vices to virtues, so that we may deserve to see our Redeemer in Galilee. May almighty God assist our desire for life—he who for us gave his only Son to death—through the same Jesus Christ our Lord, who with him lives and reigns, God in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY V. MONDAY

Reading from the Acts of the Apostles.

“In those days, Peter stood in the midst of the people and said: ‘Men, brothers, you know what word came to pass throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee, after the baptism that John preached, Jesus of Nazareth,’” etc. [Col. 0143A]

In the present reading that you have heard, dearest brothers, the Apostle Peter briefly gathered together everything contained in the Creed: that Jesus is the Christ and that he is Lord of all.

Standing in the midst of the people, he said: “Men, brothers, you know what word came to pass throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee, after the baptism that John preached: Jesus of Nazareth.” Here everything is shown together: that Christ was sent to reconcile the world to God; that he was born as herald through John’s voice; that he was anointed with the Holy Spirit; that he was manifested by miracles, with God dwelling in him; that he was crucified, raised from the dead, and manifested to his own; that he will come at the end as judge of all; and that through his Church he will illumine the whole world by faith.

Then it is added:

“How God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power.” Jesus was therefore anointed not with visible oil but with the gift of spiritual grace, which contained all things fully. This is signified by the visible ointment with which the Church anoints the baptized while the sevenfold Spirit is invoked through the laying on of the bishop’s hand. In a similar way, the Holy Spirit descended upon him after his baptism in the form of a dove.

At that time he deigned to prefigure his Church, in which the baptized especially receive the Holy Spirit. He is to be understood as having been anointed when the Word became flesh: that is, when human nature, without any preceding merits of good works, was joined to the Word of God in the Virgin’s womb, so that divine and human nature together might be one person. For this reason we confess that he was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary [Col. 0143C].

“He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, because God was with him.” This should better be understood as meaning that the Father always remained with the Son, rather than signifying that the Son’s divinity dwelt together with the man whom he assumed, lest one multiply Christ’s person and fall into the greatest error.

Then follows:

“And we are witnesses of all that he did in the region of the Jews and in Jerusalem.” They rightly testify that they are witnesses, since they were sent throughout the whole world to preach the Gospel [Col. 0143D], as we read in the Psalm: “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.”

God the Father works two natures in Christ: through one, which he shares with God the Father, insofar as he is God; through the other, by which he became man from the Virgin Mary.

Through these two natures in the one Son of God, God the Father brings about two resurrections of the human race, namely of souls and of bodies. Souls too have their death in impiety and sins. According to this death, those people were dead of whom the same Lord says: “Let the dead bury their own dead,” meaning that those dead in soul might bury the dead in body.

The death of the soul occurs when God abandons it because of the greatness of its sins [Col. 0144A]; the death of the body occurs when it is abandoned by the soul.

From these two kinds of death we speak of two resurrections of those who are raised. Now the resurrection of souls takes place in the Church through the Son of God, the Word of God, when souls, made alive by God’s grace, rise from the death of iniquity. This is the first resurrection. Those who possess it will rise happily in the second resurrection, which is the resurrection of bodies, to eternal life.

The impious too will rise, each one with his own flesh, so that they may be punished with the devil and his angels. This must be known with complete certainty: no one will be freed except through God’s unmerited mercy, and no one will be condemned except through his deserved judgment.

Then the saints will understand more fully what good his grace has bestowed, or what they would have attained if he had not chosen them by a gratuitous divine gift [Col. 0144B].

Then God himself will be the satisfaction of the saints, the joy of the blessed, and everything that they may rightly desire: life, salvation, nourishment, abundance, glory, honor, peace, eternal blessedness, and blessed eternity. To him be honor and glory now and always, and for ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY VI. ALSO ON MONDAY

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Luke.

“In that time, two of the disciples were going to a village that was sixty stadia from Jerusalem, named Emmaus, and they were speaking with one another about all the things that had happened,” etc.

Since you are laboring through a daily solemnity, dearest brothers, only a few things need be said to you, and perhaps these will be more useful, because food that is insufficient is often eaten more eagerly [Col. 0144C].

I have therefore decided to summarize the meaning of the Gospel reading rather than proceed through every word, lest a longer exposition burden your affection.

Behold, dearest brothers, you have heard that, while two disciples were walking along the road—not believing, but nevertheless speaking about him—the Lord appeared to them, though he did not show them a form by which they could recognize him.

Thus the Lord outwardly did in the eyes of their bodies what was taking place inwardly in the eyes of their hearts. Within themselves they both loved and doubted; outwardly the Lord was present among them, but he did not show what he was.

He therefore displayed his presence to them while they were speaking about him, but concealed the appearance by which they would recognize him while they doubted about him [Col. 0144D].

He exchanged words with them, rebuked their hardness of understanding, and opened the sacred mysteries of Scripture that concerned himself. Yet, though he was still a stranger to faith in their hearts, he pretended that he was going farther. For “to pretend” means “to arrange,” and hence we call those who shape mud “formers” or potters.

The simple truth therefore did nothing through duplicity; rather, he presented himself to them in the body as he was in their minds. They were being tested to see whether, although they did not yet love him as Lord, they could at least love him as a stranger.

But because they could not be strangers to charity, they invited him, with whom the truth was walking, to their lodging as though he were a stranger. Why do we say “invited,” when it is written there that “they compelled him”? From this example it is inferred [perhaps: “that”] that strangers should not merely be invited to lodging, but also drawn into it.

They set out the table and offer food, and the one whom they had not recognized in the exposition of sacred Scripture they recognize in the breaking of bread [Col. 0145A].

They were not illumined by hearing the commandments of God; they were illumined by doing them, because it is written: “It is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified.”

Therefore whoever wishes to understand what he has heard should hasten to fulfill in action what he has already been able to understand. Behold, the Lord was not recognized while he was speaking, but deigned to be recognized while he was being fed.

Therefore, dearest brothers, love hospitality; love works of charity. Hence Paul says: “Let brotherly love remain among you, and do not forget hospitality” [Col. 0145B]. Through hospitality some, having received angels as guests, pleased God. Hence Peter says: “Be hospitable to one another without grumbling.” Truth itself says: “I was a stranger, and you welcomed me.”

A remarkable story, handed down to us through the report of our elders, is told. A certain head of a household served his entire household with great devotion to hospitality. Since he received strangers at his table every day, one day a certain stranger came among the others and was led to the table.

When the head of the household, out of his customary humility, wished to pour water over the stranger’s hands, he turned to take up the pitcher, but suddenly did not find the one into whose hands he had wished to pour the water.

While he wondered about this event within himself, the Lord said to him in a vision that same night: [Col. 0145C] “On other days you received me in my members; yesterday you received me in my very self.”

Behold, when he comes in judgment he says: “What you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me.” Behold, even before the judgment, when he is received through his members, he seeks out those who received him through his own person. Yet we are sluggish in extending hospitality.

Consider, brothers, how great is the virtue of hospitality. Receive Christ at your tables, so that you may be received by him at eternal banquets. Now offer hospitality to Christ as a stranger, so that at the judgment he may not know you as strangers, but receive you as his own into the kingdom.

Our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns for ever. Amen.

## HOMILY VII. TUESDAY

Reading from the Acts of the Apostles.

[Col. 0145D]

“In those days, Paul stood up and, having commanded silence with his hand, said: ‘Men, brothers, sons of the race of Abraham, and those among you who fear God,’” etc.

All those to whom the Apostle was speaking were sons of Abraham according to the flesh, just as they themselves said elsewhere: “We are Abraham’s offspring, and we have never been enslaved to anyone”; and again: “Our father is Abraham.” And he said to them: “I know that you are sons of Abraham.”

By imitation, however, those to whom the Lord was speaking were not sons of Abraham: “You are from your father the devil.” How, then, were the Jews sons of the devil? Not by being born, but by imitating.

“You are from your father the devil,” the Lord says, “and you wish to do the desires of your father.” Behold how they are sons of the devil. What are his desires? “He was a murderer from the beginning, and you seek to kill me.” Behold how they are sons of the devil by imitation.

For those to whom the Apostle was speaking were sons of Abraham because of the origin of their flesh, and sons by imitation because of the purity of their fear, to whom he specifically said: “And those among you who fear God, the word of this salvation has been sent.”

This is the word of which Isaiah says: “The Lord sent a word into Jacob, and it fell upon Israel”—that is, God sent his Son, of whom John says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word.”

“To Jacob,” that is, to the Jews; “and it came to Israel,” that is, to the people of the Gentiles.

The Word of God is himself the Son of God. Therefore, when the Father sent him by the Word [verbum], it was through the Father and his Word that he was sent [Col. 0146B]. Thus the same Son was sent by the Father and by the Son, who is himself the Word of the Father, the Son in that Word of God which was in the beginning with God and was God.

He was in the very Wisdom of God at the time when the Word would become flesh and dwell among us. For when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made from a woman, so that the incarnate Word might appear to humanity.

“For those who lived in Jerusalem and its rulers, not knowing Jesus or the voices of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath,” etc.

Hence it is also written in the Acts of the Apostles: “For Moses, from ancient times, has in every city those who proclaim him in the synagogues.” These testimonies clearly show that the reading of the Law or of the Prophets was always read by the Jews in the synagogues on the Sabbath [Col. 0146C].

“And when they had completed everything that was written about him.” John also relates these words in this way, saying: “Afterward, knowing that everything had been completed, Jesus, so that Scripture might be fulfilled, says: ‘I thirst,’” etc.

After Jesus had accomplished everything that had to be accomplished before his death, he surrendered his spirit when he wished and in the manner he wished.

Taking him down from the tree. In the wilderness, Moses had a bronze serpent suspended from a tree, so that the Lord might be signified both as dead in the serpent and as eternal in the bronze. Thus, although he was judged dead according to his humanity, he nevertheless remained like bronze according to his divinity. This must be said in response to the Jews who object with that testimony, “Cursed is everyone who has been hanged on a tree”: the man who hangs on a tree is cursed, but the guilty man, not the innocent. For innocence cannot be the curse of the punishment of sin. Indeed, if Mordecai, after a tree had been prepared, had been hanged and had fulfilled the sentence of the king’s cruelty, would they then have judged him worthy of this curse? Certainly not. Therefore our Lord hung on a tree so that, by being hanged on the tree, he might absolve us from the offense committed on the tree of perdition.

They placed him in a tomb. Jesus was placed in a new tomb, in which no one had yet been placed, just as no one before him and no one after him was conceived in the virgin’s womb. So in this tomb, no one before him and no one after him was buried.

But God raised him from the dead. The bitter root of the cross vanished; the flower of life rose in glory with its fruits. This is Aaron’s staff, which flowered after drying up—the staff that became green after its withering. Christ is the one who rose after death: he is the flower of virgins, the crown of martyrs, and the grace of those who practice continence.

He was seen for many days—that is, for forty days. Yet he did not appear to them continuously throughout all those forty days, but appeared whenever he wished, to whomever he wished, and in whatever manner he wished.

To those who went up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, etc. While preserving the historical account, let us consider its meaning. Galilee is interpreted as “migration” or “transmigration,” and Jerusalem as “vision of peace.” Those go up with the Lord from Galilee to Jerusalem who, first rejecting here the fuel of vices, migrate to the heights of the virtues. They, namely, will migrate with our Redeemer from passion to resurrection, from death to life, from punishment to glory, and from corruption to incorruption; and at length they will joyfully see the Lord in the heavenly Jerusalem, when, having abandoned vices, they have passed over to the loftiness of the virtues.

And we announce to you the promise that was made to our fathers, etc. For it was said to Abraham, “In you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.” To Jacob, however: “And in you and in your offspring all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed.” Explaining this, the Apostle says: “He did not say ‘in offsprings,’ but ‘in your offspring,’ which is Christ.” Christ is indeed the offspring of Abraham; in his name, blessing was promised through faith to all the families of the earth, namely, to Jews and Gentiles. The same thing is signified by, “I will give you the holy and sure things of David”—that is, “Whatever David promised, I, the faithful guarantor, will fulfill for you”: namely, that Christ would be born from his lineage, and that he would grant eternal life in heaven to all who believe in him and rightly keep his commandments.

## HOMILY VIII. ALSO FOR TUESDAY  
### Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Luke

At that time, Jesus stood in the midst of his disciples and said to them: “Peace be with you. It is I; do not be afraid,” etc.

John also recalls this appearance of the Lord after the resurrection, saying: “When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were shut where the disciples were gathered because of fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in the midst and said to them: ‘Peace be with you.’” What is surprising if, after his resurrection, he entered through closed doors, since he was now to live forever, when, coming to die, he had emerged without opening the virgin’s womb? But John says that the apostle Thomas was not with them at that time, whereas according to Luke the two disciples, one of whom was Cleopas, returned to Jerusalem and found the eleven gathered together, along with those who were with them. This must doubtless be understood to mean that Thomas had gone out from there before the Lord appeared to them while they were saying these things.

**[Col. 0148A]** But they were troubled and terrified and thought that they were seeing a spirit. The first thought that arose in the hearts of the apostles was the very suspicion that the Manichaean heretics entertain and believe concerning Christ: that he did not possess true flesh but was a spirit. The Manichaeans never believe that Jesus was a man; the disciples, however, knew the man with whom they had lived for so long [variant: *tanto tempore*, “for so long”; *tantum tempus*, “so long a time”]. But after what they knew had died, how could they believe that what had been able to die could have been raised? He therefore appeared to their eyes as one whom they knew him to be; and, not believing that true flesh could rise from the tomb on the third day, they thought that they were seeing a spirit.

This error of the apostles is the sect of the Manichaeans. When this is brought against them, they usually answer in this way: “What evil do we believe, when we believe that Christ the Lord was a spirit and do not believe that he was flesh? The spirit is better than the flesh. We believe what is better; we do not wish to believe what is worse.” If there is nothing evil in this statement, let Jesus leave his disciples in this error. What did the disciples believe? They believed Christ to be a spirit. They did not think that he was nothing, but that he was a spirit. Do you think you are in danger from only a minor illness? Hear the physician’s diagnosis.

And he said to them: “Why are you troubled, and why do thoughts arise in your hearts?” What sort of thoughts, surely, except false, diseased, and destructive ones? Christ would have lost the fruit of his passion if the resurrection had not been real. “Why are you troubled, and why do thoughts arise in your hearts?” It was as though a good farmer were saying: “What I planted there, I shall find there—not thorns, which I did not plant.” Faith descended into your hearts because it is from above; but these thoughts did not descend from above. They arose within the heart itself like harmful weeds.

“See my hands and my feet, for it is I myself. Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have.” He graciously chose to demonstrate that his resurrection was certain and real by many varied proofs, in order to build up faith, drive unbelief from their hearts, and remove every doubt concerning his resurrection. It would have been little to offer himself to their eyes to be seen if he had not also offered himself to their hands to be touched. By showing the disciples bones and flesh to be touched, he indicates in part the state of the true resurrection, both the resurrection that took place in him and the one that is to take place in us. For our body in the glory of that resurrection will not be, as Eutychius, bishop of Constantinople, wrote, intangible and more subtle than winds and air. In the glory of that resurrection our body will indeed be subtle through the effect of spiritual power, but tangible according to the truth of its nature.

Nor should the Apostle’s statement be thought to contradict this assertion: “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God.” In this passage the Apostle, by the name of flesh and blood, signifies not the substance of the true body but the corruption of mortality. As he himself immediately explains: “Nor shall corruption possess incorruption.”

In sacred Scripture, “flesh” is called one thing according to nature, another according to guilt, and another according to the corruption of mortality that arose from guilt. It is according to nature when it is said: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh,” and, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” It is according to guilt when it is said: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh.” It is according to corruptibility when it is written: “And they remembered that they were flesh”—that is, fragile and mortal. The psalmist himself makes clear that this is what he meant by the name “flesh,” when he immediately adds: “A spirit that goes and does not return.”

Therefore flesh shall not possess the kingdom of God—that is, flesh according to guilt or mortality. Yet flesh will possess the kingdom of God—that is, flesh according to nature, the same flesh that the Lord, after his resurrection, displayed to the disciples to be seen and touched. Concerning this flesh blessed Job, when describing the glory of the resurrection, says: “And again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God.” Read the letter of Saint Augustine to Consent­ius, concerning the Lord’s body after the resurrection.

And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and feet—not only the hands and feet on which the marks left by the nails shone forth, but, as John testifies, he also showed them the side that had been pierced by the lance. By displaying the scar of his wounds, he healed the wound of their doubt and unbelief.

But just as after the resurrection he deigned to strengthen the disciples’ faith and hope by displaying the places of the nails and the lance, so on the day of judgment he will come to confound the impiety and unbelief of the proud by showing both these signs of his passion and the cross itself. He will show all angels and human beings openly that he is the one who died at the hands of the impious and for the sake of the impious, so that they may see, as it is written, “the one whom they pierced,” and all the tribes of the earth may mourn over him.

It should certainly be noted that at this point pagans commonly construct a calumny and mock, with foolish chatter, the resurrection we hope for. “If,” they say, “your God was unable even to heal the wounds inflicted upon him by the Jews, but, as you claim, carried the marks of his scars with him into heaven, with what rashness do you suppose that he will restore your members from the dust to wholeness?”

They must be answered that our Lord, who, when he wished and in whatever manner he wished, was able to raise from the tomb his flesh, already glorified with perpetual immortality, also raised it in whatever condition he wished. It does not follow that one who is shown to have done greater things was unable to do lesser ones. Rather, by the grace of his dispensation, the one who did the greater refrained from doing the lesser: the one who destroyed the kingdom of death did not wish to erase the signs of death.

First, he did this so that through them he might establish in the disciples the faith in his resurrection. Second, he did it so that, pleading with the Father for us, he might always show what kind of death he had endured for the life of mortals. Third, he did it so that, by continually presenting the signs of that same death, he might renew for those redeemed by his death how mercifully they had been helped, and so that they might never cease to sing the mercies of the Lord, but say, as those redeemed by the Lord: “For he is good, for his mercy endures forever.”

Finally, he did it so that at the judgment he might declare to the faithless, among the other crimes for which they are justly condemned, how justly they are condemned by displaying the scars of the wounds he received from them.

It is as if some exceptionally brave soldier, at the command of his king and for the salvation of his entire nation, had labored in single combat, received many wounds, yet killed the enemy, stripped him of his spoils, and brought victory back to his people. If, when questioned by the physician to whose care he had been entrusted, he were asked whether he wished to be healed so that no traces of the wounds would remain, or rather in such a way that the scars would remain but all disfigurement and ugliness would entirely disappear, he might answer that he wished to be healed in such a way that, after recovering his former state of health and beauty, he would forever carry with him the signs of so great a triumph.

Thus, assuredly, the Lord preferred to bring into heaven, as an everlasting sign of victory, the scars of the wounds of his passion received for us, rather than to erase them. Yet none of this prejudices our faith in the resurrection, concerning which the true promise says: “Not a hair of your head shall perish.”

But while they still did not believe and were marveling because of joy, he said:

“Do you have anything here to eat?” To make the truth of his resurrection known, he deigns not only to be touched by the disciples but also to eat with them. He did not do this because he needed food after the resurrection, nor to signify that we shall need food in the resurrection, but to establish in this way the nature of the rising body, so that they would not think it was not a body but a spirit, or that he was appearing to them only in appearance and not in solid reality. He ate by power, not by necessity. For the thirsty earth absorbs water in one way, while a glowing ray of the sun absorbs it in another: the former through need, the latter through power.

But they offered him a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb; and when he had eaten before them, he took the leftovers and gave them to them. What do we believe the broiled fish signifies, except the mediator between God and human beings who suffered? He deigned to lie hidden in the waters of the human race; he wished to be caught in the snare of our death; and he was, as it were, roasted by tribulation at the time of his passion.

But he who deigned to become a fish, broiled in the passion, became a honeycomb for us in the resurrection. Or, by wishing to be represented in the broiled fish, did he wish in the honeycomb to express both natures of his person? For the honeycomb is honey in wax; and honey in wax is divinity in humanity.

In this way the Redeemer gives us an indication so that he may lay out for us who follow him the path of imitation. For behold, in his food he wished to join a honeycomb to the broiled fish, because he receives into his body for eternal rest those who, while they experience tribulations here for God’s sake, do not depart from the love of inward sweetness. The honeycomb is taken together with the broiled fish because those who accept affliction here for the sake of truth are satisfied there with true sweetness.

And he said to them: “These are the words that I spoke to you while I was still with you”—that is, while I was still in mortal flesh, in which you also are. At that time he was in the same flesh, but he was not in the same mortality as they. After he rose, he was with them for forty days through the presentation of his bodily presence, but he was not with them in participation in human weakness.

“How it was necessary that everything should be fulfilled that was written about me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms.” See how he removed every ambiguity: he was seen, he was touched, he ate; it was certainly he. Yet, lest he seem in any way to have deceived the human senses, he turned to the Scriptures.

Let the pagans say whatever they wish: “He was a magician; he was able to display himself in this way.” But could a magician, before he was born, have prophesied himself in this way? Produce the Scriptures, because what you see was foreseen, and what you behold was foretold. “Hear, O daughter, and see”: hear what was foretold, see what has been fulfilled.

Then he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures, and he said to them: “Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day.” He offers himself to the eyes to be seen; he offers himself to the hands to be touched. That is little: he recalls the Scriptures of the Law. And that too is little: he opens their understanding, so that you may understand what you read. Then, having confirmed the reality of his body, he commends the unity of the Church.

“And repentance for the forgiveness of sins must be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.” The perversity of the heretics is not hidden: the Church has spread from one corner throughout the whole world. All nations have the Church. Let no one deceive us: she is the true Church, she is the catholic Church. She began at Jerusalem, reached us, and is there as well as here. For she did not depart from there in order to come here; she grew, she did not migrate.

And rightly it is written in the midst of the other mysteries of the Lord’s mercy that it was necessary for the ministers of the word, who were going to preach repentance and the forgiveness of sins in the name of Christ crucified and raised from the dead among all nations, to begin from Jerusalem.

This was not only because the oracles of the Lord were entrusted to them, because theirs is the adoption as sons, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the worship, and the promises; because theirs are the fathers, and from them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever. It was also so that the nations, who were entangled in various errors and crimes, might be especially moved by this judgment of divine mercy to hope for the obtaining of pardon.

They would see that even those who crucified the Son of God had been granted not only forgiveness of their guilt by the Father but also the joy of eternal life. For the Lord is merciful and compassionate, patient and abounding in mercy; he wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. To him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY IX. FOR WEDNESDAY  
### Reading from the Acts of the Apostles

In those days, Peter opened his mouth and said: “Men of Israel and those who fear the Lord, hear,” etc.

It should be noted that he summons men of the race of Israel and those who fear the Lord to hear the word of the Lord. They are called men from their strength: they do not know how to fail through endurance or to boast with some arrogance in prosperity. Rather, fixed in steadfastness of spirit and strengthened by contemplation of heavenly things, they remain always fearless.

“Those who fear the Lord,” he says, “hear”—that is, those who have reverence for his name. For no one deserves to hear his words except the one who is known also to fear him. Since the fear of the Lord is just and upright, it renews hearing, grants love, and kindles the ardor of charity.

“The God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers.” He could have said, “The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob”; but he names the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob three times, so that you may understand the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. And lest the threefold naming of God produce a scandal for you, he adds, “the God of our fathers.” Wisely he distinguished the persons and united the nature.

**[Col. 0152B]** He glorified his Son Jesus. He glorified his Son when, after the exceedingly wondrous resurrection, God granted him to possess the faith of the whole world in that nature in which he had become human. He glorified him with the glory of the resurrection; he glorified him with the glory of the ascension; and he glorified him with the glory of his sitting at the right hand.

“Whom you indeed delivered up.” For Pilate answered the Lord with these words: “Am I a Jew? Your nation and the chief priests delivered you to me.” The priests delivered the Lord through envy. The Son delivered himself for love of us. Concerning the Father the Apostle says: “He did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all.” Concerning the Son: “He loved and delivered himself up for us.”

“And you denied him before the face of Pilate, saying, ‘Crucify such a man.’ We have no king except Caesar.” “We have the Law, and according to the laws he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.”

“When he judged that he should be released.” For, as the Gospel says, Pilate was seeking an opportunity to release Jesus, saying: “I find no case against him”; and neither did Herod. Pilate sends him to Herod; Herod sends him back to Pilate. Piety moves between two acts of impiety, yet impiety cannot condemn piety. The accused is present, but no guilt is found.

“You brought this man to me,” he says, “as one who was turning the people away; and behold, having questioned him in your presence, I find no case in him concerning the matters of which you accuse him. You say that he orders tribute not to be paid to Caesar; I have proved that what you allege is false. You say that he teaches against the Law; I have proved that he does not destroy the Law but fulfills it. Everything you alleged has been found to be the opposite.”

“And you asked that a murderous man be given to you.” The Gospel says that there was one called Barabbas, bound because he had committed murder in a revolt. Barabbas is interpreted as “son of our father.” He signifies the devil, who provokes many revolts throughout the whole world—murders, adulteries, and every crime. As soon as Jesus was crucified, this Barabbas was released and strangled the Jewish people.

But you killed the author of life, etc.—the one who formed humanity from the mud of the earth and breathed into his face the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul; the one who said, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life”; and of whom John says, “This is the true God and eternal life.”

“And now, brothers, I know that you acted through ignorance.” For, as the Apostle says, “If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.”

“But God, who foretold through the mouth of the prophets that his Christ would suffer, has fulfilled it in this way,” etc. For this reason God himself said to Cleopas and the other disciple: “O foolish ones and slow of heart to believe in all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary for Christ to suffer these things and thus enter into his glory?” And, beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things that concerned himself.

If Moses and all the prophets spoke of Christ, and of his entering into his glory through the anguish of his passion, how do those glory in calling themselves Christians who, according to the measure of their strength, neither seek out how the Scriptures pertain to Christ nor desire to reach through the sufferings of tribulations the glory that they wish to possess with Christ? Scripture clearly says that those are blessed who meditate on the law of the Lord day and night and who fear God and walk in his ways.

Their labor will profit them unto eternal salvation when, after the end of this life, they are destined to reach eternal rest, through the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY X. ALSO FOR WEDNESDAY  
### Reading from the Holy Gospel according to John

**[Col. 0153C]** At that time, Jesus revealed himself by the Sea of Tiberias. He revealed himself in this way: Peter, Thomas, who is called Didymus, Nathanael, who was from Cana of Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two other disciples of his were together.
