Simon Peter said to them: “I am going fishing.” They said to him: “We are coming with you.” And they went out and got into the boat; and that night they caught nothing, etc.

It may be asked why Peter, who had been a fisherman before his conversion, returned to fishing after his conversion, when the Truth says: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.” Why does he resume what he had abandoned?

But if the virtue of discernment is applied, it becomes clear that the occupation that had existed without sin before his conversion was not a fault for Peter to resume after his conversion. For we know that Peter was a fisherman and Matthew a tax collector. After his conversion Peter returned to fishing, but Matthew did not return to the business of the tax office, because seeking one’s livelihood through fishing is one thing, while increasing one’s wealth through the profits of a tax office is another.

There are many occupations that can scarcely, or not at all, be carried on without sins. Therefore, after conversion, the mind must not return to those things that entangle it in sin.

But when morning had already come, Jesus stood on the shore; yet the disciples did not know that it was Jesus. Jesus therefore said to them: “Children, do you have anything to eat?” They answered him: “No.”

It may be asked why, after the resurrection, the Lord stood on the shore while the disciples labored at sea, when before his resurrection he walked upon the waves of the sea in the presence of the disciples. The reason for this is quickly understood if the cause that was present at that time is considered.

For what does the sea signify except the present age, which dashes itself against the tumult of events and the waves of corruptible life? What is signified by the solidity of the shore except that perpetual stillness of eternal rest?

Since the disciples were still in the waves of mortal life, they labored at sea. But because our Redeemer had already passed beyond the corruption of the flesh, after his resurrection he stood on the shore, as though speaking the mystery of his resurrection to the disciples through these events: “I no longer appear to you at sea, because I am no longer with you in the waves of disturbance.”

There was, however, great difficulty in the disciples’ fishing, so that when the master came there might be a great height of wonder. Immediately he said to them: “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.”

Twice in the Holy Gospel we read that the Lord commanded nets to be cast for fishing: once before his passion and once after his passion. But before our Redeemer suffered and rose, he commands that a net be cast for fishing, but he does not command whether it should be cast on the right or on the left. After the resurrection, however, appearing to the disciples, he commands that the net be cast on the right.

In that fishing so many were caught that the nets were torn; in this one many were caught, and the nets were not torn. Who does not know that the good are signified by the right and the evil by the left?

That fishing, therefore, in which no particular side on which the net should be cast is specified, signified the present Church, which gathers good and evil together. It does not select those whom it draws, because it does not know whom it may be able to select.

But this fishing, which took place after the Lord’s resurrection, was cast only on the right, because only the Church of the elect reaches the sight of his glory, and it will have nothing from left-hand works. In that fishing the net is torn because of the multitude of the fish, since now even with the elect so many reprobates enter the confession of the faith that they tear the Church itself through heresies. In this fishing, however, many fish, and large ones, are caught, and the net is not torn, because the holy Church of the elect, resting in the continual peace of its author, is no longer torn apart by any dissensions.

So they cast the nets, and now they were unable to draw it in because of the multitude of fish. Therefore that disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter: “It is the Lord.” When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he girded his tunic around himself, for he was naked, and threw himself into the sea. The other disciples came in the boat. For they were not far from land, but about two hundred cubits away, dragging the net of fish.

When they came down onto the land, they saw burning coals laid out, with a fish placed upon them, and bread. This should not be understood to mean that the bread too had been placed upon the coals. Rather, the sense should simply be supplied in this way: “They saw burning coals laid out, and they saw a fish placed upon them, and they saw bread.” Or it may be understood more exactly as: “They saw burning coals laid out, and they saw a fish placed upon them and bread.”

Jesus said to them: “Bring some of the fish that you have now caught.” Simon Peter went up and drew the net onto the land. After such large fish had been caught, Simon Peter went up and drew the net onto the land.

By now, I believe that your Charity understands what it is that Peter draws onto the land. The holy Church has been entrusted to him; to him in particular it is said: “Simon, son of John, do you love me? Feed my sheep.” What is later revealed is now signified in the action.

Since the preacher separates us from the waves of this world, it is certainly necessary that Peter draw the net full of fish onto the land. He draws the fish to the solidity of the shore who, by the voice of holy preaching, shows the faithful the stability of the eternal homeland. He did this through words, through letters, and he does it daily through signs of miracles. Whenever we are converted through him to the love of eternal rest, whenever we are separated from the tumult of earthly things, what else are we doing except being drawn as fish within the net of faith to the shore?

Full of large fish, one hundred and fifty-three. This number is not empty of a great mystery; rather, the depth of so great a mystery awaits your attention. For the Evangelist would not have carefully expressed the total of the number unless he had judged it to be full of sacramental meaning.

You know that in the Old Testament every work is prescribed through the commandments of the Decalogue. In the New Testament, however, the power of that same work is given to the faithful in multiplied form through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. The prophet announces this when he says: “The Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and fortitude, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord.”

But the one who recognizes the faith of the Trinity receives the operation of this Spirit, so that he believes the Father, the Son, and that same Holy Spirit to be of one power and confesses them to be of one substance.

Since the seven things mentioned above were more broadly given through the New Testament, while the ten were given through the commandments of the Old Testament, all our virtue and activity can be fully comprehended through ten and seven.

Let us therefore form the triangular number of seventeen, and we obtain fifty-one. This number is certainly not empty of a great mystery, because we read in the Old Testament that the fiftieth year was commanded to be called the Jubilee, in which the whole people was to rest from every work. But true rest is in unity: what is one cannot be divided. Where there is the division of a breach, there is no true rest.

Let us form the triangular number of fifty-one, and we obtain one hundred and fifty-three. Since all our activity and virtue, displayed in the faith of the Trinity, tend toward rest, we take seven and ten in the triangular calculation, so that we may arrive at fifty-one. Our true rest is then, when we already recognize the very glory of the Trinity, which we firmly hold to exist in the unity of the Godhead.

We form the triangular number of fifty-one, and we take the total number of the elect in the heavenly homeland as the number of the fish, one hundred and fifty-three. After the Lord’s resurrection, it was fitting that the net cast should catch as many fish as would signify only those elect who are worthy of the heavenly homeland.

There is also another calculation of this sum of seven and ten. For if you count all the numbers from one through seventeen in this way—one plus two makes three; add three, and it makes six; add four, and it makes ten; add five, and you will have fifteen—and so, as the numbers increase and are added together up to seventeen, the sum of all the numbers reckoned from one through seventeen is one hundred and fifty-three.

When this is considered together with the previous interpretation—namely, the Law in the number ten and grace in the number seven—it agrees very appropriately. But there are many more things worthy of consideration in this matter, which the urgency of the present time prevents us from saying in full.

And although there were so many, the net was not torn. The Evangelist added a necessary detail by saying: “Although there were so many”—or “so large,” as was stated above, “full of large fish”—“the net was not torn.” That is: they were large, but there were no heresies among them; and there were no heresies among them precisely because they were large.

Jesus said to them: “Come, eat.” And no one of those reclining dared ask him: “Who are you?” The meaning, then, is this: the evidence of the truth was so great, since Jesus appeared to those disciples, that no one dared either deny it or even doubt it. For if anyone had doubted, he would certainly have had to ask.

Thus it is said:

“No one dared ask: ‘Who are you?’” As though it were said: No one dared doubt that it was he.

And Jesus came, took the bread, and gave it to them, and likewise the fish. It should also be noted that the Lord is described as having his last meal with seven disciples. Peter and Thomas, Nathanael and the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples are said to have been present. Why does he celebrate his last meal with seven disciples, unless because he declares that only those who are filled with the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit will be with him in the eternal banquet? The whole of this period is also unfolded in seven days, and perfection is often signified by the number seven.

Those, therefore, feast at this last meal upon the presence of the Truth who now transcend earthly things in their pursuit of perfection, whom the love of the world does not bind, and whom—although it may in some measure assail them through temptations—it does not blunt in the desires they have undertaken. Concerning this final meal it is elsewhere said through John: “Blessed are those who are called to the wedding supper of the Lamb.” For this reason he tells us that they were called not to lunch but to supper, since a meal at the end of the day is properly supper. Those, therefore, who, when the time of the present life has ended, come to the refreshment of heavenly contemplation are called not to the Lamb’s lunch but to his supper. This supper is represented by this final meal.

Since seven disciples are mentioned as being present with Jesus, because, as we have said, he will then receive into eternal refreshment those who, now filled with the sevenfold grace, yearn in love for the Spirit, what does it mean that our Redeemer ate a roasted fish after the resurrection, while in another Gospel he is said to have eaten honeycomb with roasted fish, but in this one bread with fish? What does the roasted fish signify except Christ who suffered? What does the honeycomb signify except the sweetness of divinity? He is a fish because he deigned to lie hidden in the waters of the human race. He wished to be caught in the snare of our death and, as it were, was roasted in tribulation at the time of his Passion.

But he who deigned to become a roasted fish in his Passion became honeycomb for us in his resurrection. Or, if he wished the roasted fish to represent the tribulation of his Passion, did he wish the honeycomb to express both natures of his person? For honeycomb is honey in wax, and divinity in humanity. This interpretation also agrees with the present reading, since he ate fish and bread. He who, in his humanity, could be roasted like a fish refreshes us with bread through his divinity, saying: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven.” He ate roasted fish and bread so that by this food itself he might show us that he endured suffering through our humanity and brought about our resurrection through his divinity.

This was now the third time he had manifested himself to his disciples after he had risen from the dead. We must refer this not to the manifestations themselves but to the days—that is, first on the day when he rose, then after eight days, when the disciple Thomas saw him and believed, and now on this day, when he did this concerning the fish. After how many days he did this is not stated here; for he was seen more than once on the first day, as the combined testimony of all the Evangelists demonstrates. But, as has been said, his manifestations must be counted according to the days, so that this may be the third.

## HOMILY XI. THURSDAY. Reading from the Acts of the Apostles.

“In those days, the angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying: ‘Rise and go toward the south,’” and the rest.

It is rightly at midday that the man who, burning with devotion of heart, deserved to be consecrated to God as a kind of firstfruits of the nations is sought, found, and washed. In him that saying of the Psalmist was spiritually fulfilled: “Ethiopia will hasten to stretch out her hands to God.”

“To the road that descends from Jerusalem to Gaza; this is deserted.” And he rose and went. It is not the road but Gaza that is called deserted. For that ancient Gaza, which was once the boundary of the Canaanites near Egypt, was utterly destroyed, and another was built elsewhere in its place. Allegorically, it signifies the people of the nations, formerly deserted by the worship of God and cultivated by the preaching of none of the prophets.

The road, however, which descends from Jerusalem to that same place and opens the fountain of salvation is the Lord Jesus Christ, who says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” For the heavenly Jerusalem descended to our lowliness, whitened us with the water of baptism, and wiped away the crimes of our guilt.

“Behold, an Ethiopian man, a eunuch in authority.” He is called a man on account of the strength and integrity of his mind; and rightly so, since he had such devotion to the Scriptures that he did not cease reading them even while on the road. He also possessed such love for religion that, leaving the royal court, he came from the ends of the world to the temple of the Lord.

Therefore, in proportion to his reward, while he sought an interpreter of his reading, he found Christ, whom he was seeking; and, as Jerome says, he found more in the desert spring of the Church than in the gilded temple of the Synagogue. There was fulfilled what Jeremiah, speaking in wonder, says: “The Ethiopian has changed his skin”; that is, cleansed from the filth of sins in the washing of Jesus, he came up made white.

[Col. 0158A]

“Of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians.” In the Book of Kings we read that the queen of the South came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon. It was indeed the custom of that nation always to be ruled by women and to call them Candaces. The queen of the Ethiopians, sending her treasurer ahead to Jerusalem, signifies the Church of the nations, which would bring to the Lord the gifts of virtues and faith.

The etymology of the name also fits. For Candace can be interpreted from Hebrew as “changed”; indeed she is the one to whom Scripture says in the psalm “For those who are changed”: “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house,” and so forth.

“Then the Spirit said to Philip: ‘Approach and join yourself to this chariot.’” Philip ran up and heard him reading the prophet Isaiah, and said: “Do you think you understand what you are reading?” He replied: “And how can I, unless someone guides me?” And he asked Philip to come up and sit with him. The passage of Scripture that he was reading was this.

The Spirit was speaking to Philip in his heart. For it is a hidden force of the Lord’s Spirit to speak certain words to us and make known what must be done.

“He was led like a sheep to the slaughter.” Just as a sheep, when it is led to the sacrifice, does not resist, so he suffered these things by his own will; or, in a higher sense, just as a lamb was accustomed to be sacrificed at Passover, so Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed.

[Col. 0158C]

“And as a lamb before its shearer is without a voice.” He not only redeemed us by his blood but also covered us with his wool, so that he might warm those who were cold in faith with his garment, and so that we might hear the Apostle speaking to us: “All who have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ.”

“Thus he did not open his mouth,” when, in his Passion, he wished to give little answer to Pilate and the chief priests, and none to Herod.

“In his humiliation his judgment was taken away.” For the judge of all found the truth of the judgment, yet he was condemned without any fault through the uprising of the Jews and the voice of Pilate.

“Who will declare his generation?” This may be understood of his divinity, because it is impossible for us to know the mysteries of his divine birth, concerning which the Father says: “Before the morning star I begot you”; or it may refer to the virgin birth, which can scarcely be explained. When Mary sought its meaning, she was told through the angel: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you.” Thus the mysteries of his birth are spoken of either by the angel or by the Evangelist, whose account of it is exceedingly rare.

“How will his life be taken from the earth?” So that he would live not on earth at all but in heaven. When, in the Acts of the Apostles, the eunuch of Queen Candace was being carried in a chariot and did not understand what he was reading, he understood through Philip’s interpretation concerning the Passion and the name of the Savior. Immediately baptized in the blood of the Lamb whom he was reading about, he deserved to be called a man and was sent as an apostle to the Ethiopian nation.

[Col. 0159A]

He, therefore, was handed over to Pilate because he himself willed it, and did not answer, so that he might undergo the gallows after being condemned for us. It is as though he said: “He himself, like a sheep, was led to slaughter and, like a lamb before its shearer, became silent; for Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed.”

John the Baptist pointed him out, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.” In the Apocalypse of John the Evangelist he is also repeatedly shown as the slain Lamb. Concerning himself he says in Jeremiah: “But I was like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter, and I did not know.” Since he knew no sin, he was made sin for us; and just as a lamb, when led to the sacrifice, does not resist, so he suffered willingly, in order to destroy him who held the power of death, humbling himself unto death, even death on a cross.

This is the Lamb in whose type the lamb was sacrificed, whose blood, smeared on the doorposts, drove away the destroyer from Egypt. He not only redeemed us by his blood but also covered us with his wool, so that he might warm those who were cold in faith with his garment, and so that we might hear the Apostle speaking to us: “All who have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ”; and elsewhere: “Put on Christ Jesus.”

What follows—“From distress and from judgment he was taken away,” or, as the Septuagint translated it, “In his humiliation his judgment was taken away”—signifies either that he ascended victorious to the Father from tribulation and judgment, or that the judge of all did not find the truth of the judgment, but that he was condemned without any fault through the uprising of the Jews and the voice of Pilate. Thus the prophet marvels that the God of all subjected himself to suffering. Concerning him Paul says:

[Col. 0159C]

“For if they had understood, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.”

It follows:

“Who will declare his generation?” This is understood in two ways. It may refer to his divinity, because it is impossible to know the mysteries of his divine birth. Concerning this he speaks in Proverbs: “Before all the hills he begot me,” in accordance with what we read elsewhere: “Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?”—that is, no one.

Or it may refer to the virgin birth, which can scarcely be explained. When the angel said to Mary, “You will conceive and bear a son,” she replied: “How can this be for me, since I have not known a man?” Again the angel said to her: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.” Thus the mystery of his birth is spoken of either by the angel or by the Evangelist, whose account of it is exceedingly rare.

[Col. 0159D]

“Philip opened his mouth and, beginning from this Scripture, preached Jesus to him.” Philip is interpreted as “mouth of a lamp.” The meaning is beautiful: the mouth of the lamp opened its mouth while bringing the obscurities of prophecy into the light of knowledge. Yet, according to the historical sense, this circumlocution may also indicate that his discourse would then become somewhat longer.

“As they went along the road, they came to a certain water.” There is today Bethtur, or Bethsoro, a village in the tribe of Judah for those traveling from Aelia to Hebron, at the twentieth milestone. Near it a spring, boiling up at the foot of the mountain, is swallowed by the same earth from which it arises. The Acts of the Apostles report that the eunuch was baptized by Philip in the spring of this village.

For Aelia Bethtur is in the tribe of Judah, one thousand paces distant from Heliopolis. And the eunuch said: “Behold, here is water. What prevents me from being baptized?” And he ordered the chariot to stop; and both Philip and the eunuch went down into the water, and he baptized him.

O wondrous power of the teacher! The eunuch was in the vehicle and was reading the sacred writings, but he did not know about whom he was reading. Nevertheless, with devout mind he desired to know the one whom, unknowingly, he was reading about in the book. Philip the philosopher came and showed him Jesus, who lay hidden within it.

According to another tradition, Philip said to the eunuch: “If you believe with all your heart, you will be saved.” And the eunuch replied: “I believe in Christ, the Son of God.” At that hour he was baptized, became faithful and holy, and was transformed from a disciple into a teacher, thereafter becoming a preacher and an apostle of his nation.

[Col. 0160B]

When they had come up from the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch did not see him again. There are some who testify that this was accomplished by an angel through the Holy Spirit. As Jerome relates, something similar is also read concerning Habakkuk, who carried a meal to Daniel.

Philip, however, was found at Azotus. Azotus is a distinguished town of Palestine, called in Hebrew Isdoth, and it is one of the five cities formerly belonging to the Philistines. Azotus is interpreted as “fire of generation” or “fire of a kinsman.”

And as he passed through, he evangelized all the cities until he came to Caesarea. This is said to be Caesarea of Palestine, where Philip is later described as having a house, which is still shown today, as well as the room of his four virgin daughters who prophesied.

[Col. 0160C]

There are two Caesareas in the Promised Land. One is Caesarea of Palestine, situated on the shore of the Great Sea. Formerly called Pyrgos, that is, the Tower of Strato, it was rebuilt by Herod, king of Judea, in a more distinguished and beautiful manner and with much greater usefulness against the force of the sea. It was called Caesarea in honor of Caesar Augustus, for whom he also built a temple of white marble there. In that city his grandson Herod was struck by an angel, the centurion Cornelius was baptized, and the prophet Agabus bound Paul with his belt.

The other is Caesarea Philippi, which the Gospel mentions as a tetrarchy, built at the foot of Mount Lebanon and named in honor of Caesar. There is also a third, Caesarea of Cappadocia, its metropolis, which Luke mentions in this way: “Having gone down to Caesarea, he greeted the Church.”

## HOMILY XII, ALSO THURSDAY. Reading from the Holy Gospel according to John.

[Col. 0160D]

“At that time, Mary stood outside at the tomb, weeping,” and the rest.

We must consider how great was the force of love that had risen in this woman’s heart. Even when the disciples were leaving, she did not leave the Lord’s tomb; she sought him whom she had not found; she wept while searching; and, inflamed by the fire of her love, she burned with longing for the one whom she believed had been taken away.

The eyes that had sought the Lord and had not found him now overflowed with tears, grieving more that he had been removed from the tomb than that he had been killed on the cross, because not even the memory of so great a teacher remained for them, since his life had been taken from them.

Thus it happened that she alone saw him who remained, because perseverance is the strength of a good work, as the Voice of Truth says: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved.”

While she was weeping, she bent down and looked into the tomb, and saw two angels in white sitting, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had been placed. Let us therefore see with what fruit of love the work of searching is repeated in this woman, who loved him in such a way that she again bends toward the tomb she had already inspected.

It follows: “She saw two angels in white sitting, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had been placed.” What does it mean that two angels are seen at the place of the Lord’s body, one sitting at the head and the other at the feet, except that in Latin an angel is called a messenger? The one who was to be proclaimed from his Passion is both God before the ages and man at the end of the ages.

The angel sits, as it were, at the head when he is preached through the apostles: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” And the angel sits, as it were, at the feet when it is said: “And the Word became flesh.”

We may also understand the two angels as the two Testaments, one earlier and the other later. These angels are joined to each other at the place of the Lord’s body, because both Testaments, with equal meaning, proclaim that the Lord was incarnate, died, and rose again. Thus the earlier Testament sits at the head and the later Testament at the feet.

They say to her: “Woman, why are you weeping?” It is as though they had said: “There is no reason to weep for one whom you ought to believe alive.”

She says to them: “Because they have taken away my Lord,” and so forth. She calls the lifeless body of her Lord “her Lord,” signifying the whole by a part, just as we all confess Jesus Christ, the only Son of God, as our one Lord. He is at once Word, soul, and flesh, yet it was only his flesh that was crucified and buried.

“And I do not know,” she says, “where they have placed him.” This was the chief cause of her grief: she did not know where to go to console her sorrow. But the hour was near when her sadness would be turned into joy.

When she had said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus. It should be noted that Mary, who was still doubting the Lord’s resurrection, turned around and saw Jesus because, through that very doubt, she had, as it were, turned her back on the Lord’s face, since she did not at all believe that he had risen.

But because she loved and doubted, she saw him without recognizing him. Her love had shown him to her, while her doubt concealed him. Her continuing ignorance is expressed when it is added: “And she did not know that it was Jesus.”

Jesus says to her: “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?” The cause of her grief is questioned so that her desire may increase, and so that, when she named the one she was seeking, she might burn more ardently in her love for him.

Thinking that he was the gardener, she says to him: “Lord, if you have taken him away, tell me where you have placed him, and I will take him.” Perhaps this woman was not mistaken even in her mistake when she believed Jesus to be the gardener. Was he not spiritually a gardener to her, who planted within her breast the seeds of virtues, green with his love?

But what does it mean that, having seen the one whom she believed to be the gardener, she says to him—before telling him whom she believed him to be—“Lord, if you have taken him away, tell me”? Let no one accuse the woman because she called the gardener “Lord” and the teacher “Jesus.” There she was asking; here she was recognizing. There she honored the man from whom she was requesting a favor; here she recalled the teacher from whom she might learn human things and learned divine things.

She called him “Lord,” although she was not his servant, in order to reach the Lord whose servant she was. Thus she used “Lord” in different ways: “They have taken away my Lord”; and: “Lord, if you have taken him away.” In the first case, truthfully; in the second, as a form of honor.

She was therefore seeking, but did not name him. When she had said, “Lord, if you have taken him away,” the power of love is shown. It habitually acts in the mind in such a way that the person whom it is always thinking about is believed by it to be unknown to no one else.

This woman rightly does not name the one she is seeking, and yet she does name him when she says, “If you have taken him away,” because she does not think that the other can be unaware of the one whom she herself continuously mourns in longing.

He says to her: “Mary.” She turns and says to him: “Rabboni,” which means “Teacher.” After he had called her by a common term and by her sex, and he was not recognized, he calls her by name. It is as though he openly said to her: “Recognize the one by whom you are recognized.”

To the perfect man also he says: “I know you by name,” because “man” is a common designation for all of us, whereas “Moses” is a proper name, and it is rightly said to him that he is known by name. It is as though the Lord openly said: “I know you not generally, like the others, but individually.”

Mary, therefore, because she is called by name, recognizes her creator and immediately calls him “Rabboni,” that is, “Teacher,” because he was both the one whom she was seeking outwardly and the one who was teaching her inwardly to seek him.

Jesus says to her: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father.” He said, “Do not touch me,” so that in that woman the Church from the nations might be represented, the Church that did not believe in Christ until he had ascended to the Father. Or Jesus wished this to be understood spiritually: he is to be touched in such a way that he and the Father are understood to be one. Otherwise he is not touched rightly—that is, he is not rightly believed in.

The Evangelist does not then state what the woman did, but he hints at it through the words she heard: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father.” These words show that Mary wished to embrace the feet of the one whom she had recognized.

But the Teacher says to her: “Do not touch me,” not because after the resurrection the Lord refused to be touched by women, since it is written concerning two women at his tomb: “They approached and held his feet.” The reason why he should not be touched is also added when it follows: “For I have not yet ascended to my Father.”

For Jesus ascends to the Father in our heart when he is believed to be equal to the Father. Whoever does not believe him to be equal to the Father still does not have Jesus ascended to the Father in his heart. He, therefore, truly touches Jesus who believes the Son to be coeternal with the Father.

“Go to my brothers and say to them: ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God.’” He does not say “our Father.” Therefore my Father in one way, and your Father in another; my God, under whom I too am man, and your God, among whom I am also mediator.

Since he says “my” and “your,” why does he not say “our” in common? By speaking distinctly, he indicates that he himself possesses the same Father and Lord in a different way from us.

“I am ascending to my Father,” namely, by nature, “and your Father,” by grace; “to my God,” because I descended; “and your God,” because you ascended. Since I too am man, God is my God; since you have been freed from error, God is your God.

The Father and God are therefore distinct for me, because the one who begot the Lord as God before the ages created him as man with me at the end of the ages.

Mary Magdalene came announcing to the disciples: “I have seen the Lord,” and that he had said these things to her. Behold, the guilt of the human race is cut away at the point from which it arose. Because in paradise a woman offered death to a man, from the tomb a woman announces life to men; and she recounts the words of her life-giver, just as she had recounted the words of the deadly serpent.

It is as though the Lord were saying to the human race, not in words but in deeds: “From the hand from which the drink of death was brought to you, receive the cup of life.”

In this there is a harmony between the two readings: the angel spoke to Mary, and he also spoke to Philip; Philip preached Jesus to the eunuch, and Mary announced Jesus to the apostles. For all these things were done for his glory, by whose gift God bestows every good thing upon the elect.

Every good gift and every perfect gift belongs to our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XIII. FRIDAY. Reading from the Epistle of the Blessed Apostle Peter.

“Beloved, Christ died once for our sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, so that he might offer us to the Lord,” and the rest.

Whoever, being righteous, suffers, imitates Christ. Whoever is corrected through scourging imitates the thief who recognized Christ on the cross and, after the cross, entered paradise with Christ. Whoever does not cease from sins even amid scourging imitates the thief on the left, who went up onto the cross because of his sins and, after the cross, fell into Tartarus.

He recalls that Christ died once so that he might also remind us that an eternal reward will be given for our temporary sufferings.

“So that he might offer us to God, put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit.” Concerning this death of the flesh and life of the spirit, which those who labor for the Lord through patience possess, the Apostle Paul also says: “Even if our outward man is corrupted, nevertheless the one who is inward is renewed day by day.”

Christ therefore offers us to God the Father when, after the death of the flesh, we rejoice in being sacrificed for him—that is, he displays our praiseworthy life in the Father’s sight. Or certainly he offers us to God when, freed from the flesh, he brings us into the eternal kingdom.

[Col. 0164A]

Moreover, what is said—“made alive in the spirit”—the holy Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, refers not to the human spirit, which is more fully brought to life when the flesh has been put to death, as the Prophet says of the Lord: “To revive the spirit of the humble and to revive the heart of the contrite,” but rather to the grace of the Holy Spirit, who repays those who put their flesh to death with everlasting life.

He also uses this testimony against the Arians, who contradict the equality of the Holy Trinity. He teaches that, through the indivisible unity of divine operation, the Father gives life, the Son gives life, and the Holy Spirit gives life.

The Father gives life, and the Son also gives life, because it is written: “For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes.” The Holy Spirit is likewise declared by this testimony, which is spoken concerning the Son: “So that he might offer us to God, put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit.” Therefore, since their operation is one, their substance and essence cannot be different.

[Col. 0164B]

“In which also he came spiritually and preached to those who were imprisoned in the flesh, who had once been unbelieving.” He who, in our times, came in the flesh and preached the way of life to the world also preached in the spirit to those who had then been unbelieving and had lived according to the flesh before the Flood. For he himself was in Noah and the other saints who lived at that time through the Holy Spirit, and through their good conduct he preached to the wicked people of that age so that they might be converted to better things.

He calls those “imprisoned in the flesh” who are weighed down by carnal desires. Hence Scripture says concerning them: “All flesh had corrupted its way.”

When he says “in which,” he signifies “in that which he had promised, namely, that he would offer us to God.” Even then, if some had refused to believe the Lord’s preaching—which he held out after the life of the faithful—and thus refused to be offered to God the Father, he nevertheless rejoiced in offering them.

If some reviled the good as though they were evildoers, they were put to shame when the Flood came. The words “in which” may also be understood in both ways: “in which he also came spiritually”—that is, in the spirit—and preached to those imprisoned in the flesh, so that through the same preaching a crown of praise might arise for believers and shame for those who persisted in unbelief.

Some manuscripts read: “In which also he came in the spirit and preached to those who were in prison.” This refers to the same intention concerning the wicked and unbelieving, who, because they have their understanding darkened as though by darkness, are rightly said even in this life to be confined in prison. In that prison they are weighed down by inward darkness—that is, blindness of mind—and by unjust works, until, freed from the flesh, they are cast into outer darkness and into the prison of eternal condemnation.

Concerning this the Lord says in the Gospel: “And the judge will hand you over to the officer, and you will be thrown into prison.”

Yet the saints also rightly proclaim themselves placed in prison in this life when they thirst for the joy of their heavenly homeland, in accordance with the Psalmist’s words: “Bring my soul out of prison, that I may confess your name.”

There is a great difference between the two prisons. The wicked are in the prison of sins and ignorance; the righteous, although placed in the prison of tribulations, enjoy the ever-expanding light of righteousness in a heart directed toward the Lord.

The apostles Paul and Silas represented this when, at midnight, bound and scourged amid the deepest horror of the prison, they sang a hymn of praise to God with a voice full of joy.

Someone interpreted this passage in the following way: the saints resting in hell desired the consolation of which the Lord says to the apostles: “Many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it.” The Psalmist also speaks of this: “My eyes have failed while waiting for your word, saying: ‘When will you comfort me?’”

According to this interpretation, when the Lord descended into hell, consolation or exhortation was preached even to those who were in prison and had formerly been unbelieving in the days of Noah. This, he said, was the meaning.

But the Catholic faith holds that when the Lord descended into hell, he did not bring unbelievers out from there, but only his faithful, whom he led with him to the heavenly kingdoms. Nor did he preach salvation to souls separated from the body and condemned in the prison of hell, salvation which they had loved before death. Rather, those imprisoned in the prison of wickedness in this life are shown the way of life every day, either by the Lord himself or through the examples and words of his faithful.

He speaks of them when he says: “Who had been unbelieving when the patience of God waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was being constructed.” For the patience of God itself was his preaching, since Noah devoted one hundred years to the work of the ark. Through the daily execution of his work he showed what would happen to the world, because Paul says: “Do you not know that the patience of God leads you to repentance?” and so forth.

Another translation gives the passage in this way:

“Christ died once for our sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, so that he might lead us to God, put to death in the body but made alive in the spirit. In this spirit he also preached to those who were in prison, who had formerly not believed in those days when the patience of God waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was being constructed. In it a few—that is, eight souls—were saved through water.”

[Col. 0165C]

“And now baptism, in a corresponding form, saves you also.” He says that the form of baptism corresponds to the ark and the waters of the Flood. It is entirely right that the very construction of the ark from smoothed wood signifies the building of the Church, which is formed from the gathering of faithful souls by the architects of the Word.

The fact that, while the entire world perished, only a few—that is, eight souls—were saved signifies through the water that, in comparison with the perishing multitude of pagans, Jews, heretics, and false believers, the number of the elect is much smaller.

Hence, concerning the narrow gate and the constricted way that leads to life, it is said: “And few are those who find it.” Again: “Do not fear, little flock, because it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom.”

Concerning this little flock the following is appropriately added here: “Not the removal of bodily filth, but the appeal of a good conscience toward God.” For where is there a good conscience except where there is an unfeigned faith? The Apostle Paul teaches that “the end of the commandment is love from a pure heart and a good conscience and unfeigned faith.”

Thus, the fact that the water of the Flood did not save those outside the ark but overwhelmed them undoubtedly prefigured every heretic who, although possessing the sacrament of baptism, is plunged into hell by the very waters by which the ark is lifted toward heaven.

The number eight itself—the number of souls saved through the water—also signifies this: the holy Church receives the washing of baptism as a sacrament of the Lord’s resurrection, so that, just as he rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we, cleansed from sins through the water of regeneration, may walk in newness of life.

On the eighth day—that is, after the seventh day of the week—the Lord rose from the dead and showed us both an example of the resurrection to come and the mystery of a new way of life, by which, while placed on earth, we might live a heavenly life. Peter himself explains this further when he says:

[Col. 0166A]

“Through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who is at the right hand of God, swallowing up death so that we might become participants in eternal life, having gone up into heaven.”

Just as he himself rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God, so he signified through baptism that the way of salvation and entry into the heavenly kingdom is open to us also.

He rightly says “swallowing up death.” What we swallow is consumed by the power of our body so that it disappears completely. The Lord swallowed up death, and when he rose from the dead he consumed it so entirely that it no longer had any power against him through contact with any corruption. While the appearance of a true body remained, every stain of its former fragility was entirely absent.

The same thing is promised to happen to us at the end, as the Apostle says when speaking of our resurrection: “Then the saying that is written will come to pass: ‘Death has been swallowed up in victory.’”

It is rightly said “swallowed up,” because when we have been made participants in eternal life, the immortal power of the body will remove all former corruption in the same way that the flame of fire ordinarily consumes a drop of water cast into it by the force of its heat.

## HOMILY XIV, ALSO FRIDAY. Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Matthew.

[Col. 0166C]

“At that time, the eleven disciples went into Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them,” and so forth.

After the resurrection, Jesus is seen on the mountain of Galilee, and there he is worshiped. Although some doubt, their doubt increases our faith, since it is shown more plainly that Thomas was shown the side wounded by the spear and the hands fixed with nails.

“Jesus approached and spoke to them, saying: ‘All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.’” It was given to the one who shortly before had been crucified, who had been buried in a tomb, who had lain dead, and who afterward had risen.

Authority was given to him in heaven and on earth so that the one who had previously reigned in heaven through the faith of believers might reign on earth.

“Go, therefore, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” First he teaches all nations; then he immerses those who have been taught in water. For it cannot happen that the body receives the sacrament of baptism unless the soul has first received the truth of faith.

They are baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit so that, since they possess one divinity, there may be one gift; and the name of the Trinity is one God.

[Col. 0167A]

“Teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you.” The principal order instructed the apostles first to teach all nations, then to immerse them in the sacrament of faith, and afterward to command what must be observed after faith and baptism. But lest we think that what he commanded was insignificant or little, he adds:

“Everything that I have commanded you,” so that those who have believed and have been baptized in the Trinity may do everything that has been commanded.

I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age. He who promises that he will be with the disciples until the consummation of the age shows that they will always be victorious and that he will never withdraw from believers. But he who promises his presence until the consummation of the world does not fail to know the day on which he knows that he will be with the apostles. How did he say, “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age,” and again: “These are my words,” he says, “while I was still with you”—that is, while I was still mortal, as you also are? He was with them by the presence of his body, but he was not with them in the condition of mortality. And now he is with us by the presence of his majesty, but he is not with us by the presence of his body. In holy baptism, the readings concerning these two realities are brought into harmony. For the Apostle says: “And baptism, in a similar form, saves you”; the Gospel says: “Teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe and is not baptized will be condemned forever.”

## HOMILY XV. ON THE SATURDAY IN THE OCTAVE OF EASTER

Reading from the Epistle of blessed Peter the Apostle.

[Col. 0167C]

“Beloved, laying aside all malice, and all deceit, and hypocrisies, and envies, and all slanders, like newborn infants, desire the rational milk without deceit, so that by it you may grow into salvation,” etc.

“You who have recently been reborn,” he says, “and made sons of God through baptism, now become through zeal for a good way of life what infants newly born by nature are: innocent because of their tender age, ignorant of malice and every deceit, and wholly unaware of pretending, envying, slandering, and being enslaved to other vices of this kind. Just as infants naturally desire milk continually, so that they may grow into salvation and be able to reach the point of eating bread, so you too should first seek the simple elements of faith from the breasts of Mother Church—that is, from the teachers of both Testaments, who either wrote the divine utterances or proclaim them to you with the living voice—so that by learning well you may reach the nourishment of the living bread that came down from heaven. This is accomplished through the sacraments of the Lord’s incarnation, by which you were reborn and by which you are nourished, until you reach the contemplation of the divine majesty.”

“Desire,” he says, “the rational milk without deceit, so that by it you may grow into salvation.” By the command to desire milk he reproves those who come unwillingly and reluctantly to hear the sacred readings, ignorant of that thirst and hunger of which the Lord says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness.” For this reason they reach more slowly the perfect growth of salvation [Col. 0168A], by which they could be nourished with the solid food of the word—that is, understand divine mysteries and do greater good.

“If indeed you have tasted how sweet the Lord is.” “In this way,” he says, “with the malice and impurity of your hearts dismissed and cleansed, desire the spiritual nourishment of Christ; thus you will taste how great the sweetness of God is. For one who tastes nothing in his soul of the sweetness above has no cause for wonder if he does not avoid defiling himself with earthly allurements.”

The Psalmist rightly urges us to taste how sweet the Lord is, because there are some who do not perceive the Lord as something inwardly sweet, but as something that, once struck, gives an inward sound. Even if they grasp certain hidden things through understanding, they cannot experience their sweetness. And although they know what these things are, they do not know, as I have said, how they taste. Moreover, in the very psalm from which he took this verse, it is prefaced: “Draw near to him and be enlightened.” Accordingly, blessed Peter rightly adds:

“To whom, drawing near, a living stone, rejected indeed by human beings but chosen and honored by the Lord.” He also takes this testimony concerning the stone from the psalm, where it is written: “The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the head of the corner.” But lest anyone should think, in a Jewish sense, that the Prophet sang of a material stone which, in the construction of some earthly house, would be set in place contrary to human arrangement by divine judgment, he deliberately adds “living”: “Drawing near to him,” he says, “a living stone,” signifying that this was spoken of Christ, who is rightly called a stone. Coming in the flesh, he deigned to insert himself into the building of holy Church in order to strengthen it.

He is living because he could say: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” He was rejected by human beings when he said: “Yet I have been appointed king by him,” and so forth. He was honored because, after the death of the cross, God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, and so forth.

“And you yourselves, like living stones, are being built upon into spiritual houses.” He says that they are being built upon because without the Lord Jesus Christ, the living stone, no spiritual building can stand. “No one can lay another foundation” apart from him. Through participation in him, believers become living stones, though through unbelief they had been dead stones—hard, that is, and insensible—to whom it would rightly be said: “I will take the heart of stone away from you, and I will give you a heart of flesh.”

But they are fitted as living stones for a spiritual building. Through the discernment of a learned teacher, their superfluous actions and thoughts are cut away; like stones shaped by the stroke of an axe, they are squared. And just as the courses of stones in a wall support one another, so each of the faithful is supported by those who preceded them in the Church; they in turn support those who follow through teaching and endurance, all the way to the final righteous person. When that person is supported by those before him, whom he ought to support, he will have no one following him to support.

But the one who bears the entire building and is himself borne by no one is Christ the Lord. Hence the Prophet also calls him a precious stone, founded as the foundation [Col. 0169A].

“Be built upon,” he says, “into spiritual houses.” He says that they become spiritual houses, although there is one house of Christ, gathered from angels and elect human beings. In the same way, although there is one Catholic Church spread throughout the whole world, it is often called “churches” in the plural because of the many gatherings of the faithful, distinguished according to different tribes, peoples, and languages. Hence Christ himself says: “I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify these things to you in the churches.”

Nor should it be passed over that some manuscripts have, in the singular number, “be built upon, a spiritual house,” while others have, “be built upon into a spiritual house.” In this, the unity of the whole holy Church is more aptly commended. After he had said, “Be built upon into spiritual houses,” or “a spiritual house,” he adds:

“A holy priesthood”—that is, a priesthood, with you yourselves existing upon the foundation of Christ. He calls the whole Church a holy priesthood, although in the Law only the house of Aaron possessed the name and office. For truly we are all members of the great High Priest; we are all marked with the oil of gladness. What follows therefore applies to everyone:

“To offer spiritual sacrifices through Jesus Christ.” By spiritual sacrifices he means our works, almsgiving, and prayers, in contrast with the bodily sacrifices of the Law.

When he says in conclusion, “through Jesus Christ,” this applies to everything he had promised: through his grace we are built upon him by wise architects—that is, the ministers of the New Testament—and through his Spirit we are made spiritual houses [Col. 0169C], fortified against the rains, winds, and rivers of temptations; we share in the holy priesthood; and we are able to perform anything good and acceptable to the Lord only through him. For just as a branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you, he says, unless you remain in me.

“For this reason Scripture contains: ‘Behold, I place in Zion a chief cornerstone, chosen and precious.’” He gives this testimony from Isaiah to confirm what he had promised concerning the one to whom, drawing near as to a living stone, they come. He asserts and affirms that the Lord the Savior is called by the prophets a stone because of his firmness. He also adds:

“And everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.” He includes this because he had said: “And you, like living stones [Col. 0169D], are being built upon.” The Prophets and the Apostle’s statement harmonize beautifully here: “Drawing near to the living stone,” or “believing in him,” they are not put to shame, in accordance with the verse of that psalm in which, after saying, “Draw near to him and be enlightened,” it immediately adds: “And your faces will not blush with shame.” John says something similar: “And now, little children, remain in him, so that when he appears we may have confidence and not be put to shame by him at his coming.”

“Therefore, honor belongs to you who believe.” That honor, namely, that you may not be put to shame by him at his coming. But as he himself says: “If anyone serves me, my Father will honor him.”

“But for those who do not believe, the stone which the builders rejected” [Col. 0170A]—so that just as they rejected him when they built their deeds, refusing to place him in the foundation of their hearts, so they too may be rejected by him at his coming, when he will then refuse to receive those who rejected him into the building of his house, which is in heaven.

This distinction between the honor of believers and the rejection of unbelievers extends this far. He then proceeds concerning believers:

“This has become the head of the corner.” For just as a cornerstone joins two walls, so the Lord joined the people of the Jews and the nations to himself in one fellowship of faith. Immediately afterward he adds concerning unbelievers:

“And a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense.” Hence Paul also says: “We preach Christ: to the Jews, indeed, a stumbling block, but to the nations, foolishness.”

“For those who stumble at the word and do not believe, in which they have also been appointed.” They stumble at the word precisely because they happen to hear the word of God; they stumble in mind because they refuse to believe what they hear.

To heighten their foolishness he adds, “in which they have also been appointed.” There are those who have been appointed to this—that is, who by nature have been made human beings—in order to believe God and obey his will. Solomon bears witness to this when he says: “Fear the Lord and observe his commandments.” This means: “This is every human being”—that is, every human being has naturally been made for this purpose, to fear God and obey his commandments.

Some manuscripts have: “In which also they have been placed.” This may likewise be understood in accordance with what Paul says when speaking of the Lord: “For in him we live and move and are.”

“But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of acquisition.” This is a testimony of praise once given through Moses to the ancient people of the Lord, which the Apostle Peter now rightly gives to the nations, since they have believed in Christ. Like a cornerstone, he united the nations to the salvation that Israel had in him.

He calls them “a chosen race” on account of their faith, distinguishing them from those who, by rejecting the living stone, have themselves become rejected. He calls them “a royal priesthood” because they have been united to his body, who is both the supreme King and the true Priest: as King, granting them a kingdom; and as High Priest, cleansing their sins by the sacrifice of his blood. He names them a royal priesthood so that they may remember to hope for an everlasting kingdom and always to offer God sacrifices of blameless conduct.

They are also called “a holy nation” and “a people of acquisition” [Col. 0170D], in accordance with the statement that the Apostle Paul explains from prophecy: “But my righteous one lives by faith. And if he withdraws, my soul will not be pleased with him.” “But we,” he says, “are not of withdrawal unto destruction, but of faith unto the acquisition of the soul.”

And in the Acts of the Apostles: “The Holy Spirit has appointed you bishops to govern the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood.” We have therefore become a people of acquisition through the blood of our Redeemer, just as formerly Israel was a people redeemed from Egypt by the blood of the lamb.

Accordingly, in the following verse he also recalls mystically the ancient history and teaches that it is to be fulfilled spiritually in the new people of God, saying:

“So that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you from darkness [Col. 0171A] into his wondrous light.” Just as those who were freed from Egyptian slavery through Moses sang a song of triumph to the Lord after crossing the Red Sea and drowning Pharaoh’s army, so we too ought, after receiving the remission of sins in baptism, to repay the heavenly benefits with fitting thanksgiving.

For the Egyptians aptly signify the sins that pursue us and are blotted out in baptism, not only because they afflicted the people of God, but also because their name is interpreted as “darkness” or “tribulations.” The liberation of the children of Israel and their being led into the homeland long ago promised agree with the mystery of our redemption, through which, with the grace of Christ enlightening and guiding us, we move toward the light of our heavenly dwelling.

The light of this grace was also prefigured by that cloud and pillar of fire [Col. 0171B] which protected them from the darkness of the nights throughout that journey and led them by a venerable path to the promised dwelling places of their homeland.

“Who once were not a people, but are now the people of God; who had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy.” These verses clearly indicate that he wrote this epistle to those who had come to the faith from the nations. Once alienated from the way of life of God’s people, they were then united to his people through the grace of faith and obtained the mercy which they had not known how to hope for.

He takes this from the prophet Hosea, who, foretelling the calling of the nations, says: “I will call those who were not my people, ‘my people,’ and her who had not obtained mercy, ‘she who has obtained mercy.’ And in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they will be called sons of the living God.”

And in accordance with the Psalmist’s statement: “All nations will clap their hands and shout with a voice of rejoicing.” And again: “All nations,” he says, “will come and worship before you, and will honor your name forever, because the Lord our God is great, and there is no end to his greatness; he lives and reigns, God, in perfect Trinity and unity, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”

## HOMILY XVI. ON THE SAME FEAST

Reading from the holy Gospel according to John.

“At that time, on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene came early, while it was still dark, to the tomb, and saw that the stone had been removed from the tomb,” etc.

[Col. 0171D]

Just as at the beginning the woman was the author of guilt for the man, and the man the executor of the error, so now the woman who had first tasted death was the first to see the resurrection. And lest she who had transferred guilt to the man should endure perpetual disgrace among men, she also transferred grace.

He says, “on the first day of the week”—the day which Christian custom now calls the Lord’s Day because of the Lord’s resurrection. Matthew alone among the Evangelists called it “the first of the Sabbath.”

“So she ran and came to Simon Peter and to the other disciple whom Jesus loved, and said to them: ‘They have taken the Lord from the tomb, and I do not know where they have laid him.’” Troubled by overwhelming love, she ran to announce to the disciples that either they should search with her or grieve with her over the removal of the Lord whom she did not hesitate to call “Lord,” although she was seeking only his body in the tomb.

“So Peter went out, and the other disciple, and they came to the tomb. Now the two were running together, and the other disciple ran ahead, faster than Peter, and came first [earlier] to the tomb.”

Here one should observe and commend the recapitulation: the narrative returns to what had been passed over, and something is added as though it followed directly. For after he had already said, “They came to the tomb,” he went back to explain how they came and said: “Now the two were running together,” and so forth.

There he shows that the other disciple, who represents himself as though speaking of another in the manner customary to Holy Scripture, reached the tomb first by running ahead.

“And when he had bent down, he saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not enter.” That Mary Magdalene came to the tomb while it was still dark is noted historically as indicating the hour; mystically, it signifies the understanding of one who is seeking.

Mary was seeking in the tomb the author of all things whom she had seen dead in the flesh. Because she did not find him there, she thought he had been stolen. It was still dark, therefore, when she came to the tomb. She ran quickly and announced it to the disciples. But those who loved more than the others ran ahead of the others—namely, Peter and John. The two ran together for some time, but John ran faster than Peter, reached the tomb first, and did not presume to enter.

“Then Simon Peter came, following him, and entered the tomb.” This race of the two disciples contains a great mystery. What is signified by John, who came first to the tomb but did not enter, except the Synagogue? And what is signified by Peter except the Church gathered from the nations, which, though called later, entered first?

For the Gentiles and the Synagogue ran together through the successive periods of this age, but they did not come with equal understanding. The Synagogue came first to the tomb but did not enter, because it received certain commandments of the Law and heard the prophets concerning the incarnation and passion of the Lord, but refused to believe in the dead one.

John saw the linen cloths lying there but did not enter [Col. 0172D], because the Synagogue knew the mysteries of the sacred Scriptures and yet delayed entering, through belief, into faith in the Lord’s passion. It had long and extensively prophesied about him; it saw him present and rejected him. It despised him as a human being and refused to believe that God had become mortal flesh.

What does this mean, then, except that it ran faster and yet stood empty at the tomb? But Simon Peter came after him and entered the tomb, because the Church of the nations, following later, followed Jesus Christ, the mediator between God and human beings; it recognized him in the flesh, believed him dead, and believed him to be the living God.

The text continues:

“And he saw the linen cloths lying there, and the napkin which had been over Jesus’ head, not lying with the linen cloths, but rolled up separately in one place.” Why is the napkin of the Lord’s head not found in the tomb with the linen cloths? Paul bears witness that Christ’s head is God; thus the incomprehensible mysteries of divinity are separated from the knowledge of our weakness, and his power transcends the nature of creation.

It should also be noted that it is said to have been found not merely separately, but rolled up. A cloth that is rolled up reveals neither its beginning nor its end. The napkin of the head is therefore rightly rolled up, because the exaltation of divinity neither began to exist nor ceased to exist.

It is rightly added, “in one place,” because God is not in division of minds. God is in unity, and those deserve to possess his grace who do not divide themselves from one another because of the scandals caused by persecutors [Col. 0173B].

The napkin may also signify the passion of our Lord, whose mysteries are rolled up for unbelievers: they saw him mortal in the flesh, but did not believe that he was immortal God. The napkin that had been over his head is therefore found separately, because the passion of our Redeemer is far removed from our passion: he endured without guilt what we endure because of guilt. He willingly submitted to death, whereas we come to it unwillingly.

The text continues:

“Then the other disciple who had come first to the tomb also entered.” After Peter entered, John entered as well. The one who had come first entered later. It is known that at the end of the world Judea too will be gathered to faith in the Redeemer, as Paul bears witness [Col. 0173C] when he says: “Until the fullness of the nations enters, and thus all Israel will be saved.”

“And he saw and believed.” What did he see, and what did he believe? He saw the linen cloths lying there, and he believed what the woman had said: that the Lord had been taken from the tomb. For it was still dark in the tomb—that is, in their minds. Therefore it follows: “For they did not yet know the Scriptures, that he must rise from the dead.”

“So the disciples went away again to their own homes”—that is, to the place where they lived and from which they had run to the tomb.

It should also be noted that there is a fitting harmony between the readings in the name of the stone and in the meaning of the two peoples. According to the Apostle, the two peoples are joined in the cornerstone; according to the Gospel, both peoples are signified in the two apostles. For John represented the people of the Jews, while Peter represented the people of the nations.

Yet both preached the word of God to Jews and nations alike and faithfully proclaimed that our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, had truly risen from the dead. To him be glory with the Lord Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XVII. ON THE EIGHTH SUNDAY OF EASTER

Reading from the Epistle of the blessed Apostle John.

“Beloved, everything that has been born of God conquers the world,” etc.

The divine commandments are not burdensome because all who devote themselves to them with true devotion, and who despise equally both the adversities and the flatteries of this world, love even death as an entrance into the heavenly homeland. And lest anyone should trust that by his own strength he could overcome either the pleasures or the labors of the world, he appropriately adds:

“And this is the victory that conquers the world: our faith.” This is the faith that works through love; this is the faith by which we humbly implore the help of him who says: “In the world you will have distress; but take courage, I have conquered the world.”

“Who is it that conquers the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?” He conquers the world who, believing that Jesus is the Son of God, joins to that faith works worthy of it.

But is faith and confession of his divinity alone sufficient for salvation? Consider what follows.

“This is the one who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ.” He who was the eternal Son of God became human in time, so that he who had created us through the power of his divinity might recreate us through the weakness of his humanity.

“He came through the water and blood of his passion—not in water alone, but in water and blood.” He not only deigned to be baptized for our cleansing, consecrating and handing over to us the sacrament of baptism; he also gave his blood for us and redeemed us through his passion, so that, continually nourished by his sacraments, we might be fed unto salvation.

“And the Spirit is the one who testifies, because Christ is truth” [Col. 0174C]. When the Lord was baptized in the Jordan, the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove, bearing witness that he is truth—that is, the true Son of God, the true mediator between God and human beings, the true Redeemer and reconciler of the human race, truly clean from every stain of sin, and truly sufficient to take away the sins of the world.

The Baptist himself, seeing the coming of that Spirit and understanding it, said: “He who sent me to baptize in water said to me: ‘Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’ And I saw and bore witness that he is the Son of God.”

Since, therefore, the Spirit testifies that Jesus Christ is truth, he himself takes “truth” as his name. The Baptist preaches him as truth; the son of thunder evangelizes truth [Col. 0174D]. Let the blasphemers be silent, those who dogmatically assert that he was a phantom; let the memory of those who deny that he was truly either God or human perish from the earth.

“For there are three who bear witness: the Spirit, the water, and the blood.” The Spirit gave testimony that Jesus is truth when he descended upon him after his baptism. For if he were not the true Son of God, the Holy Spirit would never have come upon him with such a manifestation.

The water and the blood also bore testimony that Jesus is truth when they flowed from his side as he lay dead on the cross. This could not in any way have happened if he had not possessed the true nature of flesh.

Nor should it be rejected that, when he prayed before his passion, his sweat became like drops of blood running down upon the ground. This also bears witness to the truth of the flesh he assumed. Indeed, in this too the blood and water bore witness to him when they flowed vividly from the side of the dead man, contrary to the nature of a body. For this reason the event was suited to the mysteries and fitting as testimony to the truth: it signified that the Lord’s body itself would live more fully after death, resurrected in glory, and that his death itself would give us life.

The fact also that his sweat ran down upon the ground like drops of blood bore witness to the holy mystery that he would wash the whole Church throughout the world with his blood.

“And the three are one.” These realities remain indivisible, and none of them is separated from its connection with the others, because there is neither humanity without true divinity nor divinity without humanity.

But in us too these are one—not in the substance of the same nature, but in the operation of the same mystery. For, as blessed Ambrose says, “The Spirit renews the mind, the water serves for the washing, and the blood pertains to the price.” The Spirit made us sons of God by adoption, the water of the sacred font washes us, and the Lord’s blood redeemed us.

Thus one invisible testimony and another visible testimony accompany the spiritual sacrament:

“If we have received human testimony, the testimony of God is greater, because this is the testimony of God, which is greater: that he has testified concerning his Son.”

Great is the testimony of a human being concerning the Son of God, saying: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” [Col. 0175C]. And from the person of that Son: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son.” Likewise, from the person of the Father speaking about the Son: “He will call upon me: You are my Father, my God, and the protector of my salvation.”

“My Father,” because I am the Son of God; “my God,” because I am human; “the protector of my salvation,” because I am to suffer and be saved from death.

“And I,” he says, “will make him my firstborn, high above the kings of the earth.” This is a great and truthful testimony, worthy of complete acceptance: testimony concerning the Son of God. But much greater is the testimony of God, who himself testified concerning his Son when he addressed him from heaven, saying: “You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased.”

Great is the testimony of the Forerunner, who, bearing witness to the Son of God, says: “I baptized you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.” Greater is the testimony of the Father, who sent the Holy Spirit visibly upon him, although he had always been full of the Spirit.

“Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony of God within him.” Whoever believes in the Son of God in such a way that he practices by his deeds what he believes has the testimony of God within him—namely, that he too is rightly counted among the sons of God. The only Son of God himself promises this to his faithful when he says: “If anyone serves me, my Father will honor him.”

If you have been worthy to possess God’s testimony, if you have the Lord as the witness of your undefiled faith, what harm will human infamy or persecution do you? “If God is for us, who can be against us?” Jesus Christ, our Lord, who will redeem the souls of his servants and will not abandon all who hope in him, lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XVIII. ON THE SAME FEAST

Reading from the holy Gospel according to John.

“At that time, when it was evening on that day, the first of the week, and the doors were closed where the disciples were gathered because of fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in their midst,” etc.

What is surprising if, after his resurrection, when he was already destined to live forever, he entered through closed doors, when, coming to die, he emerged without opening the virgin’s womb? But because faith doubted that body which could be seen, he immediately showed them his hands and side and offered for touching the flesh that he had brought in through closed doors.

Nails had pierced his hands, and a lance had opened his side. The traces of the wounds were preserved there for the healing of doubting hearts, because he displayed in himself two wondrous things that, according to human reasoning, are greatly opposed to one another: after the resurrection he showed his body both incorruptible and yet touchable.

For what is touched must necessarily be subject to corruption, and what is not subject to corruption cannot be touched. Yet in a wondrous and immeasurable manner our Redeemer presented an incorruptible body after the resurrection and a body that could be touched. By showing it to be incorruptible, he invited us to the reward; by offering it to be touched, he formed us in faith.

He therefore showed himself both incorruptible and touchable, so that he might clearly demonstrate that after the resurrection his body was of the same nature but possessed a different glory [Col. 0176C].

He says to them: “Peace be with you.” He offered peace who came for the sake of peace. To those to whom he had previously said, “I leave you peace; I give you my peace,” he now says, “Peace be with you”—the peace which the angels proclaimed to the world at Christ’s birth.

“And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and side. Then the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord.” It would have been little to offer himself to their eyes to be seen if he had not also offered himself to their hands to be touched.

By showing the bones and flesh to the disciples for touching, he clearly signifies the state of the true resurrection that took place in him and will take place in us. For it is not as Eutychius, bishop of the city of Constantinople, wrote: that in no glory of resurrection will our body be impalpable and subtler than winds and air.

In the glory of that resurrection our body will indeed be subtle through the effect of spiritual power, but it will be touchable through the reality of its nature. Nor should the Apostle’s statement be thought to oppose this assertion: “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God.” In that passage the Apostle signifies by “flesh and blood” not the substance of the true body, but the corruption of mortality, as he immediately explained by adding: “Nor will corruption possess incorruption.”

In Holy Scripture, “flesh” is used in one way according to nature, in another according to guilt, and in another according to the corruption of mortality, which resulted from guilt.

It is according to nature when it is said: “This now is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh,” and, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”
