It is according to guilt when it is said: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh.”

It is according to corruptibility when it is written: “And they remembered that they are flesh”—that is, fragile and mortal. The Psalmist himself shows that he meant this by “flesh,” when he immediately adds: “A spirit that goes and does not return.”

Therefore flesh will not possess the Lord’s kingdom—that is, flesh according to guilt or mortality. Yet flesh will possess the Lord’s kingdom—that is, flesh according to nature, which the Lord also displayed to the disciples after the resurrection to be seen and touched.

Concerning this flesh blessed Job, when describing the glory of the resurrection, says: “And again I shall be clothed in my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God.”

Read the letter of Saint Augustine to Crescentius concerning the Lord’s body after the resurrection.

He therefore says to them again: “Peace be with you.” The repetition of the saying is a confirmation. By saying a second time, “Peace be with you,” he shows that the things in heaven and the things on earth have been reconciled through his blood.

“As the Father sent me, so I send you.” The Father sent the Son, appointing him to become incarnate for the redemption of the human race. He wished him to come into the world for suffering, yet he loved the Son whom he sent to suffer.

The Lord sends the chosen apostles not to the joys of the world, but into the world for sufferings, just as he himself was sent. Since, therefore, the Son is loved by the Father and yet is sent to suffering, so the disciples are loved by the Lord and yet are sent into the world to suffer.

Thus he says: “As the Father sent me, so I send you”—that is, I love you with the love with which the Father loves me, whom he caused to come to endure sufferings, even as I send you amid the scandals of persecutors.

“When he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit.’” We must ask what it means that our Lord gave the Holy Spirit once while remaining on earth and once while presiding from heaven.

The Holy Spirit is not openly shown elsewhere except here, when he is received through the breathing, and afterward when, coming from heaven, he is manifested in different tongues. Why, then, is he first given to the disciples on earth and afterward sent from heaven, unless because there are two commandments of love: love of God and love of neighbor?

The Spirit is given on earth so that the neighbor may be loved; the Spirit is given from heaven so that God may be loved. Therefore, just as there is one love and two commandments, so there is one Spirit and two gifts.

First he is given by the Lord while he remains on earth, afterward from heaven, because through love of neighbor one learns how one must arrive at love of God. By breathing on them, he signifies that the Holy Spirit is not the Spirit of the Father alone, but also his own.

“Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained.” Behold the love that is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit: it forgives the sins of those who share in it, but it holds fast the sins of those who do not share in it.

For this reason, after saying, “Receive the Holy Spirit,” he immediately added this concerning the forgiveness and retention of sins.

It should be understood that those who first had the Holy Spirit so that they themselves might live innocently and benefit certain people through preaching received him openly after the Lord’s resurrection for this reason: so that they might not benefit only a few, but might benefit many.

Thomas, one of the twelve, who is called Didymus, was not with them when Jesus came. This one disciple was absent. When he returned, he heard what had happened, but refused to believe what he had heard. The Lord came again and offered his side to the unbelieving disciple to touch; he showed him his hands, and by displaying the scar of his wounds he healed the wound of his unbelief. What, dearly beloved brothers, what did you observe in all this? Do you think it happened by chance that that chosen disciple was then absent? [Col. 0178B] That afterward he came, heard what had happened, doubted, and, doubting, touched—this did not happen by chance but by divine providence. For heavenly mercy acted wondrously, so that the doubting disciple, while touching the wounds of the flesh in his Master, might heal in us the wounds of unbelief. Thomas’s unbelief contributed more to our faith than the faith of the believing disciples did, because while he is brought back to faith by touching, our mind, setting aside every doubt, is established in faith.

Then the other disciples said to him, “We have seen the Lord.” But he said to them, “Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.” When John says that the apostle Thomas was not with them at that time, whereas according to Luke [Col. 0178C] the two of them—one of whom was Cleopas—returned to Jerusalem and found the eleven gathered together, along with those who were with them, it must without doubt be understood that Thomas had left before the Lord appeared to them while they were saying these things.

And after eight days his disciples were again inside, and Thomas was with them. Jesus came through the closed doors, stood in their midst, and said, “Peace be with you.” Then he said to Thomas, “Put your finger here, and see my hands; bring your hand and put it into my side; and do not be unbelieving but faithful.” Thus he permitted the disciple to doubt after his resurrection, yet did not abandon him in his doubt, just as before his birth he willed that Mary should have a betrothed husband, although that man did not reach her wedding. For the disciple [Col. 0178D] became a doubting and touching witness of the true resurrection, just as the bridegroom became the guardian of his mother’s most pure virginity. He showed not only his hands and feet, where the marks made by the nails were visible, but, as John attests, also the side that had been pierced by the lance, so that by displaying the scar of his wounds he might heal the wound of their doubt and unbelief.

But just as after his resurrection he deigned to strengthen the disciples’ faith and hope by displaying the places of the nails and the lance, so on the day of judgment he will come to confound the impiety of the proud and the unbelief of the faithless by displaying both the evidences of that same Passion and the cross itself. He will show openly to all angels and human beings that he is the very one who died at the hands of the impious and for the sake of the impious, [Col. 0179A] so that they may see, as it is written, “the one whom they pierced,” and all the tribes of the earth may mourn over him.

It should be noted that at this point pagans commonly construct an accusation and ridicule with foolish chatter the resurrection in which we hope. “If,” they say, “your God was unable even to heal the wounds inflicted upon him by the Jews, but, as you say, carried the marks of his scars with him into heaven, with what presumption do you think that he will restore your bodies from the dust intact?” We must answer them that our God, who, when he willed, was able to raise from the tomb the flesh he had already glorified with perpetual immortality, and to do so in whatever manner he willed, also raised it in whatever condition he willed. For it does not follow that the one who is shown to have done greater things was unable to do lesser ones; rather, by the grace of his providential arrangement, [Col. 0179B] he who did the greater refrained from doing the lesser.

He destroyed the kingdoms of death but did not wish to erase the marks of death: first, so that through them he might establish for his disciples the reality of his resurrection; next, so that, interceding with the Father for us, he might always show what kind of death he had endured for the life of mortals; third, so that for those redeemed by his death he might continually renew, by the visible signs of that same death, the memory of how mercifully they had been helped, and so they would never cease to sing the mercies of the Lord but would say, “For he is good, for his mercy endures forever,” those who have been redeemed by the Lord; finally, so that even to the faithless, at the judgment, the scar of the wounds he received from them might declare, among their other crimes, how justly they are condemned.

It is as though some exceptionally brave soldier, at the command of his king, had labored in single combat for the safety of his entire nation, [Col. 0179C] received many wounds, yet killed the enemy, seized his spoils, and brought victory back to his people. When he was handed over to a physician for treatment and was asked whether he wished to be healed so that no trace of his wounds would remain, or rather in such a way that the scars would remain while all deformity and ugliness were entirely removed, he might repeatedly reply that he wished to be healed in such a way that, after recovering his former condition of health and beauty, he would carry with him forever the signs of so great a triumph.

So indeed the Lord preferred, as a perpetual sign of victory, not to have the wounds of his Passion—received for us—erased, but to carry their scars into heaven. Yet this in no way prejudices our faith in the resurrection [Col. 0179D], of which it is proclaimed in a true promise: “Not a hair of your head will perish.”

Thomas answered and said to him, “My Lord and my God.” Jesus said to him, “Because you have seen me, you have believed.” Since Thomas saw and touched him, why is he told, “Because you have seen me, you have believed”? He saw one thing and believed another; for the divinity could not be seen by mortal human beings. He therefore saw the man and confessed him to be God, saying, “My Lord and my God.” Thus, by seeing, he believed: observing the true man, he cried out that this was the God whom he could not see.

“Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.” In this statement we are especially designated, we who hold in our minds the one whom we have not seen in the flesh. [Col. 0180A] We are designated, but only if our faith is followed by works; for the one who practices in action what he believes is truly a believer. When he says, “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed,” he uses the verb in the past tense, as though the one who knew in his predestination what was still future already regarded it as accomplished. But by these words, as we have said, the faith of the nations is specifically signified.

Jesus performed many other signs in the presence of his disciples that are not written in this book. The evangelist indicates that Jesus performed very many signs and miracles of salvation and preaching that were not written down because of the multitude of the things he had done.

But these things have been written so that you may believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, and so that, believing, you may have eternal life [Col. 0180B] in his name. For the one who believes that Jesus is Christ, the Son of God, has the Son himself within him through believing; and having the Son, he also has life, because he himself said, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” Moreover, he will possess eternal life with the saints, where there will be certain security, everlasting happiness, and indescribable joy, where this saying will be fulfilled: “I will be their God, and they will be my people”—that is, I will be the one with whom they are satisfied; I will be their life, salvation, nourishment, abundance, glory, honor, peace, and every good thing.

And so the Apostle’s saying will be fulfilled: “That God may be all in all.” He will be the end of our desires: he will be seen without end, loved without weariness, and praised without exhaustion—Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. [Col. 0180C] Amen.

## HOMILY XIX. WEDNESDAY

Reading from the Epistle to the Hebrews.

“Brothers, obey your leaders and be subject to them; for they keep watch as those who will give an account for your souls, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning; for this is not profitable for you.”

After he had said above, “Observing the outcome of their way of life, imitate their faith,” he then added, “Obey your leaders and be subject to them.” First he instructed them, and then he said, “Obey your leaders and be subject to them.” Someone may say, then, [Col. 0180D] “What if the leader turns out to be wicked? Are we not to obey the wicked?”

What do you mean by “wicked”? If the matter concerns the faith, flee him and avoid him—not only if he is a human being, but even if an angel should descend from heaven. But if you regard him as wicked in his entire character and conduct, do not investigate the matter further. I do not say this on my own authority, but from divine Scripture. Hear Jesus saying: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat.” After first saying many things against them, he then said, “They have sat on Moses’ seat; therefore do and observe everything they tell you, but do not do what they do.”

They possess, he says, authority, even though their lives are corrupt; but attend not to their lives, only to their words. As far as conduct is concerned, no one can be harmed. Why? Because what he does is manifest to everyone, and even if he reaches the summit of wickedness, [Col. 0181A] he will not be able to teach others evil.

But when the matter concerns the faith, what is said is not manifest to everyone, nor does the wicked hesitate to teach what is contrary. For the saying, “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged,” concerns conduct, not faith. What follows makes this clear: “Why do you see the splinter in your brother’s eye,” he says, “but do not see the beam in your own eye?” Therefore, “Everything they tell you to do,” he says, “do.” To do concerns conduct, not faith. “But do not do according to their works.” Do you see how the subject is not doctrines but life and works?

“For they keep watch on your behalf, as those who will give an account.” Let rulers hear this also—not only those who are governed by rulers—how, just as he says that those who are governed ought to be obedient, so he also says that rulers and leaders ought to keep watch. [Col. 0181B] “I say this,” he says, “so that they may do it with joy and not with groaning; for this is not profitable for you.”

Observe that when rulers are despised, they ought not to inflict vengeance; their entire vengeance consists in weeping and groaning. For when a physician is despised by a sick person, he does not take revenge but weeps and groans. But you say that he groans; God takes vengeance on you. For if, when we groan over our own sins, we bring God’s mercy upon ourselves, when we groan because of the pride and contempt of others, do we not call upon God even more? Groaning will be worse than any vengeance. For when the person himself does not understand, the one who groans calls upon the Lord. And just as when a teacher is despised by a child, the pedagogue is compelled to approach the child more severely, so also those who [Col. 0181C] do not speak to disobedient disciples [are in danger].

“Pray for us, for we are confident that we have a good conscience, wishing to conduct ourselves well in all things.” Observe how these are prayers written as though to people who had been grieved, to those who were turning away and who regarded him as a transgressor, refusing even to hear his name. How, then, did he ask such things of those who obeyed him—things that one might expect from people who loved him? For this reason he established this point here, saying, “We are confident that we have a good conscience,” as though he were saying, “I do not want you to bring any accusations against me.”

“Our conscience,” he says, “condemns us in nothing, nor are we conscious of having laid any snares for you.” “We are confident,” he says, [Col. 0181D] “that we have a good conscience in all things,” not only among the nations but also among you. “We did nothing for the sake of profit; we produced no fabricated teaching”—for perhaps he was accused of such things. “They have heard,” he says, “that you teach defection from the law.” “I do not write these things,” he says, “as an enemy or as a foe, but as a friend.” This is also shown by what follows.

“Moreover, I urge you to do this, so that I may be restored to you more quickly.” This belongs to someone who loves greatly: to pray in this way, not casually, but with complete earnestness and every possible effort. “So that I may come to you quickly,” he says. This is the disposition of one conscious of no wrongdoing, hastening to come to them swiftly, to exhort them and pray for them [Col. 0182A] that this might be granted to him. First he asks prayers from them; then he himself prays for every good thing on their behalf.

“Now may the God of peace, who brought back from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep, our Lord Jesus Christ, by the blood of the eternal covenant, equip you in every good work so that you may do his will, accomplishing in you what is pleasing in his sight through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.”

“The God of peace,” he says; therefore, if you wish to have the Lord propitious, do not disagree with us. “Who brought back,” he says, “from the earth the great shepherd.” This was spoken of the resurrection. From this point to the end of the prayer he confirms for them the truth of the resurrection and bears witness to their greater perfection. For this concerns those who have already made a beginning [Col. 0182B] and whose entire course is directed toward perfection; and he prays for them, which is characteristic of one who loves.

In the other Epistles he prays at the beginnings; here, at the end. “May he equip you,” he says, “in every good work so that you may do his will, accomplishing in you what is pleasing in his sight.” Observe how he shows that virtue can be implanted: he does not say that everything comes from the Lord, nor that it is perfected solely by us. For when he says, “May he perfect you in every good work,” he means this: “You possess virtue, but you need completion.”

What does he mean by “in every good work and word”? That they should have both an upright life and sound doctrines. “According to his will,” he says, “accomplishing in you what is pleasing in his sight.” This indeed is the greatest virtue: to do what is pleasing [Col. 0182C] in the sight of God, as the Prophet also says: “And according to the cleanness of my hands in the sight of his eyes.” For this there is truly a reward in heaven, granted by our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XX. ALSO WEDNESDAY

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Mark.

“At that time, rising early on the first day of the week, Jesus appeared first to Mary Magdalene,” etc.

John teaches most fully how and where this appearance took place. The Lord rose early from the tomb in which, when evening had already come, he had been laid, [Col. 0182D] so that the Psalmist’s saying might be fulfilled: “In the evening weeping will remain, and in the morning gladness.” He was buried on the sixth day of the week, which is called the Day of Preparation, around evening; he remained in the tomb through the following night and day of the Sabbath and the succeeding night, and thus on the third day—that is, early on the first day of the week—he rose. “He appeared,” it says, “first to Mary Magdalene,” from whom he had cast out seven demons.

She went and announced it to those who had been with him, mourning and weeping. Just as in the beginning a woman was the author of guilt for a man, and a man the executor of error, so now the woman who had first tasted death was the first to see the resurrection. And lest she suffer among men the reproach of perpetual guilt, she who had transmitted guilt to the man also transmitted grace. [Col. 0183A] Hence this woman, who first announced the joy of the Lord’s resurrection to the men who were mourning and weeping, is rightly remembered as having been healed of seven demons, so that it might be signified that she had been full of every vice but cleansed from all of them by divine gift, and that where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more.

And when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they did not believe. The fact that the disciples were slow to believe the Lord’s resurrection was not so much their weakness as, so to speak, our future firmness. For his resurrection itself was demonstrated to those who doubted by many proofs; when we recognize these as we read them, what else happens than that we are strengthened by their solid doubt? Mary Magdalene, [Col. 0183B] who believed more quickly, benefited me less than Thomas, who doubted for a long time. For while doubting, he touched the scars of the wounds and cut away the wound of doubt from our hearts.

After this he appeared in another form to two of them as they were walking and going into the country; and they went and reported it to the others. Luke explains more fully how this happened. What Mark says—“he was manifested in another form”—Luke states more clearly: their eyes were held so that they would not recognize him, until, when they arrived with him at the village to which they were going and set a table before him as though he were a stranger, they finally recognized him in the breaking of the bread.

As that same Luke immediately adds: “Rising at that same hour, they returned to Jerusalem and found the eleven gathered together, and those who were with them, saying, ‘The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon.’ And they recounted what had happened on the way and how they had recognized him in the breaking of the bread.”

When Mark says, “They announced it to the others, and they did not believe them,” while Luke says that they were already saying that he had truly risen and had appeared to Simon, what are we to understand [Col. 0183C] except that some were there who did not want to believe this? Who would not see that Mark omitted what Luke explained in his narrative—namely, what Jesus had said to them before they recognized him and how they recognized him in the breaking of the bread?

For as soon as Mark said that he had appeared in another form to those going into the country, he immediately added, “They went and announced it to the others, and they did not believe them,” as though they could announce someone whom they had not recognized, or could recognize someone [Col. 0183D] whose form had appeared different to them. How they recognized him so that they could announce him Mark undoubtedly omitted.

This should be committed to memory so that we may become accustomed to noticing the evangelists’ practice of omitting what they do not mention and joining together what they do mention. Otherwise, those who lack experience in considering such matters may be led into the greatest error by supposing that the evangelists do not agree with one another, although they had one faith, one baptism, and truly worshiped one God, who reigns in perfect Unity and Trinity forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXI. FRIDAY

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Matthew.

[Col. 0184A]

“At that time, the women went out quickly from the tomb with fear and great joy, running to announce it to his disciples,” etc.

A twofold emotion held the women’s minds: fear and joy—the one arising from the magnitude of the miracle, the other from their desire for the risen one. Yet each emotion quickened their feminine steps; they went to the apostles so that through them they might scatter the seed of faith. As the disciples ran to evangelize, Jesus met them and greeted them, showing that he comes to meet and assist all who begin the way of virtue, so that they may be able to reach everlasting salvation.

[Col. 0184B] Behold, Jesus met them, saying, “Greetings.” Those who sought him in this way, who ran in this manner, deserved to have the risen Lord meet them and to hear “Greetings” first, so that the curse of Eve the woman might be undone through women.

They approached, took hold of his feet, and worshiped him. These women approach and hold his feet because they worshiped him. But the woman who was seeking the living among the dead and did not yet know that the Son of God had risen rightly heard, “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father.”

Let us see the Lord rising from the dead in the truth of our flesh; let us see the glory of the new incorruption. Earlier it was read that he rose while the tomb was closed; now it is read that the women held [Col. 0184C] his feet and worshiped him. He rose through the closed entrance of the tomb and came out, to teach that the body which had been dead and shut within the tomb had already become immortal. He offered the soles of his feet to the women to be held, indicating that he truly possessed flesh which could be touched by mortals.

Then he said to them, “Do not be afraid.” In both the Old and the New Testament this should always be observed: whenever a more awe-inspiring vision appears, it first drives away fear, so that with a calm mind people may be able to hear what is said.

“Go, announce to my brothers that they should go to Galilee; there they will see me.” He calls those his brothers of whom it is said elsewhere, “I will announce your name to my brothers”—those who do not see the Savior in Judea [Col. 0184D] but among the multitude of the nations. Behold, he cut away the guilt of the human race at the place from which it arose. Because a woman in paradise gave death to a man, from the tomb a woman announced life to men; and she tells of the words of her life-giver who had previously recounted the deadly words of the serpent.

While they were going, some of the guards came into the city and announced to the chief priests everything that had happened. The simple quality of an uneducated and rustic mind often reveals the truth of a matter as it is, without deceit. By contrast, cunning malice and the practiced wickedness of a depraved mind, turning over its schemes, strives to commend falsehood as truth through plausible words and hastens to turn and gather many people to its agreement. [Col. 0185A] The following statement shows this.

After they had assembled with the elders and taken counsel, they gave the soldiers a large sum of money, saying, “Say that his disciples came by night and stole him while we were asleep.” Such miracles took place around the tomb that the very soldiers who had come as guards could have become witnesses if they had wished to report the truth. But that greed which had enslaved the disciple who accompanied Christ also enslaved the soldiers guarding the tomb.

“And if this comes to the governor’s ears, we will persuade him and make you secure.” The guards confess the miracle, hurry back to the city, and announce to the chief priests what they had seen and what they had witnessed. Those who had been uncertain and might have turned to repentance [Col. 0185B] and sought the risen Jesus persist in wickedness; and they turn the money that had been given for the temple’s uses into the purchase of a lie, just as earlier they had given thirty pieces of silver to Judas the betrayer. Therefore, all who misuse temple offerings and the contributions given for the uses of the Church for other purposes by which they satisfy their own desires are like the scribes and priests who purchased a lie and the blood of the Savior.

And they, having received the money, did as they had been instructed. O wicked plague, greed ever detestable to good minds, what do you leave unharmed, what unshaken? You first destroyed the human being; you confused the human race; you armed brothers of one mind for battle; you made the peaceful quarrelsome; you cast the disciple who accompanied Christ down from the apostleship; you enslaved the soldier who guarded the tomb; [Col. 0185C] you introduced the most wicked error into the world; and you led astray an ancient and once most noble people. Hence it follows:

“And this saying has been spread among the Jews to the present day.” To this day that error remains among the Jews. And just as the guilt of blood that they invoked upon themselves and their descendants presses heavily upon them as a burden of sins, so the purchase of the lie by which they deny the truth of the resurrection binds them in perpetual guilt, as they continually reject Christ and await the Antichrist. Thus those who sold the truth for a cheap price may seize the fullness of error upon their own head, and, when the just Judge repays them, receive everlasting punishment forever and ever. [Col. 0185D] Amen.

For the reading and Gospel at the CONCEPTION OF SAINT MARY, see the readings for month X, Wednesday of the second week before Christmas.

Reading from the prophet Isaiah.

“In those days the Lord spoke to Ahaz, saying: Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God, either in the depth of hell or in the height above.”

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Luke.

“At that time, the angel Gabriel was sent by God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin’s name was Mary.”

## HOMILY XXII. FIRST SUNDAY AFTER THE OCTAVE OF EASTER

Reading from the Epistle of blessed Peter the Apostle.

“Beloved, Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example so that you might follow in his footsteps. He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but handed himself over to the one who judges unjustly.”

You have heard, “Christ suffered for you,” and you rejoice because Christ died for you. Attend to what follows: “Leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his footsteps”—an example of tribulations, not pleasures; [Col. 0186C] of insults, scourging, pains, reproaches, thorns, the cross, wounds, and death. It is written in the Psalm: “Because of the words of your lips I have kept the hard ways.” Because of what words of God’s lips, if not those by which he promises eternal life?

“He himself bore our sins in his body upon the wood, so that, having died to sins, we might live for righteousness; by his death you have been healed.” Earlier he had addressed servants in particular; now he admonishes everyone in general, so that he may also remind masters what the Lord God endured for them. Indeed, he instructs the whole Church concerning what its author endured for its liberation. For he does not say “your sins,” but adds himself as well: “He himself bore our sins in his body upon the wood.”

[Col. 0186D] “For you were like wandering sheep.” How does he call them both sheep and wandering, when those who lead their lives in error are counted by the name of goats rather than sheep? Unless it is because the Lord knows who are his, and sustains many who have long lived badly, though he foresees that they will be saved among the number of his sheep.

“But now you have returned to the shepherd and bishop of your souls.” He touches on the Gospel parable in which the merciful shepherd, leaving the ninety-nine sheep in the wilderness, came to visit the one that had gone astray. For what is said there—that after finding it he placed it joyfully upon his shoulders—is anticipated here by blessed Peter: “He himself bore our sins in his body upon the wood.” For he wished to redeem us in such a way [Col. 0187A] that he would carry upon his shoulders the wood on which he would take away sins.

“To the shepherd,” he says, “and overseer of your souls.” He is the shepherd because he gives us the pastures of eternal life and, in the present, provides the pastures of temporal graces. He is the overseer of your souls because “the dayspring from on high has visited us, to enlighten those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death.” He visits daily that light which he has given us, preserving it so that it does not fail—or rather, helping it to increase. Some manuscripts have the Greek itself: “to the shepherd and bishop of your souls.” In Latin, *episcopus* means “overseer,” because truly “the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayers, and he delivered them from all their tribulations.” [Col. 0187B] To him be glory, honor, and power forever and ever.

## HOMILY XXIII. ON THE SAME FEAST

Reading from the holy Gospel according to John.

“At that time Jesus said to his disciples: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd gives his life for his sheep,” etc.

When the Lord wished to show the work of the good shepherd, he presented himself as an example, saying, “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep.” He did what he commanded; he demonstrated what he ordered: he laid down his life for his sheep. He showed us a path of contempt for death to follow and provided a pattern to which we should conform. First, we must mercifully devote our external possessions to his sheep; finally, if necessary, [Col. 0187C] we must also offer our own death for those same sheep. Whoever does not give his possessions for the sheep, how will he give his life?

We have explained—or rather, learned through the Lord’s teaching—who the shepherd is, who the door is, who the gatekeeper is, and who the sheep are; we have also learned who the thieves and robbers are. But now let us consider the hired hand and the wolf, concerning whom the Lord himself said:

“But the hired hand, who is not the shepherd and whose own the sheep are not, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees.” He is called not a shepherd but a hired hand who feeds the Lord’s sheep not out of inward love but for temporal wages. For the hired hand is one who indeed occupies the shepherd’s place but does not seek the profit of souls; he longs for earthly advantages, rejoices in the honor of authority, is nourished by temporal gains, and is pleased by the respect shown him by human beings. [Col. 0187D] These are the wages of the hired hand: that, for the very labor he undertakes in government, he finds here what he seeks and remains excluded from the flock’s inheritance in the future.

“And the wolf seizes and scatters the sheep.” The wolf seizes and scatters the sheep when he draws one person into lust, inflames another with greed, raises another up in pride, divides another through anger, goads one with envy, and trips another through deceit. Thus the devil, through temptations, disperses the flock and destroys the people of the faithful. Against all this, the hired hand is stirred by no zeal and aroused by no fervor of love, because while he seeks only external advantages, [Col. 0188A] he negligently tolerates the inner losses of the flock.

“But the hired hand flees because he is a hired hand and does not care about the sheep.” The sole reason for the hired hand’s flight is that he is a hired hand. It is as though it were openly said: He cannot stand firm in danger for the sheep who, while placed over the sheep, does not love the sheep but seeks earthly profit. While he embraces honor and rejoices in temporal advantages, he trembles to oppose danger, lest he lose what he loves.

Likewise, the wolf comes upon the sheep when any unjust and rapacious person oppresses the faithful and the humble. But the one who seemed to be a shepherd and was not one leaves the sheep and flees, because, fearing danger to himself from that person, he does not dare resist his injustice. He flees not by changing his location but by withdrawing his assistance. He flees who sees injustice and remains silent; he flees who hides himself under silence.

[Col. 0188B] But there is another wolf who every day, without ceasing, tears apart not bodies but minds: namely, the evil spirit, who prowls around the sheepfolds of the faithful, lying in wait and seeking the deaths of souls. “I am the good shepherd.” Because our Redeemer earlier made known the faults of the false shepherd, he again shows the pattern to which we ought to conform, saying:

“I am the good shepherd.” And he adds: “And I know my own”—that is, I love them. “And my own know me”—that is, they obey me because they love me.

“As the Father knows me, and I know the Father; and I lay down my life for my sheep.” It is as though he openly said: “This is how it is evident that I know the Father and am known by the Father: I lay down my life for my sheep.” [Col. 0188C] That is, by the love with which I die for the sheep, I show how greatly I love the Father.

But because he had come to redeem not only Judea but also the nations, he adds:

“And I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one flock and one shepherd.” The Lord had looked upon our redemption—we who have come from the Gentile people—when he said that he would bring in other sheep. Brothers, you see this happening every day; today you see this accomplished in the reconciliation of the nations. He has made one fold from two flocks, because he joins the Jewish and Gentile peoples in his faith, as Paul attests when he says: “He is our peace, who made both one.” For when he chooses the simple-hearted from both nations for eternal life, [Col. 0188D] he leads the sheep into his own fold.

Therefore, in these two flocks and in the one shepherd there is a fitting harmony of the readings, where the harmony of the head and the members is displayed—a harmony that exists in Christ and the Church. For Christ Jesus, the one mediator between God and human beings, rejoices and reigns together with his members, that is, with all the elect, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXIV. WEDNESDAY

Reading from the Epistle of blessed Peter the Apostle.

“Beloved, knowing that you were redeemed from your futile way of life [Col. 0189A] inherited from your ancestors, not with perishable things, gold or silver, but with precious blood, as of a spotless and undefiled lamb, Jesus Christ,” etc.

The greater the price by which you were redeemed from the corruption of bodily life, the more you ought to fear lest, by returning to the corruption of vices, you offend the mind of your Redeemer. You were reborn not from corruptible seed but from incorruptible seed, through the word of the living God that endures forever. Thus it is in the Gospel of John: “To those who believe in his name, who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of man, but of God.” Therefore, just as incorruptible is the price of the Lord’s Passion by which we were redeemed, so also incorruptible is the sacrament of the sacred font by which we are reborn. These two are so joined to one another that one cannot confer salvation upon us without the other, [Col. 0189B] because the Lord, at the time of his Incarnation, redeemed us all together by his sacred blood in such a way that we too, in our own time, must attain individually through the regeneration of baptism a share in that same regeneration.

Concerning this regeneration it is rightly said that it takes place “not from corruptible seed, but through the word of the living God that endures forever,” so that from this we may understand that, just as corruptible flesh is born from corruptible seed and itself decays, so through water consecrated by the word of God a life that knows no end is bestowed upon us. He also aptly establishes this by prophetic testimony, adding: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass; the grass withers and the flower falls, but the word of the Lord remains forever.” Therefore, just as corruptible flesh generates corruptible flesh, [Col. 0189C] so the word of the Lord, which remains forever, gives those whom it renews from water eternal life in both flesh and soul.

Saint Cyprian, in his book *On the Attire of Virgins*, recalls this testimony as follows: “God says to Isaiah: ‘Cry out: All flesh is grass, and all its brightness is like the flower of grass; the grass has withered and the flower has fallen, but the word of the Lord will remain forever.’ It is fitting for no Christian, and especially for no virgin, to reckon any brightness or honor of the flesh as valuable, but only to desire the word of God and embrace good things that will remain forever. Or, if the flesh is to glory, then plainly it should glory when it is tortured in confession of Christ’s name, because then the woman is found stronger than the men who torture her, when she endures fires, crosses, iron, or wild beasts in order to be crowned. Those are the precious [Col. 0189D] jewels of the flesh, better than bodily adornment; and through the tortures of the flesh, in which the soul is adorned by patience, he prepares everlasting glory for the holy and faithful.” This is granted by our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXV. ALSO ON WEDNESDAY

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Luke.

“At that time, very early on the first day of the week, they came to the tomb, bringing the spices they had prepared,” etc.

“On the first day of the week,” or “the first of the Sabbath,” means the first day after the Sabbath. Christian custom has called this day the Lord’s Day because of the Lord’s resurrection. As for the women coming to the tomb very early, historically this reveals the great fervor of their love in seeking and finding the Lord; mystically, however, it gives us an example: with enlightened faces and the darkness of vices dispelled, we should approach the most holy body of the Lord. That venerable tomb also represented the Lord’s altar, on which the mysteries of his flesh and blood are customarily celebrated. The spices that the women carry signify the fragrance and sweetness of the virtues and prayers with which we ought to approach the altar. Hence John, in his Apocalypse, after describing golden bowls in the hands of the angels—that is, pure consciences in the hearts of the elect—filled with incense, [Col. 0190B] added an explanation, saying: “These are the prayers of the saints.”

“And they found the stone rolled away from the tomb, and when they entered they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus.” Matthew sufficiently explained how the stone was rolled away by an angel. Mystically, however, the rolling away of the stone signifies the opening of the mysteries that had been covered by the veil of the letter. The Law was written on stone; once its covering has been removed, the dead body of the Lord is not found, but he is proclaimed alive. For although we have known Christ according to the flesh, now we know him no longer in that way.

“And it happened, while they were bewildered in mind about this, behold, two men stood beside them in shining garments.” They were bewildered in mind because they were astonished that a stone of such immense [Col. 0190C] size had been rolled away, and they grieved that a body worthy of such exceptional veneration had not been found. Just as, when the Lord was tempted in the wilderness, angels came to minister to him immediately after his victory had been completed, so, after the Savior had suffered in the flesh, following his battles with death and his victory over it, angels came to announce the glory of the triumphant one—not only with consoling words but also with radiant garments.

Since angels are said to have stood beside the Savior when he was placed in the tomb, so too we must believe that they stand by during the consecration of the mysteries of that same most sacred body. The Apostle warns that women should have a veil in the Church “because of the angels.”

“And as they were afraid and bowed their faces to the ground, they said to them: ‘Why do you seek the living among the dead?’” [Col. 0190D] “He is not here, but has risen.” “Do not,” they say, “seek among the dead”—that is, in the tomb, which is properly a place of the dead—the one who has already risen from the dead to life.

We too, following the example of these women devoted to God, whenever we enter a church and approach the heavenly mysteries, should enter with complete humility and fear, whether because of the presence of the angelic power or because of reverence for the sacred offering. We bow our faces to the ground in the sight of the angels when, contemplating the eternal joys of the citizens above, we humbly remember that we are dust and earth, as blessed Abraham said: “I shall speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes.” It should be noted that the holy women, while angels stood beside them, are said not to have fallen to the ground but to have bowed their faces toward the ground. Nor do we read that any of the saints, at the time of the Lord’s resurrection, worshiped prostrate on the earth either the Lord himself or the angels who appeared to them. Hence the ecclesiastical custom has arisen that, both in memory of the Lord’s resurrection and in hope of our own resurrection, on all Sundays and throughout the entire period of Pentecost we pray not on bent knees but with our faces bowed toward the ground.

“Remember how he spoke to you while he was still in Galilee, saying: ‘The Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinners, and be crucified, and on the third day rise again.’” On the third day the Lord celebrated his triumph of resurrection, just as he himself—something we learn from this passage—had foretold it among the disciples, to the women as well as to the men who followed him. For, handing over his spirit at the ninth hour on the day of Preparation, he was buried in the evening and rose in the morning on the first day of the week, as the evangelist Mark clearly indicates.

It was therefore not without reason that he lay in the tomb for one day and two nights: he joined the light of his single death to the darkness of our double death. He came to us, who were held in the death of spirit and flesh; he brought to us one death of his own—that is, the death of the flesh—and by taking upon himself our two deaths, he dissolved them. If he had assumed both deaths himself, he would have freed us from none. Mercifully he accepted his own single death and justly condemned both of ours; he joined his single death to our double death and, by dying, subdued our double death.

“And they remembered his words.” The women standing in the Lord’s tomb remembered the words he had spoken concerning his saving dispensation. They provide us with a model, so that while the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion are being celebrated, we may always remember with fitting reverence not only that Passion but also his resurrection from the dead and his glorious ascension into heaven.

“And returning from the tomb, they announced all these things to the eleven and to all the others.” Just as at the beginning a woman was the author of guilt for a man, while the man carried out the error, so now she who had first tasted death was the first to see the resurrection. And, lest she endure among men the reproach of perpetual guilt, she who had transmitted guilt to a man also transmitted grace.

“It was Mary Magdalene, and Joanna, and Mary the mother of James, and the other women who were with them, who told these things to the apostles.” Mary Magdalene was the sister of Lazarus, [Col. 0191D] who anointed the Lord with ointment. Joanna was the wife of Chuza, Herod’s steward; they have been mentioned above. Mary of James was the mother of James the younger and Joseph and, as the evangelist Mark says, the sister of the Lord’s mother. Hence James himself deserved to be called the Lord’s brother.

“And these words appeared to them like delirium, and they did not believe them.” That the disciples were slow to believe the Lord’s resurrection was not so much their weakness as, so to speak, a future strengthening of our faith. His resurrection itself was demonstrated to those who doubted by many proofs; when we recognize these as we read, what else do we do but become firmly established through their doubt?

“But Peter rose and ran to the tomb, and bending down he saw only the linen cloths lying there, and he went away, wondering to himself.” Luke briefly recalls what happened concerning Peter’s running. John, however, explains more fully how it occurred, saying that the disciple whom Jesus loved also ran with Peter—thereby indicating himself. It is therefore asked how Luke can say of Peter, “And bending down he saw only the linen cloths lying there,” when John seems to indicate that he himself did this, while Peter, entering the tomb, saw not only the linen cloths but also the cloth that had been over his head.

It should be understood that Peter first bent down and saw what Luke records and John passes over in silence. Afterwards he entered, so that he might examine the interior more carefully; nevertheless, he entered before John. Yet both of them, [Col. 0192B] united to their Redeemer by perfect love, will therefore rejoice with him forever, dwelling together with the holy angels in the joy of the heavenly kingdom. Amen.

## HOMILY XXVI. ON FRIDAY

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Matthew.

“At that time, the disciples of John approached Jesus, saying: ‘Why do we and the Pharisees fast frequently, but your disciples do not fast?’”

A proud question, full of Pharisaic arrogance; even if we say nothing else, it must certainly be condemned as boastful display of fasting. Nor could the disciples of John be free from blame when they slandered the one whom they knew had been proclaimed by the voice of their teacher, and joined themselves to the Pharisees whom they knew John had condemned when he said: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the wrath to come?”

Jesus said to them: “Can the children of the bridegroom mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast.” If Christ is the bridegroom, the Church is the bride. From this spiritual marriage the apostles were born; they cannot mourn as long as they see the bride in the bridal chamber and know that the bridegroom is with the bride. But when the wedding has passed and the time of the Passion and resurrection has arrived, then the children of the bridegroom will fast.

Some think that for this reason the fasts of the Passion ought to be undertaken after forty days, although the immediate arrival of Pentecost and the Holy Spirit indicates a festival for us. On the occasion of this testimony, Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla also observe a forty-day fast after Pentecost, on the grounds that, once the bridegroom has been taken away, the bridegroom’s children ought to fast. The custom of the Church, however, approaches the Lord’s Passion and resurrection through humility of the flesh, so that we may prepare ourselves for spiritual nourishment by bodily fasting.

According to the rules of allegorical interpretation, we should understand that as long as the bridegroom is with us and we are in joy, we can neither fast nor mourn. But when he has withdrawn and flown away from us because of our sins, then fasting must be imposed and mourning undertaken.

“No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth onto an old garment; otherwise it tears away its fullness from the garment, and a worse tear results. Nor do they put new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the skins will burst, the wine will be spilled, and the skins will be ruined. But they put new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved.”

What he says means this: until someone has been reborn and, having laid aside the old man through my Passion, has put on the new man, he cannot endure the stricter commands of fasting and self-restraint, lest through excessive severity he also lose the faith that he now appears to possess.

He offered two examples, of garments and of old and new wineskins. By the old we should understand the scribes and Pharisees; by the patch of new cloth and the new wine, the evangelical commandments, which the Jews cannot bear lest a greater tear result. The Galatians too wished to do something of this kind, mixing the commandments of the Law with the Gospel [Col. 0193B] and putting new wine into old wineskins. But the Apostle says to them: “O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you into not obeying the truth?”

The evangelical word, therefore, should be entrusted more appropriately to the apostles than to the scribes and Pharisees, who, corrupted by the traditions of their ancestors, could not preserve the purity of Christ’s commandments. For one thing is the purity of a virginal soul, polluted by no contagion of former vice, and another are the stains of one who has been subject to the lust of many. Hence it is necessary that each person first wash away the stains of vices and cleanse the oldness of sin through repentance; then, with the Lord’s help, knowledge of the virtues and spiritual teaching may be granted through Christ’s generosity. He lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, through [Col. 0193C] all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXVII. SECOND SUNDAY AFTER THE OCTAVE OF EASTER

Reading from the Epistle of Blessed Peter the Apostle.

“Beloved, I beseech you as foreigners and pilgrims,” etc.

In Latin, *advenae* means “proselytes.” The Jews used this name for those born among the nations who wished to believe in God, receive circumcision, and live according to Jewish custom in accordance with God’s Law. Some of those who believed in Christ at the apostles’ preaching on the holy day of Pentecost, when the apostles received the Holy Spirit in the appearance of fire, belonged to this number; Scripture says that Jews and proselytes were also present.

But if we can truthfully say to God with the Prophet, [Col. 0193D] “For we are resident foreigners with you on the earth, and pilgrims like all our fathers,” then we too ought to believe that the Epistles of blessed Peter were written for us and read as though they had been sent to us.

“Abstain from fleshly desires, which wage war against the soul.” While the flesh is weakly subjected to flattering desires, the army of vices is already firmly armed against the soul. He appropriately calls them foreigners and pilgrims, so that they may submit their souls less to earthly things because they remember that they have their homeland in heaven.

In this life there is usually this difference between the elect and the reprobate: the elect, as pilgrims and exiles, await what is to come, and they take correspondingly less delight in present and transient joys because they hope to receive future joys without end and reign with Christ forever. The reprobate, however, have their homeland here; they know how to yearn only for the desires of this life. Therefore, after this life they are banished into perpetual exile, where, deprived of every pleasure, they suffer only adversity amid torments.

“Maintain good conduct among the nations, so that, when they slander you as evildoers, they may observe your good works and glorify God on the day of visitation.” It often happens that pagans who had criticized the Christian faith because Christians had abandoned their gods later, observing their chaste conduct and unconquered spirit in Christ, ceased to slander them. Instead, they began to glorify and praise God, who was shown to be good and just by the goodness and justice of his worshipers.

“Let them glorify,” he says, “God on the day of visitation”—that is, at the time of recompense. Let unbelievers already recognize how great a glory is to be given to you by God when they see you persistently following him through dangers that stand in your way.

“Be subject to every human creature for God’s sake.” By “every human creature” he means every human dignity, every person, every authority to which divine ordering has wished you to be subject. This is what he means by “for God’s sake,” because “there is no authority except from God, and whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance.”

Then, by adding which creature he means, he explains: “Whether to the king, as superior, or to governors, as sent by him.” [Col. 0194C] He mentions only the king and governors, not masters, because at this point he is instructing specifically those whom we have said are masters of servants; afterwards he admonishes servants concerning how they should serve their masters. He therefore teaches the faithful servants of the eternal King to be subject even to the powers of the world, lest in this respect too the rights of their Christian condition and religion be disturbed.

What was said—“to every human creature”—may also rightly be understood to signify both faithful and unbelieving masters of earthly possessions.

“For the punishment of evildoers and the praise of those who do good.” This does not mean that all governors sent by kings know how to punish evildoers and praise the good. Rather, he simply describes what the conduct of a good governor ought to be: that he restrain those who do evil and reward those who do good. Even if he acts unjustly and condemns the good, what he does nevertheless contributes to their praise if they patiently resist his folly.

Hence Paul also says: “Do you wish not to fear authority? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it.” He does not say “by it” but “from it,” because even if worldly authority does not praise you—or even persecutes you, kills you with the sword as it did Paul, or crucifies you as it did Peter—you will receive praise from it, since, from the fact that it does evil to you, who are just and innocent, the patience of your virtue earns a crown of praise.

The following words show that blessed Peter intended this very point in the present sentence:

“For this is the will of God: that by doing good you silence the ignorance of foolish men.” This, then, is the praise of the good for which he says governors are sent by the king: by doing good, the good use the ignorance of foolish governors for their own perpetual praise.

“As free people, yet not using freedom as a covering for evil.” Those do good as free people who, following the example of the patriarch Joseph, although weighed down by human servitude, are compelled by no device to be servants of vices. But they turn their freedom into a covering for evil who, the less they are restrained by the yoke of human service, the more widely they become enslaved to the dominion of sins. When they serve their vices with impunity, they call it freedom; under this name they conceal their guilt.

This may also be understood generally according to the words of the Apostle Paul: “You were called to freedom, brothers; only do not use freedom as an opportunity for the flesh.” We are rightly called free [Col. 0195B] because through baptism we have been released from the bonds of sins, redeemed from demonic servitude, and made children of God.

Nevertheless, through the gift of freedom we do not receive a greater opportunity or license to sin. On the contrary, if we sin, we immediately become servants of sin, having lost our freedom. Whoever thinks that he received freedom from the Lord so that he might sin more freely turns his freedom into a covering for evil. Blessed Peter wants us to be free from the service of guilt, so that we may remain servants of our good and faithful Creator. Hence he adds:

“But as servants of God, honor everyone, love the brotherhood, fear God, honor the king.” He therefore urges us to show fitting honor to everyone, and, in accordance with the Lord’s command, to render to Caesar what belongs to Caesar and to God [Col. 0195C] what belongs to God. Well does he command free people, among other things, to love the brotherhood, so that they may remember that even those who are subject to them in temporal condition have been made their brothers in Christ, invoking with them the Father—he who judges without partiality.

“Servants, be subject in all fear to your masters, not only to the good and gentle but also to the difficult.” By “difficult” he means undisciplined people, using a term derived from Greek speech. In Greek, *scholē*—σχολή—is the name for a place where young men usually devote themselves to literary studies and spend their time listening to teachers; hence *scholē* is interpreted as “leisure” or “freedom from other occupations.”

Finally, in the psalm where we sing, “Be at leisure and see that I am God,” the Greek has *scholaste* for what we call “be at leisure.” Thus the *scholastici* are educated people; the *dyscoli*—δυσκολοί—are uneducated and rustic people. Yet he wants subjects to obey both, explaining more clearly how above he commanded us to be subject to every human creature.

Another edition has “more difficult” in place of “difficult,” and Saint Bishop Fulgentius gives the passage in his little works as follows: “Serve with fear, not only the good but also the more difficult. For this is grace in Christ Jesus, if, while doing good, you endure patiently.”

“For this is grace in Christ Jesus.” This, then, is grace before God. For you were called to this, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, etc. We should observe carefully how greatly he glorifies the condition of servants: he declares that those who do good and are beaten without guilt by cruel and wicked masters are imitators of the Lord’s Passion. [Col. 0196A] Whoever willingly and patiently wishes to share in Christ’s Passion in the present life will undoubtedly share in his glory in the future life. There he will remain forever exulting in his praises together with the holy angels. This is granted by our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who lives and reigns with the Father through ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXVIII. ON THE SAME FEAST

Reading from the holy Gospel according to John.

“At that time, Jesus said to his disciples: ‘A little while, and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me.’”

These words apply especially to those who deserved to cling to his discipleship while he preached in the flesh, and, after the sorrow of the Passion, to rejoice when they saw his resurrection and ascension. The interval from the hour of that night when he was betrayed to the hour of his Passion was also short, or it was short while the disciples saw him according to the flesh. Again, the time during which he lay shut in the tomb, destined to rise on the third day, was short, when he could not be seen by them. This is what he says: “A little while, and you will not see me.”

But when he says, “Again a little while, and you will see me,” he signifies the period after the resurrection during which he lived with the disciples and appeared to them in many ways, until he ascended into heaven while they watched, as we read in the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles. This is what he says:

“Because I am going to the Father.” It is as though he were saying plainly: “After a little while I shall be hidden from your sight within the enclosure of the tomb, and again after a little while, having destroyed the dominion of death, I shall appear for you to see, because the time has come for me, having completed the dispensation of the mortality I assumed, to return to the Father with the triumph of the resurrection.”

As we have said, these words apply specifically to those who were able to see his resurrection, though the apostles at that time could not understand them. The compassionate teacher, recognizing their ignorance, subsequently answered in accordance with the doubt in their minds, as though he were explaining what he meant by saying, “A little while, and you will not see me; again a little while, and you will see me.”

“Jesus knew that they wanted to question him and said to them: ‘Are you asking one another about this, because I said, “A little while, and you will not see me; again a little while, and you will see me”?’ Amen, amen, I say to you: you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice; you will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will be turned into joy.”

This applies both to them and to the condition of the whole Church. The lovers of Christ wept and lamented when they saw him seized by his enemies, bound, led before the council, condemned, crucified, killed, and buried. The lovers of the world rejoiced—those whom the Lord calls “the world” because of their low and earthly thinking—when they condemned to a most shameful death the one whose very presence was burdensome for them to see.

The disciples were sorrowful when he had been placed in death, but once they recognized his resurrection their sorrow was turned into joy. When the power of his ascension was revealed, they were lifted up by still greater joy and praised and blessed the Lord, as the evangelist Luke testifies. The Lord’s saying also applies to all the faithful, who strive to reach eternal joys through present tears and afflictions: “Those who sow in tears will reap in joy; going forth, they went and wept,” so that in eternal blessedness they may receive the reward of their labor.

But “the world”—that is, the lovers of the world—will rejoice. They disdain to prepare themselves for eternal joys through tears and afflictions. You, however, will be sorrowful through labors and troubles, but your sorrow will be changed into the joy of eternal blessedness.

“A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow because her hour has come.” By “the woman” he means the holy Church, because of the fruitfulness of her good works and because she never ceases to bear spiritual children for the Lord. This woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow because her hour has come.

“But when she has given birth to the child, she no longer remembers her distress because of the joy that a human being has been born into the world.” The holy Church, as long as she devotes herself in the world to progress in spiritual virtues, never ceases to be tested by the world’s temptations. But when, having conquered the struggle of labors, she reaches the palm of victory, she no longer remembers her former distress because of the joy of the reward received. “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the glory that is to be revealed in us.”

“She does not remember,” he says, “her distress because of the joy that a human being has been born into the world.” Just as a woman rejoices when a human being is born into this world, so the Church is filled with worthy exultation when the people of the faithful are born into the future life. For this birth she labors and groans greatly in the present, suffering as though in labor.

No one should find it strange that someone who has departed from this life is said to have been born. Just as one is said to be born when one comes forth from the womb of one’s mother and emerges into this light, so the one who has been released from the bonds of the flesh and raised into eternal light can most rightly be called born. Hence the ecclesiastical custom has arisen of calling the days of the blessed martyrs or confessors of Christ, on which they departed from this world, their “birthdays,” and of calling their solemn observances not funerals but celebrations of birth.

“And so you too now have sorrow; but I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.” This is readily understood of the disciples themselves, because they were sorrowful when the Lord had suffered and been buried. But once the glory of the resurrection had been accomplished, they rejoiced when they saw the Lord, and no one took their joy from them. Although they suffered hardships and persecutions in this world, they always rejoiced in hope of the future reward because they were worthy to suffer insults for Jesus’ name.

“I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.” The Lord sees the elect after their sorrow when, having condemned their adversary, he rewards their patience. “I will see you,” that is, when I take you to myself, so that where I am, you also may be. In that vision of everlasting glory your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you, because there will be no adversary, no persecutor, no one to inflict sorrow on your souls, while the God of gods is seen in Zion.

## HOMILY XXIX. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE HOLY APOSTLES PHILIP AND JAMES

Reading from the Book of Wisdom.

“The righteous stood with great confidence against those who had oppressed them and taken away their labors.”

Divine Wisdom tells what the glory of the saints and the anguish of the reprobate will be at the final judgment, when they see the saints standing at God’s right hand in the glory of incorruption and immortality, awaiting the judgment of the merciful Judge, by which he invites them to the eternal kingdom. The reprobate will then rightly be condemned because they persecuted the saints, refused to obey their saving teaching, despised them with mockery, [Col. 0198B] and did not give them fitting honor.

Thus, when the reading was being read, you heard: “Then,” he says, “the righteous will stand with great confidence against those who oppressed them and took away their labors. Seeing them, they will be troubled by terrible fear and will be astonished at the suddenness of an unexpected salvation. Groaning in anguish of spirit, they will say among themselves in repentance: ‘These are the ones whom we once held up to ridicule and made the object of reproach. We foolishly considered their life madness and their end without honor. How then have they been counted among the sons of God, and how is their lot among the saints?’”

Then, indeed, the righteous will stand with great confidence against their persecutors, who afflicted them here with undeserved punishments and reproached their labors as though they were foolish, [Col. 0198C] when, revealed in heavenly brightness, they will become judges according to the truth of those who formerly condemned them unjustly.

When the reprobate see themselves suddenly transferred from glory to disgrace, and, conversely, their adversaries transferred from temporal affliction to heavenly honor, they will complain with late and fruitless repentance that previously, while it was permitted, they could have acted fruitfully if they had wished.

Therefore, whoever has lived his life negligently and served sins must, before the end of the present life, practice worthy repentance for the evils committed. By God’s grace, he must strive through good works to merit forgiveness of sins and attain eternal life. This is granted by our Redeemer, the Lord Jesus Christ, who wills all human beings to be saved [Col. 0198D] and to come to the knowledge of the truth, reigning as God with the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXX. ON THE SAME FEAST

Reading from the holy Gospel according to John.

“At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘Let not your heart be troubled. Believe in God, and believe in me,’” etc.

So that they would not fear death as human beings and consequently become troubled, he consoles them by also declaring that he is God. For it follows that if you believe in God, you ought also to believe in me; this would not follow if Christ were not God.

“In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places.” Because the merits of the saints are different, there are many dwelling places in the Father’s house. None of them will be excluded from that house; each will receive a dwelling place according to his merit. Therefore, “Let not your heart be troubled.” For one denarius will be given to all who labor in the vineyard—that is, to all who labor in the Church through faith—as eternal life. But the many dwelling places signify different dignities of merit within the one eternal life. God will be all in all, because God is love. Each person possesses what he himself does not have when he loves it in another, because the unity of love reigns in all.

“If not, I would have told you, because I am going to prepare a place for you.” How could the members have reached those dwelling places if the head had not gone before them? He prepared a place for us when he died for us and rose again—or rather, ascended into heaven. He did all these things for us, so that he might prepare a place for us in the kingdom of his Father.

“And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again to you.” If I go away through the absence of the flesh, I will come through the presence of divinity, in which I shall be with you until the consummation of the age. Or, if I go away by ascending into heaven, I will come again to judge the living and the dead. The angels testified to this when they said: “This Jesus, who has been taken up from you, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven.” The text continues:

“And I will take you to myself, so that where I am, you also may be.” This is what he said later: “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me.”

“And you know where I am going, and you know the way.” “Where I am going”—that is, to the Father—and the way by which one comes there is known.

[Col. 0199C] Thomas said to him: “Lord, we do not know where you are going; how can we know the way?” He appeared not to know what Christ was proving that he knew when he said:

“I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” It was as though he had said: “If you know me, you know the way. I am the one to whom one goes—that is, the truth—and I am the life in which one remains. If you know me, you know the way; you know where I am going and where you will remain. Those who go to the Father go through me, and those who come to the Father come to me, because I and the Father are one. They remain in me, because this is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent.”

Hence he continued, saying:

“No one comes to the Father except through me.” Explaining what he had said, “I am the way,” he immediately added:

“If you had known me, you would certainly have known my Father also, because I am the truth in the true Father. And from now on you know him and have seen him.” If you know and see me spiritually, you know and see him, because I and the Father are one—not one in person but one in nature.

Philip said to him, without understanding this: “Lord, show us the Father, and that is enough for us.” It was as though the Father were something better than the Son, in whose vision alone blessedness would be sufficient. The teacher rebuked the disciple for this statement:

“Have I been with you for so long a time, and you have not known me? Have you not known that I am in the Father and the Father is in me, Philip?”

[Col. 0200A] Whoever sees me sees the Father also. Whoever understands me certainly understands the Father in me as well. But the teacher rebuked the disciple for he saw the heart of the one who was asking. Philip desired to know the Father as though the Father were better than the Son; and for that reason he did not know the Son either, in comparison with whom he believed that something better existed. To correct this understanding it was said: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also.”

“How can you say, ‘Show us the Father’?” I see what you mean by saying this: you are not asking to see another who is like him, but you think that he is something better.

“Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” Why do you desire to know separately those who are inseparable? Then he addresses not Philip alone but them all:

[Col. 0200B] “The words that I speak to you I do not speak from myself. But the Father, remaining in me, himself does the works.” What does “I do not speak from myself” mean except “I am not from myself, who speak”? For he attributes what he does to the one from whom he himself is. God the Father is from no one, whereas the Son is indeed God, equal to the Father, but from God the Father. Therefore the Father is God but not from God, and light but not from light; the Son, however, is God from God, light from light. Finally he adds:

“Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? Otherwise, believe because of the works themselves.” At first Philip alone was being rebuked; now it is shown that he was not the only one there who needed rebuke. “Because of the works themselves,” he says, “believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me.” For if we were separated, we could in no way work inseparably. But what follows? “Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these, because I am going to the Father.”

Let not the servant exalt himself above his lord, nor the disciple above his teacher. He said that they would do greater works than he himself did, but without him—as he said below, what could they have done? Yet what are these greater works? Perhaps it is greater that the shadow of the apostles should heal the sick even as they passed by. For it is greater that a shadow should heal than a fringe: the latter was done by him in person, the former through them; yet both were done in him. Or perhaps the apostles’ works are greater because they brought salvation to all the nations, whereas Christ brought salvation only to the Jews, and to only a very few of them. Nevertheless, he accomplished both: salvation for some in Judea through himself, [Col. 0200D] and salvation for the nations through the apostles—and not only through the apostles but also through other preachers. Hence he continued:

“Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these.” This does not mean that the disciple is greater than the teacher, or the servant greater than the lord, or the adopted son greater than the Only-Begotten, or the human being greater than God; rather, it means that he himself deigned to accomplish those greater works through them. He immediately showed how they could do greater works, saying: “Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these.” He followed this at once by adding: “Because I am going to the Father.”

“And whatever you ask in my name, I will do.” He who said “will do” later says “I will do.” It is as though he were saying: “Let this not seem impossible to you; for whoever believes in me cannot be greater than I. Therefore he does not do greater works by himself, but through me, in whom he believes.” This is not a failure of power but a compassion arising from loving-kindness.

The rich man therefore went away from him sadly, refusing to receive the words of salvation; but when the apostles preached, many rich people followed poverty willingly. Thus what one man, hearing it from him, did not do, many did when the good teacher spoke through his disciples. Behold, he accomplished greater things when preached by believers than when speaking to hearers—but this was through the preachers. Are all who believe in him preachers? Yet he says that those who believe in him do greater works. In this work of faith we shall do the works of Christ, because believing in Christ itself is also a work; and Christ works in us, certainly not without us. First I act, grace going before; then he himself also acts, grace following, because I make it possible for him to act. What works, unless that the ungodly should be made righteous?
