Perhaps it is a greater work for us, through him, to do the works of our salvation than to preach the words of salvation—which he did without us when he said: “Because I am going to the Father. And whatever you ask in my name, I will do.” In these words he promised great hope to those who pray. Thus he went to the Father in such a way that he did not leave those in need, but heard those who asked. Yet he did not mean all requests, but those that pertain to the salvation of the petitioners. Therefore he said: “If you ask me for anything in my name, I will do it.” What does “in my name” mean except “in the name of the Savior”? If you ask for what pertains to your salvation, you have asked in my name. For when evil things please us and good things do not please us, we ought rather to ask God that good things may please us than that evil things may be granted.

Whoever therefore believes in him, whatever he asks in the name that has been given to those who believe in him, he does—doing it as Savior. But if one who believes in him, through ignorance, asks for something contrary to his salvation, he does not ask in the name of the Savior, because the Savior would not be his savior. If someone were to bring about what hinders his salvation, that one would not be his Savior. What is better or more beneficial to us than to be saved ourselves? Therefore we must ask that his will be done in us—he who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXI. WEDNESDAY

Reading from the Letter of the blessed apostle John.

[Col. 0201D]

“Beloved, I write these things to you so that you may not sin,” etc.

He is not contradicting himself when earlier he declared that we cannot live without sin, but now says that he is writing to us so that we may not sin. There he wisely warned us of our weakness, because of the necessity of providing for our welfare, so that no one might please himself as though he were innocent and perish more completely by exalting himself on the basis of his merits. Here, correspondingly, he urges us that, if we cannot be free from every fault, we should nevertheless do all that we can so that we do not live negligently by acting according to the weakness of our condition, but fight vigorously and watchfully against all vices—especially the greater and more evident ones, which, with the Lord’s help, we can more easily overcome and avoid—so that, in accordance with what Paul says, temptation may not seize us except in a human way, that is, only such temptation as human weakness cannot wholly avoid.

“But if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.” Observe how John preserves the humility that he teaches. Certainly he was a righteous and great man who drank the secrets of mysteries from the Lord’s breast. Yet he did not say, “You have an advocate with the Father,” but “we have an advocate”; he did not say “you have.” He preferred to place himself among sinners, so that he might have Christ as his advocate, rather than present himself as an advocate in Christ’s place and be found among the proud who are condemned.

Nevertheless, it must not be said that bishops or superiors do not pray for the people. The Apostle prays for the people, and the people pray for the Apostle, who says: “Praying together also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word.” The Church prayed for Peter when Peter was in chains, and she was heard; and likewise Peter prayed for the Church, because all the members pray for one another, while the head intercedes for all. Of him it is written: “Who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us.”

For the Only-Begotten Son to intercede for humanity means that he presents himself before the Father who is coeternal with him; and to ask for human nature means that he has taken that same nature into the height of his divinity. The Lord therefore intercedes for us not by a voice but by compassion, because, by assuming what he did not wish to condemn in the elect, he saved it. And rightly, when he said that we have Jesus Christ as our advocate with the Father, he added “the righteous.” A righteous advocate [Col. 0202C] does not undertake unjust causes; yet he defends the righteous in judgment if we acknowledge and accuse ourselves as unjust. For why should the one who already rages against his own injustice through tears not be righteous?

“And he himself is the propitiation for sins,” he who through humility intercedes for us with the Father—that is, through his divinity he is propitious to us together with the Father.

“Not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world.” The Lord is not propitiation only for those to whom John was writing while they were then living in the flesh, but also for the whole Church spread throughout the breadth of the world, extending from the first elect to the last person who will be born at the end of the world. By these words he condemns the schism of the Donatists, who said that Christ’s Church was confined to the boundaries of Africa alone. The Lord therefore intercedes for the sins of the whole world, because throughout the whole world is the Church that he purchased with his blood.

Nor does this conflict with what he says later: “The whole world lies in the evil one,” that is, in the ancient enemy. For there are also throughout the whole world those who serve the evil one, that is, the ancient enemy.

“And by this we know that we have known him, if we keep his commandments.” In what follows he makes clear which commandments he means: love.

“Whoever says that he knows him and does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him.” Christ is called the Truth: “I am,” he says, “the way and the truth and the life.” We therefore applaud ourselves in him in vain if we do not do his commandments; nor should we consider it a great thing to know the one God, since even the demons believe and tremble. But what it truly means to know God he next shows by saying:

“But whoever keeps his word, truly the love of God is perfected in him.” Therefore the one who truly knows God is the one who proves that he possesses his love by keeping his commandments. For to know God is to love him. Whoever does not love him clearly shows that he does not know how lovable he is; he has not learned to taste and see how sweet and good the Lord is, since he does not continually strive to please him in his sight.

“And by this we know that we are in him. Whoever says that he remains in him ought himself to walk as he walked,” that is, through abundant love even to pray for enemies, saying: “Father, forgive them”; but also to despise all the world’s prosperity with a courageous spirit, and willingly to endure mockery and reproach, as he himself says: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.”

“Beloved, I am not writing a new commandment to you, but the old commandment that you had from the beginning. The old commandment is the word that you heard; again, I am writing a new commandment to you.” The same love is both an old commandment, because it was commended from the beginning, and a new commandment, because, once darkness has been expelled, it instills the desire for new light. Hence it is rightly added:

“Which is true in him and in you, because the darkness has passed away and the true light is already shining.” Behold why it is new: darkness belongs to the old human being, whereas light belongs to the new human being. Finally the apostle Paul says: “Put off the old human being and put on the new.” And again: “Once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.”

Happy is the one who rejects the deeds of the old human being and rightly desires the conduct of the new human being, in accordance with what is written: “Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, so that his works may not be exposed. But whoever does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be revealed, because they have been done in God,” through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXII. ALSO ON WEDNESDAY

Reading from the holy Gospel according to John.

[Col. 0203D]

“At that time, a dispute arose among John’s disciples and the Jews concerning purification,” etc.

John’s disciples were jealous of their teacher because they saw more people coming together for Christ’s baptism and preferring Christ’s baptism to John’s. At last they came to John himself, so that he might resolve the dispute that had arisen between his disciples and the Jews concerning the distinction between Christ’s baptism and John’s baptism. They said to him:

“Rabbi, the one who was with you beyond the Jordan—look, he is baptizing, and everyone is coming to him.” As though indignant that more people had come to Christ’s baptism, they said: “Everyone is coming to him and leaving you, although he was baptized with your baptism—the one to whose baptism everyone is now flocking.”

He answered and said: “A person cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven.” You yourselves bear witness to me that I said: “I am not the Christ.” If you believe my testimony, know that I am not the Christ; but that he and his baptism are the ones in which there is forgiveness of sins and the Holy Spirit is given—not mine, in which only repentance was given, together with faith in the one about whom you are now complaining.

“A person cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven.” I have received the ministry that was given to me from heaven. I am the herald, he the judge; I am the servant, he the Lord; he is the bridegroom, I the friend of the bridegroom. He must increase, while I must decrease. I came to prepare his way, not to exalt myself; I am the voice of one crying out, he the Word of the Father. The one who comes after me has been placed before me, that is, he has been preferred to me in dignity. I am not worthy to untie the strap of his sandal—that is, to recount the mystery of his birth, by which he was born of a virgin and came into the world.

You have heard my testimony; believe my testimony; come together to him in whose baptism there is forgiveness of sins. This John was held in such great authority that he was thought by the people to be the Christ. But he rejected the false honor so that he might possess the solid truth. He did not wish to boast of being what he was not, lest he be without the one who always was.

“Whoever has the bride is the bridegroom.” I am not the bridegroom; but what am I? The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him and rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice. Who is the bridegroom? He of whom it is said: “God is king of the whole earth,” and “all the kings of the earth will worship him; all nations will serve him.” He is the true bridegroom. The bride is the holy Church, gathered from all nations, of whom the Apostle says: “I betrothed you to one man, to present a chaste virgin to Christ.”

The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice; he does not make joy for himself out of himself. For whoever wishes to rejoice in himself will be sad, whereas whoever wishes to rejoice in God will always rejoice, because God is everlasting. John declared himself to be such a friend. “The friend of the bridegroom,” he says, “will rejoice because of the bridegroom’s voice,” not because of his own voice. “And he stands and hears him.” Therefore, if he falls, he does not hear him. Of the one who once fell it was said—and this was said of the devil—“He did not stand in the truth.” Therefore the friend of the bridegroom must stand and hear. What does “stand” mean? To remain in the grace that he received, and to hear the voice at which he may rejoice.

John was such a person: he knew the source of his joy, and he did not claim for himself what he was not. He knew that he had been enlightened, not that he was the one who enlightens.

“He must increase, while I must decrease.” What does this mean? He must be exalted, while I must be humbled. This is a great mystery. Before the Lord Jesus came, human beings gloried in themselves. He came as a human being so that human glory might decrease and the glory of God increase. For he came without sin and found everyone with sin. If he came in order to forgive sins, let God give generously and let the human being confess. For human confession is humility, human misery; God is exalted. If therefore he came to forgive sins, let the human being acknowledge his humility, and God will show his mercy.

“The one who comes from above is above all,” that is, Christ. “The one who is from the earth is from the earth and speaks from the earth,” that is, John. How then does he speak from the earth? Every human being is earthly, and while he speaks earthly things, he speaks from the earth. But the one who has been enlightened by him who is the true light speaks of divine things.

“The one who comes from heaven is above all,” the Lord Jesus Christ, of whom it was said above: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.” He is above all.

“And what he has seen and heard, this he speaks.” For the Son of God himself has the Father; he has the Father and has heard from the Father.

“What he has seen and heard, he testifies, and no one accepts his testimony.” If no one accepts it, why did he come? “No one” therefore refers to some people. A certain people is being prepared for the wrath of God, to be condemned with the devil; none of them accepts Christ’s testimony. For if “no one” meant absolutely no human being, what is the meaning of what follows?

“Whoever accepts his testimony has certified that God is true.” Certainly then there is a “no one,” if you yourself say that whoever accepts his testimony has certified that the Lord is true.

“For the one whom God sent speaks the words of God.” He is truthful; he is God, and he is our Lord Jesus Christ, of whom the Apostle says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law.” “The one whom God sent speaks the words of God.” He was speaking this about Christ, in order to distinguish himself from him.

“For God does not give the Spirit by measure.” Hear the Apostle saying: “According to the measure of Christ’s gift, he gives to human beings by measure.” He does not give to the Only Son by measure. How does he give to human beings by measure? “To one is given through the Spirit the utterance of wisdom, to another the utterance of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another prophecy, to another the discernment of spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, and to another gifts of healings.”

“The Father loves the Son.” Why? The Father loves John, yet he did not give everything into his hand. The Father loves Paul, yet he did not give everything into his hand. The Father loves the Son—but as a father loves a son, not as a lord loves a servant; as the Only-Begotten, not as an adopted son.

“Therefore he has given everything into his hand.” What does “everything” mean? It means that the Son is as great as the Father. For the Lord—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—is one and almighty God, whose will is one and whose power is one, who exists in three persons and one substance, living and reigning throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXIII. FRIDAY

Reading from the holy Gospel according to John.

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “I came as light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me may not remain in darkness.”

In one place he said to his disciples: “You are the light of the world. A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden; nor do they light a lamp and place it under a measure, but on a lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in the house. Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.”

Yet I did not say to you: “You came as light into the world, so that everyone who believes in you may not remain in darkness.” I affirm that this cannot be read anywhere. All the saints, therefore, are lights, but they are enlightened by him; if anyone withdraws from him, that person will become dark. But that light which is enlightened from itself cannot withdraw, because it is altogether unchangeable.

When he says, “Everyone who believes in me will not remain in darkness,” he clearly shows that he found everyone in darkness. But so that they may not remain in the darkness in which they were found, they ought to believe in the light that came into this world, because through it the world was made.

“And if anyone hears my words,” he says, “and does not keep them, I do not judge him.” Hear how the Son says, “I do not judge him,” when elsewhere he says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.” The explanation lies in what follows: “For I did not come,” he says, “to judge the world, but to save the world.”

Now therefore is the time of mercy; afterward will be the time of judgment, because he says: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord.” But concerning that final judgment still to come, observe what he says: “Whoever despises me and does not receive my words has one who judges him; the word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day.”

Thus he says: “Whoever despises me and does not receive my words has one who judges him; the word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day.” He does not say: “Whoever despises me and does not receive my words, I do not judge him on the last day.” The Son of God therefore came to save, not to judge. For this reason he said, “I do not judge him”—that is, now, in the present—but “I judge him on the last day.”

When he had said, “Whoever despises me and does not receive my words has one who judges him,” and those who were waiting to know who that judge might be, he cautiously added: “The word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day.” For he spoke of himself, announced himself, and set himself as the door through which he himself, the shepherd, would enter to the sheep.

Those who did not hear will therefore be judged differently from those who heard and despised. “Those who sinned without the law,” the Apostle says, “will also perish without the law; and those who sinned under the law will be judged by the law.”

“For I,” he says, “have not spoken from myself.” He again says that he did not speak from himself. We have often said that the Son is not from himself but from the Father; therefore he adds:

“But the Father who sent me himself gave me a commandment concerning what I should say and what I should speak.” The Father does not speak to the Son through spatial intervals, the articulation of syllables, or vocal sound, as a human father speaks to a human son so that the son may hear what his father commands him. Rather, the Only-Begotten Son is the Word of the Father and the Wisdom of the Father; in him are all the Father’s commandments.

The Son never at any time failed to know the Father’s commandment, as though it were necessary for him to receive in time what he had not possessed and to receive by being born what the Father gave him by begetting. Rather, the Father begot him possessing life, just as he said above: “As the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself.” That is, he begot the Son possessing life in himself.

Here too he says: “As the Father gave me a commandment.” Since that begetting is eternal, the Son, who is life, never did not exist; and just as life is eternal, so too is the commandment. This does not mean that the Son does not possess what the Father gave him. Rather, as I have said, in the Wisdom of the Father, which is the Word of the Father, all the Father’s commandments are present. For he continues:

“And I know that his commandment is eternal life.” If the Son himself is eternal life, and the Father’s commandment is eternal life, what else has been said than: “I am the Father’s commandment”?

Accordingly, when he adds and says, “The things that I speak, I speak just as the Father told me,” we must not understand “told me” as though he spoke by words to the one Word, or as though God the Word needed words from God. The Father said to the Son, “As he gave the Son life”—not something that he did not know or possess, since he himself was the Son. What does “As he told me, so I speak” mean except “I speak the Word”? The Father spoke these things as the truthful one; the Son speaks as the Truth. The truthful one begot the Truth.

What, then, would he say to the Truth? The Truth was not imperfect, as though some word needed to be added to it. Therefore he spoke to the Truth because he begot the Truth. The Truth itself speaks in the manner in which it was told, to those who understand whom it teaches, just as it was born.

But so that human beings might believe what they are not yet able to understand, words sounded from the mouth of flesh, and the sounds passed away as the brief periods of time assigned to them were completed. Yet the realities of which those sounds are signs, drawn in a certain way into the memory of those who heard them, have reached even us through letters, which are visible signs.

The Truth does not speak in this way to minds that understand. It speaks inwardly, instructs without sound, and pours itself forth with an intelligible voice. Whoever can see in it the eternity of its birth hears it speaking in this way. “As the Father told him what he should speak”: by this he has stirred us to a great desire for the sweetness within.

Let us grasp it as we grow; let us grow as we walk; let us walk by advancing, so that we may reach, through him himself, him himself, with him himself guiding us and promising himself to us. “I am the way, and the truth, and the life”: the way for those who seek, the truth for those who find, the life for those who remain. For he lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXIV. THIRD SUNDAY AFTER THE OCTAVE OF EASTER

Reading from the Letter of the blessed apostle James.

Beloved, “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights,” etc.

After teaching that the vices by which we are tempted arise not from God but from ourselves, he shows, conversely, that whatever good we do, we have received from God as giver. For this reason he calls him “the Father of lights,” because he recognizes him as the author of spiritual gifts. This agrees with the Apostle’s statement: “What do you have that you did not receive?”

“With whom there is no change or shadow of alteration.” Since there is no mutability in God’s nature, and his light, unlike the light of this world, is not cut off by any shadow of change, it is clear that he sends us only gifts of light and not also the darkness of errors.

“Of his own will he begot us by the word of truth.” And the Lord says in the Gospel: “You did not choose me, but I chose you.” And in the prophet Hosea: “I will love you freely.” Since he had said that every good gift and every perfect gift descends from God, he consequently asserts that, not through our merits but through the favor of his own will, he has changed us from children of darkness into children of light through the water of regeneration.

“So that we might be a kind of first beginning of his creation.” Lest, when he says “begot,” we should suppose that we become what he himself is, he shows that a certain primacy among created things has been granted to us through this adoption. Some have translated these verses as follows: “Willingly he begot us by the word of truth, so that we might be the firstfruits of his creatures,” that is, so that we might be better than the other creatures that we see.

For the law commands the firstfruits of crops and animals to be consecrated; it ordered the firstfruits of gold and silver to be brought for the work of the tabernacle—that is, the finest things among metals. And the prophet Jeremiah said of God’s ancient people: “Israel was holy to the Lord, the firstfruits of his harvest.”

“You know, my beloved brothers.” “It is very well known to you,” he says, “that you have fallen into vices through yourselves, but that you have been enlightened by the Lord has happened not through your own promise but because heavenly grace went before you.”

“Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.” Here he instructs the hearer with moral precepts. He rightly first urges everyone to lend an ear quickly to a teacher, but to open the mouth for teaching slowly, because it is foolish for someone to wish to preach to others what he himself has not learned.

Whoever therefore loves wisdom should first, as he advised above, ask it from God; then, as a humble hearer of truth, seek a teacher; and in the course of action he should carefully restrain his tongue not only from idle speech but also from preaching the truth that he himself has only recently learned.

Hence Solomon, writing about the distinction between times, says: “A time to keep silence, and a time to speak.” For this reason the Pythagoreans, endowed with the training of natural knowledge, order their students to remain silent for five years and only then permit them to preach.

“And slow to anger.” The maturity of wisdom cannot be received except by a tranquil mind. For it is written: “Anger rests in the bosom of a fool.” He does not forbid quickness to anger in such a way as to approve its slowness; rather, he urges us to be careful that the hour of disturbance and quarrels not steal anger upon us. Or, if it should steal upon us, we should restrain its impulse within the bounds of our mouth and, when the critical hour has passed, cleanse it completely from our heart more freely over time.

Or certainly he commands us to be slow to anger so that we do not turn the calmness of our countenance into severity for just any reason. But when a definite reason exists—for example, if we see that those close to us, especially those entrusted to us, cannot otherwise be corrected—we should show severity toward them in word or even through stricter judgment, while preserving, as far as human nature permits, the serenity of our mind.

I believe that Phinehas, Samuel, Elijah, and Peter were slow to anger, yet they destroyed sinners either by word or by the sword. Moses too, although he was an exceedingly gentle man, left Pharaoh in anger when he saw that Pharaoh was incorrigible; he threatened him with punishment and carried it out in deed.

“For the anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God.” The meaning is straightforward: whoever carelessly and viciously submits to anger, even if he appears righteous to human beings, is not yet perfectly righteous in the divine examination.

Yet it can more aptly be understood in relation to what was said by the Lord: “But you, Lord of hosts, judge with tranquility.” Whatever human judge judges a delinquent after losing the tranquility of his mind, even if he judges justly, cannot imitate the righteousness of divine judgment, into which disturbance cannot enter.

“Therefore, putting away all filthiness and abundance of wickedness, receive with meekness the implanted word.” First he commands both body and mind to be cleansed from vices, so that they may be worthy to receive the word of salvation. For whoever does not first turn away from evil cannot do good.

He calls all filthiness that of both flesh and soul; “wickedness,” however, properly concerns the depravity of the inner human being. “Receive,” he says, “the implanted word,” that is, the word of God that we implant in your hearts by preaching; receive it by learning.

Or certainly this should be understood in this way: receive more perfectly even now the Word that was implanted in you on the day of resurrection, when God willingly begot us, fulfilling in deeds what you already possess in mystery.

“Which is able to save your souls.” Even if you suffer temptations in the body or are consumed by death at the hands of the faithless, nevertheless future life will be granted to you with the holy angels in perpetual light.

## HOMILY XXXV. ON THE SAME FEAST

Reading from the holy Gospel according to John.

[Col. 0209D]

“At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, “Where are you going?”’”

He indicates that he will go to the one who sent him in such a way that no one would ask about what they would plainly see happening before their bodily eyes. For a cloud received him when he ascended from them; and when they saw him going into heaven, they did not ask with words but followed him with their eyes.

“But because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart.” Certainly he saw what those words of his were doing in their hearts. Since they did not yet possess inwardly the spiritual consolation that they would have through the Holy Spirit, they feared losing what they saw outwardly in Christ.

[Col. 0210A] “But I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away.” It is to your advantage that the form of a servant be withdrawn from your sight, so that love of the divine nature may be more suitably fixed in your minds. It is to your advantage that I bring the form familiar to you into heaven, so that through this you may sigh for heaven with greater desire.

“For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go away, I will send him to you.” He does not say this because, while present on earth, he was unable to give the Spirit to his disciples, since it is plainly written that after the resurrection he appeared to them, breathed on them, and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit.” Rather, while he was present on earth and living bodily with them, they were unable to lift their minds toward him so as to thirst for the gifts of heavenly grace.

But when he ascended into heaven, they likewise transferred all their desire to him. Thus they had already become capable of the Holy Spirit: they were no longer saddened by his death but rejoiced in the hope of his promise.

It is clear, and requires no laborious explanation, why he called that same Spirit the Paraclete, that is, the Comforter: the coming of the Spirit would console and revive the hearts of the disciples, which his departure had made sorrowful.

This does not mean that the Holy Spirit had not previously been in the hearts of the disciples or even of the saints of ancient times. But he had not previously been given in such manifest fullness as he is recorded to have been given after the ascension, on the tenth day, to the hundred and twenty persons.

Nevertheless, in no work of any person of the Father, Son, or Holy Spirit was the activity of the entire Holy Trinity absent. It was necessary, however, for the Trinity to be revealed in such a way that, although there is no difference of substance, the distinction of the persons would nevertheless be commended individually.

“And when he comes, he will convict the world.” What does he mean by saying, “When he comes, he will convict the world”? Did Christ, while he was in the world, not convict the world concerning all the matters that follow? But Christ convicted only the nation of the Jews, whereas the Holy Spirit, spread through his disciples throughout the whole world, is understood to have convicted not one nation but the world.

In what respect did he convict it? In this respect: love was poured out through the Holy Spirit into their hearts, and love casts out fear, so that they would not fear the world—that is, so that they would convict those who love the world.

[Col. 0210D] “Concerning sin, and concerning righteousness, and concerning judgment.” Christ himself explained this statement by saying:

“Concerning sin, because they do not believe in me.” He set the sin of unbelief as a particular sin, because just as faith is the origin of virtues, so persistence in unbelief is the foundation of vices. The Lord bears terrifying witness to this when he says: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he has not believed in the name of the Only-Begotten Son of God.” He said “has been judged,” that is, “has been condemned.”

Regarding righteousness, because I am going to the Father, and you will no longer see me. The righteousness of Christ’s disciples consisted in this: they believed that the Lord, whom they saw to be truly human, was also truly the Son of God; and although they knew that he had been taken away from them bodily, they continued always to worship him with steadfast love. The righteousness of the other faithful—that is, of those who did not see the Lord in the flesh—is this: they believe and love him in their hearts as true God and true man, although they have never seen him with bodily eyes. By this righteousness of faith unbelievers are certainly convicted, namely, because, although they likewise heard the word of life, they refused to believe unto righteousness. For the wickedness of the evil is condemned not only on account of its own perversity but also by comparison with the righteous, which immediately declares that they are to be condemned.

The Holy Spirit therefore convicts the world concerning sin, because it did not believe in Christ. He also convicts it concerning the righteousness of believers, because it was unwilling to follow the example of those who knew that he had ascended to the Father and would no longer dwell bodily on earth, yet could not in any way be separated from his love. This is what he says: “Because I am going to the Father, and you will no longer see me.” You will not see me after I have ascended, as you now see me, surrounded by mortal and tangible flesh; but you will see me coming in majesty for judgment and, when the judgment has been completed, appearing with the saints in greater glory. It follows:

“Concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world has been judged.” He calls the devil the ruler of the world, because he holds primacy in the hearts of unbelievers, whom he intended to be understood here by the name “world”—people who, in perverse order, love the world rather than the Creator of the world. He was judged by the Lord, who said: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven.” He was judged by him when he himself was also casting out demons and giving his disciples power to trample upon every power of the enemy.

Thus the world is convicted concerning the judgment by which the devil was judged, when human beings are terrified by the example of the archangels condemned for their pride, lest they presume to resist God’s will. Let people therefore believe in Christ, lest they be convicted of the sin of their unbelief, by which sin all sins are held fast. Let them pass into the number of the faithful, lest they be convicted by the righteousness of those whom, though justified, they refuse to imitate. Let them beware of the coming judgment, lest they be judged together with the ruler of the world, whom they imitate though he has already been judged. For lest the stubborn pride of mortals imagine that it will be spared, it must be terrified by the punishment of the proud angels.

“I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth.” It is certain that, when the Spirit came from above, the apostles attained much greater knowledge of the truth than they had previously been able to possess in the flesh, and were inflamed with a far greater desire to contend for the truth. Yet one must not suppose that anyone in this life can comprehend all truth. Hence the blessed apostle Paul himself, who was caught up to the third heaven and there heard secret words that it is not permitted a human being to speak, says: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part; but when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part will be abolished.”

We must therefore understand what he says about the Spirit—“He will teach you all truth”—as though he were saying: “He will pour out in your hearts the love that makes you love all truth. Taught inwardly by its instruction, may you advance from virtue to virtue and become worthy to reach that life in which the eternal brightness of supreme truth and true sublimity—that is, the contemplation of your Creator—will appear to you.”

“For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak.” The Spirit will not speak from himself, perhaps because he is not from himself but from the Father. For the Son is born from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. He does not speak from himself—that is, without the communion of the Father and the Son. The Holy Spirit is not divided from the Father and the Son, but the work of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one.

“But whatever he hears he will speak.” He will hear, namely, through unity of substance and the particularity of knowledge. He does not speak from himself because he is not from himself: the Father alone is not from another; the Son is begotten from the Father; and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. The Holy Spirit hears from the one from whom he proceeds, because he is not from himself but from the one from whom he proceeds. From the one from whom he has understanding, from that one he also has knowledge; therefore from him he has hearing, which is nothing other than knowledge. What he adds is this:

“And he will announce to you the things that are to come.” It is clear that some of the saints, through the Holy Spirit, foretold future events. Yet these words of the Lord must be considered more profoundly, since they can apply commonly to all the saints. Thus, when the Spirit comes, he will announce what is to come when he recalls to our memory the joys of our heavenly homeland, when, through the gift of his inspiration, he makes known to us the festivals of that heavenly city. He announces what is to come when, withdrawing us from delight in present things, he inflames our hearts with desire for the promised kingdom in heaven.

“He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you.” The Spirit glorified Christ because through him that love was kindled in the hearts of the disciples that, once carnal fear had been cast aside, they confidently proclaimed the reality of his resurrection, although shortly before, at the time of his Passion, they had fled in fear. Hence it is written: “And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spoke the word of God with confidence.”

The Spirit glorified Christ when the holy teachers, filled with spiritual grace, performed so many and such great miracles in Christ’s name that they converted the whole world to faith in Christ, and endured so many and such great struggles of suffering for Christ’s name. He glorifies him while he pours love into our hearts and inspires love of our eternal homeland.

“Because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you”—that is, from my Father. The Holy Spirit receives from the Father because he proceeds from the Father, from whom the Son also is born. But the Father alone is born from no one and proceeds from no one.

“All things whatever the Father has are mine. Therefore I said: He will receive from what is mine and announce it to you.” He spoke of those things that pertain to the very divinity of the Father, in which he is equal to the Father, and in which the Holy Spirit is equal to the Father and the Son. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one substance, one nature, one majesty, one glory, and one eternity; and they are one almighty, invisible, incomprehensible God to every creature: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. In the name of righteousness, and in the gift and sending of the Holy Spirit, the concord of these two readings is established. Blessed is the one who understands the truth and follows righteousness, because, if he perseveres in this, he will rejoice eternally together with Christ.

## HOMILY XXXVI. ON THE FINDING OF THE HOLY CROSS

Reading from the Epistle of the Blessed Paul to the Galatians.

“Brothers, I am confident in you in the Lord that you will think nothing otherwise,” etc.

With this hope he says that he is confident concerning them, because they did not go astray willingly.

“But whoever is troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be.” Just as the one who converts an erring person is to be rewarded, as the apostle James says in his Epistle: “Whoever converts a sinner will save his soul and cover a multitude of sins,” so also whoever compels one walking rightly to turn aside onto a crooked path receives condemnation, whoever he may be. He adds this on account of these people, lest anyone defend his merit on the grounds that they were sons of Abraham according to the flesh. Thus they cried out to Jesus: “We are sons of Abraham.”

“But I, brothers, if I preach circumcision, why do I still suffer persecution?” What he says is clear. For this reason the Jews hated him as an enemy and did not cease persecuting him: he taught that circumcision had already come to an end. Finally, when the Jews compelled him and repeatedly brought false accusations against him, seeing that the judge was unjust, he was forced to appeal to Caesar.

“Then the scandal of the cross has been removed.” The preaching of the cross was a scandal to the Jews because it abolished the Sabbath and circumcision. But if he admitted circumcision, there would be no scandal, and the Jews would be at peace with us. For they said of the Savior: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath.” Therefore the scandal of the cross has been removed.

“Would that those who are troubling you would even cut themselves off”—that is, would that those who are subverting you would be cut off. This is like what he says elsewhere, in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “If anyone,” he says, “does not love the Lord Jesus, let him be accursed.” These too belong to the same diseased flock; he joins them to that sentence so that they may be cut off from the mercy of God—those who stripped the Galatians of God’s grace. He curses them not only spiritually but also bodily, so that, since they were forcing the Galatians to be circumcised, they themselves might be cut off, and their bodily pain might be increased.

“Those who wish to please in the flesh compel you to be circumcised, only so that they may not suffer persecution for the cross of Christ.” To please in the flesh means to please human beings. Thus, in order to live with the Jews, whom he calls false apostles, either favorably or without provoking their hostility, they preached Christ in such a way that they also taught that the law must be observed. The Apostle never feared this, but steadfastly refused to keep silent about what is true, and took care through it for those whom he was teaching. Thus he says: “I am ready not only to be bound but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

“For those who are circumcised do not keep the law; rather, they wish you to be circumcised so that they may boast in your flesh.” This is like what was said to the apostle Peter: “If you, although you are a Jew, live like a Gentile, how do you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?” So here too, although they themselves did not keep the law and lived unjustly, they pursued circumcision so that they might appear to prevail and to be lovers of the law. Yet it is clear that the one defends and keeps the law who performs its righteous requirements and does not neglect the commandment given for life. Thus the Galatians’ ruin was their excuse, so that they might understand—even if only in this way—that they were being deceived like fools and dullards, while those people gloried in their sufferings.

“But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me and I to the world.” Just as the false apostles, ashamed of them, evaded through hypocrisy the tribulations suffered for Christ’s name, as though those tribulations would profit nothing, so the Apostle gloried in them, knowing that he would receive a great reward for them, as would Christ’s other apostles. As it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “Then,” it says, “the apostles went out from the council rejoicing, because they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Christ.”

Therefore, whoever has all his hope in Christ glories in his cross. For him the world has also been crucified, since he knows for certain that love of Christ’s cross is life, whereas love of the world prepares death. Blessed is the one who puts to death the desires of his flesh and patiently endures the tribulations of this present life, because, if he perseveres in this good endeavor to the end, he will become a participant in eternal life with Christ and his saints and will undoubtedly rejoice forever. This is granted by our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXVII. WEDNESDAY

Reading from the Epistle of the Blessed Paul to the Thessalonians.

“Brothers, you are all sons of light and sons of the day; we are not of the night or of darkness.”

How did he say, “He will come like a thief in the night,” when here he says: “Because you are not in darkness, you have recognized the truth”? Thus, even if the day is suddenly at hand, it does not claim over you the order of a thief, since you are to be helped by his coming; rather, it claims that order over those who await punitive harm. And lest they think that recognition alone is sufficient for them, he adds:

“Therefore let us not sleep as the others do, but let us watch and be sober. For those who sleep, sleep at night; and those who become drunk, become drunk at night. But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, clothed with the breastplate of faith and love, and with the helmet of the hope of salvation. For God has not appointed us for wrath but for the acquisition of salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us, so that whether we are awake or asleep, we may live together with him.”

It is therefore fitting that, rewarded with such knowledge, we should watch and be sober concerning the diligence in those things that befit us, so as to guard the night-time; nor is it necessary for us to pursue drunkenness. For one who is such can easily remain hidden. But those who, through knowledge, already stand as though in the day ought to be sober and watchful in their pursuit of virtues, as those who live in the daytime, in which it is impossible for anyone to remain hidden if he has done anything improper.

What are those works by which, as people living in the day, we may be reckoned to possess faith and love, from which hope of salvation is acquired for us, through which the Lord God, by Christ who was willing to accept death for us, has handed salvation to us rather than punishment? Although we have this according to the present life—this is what he means when he says, “Let us watch”—even if we have departed from this life, he says, “Let us sleep.” For he means that those who are then living at Christ’s coming, and those who have already died, will all acquire eternal and incorruptible life: those who went before us into death long ago will rise again, while those who are then living will be changed into incorruptibility, as the same Apostle says elsewhere: “For we shall all be changed.”

Therefore, nothing prevents us from enjoying the salvation that is to come, provided that those things which arise from us do not hinder us in any way. And saying this, he adds:

“Therefore console one another and build one another up, just as you are doing,” in Christ our Lord, to whom are honor and glory together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXVIII. ALSO WEDNESDAY

Reading from the holy Gospel according to John.

[Col. 0215C]

At that time Jesus, looking toward his disciples, said: “Holy Father, keep them in your name, those whom you have given me,” etc.

Certainly, as a human being, he asks God on behalf of his disciples, whom he received from God. Pay attention to what follows:

“That they may be one,” he says, “as we also are.” He did not say, “That they may be one with us,” or, “That we and they may be one as we are one”; rather, he said: “That they may be one as we also are.” They themselves, in their own nature, are to be one as we are one in ours. He would surely not say this unless he were speaking according to the fact that the Son is equal to the Father, as he says elsewhere: “I and the Father are one.” He was not speaking according to what he is as a human being, for according to that he said: “The Father is greater than I.” But because one and the same person is God and human being, we understand the human being in the fact that he asks, and we understand God in the fact that he and the one whom he asks are one. It follows:

“When I was with them, I was keeping them in your name.” “When I come to you,” he says, “keep them in your name, in which, when I was with them, I myself also kept them.” The Son of Man, established in human presence, kept his disciples in the Father’s name; but the Father also kept those who asked in the Son’s name and whose requests he heard. For the same Son said to them: “Amen, amen, I say to you, whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you.”

The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, who is the one true and blessed God, guard us together. When he speaks in this way, as he has spoken here, let us understand that he distinguishes the persons without separating the nature, although the bodily presence of the Son has been taken away from them. Yet spiritual protection was never lacking, concerning which he says: “Behold, I am with you all the days, even to the consummation of the age.”

“Those whom you gave me I have kept; and none of them perished except the son of perdition, that the Scripture might be fulfilled.” The “son of perdition” is called the betrayer of Christ, concerning whom the hundred and ninth Psalm especially prophesies.

“But now,” he says, “I am coming to you; and I speak these things in the world so that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves.” Behold, he says that he is speaking in the world, although shortly before he had said: “I am no longer in the world.” Therefore, because he was not departing by nature, he was still here; and because he was about to depart from here, he was in a certain sense already no longer here.

What this joy is, concerning which he says, “So that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves,” has already been expressed above, where he says: “That they may be one as we also are.” He says that this joy of his—that is, the joy bestowed by him upon them—is to be fulfilled in them, and for this reason he said that he had spoken in the world. This is that peace and blessedness in the age to come, for the attainment of which we must live temperately, justly, and devoutly in this age.

While the Lord continued speaking to the Father and praying for his disciples:

“I have given them your word,” he said. This was explained earlier.

“And the world hated them.” He signifies the sufferings they would have in the world from persecutors, whom he indicates here by the name “world.” Then, adding the reason why the world would hate them:

“Because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.” But they are so in one way, and I in another: they by regeneration, I by generation. They needed a second birth because they were born in sins; I, because I was born without sin, did not need regeneration. It was therefore granted to them not to be of the world; but I was never of the world, because I was never in sin.

He himself was never of the world because, even according to the form of a servant, he was born from the Holy Spirit, from whom they were reborn. If, therefore, they are not of the world because they have been reborn from the Holy Spirit, he was never of the world because he was born from the Holy Spirit.

“I do not ask,” he says, “that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from evil.” For it was still necessary, although they were no longer of the world, that they should nevertheless be in the world, so that what was said might be fulfilled: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.”

“Sanctify them in truth.” For they are preserved from the evil concerning which he prayed above, so that they might be freed from the evil of unbelief in which Judas the betrayer fell. The heirs of the new covenant are therefore sanctified in truth, while the sanctifications of the old covenant were shadows of that truth. And when they are sanctified in truth, they are certainly sanctified in Christ, who truly said: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life,” and “the truth will set you free.”

“As you sent me into the world, so I also sent them into the world.” Whom did he send, except his apostles? For the very name “apostles,” which is Greek, means nothing other than “sent ones” in Latin. The Lord therefore sent his Son, conceived and born without sin; the Son sent his disciples, whom he sanctified either through the sacrament of baptism or through the redemption of his blood, so that they might preach to the world sanctification, cleansing, and remission of sins. Hence he also adds:

“And for them I sanctify myself,” that is, in that I did not come to do my own will but the will of the one who sent me, the Father. The sanctification of the faithful is the obedience of the Son, who was obedient to the Father even unto death, and death on a cross; for this reason God also exalted him. But when he says:

“So that they themselves also may be sanctified in truth,” this means: in me, just as I too have been sanctified in the word of God. Therefore he adds:

“I ask not only for these”—that is, for the disciples who were then with him—

“but also for those who will believe in me through their word.” Here he intended all his own to be understood: not only those who were then present in the flesh but also those who were to come. All who afterward believed in him through the word of the apostles certainly believed, and they will continue to believe until he comes; for he had said to them: “And you also bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.”

“That they may all be one.” One in love, one in faith, one in peace, because they are destined for one kingdom. Although there are different dwelling places in that kingdom on account of the different merits of the saints, whoever is in that kingdom will be blessed, and what he possesses will be sufficient for him; he rejoices in what he possesses.

“As you, Father, are in me and I in you.” This is what he said shortly before: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.” For the whole Father is in the Son, and the whole Son is in the Father; whoever has the Son also has the Father, and whoever has the Father also has the Son. Hence he adds:

“That they too may be one in us.” That is, may they love us with one love, believe in us with one faith, and trust in us with one hope, so that there may be unity of the body in the head, and that God may be all in all.

“I in them, as the head is in the members, and you in me, as the Father is in the Son, so that they may be perfected in one”—that is, made complete, which is accomplished by the one who willed us to be one in himself and through himself.

[Col. 0217D]

“So that the world may know that you sent me and loved them as you loved me.” You loved them so that they might become what they were not; you loved me so that I might be what I always was.

“Father, those whom you have given me, I desire that where I am, they too may be with me.” Now through faith, but then through sight, when Christ our life appears; then we too will appear with him in glory. Then it will be clear what we shall be, because then the one who existed before we existed will appear.

“That they may see,” he says, “my glory, which you have given me.” Righteous Father, the world did not know you. Because you are righteous, it did not know you. Yet a certain world, born through righteousness, did not know you; but the one that was to be saved through mercy did know you. The world whom he reconciled to himself through Christ knew him not by merit but by grace. Finally, it follows:

“But I have known you.” God is by nature the very fountain of grace; but the human being, through ineffable grace, was assumed from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin into the unity of the person of the Son of God. Through him these people knew, and all who through them were to believe.

“Because you sent me”—therefore they knew; they knew, accordingly, through grace.

“And I made your name known to them,” he says, “and I will make it known.” I made it known through faith; I will make it known through sight. I made it known to those journeying as strangers in this age; I will make it known to those reigning in heaven.

“So that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them.” But how is the love with which the Father loved the Son also among us, except because we are his members and are loved in him, when he is loved in his entirety—that is, head and body? Therefore he adds, “and I in them,” as though he were saying: Since I am in them, if they persevere to the end in right faith and good works, I am ready to give them the glory of the heavenly kingdom, where they may live and rejoice forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXIX. FRIDAY

Reading from the holy Gospel according to John.

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “I am with you a little while longer,” etc.

It is as though he were saying: I will indeed be glorified immediately through the resurrection, but I will not immediately ascend into heaven; rather, I will remain with you a little while longer, signifying the forty days during which he was to appear to the disciples at appropriate times. Yet it may also be understood that he indicated that he would be with the disciples only for the short period of that night, until the hour of his Passion.

There is also another divine presence, unknown to mortal senses, concerning which he likewise says: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age.” Certainly this is not “I am with you a little while longer”; rather, “I am with you a little while longer” refers either to the time before the hour of his Passion or to the period after his resurrection. Elsewhere he said to his disciples: “These are the words that I spoke to you when I was still with you”—that is, when I was still in mortal flesh, in which you too are. For when he said these things, he had already risen in that same flesh, but he was no longer with them in the same mortality.

[Col. 0218D]

“You will seek me; and as I said to the Jews, ‘Where I am going you cannot come,’ so I say to you now.” That is, you cannot come now. When he said this to the Jews, he did not add “now.” These disciples therefore could not then come where he was going, but they could come afterward. Thus, wishing to show them how they could become fit to proceed where he was going before them:

“I give you a new commandment,” he says, “that you love one another.” These are the steps by which Christ must be followed: this is the commandment of love. It makes the hearer—or rather, the one who obeys—new, not every kind of love but this love, which the Lord distinguished from carnal love when he said: “As I have loved you.”

This love does not make us new merely so that we may be new human beings, but so that we may be heirs of the new covenant. This love gathered a new people to Christ; it renewed the ancient Fathers so that they might believe in Christ, who was to come to redeem them. Let all who wish to be brothers of the only Son of God, who gave himself for us in this love, hear and keep the commandment: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another.”

For this commandment also contains the commandment given first: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind.” Yet those who understand rightly find both commandments in each one. For the one who loves God cannot restrain himself from obeying him when he commands love of neighbor; and the one who first and spiritually loves his neighbor—what does he love in him except the Lord? This is the love distinguished from every worldly love, which the Lord marked out by adding: “As I have loved you,” when the Lord Jesus commended to his disciples the holy love by which they were to love one another.

Simon Peter said to him: “Lord, where are you going?” The disciple spoke thus to his teacher and the servant to his Lord, as one ready to follow. Therefore the Lord, who saw his heart and why he had asked this question, answered him:

“Where I am going you cannot follow me now.” It was as though he were saying: You cannot now go where you are asking about. He did not say, “You cannot”; rather, “You cannot now.” He introduced delay, not removed hope; and he confirmed the very hope he had not removed but rather given, with the following words, adding:

“But you will follow afterward.”

Peter answered: “Why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.” What desire did he see in Peter’s heart? What strength did he not see? The weak man was boasting of his will, but the physician was pointing out his weakness. Peter was making a promise; Christ knew beforehand what would happen. The one who did not know was listening, and the one who knew beforehand was teaching.

Jesus answered: “You will lay down your life for me.” What you promise, you cannot do now. First my life must be laid down for you, so that afterward you may lay down your life for me. Thus the glory of my resurrection will be completed, and the reward of your Passion will be prepared for you in the heavenly kingdom, so that you may live and rejoice with the holy angels forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XL. FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER THE OCTAVE OF EASTER

Reading from the Epistle of the blessed apostle James.

[Col. 0219D]

“Most beloved, be doers of the word and not hearers only,” etc.

Thus Paul also says concerning those who observe the law: “It is not the hearers of the law who will be justified before God, but the doers of the law are righteous.” And in the Apocalypse of John, after he had said: “Blessed is the one who reads and those who hear the words of the prophecy of this book,” he immediately added: “And keeps the things written in it.”

“For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he will be compared to a man who considers the face of his birth in a mirror; for he considered himself and went away, and immediately forgot what he was like.” By “the face of his birth” he means the face of infancy, which has not yet reached the maturity of a grown man.

[Col. 0220A]

It is customary for women to look at themselves in mirrors, so that, whatever they see to be dirty or not properly arranged, they may correct for the better and take care to please their husbands. Morally speaking, it is fitting that our souls do this. For we ought to look at ourselves in the mirror of the Gospel, or of all the divine Scriptures, and, having put away our stains and adorned the conduct of our souls, take care to please Christ indeed by merit [perhaps read *marito*, “their husband”].

“But whoever looks into the perfect law of liberty and perseveres in it.” He calls the grace of the Gospel the perfect law of liberty; for the law brought nothing to perfection. And elsewhere: “You did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons.” And again: “For where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty.” And the Lord himself: “If the Son,” he says, “sets you free, you will truly be free.”

“Not becoming a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work: this person will be blessed in his action.” Blessedness is prepared not by the useless hearing of the word but by carrying out the work, just as the Lord also said when speaking to his disciples: “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.”

“But if anyone thinks that he is religious, not restraining his tongue but deceiving his heart, his religion is worthless.” Above he had warned that one should not only hear the word of God but also do it. Now he adds that even if someone appears to practice in deeds the commandments of the Lord that he has learned, if he does not also restrain his tongue from slander, lies, blasphemies, foolish talk, excessive speech itself, and the other things by which one commonly sins, he boasts in vain about the righteousness of his works. Thus Paul too, approving the saying of a pagan poet, says: “Bad conversations corrupt good morals.”

“Pure and undefiled religion before God and the Father is this.” He fittingly added “before God and the Father,” because there are people who seem religious to human beings while they are considered profane before God. Hence Solomon also says: “There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end leads to death.”

“To visit orphans and widows in their tribulation, and to keep oneself undefiled from this age.” Since he had said that the doer of the work would be blessed in his action, he now states which deeds especially please God: namely, mercy and innocence. For in commanding us to visit orphans and widows in their tribulation, he indicates everything that we ought to do mercifully toward our neighbor. How greatly this counts will be revealed at the time of judgment, when the Judge will say: “As long as you did it for one of the least of my brothers, you did it for me.”

Moreover, by commanding us to keep ourselves undefiled from this age, he shows all the things in which we ought to preserve ourselves pure. Among these are the practices he advised above: that we be slow to speak and slow to anger, and that in patience and in the tribulation of the present life we be strong enough to endure every adversity. Thus, with right faith and good works, let us strive to reach eternal life, by the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XLI. ON THE SAME FEAST

Reading from the holy Gospel according to John.

[Col. 0221A]

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Amen, amen, I say to you, whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you. Until now you have asked nothing in my name; ask, and you will receive, so that your joy may be full.”

This can be understood in two ways: either because you did not ask in my name, since you did not know that name as it ought to be known; or because you asked for nothing, since, in comparison with the things you ought to have asked for, what you asked for must be regarded as nothing. For whoever asks for something that does not pertain to heavenly salvation and eternal joy seems to ask for nothing in comparison with the petition he ought to have made.

“Ask, and you will receive, so that your joy may be full.” It is as though he plainly said: Do not ask for the fleeting joys of the age, which are always mixed with sorrow and end in pain; rather, ask the Father for that unique joy whose fullness cannot be diminished by any disturbance whatsoever. Eternity will never be dissolved by any limit, if you provide for it by asking such things. Without doubt, you will receive what you ask, if the conduct of the one asking is in harmony with his mind. For asking rightly for heavenly things brings little benefit to one who does not cease to entangle himself in lowly things through perverse living.

“I have spoken these things to you in proverbs. The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in proverbs, but will announce the Father to you openly.” They were still little children and had not yet been able to understand how the Father was in the Son, and the Son in the Father, and the other matters pertaining to the profound mysteries of the divinity. They could not yet know these things; therefore the Lord seemed to speak to them in proverbs, as though in riddles. But he promises the hour in which he would speak openly.

He was evidently signifying that hour when, after completing his Passion and resurrection, he was to give them the grace of the Holy Spirit. For then, instructed inwardly in a spiritual way and inflamed with spiritual delight, the more perfectly they received all that mortals were able to grasp through knowledge of the divinity, the more ardently they took care to ask for and desire only those things that would help them merit its vision.

“In that day you will ask in my name.” That is, you will begin to ask for those things that pertain only to the salvation of your souls and that seem to belong to eternal joys. And especially, so that you may understand what he meant when he said: “I and the Father are one,” and that the Father is in me and I in the Father.

Then they ask in his name who ask because, in the sound of that name, they understand nothing other than the very reality that is called by that name. Such people can in some way consider our Lord Jesus Christ: insofar as he is human, interceding for us with the Father; insofar as he is God, hearing us together with the Father. I believe that he signified this when he said:

I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf. For what he says, “And I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf,” can quite appropriately be understood in this way: I do not ask now, but in the future. He used the word “I will ask,” because, once the saints have been received into inward peace, no one will then be able to ask anything on their behalf, since they are to be endowed with such great blessedness that nothing greater can exist.

For the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came forth from God. What he says, “because you have loved me,” is not to be understood as though they had loved Christ first; rather, the Father preceded them with gratuitous love and, by loving them, raised them up to love and believe in the Son. And because they preserved with devoted and watchful hearts the love and faith they had recognized in the Son, he rewards them with greater gifts of paternal love, loving them together with the Son and the Holy Spirit, whom he judges worthy of love. What he adds—“because you have loved me”—is to be understood in the same way. Therefore, whoever rightly possesses the Son loves him together with the Father and the Holy Spirit; and because those whose divine nature is inseparable also possess one and the same gifts of virtue, this is what it means: that you love and believe that I came forth from God.

I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father. He came forth from the Father and came into the world because he who was invisible with the Father in divinity appeared visibly to the world in humanity. He came forth from the Father because he appeared not in the form in which he is equal to the Father, but in an assumed creaturely form, in which he appeared lesser. And he came into the world because, in the form of a servant which he had assumed, he presented himself to be seen [Variant: to live] even by the lovers of this world. Again he left the world and returned to the Father because he removed from the sight of the world’s lovers what they had seen and taught his own lovers to believe that he was equal to the Father. He left the world and returned to the Father because, through his ascension, he brought the humanity he had assumed to the invisible things of the Father’s majesty.

These words of the Lord are indeed mystical and, as he himself testifies, were spoken in parables; but the disciples to whom they were spoken were still so carnal that they could not at all grasp their depth. They understood not only none of the hidden meaning of the words, but not even their own ignorance, thinking that what had been spoken simply and clearly was not a parable to those who did not understand it. Behold, they immediately answered:

“Now you are speaking openly, and saying no parable.” They therefore thought that he was speaking openly, although they were not yet able to comprehend the mysteries of his words. But when they add:

“Now we know that you know all things, and that you have no need for anyone to question you; by this we believe that you came forth from God,” they plainly show that, when the Lord spoke to them, he was chiefly discussing those things which they were pleased to hear; and whatever they wished to ask, he anticipated and offered to them of his own accord. Hence they rightly believe and confess that he knows all things as God and that, as the Son of God, he came from God. For knowing the secrets of thoughts is an evident sign of divinity.

In the name of God and the Father, these two readings are brought into harmony, because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one substance, one glory, and one majesty, reigning throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XLII. ON THE GREATER LITANY

Reading from the Epistle of the blessed apostle James.

[Col. 0223A]

“Beloved, confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, so that you may be saved.”

In this statement there should be the following distinction: we ought to confess our daily and slight sins to those who are our equals, and believe that we are saved through their daily prayer. But the uncleanness of more serious leprosy we should disclose to the priest according to the law, and, according to his judgment, take care to be purified in the manner and for the length of time he commands.

“For the continual prayer of a righteous person has great power. Elijah was a human being like us, subject to suffering; and he prayed earnestly that it might not rain upon the earth, and it did not rain for three years and six months.”

[Col. 0223B]

He fittingly establishes by example how much power the continual prayer of a righteous person possesses: by praying only one prayer, Elijah held back the heavens for so long, turned the rains away from the earth, and denied mortals their crops. Then again, when he wished, when he saw that the time had come, and when he saw that the heart of the proud king and the idolatrous nation had been bent toward repentance by the long wasting of famine, he prayed only one prayer and restored to the earth the crops and waters he had denied it. Thus the text continues:

“And again he prayed, and the heaven gave rain, and the earth produced its fruit.”

If, then, he prayed once both before and afterward, and one Elijah obtained so much, the passage shows how powerful the frequent prayer of many righteous people is. But lest our weakness should tremble, reasoning that it could not do what so great a prophet—who was worthy to be carried up to heaven in a fiery chariot—had done, the blessed James, intending to speak of his prayer, wisely began in this way: “Elijah was a human being like us, subject to suffering.”

He was indeed a human being, although inferior to no one in virtue: like us in the origin of his flesh, and subject to suffering as we are, both in the weakness of his mind and of his flesh. He showed that he was weak in the flesh when he sought food from the widow of Sarepta. That he was also subject to mental suffering he demonstrated when, after restoring the waters to the earth and destroying the prophets and priests of the idols, he was terrified by the threats of a single woman and fled through the wilderness.

How great a merit it is before the Lord to pray for the weak, and to restore to lost health those who confess their sins, he makes clear by adding:

“If anyone among you should wander from the truth, and someone should turn him back, he should know that whoever turns a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul from death.”

[Col. 0223D]

Since in the earlier parts of this Epistle he restrains our tongue from malicious or idle speech, he appropriately shows at the end what we ought chiefly to say. We are therefore commanded to pray and sing psalms to the Lord whenever we are assailed by adversities. Likewise, we are to confess our sins to one another and pray for one another so that we may be saved; and for the health of our neighbors, not only temporal but especially eternal, we must take as much care as we can.

For if it is a deed worthy of reward to rescue from death a body that will one day die, how great is the merit of freeing from death a soul that will live without end in the heavenly homeland? It should certainly be noted that some manuscripts read: “He will save his own soul from death.” Because of the ambiguity of the Greek, this too can rightly be interpreted in this way; and in truth, whoever corrects someone who has gone astray thereby gains for himself more abundant joys of heavenly life.

“He will save his soul,” he says, “from death, and will cover a multitude of sins.” Whoever turns a sinner back from error and, through this conversion, hides his sins from the sight of the inner Judge by the superimposition of a better life also conceals from the gaze of him who sees all things his own faults, whatever they may be, by caring for his neighbor. In accordance with the Psalmist’s words:

“Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered.”

The blessed James does not forget what he said above: “Do not become teachers in great numbers, my brothers.” There he removes those who are imperfect in their own conduct from the office of teaching, which they sought through vainglory; here, however, he teaches those who are instructed in every respect what they ought to do for the salvation of their neighbors through fraternal love.

What this teacher is said to do is elsewhere attributed to charity, as the blessed apostle Peter says: “Charity covers a multitude of sins.” Nor should it be passed over that this conversion of the one who has gone astray is accomplished not only by speaking, but often also by good conduct. For if someone, even while his tongue is silent, shows his neighbors examples of good action and turns them toward imitating the works of almsgiving, hospitality, or other virtues which they had neglected, he certainly performs the office of a teacher and, for the salvation of the brother he has corrected, will receive a sure reward from the merciful Judge.

## HOMILY XLIII. ON THE SAME FEAST

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Luke.

[Col. 0224C]

“At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘Which of you will have a friend and go to him at midnight and say to him, “Friend, lend me three loaves, because my friend has come to me from the road, and I have nothing to set before him,” etc.’”

When the disciples asked him, the Savior taught not only the form of prayer but also the persistence and frequency with which we should pray. The friend to whom one comes at midnight signifies God himself. In the midst of tribulation we must plead with him and earnestly ask for three loaves—that is, understanding of the Trinity, by which the labors of the present life may be consoled.

The friend who comes from the road is our mind whenever it departs from us, whenever it wanders outside toward the pursuit of earthly and temporal things.
