It returns and desires to be refreshed with heavenly nourishment when, having returned to itself, it begins to meditate upon things above and spiritual realities. Concerning him, the one who had asked beautifully adds: “He has nothing to set before him.” For when the soul, after the darkness of the world, sighs for God, it wishes to think of nothing but him, to speak of nothing, to look upon nothing; it strives only to contemplate the joy of the supreme Trinity, which it has recognized, and to reach a fuller vision of it.

“And the one inside will answer, saying: ‘Do not trouble me; the door is already shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot rise and give you anything.’”

The door of the divine Friend is understanding of the word. The apostle prays that this door may be opened to him for proclaiming the mystery of Christ; it is closed in the time of famine of the word, when understanding is not granted. The children of the head of the household are already in secret repose with the Lord; yet through prayer the one who desires obtains understanding from the Lord himself, even when there is no human being through whom wisdom may be preached.

“And if he persists in knocking, I say to you, even if he will not rise and give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence he will rise and give him as many as he needs. And I say to you: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.”

The comparison proceeds from the lesser: if a human friend rises from bed and gives, compelled not by friendship but by annoyance, how much more will God give, who without annoyance most generously grants what is asked. But he wants this to be sought so that those who ask may become capable of his gifts, lest the friend who has recently come from the road perish from hunger—that is, lest the spirit that has only recently recovered from the vanity of its error waste away for too long through lack of spiritual desire.

Let us ask for the banquets of the word, by which we may be nourished; let us seek the friend who gives; let us knock at the door by which we may be secretly saved. He has given, and continues to give, great hope—he who does not deceive when he promises. For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.

Therefore, in accordance with the parable just mentioned of the friend who asks, perseverance is necessary if we are to receive what we ask, find what we seek, and have opened to us what we knock upon. For if what is asked for is not given, and the seeker does not find, and the door is not opened to the one who knocks, it is evident that he has not asked, sought, or knocked properly.

“Which of you, if his son asks for bread, will give him a stone? Bread signifies charity, because of the greater appetite for it and because it is so necessary that without it all other things are nothing, just as without bread a table is poor. Its opposite is hardness of heart, which he compared to a stone.

“Or if he asks for a fish, will he give him a serpent instead of a fish?”

The fish is faith in invisible things, either because of the water of baptism or because it is caught from invisible places. Since faith, although surrounded by the waves of this world, is not broken, it is rightly compared to a fish. Its opposite he presented as a serpent, because of the poisonous deceptions which it also sowed by its evil counsel in the first human being.

[Col. 0225D]

“Or if he asks for an egg, will he offer him a scorpion?”

The egg indicates hope. For an egg is not yet a fully formed offspring, but is expected to become one through incubation. Its opposite he presented as a scorpion, whose poisonous sting must be feared from behind, just as the opposite of hope is what lies behind, since hope stretches toward the things that are ahead.

“If you, then, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the good Spirit to those who ask him?”

How do the evil give? He called them evil as lovers and sinners still attached to this age. The good things they give are to be called good according to the judgment of those who consider them good for us, although they are also good by their nature—yet temporal and belonging to this weak life. Moreover, whoever is evil does not give these things from his own possession.

“The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness,” he who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them. How greatly, then, should we hope that God will give good things to us when we ask, and that we cannot be deceived into receiving one thing instead of another when we ask him, since even we, although evil, know how to give what is requested.

For we do not deceive our children; and whatever good things we give, we give not from our own possession but from his. In another sense, the apostles, who by the merit of their election had surpassed the goodness of the human race, are nevertheless called evil in every respect in view of the goodness above, because nothing is stable in itself, nothing immutable, nothing good except divinity alone.

All creatures, however, if they attain the blessedness of eternity or immutability, attain it not through their own nature but through participation in and grace from their Creator. But when it is said, “How much more will your heavenly Father give the good Spirit to those who ask him,” in place of which Matthew wrote, “He will give good things to those who ask him,” it shows that the Holy Spirit is the fullness of God’s good things, and that the things administered by God do not subsist apart from him, because all benefits received from the grace of God’s gifts flow from this fountain.

In the requesting of prayer and in the receiving of the gift, these two readings are brought into harmony. Both come to salvation everlasting for those who rightly believe in God and firmly hope in his mercy, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XLIV. ON THE VIGIL OF THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

Reading from the Epistle to the Ephesians.

[Col. 0226C]

“Brothers, grace has been given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift. Therefore he says: ‘Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to human beings,’ etc.”

The apostle has briefly recalled here, as you have heard in the present reading, the grace and mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ which he bestowed upon the human race. For he says: “Grace has been given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift.” Spiritual grace is given according to the measure of believers, his mercy bestowing as much of the gift as the one to whom it is given is able to receive.

“Therefore he says: ‘Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to human beings.’”

We who now believe in Christ, gathered from the nations, were creatures of God but had been taken captive by the devil and distributed among his servants. Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ came, concealing divine majesty in a human being so that he would not be recognized by the devil. He proclaimed to us, who had been taken captive by the devil, forgiveness, and to those held in the bonds of death, release. He endured death for human beings in his humanity, although he cannot die in his divinity; by his death he conquered eternal death; and, rising from the earth, he raised into the heights of heaven the human being whom he had assumed.

He freed from captivity the souls of the saints who were held in hell and brought them with him to the kingdoms of heaven; and he bestowed the gifts of the Holy Spirit upon those who believed in him, as the apostle himself teaches elsewhere: “To some the grace of healings, to others the working of miracles, to others prophecy, to others the discernment of spirits, to others kinds of tongues, and to others the interpretation of speech,” distributing them individually as he wills.

“But what does ‘he ascended’ mean except that he also first descended into the lower parts of the earth?”

He ascended, clearly, according to the form of a servant, to which he descended not spatially but in condescension. He is also said to have descended into hell to preserve the souls of the righteous, so that he might call human beings back with him to heavenly things. He who descended with his soul into hell ascended with soul and body into heaven, in order to fulfill everything written concerning the glory of his triumph.

“And he himself gave some as apostles”—those sent throughout the world to preach—“some as prophets, others as evangelists, and others as pastors and teachers, for the completion of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ.”

Since the Church is understood to be the Lord’s body, built from living stones—that is, from faithful human beings—it is their task, according to the stewardship and duties entrusted to them, to build up the Church of Christ, which is his body.

“Until we all attain the unity of faith and the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.”

Therefore we must labor with every effort, first so that we may all attain unity in faith; then, within that same unity, possess knowledge of the Son of God, so that, by confidently imitating Christ in the inner person, we may receive the title of perfect human beings.

In the present feast—that is, the ascension of Christ the Lord into heaven, which today we honor in anticipation—we have been joined to God, beloved, by a wondrous reconciliation and have fully obtained heavenly mercy. Through Christ we have been given a marvelous peace, which we never wished to attain by any merits of our own.

We who seemed unworthy of the earth have been raised to heaven in this solemnity. We who did not deserve even earthly things have crossed the boundaries of heaven and, in human nature, are adorned with the royal seat itself.

Let us therefore rejoice, beloved, with spiritual joy; and, glad with fitting thanksgiving to God, let us raise the free eyes of our hearts to that height where Christ is. Let not earthly desires weigh down the minds called upward; let not perishable things occupy those who have been lifted toward eternal realities; let not worldly vanities turn back those who have entered the way of truth.

Nothing, beloved, is more powerful against the devil’s deceits than the kindness of mercy and the generosity of charity, through which every sin is either overcome or avoided. But the sublimity of this virtue cannot be grasped until what opposes it has been overthrown.

What, then, is so hostile to mercy and works of charity as greed, from whose root the seed of every evil springs? Unless it is destroyed in its own fuel, it is inevitable that, in the field where this evil planting has grown strong, thorns and thistles of vices will arise rather than any seed of true virtue.

Let us therefore resist, beloved, this most destructive evil and pursue charity, without which no virtue can shine, so that by this way of love, through which Christ descended to us, we may now also ascend to him, to whom, with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, be honor throughout ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XLV. ON THE SAME FEAST

Reading from the holy Gospel according to John.

[Col. 0228B]

“At that time Jesus, lifting his eyes to heaven, said: ‘Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son,’ etc.”

The Son could have spoken these same words of prayer to the Father silently, but the Son’s prayer is instruction for the disciples, as well as for those who would wish to follow their example or read their writings.

He said, “The hour has come”—that is, the hour of his passion is approaching. “Glorify your Son”: let the suffering of his humanity precede the glory of the resurrection, and let the glorification of the resurrection quickly follow.

The text continues:

“So that your Son may glorify you.”

The Father’s glorification is eternal and can neither increase nor diminish. But this glorification concerns the making known of God the Father, so that, through the glory of the resurrection accomplished in the Son, God the Father might become known throughout the world, whereas previously he had been known only among the Jews.

“Glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you,” as though he had said: “Raise me from the dead, so that through me you may become known throughout the world.”

The text continues:

“As you gave him authority over all flesh.”

That is, over every human being: the whole is named from a part, for he uses “flesh” to mean the whole human being. He said this to show more clearly how he would glorify the Father. “As you gave him authority,” he says, “over all flesh, so may the Son glorify you”—that is, make you known to all flesh which you gave him.

For you gave it in such a way that everything you gave him he might give them eternal life.

“Now this is eternal life: that they should know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent.”

The order of the words is this: “That they should know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent.” Full knowledge of God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is also full and perfect eternal life; it is supreme blessedness. Supreme blessedness exists only in eternal life. Therefore he said: “This is eternal life: that they should know you and Jesus Christ whom you sent, the only and true God.”

“I glorified you on earth; I completed the work which you gave me to do.”

Why did he use the past tense—“I glorified” and “I completed”—and immediately add a future-tense verb, “to do,” unless it is because all things are present to God and things future in divine predestination are to be regarded as though already accomplished? What was destined to happen was, for him, as though it had already happened.

“I glorified you,” as though he had said: “I will glorify you with the glory of preaching which I will bring about throughout the whole world through my disciples, when I complete the work of my passion and resurrection which you gave me to do.”

“And now, Father, glorify me with yourself.”

By saying, “I glorified you on earth,” and asking the Father, with the Father himself, to be glorified, he clearly showed the manner of both glorifications. He glorified the Father on earth by preaching him to the nations; the Father glorified him with himself by placing him at his right hand.

He added: “With the glory which I had with you before the world existed.” The order of the words is: “With the glory which I had with you before the world was.”

This is the force of his statement, “And now glorify me”: as then, so now; as then by predestination, so now by completion. Do in the world what existed with you before the world; accomplish in its proper time what you established before all times.

We should understand this passage as referring to the predestination of the glorification of his human nature, which was to become immortal from mortal before the Father. By predestination this had already been accomplished before the world existed, although it was to take place in the world at its proper time. As the apostle says of us: “As he chose us in him before the foundation of the world.”

“I have manifested your name to the human beings whom you gave me from the world.”

What he was going to accomplish through holy teachers throughout the whole world after the glory of his resurrection and ascension, and after the gifts of the Holy Spirit had been bestowed upon the disciples, he declared as though it had already been accomplished.

This is like what he said shortly before: “I glorified you on earth.” In both places he uses the past tense in place of the future, as one who knew that it had been predestined to happen, and therefore said that he had done what he would certainly do without any doubt.

The text continues:

“They were yours, and you gave them to me; and they have kept your word. Now they know that everything you have given me is from you; because the words which you gave me I have given to them, and they received them and truly understood that I came forth from you, and they believed that you sent me.”

Although all these things could also have been said of all future believers, in the certainty of hope while they were still future, they can nevertheless be understood especially of the disciples, to whom he was then speaking in their presence.

For what follows:

“When I was with them, I was keeping them in your name. Those whom you gave me I guarded, and none of them perished except the son of perdition.”

Since he signifies Judas, who betrayed him and was one of the Twelve, this interpretation agrees better with the sense that he was speaking specifically to the apostles.

Then he adds:

“But now I am coming to you.”

It is clear that, by saying, “When I was with them, I was keeping them,” he spoke of his bodily presence, as though that presence would no longer be with them. In this way he wished to signify the ascension that was soon to occur, of which he says: “But now I am coming to you”—going, of course, to the right hand of the Father, from which he will come to judge the living and the dead.

“I have manifested your name to the human beings whom you gave me.”

Not the name by which you are God, but the name by which you are my Father—a name that cannot be manifested without the manifestation of his Son. As for the name by which he is God, he considered that it could not be wholly unknown to any rational nature. For this is truly the power of divinity: it cannot be entirely hidden from a rational creature without being known, except in the few in whom rational nature has been excessively corrupted.

Almost all nations confess that God exists, although various errors prevent them from recognizing the true God. What is read in the Psalms—“God is known in Judah alone”—means that only among the Jews was the true God known and worshiped through legitimate worship.

“And they have kept your word. Now they know that everything you have given me is from you.”

That is, they have understood that everything is from you. For the Father gave everything at the same time as he begot the one who possessed everything, as the Lord himself says earlier in this Gospel: “For as the Father has life in himself, so he has also given the Son to have life in himself.” That is, he begot the Son possessing life in himself.

“Because the words which you gave me I have given them, and they received them.”

That is, they understood and retained them. For the word is received when it is grasped by the mind, and it is retained so that it does not perish through forgetfulness.

“And they truly understood,” he says, “that I came forth from you, and they believed that you sent me.”

Here too “truly” must be supplied. What he said—“They truly understood”—he did not explain by adding, “and they believed.” They therefore truly believed what they truly understood. For “I came forth from you” is the same as “You sent me.”

Yet the disciples were not still such as he says they would become. He used verbs in the past tense, speaking as though it had already happened, and declaring what they would become in the future once they had received the Holy Spirit, who, as promised, would teach them all things and lead them into all truth.

He gave them the words, as he said, which the Father gave him; but they received them spiritually not outwardly in their ears but inwardly in their hearts. Then they truly received them, because then they truly understood; and they truly understood because they truly believed.

But if the words which the Son says the Father gave him are understood as referring to the unity of divinity, the Father gave words to the Son in the same way that he begot the Word coeternal with himself. If, however, the statement refers to humanity, who can understand in what manner God, made human from the Virgin, gave or received them? Who can even narrate that generation which took place from the Virgin?

The text continues:

“I am praying for them; I am not praying for the world, but for those whom you gave me.”

He said this among other things while praying for those whom the Father had given him. By “the world” he now wishes to be understood those who live according to the desire of the world and do not yet possess that grace by which they may be chosen out of the world. Therefore he says that he is not praying for the world but for those whom the Father gave him.

For the fact that the Father has already given them to him has made it so that they do not belong to that world for which he does not pray. Then he adds: “Because they are yours.”

For the Father did not lose those whom he gave to the Son, since the Son continues and says: “All mine are yours, and yours are mine.” Here it is sufficiently clear how all that belongs to the Father belongs to the only Son: namely, because he too is God and was born of the Father, equal to the Father.

This was said concerning the holy and rational creature whom God chose and who is subject to the Father and the Son, and who belongs equally to the Father and the Son. Since this creature belongs to God the Father, it would not also belong to the Son unless the Son were equal to the Father. Nor is it right that the saints of whom he spoke should belong to anyone except the one by whom they were created and sanctified.

Therefore, since they belong both to the Father and to the Son, they demonstrate that the two are equal, since those creatures belong equally to both.

“And I am glorified in them,” he says.

Now he speaks of his glorification as though it had already happened, although it was still future.

“And I am glorified in them”—that is, I am glorified throughout the whole world through their preaching. And because it had been predestined to happen, he wished what was future to be certain; therefore he used a verb in the past tense.

“And now,” he says, “I am no longer in the world, and these are in the world.”

He signifies the hour when he was about to pass from this world. He used the present tense in place of the future because he said that what was soon to happen was as though it had already happened.

When he says, “These are in the world,” he signifies those to whom he was speaking. They would pass from this world more slowly, since, when he departed from the world, it was necessary for them to remain, through whom his holy name would be preached in the world.

Foreseeing what might trouble those who would not hear these things when they read them, he added: “But now I am coming to you.”

He designates the glory of the ascension, through which the human being was lifted above the heights of heaven and the dignities of all angelic powers, so that he might be placed at the right hand of God the Father. There he remains with him and reigns together with the Holy Spirit as one God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XLVI. ON THE DAY OF THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

Reading from the Acts of the Apostles.

“I composed the first account, O Theophilus, of all that Jesus began to do and teach until the day when, after giving commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen, he was taken up,” etc.

Luke the evangelist, my brothers, who wrote one of the four Gospels, also produced the book of the Acts of the Apostles, from which the present reading has just been proclaimed. In it he first makes mention both of the final meal which the Lord had with his disciples after his resurrection and of his ascension into heaven, which we celebrate today.

The beginning of that book is as follows: “I composed the first account”—that is, the Gospel—“O Theophilus, bishop,” you who compel me to write this book of the Acts of the Apostles, “of all that Jesus began to do,” first by displaying signs or doing those things which pertained to examples of life, “and afterward to teach.” For Jesus, establishing a good teacher, did nothing except what he taught, “until the day when, after giving commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen, he was taken up,” giving commands before his ascension that they should observe and fulfill what is read either in this book or in the Gospels.

[Col. 0232A]

“To whom he also presented himself alive after his passion by many proofs, appearing to them for forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God.”

Through this fellowship with the disciples during the forty days, he signifies that he would fulfill everything, both open and hidden, which he had promised to fulfill. Let us mention just one of the many things he said: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age.”

“And while eating with them, he commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to await the promise of the Father.”

He took food with the disciples in order to show, by allowing them to touch and handle it, that the same flesh which he had raised after dying was truly his flesh.

The text continues:

“Which you heard,” he says, “through my mouth: for John indeed baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.”

The apostles had already been baptized with water, but not yet fully with the Holy Spirit, whose coming is promised after that ascension. Neither the apostles themselves nor their successors have so far been able to baptize in the Church in any other way than John the Baptist—that is, in water. Yet, when the name of Christ is invoked, the inward power of the Holy Spirit is present. By plunging the human being into the water, it simultaneously purifies the souls and bodies of those who are baptized; this did not happen in John’s baptism.

Therefore, those who had gathered together questioned him, saying:

“Lord, will you restore the kingdom to Israel at this time?”

They appropriately inquire about the kingdom of God, asking whether, when the Holy Spirit immediately came, it was to be restored in the present, or whether they should believe that it was reserved for the saints in the future.

But he said to them:

“It is not for you to know the times or moments which the Father has established in his own authority.”

He showed that it is not beneficial for us mortals to know the day of our calling, so that, always uncertain of the Judge’s coming, we may live each day with such vigilance as though we must hasten to judgment on the following day.

“But you will receive,” he says, “the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and throughout all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.”

It is as though he said: “You must not think that, when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, the consummation of this world will immediately occur. Rather, he will provide you with power only to testify about me.”

[Col. 0232D]

“And when he had said these things, while they were watching, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their eyes.”

Everywhere creation renders service to its Creator: the stars announce him at his birth; they are darkened over him in his suffering; clouds receive him as he ascends; and they will accompany him when he returns for judgment.

And behold, two men stood beside them in white garments, and they said to them: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking up into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven.” That is, he will come to judge in the same form of flesh and substance in which he came to be judged.

Let us therefore prepare ourselves by worthy conduct for the ascent into heaven, and recognize that we are sojourning in this valley of the world. [Col. 0233A] Even if certain advantages flatter us here, they must not be wickedly embraced but courageously despised. Therefore, beloved brothers, if you wish to ascend into heaven, let us meanwhile strengthen this hope within us; let us burn with all our desires for it; let us meditate on earth upon the fact that we are reckoned among the inhabitants of heaven. Then, when we shall cast off the mortality of the flesh, let us now cast off the oldness of the soul. The body will easily be lifted into the heights of heaven if the burden of sins does not weigh down the spirit.

Therefore, beloved, let us raise ourselves toward him who made the dust of our lowliness into the body of his glory; and, in order that we may deserve to be companions of his ascension, let us conform ourselves in every respect to his humility and patience. We have undertaken the malice (*malitiam*) of a great name [perhaps: “military service,” *militiam*], the discipline of a great promise. The followers of Christ may not depart from the royal road, nor is it fitting for those who strive toward eternal things to be occupied with temporal matters. [Col. 0233B] And since we have been redeemed by the precious blood of Christ, let us glorify and bear God in our body, so that we may deserve to attain what has been prepared in every respect for the faithful.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XLVII. ON THE SAME FEAST

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Mark.

At that time, when the eleven disciples were reclining at table for the last time, Jesus appeared and reproached their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen him risen.

[Col. 0233C] How “for the last time”? As though they would not see him thereafter. For that was the last occasion on which the apostles saw the Lord on earth, when he ascended into heaven; this took place on the fortieth day after the resurrection. Was he then going to reproach them for not having believed those who had seen him risen, when they themselves had so often seen him after the resurrection?

We therefore understand that, after the many appearances by which he presented himself to the disciples over forty days, he appeared to the eleven while they were reclining at table for the last time—that is, on the fortieth day itself. And since he was about to ascend into heaven, we understand that on that day especially he wished to reproach them for not having believed those who had seen him risen before they themselves saw him, [Col. 0233D] since, after his ascension, as they preached the Gospel, the nations would believe what they had not seen.

After this reproach, Mark immediately says:

And he said to them: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned.”

Since they were going to preach this, how could one who did not believe be condemned, seeing that he would not have believed what he had not seen? Should not the disciples themselves first have been reproached because, before they had seen the Lord, they had not believed those to whom the Lord had appeared?

When he said to them, “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature,” was the holy Gospel to be preached to things without understanding or to irrational animals, so that the disciples were told, “Preach to every creature”? [Col. 0234A] Rather, by the name “every creature” every human being among the nations can be understood. For earlier it had been said, “Do not go into the way of the nations”; but now it is said, “Preach the Gospel to every creature,” so that the preaching rejected by Judea might then become our aid, when Judea had proudly rejected it as a testimony to its own condemnation.

“Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned.” Perhaps each person may say to himself: “I have already believed; I shall be saved.” This is true if he holds the faith by his works. For true faith is that which is not contradicted in conduct by what it says in words. Hence Paul says of certain false believers: “They profess that they know God, but they deny him by their deeds.” [Col. 0234B] Hence John says: “Whoever says that he knows God but does not keep his commandments is a liar.”

But when it is said, “Whoever does not believe will be condemned,” what shall we say here about little children, who because of their age are not yet able to believe? There is no question concerning adults. In the Church of the Savior, therefore, little children believe through others, just as from others they have inherited the sins that are remitted to them in baptism.

And these signs will accompany those who believe: “In my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will pick up serpents; and if they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them; they will lay hands on the sick, and they will be well.”

Does it follow that, because we do not perform signs, we do not believe? [Col. 0234C] These signs were necessary at the beginning of the Church. For the faith of believers to grow, it had to be nourished by miracles. We too, when we plant trees, keep pouring water on them until we see that they have become strong in the soil; but once they have firmly taken root, the watering stops. Hence Paul says: “Tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers.”

Or should we consider more subtly the signs and powers mentioned here? The holy Church indeed performs spiritually every day what it then performed bodily through the apostles. When its priests lay a hand on believers through the grace of exorcism and forbid evil spirits to dwell in their minds, what else are they doing but casting out demons? And all the faithful who have now silenced the worldly sounds of their former life [perhaps: “have cast them away”] proclaim, as far as they are able, the praise and power of their Creator. [Col. 0234D] What else are they doing but speaking in new tongues?

When, through their good exhortations, they remove wickedness from the hearts of others, they pick up serpents. And when they hear poisonous suggestions but are not drawn into wicked action, what they drink is indeed deadly, but it does not harm them. Whenever they see their neighbors weakened in good works, they come to their aid with all their strength and strengthen the lives of those who were faltering in their own conduct by the example of their action. What else are they doing but laying hands on the sick so that they may be well?

These miracles are all the greater because they are spiritual; they are all the greater because through them not bodies but souls are raised up.

And indeed, after the Lord Jesus had spoken to them, he was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God. [Col. 0235A]

We must consider what Mark means when he says, “He sits at the right hand of God.” Stephen says: “I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.” What does it mean that Mark testifies that he saw him sitting, whereas Stephen saw him standing?

We know that sitting belongs to one who judges, while standing belongs to one who fights or gives assistance. Since our Redeemer, having been taken up into heaven, now judges all things and will come at the end as judge of all, Mark describes him after his ascension as sitting, because after the glory of his ascension he will be seen as judge at the end. But Stephen, placed in the struggle of suffering, [Col. 0235B] saw him standing as his helper, because, so that Stephen might overcome the unbelief of his persecutors on earth, Christ fought for him from heaven by his grace.

But they went out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word through the signs that followed.

What should be considered here, what should be entrusted to memory, except that obedience followed the command, and signs followed obedience?

There remains, certainly, a question of no small importance: how the same evangelist could have written that the angel said to the women, “Go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you into Galilee; there you will see him, as he told you,” and yet did not subsequently report anywhere in his Gospel that the Lord was seen by the disciples there. We must understand that what was said by the angel and by the Lord was said prophetically. [Col. 0235C]

For Galilee is interpreted either as “migration” or as “revelation.” First, according to the meaning “migration,” what else should be understood by “He is going before you into Galilee; there you will see him, as he told you,” except that the grace of Christ was going to migrate from the people of Israel to the nations? The apostles would in no way have been believed by them as they preached the Gospel unless the Lord himself had first prepared the way for them in human hearts. This is what is meant by “He is going before you into Galilee.”

When they would marvel with joy that, after difficulties had been broken and overcome, a door in the Lord had been opened to them through the illumination of believers, this is what is meant by “There you will see him”: that is, “There you will find his members; there you will recognize his living body in those who receive you.”

But according to the interpretation of Galilee as “revelation,” [Col. 0235D] this should no longer be understood as referring to him in the form of a servant, but in that form in which he is equal to the Father. He promised this revelation to those who love him when he said in John: “I too will love him and will show myself to him.”

That will be the revelation, the true Galilee, when we shall be like him and see him as he is. It will also be the more blessed migration from this world into that eternity, if we embrace his commandments in such a way that we may deserve to be separated to his right hand. For then those on the left will go into eternal fire, but the righteous into eternal life.

In the Lord’s ascension the two readings are harmonized: there the glory of his resurrection and ascension from this world is revealed, as well as his judgment that will come at the end of the present [Col. 0236A] world, when he will repay each person according to his own merits. There they will remain without end throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XLVIII. THE SUNDAY AFTER THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

Reading from the Epistle of the blessed apostle Peter.

Beloved, be prudent and vigilant in prayers, etc.

And in the Gospel the Lord commanded us always to pray and keep watch in view of the uncertainty of the end. Speaking of the day of judgment, he says: “Keep watch, praying at all times, so that you may be considered worthy to escape all these things that are going to happen and to stand before the Son of Man.”

We are rightly commanded to keep watch in prayers, so that when we stand at prayer every carnal and worldly thought may withdraw, and the mind may think of nothing then except that for which it is praying. The enemy frequently slips in, and, deceiving us subtly, turns our prayers away from God, so that we hold one thing in our heart and utter another with our voice, although God ought to be prayed to by sincere intention—not by the sound of the voice, but by the feeling of the mind. [Col. 0236B]

“Above all, have constant mutual charity among yourselves.”

He rightly adds “constant,” because we are always able to love, but we cannot always keep watch in prayer, since the weakness of the flesh hinders us. Nor are we able to devote ourselves continually to the virtues he next mentions, namely, hospitality, teaching, the administration of gifts—whether common or spiritual—to our neighbors, and other things of this kind. These necessarily take place through the service of the body and at suitable times. [Col. 0236C] But charity itself, by whose impulse these outward actions are performed and which presides over the inner person, can always be possessed inwardly, even though it cannot always be displayed publicly.

“For charity covers a multitude of sins,” etc.

This is especially true when one says truthfully to God: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” It is certain that all the good works we perform can cleanse and cover the faults we have committed. But he speaks here especially of charity, by which we forgive our neighbors what they owe us, because it is most just before God that according to the measure of mercy with which we have measured, it should be measured back to us.

Conversely, the wise man rebukes the terrifying hardness of heart when he says: “A man preserves anger against another man and seeks healing from God.” [Col. 0236D] Nor should we doubt that in the person who, through charity, does everything he can for the correction of his neighbor—admonishing, reproving, and chastising—charity itself also covers a multitude of sins.

“If anyone speaks, let him speak as the words of God.”

He fears, evidently, lest he say or command anything contrary to God’s will, or contrary to what is clearly commanded in the holy Scriptures, and thus be found like a false witness or a sacrilegious person, introducing something foreign into the teaching of the Lord. Or he fears lest he suppress and pass over anything that is pleasing to God, since the Lord himself most explicitly commands preachers of the truth to instruct those whom they form in life, saying: “Teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you.” [Col. 0237A]

He commands them to hand over to their hearers for observance the things that he himself commanded—not other things, and not some of them rather than all of them.

“If anyone ministers, let him do so as from the power that God supplies.”

The more certainly each person knows that he cannot have from himself what he supplies, the more humbly should he offer his neighbor every good that he can. Thus God may be honored in all things through Jesus Christ, in accordance with the command of Jesus Christ himself, who says: “Let them see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” [Col. 0237B]

God is therefore honored in our actions when we attribute everything we do well and according to God’s will not to our own merits but to his grace. Conversely, we attribute the evils we commit solely to our own wickedness, laziness, or ignorance.

Therefore it is necessary that we order our life in all things according to God’s will and diligently do what has been commanded by him. What has been forbidden by him, however, must in no way be done. Rather, we must strive to persevere in right faith and good works until the end of life.

By the provision of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XLIX. ON THE SAME FEAST

Reading from the holy Gospel according to John.

[Col. 0237C]

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “When the Paraclete has come, whom I shall send to you from my Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father,” etc.

In many passages of the holy Gospel we find that, before the coming of the Holy Spirit, the disciples were less capable of understanding the mysteries of divine majesty and less strong in enduring the adversities of human wickedness. But when the Spirit came, an increase in divine knowledge was given to them together with steadfastness for overcoming the trials of human persecution.

Therefore he promised that they would be strengthened by the coming of the Holy Spirit, both for confidence in preaching and for steadfastness in suffering. We know that this happened in the very leader of the apostles, who previously feared confessing Christ at the voice of a single maidservant, [Col. 0237D] but later, strengthened by the Holy Spirit, preached him openly and more boldly than all the others to many thousands of Jews. We read that three thousand men believed and were baptized at his preaching, and that not long afterward another five thousand believed.

When he says, “who proceeds from the Father,” and immediately adds, “whom I shall send,” he signifies that the same Holy Spirit proceeds equally from the Father and the Son and is sent equally by the Father and the Son. But because of the distinction of persons, he is here said to proceed from the Father and to be sent by the Son. In that same distinction of persons, Christ declares that his operation and will are one with the Father’s will.

He also comes of his own accord, because he is equal to the Father and the Son, so that it may be recognized that the Holy Trinity has one will and one operation. [Col. 0238A]

“He,” he says, “will bear witness about me, and you also will bear witness.”

What they received through the inward teaching of the Spirit, they carried out outwardly by speaking and ministering to others after casting away fear. For the Spirit himself illuminated their hearts with knowledge of the truth and raised them up to teach the heights of the truth that they had come to know.

“When the Paraclete comes,” he says, “he will bear witness about me.” It is as though he said: “They hated me and killed me while seeing me; but the Paraclete will bear such witness about me that he will cause them to believe in me without seeing me.”

“And you,” he says, “will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.” The Holy Spirit will bear witness, and you also will bear witness, you who have been with me from the beginning. [Col. 0238B] You can preach what you know, but you do not do so now because the fullness of that Spirit is not yet present in you.

“I have spoken these things to you so that you may not be scandalized.”

“They will expel you from the synagogues.” The merciful teacher took care to predict to his disciples the future conflicts with wicked people, so that the things coming upon them might trouble them less. Adversities that are foreseen are usually borne more lightly than those that suddenly arise out of despair. Thus we read in secular literature that sudden disasters and disturbances often weary even the bravest soldiers in war.

“But the hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God.”

The Jews thought that they were offering service to God by pursuing the ministers of the New Testament with hatred and death. But, as the Apostle testifies concerning them, “They have zeal, but not according to knowledge.” The zealots of the Law therefore think that they are offering service to God while inflicting death upon the heralds of grace. [Col. 0238C] They defend the Law that was given through a servant, while refusing to receive the grace offered by the Son himself.

But they think in vain that they please the Father when they strive to despise, and even to persecute and blaspheme, the Son of God.

He said that two things would come upon them from the Jews: first, that they would expel them from the synagogue; second, that they would kill them. These things also contributed to the accumulation of that people’s condemnation, so that they might become beneficial to the salvation of the nations.

Thus Paul said to those Jews in the Acts of the Apostles: “Since you have judged yourselves unworthy of the word of God, behold, we turn to the nations.” [Col. 0238D] For the Lord commanded us in this way: “Behold, I have given you as a light to the nations, so that you may be salvation to them unto the end of the earth.”

It follows:

“And they will do these things because they have known neither me nor my Father.”

Since the Son is in the Father, and the Father is in the Son, and whoever sees the Son also sees the Father, it is evident that all who stubbornly reject belief in the Son are proved not to know the Father either.

“I did not tell you these things from the beginning, because I was with you.”

It is a great consolation for the disciples to remember that their teacher had foretold what they would suffer, and to know that they would have as helper and rewarder the one for whose name they had been told they would suffer such things. [Col. 0239A]

“But I have spoken these things to you so that, when the hour comes, you may remember them, because I told you.”

What are the things he did not tell them from the beginning? Even the things concerning the Holy Spirit, whom he was going to send them from the Father, and concerning the consolation and strengthening of that same Spirit, by which they would be consoled and strengthened, so that they would have no need to fear with a free mind any adversities of the world, or the scandals and persecutions of the Jews.

“I did not tell you these things from the beginning, because I was with you.”

For my presence was consoling you.

These two readings are harmonized in the duty of charity. Whoever possesses charity perfectly and strives to preserve it fully, both in heart and in works, to the end of life will undoubtedly enjoy the eternal kingdom, the contemplation of God’s face, and the holy angels forever. [Col. 0239B]

By the provision of our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY L. WEDNESDAY

Reading from the Epistle of the blessed apostle Paul to the Hebrews.

Brothers, “we have seen Jesus crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone.”

Here he shows that the cross of Christ is glory and honor, for the sake of which he was made a little lower than the angels, just as the Lord himself always calls it, saying: “So that the Son of Man may be glorified.” [Col. 0239C]

If he calls those things which he suffered for his servants glory, much more should you, a human being who suffer for the Lord, have no doubt that this pertains to your everlasting glory.

He added: “So that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone.” He names as “grace” the one who tasted death for the salvation of all. For it was not owed to us that the Son should taste death for us; grace accomplished this. He indeed died for everyone.

But what if not everyone believes? He nevertheless fulfilled what belonged to him. For this reason he said that he “tasted death”: because he remained in it for a short time, so that, having conquered it, he might immediately rise again.

For it was fitting that he for whom and through whom all things exist, who had brought many sons into glory, should perfect the author of their salvation through suffering.

“It was fitting that he should perfect through suffering”—that is, complete the salvation of all through him, through whom all things exist. By “all things” are meant those things restored both in heaven and on earth through his death, as well as all things that were created through him. [Col. 0239D]

You see how much there is in our midst: both the Son and us as sons—the Son by nature, us by adoption. But he saves, and we are saved. You see how he both joins us together and distinguishes us. When he says “bringing many sons into glory,” he joins us; when he says “author of their salvation,” he distinguishes him from us.

“For the one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one.”

Here again he joins them, honoring and consoling them, and calling them brothers of Christ, since he says that they are from one source.

Then, fortifying his statement and showing how he spoke of the one who is according to the flesh, he says: “The one who sanctifies”—that is, Christ—“and those who are sanctified”—that is, us. Do you see how great the difference is? [Col. 0240A] He sanctifies; we are sanctified.

He added, “all from one.” There is one God from whom all things come, but he is so in one way and we in another: he as the proper Son, we as adopted sons. Nevertheless, we have one God as Father. He, as the proper Son, sanctifies; we, as adopted sons, are sanctified. For this reason he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying:

“I shall proclaim your name to my brothers.”

When he says that he is not ashamed to call them brothers, he demonstrates that the brotherhood belongs to our nature, but also to his great mercy and humility, because he chose us as brothers for himself. [Col. 0240B]

He confirms this by prophetic testimony, so that it would not be thought to be something new or something not foretold long before. For he says: “I shall proclaim to my brothers.” After the sacred passion and resurrection, he says that the glory of his divinity would be proclaimed throughout the whole world.

“I shall proclaim” means “I shall cause it to be proclaimed,” just as he said to the women in the Gospel: “Go, announce to my brothers.” Those who love and those who are loved are both called brothers.

He added:

“In the midst of the Church I shall praise you.”

In the midst of the saints the Lord’s praise resounds through the one who says: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little ones.”

The true praise of the Lord is proclaimed not only with the mouth but also with the heart of one who loves and fulfills the Lord’s commandments. [Col. 0240C]

And again:

“I shall put my trust in him.”

This was said of the man who was assumed, whose entire confidence is undoubtedly in God the Father. Thus in the Gospel he himself says on behalf of those for whom he was praying: “Father, I desire that where I am, these also may be with me.”

He also exhorted them to have confidence, saying: “Take courage; I have conquered the world.”

And again:

“Behold, I and the children whom God has given me.”

The Apostle brought this testimony from Isaiah and referred it to Christ and to the apostles, whom he called children because of their innocence. Concerning them the Lord himself says: “Let the little children come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven.”

Therefore, since the children shared in flesh and blood, he himself likewise shared in the same.

Here he establishes the true brotherhood and the reality, not the fiction, of Christ’s humanity. Just as children consist of flesh and blood, so he shared in flesh and blood, so that he might have that by which to taste death for the salvation of the children. [Col. 0240D] He adds the reason for this dispensation:

“So that through death,” he says, “he might destroy the one who held the power of death”—that is, the devil.

Here he displays something remarkable: the devil was defeated by the very means through which he had exercised power. The weapons that had been strong against the world—that is, death—were used by Christ to strike him. Here he indicates the greatness of the victor’s power by showing what good death accomplished.

“And he might free,” he says, “those who through fear of death were subject to slavery throughout their whole life.”

Why do you tremble? Why do you fear what has already been condemned? It is no longer terrifying but desirable, like the end of labors and the beginning of rest.

Why, he says, were they subject to slavery throughout their whole life through fear of death? All had been slaves of death because they feared death. [Col. 0241A] They had not yet been released from fear of death, whose laws held them bound.

Now the saints mock it. Having passed through the contest and conquered death, they are going to pass into the kingdom. Hence Paul himself says: “I desire to depart and be with Christ.”

For he did not take hold of angels, but he took hold of the seed of Abraham.

Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect.

Here he honors the patriarch and those who are descended from him, to whom this Epistle was written. [Col. 0241B] He therefore recalls the benefits of God, their bodily kinship with Christ, and the promise made to Abraham: “To you and to your seed I shall give this land.”

“For all are from one”—that is, Christ according to the flesh and those to whom he was speaking were from Abraham.

But when he said above, “Since the children shared in flesh and blood, he himself likewise shared in the same,” he develops this meaning further, explaining from whom he would receive flesh and blood.

Therefore he says: “For he did not take hold of any angel”—that is, he did not assume the nature of any angel—but “he took hold of the seed of Abraham.”

The angels were not granted one common dignity such that the Son of God would be joined to their nature in one person. Rather, God the Son bestowed honor and this dignity upon human nature, so that God and man might be one person. [Col. 0241C]

Why did he say “he took hold”? Because he pursued and seized us as though we had withdrawn from him and fled far away, and he united the nature of our weakness to himself in one person.

Therefore, he says, “he had to be made like his brothers in every respect.” What does “in every respect” mean? He was born, brought up, grew, suffered everything that was fitting, and at the end died. This is what it means to be made like his brothers in every respect.

For he had said many things about his majesty and former glory; now he begins to speak about the dispensation, so that we may contemplate with what wisdom he shows that he was deeply concerned to become like us. This revealed his very great care for us.

Having said above, “Since the children shared in flesh and blood, he himself likewise shared in the same,” and here, “he was made like his brothers in every respect,” he is as if saying: He who is so great, who is the brightness of glory, the imprint of substance, who made the ages, who sits at the Father’s right hand—he willed and desired to become our brother in every respect. [Col. 0241D]

“So that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God, to make propitiation for the sins of the people.”

There was therefore no other reason for him to be made like his brothers in every respect except that he might be a faithful high priest for us and make propitiation for our sins.

“For in that which he himself suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted.”

In that is, in his humanity, in which he suffered, he is able to free those who are bound and help those who are tempted, so that they may not be overcome. He knew our temptations by experience in himself, not only as God but also as man.

Although God in his own nature is incapable of suffering, the same Son of God was capable of suffering in the nature he assumed, since he was made like our nature. In the flesh he assumed he suffered many cruel things; he knows what temptation is for those who suffer. He himself was tempted but not overcome. [Col. 0242A]

What, then, does it mean that he is able to help those who are tempted? It is as though someone were saying: “I extend my hand with great eagerness to share in suffering.”

Therefore, holy brothers, sharers in a heavenly calling, consider the apostle and high priest of our confession, Jesus Christ our Lord.

He is still speaking about the mystery of Christ’s incarnation. In the Gospel he himself testifies that he was sent only to the lost sheep, that is, to the house of Israel. [Col. 0242B]

The Greek word *apostolus* means “one who is sent” in Latin. Recognize what Jesus the priest is, and what kind of priest he is; you have no need of any other consolation or comfort.

He called him the high priest of our confession—that is, of our faith—to whom this new people has been entrusted, just as the former people was given to Moses to govern. But greater and far better things have been entrusted to this one.

For the blessed Paul wishes to raise the minds of the Israelites to the excellence of God’s promises, so that they may prepare themselves attentively to receive what God has graciously promised to bring them through Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LI. ON THE SAME FEAST

Reading from the holy Gospel according to John.

[Col. 0242C]

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “If you remain in me and my words remain in you, whatever you wish, ask, and it will be done for you.”

By remaining in Christ, what can they wish for except what is fitting for Christ? By remaining in the Savior, what can they wish for except what is not foreign to salvation? They do not wish to ask for anything except what is beneficial for salvation.

When we remain in him and his words remain in us, whatever we wish, let us ask, and it will be done for us. If we ask and it is not done, then we are not asking for what belongs to remaining in him, nor for what his words, which remain in us, persuade us to ask. Rather, we are asking for what belongs to desire and the weakness of the flesh, which is not in him and in which his words do not remain. [Col. 0242D]

His words are said to remain in us when we do what he commanded and love what he promised.

The Savior increasingly commends to the disciples the grace by which we are saved, saying:

“In this my Father is glorified: that you bear much fruit and become my disciples.”

If it is the Father’s glory that we bear much fruit and become Christ’s disciples, let us not attribute this to our own glory, as though we possessed it from ourselves. This grace belongs to him, and therefore in this it is not our glory but his.

From whom, then, are we made Christ’s disciples, except from the one whose mercy goes before us in willing, follows us in enabling, and brings about those things by which we remain continually in him? [Col. 0243A]

“As the Father has loved me, I also have loved you. Remain in my love.”

From where do good works come to us? From where could they come, except that faith works through love? And from where do we love, except that we were loved first? And how would God’s love be in us unless his grace first went before us—the grace by which he loved us when we were in sins and made us alive together with Christ?

When he says, “As the Father has loved me, and I have loved you,” he does not show an equality of nature between ours and his, as there is between the Father and himself. Rather, he shows the grace by which he is the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus.

He shows himself to be the mediator when he says, “The Father has loved me, and I have loved you.” For the Father certainly loves us also, but in him, since the Father is glorified in this: that we bear fruit in the vine, that is, in the Son, and become his disciples. [Col. 0243B]

“Remain,” he says, “in my love.” How will you remain? Listen to what follows:

“If you keep my commandments,” he says, “you will remain in my love.”

For this will show that you remain in my love: if you keep my commandments. Let no one deceive himself by saying that he loves him if he does not keep his commandments. We love him to the extent that we keep his commandments; to the extent that we keep them less, we love him less.

What does he mean by saying, “Remain in my love,” except “Remain in my grace”? And what does “If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love” mean except “By this you will know that you remain in my love, with which I love you, if you keep my commandments”?

But what does he add: “As I have kept my Father’s commandments and remain in his love”? [Col. 0243C]

What are the Father’s commandments except those he mentioned earlier: “As the Father gave me a commandment, so I do”? Explaining this, the Apostle says: “Christ became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name.”

He adds: “And I remain in his love.”

He spoke of the love with which the Father loves him. But is grace also to be understood here, by which the Father loves the Son, just as grace is that by which the Son loves us, since we are sons by grace, while the only-begotten Son is so by nature?

The Son therefore remains in the love with which the Father loved him, and for this reason he kept the commandments.

What is that man born of a virgin except one whose protector is God? [Col. 0243D] For he was the only-begotten Son of God the Father, God himself; but so that he might be given to us as mediator through ineffable grace, the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.

I have said these things to you so that my joy may be in you, and your joy may be made complete. Let my word be in you and be fulfilled. What is Christ’s joy in us except our salvation, for the sake of which he became human? And what is the joy of yours that he says is to be made complete, except having fellowship with him, as he says in what follows: “Father, I will that where I am, these also may be with me.” His joy, therefore, concerning our salvation—which was always his, since he foreknew and predestined us—began to be in us when he called us. And this we rightly call our joy, by which we too shall be blessed in the future. His joy, however, has always been perfect; it cannot diminish, nor would it have anywhere to grow. But our joy begins in the faith of those who are reborn and will be completed in the reward of those who rise again.

“This is my commandment: that you love one another, as I have loved you.” Above, when he commanded love, he said, “I give you a new commandment”; now he says, “my commandment.” He said “new,” so that we should not persist in our old condition; here he says “my,” so that we should not think it contemptible. The repetition of this commandment is itself a commendation of it. For without charity no commandment is acceptable to God. Concerning charity the Apostle says: “Love is the fullness of the law.” Where, therefore, charity is present, what could be lacking? But where it is absent, what could be beneficial? No one loves who does not believe; no one despairs who loves. These are the three things on which the Christian religion rests: hope, faith, and charity. Yet charity is greater than these, because it does not pass away but remains. When it begins here, it will be perfected there, where it remains.

Let us therefore hold to this commandment of the Lord, that we love one another, and let us do whatever else he commands, just as we possess whatever else there is. He displayed an example of this love in himself, and therefore added: “that you love one another as I have loved you.” For what purpose did Christ love us except that we might be able to reign with Christ? We must love for this purpose: that we may have God and remain in God. Thus those who love one another love God, and this is the love by which God becomes all in all. [Col. 0244C] It follows:

“Greater love has no one than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends.” Why did our Lord Jesus Christ repeat the commandments of charity so often, except because every commandment and every good work is made firm by charity alone? The commandments of the Lord are therefore many in the diversity of their works, but one in the root of love. He truly possesses this charity who loves his friend in God and loves his enemy for God’s sake.

For this reason he added, “as I have loved you”—that is, love to the end for which I loved you. Thus, while hanging on the cross, he prayed for his enemies, saying, “Father, forgive them.” “Greater love has no one than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends.” In this respect Christ’s love for us surpasses all others: he came to lay down his life for his friends, yet with the purpose of making friends out of enemies. Martyrdom, however, is not granted to everyone; nevertheless, showing mercy to the brethren is a benefit available to all. If someone does not give his possessions to a brother in need, how will he be ready to give his life for his brother in persecution? The strength of this charity is to distribute one’s possessions in peace for the love of Christ, so that one may be able, in times of turmoil, to surrender oneself for his name.

“You are my friends if you do what I command you.” Great is the dignity of being God’s friend, but we must consider by what steps one reaches this height. He adds: “if you do what I command you.” It is as though he said openly: You rejoice in the summit; consider through what labors the summit is reached. Great is the mercy of our giver: we were not worthy to be servants, yet we are called friends. Therefore he adds:

“Now I no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his lord is doing.” One kind of service is service arising from fear, another from love. Truth itself expresses these two kinds in this same Gospel, saying: “A servant does not remain in the house forever, but the son remains.” The son serves the Father out of love, whereas the servant serves out of fear. Concerning this service the Lord now says: “Now I no longer call you servants, but friends,” because they are sons, not servants, and therefore also friends; “for a servant does not know what his lord is doing.” One who serves his Lord through the bitterness of fear, rather than serving him as a Father through the sweetness of charity, does not know his Lord’s will.

“But I have called you friends, because I have made known to you everything that I have heard from my Father.” What is everything that he heard from his Father and wished to make known to his servants, so as to perfect them as his friends, except the joys of inward charity and those celebrations of the heavenly homeland that he daily impresses upon our minds through the inspiration of his love? Yet this knowledge, which now proceeds from the Father, will be perfected in that fullness of knowledge concerning which the Apostle says: “When the perfect comes, what is partial will be brought to an end.” The Lord said that he had done for his disciples what he knew he would do.

“You did not choose me, but I chose you.” This is the ineffable grace that goes before us, so that from servants we might become friends. Therefore let pride not steal upon us, as though we could accomplish anything by ourselves. Shortly before, Truth itself said: “Without me you can do nothing.”

“And I appointed you to go and bear fruit.” “I appointed”: I planted you by grace, so that you might go by willing and bear fruit by working. I said “go by willing,” because willing to do something is already a great step toward going. What kind of fruit they ought to bear, he adds:

“And that your fruit should remain, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give you.” The name of the Son is Jesus; Jesus is called “Savior,” or also “salutary.” Therefore the one who asks in the name of the Savior is the one who asks for what pertains to true salvation. For if what is not beneficial is requested, we are not asking in the name of Jesus. Therefore we must struggle to the end to attain eternal salvation; and thus we shall have consolation here in the present tribulation and, in the life to come, shall receive eternal rest. This is granted by our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LII. FRIDAY

A reading from the holy Gospel according to Luke.

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “I am sending the promise of my Father upon you.”

That the grace of the Holy Spirit is called the Father’s promise is shown more fully in the Gospel of John and is also briefly indicated here, when it follows:

“But you are to remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.” Concerning this power, that is, the Holy Spirit, the angel also says to Mary: “The power of the Most High will overshadow you.” And the Lord himself says elsewhere: “For I also know that power has gone out from me.” Luke himself speaks more plainly of this promised power from on high and of the command to remain in the city in the Acts of the Apostles. He says that he commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem but to await the promise of the Father, “which you have heard,” he says, “from my mouth: for John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.” And shortly afterward: “You will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be my witnesses.”

Then he led them out as far as Bethany, and, lifting up his hands, he blessed them. And it happened that, while he was blessing them, he withdrew from them and was carried up into heaven. Passing over everything that he may have done with the disciples during the forty days, he silently joins the first day of his resurrection to the final day on which he ascended into heaven.

Beautifully, as he is about to ascend into heaven, he leads the disciples whom he is to bless outside, as far as Bethany. First, because of the name of the city, which is interpreted as “house of obedience”: the one who descended because of the disobedience of the perverse ascended because of the obedience of those who were converted. For, as the Apostle says, he died because of our offenses and rose because of our justification.

Then also because of the location of that village, or little city, which is said to have been situated on the side of the Mount of Olives. The house of the obedient Church, worthy of apostolic hospitality, has placed the foundations of its faith, hope, and love nowhere except in the side of that highest mountain—that is, of Christ. From this side, opened by the lance, it rejoices that the mysteries of blood and water, by which it is born and nourished, flowed forth for it. From his most fruitful summit—that is, the height of his divinity—it longs for the gifts of spiritual anointing and eagerly awaits the promises of perpetual light and peace.

“And they worshiped him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy; and they were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God.” When the Lord had ascended into heaven, the disciples immediately returned to Jerusalem, worshiping in the place where his feet had last stood, because there they had been commanded to await the promise of the Father that they had heard from the Lord’s mouth. They brought back great joys, because they rejoiced that, after the triumph of the resurrection, their God and Lord had also penetrated the heavens.

They remained continually in the temple, praising and blessing God, so that in the place of prayer, amid the devotions of praise, they might await the coming of the promised Holy Spirit with hearts ready and prepared in every way. Let us too, following the example of the disciples, after celebrating at Jerusalem—that is, in the vision of the Lord’s peace—the solemnities of his passion and resurrection, immediately seek the fields of Bethany under Christ’s leadership. Thus, with a tranquil mind, pacified from every storm of discord, and nourished by the reception of Christ’s flesh and blood, we may take care to become the house of obedience, through which, by God’s mercy, we may attain everlasting glory.

## HOMILY LIII. ON THE SATURDAY OF THE VIGIL OF PENTECOST

Require on Holy Saturday of Easter:

1. From Genesis: “God tested Abraham.”
2. From Deuteronomy: “Moses wrote a song.”
3. From Isaiah: “Seven women will seize.”
4. From Jeremiah: “Hear, Israel.”
5. From Psalm XLI: “A Song: As the deer.”

### A Reading from the Book of Genesis

In those days God tested Abraham and said to him: “Abraham, Abraham.” He answered: “Here I am.” He said to him: “Take your only-begotten son, whom you love, Isaac, and go into the land of vision, and offer him there as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains that I will show you.”

Let us now see what mystery lies hidden beneath this sacrament. When Abraham brought his only son to be sacrificed, he represented the person of God the Father. But why did he receive him as an old man? God does not grow old; rather, the very proclamation concerning Christ had already, in a certain way, grown old when Christ was born. It began from Adam, when it was said, “The two shall be one flesh,” and it was completed in the sixth age of the world, which is signified by Abraham’s old age. For the sacrament of God itself was already ancient, and the sacred old age in the people of God—that is, in the multitude of the prophets—signifies the same thing: that at the end of time Christ was born from that very people of holy souls.

His barrenness, however, indicates that in this world we have been saved in hope and that in Christ, as in Isaac, we have all been born. The Church brought forth that birth at the end of time by the wondrous grace of God, not by natural fertility.

Now we must examine what the sacrament of the following narrative symbolically foreshadowed. Who, then, was represented in Abraham, as was said, by that sacrifice, except the exalted Father? And who in Isaac except Christ? For just as Abraham offered his only and beloved son to God as a victim, so the Lord God handed over his only-begotten Son for us all.

And just as Isaac himself carried the wood on which he was to be placed, so Christ carried on his shoulders the wood of his cross, on which he was to be crucified. The two servants who were left behind and did not go to the place of sacrifice signified the Jews. Since they lived as servants and understood in a carnal manner, they did not comprehend Christ’s humility. Because they did not understand Christ’s passion, they did not reach the place of sacrifice.

Why were there two servants? Because the people themselves were to be divided into two parts. This happened when Solomon sinned, when the same people were divided in the matter of the kingdom, though not by an error of impiety. To these two parts the prophets often say: “Israel the apostate and Judah the transgressor.”

But the donkey, representing the senseless folly of the Jews, carried all these mysteries in its senseless folly and did not know what it carried. Now, concerning what was said to them:

“Wait here with the donkey; after we have worshiped, we will return to you”—listen to the Apostle: “A hardening in part has happened to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved.” For a time, therefore, the Jews were given the dullness of blindness. While they were zealous for the law, they did not see that the gift promised by God and proclaimed by Christ had come. Blinded by zeal, they thought that the law of works ought never to cease.

The three-day period during which they came to the place of sacrifice signifies the three ages of the world: one before the law, another under the law, and a third under grace. Before the law extends from Adam to Moses; under the law, from Moses to John; from then onward, beginning with the Lord and including whatever remains, is the third day of grace. In this third age, as after three days, the sacrificial mystery of Christ was completed.

Then Isaac, with his feet bound, is placed upon the altar, and the Lord, suspended upon the wood, is fastened to the cross. But what was symbolized in Isaac was transferred to the ram. Why? Because Christ is the sheep: he is the Son; he is the Lamb, because he was born; he is the ram, because he was sacrificed.

But what does it mean that the ram was caught in the thickets? The cross has horns. For two pieces of wood are joined together and produce the form of a cross. Hence it is written concerning him: “Horns are in his hands.” The ram caught by its horns therefore signifies Christ crucified.

The thickets are thorns. Thorns signify the wicked and sinners who hung the Lord upon the cross. The Lord, therefore, was suspended amid the thorns of Jewish sinners, just as Jeremiah says of the same people: “This people has surrounded me with the thorns of its sins.” Others have understood this ram, bound by its horns in the thickets, as the same Christ crowned with thorns by the Jews before he was sacrificed.
