After the sacrifice had been completed, Abraham was told: “In your seed all the nations will be blessed.” When did this happen except when the ram says: “They dug my hands and my feet, and they counted all my bones”? When that sacrifice was completed in the Psalms, it was then said in the same Psalm: “All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations will worship in his presence, for the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he will rule the nations.”

After Abraham had sacrificed the ram in place of his son Isaac, he called the name of that place “The Lord sees,” because the Lord made himself visible, certainly through the incarnation that he assumed for the redemption of the human race. Through it he will lead all his elect to everlasting life: Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, through all ages of ages. Amen.

### A Reading from the Book of Deuteronomy

In those days Moses wrote a song, etc. Require on the vigil of Easter.

### A Reading from the Prophet Isaiah

[Col. 0249A]

In those days seven women will seize, etc. Require on the vigil of Easter.

## HOMILY LIV. ON THE SAME FEAST

### A Reading from Jeremiah [Baruch] the Prophet

“Hear, Israel, the commandments of life; listen with your ears so that you may learn wisdom,” etc.

This reading teaches and exhorts both the Israelites according to its historical meaning and the Christian people according to its allegorical meaning, so that they may apply the hearing of their hearts to learning God’s commandments and may receive evangelical teaching and fulfill in works what they understand in their hearts.

“What is this, Israel, that you have grown old in the land of your enemies? You have been defiled with the dead; you have been counted among those who are in hell.” Under the form of a question, he investigates the cause of the vengeance that the former people suffered in the captivity of a foreign land. But he immediately explains from where such evils came to them: namely, because they abandoned the fountain of wisdom, the true God, and our Lord Jesus Christ. For if they had obeyed God’s commandments, they would have lived in peace in their own land.

Likewise, if the ecclesiastical people guarded the evangelical commandments by believing rightly and living well, and avoided sins insofar as they could, they would dwell in everlasting peace. Hence Scripture says: “Great peace belongs to those who love your name, Lord, and there is no scandal in them,” etc.

“Learn where wisdom is, where strength is, where understanding is, so that you may know at the same time where there is length of life and livelihood, where there is light for the eyes and peace.” The prophetic admonition therefore summons its hearers to seek divine wisdom, strength, and understanding. And what is that wisdom except our Redeemer, who is the wisdom and power of God, and the Savior of all people, especially of the faithful? Concerning him the Apostle says: “I speak of Christ, the power and wisdom of God.” Nor is there any other name given to human beings under heaven by which they must be saved.

Therefore, whoever believes in him and rightly keeps his commandments will not be put to shame forever, because he is the true light that enlightens everyone coming into this world, and the firm peace that made both one and, by destroying the dividing wall, killed hostility in his flesh.

His place, therefore, is the holy Gospel and the sacred writings, where the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden—namely, the divine mysteries hidden from ages and generations but revealed to the faithful and devout through the mediator himself between God and human beings, who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood. It follows:

“Where are the rulers of the nations and those who rule over the beasts that are on the earth? Those who play with the birds of heaven, who treasure up silver and gold, in which human beings place their trust, and whose possessions have no end? Those who manufacture silver and are anxious, yet their works cannot be found. And yet they have been destroyed and have gone down to the underworld, and others have risen in their place. The young saw light and dwelt upon the earth, but they did not know the way of discipline, nor did they understand its paths, nor did their children receive it; it was made far from their presence.”

The prophet rebukes the folly of the nations, who seemed, in their rulers, to rule over the beasts of the earth and to play with the birds of heaven. They thought that they could satisfy their pleasure in this way. Through greed they had sought out much silver and gold, and they had striven to possess wealth beyond measure. They made for themselves carved images and idols of gold and silver, according to the invention that they themselves had devised.

Although they applauded themselves for their many riches and earthly resources, placing all their hope in them, nevertheless they ended their present life in mortal flesh. Their souls, because of their error and evil deeds, were plunged into hell, and others rose in their place—young people who “saw light and dwelt upon the earth.”

By “the young” we can understand the philosophers of the nations, who received some spark of knowledge in various arts and disputations and in eloquent speech. Yet they did not truly find it in every respect, because whatever they put forward in their doctrines they reduced to earthly wisdom and the folly of this world.

They did not know the way of discipline, because they did not know the way of discipline, which is Christ, nor how he is the author of every good. They did not understand the path of his commandments—neither they nor their children, that is, those who imitated their faithlessness. It was made far from their presence because they refused to receive the true faith of Christ. Hence the Psalmist says of them: “Salvation is far from sinners, because they did not seek your justifications, O God.”

It follows:

“Wisdom was not heard in Canaan, nor was it seen in Theman. The children of Hagar also, who seek the understanding that comes from the earth, the merchants of Merrha and Theman, and the storytellers, and the seekers of understanding: they did not know the way of wisdom, nor did they remember its paths.”

Through the names of the places in which the nations once dwelt, the wickedness of their error and the teaching of folly are expressed. For Canaan is interpreted as “merchant”; Theman as “south”; Hagar as “newcomer” or “converted.”

Whoever uses earthly concerns indiscriminately and eagerly devotes himself to the heat of desire, makes himself alien from the Lord’s discipline and from fellowship with the holy Church, and occupies himself with idle stories and empty amusements—although he considers himself wise, he shows himself to be foolish in every respect. For he does not choose the way of truth or the standard of wisdom, and he utterly scorns learning and keeping God’s judgments.

After the prophet had completed his discourse concerning the condemnation of the reprobate, he turned to proclaim the praise of the house of God and to demonstrate the power of divine strength, saying:

“O Israel, how great is the house of God, and how immense is the place of his possession! It is great and has no end; exalted and immeasurable. There were the giants, those renowned ones who existed from the beginning, great in stature and skilled in war. The Lord did not choose them, nor did they find the way of discipline; therefore they perished. And because they did not possess wisdom, they died through their own folly.”

The house of God therefore signifies not only the Mosaic tabernacle or the Solomonic temple, but also the holy people who existed under the Old and New Testaments, in whom God himself dwells and remains forever. This house and this place of God’s possession are great, without end, exalted, and immeasurable. For the holy Church is spread and extended throughout the whole world and has no limit, since it exists in heaven and on earth, in holy angels and good people.

When he says that there were there giants, those renowned from the beginning, great in stature and skilled in war, he signifies proud people who, before the Lord’s coming, exalted themselves above other human beings on earth through the arrogance of their position and worldly wisdom, boasting that they were wiser and more powerful.

Because they did not know the truth of true wisdom and did not observe the discipline of justice, they perished by God’s just judgment. From where true wisdom came into the world, the following discourse shows.

“Who has ascended into the heavens?” he says. No one else except the Lord Jesus Christ, who reigns in heaven with the Father and the Holy Spirit. For just as he was begotten by the Father, so he also received wisdom from him. Through his servants—that is, through the prophets and apostles, who are rightly called clouds because they carried within themselves God’s hidden gift—he poured the rain of sound words into human minds according to the divine dispensation.

Hence the Psalmist also says: “Everything that he willed he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in the abysses. He established the earth for all eternity.” For through him heaven and earth were created from the beginning. “In the beginning”—that is, in the Son—God made heaven and earth, that is, the heavenly and earthly creation.

“He filled the earth with cattle,” because various animals were also created from earthly matter. The various classes of human beings may also be understood by the cattle, since the author of all things uses them according to his own will and all things look toward him, so that whatever he decrees may be accomplished in them. For heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them remain in his power, and no creature can resist his will.

The stars—that is, the holy preachers—gave the light of sound teaching in their offices. With great joy and spiritual gladness they fulfilled the work of preaching, and they attributed the gift they had received not to themselves but to divine generosity.

“For this is our God, and no other will be reckoned beside him. For the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens.”

“This one discovered every way of discipline”—that is, the commandments of the divine law—

“and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his chosen one.” That is, to the former people, namely, to the patriarchs and prophets, and also to all who held the true faith and served him devoutly.

Afterward, at the time of his incarnation, he was seen upon the earth and lived among human beings, preaching the Gospel and healing every disease and every sickness among the people.

## HOMILY LV. ON THE VIGIL OF PENTECOST

### A Reading from the Acts of the Apostles

In those days, while Apollos was at Corinth, and Paul, having passed through the upper regions, came to Ephesus and found certain disciples, he said to them: “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” etc.

The text of the divine words most fully shows us, beloved, the cause and meaning of the present feast. We recognize that the Holy Spirit was poured out upon Christ’s disciples on the fiftieth day after the resurrection, which is the tenth day after his ascension, as had been promised and awaited. But, for your instruction, a discourse must also be added from the present reading that you have heard:

“It happened,” he says, “while Apollos was at Corinth and Paul, having passed through the upper regions, came to Ephesus and found certain disciples, he said to them: ‘Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?’” That is, did you receive, after baptism, the laying on of hands that the Holy Spirit customarily gives?

They said to him: “We have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit.” He said: “Into what, then, were you baptized?” They said: “Into John’s baptism.” Paul said: “John baptized the people with a baptism of repentance, saying that they should believe in the one who was to come after him”—that is, in Jesus.

That baptism could not give the remission of sins; it could only teach repentance. For just as circumcision among the patriarchs was a sign of the faith they possessed, so this washing was received by the repentant people as a distinctive sign of their devotion. Nevertheless, even this baptism, in a figurative way, pointed to Christ’s baptism, by which remission would be given.

When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. If, as some teach, mere participation in the body and blood of Christ could have been sufficient for such people, there would have been no need for those whom John had baptized with water to be baptized by Christ’s disciples; they would only have needed to be confirmed by participation in Christ’s body and blood.

Baptism frees one from eternal punishment, not from the punishments of the present life. If people were freed from present punishment through baptism, they would think that this was baptism’s reward, rather than the eternal reward. Nevertheless, once the guilt of sin has been removed, a certain temporal punishment remains, so that the life that will be free from every punishment may be sought more fervently.

No one denies that even after baptism, by which sins are washed away, believers must turn to the Lord daily for as long as we are in this world. Although this must be done every day without interruption, it is never enough to suppose that it has been done once.

Those who are still in their mothers’ wombs cannot be baptized with their mothers, because one who has not yet been born according to Adam cannot be reborn according to Christ. Nor can regeneration be said to occur in someone whom generation has not preceded.

Those who live wickedly within the Church and do not cease to receive communion, thinking that they are cleansed by such communion, should hear the prophet say that it does not contribute to their cleansing: “What is it that my beloved has done in my house? He has committed many crimes. Will holy flesh take away your wickedness?” And the Apostle says: “Let a person examine himself, and then let him eat of that bread and drink from that cup.”

But let us, beloved, with God’s help, disdain to serve sin, since such great blessedness is prepared for us in heaven. Therefore, while it is permitted and lies within our power, let us reject false and transitory things so that we may receive those things that are truly good from the Lord. Let us be emptied of vices and filled with virtues, through the generosity of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives with the Father and the Holy Spirit and reigns as one God through all ages of ages. [Col. 0253B] Amen.

## HOMILY LVI. ON THE SAME FEAST

### A Reading from the Holy Gospel according to John

“If you love me, keep my commandments. And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete,” etc.

What does it mean that the Spirit, the Paraclete, would be given to those who love God and keep his commandments, when God cannot be loved and his commandments cannot be kept except through the Holy Spirit? What else does it mean except that the one who loves God through the Holy Spirit merits, by loving, to possess more of the Spirit, and by possessing more, to love more?

“Paraclete” is interpreted as “Comforter,” and the Holy Spirit is rightly called the Paraclete because he lifts up and refreshes the hearts of the faithful with desires for heavenly life, so that they do not fail amid the adversities of this world.

The disciples therefore had the Holy Spirit through a certain hidden inspiration, by whom they loved the Lord; but they did not yet have him in the manner promised by the Lord. They had him secretly, but afterward they were to have him through a certain manifestation: that is, when he came in tongues of fire, sat upon them, and they spoke in tongues, magnifying God.

“I will ask my Father,” he says, “and he will give you another Paraclete,” thereby showing that he himself is also the Paraclete. Previously, they also had the Paraclete himself, namely, the Lord dwelling with them in the flesh. Through the sweetness of miracles and the work of preaching, he used to raise and strengthen them so that they would not be scandalized by the persecution of unbelievers.

“I will ask,” he said, because of his humanity; yet he gives together with the Father through his divinity, “so that he may remain with you forever.” He remains forever with the saints, whom in this life he will always illuminate inwardly and invisibly, and in the future he will lead into the perpetual contemplation of the hope of his majesty.

“The Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive because it has neither seen him nor knows him.” By “the world” he means people devoted to the love of this world. The world therefore cannot receive him—that is, worldly people, who do not possess the invisible eyes of charity, by which alone the Holy Spirit can be seen and known, and through knowing can be understood.

“But you will know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you.” He will be such that he may remain forever. Unbelievers saw the Lord and Savior in the flesh before his passion; but they could not know that he was the Son of God, the Paraclete sent by God into the world. Only believers could know this.

Unbelievers could neither see the Holy Spirit with their eyes nor know him in their minds, because he did not appear to the disciples clothed in humanity. Rather, he wished to come to them and remain with them in such a way that he would consecrate for himself a most welcome dwelling in their very hearts.

This is what he says: “But you will know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you.” The one who remains invisibly with the elect in this life also visibly grants them the grace of knowing him.

“I will not leave you orphaned; I will come to you.” It seemed to unbelievers that, by dying on the cross, the Lord was leaving the disciples orphaned. But he did not leave orphaned those to whom, after his passion, he showed himself alive by many proofs during forty days, and after ten days from his ascension gave the gifts of the Holy Spirit from heaven. No one doubts that Christ himself came to them when he recognizes the inseparable nature of the Holy Trinity in its power and operation.

“Yet a little while, and the world will no longer see me, but you will see me.” The little while extended until the time when his passion was completed. After that, the wicked were unable to see him; only the righteous, who had been saddened by his death, were found worthy to see the joy of his resurrection.

“Because I live, you also will live.” What does “because I live, you also will live” mean? Why did he say that he lives in the present, but that they would live in the future, unless he promised them also the life of the flesh—the life of resurrection—that was already going before them in him?

Since his resurrection was soon to occur, he used the verb of the present tense to signify its nearness. But because their resurrection is deferred until the end of the world, he did not say, “you live,” but “you will live.” Thus, in two words—one in the present tense and one in the future—he elegantly and briefly promised two resurrections: his own, soon to come, and ours, to follow at the end of the world.

“On that day,” he says, “you will know that I am in my Father, and you are in me, and I am in you.” On what day except the day concerning which he said, “you also will live”? The apostles knew that Christ was then in the Father through the unity of undivided divinity. They knew that they were in Christ through their reception of his faith and sacraments. They knew that Christ truly lived, that he was in the Father, and that he was in them through their love and observance of his commandments.

The holy Church of God also knows this, but far better and more fully on that day about which he said, “you will live”—the day of the resurrection—when they begin truly to live. Then they will see all that must be known more perfectly, the nearer and without end they behold the very fountain of knowledge himself. Therefore, in order to promise this blessedness to everyone, not only to the apostles, he immediately added:

Whoever has my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me. Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him.

Here we must consider with complete attention that truly to love Christ means not to seek the love itself merely by professing it, but to have Christ’s commandments by learning them and to keep them by putting them into practice. “Whoever has my commandments,” he says, “and keeps them, he is the one who loves me”—who has them in memory and keeps them in life; who has them in speech and keeps them in conduct; who has them by hearing and keeps them by doing; or who has them by doing and keeps them by persevering. He, he says, is the one who loves me.

It should be noted that, when he said with a present-tense verb, “Whoever loves me,” he added in the future: “will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him.” For the Son, together with the Father, loves those who love him even now; but now he loves them so that they may live rightly by faith working through love, whereas then he will love them so that they may attain the vision of the truth which they had tasted through faith. He did not add without reason, “and I will manifest myself to him.” For although he will manifest himself to all at the judgment according to his humanity, he will manifest to the just and holy alone the glory of his divinity—in which he is equal to the Father and the Holy Spirit—for eternal blessedness, so that they may live and rejoice with him forever in the heavenly kingdom, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LVII. SUNDAY OF PENTECOST

### Reading from the Acts of the Apostles

“In those days, when the days of Pentecost were being completed, they were all together in the same place. And suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a violent wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting,” etc.

Beloved, it was the coming of the Holy Spirit that consecrated this day’s festival, venerable throughout the whole world. Fifty days after the Lord’s resurrection, as had been hoped, he flowed into the apostles and the people of believers, just as you heard when the present reading was read.

“When the days of Pentecost were completed,” he says, “they were all together in the same place”—that is, in the upper room where they had gathered immediately after the Lord’s ascension, where they were awaiting the promise of the Holy Spirit. For whoever desires to be filled with the Holy Spirit must necessarily rise above the dwelling of the flesh through contemplation of the mind.

“And suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a violent wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting.” The Lord appeared to the disciples in the likeness of fire, but through himself he produced speech inwardly. Neither the fire nor that sound was itself the reality; rather, by what he displayed outwardly, he expressed what he accomplished inwardly.

“And there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire.” The Holy Spirit appeared in tongues of fire because he makes all whom he fills both burning and speaking at once, since the holy Church, extended throughout the ends of the world, was destined to speak in the voice of all nations.

“And it rested upon each of them.” Certainly, his resting is signified in the saints.

**[Col. 0256A]** “And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they began to speak in various tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance.” The variety of tongues signifies the gifts of various graces.

Indeed, it is not inappropriately understood that the Holy Spirit first gave the gift of tongues to human beings, among whom human wisdom is both examined and taught outwardly, in order to show how easily the wisdom of God, which is upon the earth, can make the wise truly wise.

“Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men from every nation under heaven. And when this sound occurred, the multitude gathered and was bewildered, because each one heard them speaking in his own language.” Their speech itself possessed this power: although hearers from different nations were present, each received hearing and understanding according to his own language from the one speech that had been uttered by the apostles.

By these and other teachings, through which the authority of the divine utterances flashes forth innumerably, let us be moved with one mind to venerate Pentecost, rejoicing in the honor of the Holy Spirit, through whom the whole catholic Church is sanctified, every rational soul is instructed, and who is the inspirer of faith, the teacher of knowledge, the fountain of love, the seal of chastity, and the source of every virtue.

Let the minds of the faithful rejoice that throughout the whole world the one God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is praised in the confession of every language. That signification which appeared in the form of fire continues both in its effect and in its gift. For the Spirit of truth makes the gift of his glory shine with the brilliance of his light, and in his temple he desires nothing to be dark or lukewarm.

From this work and teaching there has also been bestowed upon us purification through fasting and almsgiving. For this venerable day is followed by the practice of a most salutary discipline, which all the saints have always found most beneficial for themselves. We urge you diligently to observe it with pastoral concern, so that if heedless negligence has contracted any stains in recent days, the strictness of fasting may chastise them and devotion to piety may correct them. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LVIII. ON THE SAME FEAST

### Reading from the Holy Gospel according to John

**[Col. 0256D]**

“At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him,’” etc.

The proof of love is the performance of a work. Hence the same John says in his Epistle: “Whoever says, ‘I love God,’ and does not keep his commandments, is a liar.” We truly love God if we observe his commandments and restrain ourselves from our own pleasures in order to obey them.

“And my Father loves him.” Since the works that the Father does, the Son likewise does; whoever loves the Son also loves the Father; and whoever is loved by the Son is loved by the Father. “And we will come to him and make our dwelling with him.” For when someone truly loves God and does not withdraw from God’s love even in a time of temptation, the Father and the Son come to him through spiritual approach and make their dwelling with him.

That person truly loves whose mind is not overcome by an evil pleasure through consent. For each person is separated from heavenly love to the extent that he finds delight in lower things. Love distinguishes the saints from the world; it made them dwell together in one house. In that house the Father and the Son make their dwelling, and they grant the very love itself to those to whom they give it, together with their manifestation at the end. It was concerning this manifestation that the disciple asked and heard that one must come to it through love.

“Whoever does not love me does not keep my words.” These are the ones who never see the Father and the Holy Spirit, while they see the Son for a short time—not so that they may be blessed, but so that they may be judged. They see him not in the form of God, where he is equally invisible with the Father and the Holy Spirit, but in the form of a human being, in which he willed to be contemptible to the world through suffering and terrifying in judgment.

“And the word that you have heard is not mine, but the Father’s who sent me.” Why did he first say “words” in the plural, but now “word” in the singular? Perhaps there he indicated the words of preaching, while here he indicated himself, who is the Father’s Word. For this reason he said that it was not his own, because he is not from himself but from the Father—just as the image is not his own but the Father’s, and the son is not his own but the Father’s. Rightly, therefore, he attributes to the source whatever the equal one does, since he has from that source the very fact that he is equally equal to him.

“I have spoken these things to you while remaining with you.” The dwelling of which he spoke above is spiritual and is given to the saints alone. The dwelling of which he now speaks is bodily; he spoke only of his bodily presence, which both the just and the wicked were able to see. The former grants eternal blessedness to those who have been liberated; the latter visits those who are to be liberated in time.

“These things,” he says, “I have spoken to you while remaining with you”—that is, in bodily presence he was speaking visibly together with them.

“But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things and remind you of everything that I have said to you.” He said many things to unbelieving hearers that found no place in their hearts, because the Holy Spirit was not teaching them inwardly. He says many things every day through holy preachers that those who hear do not receive inwardly, because the Holy Spirit does not inwardly remind them of what they heard outwardly.

Concerning him it is rightly promised: “He himself will teach you all things.” For unless that same Spirit assists the heart of the hearer, the teacher’s speech is fruitless. No one should attribute to the human teacher what he understands from the teacher’s mouth, because unless there is one who teaches inwardly, the teacher’s tongue labors outwardly in vain.

The Jews therefore heard Christ preaching in one way, and the apostles in another: the former for judgment, the latter for salvation. For the Spirit taught these in their minds what they had heard outwardly with their ears.

“I leave peace with you; I give you my peace.” I leave you in peace; in peace I will find you. Here I leave it; there I give it. I leave it to those who are following; I give it to those who have arrived. He left us his peace so that we might love one another; he will give us his peace where we can never disagree with one another.

Why does he say, “I give you my peace,” and not, “I leave you my peace”? Perhaps because peace will be different now and then. Here we have wars with vices, and for that reason he did not add “my”; there, in eternal peace, there will be eternal tranquility and harmony, and such peace as he had with himself, since he had no sin within himself.

“Not as the world gives do I give to you.” That is, not as people in the world often agree with one another in their wickedness, but as those who agree with one another in holiness and unite themselves in the love of Christ.

**[Col. 0258B]** “Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid. You have heard that I said to you: ‘I am going away and I am coming to you.’” Their hearts could be troubled and afraid because he was going away from them, although he was going to come to them, lest perhaps the wolf attack the flock while the shepherd was absent.

But from those whom the human being was leaving, God was not departing; and that same Christ was both human and God. He was therefore going away by what he was as human, and remaining by what he was as God. Thus God, whom no place contains, departs from the hearts of those who abandon him in their conduct, not with their feet; and he comes to those who turn to him, not with their faces but with faith, and draw near to him, not in the flesh but in love.

“If you loved me, you would certainly rejoice, because I am going to the Father, because the Father is greater than I.” By that in which the Son is not equal to the Father, he was going to the Father—the one who will come in that same nature to judge the living and the dead. But by that in which he is equal to the Father, he never departed from the Father; rather, by his divinity, which no place contains, he is wholly everywhere with him.

Let us recognize the twofold substance of Christ: the divine, by which he is equal to the Father, and the human, by which the Father is greater. Yet the two together are not two but one Christ, so that God is not a quaternity but a Trinity. For just as one human being consists of a rational soul and flesh, so one Christ is God and human being. Accordingly, Christ is God, rational soul, and flesh; we confess Christ in all these and Christ in each one.

Who, then, is the one through whom the world was made? Christ Jesus—but in the form of God. Who was crucified under Pontius? Christ Jesus—but in the form of a servant. Again, concerning the individual elements of which a human being consists: Who was not abandoned in hell? Christ Jesus—but in the soul alone. Who lay in the tomb for three days, destined to rise again? Christ Jesus—but in the flesh alone.

Christ is therefore spoken of in each of these particulars; yet all these together are not two or three, but one Christ. Thus he said: “If you loved me, you would certainly rejoice, because I am going to the Father.” Human nature should rejoice in this: that it was assumed by the only-begotten Word so as to be established immortal in heaven.

For this is the way in which he said that he would go to the Father. He was certainly not going to the one who was already with him; rather, going to him meant receiving from us what was mortal, making immortal what he had received from us as mortal, and establishing at the Father’s right hand that by which he had been on earth for us.

Then the Lord Jesus himself added:

“And now I have told you before it happens, so that when it happens you may believe.” He is speaking of what would happen: that after his death they would see him alive and ascending to the Father, and, on seeing this, would believe what they had previously doubted. Christ, the Son of God, was already able to do this when he said it, and to proclaim it before he accomplished it.

They could doubt whether he was the Son of God when they saw him about to die. But when they saw him risen again, they believed what they had previously doubted. Their faith was confirmed in their hearts by the one who both promised with his mouth what he was going to do and fulfilled by his work what he had foretold.

Then he says:

“I will no longer speak much with you, for the prince of this world is coming.” Who else but the devil?

“And he has nothing in me”—that is, absolutely no sin.

Here he shows that the devil is prince of sinful human beings, not of God’s creatures. Whenever “world” is used in an evil sense, it indicates nothing except the lovers of this world and not of God. Far be it from us to believe that he is prince of heaven and earth and of all creatures that are generally called “the world.”

The whole world therefore serves its Creator, not its deceiver; its Redeemer, not its destroyer. It is governed by divine providence, not overturned by the enemy’s cunning—except for those human beings belonging to that portion who subject themselves to the devil by their own will, not by any necessity.

Hence the Apostle says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood”—that is, against human beings—“but against powers and rulers of this darkness”—that is, of sins—which remain in the darkness of iniquity. By calling them rulers, he indicates that they are fallen angels. Yet there are those who, through the grace of God and not through their own merits, are rescued from them. Concerning these the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light.” And again, as the same Apostle says: “Thanks be to God, who has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love.”

In this kingdom the prince of the world—that is, of this darkness—had nothing, because God did not come with sin, nor had the Virgin borne his flesh from the propagation of sin. And as though someone might say to him, “Why then do you die, if you have no sin to which the punishment of death was owed?” he immediately added:

“But so that the world may know that I love the Father, and that just as the Father commanded me, so I do.” In the fulfillment of God’s commandments, therefore, Christ’s love for his Father was made manifest. For just as the Father established him, once incarnate, as the Savior of the world, so he himself, by doing good and keeping the Father’s commandments, rescued from death those oppressed by the devil. He lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LIX. MONDAY AFTER PENTECOST

### Reading from the Acts of the Apostles

**[Col. 0260A]**

“In those days, Peter opened his mouth and said: ‘Men, brothers and fathers, the Lord commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead,’” etc.

The holy Apostle Peter, wishing to show that our Lord Jesus Christ is the true judge of the living and the dead, says that this was entrusted to him and to the other apostles by the Lord himself: they were to preach it to the peoples by word and testify to it through the sayings and examples of the holy prophets, who had long ago proclaimed it.

That is, all who believe in him receive forgiveness of sins through his name, because salvation is in no other, except in him whom God the almighty Father sent into the world, so that everyone who believes in him might be saved through him—having received forgiveness of sins through his name by the washing of sacred baptism, confirmation by the Holy Spirit, and the proof of good works, which must be displayed in right faith.

Accordingly, it is read afterward that, when Peter had preached the word of God to the Gentiles, the Holy Spirit immediately fell upon all who heard the word. The faithful of the circumcision who had come with Peter were astonished, because the grace of the Holy Spirit had also been poured out upon the nations. For they heard them speaking in tongues and magnifying God.

So that he might not hesitate to confer baptism upon the Gentiles, he was confirmed by the testimony of the Holy Spirit, who in a new order had gone before even the waters of the washing which he is accustomed to sanctify. This is found to have happened once as a testimony to the faith of the Gentiles, but never among the Jews.

“And he ordered them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ.”

Although it is the rule of the Church that the faithful be baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity, it is asked why Luke, throughout the entire text of this book, testifies that baptism was given in no other way than in the name of Jesus Christ.

The blessed Ambrose resolves this as follows: the mystery is fulfilled through the unity of the name. For whether you say “Christ,” you have designated God the Father, by whom the Son was anointed; the Son himself, who was anointed; and the Holy Spirit, with whom he was anointed. For it is written: “Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit.”

Or whether you say “Father,” you have likewise indicated his Son and the Spirit of his mouth—provided that you also comprehend this in your heart. Or whether you say “Spirit,” you have named God the Father, from whom the Spirit proceeds, and the Son, because the Spirit is also called the Son’s Spirit.

Thus authority is joined to reason. Scripture also indicates that one may rightly be baptized in the Spirit, when the Lord says: “You will be baptized in the Holy Spirit,” and the Apostle says: “For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body.”

It is especially fitting that we should be baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ because, as the Apostle says: “All of us who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death. For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also share in his resurrection.”

May this be granted by our Redeemer Jesus Christ himself, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LX. ALSO MONDAY

### Reading from the Holy Gospel according to John

“At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life,’” etc.

It should be noted that he repeats concerning the only-begotten Son of God what he had promised concerning the Son of Man exalted upon the cross, saying: “so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.”

For our same Redeemer and Creator, the Son of God existing before the ages, became the Son of Man at the end of the ages. He who had created us through the power of his divinity for the enjoyment of perpetual blessed life restored us through the weakness of our humanity, so that we might receive the life we had lost.

It follows:

“For God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him.” Thus, as far as the physician is concerned, he came to heal the sick; the one who does not wish to obey the physician’s instructions destroys himself. The Savior came into the world. Why is he called the Savior of the world, except to save the world, not to judge the world?

You do not wish to be saved by this very one; you will be judged by yourself—and what do I say, “you will be judged”? Consider what he says:

“Whoever believes in him will not be judged, but whoever does not believe”—what did you expect him to say, except “has been judged”? “He has already been judged.”

Judgment has not yet appeared, but judgment has already taken place. For the Lord knows those who are his. He knows those who will remain for the flame; he knows his wheat in his ark; he knows the chaff, the crop, and the weeds. The one who does not believe has been judged.

Why has he been judged? Because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God. “And this is the judgment: that the light has come into the world, and people loved darkness more than the light, for their works were evil.”

My brothers, whose good works did the Lord find? No one’s. For he found all works evil. How, then, did some practice the truth and come to the light? For this follows:

“But whoever practices the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be made manifest, because they have been done in God.”

How, then, did some do a good work so that they might come to the light—that is, to Christ? And how did some love darkness, if he found all to be sinners, if he heals all from sin, and if that serpent in which the death of the Lord was prefigured heals those who had been bitten? The serpent was raised because of the bites of the serpent: that is, the Lord’s death was raised up for mortal human beings, whom he found unrighteous.

How is this understood: “This is the judgment, that the light has come into the world, and people loved darkness more than the light, for their works were evil”? What does this mean? Whose works were good? Did you not come to justify the ungodly?

But he says, “They loved darkness more than the light.” There he placed the emphasis. For many loved their sins more. The one who confesses his sins and accuses his sins is already acting together with God. The Lord accuses your sins; if you also accuse them, you are joined to God, as though there were two things: the human being and the sinner.

What you hear called “human being,” God made. What you hear called “sinner,” the human being himself made. Destroy what you made, so that God may save what he made. You must hate in yourself your own work and love in yourself God’s work.

When what you have done begins to displease you, your good works begin there, because you accuse your evil works. Confession of evil works is the beginning of good works.

You practice the truth and come to the light. What does “you practice the truth” mean? You do not flatter yourself, you do not cajole yourself, you do not praise yourself, and you do not say, “I am righteous,” when you are wicked. You begin to practice the truth, and you come to the light, so that your works may be made manifest because they have been done in God.

Even the fact that your sin displeases you would not displease you unless God were shining upon you and his truth were showing itself to you. But the one who, even after being admonished, loves his sins hates the light that admonishes him and flees from it, so that his evil works, which he loves, may not be exposed.

But the one who practices the truth accuses his evil within himself. He does not spare himself; he does not forgive himself, so that God may forgive him. What he wants God to acknowledge, he himself forgives. And he comes to the light, to which he gives thanks, because the one who showed that he had killed himself says to the Lord: “Turn your face away from my sins.”

With what confidence does he say this, unless he also says: “For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me”? Let what you do not want to be before God be before you. But if you place your sin behind you, God turns it back before your eyes. He does this when there will no longer be any fruit of repentance.

Run, lest darkness overtake you. Whoever in the present life labors well in the service of God will receive eternal rest and glory in the future. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXI. TUESDAY, AT SAINT ANASTASIA

### Reading from the Acts of the Apostles

**[Col. 0262D]**

“In those days, when the apostles who were in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them,” etc.

After the martyrdom of Stephen, as the book of the Acts of the Apostles relates, a great persecution arose against the Church that was in Jerusalem, and all except the apostles were scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria.

Philip, however, went down to a city of Samaria and preached Christ to them. The crowds paid unanimous attention to what Philip said, hearing and seeing the signs that he performed. For many of those who had unclean spirits came out crying with a loud voice. Many paralytics and lame people were healed. Thus great joy arose in that city.

When the apostles who were in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. When they arrived, they prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit, for he had not yet come upon any of them; they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Then they laid hands upon them, and they received the Holy Spirit.

The companionship of Peter and John in preaching the Gospel signifies the chastity of right faith, which holy preachers must always teach to be present in the word of doctrine and in the gift of the Holy Spirit. The poet Arator beautifully explains this in verse, saying:

“Peter often makes John his companion,  
because the virgin Church pleases him.”

It should be noted, however, that Philip, who was evangelizing Samaria, was one of the seven. If he had been an apostle, he himself would certainly have been able to lay hands upon them so that they might receive the Holy Spirit.

For this is owed to bishops alone. Presbyters may anoint those who have been baptized with chrism, whether outside the presence of the bishop or in the bishop’s presence, when they baptize—but with chrism that has been consecrated by the bishop. They may not, however, sign the forehead with that same oil, since this belongs to bishops alone when they impart the Paraclete Spirit to the baptized.

Each person should therefore observe the rite of his order and the measure of his rank, because God is not a God of discord but of peace. “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit,” and “wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul.”

Hence the Savior commanded his disciples, saying: “Whoever wishes to become greater among you, let him become as the lesser,” because “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”

Let each person strive to possess humility in his heart and to display good works in his example. Thus he will have praise not only before God but also before human beings, and he will find grace in the sight of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXII. ALSO TUESDAY

### Reading from the Holy Gospel according to John

“At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever does not enter the sheepfold through the door, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber,’” etc.

Jesus spoke this proverb to them, but they did not understand what he was saying to them. Because of the poisonous, proud, and incurable arrogance of the Pharisees, who boasted that they could see although they were blind, the Lord Jesus composed these words that are read in this parable. In it, if we pay attention, he usefully admonished us not to glory in human wisdom or in moral distinction if the humility of Catholic faith in Christ is absent.

For there are many pagans who, according to a certain manner of life in this world, are called good and innocent people, as though observing the things commanded in the law: honoring their parents, not committing adultery, not perpetrating murder, not committing theft, not bearing false witness against anyone, and observing the other commands of the law as well. Yet they are not Christians. Often they boast, like those Pharisees, saying: “Are we also blind?”

But they do all these things in vain, because they do not enter through the door. Instead, in their swollen pride, they seek to climb up by another way, as though by themselves. Therefore the Lord offered a likeness concerning his flock and the door by which one enters the sheepfold.

For what benefit is there in the empty inflation of those who boast about living well, if their life does not reach the everlasting goal of living well? Living well ought to benefit each person precisely so that he may be granted to live well forever. For if someone is not granted to live well forever, what benefit is it for him to live well for a time?

Therefore those should not even be called people who live well who, through blindness, do not know the end of living well, or who despise it through self-inflation. No one has true and certain hope of living forever unless he recognizes the life that is Christ and enters the sheepfold through the door.

There are some people who glory in their own conduct and seek to draw others after them. They do not instruct their followers in Christ’s commandments, but persuade them to live according to their own examples. Concerning such people the Truth himself says elsewhere: “Teaching human doctrines and neglecting the commandments of God.” They seek to climb up by another door in order to rob and kill, not to save and preserve as the shepherd does.

It is of such people that it is said here: “Whoever climbs in by another way is a thief and a robber.”

Such teachers are found not only among those who are without the name of Christ, such as many philosophers who proclaimed their wisdom with swelling mouths and promised their followers a blessed life. They are also found among very many who are called Christians and boast that they have been enlightened by Christ, inventing new names for themselves from Christ and doctrines contrary to the Catholic faith. Countless heretics did this, falsely thinking that they entered through the door, which is Christ.

Sabellius says: “The one who is Son is himself the Father.” But the Son is not the Father. Whoever says that the Son is the Father does not enter through the door.

Arius says: “The Father is one thing, the Son another.” He would speak correctly if he said “another person,” not “another thing.” For when he says “another thing,” he contradicts the one from whom he hears: “I and the Father are one.” He too, therefore, does not enter through the door. He preaches Christ as he imagines him, not as the truth possesses him.

Photinus says: “Christ is merely human, not God.” He too does not enter through the door, because Christ is both human and God.

A new heresy that has arisen in our own time also seems to agree with this, asserting and preaching that Christ is, like any one of the saints, merely a titular god and not the true God.

Why pursue many details and enumerate the many vanities of heresies? Hold fast to this: believe that the Catholic Church is the sheepfold of Christ. Whoever wishes to enter the sheepfold should enter through the door—that is, through Christ—and should preach Christ as true God and true Son of God. He should not merely preach Christ but seek Christ’s glory, not his own. For many, in seeking their own glory, have scattered Christ’s sheep rather than gathered them.

Christ the Lord our God is a humble door. Whoever enters through this door must humble himself in order to enter with a sound head. These are the ones who hear the voice of the true shepherd. These are the ones whom the true shepherd calls by name as his own sheep. Concerning them it is said: “Rejoice and exult, because your names are written in heaven.”

He calls them by name, and who else leads them out except the one who forgives their sins, so that, freed from their harsh bonds, they may be able to follow him? And who went before them, so that they might follow him, except the one who, having risen from the dead, no longer dies, and over whom death will no longer have dominion?

He leads these out from faith to sight, and he goes before them because he first of all ascended into heaven. His sheep follow him because they know the voice of his teaching.

They will not follow alien guides but will flee from them, because they do not know the voice—that is, the teaching—of strangers. But when the Lord Jesus was speaking, those who heard did not understand, because they had a fattened heart and heard with difficulty.

He names the door, he names the sheepfold, he names the sheep, and he commends all these things, but he does not yet explain them. Let us hear the one explaining whom we heard proposing them:

“Again Jesus said to them: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you, I am the door of the sheep.’”

Behold, he has opened the very door that he had presented as closed. He himself is the door. We have recognized him; let us enter, so that we may rejoice that we have entered.

All who came came are thieves and robbers. What is this, Lord? “All who came”—for did you not come? But understand that when he said “all who came,” he meant everyone except me. Let us therefore recall what happened before his coming. Prophets came; were they thieves and robbers? By no means. They did not come apart from him: they were heralds of the one who was to come, and he possessed the hearts of those whom he had sent. Thus those who came with the word of God came with him, for he says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” He is the truth; those who were truthful and preached the truth came with him. But all who came apart from him are thieves and robbers: they came on their own, because they were not sent by him [Col. 0265D], not adhering to sound doctrine. Of them it is said that they are thieves and robbers—that is, they came to steal and kill.

But the sheep did not listen to them. They are true sheep, not those who, beneath a sheep’s skin, conceal a wolfish heart. Therefore those who preached before Christ’s coming preached by the same Spirit by whom the apostles and holy teachers, after Christ’s coming, showed the way of truth to the world. But all who believed at that time—whether in Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, or Moses, or in the other patriarchs and prophets who proclaimed Christ—were sheep and heard Christ. They did not hear a stranger’s voice, but Christ’s own voice. For the judge cries out in the herald, while the herald announces that the judge is coming [Col. 0266A].

There are therefore others whom the sheep did not hear, in whom the voice of Christ was absent: men who went astray, spoke falsely, chattered empty things, invented vanities, and led the wretched astray—such as the false prophets, and the scribes and Pharisees in the time of the Lord himself. These are the ones who came on their own and were not sent by the judge. Having driven them and their doctrines far away, let us see where the good shepherd calls us. For he says:

> I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he will be saved; he will enter and go out, and will find pasture.

By this he clearly shows that not only shepherds but also sheep enter through the door. But what does “he will enter and go out, and will find pasture” mean? To enter the Church through Christ, the door, is very good; but to leave the Church, as John the Evangelist himself says in his Epistle, is this: “They went out from us, but they were not of us.” “I came so that they may have life, and have it more abundantly.”

He appears to have said that those who enter should have eternal life. Yet no one can go out through the door—that is, through Christ—to the eternal life that will exist in the wise, unless through that same door, Christ, he has entered his Church, which is his sheepfold, into the temporal life that exists in faith. Therefore he says: “I came so that they may have life”—that is, faith, which works through love. Through this faith they enter the sheepfold in order to live, because “the righteous lives by faith.” And “that they may have it more abundantly”: the one who perseveres to the end will be saved.

Through that door, that is, through faith in Christ, they go out when true believers die [Col. 0266C], and they will have life more abundantly when they come to the place where that shepherd has gone before them, where thereafter they will never die, but will live with that shepherd in eternal blessedness and reign forever and ever.

## HOMILY LXIII. WEDNESDAY

### Reading from the Acts of the Apostles

> In those days, Peter, standing with the eleven, raised his voice and spoke to them: “Men of Judea, and all you who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and hear my words,” etc.

After the grace of the Holy Spirit, which was poured out on the day of Pentecost upon the one hundred and twenty believers who were gathered in the upper room of Zion and were speaking [Col. 0266D] in various languages, those who were present were astonished, marveling at so admirable a wonder. Some praised God for this, while others attributed their different speech to drunkenness, failing to understand correctly what had happened. Therefore the apostle Peter, as has just been read, raised his voice and spoke to them, making known God’s admirable gift.

“Not only,” they said, “did those who are Jews by birth gather from various parts of the world, but those born in uncircumcision also adhered to their observance.” Others, however, mocking them, said: “These men are full of new wine.” Though mocking, they nevertheless testify mystically to the truth: they were filled not with the old wine that failed at the wedding of the Church, but with the new wine of spiritual grace. For new wine had already come into new wineskins, when the apostles proclaimed God’s mighty works, not in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the Spirit [Col. 0267A].

> For these men are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is the third hour of the day.

The Holy Spirit, about to proclaim the glory of the undivided Trinity to the world, fittingly descended at the third hour. And since it is said above, “They were persevering in prayer,” they rightly received the Holy Spirit at the hour of prayer, so that readers might understand that the grace of the Holy Spirit is not easily received unless grace lifts people from carnal things toward heavenly concerns.

The three times at which Daniel is read to have bent his knees and worshiped during the day—the third, sixth, and ninth hours—are understood by the Church. For the Lord, sending the Holy Spirit at the third hour, ascending the cross at the sixth, and laying down his life at the ninth, graciously chose to make those same hours more clearly known and sacred to us than the others.

> I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh.

The word “pouring out” shows the generosity of the gift: not, as formerly, only upon prophets and priests, but upon everyone indiscriminately, of either sex, condition, and rank, the grace of the Holy Spirit was to be bestowed. What “all flesh” means, the prophet goes on to explain:

> And your sons and your daughters shall prophesy,

and so forth.

> And I will give wonders in heaven above and signs on the earth below.

Wonders in heaven: when the Lord was born, a new star appeared. When he ascended the cross, the sun was darkened and heaven itself was covered with darkness. Signs on earth: when the Lord gave up his spirit, the earth trembled, opened tombs, split rocks, and brought forth again many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep [Col. 0267C].

> Blood and fire and vapor of smoke.

The blood was that of the Lord’s side; the fire was the Holy Spirit; the vapor was the compunction and tears. For just as we come from fire, so from the burning of the Holy Spirit arises the fire of love. And since blood flowing in a living stream from dead flesh is contrary to the nature of our bodies, we must believe that this too was done as a sign. Whose sign was it, if not of our salvation and life, which unquestionably arises from his death?

The fire may also signify the illumination of the faithful, while the vapor of smoke may signify the blindness of the Jews who refuse to believe. Hence, too, when the Lord was about to give the law, he descended in fire and smoke: he illuminates the humble through the brightness of his manifestation, and obscures the eyes of the proud through the darkness of error.

> The sun will be changed into darkness and the moon into blood.

This is believed to have happened partly in the Lord’s Passion and partly to be destined to occur before the great day of the Lord, that is, the day of judgment. For then the sun was darkened. But could the moon, turned into blood, openly appear to human beings? At that time, since it was the fifteenth day of Passover, it was sometimes hidden from mortal sight by the intervening earth.

> And it shall be that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved.

This is what Peter says elsewhere: “God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to him.”

Blessed is the one who strives to bring his days in the present life to an end in right faith and good works, because, when the Lord recompenses him, he will deserve to receive, for all his labor, a full reward and everlasting glory in the future life with the holy angels, through our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen [Col. 0268A].

## HOMILY LXIV. ALSO WEDNESDAY

### Reading from the Holy Gospel according to John

> At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him; and I will raise him up on the last day,” etc.

When he said, “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him,” he immediately added, “And I will raise him up on the last day.” Let him believe what he has hoped for. He will see what he has believed without yet seeing; he will eat what he has not hungered for; he will be satisfied with what he thirsts for. Where? In the resurrection of the dead, because “I will raise him up on the last day” [Col. 0268B].

For it is written in the Prophets:

> And they shall all be taught by God.

Why did he say this? O Jews, the Father did not teach you how you could know me. All the people of his kingdom will be taught by God; they will not hear from human beings. And even if someone hears from human beings, what they understand is given within, flashes within, and is revealed within. Human beings can sow the word outwardly, but they labor in vain unless God, teaching within, opens the senses. The one is taught by God whom the Lord inwardly instructs in the knowledge and love of truth.

> Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me.

How does the Father draw? He delights by teaching. He does not believe by compulsion but by will. The Son was speaking, the Father was teaching; the man who was seen was speaking, but God [Col. 0268C] was teaching inwardly in the heart of the hearer. Therefore he added:

> Not that anyone has seen the Father, except the one who is from God; he has seen the Father.

Do not suppose that the Father is visible to you. No one has seen the Father except the one who is from God; he has seen the Father. “I am from the Father, and therefore I see the Father.” But what does it mean for you to be drawn by the Father, except to learn from the Father? And what does it mean to learn from the Father, except to hear the Father—to hear the Word of the Father? That is, to hear me.

Lest, therefore, when I say to you, “Everyone who hears from the Father and learns,” you should say among yourselves, “But we have never seen the Father—how could we have learned from the Father?” Hear from me: “Not that anyone has seen the Father, except the one who is from God; he has seen the Father.” I know the Father; I am from him. But how is the Word from him whose Word he is? Not a word that sounds and passes away, but one that remains with the speaker [Col. 0268D] and draws the hearer.

> Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever believes in me has eternal life.

He did not wish to reveal what he was. He could have said briefly, “Whoever believes in me has me,” for Christ himself is the true God and eternal life. Whoever therefore believes in me comes to me, and whoever comes to me has me. But what does it mean to have me? To have eternal life.

Eternal life assumed death and was willing to die—but from what was yours, O human being, not from what was its own. It received from you the place in which it might die for you. Thus life assumed death so that life might kill death.

For he says, “Whoever believes has eternal life”—not what is apparent, but what is hidden. For eternal life is the Word who “in the beginning was with God,” and “the Word was God,” and was “the light of human beings.” He came to die, but on the third day he rose again [Col. 0269A].

> I am, he says, the bread of life.

And this is where they were arrogant.

> Your fathers ate manna and died.

Why did they eat and die? Because they believed what they saw and did not understand what they did not see. Therefore your fathers—because you are like them—ate. Moses and Aaron and the other holy people who were among the people ate manna and did not die: they understood the visible food spiritually and hungered spiritually.

Others, however, ate and remained in unbelief, just as the Jews heard Christ speaking but did not understand his words spiritually. Therefore he said to them:

> Your fathers ate manna in the desert and died.

By what death, if not the death of unbelief? The saints who were among them also died the common death. Therefore by these words the Lord signified spiritual, not bodily, death.

Thus their fathers were the fathers of these people—that is, evil fathers of evil people, unbelieving fathers of unbelievers, murmuring fathers of those who murmur. For that people is said to have offended God in nothing more than by murmuring against him. Therefore, wishing to show that their children were like them, the Lord began by saying to them: “Why are you murmuring among yourselves, you children of murmurers? Your fathers ate manna and died.” Not because the manna was evil, but because they ate it evilly.

> This is the bread that came down from heaven.

The manna signified this bread; the altar of God signifies this bread. Those sacraments differed in their signs, but in the reality signified they are equal. Hear the Apostle:

> I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate spiritual food.

Spiritual, certainly, not bodily food. Their bodily food was different—for they had manna, while we have something else—but their spiritual food was the same as ours. Yet they were our fathers, not the fathers of those Jews: we are like them, not like those Jews.

This, then, is the bread descending from heaven, so that if anyone eats of it, he will not die. But as regards the power of the sacrament, does this refer to the visible sacrament? The one who eats inwardly, not outwardly; who eats in the heart, not the one who, with another thing preceding—

> I am the living bread that came down from heaven.

It is living for this reason: manna also came down from heaven, but manna was a shadow; this is the truth.

> If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever; and the bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world.

When could flesh grasp what he said—bread, flesh? Flesh is called what flesh cannot grasp. And for this very reason flesh grasps it all the less, because it is called flesh. This is what they recoiled from; this is what they claimed was impossible; this is what they thought could not happen.

> My flesh, he says, is for the life of the world.

The faithful know the body of Christ. If they do not neglect to be the body of Christ, they become the body of Christ, if they wish to live by the Spirit of Christ. No one lives by the Spirit of Christ except the body of Christ. Whoever wishes to live, let him believe in Christ; let him eat spiritually the spiritual food; let him be incorporated into the body of Christ, and let him not be a rotten member deserving to be cut off. Let him be beautiful, healthy, and fitting for his head, namely Christ the Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY LXV. THURSDAY

### Reading from the Acts of the Apostles

> In those days, Philip, going down into the city of Samaria, preached Christ to them, etc.

After the passion of Stephen, the first martyr, as the book of the Acts of the Apostles testifies, a great persecution arose against the Church that was in Jerusalem, and all were scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles. Therefore Philip, one of the seven deacons, as the present reading recalls, went down into the city of Samaria and preached Christ to them [Col. 0270B].

> The crowds paid attention to what Philip was saying, hearing the word of God with one accord and seeing the signs that he performed.

They were summoned to perfect faith in the Lord by the benefits of heavenly grace.

> For many who had unclean spirits came out, crying with a loud voice; and many paralytics and lame people were healed.

The account agrees with that passage of the holy Gospel in which the history relates that Jesus summoned the twelve disciples and gave them power and authority over all demons, so that they might also cure diseases, and sent them to preach the kingdom of God and heal the sick. Having gone out, they went through the villages, evangelizing and healing everywhere.

The book of the Acts of the Apostles also plainly recounts the fulfillment of this, when the apostles bore witness with great power to the resurrection of Jesus Christ our Lord, and great grace was upon them all. Hence it is also read here that, because of the miracles Philip performed in Samaria, there was great joy in that city, since those who truly believed in Christ were healed in soul and body.

But those who pretended to believe and, with a treacherous heart, had chosen to serve the devil rather than Christ received the just recompense for their wickedness. Thus it is subsequently read here that Simon, who had previously been a magician in the city and had led the people of Samaria astray, claiming to be someone great, although he had been baptized by Philip, nevertheless did not escape punishment for his pretense and hypocrisy [Col. 0270D].

Overcome, therefore, by the words and power of blessed Philip, he pretended to believe truly until he received baptism. As he was exceedingly eager for praise and wished to be believed to be Christ, he learned from Philip, as the histories relate, the arts by which he could perform miracles. His successors are said to have done the same: trained in the evil arts of their founder, they entered the Church by fraud of one kind or another and made a practice of stealing baptism.

When Peter and John, who had been sent to Samaria, laid hands on the believers so that they might receive the Holy Spirit, many believers showed by evident signs that they had received the gift of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0271A]. Seeing this miracle—that the Holy Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands—Simon offered them money, saying:

> Give me this power, so that whoever I lay my hands upon may receive the Holy Spirit.

But Peter said to him:

> May your money be with you for destruction, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed with money. You have neither part nor share in this matter. For your heart is not right before God. Therefore repent of this wickedness of yours and pray to God, if perhaps this thought of your heart may be forgiven you, for I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity.

Although Simon pretended that he wished to repent, he persevered in the wickedness he had begun and received, through heavenly judgment, the fitting reward of his iniquity.

For this reason the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove upon the baptized Savior: to teach those who wish to receive him that they must be simple. Whoever keeps the gall of bitterness in his heart, no matter how baptized he may appear, has not been freed from the bonds of his iniquity. Even if he is cleansed for the brief moment of the hour of baptism, he is soon afterward oppressed sevenfold by a harsher demon.

In vain, therefore, does one try to purchase the grace of the Spirit if one has not taken care to strip off the raven-like mind. It is therefore extremely necessary for every Christian, in accordance with Paul’s teaching, to believe with the heart for righteousness and confess with the mouth for salvation. Let him hasten to adorn this faith with good works and persevere in it to the end of life, so that through the grace of the Savior he may deserve to possess heavenly joy with the holy angels in eternal blessedness, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever [Col. 0271C].

## HOMILY LXVI. ALSO THURSDAY

### Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Luke

> At that time Jesus summoned the twelve disciples and gave them power and authority over all demons, so that they might cure diseases. And he sent them to preach the kingdom of God and heal the sick. And he said to them: “Take nothing for the journey, neither a staff, nor a bag, nor bread, nor money; and do not have two tunics. And into whatever house you enter, remain there, and do not leave from there. And whoever does not receive you, when you leave that city, shake even the dust from your feet as a testimony against them,” etc.

Having first granted them the power to perform signs, he sent them to preach the kingdom of God, so that the greatness of their deeds might also attest to the greatness of the promises, and the power displayed might give credibility to their words; those who preached new things would perform new things.

Hence now also, although the number of the faithful has increased within the holy Church, there are many who possess a virtuous life but do not possess signs of virtue, because a miracle is displayed outwardly in vain if what should operate inwardly is lacking. For according to the voice of the teacher of the nations, tongues are for a sign not to believers but to unbelievers.

> And he said to them: “Take nothing for the journey, neither a staff, nor a bag, nor bread, nor money; and do not have two tunics.”

It is usually asked how Matthew and Luke recall that the Lord told the disciples not to carry a staff, when Mark says that he commanded them to take nothing on the journey except a staff. This is resolved by understanding that the staff is spoken of under one meaning in the passage according to Mark, where it is to be carried, and under another meaning in the passages according to Matthew and Luke, where it is not to be carried.

The same distinction applies to the temptation of which it is said: “The Lord your God is testing you, to know whether you love him.” One temptation is enticement; the other is testing. Both, therefore, should be understood as having been said by the Lord to the apostles: both that they should carry no staff and that they should carry nothing except a staff.

For when, according to Matthew, he said to them, “Do not possess gold or silver,” and so forth, he immediately added: “The laborer is worthy of his food.” Thus he sufficiently showed why he did not want them to possess or carry these things—not because they are unnecessary for the sustenance of this life, but because he was sending them in such a way that he might show that these things were owed to them by those to whom they proclaimed the Gospel and who believed it.

It is clear that the Lord did not command this as though evangelists ought to live from no other source than what those to whom they proclaim the Gospel provide. Otherwise the Apostle acted against this command when he obtained his livelihood through the labor of his own hands, so as not to be burdensome to anyone. Rather, the Lord gave them authority by which they would know that these things were owed to them.

When something is commanded by the Lord, failure to do it is a fault of disobedience. But when authority is given, anyone may choose not to use it and may yield what is, as it were, his own right.

The Lord therefore established this order—as the Apostle says, that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel—and spoke those words to the apostles so that, secure in God’s provision, they would possess or carry neither great nor small necessities of this life. For this reason he said, “not even a staff,” showing that all things were owed by his faithful to his ministers, who sought no superfluity. By adding, “For the laborer is worthy of his food,” he completely revealed and illuminated the reason for all these instructions.

He signified this authority under the name of the staff when he said that they should take nothing on the journey except a staff, so that it might be understood that, through the authority received from the Lord—which is signified by the name “staff”—even what they did not carry would not be lacking.
