The same should be understood concerning two tunics: none of them was to worry about carrying another besides the one he was wearing, lest it be needed, since he could receive one through that authority [Col. 0272D]. But when, according to Mark, he prohibits not merely the carrying or possession of two tunics but more explicitly their wearing them, saying that they should not put on two tunics, what does he teach them except to walk not in duplicity but in simplicity?

Alternatively, it seems to me that “two tunics” signifies a double garment—not that in the cold regions of Scythia and Galatia one should be content with a single tunic, but that by “tunic” we should understand clothing: let us not reserve one garment for yourselves and another for us out of fear of future things.

> And into whatever house you enter, remain there, and do not leave from there.

He gives a general command of steadfastness, so that they may observe the obligations of hospitality, asserting that it is foreign to a preacher of the heavenly kingdom to run about from house to house and violate the inviolable rights of hospitality. Nor is it without purpose that, according to Matthew, the house into which the apostles are to enter is to be chosen, so that there may be no occasion for changing lodgings and violating the bond of hospitality.

> And whoever does not receive you, when you leave that city, shake even the dust from your feet as a testimony against them.

The dust is shaken from their feet as a testimony to their labor: that they entered the city and that apostolic preaching reached those people. Or the dust is shaken off so that they receive nothing from those who rejected the Gospel—not even what is necessary for sustenance.

Allegorically, those who attend humbly to the word, if they are obscured by certain blemishes of earthly levity, are cleansed of them at once by the traces of evangelical preaching that they receive. But those who despise it through unbelief, negligence, or even deliberate intent are judged to have communion with them avoided and their synagogue fled; the dust of the feet is to be shaken off, lest the trace of a pure mind be polluted by empty deeds comparable to dust [Col. 0273B].

> Having gone out, they went through the villages, evangelizing and healing everywhere.

Mark explains more fully what the apostles preached and how they healed:

> They preached that people should repent, and they anointed many sick people with oil and healed them.

James also says:

> Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him.

Hence it is clear that from the apostles themselves the holy Church has received the custom that the sick should be anointed with oil consecrated by pontifical blessing [Col. 0273C].

They preached that people should repent. And above he says, “He sent them to evangelize the kingdom of the Lord.” For, following both the example of John the Baptist and that of the Savior himself, they preached both things:

> Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near.

For each person to draw near to the gates of the kingdom of heaven is to repent of those things by which he had departed from it and to hasten through works of righteousness toward everlasting life, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY LXVII. FRIDAY

### Reading from the Acts of the Apostles

[Col. 0273D]

> In those days Peter opened his mouth and said: “Men of Israel, hear these words: Jesus the Nazarene, a man approved by God among you through mighty works, wonders, and signs, which God performed through him in your midst, as you yourselves know—this man, delivered up by the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you killed by the hands of lawless men, fastening him to the cross,” etc.

Like a learned teacher, he first reminds the unbelievers of the guilt they had incurred, so that afterward, when they had been pierced by righteous fear, he might offer them the counsel of salvation at the proper time. Because he is speaking to people who know the law, he shows that Christ is the one promised by the prophets. Yet he does not call him the Son of God on his own authority, but a man approved, a just man, a man raised from the dead [Col. 0274A].

He was not raised with the others in the common resurrection—that is, one postponed until the end of the world—but on the third day, so that the testimony of a singular and glorious resurrection might obtain proof of eternal divinity. For while the bodies of others were shown after death to be subject to corruption, this one, of whom it is said, “You will not allow your holy one to see corruption,” is shown to be free from human frailty. He is also shown to have surpassed the limits of the human condition, and therefore to be attributed to God rather than to human beings.

What beginnings the apostles use in preaching to the Gentiles you will learn from the history of Cornelius the centurion and from the sermon of the apostle Paul delivered at Athens.

> I kept the Lord always before me, because he is at my right hand so that I may not be shaken,

and so forth.

He says: “When I came into those things that pass away, I did not turn my eyes away from the one who always remains. I kept him before me so that, after temporal things had been accomplished, I might return to him. How he favors me, so that I may remain steadfastly in him! And this fact—that I did not sin and that deceit was not found in my mouth—I shall attribute not to humanity but to divinity.

Therefore there was joy in my thoughts and exultation in my words, namely because of the resurrection, since through it the world was delivered. Moreover, my flesh will not perish into destruction but will sleep in the hope of resurrection, because you will neither abandon my soul to be possessed by the underworld nor allow the sanctified body, through which others too are to be sanctified, to undergo corruption.

For you have made known to me the paths by which one goes to eternity; along them, after the sadness of the Passion, you will fill me with joy in your presence [Col. 0274C]. And to the one ascending into heaven you will grant delights at your right hand forever.”

For although he was not abandoned in the underworld—Christ descended in soul to the underworld to help those whom it was fitting to help—he was not abandoned there, since in the swiftest return he sought the body that was to rise again.

On the third day, therefore, he rose from the dead; afterward, on the fortieth day, he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God the almighty Father. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire.

## HOMILY LXVIII. ALSO FRIDAY

### Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Luke

[Col. 0274D]

> At that time, it happened that on one of the days Jesus was sitting and teaching, and the Pharisees were sitting there, etc.

Luke passed over, for the sake of brevity, where the Lord taught while seated, when he cured the paralytic while the scribes and Pharisees were seated. But Matthew and Mark, who relate the event, seem to create a question, since Matthew testifies that he did this in his own city, while Mark says that he did it in Capernaum.

This is more difficult to resolve unless, following Matthew, Nazareth is also understood to be called Christ’s city, evidently to distinguish it from the region of the Gerasenes beyond the sea, from which he had crossed over into Galilee, as Matthew writes. Or certainly Capernaum itself was called Christ’s city, which he made his own not by being born there but by glorifying it with his miracles [Col. 0275A].

> And behold, men were carrying on a bed a man who was paralyzed; and they were seeking to bring him in and place him before him.

The healing of this paralytic signifies the salvation of the soul that, after the prolonged sluggishness of carnal enticement, sighs for Christ. First of all it requires ministers to lift it up and bring it to Christ—that is, good teachers who offer the hope of healing and the help of intercession.

According to Mark’s account, these men are found to have been four, either because the entire power and speech of preachers is confirmed by the four books of the Gospel, or because there are four virtues by which the confidence of the mind is raised to obtain health. Of these it is said in praise of eternal wisdom:

> For it teaches sobriety and wisdom, justice and virtue, and nothing is more useful to human beings in life.

Some, using different names, call these prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice [Col. 0275B].

> And not finding by what way they might bring him in because of the crowd, they went up onto the roof through the tiles.

They desire to bring the paralytic before Christ, but because a crowd intervenes, they are shut out on every side. So often the soul, recovering toward God after the sluggishness of an infirm body and desiring to be renewed by the remedy of heavenly grace, is held back by the obstacle of an old habit. Often, even amid the sweetness of secret prayer and what is almost a pleasant conversation with the Lord, a crowd of thoughts intervenes and blocks the mind’s vision, so that Christ cannot be seen.

What should be done in these circumstances? Certainly one must not remain outwardly below, where the crowd is making a tumult, but must climb onto the roof of the house in which Christ is teaching [Col. 0275C]. That is, one must seek the loftiness of Sacred Scripture and meditate day and night on the law of the Lord with the Psalmist:

> In what way does a young person correct his path? By keeping your words.

> And they lowered him with the bed into the midst before Jesus.

When the roof has been opened, the sick man is lowered before Jesus, because Christ is reached through the mysteries of Scripture once they have been opened. This means that one descends to his humility through the piety of faith.

The house of Jesus is rightly described as covered with tiles, because beneath the contemptible covering of letters, if there is a teacher to open them, the divine power of spiritual grace will be found. But the fact that the man is lowered with his bed signifies that Christ must be known by a person who is still established in this flesh.

> When he saw their faith, he said: “Man, your sins are forgiven you.”

As the Lord was about to heal the man from paralysis, he first released him from the bond of sins, showing that he was condemned because of the chains of his faults and that he could not be healed in his limbs unless those chains were loosened.

Thus also, to the paralytic who had long and vainly awaited movement beside the Pool of the Sheep, the Lord says after healing him:

> Behold, you have been made well; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you.

It is fitting that the one whose sins were forgiven is called “man,” since merely because he was human he could not say, “I have not sinned.” At the same time, this was so that the one who forgave the man might be understood to be God.

Consider carefully how great the value of each person’s own faith is before God, since the faith of others was so valuable that the entire man—that is, outwardly [Col. 0276A] and inwardly—rose suddenly already healed, and through the merit of some, the errors of others were forgiven.

> And the scribes and Pharisees began to think, saying: “Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins except God alone?”

The scribes speak truly, because no one can forgive sins except God, who also forgives through those to whom he grants the power of forgiving. And therefore Christ is proved truly to be God, since he can forgive sins as God.

They bear true witness to God, but they err by denying Christ’s person. Thus the Jews are mistaken: although they believe that Christ is God and can forgive sins, they do not believe that Jesus is the Christ.

But the Arians err far more foolishly. Although, overcome by the words of the Gospel, they do not dare deny that Jesus is the Christ and that he can forgive sins, they nevertheless are not afraid to deny that he is God. But he, desiring to save the faithless, manifests himself to be God both through his knowledge of hidden things and through the power of his works.

Responding, he said to them: “What are you reasoning in your hearts?” For to that same Lord God who says, “I am, I am he who blots out your iniquities,” the most wise worshiper says: “For you alone know the hearts of all the children of men.” Therefore, he says, “By the same majesty and power by which I see your thoughts, I can also forgive sins to human beings. From what happens to the paralytic, understand what you ought to conclude.”

“Which is easier to say: ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say: ‘Rise and walk’?” In truth, only the one who forgave knew that the paralytic’s sins had been forgiven; but “Rise and walk” could be confirmed both by the man who rose and by those who saw him rising. Thus a bodily sign is performed so that a spiritual reality may be proved.

“But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins.” If, according to the testimony of Isaiah just mentioned, God is the one who blots out our iniquities, and the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, then he himself is both God and Son of Man. Thus Christ, as man, could forgive sins through the power of his divinity, and the same Christ, as God, could die for sinners through the weakness of his humanity.

He said to the paralytic: “I say to you, rise, take up your bed, and go into your house.” Spiritually, to rise from one’s bed means to withdraw the soul from carnal desires, in which it had been lying sick. To take up the bed means also to restrain the flesh itself by the bridle of self-control and, in hope of heavenly rewards, to deprive it of earthly pleasures. For this is the bed that David washes each night—that is, the bed is chastened by a worthy stream of repentance for the stains of each individual sin. Once the bed has been taken up, to go home means to return to paradise. For that is the true home that first received the human being, lost not by right but by deceit, and finally restored through him who owed nothing to the deceitful enemy. Alternatively, the man who had been ill, now healed, carries his bed back home when the soul, having received forgiveness of sins, carries it back with the body into its inner custody, lest after pardon it commit something for which it might again justly be struck.

[Col. 0277A] “And immediately he rose before them, took up the bed on which he had lain, and went to his house, glorifying God,” and so forth. Wonderful is the power of divine might, when, with no intervening delay, swift health accompanies the Savior’s command. Deservedly, those who had been present, whose hearts had been turned from the darts of blasphemy to praise of such great majesty, glorified God the Lord—namely, our Jesus Christ—when they recognized the true power of God. With the Father and the Holy Spirit, he reigns in power as one God and truly lives throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXIX. SATURDAY. Reading from the Acts of the Apostles

[Col. 0277B] “In those days the whole city gathered to hear the word of God,” and so forth.

In the preceding statements of this chapter it is recounted how Paul preached by proofs that Christ had been foretold by the prophets, that he was to be sent for the salvation of the human race, and that through his passion he would redeem the human race. He confirmed this with prophetic testimonies. But because the Jews who heard these things were unwilling to believe them readily, they asked Paul to speak to the people again about the same matter on the following Sabbath.

When the synagogue had been dismissed, many of the Jews and of the devout Gentile converts followed Paul and Barnabas. They spoke to them and urged them to remain in the grace of God. For they had heard from those preachers of the word of God that God had promised that the Christ would come from the stock of David. Thus Isaiah, anticipating the mysteries of the New Testament, says: “And I will establish with you an everlasting covenant, the holy and faithful promises of David.” In the Hebrew text this is read: “And I will make with you an everlasting covenant, the faithful mercies of David.” Hence many of the Jews and of the devout Gentile converts followed them. This is better rendered “those who worship God,” as we have seen in the Greek. It signifies those who by nature were Gentiles but by religion were Jews, whom the Greeks call *proselytes*. But because the apostles themselves perceived that the Jews were unbelieving and rebellious, since they were unwilling to receive the word of God—

Then Paul and Barnabas said boldly: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you. But since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles. For so the Lord has commanded us: ‘I have appointed you as a light to the Gentiles, so that you may be for salvation to the ends of the earth.’”

When the Gentiles heard this, they glorified the word of the Lord, and all who had been ordained for eternal life believed. The word of the Lord was spread throughout the whole region. But the Jews stirred up devout and honorable women, as well as the leading men of the city, and aroused persecution against Paul and Barnabas; and they drove them from their territory. But they shook the dust from their feet against them and came to Iconium. The disciples also were filled with joy and the Holy Spirit.

In accordance with the Gospel’s command, the dust is shaken from their feet as a testimony to their labor: they had entered the Jews’ city, and apostolic preaching had reached them. Or the dust is shaken off so that they may receive nothing from them—not even what is necessary for food—since they had rejected the Gospel. “The disciples also were filled with joy and the Holy Spirit.” In the Greek it reads, “But the disciples”; this enables us to understand that, while the Jews persecuted the faith, the disciples were, by contrast, enriched with spiritual joy. And deservedly so, because everyone who rightly believes in God and adorns that faith with good works throughout his life will receive the joy of the Holy Spirit and true blessedness in the contemplation of God. By contrast, those who were unbelieving toward God and opposed his words with wicked deeds will receive the punishment of Gehenna in the future. For at the final judgment the wicked will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.

## HOMILY LXX. ALSO SATURDAY. Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Luke

“In that time Jesus rose from the synagogue and entered the house of Simon. Simon’s mother-in-law was held by a severe fever,” and so forth.

If we say that the man freed from a demon signifies morally a mind cleansed from unclean thought, then, correspondingly, the woman afflicted with fever but healed at the Lord’s command represents the flesh restrained from the heat of its desire by the precepts of self-control. For every bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy is the fury of an unclean spirit. Understand fornication as uncleanness, lust as evil desire, and greed—which is the service of idols—as the fever of seductive flesh.

“And they asked him concerning her. And standing over her, he commanded the fever, and it left her.” At one time the Savior heals the sick when asked; at another he heals them unprompted. In this way he shows that, even regarding the passions of sins, he always responds to the prayers of the faithful, and grants them understanding of those things that they themselves scarcely understand, or forgives even what they do not understand, in accordance with the Psalmist’s request: “Who understands his offenses? Cleanse me from my hidden faults, O Lord.”

“And immediately she rose and served them.” It is natural for those suffering from fever, when health begins, to grow weak and feel the distress of their illness. But the health granted by the Lord’s command returns all at once, and is accompanied by such strength that she is immediately able to serve those who had helped her. Thus, according to the laws of tropology, the members that had served uncleanness for iniquity and produced fruit for death should serve righteousness unto eternal life.

“When the sun had set, all who had sick people suffering from various diseases brought them to him. But he laid his hands on each one of them and healed them.” The setting of the sun signifies the passion and death of the one who said: “As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.” When the sun sets, more demoniacs than before are healed, as are the sick. For the one who, while living temporarily in the flesh, taught only a few Jews, after trampling down the kingdom of death, transmitted the gifts of faith and salvation to all the nations throughout the world. Concerning his ministers, as heralds of life and light, the Psalmist mystically sings: “Make way for him who ascends above the setting.” The Lord indeed ascended above the setting, for from the place where he fell in his passion, from that same place he manifested his greater glory by rising again.

“But demons also came out from many, crying out and saying: ‘You are the Christ, the Son of God.’ And rebuking them, he did not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ.” The demons confessed that he was the Son of God, and, as the Evangelist testifies, they knew that he was the Christ. The devil had recognized him as a man when he was exhausted by forty days of fasting, but, unable to discover through temptation whether he was also the Son of God, the devil now either understood—or rather suspected through the power of his signs—that he was the Son of God.

Therefore, he did not persuade the Jews to crucify him because he thought that he was not the Christ or the Son of God, but because he did not foresee that he himself would be condemned by Christ’s death. For the Apostle truly speaks of this mystery, hidden from the ages: “None of the rulers of this age understood it; for if they had understood it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.” Why, then, did the Lord forbid the demons to speak? The Psalmist makes this clear when he says: “But to the sinner God says, ‘Why do you recite my statutes?’” and so forth. He did this lest anyone, hearing the demons preach, should follow them in their error. For the devil is a wicked teacher, who often mixes falsehoods with truths so that, under the appearance of truth, he may conceal the testimony of fraud.

Elsewhere, however, not only demons—who confessed unwillingly—are ordered to keep silent about Christ, but also those who had been healed by him and wished freely to confess him. Indeed, even the Apostles, who after the resurrection would preach him throughout the whole world, were commanded to remain entirely silent about him before his passion, lest, once his divine majesty had been preached, the dispensation of his passion should be delayed, and, if the passion were delayed, the salvation of the world—which was to come through it—should be denied.

“But when day came, he departed and went into a deserted place. The crowds sought him, and they came even to him,” and so forth. If the Lord’s death is expressed by the setting of the sun, why should his resurrection not be indicated by the return of day? Once its light had been revealed, he was sought by crowds of believers and, having been found in the desert of the Gentiles, was held fast lest he depart. This is especially appropriate because the departure, seeking, and finding occurred on the first day of the week, on which the resurrection was celebrated. In all these events the goodness and mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ are manifested. In him we live, move, and exist, and through his clemency we hope to reach the life to come, with our Creator and Redeemer himself, Jesus Christ, granting it—he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXI. EIGHTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST. Reading from the Book of Revelation

“In those days, I saw a door standing open in heaven, and the first voice that I heard was like a trumpet speaking with me, saying: ‘Come up here, and I will show you what must take place,’” and so forth.

Having described the works of the Church—what it was and what it would be—he recapitulates them from Christ’s birth onward. He is about to speak of the same things in another way, for throughout this book he repeats the entire period of the Church under various figures.

“Behold,” he says, “a door standing open in heaven.” It is fitting that the one who is about to ascend should look upon a heavenly door, since lofty mysteries are promised to be opened to him. Or, because Christ is the door, whoever believes that he was born and suffered ascends into heaven—that is, into the height of the Church—and sees future spiritual effects, as he says: “And immediately I was in the spirit.”

“And the first voice that I heard was like a trumpet speaking with me, saying: ‘Come up here, and I will show you what must take place after these things.’ Immediately I was in the spirit.” This is evidently similar to the earlier voice that had said: “What you see, write in a book.”

“And behold, a throne was set in heaven, and above the throne was one seated.” The Lord inhabits the Church, established in heavenly conduct. Pope Gregory interprets the throne of God in Micah’s vision as the angelic powers; presiding more exaltedly over their minds, he arranges all things below.

“And the one who was seated was like the appearance of a jasper stone and a sardius.” The color of jasper signifies water, and that of sardius fire; by these two we know that judgment is celebrated. For, he says, “as it was in the days of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.”

“And there was a rainbow around the throne, like the appearance of an emerald.” The rainbow is produced when the sun illuminates the clouds, and after the flood it first appeared as a judgment of reconciliation. It signifies that, through the intercession of the saints whom the Lord illuminates, the Church is protected. It is fittingly compared with the emerald, a stone of intense greenness: the more firmly they await the imperishable inheritance through advancing faith, the more powerfully they protect others by praying.

“And around the throne were twenty-four seats, and upon the seats twenty-four thrones, and seated upon them were elders.” The Church, which he had seen on one throne because of the unity of faith, he now sees generated through the two Testaments from the patriarchs and the Apostles and seated on twenty-four seats. It is seated because of its judicial dignity in Christ. All its members sat and judged, but in one head and through one head. For how could the saints sit in judgment if they stood at the judge’s right hand?

The twenty-four elders may also be understood as those who complete the perfection of works—commended by the number six—through the clear preaching of the Gospel. For four times six makes twenty-four.

“They were clothed all around in white garments, and on their heads were golden crowns.” That is, they were clothed in good works and, through the perpetual remembrance of their minds, sought the joys above. For the name “head” often signifies the mind.

“And from the throne came flashes of lightning, voices, and thunder.” This is what Mark says: “But they went out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word by the signs that followed.”

“And seven burning lamps before the throne, which are the seven Spirits of God.” He speaks of one Spirit who is sevenfold. For the Spirit is one; sevenfoldness is perfection and fullness. After the Holy Spirit has been mentioned, the water of baptism appropriately follows, in which that same Spirit is believed to be received.

“And before the throne there was something like a glass sea, resembling crystal.” Because of faith in true baptism, it is compared with glass, in which nothing appears outwardly other than what it contains within. Its comparison with crystal also represents the grace of baptism, which changes water into ice and precious stone.

“And in the midst of the throne and around the throne were four living creatures, full of eyes before and behind.” The light of the Gospel fills all the parts of the throne of God—that is, of the Church—with knowledge of past and future things.

“And the first living creature was like a lion,” and so forth. These living creatures are interpreted in many ways. Blessed Augustine, following the order of this book, says that Matthew is understood in the lion, since he narrates Christ’s royal ancestry: “The lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered.” For Judah is a lion’s cub; Christ is feared as king by kings and adored by the Magi. There too the king settles accounts with his servants; the king makes a wedding for his son; and finally the king separates the sheep from the goats.

Luke is understood in the calf, because it was a great sacrificial victim in the Law. Not only do the beginnings of his Gospel concern the temple and sacrifices, but it also concludes in this way: “And they were always in the temple, praising and blessing God.”

The face of a human being signifies Mark, who said nothing about the Lord’s royal and priestly power but simply narrated the deeds of Christ as a man.

The eagle is John, who gazes perceptively upon the birth of the Word as upon the rising of the sun. These living creatures sometimes signify the Evangelists and sometimes the whole Church, whose strength is shown in the lion, its sacrificial offering in the calf, its humility in the human being, and its sublimity in the flying eagle.

“Each of them had six wings.” Through the perfection of its teaching, the Church is lifted to the heights. For the number six is called perfect because it is first completed by its own parts: one, which is one-sixth of six; two, which is one-third; and three, which is one-half—all together make six.

Alternatively, the six wings of each of the four living creatures, which total twenty-four, signify the same number of books of the Old Testament. These support the authority of the Evangelists and confirm its truth.

“And around them and within they were full of eyes.” The holy Church watches over itself attentively before God and before human beings. The Psalmist had seen its inner eyes when he says: “All the glory of the daughter of kings is within”; and its outer eyes when he immediately adds: “Clothed all around in embroidered garments with golden borders.”

Alternatively, whether one attends to the literal sense or seeks an allegory, one always finds light in the Gospel. Another translation reads: “Full of eyes before and behind,” because the light of the Gospel illuminates the enigmas of the Law and pours the lightning of new grace upon the world.

“And they have no rest day or night, saying: ‘Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty.’” The holy living creatures throughout the entire course of the age affirm the one lordship of the Godhead, the omnipotence, and the eternity of the Holy Trinity, while the perpetual praise of rational creation remains in the heavenly realms.

“The twenty-four elders fell before the one seated on the throne and worshiped him who lives throughout the ages of ages.” When the living creatures sound forth praise—that is, when the Evangelists preach Christ’s dispensation—the whole Church, which consists of its leaders and peoples—for this is signified by the doubled number twelve—immediately falls on its face and worships him who lives throughout the ages of ages.

“And they cast their crowns before the throne,” assigning to God whatever virtue and whatever dignity they possessed. For he had created all things from nothing and is the ruler of all things; he lives and reigns as God in unity and perfect Trinity throughout all ages of ages.

## HOMILY LXXII. ON THE SAME FEAST. Reading from the Holy Gospel according to John

“At that time there was a man from the Pharisees, named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. He came to Jesus by night,” and so forth.

[Col. 0282B] The ruler of the Jews came to Jesus by night. Desiring privately to learn more fully, through conversation with him, the mysteries of the faith, whose beginnings he had already grasped to some extent through the open display of signs, he approached him. Because he wisely took care to understand what he saw Jesus doing, he deserved to investigate subtly the things he asked him.

“Rabbi, we know that you have come from God as a teacher. For no one can perform these signs that you perform unless God is with him.” He confessed, then, that Jesus had come from God to present heavenly teaching to the world. He understood from the miracles that God was with him, but he did not yet recognize that Jesus himself was God.

Yet because he approached earnestly to be taught by the one whom he knew as a teacher of truth, he deserved to be perfectly instructed in the knowledge of his divinity. He accordingly learned the mysteries of both his births—namely, his divine and human birth—as well as of his passion and ascension. By God’s revelation, he also learned the manner of the second generation, entrance into the heavenly kingdom, and many other mysteries of Gospel teaching.

Jesus answered and said: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.” This statement shines so clearly for all the faithful because it is certain that without its light they cannot be faithful. For who can obtain forgiveness of sins and enter the kingdom of heaven without the washing of regeneration?

But Nicodemus, who came to the Lord by night, did not yet know how to grasp the mysteries of the light. The night in which he came signifies the ignorance that oppressed him. He had not yet been joined to those to whom the Apostle says: “Once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.” Rather, he still remained among those to whom Isaiah says: “Arise, shine, Jerusalem, for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you.”

Nicodemus says to him: “How can a human being be born when he is old? Surely he cannot enter his mother’s womb a second time and be born again?” Since he still remained ignorant of the second birth, yet had already become concerned about his salvation, he necessarily asked whether the one birth he knew could be repeated, or by what process regeneration could be accomplished, lest, remaining without it, he should be unable to share in heavenly life.

It must be noted that what he said about bodily birth must also be understood of spiritual regeneration. Once it has been completed, it cannot in any way be repeated. Whether a heretic, a schismatic, or any criminal person baptizes in the confession of the Holy Trinity, the one who has been baptized cannot be rebaptized by good Catholics, lest the confession and invocation of so great a name appear to be annulled.

Because Nicodemus carefully asks how the Lord’s first answer is to be understood, he deserves to be instructed more clearly. Since the second birth is not bodily but spiritual, he deserves to hear:

Jesus answered: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone is born of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.” Then, explaining the manner of this birth and distinguishing it completely from bodily birth, he says:

“What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit.” Spiritual nature is invisible, while bodily nature is visible. Therefore bodily generation is administered visibly, with visible growth: the one born in the flesh progresses through the stages of age. Spiritual generation, however, takes place entirely invisibly.

The person who is baptized is indeed seen descending into the font, being immersed in the waters, and rising from the waters. But what takes place in him through the washing of regeneration cannot be seen at all. The devotion of the faithful alone knows that sin descends into the font but the purified person rises; a child of death descends but a child of resurrection rises; a child of transgression descends but a child of reconciliation rises; a child of wrath descends but a child of mercy rises; a child of the devil descends but a child of God rises. Only the Church, that mother who gives birth, knows this.

To the eyes of the foolish, however, such a person seems to come out of the font just as he entered it, and everything that has been done appears to be a game. Therefore, at the end, when they see the glory of the saints, they will say, groaning in torment: “These are the ones whom we once held in derision and made a reproachful example of. How, then, have they been counted among the children of God?”

The apostle John says: “Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be.” Therefore, what is born is from the Holy Spirit, because the one who is regenerated invisibly through water and the Spirit is changed into a new human being and, from being carnal, becomes spiritual.

For this reason he is rightly called not only spiritual but also “spirit,” because just as the substance of spirit is invisible to our eyes, so the one who is renewed by God’s grace becomes invisibly spiritual and a child of God, while visibly appearing to all as flesh and as the Son of Man.

“Do not marvel that I said to you: ‘You must be born again.’ The Spirit blows where he wills, and you hear his voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.”

“The Spirit blows where he wills,” because he has power over whose heart he will illuminate by the grace of his visitation. You hear his voice when, in your presence, the one who has been filled with the Spirit speaks. But you do not know where he comes from or where he goes. Even if the Spirit fills someone for a time in your presence, you cannot see how he entered or how he returned, since he is invisible by nature.

“So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.” Through the invisible action of the Spirit, such a person begins to be what he was not. Thus the faithful do not know where he comes from or where he goes—that is, he comes by the grace of regeneration into adoption as a child of God and goes on to receive the heavenly kingdom.

While Nicodemus was still asking how these things could happen,

Jesus answered and said to him: “You are a teacher in Israel, and you do not know these things?” He did not say this as though he wished to insult one who was called a teacher yet was ignorant of heavenly mysteries, but to call him to the way of humility, without which the heavenly door cannot be found.

[Col. 0284B] “Amen, amen, I say to you: We speak what we know and testify to what we have seen, and you do not accept our testimony. If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?”

He told them earthly things, as we find in the preceding reading, when he spoke of the passion and resurrection of his body, which he had taken from the earth, saying: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” Yet they did not believe the word he had spoken; indeed, they were not even able to understand that he was speaking of any temple other than the temple of his body.

Therefore, if they did not grasp earthly things when they heard them, how much less were they capable of grasping heavenly things—that is, the mysteries of divine generation? The Lord nevertheless continues to instruct the one whom he sees attending wisely and diligently to what he hears, both in heavenly and earthly mysteries.

His ascension to eternal life is heavenly; his exaltation to temporal death is earthly. Therefore he speaks of heavenly things:

“And no one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.”

It is rightly asked how the Son of Man can be said either to have descended from heaven or, at the time when he was speaking these words on earth, already to have been in heaven. For Christ’s flesh did not descend from heaven, nor was it in heaven before the time of the ascension. How, then, can he say, “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven”?

The answer is that there is one person of Christ existing in two natures. Therefore the Son of Man is rightly said both to have descended from heaven and to have been in heaven before his passion, because what he could not possess in his own nature he possessed in the Son of God by whom he was assumed.

It must also be asked how he could have said, “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven,” since all the elect confidently believe that they will ascend into heaven, as the Lord promises them: “Where I am, there my servant will be also.”

The clearest reasoning resolves this difficulty. The mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, is the head of all the elect. Likewise, all the elect are members of that same head, as the Apostle says: “He gave him as head over the whole Church.” And again: “You are the body of Christ, and members individually.”

No one ascends into heaven except Christ in his body, which is the Church. He first ascended in himself, in the sight of the Apostles, who were his most distinguished members; and from that time he ascends daily in his members and gathers them into heaven.

Whoever desires to ascend into heaven joins himself in true unity of faith and love to the one who descended from heaven and is in heaven. He clearly understands that no one can ascend into heaven by any other path than through the one who descended from heaven. Hence he himself says elsewhere: “No one comes to the Father except through me.”

“And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up.” With wondrous skill in heavenly teaching, the Lord leads the teacher of the Mosaic Law to the spiritual meaning of that same Law. He recalls the ancient history and explains it as a figure of his passion and of the salvation of the human race.

The Book of Numbers relates that, wearied by the long journey and labor in the wilderness, the people of Israel murmured against the Lord and Moses. Therefore the Lord sent fiery serpents among them. When many cried out to Moses because of their wounds and bites, and Moses prayed, the Lord commanded him to make a bronze serpent and set it up as a sign. “Anyone who is bitten,” he says, “who looks at it shall live.” And so it happened.

The wounds inflicted by the fiery serpents are therefore the poisons and incitements of vices, which kill with spiritual death the soul they touch. It was fitting that the people who murmured against the Lord should be struck down by the bites of serpents, so that, through the sequence of the outward scourge, they might recognize the great destruction they were suffering inwardly through murmuring.

The lifting up of the bronze serpent, by looking upon which those who had been bitten were healed, is the passion of our Redeemer on the cross. Through faith in him alone, the kingdom of death and sin is overcome.

Sins are rightly expressed by serpents, since they drag both soul and body to destruction—not only because the serpents were fiery, poisonous, and appointed to kill, but also because our first parents were persuaded to sin through a serpent and, by sinning, were changed from immortal to mortal beings.

The Lord is rightly shown by the bronze serpent, because he came in the likeness of sinful flesh. As the bronze serpent had an image resembling the fiery serpents but possessed no burning poison at all in its members, and by being lifted up healed those who had been bitten by the serpents, so the Redeemer of the human race did not assume sinful flesh but the likeness of sinful flesh. By suffering the death of the cross in that flesh, he freed those who believe in him from every sin and from death itself.

“So that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.” The meaning of this statement is clear: whoever believes in Jesus not only escapes the punishment of perdition but also receives eternal life.

This is the difference between the figure and the reality: through the former, temporal life was prolonged; through the latter, life is given that will remain without end.

But one must diligently ensure that right understanding is completed by worthy conduct, so that our true confession of faith may, through pious and sober living, deserve to reach the perfection of the life promised to us.

Yet because these things are said of the Son of Man, who deserved to be lifted up and was able to suffer death, the Lord took care to reveal to Nicodemus also the mystery of his divinity. He showed him that the one and same Son of Man is the Savior of the world, who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXIII. WEDNESDAY. Reading from the Epistle of the Holy Apostle Paul to the Corinthians

“Brothers, if Christ is preached as having risen from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? But if there is no resurrection of the dead, neither has Christ risen. And if Christ has not risen, then our preaching is empty, and your faith is also empty,” and so forth.

These teachings had been handed down by false apostles, who asserted that Christ had neither been born, nor suffered in the flesh, nor risen again. The Apostle John also identifies them: they denied that Christ had come in the flesh. Hence he says: “Whoever denies that Christ has come in the flesh is the Antichrist.” And: “Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father.”

These false apostles were active among them and were overturning the faith of some, lest they should be judged foolish by the wise people of the world. For the wise of this age consider it foolish when they hear of the resurrection of the dead.

“If,” he says, “it is true that Christ has not risen, then we are false preachers and our faith is empty.” They had believed this because the Apostle preached that the dead would rise, and they had been drawn to the faith by this hope. He therefore asserts that it would be to their detriment if they believed something that will not happen. It is shameful for anyone to confess that he believed what is false.

Thus he brings shame upon them and declares their labors fruitless if what they heard from the false apostles is true—namely, that the dead will not rise. No one willingly endures hearing this about himself; therefore, when they see that this is against them, they will return to their former faith.

“But we are also found to be false witnesses of God, because we testify against God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise.” Whoever asserts that God raised Christ from the dead is a false witness if the event did not happen. Yet he proclaims God’s power, not as an enemy would, since he attributes so marvelous a deed to God’s power.

But if it is true that God raised Christ from the dead, what will this person say, since he has both become a witness against God and declared God’s work to be foolishness?

“For if the dead are not raised, neither has Christ been raised. And if Christ has not been raised, you are still in your sins; therefore those who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished.”

He terrifies them so that, since no one wishes evil upon himself, they may grieve that they have begun to believe what is against them. For who would not wish to hear that his sins have been forgiven? “And those who have fallen asleep,” he says, “in Christ have perished.”

He adds this to increase their fear, because they did not wish to regard the deaths of their loved ones as destruction. Those who departed from this world in that hope—or who did not fear being killed because they believed that they would rise following Christ’s example—have perished, if this is not true.

He tells them what, because of their love for their dead, they do not wish to hear, so that they may realize that what they previously wanted to hear in error is being charged against them.

There are also valid connections in an argument that contain false conclusions—conclusions that follow from the error of the person being addressed. A good and learned person nevertheless introduces such conclusions so that the one whose error they follow may become ashamed of it and abandon the same error. For if he wishes to remain in it, he must necessarily be compelled to hold even those conclusions that he condemns.

If our hope in Christ is only for this life, [Col. 0287B] we are more pitiable than all human beings. It is clear that we hope in Christ both in this present life and in the future one. For Christ does not abandon his servants here, but grants them grace, and in the future they will be in eternal glory. But if there were no hope of the future life, we would be more pitiable than all human beings, as he said. For what purpose would there be fasts, vigils, departures, a pure life, justice, mercy, and death, if there will be no reward for these things in the future? But unbelievers at least enjoy this life.

Now Christ has risen from the dead, the first fruits of those who sleep; for since death came through a human being, the resurrection of the dead also comes through a human being. In saying this he touches upon the false prophets who denied that Christ had been born and, consequently, that the flesh had risen. For one who was not born does not die. Thus he proves that Christ rose from the dead because he was human: so that there can be no doubt that a human being was raised by God from the dead; and since death was brought forth through human sin, Christ’s righteousness merited the resurrection of the dead.

For just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ. He says this because, just as Adam, by sinning, found death and held all his descendants in its power so that they might be dissolved, so Christ, by not sinning and thereby conquering death—for whoever does not sin conquers death, since death is the expectation of the righteous—acquired life, that is, resurrection, for all who belong to his body. Although he granted a general resurrection, so that just as in Adam all, whether righteous or unrighteous, die, so also in Christ all, both believers and unbelievers, may rise, nevertheless the unbelievers appear to be made alive for punishment, because they will receive their bodies, no longer to die but to suffer punishment in them without end, since they were unwilling to believe. “Just as,” he says, “all die in Adam, so also they will be made alive in Christ.” For just as no one is without Adam in the kingdom of death, so no one is without Christ in the kingdom of life; just as through Adam all mortals became sons of the age in punishment, so also through Christ all immortals become, by grace, sons of God.

But each in his own order: now he wishes to explain the orders of the resurrection, lest they should think God’s promise fictitious because it has not yet happened in the rest. He explains to them the orders and the times when it has happened [Col. 0288A] and when it will happen that the dead rise: Christ the first fruits, as it is also attested in the Acts of the Apostles, where it is written in Moses: “If Christ is subject to suffering, if he is the first to rise from the dead,” and so forth. He therefore rose first, so that he might become an example for those who believe in him.

Then [ii] those who belong to Christ, who believed at his coming. This is to be understood in two ways, because the saints will also rise at his second coming, according to the faith of the Apocalypse of John, just as at his first coming, when he rose, many holy bodies rose as a testimony that death had been defeated and despoiled. Thus, under one signification, he encompasses the Lord’s two comings: the first, when he came to save the human race, and the second, when he will come to judge the living and the dead and the age by fire. [Col. 0288B]

# HOMILY LXXIV. ALSO ON WEDNESDAY

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Luke.

At that time certain Sadducees approached Jesus, who deny that there is a resurrection, and so forth.

There were two heresies among the Jews: one of the Pharisees and the other of the Sadducees. The Pharisees put forward the traditions and observances that they call *deuteroseis* [“second traditions”], and for this reason they were also called “separated” by the people. The Sadducees, whose name is interpreted as “just,” claimed this title for themselves although they were not just. While the former believed in and confessed the resurrection of both body and soul, and acknowledged angels and spirits, the latter denied everything, as is related in the Acts of the Apostles.

[Col. 0288C] And they questioned him, saying: “Teacher, Moses wrote for us: If someone’s brother has died, having a wife, and he was childless, his brother must take his wife and raise up offspring for his brother.” Observe the difference between letter and spirit. According to the letter, a man is compelled to marry during life so that the brother may raise up the dead man’s offspring; but the Spirit is the teacher of chastity.

Now there were seven brothers. The first took a wife and died childless; the next took her, and he too died without a child; and the third took her, and similarly all seven, and they left no offspring and died. Last of all the woman also died. Those who did not believe in the resurrection of bodies, judging that souls perished with their bodies, rightly invent such a story, which exposes as madness those who affirm the resurrection of the dead. Yet it may be that something of this kind once actually happened among their people.

In the resurrection, then, whose wife will she be, since all seven had her as wife? They set the indecency of the story against the truth of the resurrection in order to deny it. Mystically, however, these seven brothers who died childless correspond to the reprobate, who throughout the whole life of this age—which revolves through seven days—remain barren of good works. When each of them has been taken away by miserable death, the worldly way of life itself, which they passed without the work that gives life, will at last pass away like a barren wife.

And Jesus said to them: “The children of this age marry and are given in marriage.” When the Lord says, “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine,” he is not to be thought to have given what is holy to dogs or thrown pearls before swine when he is found to have spoken, either here about the glory of the resurrection or elsewhere about the mystery of his dispensation or even of his divinity—things that many who heard them, whether by resisting or despising them, did not receive. For he did not give these things to those unable to receive them, but to those who could receive them and were present at the same time. They ought not to have been neglected because of the uncleanness of others. And when tempters questioned him, he answered them in such a way that they had something to contradict, although they wasted away on their own poisons rather than being filled with his food. Others, however, who were able to receive it, heard many useful things because of their questioning. [Col. 0289B]

“But those who are considered worthy of that age and of the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage.” This is not to be understood as though only the worthy will either rise or exist without marriage, while the unworthy—that is, sinners—are to be believed either not to rise at all or to rise for marriage. Rather, it should be understood that everyone will rise and remain in that age without marriage; but the Lord and Savior, in order to stir minds to seek the glory of the resurrection, wished to speak only about the elect.

But if in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, then the bodies rise—bodies capable of marrying and taking wives, that is, the distinct members of women and men, differentiated by their particular forms—yet enslaved neither to the pleasure nor to the necessity of intercourse. For no one says of a stone, a tree, or things that have no genital members that they do not marry or take wives, but of those who, although able to marry, nevertheless do not do so for another reason.

For they can no longer die. Marriages exist for the sake of children, children for the sake of succession, and succession for the sake of death. Where, therefore, there is no death, there are no marriages either.

“For they are equal to angels, and are children of God, since they are children of the resurrection.” They are equal to angels and are children of God who, renewed by the glory of the resurrection, without any fear of death, without any stain of corruption, and without any activity belonging to an earthly condition, enjoy the perpetual vision of God. Whoever then desires to attain the equality of angelic dignity must now stoop down to the least of his brothers. [Col. 0289D]

“But that the dead rise, Moses also showed at the bush, when he calls the Lord ‘the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.’” To establish the truth of the resurrection, he could have used many other clearer examples, among them this one: “The dead will be raised, and those in the tombs will rise.” It is therefore asked what the Lord intended by bringing forward this testimony, which appears ambiguous or not sufficiently relevant to the truth of the resurrection. But the Sadducees accepted only the five books of Moses and rejected the prophecies of the prophets. It would therefore have been foolish [Col. 0290A] to produce testimonies whose authority they did not follow. Moreover, to prove the immortality of souls, he gives an example from Moses: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” And immediately he adds:

“God is not the God of the dead, but of the living.” He wished to prove that souls remain after death, something they denied among other things. For it could not be that he was the God of those who did not exist at all. Consequently, the resurrection of bodies was also introduced, since together with their souls they had done either good or evil. For all live to him—namely, all those whose God the Lord is live to him—with that true life by which the righteous live even when they die in body. Concerning this the Lord says elsewhere: “Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live.” Believe, therefore: even if you have died, you will live; but if you do not believe, even while you live you are dead. For the widow who lives in pleasure is dead.

Some of the scribes answered and said to him: “Teacher, you have spoken well.” And they no longer dared to question him about anything. The chief priests, the Sadducees, and the scribes had been seeking an opportunity for slander and some word that would expose him to their plots. Since they had been refuted in argument, they questioned him no further but openly handed him over to the Roman authorities. From this we understand that the poisons of envy can indeed be overcome, but are slow to become quiet. Hence it is written: “Through the envy of the devil death entered the world.” Those who belong to his party imitate him. Through the love and mercy of our Creator, however, eternal salvation and perpetual life have been granted to us; if we rightly obey his commandments, we will receive eternal life in the heavenly kingdom, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, through all ages of ages. Amen.

# HOMILY LXXV. THURSDAY

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Luke.

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “When they bring you into synagogues and before magistrates and authorities, do not be anxious about how or what you should answer, or what you should say; for the Holy Spirit will teach you at that hour what must be said,” and so forth.

[Col. 0290D] Therefore, when we are brought before judges because of Christ, we ought to offer only our will for Christ; Christ himself, who dwells in us, will speak for himself, and the Holy Spirit will supply grace in our answer.

But someone from the crowd said to him: “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” But he said to him: “Man, who appointed me judge or divider over you?” This brother is rightly rebuked: while the Teacher was commending the joys of heavenly peace and unity, he wished to intrude upon him the trouble of dividing earthly possessions. He is rightly designated by the word “man.” For when there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal? Are you not human, and walking according to human ways? The Lord denies that he is a divider among human beings, since he had come to reconcile them both with himself and with the angels. “God is not of dissension but of peace,” and the heart and soul of the multitude of believers were one; no one said that any of the things they possessed was his own, but everything was common to them. The sole divider and author of dissension among brothers is the one of whom it is said above, “He who does not gather with me scatters”; and of those members it is said: “Every kingdom divided against itself is desolated, and house falls upon house.”

And he said to them: “See and beware of all greed, because one’s life does not consist in the abundance of what one possesses.” Just as the Lord had previously said many things against blasphemers and hypocrites, so here, taking occasion from this foolish petitioner, he strives to arm both the crowds and the disciples by precepts and examples against the plague of greed, with which most mortals labor excessively. It should be noted that he does not say merely, “Beware of greed,” but adds, “of all,” because some actions appear simple to human beings, but the inner judge, who sees with what intention they are done, passes judgment. For who, while dividing an inheritance with his brother, would count it a crime to store the mature fruits of his own field in barns? Yet God himself is the witness and judge, as it is written.

“The field of a certain rich man produced abundant crops. And he thought within himself, saying: ‘What shall I do? For I have nowhere to gather my crops.’ And he said: ‘I will do this: I will pull down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will gather all that has grown for me and my goods.’” The rich man is not condemned because he cultivated the soil and gathered its produce into barns, but because he placed all his confidence for life in that abundance of possessions. Counting the unusually abundant crops that the earth had produced as “his crops” and “his goods,” he did not distribute them to the poor, in accordance with the Lord’s command: “What remains, give as alms.” Instead, after making larger storage places, he intended to reserve them for his future luxury.

“‘Soul, you have many good things stored up for many years; rest, eat, drink, feast.’” A similar saying is read in Ecclesiasticus: “There is one who becomes rich by acting sparingly, and this is his reward,” in what he says: “I have found rest for myself, and now I shall eat my goods alone,” not knowing that time will pass and leave everything to others.

But the Lord said to him: “Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you; and whose will the things you have prepared be?” You foolishly promised yourself many years of delights in life; but, seized by death on the coming night, you will leave to others what you gathered. That God says this to the human being means that he restrains his wicked schemes by sudden correction. Alternatively, the soul was taken away “in the night” because it was lost in the darkness of the heart; it was taken away in the night because it did not wish to have the light of reflection, so as to foresee what it might suffer. Hence the apostle Paul rightly says to disciples who were thinking about the future: “But you, brothers, are not in darkness, so that that day should overtake you like a thief. For you are all sons of light and sons of day; we are not of night or darkness.” The day of departure overtakes like a thief in the night when it drives out the souls of fools who have not considered the future beforehand.

“So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.” He is a fool and will be snatched away in the night. Therefore, whoever wishes to be rich toward God should not store up treasure for himself, but distribute his possessions to the poor. In this way he will deserve to be wise and a child of light. Hence the Psalmist, having first spoken of some greedy rich man, says: “And yet he is troubled in vain; he stores up treasure and does not know for whom he will gather it.” Then he immediately reveals where he has placed the treasure of his heart, saying: “And now what is my expectation? Is it not the Lord? And my substance is with you.” That substance is with God which the faithful distribute to the poor and needy with a good disposition and humble heart, because for this an eternal reward will be repaid to them in the heavenly kingdom by the judge of the living and the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord, who will repay each according to his works: rewards of eternal life to the good, perpetual punishment to the wicked. To him be honor and glory through ages of ages. Amen.

# HOMILY LXXVI. SECOND SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

Reading from the Epistle of the blessed apostle John.

Beloved: “God is love. In this the love of God was revealed among us, because God sent his only-begotten Son into the world, so that we might live through him,” and so forth.

We must listen attentively, dearest brothers, carefully commit to memory, and also fulfill in our works what the apostle John teaches us in the present reading when he says: “God is love.” Love is pure and undefiled affection: pure from every stain of sin; pure from perverse thought; pure from idle and useless speech; pure from every evil work; pure from every evil desire; and pure from every wickedness. It is chaste love, sincere affection, true affection, faithful love that nourishes every good; love that flees and hates every evil; love without which nothing is good; love from which every good proceeds. Whoever possesses this possesses every good, because he possesses God himself, for God is love.

“In this the love of God was revealed among us, because God sent his only-begotten Son into the world, so that we might live through him.” The love of God the Father toward us is proved by this: he sent his only Son to die for us. The love of Christ, the Son of God, toward us is proved by this: he died for us, the just for the unjust, so that we might be justified and made worthy of God through good works and a pure will in the Lord. And he died for the dead, so that we who were dead in sins and slain in transgressions might be freed from every sin, receive forgiveness of all crimes, and be brought back from death to life. Christ died as salvation for the sick, so that he might grant us eternal salvation.

“In this is love: not that we loved God, but that he first loved us and sent his Son as an expiation for our sins.” For God the Father did not love human beings because of any merits of theirs, but solely through his free mercy. He loved them so greatly that he sent his only Son to die for the sins of humanity, so that human beings who obeyed his commandments would no longer die in sins. And because through the disobedience of the first human being, Adam, all human beings were dying to God in sins, God the Son himself deigned to become obedient to the Lord his Father unto death, so that he might die for the life and salvation of human beings, open the way of life to all who believe in him, and lead them with himself to the eternal and blessed immortality from which they had fallen through guilt.

Dearest brothers, if God loved us in this way, we also ought to love one another. Since God loved us so greatly without any preceding merits of ours, as we have said, why do we hate one another, unless to satisfy the devil and resist God’s will? Why are we stirred by envy of our neighbor, unless to make our love ungrateful? Why do we bite our neighbors with anger and jealousy, unless to despise God’s commandments and enslave ourselves not to God but to the devil? Since these things are so, brothers, with complete attention, every precaution, all haste, and every concern, we must flee these and similar evils and avoid them with every effort through God’s mercy, so that we may escape eternal punishments.

We must carefully remember that God loved us so greatly that he sent his only Son to die for us; and because the Son of God also died for us, and because we are unable to repay God worthily for such great and immeasurable goodness, we must love one another with a pure heart and chaste, sincere love in God, not with an unjust and harmful worldly love. Let us do nothing to our neighbors that we do not wish to be done to ourselves; let us envy our neighbors none of the good things we desire for ourselves. From such words, my brothers, we can understand that acting against such love, as you have heard, is acting against God, because God is love.

Let no one say, “I sin against a human being when I do not love my brother.” If you dare, act against God and do not love your brother. For “whoever does not love remains in death.” But whoever loves has God the Holy Spirit dwelling in him. Since God is love, whoever remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him. For everyone who does not love is alienated from God, and this is Antichrist. Even if he enters a basilica, he cannot be counted among the children of God. He may possess baptism and still be evil; he may receive the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood and still be evil. For concerning such people it is written: “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.” He may be called a Christian and still be evil; but he cannot possess love and still be evil.

This, then, is the distinctive gift God gives to human beings; it is the saving fountain. The apostle teaches us to drink from it, and the Holy Spirit urges us to drink from it, because if we love one another, God remains in us and his love is perfected in us. He grants this, our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be praise, honor, and glory through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

# HOMILY LXXVII. ON THE SAME FEAST

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Luke.

At that time: “There was a certain rich man, and he was clothed in purple and fine linen, and he feasted splendidly every day,” and so forth.

Almost no one doubts that purple is the color of royal clothing, obtained from marine shells. For shells cut open with iron emit tears of purple color with which wool is dyed. Fine linen (*byssus*) is a kind of linen, exceedingly white and soft, which the Greeks call *papaten*.

The Lord had previously instructed them to make friends from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when we have departed from this life, they might receive us into eternal dwellings. Hearing this, the Pharisees mocked him. But he supported what he had proposed with examples and showed that the rich man dressed in purple was tortured irredeemably in hell because he had neglected to make the poor Lazarus his friend, by whom he could have been received into the dwellings of life.

Some think that the commandments of the Old Testament are stricter than those of the New; but they are deceived by an incautious judgment. In the former, it is not stinginess but robbery that is punished; there an unjustly taken possession is punished by fourfold restitution. Here, however, this rich man is not reproved for taking another’s property but for not giving his own. He is not said to have oppressed anyone by force, but to have exalted himself in the things he had received. From this we must draw the greatest possible conclusion: what punishment must be imposed on one who seizes another’s property, if one who does not give his own is struck by condemnation to hell?

There are also some who do not think that the adornment of delicate and expensive clothing is a sin. Yet if it were not a fault, the word of God would never so carefully state that the rich man who is tormented in hell had been clothed in fine linen and purple. No one seeks exceptional clothing except for empty glory—that is, so that he may appear more honorable than others. We can also gather this fault even from the opposite case: if the rejection of cheap clothing were not a virtue, the Evangelist would not carefully have said of John, “He was clothed in camel’s hair.”

But we must pay close attention to the order of the narrative in the mouth of Truth concerning the proud rich man and the humble poor man. For it says: “There was a certain rich man,” and immediately adds:

“There was also a beggar named Lazarus.” Certainly, the names of the rich are usually better known among the people than those of the poor. What does it mean that, when the Lord speaks about the poor man and the rich man, he gives the poor man’s name but does not give the rich man’s name, unless that God knows and approves the humble but ignores the proud? Hence, concerning some who grow proud of the power of miracles, he will say at the end: “I do not know you; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity.” But to Moses, by contrast, he says: “I know you by name.”

Thus he says of the rich man, “A certain man”; of the poor man, “A needy man named Lazarus.” As though he were plainly saying: I know the humble poor man; I do not know the proud rich man. I possess the former as one known through approval; I ignore the latter through the judgment of rejection.

“He lay at his gate, full of sores, desiring to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table. Moreover, dogs came and licked his sores.” The beggar Lazarus, full of sores, lay before the rich man’s gates. Through this one circumstance the Lord fulfilled two judgments. The rich man might perhaps have had some excuse if the poor and sick Lazarus had not lain before his gate; if he had been far away; if his poverty had not been an unwelcome sight before his eyes. Conversely, if the rich man had been far from the eyes of the sick poor man, the poor man would have endured a lesser temptation in his heart.

But by placing the needy and sick man before the gate of the rich man, who was overflowing with pleasures, God brought upon the rich man the accumulation of condemnation from seeing the poor man without pity; and, in turn, by placing the rich man before the poor man’s eyes, he tested the poor man daily. Poverty alone could certainly have sufficed as a punishment for him, even if he had been healthy; sickness alone would also have sufficed, even if assistance had been present. But, so that the poor man might be tested more fully, both poverty and sickness weakened him, and on top of this he saw the rich man going out supported by attending crowds, while no one visited him in his illness and need. For that no one came to visit him is demonstrated by the dogs, which freely licked his wounds.

Thus, through one circumstance, almighty God displayed two judgments when he permitted poor Lazarus to lie before the rich man’s gate: the wicked rich man increased the vengeance of his own condemnation, while the tested poor man grew toward his reward.

It happened that the beggar died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom. The rich man also died and was buried in hell. Abraham’s bosom is the rest of the blessed poor, whose is the kingdom of heaven, into which they are received after this life. The burial in hell is the depth of punishments that devours the proud and merciless after this life.

“Lifting up his eyes while he was in torments, he saw Abraham from afar and Lazarus in his bosom. And he himself cried out and said: ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame.’”

O how lofty are the judgments of God! How strictly the repayment of good and evil deeds is carried out! It was said above that in this life Lazarus sought the crumbs falling from the rich man’s table, and no one gave him any. Now, concerning the rich man’s punishment, it is said that he desires water to drip into his mouth from the tip of Lazarus’s finger. Therefore, the one who refused to give even the smallest things from his table, placed in hell, came to seek the smallest things.

But it must be noted very carefully why the rich man, placed in the fire, asks that his tongue be cooled. It is the custom of sacred expression sometimes to say one thing while implying another through the same statement. Above, the Lord had not described this proud rich man as devoting himself to talkativeness, but as feasting excessively. He did not narrate that he had sinned through talkativeness, but that he had sinned through gluttony, with arrogance and stinginess. Yet because talkativeness is usually abundant at feasts, the one who is said to have feasted badly here is said to burn more grievously in hell in his tongue.

But what follows must be weighed with very great fear:

“And Abraham said to him: ‘Son, remember that you received good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted, while you are tormented.’” Behold, when it says, “You received good things in your life,” it indicates that this rich man had possessed some good from which he received good things in this life. Again, when it says of Lazarus that he received evil things, it plainly shows that Lazarus too had some evil that needed purification. The fire of poverty purified Lazarus’s evils, while the prosperity of passing life rewarded the rich man’s goods.

“And in all these things a great chasm has been fixed between us and you, so that those who wish to cross from here to you cannot, nor can they cross from there to here.” In this matter it must be carefully asked how it is said that those who wish to cross to them cannot do so. For there is no doubt that those who are in hell wish to cross over to the lot of the blessed. But how is it said that those already received into the lot of blessedness wish to cross over to those being tormented in hell?

Just as the reprobate wish to cross over to the elect—that is, to move away from the affliction of their punishments—so the righteous wish to cross over to those who are afflicted and placed in torments: they go to them in mind through mercy and wish to free them. But those who wish to cross from the seat of the blessed to the afflicted and tormented cannot do so, because although the souls of the righteous possess mercy according to the goodness of their nature, they are now so closely joined to the justice of their Creator and bound by such uprightness that they are moved by no compassion toward the reprobate.
