After the burning rich man’s hope concerning himself has been removed, his mind turns back to the relatives he had left behind, because punishment sometimes teaches the mind of the reprobate, though uselessly, to love, so that they then love even their own spiritually, although while they were here loving sins, they did not love themselves. Hence it now follows:

“And he said: ‘I ask you, Father, to send him to my father’s house, for I have five brothers, so that he may testify to them, lest they too come to this place of torment.’”

Here it should be noted how many things are heaped upon the burning rich man for his punishment. Knowledge and memory are preserved for his punishment. He recognizes Lazarus, whom he despised, and he remembers his brothers, whom he left behind. The punishment inflicted on him on account of the poor man would not be complete if he did not recognize him in his recompense. Nor would his punishment in the fire be complete if he did not fear for his own what he himself suffers. Thus sinners are punished more severely in their torment: they see the glory of those whom they despised and are tormented also by the punishment of those whom they loved uselessly.

It should be believed that, before the retribution of the final judgment, the unjust see certain righteous people in rest, so that, seeing them in joy, they may be tormented not only by their own punishment but also by the good fortune of the righteous. The righteous, however, always behold the unjust in torments, so that their joy may increase when they see the evil from which they mercifully escaped. And they give greater thanks to their Deliverer the more they see in others what they themselves could have suffered had they been neglectful. For those who see the glory of their Creator see everything that takes place in creation.

“And Abraham said to him: ‘They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them.’” But the rich man, who had despised the words of God, thought that his followers could not hear this. Therefore he replied:

“‘No, Father Abraham; but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent.’” To him a true statement is immediately spoken:

“‘If they do not hear Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe if someone rises from the dead.’” For surely those who despise the words of the law will fulfill the commands of the Redeemer, who rose from the dead, even less. Indeed, it is evident that those who refuse to fulfill someone’s words plainly refuse to believe him.

In the midst of this it should be noted that he is told, “Remember, son.” For Abraham calls him “son” but nevertheless does not free him from torment, since the faithful forefathers of this faithless people, seeing that many have departed from their faith, do not rescue them from torments through any compassion, although they recognize them as sons according to the flesh.

The rich man, placed in torments, declares that he has five brothers, because that proud Jewish people, much of which has been condemned, recognizes that its followers whom it left on earth are devoted to the five bodily senses. He expresses the brothers whom he left behind by the number five because, placed in hell, he laments that they do not rise to spiritual understanding.

He asks that Lazarus be sent to them, and he is told that they have Moses and the prophets. But he [apparently says] that they will not believe unless someone rises from the dead. To this the answer is immediately given: “If they do not hear Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe him if someone rises from the dead.”

Certainly Truth says concerning Moses: “If you believed Moses, you would also believe me, for he wrote about me.” Thus what is said through Abraham’s reply is fulfilled: the Lord rose from the dead, but because the Jewish people refused to believe Moses, it also scorned belief in the one who rose from the dead. And because it refused to understand Moses’ words spiritually, it did not reach the one about whom Moses had spoken.

For Moses pronounced this concerning our Lord Jesus Christ to his hearers, saying: “The Lord will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall hear him.” Hence it is also written: “And whoever does not hear that prophet shall be exterminated from his people,” because he is the Ruler of heaven and earth. To him be honor and glory through ages of ages. Amen.

# ON THE FEAST OF THE HOLY NABOR AND NAZARIUS

Seek the reading and the Gospel for the feast of many saints.

Reading from the Epistle of the blessed apostle Peter.

Blessed is the Lord, the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy regenerated us into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.

[Col. 0298A] Reading from the holy Gospel according to Luke.

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Let your loins be girded,” and so forth.

# HOMILY LXXVIII. WEDNESDAY

Reading from the Epistle of the blessed apostle Paul to the Colossians.

Brothers: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth,” and so forth.

Because, once made immortal after the resurrection, we will no longer be able to sin; but mortal people, by contrast, are destined to sin. Thus, just as he posits a mortal human being composed of various sinful members, so that mortals may be able to do such things, when he said “the members that are upon the earth,” he meant the evil acts that mortals are accustomed to pursue. Therefore, having put these members to death, we first rise in faith. Just as death according to the spirit precedes resurrection according to the spirit, so death according to the flesh will precede the resurrection that is to come according to the flesh.

“Fornication, impurity, lust, evil desire, and greed, which is the service of idols.” For the blessed Apostle does not compel us by a harsh command to cut off hands, feet, or genitals; rather, he explains in due order what the body of sin is and how it is destroyed. “So that,” he says, “we may no longer serve sin,” from which he also asks to be freed with a groan, saying: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” This body of sin is therefore shown to be constructed from many members of vices, and whatever is sinned by deed, word, or thought belongs to its portion. It should be noted that he called the worship of idols “greed,” as though it were something that could tear them away from the likeness of God. For it is impossible for someone to abstain from wicked dealings when he is held by the desire to possess more; therefore he compares greed to the service of idols.

Nor, I think, should this be passed over: just as there are three kinds of fornication—one accomplished through the intercourse of the sexes, another committed without female contact, for which a son of the patriarch Judah—whose name is corrupt in the Latin here—is recorded to have been struck down by the Lord, and which is called “impurity” in the holy Scriptures—and concerning this the Apostle says, “I say to the unmarried and widows: it is good for them if they remain as I am. But if they cannot contain themselves, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn”—so there is a third kind, conceived in the soul and mind, concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”

So also there are three kinds of *philargyria*—that is, love of money: the first, which does not allow those who renounce riches to be stripped of their possessions; the second, which persuades us, with greater greed, to take back what we have dispersed or distributed to the needy; and the third, which compels us to desire and acquire things that we had not previously possessed. To show how no one can do these things without guilt, he says: “Because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the children of disobedience.” It is not only absurd for us to sin; even if we sin after rising, a necessary punishment awaits us. “In these things you too once walked, when you were living in them”—things that you formerly practiced when you measured your entire hope by the present life, expecting nothing more.

[Col. 0299A] But now you too must put away everything. It is no longer fitting for you to live according to those things, since you will especially be in immortality, whose likeness you are now thought to share. We must therefore depart from all these things and put away anger, indignation, malice, blasphemy, and shameful speech from our mouths.

It should be understood that there are three kinds of anger: one that burns inwardly; another that bursts forth into speech, action, and effect, and is called hatred—concerning these the Apostle says, “But now put away from yourselves anger and indignation”; and a third that, unlike the first, which burns and is discharged for an hour, is stored up for days and periods of time, and is called “anger of a hundred years.” All these must equally be condemned by us with horror. Therefore, if we desire to attain that highest divine reward of which it is said, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God,” this must not only be cut away from our actions, but also uprooted from the inmost depths of the soul.

Do not lie to one another. He did not say “to each other” but “to one another,” for he means that you should not speak to one another with pretense, but with a sincere mind. And because he has mentioned members, he adds the acts that follow from them.

“Stripping off the old human being with his acts.” In its entirety, he says, it is fitting for you, while laying aside the mortal human being, to lay aside also the acts that follow him.

“And put on the new, which is being renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of the one who created him.” You ought to act in accordance with this new person whom you have put on, renewed and made according to the image of the one who became the author of this recreation for us, so that you may be called Christians. Therefore it is fitting for you to remain wholly unchanging in goodness; this will benefit you in the future according to the possibility present in this life. Then, showing the goodness of this recreation, he says:

“Where there is neither Gentile nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, barbarian nor Scythian, slave nor free, but Christ is all and in all.” When, he says, we have stood in that transformation, there will no longer be a distinction between Jew and Gentile, for the distinction between circumcision and uncircumcision has been abolished because we have been made immortal. Thus neither barbarian, nor free person, nor slave will any longer be discernible, since Christ will appear in all; in his likeness we shall possess immortality, through the gift of the giver of all good things, who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXIX. ALSO ON WEDNESDAY

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Matthew.

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish but to fulfill,” and so forth.

[Col. 0300A] After he had exhorted his hearers to prepare themselves to endure everything for truth and justice, and not to conceal the good that they were going to receive, but to learn it with such goodwill that they might teach others, referring their good works not to their own praise but to the glory of God, he begins to instruct them and teach them what they should teach—as though they were asking: “Behold, we wish to endure everything for your name and not conceal your teaching. But what exactly is this which you forbid to be concealed, and for which you command that everything be endured? Are you perhaps going to say something contrary to what is written in the Law?”

“No,” he says. “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets. I have not come to abolish but to fulfill.” This statement has a twofold meaning and must be interpreted in both ways. [Col. 0300B] For one who says, “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it,” either says this by adding what it lacks, or by doing what it contains. Let us therefore first consider the meaning I mentioned first. One who adds what is lacking does not abolish what he finds; rather, by perfecting it, he confirms it. Whether, therefore, he came in human form to fulfill what had been prophesied about him, or to complete those things that earlier, because of the weakness of his hearers, had been rudimentary and imperfect—removing anger, excluding retaliation, and forbidding the possession of hidden desire in the mind—

“Amen, I say to you: until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one stroke will pass from the Law until all things come to be.” New heavens and a new earth are promised, which the Lord God will make. If new things are to be created, then consequently these present things will pass away. But what follows—“Not one iota or one stroke will pass from the Law until all these things come to be”—is shown through the form of the letter: even those things that are considered least in the Law are filled with particular mysteries, and everything is recapitulated in the Gospel. Among the letters, the iota is smaller than the others; a stroke is even some very small part of the iota itself. By these words he shows that even the smallest things in the Law are brought to fulfillment.

Appropriately he used the Greek *iota*, and not the Hebrew *yod*, because *iota* signifies ten in number and enumerates the Decalogue of the Law, whose stroke and perfection is the Gospel.

“Whoever therefore abolishes one of these least commandments and teaches people accordingly will be called least in the kingdom [Col. 0300D] of heaven.” Thus he declares that not even the least of God’s commandments may be abolished without sacrilege, and that those who abolish the least commandments will be called the least—that is, the last and almost nothing.

Nothing can be less than those things that are least. The least of all, however, is the Lord’s passion and death on the cross; if someone does not confess it, as though he were ashamed of it, he will be least. But to the one who confesses it he promises the glory of a great calling in heaven.

In another way, by this passage he censures the Pharisees, who, having disregarded God’s commandments, established their own traditions. Their teaching will not benefit the people if they destroy even a small commandment that is prescribed in the Law. The least commandments are therefore signified by one iota or one stroke, as was shown above. Whoever abolishes one and teaches accordingly—that is, according to what he abolishes, not according to what he finds and reads—will be called least in the kingdom of heaven, where no one can be anything except great.

This may also be understood morally. The one who does not fulfill God’s commandment abolishes it—not by effecting its abolition in the commandment itself, but in himself. God’s commandment is firm, and Scripture can be abolished; the Law is therefore, in a certain sense, a bond. Whoever cuts away God’s bonds abolishes the commandments in himself, not in the commandments themselves. Such a person will indeed be called least in the kingdom of heaven, because he is most despised in the assembly of the saints.

Here, too, “the kingdom of heaven” signifies the present Church, as elsewhere, where it is written: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea”; and, “The kingdom of God is within you.” But “whoever does and teaches will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.” By doing the commandments of the Law, the one who teaches earns the name of great, because not teachers or hearers, but doers of the Law, will be justified before God. Their reward will be given in the future by the giver of all good things, namely the Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXX. ON FRIDAY

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Luke.

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “It is impossible that stumbling blocks should not come; but woe to the one through whom they come,” and so forth.

The Apostle also says: “There must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may be made manifest among you.” In this world, therefore, which is full of errors and troubles, it is impossible that stumbling blocks should not very often arise. But woe to the one who, through his own fault, makes what cannot fail to come arise through himself.

Although, according to the general sense, either some false brother or Judas himself, who was preparing his heart for betrayal, may be understood here, nevertheless, in accordance with the sequence of the discourse, this passage looks back to what precedes, where the Lord spoke about giving alms and was mocked by the Pharisees. Whoever censures one who speaks rightly certainly provides a stumbling block—that is, an offense and a downfall—to weak hearers, especially if he himself appears, together with the Pharisees, to possess knowledge of the Law. The Apostle rebukes such a person, saying: “And the weak brother for whom Christ died will perish through your knowledge.”

[Col. 0301D] “It would be better for him if a millstone were placed around his neck and he were thrown into the sea than that he should cause one of these little ones to stumble.” He speaks according to the custom of the province, since among the ancient Jews this was the punishment for greater crimes: those bound with a stone were cast into the depths. In truth, it is better for an innocent person to end bodily life through punishment, however atrocious but nevertheless temporary, than for one who harms his brother to deserve the everlasting death of the soul.

“Pay attention to yourselves. If your brother sins against you, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him.” We read something similar in Deuteronomy: “You shall not hate your brother in your heart, but publicly rebuke him, lest you bear sin because of him.” He therefore indicates the order by which we can avoid stumbling blocks and escape everlasting woe: if we pay attention to ourselves so that we do not harm anyone; if we rebuke the sinner with the justice of heaven; and if, when he repents from the heart, we open to him the inward compassion of mercy and kindness.

“And if he sins against you seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turns back to you, saying, ‘I repent,’ forgive him.” The number seven does not establish a limit for granting forgiveness; rather, it commands either that all sins be forgiven or that forgiveness be granted to one who is always repentant. For universality of any thing or period of time is often indicated by seven; hence it is also sung in the Psalm: “Seven times a day I have given you praise.”

And the apostles said to the Lord: “Increase our faith.” The Lord had said above: “The one who is faithful in the least is faithful also in much; and if you have not been faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours?” Therefore the apostles, who had already been faithful in what belonged to another and in what was least—that is, in contempt for earthly things—ask that faith in what is their own and in what is greater be increased for them.

But the Lord said: “If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you would say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea,’ and it would obey you.” He compares perfect faith to a grain of mustard, which is humble in appearance yet ardent within: insignificant to those who look at it casually and seemingly without strength, but showing, when crushed by pressures, what it contains inside.

It should also be noted that mustard seed is very beneficial for cleansing the head. If it is thoroughly ground and sifted, mixed with warm, rich honey-wine, and gargled while fasting in the heat of the sun or in a bath, it cleanses every harmful humor from the head, even if it is thicker, and also prevents the dangers of impending weaknesses. Thus faith, tested by the pestle of temptations, chastened by the sieve of discernment from every superficial, fleeting thought, and sweetened with the honey of perfect love, drains from the heart—the head of our inward person—all the sewers of vices, not only for the present, but also guarding against their gathering again in the future.

The mulberry tree that is to be uprooted and planted in the sea may be understood simply as indicating that the sign of consummate faith is to command the elements by word, so that what was said specifically of one thing may be believed to be understood generally of all.

[Col. 0302D] “Which of you, having a servant plowing or tending sheep?” This parable teaches that the more faith excels outwardly in virtues, the more inwardly it should become humble in the conscience. The servant who plows or tends sheep signifies any teacher of the Church, of whom the Lord says: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.” To another who testified his love, he replied the third time: “Feed my sheep.”

“Will say to him when he returns from the field, ‘Come at once and recline,’ and will not say to him, ‘Prepare what I may eat.’” The servant returns from the field later, when, having interrupted his preaching for a time, he returns to his conscience; coming back from public speech to the court of the heart, he privately reviews with himself his deeds and words. The Lord does not immediately say to him, “Come, recline”—that is, “Pass from this mortal life and rest in the blessed seat of eternal life.” For, before saying this, he commands him in the meantime, after the work of tending and cultivating, to prepare at home what he may eat: that is, after the labor of open speech, to display also the humility of self-examination.

“And gird yourself and serve me until I eat and drink.” To gird oneself is to restrain a humbled mind from all the channels of wavering thoughts, by which the progress of one’s works is usually hindered. For one who girds his garments does so so that, as he walks, he may not become entangled and fall. To serve God is to profess oneself least in all things and to have no strength without his grace. The word “servant” derives its name from a lower state, that is, subjection, just as “master” derives its name from a higher one. Therefore the one who considers the Creator’s nature and fears his judgments serves him, humbling himself concerning his own virtues.

“And afterward you will eat and drink.” After I, he says, have delighted in the work of your preaching and been refreshed by the feasts of your contrition, then at last you will pass over and recline, and you will be eternally refreshed by the everlasting banquets of my wisdom.

“Does he thank that servant because he did what was commanded him? I do not think so. So you also, when you have done everything that was commanded you, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants.’” If, he says, one human being demands from a human servant not a uniform but a varied service, and nevertheless does not thank him, how much more must you, who can do nothing without me, not weigh the length of time or the merits of your labors, but continually increase your former efforts through love and willing service. Therefore say: “We are unprofitable servants.” Servants, indeed, because you were bought at a price; unprofitable, because the Lord has no need of your goods.

“We have done what we were obliged to do.” Indeed, we were obliged, because he who came not to be served but to serve made us his debtors, so that we should not trust in our own works but always fear his judgment. With the prophet we should say: “What shall we render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to us?” For in the future judgment he will give each person a fitting reward: eternal life to the good, and everlasting punishment to the wicked. To him be praise, honor, and power throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXXI. THIRD SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

Reading from the Epistle of the blessed Apostle John.

Beloved: “Do not be surprised if the world hates you. We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love the brethren,” and so forth.

We are admonished by the present reading, as you have heard, beloved, concerning kindness toward our neighbors and avoidance of hatred: “Do not be surprised,” he says, “if the world hates you.” In the Scriptures, lovers of the world are very often called “the world.” “We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love the brethren.”

[Col. 0304A] Through the great mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ we have been transferred, through his passion, death, and resurrection, from death and the power of the devil to the free service of the Lord our God; from the darkness of eternal punishment we have been led to the joys of eternal blessedness. And this lies within our power: whether we choose death or life. We choose death if we persist in hatred of our neighbor and love of the world. We choose life if we love God with our whole heart, whole mind, and whole strength, and our neighbors as ourselves.

“Whoever does not love remains in death.” Let each person return to his own heart. If he finds there charity—that is, pure love of God and neighbor—he may be secure, because he has passed from death to life. Therefore, brothers, do not think it a light matter to hate or not to love a brother. Hear what follows:

“Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer.” If someone harbors brotherly hatred, does he not despise murder in his heart? Although he does not move his hand to kill a person, through hatred of his neighbor he is already guilty before God as a murderer. One is alive, and the other is already judged a killer, because even if he has not killed his neighbor, he has killed himself and his own soul through hatred or envy of his neighbor.

“And you know that no murderer has eternal life remaining in himself.” For “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit,” and where hatred or envy remains, charity—which is God—has no place, unless it is corrected through long-standing kindness, humane treatment of one’s neighbor, confession, and repentance. For where charity is absent—that is, where the Holy Spirit has no place in a person’s heart—the devil has a dwelling place. Therefore, beloved, cast hatred and envy from your hearts, for they prepare a dwelling for the devil within you. Be kind toward your neighbors and love them; through confession, sincere repentance, and works of mercy, prepare in your hearts a worthy dwelling place for the Holy Spirit.

“In this we have known the charity of God: that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren.” We must imitate the example of Christ and the apostles, so that our teaching and preaching may be confirmed by our works. Nothing is more shameful than for someone to neglect fulfilling by his deeds the good that he preaches; preaching is useful only when it is effectively carried out.

Therefore priests must fear the enmity of no one. They must openly rebuke oppressors of the poor and those who act unjustly in power, and earnestly urge them toward mercy for the needy and correction of themselves. If they rebuke such people in the charity of God and neighbor, they are proved faithful. But if priests do not rise to correct the rich who act unjustly, they show themselves to be hirelings rather than shepherds, and strangers to the charity of God, because they see the wolf coming and flee while they fear to rebuke the wicked. They are condemned for the iniquity of others if they either do not instruct the ignorant or do not rebuke sinners.

[Col. 0305A] “Whoever has the world’s possessions, and sees his brother in need, and closes his compassion against him—how does the charity of God remain in him?” If you are not yet capable of dying for your brother, become capable now of giving your possessions to your brother; let charity already strike your inward parts. Do not do this from boastfulness, but from the innermost richness of mercy, so that you may consider him lying in poverty.

If you do not care to give your surplus to your brother, how will you be able to lay down your life for your brother? Money lies in your bosom, and thieves can take it from you; and even if thieves do not take it, you will abandon it when you die, even if it does not abandon you while you live. What will you do with it then? Your brother is hungry; he is in need; he has nothing, while you have something. Consider that you were both bought together: the price paid for both of you is one. You were redeemed by the blood of Christ. How can you boast that you are a Christian if you do not perform the works of Christ? The name “Christian” benefits you nothing if you do not prove by your works that you are a Christian.

“My little children, let us not love in word or with the tongue, but in deed and in truth,” through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXXII. ON THE SAME FEAST

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Luke.

At that time Jesus spoke this parable: “A certain man made a great supper and invited many. And he sent his servant at supper time to say to those who had been invited that they should come, because everything was now ready,” and so forth.

Who is this man except the one of whom it is said through the prophet, “He is both a man and who can know him?” He made a great supper because he prepared for us the fullness of inward sweetness. He calls many, but few come, because sometimes even those who are subject to him through faith oppose his eternal banquet by living badly.

“And he sent his servant at supper time to say to those who had been invited that they should come, because everything was now ready.” What is the supper hour except the end of the world? We are surely in it, as Paul testified long ago, saying: “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come.” If, then, it is already supper time when we are called, we should excuse ourselves from God’s banquet all the less, since we see that the end of the age has already drawn near.

This banquet of God is called not lunch but supper because after lunch supper remains, whereas after supper no banquet remains; and because God’s eternal banquet will be prepared for you at the end, it was right that it should be called not lunch but supper.

But whom does this servant, sent by the head of the household to invite people, signify except the order of preachers? To repel our pride, everything is already prepared, because, to wipe away the torpor of our minds at God’s supper, that unique Lamb has been slain for us who took away the sins of the world.

[Col. 0306A] “And they all began together to make excuses.” God offers what should have been requested. Unasked, he wishes to give what could scarcely have been hoped for, so that he might graciously bestow it when asked—and yet he is despised. He announces that the delights of eternal refreshment are ready, and yet all together make excuses.

But some say: “Let us not wish to make excuses; for we rejoice that we are both called to and will reach that banquet of heavenly refreshment.” They speak truly if they do not love earthly things more than heavenly things, and if they are not more occupied with bodily matters than with spiritual ones. Hence the cause of those making excuses is added immediately, when it follows:

“The first said to him: ‘I have bought a farm, and I must go out and see it; I ask you to excuse me.’” What is signified by the farm except earthly substance? He goes out to see it who thinks only of external things because of his possessions.

“And another said: ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I am going to test them; I ask you to excuse me.’” What do we understand by the five yoke of oxen except the five bodily senses? They are rightly called yokes because they are doubled in each sex. Since these bodily senses cannot grasp inward things but know only external things, and, abandoning what is within, touch what is outside, curiosity is rightly signified through them.

Curiosity is a grave vice. While it drives a person to investigate the outward life of his neighbor, it always conceals his own inward life. It follows: “I ask you to excuse me.” For while he says “I ask,” yet refuses to come, humility sounds in his voice but pride in his action. And behold, every wicked person judges this when he hears it, yet does not cease doing what he judges.

[Col. 0306C] “And another said: ‘I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.’” What is signified by the wife except the pleasure of the flesh? Although marriage is good and was established by divine providence for the propagation of offspring, some people seek in it not the fruitfulness of children but the desires of pleasure. Therefore, through a just matter, an unjust matter may not inappropriately be signified.

The supreme head of the household therefore invites us to the supper of the eternal banquet. But while one person is occupied with earthly care, another is consumed by keen attention to the actions of others, and the mind of yet another is defiled by pleasure of the flesh. Each fastidious person fails to hasten to the feasts of eternal life.

“And the servant returned and reported these things to his master. Then the head of the household, being angry, said to his servant: ‘Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in here the poor, the weak, the blind, and the lame.’” Behold, the one who clings to earthly possessions more than is right refuses to come to the Lord’s supper. The one who labors at the vice of curiosity rejects the nourishment prepared for life. The one who clings to carnal desires spurns the food of the spiritual banquet.

Because the proud refuse to come, the poor are chosen. Why? Because, in Paul’s words, “God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong.” The poor and weak are those who are weak in their own judgment of themselves. For there are poor people who are, as it were, strong, because they are proud even when placed in poverty. The blind are those who possess no light of understanding; the lame are those who do not have upright steps in their actions.

But when vices of character are signified by weakness of the limbs, it is clearly evident that, just as those who were called but refused to come were sinners, so these poor people who are invited and come are also sinners. Yet proud sinners are rejected, while humble sinners are chosen. But after the poor have been led to the supper, let us hear what the servant says next:

[Col. 0307A] “Lord, it has been done as you commanded, and there is still room.” Many such people have been gathered from Judea to the Lord’s supper. But the multitude from the Israelite people who believed did not fill the place at the heavenly banquet. A considerable number of Jews has already entered, but room still remains vacant in the kingdom where the multitude of the Gentiles is to be received. Hence the same servant is told:

“Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel them to enter, so that my house may be filled.” When the Lord invites people to the supper from the lanes and streets, he signifies that people who knew how to keep the Law within an urban way of life. But when he commands that his guests be gathered from roads and hedges, he clearly seeks to gather a rustic people—that is, the Gentiles.

It should be noted that in this third invitation he does not say “invite,” but “compel to enter.” For there are some who understand that good things ought to be done but desist from doing them. As we said above, it often happens to such people that the adversity of this world strikes them in their carnal desires. Frequently they waste away through prolonged illness, collapse under injuries, or are afflicted by heavier losses; then, reproving themselves for their desires, they turn their hearts to the Lord.

Those who, broken by the adversities of this world, return to the love of God and are corrected concerning the desires of the present life—what are such people except those who are compelled to enter? But the sentence that follows immediately is exceedingly fearful. For he says:

“I tell you that none of those men who were invited will taste my supper.” Behold, he calls through himself; he calls through angels; he calls through the patriarchs; he calls through the prophets; he calls through the apostles; he calls through shepherds; often he calls through miracles; often he calls through scourges; sometimes he calls through the prosperity of this world, sometimes through adversity. Let no one despise him, lest, while making excuses when called, he be unable to enter when he wishes.

## HOMILY LXXXIII. ON WEDNESDAY

Reading from the Book of Wisdom.

In those days Solomon said to the children of Israel: “Love justice, you who judge the earth.”

Divine Wisdom admonishes the leaders of God’s people, to whom the power of judging has been given, to love justice and preserve equity in judgment. Alternatively, this statement may apply generally to all who possess reason and an understanding mind: while judging the earth—that is, their own flesh—they should love justice, so that they do not make provision for the flesh in its desires, [Col. 0308A] but subjecting it to the command of the spirit, devote themselves especially to the virtues by which the soul is nourished. Then they should care for their body according to necessity, not according to pleasure, always recalling that statement of the Law: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.”

“Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart.” One thinks rightly of the Lord in goodness who reads and understands Holy Scripture according to piety. One seeks him in simplicity of heart who humbly submits himself to his will, namely, in order to keep his commandments. For the one who seeks God devoutly honors Holy Scripture and does not criticize what he does not yet understand, and therefore does not resist it. This is what it means to be meek, concerning which he says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.”

“For he is found by those who do not test him, and he appears to those who have faith in him.” It is dangerous to test God through human presumption, since it is written: “You shall not test the Lord your God.” But it is salutary to honor him with upright faith, because “the righteous person lives by faith.”

“For perverse thoughts separate from God, and tested virtue rebukes the foolish.” It is clear that every impious thought and wicked will cannot in any way be joined to God; it does not agree with the highest good, because “there is no fellowship between light and darkness,” nor “agreement between Christ and Belial.” But wherever a good intention and devotion to sacred virtues are present in the heart, they always condemn and rebuke the vices and errors of the foolish. Therefore lovers of true wisdom must cleanse their hearts and turn the whole intention of their mind toward love of their Creator.

“For wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul, nor dwell in a body enslaved to sins.” The Apostle James, sharing the same understanding, wrote similarly in his Epistle, saying: “Can a fig tree, my brothers, produce olives, or a vine figs? So neither can salt water produce sweet water. Who is wise and disciplined among you? Let him show his good conduct in the gentleness of wisdom. But if you have bitter zeal and contentions in your hearts, do not boast and become liars against the truth. This is not the wisdom that descends from above, from the Father of lights, but is earthly, animal, demonic. For where there is zeal and contention, there are instability and every evil work.” True wisdom by no means enters a malevolent mind, nor can it dwell in a criminal person.

“For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit and withdraw from thoughts that lack understanding.” Hence it is completely certain that Mani, Arius, Eunomius, and the other heretics established their doctrines, full of errors, without the grace of the Holy Spirit. For the good Spirit of the Lord always leads people along the right path, whereas the evil spirit misleads and drags its followers with itself into the snare of eternal destruction. Concerning this it is also added:

“He will be rebuked when iniquity arrives.” For when the time of recompense comes, all the impious and sinners will receive everlasting punishment for their iniquities.

For the spirit of wisdom is benevolent and will not acquit the evil speaker on account of his lips, because God is the witness of his reins, the true scrutinizer of his heart, and the hearer of his tongue. This statement destroys the error of those who, just as they acknowledge that good thoughts are inspired in us by God, likewise suppose that bad thoughts are generated in our minds at his instigation. Yet God, who is supremely good and desires all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, in no way imposes upon anyone the necessity of an evil word or wicked deed by which that person might perish. As the Apostle James shows when he says: “Let no one, then, when he is being tempted, say that he is tempted by God; for God is not a tempter of evils, and he himself tempts no one.”

For the spirit of the Lord has filled the world. Therefore the Holy Spirit, who at the beginning of creation was borne by invisible power over the waters, by his majesty both fills and contains every creature; without the gift of his power, he fills the entire world of the Church, in which every day he displays his generosity to all. Hence what follows:

And he who contains all things has knowledge of the voice. For, as Paul says, “To one through the Spirit is given a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit. To one is given the grace of healings in one Spirit, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the discernment of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of utterances.” For one and the same Spirit brings about all these things, distributing them to each one as he wills. He lives and reigns with the Father and the Son, one God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXXIV. ALSO ON WEDNESDAY. Reading from the Prophet Isaiah.

Thus says the Lord God: “Listen, Jacob, my servant, and Israel, whom I have chosen, the one forming and fashioning you, your helper from the womb,” etc.

Now, when the prophetic reading was being read, you heard, dearest brothers, the prophet urging the Israelite people to faith and promising them spiritual blessings, saying: “Listen, Jacob, my servant, and Israel, whom I have chosen.” He rightly first called him a servant and afterward the chosen one, because through service to the holy name of God each person will merit election before God, so as to be made righteous. Then, when someone tramples down vices and sins and follows the will of his Lord, he may rightly be called Jacob—“supplanter,” as the name is interpreted—and finally Israel, which means “a man seeing God”: namely, one who now hastens by good works toward the eternal vision of God.

“Forming and fashioning you from the womb, your helper.” For at the beginning of the Church’s birth I preserved all believers who obeyed my commandments from the hands of persecutors and from the cruelty of their savagery. [Col. 0310A] For I am the one who blots out your iniquities for my own sake, and I will remember your sins no more. For I am merciful and rich in compassion; I will blot out all your iniquities in the sprinkling of my blood, which I shall pour out for the redemption of the whole world, erasing the bond of the curse that Adam earned in paradise by transgressing the commandment, which had been written against the human race. I will remember your sins no longer.

O faithful people, if you believe rightly and sincerely in me, I shall forgive these things to you in baptism. “Bring me to remembrance, and let us judge together; tell me if you have anything by which you may be justified.” Consider and reflect together upon the things that you deservedly endured, because the many sins that you committed merited this for you: that for so long you should lie under the power of the devil, whom for so long you served, abandoning me and despising my commandments as though they were nothing. But now also know that I have mercy on you not because of your merit, but solely because of my clemency.

“Do not fear, my servant Jacob, and most rightly so, whom I have chosen.” Now that you have turned away from your wickedness, abandoned the vain and mute idols that did you no good, and turned back to me through repentance for your crimes, by pleading for mercy and abandoning vices and sins, you will be called my chosen one, because you have now followed my commandments.

“For I shall pour out waters upon the thirsty.” Upon the one who thirsts for the fountain of saving doctrine, I shall pour it through the mouths of the holy teachers in the Church. Or I shall pour out upon the faithful the fountain of baptism, so that they may be cleansed [Col. 0310C] from all their crimes and receive forgiveness of all their sins. I shall pour out the streams of evangelical doctrine upon arid hearts, which until now, before baptism, have produced no fruit of good works.

“And I shall pour out my spirit upon your offspring, and my blessing upon your descendants,” says the Lord Almighty. It is as though he were saying: “Through the laying on of the hands of my holy priests, after the sacrament of baptism, I shall pour out upon my children, whom the bride Church has borne for me, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety. I shall fill them with the spirit of my fear and love, and I shall give them an everlasting inheritance in blessing, if they faithfully take care to obey my commandments.”

Let the Catholic Christian therefore recognize the fruit of his work, because the good things he has done are nothing unless they have proceeded from the watering of the Holy Spirit. Hence the Apostle says that no virtues profit a person without love. He likewise says that “the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.” We must therefore beware lest we lose the good things we do through arrogance. For anyone who glories more in himself than in the Lord over the zeal and diligence of his own efforts strips himself of all merit.

For vain and harmful are the things in which the world, destined to perish with its lovers, wants us to glory. We must reject them altogether, so that with a good conscience we may glory unspeakably in holiness of conduct, in the acquisition of virtues, in the gift of God, and in the promise of the future kingdom, through Jesus Christ [Col. 0311A] our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXXV. ALSO ON WEDNESDAY. Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Luke.

At that time the disciples approached Jesus and said to him: “Dismiss the crowds, so that they may go away to the surrounding villages and farms and find food,” etc.

As the day was declining, the Savior refreshes the crowds, because either when the end of the ages was approaching, or when the Sun of righteousness set for us, we were saved from the corruption of spiritual hunger.

But he said to them: “You give them something to eat.” He urges the apostles to break the bread, so that when they testify that they do not have enough, the greatness of the sign may become more evident; at the same time he intimates that through them our hearts, daily afflicted by fasting, must be nourished. For what does Peter do when he speaks through his letters except satisfy our wretchedly fasting hearts with the nourishment of the word? What does Paul do? What does John do when they speak through their letters, except ensure that our minds receive heavenly nourishment and overcome the disgust of their hunger by which they were dying?

But they said: “We have no more than five loaves and two fish.” The apostles did not yet have more than the five loaves of the Mosaic Law and the two fish of the two Testaments, which for a long time lay hidden beneath the mysteries of concealed things and were nourished, as it were, in the naked depths of the abyss.

Now there were about five thousand men. Because there are five external senses of the human being, the five thousand men who followed the Lord signify those who, still placed in a secular way of life, knew how to use well the external things they possessed. Such people are rightly nourished by five loaves, because they still need to be instructed by the commandments of the Law.

For those who renounce the world completely number four thousand and are refreshed by seven loaves: that is, they are raised up by evangelical perfection and instructed by spiritual grace. To signify this distinction, I think it was mystically ordered that five gilded columns be placed at the entrance of the tabernacle, but four before the oracle, that is, the Holy of Holies: beginners are chastened through the Law lest they sin, whereas the perfect are admonished through grace to live more devotedly for God.

But he said to his disciples: “Have them sit down in groups of fifty for a meal.” And they did so. The various arrangements of those reclining at the meal signify the various gatherings throughout the world of the Churches that make up the one Catholic Church. They reclined not only in groups of fifty, as Mark attests, but also in groups of one hundred. For since the fiftieth Psalm is the Psalm of repentance, while the number one hundred passes from the left to the right, groups of fifty recline at the Lord’s banquet because, still occupied with repentance for their sins, they receive the hearing of the word; groups of one hundred do so because, already confident in the hope of forgiveness, they sigh only from desire for eternal life.

When he had taken the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and blessed them; then he broke them and distributed them to his disciples to set before the crowds. And [Col. 0312A] they all ate and were satisfied. When the crowds were hungry, the Savior did not create new food, but, taking what the disciples had, he blessed it, because when he came in the flesh he preached nothing other than what had been foretold; rather, he showed that the sayings of the prophets were pregnant with the mysteries of grace.

He looks toward heaven, teaching that the eye of the mind must be directed there and that the light of knowledge must be sought there. He breaks the loaves and distributes them through the disciples to be set before the crowds, because our Lord Jesus Christ, the giver of all good things, discloses to them the closed mysteries of the Law and the prophecy, so that they may preach them throughout the world. He lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXXVI. ON FRIDAY. Reading from the Prophet Joel.

Thus says the Lord God: “Rejoice, daughters of Zion, and be glad in the Lord your God, because he has given you a teacher of righteousness, and he will cause the early rain and the late rain to descend upon you, as at the beginning. The threshing floors will be filled with grain, and the winepresses will overflow with wine and oil. I shall restore to you the years that the locust, the young locust, the mildew, and the caterpillar consumed: my great army, which I sent against you. You shall eat, eating, and be satisfied, and you shall praise the name of the Lord your God, who has done wonders with you; and my people shall not be put to shame forever. And they shall know that I am in the midst of Israel, and that I am the Lord your God, and there is no other; and my people shall not be put to shame forever.”

“God the Father,” he says, “has given you a teacher of righteousness,” or “has bestowed upon you the nourishment of righteousness,” and has caused the seasonal and late rains to descend upon you. The seasonal rain is when we first receive instruction; the late rain is when we receive the fruit of our labor and arrive at perfect knowledge of the Holy Scriptures. The seasonal and late rains may also be understood as the Old and New Testaments.

“And not only this,” he says, “has he given, but he has caused you to abound in new fruits of virtues, to be satisfied, and to be made drunk with grain, wine, and oil,” concerning which we have often spoken. And he has restored the years that you lost while disturbances reigned among you, when the locust, the young locust, the mildew, and the caterpillar had consumed your works. God did not permit you to perish. Then you shall eat the fruits of righteousness [Col. 0312D] and be satisfied, and you shall praise the name of the Lord your God, who has done wonders with you.

But if after repentance God promises such great abundance of all things, what will the Novatian answer, denying repentance and claiming that sinners cannot be restored to their former state if they perform worthy works of repentance? God receives penitents to such an extent that he calls them his people, by no means declares that they will be put to shame, promises that he will dwell in their midst, and assures them that they will have no other god, but will trust with their whole heart in him who dwells among them and reigns eternally in heaven and on earth.

Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages, will not abandon all who hope in him, but will grant them life in the heavenly kingdom and everlasting rest. [Col. 0313A] Amen.

## HOMILY LXXXVII. ALSO ON FRIDAY. Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Luke.

At that time a man named Jairus came to Jesus; he was the ruler of the synagogue, etc.

Following the previous reading, which we interpreted as concerning the rejection of the Synagogue, the faith of the Church, and then again the restoration of the Synagogue, the dying daughter of the ruler of the synagogue is introduced. While the Lord hastens to raise her, a woman with a hemorrhage intervenes first and snatches the healing, so that she who came afterward receives salvation first. For “Ethiopia will stretch out her hands to God,” and “when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved.”

And he fell at the feet of Jesus, asking him to enter his house. If God is the head of Christ, then his feet are to be understood accordingly as his incarnation, by which he touched the earth of our mortality. The ruler of the synagogue therefore fell at the feet of Jesus: he, the lawgiver, recognized, together with the entire line of the fathers, that Christ appearing in the flesh was far superior to him in the glory of dignity.

For he had an only daughter, about twelve years old, and she was dying. The Synagogue itself, formed solely by legal instruction and born, as it were, as Moses’ only daughter, was dying when it was almost twelve years old—that is, as it approached the time of puberty. Nobly raised by the prophets, after it had reached the age of understanding, after it ought to have produced spiritual fruits for God, it was suddenly overwhelmed by the sickness of error and hopelessly abandoned the paths of spiritual life. Unless Christ came to its aid, it would have fallen utterly into a dreadful death.

And it happened that, as he went, he was pressed by the crowd. As the Lord went to heal the girl, he was pressed by the crowd, because while offering the Jewish people saving admonitions by which he might raise up its sick inner conscience, he was burdened by the harmful custom of carnal peoples.

And there was a woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years. The woman suffering from the flow of blood is the Church gathered from the Gentiles. Polluted by the congenital flow of carnal pleasures and already separated from the assembly of the faithful, while the word of God determined to save Judea, she seized, with firm hope, the salvation already prepared and promised for others.

It should be noted that the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter was twelve years old, while this woman had suffered from the flow of blood for twelve years. That is, at the very time when the one was born, the other began to grow ill. For at nearly the same age of this world, the Synagogue began to be born in the patriarchs, and the nation of the Gentiles began throughout the world to be defiled by the corruption of idolatry. The twofold flow of blood may also be understood as referring both to the superstition of idolatry and to the things performed through the delight of flesh and blood.

She had spent all her substance on physicians, and could not be healed by anyone. The physicians may mean either false theologians or philosophers and teachers of secular laws, [Col. 0314A] who, discoursing most subtly about virtues and vices, promised that they were giving mortals useful rules for living and believing.

She came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately the flow of her blood stopped. The Church also approaches and touches the Lord, because she draws near to him through the truth of faith. She comes up behind him, or alongside him, in accordance with what he himself says: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me.”

And Jesus said: “Who touched me?” He did not ask because he himself was unaware, but so that the power of faith, which he knew—or rather, which he himself had given—might be declared in the woman.

When all denied it, Peter and those who were with him said: “Master, the crowds press upon you and afflict you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” While the crowds accompanying him press upon him indiscriminately, one believing woman touches the Lord, because although he is afflicted by the various heresies of those who gather disorderly together, he is sought faithfully in heart by the Catholic Church alone.

And Jesus said: “Someone touched me, for I know that power has gone out from me,” etc. Therefore the one who touched the fringe is not hidden: that is, the one who has believed with perfect love in the mysteries of the incarnation until reaching the capacity to grasp greater things.

But he said to her: “Daughter, your faith has saved you; go in peace.” He calls her daughter because her faith has saved her. He did not say, “Your faith will save you,” but “has saved you.” Because you believed, you have already been saved.

While he was still speaking, someone came from the ruler of the synagogue, saying to him: “Your daughter has died; do not trouble him.” After the woman was saved from the flow of blood, the ruler’s daughter is immediately reported dead, because when the Church had been cleansed from the stain of vices and, on account of the merit of faith, had been called daughter, the Synagogue was immediately overcome by the death of unbelief and envy: unbelief, because it refused to believe in Christ; envy, because it was grieved that the Church had believed.

But when Jesus heard this, he answered the girl’s father: “Do not fear; only believe, and she will be saved.” The girl’s father is understood as the assembly of teachers of the Law, concerning whom the Lord says: “The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat.” If they themselves should wish to believe, the Synagogue subject to them will also be saved.

When he had entered the house, he allowed no one to enter with him except Peter, James, and John, and the girl’s father and mother. Above, the son of the widow is raised publicly; here, many witnesses are removed. I think, therefore, that the Lord’s compassion is also shown in this: the widowed mother could not bear delay regarding her only son, and therefore greater speed is added, lest she be afflicted any longer.

There is already a form of wisdom here: in the case of the widow’s son, the Church will quickly believe; in the case of the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter, the Jews will indeed believe, but only a smaller number from among them.

All were weeping and mourning for her. “Can the children of the bridegroom,” he says, “mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast.” Therefore the Synagogue, because it has lost the joy of the bridegroom by which it could live, lies as though dead among those who mourn, without even understanding why it is being mourned.

But he said: “Do not weep; she is not dead, but sleeping.” To human beings, who could not raise her, she was dead; to God she was sleeping. Under his authority her soul lived after being received, and her flesh rested, awaiting resurrection.

And they laughed at him, knowing that she was dead. Since they preferred to ridicule the word of the one raising her rather than believe it, they were rightly excluded outside, unworthy to see the miracle of the one rising.

But he took her hand and cried out, saying: “Girl, arise.” Jesus therefore took the girl’s hand and healed her, because unless the hands of the Jews, which are full of blood, are first cleansed, their dead Synagogue does not rise.

[Col. 0315B] And her spirit returned, and she immediately arose. Mark says: “The girl immediately arose and walked,” indicating spiritually that whoever recovers from the death of the soul, strengthened by Christ extending his hand to him, must not only rise from the filth of vices but also immediately advance in good works.

And he ordered that food be given to her. As a testimony to life, he commands that the one who has been raised eat, so that she might be believed to be not a phantom but a reality. Likewise, if anyone rises from spiritual death, he must immediately be satisfied with heavenly bread, becoming a participant in the divine word and in the most holy altar.

And her parents, he says, were astonished, and he commanded them to tell no one what had happened. A young man is raised outside the gate, with a large crowd accompanying and looking on. Lazarus, called from the tomb, became so widely known among the people that, on account of the testimony of those who had seen it, very large crowds went out to meet the Lord with palms, and many Jews departed because of him and believed in Jesus.

But the Lord recognizes a fourth dead man when a disciple reports him. Since there were no living people who would ask the Lord for his rescue, he says: “Let the dead bury their dead”—that is, let the wicked burden the wicked with harmful praises. Because there is no righteous person present to rebuke him, “the oil of the sinner will fatten his head.”

It is just and entirely fitting that we should offer due praises and thanks in all things to our Creator and Savior, Jesus Christ, and, rejoicing over his benefits and gifts, persevere devotedly in his service to the end. For if this is done, we shall forever share in heavenly joy with his holy angels, through the favor of him who lives and reigns throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXXVIII. ON SATURDAY, WITH TWELVE READINGS. Reading from the Prophet Joel.

Thus says the Lord God: “I shall pour out my spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy; your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions. Moreover, upon my servants and my handmaids I shall pour out my spirit. And I shall give signs in heaven and on earth, blood and fire and a vapor of smoke. The sun shall be turned into darkness and the moon into blood, before the great and dreadful day of the Lord comes. And it shall be that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved,” etc.

The blessed Apostle Peter explained this passage as fulfilled at the time of the Lord’s Passion, when, descending on the day of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit was given to the apostles, so that those who were present marveled and said: “Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? And how is it that we each hear our own language in which we were born: Parthians, Medes, and Elamites?” etc.

Yet not everyone who receives the Holy Spirit immediately possesses spiritual grace as well. Rather, through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit they will receive various graces: some prophecy, like the sons and daughters who possess greater merit; some dreams, like the old men who are already advanced in age; others visions, like the young men who have conquered the evil one.

But the servants and handmaids, who still possess the spirit of fear and not of love—for “perfect love casts out fear”—will have neither prophecy, dreams, nor visions. Content with the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, they will possess only the grace of faith and salvation.

Then the Lord will give signs in heaven and on earth: in heaven, because the sun was turned into darkness and the moon into blood; on earth, because the earth trembled with such a violent and unusual movement that tombs were opened and rocks split apart.

As for what he says, “blood and fire and a vapor—or terror—of smoke,” that blood is the one concerning which we also read in the Psalmist: “That your foot may be dipped in blood,” and in Isaiah: “How red are your garments!” It is also the blood that the Roman soldier poured out, mixed with water, when he pierced the Savior’s side. The fire is the fire of the Holy Spirit that descended from heaven, concerning which we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “There appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, and it rested upon each one of them; and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance.”

This is the fire that the Lord came to cast upon the earth, and which, before he suffered, he desired to burn in his disciples. The sun also was turned into darkness when it did not dare to look upon its Lord hanging on the cross. And the moon was turned into blood—a thing that we may believe happened according to the historical account but was passed over in silence by the evangelists. For not everything that Jesus did is recorded in writing: “If they were written down one by one, I do not think that the world itself could contain the books that would have to be written.”

He describes all these things as occurring before the great and dreadful day of the Lord comes. The great and dreadful day of the Lord must either be understood as the day of the resurrection or, certainly, as the day of judgment after a long period of time, which is truly great and dreadful.

But what follows—“and it shall be that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved”—the Apostle Paul also refers to the time of the Lord’s Passion; it is more properly to be understood of the day of the resurrection.

## HOMILY LXXXIX. ON THE SAME FEAST. Reading from the Book of Leviticus.

In those days the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: When you have entered the land that I shall give you, and have reaped its grain, you shall bring sheaves of ears of grain, the firstfruits of your harvest, to the priest. He shall lift up the bundle before the Lord, so that it may be acceptable for you,” etc.

We have often taught that the land given by the Lord means evangelical doctrine and conduct. It is called land because of the fruits of virtues that arise from it; it was given by him, and he did not use a mediator for it, but announced it with his own mouth.

When, therefore, those who received the saving word entered and reaped its grain, they were the reapers of the intelligible harvest, to whom the Lord said: “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the workers are few. Therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to [Col. 0317B] send workers into his harvest.”

The intelligible Priest, Christ, offered his own body as the sheaf of firstfruits. For since the head, or sum, of the harvest—that is, the resurrection of the dead—was the word of the Savior and divine preaching, the true sheaf and true firstfruits of our intelligible harvest, Christ the Priest, then raised his own body from the dead. Concerning him Paul said: “But now Christ has risen from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep.”

But when did this happen? On the second day of the Sabbath. “And the priest shall sanctify it.” The things we have said earlier showed that the first day was the day of the Lord’s Passion, on which the Lord distributed his offering for a reason. He commanded fifty days to be counted from the second day of the Sabbath, wishing the Lord’s Day to be understood without doubt. For this is the second day of the Sabbath. On this day the resurrection took place; from it seven weeks are counted until the second day completing the seventh week, and on the Lord’s Day once again we celebrate the festival of Pentecost, on which we merited the coming of the Holy Spirit.

“And thus you shall offer a new sacrifice to the Lord from all your dwelling places: two loaves of firstfruits, from two tenths of fermented fine flour, which you shall bake as firstfruits for the Lord.”

By saying “a new sacrifice,” he excluded the old sacrifices of the Law and introduced the evangelical sacrifice in their place. Then, by adding “from your dwelling places,” he signified the Church. The two loaves of firstfruits mean the Law and the Gospel. They are made from two tenths of fermented fine flour, from a teaching that transmits the perfect divinity and the perfect humanity of God; nor can they be baked in any other way except through such teaching.

But they are firstfruits for the Lord. First the Lord perfected the Law, and afterward he taught the Gospel: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not kill’; but I say to you, everyone who is angry with his brother without cause will be liable to judgment.” Here he joined the Law to the Gospel, and for this reason they are called his firstfruits.

“And you shall call this day most celebrated and most holy; you shall do no servile work on it. It shall be a perpetual ordinance in all your dwellings and throughout your generations.”

What, then, does it have that surpasses the others? For he also calls other days holy. But concerning this day he first says: “You shall call this day most celebrated,” and afterward “most holy,” so that you might recognize what it has in common with the others and what is proper to it.

On this day the calling of the Gentiles began not only to be preached but also to be enacted, when Parthians, Medes, Elamites, those who inhabited Mesopotamia, Judea, and Pamphylia, and all the remaining nations whom Luke enumerated began to hear the apostles speaking and proclaiming the great things of God in their own languages.

Let us therefore do no servile work on that day—that is, nothing pertaining to slavery—but let us preserve the perpetual ordinance in all our dwellings and generations. We must perform nothing servile at the time when the Spirit came to us, because “where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.” To him, with the Father and the Son, praise, honor, and glory remain throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XC. ON THE SAME FEAST. Reading from the Book of Deuteronomy.

In those days Moses said: “Listen, Israel, to what I command you today. When you enter the land that the Lord your God is about to give you to possess, and you have obtained it and dwell in it, you shall take the firstfruits of all your crops and place them in a basket. Then you shall go to the place that the Lord your God will choose, so that his name may be invoked there,” etc.

Through these words, by which the Israelites were instructed how they should offer the firstfruits to the Lord in a basket in the land of their possession, in thanksgiving because they had been rescued from Egypt, we too are instructed to enter through the spiritual Jordan—that is, through baptism and faith in the Holy Trinity—into the land of the Church. There we are to place, in the basket of our conduct, the firstfruits of good works and bring them to God upon the altar of Catholic faith, so that our priest may receive them there—namely, the one who, according to the order of Melchizedek, was made a high priest for us by God.

There we should confess to the Lord and say to him that the spiritual Syrian—interpreted as “exalted” or “one who moistens”—persecuted our father, namely the first-formed ancestor, so that he deceived him through pride and gluttony, made him a transgressor, and deprived him of possession of paradise.

Therefore he became an inhabitant of Egypt, this world, where, as a sojourner, he remained with very few companions, because, while many followed idolatry, few remained faithful. But after more had grown in number through the ordering of the Law, those who received knowledge and belief in the one God, the spiritual Egyptians afflicted them—that is, evil spirits. By placing the heaviest burdens of sins upon them, they oppressed the human race.

But God Almighty, our maker and creator, regarded our humility, labor, and distress, and sent his only-begotten Son, who is called the hand and arm of God, to rescue us from the power of darkness and transfer us to a place of peace, so that we might become children of light.

He gave us a land flowing with milk and honey: namely, the present Church, in which there is the milk of innocent and simple doctrine, by which the little ones in understanding may be nourished, and the honey of sweet and manifold knowledge, by which the perfect in understanding may be satisfied.

Whoever offers such gifts to God can hold a spiritual banquet in the house of God with the true Levites and resident foreigners. For together with God’s ministers, with his brothers, and with all who understand that they are resident foreigners and pilgrims in this world, he will be happily nourished and filled with the dishes of virtue and spiritual knowledge.

Thus, when the appointed time of mortal life has been completed, by God’s generosity he will arrive at the heavenly kingdom, where he will rejoice forever with God’s saints, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who lives and reigns with God the Father throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XCI. ON THE SAME FEAST. Reading from the Book of Leviticus.

In those days the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “If you walk in my precepts, keep my commandments, and carry them out, I shall give you rain at its proper times. The earth shall produce its fruit, and the trees shall be filled with fruits. The threshing of the harvest shall overtake the vintage, and the vintage shall overtake the sowing; you shall eat your bread to satisfaction, and dwell without fear in your land.

“I shall give peace within your borders; you shall sleep, and there will be no one to terrify you. I shall remove evil beasts, and the sword shall not pass through your borders. You shall pursue your enemies, and they shall fall before you. Five of your men shall pursue a hundred foreigners, and a hundred of you shall pursue ten thousand. Your enemies shall fall before your eyes by the sword.

“I shall look favorably upon you and make you increase; you shall multiply, and I shall establish my covenant with you. You shall eat the oldest of the old, and you shall cast out the old when the new has arrived.

“I shall place my tabernacle in your midst, and my soul shall not reject you. I shall walk among you and be your God, and you shall be my people. I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of the Egyptians so that you would not serve them, and who broke the chains of your necks so that you might walk upright,” etc.

How shall we find all these things fulfilled literally by the Jews, when many prophets of God, keeping his commandments and walking in his precepts, were subjected to great affliction and ate their bread not in satiety but in want, [Col. 0319D] as did Ezekiel, to whom this very God gave the command? Paul too, explaining that those who were justified in the Law and the Prophets, said: “They went about in sheepskins and goatskins, humbled and afflicted—men of whom the world was not worthy.”

Rather, we ought to understand more deeply what has been said: for those who keep God’s commandments, the Law has set forth thirty blessings in the present age. You will find this number if you distinguish each blessing from the next by the conjunction in the Septuagint edition. For the Lord, being thirty years old, as Paul describes when he says, “until we all attain to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ,” came to baptism so that by the age at which he was baptized he might signify and manifest the perfection of the gift. [Col. 0320A] Thus, having been made perfect according to the time, he began to preach the Gospel, in which there is the fullness of all life, of the gift, of conduct, and of recompense—things which he signified here.

For he says: “And I will give you rain in its seasons.” He calls the word of God “rain,” as though it descends from heaven as grace; concerning it Moses said: “Give ear, O heaven, and I will speak; let the earth hear the words from my mouth. Let my speech be expected like rain.”

“And the earth will yield its fruit,” that is, our body; for the fruits of this good are chastity, sobriety, and abstinence. “And the trees will be filled with fruit,” or, as the Septuagint translated it, “The trees of the field will yield their fruit.” The trees of the field are the movements of the soul, since they are higher than the movements of our intelligible earth, namely, the flesh. [Col. 0320B] Their fruit is truth, justice, gentleness, compassion, and things of this kind.

“The threshing of the grain will overtake the vintage, and the vintage will overtake the sowing.” Since the threshing of the earth gathers the fruits, while the vintage properly refers to the fruits of the trees, he says that the fruits of the body will grasp or overtake the fruits of the soul. For this is the greatest blessing: to possess, at one and the same time, a body and soul that are stable and fruitful in the virtues.

“And you will dwell without fear in your land; I will give peace within your borders.” For if the body is stable and the soul bears fruit, we shall dwell securely in our land, because the flesh does not desire against the spirit. Therefore no war will pass through the land, nor will there be time for the resurrection of desires, concerning which James says: [Col. 0320C] “From where do wars and quarrels arise among you? Is it not from this—from your desires that wage war in your members?” When these have been destroyed, peace in our land, restrained by the law of God, is established.

“And you will sleep,” he says. Scripture has also placed this in the likeness of recompense, for sleep, being rest, is called the death of the saints. “And there will be no one to frighten you.” Whoever has lived in the manner described above will have no one to frighten him at the time of death, which for us is sleep because of the hope of the resurrection of the dead. He will have no one, then, who terrifies him—being conscious of nothing for which he might be terrified.
