“I will remove evil beasts,” namely, demons. They are called beasts because of their similar wickedness: first, because they lie in wait; then, because they possess unbearable and deadly poison.

“You will pursue your enemies.” [Col. 0320D] For they cannot stand before the face of those who live according to the Law. “And they will fall before you.” By what death? Certainly by fasting and prayer. In this way our intelligible enemies, the demons, are killed, so that they can never rise again against us.

“Five of you will pursue a hundred strangers,” or, as the Septuagint translated it, “Fifty will put ten thousand to flight.” We call the number fifty spiritual because on the day of Pentecost the Spirit descended from heaven. Thus that spiritual person of whom Paul said, “The spiritual person judges all things, and he himself is judged by no one”—that is, the person who possesses perfect knowledge for the subtle discernment of what ought to be done—can overcome and conquer even a powerful demon, for example one who is among those above a hundred and is called Legion because of the multitude of evil spirits obedient and cooperating with him. [Col. 0321A]

“And a hundred of you will pursue ten thousand.” Whoever possesses not only subtle knowledge but also a perfect and consummate life is, in a certain sense, doubly spiritual. Therefore the number one hundred is more dreadful, as bearing a twofold and perfect fruit in the spirit.

For he says: “And your enemies will fall before you by the sword.” He means the sword which Paul explained when, after first speaking of the thousands of enemies—that is, “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places”—he adds: “Therefore take up the armor of God,” and, counting its parts individually, says: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.” [Col. 0321B]

“I will look upon you.” For what is better than to be looked upon by God? His regard is salvation, but for the adversary it is death.

“And I will make you increase, and you will multiply.” He increases us when he makes the small good things we do appear great.

“You will eat the very oldest of the old,” or, as the Septuagint translated it, [Note: [Col. 0321D] In this place, the translation of the Septuagint had been deleted in the manuscript exemplar.] that is, the things promised to you through the Law and the Prophets.

“And the old things of old”: those which he promised through the patriarchs in their blessings.

“And you will cast out the old things when new things arrive.” What are the “new” things? The Gospel, of course. For although the things promised through the patriarchs, the Law, and the Prophets are very great, the promises made through the Gospel are greater; [Col. 0321C] therefore, in comparison with these, those former things are judged by us to be superfluous.

Behold, he introduces a statement that confirms the whole blessing: namely, that the things enacted and fulfilled through the Gospel by grace are these: “I will place my tabernacle in your midst”; or, according to the Septuagint, “I will establish my covenant with you.” This is that in which he set forth the new things, of which the prophet Jeremiah speaks: “And I will establish for you a new covenant, not according to the covenant which I made with your fathers.”

These statements are joined to what follows, especially: “And my soul will not abhor you.” God calls his will his soul.

“I will walk among you, and I will be your God, and you will be my people.” These things too were plainly foretold by the Prophet, as the Septuagint edition contains them in writing: “This your God will not be reckoned as another; after this he was seen on earth and lived among human beings.” He would not have done this if he had rejected us. Therefore he did not abhor us; rather, he wished to walk within us through the flesh and to become our God, although he had been so previously—but unknown, because we were joined to error. Afterwards, washed from sins by his grace and abundantly filled with the gifts of the virtues, we shall attain everlasting light.

## HOMILY XCII. ON THE SAME FEAST

Reading from the Epistle of Blessed Paul the Apostle to the Romans.

“Brothers, justified by faith, let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,” etc.

When the apostle Paul had explained that no one could be saved through the works of the old Law, he added what you have heard in the present reading: “Justified, therefore, by faith,” following the example of Abraham, whose children all believers are said to be, since Abraham is interpreted as “the father of all believers.” By this reasoning it is shown that no one is justified before God by nobility of birth, except the one who has rightly believed in God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the holy and undivided Trinity, one God of one substance [Col. 0322B] and one majesty, coequal in all things and through all things.

For this reason he exhorts us to have peace, saying: “Let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.” Since we have all been saved together not by any merits of our own but by the great grace and mercy of God, we ought to be subject to God, to preserve God’s peace—not merely as holy people toward one another—and to live among ourselves in harmonious charity, because we are all brothers in Christ and have all been redeemed at the one price of Christ’s blood.

It follows:

“Through whom we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand.” Through Christ’s passion and death, and through his resurrection and ascension in human flesh into heaven, we have access to God and have been faithfully reconciled to God in the same [Col. 0322C] grace by which we were redeemed, if we desire to remain in worthy conduct and right faith. For all of us who were far from God through sin have, through Christ’s grace, been brought near; and we who previously lay in death have now been raised up to Christ and stand in life, if we remain in his commandments.

“And we glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God.” We hope, through the adoption of God’s grace, that we have been counted as children of God and that we shall possess eternal glory together with him and with all his saints.

“Not only this, but we also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces perseverance, and perseverance produces testing.” God’s faithful and devoted servants glory not only in the hope of eternal blessedness but also, in salutary tribulations, [Col. 0322D] consider the greatness of the reward, as James says: “Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various trials and tribulations for Christ’s name,” because enduring adversity for God’s sake awaits great joy in the future. Therefore we ought to rejoice in suffering something for God’s name, so that from tribulation, once ended, we may gain an infinite reward. For when we consider the rewards, we cannot judge any labor to be worthy of them.

We have something of which to glory honorably and without danger. For it is a great glory to rise from the lowest things to the highest, to reach the greatest things from nothing; indeed, we are called from clay to heaven and from slavery to a kingdom, provided that, [Col. 0323A] having rejected every worldly glory and pleasure, we glory in that alone which is promised to us as our future portion.

“Testing produces hope, and hope does not disappoint.” The hope of future goods drives away every shame. Therefore the one who is put to shame in Christ’s commandments is shown not to have this hope.

It follows:

“Because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts.” The greatness of the promised benefits awakens in a person a great love, which trusts perfectly and knows neither fear nor despair.

“Through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.” We know from this how God loves us: not only has he forgiven us our sins through the death of his Son, but he has also given us the Holy Spirit, who shows us all future [Col. 0323B] goods and strengthens us in right faith, firm hope, and perfect love, if we prepare ourselves through good works to be worthy of his dwelling.

For if we love him with our whole heart, there will be nothing in us by which we might serve the desires of sin. And what is it to love God except to occupy the mind with him, to conceive an affection for enjoying his vision, hatred of sin, and disdain for the world; also to love one’s neighbor, whom he himself judged ought to be loved; and in that love to preserve the proper measure through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be honor and glory, now and forever, world without end. Amen.

## HOMILY XCIII. ON THE SAME FEAST

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Matthew.

[Col. 0323C] “At that time, as Jesus was leaving Jericho, a great crowd followed him; and behold, two blind men sitting beside the road heard that Jesus was passing by, and they cried out, saying: ‘Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David.’ But the crowd rebuked them so that they would be silent. Yet they cried out all the more, saying: ‘Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David,’” etc.

There were many robbers in Jericho who were accustomed to kill and wound those descending from Jerusalem to Jericho. Therefore the Lord came to Jericho with his disciples, to free the wounded and draw a great crowd after him. Finally, when he wished to leave Jericho, a great crowd followed him.

If he had remained in Jerusalem and had never descended to lowly places, the crowd would still be sitting in darkness and [Col. 0323D] the shadow of death. There were also two blind men beside the road. He calls them blind because they could not yet say, “In your light we shall see light.” They were beside the road because they seemed indeed to possess knowledge of the Law, but they did not know the road, which is Christ. Many understand them as the Pharisees and Sadducees; others understand both peoples, that of the Old Testament and that of the New: the one following the written Law, the other the natural law, and both blind without Christ.

Since these men could not see by themselves, they heard the praises of the Savior and confessed him to be the Son of David. But if the two blind men refer to the Jewish people, the following statement—“the crowd rebuked them”—is to be understood of the Gentiles. The Apostle warns them not to boast and become proud against their root [Col. 0324A], but, since they themselves were grafted from a wild olive into a good olive after being removed from the error of their predecessors, they must not envy the salvation of those who came before them.

“Have mercy on us, Son of David.” They are rebuked by the crowd, yet nevertheless do not remain silent; instead, they repeat the same words more frequently, showing their desire for the true light.

“Jesus stood still, called them, and said: ‘What do you want me to do for you?’ They said: ‘Lord, that our eyes may be opened.’”

They were blind and did not know where to go. They could not follow the Savior: there were many pits in Jericho, many cliffs and steep places descending into the depths. Therefore the Lord stood still so that they could come; he commanded them to be called, lest the crowds prevent them; and he asked them, as though ignorant of what they wanted, so that from the blind men’s answer their weakness might be made manifest and his power recognized through the remedy.

[Col. 0324B] “Moved with compassion, Jesus touched their eyes. And immediately they saw, and followed him.”

He touches their eyes and the craftsman provides what nature had not given; or rather, mercy grants what weakness had taken away. Immediately they saw and followed him—those who had previously sat crouched in Jericho and knew only how to cry out. Afterwards they followed Jesus not so much with their feet as with their virtues, because he himself is the way, the truth, and the life: namely, our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XCIV. FOURTH WEEK AFTER PENTECOST

Reading from the Epistle of the blessed Apostle Peter.

[Col. 0324C] “Beloved, humble yourselves under the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt you at the time of his visitation; casting all your anxiety upon him, because he cares for you,” etc.

A moment ago, dearly beloved brothers, we heard the blessed apostle Peter exhorting us to humility and saying: “Humble yourselves under the powerful hand of God.” The hand of God signifies his power, because there is no joining of bodily members in God, who is everywhere wholly full and perfect in all things. Scripture nevertheless speaks of God in human fashion so that people may understand more clearly the majesty and power of their Creator and, understanding them, strive to fulfill God’s will in their works, by which they may acquire everlasting joys.

It follows: “So that he may exalt you at the time of his visitation.” Whoever in the present world submits himself to God’s will, gives assent to his commandments, and strives to fulfill them in works insofar as divine grace grants the ability, crushing the pride of the flesh, will be exalted by the Lord on the day of final recompense and led to the rewards of eternal blessedness.

“Casting all your anxiety upon him, because he cares for you.” The Psalmist admonishes us when he says: “Cast your thought upon God, and he himself will nourish you.” And elsewhere: “Those who seek the Lord will not lack any good thing.” The Lord himself also says in the Gospel: “Do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or, ‘What shall we drink?’ For your Father knows that you need all these things. Seek first [Col. 0325A] the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.”

“Be sober and watchful.” Always conduct your life with sobriety and moderation, continually avoiding the devil’s cunning, and watch constantly in keeping God’s commandments and guarding your souls.

It follows:

“Because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour.” The devil never sleeps and never rests from laying snares for human beings. Day and night he continually goes about, tempting and setting traps for people, seeking how he may deceive any one of them who are subject to God’s will through his suggestion. “Seeking whom he may devour”—not in body, but in soul, so that he may draw each person toward harmful and useless [Col. 0325B] carnal desires.

“Resist him, strong in faith.” Following the example of Christ and his saints, despise the sweetness of carnal desire and continually remember what bitterness is prepared for those who serve earthly desires and do not wish to turn from their wickedness through repentance.

Let us therefore strive faithfully to cling to the Lord, continually meditate on his commandments, crush the desires of our flesh, and resist with strength the devil, our most wicked enemy, in right faith and firm hope, and in perfect love, through the mercy of the Lord God almighty, serving him in works of mercy and compassion, so that, by his gracious gift, we may deserve both triumph over the enemy and the reward of eternal blessedness.

It follows:

[Col. 0325C] “The God of all grace, who has called us into his eternal glory in Christ, through the incarnation of his only-begotten Son, whom he sent to die for the salvation of the world.”

“After suffering briefly.” Although in this world he suffered many insults for us during a brief period, in the end he was also crucified and killed for our redemption. He graciously consented to die for us and, held by death for a brief time, rose immediately on the third day. He himself will perfect in us the good work he had begun; he will confirm and strengthen us always in his will and in divine religion, and in perseverance in good works.

To him be glory and dominion, praise and thanksgiving, world without end. Amen.

## HOMILY XCV. AS ABOVE

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Luke.

“At that time, tax collectors and sinners were drawing near to Jesus in order to hear him. And the Pharisees and scribes murmured, saying: ‘This man receives sinners and eats with them.’”

Because not only can the righteous sin through negligence, but the sinner can also repent through diligence, after it had been said that salt which has lost its savor ought to be thrown outside, the company of penitents is immediately described as being admitted within. They drew near to hear the word of God and were received not only for conversation but also for eating together. [Col. 0326A] When the Pharisees saw this, they were indignant, because true righteousness has compassion, whereas false righteousness has disdain—although even righteous people may rightly be indignant toward sinners.

Yet one thing is done in the image of pride, and another through zeal for discipline. But because they were sick in such a way that they did not know themselves to be sick, the heavenly physician, in order that they might recognize what they were, treats them with gentle remedies, offers them a kindly example, and presses upon their hearts the swelling of their wound. For he says:

“Which one of you, having a hundred sheep, if he loses one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one that was lost until he finds it?”

[Col. 0326B] Behold, by a wondrous dispensation of mercy, Truth gave an allegory in which the human being might recognize himself, while it nevertheless referred especially to the author of humanity. Because one hundred is a perfect number, he himself had one hundred sheep when he created the nature of angels and human beings. But one sheep was lost when, by sinning, humanity abandoned the pastures of life.

He left the ninety-nine sheep in the wilderness because he left the highest choirs of angels in heaven. Why is heaven called a wilderness, unless because a wilderness is called an abandoned place? Humanity deserted heaven when it sinned. The ninety-nine sheep remained in the wilderness while the Lord sought the one on earth, because the number of rational creatures—namely, angels and human beings—who had been created to behold God, had been diminished by the loss of humanity. In order that the fullness of the sheep might be restored more perfectly in heaven, the lost human being was sought on earth. [Col. 0326C]

“And when he has found it, he places it on his shoulders, rejoicing.” He placed the sheep on his shoulders because, taking human nature upon himself, he himself bore our sins.

“And when he comes home, he calls together his friends and neighbors, saying to them: ‘Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep which was lost.’”

Having found the sheep, he returned home, because our Shepherd, with humanity restored, returned to the kingdom. There he found friends and neighbors: namely, the choirs of angels, who are his friends because they continually preserve his will in their own steadfastness. They are also his neighbors because they continually enjoy the brightness of his vision.

[Col. 0326D] It should be noted that he does not say, “Rejoice with the sheep that was found,” but “with me,” because our life is his joy; and when we are brought back to heaven, we complete the solemnity of his rejoicing.

“I tell you that in this way there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous people who have no need of repentance.”

There will be more joy in heaven over converted sinners than over righteous people who remain standing, because often those who know that they are oppressed by no burdens of sin do indeed stand in the way of righteousness and commit no unlawful acts, yet they do not anxiously yearn for their heavenly homeland. They allow themselves the use of lawful things to the same extent that they remember having committed no unlawful things. Often they remain sluggish in practicing the more excellent good deeds because [Col. 0327A] they are very secure in having committed no more serious evils.

“Or what woman, having ten drachmas, if she loses one drachma, does not light a lamp, sweep the house, and search carefully until she finds it?”

The one signified by the shepherd is also signified by the woman. He is God himself and the Wisdom of God. Because an image is stamped on the drachma, the woman lost the drachma when humanity, created in the image of God, withdrew through sin from the likeness of its Creator.

But the woman lights a lamp because the Wisdom of God appeared in humanity. A lamp is light in an earthen vessel; light in an earthen vessel is divinity in flesh. Once the lamp has been lit, she sweeps the house, because as soon as his divinity shone forth through the flesh, our entire [Col. 0327B] conscience was shaken. The house is swept when the human conscience is disturbed by consideration of its guilt. Once the house has been swept, the drachma is found, because when the human conscience is disturbed, the likeness of the Creator is restored in humanity.

“And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying: ‘Rejoice with me, because I have found the drachma which I had lost.’”

Who are these friends and neighbors except the heavenly powers already mentioned? They are close to heavenly Wisdom to the extent that they approach it through the continual vision granted by grace.

But we must consider why this woman is said to have had ten drachmas. The Lord created the nature of angels and human beings so that they might know him; and when he willed that this nature should endure unto eternity, he undoubtedly created it in his own likeness. The woman had ten drachmas because there are nine orders of angels; but, in order that the number of the elect might be complete, the human being was created as the tenth. Humanity did not perish entirely from its Creator even after its fault, because eternal Wisdom, shining with miracles through the flesh, restored it from the light of the earthen vessel.

“So I tell you, there will be joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.”

To repent is both to mourn the evils one has committed and not to commit again the things that ought to be mourned. For someone who laments some sins while continuing to commit others either does not know how to repent or pretends to do so. What good does it do if someone weeps over sins of lust yet still burns with the passions of greed? Or what if, having already mourned the faults of anger, he still wastes away in the flames of envy? [Col. 0327D]

But what we have said is still far too little: the person who laments sins must be especially careful not to commit them again. He should also remember that, having committed unlawful acts, he ought to abstain even from certain lawful things, so that by this he may satisfy his Creator. Whoever has committed forbidden acts ought to deny himself even things already done [perhaps read: permitted things, concessa], and thus, living religiously in right faith and good works, he will reach eternal glory with God’s help.

## HOMILY XCVI. WEDNESDAY

Reading from the Epistle of the blessed Apostle Peter to the Colossians.

“Brothers, whatever you do in word or [Col. 0328A] deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him,” etc.

“Whatever,” he says, “you say or do, looking to Christ, hasten to return due thanksgiving to God and the Father for the things granted to you through Christ.” For he called this thanksgiving when he said: “Give thanks to God in your hearts with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs.” Whatever you say or do, say and do it as is right for those who have been judged worthy to attain such things.

This is true thanksgiving. Then, in this part also imitating what he had written to the Ephesians, he turns to a particular consolation, saying:

[Col. 0328B] “Wives, be subject to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.” He commands wives to be subject to their husbands.

“Husbands, love your wives and do not be harsh toward them.” He admonishes husbands to love their wives and not to deal harshly with them.

“Children, obey your parents in everything, for this is pleasing to the Lord.” He urges children to obey their parents.

“Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, lest they become discouraged.” He advises fathers not to grieve their children excessively.

“Servants, obey in everything your earthly masters, not serving merely for appearances, as those who please human beings, but in sincerity of heart, fearing God. Whatever you do, work from the soul, as for the Lord and not for human beings, knowing that you will receive the reward of the inheritance from the Lord. Serve the Lord Christ.”

[Col. 0328C] He also commands servants to obey their masters, looking toward the reward of recompense that will be given them by God for faithful service. Let them act as it is right for those who expect God to grant them their reward—not as serving human beings, but as serving the one from whom they expect their reward in return.

Whoever rightly keeps the apostolic commandments and strives to please God through faith and good works will undoubtedly share in the heavenly reward, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XCVII. ALSO ON WEDNESDAY

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Matthew.

“At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘Be reconciled quickly with your adversary while you are on the way with him, lest perhaps your adversary hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and you be thrown into prison. Truly I say to you, you will not come out from there until you have paid the last quadrans,’” etc.

From what precedes and follows, the meaning is clear: while we are running along the road of this age, the Lord and Savior exhorts us to peace and concord, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “If it is possible, insofar as it depends on you, live at peace with all people.”

For in the preceding passage he had also said: “If you offer your gift at the altar and there remember [Col. 0329A] that your brother has something against you,” and immediately he adds this: “Be well disposed or kind toward your adversary,” and the rest. In what follows he commands: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute you.”

I understand the judge to be Christ: “The Father judges no one but has given all judgment to the Son.” I understand the officer to be an angel: “And angels ministered to him”; and we believe that he will come with his angels to judge the living and the dead.

I understand the prison to be punishments of darkness, which elsewhere he calls “outer” punishments. I think this is because they are within and remain in the prison itself; or, if something more hidden may also be understood, it may refer to the joy of divine rewards, of which it is said to the deserving servant: “Enter into the joy of your Lord.” [Col. 0329B] Likewise, in the administration of the state, a person is sent out either from the secretary’s office or from the judge’s tribunal when he is thrust into prison.

A quadrans is a kind of coin that contains two small coins. Thus in one Gospel that poor widow is said to have put a quadrans into the treasury, while in another she is said to have put two small coins—not because the Gospels disagree, but because one quadrans contains two small coins.

This, therefore, is what he says: “You will not leave the prison until you have paid even your smallest sins.” Concerning the payment of the last quadrans, it may reasonably be understood either as meaning that nothing will be left unpunished—just as we say “down to the dregs” when we wish to express that something has been so completely exhausted that nothing remains—[Col. 0329C] or as signifying earthly sins by the name “the last quadrans.” For the fourth part of the distinct members of this world is found to be the earth, if you begin with heaven, count the air as the second, water as the third, and earth as the fourth.

[Col. 0329D] “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”

The lesser righteousness of the kingdom of God is not to commit adultery through bodily union; the greater righteousness of the kingdom of God is not to commit adultery in the heart. Whoever does not commit adultery in the heart much more easily guards against committing adultery in the body. Therefore the one who gave this command confirmed the Law by saying: “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it.”

It should carefully be considered that he did not say, “Everyone who desires a woman,” but, “Everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her”—that is, who looks with this purpose and intention, so that he may desire her. This is no longer merely to be tickled by the pleasure of the flesh, but plainly to consent to lust, so that the unlawful desire is not restrained but, if opportunity is given, is satisfied.

In these two matters the ancients wished to distinguish the terms: they called one “pre-passion” and the other “passion.” The difference between passion and pre-passion is that passion is counted as a fault, whereas pre-passion, although it bears guilt, is not held as a crime. Therefore, when someone looks at a woman and his soul is tickled, he has been struck by pre-passion. But if he consents and turns the thought into affection, as it is written concerning David, “They passed into the affection of the heart,” he has passed from pre-passion to passion. [Col. 0330A]

In such a person the will to sin is not lacking, but only the opportunity. Whoever, therefore, looks at a woman in order to desire her—that is, looks in such a way that he desires her and intends to act—is rightly said to have committed adultery with her in his heart.

“If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you; for it is better for you that one of your members perish than that your whole body be cast into Gehenna.”

Because he had spoken above about desire for a woman, he now rightly calls the thought and sense that turn in various directions an eye. By the right side and the other parts of the body he indicates the beginnings of the will and affections, so that what we conceive in the mind we may not complete in action. [Col. 0330B] We must therefore beware lest what is best in us quickly slide into vice.

For if the right eye and right hand cause us to stumble, how much more those things that are on the left in these members? If the soul falls, how much more the body, which is more inclined toward sin?

“And if your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you; for it is better for you that one of your members perish than that your whole body go into Gehenna.”

The right hand, therefore, is understood as a beloved helper and minister in divine works. For just as contemplation is rightly understood in the eye, so action is understood in the hand. The left hand signifies the works necessary for this life, while the right signifies those deeds in which God’s elect labor in the present life, so that through them eternal glory may be repaid to them in the future [Col. 0330C] by our Creator and Redeemer Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the same Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XCVIII. FRIDAY

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Mark.

“At that time, when Jesus had entered Jerusalem and the temple,” etc.

[Col. 0330D] By entering the city and going first to the temple, the Lord sets before us a pattern of religious practice for us to follow: whenever we enter a village, town, or any elevated place in which there is a house of prayer consecrated to God, we should first turn aside to it. After commending ourselves to the Lord through earnest prayer, we may then depart to conduct the temporal business for which we came.

And when he had looked around at everything, since it was already evening, he went out to Bethany with the Twelve. He did not do this only once, but throughout all five days from the time he had gone up to Jerusalem until the time of his Passion he habitually did the same: by day he taught in the Temple, but at night, going out, he stayed on the Mount of Olives, as we read in Luke. For by teaching he diligently performed the duty of correction toward unbelievers, but by staying among the faithful he graciously bestowed upon them the favor of his kindness. It is rightly said that, after looking around at everything, he went out to Bethany. The inward Judge indeed examines the hearts of all; and when he finds nowhere to lay his head among those who contradict and resist the truth, he withdraws to the faithful and rejoices to make his dwelling with the Father among those who obey the word. Bethany, moreover, is interpreted as “house of obedience.”

And on the following day, when they were going out from Bethany, he was hungry. He was hungry either to show the reality of his human flesh, or because he hungered for the salvation of believers and burned with zeal over Israel’s unbelief.

And when he saw from a distance a fig tree with leaves, he came to see whether he might perhaps find something on it; and when he came to it, he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs. And Jesus answered and said to it: “May no one ever again eat fruit from you.” Just as the Lord often spoke many things in parables, so also he was accustomed to do certain things in parables. For what reason would he, being hungry, seek fruit on a fig tree when anyone could know that its season had not yet come, and condemn the tree—because at that time it had no fruit—to the curse of eternal sterility, unless it was because he was terrifying by this deed the people whom he taught by word, lest anyone, having leaves but no fruit—that is, displaying words of righteousness without works—should be cut down and deserve to be thrown into the fire? For every tree is known not by its flowers or its leaves but by its fruit; that is, every person is proved not by reputation or the display of speech but by the testimony of his actions.

And they came to Jerusalem; and when he had entered the Temple, he began to drive out those who were selling and buying in the Temple. He overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves. What the Lord had done figuratively by cursing the fruitless fig tree, he immediately demonstrated more openly by driving the wicked from the Temple. For the tree had committed no sin by having no fruit for the hungry Lord, since its season had not yet arrived; but the priests had sinned, because they were conducting worldly business in the house of the Lord and had ceased to bear the fruit of piety which they ought to have borne and which the Lord hungered to find in them. The Lord caused the tree to wither by his curse, so that those who saw or heard these things might understand all the more that they would be condemned by divine judgment if, without the fruit of works, they merely flattered themselves with the applause of religious speech as though with a sound, and with the covering of green leaves.

**[Col. 0331D]** And he did not allow anyone to carry a vessel through the Temple. He is speaking of the vessels that were brought in for the sake of trade. Far be it, however, that the Lord should have driven from the Temple, or forbidden to be brought into the Temple, vessels dedicated to God, where he set forth an exemplary sign of his future judgment. Rather, he removes unclean and profane vessels from the Temple and forbids them to be brought in again, since he not only drives all the reprobate away from the Church, but also restrains them with eternal punishment so that they may not enter again to disturb the Church.

And he was teaching, saying to them: “Is it not written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations’?” “For all nations,” he says—not for the Jewish nation alone, nor in one place within the city of Jerusalem, but throughout the whole world—and not a house of bulls, goats, and rams, but of prayer.

“But you have made it a den of thieves.” Those who sat in the Temple to receive gifts plainly sought grounds for injuring those who did not give them; there could be no doubt of this. The house of prayer, therefore, had been made a den of thieves, because they knew how to stand in the Temple for this purpose: either to persecute bodily those who did not give gifts, or to kill spiritually those who did give them.

And when they passed by in the morning, they saw the fig tree dried up from the roots. Not only the branches or trunk of the fruitless fig tree, but its very root also, by being dried up, displayed the sentence of divine rejection against it; and John says that “the axe has been laid to the root of the trees.” The fig tree was therefore dried up from the roots, so that it might be shown that the wicked nation was not merely to be corrected for a time and in part by external attacks and then, after repentance, restored by the Lord’s mercy to its former freedom, as sacred history often reports; rather, it was dried up by the roots to be struck with eternal condemnation. This signified that the abominable people would be utterly deprived not only of external human glory but also of the divine favor within.

And Jesus answered and said to them: “Have faith in God. Amen I say to you, whoever says to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and cast into the sea,’ and does not waver in his heart but believes that whatever he says will happen, it shall be done for him.” Pagans who have written insults against the Church are accustomed to reproach us by saying that we have not had complete faith in God, since we have never been able to move mountains. To them it must be answered that not everything done in the Church has been written down, just as our Scripture bears witness to this even concerning the deeds of Christ himself, our God and Lord. Thus it could also have happened that, if necessity had demanded it, a mountain might have been removed from the land and cast into the sea, as we read happened through the prayers of blessed Father Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, a man distinguished in merits and virtues: the mountain yielded its place on the land by as much as the inhabitants of the city required.

Yet because the devil is sometimes signified by the name “mountain,” namely on account of the pride by which he raises himself against God and wishes to be like the Most High, the mountain is lifted from the land at the command of those who are strong in faith and is cast into the sea when, through holy teachers preaching the word, the unclean spirit is driven from the hearts of those who have been ordained to life and is allowed to exercise the madness of his tyranny in the turbulent and bitter minds of unbelievers. This does not mean that he had not previously possessed a seat and kingdom there, but that he rages all the more fiercely against those whom he can, the more deeply he grieves at having been driven away from harming the devout. Nevertheless, through the victory of our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who frees his chosen ones from his hands, he will condemn that enemy of the human race forever to the prisons of hell for his wickedness.

## HOMILY XCIX. FIFTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

Reading from the Epistle to the Romans.

“Brothers, I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us,” etc.

That no one in this age can endure any suffering worthy of comparison with the eternal glory that God prepared for his saints before the ages, the Apostle Paul briefly declares in the present reading, saying: “For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us.” For what mortal thing can be compared with what is immortal, or what is visible with what is invisible, or temporal things with eternal things? Yet if in the present life certain seeds of glory can somehow be gathered, these future seeds are gathered from the tribulations and sufferings endured for the Lord. As the same Apostle says elsewhere: “For what is momentary and light in the present is producing an immeasurable weight of future glory” for us who do not look to the things that are seen but to those that are unseen and eternal. Therefore every tribulation, whatever it may be, however savage or however long it may seem, ought to be considered momentary and light. For whoever looks toward the future glory that has been revealed and sought for us, when our mortal body will be transformed and made conformed to the glory of the body of the Son of God, [lacuna] the greater the tribulations we endure in this world for Christ, the more we should believe that the greatness of glory is being accumulated for us.

For “the expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the sons of God.” The expectation of creation is the expectation of rational humanity, which awaits the day of judgment, when the greatness of the glory prepared for those who faithfully endure tribulations for God in this age and labor according to the Lord’s will will be revealed.

For creation has been subjected to vanity. That is, every human being is unwillingly subjected to the vanity of this world so long as he is devoted to temporal things, or so long as he uses these passing things, which pass away like a shadow.

Not willingly. For just as man sinned voluntarily, so he was not condemned voluntarily, but by the will of him who orders all things, whose commandments man also despised. Man is subject to vanity so long as he lives in this mortal flesh. It follows:

Because creation itself will be freed from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God. “Creation” is rightly called man so long as he serves creation rather than the Creator. But when he has received faith, recognized the Lord his God, and begun to obey his will, he is no longer called creation but a son of God. This creation—that is, man—when he believes through the inspiration of divine grace, will be freed from the slavery of corruption, so that he may no longer serve destruction, to which all sinners are enslaved so long as they remain in sins. He will be freed from this corruption and wickedness through faith into the freedom of the glory of the children of God, so that he may no longer serve the flesh or earthly desires, nor the devil, but Christ, by whose grace he will become a participant in and co-heir of his glory.

For we know that all creation groans. By “all creation” he now means the nature of angels and human beings, because, as the Lord says in the Gospel, just as the angels rejoice over penitents, so they grieve and groan over those unwilling to be converted. Watching our struggles every day, they grieve greatly when we are overcome by the devil; but when we conquer, they rejoice much more. Therefore, if we wish to rejoice with the holy angels in heaven, we ought now to perfect their joy through our good conduct and worthy behavior, with great zeal in the purity of our life, so that when we depart from this carnal life they may receive us into the eternal dwellings, to rejoice together with them.

And not only that, but we ourselves. That is, the apostles and apostolic men, the successors of the apostles in the Church of the saints.

Having the first fruits of the Spirit—that is, possessing the pledge and gifts of the Holy Spirit—we groan inwardly while awaiting adoption as sons, the redemption of our body. For we groan over our adoptive sons of God, our brothers, whom we have been sent to teach and instruct, until we see them make progress in every good work, so that they may deserve to become sons of God and heirs of Christ. Therefore, so long as we—those, I mean, who are being instructed by them—neglect and delay, prolong the time of our correction, and take pleasure in things that are not seen, we move the apostles to sorrow and likewise bring grief and mourning to the holy preachers who teach discipline. When they see our iniquities, they afflict themselves with great mourning over our transgressions, imploring divine mercy for us, humbly asking forgiveness for the past and protection for the future.

Therefore, thinking carefully and faithfully about these and similar matters, let us not give heed to those who, lifted up in pride through free will, try to cast themselves down rather than raise themselves up. Instead, let us humbly consider what the Apostle says: “God is the one who works in you both to will and to accomplish.” Let us give thanks to our Lord and Savior, who, though we had been wounded without any preceding merits of our own, healed us, reconciled us when we were enemies, redeemed us from captivity, brought us back from darkness to light, and recalled us from death to life. Let us humbly confess our weakness and implore his mercy. Since, according to the Psalmist, his mercy has gone before us, may he deign not only to preserve in us but also to increase his gifts and benefits, which he himself has deigned to grant—the one who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, now and always, and forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY C. ON THE SAME FEAST

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Luke.

“At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘Be merciful, just as your Father also is merciful.’”

**[Col. 0335A]** God is merciful toward the ungrateful, both through the greater—or, more precisely, manifold—mercy by which he also saves animals, granting temporal goods, and through the singular grace by which he glorifies only the elect, inspiring them with heavenly goods. But whether you understand this in one way or the other, or both ways together, it is accomplished by God’s great goodness, which we are commanded to imitate if we wish to be sons of God and obtain the glory of the children of God.

“Do not judge, and you will not be judged; do not condemn, and you will not be condemned.” Here, I think, nothing else is commanded us except that, when it is uncertain with what intention actions are done, we interpret those actions for the better.

“Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you.” He commands us to forgive injuries and give benefits, so that our sins may be forgiven and eternal life given to us. With this brief but excellent saying he gathers and concludes everything he had commanded at length concerning conduct toward enemies.

“A good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing, they will give into your lap.” This resembles what he says elsewhere: “that they may receive you into the eternal dwellings.” For it is not the poor themselves who will repay those who give alms, but Christ. Yet they are said to give the reward into the giver’s lap because, by earning it, they provided the occasion for that reward, whenever they showed mercy to the needy, endured those raging wickedly with the patience of the stronger, sustained them by their generosity, and on several occasions tested them through the grace of indulgence.

For “with the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you.” And the Apostle, exhorting the Corinthians to almsgiving, says among other things: “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows in blessings will also reap in blessings.” This can be understood of everything we do in mind, hand, and tongue, because, he says, “you will repay each one according to his works.”

And he also told them a parable: “Can a blind man lead a blind man? Will not both fall into a pit?” The meaning of this saying depends on what precedes, where he commands that alms be given and injuries forgiven. If, he says, anger against one who is violent and greed against one who is powerful have blinded you, will you be able to cure his fault while your own mind is corrupted? Or will only the one who committed the injury be judged guilty, and not also you, who did not know how to endure it? But if the wickedness of the other finds you gentle and tranquil in heart, he will be moved to repentance and you will be rewarded for your patience, because, with the eye of one who sees—that is, with a serene heart—you were concerned to lead the blind man toward the light.

“A disciple is not above his teacher; but everyone, when perfected, will be like his teacher.” If the teacher, who, being God, could certainly have avenged his own injuries but preferred to make his persecutors gentler through suffering, then it is necessary that disciples, who are merely human beings, follow the same rule of perfection.

“But why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye, while you do not consider the beam that is in your own eye?” Here “eye” signifies the mind’s understanding, and this refers back to what was said above, where he warned that the blind cannot be led by the blind—that is, that a sinner cannot be corrected by a sinner. Many, overcome by pride or hatred, greed or avarice, or some other crime, judge these things slight or nonexistent and sharply rebuke those whom they see suddenly disturbed by anger, as though a speck had entered and changed the eye of their mind from its customary state of purity. Forgetful of the Lord’s command, “Do not condemn, and you will not be condemned,” they prefer to blame and condemn rather than to amend and correct.

“And how can you say to your brother, ‘Brother, let me remove the speck from your eye,’ while you yourself do not see the beam in your own eye?” You do this to your brother, for example, when he has sinned through anger and you rebuke him through hatred. As great as the difference between a speck and a beam is, so great is the difference between anger and hatred. Hatred is anger grown old, which through the very passage of time has become so great that it is rightly called a beam. It may happen that, if you are angry with a person, you may wish him to be corrected; but if you hate a person, you cannot wish him to be corrected. Therefore it is said to be impossible for one who carries a beam in his own eye to remove the speck from his brother’s eye.

“Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.” That is, first drive hatred away from yourself, and afterward you will be able to correct the person whom you love. It is truly necessary to be very cautious about the troublesome class of hypocrites—that is, pretenders—who, though they receive accusations of every vice out of hatred and envy, nevertheless wish to appear to be advisers. Therefore we must watch carefully and piously, so that whenever necessity compels us to rebuke or reprimand someone, we first consider whether the vice is one we have never had or from which we have been freed. If we have never had it, let us remember that we too are human beings and could have had it. But if we have had it and no longer have it, let the memory of our common weakness touch us, so that mercy, not hatred, precedes that rebuke or reprimand. Thus sound instruction, confirmed by love of God and neighbor, will lead both teacher and hearer to eternal salvation, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY CI. ON THE VIGIL OF SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST

Reading from the prophet Jeremiah.

“Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you, and appointed you a prophet among the nations.”

This does not mean that Jeremiah existed before conception, as the heresy supposes, but that the Lord foreknew that he would exist; to him things not yet done are already done, according to the Apostle’s statement about him “who calls things that are not as though they were.” Some understand this passage concerning the Savior, who is properly the prophet of the nations and, through the apostles, called all peoples. He truly was sanctified in the womb before he was formed in the virginal womb and before he came forth from his mother’s womb, and he was known to the Father, since he is always in the Father and the Father is always in him.

“And I said: ‘Lord God, behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am a child.’ And the Lord said to me: ‘Do not say, “I am a child,” for you will go wherever I send you, and you will speak everything that I command you. Do not fear their presence, for I am with you to rescue you,’ says the Lord.”

When he came in human flesh, he says at the beginning: “I do not know how to speak, for I am young.” Young on account of the dispensation, but old according to the fact that he is the firstborn of all creation. Young because he came at the consummation of the age, at the final period of this life. Therefore he says, “I do not know how to speak”: I know how to speak certain greater things; I know your utterance; I know your word, O Zion; I know how to speak to you, but I do not know how to speak to human beings. I am young.

And the Lord stretched out his hand and touched my mouth; and the Lord said to me: “Behold, I have put my words in your mouth; and I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, to uproot, destroy, and devastate, to overthrow, and to build and plant,” says the almighty Lord. It should be noted that two joyful things follow four sorrowful ones. For good things could not be built unless evil things had been destroyed, nor the best things planted unless the worst had been uprooted. Every planting that the heavenly Father did not plant will be uprooted, and a building that has no foundation upon rock but has been erected on sand is undermined and destroyed by the word of God. This is the building that Jesus will consume with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the appearance of his coming; that is, he will destroy forever every sacrilegious and perverse doctrine. Moreover, he will overthrow and cast down those things that are raised against the knowledge of God and trust in their own wisdom, which is folly before God, so that humble things may be built in their place, and in the place of what has been destroyed and uprooted there may be constructed and planted things that accord with the truth of the Church, fulfilling what the Apostle says: “You are God’s building, God’s cultivation.”

## HOMILY CII. ON THE SAME FEAST

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Luke.

“There was in the days of Herod, king of Judea, a certain priest named Zechariah.”

The most sacred nobility of the Lord’s forerunner descended gloriously not only from his parents but also from his ancestors, so that the faith in his coming might be preached more freely—not as something conceived through a sudden inspiration, but as something received through an established succession.

“Of the division of Abijah.” Solomon divided the twenty-four orders of priests serving in the house of the Lord by lot. Among them, the eighth lot fell to the family of Abijah, from which Zechariah was descended. It was not without reason that the first herald of the New Testament was born in the service of the eighth lot. For just as the Old Testament is often expressed by the number seven on account of the Sabbath, so the New Testament is sometimes expressed by eight on account of the mystery of the resurrection. Since the court of the heavenly kingdom is entered only through observance of both Testaments, it is rightly also related that in Solomon’s Temple there was a mystical ascent of fifteen steps.

“And his wife was from the daughters of Aaron.” Thus the praise is complete, encompassing lineage, character, office, conduct, and judgment: lineage in one’s ancestors, character in equity, office in the priesthood, conduct in obedience to the commandment, and judgment in justification.

“Both were righteous before God.” Blessed is the one who is righteous and praiseworthy in God’s sight. It happens that people praise one who is not praiseworthy and disparage one who is entirely undeserving of disparagement. God alone is a just judge both in praise and in blame.

“Walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord, without complaint,” etc. Human righteousness is often more severe and provokes anger; but righteousness tempered with moderation, by the grace of its own sweetness, avoids even the complaint of envy. For when we fulfill God’s commandment but scatter the stains of vain glory over our desire, so that we may please human beings, we do not fulfill it without complaint.

“And it happened that, while he was serving as priest in the order of his division,” etc. One who is chosen by lot is not selected by human judgment. He was therefore sought as a figure of the true eternal priest, to whom it is said: “You are a priest forever.” He would reconcile God the Father to the human race not by the blood of victims but by his own blood. At that time blood was poured out in figure and a priest was appointed; now that the truth has come, let us leave the figure and follow the truth. **[Col. 0338C]** At that time there were rotations of service; now there is perpetuity. Whom else did the priest Zechariah signify except that priest whose sacrifice would not be common with the others, who would sacrifice for us not in temples made by human hands but in the temple of his own body, wiping away our sins?

“It fell to him by lot to offer incense,” etc. It was commanded that the high priest carry incense into the Holy of Holies on the tenth day of the seventh month, while all the people waited outside the Temple. This day was called the Day of Atonement or Propitiation. Among us, because of the varying course of the moon by which the Hebrews calculate the months, it falls sometimes in September and sometimes in October. That month, in which the Passover is celebrated, holds the beginning of the year both by the order of creation and by the decree of the Law, as the Lord says: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year.”

And an angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing at the right side of the altar of incense, etc. It was not without reason that the angel appeared in the Temple, because the coming of the true priest was already being announced and the heavenly sacrifice was being prepared, in which angels would minister. The angel rightly appears both in the Temple and beside the altar, and on the right, because he proclaims both the coming of the true priest in the mystery of the universal sacrifice and the joy of the heavenly gift. For just as present things are often signified by the left, so eternal goods are often foretold by the right.

But the angel said to him: “Do not fear, Zechariah, because your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John.” By saying that the prayer had been heard, he immediately promises the wife’s childbirth—not because the man who had entered to offer sacrifice for the people could have left aside the words of prayer and prayed to receive children, but because the statement “Your prayer has been heard” signifies the redemption of the people. What he adds, “Your wife will bear you a son,” discloses the order of that same redemption: namely, that the son born to Zechariah would go before the redeemer of that people by proclaiming him.

“And you will have joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth.” It should be noted that many rejoice at the birth of the forerunner, whereas, at the birth of the Lord, the angel announces “great joy that will be for all the people,” because the former came to proclaim salvation to many, while the latter came to grant it to all who are willing.

“And he will be great before the Lord.” This declares not greatness of body but greatness of soul. Before the Lord there is greatness of soul and greatness of virtue, just as there is smallness of soul and childishness of virtue.

“He will drink neither wine nor strong drink.” “Strong drink” is interpreted as drunkenness. By this term the Hebrews signify every drink capable of causing intoxication, whether made from fruits, crops, or any other material. It was characteristic of the law concerning Nazirite vows to abstain from wine and strong drink during the time of consecration. Therefore John, Samson, Jeremiah, and others of this kind, in order that they might remain Nazirites—that is, holy—always took care to abstain from these things.

“And he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb.” There is no doubt that this was truly promised by the angel, since holy John, before he was born, while still situated in his mother’s womb, manifested the grace of the Spirit he had received.

“And he will turn many of the sons of Israel to the Lord their God.” Since John, bearing witness to Christ, baptized peoples in faith in him, he is said to have turned the sons of Israel to the Lord their God. It is therefore plainly evident that Christ is their Lord God.

“And he himself will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah.” He is rightly said to go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, because just as Elijah was the herald of the Judge who was to come, so John became the herald of the Redeemer.

“To turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the unbelieving to the prudence of the righteous, to prepare for the Lord a perfect people.” To turn the hearts of the fathers to the children is to pour the spiritual knowledge of the holy ancestors into the peoples by preaching it. The true prudence of the righteous is not to presume upon righteousness from works of the Law but to seek salvation through faith. Thus the people are perfectly prepared for the Lord when they are completely converted to the Lord’s service in right faith and holy conduct.

## HOMILY CIII. ON THE NATIVITY OF SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST

Reading from the prophet Isaiah.

“Thus says the Lord: ‘Listen, islands, and attend, peoples from afar.’”

After the calling of the remnant of the people of Israel and the rejection of the unbelieving people who remained—concerning whom he had said, “There is no peace for the wicked,” says the Lord—he turns to the churches gathered from the nations and speaks to them under the name of “islands.” They are exposed to persecutors like islands to the waves of the sea and, though shipwreck rages on every side, are established rather than moved. And lest anyone think that our interpretation is forced and that what is said does not concern the nations but the synagogues of the Jewish people, what follows says: “And attend, peoples,” or “nations from afar”—that is, from the farthest ends of the earth—or, as the Septuagint translated it: “After a long time he will stand,” meaning that these things will not occur at the time when they are spoken of but after many ages.

“The Lord,” he says, “called me from the womb; from my mother’s belly he remembered my name.” What now seems obscure to those hearing it will afterward become known to all the nations, when Gabriel says to Joseph concerning the virgin birth: “You shall call his name Jesus,” for “he himself will save his people from their sins.”

“And he made my mouth like a sharp sword.” He made his mouth like a sharp sword so that by the breath of his mouth he might slay the wicked. Concerning this sword he himself speaks in the Gospel: “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth but a sword,” separating the wicked from the good. “For I have come to divide a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law.”

“And in the shadow of his hand he protected me.” He asserts that he was protected in the shadow of God’s hand, so that the lowliness of the flesh might be concealed by the power of divinity, when the angel announced to the Virgin: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.”

“He made me like a chosen arrow; in his quiver he hid me.” When he says “chosen arrow,” he shows that God has many arrows, but not all are chosen. These arrows are the prophets and apostles who travel throughout the whole world. Concerning them it is sung elsewhere: “The sharp arrows of the mighty: peoples will fall beneath you”; and again: “Mighty sharp arrows with desolating coals.” But Christ, among many arrows and many sons, is one chosen arrow and the only-begotten Son. He hid this arrow in his quiver—that is, in a human body—so that the fullness of divinity might dwell bodily in him, and the faith of believers might be rare; of him it is said above: “You are a hidden God, and we did not know you.” The bride, having received the wound of this arrow, also speaks of it in the Song of Songs: “I am wounded by love.”

“And he said to me: ‘You are my servant, Israel, because I will glory in you.’” He is a servant because, although he was in the form of God, he deigned to assume the form of a servant. He shows that he is called a servant who was formed in the womb, and who also says in the Psalm: “From my mother’s womb you are my God.” And “Israel,” because he was born from the seed of the Jews. What cannot be understood of any other servant is added: “Because I will glory in you.” He himself says in the Gospel: “Father, I have glorified your name”; and in the Psalm he says: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and lyre”—that is, the choir of all virtues. “I have given you as a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.” That is, so that you may enlighten the whole world and bring my salvation, through which all may be saved, to the ends of the earth.

We know that these things were accomplished through the preaching of the apostles, concerning whom the Psalmist proclaims: “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.” “Kings will see and rise; princes will adore because of the Lord your God and the Holy One of Israel, who chose you.” These things will happen when Christ comes in the glory of his Father with his angels and sits upon the throne of his glory to judge the living and the dead. Then all will adore him because of the Lord God his Father, for he is faithful who chose him.

Or it may be understood in this way: the kings whose heart is in God’s hand, and who are princes of the Church, will adore him because the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, is faithful. The following words can also be understood of Christ. For he says: “In an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you.” The Apostle uses this testimony, saying: “In an opportune time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you. Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.” The acceptable and opportune time and the day of salvation are the Savior’s Passion and resurrection.

To him the same Father says in what follows: “I have given you as a covenant of the people, to raise up the earth and possess the scattered inheritances, to say to those who are bound, ‘Come out,’ and to those who are in darkness, ‘Be raised up.’” “As a covenant of the people” means, implicitly, of the Jewish people—that is, of those among them who wished to believe. He will raise up the earth that lay in the errors of idolatry, and he will possess the deserted inheritances that had no Lord dwelling in them. He says to those bound by the chains of sins, “Come out,” for each person is bound by the cords of his sins. And to those who sat in darkness and could not see the light he says, “Be raised up.” After all these people have been converted and have looked upon the clear light of Christ, they will be nourished along the roads and paths of the holy Scriptures and will say: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing. He will settle me in a place of pasture; he will lead me beside the waters of refreshment.” He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY CIV. ON THE SAME FEAST

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Luke.

**[Col. 0341D]** “At that time, the time for Elizabeth to give birth was fulfilled, and she bore a son.”

The word “fulfillment” Holy Scripture is accustomed to use only in connection with the birth, death, or deeds of the good, signifying that their life possessed the fullness of perfection. Thus, “the time came for Elizabeth to give birth”; “Mary’s days were fulfilled, so that she might give birth”; “Solomon completed building the house of the Lord”; Abraham—or some other patriarch—died “old and full of days”; and, “when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son.” But, in contrast, the days of the wicked are empty and void: “Men of bloodshed and deceit will not live out half their days.”

“And his neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had magnified his mercy toward her, and they rejoiced with her.” The bringing forth of the saints possesses the joy of many, because it is a common good; for righteousness is a common virtue. Therefore, at the birth of the righteous person, it announces in advance the sign of the life to come, and the grace of the virtue that will follow is marked out by the rejoicing of the neighbors, which prefigures it.

“And it came to pass that on the eighth day they came to circumcise the child, and they were calling him by the name of his father, Zacharias. But his mother answered and said: ‘By no means; he shall be called John.’” The holy Evangelist remarkably thought it necessary to state beforehand that many would suppose the infant should be called by his father’s name, so that you might perceive that his mother rejected the name of someone degenerate, but, filled with the Holy Spirit, uttered the name that had been foretold by the angel before Zacharias. Indeed, he, being mute, could not communicate the child’s name to his wife, but Elizabeth learned through prophecy [Col. 0342B] what she had learned from her husband.

“And they said to her: ‘No one in your family is called by this name.’” They were indicating to his father how he wished the child to be called. “And asking for a writing tablet, he wrote, saying: ‘John is his name.’ And they were all amazed.” “‘John is his name,’ he says—that is, we are not giving him a name, because he has already received a name from God; he has his own name, which we have recognized, not one that we have chosen.” Nor should you be surprised that the woman asserted a name she had not heard, since the Holy Spirit, who had given the command to the angel, revealed it to her. Nor could she have been ignorant of the Lord’s herald who had prophesied Christ. And it is rightly added that no one in his family was called by this name, so that you may understand that the name belonged not to the family but to the prophet.

[Col. 0342C] “Immediately his mouth and tongue were opened, and he spoke, blessing God, and fear came upon all their neighbors.” Because the voice of one crying in the wilderness had been born, the parent’s tongue was rightly released. For it was not fitting that the father should remain silent from praise when he rejoiced that the herald of the Word had been born to him; his lips, which unbelief had bound, faith had now released.

But if anyone wishes to investigate these matters allegorically as well, the celebrated birth of John is the beginning of the exalted dignity of the grace of the New Testament. His neighbors and relatives preferred to impose upon him his father’s name rather than John’s, because the Jews, who were joined to him by observance of the Law as by kinship, desired rather to pursue the righteousness that comes from the Law than to receive the grace of faith. But John—that is, the name “grace of God”—is communicated by the mother in words and by the father in writing, because the Law itself, together with the Psalms and the Prophets, openly proclaims Christ’s grace in the clear utterances of its statements, while that old priesthood also bears witness to it through the figurative shadows of ceremonies and sacrifices. Zacharias speaks fittingly on the eighth day after the child’s birth, because through the Lord’s resurrection, which took place on the eighth day after the seventh day of the week, the hidden mysteries of the royal priesthood were revealed, and the tongue of the Jewish priests, which the bonds of distrust had constrained, was released in the voice of rational understanding.

“And throughout all the hill country of Judea all these things were being spoken of, and all who heard them laid them up in their hearts, saying: ‘What, then, will this child be?’ For the hand of the Lord was with him.” “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his desires.” Behold, the single silence of Zacharias benefits not only the one to whom it was given as a punishment for unbelief and as a sign of faith, but, when it is removed, it also fills all his neighbors with amazement at the miracle and with fear; it spreads the fame of the prophet’s birth throughout all the surrounding hill country; and it prompts all who could hear to inquire more carefully into the origin and condition of the child who had been born. Thus, by these and similar auspices, the future prophet of Christ might be commended, and, so to speak, the signs preceding the truth might provide signs in advance of its forerunner.

“And Zacharias, his father, was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying: ‘Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, because he has visited and accomplished redemption for his people Israel.’” [Col. 0343B] Behold, the speech that alone had been taken from the unbelieving man was restored to the believer together with the spirit of prophecy. The Lord visited his people, who were wasting away as though from a long illness, and, as though they had been sold under sin, redeemed them by the blood of his only Son, who, with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

HOMILY CV. ON THE SIXTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST. Reading from the Letter of Blessed Peter the Apostle.

“Beloved, be all of one mind in prayer, compassionate, loving the brotherhood, merciful, humble, not repaying evil for evil or abuse for abuse, but, on the contrary, blessing,” etc.

[Col. 0343C] Because above he had taught persons of different condition and sex with appropriate discrimination, now he admonishes everyone together to have one heart and one soul in the cause of the Lord’s faith.

“For to this you were called, that you may possess a blessing as your inheritance.” Namely, when the Judge says: “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom.” The blessing of inheritance can also be understood as that blessing with which he blessed the Church in the future life everlasting. Hence even now, rejoicing in hope of the future, she sings: “I will exalt you, my God and King, and I will bless your name forever and ever.” Therefore, whatever each person desires to find in the future, let him strive to meditate upon and practice in the present: to bless the Creator and his neighbor with a sincere voice, and likewise to make himself worthy of divine and fraternal blessing, because

“The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayers; but the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.” Since blessed Peter had forbidden us to return evil for evil, and had rather commanded us to bless those who curse, he rightly establishes by prophetic testimony that, through heavenly observation, the good are always seen, and the wicked likewise—so that we may remember both that our patience, by which we endure the wicked, and our benevolence, by which we wish good upon our persecutors, will be rewarded with an eternal recompense, and that our persecutors, if they refuse to repent, will be punished with a fitting penalty. But if they repent, we too, for their salvation—which we had entreated from the Lord—will receive the crown of rightful rejoicing.

“And who is there who can harm you, if you are zealous for what is good?” He speaks of those things that come upon us from adversaries through insulting words, loss of temporal possessions, and bodily torments. For when these and all similar things are inflicted upon the faithful—provided they are zealous for what is good and do so according to knowledge—they can in no way harm them, but rather bring the palm of patience to those who endure them with equanimity; conversely, they greatly harm those who inflict them by heaping up eternal punishment. But if anyone, overcome by such adversities, falls away, it was not the one who inflicted the evil who harmed him, but he harmed himself by refusing to endure it patiently.

[Col. 0344B] “But even if you suffer for righteousness’ sake, you will be blessed.” He says: Not only does the one who inflicts evil upon those who do good do you no harm, but when the enemy persecutes you because of the good things he detests, he provides you with the cause of greater blessedness, since he exercises the strength of your patience, in accordance with the Gospel saying: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake.”

“But sanctify the Lord Christ in your hearts.” What is it to sanctify the Lord in our hearts except to contemplate, with the innermost affection of the heart, his holiness and how incomprehensible his glory is, and how much strength for conquering he is able to give those who hope in him, whose inestimable holiness shines forth? He, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

HOMILY CVI. ON THE SAME FEAST. Reading from the holy Gospel according to Luke.

“At that time, when the crowds were pressing upon Jesus to hear the word of God, he was standing beside the lake of Gennesaret.”

They say that the lake of Gennesaret is the same as the Sea of Galilee and the Sea of Tiberias. It was called the Sea of Galilee from the neighboring province, and the Sea of Tiberias from the nearby city, which was formerly called Cennerech but was rebuilt by Herod the tetrarch in honor of Tiberius Caesar and called Tiberias. Moreover, Genezar is said by a Greek expression to mean “generating a breeze for itself,” from the nature of the lake, which is said to raise a breeze from its own rippling waters.

[Col. 0344D] “And he saw two boats standing beside the lake.” The two boats placed beside the lake represent circumcision and uncircumcision. Jesus is rightly said to have seen them, because the Lord knows who are his in both peoples, and, by seeing—that is, by mercifully visiting—their hearts, he leads them from the waves of this age to the tranquility of the life to come, as to the firmness of the shore.

“But the fishermen had gone down and were washing their nets.” The fishermen are the teachers of the Church, who bring those caught in the net of faith and raised from the depths into the light, like fish to the shore, to the land of the living. The sayings of the preachers are like certain nets of fishermen: those whom they begin to seize in faith, they do not let go. Hence the nets are called *retia*, as though they were things that retain.
