[Col. 0345A] But these nets are now spread out for a catch, now washed and folded, because not every time is suitable for teaching: now the teacher’s tongue must be exercised, now care must be taken of oneself.

“Getting into one of the boats, which was Simon’s, he asked him to put out a little from the land. And sitting down, he taught the crowds from the boat.” Simon’s boat is the primitive Church, of which Paul says: “He who worked through Peter for the apostleship to the circumcised worked also through me among the nations.” It is rightly called one, because the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul. From it he taught the crowds, because from the authority of the Church he teaches the nations even to this day.

“When he had ceased speaking, he said to Simon: ‘Put out into the deep, and lower your nets for a catch.’” His first request that Simon put the boat out a little from the land signifies either that the word should be used moderately with the crowds, so that neither earthly things are commanded to them nor do they withdraw so far from earthly matters into the depths of the mysteries that they fail to understand them; or that the Gospel should first be preached among the nearby nations, so that when he likewise says to Peter, “Put out into the deep and lower your nets for a catch,” this may refer to the more distant nations to whom it was later preached.

“And Simon answered and said to him: ‘Master, we have labored all night and caught nothing; but at your word I will lower the net.’” “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain.” Unless the Lord illumines the hearts of those who hear, the teacher labors in the night. Unless the instruments of disputation are lowered at the word of heavenly grace, the preacher will cast the dart of his voice in vain, because the faith of peoples is preceded not by the wisdom of polished speech but by the gift of the divine calling.

“And when they had done this, they enclosed a great multitude of fish, and their net was breaking.” The net was breaking because of the multitude of fish, since now, even among the elect, so many reprobates enter through the confession of faith that they tear the Church herself apart through heresies. The net is broken, but the fish does not fall out, because the Lord preserves his own even amid the scandals caused by persecutors.

“And they signaled to their companions who were in the other boat to come and help them.” The other boat, as we said earlier, is the Church from the nations. Even it, since one little boat is insufficient for the fish, is filled with the elect, because the Lord knows who are his, and the number of his elect is certain with him. Since he does not find as many in Judea who will believe as he knows have been predestined to faith and eternal life, he seeks, as it were, another boat as a receptacle for his fish and fills the hearts of the nations also with the grace of faith. The companion boat is fittingly summoned when the net has broken, because Judas the betrayer was caught first, and Simon Magus, the most wicked of fish; Ananias and Sapphira deceitfully attempted to enter the net of faith; before this, as John testifies, many of his disciples went back and no longer walked with him; and afterward Barnabas and Paul were set apart for the apostleship to the nations.

“And they came and filled both boats, so that they were sinking.” The filling of these boats will increase until the end of the age. But that they sink when filled—that is, that they are pressed toward submersion—does not mean that they are submerged, but that they are endangered. The Apostle explains this when he says: “In the last days perilous times will come, and people will be lovers of themselves,” etc. For the sinking of the boat means that people, having been lifted from this world by faith, fall back into it through the depravity of their conduct. Peter himself, while still in a condition of weakness, demonstrates this in the present passage. Hence it follows:

“When Simon Peter saw this, he fell at Jesus’ knees, saying: ‘Depart from me, Lord, because I am a sinful man.’” Carnal people in the Church, in a way, drive away from themselves the governance of spiritual persons, in whom the person of Christ is especially manifest. They do not say with the voice of the tongue to God’s good ministers that they should withdraw from them, but by the voice of their conduct and actions they persuade them to depart. They refuse to be governed by good men, and the more earnestly they honor them, the more their deeds urge them to withdraw. Thus Peter’s falling at the Lord’s feet signifies their honor, while his words—“Depart from me, Lord, because I am a sinful man”—signify their conduct. Yet the Lord did not do this, for he did not withdraw from them but brought them to the shore after drawing in the boats. This signifies that good and spiritual men ought not to have the desire to abandon ecclesiastical office because they are disturbed by the sins of the crowds and wish to live more securely and peacefully.

“And Jesus said to Simon: ‘Do not be afraid.’” The Lord strengthens the fear of carnal people and raises up the minds of the weak by consoling them, so that no one, trembling either from awareness of his own guilt or from astonishment at the innocence of others, may fear to undertake the path of holiness. What follows—

“From now on you will be catching people”—applies particularly to Peter. The Lord explains to him what this catch of fish signifies: namely, that just as he now catches fish through nets, so at some time he will catch people through words. The whole order of this event shows what is enacted daily in the Church, whose figure he bears. But what follows—

“And having drawn the boats to land, they left everything and followed him”—can signify the end of time, when those who have clung to Christ will withdraw completely from the sea of this world.

It should be understood, however, that this is not the same passage in which Matthew and Mark relate that the Lord first called two fishermen from the boats—Peter and Andrew, and then the sons of Zebedee. For Luke does not now indicate that they were called by the Lord, but only that it was foretold to Peter that he would catch people. We also read that they went fishing after the Lord’s resurrection. From this it may be understood that they had returned, according to their custom, to catching fish, so that what Matthew and Mark relate would happen later, when he called those two. At that time, although they did not draw the boats to land, as though intending to return, they followed him as one who was calling and commanding them to follow. Later, having been imbued with right faith and fully instructed in the teaching of their Savior, they remained firmly and steadfastly with their Lord and Master, by whose grace they were brought to eternal life, and there they will reign with him through ages of ages. Amen.

HOMILY CVII. ON THE VIGIL OF SAINT PETER THE APOSTLE. Reading from the Acts of the Apostles.

“In those days Peter and John were going up into the temple at the ninth hour of prayer,” etc.

In the reading from the Acts of the Apostles that has now been read in remembrance of the blessed apostles, whose anniversaries we piously anticipate today, you heard, beloved, that “Peter and John were going up into the temple at the ninth hour of prayer.” Entering the temple at the ninth hour, the apostles first healed a lame man, then a weak man, and afterward, laboring until evening, instructed many thousands of people in the word of faith. By their very action they showed figuratively that they were doing this because our Lord had come into this world, as the end of the world drew near, to save all who believed in him, and had sent his apostles throughout the whole world, as though toward the very evening of the world, to teach the multitude of human beings.

“And a certain man who had been lame from his mother’s womb was being carried. They placed him daily at the temple gate called Beautiful, so that he might ask alms from those entering the temple. When Peter and John saw him, Peter said: ‘Look at us.’ He looked at them, hoping to receive something from them, but Peter said:

“‘Silver and gold I have none, but what I have I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, rise and walk.’” [Col. 0347C] And he immediately rose. If we consider the mystical mysteries in this lame man, we recognize what was prefigured. By the temple gate called Beautiful, where this lame man was healed, we can understand the preaching of the Gospel, through which the temple of God—that is, the Church of Christ—is adorned with spiritual beauty. In it, those who are weak in mind through unbelief and ignorance of Christ’s name, and who are therefore lame in soul as well, receive the remedy of salvation through the preaching of Christ’s Gospel.

Indeed, that Beautiful gate of the temple, which we said should be understood as the preaching of the Gospel, receives the lame man—that is, unbelievers—and makes him whole, leading them to the perpetual health of the soul by moving, exhorting, and teaching them. Just as this lame man, while he was at the Beautiful gate of the temple, received healing by looking toward Peter and John, so we too, before coming to the knowledge of Christ, were truly lame, because we limped along the way of righteousness. We limped not in bodily gait but through the wandering of the inner mind. For whoever is alien to the way of righteousness, to the way of truth—that is, to faith in and knowledge of Christ, the Son of the living God—even if he has straight bodily feet, is entirely lame, because he limps in mind and soul. The path of faith and truth, in obedience to Christ’s commandments, is traversed not merely by bodily movements but by the movements of the inner mind. Hence there is no doubt that we formerly limped along the way of righteousness when we did not know Christ our Lord, the true way of salvation and life.

But after we came to the Beautiful gate of the temple, as we said, by hearing, understanding, and likewise practicing the word of life, and by looking in faith toward the apostles—that is, toward their examples—through the preaching of their holy successors, then the steps of our mind were steadied and strengthened, so that we no longer limped along the way of iniquity but walked by the straight steps of good works along the path of righteousness.

“And Peter took the lame man by the right hand and lifted him up.” Fittingly, the one whom he raised by his word he also strengthens with his right hand, because the speech of the teacher has less power in the heart of the hearer if it is not also commended by examples of personal action.

“And leaping up, he stood and walked, and entered the temple with them.” The order of perfection is excellent: first to raise up the one who had been lying down, then to undertake the path of good action, and thus to enter the gate of the eternal kingdom together with the holy apostles. Therefore, dearest brothers, whenever we celebrate the memory of the most blessed apostles, we ought, setting aside all the activities of the world, to hasten without any delay toward the progress of good works and to render them due honor in the praises of God. They obtained eternal salvation for us through the shedding of their blood, and offered such a great sacrifice in themselves to the Lord for our reconciliation, especially since the Lord himself said to them: “Whoever honors you honors me, and whoever despises you despises me.” Therefore, whoever honors the apostles and martyrs of Christ with due reverence honors Christ, whom he loves, and, together with those holy apostles and martyrs and with all the saints, will obtain the rewards of eternal blessedness, by the generosity of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor and glory through immortal ages. Amen.

HOMILY CVIII. ON THE SAME FEAST. Reading from the holy Gospel according to John.

“At that time Jesus said to Peter: ‘Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?’ He said to him: ‘Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.’”

Our Lord’s present question shows us the perfect virtue of love. Perfect love is that by which we are commanded to love the Lord with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength, and our neighbor as ourselves. Neither of these loves can be perfect without the other, because neither can God truly be loved without one’s neighbor, nor one’s neighbor truly without God.

“He said to him: ‘Feed my lambs.’” As though he were saying openly: This alone is the true proof of a complete love of the Lord, if you strive diligently to perform your labors toward the brothers. For whoever neglects to provide his brother with whatever work of mercy he is able to offer shows that he loves the Creator less justly, since he disregards his commandments in supporting his neighbor’s need.

“He said to him again: ‘Simon, son of John, do you love me?’ He said to him: ‘Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.’” Simon is called obedient, and John means “grace of God.” Therefore, when he is questioned about his love, the first of the apostles is rightly called Simon son of John—that is, “obedient by the grace of God”—so that it may clearly be shown to everyone that the fact that he obeys the Lord’s commands with greater obedience than the others, and embraces him with more ardent charity, is not a matter of human merit but of divine gift. With a cautious, measured, and simple utterance he says: “Lord, you know that I love you.” This is plainly to say: I certainly know that I love you with an undivided heart, as you yourself know better; but how others love you is unknown to me, while everything is known to you.

“Peter was grieved because he said to him the third time, ‘Do you love me?’ and he said to him: ‘Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you.’ He said to him: ‘Feed my lambs.’” In provident mercy the Lord asks Peter three times whether he loves him, so that by the threefold confession he may release the bonds by which Peter had been bound through his threefold denial. As often as, terrified by his passion, he had denied knowing him, so often, restored by his resurrection, he testifies that he loves him with his whole heart.

But this must be firmly held in the heart by a shepherd: he must remember that those over whom he presides are not his own flock but the flock of his Lord. This accords with what is said to Peter: “If you love me, feed my sheep.” “My,” he says, not “yours.” Know that my sheep have been entrusted to you, and, if you love me perfectly, remember to govern them as mine, seeking in them my glory, my lordship, and my interests—not your own.

“Love” (*dilectio*) possesses a quality greater than “affection” (*amor*). Therefore, when the Lord says, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” Peter does not dare to confess that he possesses the measure of that higher love, but humbly declares that he has affection. Love is found to be superior to affection. Finally, when the Lord questions Peter for the third time, he does not say, as in the previous two instances, “Do you love me?” but “Do you have affection for me?” Peter is grieved because, in the third question as well, he did not say “Do you love me?” but “Do you have affection for me?”—as though he were no longer being questioned about the higher order of love but about the lower grace of affection.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: when you were younger, you girded yourself and walked where you wished; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish.” It is as though he were saying openly: You will one day prove with how great a love you love me, when, striving even unto death for the life of my little ones, you arrive at death. And so that they may be saved in body and mind, you will endure with steadfast courage of mind all the torments of the body that the adversary may wish to inflict. By the stretching out of the hands he indicates the position of the limbs of one who was to be fastened to the cross. By another’s girding he expresses the imposition of the bonds by which the persecutor was to restrain him. By being led where he did not wish, he indicates the bitterness of death and passion itself, which his bodily weakness shrank from, while the spiritual weakness of his soul rejoiced to endure every adversity for the Lord. For he did not seek his own will but the will of Christ, who sent him.

“He said this, signifying by what death he would glorify God.” Peter glorified God by his death when, through this judgment, he showed how greatly God ought to be worshiped and loved: when given the choice, he preferred to undergo the torments of the cross rather than cease preaching the heavenly word. May the one who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages, make us imitate him. Amen.

HOMILY CIX. ON THE NATAL DAY OF SAINT PETER. Reading from the Acts of the Apostles.

“In those days King Herod laid hands upon some of the Church to afflict them,” etc.

History relates that this Herod was struck down by an angel in the year … of Claudius, and in the seventieth year of his own reign.

“And he killed James, the brother of John, with the sword.” Concerning this James, Clement of Alexandria relates a memorable story: “And the one who had handed James over to the judge for martyrdom, moved by this, also confessed that he was a Christian. Both were led together to execution, and as they were being taken along the road, he asked James to grant him forgiveness. After pausing briefly to consider, James said, ‘Peace be with you,’ and kissed him. Thus both were beheaded together.”

“When he saw that this pleased the Jews, he proceeded to arrest Peter. After arresting him, he put him in prison,” etc. How holy Peter was sent into prison, bound with two chains and handed over to four companies of soldiers, and how he was freed from there by the angel of the Lord, your belovedness heard in due order. Holy Peter was therefore sent into prison on account of the name of Christ, but he could not dread the punishment of imprisonment, since he himself was the temple of God in the prison. He was bound with two chains, but in that very prison he was removing the chains of sins from believers. He was guarded by four companies of soldiers—that is, by sixteen men. For just as a centurion has one hundred men under him, so a company of four has four soldiers under it. Yet under that very guard he was presenting the four Gospels to those coming to the faith. He could not fear human custody, since he was protected by divine custody.

While Peter was therefore being carefully guarded in prison by four companies of soldiers and bound with two chains, the angel of the Lord came to him, as your belovedness heard, opened the prison doors for him, and said:

“‘Rise, take up your garment, cover yourself, put on your footwear, and come; follow me.’ And rising, he followed him. When he had come with the angel to the iron gate, the gate immediately opened by itself for them.” It is certainly no wonder that the iron gate opened of its own accord for holy Peter, since he had already received the gates of hell under his power, when the Lord said to him: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it. Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.” The one who opened the gates of hell opened the iron gate for holy Peter. The one who conquered death itself rescued Peter from death.

But what was then done literally around holy Peter, we understand to be done mystically around us also if we follow Peter’s faith. For we too are placed in this world as though in a prison. Therefore, if we deserve to be visited by God, God’s angel is sent to us and says to each one of us: “Gird yourself, put on your sandals, cover yourself with your garment, and follow me.”

We gird ourselves if we encircle the loins of our body with the belt of chastity, as the Apostle says: “Let your loins be in purity.” We put sandals on our feet if we fortify the steps of our life with the commandments of the Gospel and with faith, so that we may safely trample upon the thorns of sins and the thistles of iniquity. We cover ourselves with our garment if we preserve within us that wedding garment—that is, the grace of baptism—whole and undefiled.

If we faithfully fulfill these things, the chains will immediately fall from our hands: the chains of sins by which, according to the soul, we were held bound and fettered. But we cannot otherwise escape from prison—that is, from the error of this world—unless the Lord visits us through an angel. The iron gate will be opened for us—that is, the gate of death—and the punishment that the Son of God has shattered by the power of his passion.

Then we come to the house of Mary, to the Church of Christ, where Mary, the mother of the Lord, dwells; and there a girl named Rhoda meets us. Fittingly, this name, Rhoda, expresses the mystery of our salvation. For *Rhoda*, according to the Greek language, is called “rose.” When we come, therefore, to Mary’s house, Rhoda meets us—that is, the congregation of the saints, which shines like a precious rose in the glorious blood of the martyrs. Through the grace of baptism it is entrusted to us in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and through it we are cleansed from every stain of sin so that we may be made pure.

Since, therefore, we recognize such great mercy of God toward us—that we, though unworthy, have been called to such great grace—we ought piously and justly to live and conduct ourselves in his sight, so that at the coming of his glory we may receive not punishment with the impure and ungodly, but, with his saints and elect, the promises of the heavenly kingdom and the reward of everlasting life, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who, with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God in true unity through all ages of ages. Amen.

HOMILY CX. ON THE SAME FEAST. Reading from the holy Gospel according to Matthew.

“At that time Jesus came into the region of Caesarea Philippi.”

This Philip is the brother of Herod, whom we mentioned above, tetrarch of the regions of Iturea and Trachonitis. In honor of Tiberius Caesar he named Caesarea—now called Paneas—which lies in the province of Phoenicia.

“And he was questioning his disciples, saying: ‘Who do people say the Son of Man is?’” He did not say, “Who do people say that I am?” but “the Son of Man,” so that he would not appear to be asking about himself boastfully. And note that wherever “son of man” is written in the Old Testament, it is rendered in Hebrew as “son of Adam.” Likewise, what we read in the Psalm, “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” is said in Hebrew as “sons of Adam.” He fittingly asks who people say the Son of Man is, because those who speak of the Son of Man are human beings, whereas those who understand his divinity are called not human beings but gods.

“But they said: ‘Some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, and others Jeremiah or one of the prophets.’” I am astonished that certain interpreters inquire into the causes of each person’s error and weave an exceedingly long discussion about why some thought our Lord Jesus Christ was John, others Elijah, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets, when they could have erred about Elijah and Jeremiah just as Herod erred about John, saying: “John, whom I beheaded, has risen from the dead, and powers are working in him.”

“But you, who do you say that I am?” Simon Peter answered: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Prudent reader, observe that from what follows and from the wording of the discourse the apostles are called not human beings but gods. For after he had said, “Who do people say the Son of Man is?” he added, “But you, who do you say that I am?” To those who, because they are human beings, formed human opinions, he says: You who are gods, who do you think I am? Peter, speaking in the person of all the apostles, confesses: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” He calls him the living God in comparison with those who are thought to be gods but are dead—Saturn, Jupiter, Ceres, Liber, and the other monstrosities of idols.

“Jesus answered and said to him: ‘Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.’” What flesh and blood could not reveal—that is, human teaching—was revealed by the grace of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, from his confession he receives his name, because he has revelation from the Holy Spirit; and he should also be called its son, since *Bar-Jonah* in our language sounds like “son of a dove.”

Others take it simply to mean that Simon—that is, Peter—is the son of John, in accordance with the question found in another passage: “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” He answered: “Lord, you know.” They maintain that, through an error of the scribes, *Bar-Jonah* was written instead of *Bar-Joanna*, that is, “son of John,” with one syllable omitted. *Joanna* is interpreted as “grace of the Lord.” Both names, however, can be understood mystically: the dove signifies the Holy Spirit, and the grace of God signifies a spiritual gift.

The statement “flesh and blood has not revealed this to you” also corresponds to the apostolic account in which he says: “Immediately I did not consult flesh and blood.” There he wished Jews and Pharisees to be understood by “flesh and blood,” so that this too might be demonstrated under another sense: Christ the Son of God was revealed to him not through the teaching of the Pharisees but through the grace of God.

And I say to you. What does “And I say to you” mean? Because you said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” I say to you—not with an empty word that accomplishes nothing, but I say to you because for me to say is to do.

Because you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church. Just as he himself gave light to the apostles, so that they might be called “the light of the world,” and just as the other names they received from the Lord were bestowed upon them, so also he granted Simon, who believed Christ to be the rock, the name Peter. This is rightly said to him according to the metaphor of the rock: “I will build my Church upon you,” or “upon this rock”—that is, upon the one whom you have just confessed by saying, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God”—or “upon this rock,” that is, upon Peter’s confession.

And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. I believe the gates of hell to be vices and sins, or certainly the teachings of heretics, through which deceived people are led down to Tartarus. Therefore no one should think that this is spoken of death, as though the apostles had not been subject to the condition of death, whose martyrdoms we see shining forth.

And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven. Bishops and presbyters, not understanding this passage, assume for themselves something of the Pharisees’ arrogance, so that they either condemn the innocent or presume that they can absolve the guilty, whereas before God it is not the priests’ sentence but their life that is examined. We read in Leviticus concerning lepers, where they are commanded to show themselves to the priests; and if they have leprosy, then they are to be declared unclean by the priest—not because priests make lepers unclean, but because they possess knowledge of who is leprous and who is not, and can discern who is clean and who is unclean. Therefore, just as there the priest makes the leper unclean, so here too the bishop and presbyter bind or loose—not those who are innocent or guilty, but in accordance with their office: when they have heard the various kinds of sins, they know who is to be bound and who is to be loosed. Authority to bind and loose penitents is therefore given to all the Church’s elect according to the measure of their faults. But blessed Peter, who confessed Christ with true faith and followed him with true love, specially receives the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the primacy of judicial power, so that all believers throughout the world may understand that whoever in any way separates himself from the unity of the faith or from fellowship with him can neither be freed from the bonds of sins nor enter the gate of the heavenly kingdom.

Therefore, dearest brothers, we must devote our whole attention both to learning the mysteries of the faith that he taught and to demonstrating works consistent with the faith. With complete vigilance we must beware of the manifold and subtle snares of the gates of hell, so that, with the Lord’s help, we may be rescued from them, according to the Psalmist’s words, and may deserve to enter the gates of the daughter of Zion—that is, the joys of the heavenly city—in order to proclaim his praises. Nor should we think that salvation is sufficient for us if we merely equal the faith or conduct of crowds of negligent people or of any uninstructed persons, for the sacred writings prescribe a single rule both of believing and of living. Whenever examples of those who err are thrust before us, we should immediately turn away the eyes of our mind, lest they see vanity, and instead diligently search in our hearts what the truth itself decrees, following the example of blessed Peter. He rejected the sects of those who erred, openly uttered the mystery of the true faith that he had come to know in an unwavering confession of his mouth, and preserved it with the unceasing devotion of his heart.

Thus it will come about that, building upon the rock of faith gold, silver, and precious stones—that is, the perfect works of virtue—no fire of tribulations will harm us and no storm of temptations will prevail, because, tested by adversities, we will receive the crown of life that he promised us before the ages, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY CXI. ON THE BIRTHDAY OF SAINT PAUL

Reading from the Acts of the Apostles.

“In those days: Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord,” etc.

The present reading from the Acts of the Apostles, dearest brothers, declares how the apostle Paul, whose singular feast we celebrate today, was made from a persecutor of Christians into a preacher and teacher of Christians. For Christ killed savagery in him and made true gentleness live again in him. The prophecy of blessed patriarch Jacob was fulfilled in him, when, blessing his son Benjamin, he said: “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he devours the prey, and in the evening he divides the spoils.” He who is now called Paul after his conversion had previously been called Saul while he remained in impiety, because when he changed his actions, he also changed his name. He was of the tribe of Benjamin, and he was a wolf in the morning—that is, at first a persecutor of Christians; in the evening—that is, afterward—changed through Christ’s grace, he divided the spoils, that is, he wondrously distributed the mysteries of the Gospel among the nations.

Let us hear him devouring the prey in the morning: “Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord,” asks for and receives letters from the chief priests to Damascus, where a large part of the faithful already lived, so that he might bring bound to Jerusalem for martyrdom any men and women of this way whom he found believing in Christ.

And while he was making the journey, it happened that he was approaching Damascus, and suddenly a light from heaven shone around him. Falling to the ground, he heard a voice saying to him: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” For whatever you do by persecuting one of my faithful, know that you are doing it to me. Why do you rage in vain against my name, since long ago you killed my martyr Stephen by the hands of all the Jews? Long ago, indeed, I ought to have destroyed you, but my Stephen prayed for you.

And he said: “Who are you, Lord?” And the Lord said to him: “I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you, unbeliever, are persecuting. But rise and enter the city; there you will be told what you must do.” And when he arose, he saw nothing. Thus he was for three days without sight, and he neither ate nor drank. For a time he lost this bodily light so that through this punishment he might perceive spiritual light more truly. He lost it for three days because he had not believed that the Lord had risen on the third day.

A certain disciple of Christ named Ananias was in Damascus. The Lord said to him: “Rise, go to the street called Straight, seek Saul, approach him, and mark him with my sign, for he will suffer many things for my name.” And he said: “Lord, I have heard about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints.” The Lord said to him: “Go, for he is a vessel chosen for me, to carry my name among the nations before kings and rulers of the earth.”

His pride was therefore struck down so that humility and the devotion of obedience might be raised up in him. His vices had now been struck down so that holiness might be raised up. Ananias therefore came, baptized the impious Saul, and made Paul a devout preacher for us; he baptized a wolf and made him a lamb. Afterward we began to have as a preacher the one whom previously we had had as a persecutor. See how, in the evening, he divided the spoils.

For he immediately began everywhere to preach Christ, whom previously he had vigorously opposed. Now Paul suffered what Saul had done: Saul stoned Stephen; Paul was stoned for Christ. Saul beat Christians with rods; Paul received five times forty lashes less one for Christ, so that he might again be beaten for Christ. Indeed, all the punishments that he had previously inflicted upon the faithful, he himself endured for Christ in much greater tortures.

If we consider it, dearest ones, Christ is our way. Look to Christ: he came to suffer, but also to be glorified; to be despised, but also to be exalted; to die, but also to rise again. Thinking on these things, dearest brothers, let us not despair, because although we are sinners, we have a great physician. Hear the physician himself: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”

The benefit of this event is the following. The apostle himself recalls in his letters that forgiveness of all his sins was granted to him for this purpose: so that no one who has been entangled in great sins and ensnared in great crimes may despair of himself, as though he would not receive forgiveness if he turned to the one who, hanging on the cross, prayed for his persecutors, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”

He who had been a persecutor became a preacher and teacher of the nations. “For previously,” he says, “I was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man.” You see his desert: punishment is due. Therefore punishment is not repaid, but he obtains mercy in place of punishment. For by grace we are saved from our sins, through the generosity of our Lord himself, who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY CXII. ON THE SAME FEAST

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Matthew.

“At that time, Simon Peter, answering, said to Jesus: ‘Behold, we have left everything and followed you; what therefore will there be for us?’” etc.

Then Peter answered and said: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you; what therefore will there be for us?” Great confidence! Peter was a fisherman; he had not been rich. He sought his food by hand and by skill, and yet he speaks confidently: “We have left everything.” And because merely leaving is not enough, he adds what is perfect: “and we have followed you.” We have done what you commanded; therefore what reward will you give us?

But Jesus said to them: “Amen I say to you, that you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

He did not say, “You who have left everything”—for the philosopher Socrates did this too, and many others despised riches—but “you who have followed me,” which properly belongs to the apostles and believers. “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty”: when the dead rise incorruptible from corruption, you too will sit on thrones of judgment, condemning the twelve tribes of Israel because, while you believed, they did not wish to believe.

Here we learn that Jesus will judge with his disciples. Hence elsewhere he said to the Jews: “If I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they themselves will be your judges.”

Nor, because he says that they will sit upon twelve thrones, should we think that only twelve men will judge with him. For by the number twelve a certain totality of judges is signified, because of the two parts of the number seven, by which universality is usually signified. These two parts—that is, three and four—multiplied one by the other make twelve. For four times three and three times four are also twelve, as are other signs of this number twelve that reason discovers to be relevant here.

Otherwise, since we read that Matthias the apostle was appointed in the place of Judas the betrayer, where will the apostle Paul, who labored more than all of them, sit to judge? Yet he plainly shows that he belongs with the other saints to the number of judges when he says: “Do you not know that we will judge angels?”

The same reasoning applies to those who are to be judged in this number twelve. For because it is said, “judging the twelve tribes of Israel,” we should not suppose that the tribe of Levi, which is the thirteenth among them, will not be judged, or that they will judge only that people and not the other nations as well.

When he says “in the regeneration,” there is no doubt that by the name of regeneration he intended the resurrection of the dead to be understood. Thus our flesh will be regenerated through incorruption, just as our soul has been regenerated through faith.

“And everyone who has left a house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields, for the sake of my name, will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life. But many who are first will be last, and the last first.”

This passage agrees with that saying in which the Savior declares: “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. For I have come to separate a man from his father, and a daughter from her mother, and a daughter-in-law from her mother-in-law; and a man’s enemies will be those of his household.”

Those who, therefore, for the sake of faith in Christ and the preaching of the Gospel have despised all affections, as well as the riches and pleasures of the world, will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life.

Taking this saying as an occasion, some introduce a thousand years after the resurrection, saying that then a hundredfold of everything we have left, together with eternal life, will be returned to us. They do not understand that, if the promise is worthy in other respects, it becomes shameful with regard to wives, so that whoever has left one wife for the Lord would receive a hundred in the future.

The meaning, therefore, is this: whoever has left carnal things for the Savior will receive spiritual things, which in comparison and according to their worth will be as though a hundredfold number were compared with a small number. Hence the Apostle also says that he who had left one house and the small fields of one province was as having nothing and possessing everything.

For whoever has God favorable toward him and has served him rightly will suffer no lack of anything that pertains to salvation. Rather, through him he will have suitable consolation in this world and will possess eternal joy in the life to come, through Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY CXIII. THE SEVENTH WEEK AFTER PENTECOST

Reading from the Epistle of Paul to the Romans.

“Brothers, all of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death. For we have been buried with him through baptism into death,” etc.

You heard, dearest brothers, the Apostle saying in the present reading: “Or are you unaware that all of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death? For we have been buried with him through baptism into death.” Thus, just as Christ rose from the dead on the third day, so also we, plunged into the water and made dead to the world and to the devil, and buried with Christ, are raised from the font after the third immersion as though Christ were rising: new and undefiled, having laid aside the filth of all sins.

“So that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life.” Baptism is understood in Scripture in three ways: baptism of water; of the Holy Spirit, who, like fire, consumes all sins; and of blood in martyrdom, poured out for the name of Christ. Concerning this the Savior says: “I have a baptism with which I am to be baptized in my blood.” He shows that we are baptized for this reason: that through the mystery we may be buried with Christ, dying to our crimes and renouncing our former life. Thus, just as the Father was glorified in the resurrection of the Son, so after baptism Christ may be glorified by all through the newness of our conduct, so that not even the signs of our former wickedness may be recognized in us. Nor should we desire or seek anything that those who are still entangled in the errors of their former life desire or seek.

“For if we have been grafted together in the likeness of his death, we will also be so in the likeness of his resurrection.” If we die to the world and its desires, and now desire to be buried with Christ in the death of sin, then in the death of our body we will deserve to share in his resurrection. And if in this life we are new and changed, remaining in holy conduct, we will be new and changed with Christ in eternal glory.

Knowing this, that our old man was crucified together with him. The Apostle says that all Christ’s faithful were crucified together with Christ. Previously, before renouncing sin and the service of the devil, they sinned by imitating the old man Adam; but through the renunciation of vices and through baptism [lacuna] because they have become members of Christ’s body through the mystery of the holy washing.

Christ hung his innocent body so that we might suspend our guilty body from vices, so that the body of sin might be destroyed and we might no longer serve sin. This means that all the vices we committed after baptism must be completely destroyed through pure confession and true repentance, together with the generosity of almsgiving, because one vice is a member of sin. Just as Christ was crucified whole, not in part, so, as we have said, through confession it is necessary that the whole body of sin be destroyed in us, so that our flesh may become a slave to righteousness, whereas it had been accustomed to be a slave to wrongdoing. For everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.

For he who has died to sin through confession and hatred of sin has been justified from sin. He is altogether dead who does not sin; and he who has been crucified to sins through repentance, through grief and contrition for sin, will scarcely be able to sin again.

But if we have died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him. If we have not died with Christ, we will not live with Christ, because we are not his members.

Knowing that Christ, rising from the dead, no longer dies, death will no longer rule over him. So also, if here we have died to sins by our will, we do not fear a second death, nor will we be held by Gehenna.

For he died to sin once; that is, we cannot be baptized in water again, because Christ cannot be crucified again for us. As it is said elsewhere: “For it is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, who have also tasted the heavenly gift and have become participants in the Holy Spirit, to be baptized again,” because that passage does not deny repentance but denies the repetition of baptism.

But what lives, lives for God, in the glory of divinity.

So also you should consider yourselves dead to sin—if you have confessed purely—but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord, in good works and holy conduct, with God’s mercy protecting you. To him be honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY CXIV. ON THE SAME FEAST

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Matthew.

“At that time, Jesus said to his disciples: ‘Amen, I say to you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven,’” etc.

That is, unless you fulfill not only those least commandments of the Law that initiate a person, but also these commandments that I add—I who have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it—you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.

The righteousness of the Pharisees is that they do not kill. The righteousness of those who are to enter the kingdom of God is that they do not become angry without cause. It is therefore a small thing both not to kill, and for one who violates that commandment to be called least in the kingdom of heaven. But whoever fulfills it by not killing will not immediately be great or fit for the kingdom of heaven; nevertheless, he has ascended one step. He is perfected if he does not become angry without cause. If he has perfected this, he will be much farther from homicide. Therefore he who teaches us not to become angry does not abolish the commandment against killing; rather, he fulfills it, so that outwardly, by not killing, and inwardly, by not becoming angry, we may preserve innocence.

“You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not kill; whoever kills will be liable to judgment.’” For in the Law it was decreed that whoever killed should himself be killed.

“But I say to you.” That is: “I speak new things to you, new people.” “For everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment.” We must consider how great the difference is between the righteousness of the Pharisees and that of Christians, which introduces one into the kingdom of heaven. There, killing makes one liable to judgment; here, anger likewise makes one liable to judgment.

“Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ will be liable to the council.” This word properly belongs to the Hebrews. For *raca* is called κήναι—that is, “empty” and “void”—whom we may call, in ordinary abuse, “brainless.” If we will have to give an account of an idle word, how much more of an insult? It is also significantly added, “whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca.’” For no one is a brother except one who has the same father as we do. Therefore, when he likewise believes in God and knows the wisdom of God in Christ, by what reasoning can he be branded with the epithet of folly?

What is the difference between being liable to judgment, being liable to the council, and being liable to the fire of Gehenna? The last sounds most serious and indicates that certain steps have been made from lighter matters to graver ones, until one arrives at the fire of Gehenna. Therefore, if it is lighter to be liable to judgment than to be liable to the council, it is likewise lighter to be liable to the council than to be liable to the fire of Gehenna.

It must therefore be understood that becoming angry with one’s brother without cause is lighter than saying “Raca,” and again that saying “Raca” is lighter than saying “Fool.” For guilt itself would not have degrees unless sins too were mentioned by degrees.

“Raca” is obscure, since it is neither Greek nor Latin. Some have wished to derive its interpretation from Greek, thinking that it means “ragged,” for in Greek a rag is called *rachus*. More probably, however, it is said to be a word signifying nothing other than an expression of an indignant movement of the spirit, like the interjections among grammarians, when someone in grief says “Alas!” or someone in anger says “Hem!” Such words belong properly to their respective languages and are not easily transferred into another language. This is what compelled both the Greek and Latin translator to place the word itself, since they could not find how to interpret it.

There are therefore degrees in these sins. First, someone becomes angry and retains the movement in his heart, conceived in his mind. If the indignant emotion then forces out a sound—not signifying anything, but by its very eruption testifying to the movement of the spirit by which the person against whom he is angry is struck—that is certainly more serious than if the anger were suppressed in silence. But if not only the sound of indignation is heard, but also a word that clearly indicates and marks the insult directed against the person to whom it is spoken, who would doubt that this is more serious than if only the sound of indignation were uttered?

Thus in the first there is one thing alone: anger. In the second there are two: anger and a voice signifying anger. In the third there are three: anger, a voice signifying anger, and in the voice itself an expression of a definite insult.

Now consider also the three liabilities: judgment, council, and the fire of Gehenna. In judgment, room is still given for a defense. In the council, although judgment also ordinarily takes place, the distinction itself compels us to acknowledge that something different is meant here. It appears to pertain to the council’s determination, when the matter is no longer being debated with the accused as to whether he should be condemned, but those who judge discuss among themselves by what punishment one who is known to be condemnable ought to be condemned. Gehenna, however, involves neither a condemnation still in doubt, as judgment does, nor merely the punishment of one already condemned, as the council does. In Gehenna both the condemnation and the punishment of the condemned are certain.

The name *Gehenna* is composed of *ge* and *henna*. For *ge* is interpreted as “valley,” while Gehenna means “a fertile valley.” It was the Valley of the Sons of Hinnom beside Jerusalem, in which many corpses of the dead lay. Hence the Gehenna of hell appropriately corresponds to the name.

“If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there you remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go first to be reconciled with your brother, and then come and offer your gift.”

He did not say, “If you have something against your brother,” but “If your brother has something against you,” so that a more demanding necessity of reconciliation might be imposed upon you. Therefore, as long as we cannot appease him, I do not know whether we can fittingly offer our gifts to God. He teaches, certainly, that one who is unreconciled with his brother cannot rightly offer the sacrifice of peace to the Lord.

If it comes to mind that a brother has something against us—that is, if we have injured him in some way—then the brother has something against us. For we have something against him if he has injured us, in which case there is no need to go to reconciliation. You will not ask forgiveness from one who has wronged you; you merely forgive him, just as you desire the Lord to forgive what you yourself have committed.

Therefore, when it comes to mind that we may have injured our brother in some way, we must proceed to reconciliation—not with bodily feet, but with the movements of the heart—so that with humble affection you may prostrate yourself before your brother, running toward him in loving thought, in the presence of the one to whom you are about to offer your gift.

Spiritually, our temple is the inner person; the altar is faith; the gift is prophecy, teaching, prayer, hymn, psalm, and anything of that kind among spiritual gifts. Thus, even if your brother is physically present, you will be able to calm him with a sincere heart and restore him to favor by asking forgiveness, if you have first done this before the Lord, going toward him not with the sluggish movement of the body but with the swiftest affection of love.

Then, returning from there—that is, recalling your intention to what you had begun to do—you will offer your gift. For every gift that anyone offers to God with right faith and perfect love is graciously received by him, and he himself will grant the giver a worthy reward in the heavenly kingdom: he who lives and reigns, God, in perfect unity and Trinity, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY CXV. ON THE OCTAVE OF THE APOSTLES

Reading from the Book of Ecclesiasticus.

“These are men of mercy, whose righteousness has not been forgotten. Their good works remain with their offspring; their inheritance is holy; their descendants endure, and their seed stands firm in their covenants. Their children remain forever because of them; their generation and their glory will not be abandoned. Their bodies are buried in peace, and their names will live for ages. All peoples will recount their wisdom, and the whole assembly of the saints will proclaim their praise.”

These words of the wise man apply not only to the holy apostles and prophets but also to all the saints and faithful who, holding the catholic faith, do not cease daily to exercise themselves in good works through devout labor. They provide not so much for themselves, by living well in order to obtain eternal rest, as they strive to make God’s will known to all their hearers, so that through right faith and good works they may strive to reach perpetual salvation.

“These,” he says, “are men of mercy,” who through right faith and good works have earned the Lord’s mercy. For his mercy is from generation to generation toward those who fear him. Their good deeds were not without recompense; and, together with their offspring—that is, the worshipers of the one God who became the descendants and heirs of their faith and religious conduct—the covenant of God’s Law stood firm, and the offspring of their descendants remained for a long time because of their merits. The glory of the holy fathers will not be erased by any forgetfulness, but their bodies, resting in peace, await the day of resurrection so that they may receive the glory of incorruption. Their name remains renowned among their descendants, who everywhere proclaim their wisdom and daily exalt their praiseworthy life with great praises in the assembly of the saints.

According to the historical sense, these things appear to pertain to the patriarchs and prophets, whose offspring—that is, the Israelites—were often delivered from distress because of their merits and the promises made to them, and obtained forgiveness of sins not through their own righteousness but through the faith and good works of their ancestors.

Hence there is that passage in which Moses, praying for the same sinful Israelite people, calls to mind Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, to whom the promises had been given, so that, appeased by their merits, the Lord might grant indulgence to their sinful children. Likewise, David’s merit assists his children in many matters; because of his memory, the Lord also preserved the kingdom for his children for a very long time.

In a more sacred sense, however, the men of mercy are the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ and the preachers of the New Testament. Through the word of the Gospel and holy baptism they daily beget children worthy of God; having become imitators of their parents, these follow the examples of their faith and conduct. Their bodies, certainly, after the end of the present life, sleep in the hope of resurrection, awaiting future glory, when the seed of their good works will be rewarded with a heavenly recompense by the supreme Judge, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God for ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY CXVI. ON THE SAME FEAST

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Matthew.

“At that time, Jesus ordered his disciples to get into the boat and go ahead of him across the strait, until he dismissed the crowds,” etc.

He commands the disciples to cross and compels them to get into the boat. By this wording it is shown that they departed from the Lord unwillingly, since out of love for their teacher they did not wish to separate from him.

Why he compelled the disciples to enter the boat, and why he himself, after dismissing the people, immediately went up into the mountain to pray, John clearly declares. After completing that heavenly meal, he immediately adds: “When Jesus therefore knew that they were about to come and seize him and make him king, he fled again into the mountain, alone.” Here he shows us a necessary example for living: in the good things we do, we should avoid the reward of human favor, and the performance of spiritual virtues should not turn us toward the desire for temporal pleasures.

For it has happened to some that, while through the merit of a higher life they were admirable and praiseworthy to those of lesser standing and were rightly thought worthy of honor, they lost the beginnings of their justice after receiving money or estates. When, through carelessness, they corrupted themselves with carnal enticements and greed, they came to be regarded by those who had honored them for their good deeds as objects not only of disgust but even of hatred because of their evil actions.

It is far less dangerous to be wearied by the wickedness of adversaries in the things we do rightly than to be caressed by the favor of those who honor us. The latter often corrupts the soul when it feels secure; the former always makes it watchful and cautious.

Thus, when announcing to us the way of life that we should follow, the Lord, when those who admired his virtues wanted to make him king, fled into the mountain to pray. But when those who envied his virtues were planning to hand him over to death, he came forward readily and offered himself to the enraged men to be bound and crucified.

By this evident example he instructs us to be ready to endure the adversities of the world, cautious about avoiding its flatteries whenever they smile upon us, and to ask the Lord in frequent prayers that the prosperity of the world, should it abound, may not soften and deceive us.

That the disciples went ahead of the Lord, Mark shows. He relates that the Lord compelled his disciples to get into the boat and go ahead of him across the strait to Bethsaida while he dismissed the people.

Bethsaida is therefore a city in Galilee belonging to the apostles Andrew, Peter, and Philip, near the lake of Gennesaret, as we find in the books of *Locations*. Here it is worth considering how Mark says that, after the miracle of the loaves had been completed, the disciples came across the strait to Bethsaida, when Luke appears to say that the memorable miracle and heavenly meal took place in the region of Bethsaida.

For he says: “Taking them, he withdrew privately into a deserted place that is Bethsaida.” When the crowds learned this, they followed him, and he received them, and so forth, through the remainder of that sacred account of the meal.

Unless perhaps we understand that when Luke says “into a deserted place that is Bethsaida,” he does not designate the vicinity of the city itself but the deserted places belonging to it. For Mark clearly says that they were to go ahead of him to Bethsaida, where it is evident that the boundaries of the city itself are indicated.

Luke, however, who says “into a deserted place that is Bethsaida,” can, if I am not mistaken, rightly be understood not to mean Bethsaida itself but its deserted place—that is, a place belonging to its boundaries.

The Evangelist John, moreover, relates that the crowds ate bread near Tiberias, and that the disciples, having boarded the boat, came across the sea to Capernaum. Both are cities in Galilee beside the lake of Gennesaret, which is also called the Sea of Tiberias after the city of Tiberias.

And dismissing the crowd, he went up onto the mountain to pray alone. If the disciples Peter, James, and John, who had seen the glory of the Transfigured One, had been with him, perhaps they would have gone up the mountain with him. But the crowd could not follow to the heights unless he had first taught it beside the sea on the shore and fed it in the wilderness. That he went up alone to pray, however, should not be referred to the one who fed five thousand men from five loaves, women and children excepted, but to the one who, after hearing of John’s death, withdrew into solitude. This does not mean that we separate the Lord’s person, but that his works are divided between God and man. Here it should be noted that not everyone who prays ascends the mountain: there is a prayer [Col. 0363D] that produces sin; but the one who seeks God by praying prays well. Advancing here from earthly things to higher ones, he ascends to the summit of a loftier concern. But the person who pleads anxiously over wealth, worldly honor, or even an enemy’s death, lying in weakness, sends worthless prayers to God. The Lord prays, not to plead for himself, but to obtain favor for me. For although the Father has placed everything under the Son’s authority, the Son nevertheless, in fulfilling the form of a human being, considers that the Father should be entreated on our behalf, because he is our advocate. “We have an advocate with the Father,” John says, “Jesus Christ.” If he is an advocate, he must intercede for my sins; therefore he pleads not as one weak, but as one compassionate. Would you know that he can do everything [Col. 0364A], and that he is both advocate and judge? In the one role there is the duty of compassion; in the other, the mark of power.

But when evening came, he was there alone. Meanwhile the boat was being tossed about in the middle of the sea by the waves, for the wind was against them. It was rightly as though the Apostles, unwilling and holding back, had withdrawn from the Lord, lest, in his absence, they suffer shipwreck. Indeed, while the Lord remained on the mountain’s summit, the contrary wind immediately arose, the sea was disturbed, the Apostles were endangered, and the threatening shipwreck continued for as long as Jesus did not come. The disciples’ labor in rowing, and the contrary wind that opposed them, signify the various labors of the holy Church, which amid the opposing waves of the world and the blasts of unclean spirits strives to reach the repose of the heavenly homeland, as though a secure anchorage on the shore. [Col. 0364B] It is rightly said that the boat was in the middle of the sea while he himself was on land, because sometimes the Church is so afflicted and even defiled by the pressures of the nations that, if it were possible, her Redeemer might seem for a time to have utterly abandoned her. Hence comes her voice, caught amid the waves and storms of sweeping temptations and seeking the help of his protection with a mournful cry: “Why, Lord, do you stand far off? Do you disregard in times of need, in tribulation?” This also sets forth the voice of the enemy pursuing her, as the same psalm continues: “For he said in his heart, ‘God has forgotten; he has turned his face away, so as never to see.’” Yet he does not forget the prayer of the poor, nor does he turn his face away from those who hope in him. [Col. 0364C] Rather, he helps those struggling with their enemies so that they may conquer, and crowns the victorious eternally. Hence in this passage it is also appropriately said through Mark that he saw them laboring at the oars. The Lord sees his own laboring on the sea, although he is situated on land; and even if he should seem to delay lending aid to the afflicted for a time, nevertheless, out of regard for his compassion, he strengthens them so that they do not fail amid tribulations. At times, too, by manifest assistance, once adversities have been overcome, he frees them—as though he were trampling down and stilling the billowing waves—as is subsequently indicated here when it says:

But during the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking upon the sea. Military stations and watches are divided among the intervals of the hours. Therefore, when it says that the Lord came to them during the fourth watch of the night, it shows that they had [Col. 0364D] been in danger throughout the entire night and that help was granted them at the night’s final hour. They labor, then, throughout the whole darkness of night; but as dawn approaches, and the morning star promises the rising of the sun and the day, the Lord comes and, walking upon the swollen surface of the sea, presses it down. For when fragile humanity, burdened by afflictions, considers the weakness of its strength, it sees nothing around itself except the darkness of distress and the heat of hostile forces contending against it. But when it raises its mind toward the light of heavenly protection and the gifts of eternal recompense, it suddenly sees, as though amid the shadows of night, the rising of the morning star that announces the coming day. The morning star, it is said, illuminates for nearly three hours of the night—that is, the entire morning watch. [Col. 0365A] The Lord will be present, granting to those whose temptations have been lulled a full confidence in freedom through his protection.

It follows:

And when they saw him walking upon the sea, they were troubled, saying, “It is a phantom.” If, according to Marcion and Manichaeus, our Lord was not born of a virgin but appeared as a phantom, why are the Apostles now afraid that they are seeing a phantom? Even now the heretics suppose that the Lord was a phantom and did not truly assume flesh from the virgin. Indeed, Theodorus Pharanitanus, once a bishop, wrote that the Lord, according to the flesh, did not possess bodily weight, but walked upon the sea without weight or body. In opposition to this, the Catholic faith proclaims both that he possessed weight according to the flesh and that he bore a bodily burden, [Col. 0365B] and that, with bodily weight and burden, he walked upon the waters without sinking his feet into them. For Dionysius, an eminent ecclesiastical writer, speaks in this way in his treatises On the Divine Names: “For we do not know how he was formed from virginal blood by another law beyond nature, nor how, without sinking his feet, he walked upon the fluid and unstable substance while possessing bodily weight and material burden.”

It must therefore be considered how Mark says that, around the fourth watch of the night, the Lord came to them walking upon the sea and wished to pass them by. But how did the Lord wish to pass them by as though they were strangers, when he had come to free them from the danger of shipwreck? Unless it was so that, after being troubled [Col. 0365C] and frightened for a moment but immediately delivered, they might marvel more greatly at their rescue and offer greater thanks to their rescuer. For amid the storms of sufferings inflicted by the faithless against the steadfastness of faith, such providence is sometimes revealed by God. Often the divine compassion has seemed to abandon the faithful who are placed in tribulation, so that Jesus might be thought to have wished to pass by the disciples laboring on the sea. Hence comes the Church’s cry as she sweats through the contest of martyrdom: “Why have you forgotten me? Why have you rejected me? And why do I go about sorrowfully while my enemy afflicts me and all my bones are crushed?” Yet let the enemies who terrify them say, “Where is their God?” As though announcing shipwreck to the exhausted Apostles, their God himself says: “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you, and the rivers [Col. 0365D] will not overwhelm you. When you walk through fire, you will not be burned, and the flame will not consume you.”

What follows—“and because of fear they cried out”—is a confused cry and an uncertain voice, an indication of great fear. But the Psalmist’s testimony is true: “The Lord is near to those who fear him,” and he does not abandon all who hope in him. Hence it is added:

Immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying, “Take courage; it is I; do not be afraid.” He cures what was foremost in the matter and commands those who were afraid, saying, “Take courage.” “Do not be afraid”; and when he adds, “It is I,” he does not specify who he is. Either they could recognize him from his familiar voice, since he was speaking through the dark shadows of night, or they could know that he was [Col. 0366A] the one whom they knew had spoken to Moses: “You shall say this to the children of Israel: ‘He who is’ has sent me to you.”

Then Peter answered him, saying, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters.” And he said, “Come.” In every passage Peter is found to possess the most ardent faith. When the disciples are asked whom people say Jesus is, he confesses him to be the Son of God. When he intends to go to his Passion, although he errs in his action, he does not err in his affection: he does not wish the one whom he had shortly before confessed to be the Son of God to die. He ascends the mountain with the Savior among the first, and in the Passion follows him alone. The sin of denial, which arose from sudden fear, he immediately washes away with the bitterest tears. After the Passion, when he was at the lake of Gennesareth and they were fishing, while the Lord stood on the shore and the others were gradually sailing toward land, [Col. 0366B] he could not tolerate delay but, having girded himself, immediately plunged into the waves.

With this same ardor of faith by which he always excelled, he now too, while the others were silent, believed that he could do the will of his Master—something he could not do by nature. “Command me,” he said, “to come to you upon the waters.” You command, and immediately they will become solid, so that the body, which is heavy in itself, may become light.

And Peter, coming down from the boat, walked upon the water to come to Jesus. Let those who think that the Lord’s body was not real because he walked upon soft waters with a soft and aerial step answer how Peter walked, whom they certainly will not deny to have been a real human being.

But when he saw the strong wind, he was afraid; and when he began to [Col. 0366C] sink, he cried out, saying, “Lord, save me!” The faith of his spirit was burning, but human frailty was dragging him into the depths. He is therefore left for a little while to temptation, so that his faith may be increased and he may understand that he was preserved not by the ease of his petition but by the Lord’s power.

And immediately stretching out his hand, he seized him. If the Lord had not stretched out his hand—he who elsewhere looked upon Peter when he was denying him—Peter himself would immediately have sunk into the depths and would not even have escaped hell. The Lord looked upon him and turned him toward repentance; he stretched out his hand and granted pardon; and thus the disciple found perfect salvation. For, in Paul’s words, it does not depend on the one who wills or on the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy. We are not saved by our own merit, but by his gift.

And he said to him, “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” If the Apostle [Col. 0366D] Peter, whose faith and ardor of mind we have described above, confidently asked the Savior, saying, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters,” and because he was afraid for a moment was told, “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” what should be said of us, who possess not even the smallest portion of this little faith?

Mystically, however, the fact that Peter, commanded by the Lord to come, treads upon the waves of the sea in order to come to Jesus signifies the Church, of which he is the shepherd, striving toward the heavenly homeland. By the footprints of right faith and the steps of good works, she must overcome and tread beneath her feet the waves of this world. And the fact that Peter, terrified by the storm, began to sink in the waves represents the weaker members of the Church, whom the storm of persecutions or the whirlwind of temptations frightens and turns aside for a moment from the course of faith or from the practice of good works. Yet, lest they [Col. 0367A] sink completely into unbelief and the abyss of sins, the outstretched right hand of divine mercy draws them out. And just as he will set Peter, rescued from the abyssal sea, beside himself on the firm ground of heavenly repose, so he will set those rescued from the snare of persecutors beside himself. For it is impossible that any of those whom the judgment of the just Judge has predestined to eternal life should perish. Hence Truth itself says: “Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out.” For the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from temptation, and he is not powerless, amid the storms of this world, to keep his own unharmed by every wickedness of the evil.

But let us see what follows:

[Col. 0367B]

And when he had gone up into the boat, the wind ceased. The first assistance, then, given to those who are trembling and in danger is to drive fear from their hearts; the second is to restrain the violence of the storms by the power of his presence. Nor is it surprising that, when the Lord went up into the boat, the wind ceased. For in whatever heart God is present through the grace of his love, all the battles of vices, of the hostile world, and of evil spirits are immediately subdued and brought to rest.

And those who were in the boat came and worshiped him, saying, “Truly, you are the Son of God.” At the restoration of calm to the sea through a single sign—something that can sometimes happen by chance after excessive storms—the sailors and passengers confess him truly to be the Son of God, while Arius proclaims in the Church that he is a creature. Let us therefore believe and confess that he is not [Col. 0367C] a creature—as the madness of the heretics claims—created among all created things, but the Creator, existing and remaining before all things together with the Father and the Holy Spirit. In this confession, let us venerate and proclaim him with fitting praises of good works before the children of men as the only-begotten Son of God. Let us recount his powers and his wonders, he who, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY 117. WEDNESDAY

Reading from the Epistle of the blessed Apostle Paul to the Hebrews.

Brothers, we have grace by which we may serve God acceptably [Col. 0367D], with fear and reverence; for our God is a consuming fire.

Just as elsewhere he said that “the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal,” and from this he drew an argument for exhortation and consolation in view of the evils that we endure in the present time, so he does here also. He says that we must remain steadfast so that we may have grace—that is, so that we may give thanks to God. We must not only bear present evils with equanimity, but also offer him thanks for future blessings. “By which,” he says, “we may serve in a manner pleasing to God.” That is, we serve God pleasingly when thanks are rendered to him in all things. “Do everything,” he says, “without murmuring and without hesitation.” Whatever someone does while murmuring [Col. 0368A] will be cut off, and his reward will perish. Consider also what judgment the Israelites received because of their murmuring. Therefore he says, “Do not murmur.” For it does not please God when he is served with murmuring and when thanks are not rendered to him for everything—for temptations as well as for spiritual things. Let us therefore say nothing sluggish, nothing shameless, but let us submit ourselves so that we may conduct ourselves with veneration and reverence, that is, with reverence and fear of the Lord.

Let brotherly love remain, and do not forget hospitality; for through it some, by receiving angels as guests, pleased God. Observe how he commands them to keep the present commandments. He does not impose others upon them; he did not say, “Become lovers of the brethren,” but “Let brotherly love remain.” Again, he did not [Col. 0368B] say, “Become hospitable,” as though they were not already so, but “Do not forget hospitality,” since this might perhaps have happened because of their tribulations. “For through it,” he says, “some pleased God by receiving angels as guests.” Do you see how great the honor and the profit are? Or, according to another edition, “some were unaware”—that is, they received them as guests without knowing. Therefore the reward is also great for the person who received them as guests without knowing that they were angels. For if he had known, there would have been nothing remarkable. Some say that Lot is also signified in this passage.

Remember those who are imprisoned, as though imprisoned together with them; and those who suffer hardship, as though you too were remaining in the body. Marriage is honorable in all, and the marriage bed undefiled. God will judge fornicators and adulterers.

Consider [Col. 0368C] how extensively he develops his discourse on chastity. “Pursue peace,” he says, “with all people, and holiness, without which no one will see the Lord; let there be no fornicator or polluted person among you.” And again, “God judges fornicators and adulterers.” But let us now see how he says that marriage is honorable in all and the marriage bed undefiled, since he evidently makes the faithful person live in the holiness of chastity. Here he also strikes at the Jews, who thought marital intercourse polluted and said that a person who rose from the bed of his spouse could not remain clean. Therefore what is permitted by nature is not polluted, O most ungrateful and senseless Jews, but what proceeds from a depraved will. For if some marriages are honorable, they are also clean. Why, then, do you think that pollution arises from them? By first saying, [Col. 0368D] “Marriage is honorable in all and the marriage bed undefiled,” he shows that he has rightly introduced what follows. If marriage is permitted, then the fornicator is rightly punished, and adulterers are rightly punished.

Here he contends against the heretics. See how well he did not say, “Again, let no one be greedy,” but said it together with the preceding matters. Then he introduced it as a general exhortation, not as though addressing these words to them alone.

Let your conduct be free from greed, and be content with what you have. He says, “Let your conduct be free from greed.” He did not say, “Do not possess anything,” but “Let your conduct be free from greed,” thereby revealing the philosophical disposition of each person’s will. For above he had said, “You joyfully accepted the plundering of your possessions,” thereby showing that they were not devoted to greed. Rightly [Col. 0369A], therefore, he admonishes them to have sufficiency.
