He says, “Be content with what is present,” because many, after the emptying of their possessions, later desire to gather wealth again under the pretext of almsgiving. Therefore he says, “Let your conduct be free from greed”—that is, let us await what will be useful and care only for necessities. Whatever someone may say—that perhaps we may have the support of those very necessities—believe me, this is not so; it is not so.

For he himself said, “I will not abandon you, nor will I forsake you,” so that we may confidently say, [Col. 0369B] “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me.” Again, this is consolation in temptations. For he himself made the promise and immediately, in no respect lying, said, “I will not forsake you.” Therefore we can confidently say, “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me.” You have a promise; you must not hesitate. He himself promised; do not doubt. When he says, “I will not abandon you,” he is not speaking only about money, but also about everything else. “The Lord,” he says, “is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me.” And rightly so. Let us therefore cry this out amid all temptations, and, having God favorable to us, let us mock all human things. For just as nothing will benefit us if God is angry, even if all our friends stand with us, so, if God loves us, we will have no need and suffer no injury even if all our enemies pursue us with hostility. “I will not fear,” he says, “what man can do to me.”

Remember your leaders, who spoke the word of God to you; considering the outcome of their manner of life, [Col. 0369C] imitate their faith. In this passage I think he is also speaking about assistance to the brethren. For this is what he says: they spoke the word of God to you; observing the outcome of their manner of life, imitate their faith. What does “observing” mean? Turning it over frequently in the mind, examining it within ourselves, considering it, and discussing it carefully. He says, “the outcome of their manner of life,” that is, perseverance to the end, because their manner of life had a good ending. “Observing,” he says, “the excellence of their life, imitate their faith.” He says that faith is confirmed by a pure life. How? Because they believe in future things. For they would not display a pure life if they hesitated about the future.

Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today, and throughout the ages of ages. “Yesterday” signifies all past time; “today,” [Col. 0369D] the present; “throughout the ages of ages,” the future without end. It is as though he were saying: You have heard of a high priest, but not of a high priest who will cease to exist; he is always the same. It is as though there were some who said—though it is not so—that another was going to come. To this he replies that the one who was yesterday is himself today and forever. Even today the Jews say that another is going to come. Deprived of themselves and turning away from the one who is the true high priest, they have fallen into error and think that the Antichrist is going to come. Whoever follows this error, unless he corrects himself and performs worthy repentance for it, will in no way escape the torment of hell.

## HOMILY 118. ALSO WEDNESDAY

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Mark.

[Col. 0370A]

At that time, when Jesus had gone out onto the road, a certain man ran up, knelt before him, and asked him, saying, “Good Teacher, what must I do to receive eternal life?”

I believe that this inquirer after eternal life had heard from the Lord that only those who wished to become like little children were worthy to enter the kingdom of heaven. Therefore, taking care to obtain a more certain teaching, he sought to have it explained to him—not through parables, but openly—by what merits of works he could attain eternal life.

But Jesus said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except one, God.” Because he had called him a good teacher [Col. 0370B] and had not confessed him to be God or the Son of God, he learns that even a holy human being is not good in comparison with God. Of him it is said, “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good.” The one good God, however, must not be understood as the Father alone, but also as the Son, who says, “I am the good shepherd”; and also as the Holy Spirit, because “the Father from heaven will give the good Spirit to those who ask him.” That is, the one undivided Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—is the one and only good God. Therefore the Lord does not deny that he is good; he signifies that he is God. He does not testify that he is not a good teacher, but that no good teacher exists apart from God.

You know the commandments: “Do not commit adultery; do not kill; [Col. 0370C] do not steal; do not bear false witness; do not defraud; honor your father and your mother.” This is the chastity of childlike innocence, which is proposed for our imitation if we wish to enter the kingdom of God. It should certainly be noted that the righteousness of the law, when observed in its own time, conferred not only the goods of the earth but also eternal life upon those who practiced it.

And he answered and said, “Teacher, I have observed all these things from my youth.” But Jesus, looking at him, loved him and said to him, “One thing you lack.” This man should not be thought to have questioned the Lord as a test, as some have believed, or to have lied about his life when he said that he had kept the commandments of the law. Rather, he simply confessed how he had lived. For if he had been guilty of the wrongdoing of lying or pretence, Jesus would certainly not be said to have looked into the secrets of his [Col. 0370D] heart and loved him. The Lord loves those who keep the commandments of the law, even though they are lesser commandments; nevertheless, he shows those who desire to be perfect what was lacking in the law, because he came not to abolish the law or the prophets but to fulfill them. The command that he adds here next certainly belongs to that fulfillment.

Go, sell whatever you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me. Whoever wishes to be perfect must sell what he possesses, and must not sell only part of it, as Ananias and Sapphira did, but sell everything and, once he has sold it, give it all to the poor. Thus he prepares treasure for himself in the kingdom of heaven. Yet this is not sufficient for [Col. 0371A] perfection unless, after scorning riches, he follows the Savior—that is, after abandoning evil, he does good. For a purse is more easily scorned than the will. Many abandon their riches but do not follow the Lord. The one who follows the Lord is his imitator and walks in his footsteps. Whoever says that he believes in Christ ought himself to walk as Christ walked, and in this way he will reach the heavenly kingdom.

## HOMILY 119. FRIDAY

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Mark.

At that time Jesus came into the region of the Gerasenes. And as he was getting out of the boat, immediately a man with an unclean spirit came toward him from the tombs. He lived among the tombs, and so forth.

[Col. 0371B]

This man, who was tormented by an unclean spirit and, though mad before the Lord, immediately came to be healed, represents the figure of the gentile people, who, until the time of the Lord’s incarnation, deceived by demonic teachings, worshiped idols instead of God. He lived among the tombs because he delighted in dead works—that is, in sins. For what are the bodies of unbelievers except certain tombs of the dead, in which the word of God does not dwell but a soul dead through sins is confined?

And no one could now bind him, even with chains, because he had often broken the chains and shattered the fetters, and no one could subdue him. Chains and fetters signify the severe and harsh laws of the nations, by which sins are restrained even in their public administration. [Col. 0371C] After breaking the chains, as Luke writes, he was driven by the demon into the wilderness, because, even after transgressing the laws, he was led by desire toward crimes that exceeded ordinary custom.

And he was always, night and day, among the tombs and in the mountains, crying out and cutting himself with stones. The demoniac raged continually, night and day, because the gentile world—whether it was suffering under adverse circumstances or whether some peace and prosperity of the flattering world smiled upon it—did not know how to shake the neck of its mind free from the service of evil spirits. Rather, through the foulness of its works, it lay as though among tombs. Through the arrogance of pride, it wandered on the mountain peaks; [Col. 0371D] through words of the harshest unbelief, it cut itself in a frenzy with stones seized up, as it were. But, as John the Baptist bears witness, the Lord raised up children for Abraham from stones when he converted the hard hearts of unbelievers to the grace of mercy.

When he saw Jesus from far away, he ran and worshiped him; and crying out with a loud voice, he said, “What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of the Most High God?” What madness of Arius—to believe that Jesus is a creature and not God, when the demons believe that he is the Son of the Most High God and tremble! What impiety of the Jews—to say that he cast out demons by the prince of demons, when the demons themselves confess that he has nothing in common with them! The very thing that they then cried out through the demoniac’s frenzy they later did not cease to say and confess in the temples of idols: namely, that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the Most High God [Col. 0372A], and that they have no peace or fellowship with him.

I adjure you by God, do not torment me. For he was saying to him, “Come out of the man, unclean spirit.” The enemy of human salvation considers it no small torment to cease harming a human being. The longer he has been accustomed to possess someone, the more unwillingly he consents to leave him. Therefore we must strive with the greatest care so that, if at any time we human beings are overcome by the devil, we may immediately hasten to escape his snares. Otherwise, if resistance is delayed for some time, he will at length be driven out only with greater difficulty.

And he asked him, “What is your name?” And he said to him, “My name is Legion, because we are many.” He does not inquire the name as though he were ignorant, but so that, once the plague which the madman suffered had been publicly confessed, the power of the healer might shine forth more gloriously. [Col. 0372B] The priests of our own time, too, who know how to cast out demons through the grace of exorcism, commonly say that those afflicted cannot otherwise be healed unless, as far as they are able to understand, they openly disclose by confession everything that they have endured from unclean spirits—whether awake or asleep—through sight, hearing, taste, touch, or any other sense of body or mind.

But when the spirit said, “My name is Legion, because we are many,” it signifies that the gentile people were enslaved not to one particular form but to innumerable and diverse practices of idolatry. In opposition to this it is written that the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul. Thus, in the construction of Babylon, the unity of languages, divided by the spirit of pride, was scattered; but in Jerusalem, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, the diversity [Col. 0372C] of languages was united. The former is interpreted as confusion, the latter as a vision of peace, because one faith and devotion confirm that the elect, though spread among many languages and nations, are to be made peaceful throughout the whole world, while the reprobate are divided and confused by more sects than languages.

And he begged him insistently not to drive him out of the region. In Luke’s Gospel it is written, “And they begged him not to command them to go into the abyss.” The demons therefore knew that at some future time, through the Lord’s coming, they would be sent into the abyss—not because they themselves were foretelling the future, but because they remembered what the Prophets had said about them. Therefore the glory of the Lord’s coming, which they marveled at, they feared would lead to their own condemnation.

[Col. 0372D]

Now there was there, near the mountain, a large herd of pigs feeding. And the spirits begged him, saying, “Send us into the pigs, so that we may enter them.” And Jesus immediately granted their request. He permitted them what they asked so that, through the destruction of the pigs, an opportunity for human salvation might be provided; for when the herdsmen saw these things, they immediately reported them to the city. Let Manichaeus be ashamed. If the souls of human beings and beasts are of the same substance and from the same creator, how can two thousand pigs be drowned for the salvation of one human being? Yet in their destruction, human beings who are unclean and without voice or prayer are indicated figuratively. Feeding on the mountain of pride, they delight in muddy actions; and demons can dominate such people through the worship of idols. For unless someone has lived like a pig, the devil will not [Col. 0373A] receive power over him. Even when he does receive it, it is only for testing, not for destruction.

And the unclean spirits went out and entered the pigs; and the herd, numbering about two thousand, rushed down into the sea with great force, and they were drowned in the sea. This signifies that, once the Church had been glorified and the gentile people freed from the domination of demons, those who refused to believe in Christ practice their sacrilegious rites in hidden places, having been submerged by blind and profound curiosity. It should also be noted that the unclean spirits would not have gone even into the pigs unless the merciful Savior himself, when they asked, had granted them permission—although he could have banished them into the abyss. He wished to teach us something necessary: namely, that we should know how much less they can harm human beings by their own power, since they were unable to harm even animals of any kind. God, in his goodness, can give us this power through hidden justice; [Col. 0373B] he cannot give it through injustice.

But those who tended them fled and reported the matter in the city and in the countryside. The fact that the swineherds fled and reported these events signifies that some leaders of the impious, although they flee the Christian law, nevertheless continue to proclaim its power in amazement and wonder.

And they went out to see what had happened. They came to Jesus and saw the man who had been tormented by the demon sitting, clothed, and in his right mind, and they were afraid, and so forth. In Luke’s Gospel it is written that he was sitting at his feet. This signifies that the multitude, delighted by its ancient pleasures, indeed pays honor, but does not wish to endure the Christian law. They say that they cannot fulfill it, yet they marvel at the faithful people healed from their former ruined manner of life. To sit at the Lord’s feet means to observe, with fixed attention of mind, the footsteps of the Savior from whom the demons had departed, so that those who have been corrected from their sins may follow them. To put on clothing means to take up again, with a sound mind, the practice of virtues that the madman had lost.

This figure is aptly matched by the Lord’s parable in which the returning prodigal and dissolute son is immediately clothed with the first robe and the ring. It clearly suggests that anyone who truly repents from the heart of his offenses can, by the grace of Christ, recover the first works of righteousness from which he had fallen, together with the ring of inviolate faith.

[Col. 0373D]

And they began to beg him to depart from their borders. The Gerasenes, conscious of their weakness, judged themselves unworthy of the Lord’s presence. They could not comprehend the word of God, nor could their still feeble minds bear the weight of wisdom. The same thing is also said to have happened to Peter when he saw the miracle of the fish, and to the widow of Sarepta, who experienced the blessing of the hospitality of blessed Elijah but nevertheless thought herself burdened by his presence. “What have I to do with you,” she said, “man of God? You have come to me so that my iniquities might be remembered and my son killed.”

And as he was getting into the boat, the man who had been tormented by the demon began to beg him to let him remain with him. But he did not permit him; rather, he said to him, “Go to your house and to your own people, and announce to them how much the Lord has done for you and how he has had mercy on you.” These words can rightly be understood in light of the Apostle’s statement [Col. 0374A]: “I desire to depart and be with Christ, which is much better; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake.” Thus each person should understand that, after receiving remission, he must return to a good conscience and serve the Gospel for the salvation of others also, so that afterward he may rest with Christ. He must not, by wishing too hastily to be with Christ, neglect the ministry of preaching, which is directed toward the redemption of the brethren.

But why does Matthew say that two men were healed from the demonic legion, while Mark and Luke mention one? You should understand that one of them was a person of greater distinction and fame, whom that region especially mourned and for whose salvation it exerted itself greatly. The two Evangelists, wishing to indicate this, judged that only he should be mentioned [Col. 0374B], since the fame of what had happened to him had spread more widely and more brilliantly. The overall allegory also agrees, because just as one possessed man represents the gentile people, so two men can appropriately signify two gentile peoples. For although Noah fathered three sons, only one family was admitted into God’s possession; from the other two were born peoples of various nations enslaved to idols. Nevertheless, those among them who came to the faith of Christ and were washed from sins in his baptism deserved to become sharers in the kingdom of God, according to the Savior’s judgment: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned.” Through the same Lord.

## HOMILY 120. THE EIGHTH WEEK AFTER PENTECOST

Reading from the Epistle of the blessed Paul to the Romans.

[Col. 0374C]

Brothers, I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. For just as you presented your members as servants to impurity and iniquity, leading to iniquity, so now present your members as servants to righteousness, leading to sanctification, etc.

The great concern and care for your salvation, and your devotion to eternal progress before God, urge us to discuss with you briefly the apostolic reading that you have heard. “I speak in human terms,” he says, “because of the weakness of your flesh,” since you are not yet able fully to hear divine things. Or else I speak in a manner suited to human reasoning, which everyone can understand with me, so that no one may reject it. “For just as,” he says, “you presented your members as servants to impurity and iniquity, leading to iniquity, so now present your members as servants to righteousness, leading to sanctification.”

It is certainly disgraceful for someone to serve virtues in the same way as vices; righteousness, after all, deserves to be honored much more and much more earnestly. Therefore he says that he is speaking humanly. “If, then,” he says, “I act in a human and ordinary manner, I ask for the same things and require similar conduct.” Formerly, then, the feet of our ancestors ran to the temples of demons; let our feet now run to the Church of God. Let the feet that once willingly ran to shed the blood of a neighbor now run much more willingly to deliver a neighbor. Let the hands that were once swift to seize another’s property now be much swifter to give away their own. Let the eyes that once gazed upon the beauty of women, or upon something belonging to another, in order to covet it, now look much more intently upon the poor, the weak, and the needy, so as to show compassion. Let the ears that delighted in hearing empty talk now turn to hearing the word of God, explaining divine commands, and acquiring the discipline of wisdom. Let the tongue that was accustomed to insults, curses, or shameful speech now turn to blessing God; let it always speak sound and honorable words that build up those who hear, abandon falsehood, and speak the truth with its neighbor.

But why pursue each point individually, when it is clear to everyone what service belongs to each member, and that whatever someone formerly offered to vices he should now strive to adapt to virtues and works of righteousness? Let the act that he formerly offered to adultery be wholly turned now toward chastity and sanctification. Thus let all the members that formerly depended upon serving iniquity, through this conversion proposed for the better, depend upon serving righteousness and sanctification. It continues:

> For when you were servants of sin, you were free from righteousness.

That is, you were alienated from all righteousness, since it is not acceptable to God to serve righteousness and sin at the same time. Hence it continues:

> What fruit, then, did you have at that time in those things of which you are now ashamed?

The recollection of these things brings the greatest shame to those who love righteousness and truth. For everyone who recognizes or loves goodness is ashamed of his evil deeds.

**[Col. 0375C]**

> For the end of those things is death.

That is, their recompense is everlasting punishment.

> But now, having been freed from sin and having become servants of God, you have eternal fruit in sanctification, and the end is eternal life.

It should be noted that there is a blameworthy freedom—being alienated from works of righteousness—and a praiseworthy servitude—servitude to righteousness leading to sanctification. Whoever is a servant of righteousness is free from sin, and at the same time is a servant of wisdom and piety, modesty and chastity, and every virtue; their end, that is, their recompense, is eternal life.

Therefore, brothers, we must examine ourselves unceasingly in each thing we have done or are doing, and in every action consider whom we are serving: whether sin, leading to iniquity and destruction for ourselves unless we abandon it quickly, or righteousness, leading to sanctification and to earning for ourselves the joys of eternal life. For unless we first die to sin through repentance, we cannot live to God through righteousness.

**[Col. 0375D]**

> For the wages of sin is death.

Unless sin is destroyed through confession, repentance, and generous almsgiving, it receives its recompense: eternal punishment.

> But the grace of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

It is rightly added, “eternal life in Christ Jesus,” because those who rise to confusion and everlasting disgrace do indeed have eternal life, but in confusion and eternal punishment. The righteous, however, who rise to everlasting joys have eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord, possessing eternal joys with him, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY CXXI. ALSO AS ABOVE. Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Mark

At that time, when a great crowd was with Jesus and they had nothing to eat, he summoned his disciples and said to them: “I have compassion on the crowd, because, behold, they have already been with me for three days and have nothing to eat; and if I send them away fasting, they will collapse on the way,” etc.

In this reading we must consider, in one and the same Redeemer, the distinct operation of divinity and humanity. For who does not see that the Lord’s compassion for the crowd, lest they should fail either from hunger or from the exertion of a longer journey, is an affection and compassion belonging to human weakness? But that he fed four thousand people with seven loaves and a few small fish is plainly a work of divine power.

Mystically, however, this miracle signifies that we cannot cross the road of the present age safely in any other way unless the grace of our Redeemer refreshes us with the nourishment of his word. The typological difference between this feeding and that of the five loaves and two fish is that there spiritual grace was signified as being full in the books of the Old Testament, whereas here the truth and grace of the New Testament are shown to be supplied to the faithful.

Both feedings, as the account of the other Evangelists makes clear, took place on a mountain, because, rightly understood, the Scripture of both Testaments proclaims with harmonious voice both the height of heavenly commands and the height of rewards, and proclaims Christ as their height—Christ who is the mountain, the house of the Lord at the summit of the mountains. He who raises on high the city or house of the Lord—that is, the Church—built upon himself by the loftiness of good works, and displays it openly to all nations, himself refreshes it, having drawn it away from lowly pleasures, with the bread of heaven and, by giving the pledge of spiritual food, kindles its desire for heavenly sweetness.

> I have compassion on the crowd, because, behold, they have already been with me for three days and have nothing to eat.

The crowd remains with the Lord for three days because of the healing of its sick, when each of the elect, enlightened by faith in the Holy Trinity, perseveres in earnest prayer to the Lord for the sins of himself and his own—that is, for the sicknesses of their souls. Again, the crowd remains with the Lord for three days when the multitude of the faithful, turning away through repentance from the sins it has committed, converts itself in deed, speech, and thought.

> And if I send them away fasting to their homes, they will collapse on the way.

The Lord does not wish to send them away fasting to their homes, lest they collapse on the way. For converted sinners plainly collapse on the road of the present life if they are sent away in their own conscience without the holy nourishment of instruction. Therefore, lest they grow weary on the journey of this pilgrimage, they must be fed with sacred admonition.

> For some of them have come from far away.

There is one who, having experienced no deceit and no carnal corruption, hastened to the service of almighty God. He did not come from far away, because through incorruption and innocence he was near. Another, stained by no impurity and no disgraceful acts, but having experienced marriage alone, was converted to spiritual service. He too did not come from far away, because, having used a permitted union, he did not go astray through unlawful practices.

Others return to repentance after sexual offenses, others after false testimonies, others after committing thefts, others after inflicting violence, and others after committing murders; they turn to the service of almighty God. These indeed come to the Lord from far away. For the more someone has gone astray in an evil deed, the farther he has withdrawn from almighty God.

Let nourishment therefore also be given to those who come from far away, because food of holy instruction must be offered to converted sinners, so that they may seize from God the strength they lost in their offenses.

Likewise, those Jews who believed in Christ came to him from nearby, because they had been instructed about him through the letters of the Law and the Prophets. But those who believed from among the Gentiles certainly came to Christ from far away, because they had not been forewarned of his faith by any records of the sacred writings.

And his disciples answered him: “Where can anyone satisfy these people with bread here in the wilderness?” And he asked them: “How many loaves do you have?” They said: “Seven.”

The seven loaves are rightly understood as belonging to the ministry of the New Testament, in which the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit is more fully revealed to all the faithful for belief and given to those who believe. They are not reported to have been barley loaves, as were the five by which five thousand people were fed, lest once again, as under the Law, the life-giving nourishment of the soul be hidden beneath bodily sacraments; for the marrow of barley is covered by an extremely tough husk.

And he commanded the crowd to sit down upon the ground. Above, in the feeding of the five loaves, the crowd sat upon green grass. Now, when it is to be refreshed with seven loaves, it is commanded to sit upon the ground, because through the Scripture of the Law we are commanded to trample down and restrain the desires of the flesh:

> All flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass.

In the New Testament, however, we are also commanded to abandon the earth itself and temporal possessions. Or certainly, because the mountain on which the crowd was refreshed with the Lord’s loaves signifies, as we said above, the height of our Redeemer, there the crowd is refreshed upon grass, here upon the ground. There, the loftiness of Christ is covered, on account of carnal people and earthly Jerusalem, by carnal hope and desire; here, with every carnal appetite removed, the guests of the New Testament were held by the firmness of abiding hope, like the solidity of the mountain itself, with no grass interposed.

And taking the seven loaves, giving thanks, he broke them and gave them to his disciples to set before the people; and they set them before the crowd. The Lord took the loaves and gave them to his disciples so that they themselves might set before the crowd what they had received, because, granting the Apostles spiritual gifts of knowledge, he wished the nourishment of life to be distributed throughout the world to his Church through their ministry.

That he broke the loaves which he was to give to the disciples signifies the opening of the mysteries by which the world was to be nourished for eternal salvation. For the Lord himself says:

> No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.

By this he showed that the bread of life must be opened to us by him, since we cannot penetrate by ourselves to behold its interior. Concerning this, the Prophet, lamenting the extraordinary hunger of certain people, said:

> The little ones asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them.

In other words, the unlearned sought the nourishment of God’s word, by which they might be refreshed and strengthened for the practice of virtue, but, when teachers were lacking, there was no one to disclose the secrets of Scripture to them and instruct them in the way of truth.

When the loaves were received for breaking, the Lord gave thanks, both to show how much he rejoiced in the salvation of the human race and to teach us always to give thanks to God, whether we refresh the flesh with earthly bread or the soul with heavenly grace bestowed from above.

And they had a few small fish, and he blessed them also and commanded them to be set before the people. If the seven loaves signify the Scripture of the New Testament, in whose reading we find, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, inward feasts for our minds, whom should we understand by the fish, which the Lord likewise blessed and commanded to be set before the crowd, except the saints of the time in which that Scripture was composed, or those whose faith, life, and sufferings that Scripture itself contains? Rescued from the turbulent waves of this age and consecrated by divine blessing, they supplied us with inward refreshment, lest we should fail in the course of this passing world, by the example either of their life or of their death.

And they ate and were satisfied. They eat of the Lord’s loaves and fish and are satisfied who, hearing the words of God and contemplating examples, hasten to be awakened and rise toward the improvement of their lives through these things. To them the Psalmist’s statement appropriately applies:

> The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and they shall praise the Lord, etc.

And they took up what remained of the fragments, seven baskets. What remains after the crowds have been satisfied the Apostles take up and fill seven baskets, because there are higher commands—or rather exhortations and counsels—of perfection, which the general multitude of the faithful cannot reach by observing and fulfilling them. Their execution properly belongs to those who, filled with a greater grace of the Holy Spirit, surpass the general people of God in the loftiness of their way of life in mind and deed.

To such people it is said:

> If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have, etc.

Thus the baskets in which the fragments of the Lord’s food were stored are rightly said to have been seven, on account of the sevenfold grace of the Spirit. Since baskets are usually woven from rushes and palm leaves, they are rightly used as a sign of the saints. The rush, indeed, commonly grows upon waters, while the palm adorns the victorious hand.

The elect are rightly compared with vessels of rushes when they place the root of their heart at the very source of life, lest it wither away from the love of eternity. They are likewise compared with things woven from palm leaves when, in their very failing, they retain in a pure heart the memory of eternal reward.

The crowd is rightly said to have eaten and been satisfied, although it could not contain the remnants of the Lord’s meal, because there are some who, although unable to abandon all that they possess, nevertheless hunger and thirst for righteousness and are satisfied when, by hearing the commandments of God’s Law, they attain eternal life.

The four thousand are also fittingly mentioned, so that by this number itself they might be taught that they had been fed with Gospel nourishment by our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY CXXII. WEDNESDAY. Reading from the Epistle of the blessed Apostle Paul to the Romans

**[Col. 0379B]**

Brothers, there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, etc.

There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed me from the law of sin and death. From this it is understood that the daily grace of Christ frees all the saints from this law of sin and death, into which they continually fall, even unwillingly, when they ask the Lord to forgive and release them from their debts.

It therefore appears that the blessed Apostle uttered this statement not in the person of sinners, but in the person of those who are truly holy and perfect:

> For I do not do the good that I wish, but the evil that I hate is what I do; and I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members.

“For the law,” he says, “of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed me from the law of sin and death.”

Here he gives great assurance, because what was impossible for the Law, in which it was weakened through the flesh, God accomplished by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and, because of sin, condemning sin in the flesh. He says this to make the baptized secure, since they have been freed from sin. “What was impossible,” he says, “for the Law”—for whom was it impossible? It was impossible for us to fulfill the commandment of the Law, because we were subject to sin—God accomplished so that the justification of the Law might be fulfilled in us who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.

Through this sacrifice of the flesh, which was offered for sin, he condemned sin—that is, he drove sin away and removed it—so that the justification of the Law might be fulfilled in us who keep the Law according to the Spirit and not according to the flesh. In this respect, according to what we explained above, the Law was impossible and weak.

For the Lord’s death accomplished this: death was no longer to be feared, and therefore temporal goods were no longer to be desired nor temporal evils feared. In these things was that carnal wisdom by which the commandments of the Law could not be fulfilled. But when this wisdom was extinguished and removed in the Lord’s human nature, the righteousness of the Law is fulfilled when one does not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.

Thus it was said most truly:

> I have not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it.

The fullness of the Law, therefore, is love, and love belongs to those who walk according to the Spirit. These things belong to the grace of the Holy Spirit. When there was not the love of righteousness but fear, the Law was not fulfilled.

Therefore he says that sin was condemned so that the justification of the Law given through Moses might be fulfilled in us. For, removed from the condition of the Law, we have become its friends; those who are justified are friends of the Law.

But how is justification fulfilled in us except when the forgiveness of all sins is granted? Once sins have been removed, the justified person appears, in mind, to serve the Law of God—that is, not to walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit—so that the devotion of the soul, which is spirit, does not consent to the desire of sin, because through the flesh the desire of the soul, which is sin, is sown.

Those who are according to the flesh understand the things of the flesh; but those who are according to the Spirit perceive the things of the Spirit. Here, placing the Law of Moses, as it were, between us and the Jews, he says: “Those who are according to the flesh understand the things of the flesh,” that is, the Jews, whom he calls Israel according to the flesh, understand the things of the flesh insofar as they understand the Law according to the flesh.

But when he says, “Those who are according to the Spirit perceive the things of the Spirit,” he is speaking of those whom he calls Jews in spirit, not in letter.

For the wisdom of the flesh is death, but the wisdom of the Spirit is life and peace in Christ Jesus our Lord. Is it not one and the same thing that he says: “The wisdom of the flesh is death”? To whom is it death? To the soul, undoubtedly. For whoever understands the Law according to the flesh—that is, according to the letter—does not come to Christ, who is life. Therefore the wisdom of the flesh is death.

But the wisdom of the Spirit is life and peace, for whoever understands the Law spiritually and fulfills through good works what he rightly understands to have been commanded to him in God’s commandments possesses the life and peace that is Christ. With Christ himself granting it, he will reign in eternal life, Christ who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY CXXIII. ALSO WEDNESDAY. Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Matthew

At that time the Pharisees and Sadducees approached Jesus, testing him, and asked him to show them a sign from heaven, etc.

They ask for a sign from heaven because, just as he had twice fed many thousands of people with a few loaves, they now wanted him, following the example of Moses, to refresh the whole people for a long time with manna sent from heaven and scattered everywhere. In the Gospel according to John we read that, after the feeding with bread, the crowds asked this of him, saying:

> What sign, then, do you perform, so that we may see and believe you? What do you work? Our fathers ate in the wilderness, as it is written: He gave them bread from heaven to eat.

But he answered them: “In the evening you say, ‘It will be fair weather, for the sky is red’; and in the morning, ‘Today there will be a storm, for the sky is red and gloomy.’ You know how to judge the appearance of the sky, but you cannot judge the signs of the times?”

According to the historical sense, the meaning is clear: fair and rainy days can be predicted from the order and harmony of the elements. But the scribes and Pharisees, who appeared to be teachers of the Law, could not understand the Savior’s coming from the prophecies of the Prophets.

Spiritually, however, when the Lord said, “In the evening you say, ‘It will be fair weather, for the sky is red,’” he signifies that through the blood of Christ’s Passion the forgiveness of sins is given at his first coming. And when he says, “In the morning, ‘Today there will be a storm, for the sky is red and gloomy,’” he signifies that at his second coming he will arrive with fire going before him.

“You know how to judge the appearance of the sky, but you cannot judge the signs of the times.” By “the signs of the times” he meant the signs of his coming or Passion, to which the rosy evening sky is similar, and likewise the tribulation that will occur before his coming, to which the rosy morning sky with its gloom is similar.

An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah. A sign is therefore not given to that generation—that is, to those who test the Lord and insult his words—of the kind they were seeking, namely, a sign from heaven, although he was giving them many heavenly signs on earth.

To the generation that seeks the Lord and searches for the face of the God of Jacob, however, he displayed a sign from heaven when, in the sight of the Apostles, he ascended into heaven; when, after sending the Spirit, he filled the first Church; and when, at the laying on of the Apostles’ hands in Samaria, Caesarea, Ephesus, and many other cities and places, he supplied from heaven the grace of the Holy Spirit to those who believed.

What the sign of Jonah means has already been stated above. It continues:

And leaving them, he went away. Leaving the scribes and Pharisees, to whom he had said, “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah,” he rightly crossed the lake, and the people followed him from among the Gentiles.

And when his disciples had come across the lake, they had forgotten to take bread. Someone may ask how they had no bread when, immediately after the seven baskets had been filled, they went up into the boat and came to the region of Magadan, where they heard, while sailing, that they should beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees. But Scripture testifies that they had forgotten to take it with them.

That they forgot to take provisions with them when they were about to cross the lake indicates how little care they had for the flesh. The very necessity of refreshing the body, which naturally belongs to all mortals, had slipped from their minds because of their attention to the Lord’s company.

The one loaf that they had with them in the boat mystically signifies the Lord himself, the bread of life, namely, the Savior. Because they were continually refreshed inwardly in their hearts by love for him, they cared less about the earthly bread by which the body is usually nourished.

He said to them: “Pay attention and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” In Mark it is written: “See and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod.”

The leaven of the Pharisees is to place the decrees of the divine Law after human traditions, or certainly to preach the Law in words while opposing it by one’s deeds. The leaven of the Sadducees is to test the Lord and to believe neither his teaching nor his works, but, by insulting him, to ask for other things in which they should believe. The leaven of Herod is adultery, murder, rashness in swearing oaths, religious pretense, and—what is the head and source of every crime—hatred and persecution of Christ and of his forerunner and first herald of the heavenly kingdom.

Against the leaven of both, the Apostle also prohibits us, saying:

> Therefore let us celebrate the feast, not with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

But they were thinking among themselves, saying: “Because we did not take bread.” Knowing this, Jesus said: “Why are you thinking among yourselves, you of little faith, because you have no bread? Do you not yet understand, nor remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you took up? Nor the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many baskets you took up? Why do you not understand that I did not speak to you about bread when I said, ‘Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees’?”

Taking the opportunity provided by the command in which the Savior had ordered them, saying, “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod,” he teaches them what the five loaves and the seven loaves, or the small fish, signify, and what is signified by the five thousand and the four thousand who were fed in the wilderness. Although the greatness of the signs is evident, spiritual understanding reveals another meaning.

For if the leaven of the Pharisees, the Sadducees, and Herod does not signify bodily bread but perverse traditions and heretical doctrines, why should the foods with which the people of God were nourished not signify true and complete teaching?

Marcion and Valentinus, and all the heretics, possessed this kind of leaven, which must be avoided in every way. Leaven has this power: if it is mixed with flour, what appeared small grows larger and draws the whole lump toward its own taste. So too, if heretical teaching casts even a small spark into your heart, in a short time a great flame will grow and draw the whole possession of the person toward itself.

This is what the Apostle also says:

> A little leaven corrupts the whole lump.

Then they understood that he had not told them to beware of the leaven of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees. He persuaded them of what was useful and commanded them to avoid what was harmful. Superstitious and heretical teaching weighs down more than it helps; it sinks rather than raises up.

Thus, instructed by the good Teacher, the disciples understood that in the leaven the deception of the Pharisees and Sadducees—indeed, of all heretics who hold opinions contrary to the truth—was expressly represented and had to be avoided. They themselves avoided it altogether and judged that we too must flee from it, so that, scorning every error and following the way of truth in all things, we may hasten to escape eternal punishment and earn eternal life, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY CXXIV. FRIDAY. Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Matthew

**[Col. 0383A]**

At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath; his disciples, being hungry, began to pluck the ears of grain and eat, etc.

As we read in another Evangelist, because of the crowd's excessive importunity they did not even have an opportunity to eat, and therefore they were hungry like other human beings. That they rubbed the ears of grain in their hands and relieved their hunger is an indication of a stricter way of life: they sought not prepared dishes but simple foods.

But the Pharisees, seeing this, said to him: “Behold, your disciples are doing what is not lawful for them to do on the Sabbath.”

Note that the first Apostles of the Savior destroy the literal observance of the Law on the Sabbaths, against the Ebionites, who accept the other Apostles but reject Paul as a transgressor of the Law.

But he said to them: “Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him—how he entered the house of God and ate the bread of the Presence, which was not lawful for him to eat, nor for those who were with him, but only for the priests?”

To refute the Pharisees’ accusation, he recalls the ancient history of David, when, fleeing from Saul at Nob, he was received by the priest Ahimelech and asked for food. Since he had no ordinary bread, Ahimelech gave him consecrated bread, which no one except the priests and Levites was permitted to eat. He asked only whether they were pure from women.

When David answered that they had been so since yesterday and the day before yesterday, he did not hesitate to give them the bread, judging that, as the Prophet says, “I desire mercy and not sacrifice,” it was better to free people from the danger of hunger than to offer sacrifice to God; for a sacrifice pleasing to God is the salvation of human beings.

The Lord therefore puts forward this argument and says: If David is holy and the high priest Ahimelech is not reproached by you, but both transgressed the commandment of the Law with a plausible excuse, and hunger was the reason, why do you not approve the same hunger in the Apostles that you approve in others?

There is, moreover, a great difference here. These men rub ears of grain with their hands on the Sabbath; those men ate Levitical bread. And the days of the new moons, on which they approached the solemnity of the Sabbath, were at hand when he, summoned to a feast, fled from the royal court.

Observe that neither David nor his young men took the bread of the Presence before they answered that they were pure from women.

Or have you not read in the Law that on the Sabbaths the priests in the temple violate the Sabbath and are without guilt? You slander my disciples, he says, because, passing through the grainfields, they rubbed the ears of grain, and they did this because hunger compelled them. Yet you yourselves violate the Sabbath in the temple by sacrificing victims, slaughtering bulls, burning burnt offerings in the fire upon a heap of wood, and, according to the testimony of another Gospel, circumcising infants on the Sabbath. While you wish to keep one law, you destroy the Sabbath.

The laws of the Lord are never opposed to one another. Wisely, then, where his disciples could be accused of transgression, he cites the examples of David and Ahimelech. But he attributes a true violation of the Sabbath, without the excuse of necessity, to those who had made the accusation.

But I say to you that here is something greater than the temple. “Here” should be read not as a pronoun but as an adverb of place: the place that contains the Lord of the temple is greater than the temple.

If you had known what this means—“I desire mercy and not sacrifice”—you would never have condemned the innocent. We explained above what “I desire mercy and not sacrifice” means. What follows, “you would never have condemned the innocent,” is to be understood of the Apostles.

The meaning is this: You approved Ahimelech’s mercy because, when David was endangered by hunger, he refreshed him and his young men. Why, then, have you not shown similar compassion to my disciples when they suffer from hunger, although they feed you daily with the bread of heavenly speech, so that, filled by its satisfaction, you may be able to attain everlasting life? This is granted by our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY CXXV. NINTH WEEK AFTER PENTECOST. Reading from the Epistle of the blessed Apostle Paul to the Romans

Brothers, we are debtors not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live, etc.

**[Col. 0384C]**

In the reading you have heard today, the blessed Apostle teaches us most openly, beloved brothers, that we must not serve the desires of the flesh, saying: “Therefore, brothers, we are debtors not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh.” God did not make us in his image so that we should be subject to the service of the flesh, but rather so that the soul, serving its Creator, might use the flesh itself through that service and ministry.

But perhaps someone may ask how we are not debtors to the flesh, since the necessity of nature compels us to provide it with food and clothing. The Apostle therefore added this to show that he does not mean that providing something for the flesh as necessity requires is blameworthy, but that surrendering life itself to the desires of the flesh is blameworthy: “For if you live according to the flesh, you will die.”

To live according to the flesh is to indulge carnal desires. In this respect, then, the Apostle denies that we are debtors, just as he says elsewhere:

> Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires.

He certainly does not deny that care must be taken for the flesh in the necessities of life; rather, he forbids consenting to its desires.

It continues: “But if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live.” Whoever therefore lives according to spiritual desires and puts to death the actions of his flesh lives because of the Spirit of life dwelling within him.

But in what way can someone put to death the actions of the flesh? The fruit of the Spirit is love; hatred is an action of the flesh. Hatred is therefore put to death and extinguished by love. Joy in God is likewise a fruit of the Spirit. The sorrow of this world, which produces death, is an action of the flesh; it is therefore extinguished if perfect joy in God is present in us.

Peace is a fruit of the Spirit; disagreement and discord belong to the flesh. It is certain that discord can be put to death through peace. Chastity and self-control are fruits of the Spirit; adultery and fornication belong to the flesh. It is true that lust can be put to death through self-control, and evil deeds—adulteries and fornications—can be cleansed.

Likewise, repentance [perhaps: patience] extinguishes impatience, kindness destroys wickedness, gentleness kills ferocity, and chastity kills immodesty. In this order, whoever puts to death the actions of the flesh through the Spirit will live. It continues:

> For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.

Those who are in sins are led by the spirit of the Devil; but those who are deemed worthy to be governed by the Holy Spirit, and who live according to the teaching of the Holy Spirit, are led by the Spirit of God.

For you have not received the spirit of servitude again in fear—not that spirit in which you should serve the Lord only in fear, but the law by which you should serve God rather through love. Yet there is a spirit of servitude in fear, which is the beginning of wisdom and knowledge of God. When someone first begins to fear the Lord and resist the Devil, he must serve the Lord in this spirit of fear at the beginning of a good way of life, like a child under tutors, so that he may learn to fear the Lord and keep his commandments, until he reaches maturity in good works and deserves to receive the spirit of adoption and already to be a son of God through his habitual good works, as the same Apostle says in what follows:

But you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons of God, so that we may no longer serve God through fear of punishment, but with pure and perfect love, which casts out the previously mentioned fear. When, therefore, through repentance and confession we have died to sins and have ceased to be what we were—slaves of sin—serving him through habitual works of piety and righteousness, then, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, we may deserve both to be called and actually to be sons of God.

In him we cry, “Abba, Father.” For now, through the sanctification of the Holy Spirit, whom we deserve to have dwell within us by good and holy conduct, we have the confidence to call God our Father, since we recognize ourselves to be his sons in the fulfillment of his will [Col. 0385D]. Let us therefore perform every good work we can with single-hearted devotion, so that we may prove ourselves to be God’s sons, serving in love and no longer in fear. For whoever calls him “Father” professes himself to be a son. A son must therefore be found pleasing through the character of his fathers, lest, even on account of the name which he has presumptuously assumed, he be subjected to a greater punishment.

For the Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are sons of God. Indeed, that Spirit of servitude through which we served the Lord only in fear bears witness to the Spirit of adoption, in which we have served God perfectly through love: that we are sons of God. For only the sons of God deserve to receive the pledge of his Spirit.

[Col. 0386A] But if sons, then heirs—heirs, indeed, of God, and fellow-heirs with Christ. A slave awaits a wage, but a son hopes for an inheritance. Let us therefore strive not to remain servants of the Lord through fear, but to do every good thing through love of the Father, so that we may deserve to possess the inheritance of incorruption and immortality, together with eternal glory, and also to attain what the Savior himself adopted for us from the Father, saying: “Father, I desire that where I am, there my ministers also may be.”

In this way Christ brings his fellow-heirs not only to a share in the inheritance, but also into fellowship with eternal blessedness. To him be honor, praise, and thanksgiving, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY CXXVI, ALSO AS ABOVE

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Matthew.

[Col. 0386B]

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves,” and so forth.

This can indeed be understood of all who promise one thing in appearance and speech but demonstrate another in their conduct. More particularly, however, it must be understood of heretics, who seem to wrap themselves in a garment of piety through continence, chastity, and fasting, while inwardly possessing a poisoned mind and deceiving the hearts of their simpler brothers. They are therefore compared to ravenous wolves because of the fruits of their souls by which they drag the innocent to ruin.

“A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a bad tree [Col. 0386C] bear good fruit.” Let us ask the heretics, who say that there are two natures opposed to one another: if, according to their understanding, a good tree can never bear bad fruit, how was Moses, a good tree, to sin at the waters of contradiction? And how did David, after Uriah had been killed, lie with Bathsheba? How also did Peter deny God during the Passion, saying, “I do not know the man”? Or by what reasoning did Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law—a bad tree who certainly did not believe in the God of Israel—give good counsel to Moses? And did Achior say something useful to Holofernes? Did the comic poet say what the Apostle confirms as well said: “Bad conversations corrupt good morals”? And when they have found nothing to answer, we shall add that Judas too, once a good tree, bore bad fruit after betraying the Savior, while Paul, a bad tree when he was persecuting the Church of Christ, later bore good fruit when he was transformed from a persecutor into a vessel of election.

A good tree, therefore, will not bear bad fruit so long as it perseveres in the pursuit of goodness; and a bad tree remains in the fruits of sin so long as it does not turn to repentance. For no one, while remaining in what he was, begins to be what he had not yet begun to be.

“Every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.” For every wicked person who is not found to have produced the fruit of a good work is uprooted from the land of the living by the forceful sentence of judgment and thrown into the fire of Gehenna.

[Col. 0387A] “Therefore, by their fruits you will know them.” What, then, are the fruits by which we may recognize a bad tree when they are found? The Apostle says: “The works of the flesh are manifest: fornications, uncleanness, licentiousness, the service of idols, sorceries, enmities, quarrels, rivalries, hostilities, dissensions, heresies, envies, drunkennesses, revelries, and things like these, which I warn you of, as I warned you before, because those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God.”

And what are those by which we recognize a good tree? The same Apostle immediately says: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control,” and so forth.

“Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father [Col. 0387B] who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven.” The kingdom of heaven is not obtained by verbal service alone, nor will those who say, “Lord, Lord,” be his fellow-heirs. What merit is there in saying “Lord” to the Lord? Will he not be Lord unless he is called so by us? And what sanctity of service lies in pronouncing a name, when the path to the heavenly kingdom is to be found rather in obedience to the will than in naming God?

Therefore, just as he had said above that those who wore the garment of a good life were not to be received because of the wickedness of their doctrines, so now, conversely, he asserts that faith is not to be granted even to those who possess integrity of faith but live shamefully and destroy the integrity of their teaching by evil works. Both things are necessary for God’s servants: that deed be confirmed by speech and speech by deeds. To this judgment the statement may seem contrary: “No one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit.”

But it is customary in Scripture to understand words as standing for deeds, as is immediately confirmed by what follows, when those who boast of knowing the Lord through their works are rejected and hear from the Savior: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity; I do not know you.” The Apostle expresses this meaning: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him.”

For, according to the Savior’s judgment, the one who rightly believes God’s commandments, completes them through good works, and teaches them to others will be called great in the kingdom of heaven. But the one who teaches and does not do them will be called least in the kingdom of heaven.

## HOMILY CXXVII, WEDNESDAY

Reading from the Epistle of blessed Paul the Apostle to the Romans.

[Col. 0387D]

Brothers, if, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us, much more, now that we have been justified by his blood, shall we be saved from wrath through him, and so forth.

He says this because, if God permitted his Son to be killed for sinners, what will he do for the justified except preserve them from wrath—that is, keep them safe from the devil’s assault? Thus they may be secure on the day of judgment, when vengeance begins to devastate the faithless. Since God’s goodness wishes no one to perish, he gave the most worthy death, so that, for those who understand God’s grace toward them, he might increase dignity and glory.

Those are ungrateful who resist when God calls, rejecting God’s grace so that they may remain in their chosen error and wickedness. I certainly do not think that Paul’s variation of words is purposeless [Col. 0388A], when he sometimes calls those for whom Christ died “weak,” sometimes “ungodly,” and sometimes “sinners.” Although he confesses himself unskilled in speech, I do not think that in this matter he displayed lack of skill; rather, he varied his language out of profound knowledge.

For through these three terms every kind of sin is gathered. Someone may be ignorant of God and unwilling to keep his commandment, overcome by the weakness of the flesh and deceived by the attractions of the present life; such a person is called weak. Or someone may knowingly and willingly despise the commandment, hate God’s discipline, and cast his words behind him; such a person is called a sinner.

Thus Paul, who—as we said—professes himself unskilled in speech, has embraced in these three distinctions the whole class of those for whom Christ is proclaimed [Col. 0388B] to have died.

If at times even those who are under the Law and appear to worship God are called ungodly in the divine Scriptures, this is because, abandoning the God of their fathers, they worship the gods of the nations. But when Paul counts himself among sinners, although he says to others, “We are Jews by nature and not sinners from the nations,” this is the virtue of his humility. For he imitates the one who, though he had not committed sin, became sin for us, and, though he was God, lived among human beings.

“God commends his love in us.” Here he commends, confirms, and makes his love evident through the benefits he has bestowed. For the fact that Christ died for us while we were still sinners gives us hope that he will save us from the wrath [Col. 0388C] that threatens sinners, now that we have been cleansed and justified from sin through him. He loved strangers and enemies so greatly that he gave his only Son to death for us; much more, now that we have become his own and have been reconciled to him, will he grant us eternal salvation.

“Much more,” he says, “now that we have been justified by his blood, shall we be saved from wrath through him.” Above he had said: “Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace with God.” Now he says: “Much more, now that we have been justified by his blood, shall we be saved from wrath through him.”

From this he shows that neither does our faith justify us without Christ’s blood, nor does Christ’s blood justify us without our faith. Yet, from both together, Christ’s blood justifies us much more than our faith does. Therefore it seems to me that, although above he simply said, “Justified by faith,” here he added, “Much more, therefore, now justified by his blood” [Col. 0388D], in order to teach that, even if our faith saves us from the coming wrath, and even if works of righteousness do so, nevertheless, above all these things, Christ’s blood will save us much more from the wrath to come.

For if, when we had been reconciled, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved by his life. It is clear that if, in order to reconcile us to himself, God handed his Son over to death, how much more will he save those who have been reconciled through his life.

If the Savior’s death benefited us, how much more will his life benefit us when he rises from the dead? For just as his death rescued us from the devil, so his life will free us on the day of judgment.

Christ, therefore, died for the ungodly, and Christ is God. How will he not reign, found righteous in the life of God, when the ungodly was sought out so that he might not perish through the death of God? [Col. 0389A] We shall be saved in the life of God, because in our own life we had perished.

But when we hear both of God’s life and God’s death, let us distinguish what belongs to each. He brought us life; he received death from us—not, however, on account of his own merit, but on account of ours. For we too, he says, “were by nature children of wrath, like the rest.”

When human beings were in this wrath through original sin, all the more grievously and perniciously because they added greater or more numerous sins besides, a mediator was necessary—that is, a reconciler—who would appease this wrath by the offering of a singular sacrifice, of which all the sacrifices of the Law and the Prophets were shadows.

When God is said to be angry, this does not signify a disturbance in him such as exists in the mind of an angry human being. Rather, through a word transferred from human emotions, his vengeance—which is never anything but just—has received the name “wrath.”

[Col. 0389B] Through the mediator, therefore, we are reconciled to God and receive the Spirit, so that from enemies we may become sons of God. “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God.” This is the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

“For if,” he says, “when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved by his life.” And so forth.

It is clearly shown that there is no substance which, according to the definition of Marcion and Valentinus, is naturally hostile to God. Otherwise, if what is hostile were so by nature and not by will, those who are hostile to God would certainly have no reconciliation. But when someone who was an enemy becomes a friend, it is clear that, while he performs the works God does not love, he is an enemy of God; and each person becomes God’s enemy as gravely and hatefully as he multiplies works deserving of enmity.

[Col. 0389C] There are therefore certain measures and degrees among sins, distinguished by their quality and quantity, and those who are enemies of God possess them. Hence the one who sinned above all others is remembered by Paul as the last enemy to be destroyed.

Conversely, and in due order, those who have been reconciled through the death of his Son are certainly counted among his friends. Someone may be as much a friend as Moses, who was called God’s friend. There are also others to whom the Savior says: “I no longer call you servants, but friends.”

I believe that there are still more intimate friends in heaven with God: either those who always see the face of God, or those who always stand in the presence of the Most High. As we said above, there is a certain last enemy; so, according to the merits of their virtues, there are also some highest friends and others who are later in rank.

[Col. 0389D] Since these things are so, I do not know whether someone who still persists in the works God hates, and on account of which there is enmity between God and human beings, can rightly be said to have been reconciled to God through Christ’s blood. For how has one who is an enemy been reconciled?

Paul therefore rightly says both of himself and of those like him: “When we were enemies, we were reconciled through the blood of his Son.” It is a great shame, where such reconciliation has been made—where enmity between God and human beings has been removed not by the sinner’s speech but by the mediator’s blood—to return again to enmity [Col. 0390A] and to do what he hates, the one who reconciled us to himself only through the outpouring of sacred blood.

“Not only this, but we also glory in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.” He teaches us to give thanks to God not only for the salvation and security we have received, but also to glory through Jesus Christ in God, who has deigned to call us, though ungodly and enemies, his friends. Thus we may rejoice that we have obtained every benefit through Christ, and because through him we have come to know the Lord, we may glorify him and render him honor equal to that given to God the Father, as he himself testifies by proclaiming: “That they may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.” He lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY CXXVIII, ALSO ON WEDNESDAY

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Mark.

[Col. 0390B]

At that time John said to Jesus: “We saw someone casting out demons in your name, one who does not follow us, and we forbade him,” and so forth.

John, loving the Lord with exceptional devotion—and therefore worthy of being loved in return—thought that one who did not use the office should be excluded from the benefit. But the Lord teaches that no one should be kept from the good which he possesses in part; rather, he should be encouraged toward what he does not yet possess.

For it follows:

“But Jesus said: ‘Do not forbid him, for no one who performs a mighty deed in my name can quickly speak evil of me. For whoever is not against you is for you.’”

[Col. 0390C] Taught by this saying, the Apostle says: “Whether Christ is proclaimed in pretense or in truth, I rejoice in this, and I will also rejoice.”

Although he rejoices even over those who proclaim Christ insincerely, and although people of this kind may sometimes perform signs in Christ’s name and, for the sake of others’ salvation, may be judged not to be prevented, such signs do not give them a secure conscience. On the contrary, on that day, when they say, “Lord, Lord, in your name we prophesied, in your name we cast out demons, and in your name we performed many mighty works,” they will receive the answer: “I never knew you; depart from me, you who work iniquity.”

Therefore, in heretics and evil Catholics we must not detest or forbid the common sacraments in which they are with us and are not against us, but rather the division contrary to peace and truth by which they are against us and do not follow the Lord.

[Col. 0390D] “For whoever gives you a cup of water in my name, because you belong to Christ—truly I tell you, he will not lose his reward.”

We read in the prophet David, “to provide excuses for sins,” because many put forward apparently just reasons for their sins, so that what they do voluntarily may appear to be done from necessity. But the Lord, who searches the heart and the kidneys and observes the future thoughts of each person, had said: “Whoever receives one little child in my name receives me.”

Someone might make this excuse and say: “I am prevented by poverty; my small means hold me back, so that I cannot practice hospitality.” [Col. 0391A] He removes this excuse with a very slight command, so that we may offer a cup of water—and, according to Matthew, even cold water—with our whole heart. He says “cold water,” not hot water, so that poverty and lack of firewood might not be offered as an excuse in the case of hot water.

The Apostle likewise commands something of this kind to the Galatians: “Let the one who is instructed in the word share all good things with the one who instructs him.” He encourages disciples to provide refreshment for their teachers. And because someone could in any way plead [perhaps: “pretend”] poverty and evade the command, before presenting it he removes the impending objection, saying: “Do not be deceived; God is not mocked. For whatever a person sows, that he will also reap.”

“And whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it is better for him if a millstone [Col. 0391B] were fastened around his neck and he were thrown into the sea.”

Although this can be a general judgment against all who cause anyone to stumble, according to the sequence of the passage it may also be understood as spoken against the Apostles. They were arguing among themselves about which of them was greater, and, if they had persisted in this fault, they could have destroyed by their scandal those whom they were calling to the faith, since they would see the Apostles fighting among themselves for honor.

When he says, “It is better for him if a millstone were fastened around his neck,” he speaks according to the custom of the province. Among the ancient Jews this was the punishment for greater crimes: people were thrown into the depths with a stone fastened to them.

Indeed, it is better for an innocent person to end bodily life through a punishment, however atrocious but nevertheless temporary, than to earn the perpetual death of the soul by harming a brother.

[Col. 0391C] The person who can be caused to stumble is rightly called “little.” One who is great does not depart from the faith whatever he sees or suffers; but one who is small and little in spirit seeks opportunities to be scandalized. For this reason we must take special care of those who are little in faith, lest they be offended by our example, depart from the faith, and fall away from salvation.

It should certainly be noted that in our good works we must sometimes avoid causing a neighbor to stumble, while at other times we must disregard it as nothing. Insofar as we can do so without sin, we ought to avoid causing our neighbors to stumble. But if a stumbling block is created by the truth, it is better to permit the stumbling block to arise than to abandon the truth.

[Col. 0391D] Likewise, the millstone signifies the circuit and labor of secular life, while the depth of the sea indicates the final condemnation. As for one who has been led to the appearance of holiness but destroys others either by word or by example, it would certainly have been better if earthly actions had bound him beneath an outward appearance and brought him to death, than that he should make sacred offices, through his guilt, an unavoidable example to others. For if he fell alone, the punishment of hell would torment him in some degree more bearably.

“And if your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life maimed than, having two hands, to go into the unquenchable Gehenna.”

Since above he had taught us not to cause those who believe in him to stumble [Col. 0392A], he now accordingly warns us how greatly we must beware of those who strive to cause us to stumble—that is, to drive us toward the ruin of sin by their word or example.

He calls our hand a necessary friend, whose work and assistance we need daily. But if such a person wishes to harm us in the matter of the soul, he must be excluded from our companionship, lest, if we wish to share in this life with one who is ruined, we should perish together with him in the future.

What follows is:

“Where their worm does not die and the fire is not extinguished.”

[Col. 0392B] In the worm he signifies the rottenness of Gehenna, and in the fire its burning; or by the worm he means the belated repentance for sins, which will never cease to gnaw the conscience of the afflicted amid their torments. Thus the fire is punishment serving from without, while the worm is pain accusing from within.

“And if your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off. It is better for you to enter eternal life lame than, having two feet, to be thrown into the unquenchable fire of Gehenna.”

In the foot, as also in the hand, he teaches that dear but incorrigible persons are to be separated from us, lest, through the uncleanness of those whom we cannot correct, we ourselves should be polluted and perish. The hand refers to such persons because of their necessary work for us; the foot refers to those who are spoken of because of their service and their movement about in matters useful to us.

[Col. 0392C] “But if your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out. It is better for you to enter the kingdom of God with one eye than, having two eyes, to be thrown into the fire of Gehenna.”

In the eye also, which is to be torn out because of the stumbling block, the same persons are signified: carnally our friends, but spiritually our adversaries. We need their counsel and foresight, but they seek to deceive us with wicked advice and turn us aside onto the path of error.

The Greek word *scandalum* (“stumbling block”) may be rendered by “offense,” “ruin,” or “tripping of the foot.” We must avoid it as far as we can, so that, escaping the punishment of Gehenna, we may reach everlasting life, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY CXXIX, FRIDAY

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Matthew.

[Col. 0392D]
