At that time Jesus said to the crowds of the Jews and to the chief priests: “Woe to you, scribes and hypocritical Pharisees, because you shut the kingdom of heaven before human beings. For you yourselves do not enter, nor do you allow those entering to enter,” and so forth.

The scribes and Pharisees possess knowledge of the Law and the Prophets. They know that Christ is the Son of God; they are not ignorant that he was born of a virgin. But while the bodily advent of Christ, proclaimed by the Prophets, is concealed by a pretended doctrine, and while they seek profit from the people subjected to them, they themselves do not enter the kingdom of heaven, nor do they permit those who could enter to do so.

This is what the Lord condemns through the prophet Hosea, saying: “The priests concealed the way; they killed Shechem.” And again, the priests did not say, “Where is the Lord?” [Col. 0393A] Or certainly, every teacher who builds by his words but scandalizes his disciples through evil works shuts the kingdom of heaven before them.

“Woe to you, scribes and hypocritical Pharisees, because you travel around sea and land to make one proselyte; and when he has been made, you make him a son of Gehenna twice as much as yourselves.”

We do not preserve what we seek with the same zeal with which we seek it. The scribes and Pharisees, traveling throughout the whole world for commercial dealings and various profits—both profits to be extracted from disciples and profits sought through images of holiness—were intent on making a proselyte from the nations, that is, on taking a foreigner and one who was uncircumcised and joining him to the people of God.

But the person who, while previously a pagan, wandered simply in error and was once a son of Gehenna, seeing the vices of his teachers and understanding that by their deeds they were destroying what they taught in words, returns to his vomit. Having become a pagan, like a transgressor, he will be worthy of a greater punishment.

[Col. 0393B] He is called a son of Gehenna, just as one is called a son of destruction or a son of this age. He is called a son of Gehenna because he has been prepared for it, not generated from it. For each person is called the son of the one whose works he performs.

“Woe to you, blind guides, who say: ‘Whoever swears by the temple, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the temple is bound.’ Foolish and blind people, which is greater: the gold, or the temple that sanctifies the gold? And whoever swears by the altar, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gift that is upon it is bound.”

“Blind people, which is greater: the gift, or the altar that sanctifies the gift? [Col. 0393C] Therefore, the one who swears by the altar swears by it and by everything that is upon it. And the one who swears by the temple swears by it and by the one who dwells in it. And the one who swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by the one who sits upon it.”

Above, as it seemed to us, we explained what was signified by the Pharisees’ tradition that said, “Whatever gift is from me will profit you.” Now the Pharisees’ tradition is condemned in a twofold manner and is directed toward a single occasion of greed, so that they may be exposed as doing everything for profit and not out of fear of God.

For just as, through broad phylacteries and enlarged tassels, they sought glory through the appearance of holiness, and through the opportunity for glory sought profits, so another trick invented by their tradition exposes the teachers’ impiety.

[Col. 0393D] If someone had sworn in the temple during a dispute, quarrel, or ambiguous case, and afterward had been convicted of lying, he was not held guilty of the offense. But if he had sworn by the gold and money offered in the temple to the priests, he was immediately compelled to pay what he had sworn.

Again, if someone had sworn by the altar, no one held him guilty of perjury. But if he had sworn falsely by the gift or offerings—that is, by the sacrificial victim, victims, fine flour, and other things offered to God upon the altar—they demanded these most insistently.

The Lord therefore rebukes them both for foolishness and for fraud: the temple is much greater than the gold sanctified by the temple, and the altar is greater than the sacrifices sanctified by the altar. Yet they did everything not out of fear of God but out of desire for riches.

[Col. 0394A] Spiritually, however, the Lord’s words—“Which is greater, the gold or the temple that sanctifies the gold?” and again, “Which is greater, the gift or the altar that sanctifies the gift?”—are to be understood in this way: the temple and altar are Christ himself; the gold and gift are the praises and sacrifices of prayers that we offer in him and through him. For he is not sanctified by these; rather, these are sanctified through him.

“Woe also to you, scribes and hypocritical Pharisees, because you tithe mint, dill, and cumin, and have abandoned the weightier matters of the Law: judgment, mercy, and faith. These you ought to have practiced, without neglecting the others.”

There are many commandments in the Law that present types of future things. Others are open and illuminate the eyes, according to the Psalmist’s saying: “The commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes.” These immediately require action, for example: “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness,” and so forth.

[Col. 0394B] But because the Lord had commanded that, for the support of the priests and Levites—whose portion was the Lord—tithes of all things should be offered in the temple, the Pharisees had only this concern: that what had been commanded should be brought in. They paid little attention to whether the other, greater matters were practiced or not.

In this passage, therefore, he also accuses them of greed: they carefully demand tithes even of cheap herbs, but neglect judgment in the settlement of disputes, mercy toward the poor, orphans, and widows, and faith in God, though these are the greater matters.

“These,” he says, “you ought to have practiced”—that is, judgment, mercy, and faith—so that, truly judging our own misery and loving the love of God which he himself has bestowed, we may live piously and rightly.

[Col. 0394C] We confess his just judgment, by which we were made miserable; of this the Apostle says: “Judgment from one offense led to condemnation.” And we give thanks for his great love, of which the same Apostle, the preacher of grace, says: “God commends his love in us, because, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”

“And those others you ought not to have neglected”—that is, the almsgiving of earthly produce. Through right faith and the practice of sacred virtues, together with generous almsgiving, everyone must strive to reach eternal life, granted by the mediator of God and human beings, our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy [Col. 0394D] Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY CXXX, TENTH WEEK AFTER PENTECOST

Reading from the Epistle to the Corinthians.

Brothers, let us not be desirous of evil things, as they also desired them, and so forth.

See what a skilled physician the Apostle Paul is, a true and faithful disciple of Christ, the heavenly physician. He was sent to us by the Lord to remove our longstanding illness and restore health of body and soul within us. Throughout his preaching he has shown us the remedies that must be retained and demonstrated everywhere what is harmful and what must be avoided.

Thus, in the present reading that you have heard [Col. 0395A], under the figure of the faithless Israelite people, he admonishes us, saying: “Brothers, let us not be desirous of evil things, as they also desired them.”

For they were struck down in the wilderness because of their evil desire, so that none of that innumerable people who had come out of Egypt, except two, entered the promised land. This is something we must avoid in their example.

Egypt signifies this world. From it we have departed through renouncing the devil and all his works, and, denying all the desires of the flesh, we have promised to serve God, so that we may deserve to receive the promised land—which is the heavenly kingdom, or the land of the living—as an inheritance.

But if, in the wilderness—that is, in the vast solitude of the world—after the promise we made to the Lord [Col. 0395B] we again fall into desire for the world, we must fear lest, through a sudden interruption by death, the gate of the heavenly kingdom be closed. It is open to us so long as we remain in righteous action.

We must flee, dearest brothers, the insane desire for temporal things, which entangles a person in deadly snares, occupies and torments him in this world, and in the future delivers him over to unquenchable flames.

“Nor become idolaters, as some of them did; as it is written: ‘The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.’”

For we know that an idol is nothing except empty superstition and an offense against God. Whoever worships idols worships the devil and gravely offends God [Col. 0395C]. Hence the idolater is said to be like it, as is the one who trusts in it; yet the idol passes away in a single moment, while the punishment prepared for those who worship idols will never pass away but is eternal.

“Nor let us commit fornication, as some of them committed fornication, and twenty-three thousand fell in one day.”

Fornication likewise belongs to the worship of idols, when the creature is worshiped instead of the Creator and the soul commits fornication with false gods, despising Christ, its true bridegroom.

Similarly, whoever makes his body—which God desired to be his temple through the gift of the Spirit that he gave to those immersed in baptism—a temple of the devil through the uncleanness of fornication, God will destroy him unless he quickly turns back to the Lord his God through repentance and confession and through the good of chastity.

He must cleanse God’s temple with fasts, vigils, prayers, and the other works of piety, and, through generous almsgiving, prepare his heart [Col. 0395D] once again as a dwelling worthy of the Lord, holy and adorned with the flowers of good works.

“Nor let us put Christ to the test, as some of them tested him and perished by serpents.”

The person who gives himself over to uncertain danger beyond the protection proper to him tests his Lord. Likewise, anyone who knowingly [does] what the Lord forbade him to do, and for which he threatens those who do it with death—not ordinary death but eternal death—tests him, unless they quickly turn back and are reformed through repentance.

“Nor murmur, as some of them murmured and perished by the destroyer.”

We must therefore be extremely careful [Col. 0396A], whenever we fall into bodily illnesses or other difficulties of this world because of our sins, not to murmur against the Lord. For we either suffer these things because of our evil merits, for our correction, or for our testing, so that, if we bear such great and serious things patiently in the Lord’s name with thanksgiving, we may be made more righteous before him.

“All these things happened to them in a figure, but they were written for our correction.”

The faithless Jews received everything that happened to them according to their merits. Nevertheless, these things were written so that we would not suppose that we can sin with impunity.

Therefore, let the one who thinks he is standing in the perfection of good works take care lest he fall through empty glory [Col. 0396B]. Let no temptation seize you except what human weakness can endure and overcome. But God is faithful: he will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear. He has always promised that he would be present for those afflicted on account of his name, as in the Psalm: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and the Lord delivered them from them all.”

But he will provide, along with the temptation, a way out, so that you may be able to endure it. He himself removes from us the devil’s temptations that are impossible to overcome, just as he taught us to pray in the prayer that he composed, saying: “And do not lead us into temptation”—that is, do not allow the devil to tempt us beyond what our weakness can endure—but deliver us from every evil, Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY 131. ALSO AS ABOVE

A reading from the holy Gospel according to Luke.

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “There was a certain rich man who had a steward, and this man was reported to him as having squandered his property. He summoned him and said to him: ‘What is this that I hear about you? Give an account of your stewardship, for you can no longer be steward,’” and so forth.

In this steward, whom the Lord was dismissing from his stewardship yet praised because he had provided for his future, we must not take everything as something to imitate. For we must not commit fraud against our Lord in any respect so that we may make alms from that fraud; nor is it right to understand those from whom we wish to receive into eternal dwellings as debtors of God and our Lord. Rather, those who bring them into the eternal dwellings are signified here as the righteous and holy, who shared earthly goods with them in their necessities. Of such people he also says that if anyone gives one of them merely a cup of cold water in the name of a disciple, he will not lose his reward.

Yet these comparisons are also spoken in the opposite direction, so that we may understand this: if that man could be praised by the lord whom he was defrauding, how much more do those please the Lord God who perform any works according to his command. By the term “stewards,” therefore, we understand those who possess money but must be regarded not as masters of their own property, but rather as administrators of another’s. If, following the example of this servant, they carefully foresee the approaching end of their stewardship and the time when an account must be rendered, then, easily stripped both of delight in and love for earthly things, they will take care to provide more for acquiring friends in the future than for accumulating riches in the present.

But the steward said within himself: “What shall I do, since my lord is taking the stewardship away from me? I cannot dig.” Once the stewardship has been taken away, we cannot dig, because when this life is ended—in which alone it is permitted to work—we can no longer seek the fruit of a good way of life with the spade of devoted repentance.

“I am ashamed to beg,” and so forth. Begging is a matter of disgrace, namely, that worst kind of begging by which those foolish virgins are reported to have begged. When the time of the wedding approached and the oil of their virtues had failed, they said to the wise: “Give us some of your oil, because our lamps are going out.” Solomon speaks of the same kind when he says: “Because of the cold the sluggard would not plow; therefore he will beg in summer, and it will not be given to him.”

Therefore, having summoned each of his master’s debtors, he said to the first: “How much do you owe my master?” He replied: “A hundred measures of oil.” He said to him: “Take your bond, sit down quickly, and write fifty.” Then he said to another: “But you, how much do you owe?” He replied: “A hundred measures of wheat.” He said to him: “Take your document and write eighty.” A *cadus* in Greek is an *amphora*, containing three urns. A *corus* amounts to thirty *modii*.

As for the fact that he had the debtor write fifty in place of one hundred measures of oil, and eighty in place of one hundred measures of wheat, I think it has no other significance than this: whatever each person does similarly among the Jewish priests and Levites in the Church of Christ, his righteousness should exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees. Thus, when they gave tithes, these should give divine [possibly, “riches”]—as Zacchaeus did, not from his produce but from his very possessions—or at least double the tithes, or surpass the expenditures of the Jews by giving two tithes.

Unless someone thinks the passage should be understood simply to mean that anyone who relieves the need of one of the poor saints by half, or indeed by a fifth—for twenty or fifty are to one hundred—will certainly be rewarded with the recompense of his mercy.

And the lord praised the steward of iniquity because he had acted prudently, “for the children of this age are more prudent in their generation than the children of light.” Let the wise of this age hear, so that they may abandon foolish wisdom and learn the wise foolishness of God; let them learn how highly divine justice evaluates their wisdom. It does not call them truly prudent, but prudent in their own generation.

This accords with what is said elsewhere: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight.” And by calling lovers of eternal life “children of light,” he indicates that those who are wise in doing evil but have not learned to do good are nothing other than children of darkness. “Children of light” and “children of this age” are named in the same way as “children of the kingdom” and “children of perdition.” For each person is called the child of the one whose works he performs.

[Col. 0398A] “And I say to you: Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail, they may receive you into the eternal dwellings.” He calls the money that we possess for a time “the mammon of iniquity” because *mammon* is interpreted as “riches.” Yet these are riches only to the wicked, who place in them the hope and abundance of their blessedness. When the righteous possess such things, it is indeed money for them, but their riches are heavenly and spiritual: by spiritually supplying their need with these, they will be enriched with an abundance of blessedness once the poverty of misery has been excluded.

If those who give alms from iniquitous mammon make friends for themselves by whom they may be received into eternal dwellings, how much more should those who provide spiritual feasts, who give food to their fellow servants at the proper time, be raised up by the most certain hope of the supreme recompense through our Lord Jesus Christ, the giver of all good things, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY 132. WEDNESDAY

A reading from the Epistle of blessed Paul the Apostle to the Romans.

“Brothers, do you not know that when you presented yourselves as slaves for obedience, you became slaves of the one whom you obeyed, whether of sin, leading to death, or of obedience, leading to righteousness?”

So that we do not profess one thing while doing another, and, although we are called servants of God, are found by our deeds to be servants of the devil, he warns and declares that we are servants of the one whose will we fulfill by our works. It is no small harm to confess God as Lord while serving the devil by our actions.

For God once denounced and accused this very thing, saying: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.” And the Lord says in the Gospel: “No one can serve two masters.” It is also said in the Law: “God is not mocked.”

This, then, is what the Apostle teaches in this passage: each person has it in his own hand and within the power of his free choice either to be a servant of sin or of righteousness. For whichever side he obeyingly inclines toward, and whichever he wishes to obey, that side claims him as its servant. Thus, as I have said, he shows that freedom of choice exists within us without any hesitation: it is in us to offer our obedience either to righteousness or to sin.

No one, however, can serve two masters at the same time, sin and righteousness. He will either hate one—namely, sin—and love the other—that is, righteousness—or he will tolerate one, sin alone, and despise the other—that is, righteousness. The Apostle’s statement is therefore similar: “You are slaves of the one whom you obey, whether of sin or of righteousness.”

Moreover, everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin. This is what the Apostle has in view, although he did not add that everyone who practices righteousness is a servant of righteousness. Perhaps someone might think that this was left for others to supply, so that it should be understood as a consequence. Yet it seems to me that it was deliberately not added. For it was not appropriate to say that everyone who practices righteousness is a servant of righteousness, just as everyone who commits sin is a servant of sin. The devil himself is undoubtedly a servant of sin, since he departed from service to righteousness and rebelled in the presence of the almighty Lord; for this reason he was also called an apostate.

It is therefore clear from these words of Paul—when he says, “You present yourselves as slaves for obedience, and you are slaves of the one whom you obey, whether of sin or of righteousness”—that by our own will, with neither sin nor righteousness compelling us, we present ourselves either to serve sin or to serve righteousness through our obedience.

For this reason we must always remember these things, lest we utter empty complaints in excuse for sin, saying that the devil made us sinners, or that necessity of nature, or a fatal condition, or the course of the stars did so. Instead, let us hear Paul’s clear judgment: “You present yourselves as slaves for obedience, and you are slaves of the one whom you obey, whether of sin or of righteousness.”

[Col. 0399B] “But thanks be to God that, although you were slaves of sin, you obeyed from the heart the form of teaching to which you were handed over.” By believing in Christ we have become servants of righteousness. We are called the servants of the one whom we obey. Since it is righteous to obey Christ—for he himself is righteousness, and what he commanded is righteous—he therefore says that we have become servants of righteousness, from the heart and not from the Law, so that our profession may arise from the judgment of the soul.

By nature we have been led to faith, not by the Law. We were handed over to this form of teaching by God’s command, by him who fashioned nature. For in nature we possess the capacity to know from whom, through whom, and in whom we were created.

The form of teaching, therefore, is that into which the Creator has naturally handed us. This is what he said above: “They are a law to themselves,” when they see that what they believe belongs to their own nature. Thus what the Law and the prophets proclaimed to the Jews about Christ, the Gentiles trust from the heart.

For this reason he gives thanks to the Lord: although we were slaves of sin, we obeyed from the heart, believing in Christ so that we might serve God—not through the Law of Moses, but through the law of nature.

When he says, “Thanks be to God that you were slaves of sin,” he shows that all human beings first serve sin. For it is written: “There is no righteous person upon earth who does good and does not sin.” First, what is written must necessarily be fulfilled in every human being: “But when the commandment came, sin revived.”

Yet what follows is said only of the few, namely, those who are already being corrected: “But thanks be to God that, although you were slaves of sin, you obeyed from the heart the form of teaching to which you were handed over.”

We were therefore all slaves of sin. But when the form of teaching was handed over to us, and we chose to obey it—not casually, nor with words alone, but from the heart, from the soul, and with complete devotion—we were freed from slavery to sin and made servants of righteousness.

As for his statement, “the form of teaching to which you were handed over,” I think we must inquire how each person is handed over. We find that God hands over those who do not approve of having God in their knowledge to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they dishonor their own bodies among themselves. He also hands over others, who exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God, to dishonorable passions. We have discussed these matters in their proper places as best we could.

Here, too, God hands over those who present themselves as servants of righteousness through obedience, so that they may be instructed and formed according to the form of righteousness.

I am also moved by the fact that he did not say, “You obeyed from the heart the teaching into which you were handed over,” but inserted the expression “the form of teaching.” I do not think that the Apostle considered “teaching” and “the form of teaching” to be the same thing. Rather, it seems to me that he knew the form of teaching to be less than the teaching itself.

In the present life, while we are in the body and this earthly dwelling weighs down the mind that thinks of many things, we possess the form of teaching, not the teaching itself. The same Apostle says elsewhere: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma.” But the teaching itself is that of which he says: “Then we shall see face to face.”

Therefore, in the present life I think we can grasp the form and shadow of the virtues; the virtues themselves, however, will be ours when those things that are perfect have come. For this reason, the righteous person now, as it seems to me, lives more in the shadow of the virtues than in the virtues themselves.

[Col. 0400B] “But having been freed from sin, you became servants of righteousness.” This is an explanation of what we said above. If you will no longer serve sin, it is certain that, having been freed from it, you have become servants of righteousness.

But the question is: who is the one who frees from sin? Without doubt, it is the recognition of the truth. Thus Jesus said to the Jews who believed him: “If you believe my word, you will recognize the truth, and the truth will set you free.”

It is therefore the truth, and the recognition of the truth, that frees from sin. It is certain that everyone who has been freed from sin serves righteousness.

When we say “serve righteousness,” since righteousness is one member of the chorus of virtues, the meaning is similar to saying: if anyone has been freed from sin, he will serve truth, serve wisdom, serve chastity, and serve piety.

Together with the other forms of virtue, all these things are necessary for the servant of God, so that by doing good in them and persevering to the end, he may attain eternal life, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY 133. ALSO WEDNESDAY

A reading from the holy Gospel according to Luke.

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Whoever is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much; and whoever is unrighteous in a very little is unrighteous also in much.”

There are people who, ignorant of the compassion and works of mercy owed to their neighbors, regard themselves as truly faithful on the basis of the merit of their chastity, vigils, long prayer, complete faith, fasting, and the other virtues that the love of God usually produces. Yet the judge himself bears witness that “whoever is faithful in a very little”—that is, in sharing money with the poor—is faithful also in much, namely, in that act by which he especially desires to cling to the Creator and become one spirit with him.

But whoever neglects to distribute properly the temporal goods he possesses empties for himself the glory of eternal things in which he takes pride. For “whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” And, as the same Apostle says: “If anyone has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need but closes his heart against him, how does the love of God remain in him?”

“If, therefore, you were not faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will entrust to you what is yours?” It has already been explained above that the unrighteous mammon signifies the riches of the wicked. Referring to these elsewhere, the Savior says: “The deceitfulness of riches chokes the word.”

But true riches signify either the joys of eternal life, of which it is written, “What are the riches of his inheritance among the saints,” or the abundance of spiritual virtues by which one reaches life. Of these Isaiah says: “The riches of salvation are wisdom and knowledge; the fear of the Lord itself is his treasure.”

“And if you were not faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours?” The resources of this age are alien to us—that is, they lie outside our nature. For we brought nothing into this world, and there is no doubt that we can take nothing away.

Our possession, however, is the kingdom of heaven; our life is there; our riches are the fruits of spiritual works, of which Solomon says: “The redemption of a man’s soul is his own riches.”

He therefore accuses the Pharisees of fraud and greed. Because they were not faithful with their possessions, preferring to hold privately the Creator’s common goods, they were not worthy to receive Christ. Yet the publican Zacchaeus, whom I mentioned shortly before, offered half of his possessions so that he might acquire Christ.

“No servant can serve two masters.” For one cannot love both transitory and eternal things at the same time. If we love eternity, we possess all temporal things for use, not with affection.

“He will either hate the one and love the other, or he will cling to the one and despise the other.” These words must be considered carefully, for he subsequently explains who the two masters are, saying:

“You cannot serve God and mammon.” Let the greedy person hear this; let the person who is regarded as Christian by name hear that one cannot serve mammon—that is, riches—and Christ at the same time.

Yet he did not say, “the one who has riches,” but “the one who serves riches.” For the servant of riches guards riches as a servant; but the person who has shaken off the yoke of servitude distributes them as a master.

Whoever serves mammon, however, serves the one who, because of his perversity, has been rightly placed over these earthly things and is called by the Lord “the prince of this age.”

Therefore, he will either hate the one and love the other, as he ought: he will hate the devil and love God. Or he will cling to the one and despise the other. He will cling to the devil when he pursues temporal rewards as though they were his; he will despise God—not, he says, “hate” him, but, as those who postpone threats to their desires usually do, flatter themselves into impunity because of God’s goodness. To such people Solomon says: “My son, do not add sin upon sin and say, ‘The mercy of God is great.’”

The Pharisees, who were greedy, heard all these things and mocked him. He was warning the scribes and Pharisees not to be proudly wise, not to presume upon their own righteousness, but also to receive repentant sinners and publicans, and to redeem their sins by almsgiving if such sins should occur.

But they mocked the teacher of mercy, humility, and frugality chiefly for two reasons: either because he was commanding things that were less useful and should never be done, as though he were harmful; or because he was needlessly urging upon them useful things that they had already done.

And he said to them: “You are those who justify yourselves before human beings, but God knows your hearts, because what is exalted among human beings is an abomination before God.”

They justify themselves before human beings when they despise sinners as weak and hopeless, while believing themselves perfect in everything and free from every weakness, so that they have no need of the remedy of almsgiving.

But the height of this harmful swelling—and how justly it must be condemned—is seen by him who “will bring to light the things hidden in darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts,” Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY 134. FRIDAY

A reading from the holy Gospel according to Luke.

At that time a certain Pharisee asked Jesus to dine with him, and he entered and reclined. The Pharisee began to reason within himself, saying why he had not been washed before dinner, and so forth.

The Evangelist Mark disclosed the reason for the Pharisee’s thought when he said: “For the Pharisees and all the Jews, unless they wash their hands frequently, do not eat, holding to the tradition of the elders; and when they come from the marketplace, unless they baptize themselves, they do not eat.”

And Jesus said to him: “Now you Pharisees cleanse what is outside the cup and the dish, but what is within you is full of plunder and wickedness.”

Mark reports that they were accustomed to observe the washing of cups, jugs, couches, and bronze vessels. But under the name of vessels they are more truly accused of falsehood and hypocrisy: they display one thing outwardly to human beings and do another at home. They have the appearance of piety outwardly, but inwardly are disfigured by the filth of their vices. The Lord wishes to explain more fully what he had briefly stated above about cleansing the eye of the heart.

“Fools! Did not the one who made what is outside also make what is inside?” He means that he desires both to be cleansed.

This is directed against the Manichaeans, who think that the soul alone was created by God, while the flesh was created by the devil. It is also directed against those who detest bodily sins—namely, fornication, impurity, lust, theft, robbery, and other such things—as though they were the gravest sins, but regard spiritual sins, which the Apostle condemns no less—bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, blasphemy, pride, and greed, which is the service of idols—as trivial.

“Nevertheless, give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you.” Give to the poor whatever remains after what is necessary for food and clothing, in accordance with John’s command: “Let the one who has two tunics give to the one who has none.”

Almsgiving is not commanded in such a way that you consume yourself through poverty. Rather, once you have cared for your own body, you should support the needy as much as you are able.

Or the phrase “whatever remains” should be understood in this way: because you are preoccupied with so many crimes, the only remedy left is to give alms. This saying applies to everything done in useful compassion.

For not only does the person who gives food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the naked, lodging to the traveler, and other things of this kind give alms; the person who grants forgiveness to one who sins also gives alms. Likewise, the person who corrects with a blow someone over whom authority has been given, or restrains him by some discipline, while forgiving from the heart the sin by which he was harmed or offended, or praying that it may be forgiven him, gives alms—not only in what he forgives and for which he prays, but also in what he rebukes and punishes with some corrective penalty, because he shows mercy.

There are therefore many kinds of almsgiving. When we perform them, we are helped so that our sins may be forgiven. Yet none is greater than that by which we forgive from the heart whatever each person has sinned against us.

But are we to understand the statement, “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you,” in such a way that everything is clean for the Pharisees—even if they do not believe in Christ and have not been reborn from water and the Holy Spirit—provided only that they give alms? Some people think alms should be given, although all whom the faith of Christ does not cleanse are unclean; yet it is written of that faith: “Cleansing their hearts by faith.”

Nevertheless, what they heard is true: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you.” Whoever wishes to give alms in the proper way must begin with himself and give alms first to himself. Almsgiving is an act of mercy, and it is most truly said: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God.”

For this reason we are reborn, so that we may please God, whom what we contracted by birth rightly displeases. This is the first almsgiving that we gave ourselves, since through the mercy of the merciful God we sought out ourselves in our misery.

Because of the order of love it is said: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” When, therefore, he rebuked them because they washed themselves outwardly while inwardly being full of plunder and wickedness, he reminded them of a kind of almsgiving that a person must first give himself, cleansing his interior.

“Nevertheless,” he says, “whatever remains, give as alms, and behold, everything is clean for you.” Then, to show what he had advised and what they themselves did not care to do—and lest they think that he was unaware of their almsgiving—he says: “But woe to you, Pharisees.” It is as though he were saying: “I have indeed urged you to give alms, through which everything may be clean for you.”

“But woe to you, Pharisees, because you tithe mint and rue and every herb.” I know these almsgivings of yours; do not think that I am now advising you about them.

“And you pass over judgment and the love of God”—the almsgiving by which you could be cleansed from every interior defilement, so that your bodies also, which you wash, might be clean.

For this is “everything,” namely, both the interior and the exterior, as it is read elsewhere: “Cleanse what is within, and what is outside will be clean.”

But lest he seem to reject those alms that are made from the fruits of the earth, he adds:

“These things you ought to do”—that is, judgment and the love of God—so that, judging our misery truthfully and loving the love of God that he himself has given, we may live piously and rightly, confessing his just judgment, since we have been made miserable.

Of this the Apostle says: “Judgment from one transgression brought condemnation.” And we should give thanks for his great love, of which the same preacher of grace says: “God commends his love toward us, because while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”

“These things you ought to do, and not omit the others”—that is, alms from earthly produce.

Let those who think they can purchase impunity through alms, however lavishly they distribute their produce or any money, not deceive themselves while remaining in the enormity of crimes and the wickedness of shameful acts.

“Woe to you Pharisees, because you love the first seats in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplace.” Woe to us wretched people, to whom the vices of the Pharisees have passed. We do not fear adding further burdens to our sins by proudly competing with one another for precedence during the brief and uncertain course of our life, in which we ought humbly to have mourned our sins.

“Woe to you, because you are like unmarked tombs, and people walk over them without knowing it.” This saying also rebukes the superstition of the Pharisees, because outwardly they display the appearance of sound teaching, but inwardly conceal the foulness they carry. They are like tombs which, while showing the common surface of the earth, are inwardly full of worm-ridden corpses.

When the Psalmist said of these, “Their throat is an open tomb,” he immediately explained what he meant by adding: “With their tongues they acted deceitfully.”

One of the lawyers answered and said to him: “Teacher, by saying these things you insult us also.” How wretched is the conscience that thinks itself insulted when it hears the word of God and, whenever the punishment of the faithless is mentioned, understands that it is always being condemned.

Therefore, for me and those like me, the one refuge is always to beseech the Lord with the Prophet: “Would that my ways were directed toward keeping your statutes; then I shall not be put to shame when I look upon all your commandments.”

But he said: “Woe to you also, lawyers, because you load people with burdens that they cannot carry, while you yourselves do not touch the burden with one of your fingers.”

The burdens of the Law could not be carried in the manner in which these lawyers imposed them on people. Thus he rightly heard that they did not touch their burdens with even one finger—that is, they did not fulfill the Law even in the smallest matters, which they presumed, without faith in and the grace of Jesus Christ, both to keep themselves and to hand down for observance contrary to the [possibly, “custom” of their] fathers.

For this reason they attempted to cast far away and abolish the yoke of Christ, which is easy, and his burden, which is light and in which souls find rest, although it is written: “The righteous lives by faith.” The Apostle Peter also protested against those who taught believing Gentiles to be circumcised, saying: “Why, then, are you testing God by placing upon the neck of the disciples a yoke that neither our fathers nor we were able to bear? But we believe that we shall be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they were.”

He lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY 135. THE ELEVENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

A reading from the Epistle of blessed Paul to the Corinthians.

“Brothers, you know that when you were Gentiles, you went to mute idols, being led wherever you were led. Therefore I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says, ‘Anathema to Jesus,’” and so forth.

While briefly discussing the divine gifts and the distribution of the gifts of the Holy Spirit—which almighty God distributes to his faithful through his Holy Spirit—the Apostle Paul said, as you heard in the present reading: “You know that when you were Gentiles, you went to mute idols, being led wherever you were led.” That is, before you had understood the account of the true faith, and before the knowledge of the Son of God, you worshiped mute and vain idols.

“Therefore I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says, ‘Anathema to Jesus.’” The Apostle wants you no longer to be irrational and immovable. Along with religion, you must examine your conduct and recognize the account of the faith.

“And no one can say, ‘The Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit.” For just as the Lord does not acknowledge workers of iniquity, even though they perform miracles, so Christ does not know those who confess him as Lord Jesus with their voice alone and not by righteous works.

As he himself says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven.”

“There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; there are varieties of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of works, but the same God, who works all things in all.”

Here he wishes to show that the gifts of the Holy Spirit are many and diverse, but that the divine substance itself—the source from which these gifts are bestowed—is not divided. By continually saying “the same,” he declares that he is speaking of the Holy Spirit in all cases. Hence what follows: “But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit.”

The preaching of one Godhead and one substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is evident. In his own power the Lord God bestows the gifts of grace upon each person according to his will.

“To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.” This is so that it may appear that he has received the Holy Spirit, so that unbelievers may believe and believers may be strengthened.

“To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom.” A word of wisdom is to speak wisely, clearly, and rationally, and to be able to discuss or teach what one knows.

Indeed, the one who possesses wisdom as a gift speaks without his own exertion or labor, and no one can resist him.

Then follows:

“To another, a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit.” This is so that he may know how to explain the mysteries of the Law and also understand things concerning the past.

“To another, faith in the same Spirit.” For to one person a more truthful and clearer understanding is given for faith.

“To another, gifts of healings in one Spirit.” Through the Holy Spirit it is given to him that he may be able to cure the sick.

“To another, prophecy.” Such people proclaim future things.

“To another, discernment of spirits.” This is so that he may understand with what kind of spirit someone comes or speaks.

“To another, kinds of tongues.” This enables him to speak in many and diverse languages.

[Col. 0406B] “To another, interpretation of discourses.” Thus what others speak in different languages may, through the gift of the Holy Spirit, be interpreted by another for the knowledge of those who hear.

“But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills.”

It is rightly written of the same Spirit: “He will teach you everything and remind you of everything I have said to you.” The same Paraclete Spirit is therefore a good teacher, teaching us everything that Christ promised to teach.

We must celebrate this not only on the day of Pentecost—that is, at the coming of the Holy Spirit—but must act in such a way that every day we invite him to ourselves through pure works and pure hearts.

We must be pure and cleansed in our perceptions and thoughts. We must guard our mouths and hearts so carefully that we may always make ourselves worthy of his visitation and illumination, so that we may appear free from every impurity of thought. For, as I have said, perverse thoughts separate us from God.

Let us strive to be free from every slander and every wickedness, because wisdom does not enter a malevolent soul, nor does it dwell in a body subjected to sins.

Through anger and pride, the souls of the negligent are stripped of the guardianship and protection of the Holy Spirit. Let us not, therefore, grieve the Holy Spirit through such passions. Rather, let us summon him to the seat of our heart through the grace of humility, peace, and gentleness, and gladden him by our works, so that, thoroughly cleansed and purified, we may become the dwelling of God.

May the Holy Spirit, who is read to have descended on the eighth day, deign always to be in us, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom with the eternal Father and the same Holy Spirit be honor and glory throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY 136. ON THE SAME FEAST

A reading from the holy Gospel according to Luke.

At that time, as Jesus drew near to Jerusalem, seeing the city, he wept over it, saying: “For if you too had known,” and so forth.

That the destruction of Jerusalem was being described as the Lord wept—a destruction carried out by the Roman rulers Vespasian and Titus—is known to everyone who has read the history of its overthrow.

But we must first ask what is meant by the statement: “Seeing the city, he wept over it, saying, ‘For if you too had known.’” The compassionate Redeemer wept over the ruin of the faithless city, which did not recognize that ruin was coming upon it. The weeping Lord rightly says to it: “For if you too had known”—with “you would have wept” understood—but now, because you do not know what is impending, you rejoice.

Hence it is added:

“And indeed, on this your day—what is for your peace.” Since it was giving itself over to the pleasures of the flesh and did not foresee the evils that were to come, it possessed in its day the things that could have been for its peace.

Why it possessed present goods for its peace is made clear when it adds:

“But now they are hidden from your eyes.” If the evils that were impending had not been hidden from the eyes of its heart, it would not have been joyful amid its present prosperity.

Its punishment, which, as I said, was impending from the Roman rulers, is then immediately added in these words:

For days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart; they will surround you and hem you in on every side. They will cast you and your children who are within you down to the ground. This too, which is added—“They will not leave in you one stone upon another”—is attested by the very subsequent history of that city: since the city now built in the place outside the gate where the Lord was crucified, that former Jerusalem was utterly overthrown. The guilt for which the punishment of its overthrow was inflicted is then added:

“Because you did not recognize the time of your visitation.” For the Creator of all things deigned to visit her through the mystery of the Incarnation, but she did not remember him with fear and love. Hence, too, in the prophet’s rebuke of the human heart, the birds of the air are brought forward as witnesses, when it is said: “The kite in the sky knows its time; the turtledove, the swallow, and the stork have kept the time of their coming; but my people have not known the judgment of God.”

“And entering the temple, he began to drive out those who sold and bought in it, saying to them: ‘It is written: My house is a house of prayer.’” He who had narrated the evils to come immediately entered the temple in order to drive out from it the sellers and buyers. He clearly indicated that the ruin of the people arose chiefly from the guilt of the priests. For, while describing the overthrow and striking the sellers and buyers in the temple, he showed by the very effect of his action from what root destruction had sprung:

“But you have made it a den of robbers.” Those who sat in the temple to receive gifts undoubtedly sought to inflict harm upon those who did not give them. Thus the house of prayer had been made a den of robbers, because they knew how to attend the temple for this purpose: either to persecute bodily those who did not give gifts, or to kill spiritually those who did give them. But because our Redeemer does not withhold the words of preaching even from the unworthy and ungrateful, after he had maintained the rigor of discipline by driving out the perverse, he immediately displayed the gift of grace. For it follows:

“And he was teaching daily in the temple.”

We have briefly passed through these matters according to the historical sense; now let us return to examine the same things according to their moral meaning.

“He saw the city and wept over it, saying: ‘If you had known—even you.’” He did this once when he announced that the city would perish; our Redeemer does this continually through his elect whenever he sees that certain people have fallen from a good life into reprehensible conduct. He mourns those who do not know why they are mourned—those who, in Solomon’s words, rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things. If they had recognized the condemnation hanging over them, they would have mourned themselves with tears for their sins.

“And indeed, in this your day, the things that are for your peace.” Here the perverse soul has its own day: it rejoices for a fleeting time, and the things present are for its peace. While it delights in temporal possessions, while it is lifted up by honors, while it is relaxed in carnal pleasure, while it is terrified by no fear of the punishment to come, it has peace in its own day—a peace that will have a grave stumbling-block of condemnation in another’s day. For there it must be afflicted where the righteous will rejoice.

“But now they are hidden from your eyes.” The perverse soul, devoted to present things and relaxed in earthly pleasures, hides from itself the evils that follow, because it refuses to foresee the future things that would disturb its present joy. And while it abandons itself to the delight of the present life, what else is it doing than going to the fire with its eyes closed?

“For days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart.” Who could be greater enemies of the human soul than evil spirits? They besiege it as it departs from the body, and they cherish it, placed in the love of the flesh, with deceptive pleasures. They surround it with a rampart when, bringing before its mind’s eyes the iniquities it has committed, they hem it in as they drag it toward fellowship in their condemnation.

“And they will surround you and hem you in on every side.” Evil spirits hem the soul in on every side when they recall to it not only the iniquities of its actions, but also those of its speech and, beyond these, of its thoughts—so that the soul which previously expanded itself through many crimes is finally constricted by all of them in retribution.

“And they will cast you and your children who are within you down to the ground.” The soul is then cast down to the ground through knowledge of its guilt, when the flesh—which believed it would return to life—is forced back to dust. Its children fall in its death when the unlawful thoughts that now proceed from it are scattered in the final punishment of life, as it is written: “On that day all their thoughts will perish.”

Those harsh thoughts can also appropriately be understood through the symbolism of stones. For it follows: “They will not leave in you one stone upon another.” When the perverse mind adds further perversity to a perverse thought, what else is it doing than placing one stone upon another? But in the destroyed city, no stone is left upon another, because when the soul is led to its punishment, the whole structure of its thoughts is scattered.

“Because you did not recognize the time of your visitation.” Almighty God is accustomed to visit every perverse soul in many ways. He visits it continually through a commandment, sometimes through a scourge, and sometimes through a miracle, so that it may hear truths of which it was unaware and, although it still remains proud and contemptuous, may either return, pierced by suffering, or, overcome by benefits, blush for the evil it has done. But because it does not recognize the time of its visitation, it is finally handed over to those enemies with whom it is joined in the fellowship of its condemnation at the eternal judgment.

“And entering the temple, he began to drive out those who sold and bought in it.” Just as the temple of the Lord is in the city, so in the faithful people the life of religious persons is a temple. Often certain people assume the religious habit, but when they obtain a place among the sacred orders, they turn the office of holy religion into a business of earthly commerce.

Those who sell in the temple are those who distribute for a reward what they ought rightly to grant to certain people. For to sell justice is to preserve it in exchange for receiving a reward. Those who buy in the temple are those who do not wish to render to their neighbor what is just; while they refuse to do what is legally owed, they buy sin by paying a reward to their patrons.

To such people it is rightly said: “My house is a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of robbers.” For when perverse people occupy a place of religion, they kill there with the swords of their malice where they ought to give life to their neighbors through the intercession of their prayer.

The temple and house of God is also the mind and conscience of the faithful. If it produces perverse thoughts that harm its neighbor, robbers are, as it were, sitting in a den, and they kill those who walk innocently when they drive the swords of injury into people who are guilty of nothing. The mind of the faithful is no longer a house of prayer but a den of robbers when, having abandoned innocence and holy simplicity, it strives to do what may enable it to harm its neighbors.

But because we are continually instructed against all these perversities by the words of our Redeemer through the sacred pages, what was forbidden to be done is nevertheless done even now, as is said:

“And he was teaching daily in the temple.” When he subtly teaches the minds of the faithful to avoid evils, the Truth teaches daily—namely Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY CXXXVII. WEDNESDAY

A reading from the Epistle of blessed Paul the Apostle to the Corinthians.

“Brothers, not every flesh is the same flesh: there is one kind among human beings, another among cattle, another among birds, and another among fish. There are also heavenly bodies and earthly bodies; but one is the glory of heavenly bodies and another that of earthly bodies; one is the brightness of the sun, another the brightness of the moon, and another the brightness of the stars. For star differs from star in brightness; so also is the resurrection of the dead,” etc.

The meaning in all these statements is as follows. Although all kinds of flesh are mortal, they nevertheless differ among themselves according to the varieties of living creatures. Although all bodies are visible, they likewise differ among themselves according to the variety of their places; hence one is the glory of heavenly things and another that of earthly things. And if, in the higher regions, all heavenly things differ even in the brightness of their lights, it is not surprising that in the resurrection of the dead the glory of merits will differ, since all flesh comes from the same substance.

Therefore, let the sophists of the world and the investigators of the stars now say, if they can understand how such great diversity exists in these things, when they do not know what is within themselves. Indeed, all worldly philosophers, because they refused to humble their minds before the law of God in order to receive its faith, always asserting diverse and contrary opinions, confused one another in utterly empty disputations, because none of them bears witness to the sign of truth.

It has been understood that the word previously set forth commends the doctrine, just as God also has distinguished our discipline, which is proved not by words but by power—a power which words cannot resist. For just as flesh of different living creatures comes from one substance, so the ranks of human beings, though of one flesh, will differ in the resurrection, so that each person will appear according to the quality of his merit.

For even here we see a diversity of bodies: “There are,” he says, “heavenly bodies and earthly bodies; but one is the glory of heavenly bodies and another that of earthly bodies.” Heavenly bodies are those of the risen; earthly bodies are those of people before they die or rise, since Christ is heavenly and therefore heavenly bodies are named from him. But from Adam, because he is earthly, come earthly bodies.

“One is the brightness of the sun, another the brightness of the moon, and another the brightness of the stars; for star differs from star in brightness.” He uses a comparison drawn from one nature to explain the distinction of an undivided substance. Just as the sun, moon, and stars are indeed of one nature but differ in brightness, so human beings, although of one kind, will nevertheless differ in glory according to merit.

Their dignity will equal the brightness of the sun who have the hundredfold number, who, in order to be perfect, were emulators of the first degree. Of them it is said: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.” Those who have earned the sixtyfold number through good works, so as to possess the merit of the second degree, are to be compared with lunar brightness. The merits of those who have sought through righteous labors the thirtyfold number and the dignity of the third degree are to be compared with the brighter stars.

People who are sinners, who did not wish to attain the honor of any degree among the three, are to be likened to the stars that follow—those that are midway between the bright and the darker stars. But the resurrection of the unbelieving is like that of the darkest stars [Tetricis]; because they followed error, they are to be compared with stars that lead into error. As the apostle Jude says in his Epistle, unbelief cannot have a bright resurrection. Just as a coal covered with its own ash is darkened, so they, surrounded by the darkness of error through their unbelief, will lack light.

“So also is the resurrection of the dead.” He gives examples so that there may be no doubt that the dead will rise; once the explanation has been received, no one should hesitate.

“It is sown in corruption; it will rise in incorruption.” To sow is to bury, so that the body may decay; to rise in incorruption is for what has already been raised no longer to be able to decay, but to possess the brightness of immortality.

“It is sown in dishonor; it will rise in glory.” It is sown in dishonor when it is placed in a gloomy place, becomes fetid, and swarms with worms. But to rise in glory is for what has been raised to become light and suffer no injury from foulness.

“It is sown in weakness; it will rise in power.” It is sown in weakness because it is immobile and incapable of movement; but it rises in power because it will then be wholly alive and vigorous.

“It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body.” Although we declare that some natures are spiritual—such as angels, archangels, and the other powers, as well as our own soul, or certainly this subtle air—nevertheless they are in no way to be considered incorporeal.

[Note: See Dionysius Petavius, *Dogmata theologica*, volume 1, treatise “On Angels,” book 1, chapter 2, page 3, Antwerp edition. — EDITOR.]

For they possess, according to their own nature, a body by which they subsist, although it is much more subtle than our bodies, according to the Apostle’s statement: “There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies”; and again: “It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body.”

From these statements it is clearly gathered that nothing is incorporeal except God alone. Therefore only to him can all spiritual and intellectual substances be penetrable, because he alone is wholly and everywhere and in all things, so that he sees and examines the thoughts of human beings, their inward movements, and all the recesses of the mind.

Of him alone blessed Paul declared: “The word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart; and no creature is invisible in his sight, but all things are naked and open to his eyes.” And blessed David says: “He who fashioned their hearts individually.” And again: “For he himself knows the secrets of the heart.”

The body is animal while it is sustained by food, so that it may live; but it is spiritual when, transformed into life, it will need none of these things. All the foregoing statements are enclosed within this meaning. For the animal body cannot always have the Holy Spirit here. But then, that is, in the resurrection, it will always remain in the saints. It will rise a spiritual body, able to go out to meet Christ.

“As it is written: ‘The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam a life-giving spirit.’” It must be noted that when he speaks of two Adams, he shows that both are of the same nature. This is directed against the Manichaeans and the Apollinarists, who deny that a perfect human being was assumed by the Word of God.

“But not first the spiritual, but the animal; afterward the spiritual.”

“The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man from heaven, heavenly.” He is called heavenly because he was conceived and born not according to the custom of human weakness, but by the will of divine majesty. For he possessed our nature to such a degree that he is called the second Adam, and a human being: Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY CXXXVIII. ALSO ON WEDNESDAY

A reading from the holy Gospel according to Luke.

“At that time, Jesus, answering his disciples, said: ‘When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army, then know that its desolation is near,’” etc.

Up to this point, the things that were to occur over the course of forty years, before the end arrived, have been explained. From here onward, the Lord’s words explain the very end of the desolation carried out by the Roman army.

“Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains.” Ecclesiastical history relates that all the Christians who were in Judea, having been warned by the Lord as the destruction of Jerusalem approached, departed from the place and lived across the Jordan in a certain city called Pella until the desolation of Judea was completed.

“And those who are in its midst, let them depart; and those who are in the regions, let them not enter it. For these are the days of vengeance, so that all things that are written may be fulfilled.” This seems to belong to a fitting warning: those who are outside should not enter it. But how will those who are in its midst depart from an army that has already surrounded the city? Perhaps we should say that the preceding statement—“then, that is, then let those who are in Judea flee”—refers not to the actual time of the siege, but to the immediately preceding period, when the Roman soldier first began to spread through the territories of Galilee and Samaria. Thus each person was to hasten to flee while there was still time to flee.

“These are the days of vengeance,” namely, days demanding vengeance for the Lord’s blood.

“But woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in those days.” Woe to those who are pregnant or nursing, or suckling, as some interpret it, during the captivity that was then present. The burden of their wombs and the weight of their children in their arms greatly impede the necessity of flight. Read the history in the Books of Kings, where Jonathan’s wife, hastening to avoid the evil of captivity by flight, received her son permanently lame after he had fallen.

“For there will be great distress upon the earth, and wrath against this people.” This distress and wrath remain an inseparable companion of that people, dispersed among all nations to this day; nevertheless, it should not be believed that they will remain forever. For after the Lord had shown the course of that distress and wrath, saying:

“And they will fall by the edge of the sword, and will be led captive into all nations, and Jerusalem will be trampled by the nations,”

he immediately added, in accordance with the prophecy that sings, “In wrath you will remember mercy,” and said:

“Until the times of the nations are fulfilled.” The times of the nations are those of which the Apostle speaks: “A hardening has come upon Israel in part, until the fullness of the nations enters, and thus all Israel is saved.” Once Israel has obtained the promised salvation, it is hoped that it will also return to its ancestral land and regain possession of and residence in its former capital. For it is said to be oppressed by wrath not forever, but only until the times of the nations are fulfilled.

What will follow when the times of the nations have been fulfilled and all Israel has thus been saved, the Lord makes clear in order. For when questioning him according to Matthew, the disciples asked not only about the time of the temple’s destruction, but also about the sign of his coming and the consummation of the age.

“And there will be signs in the sun, and moon, and stars, and upon the earth distress among the nations because of the confusion caused by the roaring of the sea and the waves.” Since, as the Lord intimates in what follows, heaven and earth will pass away when the universal judgment appears, and since we read in John’s Apocalypse that the sea will no longer exist, it is fitting that, as the judgment presses upon everything, the roaring of the sea and the waves should be thrown into confusion.

The inhabitants of the world are afflicted as they press upon one another; the greatest lights of heaven, struck by a new horror, veil their troubled faces with their rays. And just as trees driven toward falling usually give beforehand signs of their crash and movement, so, as the end approaches, the elements, as though afraid, sway and tremble.

Therefore, when Matthew says, “The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven,” he signifies the very presence of the judgment, when, as the glory of the true light appears, all the lights of the world are compared with darkness and shadows.

But when Luke says, “There will be signs in the sun and moon and stars,” he indicates the precursors of that approaching judgment, as though they were messengers announcing it. Among these is the prophet’s statement: “The sun will be turned into darkness and the moon into blood before the great and manifest day of the Lord comes.”

Likewise, when Luke says, “And upon the earth distress among the nations,” I think this is the very event that Matthew describes when, speaking of the times of Antichrist, he says: “For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor will ever be.”

But what Luke adds—“because of the confusion caused by the roaring of the sea and the waves”—is a proclamation of what John saw: that, among the other mutable things of the world, the sea would pass away.

“People fainting from fear and expectation of what will come upon the whole world.” I believe that this sentence designates the very coming of the Judge. Then, in accordance with the parable found elsewhere, all—the wise virgins as well as the foolish—will be awakened by an unaccustomed cry and trim their lamps. Each will reckon up the works that belong to him, for which, in the greatest fear, they await the event of the eternal judgment that is already, already at hand.

Until that time, almost the whole world will act without any fear of the Judge, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them.” When fear of the whole world and expectation of the searching judgment therefore arrive, many who seemed to flourish in this world will wither when they see themselves without fruit.

Then the faith that had flourished without works will wither when tested by the fire of the just Judge, because faith without works is dead in itself. For then our Lord Jesus Christ, the Judge of the living and the dead, will repay each person according to his works.

## HOMILY CXXXIX. FRIDAY

A reading from the holy Gospel according to Luke.

“At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘Pay attention to yourselves, lest your hearts be weighed down by overeating, drunkenness, and the cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly. For it will come like a snare upon all who sit upon the face of the whole earth,’” etc.

O foolish presumption of the human heart! It foresees neither the lamentable end of desire, drunkenness, and overeating, even though the Judge himself bears witness to it; instead, like a wicked servant, once it has learned the edict of the eternal King, it despises it.

If some skilled and wise physician instructed us in this way—“Pay attention to yourselves,” he might say, “lest someone, for example, take too much of the juice of this or that herb, for if he does so, sudden death will overtake him”—with what diligence would everyone obey the physician’s warning, lest he perish by tasting what was forbidden?

But now the Savior and Lord of souls and bodies commands that the herb of drunkenness and overeating, as well as the juices of worldly cares, be avoided as deadly substances. Yet how many of us do not fear being merely wounded by these things, but even consumed by them! I believe there is no other reason than that they refuse to give to the Lord’s words the faith they give to physicians.

For if they had believed, they would certainly have feared through believing; and fearing, they would have guarded against the impending danger. But by their contrary torpor they prove how rightly it was said: “When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith on earth?”

“Watch, therefore, at all times, praying that you may be worthy to escape all these things that are to come and to stand before the Son of Man.” Whoever desires to stand before the Son of Man and, according to John’s Apocalypse, serve him day and night in his temple, and not be cast away accursed from his sight into eternal fire, must be restrained not only from worldly allurements but also pray and keep watch—not on certain days only, but at all times.

As the Psalmist says: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise will always be in my mouth.” Thus he will deserve to dwell in the house of the Lord and praise him forever and ever.

By the gift of that Redeemer and Savior of the human race, namely our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit reigns in perfect unity forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY CXL. TWELFTH WEEK AFTER PENTECOST

A reading from the Epistle of blessed Paul to the Corinthians.

“Brothers, I make the Gospel known to you,” etc.

Here, setting aside the order of preaching, he turned to the teaching of the resurrection, because some of the Corinthians doubted the resurrection.

“Which you also received.” That is, which you had received. He says this so that they might not appear not to have believed it.

“In which also you stand.” That is, persevering in good works, by whose teaching you have been raised toward heavenly things.

“Through which also you are saved.” That is, through whose teaching you hope for salvation, both of souls and from various bodily infirmities, because without faith in the resurrection the hope of salvation perishes entirely.

“According to the manner in which I preached to you.” It is as if he were saying: “The whole purpose of our preaching is this: that you believe in the resurrection.” For this is the reward of all who have believed in Christ; otherwise all the labor of fasts and all the tribulations that you suffer for Christ in this life are useless.

“If you hold fast to it, unless you believed in vain.” That is, unless you have forgotten, or certainly unless you do not hope to receive the reward of your faith and labor by rising again, you believe in vain.

“For I delivered to you as of first importance.” That is, from the beginning, when I first preached to you, I delivered the mystery of the resurrection, which consists either in ours, or first [lacuna].

“Which I also received.” He says that he received it either from the Law, or from the elders, or from the Lord himself through revelation.

“That Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures.” So that blessed Paul might establish with greater authority what he preached, he says that this is the Christ, the Savior of the world, whom Moses and the Prophets announced. Therefore he recalls that it was foretold according to the Scriptures: “He will be led like a sheep to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he will be silent”; and: “He was handed over because of our iniquities, and by his bruising we have been healed”; and you will find many other passages concerning his passion in the divine Scriptures.

“And that he was buried.” This accords with Isaiah: “He will give the impious in exchange for his burial, and the rich for his death.” Likewise, he himself says: “His burial was taken away from the midst.”

“And that he rose on the third day according to the Scriptures.” You have this in Hosea: “He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we will live in his sight.”

“And that he was seen by Cephas,” that is, Peter. For Cephas is a Syriac name. He appeared to Peter, as it is written in the Gospel, that he appeared to Simon.

“And afterward by the eleven.” This was when he entered to them while the doors were closed. It must be understood that not all the appearances are written in the Gospel, but only those sufficient for the faith of the hearers.

“Then he was seen by more than five hundred brothers at once, of whom many remain until now, but some have fallen asleep.” To establish greater faith, he inserted a multitude of witnesses. Many of them are said to be alive, able, if questioned, to relate what they saw. Others are said already to be sleeping in death.

“Then he was seen by James.” He appeared separately to James the son of Alphaeus. For they report that this James the son of Alphaeus testified at the Lord’s Supper, saying that he would not eat bread until he saw Christ risen from the dead.

“Then by all the Apostles.” Many wish these to be understood as all the seventy Apostles whom the Lord sent out to preach.

“Last of all, as to an untimely birth, he was seen also by me.” He appeared to him on the road, when light surrounded him, or in the temple. He says this so that they would not think he was reporting things heard rather than seen.

He says “as to an untimely birth” because he died to the synagogue and was born to the Church—like an untimely birth whose life would have been despaired of unless it had been forcibly drawn forth by the grace of the Lord. He was drawn forth by preachings, not by chains, and through the astonishment of novelty he came unwillingly, although he was perfect in his knowledge of the Law. Or he is called untimely because the synagogue deservedly conceived and bore him wrongly and imperfectly.

“For I am the least of the Apostles.” He says this about himself out of humility. Otherwise, he was least in time, not in labor, for elsewhere he says: “I labored more than all of them.”

“Who am not worthy to be called an Apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God.” Explaining why he is not worthy, he says: “Because I persecuted the Church of God.” By his own example he teaches us that, even if we make progress in the present, we should mourn our past. It is better to remember sins that have been forgiven than to forget those we have committed. For it is written: “Son, you have sinned; do not add again,” but also: “Pray concerning your past sins.”

“But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me has not been empty.” The grace by which we were redeemed did not seek the merit of our efforts. But daily grace after baptism expects daily service of labor, in which whoever performs good works and perseveres to the end will be saved forever.

## HOMILY CXLI. ALSO AS ABOVE

A reading from the holy Gospel according to Luke.

“At that time, two men went up into the temple to pray: one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector,” etc.

The tax collector praying humbly belongs to the members of that widow previously mentioned, that is, the Church, concerning whom it was said above: “But God will avenge his elect who cry out to him.” The Pharisee, boasting of his merits, belongs to those concerning whom the terrible sentence is added at the conclusion: “Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith on earth?”

“The Pharisee, standing, prayed this within himself, saying: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of humanity: robbers, unjust, adulterers—or even like this tax collector.’” There are four forms in which all the arrogance of the proud is displayed.
