It appears when people think they possess good from themselves; or, if they believe it has been given to them from above, think they received it on account of their own merits; or when they boast of possessing what they do not possess; or when, despising others, they seek to appear uniquely possessed of what they do possess.

This Pharisee is found to have been afflicted by the plague of boasting. For he descended from the temple without justification because, attributing the merits of good works to himself as though they were uniquely his own, he placed himself above the praying tax collector.

“I fast twice a week; I give tithes of everything I possess.” The prophet Ezekiel writes concerning the living creatures of heaven shown to him: “Their whole body was full of eyes all around the four of them.” The bodies of the living creatures are described as full of eyes because the conduct of the saints is watchful on every side: it foresees desirable things with longing and carefully avoids evil. But often, while we attend to other things, we neglect some others, and there we certainly have no eye.

For behold, the Pharisee had an eye for displaying abstinence, fulfilling mercy, and giving thanks to God, but he had no eye for guarding humility. And what benefit is there if nearly the whole city is carefully guarded against the enemy’s ambushes, when one open hole is left through which the enemy may enter?

“But the tax collector, standing far off, did not even wish to raise his eyes toward heaven, but was beating his breast, saying: ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner.’ I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other.” What confidence in forgiveness this rightly offers to penitents! The tax collector perfectly recognized the guilt of his wickedness, wept, and confessed; although he came to the temple unjustified, he returned from the temple justified.

In a typological sense, the Pharisee is the people of the Jews, who exalt their merits through the justifications of the Law. The tax collector is the Gentile, who, placed far from God, confesses his sins. One of them withdrew in pride and was humbled; the other, by lamenting, deserved to draw near and was exalted.

“For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” This can rightly be understood both of the two peoples mentioned above and of every proud or humble person, just as can the statement we read elsewhere: “Before a fall the heart is exalted, and before glory it is humbled.”

Therefore, from the words of the haughty Pharisee, by which he deserved to be humbled, we can take the opposite pattern of humility by which we may be exalted. Just as he, considering the vices of worse people and his own virtues, was exalted toward ruin, so let us, examining not only our own laziness but also the virtues of those who are better, humble ourselves toward glory.

Thus each of us should entreat with a submissive and humble heart:

“Almighty God, have mercy on your suppliant, because I am not like the countless servants of yours who are exalted by contempt for the world, glorious through the merit of justice, or angelic in the praise of chastity; nor am I like the many who, after public crimes, deserved through repentance to become devoted to you. And even if, by your grace bestowing it, I do something good, I do not know toward what end I do it, or with what strictness it is weighed by you, because, as Scripture says, ‘the judgments of God are a great abyss.’

“For you alone know all things, and nothing is hidden before your eyes. You alone live and reign as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”

## HOMILY CXLII. WEDNESDAY

A reading from the Epistle of blessed Paul the Apostle to the Corinthians.

“Brothers, do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?” etc.

Our bodies are members of Christ, but in the new human being, who was created according to God, because he is the head of the Church.

“Taking therefore the members of Christ, shall I make them members of a prostitute? By no means.” For members joined to a prostitute cease to be members of Christ.

“Or do you not know that whoever is joined to a prostitute is one body?” He says this because whoever mingles himself with defilement becomes one with that to which he mingles himself. For fornication makes the two one, so that they are one both in nature and in stain.

“They will be,” he says, “two in one flesh.” The meaning is clear: because the woman is from the man, the two are one flesh.

But whoever adheres to the Lord is one spirit. For among those who act rightly, the Spirit of God is shared by God and human beings. When “one” is said without adding what the one thing is, and several things are called “one,” a sameness of nature and essence, without disagreement or dissent, is signified. But when what the one thing is is added, something formed from several things may be signified, even though they differ in nature—as soul and body are certainly not one; for what is so different?—unless one adds or understands what the one thing is, namely, one human being or one animal.

Thus the Apostle says that whoever adheres to a prostitute is one body. He did not say “they are one” or “he is one,” but added “body,” as though one body had been composed by the addition of two different beings, male and female. And whoever adheres to the Lord, he says, is one spirit. He did not say, “Whoever adheres to the Lord is one,” or “they are one,” but added “spirit.” For the spirit of a human being and the Spirit of God differ in nature; yet through adherence one spirit is formed from two different beings, so that without the human spirit the Spirit of God is blessed and perfect, whereas the human spirit is blessed only with God.

Therefore, whether one says “God from God,” so that this name applies also to each individually, it is nevertheless not the case that the two together are two gods, but one God. For they adhere to one another in this way. The Apostle bears witness that the same can occur even in substances that are distinct and different. For the Spirit of the Lord alone is certainly spirit, and the spirit of a human being alone is certainly spirit; yet if it adheres to the Lord, it is one spirit. How much more, then, where the connection is wholly inseparable and eternal?

The mind has been ordered according to the order of natures, not of places, so that above it there is nothing except God. Therefore, when it has wholly adhered to him, it will be one spirit—a matter to which the Apostle bears witness when he says: “But whoever adheres to the Lord is one spirit.” It approaches participation in his nature, truth, and blessedness, but he does not thereby increase in his nature, truth, or blessedness. In that nature, then, to which it has happily adhered, it will see everything it sees as immutable. Then, as divine Scripture promises it, “its desire will be satisfied with good things”—with immutable things, [Col. 0419A] that is, with the Trinity itself, its God, whose image it is. And, so that it may never again be violated anywhere, it will be in the hidden place of his countenance, filled with such abundance of him that it will never take pleasure in sinning.

Flee fornication. He rightly urges that fornication be fled, through which the sons of God become sons of the devil.

Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but whoever commits fornication sins against his own body. He shows that fornication is the gravest sin, because through it the whole body is destroyed, whereas in other sins only a part perishes, not the whole. For the whole body is man and woman, since the woman is a part of the man. Whoever commits any other sin sins outside himself; but the fornicator sins against his own flesh.

Suppose that someone ends his life by hanging, or kills himself with a sword: does he not appear to sin against his own body? He does not sin against his body, but against the soul to which he does violence. Fornication, however, is a bodily offense that affects both body and soul—not without the desire of the flesh, since the flesh too has its own movement: the soul lusts in order to sin against the flesh, although without the soul it can accomplish nothing through that by which it sins against the flesh that comes from itself.

He refers this to the origin, saying that one sins against one’s own body, so that a person may cease from fornication as though sparing himself. Yet according to Novatian, the one who commits fornication does not seem to sin against his own body but against Christ’s. For he interprets this differently, so as to say that the fornicator also sins against the Holy Spirit, because of the reason for which he was cut off from the Church.

This cannot be established by any reasoning. The body of Christ is not one or two Christians, but all of them; each individual, however, is a member. How, then, does the fornicator sin against Christ’s body, when he does not contaminate everyone? If this were so, as it appears to Novatian, all other sins would be outside God, and fornication alone would be sin against God. Even the one who goes to idols would not sin against God, nor the one who denies Christ during persecution, since, according to that view, every sin that a person commits is outside Christ’s body.

But if he wishes to interpret this differently, so as to deny that any sin is outside the body, he will be compelled to say that everyone who commits any sin sins against God and against the Holy Spirit—so that the thief, the perjurer, and the liar would also be said to sin against the Holy Spirit. How, then, does the Lord’s statement stand, that [Col. 0419D] “all sins and blasphemies will be forgiven human beings,” but whoever sins against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come? It is plainly evident that, apart from the other sins, there is another sin called sin against the Holy Spirit.

Others, again, think that the fornicator is said to sin against his own body because he is a member of the Church, and by contaminating himself sins against the Church, whose member he is. Since, therefore, he is a member of the Church, they say that when he commits fornication he should be told that he sins not against himself but against the Church.

Yet the Apostle says that the fornicator sins against his own body by the fact that he has offended against his own portion. “Do you not know,” he says, “that whoever adheres to a prostitute is one body? For,” he says, “the two will be one flesh.” Could this be said of various other human crimes? In other kinds of wickedness, the human mind is free both to carry out some one act and, at that very time, to be distracted elsewhere in thought. But in the act and moment of fornication, the mind is not free to think about something else. Thus the whole person is absorbed by the act itself and by the body, so that the mind can no longer be said to belong to itself; rather, the whole person can be called flesh, “and a spirit that goes away and does not return.”

Thus we can understand the statement as follows: every sin that a person commits is outside the body, but whoever commits fornication sins against his own body. The Apostle seems to have wished to exaggerate the evil of fornication to such an extent that, by comparison with it, he said that all other sins were to be regarded as outside the body, and that only in this particular evil of fornication one sins against one’s own body—because the pleasure of the body holds a person enslaved and makes him captive through the greater heat of lust, beyond which there is none more intense.

He says: “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of God?” He said, “the temple of the Holy Spirit whom you have from God.” Earlier he called it the temple of God; here, the temple of the Holy Spirit, because in substance—that is, as Spirit—the Holy Spirit is God. He said this so that we might keep our bodies undefiled, so that the Holy Spirit might be able to dwell there.

And you are not your own, for you were bought at a great price. It is clear that the one who has been bought is not free to act according to his own will, but belongs to the one by whom he was bought, so that he does not do his own will but that person’s. And because we were bought at a high price, we ought to serve our God all the more earnestly, lest, offended by us, he who redeemed us hand us over to death. For at how precious a price did he purchase us, giving his blood for us!

Glorify and bear God in your body. That is: glorify and bear God in your body by walking according to his law; for through his law he himself is seen in us. “Bear God,” he says—that is, display the image of God in good deeds.

There are two sins and two kinds of sin: a person sins either against God or against another human being. One also sins against God by corrupting his temple within oneself. Indeed, the Lord redeemed you by the blood of his Son, although even before you were redeemed you belonged to someone—if not to the one who created all things? Yet in a particular way he wished to possess you as one redeemed by the blood of his Son.

“You are not your own,” he says; “you were bought at a great price. Glorify and bear the Lord in your body.” Therefore the one by whom you were redeemed makes you his house. Would you wish your own house to be overthrown? Surely not—nor would God wish his house, that is, yourself, to be overthrown. If you do not spare yourself for your own sake, spare yourself at least for the sake of God, who made you his temple. “The temple of God is holy, and that is what you are”; and whoever violates God’s temple, God will destroy.

Therefore each person must strive to cleanse his heart from every evil desire, and his life from every stain of sin and wicked deed, so that he may deserve to have God as an inhabitant within him—God almighty, who in perfect unity and Trinity reigns throughout all ages. Amen.

## HOMILY CXLIII. ALSO ON WEDNESDAY. Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Matthew

At that time Jesus said to the Pharisees: “Whoever is not with me is against me; and whoever does not gather with me scatters,” etc.

No one should think that this was spoken about heretics and schismatics—although it may also be understood in that secondary sense. From what follows and from the sequence of the discourse, it refers to the devil: the works of the Savior cannot be compared with the works of Beelzebul. The devil desires to hold human souls captive; the Lord desires to free them. The devil preaches idols; the Lord, knowledge of the one God. The devil draws people toward vices; the Lord calls them back to virtues. How, then, can there be agreement between those whose works are divided?

Therefore I say to you: Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven human beings. Not all sins and blasphemies are indiscriminately forgiven to all human beings, but to those who in this life have performed worthy repentance for their errors. Nor does Novatian have any place for his perverse assertion, when he denies that pardon should be granted to those who repent after having fallen during martyrdom; nor does Origen, when he claims that, after the universal judgment and after countless ages have passed, all sinners and blasphemers will obtain forgiveness of sins and be led to the heavenly kingdom. The Lord’s following words also refute this error, when he continues:

But blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven. Whoever, therefore, knowingly understands the works of God but, unable to deny God’s power, is provoked by envy to slander Christ and God’s Word, and says that the works of the Holy Spirit are Beelzebul—this person will not be forgiven, either in the present age or in the future. We do not deny that even this sin could be forgiven if the person wished to repent, by him who wishes all people to be saved and to come to knowledge of the truth. But because we believe the Judge and giver of forgiveness, who says both that he always accepts repentance and that this blasphemy will never be forgiven, we believe that this blasphemer, because of the demands of his merits, will reach neither forgiveness nor even the fruits of worthy repentance.

This accords with what the evangelist John wrote most truly about certain people blinded because of the merit of their blasphemy: “Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said again: ‘He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, so that they should not see with their eyes, understand with their heart, and be converted, and I should heal them.’”

Therefore only blasphemy against the Holy Spirit—by which a person, in the likeness of the devil and his angels, does not hesitate to attack the majesty of the Godhead against his own conscience—has no forgiveness forever; rather, he will be guilty of an eternal offense. The evangelist Mark makes this plainly clear: after setting down this testimony of the Lord, he added: “Because they were saying, ‘He has an unclean spirit.’” [Col. 0422A]

For neither those who believe that the Holy Spirit does not exist, nor those who believe and profess that he is indeed God but lesser than the Father and the Son, are held by this crime of unforgivable blasphemy, since they act under the influence not of diabolical envy but of human ignorance. Therefore the leaders of the Jews, and all who are corrupted by a similar plague of envy and blaspheme the majesty of God, will perish without end.

And whoever says a word against the Son of Man, it will be forgiven him. It is as though he were saying in other words: Whoever speaks insults against me, scandalized by my flesh and judging me to be merely human—thinking that I am the son of a carpenter, that I have brothers named James, Joseph, and Judas, and that I am a glutton and a drinker of wine—such an opinion and blasphemy, although it is not free from the guilt of error, nevertheless has forgiveness because of the lowliness of the body.

For in what follows:

But whoever says something against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come,

these words make it understood that God releases certain offenses in this age and certain others in the age to come. For what is denied concerning one case makes it clear by consequence that it is granted concerning others. Yet this should be believed possible only with regard to small and very minor sins, such as continual idle speech, immoderate laughter, or the sin involved in managing one’s household affairs—matters that are scarcely handled without fault even by those who know how fault should be avoided—or offenses that are not serious, resulting from ignorant error. All these weigh even after death if they have not been released while the person still lives in this life.

This must be understood, however: there, at least, no one will obtain purification even from minor faults unless, while still living in this present life, he has deserved to obtain it there through good works.

Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad; for the tree is known by its fruit. He constrains them by a syllogism, which the Greeks call *Aphucton* [ἄφυκτον], while we may call it “inescapable.” It encloses those questioned from both sides and presses them between its two horns. “If,” he says, “the devil is evil, he cannot perform good works; but if the things you see being done are good, it follows that the one doing them is not the devil. For it cannot happen that good comes from evil, or evil from good.”

Offspring of vipers, how can you speak good things when you are evil? He calls them offspring of vipers because he calls them sons of the devil. A person is his son to the extent that he imitates him by sinning. By saying, “How can you speak good things when you are evil?” he shows that they are a bad tree and that they produce fruits overflowing with blasphemy, such as the devil’s seeds had within them.

For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. Human judgment often errs because it does not know the heart of one’s neighbor, except by weighing it from the mouth and from conduct. But the Lord judges our very works and speeches, which the mouth of the heart speaks; he is not ignorant of the intention from which words proceed.

A good person brings good things out of a good treasure, and an evil person brings evil things out of an evil treasure. The treasure of the heart is the intention of thought, from which the eternal Judge judges the outcome of a deed. Thus it often happens that some people perform lesser good works yet receive a greater reward of heavenly grace—namely, because of the intention of the heart, by which they had wished to accomplish greater good if they had been able. Others, while displaying greater works of virtue, receive lesser rewards from the Lord because of the negligence of a lukewarm heart.

But in this passage the Lord either shows the Jews themselves, while blaspheming, from what sort of treasure—that is, from what hidden place of the heart—they bring forth blasphemy; or the statement remains connected with the preceding question: just as a good person cannot bring forth evil, nor an evil person perform good works, so Christ cannot perform evil works, nor the devil good works.

[Col. 0423B] But I say to you that for every idle word that human beings speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment. This too is connected with what precedes, and the meaning is as follows: If an idle word, which in no way builds up those who hear it, is spoken by the one who speaks it without escaping danger, and each person will have to give an account on the day of judgment for his words, how much more will you have to give an account of your slander, when you slander the works of the Holy Spirit and say that I cast out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons?

An idle word is one spoken without benefit to either the speaker or the hearer—that is, when we speak about frivolous matters without rational purpose and tell old stories. But whoever repeats vulgarity, loosens mouths into laughter, and brings forth something shameful will be held guilty not of idle speech but of criminal speech.

By your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned. The statement still depends on what preceded, where he says: “For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.” There is no doubt that a person who brings forth evil words is condemned by God because of them. But no one can be justified by good words unless he speaks them with a right intention from the depths of his heart. Even if words are good, if they are spoken without a right purpose, they cannot justify the speaker—as Caiaphas too was not found righteous in prophesying when he said: “It is better that one man should die for the people than that the whole nation should perish.”

Those words, therefore, justify the speaker when he holds inwardly in his heart the good that he brings forth with his mouth and utters it with a sound intention. For the testing of human life consists in the weight of words, since, as Solomon says, “death and life are in the power of the tongue,” and “whoever guards his mouth guards his soul from distress.” But whoever is careless in speaking will experience evils.

## HOMILY CXLIV. ON FRIDAY. Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Luke

At that time, when Jesus was asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, he answered and said: “The kingdom of God does not come with observation,” etc.

They were asking about the time of the kingdom of God because, as Luke later makes clear, they supposed that when the Lord came to Jerusalem the kingdom of God would immediately be revealed. The Apostles themselves were led by this opinion, so that after his resurrection they asked him: “Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” Elsewhere Cleopas said: “But we were hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel.”

But the kingdom of God does not come with observation, nor will they say, “Look, here it is.” For its coming cannot be observed either by angels or by human beings, unlike the time of the Lord’s incarnation, which was fixed by the most certain prophecies and announced by the proclamations of angels. Thus his conception, birth, baptism, preaching, death, resurrection, and return to heaven were continually declared by signs—whether of angels, human beings, or certainly miracles.

[Col. 0424B] For behold, the kingdom of God is within you. He calls himself the kingdom of God, placed within them—that is, in their hearts, where they believed that he reigned. Hence it is written: “The word is near you, in your mouth,” that is, the word of faith that we preach.

And he said to his disciples: The days will come when you will desire to see one day of the Son of Man, and you will not see it. This is the kingdom of God that we hope will come: namely, to see the day of Christ. He rightly says “one day,” because in that glory of blessedness about which the Prophet sighed, saying, “One day in your courts is better than thousands”: no interruption of darkness, and no memory of misery or pain—the things that first passed away—will obscure the everlasting light of peace.

It is good, therefore, to desire the presence of this God, but the magnitude of our desire must not make us imagine that everything is already present, as though the day of the Lord were at hand. Therefore the Lord appropriately added a prediction of what was to come:

And they will say to you, “Look here,” or “Look there”; do not go away, nor follow them. Although this statement can be understood not only of a time but also of a person. Of a time, because there have been some who, calculating the courses of the ages, claimed that they had discovered the definite year, day, and hour of the consummation of the world—against the authority of the Lord, who says: “It is not for you to know the times or moments.” Of a person, because many have come against the Church, and many heretics will come, claiming that they are Christs. The first of these was Simon Magus; the last, and greater than the others, is the Antichrist.

If, then, some say, “Look here,” or “Look there”—that is, that the kingdom of God has come or will come in this or that person, or at this or that hour—they must not be followed, because they are not afraid to seek things higher than themselves and to utter unspeakable claims.

For as lightning flashing from beneath the sky shines upon the things that are beneath the sky, so will the Son of Man be in his day. This is what the Psalm says: “God will come openly; our God, and he will not be silent.” For the second coming of the Savior will not be in humility, as before, but in glory and majesty. He aptly says “flashing from beneath the sky”: that is, it will take place in the middle of the air, as the Apostle bears witness when he says, “We shall be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air.”

But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation. While speaking much about the glory of his coming, the Lord also took care to insert a brief reference to the terror of his Passion, so that when they saw dying the one whom they had heard would be glorified, the pain of his Passion might be eased by hope of the promised glorification. At the same time, they would prepare themselves, if they loved the glory of the kingdom, not to dread the danger of death.

He calls “this generation” not only the Jews but all the reprobate, from whom even now the Son of Man suffers and is rejected in his body, that is, in the Church.

And just as it happened in the days of Noah, so will it be in the day of the Son of Man. He confirms by many examples that the day of his coming will be sudden. For the day that he had compared to lightning swiftly passing over everything, he likewise compares with the days of Noah and Lot, when sudden destruction came upon mortals.

They were eating and drinking, marrying wives, and being given in marriage. Here he does not condemn marriages or food according to the insane doctrine of Marcion, Manichaeus, and Tatian, the leader of the Encratites, since in the former are found the means of succession and in the latter the provisions of nature. Rather, he censures the immoderate use of permitted things, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “All things are lawful for me, but not all things are beneficial.” For they did not perish by water or fire because they did these things, but because, devoting themselves entirely to them, they despised God’s judgments.

Until the day when Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all. Noah builds the ark while the Lord constructs the Church by gathering together faithful men as though they were smoothed pieces of wood. Once the ark has been perfectly completed, he enters it when the eternal inhabitant illumines it with the presence of his vision on the day of judgment. But while the ark is being built, the wicked indulge themselves; when it is entered, they perish. For those who here insult the saints while they struggle will there be punished with eternal condemnation when the saints are crowned.

Likewise, just as it happened in the days of Lot: they were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building. The Lord passes over that greatest and unspeakable crime of the Sodomites and mentions only those offenses that might be considered light or even no offenses at all, so that you may understand with what punishment unlawful acts are struck, if permitted acts—and acts without which this life cannot be lived—are punished with fire and sulfur when carried out immoderately.

But on the day when Lot went out from Sodom, fire and sulfur rained from heaven and destroyed them all. So long as Lot remains in Sodom—that is, the people of the elect dwell as strangers among the reprobate—he is righteous in sight and hearing, avoiding their crimes as far as he can, in accordance with the interpretation of the name Lot.

But when Lot goes out, Sodom will perish, because at the consummation of the world the angels will go out and separate the wicked from among the righteous and cast them into the furnace of fire. Here it should be noted that the fire and sulfur which he says rained from heaven signify not the flame of everlasting punishment itself but the sudden coming of that day. For the perpetual fire will not come upon the wicked and punish them; rather, they will be cast into eternal fire after being expelled from the sight of the Judge.

Nevertheless, we do not doubt that sulfur is also present in that fire, as John testifies when, describing both the fire of sudden correction and the fire of everlasting burning, he says: “And fire came down from God out of heaven and devoured them; and the devil who deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast and the false prophets will be tormented day and night forever and ever.”

According to these things will it be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed. He is rightly said to be “revealed,” since, though he is meanwhile unseen, he will then appear and judge all things.

In that hour, whoever is on the roof, with his possessions in the house, must not come down to take them. Thus far he has spoken of the fact that the kingdom of God—that is, Christ—comes not with observation but unexpectedly. Now he shows what sort of people ought to await that coming.

The one who is on the roof is someone who, having transcended earthly things, lives spiritually as though in the free air. His possessions in the house are the bodily desires that he had loved below but had left in this world while seeking what is above. When judgment approaches, he must not in any way return to them. He speaks not of the hour in which the Judge comes, but of the hour in which he will come.

And whoever is in the field must not turn back. Whoever works in the Church, and like Paul and Apollos plants and waters, must not look back toward the world to which he has renounced his allegiance.

Remember Lot’s wife. Lot’s wife signifies those who, in tribulation, look back and turn themselves away from hope in the divine promise. Therefore she was made into a pillar of salt, so that by warning people not to do this she might, as it were, season their hearts, lest they be foolish.

Whoever seeks to save his life will lose it. This statement can rightly be understood in two ways, but both interpretations refer entirely to one end: we must not fear suffering adversity for Christ, or even undergoing death itself. When a persecutor threatens death, whoever denies Christ in order to choose to save his life temporarily thereby prepares it unquestionably for eternal destruction. Likewise, whoever seeks the eternal salvation of his soul does not hesitate to lose it temporarily among the hands of persecutors—that is, to give it over to death.

Which of these interpretations agrees with what follows:

And whoever loses it will make it alive. That is, whoever loses it here will make it alive there. Whoever hands it over to death for Christ, esteeming it all day long as a sheep for slaughter, will then find it free, when Christ rises and helps it, on account of the name of Christ.

I tell you: On that night two will be in one bed. Above, the Lord had said that the person who is in the field must not return. So that you would not think this was spoken only about those who will openly return from the field—that is, those who will openly deny the Lord—he continues by showing that there are some who, although they seem to keep their faces directed forward, nevertheless look back in spirit and mind.

Therefore, on that night—which is so dark a tribulation that, if possible, even the elect might be led into error—he says that two will be in one bed: namely, those who choose leisure and rest, occupied neither with secular affairs nor with ecclesiastical affairs. Their rest is signified by the name “bed.”

[Col. 0427A] One will be taken and the other will be left. This is not to be understood as spoken of two people, but of two kinds of disposition. Whoever has devoted himself to continence for God’s sake, so that, living without anxiety, he may think about the things of God, will be taken by God. But whoever, whether out of love of human praise or through some other seizure by vices, has harmed the state of monastic life with which he was imbued, will be left behind. Where he is to be left, the Lamentations of Jeremiah indicate: describing under the figure of Judaea the fall of any idle and sinful soul, he says, “Her enemies saw her and mocked her Sabbaths.”

Two will be grinding together. He calls those who are established among the common people and are governed by teachers “grinders,” as they do the things of this world. He also signified them by the name “women,” because, as I have said, it is advantageous for them to be governed by the counsel of the experienced. He called them “grinders” because of the circle and circuit of temporal affairs. Yet he says that they are grinding together insofar as, from these very affairs and occupations, they provide for the uses of the Church.

Every activity of this world is a millstone: while it piles up many cares, it turns human minds around as though in a circle and throws out from itself something like flour, because with its restless heart it continually produces the finest thoughts.

One will be taken and the other will be left. The part that has practiced marriage solely for love of offspring, and has distributed earthly possessions in order to acquire heavenly things, will be taken. But the part that has devoted itself to marriage for the allurements of the flesh, and, if it has offered any earthly goods to the Church or the poor, has done so in order that these goods might abound to it still more, as though by the Lord’s redemption, will be left.

[Col. 0427C] Two will be in the field; one will be taken and the other will be left. Just as above he placed the two in one bed and the two grinders together, so here too I think it should be understood as two in one field. It signifies those who work in the ministry of the Church, as in the field of God, of which its own farmer said: “You are God’s cultivation.”

The one who does not adulterate the word of God, but speaks in Christ as from God and before God, will be taken. But the one who announces Christ not chastely, but from opportunism, will be left by him.

They answered and said to him: Where, Lord? He said to them: Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered. Asked where the good would be taken and where the wicked would be left, the Savior stated one thing and left the other to be understood. By asserting that the saints would be with him, he indicated that the reprobate would certainly be separated from his vision and therefore condemned elsewhere only with the devil.

Wherever, then, the Lord’s body is, there the elect will be gathered—those who, by imitating his Passion and humility, are nourished as though on his flesh. Through the resurrection their youth will be renewed like that of eagles, so that they may live and reign with their Savior forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY CXLV. ON THE VIGIL OF SAINT LAWRENCE. Reading from the Book of Ecclesiasticus

I will give thanks to you, Lord and King, and praise you, God my Savior. I will confess your name, for you have become my helper and protector, and you have delivered my body from destruction, from the snare of an evil tongue and from the lips of those who practice deceit, etc.

For the Lord Jesus Christ is God, King, and Savior of the Church; he is also her head and bridegroom. Hence the Apostle, admonishing wives to be subject to their husbands, wrote to the Ephesians, saying: “Let wives be subject to their husbands as to the Lord, because the husband is the head of the wife, just as Christ is the head of the Church; he is the Savior of the body.” And again: “Husbands,” he says, “love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church and gave himself for her, so that he might sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word, so that he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind, but holy and immaculate.”

This helper and protector, therefore, became the bride’s helper when he gave himself for her, so that he might deliver her from destruction, into which she had fallen through the transgression of the first human being; and from the snare of an evil tongue—that is, from the blasphemy of idolatry, so that she might neither sacrifice nor serve the creature rather than the Creator—and from the lips of those who practice deceit, that is, from the false teachings of philosophers and heretics.

And you became my helper in the sight of those who stood by. And you delivered me, according to the abundance of the mercy of your name, from those roaring and prepared for prey. By this testimony he expresses the persecutors of the Church, who, out of hatred for the name of Christ, persecute the faithful and hand them over to various torments and death, in order to turn them away from confessing the catholic faith and from worshiping the true and one God.

He aptly compares them to savage beasts, which with a powerful roar and ferocious gape seek their prey. But from them the Lord delivers his elect, preserving their souls unharmed amid the heat of persecutions, on account of whose destruction the savage persecutors chiefly tear their bodies. Hence it follows:

From the hands of those seeking my life, and from the gates of tribulations that surrounded me. What can we better understand as the gates of tribulations than the mouths of rulers and tyrants, from which threats, deceitful persuasions, and declarations of punishments proceed, so that by either feigned blandishments or savage tortures they may make God’s servants deny the faith of Christ? Yet the Lord sends an angel around those who fear him, and he will deliver them.

And from the pressure of the flame that surrounded me; and in the midst of the fire I was not burned. We often read that this occurred historically in the sufferings of martyrs: just as the three youths were preserved unharmed from the heat of the flame in the furnace of fire, so these too were preserved undefiled from the blaze of fire.

But because this was not granted to all the martyrs of God, since very many of them were bodily consumed in the fire, and yet their souls freely sought the hidden places of heaven, we understand “fire” and “flame” here better as the powerful heat of persecution. Although it could afflict the saints of God temporarily, it could not reach the destruction of their souls. Therefore he adds:

From the depth of the belly of hell, and from a defiled tongue, and from a deceitful word, from an unjust king, and from an unjust tongue. [Col. 0429A] “He delivered me” is understood. For the wicked force of the enemies could not prevail so as to reach the destruction of souls, which he here calls “the belly of hell.” Nor could a defiled tongue with blasphemies, nor deceitful words spoken by an unjust king and an unjust tongue, in any way violate the inmost hearts of the saints. Although they afflicted their bodies with various punishments and condemned them to temporal death, their souls nevertheless remained steadfast in confessing the name of Christ to the end of life.

Therefore, more happily after death, they will rejoice without end in eternal life with God’s holy angels. Concerning this he adds:

My soul will praise the Lord until death, and my life was drawing near to the underworld below. He says that his life is drawing near to the underworld because the life of the flesh, failing day by day, approaches death. [Col. 0429B] Here “the underworld” is used for death, since the death of the flesh is the punishment for the first transgression, just as the underworld is the perpetual punishment of sinful souls. But no one escapes bodily death. For who is the human being who lives and will not see death? Hence it is written elsewhere: “There is no one, therefore, who always lives and has confidence in this.” But holy people can escape the torment of the underworld through the grace of Christ, because, released from the bond of the flesh, they will immediately pass over to heavenly joy.

They surrounded me on every side, and there was no one to help. Looking around for human assistance, there was none. I remembered your mercy, Lord, and your work, which is from eternity; for you rescue those who endure for you, Lord, and you free them from the hands of distress. [Col. 0429C] The Lord our God, seeing the Church—its members—surrounded on every side by enemies, and human consolation failing, seeks assistance from the source from which he knows the success of all good things to come. Therefore he attributes it not to his own merits, nor to human deeds, but to the mercy of God, acknowledging that she has been snatched away and freed from her enemies; and not merely freed, but also exalted by the honor of her virtues and glorified by the radiance of miracles. For from him, through him, and in him are all things; to him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY 146. ON THE SAME FEAST

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Matthew.

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “If anyone [Col. 0429D] wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me,” etc.

After showing his disciples the mystery of his passion and resurrection, he urges them to follow the example of his passion and promises salvation in the future to all who suffer tribulation for his sake. Yet he did not disclose to everyone, but only to those who were more perfect, how much he himself would suffer and that he would rise from the dead. “If anyone wishes,” he says, “to follow after me, let him deny himself.” We deny ourselves, then, when we avoid what we were through our old condition and strive toward that to which we are called through renewal. “And let him take up his cross and follow me.” For the cross is taken up in two ways: either when the body is afflicted through abstinence, [Col. 0430A] or when the spirit is afflicted through compassion for one’s neighbor. Let us consider how Paul carried his cross in both ways. He said: “I chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, while preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified.” Behold, in the affliction of the body we have heard of the cross of the flesh; now, in compassion for one’s neighbor, let us hear of the cross of the mind. He says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?” The perfect preacher, then, to give an example of abstinence, carried the cross in his body; and the one who bore within himself the injuries caused by another’s weakness carried the cross in his heart.

For whoever wishes to save his soul will lose it; but whoever loses his soul for my sake will find it. Great and wondrous is the saying: how can [Col. 0430B] a person’s love for his own soul cause it to perish, and hatred preserve it? If you have loved wrongly, then you have hated; if you have hated rightly, then you have loved. Blessed are those who hate in order to preserve themselves, lest by loving they perish.

For what does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul? When persecution from adversaries is absent, the heart must be guarded with even greater vigilance. For in a time of peace, because it is permitted to live, there is also a desire to seek advancement; and often we overcome greed, but there still remains the obstacle that we maintain the paths of righteousness with too little watchfulness for perfection. For often we despise all passing things; yet we are still hindered by the force of human shame, so that we cannot yet express in speech the righteousness we preserve in our mind. And we neglect the face of God in defense of justice [Col. 0430C] to the extent that we fear human faces in opposition to justice.

Or what exchange can a person give for his soul? For Israel, Egypt and Ethiopia are given as an exchange; but for the human soul there is that one repayment which the Psalmist sings: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord.”

For the Son of Man is going to come in the glory of his Father with his angels. Because he who is lesser than the Father in human nature is himself, in the unity of one and the same glory, with the Father.

And then he will repay each person according to his works. Peter, scandalized by the preaching of the Lord’s death, had been rebuked by the Lord’s judgment. When he had urged his disciples [Col. 0430D] to deny themselves, take up their cross, and follow their teacher with the disposition of those who are dying, great terror seized the listeners; and what could have instilled fear in the other Apostles as well as in the terrified chief of the Apostles? Therefore, joyful words follow sorrowful ones, and he says: “The Son of Man is going to come in the glory of his Father with his angels.” You fear death—hear of the glory of the triumphant one. You dread the cross—listen to the ministry of the angels. “And then,” he says, “he will repay each person according to his works.” There is no distinction between Jew and Greek, man and woman, poor and rich, where not persons, but works, are considered.

Amen, I say to you: there are some of those standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man [Col. 0431A] coming in his kingdom. The kingdom of God, in which the Son of God—the same one who is also the Son of Man—reigns, is here called the present Church. And because some of the disciples were destined to live in the body long enough to see the Church of God established and raised up, through the power of its founder, against the glory of this world, it is now said by way of consoling promise: “There are some of those standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom,” that is, displaying his power. But since the Lord was issuing such serious commands concerning the death he would undergo, why did he suddenly proceed to this promise? If we attend to it carefully, we recognize with what dispensation of mercy this was done. For something concerning the present life also had to be promised to inexperienced disciples, so that they might be [Col. 0431B] strengthened more firmly for the future life. Wherever this has occurred, it will have been accomplished by the grace of God, who wishes all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY 147. ON THE BIRTHDAY OF SAINT LAWRENCE

Reading from the Epistle of blessed Paul the Apostle to the Corinthians.

Brothers, whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly; and whoever sows in blessings will also reap from blessings eternal life, etc.

Dearest brothers, today we celebrate the feast of blessed Lawrence, who was found faithful in all things as the steward of his Lord. For just as he faithfully administered the resources of the Church entrusted to him by his teacher, so he deserved [Col. 0431C] happily to be crowned by the Lord his God. Hence the present reading has spoken to us, as you have heard, about the faithful steward: “Whoever sows sparingly,” it says, “will also reap sparingly,” because whatever each person gives here to the Lord from these earthly and transitory things, he will receive an equal reward in the future, if he gives it with a good and simple heart. For many who give much lose their reward because they receive from human beings the praise they seek. Hence it continues: “And whoever sows in blessings will also reap from blessings,” as though it were saying: Whoever does whatever good he can with the sole intention of receiving future and eternal rewards from the Lord will reap the fruit of his good seed in the heavenly homeland.

Let each person give as he has decided in his heart, not from [Col. 0431D] sadness or compulsion. That is, voluntarily, not under coercion. It continues:

For God loves a cheerful giver. Therefore let us act according to that saying of Solomon: “In every gift show a cheerful face,” because God searches out the secrets of the heart. He wishes a teacher to be cheerful in his labor. Hence Paul says elsewhere: “If I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship, and if I do not carry it out worthily, I receive punishment.”

For God is able to make every grace abound in us. God always exercises his own abundance of mercy in all things for all who seek his goodness with a sincere heart. Therefore it is our task only to commend our will purely to God [Col. 0432A] and to attribute to his mercy, never to our own merits, all the good things we are able to accomplish through the generosity of his grace. He himself will deign to fulfill all his grace in us:

So that, always having complete sufficiency in all things, we may abound in every good work. As it is written: “He scattered abroad, he gave to the poor; his righteousness remains forever.” For whoever faithfully administers here what has been entrusted by his Lord deserves to hear that desirable sentence of the Gospel servant: “Well done, good servant; because you have been faithful in a little, enter into the joy of your Lord.” For what is more glorious for a person than to give earthly and transitory things and purchase the heavenly kingdoms? To offer the Lord, as a most acceptable gift, sincere willingness, the diligence of a devoted mind, and an unfailing voice of praise; and to accompany [Col. 0432B] Christ when he begins to come to judge; to become Christ’s coheir; to be made equal to the angels? Let us therefore honor, dearest brothers, blessed Lawrence, who, by overcoming the flames of his persecutor through his faith, showed us that through the fire of faith the fires of Gehenna are overcome. Let us also rejoice with spiritual joy and glory in the Lord over the end of this most blessed man. We trust that we are continually assisted by his prayer and patronage if we celebrate his solemnity with worthy conduct and holy works. Let us strengthen one another in the spirit of charity so as to overcome all temptations and snares; let us be remarkably steadfast, united in every good work, and fortified by the shield of faith against the goads of every vice, through him who conquered the devil and gave us the power to conquer him: Jesus Christ our Lord, [Col. 0432C] to whom be praise and glory throughout all ages. Amen.

## HOMILY 148. ON THE SAME FEAST

Reading from the holy Gospel according to John.

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless a grain of wheat falling into the ground dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.”

He was saying that he himself had to be put to death and multiplied: put to death through the unbelief of the Jews, multiplied through the faith of all peoples. Now, exhorting them to follow the footsteps of his passion, he adds:

[Col. 0432D] Whoever loves his soul will lose it. This can be understood in two ways. “Whoever loves will lose,” that is, if you love it, lose it; if you desire to preserve life in Christ, do not fear dying for Christ. Or in another way: “Whoever loves his soul will lose it”: do not love it in this life, lest you lose it in eternal life. The latter meaning, however, seems more consistent with the Gospel sense. For it continues:

And whoever hates his soul in this world preserves it for eternal life. Therefore, when it was said above, “Whoever loves,” we should understand “in this world”: that person will certainly lose it. But whoever hates it—again, in this world—will certainly preserve it for eternal life. Great and wondrous is the saying: how can a person’s love for his own soul cause it to perish, and hatred preserve it? If you have loved wrongly, [Col. 0433A] then you have hated; if you have hated rightly, then you have loved. Blessed are those who hate in order to preserve themselves, lest by loving they perish. Here the soul signifies the present life, or even the pleasure of this life, which is lost so that you may happily find your will in the kingdom of God, having bravely conquered it in this world. For the holy martyrs hated this present life for Christ’s name: they preferred to lose this present life rather than deny Christ, fulfilling what follows:

If anyone serves me, let him follow me. What does “let him follow me” mean except “let him imitate me”? For Christ suffered for us, as the Apostle Peter says, leaving us an example so that we might follow his footsteps. Behold what is meant by the words: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me.” With what fruit? With what payment? With what reward?

[Col. 0433B] And where I am, he says, there also my servants will be. The reward of love and the payment for the work by which Christ is served is to be with the one whom one serves. For where can it be well without him, or how could it be bad to be with him? Hear this more clearly:

And if anyone serves me, my Father, who is in heaven, will honor him. With what honor, except that he may be with his Son? For what he said earlier—“Where I am, there also my servant will be”—he explains when he says, “My Father will honor him.” For what greater honor could an adopted child receive than to be where the only Son is—not made equal to him in divinity, but admitted to eternity?

What it means to serve Christ, for which so great a reward is promised, must be considered. “If anyone serves me, let him follow me”: he intended this [Col. 0433C] to be understood as though he were saying, “If anyone does not follow me, he does not serve me.” Those, therefore, serve Jesus Christ who seek not their own interests but those of Jesus Christ. For this is what “let him follow me” means: let him walk in my ways, not his own, as it is written elsewhere: “Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked.” Therefore whoever follows the Lord Christ in this manner—namely, by keeping his commandments and persevering in right faith to the end—will rejoice with him forever in the heavenly kingdom.

## HOMILY 149. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF HOLY MARY

Reading from the Book of Ecclesiasticus.

“In all these things I sought rest, and I will dwell in the inheritance of the Lord. Then the Creator [Col. 0433D] of all commanded and said to me: And he who created me rested in my tabernacle,” etc.

The Son of God, the Word and Wisdom of God the Father, speaking through Solomon in the person of Wisdom, who is himself, announces to the human race that he desires to rest in them and dwell among them. Since the human being was made in the image of God, if he wishes to remain in God, then, with a pure heart and sincere will, God remains in him and he himself in God. Hence in the present reading that you have heard, the Wisdom of God, the Son of God, speaks to human beings: “In all these things I sought rest,” as in the saying of the Apostle: “For God wishes every person to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth,” so that, abandoning the error of earthly desire and conquering carnal [Col. 0434A] longings, each person may prepare within himself, with a pure heart and chaste body, a dwelling worthy of the Wisdom of God. For it follows: “And I will dwell in his inheritance.” God’s inheritance is all who love God and are faithful fellow workers of his will for their own salvation.

“Then the Creator of all commanded and said to me, and he who created me rested in my tabernacle.” The Wisdom of God—that is, the Son of God—remaining in eternity with the Father, equal to the Father in every respect in majesty, established the human being whom he made in his own image as an heir of eternal immortality. But when that human being had been led astray by the devil and made mortal through sin, in his mercy he resolved to clothe himself in human mortality, so that he might restore humanity once again to eternal immortality.

And he said to me. Earlier, through patriarchs [Col. 0434B] and prophets, he had announced his coming into this world in many ways.

Dwell in Jacob. For he promised to dwell in those who overthrow vices and sins and trample them down through zeal for good works, with divine grace bestowing the ability. It continues:

And inherit in Israel. That is, in those who show themselves worthy of the vision of God through chastity and the holiness of good works, as in the saying: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.”

And send down roots among my elect. For these are God’s elect: those who entirely abandon, by their whole will, all the delights of this world; who cling to this world only from necessity. Of them the Apostle says: “Those who use this world as though they did not use it,” that is, [Col. 0434C] from necessity alone and not with the consent of pleasure.

And so I was established in Zion, and likewise I rested in the sanctified city, and my power was in Jerusalem. In such people the Wisdom of God, the Son of God, deigns to dwell. By examples of good works they offer to others a mirror of life; and in the holy Church, through holy conduct, they work salvation for themselves and others and hasten toward the vision of eternal peace.

I took root among an honored people, and in the portion of my God is his inheritance. For God chose the Israelite people as his special people above all nations, because Israel is said to mean “a man seeing God.” They are to be understood spiritually as those who, through chastity of life in holy conduct, continually hasten to contemplate eternal joys. This gift belongs only to those who, by the generosity of divine grace, [Col. 0434D] preserve a commitment to continence or even virginity solely from desire for eternal glory.

I was exalted like a cedar in Lebanon and like a cypress on Mount Zion. The cedar and the cypress, trees of the highest fragrance and taller than the other trees in Lebanon, signify the men of more exalted virtue within the Church. We may understand these as virgins, who deserve to reap a hundredfold fruit.

This was clearly signified in the most blessed Mary, Mother of God, whose annual day of most blessed assumption into heaven we celebrate today. For the promise that God, the Son of God, had made—that he would come into this world for the redemption of the human race—he fulfilled not through a married woman, however holy, as we read in many Scriptures, nor [Col. 0435A] through a chaste widow, but through this one virginal body alone. For, like a bright-rising sun, free from every stain of pollution, he proceeded from the womb of the virgin mother—a woman certainly blessed and worthy of all praise, who received offspring from heaven and gave birth to the Savior for the world.

Although the merits of virginity are so great, the marriage bed of chastity must nevertheless not be rejected, because the good of virginity proceeds only from the marital bed. Chastity in a virgin is high and supreme if it remains simultaneously in heart and body. But marital chastity is holier when it remains simultaneously in the heart and is established in the body than that which is chaste only in the heart but is adulterated in the heart in various ways, whether through boastfulness, pride, or even the desire for lust.

Therefore, dearest ones, let us diligently preserve not only our body [Col. 0435B] but also our heart from everything the Lord hates, and let us ask his mercy to strengthen our heart in everything that pleases him. Amid all this, let us implore the aid of the blessed Virgin with the whole affection of our heart, because while we attend upon her on earth with humble devotion, she deigns to commend us through persistent prayer to Christ our Lord in heaven. May he himself grant this, he who reigns and rules in perfect Trinity throughout all ages. Amen.

## HOMILY 150. ON THE SAME FEAST

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Luke.

At that time Jesus entered a certain village; and a woman named Martha welcomed him [Col. 0435C] into her house. And she had a sister named Mary, etc.

This reading is connected with the preceding one in a most beautiful manner, because the former signifies love of God and neighbor in words and parables, while this one signifies it in deeds themselves and in truth. These two sisters, beloved by the Lord, demonstrate the two spiritual lives by which the holy Church is exercised in the present. Martha represents the active life, through which we join ourselves to our neighbor in charity; Mary represents the contemplative life, through which we sigh with love for God.

The active life is to give bread to the hungry, to teach the ignorant with the word of wisdom, to correct the one who has gone astray and lead him back to the way of humanity, to recall a proud neighbor, to care for the sick, to distribute to each person whatever is useful, and to provide for those entrusted to us in such a way [Col. 0435D] that they may be able to endure. The contemplative life, however, is to retain the love of God and neighbor with the whole mind, but to rest from exterior action and cling solely to the desire for the Creator, so that one wishes to do nothing, but, with all cares trampled down, the spirit burns to see the face of its Creator. Thus one already knows how to bear with sorrow the burden of corruptible flesh and, with every desire, longs to take part in the hymn-singing choirs of the angels, to be joined to the heavenly citizens, and to rejoice in incorruption eternally in the presence of God.

She sat beside the Lord’s feet and was listening to his word; but Martha was busy with extensive service. No one can doubt that this applies to both lives. The perfection of the contemplative life is [Col. 0436A] to have the mind stripped of all earthly things and, as far as human weakness permits, to unite it with Christ. But how extensive the ministry of the active life is, the teacher of the nations teaches us, for in the frequent statements of his letters he recounts his labors and dangers for Christ by land and sea. In these same writings, while commending the Lord’s visions and revelations, he indicates that he was no less perfected in the contemplative virtue, insofar as it is imitable. Hence he says: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober, it is for you.”

She stood and said: “Lord, is it no concern to you that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her, therefore, to help me.” She speaks as one of those who are still ignorant of divine contemplation and who consider only the work of fraternal love that they have learned to be pleasing to God. Therefore they maintain that all who wish to be devoted to Christ must be assigned to this work. [Col. 0436B]

And the Lord answered and said to her: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things; but one thing is necessary.” Blessed David, likewise defining this one thing as necessary for a human being, desires to cling to God continually, saying: “But it is good for me to adhere to God, to place my hope in the Lord God”; and elsewhere: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to see the will of the Lord and visit his holy temple.” There is therefore one and only one *theoria*, that is, contemplation of God, to which all the merits of justification and every pursuit of virtue are rightly subordinated.

Mary chose the better part, which will not be taken away from [Col. 0436C] her. Behold, Martha’s portion is not condemned, but Mary’s is praised. For he does not say that Mary chose a good portion, but the better one, so that Martha’s portion too might be judged good. Why Mary’s portion is better is added when he says, “which will not be taken away from her.” The active life indeed fails with the body. For who will offer bread to the hungry in the eternal homeland, where no one hungers? Who will give drink to the thirsty, where no one thirsts? Who will bury the dead, where no one dies? With the present age, therefore, the active life is taken away. The contemplative life, however, begins here so that it may be perfected in the heavenly homeland, because the fire of love that begins to burn here grows still more ardent when it sees the one whom it loves. The contemplative life, therefore, is by no means taken away; when the light of the present age has been withdrawn, it is perfected in eternal glory through [Col. 0436D] Jesus Christ our Lord, who with God the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God throughout all ages. Amen.

## HOMILY 151. THE THIRTEENTH WEEK AFTER PENTECOST

Reading from the Epistle to the Corinthians.

Brothers, we have such confidence through Christ toward God—not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as though from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God, etc.

There can be no doubt, dearest ones, that every Christian observance is of divine origin, and that whatever has been received into the custom of the Church proceeds from apostolic tradition and the teaching of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0437A] Hence in the present reading the Apostle says: “We have such confidence through Christ toward God,” because we know that you were not able to believe through yourselves, but only through divine grace at work: “not that we are sufficient to think anything from ourselves, as though from ourselves.” As though he were saying: We can do nothing through our own prudence and strength, as the Lord himself says: “Without me you can do nothing.” Nor could it ever have happened through us, rustic people, that such a great multitude of believers should hasten toward salvation without the grace of God. Hence it continues:

But our sufficiency is from God, who accomplishes in his servants whatever he wills.

He also made us competent ministers of the New Testament. Thus the prophecy might be fulfilled that says: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it”; and the Lord himself: “For it is not you [Col. 0437B] who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you”; and again: “For I will give you a mouth and wisdom.” From where, except from the Holy Spirit, did the Apostles become so competent that through them such great divine mysteries were revealed to believers? It continues:

Not of the letter. For they did not discover all these things in the letters of the old law, but learned them through the grace taught by the Holy Spirit.

For the letter kills. Because in the letter of the law there is no forgiveness, but punishment is always carried out, as in this statement: “If anyone does this or that, let him die the death.”

But the Spirit gives life. That is, the law of spiritual grace wishes every person to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, and grants eternal life to all who seek it faithfully.

[Col. 0437C] Now if the ministry of death, engraved in letters on stones, was in glory—the ministry that kills sinners and condemns them, promises only present goods to those who observe it, says nothing about future things, and nevertheless had to be observed in great glory because it displayed a shadow of future goods—so that the children of Israel could not gaze upon the face of Moses because of the glory of his countenance, which is brought to nothing through Christ’s passion and resurrection, whose grace surpasses all others—

how will the ministry of the Spirit not be still more in glory? For if what can be brought to an end is in glory, how much more must what leads to eternal glory be glorified through holy and righteous works, so that eternal glory may also be earned through them? For just as, when the sun has risen, [Col. 0437D] the light of the moon is dulled, although in its proper time it has great light, so, in comparison with the glory of the Gospel, all the glory of the old law is overshadowed.

For if the ministry of condemnation is glory, how much more is the ministry of righteousness—by which sins are forgiven to human beings and children of God are made from children of the devil—glory? By contrast, there are those who are called blessed in this life, whose lot consists in all the prosperity of this world; but that blessedness vanishes together with the world’s prosperity. Those, however, are truly called blessed who are blessed in hope of future blessedness, who here endure many adversities for God. The greater and more numerous the injuries of this age that they endure, the more joyful they always are in spirit, because the greater glory is being heaped up for them. They will not be blessed here, but in [Col. 0438A] that life, because there the blessedness of all the blessed will be perfect.

Therefore, if we wish to reach that blessed life, we must live carefully and always consider attentively the end of this life. Let each one of us, in contemplation of that life, beware of the prosperity of this age. For it is written: “In all your works remember your last things, and you will never sin.” A person must therefore die in the flesh to the world, lest he die in soul to Christ. For each person is believed to live when, dying to the desires of the age, he takes delight in living for God alone. May our Lord Jesus Christ grant this, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit as God throughout all ages. Amen.

## HOMILY 152. ALSO AS ABOVE

Reading from the holy Gospel according to Mark.

[Col. 0438B]

At that time, leaving the territory of Tyre, Jesus came through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, between the territories of the Decapolis, etc.

The Decapolis is, as the name itself indicates, a region of ten cities east of the Jordan, around Hippos, Pella, and Gadara, opposite Galilee. Therefore, when it is said that the Lord came to the Sea of Galilee between the territories of the Decapolis, it signifies that he entered the territories of the Decapolis themselves. For it is not said that he crossed the sea by ship, but rather that he came as far as the sea and reached the place that looked toward the territories of the Decapolis, situated far across the sea.

And they bring him a deaf and mute man, and they beg him [Col. 0438C] to lay his hand upon him. A deaf and mute person is one who neither has ears for hearing the word of God nor opens his mouth to speak. It is necessary that those who, through long practice, have already learned to speak and hear the divine words should offer such people to the Lord for healing, so that those whom human weakness cannot save may themselves be saved by the right hand of his grace.

And taking him aside from the crowd. For he takes the sick man aside from the crowd when, illuminating a mind weakened by sins through the visitation of his mercy, he calls it away from the customary ways of human society and urges it to follow the paths of his commandments.

He put his fingers into his ears. To put fingers into the ears is, through the gifts of the Holy Spirit, to open the ears of the heart for understanding and receiving the words of salvation. For the Lord himself testifies [Col. 0438D] that the Holy Spirit is called the finger of God when he says to the Jews: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God, by whom do your sons cast them out?” Another Evangelist, explaining this, says: “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God?” And the Egyptian magicians, when defeated, said: “This is the finger of God.” The law was also written on stone tablets by the finger of God.

The fingers of God, therefore, placed in the ears of the man who was to be healed, are the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Through these gifts he opens hearts that have strayed from the way of truth to know, hear, and learn the way of salvation. And because confession should follow the light of truth once it has been recognized, it is fittingly added:

And spitting, he touched his tongue. The Lord, spitting, touched the sick man’s tongue when, through the touch of his mercy, he trained [Col. 0439A] mouths that had long been mute to utter words of wisdom and instructed the mouths of catechumens for the confession of faith. For the Lord’s spittle signifies the savor of wisdom.

And looking up toward heaven. He looked up toward heaven in order to teach that from there speech should be sought for the mute, hearing for the deaf, and healing for all who are sick.

He groaned. He groaned not because he himself needed to ask the Father for something with a groan—he who, with the Father, grants all things to those who ask—but to give us an example of groaning when we invoke the aid of heavenly mercy either for our own errors or for those of our neighbors.

And he said to him: “Ephphatha,” which means “Be opened.” The word *Ephphatha*—that is, “Be opened”—[Col. 0439B] properly concerns the ears. For the ears had to be opened for hearing; but the tongue, so that it could speak, had to be released from the restraints of its sluggishness.

And immediately his ears were opened, and the bond of his tongue was released, and he spoke correctly. Only that person speaks correctly—whether confessing God or preaching to others—whose hearing divine grace opens so that he can listen to heavenly things and obey the commandments, and whose tongue the Lord, through the touch of wisdom, which he himself is, trains to speak.

Such a person can rightly say with the Psalmist: “Lord, open my lips, and my mouth will proclaim your praise”; and with Isaiah: “The Lord has given me a trained tongue, that I may know how to sustain the weary with a word; morning by morning he awakens, morning by morning [Col. 0439C] he awakens my ear, that I may hear as a teacher.”

And he commanded them not to tell anyone. But the more he commanded them, the more they proclaimed it, and all the more they marveled, saying: “He has done all things well; he makes the deaf hear and the mute speak.” If he knew—as did the one who knew both the present and future wills of human beings—that they would preach all the more the more he commanded them not to preach, why did he command this? He did so to show the sluggish how much more diligently and fervently those whom he commands to preach ought to proclaim him, since those who were forbidden could not remain silent.

Everyone who wishes to enter into life must strive to complete the present life by teaching well and acting well, because in this way, without any doubt, by God’s mercy he will reach eternal joys. [Col. 0439D]

## HOMILY 153. WEDNESDAY

Reading from the Epistle of blessed Paul the Apostle to the Corinthians.

Brothers, we do not preach ourselves, but our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

That is, we do not proclaim our own glory, lest anyone say that we evangelize for our own sake, perhaps so that it might profit us for a time. Rather, we proclaim Jesus Christ our Lord, subjecting ourselves to his power and majesty. Therefore, when we shake no one, burden no one, and confess Christ our Lord, why should we be judged arrogant, as though we preached for our [Col. 0440A] own advantage so that we might appear glorious?

But ourselves as your servants through Jesus. He proves himself so completely to be Christ’s servant that, at Christ’s command, he testifies that he is their minister in preaching and subject to them in the ministry of the Gospel for their benefit. By saying “servants,” therefore, he signifies ministers; but he spoke humbly in order to show clearly that the Gospel was not preached by him for his own glory, but for the glory of the Lord Christ, whom he obeys and serves, as the Lord himself says: “I am among you not as one who is served, but as one who serves.” This is not on account of the merit of those whom he serves, but because of the Lord’s command.

Because God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” has shone in our hearts for the illumination of the knowledge of God’s glory in the face of Christ Jesus. He says this [Col. 0440B] because it was accomplished by God’s mercy: “so that we,” he says, “who were formerly unbelieving in ignorance”—that is, in darkness—“might be the means by which God would give light to the other nations.” How greatly he still humbles himself, so as to proclaim the glory of God and Christ alone! For they are illuminated so that they may possess knowledge of God’s glory through Christ. Therefore he says “knowledge of the glory of God,” that is, not of God alone but also of Christ, who is his glory, signifying that it is not God alone who is known, but also his works, mercy, and providence, by which he both created and saved the human race, appearing in Christ through the glory of his power.

But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing greatness of God’s power may be shown to be not from us. By “treasure” God signified the mystery in Christ, which is revealed to believers but covered by a certain [Col. 0440C] veil from unbelievers. For just as a treasure is placed in concealment, so the mystery of God is hidden within a human being, that is, in the human heart. He therefore says that this treasure has been given by God in soul and body, so that the excellence of his power may appear through human beings—namely, through preachers—so that every tongue may be reconciled to its Creator.

In everything we suffer affliction, but we are not crushed. He now shows why they were suitable as preachers: God was always present with them in their need.
