Therefore he says that they suffered pressure but were not hemmed in; that is, God did not permit us to be so oppressed that we would give way. We suffered want but were not abandoned; that is, while placed in poverty, God the shepherd was present.

We suffer persecution, but we are not forsaken. Truly [Col. 0440D] so, because God was watching over them, lest their enemies should satisfy their desires against them.

We are cast down, but we do not perish. That is, struck down by blows but, with God resisting, not killed. Whether shut up or bound, they escaped the hands of their enemies through God’s help. Indeed, when Paul and Silas had been imprisoned after being beaten and their feet had been fastened in the stocks, they joyfully sang a hymn to God, having been made stronger by these sufferings than those who had not been beaten.

Always carrying in our body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our bodies. There is no doubt that Christ is killed in the martyrs, and that in those who suffer for the faith—whether in execution, imprisonment, or beatings—the sufferings of Christ are present, [Col. 0441A] so that his life may also be openly displayed in their bodies. For these sufferings reveal the merit that leads to the future life promised by Christ. Hence elsewhere he says: “When I am weak, then I am strong”; and again: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.” May our Lord Jesus Christ himself grant this to us, he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY CLIV. ALSO ON WEDNESDAY. Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Matthew.

[Col. 0441]

At that time, as Jesus was passing on from there, two blind men followed him, crying out and saying, “Have mercy on us, Son of David.” When he had come into the house, the blind men approached him, etc.

[Col. 0441B] As the Lord Jesus passed through the ruler’s house and proceeded to his own house, as we read above—“Getting into a boat, he crossed over and came to his own city”—two blind men cried out, saying, “Have mercy on us, Son of David.” Yet they were not healed on the way, as though incidentally, as they supposed; rather, after he came into his house, they approached him and entered. When the blind men call him “Son of David,” let Marcion and Mani and the other heretics who tore apart the Old Testament hear it, and let them learn that the Savior is called the son of David. For if he was not born in the flesh, how is he called the son of David?

And Jesus said to them, “Do you believe that I can do this for you?” Knowing their faith himself, he questions them so that confession may bring forth faith, power may follow confession, [Col. 0441C] and salvation may accompany power; for, as the Apostle says, “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.”

They said to him, “Yes, Lord.” Then he touched their eyes, saying, “According to your faith, let it be done for you.” By “yes” they outwardly affirm what they carry inwardly in a believing heart, and their firm profession obtained the deed through divine mercy. “According to your faith,” he says, “let it be done for you.” That is: because faith already illuminates the mind, may faith itself restore the light of your eyes to you.

And their eyes were opened. For, according to the prophet’s declaration, “Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.” For he himself is the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world.

[Col. 0441D] And Jesus sternly charged them, saying, “See that no one knows.” But when they had gone out, they spread his fame throughout that whole region. The Lord gave this command because, in his humility, he avoided the glory of self-display; they, however, because they remembered the grace they had received, could not keep the benefit silent. Observe, therefore, that something apparently contrary to the other is nevertheless just in each case.

When they had gone out, behold, they brought him a mute man possessed by a demon. And when the demon had been cast out, the mute man spoke. This man signifies the gentile people, who were mute because they did not have the confession of true faith in their mouth, and also deaf because they did not consent to hear the law of God. The Greek word κωφός (*kōphos*) is more commonly used in ordinary speech to mean “deaf” rather than “mute,” but it is the custom of the Scriptures to use κωφόν (*kōphon*) indiscriminately for either “mute” or “deaf.” [Col. 0442A] This man therefore had a demon because he was wholly devoted to idolatry. When he was brought to the Savior through the preachers of the holy Gospel, the error of paganism was removed, and he began to make the confession of God’s name resound more clearly.

And the crowds marveled, saying, “Never has anything like this appeared in Israel.” But the Pharisees said, “By the ruler of demons he casts out demons.” The crowd confesses God’s works and says that nothing like this has ever appeared in Israel; in the crowd there is a confession of the nations. But because the Pharisees could not deny God’s power, they slandered his works and said, “By the ruler of demons this man casts out demons,” displaying through their slander the unbelief of the Jews even to the present day.

And Jesus went around all the cities and villages, teaching [Col. 0442B] in their synagogues, proclaiming the Gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every infirmity. You see that he preached the Gospel equally in villages, cities, and fortified towns—that is, among great and small alike—so that he did not consider the power of the noble but the salvation of believers. He went around the cities, carrying out the work that the Father had commanded, and possessing this hunger: to save unbelievers through his teaching. He taught the Gospel of the kingdom in the synagogues and villages, and after preaching and instruction he healed every disease and every infirmity. Nothing is impossible for him who created all things and rules over all: Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY CLV. ON FRIDAY. Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Matthew.

[Col. 0442C]

At that time Jesus began to reproach the cities in which many of his mighty works had been performed, because they had not repented, etc.

The reproach of the cities of Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum is laid out in the heading of this chapter: he reproached them because, after very many mighty works and signs had been performed, they had not repented.

Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida. Let us ask where it is written that the Lord performed signs in Chorazin and Bethsaida. Above we read: “And Jesus went around the cities and healed every infirmity,” etc. Therefore, among the other cities and villages, we must also suppose [Col. 0442D] that the Lord performed signs in Chorazin and Bethsaida.

For if the mighty works that were performed in you had been performed in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes. It should be noted that Tyre is the metropolis of Phoenicia in the tribe of Naphtali. It was formerly an island situated in the open sea, but is now joined to the mainland. Sidon also is a distinguished city of Phoenicia, formerly the northern boundary of the Canaanites, and afterward of the region of Judea. It fell by lot to the tribe of Asher, but he did not possess it, because he was entirely unable to drive out its enemies. Tyre is interpreted as “distress,” and Sidon as “hunt,” signifying the nations whom the hunter, the devil, encloses in the distress of sin, but whom the Savior Jesus releases through the Gospel.

[Col. 0443A] And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You will descend to hell. In another copy we find: “And you, Capernaum, which have been exalted to heaven, you will descend to the lower regions.” There is a twofold interpretation: either you will descend to the lower regions because you resisted my preaching with the greatest arrogance, or because, having been exalted to heaven through my hospitality and having received such great privilege through my signs and mighty works, you will be punished with greater penalties because you were unwilling to believe these things also. In Capernaum, which is interpreted as “most beautiful village,” unbelieving Jerusalem is condemned. To it Ezekiel says: “Your sister Sodom has been justified in comparison with you.” Consequently he adds:

[Col. 0443B] For if the mighty works that were performed in you had been performed in Sodom, perhaps it would have remained to this day. Sodom is therefore said to have the lesser injustice, and almost to be just, in comparison with the greater injustice. For Sodom was not corrected by the examples of Lot, while Jerusalem had always shown itself ungrateful for the words and miracles of the Son of God; indeed, it killed the prophets and the Savior himself and persecuted his apostles.

Nevertheless I tell you, it will be more bearable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment than for you. Their punishment will be more bearable because their guilt is less, and vengeance will proceed more forcefully against those whose offense is greater. For the Lord is just in all his ways and holy in all his works; he will repay each person according to his works.

## HOMILY CLVI. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT BARTHOLOMEW THE APOSTLE. Reading from the Epistle to the Ephesians.

[Col. 0443C]

Brothers, you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, etc.

To what he had said above about the foreigners to the covenants of promise, he now responds: therefore you are no longer strangers, that is, foreigners. And to what he had promised concerning those alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, he now responds: you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household. For although you were once far away, having no promises concerning Christ or your salvation, now you are near—and not merely near, but also fellow citizens with the saints.

Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets. That is, placed upon the New and Old Testaments [Col. 0443D]: what the apostles preached, the prophets foretold as future. Although he says to the Corinthians, “God first appointed in the church apostles, second prophets,” these are different prophets. There he discusses the ordering of the Church; here, however, he discusses the foundation of the Church. The prophets prepared the arrangement, but the apostles laid the foundations. Hence the Lord says to Peter, “Upon this rock I will build my Church,” that is, I establish believers for life upon the confession of the catholic faith. David also arranged the house of God and indicated the place where it would be; Solomon, however, founded it.

With Christ Jesus himself as the chief cornerstone, in whom the whole structure, constructed, grows into a holy temple [Col. 0444A] in the Lord; in him you also are built together into a dwelling place of God in the Holy Spirit; in him you Ephesians are also built into a temple for the Most High God from living stones. If the whole structure, whether built and joined together from Jews or from gentiles, grows into one temple of the one God through the cornerstone that joins two walls, should we not strive with every effort to become those stones of which it is written, “Holy stones are rolled upon the earth”? When we have become living stones, shaped on every side, smooth, polished, and possessing no roughness, may we be built into a temple and make within ourselves a dwelling place for God, so that he may deem it worthy to dwell in us through the Holy Spirit. For the Savior took two peoples into himself and made them one in the Lord, just as the cornerstone holds two walls [Col. 0444B] together, firmly joined in the unity of the house. Believers are the surfaces of God’s temple, living in the Spirit so that they may become heirs of the heavenly dwelling. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Luke.

At that time a dispute also arose among the disciples as to which of them seemed to be the greater, etc.

See in the Passion of the Lord, which is read on Wednesday.

## HOMILY CLVII. ON THE PASSION OF SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST. Reading from the Book of Wisdom.

[Col. 0444C]

The expectation of the righteous is joy, but the hope of the wicked will perish, etc.

See under the Feast of Many Martyrs.

Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Mark.

At that time Herod sent and seized John and bound him in prison because of Herodias, the wife of Philip his brother, because he had married her. For John said to Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife,” etc.

Ancient history relates that Philip, the son of the elder Herod—under whom the Lord fled into Egypt—and the brother of this Herod, under whom Christ suffered, had married Herodias, the daughter of King Aretas. Later, after certain quarrels had arisen between her father and her husband, he took his daughter away and, to the grief of her former husband, joined her in marriage to his enemy. [Col. 0444D] Who this Philip was, the evangelist Luke teaches more fully when he says: “In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, while Philip his brother was tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis.” Therefore John the Baptist, who came in the spirit and power of Elijah, with the same authority by which Elijah rebuked Ahab and Jezebel, reproved Herod and Herodias for contracting an unlawful marriage: while the brother was alive, it was not lawful to take his wife. He preferred to risk himself before the king rather than, through flattery, become forgetful of God’s commandments.

And when the opportune day had arrived, Herod held a dinner on his birthday for the leading men, the tribunes, and the prominent people [Col. 0445A] of Galilee. Herod and Pharaoh alone among mortals are read to have celebrated their birthdays with festive rejoicing, but each king stained his festivity with blood under an ill-fated omen. Herod, however, did so with much greater wickedness, because he killed a holy and innocent teacher of truth and herald of life and the heavenly kingdom, and did so at the wish and request of a dancing girl. He was not even ashamed to bring the head of the murdered man before his guests. Pharaoh, by contrast, is not read to have committed any such madness, but only ordered that a eunuch who had sinned against him be deprived of life. The farther he was from the worship of true religion, the lighter was his offense in violating his festivity. Nevertheless, from the example of both it is proved that it is more useful for us, by fearing and living chastely, to recall frequently the day of our future death than to celebrate the day of our birth in luxury. [Col. 0445B] For a human being is born into the world for labor, and the elect pass from the world through death into rest.

And when Herodias’s daughter herself had entered, danced, and pleased Herod, and while they were reclining together, the king said to the girl, “Ask me for whatever you wish, and I will give it to you,” and he swore to her, etc. Herod is not excused on the grounds that he committed murder unwillingly and reluctantly because of his oath; for perhaps he swore this in order to prepare the machinery for the future killing. Otherwise, if he claims that he acted because of his oath, if she had requested the death of her father or mother, would he have done it or not? What he would have rejected in his own case, he ought to have rejected and disregarded in the case of the Prophet as well.

When she had gone out, she said to her mother, “What shall I ask for?” But she said, “The head of John the Baptist.” Herodias feared that Herod might at some time come to his senses, or become reconciled with Philip [Col. 0445C] his brother, and that the unlawful marriage might be dissolved by repudiation. She therefore instructed her daughter to demand John’s head immediately at that very banquet—a deed worthy of the dance, a reward of blood worthy of it.

And the king was grieved; but because of his oath and those reclining with him, he did not wish to grieve her. Instead, he sent an executioner and ordered that his head be brought on a platter, etc. It is the custom of the Scriptures for the historian to narrate the opinion of the many in the manner in which it was believed by everyone at the time. Just as Joseph is called the father of Jesus even by Mary herself, so Herod is now said to have been grieved because this is what those reclining at table thought. For, concealing his mind and being a murderous schemer, he displayed grief on his face while possessing joy in his mind, and excused his crime by an oath, so that under the pretext of [Col. 0445D] piety he might become impious. When he adds, “and because of those reclining with him,” he wishes all of them to be accomplices in his crime, so that bloody dishes might be served at a luxurious and impure banquet.

And he brought his head on a platter and gave it to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother. When his disciples heard this, they came and took his body and placed it in a tomb. Let this be understood according to the literal event. We, however, see to this day in the head of the prophet John that the Jews lost Christ, who is the head of the prophets. Alternatively: John’s beheading signifies the diminution of his renown, by which Christ was believed by the people, just as the exaltation of the Lord Savior on the cross signified the growth of faith. Through that faith, the one who had previously been thought by [Col. 0446A] the crowds to be a prophet was acknowledged by all believers as the Lord of the prophets and the Christ, the Son of God. John, therefore, was diminished by being beheaded, while the Lord was exalted on the cross, because, as John himself says, “He must increase, but I must decrease.” The one who was regarded as a prophet was to be recognized as the Christ, while the one who was thought to be the Christ because of the greatness of his works was to be understood as Christ’s prophet and forerunner. This was also clearly signified by the distinction in the season in which each of them was born: John, who had to decrease, was born when the daylight begins to diminish; but the Lord, who is the true light of the world, at that season of the year when the days begin to increase, displayed to us the light-bearing gifts of his birth. He lives and reigns with [Col. 0446B] God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY CLVIII. FOURTEENTH WEEK AFTER PENTECOST. Reading from the Epistle to the Galatians.

Brothers, the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his offspring. He does not say, “And to offspring,” as though referring to many, but as referring to one: “And to your offspring,” who is Christ, etc.

Treating of the law given through Moses to the people of Israel and of the promises made to the most holy patriarch Abraham, the Apostle says—as your love has heard in the present reading—“The promises of the redemption and salvation of the human race were spoken to Abraham and to his offspring,” as it is said to him: “In your offspring all the tribes of the earth will be blessed,” so that the first part of the curse might be removed and blessing might be given in place of the curse to all who wished to believe and obey God’s commandments. He does not say, “And to offspring,” as though referring to many, but as referring to one: “And to your offspring,” who is Christ. For neither the promise nor the blessing was given through the merits of any human being, nor was redemption accomplished through any human being, but solely through the freely given mercy of Christ, the Son of God.

Now this I say: the covenant confirmed by God does not invalidate the promise by means of the Law, which came four hundred and thirty years later. Here the Apostle teaches that the promises made earlier to Abraham cannot be destroyed by the Law given afterward, and that what came later cannot prejudice what came first. The promises had been given to Abraham [Col. 0446D] four hundred and thirty years before the Law: all the nations would be blessed in his offspring, that is, in Christ, and would be freed from every bond of the curse.

For if the inheritance comes from the law. As though it were said: If the inheritance of the eternal homeland, which was lost through Adam, were restored to us through observance of the law, then it would no longer come from the promise. For the Law was not given to annul or destroy the promise, as is said in what follows:

Why then the Law? It was established altogether because of transgressions. Because of the many offenses committed by God’s people, the law was given to prohibit transgressions until the offspring should come—that is, Christ—to whom he had [Col. 0447A] promised the liberation of the world. The Law, arranged through angels, remained prohibiting sins, so that those who, through the freedom of their will, were unwilling to await the promised one in innocence might be restrained by legal bonds and reduced to servitude under commandments, and thus be kept until the coming of the faith that was to be revealed in Christ, which would bring the promise to fulfillment. When he says “arranged through angels,” he wishes it to be understood that throughout the whole Old Testament, wherever an angel is first said to have appeared, he is afterward introduced as speaking like God. The Mediator in that passage—that is, God himself, the judge and ruler—was speaking. He said: “I am the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob,” the mediator between God and human beings. He is called mediator between the one who gives the Law and the one who receives it. Thus the Law itself, which was given after the promise and intervened between the promise [Col. 0447B] and its fulfillment, was given to guard that same promise, not to overturn it.

Now a mediator is not of one party, but he is mediator between God and a human being; that is, he is the one who promised his coming into this world to the human race, so that he might make peace between human beings and God and reconcile them.

But God is one. He adds this so that no one might think Christ could be divided from the unity of the divine nature because he had assumed the office of mediator. The mediator between God and human beings, Christ Jesus, is by no means one person in his humanity and another in his divinity, but in both he is the same one. He was neither conceived as a mere human being nor born as a mere human being; rather, God the Word [Col. 0447C] of God assumed flesh for the salvation of humanity. In that flesh, God, who was impassible, appeared as a suffering human being; in it, the immortal God, who could not die, and mortal humanity, which could die, were shown forth. He did not commit sin, but accepted punishment for us, so that through an undeserved death he might cleanse our guilt.

Let us therefore give thanks, beloved, to God the Father through his Son in the Holy Spirit, because, on account of the great love with which he loved us, he had mercy on us. Although we were dead in sins, he made us alive together with Christ, so that we might be a new creation and a new work in him. Let us therefore put off the old human being with his deeds, and, having obtained a share in Christ’s birth, let us renounce the works of the flesh. Recognize, O Christian, your dignity, and, having become a participant in the divine [Col. 0447D] nature, do not return through degenerate conduct to your former baseness. Remember your head, and recall whose body you are a member of. You have been rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into God’s light and kingdom; through the sacrament of baptism you have become a temple of the Holy Spirit. Do not drive out so great an inhabitant through evil deeds and again submit to the service of the devil, because the price of your redemption is the blood of Christ. He himself, Jesus Christ our Lord, will judge in truth—the one who redeemed you in mercy—who lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit as God in unity, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY CLIX. ALSO AS ABOVE. Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Luke.

[Col. 0448A]

At that time Jesus said to his disciples, “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see,” etc.

Not the eyes of the scribes and Pharisees, which saw only the Lord’s body, but those eyes are blessed that are able to recognize his mysteries. Of these it is said: “And you have revealed them to little ones.” Blessed are the eyes of the little ones, to whom the Son deigns to reveal both himself and the Father.

For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it. Abraham rejoiced that he might see Christ’s day; he saw it and was glad. [Col. 0448B] Isaiah, Micah, and many other prophets also saw the glory of the Lord, and for this reason they were called seers. But all of them, looking from afar and greeting it, saw through a mirror and in an enigma. The apostles, however, having the Lord present and dining with him, and learning by asking him whatever they wished, had no need to be taught through angels or various kinds of visions. What Luke calls “many prophets and kings,” Matthew more openly calls “prophets and righteous people.” For these are the great kings who did not fall by yielding to the impulses of their temptations, but advanced by ruling them.

And behold, a certain lawyer stood up, testing him and saying, “Teacher, what must I do to possess eternal life?” [Col. 0448C] The lawyer who questioned the Lord, testing him about eternal life, took the opportunity for testing, I think, from the Lord’s own words, where he says: “Rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” But by this very testing of his he demonstrates how true the Lord’s confession is when he speaks to the Father: “You have hidden these things from the wise and intelligent and revealed them to little ones.”

He said to him, “What is written in the Law? How do you read?” He answered: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength, and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself.” While responding to the lawyer, the Savior shows us the perfect path of heavenly life. [Col. 0448D] To the one who first presented the Law’s writings concerning love of God and neighbor, he says: “You have answered correctly; do this and you will live.” Then, after introducing the parable, when the lawyer answered that the one who showed mercy to the wounded man had been his neighbor, he added: “Go, and you do likewise.” That is: remember that you must love and support your neighbor in need with such zeal for mercy. He most clearly declares that love alone—and love not displayed in words but proved by the execution of a deed—is what leads to everlasting life.

But wishing to justify himself, he said to Jesus, “And who is my neighbor?” What empty-glory madness! The lawyer, seeking to win the favor of the crowd so that he might boast of having answered wisely, first [Col. 0449A] admits that he does not know the commandment of the Law. Truly, according to the Savior’s judgment, he was wise and intelligent in the Law; but because he did not wish to humble himself with Christ’s little ones and desired to justify himself, he refused to receive the blessed eyes of doves washed in the milk of innocence, by which he could see Christ’s mysteries. The Lord therefore so tempered his answer that he would both teach that anyone who shows mercy is everyone’s neighbor and, nevertheless, through this same parable specifically designate the Son of God, who deigned to become our neighbor through his humanity. We must not interpret “neighbor,” whom we are commanded to love as ourselves, concerning Christ in such a way that we attempt to weaken or remove the moral institutions of mutual brotherhood under the rules of allegory.

[Col. 0449B] But Jesus looked up and said: “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho.” This man is understood as Adam in the human race. Jerusalem is that heavenly city of peace, from whose blessedness he fell and came into this mortal and wretched life. Jericho, which is interpreted as “moon,” aptly signifies this life, always uncertain through the varied labors and errors of its waning.

And he fell among robbers. Understand the robbers as the devil and his angels, into whom the one who was descending fell. For unless he had first become inwardly swollen with pride, he would not so easily have departed after being tempted outwardly. The saying is indeed very true: “Before destruction the heart is exalted.”

They also stripped him. That [Col. 0449C] is, they deprived him of the garment of the glory of immortality and innocence. For this is the first robe by which, according to another parable, the extravagant son is adorned through repentance with rings, and which the first-formed human beings, having lost it, recognized that they were naked and put on tunics of skins belonging to mortal nature.

And after inflicting wounds upon him, they went away, leaving him half-dead. The wounds are sins, by which, violating the integrity of human nature, they implanted in its exhausted entrails, so to speak, a kind of seedbed for increasing death. They went away not by ceasing their ambushes in any respect, but by concealing the deceits of those same ambushes. They left him half-dead because they were able to strip away the blessedness of immortal life but not to abolish the power of reason. For in that part by which a human being can understand and know God, he is alive; but in that by which he wastes away through sins [Col. 0449D] and fails through misery, he is dead and disfigured by a deadly wound.

Now it happened that a certain priest went down the same road, and when he saw him, he passed by. Likewise, when a Levite was near the place and saw him, he passed by. But a certain Samaritan, making his journey, came near him, and when he saw him, he was moved with compassion. The Samaritan, whose name is interpreted as “guardian,” signifies the Lord, to whom the Prophet most appropriately prays that he may not fall among these robbers: “Guard me,” he says, “from the snare that they have set for me and from the stumbling blocks of those who work iniquity.” For our sake and for our salvation, descending from heaven, he undertook the journey of this present life and came near the one who was wasting away from the wounds inflicted upon him, [Col. 0450A] that is, having been made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being, he became near through taking on our compassion and neighbor through the gift of mercy.

And approaching him, he bound his wounds, pouring in oil and wine. He restrained the sins he found in human beings by rebuking them, instilling hope of forgiveness in the penitent and fear of punishment in sinners. For he binds wounds when he commands: “Repent”; he pours in oil when he adds: “For the kingdom of heaven will draw near”; he pours in wine when he says: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.”

And placing him on his beast, he led him to an inn and took care of him. His beast is [Col. 0450B] the flesh in which he deigned to come to us. Upon it he placed the wounded man, because he bore our sins in his body upon the wood; and, according to another parable, he placed the lost sheep he had found upon his shoulders and carried it back to the flock. Thus, to be placed upon the beast means to believe in Christ’s incarnation and to be initiated into its mysteries, while also being protected from the enemy’s attack. The inn is the present Church, where travelers are refreshed from this pilgrimage as they return to the eternal homeland. He carried him, already placed upon the beast, to the inn because no one except one who has been baptized and united to Christ’s body will enter the Church.

And on the next day he brought out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper and said, “Take care of him.” The next day is after the Lord’s resurrection. Before this, through [Col. 0450C] the grace of his Gospel, he had indeed illuminated those who sat in darkness and in the shadow of death; but after the resurrection had been celebrated, the splendor of perpetual light shone forth more powerfully. The two denarii are the two Testaments, in which the name and image of the eternal King are contained. For Christ is the end of the Law. They were brought out on the next day and given to the innkeeper because then he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures. On the next day the innkeeper received the denarii, by whose value he was to care for the wounded man, because the Holy Spirit, coming upon them, taught the apostles all truth, so that they would be sufficient to devote themselves to instructing the nations and preaching the Gospel.

And whatever more you spend, when I return I will repay you. The innkeeper spends beyond what he received in the two denarii when the Apostle says: “Concerning [Col. 0450D] virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give advice.” Likewise, the Lord appointed that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel; but we have not used this power, so that we might not burden any of you. When he returns, the Lord will repay the debtor what he promised, for at his coming in judgment he says: “Because you were faithful over a little, I will set you over much; enter into the kingdom of your lord.”

Which of these three seems to you to have been neighbor to the one who fell among the robbers? He said, “The one who showed mercy to him.” According to the literal sense, the Lord’s judgment is clear: no one is more our neighbor than the one who shows mercy. Thus, for the citizen of Jerusalem, it was not a priest or a Levite from the same people—indeed, [Col. 0451A] people born and raised in the same city—but a resident of a foreign nation who, because he showed greater mercy, became his neighbor. In a more sacred interpretation, since no one is more our neighbor than the one who healed our wounds, let us love him as the Lord our God and love him as our neighbor. For nothing is as near as the head is to the members. Let us also love the one who imitates Christ; for this is what follows:

And Jesus said to him, “Go, and you do likewise.” That is: to show truly that you love your neighbor as yourself, devote yourself to doing whatever you can to assist him in his bodily or spiritual need; and thus you will be able to attain the rewards of the heavenly kingdom.

## HOMILY CLX. ON WEDNESDAY. Reading from the Epistle of the blessed Apostle Paul to the Hebrews.

[Col. 0451B]

Brothers, since we have confidence to enter the holy places through the blood of Christ, the way that he inaugurated for us—a new and living way through the veil, that is, through his flesh—and since we have a great priest over the house of God.

He here shows the difference between the high priest, the sacrifices, the tabernacle, the Testament, and the promise, and a great difference indeed: the former are temporal, whereas the latter are eternal; the former are weak, whereas the latter are perfect; the former are figures, whereas the latter are the truth. “For,” he says, “not according to the law of a fleshly commandment, but according to the power of an indestructible life: You are a priest forever.” Behold the perpetuity of the priesthood. He said of that Testament that it was old; but “what grows old and becomes aged is near to destruction.” This, moreover, is the New Testament and has the remission of sins, whereas the former has nothing of this kind; the former was made by hand, whereas this was not made by hand; the former had the blood of goats, whereas this has the Lord’s blood; the former had a priest standing, whereas this has one seated.

Since, therefore, all those things are lesser, while these are greater, he says: “Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence.” From what source? For just as sins produce shame, so the remission of all sins produces confidence, as does the fact that we have become fellow heirs and enjoy such great love. “At the entrance,” he says, “of the holy places.” Here he calls heaven the entrance and access to spiritual realities. “Which he dedicated”—that is, which he constructed, prepared, and inaugurated. For “dedication” means the beginning of use. “Which he prepared,” he says, “and through which he himself proceeded—a new way.” Here he declares the ground of hope by calling it new, for he is striving to show that we possess all things in a greater form. For now the gates of heaven are open, something that did not happen even to Abraham. He called it a new way of life, but he called the way itself—that is, the commandments—new; and he dedicated it, for this reason, because he himself proceeded along it. He called it a veil, moreover, for when he was lifted up on high, then the heavenly things appeared.

“Let us draw near with a true heart in the fullness of faith, our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our body washed with pure water.” By what means should we draw near? By faith—that is, by spiritual worship—with a truthful heart, without hypocrisy, in the assurance of faith; for none of these things is visible: no priest now, no sacrifice, no altar. Therefore, he says, “in the fullness of faith”; one must believe in this way, as certain as we are of visible things, and even more so. For formerly the senses of the flesh were at work in things that are seen; there, however, this is by no means so, because by the Spirit we perceive spiritual things, and it is not permitted to hesitate concerning them. Therefore he says, “our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience,” showing that not faith alone is sought, but also a life accompanied by virtue, because faith without works is idle. They cleansed their bodies, but we cleanse our conscience. “And washed with pure water.” In this passage he means the washing of baptism. Baptism is not the cleansing of the body, but of the soul, if faith is present in the one being baptized—whether the faith of the parents or of the person himself, if he has reached the age of reason.

“Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who promised is faithful.” Do not scrutinize anything, and expect no rational demonstration: all these things require faith, because without faith it is impossible to please God. Just as God is faithful in his promises, so he wants us to be faithful in our promises—the promises by which we vowed to renounce the devil and confess Christ.

“And let us consider one another for the incitement of love and good works, not abandoning our assembly, as is the custom of some.” What does “let us consider one another” mean? If someone is endowed with virtue, let us imitate him and fix our attention upon him, so that we may love and be loved; for good works arise from love. A congregation is a great good: it produces more fervent love, and from it all good works are generated. Nothing is good that is not done through love. Let us therefore strengthen one another in this, because love is the fullness of the Law. We do not need labor or sweat: if we love one another, a spontaneous way of life is laid before us, leading to virtue and to heavenly things. For just as on a journey, if someone gains the beginning of the right road, he is led where he ought to go, so also seize only the beginning in love, and immediately love itself, extending its hand to you, leads and directs you.

“As is the custom of some.” In this passage he not only admonished them, but also reproved and terrified those who were dividing the unity of love.

[Col. 0452D]

“But encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the day approaching.” What day does he designate except the day of judgment, on which the merits of each person are examined? Or perhaps the final day of our life. For elsewhere he says: “The Lord is near; do not be anxious about anything”—that is, about earthly things—and again:

“Now our salvation is nearer than when we believed; for the time has been shortened.” For when we sin deliberately, after receiving the knowledge of the truth, no sacrifice for sins remains for us. When we sin willingly, after we have received the knowledge of the truth, no sacrifice for sins remains any longer, just as under the Old Law it was permitted to offer sacrifices repeatedly for sin. For Christ himself is not to be sacrificed again for our sins: this was done once, and there is no need for it a second time. Rather, after receiving grace, what is needed is to remain in faith and in the love that produces good works.

Trees that have been planted and have received the further care of farmers, applied by their hands and labors, if they produce no return for the labor, will be uprooted and handed over to the fire. Something similar occurs in the case of baptism. For when Christ has established us and we have received spiritual irrigation, if afterward we bear no fruit, the fire of Gehenna and the unquenchable flame will await us. Paul therefore exhorts us to love and to produce good works, inviting us by means of beneficial considerations. What are these beneficial considerations? We have access to the holy places; he has dedicated a new way for us. After moving from beneficial considerations to good works, he now also wishes to make the same transition by means of fearful and sorrowful things. For after saying, “Let us not abandon our assembly, as is the custom of some, but let us encourage one another, and all the more as you see the day approaching,” he added:

“For when we sin willingly, after we have received the knowledge of the truth”—he says that good works are necessary; they are necessary, indeed, very necessary—“when we sin willingly, after we have received the knowledge of the truth, no sacrifice for sins remains any longer.” You have been cleansed; you are free from crimes; you have been made a child of God. If you return to your first vomit, another judgment awaits you, unless you are renewed through repentance. Therefore he says next:

[Col. 0453C]

“But a terrifying expectation of judgment remains, and the fury of fire that will consume the adversaries.” In saying this he did not exclude repentance, nor the reconciliation that comes through repentance; nor does he drive the sinner to despair. For he is not so hostile to our salvation that he would exclude the washing of a second baptism—that is, repentance. He did not say, “There is no repentance any longer,” nor did he say, “There is no remission any longer.” Rather, he says, “There is no sacrifice any longer”—that is, there is no second cross any longer. For one sacrifice has perfected forever those who are sanctified, unlike the sacrifices of the Jews. He wishes to make us cautious, so that we do not expect either the cross of Christ or Jewish sacrifices again for our sins. And whoever neglects the remedy of repentance will be devoured by the fury of fire. Therefore let each person flee to the remedy of repentance while he has time, lest he be handed over to eternal fire, because, according to the judgment of sacred Scripture, “Those who have done good will go to eternal life, but those who have done evil to eternal punishment.”

# HOMILY CLXI. ALSO ON WEDNESDAY

*Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Matthew.*

At that time, the Pharisees went out and took counsel against Jesus about how they might destroy him, and so forth.

When it says that they “went out,” it means that they did not approach or draw near, because their perverse mind was always turned away from the Lord; nor did they belong to the company of those to whom Scripture says: “Draw near to him, and be enlightened,” and so forth. They went out, evidently, with their master the devil, of whom it is written: “Satan went out from the presence of the Lord.” They took counsel about how they might destroy life—not how they themselves might find life. That the wicked lay snares for the Lord is caused by envy. For what had he done to provoke the Pharisees to seek his death? Simply that he had stretched out a man’s hand. Which of the Pharisees had not stretched out his hand on the Sabbath—carrying food, offering a cup, and doing the other things necessary for nourishment? If, then, stretching out a hand and providing food, or offering drink, on the Sabbath is not a crime, why do they charge as evil what they themselves are compelled to do, especially since this mason (caementarius) had carried nothing of the kind, but at the Lord’s command had stretched out his hand restored to health? Indeed, the one who said, “And all things came to be,” could not be convicted of working on the Sabbath.

“But Jesus, knowing this, withdrew from there.” Knowing their snares, that they wished to destroy their Savior, he withdrew from there, in order to take away from the Pharisees the opportunity for impiety against him. He withdrew as a human being, fleeing the snares of his pursuers, because the hour of his passion had not yet come, nor was the place of his passion outside Jerusalem. He withdrew, fleeing those who pursued him out of hatred, but went to the place where he found more people following him out of love. For it follows:

“And many followed him, and he healed them all.” Behold: the Pharisees, the teachers of the people, seek with one accord to destroy the Lord; but the unlearned crowd and the populace gathered from everywhere follow him with unanimous love. Those, seeing his mighty works and hearing the words of his teaching, wished to learn nothing more than how to persecute him; these, moved merely by the report of his mighty works, come in a very great throng to hear him and to ask for the help of salvation.

“And he commanded them not to make him known.” He commanded this not out of fear of death, lest he perhaps be betrayed and killed already—for his soul was in his own power—but out of mercy toward the Jews, lest they themselves be slaughtered by persecuting an innocent man out of envy. Of such people it is read elsewhere: “Anger truly kills fools, and envy slays the little ones.” Tropologically, he instructs us not to seek outward praise when we have done something great.

“So that what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled, saying: Behold, my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved, in whom my soul is well pleased.” What the prophet foretold would happen concerning him necessarily had to be fulfilled in him, so that his innocence and gentleness might confirm the prophets’ oracle as true. Jesus, therefore, is the Lord’s servant because he took the form of a servant and was found in appearance as a human being. Yet he is the chosen one, because he himself, as Scripture says, was chosen from among thousands—namely, the true David, a man found to be according to the Lord’s heart, who did all his will. He was chosen for a work that no one else performed: to redeem the human race and reconcile the world with God. When he is chosen, he is human; when he chooses, he is God. In two natures Christ is one person. In him, moreover, the soul of God was well pleased, because he alone is the Lamb without the stain of sin, of whom the Father’s voice also says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

“I will put my Spirit upon him, and he will proclaim judgment to the nations.” This is said by the prophet in the person of the Father. For the Spirit is not placed upon God the Word, nor upon the Only-Begotten who proceeded from the Father’s bosom, but upon him of whom it was said: “Behold my servant”; and again: “The Spirit of the Lord,” he says, “will rest upon him—the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety—and he will fill him with the spirit of the fear of the Lord.”

The Lord Jesus therefore proclaimed God’s judgment to the nations, because through his Gospel and through the preachers of the New Testament he revealed the judgment that was to come, which they had not believed at all; and he taught them now to practice just judgments and to avoid unjust judgments. It follows:

“He will not contend, nor cry out, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets.” Christ therefore did not contend or cry out, nor was his voice heard in the streets, because when he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but entrusted himself to the one who judged unjustly. He gave his body to those who struck him and his cheeks to those who wished [to do so; the Latin is elliptical]; he was led like a sheep to slaughter and did not open his mouth. Allegorically, no one heard Christ’s voice in the streets because broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter through it. These many do not hear the Savior’s voice because they are not on the narrow way, but on the spacious one.

“A bruised reed he will not break, and a smoking flax he will not extinguish.” By the bruised reed he means the Jews, because they were one people yet differed from one another. “A smoking flax he will not extinguish”—namely, the people gathered from the nations, which, after the flame of the natural law had been extinguished, was enveloped in the errors of the most bitter smoke, harmful to the eyes and full of dark obscurity. He not only did not extinguish it and reduce it to ashes; on the contrary, from a small and almost dying spark he raised up an immense fire, so that the whole world burned with the fire of the Lord and Savior, which he came to cast upon the earth.

Or, in another sense, whoever does not extend a hand to a sinner or bear his brother’s burden breaks the bruised reed; and whoever despises a small spark in little ones extinguishes the smoking flax. Christ did neither of these things. For he came to save what had perished and to carry the wandering sheep back to the flock upon his sacred shoulders. Hence it follows:

“Until he brings judgment to victory.” This one, who did not crush the bruised reed or extinguish the flashing flax (linum fulminans), also brought judgment to victory. His judgments are true and have been justified in themselves. His preaching continues to shine as a light in the world, and no one is crushed or overcome by snares, until he sets judgment upon the earth and what is written is fulfilled: “Your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth.”

“And in his name the nations will hope.” Rightly, therefore, the nations will hope in his name, because he is the seed concerning which it was promised to Abraham that in his seed all the nations of the earth would be blessed. Concerning him the aforementioned Isaiah also says: “The root of Jesse, who will arise to rule the nations; in him the nations will hope,” and they will supplicate him.

All the nations will hope in his name because, as Peter says, “There is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which they can be saved.” But in the name of Jesus, according to Paul’s declaration, “every knee will bow”—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and “every tongue will confess” that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father. He lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# HOMILY CLXII. ON FRIDAY

*Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Luke.*

At that time, while Jesus was going through the cities and villages, teaching and making his journey toward Jerusalem, someone said to him: “Lord, are those who are saved few?” But he said to them: “Strive to enter through the narrow gate,” and so forth.

Through the narrow gate one enters the hall of salvation, because it is necessary that the allurements of the deceitful world be overcome through labors and fasts. And he rightly said, “Strive to enter,” because unless the exertion of the mind burns fervently, the wave of the world cannot be overcome—through that wave the soul is continually dragged back to the depths.

“For many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able.” They seek to enter, moved by love of salvation, but will not be able, deterred by the roughness of the way. They seek this through ambition for rewards, but soon withdraw from it through fear of labors—not because the Lord’s yoke is harsh or his burden heavy, but because they do not wish to learn from him that he is gentle and humble in heart, so that they may find rest for their souls. Thus the gate by which one enters into life is narrow.

“But when the master of the house has entered and shut the door, then you will begin to stand outside and knock at the door, saying: Lord, open to us.” The master of the house is the Lord Christ, who in his divinity is wholly present everywhere. He is within for those whom his present vision gladdens in the heavenly homeland, but he is, as it were, outside for those whom, while they struggle in this pilgrimage, he assists as a hidden consoler, according to his promise: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age.” He will enter and shut the door when, bringing his entire body, which is the Church, glorified by the glory of the resurrection, to the joy of contemplating him, he removes from the reprobate the opportunity for repentance—an opportunity he now opens to those who piously knock. For those who stand outside and knock at the door is for those separated from the lot of the blessed to ask God in vain for the mercy they had neglected.

[Col. 0457A]

“And he will answer and say to you: I do not know where you are from.” How does he not know where they are from, when the Psalm says: “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, for they are vain,” and elsewhere it is written: “He knows the deceiver and the one who is deceived”? It is because “to know” is sometimes said of God’s recognizing and sometimes of his approving. “God knows the way of the righteous”; but “whoever is ignorant will be ignored.” He therefore knows the reprobate, judging them by knowing them; for he would not have judged those whom he did not know at all. Yet in a certain sense he does not know where they are from, because he does not approve in them the mark of his faith and love.

“Then you will begin to say: We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets.” This may be understood simply: the Jews, despising the mysteries of faith, imagine that they are known to the Lord if they merely bring victims to the temple, feast in the Lord’s presence, and listen to the reading of the prophets, not knowing the Apostle’s saying: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit”; and elsewhere: “Their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame”—that is, in carnal circumcision.

Or it may be understood mystically: those eat and drink before the Lord who receive the nourishment of the word with worthy eagerness. Hence, as though explaining these words, they add: “And you taught in our streets.” For sacred Scripture is sometimes food for us and sometimes drink. In its more obscure passages it is food, because it is broken up as though by explanation and swallowed by chewing. It is drink in its more open passages, because it is imbibed just as it is found. Those who complain to the judge who rejects them that they ate and drank before him therefore testify that they understood both the hidden and the open commands of sacred discourse. But what follows is greatly to be feared:

“And he will say to you: I do not know where you are from; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity.” The eating of legal festivals, he says, does not help one whom the piety of faith does not commend; knowledge of the Scriptures does not make one known to God whom the iniquity of his works shows to be unworthy in his sight.

“There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” Weeping usually arises from heat, while gnashing of teeth arises from cold. Here a twofold Gehenna is indicated: one of excessive cold and one of intolerable heat. The statement agrees with blessed Job, who says: “They will pass from waters of snow to excessive heat.” Or certainly the gnashing of teeth reveals the feeling of one who is indignant, because each person repents too late, groans too late, and too late becomes angry with himself for having sinned with such obstinate wickedness.

“And behold, there are last who were first, and there are first who were last.” The principal meaning of this statement is clear from what precedes: the peoples of the nations, who had long lived without faith, were to be called to faith, while the Jews, who had held the headship of faith and righteousness for so many ages, were to become the tail.

It may also be understood in this way: some who are despised in this age will possess great glory in the future, while others who are glorious among human beings will be condemned by the strict judge. It may also be understood thus: many who come late to the service of God surpass others through great merits of life, while others who from their earliest age burn with spiritual zeal finally become sluggish and hidden through idleness.

Nevertheless, this must be known: our Savior, who is the judge of the living and the dead, will restore to each person his proper reward on the day of judgment, and the impious will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.

# HOMILY CLXIII

*Beginning of the Holy Gospel according to Matthew.*

“The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham,” and so forth.

“The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham.” The order is reversed, but necessarily changed. For if he had first placed Abraham and afterward David, he would again have had to repeat Abraham in order to weave together the sequence of the generation. He called him the son of these men alone, omitting the others, because the promise concerning Christ was made only to them. To Abraham it was said: “In your seed all the nations will be blessed”; to David: “I will place upon your throne the fruit of your womb.” Or David was placed first for this reason: because he was nearer to Christ.

“Abraham begot Isaac.” Properly, the genealogy is directed from the head of faith and the very beginning of the promise of Christ all the way to Christ himself: a hook, as it were, in faith [perhaps, “at the head of the net”], placed at the end of the genealogy, by which Leviathan was hooked and his jaw pierced, and the gate of repentance was opened. He says “begot,” not “was,” nor “generated.” He shows the divinity of Christ by saying: “Today I have begotten you”; and again: “Before the morning star I begot you.” Matthew says “begot,” because he speaks of natural sons; Luke says “was,” because he speaks of sons according to the law.

“Jacob begot Judah and his brothers.” Ishmael, Abraham’s firstborn, and Esau, Isaac’s firstborn, were passed over as foreigners to the people of God, while Judah’s brothers are mentioned. Since they were the patriarchs of the twelve tribes and belonged to the people of God, they are not strangers to Christ’s genealogy.

“Judah begot Perez and Zerah.” These were not Judah’s firstborn, but since they were born together, they are rightly mentioned together. Neither of them was considered guilty of any offense that would exclude him from the genealogy.

“By Tamar.” Passing over the legitimate wives, four foreign women are taken into Christ’s genealogy: Tamar, who sat at a crossroads in the guise of a prostitute; Rahab the prostitute, who joined herself at Jericho to Salmon, the prince of the tribe of Judah; Ruth, who came from the Moabite region after her husband’s death and joined herself to Boaz; and Bathsheba, who conceived through the adultery of King David.

This was done so that, according to the literal sense, we might admire the Lord’s supreme clemency: in order to destroy human sin, he deigned to be born not only from human beings but also from sinners and prostitutes. According to the spiritual sense, these three women signify the Church, which was to come to the Lord from the error of the nations. Formerly alien and barren, she was afterward joined to the Lord as a matron and bore more adopted children to God than the Synagogue, which, while she formerly had her own husband, produced children.

He called David king, not as though he were the only king of Judea, but because he was the first of the kings up to the Babylonian captivity; or, as others distinguish, from David the soldier.

“By her who had been Uriah’s.” Bathsheba alone is not named, because of the crime of adultery, without repentance. The other three not only ought not to be blamed, but also deserved praise. Uriah, however, is named because he was just and was killed. David, although an adulterer and murderer, is named here as an example of true repentance; and from his adultery such a son was born, from whose seed Christ was generated.

From Abraham to David there were patriarchs and leaders; from David to the captivity, kings; and from the captivity onward, the genealogy is continued.

“Joram begot Uzziah.” In the history of the Kings we read of Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah—three kings whom this evangelist omitted. The evangelist therefore proposed to place three groups of fourteen according to the differing periods of time. Since he wished to set down the sacred number forty-two, it was more fitting that three wicked kings be omitted than that none of the good ones be omitted.

And because Joram had mingled himself with the most wicked line of Jezebel, taking Ahab’s daughter Athaliah in marriage, by whom he begot Ahaziah, for this reason his memory is removed from the order of the holy birth through the third generation. The Lord says in the Law: “I am a jealous God, visiting the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third generation of those who hate me.” The sins of the fathers are visited upon those who have persisted in sins through hatred of the Lord; but mercy is shown in those who remain in the love of the Lord. A good man, “passing through whomever” (a quovis pertransit; the wording is uncertain), is worthy of mercy; an evil person, of punishment.

Joram took Athaliah, who, after Ahaziah’s death, killed his son and her own grandsons, Ahaziah’s sons, and herself reigned for seven years in Judea. After these had been killed, Joab was hidden; Jehosheba, King Joram’s daughter and Ahaziah’s sister, rescued him from the slaughter being carried out by Athaliah and brought him into the temple. After his grandmother was killed, he was appointed king by the priest Jehoiada, his guardian. After Jehoiada his guardian died, he killed his son Zechariah the priest between the temple and the altar. Amaziah, for his part, rejected the Lord and worshiped idols. These three—Ahaziah, Joab, and Amaziah—heirs of Joram’s impiety, are rightly excluded by everyone from Christ’s genealogy.

[Col. 0459D]

“Josiah begot Jeconiah and his brothers.” Because of their shared impiety, equal disgrace, and common captivity, he mentioned Jeconiah and his brothers together. For after Josiah was killed in battle against Necho, king of Egypt, his son Jehoahaz reigned in Jerusalem for three months. The king of Egypt carried him away to Egypt and appointed in his place his brother Eliakim, also called Jehoiakim. He reigned for twelve years. Because he was evil before the Lord, Nebuchadnezzar bound him in chains and led him to Babylon. Jehoiakim, also called Jeconiah, his son, reigned in his place for three months. Because he too was evil before the Lord, Nebuchadnezzar sent for him and led him to Babylon, appointing in his place Zedekiah, his uncle, as king over Judea. Because Zedekiah was evil before the Lord, Nebuchadnezzar burned the temple, carried away the vessels of the Lord, and led him to Babylon.

If we wish to place the first Jeconiah at the end of the first group of fourteen, then there follow not fourteen but thirteen. It remains, therefore, for us to understand that the first Jeconiah is Jehoiakim himself (Joachim in the Latin), the father of Jeconiah, who is mentioned at the beginning of Daniel; and that the second Jeconiah is Jehoiachin himself (Joachimum in the Latin), Josiah’s grandson, who is mentioned at the beginning of Ezekiel. The former is written with κ and μ, the latter with χ and μ. This has become confused among Greeks and Latins through the fault of scribes and the passage of time, so that those in error suppose that the same person is mentioned at the beginnings of the two prophets.

Furthermore, if you say that Jeconiah was begotten by Josiah, he is a grandson, not a son.

[Note: [Col. 0459D] The passage is corrupt, as are many others, as is abundantly clear to the reader. EDIT.]

Although Christians called Jehoiakim “Jeconiah,” even though elsewhere in the Gospel we read the passage differently, no one will say “of the sons”; but if he finds it, let it be read through to the evangelist. He now calls him the father of Jeconiah because he was the Lord’s preparation, because the Lord rightly prepared this man, just as he prepared the other, for the captivity. Hence in the captivity he says that the sons of Josiah were begotten, although they had been born earlier: they were born for this purpose, by God’s foreknowledge, that they might be taken into captivity on account of their sins.

According to Augustine, Jeconiah is counted twice: at the end of the first group and at the beginning of the turning toward the foreign nations of Babylon. But why is his father omitted? It is because this signifies that Christ would in a certain way migrate from circumcision to uncircumcision, just as from Jerusalem to Babylon, and hence become for both peoples who believe in him the cornerstone.

“Jacob begot Joseph.” The genealogy of Christ is traced through Joseph, although he was not his father, first because it is not the custom of Scripture to weave a genealogy through the female line; second, so that Mary’s origin might be shown through Joseph, since they belonged to the same tribe, the Law testifying that no one should take a wife except from his own tribe.

Luke, however, says: “He had one father according to nature and another according to law.” For we know this commandment was given through Moses at the Lord’s order: if a brother or relative died without children, another was to take his wife in order to raise up offspring for his brother or relative.

Jacob and Heli were uterine brothers—that is, they had one mother, named Estha, who after Melchi was joined to Matthan by the right of kinship. When Heli, the elder, took a wife and died without children, Joseph was raised up in his name, having been physically begotten by Jacob. Pamphilus and Eusebius, Jerome, Ambrose, and Eucherius used this explanation of the two fathers.

Augustine, however, says that Joseph had two fathers: one by whom he was begotten, and another by whom he was adopted. For the ancient custom of adopting sons existed among the people of God, as when Jacob adopted his grandsons, Joseph’s sons Ephraim and Manasseh, as his own sons, thereby increasing the number of the tribes of Israel; and likewise Moses was adopted by Pharaoh’s daughter.

This also took place in Christ, as Mary says: “Son, why have you done this to us? Behold, your father and I have been seeking you.” Joseph therefore did not beget Jesus, but adopted him.

Luke placed forty-three generations from Christ to David, while Matthew placed twenty-eight from David to Christ, either because one person is counted twice after the captivity, or because Luke, who names the maternal grandfather, resolves the question through the reason for adoption.

[The supplied source ends here.]
the husband of Mary, that is, her betrothed, because wives are called betrothed women, just as men are called betrothed husbands and spouses. Matthew placed the genealogy at the beginning of his book, which he wrote to the Jews, so that they might understand that the one whom the prophets had foretold would come from these fathers had already come. Luke, however, placed the Lord’s genealogy not before but after his baptism, so that no one, after hearing the Lord’s voice saying, “This is my beloved Son” [Col. 0461B], would believe that he had been Joseph’s son.

From Abraham to Christ, according to Matthew, there are forty-two persons in the genealogy—that is, from the beginning of faith to the land of the living, having abandoned the error of paganism—represented by the forty-two encampments of the children of Israel from Egypt to the Promised Land. Three encampments are omitted: where Aaron died; where the people murmured against the Lord and Moses out of disgust with the manna; and where they were wounded by serpents. These signify the three kings who are removed from the genealogy.

According to Luke, however, there are seventy-seven persons in the genealogy, between Adam and Christ, on account of the forgiveness of sins, as the Lord said to Peter: “I do not say to you seven times, but seventy times seven.”

Likewise, the interpretation of the names. [Col. 0461C] The first name, that is, the father Abram, is interpreted as “exalted father”; Abraham is interpreted as “father of many,” understood as “of nations.” He signifies Christ, because he has sons from many nations, as it is said: “If your sons will have kept my law.”

Isaac is interpreted as “laughter,” because Sarah and Abraham laughed for joy. He signifies Christ, as in: “Behold, I announce to you great joy.”

Jacob is interpreted as “supplanter,” because he supplanted his brother three times: first from his mother’s womb, second through the lentils, third through the blessing. He signifies Christ, because Christ supplanted the devil three times: first, “Man shall not live by bread alone”; second, “You shall not tempt the Lord your God”; third, “You shall adore the Lord your God.” Elsewhere it is said: “No one can plunder the strong man’s goods unless he first binds the strong man.”

Judah is interpreted as “confession” [Col. 0461D]. Thus his mother said: “Now I will confess the Lord, because he has given me a fourth son.” He signifies Christ, as in: “I confess to you, Father of heaven and earth.”

Phares is interpreted as “division” or “he divided,” as the midwife said: “Why have you divided the wall?” He signifies Christ, as in: “You will place the sheep at your right hand, but the goats at your left”; and: “He will divide him and assign him his portion with the hypocrites.”

Zerah is interpreted as “east” or “scarlet.” “East,” because he was destined to arise first; “scarlet,” because a scarlet thread was bound to his finger. He signifies Christ, as in: “The Dawn from on high has visited us”; and: “Why is your garment red?”

Thamar is interpreted as “palm,” and as “bitter,” “hunger,” or “impetus.” “Palm,” because of victory, since she raised up her husband’s offspring; “bitter,” [Col. 0462A] because of widowhood; “hunger,” because of her longing for children; “impetus,” because they rushed upon her to burn her. She signifies the Church.

Esron is interpreted as “he saw an arrow” or “their courtyard.” “Arrow,” because he was born at the time when the Canaanites were waging hostilities against Israel on account of the killing of Shechem and Hamor; “courtyard,” because in his time Israel lived in tabernacles and tents. He signifies Christ, as in: “Your arrows are sharp”; and: “Our feet were standing in your courtyards, Jerusalem.”

Aram is interpreted as “chosen” or “exalted.” He signifies Christ, as in: “This is my beloved Son”; and: “The Lord is exalted above all nations.”

Aminadab is interpreted as “my spontaneous people,” because at the time of his birth the people of Israel were living voluntarily in the land of Egypt. [Col. 0462B] He signifies Christ, as in: “No one takes my life from me.”

Naason is interpreted as “divining” or “a strong diviner,” because in his time Israel began in Egypt to practice divination and worship idols. He signifies Christ, because he divined concerning the past, as in: “Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day”; concerning the present: “Why are you thinking evil in your hearts?”; and concerning the future: “People will be like the angels of God.”

Salmon is interpreted as “perceptive” or “sense,” and for this reason he was made leader of the tribe of Judah. He signifies Christ, as in: “Who touched me? I perceive that power has gone out from me.”

Raab is interpreted as “breadth,” because first she enlarged the sin of her flesh as a prostitute, and afterward her offspring was spread widely among the children of Israel. She signifies the Church spread throughout the whole world.

Booz is interpreted as “in whom there is strength” or “in him is strength.” He appeared to perform an act of strength when he accepted Ruth in order to raise up the offspring of his kinsman, which another man had refused to do. He signifies Christ, as in: “If I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw the way with me” [Col. 0462C].

Obed is interpreted as “serving,” because he served God well. He signifies Christ, as in: “The Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve.”

Ruth is interpreted as “hastening,” because she hastened from a foreign land to the people of God. She signifies the Church, which hastened to Christ.

Jesse is interpreted as “sacrifice in the sun” or “incense.” From him was born a son who repeatedly ordained sacrifice or incense to be offered to God. He signifies Christ, as in: “He has set his tabernacle in the sun”; and: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?”

David is interpreted as “strong of hand” or “desirable,” because he conquered Goliath and all Israel loved him [Col. 0462D]. He signifies Christ, as in: “The Lord is strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle”; and: “Behold, the Desired One will come to all the nations.”

Bathsheba is interpreted as “daughter of the oath” or “well of satiety.” She signifies the Law, which was joined to another man, that is, to Christ, after the death of her husband, that is, after the death of Moses.

Uriah is interpreted as “God is my light.” He signifies Moses, as we said above.

Solomon is interpreted as “peaceful,” because God gave him peace in his kingdom. He signifies Christ: “For he is our peace, who made both one.”

Rehoboam is interpreted as “breadth” or, by antiphrasis, “the people’s impetus,” because he had a narrow kingdom, that is, a small one; or because eleven tribes separated themselves from his kingdom. He signifies Christ [Col. 0463A], as in: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened.”

Abijah is interpreted as “the Lord is father,” because he was a father to the people and at first did what was good before the Lord. He signifies Christ: “Do not call anyone your father on earth; one is your Father, who is in heaven.”

Asa is interpreted as “grieving,” “taking away,” or “raising up.” He grieved over the people’s sins, removed idols from his kingdom, and raised up many cities. He signifies Christ, as in: “The Lord saw Jerusalem and wept over it”; and: “Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world”; and: “Lift up your gates, O princes.”

Jehoshaphat is interpreted as “he himself judging,” or “the judgment of the Lord,” or “the Lord has judged,” because he judged his people well, or because he distinguished by judgment between the prophets of the Lord and Ahab; and because the Lord judged between him and Ahab when the Syrians were pursuing them. He signifies Christ, as in: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” [Col. 0463B].

Joram is interpreted as “exalted” or “he exalted.” He signifies Christ, as in: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.”

Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah are not counted in Christ’s genealogy, for the reasons stated above.

Uzziah is interpreted as “strong of the Lord.” He fought against every nation and conquered. He signifies Christ, as in: “Lazarus, come out.”

Jotham is interpreted as “completed” or “perfect,” because he completed the Lord’s commandments. He signifies Christ, as in: “When Jesus had finished all these words.”

Ahaz is interpreted as “apprehending,” because he apprehended and worshiped idols. He signifies Christ, who took the girl by the hand [Col. 0463C] and raised her up.

Hezekiah is interpreted as “the Lord is strong” or “the Lord has strengthened,” because the Lord strengthened him against iniquity and added years to his life. He signifies Christ, as in: “Take courage, because I have conquered the world.”

Manasseh is interpreted as “forgetful,” because at first he forgot God’s commandments, and afterward, forgetting the idols, he did God’s commandments. He signifies Christ, as in: “Your sins are forgiven you,” that is, “let them be forgotten.”

Amon is interpreted as “faithful” or “honorable,” because his father was faithful, and he himself was honorable in the beauty of his appearance. He signifies Christ, as in: “Ask and it will be given to you”; and: “Beautiful beyond the sons of men.”

Josiah is interpreted as “Where is the Lord’s incense?” because he not only did the Lord’s will in everything, but also made for the Lord such a Passover as had never previously been made. He signifies Christ [Col. 0463D], as in: “He prayed at greater length”; and: “Let my prayer be directed like incense.”

Likewise, Eliakim, also called Jehoiakim, who is written of at the beginning of the Book of Daniel: he was the son of Joash, who is not written in the genealogy. He is interpreted as “the Lord’s resurrection,” because he migrated from Judea to Babylon in captivity. So too Christ passed from circumcision to uncircumcision, as in: “When I have risen, I will go before you into Galilee”; and: “Ascending on high, he led our captivity captive by his own power,” that is, from earth to heaven.

Joarim is interpreted as “the Lord’s preparation.” He is written of at the beginning of the Book of Ezekiel; he is the same as Jeconiah, and was Josiah’s grandson, not his son. He is interpreted as “the Lord’s preparation,” as in: “Come, blessed of my Father, [Col. 0464A] receive the kingdom prepared for you”; and: “If I go and prepare a place for you.”

Babylon is interpreted as “confusion,” as in: “Let those who worship carved images be confounded.”

Galathiel is interpreted as “God is my petition,” because in his time the captive people asked to return to their land. He signifies Christ, as in: “Father, sanctify those whom you have given me.”

Zerubbabel is interpreted as “this master from Babylon.” He signifies Christ, sometimes in relation to confusion, as in: “Come to me, all,” and so forth; sometimes in relation to shame, as in: “This man eats with tax collectors and sinners.”

Abiud is interpreted as “this is my God.” He signifies Christ: “I and the Father are one.”

Eliakim is interpreted as “the resurrection of God.” He signifies Christ, as in: “Whoever believes in me will not die forever, but I will raise [Col. 0464B] him up.”
