Azor is interpreted as “helped.” He signifies Christ, as in: “I am not alone, but the Father is with me.”

Zadok is interpreted as “justified” or “just.” He signifies Christ, as in: “I speak the truth, because the one who is with me is truthful.”

Achim is interpreted as “my brother,” as in: “Tell my brothers to go into Galilee.”

Eliud is interpreted as “You are my God.” He signifies Christ, as in: “My God and my Lord.”

Eleazar is interpreted as “God my helper.” He signifies Christ, as in: “The one who sent me is with me.”

Matthan is interpreted as “giving.” He signifies Christ, as in: “I forgave you every debt.”

Jacob is interpreted as “supplanter.”

Joseph is interpreted as “increased.” He signifies Christ, as in: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold.”

Mary is interpreted as “star of the sea,” or “illuminating woman,” or “lady” [Col. 0464C]. A star is sweet to sailors, while the sea is bitter; thus Mary was in the sea, that is, in the world, among sinners. And because it is customary for a star to lead men to port, so Mary, in the world where Christ was born, is called illuminating woman and lady, since she bore for us the true Light and Lord, who leads all to life as they follow him.

Why are women, including sinful women, also included in the genealogy? Because they come to eternal life just as men do. And therefore sinners are received, because he himself said: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”

Why are Abraham and David placed at the head of the genealogy according to Matthew? Because Christ’s coming was promised to them. It was said to Abraham: “In your offspring all nations will be blessed”; and it was said to David [Col. 0464D]: “From the fruit of your womb,” and so forth.

Why does Matthew begin the genealogy with Abraham, while Luke proceeds from Christ to Abraham? Matthew begins with Abraham because Abraham is the author and head of faith, as in: “Abraham believed.” Luke begins with Christ because Christ is the true progenitor of the human race.

Why does the genealogy precede the baptism according to Matthew, whereas according to Luke the baptism precedes the genealogy? Matthew places the genealogy first so that he might speak of Christ’s lineage before speaking of the gift of his grace. Luke, however, wished to proclaim divine grace before human lineage; or he spoke after the baptism in order to show the Father’s voice and the angels [Col. 0465A] testifying about the Son, and because no one ascends to the Father except after baptism.

Why does Matthew list forty-two from Abraham to Christ, while Luke lists fifty-seven? Because Matthew traced the greater ancestors of the Lord’s lineage, whereas Luke wove it in order through the adoption of generation.

Why did Matthew trace the genealogy through Solomon, and Luke through Nathan? So that they might show Christ’s generation through a royal and priestly family: according to the flesh he was a king from kings and a priest from priests, as in: “O God, give your judgment to the king”; and: “You are a priest forever.”

Why does Matthew divide the generations into groups of fourteen? To show the patriarchs from Abraham to David, the kings from David to the Babylonian captivity [Col. 0465B], and that afterward the kingdom departed from the Jews until Christ.

Luke gives fifty-seven from Abraham to Christ to show the mystery of the fiftieth number in the Old and New Testaments, which pertains to repentance, and of the seventh number, which pertains to man as a sevenfold being: heart, soul, mind, earth, water, fire, and air.

Luke leads from Christ back to Adam, showing that through Christ the race of Adam is freed from sin; or that those who return to the Father proceed from Christ.

Likewise, what does coming to Christ through four generations signify except faith, hope, and charity? What does fourteen signify except the ten words of the Law and the four virtues of the soul? First, prudence: to serve God, not idols. Second, temperance: [Col. 0465C] not to covet. Third, justice: not to commit adultery. Fourth, fortitude: to forgive, not to kill.

Likewise, seven times six, or six times seven, makes forty-two. According to Matthew, this signifies the Church laboring with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Likewise, if in ascending number you join one, two, three, and four together, they make ten, which signifies that the Old Law is to be fulfilled in the grace of the Gospel. Through one, the law of nature; through two, the law of Moses; through three, the law of the prophets; through four, the grace of the Gospel. For just as these produce ten, so the whole Law is fulfilled in these four Gospels, or in the four virtues of the soul.

Likewise, the two that remain after forty, if you count Jeconiah twice; but otherwise [Col. 0465D] they signify the two Testaments. The first stands above them, signifying Christ, who is above all.

Likewise, fourteen three times signifies faith in the Holy Trinity, which is the threefold cord that is not easily broken.

Likewise, according to Luke, seventy-seven. In this number there are eleven sevens. Through ten it signifies the Law, and through the one that remains beyond ten, the transgressor of the Law; through seven it signifies man, who is sevenfold. And it was fitting that the one who transgresses the Law in this number should be redeemed through the same number.

Why is Ruth the Moabite placed in the Lord’s genealogy, when it is written: “Moabites shall not enter the assembly of God forever”? Because she was holy and blameless in conduct and rose above [Col. 0466A] the Law. For if the Law was established for the impious and sinners, then Ruth, who exceeded the definition of the Law, certainly entered the Church.

And why does Matthew always say “begot,” whereas Luke says “was”? Because Matthew spoke of actual generation, while Luke spoke chiefly of adoption.

Likewise, Matthew says “son,” and now the same person afterward becomes “father”; whereas Luke’s “father” is now afterward “son.”

Why did Luke place only four names of the patriarchs in the genealogy—Judah, Joseph, Simeon, and Levi? For the sake of symbolism: in that earlier Judah, the mystery of the Lord’s Passion is signified; in Joseph, the example of chastity; in Simeon, vengeance for violated modesty; in Levi, the office of the priesthood.

Why did Christ wish to be born from no other tribe except Judah? Because Judah was Jacob’s fourth son. [Col. 0466B] Reuben defiled his father’s bed and committed a great crime there. Simeon and Levi killed the peaceful men Shechem and Hamor, concerning whom their father said: “You have made me hateful to the Canaanites.” Therefore they were not worthy to be Christ’s fathers. He was from the tribe of Judah, which was the fourth son, because he came to redeem us under the fourth law, that is, the grace of the Gospel.

Why did Christ deign to come through a woman and not through another creature? Because the world perished through a woman, it was fitting that through a woman it should be restored, as Sedulius says:

> The woman alone was there through whom the gate to death was opened,  
> and the woman alone through whom life returns.

Likewise, the world’s destruction occurred through four: through a woman, a man, a tree, and a serpent. It is restored through [Col. 0466C] four: through Mary, Christ, the cross, and Joseph. For the serpent that was in Israel signifies Christ. It was made of bronze, with four round forms, and was raised upon the top of a staff so that they might look at it, while the desert animals fled from fear of the wheels. Thus each person is healed if he looks upon the one hanging at the top of the staff, that is, upon the cross.

The fear of the wheels is the fear of the preaching of the four Gospels. Thus the animals—that is, demons or thoughts—will flee from our hearts.

Likewise, the cluster of grapes carried through the desert by two men on a pole: the cluster is Christ; the two men are the Jews and the nations. The one who went before and turned his back toward the cluster signifies the Jews, who seemed to go before in the Law and the prophets, possessing God’s commandments and having [Col. 0466D] Christ promised to them. Therefore they saw him hanging on the pole—that is, on the cross—with his back, not his face, turned toward them. Those who went behind are the nations, which were converted to Christ hanging on the cross.

Christ’s generation, therefore, was as it was stated in the genealogy: “Jacob begot Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom Christ was born.” Or it was arranged so that the genealogy would be counted through Joseph, from whom Christ was not born, and not through Mary, from whom Christ was born, because it was not customary to count genealogies through women.

# OF THE SEVEN SIGNS OF THE LORD’S NATIVITY

The Lord sent many signs before his birth, foreshadowing his coming into the world; he also displayed many at the very time of his birth. Of these, the first sign was that one ruler reigned throughout the whole world, something that had never happened before, announcing in advance that Christ, the one Lord of all creation, was coming [Col. 0467A].

The second sign was an astonishing peace over the whole earth, such as had never existed before or afterward. This signified the true peace of the world, which is Christ, who made peace between God and human beings.

The third sign was that, by Caesar’s decree, once captives had been released, wherever they had been held captive, their property was restored to them; and each person professed that he owed tribute to Caesar. Those who had a payment of three denarii were assessed under the name of the drachma. This foreshadowed that the human race would be freed through Christ from captivity and the dominion of the devil and, if it professed faith in the Holy Trinity, would be brought back to its homeland, Paradise [Col. 0467B].

The fourth sign was that on a single day one thousand and thirty slaves refused, after their captivity had been released, to return to their own masters [Col. 0468A]. This foreshadowed that whoever refuses to return from vices to Christ will perish eternally.

The fifth sign was the new star that arose in the East, by whose guidance the Magi came to Christ. Its marvelous brightness, surpassing all stars, signified the grace of God, through which not only many from the Jews but also far more from the nations are led to life, which is Christ.

The sixth sign was a great circle shining with a golden radiance around the sun throughout the entire day of Christ’s birth. It signified the one whose circumference contains even the most exalted natures.

The seventh sign was that on that very day a stream of oil flowed abundantly throughout the city of Rome beyond the Tiber [Col. 0468B]. It signified the free mercy of God, through which Christ came to seek and save the human race, which had perished.

These seven signs also signify the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0467]

## (A.D. 841) PENITENTIAL OF THE BLESSED RABANUS MAURUS, ABBOT OF FULDA AND ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ

*(In Canisius, Ancient Readings, vol. II.)*

## PREFACE TO HERIBALD, BISHOP OF AUXERRE

[Col. 0467C] To his beloved brother Heribald, bishop, Rabanus, a sinner and the least worthy servant of the servants of God: greetings in Christ.

Certain chapters written on a petition [*pittatio*], brought to me by the messenger of Count Conrad, compelled me to answer you concerning various questions. But since I was not able to answer everything one by one, I have taken care to record the matters briefly. There were some passages concerning a homicide that had been committed; some concerning fornication and adultery; some concerning those who had defiled themselves through lust before receiving an ecclesiastical rank; and some concerning those who had polluted themselves after receiving such a rank, yet did not wish to withdraw from ecclesiastical office and ministry at the altar. Besides these, I also found other chapters written there [Col. 0467D], about which you asked me to respond to you.

I have not delayed inserting into this present letter whatever I found explicitly set out concerning these matters in the sacred canons. You, however, should do what seems just to you and what Holy Scripture teaches you to do. [Col. 0468C] For the books of the Old and New Testaments make abundantly clear how abominable before God are homicides, fornications, greed, sorceries, the crimes of magic, and every action of evil works. I have taken care to insert some of these here. As for the divine books themselves, if you wish to gather their teaching attentively and decide to obey them, you are able yourselves to investigate what ought to be done and what is beneficial, and to derive useful instruction from them.

May God direct your heart and your efforts toward every good work, so that in this present life you may teach and do what is pleasing to him; and so, through his grace, may you attain full reward and eternal life.

For homicides and adulteries are prohibited in the Lord’s Law [Col. 0468D], as was said above, along with all vices. Thus it is written in Leviticus that the Lord commanded his people, saying:

> “Sanctify yourselves and be holy, because I am holy, the Lord your God. Do not commit anything unjust in judgment, in measure, or in weight. You shall not stand against the blood of [Col. 0469A] your neighbor. You shall not hate your brother in your heart, but openly rebuke him, lest you incur sin on his account. You shall not seek revenge, nor remember the injury done by your fellow citizens. Whoever curses his father or mother shall die the death. Whoever curses father or mother, his blood shall be upon him.
>
> “If a man commits adultery with another man’s wife and perpetrates adultery with his neighbor’s spouse, both the adulterer and the adulteress shall die. Whoever sleeps with his stepmother and uncovers his father’s shame, both shall die, and their blood shall be upon them. Whoever sleeps with a male in a woman’s intercourse, and both have committed the crime, they shall die; their blood shall be upon them. If anyone sleeps with his daughter-in-law, both shall die [Col. 0469B], because they have committed a crime; their blood shall be upon them.
>
> “If a man takes a woman together with her daughter and marries her mother, he has committed a crime; their blood shall be upon them. He shall be burned alive with them, and such an enormity shall not remain among you. Whoever lies with an animal or beast shall die; you shall also kill the animal. A woman who lies with any animal shall be killed together with it; her blood shall be upon her.
>
> “Whoever takes his sister, the daughter of his father or the daughter of his mother, and sees her nakedness, and she sees her brother’s shame, they have committed an abominable act. They shall be killed in the sight of the people, because they have mutually uncovered their nakedness, and they shall bear their iniquity.
>
> “Whoever lies with a menstruating woman [Col. 0469C] and uncovers her nakedness, and she opens the source of her blood, both shall be killed from the midst of the people. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your paternal aunt or your maternal aunt. Whoever does this will expose the shame of his flesh; both shall bear their iniquity.
>
> “Whoever lies with the wife of his paternal uncle or his maternal uncle and uncovers the shame of his kinship, they shall bear their sin; they shall die without children. Whoever takes his brother’s wife commits an unlawful act; he has uncovered his brother’s nakedness, and they shall be without children.
>
> “Do not pollute your souls with beasts, birds, or all things that move upon the earth, which I have shown you to be unclean. A man or woman in whom there is a Pythonic or divining spirit shall die. They shall overwhelm them with stones [Col. 0469D], and their blood shall be upon them.
>
> “Keep my laws and judgments, and do them, lest the land into which you are about to enter and dwell vomit you out. Do not walk according to the ordinances of the nations that I am about to drive out before you.”

But such conduct is not forbidden only in the Old Testament; it is likewise entirely prohibited to the worshipers of God in the New Testament.

Concerning carnal desires, Paul writes to the Galatians as follows:

> “I say, walk by the Spirit [Col. 0470A], and you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh. For the flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh. These are opposed to one another, so that you do not do whatever you wish. But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the Law.
>
> “Now the works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, licentiousness, service of idols, sorceries, enmities, quarrels, jealousies, angers, disputes, dissensions, factions, heresies, envies, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God.
>
> “But the fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, gentleness, faith, modesty, self-control, chastity. Against [Col. 0470B] such things there is no law. Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires. If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit. Let us not become desirous of empty glory, envying one another and provoking one another.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Do not be deceived: God is not mocked. For whatever a person sows, that person will also reap. Whoever sows in his flesh will reap corruption from the flesh; but whoever sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit. Let us not grow weary in doing good, for in due time we shall reap.”

Since all the vices named above are prohibited as harmful both by the Lawgiver and by the Apostle, and divine authority forbids God’s worshipers to commit them, threatening those who do so with everlasting punishment [Col. 0470C], while on the other hand the Apostle praises spiritual gifts and urges that they be followed in every way, it is good for us to beware of every sin and every scandal, as far as the Lord grants us power; to do what pleases him; and to carry out what the Lord’s Law commands us. For in this way, both in the present and in the future, we shall find his mercy and protection.

If, according to the historical sense, the Lawgiver threatened transgressors of God’s commandments with the death of the flesh and the end of the present life, how much more ought we, according to the Savior’s command and evangelical teaching, to fear the death of the soul and eternal punishment, compared with that punishment which in some manner had an end? This punishment will torment the guilty without end.

Therefore it is necessary that in the present life, according to the Apostle, we put to death our members that are upon the earth [Col. 0470D], that is, that we strive to extinguish within ourselves the desires of our flesh and earthly pleasures; that, as far as the Lord grants us power, we drive away every vice; and that we earnestly obey God’s will and his commandments. For in this way, by the Lord’s generosity, we can escape everlasting death and attain eternal life.

From this point onward, let us also endeavor to answer the questions, as far as we can, briefly and in accordance with the provisions of the canons.

# THE PENITENTIAL BEGINS [Col. 0471]

## CHAPTER ONE [Col. 0471A]  
### On Homicides Committed Willingly

First, therefore, we have taken care to record briefly what the sacred canons decree concerning the commission of homicide, and how penitence should be performed by those who have committed it.

In the Council of Ancyra, chapter 21, it is written concerning homicides:

> “Those who have committed voluntary homicide shall continually submit themselves to penitence; but they shall attain perfection toward the end of life.”

## CHAPTER II  
### Likewise, on Homicides and False Witnesses

In the Council of Agde, chapter 37, it is written concerning homicides and false witnesses:

> “Accordingly, we have decreed that homicides and false witnesses are to be removed from ecclesiastical communion, unless they cleanse away the crimes committed through the satisfaction of penitence” [Col. 0471B].

## CHAPTER III  
### On Those Who Kill Their Own Slaves without Judgment; and on the Mistress Who Kills a Maidservant through Jealousy

Likewise, in the Council of Agde, chapter 62, it is written concerning those who kill their own slaves without judgment:

> “If anyone kills his own slave without the knowledge of the judge, he shall cleanse the guilt of bloodshed through excommunication or two years of penitence.”

Likewise, in the Council of Elvira, chapter 5, this is written concerning a mistress who killed a maidservant through jealousy, so that within the third day she gave up her soul amid suffering, since it is uncertain whether she killed her by intention or by accident:

> “If intentionally, after seven years; if accidentally, after five years, once the prescribed penitence has been performed, it has been decided that she may be admitted to communion. But if she should become ill during the appointed periods, she shall receive communion” [Col. 0471C].

## CHAPTER IV  
### On Homicides Committed Unwillingly; and on Those Who Kill Anyone at the Command of a Ruler

In the Council of Ancyra, chapter 22, it is written concerning those who have committed homicide unwillingly:

> “Concerning homicides committed unwillingly, the earlier decision ordered that perfection be attained after seven years of penitence; the second, however, ordered that a period of five years be completed.”

Some excuse a certain homicide recently committed in the sedition and battle of powerful men, as though no one needed to perform penitence for it, since it was carried out at the command of our rulers and ended by God’s judgment [Col. 0471D].

We know that God’s judgment is always just and worthy of no reproach. Concerning it, it is also written: “The Lord is just in all his ways and holy in all his works, who judges the world in righteousness and the peoples in his truth.” Without him, not even a sparrow falls to the ground. But no one can penetrate God’s judgments, since it is written: “Your judgments are a great abyss.”

[Col. 0472A] Therefore those who wish to defend this wicked killing must consider whether they can excuse before God’s eyes as innocent those who, because of greed—which is the root of all evils and is compared with the service of idols—and because of favor toward their temporal lords, despised the eternal Lord and, scorning his commandments, committed homicide not by accident but deliberately.

For concerning such matters we read that, for those who kill people unwillingly, God appointed through the Lawgiver cities of refuge, to which fugitives could flee and be saved from the avenger of their neighbor’s blood and not die. Thus it is written in Deuteronomy:

> “This shall be the law for the homicide: the city shall be preserved. Whoever strikes his neighbor unknowingly, and is shown not to have held any hatred against him yesterday or the day before, but to have gone with him simply into the forest to cut wood; and, while cutting the wood, the axe flies from his hand, or the iron slips from its handle and strikes and kills his companion—let him flee to one of the cities mentioned above and live, lest the near relative of the one whose blood has been shed, moved by the sting of grief, strike his soul” [Col. 0472B].

But concerning one who kills someone deliberately, it is commanded in Exodus:

> “If anyone kills his neighbor deliberately and by ambush, you shall drag him away from my altar, so that he may die.”

And in Deuteronomy:

> “If anyone, hating his neighbor, lies in wait for his life, and rising up strikes him, and he dies, and he flees to one of the cities mentioned above, the elders of that city shall send and seize him from the place of refuge and deliver him into the hands of the near relatives of the one whose blood has been shed, and he shall die; you shall not pity him” [Col. 0472C].

If, therefore, someone says that the one whom the Lord judged worthy of death is not guilty, how is that person not acting contrary to God’s Law, since he claims that what the Lord commanded happened by accident? He must therefore take care lest he himself belong to the number of those to whom it is said through the prophet:

> “Woe to you,” he says, “who call evil good and good evil; light darkness and darkness light; or bitter sweet and sweet bitter.”

Such people kill souls that do not die and give life to those that do not live.

Whoever, then, says that anyone can receive pardon from God for evil deeds without fitting penance is himself mistaken; and when, having been deceived, he hastens to deceive others, he is bound by a double guilt: namely, that of his own error and that of deceiving another. But amid these matters it must be understood that there is a great difference between a legitimate ruler and a seditious tyrant; between one who strives to overturn the tranquility of Christian peace and one who fights with weapons to defend justice against iniquity. Concerning this, many examples of courageous men are found under the Old Law and under the New Testament, examples that can instruct us about what we ought to think concerning such matters.

## CHAPTER V. On administrators and those who draw up criminal petitions

As for administrators who exercise secular judgments according to the law of their ancestors, it is easy to discover what the sacred canons think. For in the decretals of Pope Innocent, chapter 22, we read:

> It was also asked concerning those who, after baptism, have administered [justice], or have merely carried out tortures, or even have pronounced a capital sentence. Concerning these, we find nothing defined by our predecessors. For they remembered that these powers had been granted by God, and that the sword had been permitted to their authority for the punishment of the guilty; that God’s minister had been appointed as an avenger in such matters. How, then, could they condemn an act that they saw had been permitted by God as its author? Concerning these matters, therefore, we hold that things should remain as they have hitherto been observed, lest we seem either to overturn discipline or to act against the Lord’s authority. Their deeds, however, will all be preserved for them when they render an account.

Likewise, in the same decretals, chapter 25, it is written that those who draw up criminal petitions are to be regarded as free from guilt.

You also wished to inquire whether those who draw up criminal petitions are granted permission—certainly after the regeneration of baptism—to ask rulers for someone’s death or for bloodshed as punishment for a crime. Rulers, however, never grant this without investigation; rather, they always refer the matters or crimes entrusted to them to judges [Col. 0473C], so that, after the case has been examined, judgment may be rendered. When these matters have been presented to the examiner, either acquittal or condemnation is pronounced according to the nature of the case. And while the authority of the laws is exercised against criminals, the one who draws up the petition will be free from guilt.

## CHAPTER VI. On the necessary offense committed by the people

As for a necessary offense committed by the people, and how it is customarily allowed to pass unpunished, the same pope, replying to certain bishops of Macedonia concerning their questions, writes as follows:

> Let your charity take care that such matters have gone no further, and observe that necessity, as you say, compelled this; yet even churches established in peace must not presume to do such things. But it often happens that, whenever a people or crowd commits a sin, much is customarily allowed to pass because punishment cannot be inflicted upon everyone on account of their number. I therefore say that the earlier matters should be set aside from judgment, but that henceforth the greatest care must be taken to prevent such things.

For, as it seems to me, this apostolic teacher is not saying that the people need not do penance for evil deeds. Rather, because punishment cannot be inflicted upon everyone on account of their number, he says that the earlier matters should be set aside from judgment, while from then onward the greatest care must be taken lest such things occur.

## CHAPTER VII. On parricide

How detestable a crime parricide is, the Lord himself showed by the judgment rendered between Cain and his brother Abel, when he said to Cain the parricide:

> You shall be cursed upon the earth, which opened its mouth and received your brother’s blood from your hand. When you work it, it shall not give you its fruit. You shall be a wanderer and a fugitive upon the earth.

He also placed a sign upon him, namely, that he should live always groaning, trembling, and in exile, and should have no settled dwelling anywhere. But because in modern times parricides in exile wander through various places and devote themselves to various vices and the enticements of gluttony, it seems better to me that, remaining in one place, they should chastise themselves with strict penance, if perhaps they may deserve to receive pardon for their crime from the Lord’s goodness. For they will not be permitted thereafter to take up the military belt, or to enter marriage and the bond of wedlock, because the sacred canons do not allow this to them, as we shall subsequently show when we set out the synodal decrees concerning penitents for grave offenses.

## CHAPTER VIII. On those who kill children conceived through fornication

Accordingly, in the Council of Ancyra, chapter 20, it is written concerning women who kill in various ways the children conceived through fornication:

> Concerning women who commit fornication and kill their children, or who act to expel from the womb what they have conceived: the ancient definition ordered that they be removed from the Church until the end of their lives; but now we have determined more humanely that a period of ten years of penance should be granted to them.

Likewise, in the Council of Eliberis, chapter 63, it is written concerning those who kill children conceived through adultery:

> If any woman, having conceived through adultery in the absence of her husband, kills the child after the crime, it has been decided that communion should scarcely be granted to her even at the end of life, because she has doubled her crime.

## CHAPTER IX. On those who cause abortions

Likewise, in the Council of Ilerda, chapter 11, it is written concerning those who cause abortions or destroy children after birth:

> Those who have attempted to kill fetuses ill-conceived through adultery, whether unborn or born, or who have crushed them in their mothers’ wombs by means of some potions, shall grant communion to adulterers of either sex after the completion of seven years, provided that throughout the whole time of their lives they devote themselves to tears and humility.

## CHAPTER X. On those who commit capital crimes after sacred ordination, and on their penance or excommunication

[Col. 0474D] It has therefore seemed appropriate to you that we write about those who hold sacred orders and confess themselves to have been stained by capital crimes, whether before or after ordination. In their case, as it seems to me, this distinction ought to be made: those who have been publicly discovered or apprehended in perjury, theft, fornication, or other crimes of this kind should, according to the institutions of the sacred canons, be deposed from their rank. For it is a scandal to the people of God to have over them persons who are plainly exceedingly vicious. Indeed, by such people they detract from God’s sacrifice, just as they are read to have done formerly because of the sinning sons of Eli; and, becoming rebellious and hostile on this account, they grow worse each day through their evil examples.

But those who confess secretly, through private confession, the evil they have secretly committed before the eyes of God, in the presence also of the priest who is to impose penance upon them, and who accuse themselves of having grievously sinned—if they truly repent and continually strive to cleanse themselves through fasts, almsgiving, vigils, and sacred prayers with tears—should be promised hope of pardon from God while retaining their rank. He wills all people to be saved and to come to knowledge of the truth, and not the death of the sinner, but rather that he should be converted and live.

For concerning those who have been advanced to the honor of the priesthood without examination, it is written in the Council of Nicaea, chapter 9:

> If any presbyters have been advanced without examination, or, when examined, have confessed their sins, and people, stirred up against the canons, have attempted to impose hands upon those who confessed, the rule does not admit such men, because the Catholic Church defends what is irreprehensible.

Likewise, in the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 9, it is written concerning them:

> If a presbyter is advanced after having been overtaken by a bodily sin and confesses that he sinned before his ordination, he shall not consecrate the offerings, but shall remain in the other offices because of his good zeal. For many have said that other sins can be remitted through the laying on of hands. But if he has not confessed concerning himself, and cannot be openly accused, he shall be left to the judgment of his own authority.

Likewise, in the same council, chapter 10, concerning a deacon in similar fashion:

> If he has fallen into the same sin, he shall be removed from the rank of the ministry.

Concerning those who have sinned after receiving their rank, the third Apostolic Canon reads:

> A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who is caught in fornication, perjury, or theft shall be deposed, but shall not be deprived of communion. For Scripture says: “The Lord will not judge twice for the same thing.”

Likewise, in the Apostolic Canon, chapter 29:

> If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon, having been justly deposed for certain crimes, dares to take up again the ministry formerly entrusted to him, let him be entirely cast out of the Church.

The Apostle teaches that an accusation against men of sacred order should not easily be received, but that the case must first be carefully examined and judgment imposed afterward, writing to Timothy:

> Do not receive an accusation against a presbyter, unless it is brought by two or three witnesses. Those who sin, rebuke before all, so that the others may have fear.

What sort of witnesses these ought to be is made clear in the African Council, where, in chapters 6 and 15, it is written:

> It has been decided that all slaves and personal freedmen are not to be admitted to an accusation; nor all those whom the public laws do not admit to the accusation of public crimes; nor all who are stained with the marks of infamy, actors, and persons subject to disgraceful practices. Heretics also, whether pagans or Jews. Nevertheless, for all those to whom an accusation is denied, permission to accuse in their own cases is not to be denied.

Likewise, in the same council, chapter 99:

> Witnesses are not to be admitted for testimony if they are not ordered to be admitted for an accusation, nor those whom the accuser himself has produced from his own household.

No one under fourteen years of age is to be admitted as a witness. Likewise, chapter 97:

> It has been decided that whenever many crimes are brought against clerics by their accusers, and the accuser has been unable to prove one of those charges, the charge which he first pursued, he is not to be admitted to the remaining charges.

Concerning those whose sins are hidden and cannot be openly accused by anyone: if they are healthily contrite and do penance for their sins before a bishop or presbyter, secretly, it seems good to me that, according to what has been decreed for them by the bishop or presbyter, they should do penance—not lukewarmly or slowly, but fervently and diligently—as though they trusted that they would receive pardon from the Lord and recover their rank.

The blessed Pope Gregory also approves this in a letter that he wrote to Secundinus, a servant of God living in confinement, saying:

> Your holiness has therefore asked us to write back to you concerning the authorities on rising again to priestly office after a fall, since you say that you have read various canons about this and found various opinions—some allowing restoration, others denying that it is possible. Beginning with Nicaea, we venerate this council together with the other four, because, when the others follow it, they agree with it in all their judgments. We therefore follow the Fathers who preceded us, because, by God’s authority, we do not depart from their teaching.
>
> Beginning at the head and proceeding to the fourth minister of the altar, we recognize that this rule is to be observed: just as the lesser is preceded by the greater in honor, so also in crime; and the greater the guilt by which a person is involved, the greater the punishment that must be imposed upon him. In this way, afterward, his penance may be believed to be fruitful. For what good is it to sow wheat and not gather its fruit, or to construct a house and not dwell in it?
>
> After worthy satisfaction, we believe that it is possible to return to honor, since the prophet says: “Will not the one who falls rise again?” (Psalm XL.) And: “Will the one who has turned away not return?” (Jeremiah VIII.) The same is said to the sinner: “On whatever day you turn and groan, you shall be saved.” (Isaiah XXX.) Hence the Psalmist also says: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. Do not cast me away,” and so forth. (Psalm L.)

> For in asking not to be cast away after falling into sin, the king was afraid because he had seized another man’s wife; when the prophet revealed his crime, he did penance and added: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a governing spirit.” For if he had not done penance worthy of God, he would never have preached to others: “I will teach transgressors your ways.” When the prophet looked upon his sins, cleansed through penance, he did not hesitate to rebuke the sins of others by preaching; and thus he strove to offer a sacrifice from himself when he said: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God.”

> These things would be sufficient; but every judgment is believed more readily insofar as it is confirmed by more testimonies of sacred Scripture. Concerning this the prophet says: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live.” (Ezekiel XVIII.) Concerning sinners it is said: “On whatever day the sinner turns and groans, all his iniquities shall be delivered into oblivion.”
>
> If our Redeemer came not to destroy sinners but to give them life, leaving the sins of sinners in oblivion, who among human beings would reserve them for condemnation, when the Apostle says: “If God justifies, who is he who condemns?” (Romans VIII.)
>
> Returning to the fountain of mercy, let us bring forth the evangelical judgment (Luke XV): “There is joy among the angels,” he says, “over one sinner doing penance, more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of penance.” And, leaving the ninety-nine sheep that had not strayed, he carried the lost sheep back to the sheepfold upon his shoulders.
>
> If a wandering sheep is carried back to the fold after being found, why should this person not be recalled to the ministry of the Church after penance? What is more serious: to commit a carnal offense, without which [perhaps, few] are found prepared, or to deny the Son of God through fear?
>
> We know that the blessed Peter himself, the chief of the Apostles, at whose body we now sit unworthy, fell into this sin; but after the denial penance followed, and after penance mercy was granted, because the one who had foretold that he would deny him did not cast him out of the apostolate.

> Let these things, dearest son, be sufficient for you, so that you may not doubt that the one whom you see erasing his sins with weeping obtains mercy in the sight of the divine majesty, since he who came to redeem sinners by his blood despises no sinner as guilty.

The blessed Augustine, writing to the deacon Peter concerning the faith, likewise says:

> Penance can be useful to every person in this life. Whenever a person undertakes it—however wicked, however old he may be—if he renounces past sins completely, and pours out before God tears not only of the body but also of the heart for them, and takes care to wash away the stains of evil deeds through good works, he will immediately have the forgiveness of all sins.
>
> The Lord promises this to us in prophetic speech, saying: “If he turns and groans, he shall be saved.” And elsewhere it is said: “Son, you have sinned; do not add again, but pray concerning your past sins, so that they may be forgiven you.”
>
> Prayer for sins would never have been prescribed for the sinner if forgiveness were not to be granted to the one who prays. Penance for sins is also beneficial if someone performs it in the Catholic Church, to which God, in the person of the blessed Apostle Peter, granted the power of binding and loosing, saying: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.”

At whatever age, therefore, a person performs true penance for his sins and, with the Lord’s illumination, corrects his life, he will not be deprived of the gift of pardon. For God, as he says through the prophet, does not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn from his evil way and that his soul should live.

Nevertheless, no one ought to remain longer in his sins under the hope of God’s mercy, since even in the body no one wishes to remain sick longer under the hope of future health. For such people, who neglect to withdraw from their iniquities and promise themselves pardon on that account, are sometimes overtaken by God’s sudden wrath in such a way that they find neither time for conversion nor the benefit of remission.

Therefore Holy Scripture warns each of us beforehand, saying: “Do not delay turning to the Lord.” And: “Do not postpone from day to day, for his wrath will come suddenly”; and: “In the time of vengeance he will destroy you.” The blessed David also says: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.” The blessed Paul agrees with him in these words:

> See, brothers, lest there perhaps be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, departing from the living God; but exhort one another each day, while it is called “today,” so that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.

A person lives with a hardened heart if he does not convert, despairing of pardon for sins—or if he hopes for God’s mercy in such a way that he remains until the end of his present life in the perversity of his crimes. Therefore, loving God’s mercy and fearing his justice, let us neither despair of the remission of sins nor remain in sins, knowing that if the equity of the most just Judge demands from all people what is owed, what will mercy, the most compassionate Redeemer, not forgive?

For just as mercy receives and absolves those who have converted, so justice will seize and punish those who are hardened. These are the people who, sinning against the Holy Spirit, will receive forgiveness of sins neither in this age nor in the age to come.

Concerning this matter Isidore, bishop of Seville, writes as follows in response to the inquiry of Bishop Mason:

> As for what your venerable brotherhood subsequently brought to our attention, no diversity of judgment among the decrees in such matters should be understood: in one place it is read that, after penance, the rank of honor is to be restored following a bodily fall; elsewhere, after such an offense, the dignity of the former order is said never to be restored.
>
> This difference is distinguished in the following way. The canon commands that those be restored to their former ranks of office whose satisfaction through penance preceded their restoration. But those who are not corrected from the vice of corruption, and who, with a kind of superstitious recklessness, attempt even to defend the very carnal sin they commit, receive neither the rank of honor nor the grace of communion.
>
> Thus both judgments must be distinguished: those who have deserved reconciliation through penance by the divine mercy must necessarily be restored to their place of honor. They not undeservedly regain the status of the dignity they had acquired, since they are known to have received the remedy of life through correction and penance.
>
> So that this may perhaps be less ambiguous, let it be confirmed by the judgment of divine authority. For the prophet Ezekiel, under the figure of Jerusalem’s transgression, shows that after the satisfaction of penance it is possible for former honor to be restored: “Be ashamed, O Judah, and bear your disgrace.”
>
> And shortly afterward: “You and your daughters,” he says, “return from your iniquity.” By saying “Be ashamed,” he shows that after the work of shame and supplication a person ought to be ashamed and, for the crimes committed, lower his bashful face to the ground because he has perpetrated a deed worthy of shame. Then he commanded that he bear the disgrace of his deposition, mourning with humility that he had sinned; and thus, according to the prophet, he may be recalled to his former state.

Likewise, the evangelist John writes something similar, among other things, to the angel of the church of Ephesus:

> Remember from where you have fallen, and do penance, and do the first works; otherwise I will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place.

By “the angel” of the church he clearly indicates its overseer, that is, the priest, in accordance with Malachi, who says: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.”

The overseer who has fallen into vice is therefore admonished through the evangelist to remember from where he has fallen and to do penance, and to perform his first works, so that his lampstand may not be removed. For the lampstand of the angel is understood as the priestly teaching or the honor of the authority that he bears, according to what is written concerning the condemnation of Eli in Samuel: “His eyes had grown dim, and he could not see the lamp of God before it was extinguished.”

The lamp of God had been his when, possessing priestly dignity, he shone with the brightness of justice. The prophet declares that it was extinguished when, on account of his sons’ crimes, he lost the priestly authority and the light of his merits. The priest’s lampstand, or lamp—understood as the gifts of honor—is completely extinguished and removed, according to John, when, after the fall into sin, penance is neglected and the crimes committed are not mourned.

For he did not say, “Because you have fallen, I will remove your lampstand from its place.” Therefore, if penance for his offense comes first for any overseer who sins, his merit will surely follow. It is also written in Proverbs: “He who conceals his crimes will not prosper; but he who confesses and abandons them will obtain mercy.”

The fact that the censure of the canons orders a penitent to return to his former state after seven years was not decreed by the holy Fathers according to their own choice, but rather established from the judgment of divine justice. For it is read that Mary, Aaron’s sister, when she incurred the offense of stubbornness against Moses, was immediately covered with the mark of leprosy. When Moses asked that she be cleansed, the Lord commanded her to go outside the camp for seven days and, after her cleansing, to be admitted into the camp again.

Mary, the sister of Aaron, therefore signifies the flesh of the priest. When it is devoted to pride and stained by the foulest contagions of corruption, it is cast outside the camp for seven days and outside the fellowship of the holy Church for seven years. There, after the cleansing of its vices, it will recover the merit of its place or former dignity.

Thus, insofar as I have been able, I have explained through sacred testimonies the ancient, clear, and complete authority [and] judgment of the Council of Ancyra, showing that the person who has learned to mourn his own sins through the satisfaction of penance can be restored to his proper honor. But the person who does not mourn what he does, and commits things that ought to be mourned without any shame for religion or fear of divine judgment, cannot be restored.

Thus far Isidore.

Augustine, writing to Boniface, says:

> That it was decreed in the Church that no one, after doing penance for any crime, should receive the clerical office, return to the clerical office, or remain in the clerical office was done not out of despair of pardon, but through the rigor of discipline. Otherwise an argument would be made against the keys given to the Church, concerning which it was said: “Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.”
>
> But lest perhaps a mind swelling with hope of ecclesiastical honor on account of crimes should perform penance arrogantly, it was most strictly decreed that, after penance had been done for a damnable crime, no one should be a cleric, so that, through despair of temporal elevation, a truer and greater medicine of humility might be provided.
>
> David also did penance for deadly crimes, yet remained in his honor. But for that reason the later diligence should not be considered pointless: where nothing was taken away from salvation, they added something to humility, so that salvation might be more securely protected. I believe they had experienced the false penances of some people, undertaken through an affected desire for honors and power. The experience of many diseases compels the discovery of many remedies.

In the Council of Ilerda, chapter 5, it is written concerning those who serve at the altar if they suddenly fall through the frailty of the flesh:

> Those who serve at the altar, if they suddenly fall through the lamentable frailty of the flesh, and, with the Lord looking upon them, do worthy penance, so that, having mortified the body, they offer to God the sacrifice of a contrite heart, shall remain under the authority of the bishop. He may either not suspend those who are genuinely afflicted for long, or separate the negligent from the body of the Church for a longer period; provided, however, that if they retain their places in their offices, they may not thereafter be promoted to higher offices. But if, like dogs returning to their vomit, they fall back into the same behavior, they shall not only lose the dignity of their office, but shall also receive holy communion only at the end of life.

[Col. 0480D] Likewise, in the Council of Carthage, chapter 27, it is written that presbyters and deacons convicted of a more serious offense should by no means receive the laying on of hands as laymen. It was established instead:

> If at any time a presbyter or deacon is convicted of some more serious offense on account of which it is necessary to remove him from the ministry, hands are not to be imposed upon him either as upon a penitent or as upon a faithful layman; nor is it to be permitted that those who have been rebaptized be promoted to the clerical rank.

## CHAPTER XI. On presbyters who have taken wives or committed fornication

Likewise, concerning presbyters who have taken wives or committed fornication, it is written in the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 5:

> If a presbyter takes a wife, he shall be deposed from the order; but if he has committed fornication or adultery, he must be expelled still more severely and reduced to penance.

Likewise, from the decretals of Pope Innocent, chapter 26:

> Because it is worthy, chaste, and honorable, the Church must maintain this absolutely: that priests and Levites do not have intercourse with their wives, because they are occupied with the necessities of their daily ministry.
>
> For it is written: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy.” In former times, priests did not leave the temple of God during the year of their service, as we read concerning Zechariah; nor did they touch their own house at all. To them, certainly, the use of a wife had been permitted for the succession of offspring, because no one from another tribe and outside the seed of Aaron had been commanded to approach the priesthood.
>
> How much more, then, ought priests or Levites to preserve chastity from the day of their ordination, since their priesthood or ministry exists without succession? Nor does a day pass on which they are not occupied either with divine sacrifices or with the ministry of baptism.
>
> For if Paul, writing to the Corinthians, says: “Abstain from one another for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (1 Corinthians VII)—and he certainly commanded this to laypeople—how much more should priests, whose duty of praying and sacrificing is continual, always abstain from such intercourse?
>
> If someone has been defiled by carnal desire, with what shame will he perhaps presume to sacrifice, or with what conscience or merit does he believe that he will be heard, when it has been said: “All things are clean to the clean; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean”?

Likewise, from the decretals of Pope Leo, chapter 17, it is written:

> The law of continence is the same for ministers of the altar as for bishops and presbyters. When they were laymen or readers, they could lawfully marry and beget children; but when they reached the aforementioned ranks, what had been lawful for them began to be unlawful. Thus a carnal marriage is to become spiritual.
>
> They must not dismiss their wives, but, while having them, live as though they did not have them, so that the affection of marriage may remain intact while the practice of marital intercourse ceases.

Likewise, in the Council of Carthage, chapter 25, Bishop Aurelius said:

> We add this, dearest brothers. Moreover, since continence toward their own wives has been reported concerning certain clerics, even readers, it has been decided—as has also been confirmed by various councils—that subdeacons who handle the sacred mysteries, as well as deacons, presbyters, and bishops, according to the statutes of their predecessors, must abstain from their wives, so that they may be regarded as though they did not have them. If they do not do this, they shall be removed from ecclesiastical office. The other clerics, however, are not to be compelled to this except at a more mature age.

## CHAPTER XII. On those who violate their penance and transgress again

In the Council of Orléans, chapter 7, it is written concerning those who violate their penance:

> Those who, having forgotten the penance they received and the religious character of their profession, relapse into secular life are to be suspended from communion and separated from the banquets of all Catholics. If, after the prohibition, anyone presumes to eat with such a person, that person too shall be deprived of communion.

In the Council of Toledo, chapter 55:

> Whoever among the secular people, having received penance, has had his hair cut and has again become a layman through transgression shall, when apprehended by his bishop, be recalled to the penance from which he departed.
>
> But if some are incorrigible and do not return even after admonition, they shall afterward be condemned before the Church by anathema, just as those who were tonsured by their parents, or who, after losing their parents, voluntarily devoted themselves to religion and afterward assumed secular dress.
>
> Such people, when discovered by a priest, shall be recalled to religious observance after first performing penance. But if they cannot return, they shall be subjected to the sentence of anathema against apostates.
>
> The same rule shall also be observed concerning widows, consecrated virgins, and women doing penance who have put on the religious habit and afterward either changed their clothing or entered into marriage.

From the decretals of Pope Siricius, chapter 10:

> Concerning such people, your charity rightly believed that the Apostolic See should be consulted: those who, after performing penance, like dogs and swine returning to their former vomit and wallowing places, again sought the military belt, slippery pleasures, new marriages, and forbidden intercourse. Their professed incontinence was revealed by children born after their absolution.
>
> Concerning them, because they have no further recourse to penance, we have decided that they should be joined to the celebration of the sacred mysteries only by prayer within the Church, although they do not deserve to participate. They are to be separated from the banquet of the Lord’s table, so that, corrected at least by this severity, they may chastise their own errors within themselves and provide an example to others, so that they may be withdrawn from shameful desires.
>
> Nevertheless, because they fell through carnal frailty, we wish them to be aided by the grace of communion with the viaticum when they begin to depart to God. We judge that this rule should also be observed concerning women who, after penance, have bound themselves to such defilements.

Likewise, in the Council of Arles, chapter 11:

> Penitent women who, after their husband’s death, have presumed to marry another, or who have joined themselves to a stranger through a relationship that is suspect or forbidden, are to be kept away from the threshold of the Church together with that man. It has likewise been decided that this should be observed concerning a man in penance.

## CHAPTER XIII. That penance should be remitted to penitents on the Lord’s Supper

Likewise, from the decretals of Pope Innocent, chapter 7, it is written:

> As for penitents who have done penance either for graver offenses or for lesser ones, if no illness intervenes, the custom of the Roman Church shows that their penance should be remitted on the Thursday before Easter.
>
> In judging the seriousness of the sins, however, it is the priest’s responsibility to consider the penitent’s confession and the weeping and tears of the one who is correcting himself, and then to order the penance remitted when he sees that satisfaction has been sufficiently appropriate.
>
> But if someone falls ill and reaches the point of despair, his penance should be relaxed before Easter, so that he does not depart from this world without communion.

## CHAPTER XIV. That final penance is to be denied to no one

In the decretals of Pope Celestine, chapter 15, it is written that final penance is to be denied to no one:

> We have learned that penance is denied to the dying and that the wishes of those who desire assistance for their souls at the time of death are not granted. I confess that we shudder to find anyone guilty of such great impiety that he despairs of God’s mercy, as though he could not come to the aid of one who turns to him at any time, and free a person endangered beneath the burden of sins from the weight by which he desires to be released.
>
> What else, I ask, is this than to add death to one who is dying, and by cruelty to kill his soul so that it cannot be absolved, when God is fully prepared to help and, inviting the sinner to penance, promises him:
>
> “On whatever day he turns, his sins shall not be counted against him.”
>
> And again:
>
> “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but only that he should turn and live.”
>
> Whoever denies penance to a person at the time of death therefore takes salvation away from him. And he despairs of God’s clemency who does not believe that it can suffice, even in a moment, to assist the dying.
>
> The thief hanging at Christ’s right hand would have lost his reward if the penance of a single hour had not helped him. While he was in punishment, he repented, and through the confession of a single sentence he merited, by God’s promise, a dwelling in paradise.
>
> True conversion to God in those who are placed at the end of life must therefore be judged by the mind rather than by the amount of time. The prophet asserts this in such words: “When you turn and groan, you shall be saved.”
>
> Since the Lord is the examiner of the heart, penance is not to be denied at any time to one who asks for it, since the person asking binds himself to the Judge to whom all hidden things are known to be revealed.

## CHAPTER XV. That whoever asks pardon for illicit acts must also abstain from many licit acts and must not pursue the profits of commerce during the time of penance
In the decrees of Pope Leo, chapter 22, it is written [Col. 0483D] that one who seeks pardon for illicit acts ought also to abstain from many licit ones:

“Something else is to demand what is justly owed; something else is to despise what is one’s own out of love for perfection. But one who seeks pardon for illicit acts ought also to abstain from licit ones, as the Apostle says: ‘Everything is permitted, but not everything is beneficial.’ Therefore, if penitents have a case which perhaps they ought not neglect, it is better to seek ecclesiastical judgment than a secular court.”

Likewise, in the same decrees, chapter 23, it is written that no business activity is suitable for a penitent:

“The character of profit either excuses or condemns the person engaged in trade, for there is honest gain and there is shameful gain. Nevertheless, for a penitent it is more useful to suffer losses than to be bound by the dangers of commerce, because it is difficult for sin not to intervene in the dealings between buyer and seller.”

Isidore, in the book *On Offices*:

“Those who perform penance should grow their hair and beard, so as to demonstrate the abundance of their crimes, by which the sinner’s head is weighed down. For hair is understood as representing vices, as it is written: ‘Each person is bound by the hairs of his sins.’”

## CHAPTER XVI. That no one should return to military service after penance

Likewise, in the same decrees, chapter 24, it is written that no one should return to secular military service after penance:

“It is wholly contrary to ecclesiastical rules, after undertaking penance, to return to secular military service, since the Apostle says: ‘No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs.’ Therefore, whoever wishes to entangle himself in worldly military service is not free from the devil’s snares.”

## CHAPTER XVII. That certain penitents may resume their former marriages

In the Council of Toledo it is written that certain penitents may have their former marriages restored:

“It is the judgment of the ancient and most holy Father, Pope Leo, that if someone, situated in the age of youth and fearing the danger of death, has come to the remedy of penance—if he is married and perhaps incontinent—then, lest he afterward fall into adultery, he should return to his former marriage until, with the maturity of time, he can attain a state of continence. What we judge concerning women, we likewise decree concerning men—not indeed as a general and lawful precept, but as an indulgence granted by us because of human frailty—provided only that, if the person who is not bound by the laws of penance should depart this life before they come to continence by mutual agreement, the survivor may not again return to the embrace of the spouse. But if the person who does not accept the penitent’s blessing survives, let him or her marry if unable to remain continent and enjoy the companionship of another spouse. We clearly decree the same concerning both sexes, namely, that in all these matters the priest’s decision must be awaited, so that, after considering the age appropriate to the case, he may impose the rule of continence, absolution, or strictness.”

## CHAPTER XVIII. On perjury

Perjury is wholly prohibited in divine law, as the lawgiver says:

“You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain. For the Lord will not hold guiltless anyone who takes the name of his God in vain.”

Hence Truth itself says in the Gospel:

“Do not swear at all, neither by heaven nor by earth,” and so forth.

Accordingly, it is also written in a canon:

“Whoever knowingly commits perjury shall submit to seven years of penance and thereafter return to communion.”

Likewise Ecgberht, bishop of the English, defines the matter as follows:

“If someone swears an oath in a church, or on the Gospel, or on the relics of the saints, let him do penance for seven years; others assign eleven. If he swears by the hand of a bishop, presbyter, or deacon, or upon a consecrated cross, let him do penance for one year; others assign seven years. If upon an unconsecrated cross, let him do penance for one year, or seven months, as others judge. But whoever is deceived and swears in ignorance, and afterward comes to know the truth, let him do penance for one year or three Lents. If anyone is compelled by some necessity, let him do penance for three Lents; others assign three years, one of them on bread and water. Likewise, for perjury, let him do penance for three years. Whoever suspects that a perjurer is being led into an oath, yet nevertheless swears by consent, let him do penance for two years. But because in many places perjury is frequently committed by those who, through greed for earthly possessions, offer money for ecclesiastical offices in order to acquire an abundance of earthly goods for themselves, it is just that an appointed punishment be inflicted upon those who do this, for those deceived by this scandal. For the canons have established the following concerning such persons.”

## CHAPTER XIX. On bishops or presbyters who acquired an ecclesiastical rank and church by payment

In the Synod of Reims, chapter 21, it is written:

“Any presbyter who has acquired his rank by payment shall be deposed.”

From the Council of Orléans, chapter 10:

“No presbyter is to give gifts at the entrance to a church.”

In the Council of Tours, or Mainz, chapter 15, it is written:

“Any presbyter who has obtained a church by payment shall be deposed in every respect, since he is clearly acting contrary to the discipline of ecclesiastical rule. Likewise, the person who has expelled another presbyter lawfully ordained to a church by means of money and has claimed the church for himself in this way shall also be deposed. This widely spread vice must be corrected with the greatest diligence. It also seems necessary to forbid clergy and laity alike to presume to give any presbyter a church without the permission and consent of his bishop.”

## CHAPTER XX. On incestuous unions, and on the man who takes his goddaughter or mother as wife

Concerning incestuous unions, the Council of Agde, chapter 61, states:

“For incestuous marriages we reserve absolutely no pardon, unless they have healed the adultery through separation. We judge that incestuous persons are not to be considered married at all—indeed, it is fatal even to name them. If anyone violates carnally his brother’s widow, who had previously almost been his sister; if anyone takes his brother’s full sister as wife; if anyone marries his stepmother; if anyone joins himself to his female cousin—we prohibit this at the present time in such a way that we do not dissolve what was established before us. If anyone has intercourse with his uncle’s widow or daughter, or with his father’s daughter, or is defiled by intercourse with his stepdaughter—those whose illicit union is prohibited shall have the freedom to enter a better marriage.”

[Col. 0486A] Likewise, concerning the same matters, the Council of Orléans, chapter 14, states:

“Let no brother ascend the bed of his deceased brother; let no man dare join himself to his wife’s sister after losing his wife. If he does so, let him be struck by ecclesiastical discipline.”

Likewise, concerning the same matters, the Council of Ilerda, chapter 4:

“Those who defile themselves with incestuous pollution are to be permitted in church only as far as the Mass of the catechumens, for as long as they persist in that detestable and illicit intercourse of the flesh. With such persons, no Christian ought even to eat, as the Apostle commanded.”

Likewise, concerning these matters, the Council of Ancyra, chapter 23:

“A certain man had a fiancée, violated her sister, and made her pregnant; afterward he took the woman who had been betrothed to him as his wife. The woman who had been violated killed herself with a noose. All who were aware of such an act are to be reduced to ten years of penance, according to the established canons.”

In the decrees of Pope Siricius, chapter 4:

“We altogether prohibit anyone from taking another man’s fiancée as wife, because the blessing which the priest lays upon women about to marry is, among the faithful, like a kind of sacrilege if it is violated by any transgression. Betrothed girls, especially those who have been abducted, are to be rescued and restored to those to whom they had previously been betrothed, even if it is established that force was inflicted upon them by their abductors.”

Concerning women who have married two brothers, or men who have taken two sisters as wives, the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 2, states:

“If a woman marries two brothers, let her be cast out until death. Nevertheless, at the hour of death, out of mercy, if she promises that, once restored to health, she will dissolve the bonds of this union, let her obtain the fruit of penance. But if a man or woman dies in such a marriage, penance will be difficult for the one who remains alive.”

Likewise, concerning those joined to two sisters, the Council of Elvira, chapter 61, states:

“If anyone, after the death of his wife, takes her sister as wife, and she is a believer, let him abstain from communion for five years, unless necessity caused by illness should perhaps require that it be granted sooner.”

Likewise, concerning the woman who marries two brothers, it is written in the canons of Bishop Martin:

“If a woman takes two brothers, or if a man takes two sisters, let them be excluded from communion until death. At death, let communion be given them out of mercy. If they survive after receiving communion and recover from their illness, let them perform full penance for the appointed period. Whoever takes two sisters, or his brother’s daughter, in marriage cannot be a cleric.

“As for what you asked: whether the man who took his goddaughter—whom he received from the sacred baptismal font—or the man who had intercourse with his spiritual godmother, or the man whose baptized son was received from the font by the woman who later became his wife, may afterward remain in such a union: we judge this to be wholly illicit. For in the Council of Mainz, chapter 55, the following is written concerning such persons:

“‘Let no one receive his own son or daughter from the baptismal font; nor let him receive his goddaughter or his godmother as wife; nor the woman whose son or daughter he has taken for confirmation. Wherever this has occurred, let them be separated.’”

Likewise, in the Synod of Mainz, chapter 56:

“If anyone has taken a widow as wife and afterward has committed fornication with his stepdaughter, or has married two sisters; or if a woman has married two brothers, or a father and son: we command that such unions be anathematized and dissolved, and that they never again be joined in marriage, but that this be done under severe discipline.

“How detestable and abominable a crime it is for any Christian to join his goddaughter to himself for lust, Saint Pope Gregory testifies in his *Dialogues*. There he relates that a certain man violated his goddaughter and was granted three days for the satisfaction of doing penance. But that wretched man, hoping either that God would not know his sin or that it had mercifully been consigned to oblivion, neglected to do penance. Not long afterward he was seized by a pitiable death and expired, so that his tomb was consumed by fire. In this event the ineffable mercy of God appeared, for God wished to preserve the man for pardon if only he would not delay in converting.”

Likewise, in the Synod of Mainz, concerning incestuous marriages, it is written:

“If anyone has committed fornication with two sisters, or with his stepmother, or with his sister, or with his paternal aunt, or with his maternal aunt, or with the daughter of his paternal uncle, maternal uncle, paternal aunt, or maternal aunt, or with his niece, or with his godmother, or with his goddaughter whom he received from the baptismal font [Col. 0487C], or whom he held before the bishop for confirmation; or if any woman has committed fornication in a similar manner: let that person abstain from entering the house of God for one year, and during that same year let him use only bread, water, and salt, except on feast days and the chief festivals. Let him carry no weapons of war; let him give no kiss to anyone; let him receive the sacrifice only as viaticum.

“For the following six years let him enter the house of God, but let him not use meat, wine, or beer, except on the chief feast days. Concerning weapons, the kiss, and the sacrifice, let him act as stated above. Thereafter, for two years, whenever he eats meat, let him abstain from every drink capable of causing drunkenness. If he drinks such a beverage, he is not to eat meat, except on the chief feast days. From that time until his death, let him abstain from meat except on the aforementioned feast days. Let him duly observe three lawful fast days each week and three Lents each year. Concerning weapons, let him act as already stated, and let him never be joined in marriage.

“This same penance is to be imposed upon parricides, fratricides, and those who kill their blood-relatives—except that it does not apply to those who voluntarily kill an innocent person through fraud and greed, which is called *mordicum* in the German language.”

## CHAPTER XXI. On those who commit adultery

Adultery is condemned not only by the law but is also wholly forbidden by evangelical authority. Therefore the holy Fathers, instructed by heavenly teaching, established what must be observed in this matter. For in the Council of Ancyra, chapter 17, it is written:

“If anyone’s wife has committed adultery, or if he himself has committed adultery, after completing seven years of penance they ought to attain perfection according to their former degrees.”

Likewise, in the African Council, chapter 69, concerning those who abandon their wives, or women who abandon their husbands, in order to remain so, it is written:

“It was decided, according to evangelical and apostolic discipline, that neither a man dismissed by his wife nor a woman dismissed by her husband should join himself or herself to another, but should remain as they are, so that they may be reconciled to one another. If they despise this, let them be reduced to penance.”

Likewise, in the decrees of Pope Innocent, chapter 24, it is written that men should not associate with adulterous women:

“It was also desired that this be known: why do men who communicate not associate with adulterous women, when they appear to remain in fellowship with wives who have committed adultery with other men? Christian religion condemns adultery equally in both sexes, but women do not readily accuse their husbands of adultery. Hidden sins do not incur punishment. Men, however, are accustomed to report adulterous wives more freely to priests, and therefore, when their crime has been disclosed, communion is denied them. But when the offense of men remains hidden, no one is easily excluded on the basis of suspicions. He is indeed removed if his disgrace is uncovered. Therefore, although the cause is equal, when proof is lacking the application of punishment sometimes comes to a halt.”

Likewise, in chapter 27 of the decrees of the same pope, it is written:

“Your affection has also inquired about those who, after a divorce has intervened, have joined themselves to another marriage. It is clear that such persons are adulterers on both sides: while the man or woman is alive, although the marriage may appear to have been dissolved, they have hastened to another union. Nor can they fail to be regarded as adulterers, to such an extent that even those persons joined to them appear to have committed adultery, according to what we read in the Gospel: ‘Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.’ Therefore all such persons are to be excluded from communion. But concerning their parents and relatives, nothing of this kind can be decreed unless they are discovered to have encouraged the illicit union.”

Likewise, in the Council of Elvira, chapter 9, concerning women who have left adulterous husbands and married others, it is written:

“A believing woman who has left an adulterous husband and marries another is to be prohibited from marrying. If she does marry, she is not to receive communion before the man whom she left has departed this life, unless necessity caused by illness should compel it.”

## CHAPTER XXII. On those who commit fornication

Likewise, concerning fornicators, the Council of Elvira, chapter 30, states:

“Those who committed fornication in their youth are not to be ordained subdeacons, because afterward they might perhaps have been promoted by stealth to a higher rank. Those who have already been ordained are to be removed.”

Likewise, in the same council, chapter 31, concerning young men who commit fornication after baptism, it is written:

“Young men who have committed fornication after the faith of saving baptism are, once they have taken wives and completed lawful penance, to be admitted to communion.”

Likewise, in the same council, chapter 47, concerning one who, while having a wife, repeatedly commits fornication, it is written:

“If any believer who has a wife has committed fornication not once but repeatedly, he is to be challenged at the point of death. If he promises that he will cease, let communion be given him. If, after being restored, he commits fornication again, it was decided that he should no longer be allowed to trifle with communion of peace.”

## CHAPTER XXIII. On virgins consecrated to God, or secular virgins, if they commit fornication

Likewise, in the same council, chapter 13, concerning consecrated virgins, it is written:

“If virgins who have dedicated themselves to God commit fornication, if they have broken their pact of virginity and have served the same lust, not understanding what they have lost, it was decided that communion is not to be given them even at the end of life. But if, having once been persuaded, they have fallen through the weakness of the body, and during their lifetime such women perform penance so as to abstain from intercourse, it was decided that they ought to receive communion at the end of life.”

Likewise, in the same council, concerning secular virgins if they have committed fornication:
