“Virgins who have not preserved their virginity, if they marry and keep as husbands the very men who violated them, because they violated only the marriage bond, are to be reconciled after one year without penance. But if they have known other men, because they have committed fornication, it was decided that, after five years and after completing lawful penance, they may be admitted to communion.”

Likewise, in the Council of Ancyra, chapter 9, concerning those who have professed virginity, and those who live with men under the appearance of sisters, it is written:

“All who promise virginity but render their vow void are to be counted among those who have married twice. But we prohibit virgins who wish to live with men as sisters from that association.”

## CHAPTER XXIV. On those who join themselves to consecrated virgins, and on non-veiled virgins if they commit fornication

In the decrees of Pope Gelasius, chapter 20, concerning those who join themselves to consecrated virgins, it is written:

“We have learned that certain men rashly associate themselves with sacred virgins, mixing with a dedication consecrated to God incestuous unions and sacrilegious bonds. It is immediately just that such men be expelled from sacred communion and that they not be received at all except through public and approved penance. Nevertheless, if they have repented, viaticum must certainly not be denied them when they are departing from this world.”

Likewise, in the decrees of Pope Innocent, chapter 20, concerning non-veiled virgins if they deviate, it is written:

“But those who, although not yet covered by the sacred veil, have nevertheless always pretended to remain in the profession of virginity—even if they are not veiled—if they should happen to marry, must perform penance for some time, because their vow was held by the Lord. For if among human beings a contract made in good faith is ordinarily dissolved by no means, how much more must this promise, which she made with God, not be dissolved without punishment? For if the Apostle said that those who depart from their purpose of widowhood have condemnation because they have made their first faith void, how much more so virgins who have attempted to break faith with their earlier promise?”

## CHAPTER XXV. On women who fornicate with one another, and on women who mix their husbands’ semen with food or drink out of lust

Concerning women who fornicate with one another, the Council of Ancyra states:

“If a woman has fornicated with a woman, let her do penance for three years.”

Likewise:

“If a woman has joined herself to another in the manner of fornication, let her do penance for three years, like a fornicator. Likewise, let the woman who mixes her husband’s semen into food in order to receive more of his love do penance. A woman alone who has intercourse with herself is to do penance for three years.”

## CHAPTER XXVI. On those who have joined themselves to pagans or Jews

Likewise, concerning women who have joined themselves to pagans or Jews, the Council of Arles states:

“It was decided that believing girls who join themselves to pagans should be separated from communion for some time.”

Likewise, in the Council of Elvira, chapter 78, concerning married believers who commit fornication with a Jewish woman or a pagan woman, it is written:

“If any believer who has a wife commits fornication with a Jewish woman or a pagan woman, let him be excluded from communion. But if another man marries her, the Christian man may, after five years and after completing lawful penance, be joined to the Lord’s communion.”

## CHAPTER XXVII. On those who eat with Jews

Likewise, in the Council of Elvira, concerning Christians who eat with Jews, it is written:

“If any cleric or believer eats food with Jews, it was decided that he should be excluded from communion, so that he may be cleansed.”

Likewise, in the Council of Toledo, chapter 14, concerning Jews, it is written:

“At the suggestion of the council, our most glorious lord ordered this to be inserted into the canons: Jews are not to be permitted to have wives or concubines, nor to purchase Christian slaves for their own use; rather, the children born from such a union are to be taken for baptism. They must not perform public offices through which an opportunity might be provided for them to inflict punishment upon Christians. If any Christians have been defiled by them according to the rite of Judaism, or have even been circumcised, they are to return to freedom and to the Christian religion without the price being repaid.”

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On those who have both a wife and a concubine

Likewise, concerning those who have a wife and take a concubine, the Council of Toledo, chapter 17, states:

“If any believer who has a wife also has a concubine, let him not communicate. But whoever has no wife and has a concubine in place of a wife is not to be excluded from communion, provided that he is content with the union of one woman only—either a wife or a concubine, according to his preference. If he lives otherwise, let him be cast out until he ceases and returns to penance.”

## CHAPTER XXIX. On married persons who cannot consummate a marriage

As for what you asked concerning those joined in marriage who cannot consummate it—whether he may take another woman, or she another man—we answer not with authority but from the regulations of certain persons, in which it is written:

“If a man and woman have joined themselves in marriage, and afterward the woman says of the man that he cannot have intercourse with her [Note: [Col. 0491D] That is, have carnal intercourse.], if she can prove by proper evidence that this is true, let her take another man.”

## CHAPTER XXX. On women who give menstrual blood to others in food or drink, and on those who observe magic, divination, and augury

[Col. 0491B] You also asked about the following matters: the woman who mixed her menstrual blood into food or drink and gave it to her husband to eat; the woman who drank her husband’s semen in a beverage; and the woman who burned a human skull in a fire and gave it to her husband to avert illness—what penance should be imposed upon them? In our view, they should be punished by the same sentence as magicians and diviners, who are known to practice magic. For concerning those who practice magic, observe auguries, and attend to divination, we have the regulations of Theodore, archbishop of the English people, in which it is written:

“Whoever sacrifices to demons in small matters shall do penance for one year; whoever does so in great matters shall do penance for ten years. If a woman places her daughter upon a roof or in a furnace for the sake of curing a fever, let her do penance for seven years. Whoever causes grains to be burned where a person has died, for the health of the living and of the household, shall do penance for five years. If a woman performs incantations or divinations, let her do penance for one year, or three Lents, or forty days, according to the character of the offense.”

Concerning this, the Council of Ancyra, chapter 22, states:

“Those who observe auguries, auspices, dreams, or any kinds of divination according to pagan customs, or who bring such people into their homes to seek something by a magical art, or to purify their houses: if they are clergy, let them be cast out; if they are laypeople, let them do penance for five years.

“Whoever eats food sacrificed to idols and afterward confesses it—the priest must consider the person: at what age it occurred, how he was instructed, or in what manner it happened. Thus priestly authority is to be exercised with moderation toward the sick person, and in every penance confession is always to be maintained with every diligence, insofar as God deigns to help.”

## CHAPTER XXXI. On sorcerers and augurs

Likewise, in the Council of Agde, concerning sorcerers and those who observe augury, it is written:

“Lest it perhaps appear that the matter most threatening the faith of the catholic religion has been omitted: certain holy clerics or laypeople devote themselves to auguries and, under a fictitious name of religion, profess to possess the knowledge of divination through ‘the lots of the saints,’ or promise the future by examining any sort of writings. Whoever, whether cleric or layperson, is discovered either consulting or teaching such practices is to be regarded as an outsider by the Church.”

## CHAPTER XXXII. On those who fornicate unnaturally

Likewise, in the Council of Ancyra, chapter 15, concerning those who fornicate unnaturally—that is, with animals and with males—it is written:

“All who have committed such a crime before the age of twenty, after completing sixteen years of penance, may merit communion in prayers. Then, remaining in this communion for five years, they may at last receive the sacrament of the offering. Their life is to be examined, as to what it was like during the time of their penance, and accordingly they may obtain mercy. If they have clung to these crimes without restraint, let them spend a longer period performing penance.

“But all who, after the age of twenty, having wives, have fallen into this sin are to be received into communion in prayer after doing penance for twenty-five years. After remaining in it for five years, let them then receive the sacraments of the offering. But if, while having wives and being over fifty years old, they have committed such an offense, let them obtain the grace of communion at the end of life.”

Likewise, in the same council, chapter 16:

“The holy synod has commanded that those who have lived unnaturally and polluted others with the leprosy of a justly punishable crime should pray among those who are endangered by an unclean spirit.”

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the Eucharist

As for what you asked: whether, after the Eucharist has been consumed and expelled into the privy in the manner of other foods, it returns again to the original nature it possessed before it was consecrated on the altar.

[ [Note: [Col. 0491D] These words had been added in the margin by a scribe and were afterward inserted into the text either by Stewart or by someone else. Baluzius, a man of keen judgment, saw that they evidently contradicted Rabanus’s meaning; therefore he deleted them as far as the words “This question is superfluous.” Mabillon himself does not disagree, in the preface to the fourth century of the Benedictines. [Col. 0492D] B.] This statement is contrary to the opinions of Pope Clement and many other holy Fathers, who say that the Lord’s body is not expelled through the intestines into the privy together with ordinary foods.] This question is superfluous, since the Savior himself said in the Gospel:

“Everything that enters the mouth goes into the belly and is expelled into the privy” (John VI).

The sacrament [Note: [Col. 0492D] In Mabillon’s codex it reads: “Therefore, the sacrament.”] of the body and blood—that is [Note: [Col. 0492D] The words “that is” should be deleted: they are absent from the manuscript codex and invert the sense. MAB.]—is made from visible and bodily things; but it effects invisible sanctification [and] salvation of both body and soul. For what reason should what is digested in the stomach and expelled into the privy return again to its former state, when no one has ever asserted that this happens?

[Col. 0493A] For some people recently, not thinking correctly about the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, said:

“This same body [Note: [Col. 0493C] Codex of Antonius Faurius adds: “to be.”] and blood of the Lord, which was born from the Virgin Mary, in which the Lord himself suffered on the cross and rose from the tomb [Note: [Col. 0493C] There is a lacuna here in the manuscript copy of Canisius, but Baluzius filled it as follows: “to be the same as what is received from the altar.” [Col. 0494C] B.] [lacuna]”

To counter this error, as far as we could, we wrote to Abbot Egil and explained what ought truly to be believed concerning the body itself.

For the Lord himself says in the Gospel concerning his body and blood:

“I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life.”

Therefore, whoever does not eat that bread and drink that blood does not have this life. For people who are not in his body through faith can in some fashion possess that temporal life in this world without him; but they can never possess the eternal life promised to the saints.

But lest they should suppose that eternal life is promised in such a way through this food and drink—which they receive bodily but do not understand spiritually—that those who consume it would die neither in soul nor in body, he deigned to anticipate this thought. For after saying, “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life,” he immediately added:

“I will raise him up on the last day.”

Thus, in the meantime, he may have eternal life according to the spirit. On the last day, therefore, when the soul receives an incorruptible body, the soul and body of every saint, joined together as one, will possess eternal life, because head and members are united together, and thus the entire body of Christ will rejoice forever.

For my flesh “is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.” Since people desire food and drink so that they may not hunger or thirst, nothing truly provides this except that food and drink which makes those who receive it immortal and incorruptible—that is, the fellowship itself of the saints, where there will be peace and complete and perfect unity.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. [Note: [Col. 0494C] These words were added to the *Penitential*. B.] On the restoration of Bishop Ebo

I do not think it necessary to answer your question concerning the deposition and restoration of Ebo, bishop of Reims. Let those who carried this out see whether they did so justly or unjustly. When I, unworthy as I am, was placed in the episcopate of the Church of Mainz, I found him occupying an episcopal see at Hildesheim [Note: [Col. 0494C] Commonly Hildesheim.] in Saxony. I did not prevent him from carrying out the office of a bishop [Col. 0494B], because I had heard that he had been restored to his own position by the Apostolic See. Thus he remained in his office until the end of his life.

At the request of certain brothers, I recently sent a letter to Bishop Hincmar of Reims concerning this very matter, because I had heard that he had removed from priestly and clerical office those whom Ebo had consecrated after his restoration. Once I have received a suitable reply concerning this, I will make it known to you.

Thus, holy brother, in accordance with your request, I have taken care to answer your questions, insofar as the illness of my weakened body allowed and the convenience of the time permitted, according to the statutes of the holy canons and the judgments of the holy Fathers. But you, who are in good health and able to acquire and read a great many books, if you are able to find anything better and more suitable, do not hesitate to make it known to my small self in an epistolary writing.

[Col. 0493]

(Year 842) Twenty Books of the Commentaries on Ezekiel by Blessed Rabanus Maurus, Abbot of Fulda and Archbishop of Mainz.

[Col. 0493]

[Col. 0493D]

## Letter of Lothar Augustus to Rabanus

The illustrious and orthodox Lothar Augustus sends greetings to his own Rabanus Maurus.

Desiring to return the duties of mutual address in response to your greeting, I confess that, surrounded by the tumult of the crowd deafening my ears, I am held back by a horror of eloquence; yet the ardor of affection compels me, and by the privilege of its support I discharge what is owed. The charity of God, poured out into the heart, gives strength to the mind: for it suggests words to those who speak and grants them speech to utter who are unable to speak; it seeks everyone, invites all, and comes to those ages that do not know how to express their wishes.

Let our absence not constrain your longing. Although the bodily appearance [or perhaps: “the bodily sight is denied”] may be removed, the sight of the eyes does not narrow the breadth of the mind, if the mind is suddenly carried away in transference; rather, ranging abroad in immense expansiveness, it represents bodily absence through spiritual service: thus the affection of those who love purely makes its garments wander [sic]. And therefore we earnestly ask that your longing for our presence may frequently grow in your heart; and that you, not far removed from your sight, remaining always in your mind with devoted spirit, may unceasingly beseech the almighty Lord through your constant entreaty for our well-being, that, our grief restrained, we may rejoice together with the kingdom granted and with its blessings. For there is a kingdom far superior to the kingdom and rule of this age, where nothing adverse now occurs by which you may be afflicted with sorrow, but where you will exult in everlasting joy: this is true judgment, and the victory has been attained.

Others contribute small or great things out of the devotion of their faith; you have enclosed among your gifts for us the great book of the most noble leader Jesus son of Nun, who bore the figure of the true eternal king, Jesus Christ, so that we may follow Jesus armed, nor are we able to approach the attainment of victory in any other way than by cleaving to the Lord of hosts. It is indeed to be desired by us, and sought with every prayer, that under such a teacher we may endure the victorious campaign and complete it in his triumph. This, then, is the pattern of striving and of completing the course by which victory is obtained: it surpasses the form of earthly condition and, through the grace of the divine Spirit, is raised beyond the capacity of the body.

As your promise and exposition concerning other divine books have informed us through the bearer, we must seek the way by which they may be obtained; and let us seek it so that you do not delay satisfying our thirst: from the beginning of the book of Genesis, according to the literal sense, as far as the way of the tree of life, [Note: [Col. 0495C] The passage is corrupt.] join your resources, abilities, and intentions with those of Bede, so that what one desired may benefit both.

I ask that you expound the discourses of Jeremiah, in which the exposition of the great interpreter Jerome is not found, up to the place where the Lamentations are completed, together with the prayer, in a spiritual sense. As for Ezekiel, in the final vision, from the place at which the homilies of the most blessed Pope Gregory end to the conclusion of the prophecy, in which the meaning of our interpreter is examined according to the anagogical sense, may your generosity also disclose the ethical interpretation that we seek.

Weigh the benefits that you bestow, and examine on equal scales what is returned. If you receive a part, you will have a debtor for what remains; if you have ceased to be a creditor because you have received everything, how much better it is to consider both things together, so that one may fill the principal and the other multiply the interest—one in the present, the other in the future, where it cannot perish.

I say that we approve of your dwelling, if it is believed to be free from all ostentation. For rustic solitude among the mountains delights the inner person more than the royal beauty of cities; there no envy with its livid gaze falsely presents a tranquil heart with a cheerful appearance, nor does the cunning of mutual scheming construct, through the flatteries of affected speech, a shadowy semblance of affection. Whatever lies before the inward gaze delights the mind as it passes over it: now to raise the eyes from the depths, now to look down upon the valleys from the heights, and to reach toward higher things with a fiercer ardor, the more eagerly one has attained the heights.

Farewell in the Lord, and remember our requests, which were inserted in two letters, so that your diligence may grant what your kindness seeks. Because of the length of time, we earnestly implore that your memory not depart from the moderation of delay. I sent you two letters: one of them is only to be read, but this other is both to be read and to be placed at the beginning of your work.

[Col. 0495]

## Preface Written in Reply to the Aforementioned Prince

[Col. 0495C]

To the most serene and excellent emperor, Lothar Augustus, Rabanus, the least of the servants of God, wishes eternal salvation in Christ.

God is witness to how greatly the intention of my mind loves you: for I always desire that prosperity be present with you here and that good things may follow you into eternal life in the future. I pray continually that the mercy of almighty God may preserve you here for a long time, protected and unharmed from all enemies, and may make you participants, together with his saints, in eternal blessedness in the heavenly kingdom.

Therefore I also intend, according to your request and in accordance with the tenor of the letter that you sent me, to fulfill your wish and to direct especially to your presence whatever, by the gift of divine grace, I may be able to accomplish in the study of sacred literature or in treatises on divine Scripture. Thus you may possess it and, examining it together with your learned teachers, attribute whatever you find well and appropriately stated to the grace from which every good thing comes. But if anything there seems to you to have been set down otherwise than the rule of truth teaches, take care to inform me of this promptly, so that I may either correct my error or, if something has been expressed too obscurely, state it more clearly. In this way I shall obtain the fruit of my labor, if it proves useful to those who choose to use it.

As for what you added in your letter by setting down three requests together—namely, that I should explain the historical sense at the beginning of Genesis for you, supply from the treatise of the blessed Jerome on the prophet Jeremiah what remains after the sixth book of his exposition to the end, and address Ezekiel in the present work—I have done as much as I could. In composing an exposition of the book of Genesis, I explained its historical sense and also its allegorical sense at appropriate places, in accordance with the teaching of the holy Fathers, insofar as I considered sufficient. If anyone seeks more extensive treatment, let him read the books of the blessed Augustine, *On Genesis Literally*, and there he will find everything explained adequately.

As for the exposition of Jeremiah, insofar as I found it explained from the opinions of the holy Fathers, and insofar as I was able to infer from my own understanding, I have now sent it to you, contained in twenty books.

As for what you requested thirdly, concerning Ezekiel in the present work, you now have it completed insofar as the weakness of my body and the smallness of my intellect allow. I did this not as the successor of Pope Gregory and preacher of the people of God, supplementing what he began when teaching the people through the form of homilies but did not bring through to the end of the prophet; rather, I did it as an imitator and disciple, following the footsteps not only of that aforementioned pope but also of the other holy teachers.

I composed the work you requested not merely on the final part but on the whole prophet; and I set down the opinions of the individual teachers whose statements I read at the several passages, together with an indication of their names. Whatever divine grace additionally granted me to investigate, I inserted as well. And just as I completed the treatise on Jeremiah in twenty books, so I also brought this one to an end in the same number. I ask the reader not to find the length of this work tedious, but to read from it whatever he chooses if he disdains to read it all, knowing that I have done this not thoughtlessly but rather usefully.

For if, by pursuing brevity beyond measure, I had passed over untouched those things that the holy teachers judged necessary for readers, I might perhaps have harmed rather than helped those wishing to know the difficulty of the prophetic book. I have not set down here everything that I found expounded concerning it, but only what I judged necessary.

I omitted the Septuagint edition in most places where I considered it unnecessary to include it, observing in this matter the instruction of the blessed Jerome, who, concerning the dispute among interpreters, says the following in the first book of his treatise on the prophet Isaiah: “In the exposition of the holy Scriptures we ought to follow truth, not contention.” He also says in his treatise on Ezekiel: “I warn the reader not to be disturbed by the diversity of translations, but to be content in the present passage with the Hebrew truth concerning the measurements of the temple.”

Nor do I think that the following should be left unmentioned. From the reports of certain people I learned that some little know-it-alls had criticized me for indicating the names of the holy Fathers when making excerpts from their writings, or because they thought I relied more on the opinions of others [or perhaps: “was more supported by the opinions of others”] than I composed from my own. I can easily answer them on this point: what fault did I commit in judging the teachers of the Church worthy of veneration, and in inserting their opinions into my little works at appropriate places, just as they themselves had expressed them, together with an indication of their names?

It seemed to me much more salutary, while preserving humility, to rely upon the teaching of the holy Fathers than, through arrogance and the pursuit of personal praise, to put forward my own thoughts improperly, when the Lord himself, the supreme example and teacher of humility, appears in a certain way to have taught by his own example that this should be done. In the Gospel, arguing against the unbelieving Jews who reproached him, he says (John VII): “He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory; but he who seeks the glory of him who sent him is truthful, and there is no injustice in him.”

Accordingly, the most noble teachers, namely the blessed Jerome and Augustine, and likewise others, are found not only to confirm their writings by testimonies from the sacred books, but also to strengthen their own opinions by the sayings of earlier Fathers, so that their works would be more acceptable to readers insofar as they recognized them to be more certain and firmer through the testimony of reliable witnesses.

Let those who seek praise and desire to be seen by human beings dictate or write whatever they wish, and acquire for themselves from wherever they can admirers and flatterers. But for me, it is good to cling to God at all times of my life and to place my hope in the Lord God, so that I may proclaim all his praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion (Psalm LXXII)—namely, in those gates of which it is written: “Blessed are those who walk in the paths of life and enter the city through the gates” (Revelation XXII). Thus may they reach those gates of the heavenly Jerusalem of which the Psalmist says: “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion, for he has strengthened the bars of your gates; he has blessed your children within you” (Psalm CXLVII).

This will occur when the bridegroom has entered, as we read in the Gospel concerning the virgins: “Those who were ready entered with him into the wedding feast, and the door was closed” (Matthew XXV)—closed, that is, not as a punishment of imprisonment, but unto everlasting blessedness, because no one will thereafter go out from it, nor will anyone new enter afterward.

May almighty God deign to bring your life, long and long preserved in safety, to completion in eternal blessedness!

[Col. 0497C]

# Here Begin the Commentaries on Ezekiel

## Book One

[Col. 0497]

## Chapter One

The vision of the four living creatures; the vision of the wheels; the vision of God’s throne and of the image of God above the throne.

“And it came to pass in the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, on the fifth day of the month.” (Gregory.) It is the practice of prophetic speech first to describe the person, the time, and the place, and afterward to begin speaking the mysteries of prophecy, so that, in order to display the truth more solidly, it may first fix the root of the historical account and then bring forth the fruits of the Spirit through signs and allegories.

Thus Ezekiel indicates the time of his life, saying: “And it came to pass in the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, on the fifth day of the month.” He adds an indication of the place: “When I was among the captives beside the river Chebar, the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of the Lord.” He also indicates the time of the captivity, adding:

“On the fifth day of the month—it was the fifth year of the captivity of Jehoiachin.” And, in order to identify the person more fully, he also relates his lineage, when it follows: “And the word of the Lord came to Ezekiel the son of Buzi, the priest.”

But the first question that arises for us is why he who had said nothing previously began in this way, saying: “And it came to pass in the thirtieth year.” For “and” is a connective word, and we know that what follows is not connected unless there is a preceding statement. Why, then, does one who had said nothing say “and it came to pass,” when there is no preceding speech to which what he begins may be attached?

In this matter we must observe that just as we perceive bodily things, so the prophets’ minds perceive spiritual things; and things that appear absent to our ignorance are present to them. Thus it happens that, in the minds of the prophets, inner things are so joined to outward things that they see both together, and in them there occurs simultaneously, within, the word they hear and, without, what they speak.

The reason is therefore clear why he who had said nothing began by saying, “And it came to pass in the thirtieth year”: he joined the word that he uttered outwardly to the word that he had heard inwardly.

(Jerome.) The thirtieth year does not mean, as most think, the prophet’s age, nor the year of the jubilee, which is the year of remission. Rather, it extends from the eighteenth year of Josiah, king of Judah, when the book of Deuteronomy was found in the temple of God, to the fifth year of the captivity of Jehoiachin, also called Jeconiah, who was led into Babylon with his mother, with Daniel, the three boys, and Ezekiel. This was the first captivity of Judah, when the wrath of God was poured out upon Jerusalem.

According to the anagogical sense, however, the Lord and Savior is prefigured, who, being thirty years old, came to baptism; this is the perfect age in a human being. Therefore, in the book of Numbers, according to the Hebrews, the priests begin to minister in the temple not, as the Septuagint has it, from the twenty-fifth year of age, but from the thirtieth. Joseph also preceded this as a sign, when in Egypt he distributed grain to the people suffering from famine; and John the Baptist came to the streams of the Jordan and preached the baptism of repentance.

Since the sentence is left incomplete, when it says “in the fourth,” the word “month” is understood; for immediately afterward it says, “on the fifth day of the month.” To make this clearer, the Septuagint added above: “When I was among the captives beside the river Chebar, the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God; on the fifth day of the month—it was the fifth year of the captivity of Jehoiachin.”

(Jerome.) David prophesies in the Spirit that the captive people sat beside the rivers of Babylon: “By the rivers of Babylon,” he says, “there we sat and wept” (Psalm CXXXVII). Chebar is either the name of a river or, according to its interpretation, which means “heavy,” signifies the Tigris and the Euphrates, and all the great and very considerable rivers that are said to exist in the land of the Chaldeans.

Understand the opened heavens not as a division in the firmament, but as the result of the believer’s faith, because heavenly mysteries were opened to him. Thus we also read of the Savior’s baptism, when the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove, that the heavens were opened. Once they have been opened, the visions of God are revealed—not one vision but many, as the Lord says through the prophet: “I multiply visions, and through the hands of the prophets I have been represented” (Hosea XII).

These are the visions woven together throughout Ezekiel’s entire prophecy. More significantly, according to the Hebrews and the other interpreters, Jehoiachin’s departure is called a “transmigration,” not a “captivity,” as the Septuagint translated it. For he was not captured after the city had been conquered; rather, he surrendered himself voluntarily and was led into Babylon. Therefore, let the first transmigration be called that of Jehoiachin, that is, Jeconiah; but let Zedekiah’s be called the second or final captivity.

(Gregory.) The Hebrew words themselves, however, are of great value to us in interpreting the mystery. For Chebar means “weight” or “heaviness”; Ezekiel means “strength of God”; Buzi means “despised” or “contempt”; and Chaldeans means “captivating,” or “as demons.”

Ezekiel therefore comes beside the river Chebar because the strength of God, through the mystery of his incarnation, deigned to draw near to the human race, which bears the burdens of its sins and from its origin flows daily toward death, as the Psalmist says of it: “He shall be like a tree planted beside the flowing waters” (Psalm I). It is planted beside the flowing waters because he was incarnate beside the falls of peoples who are flowing away. The strength of God therefore arises from contempt or disdain, because our Redeemer deigned to assume humanity from a lost and despised people.

He therefore comes into the land of the Chaldeans. As we have said, Chaldeans are interpreted as “captivating” or “as demons.” The wicked, who themselves perpetrate iniquities and by persuasion draw others into iniquity, are truly “captivating”; and they are rightly also interpreted as “demons,” because those who persuade and drag others into iniquity receive within themselves the ministry of demons for iniquity, although they are not demons by nature.

The strength of God therefore comes into the land of the Chaldeans because the only-begotten Son of the Father appeared among those who had themselves lapsed into sin and, by captivating them, had dragged others into sins.

But let the discourse of the exposition now return to the person of the prophet: “And the hand of the Lord was there upon him.”

(Jerome.) In order that we may behold the visions of God and understand them, the hand and strength of God are necessary upon us. By that hand and arm the people of Israel were led out of Egypt. The magicians also understood a part of this strength when they said: “This is the finger of God” (Exodus VIII). And the Savior says in the Gospel: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God”; in another Gospel it is written instead: “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God” (Luke XI).

“And I saw, and behold, a whirlwind was coming from the north, and a great cloud, with fire enveloping it, and brightness around it.”

(Gregory.) We must consider what order of speech is present in the prophet’s words. Earlier, having spoken of himself, he had said: “The heavens were opened, and I saw visions of the Lord.” Later he adds, as though he were speaking of someone else: “And the hand of the Lord was there upon him.” Then, as though returning to himself, he says: “And I saw, and behold, a whirlwind was coming from the north.”

What does this mean—that Ezekiel now speaks, and now speaks about Ezekiel? If he spoke about himself throughout, there would be no question; if he spoke throughout as though about another, there would likewise be no question. What, then, does it mean that prophetic speech is so varied that at one moment the prophet speaks about himself, while at another he appears to speak about himself as though someone else were speaking?

We must know that those who are filled with the spirit of prophecy indicate by this fact—that sometimes they speak openly about themselves and sometimes utter words about themselves as though about others—that it is not the prophet but the Holy Spirit who speaks through the prophet. When the speech occurs through them, they speak about themselves; but when they speak under the breath of the Holy Spirit, that same Holy Spirit speaks through them about them, as the Truth bears witness when it says: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.”

Moses also says: “Now Moses was the meekest man above all the people who dwelt on the earth.” By saying not “I was” but “Moses was,” he plainly indicates that the one who was speaking through him about him was another. John likewise says: “I saw that disciple whom Jesus loved” (John, the final chapter). And Paul, to show that it was not he who was speaking, said: “Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (II Corinthians XIII).

Since, therefore, in prophetic speech one is the master and another the servant, when the prophet speaks about himself, the person of the servant is present; but when the Spirit speaks through the prophet, the majesty of the master is revealed concerning the prophet. Thus it is rightly said, as though of another: “The hand of the Lord was there upon him.” And he immediately adds concerning himself:

“And I saw, and behold, a whirlwind was coming from the north.”

(Jerome.) For the consolation of the people undergoing transmigration and for the revelation of God’s judgment, the prophet sees a very great vision. In interpreting it, all the synagogues of the Jews are silent, saying that it is beyond human understanding, and attempting something concerning this vision and concerning the building of the temple, which is written at the end of this prophecy.

But we, comparing spiritual things with spiritual according to the measure of our little understanding, can conjecture rather than explain what we have received from our predecessors. We ask pardon from benevolent and faithful readers, that they may favor rather than be angry with an audacity—or rather, with a faith—that does not know its measure.

First, it must be known that the spirit which carries away or lifts up, which we have interpreted, following Aquila, as “a whirlwind,” and which, following Symmachus and Theodotion, others render as “a breath” or “spirit of storm,” is understood by some in a good sense and by others in an adverse one. For the Hebrew word *ruaḥ*, according to the context, may mean spirit, soul, or wind.

“Spirit,” as in: “Send forth your spirit, and they shall be created” (Psalm CIII).

“Soul,” as in: “His spirit shall go forth, and he shall return to his earth” (Psalm CXLV).

“Wind,” as in: “With a vehement wind breaking the ships of Tarshish” (Psalm XLVII).

And elsewhere: “Fire, sulfur, and the spirit of storms are the portion of their cup” (Psalm X).

Those who read “wind” and “breath of storm” understand this to mean that the wrath and fury of God are coming from Babylon—that is, from Nebuchadnezzar—and that Jerusalem is to be captured six years after this vision. For the vision is seen in the fifth year of the transmigration of King Jehoiachin, which was also the fifth year of Zedekiah’s reign in Jerusalem; and we read that six years afterward, that is, in the eleventh year of his reign, he was led into Babylon after the city had been captured.

To those who were dwelling beside the river Chebar and had voluntarily surrendered themselves to the king, it is therefore revealed that they had done well to obey God’s judgment. For in a short time both the province of Judea and the city of Jerusalem would be captured.

Since the cloud is described as great, let us understand that it carries showers of overthrow and rains of destruction over Judea. The enveloping fire indicates the punishments and evils of captivity that were to come. “And brightness around it” signifies the manifest judgments of God.

Those who understand the passage in the contrary, that is, the good sense, interpret the spirit that carries away or lifts up as the Holy Spirit, who takes away vices and sins from human beings, or raises those who lie prostrate to sublime things, causing them to withdraw from the north wind, the coldest wind, from which evils blaze over the whole earth. In Jeremiah also that terrible pot is kindled from the face of the north.

They refer the great cloud to the person of Christ, who came into Egypt, this world, upon a light cloud. It is called great in comparison with the lesser clouds, namely, all the prophets and apostles and saints, of whom it is written: “And your truth reaches to the clouds” (Psalm XXXV); and, “I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon Jerusalem” (Isaiah V); and elsewhere, “Clouds are the dust of his feet” (Nahum I); and again, “Cloud and darkness are around him” (Psalm XCVI).

They also understand the flashing fire and brightness around it according to what is written: “God is a consuming fire” (Deuteronomy IV). The Savior says that he came to send this fire upon the earth (Luke XII), and desires it to burn in us and in all believers. Although it brings terror and punishments upon sinners, it nevertheless shines brightly and is full of light and radiance; therefore it purifies us by fire, so that it may grant more joyful things to those who have been made pure and cleansed.

(Gregory.) The sending of a malign spirit is rightly called “a whirlwind.” A whirlwind, by shaking, overthrows the building that it strikes. Every temptation of the ancient enemy that arises in the mind is a whirlwind, because by shaking a person through desires it tears him away from the stability of his uprightness.

But, leaving aside what the cunning enemy will bring upon the human race at the end, let us turn the words to Judea alone, from which the prophet came and whose destruction he sees in prophecy. After the Lord had become incarnate, Judea endured the whirlwind from the north all the more grievously because, shaken from its uprightness and falling, it remained in the coldness of unbelief through the torpor of its mind. The whirlwind therefore comes from the north because the malign spirit shook the life of the Jewish people through temptation.

And rightly it is added: “And a great cloud.” For the more anyone has blazed with unbelief, the more he has deserved to be blinded by the darkness of his ignorance. They saw and denied the Redeemer of the human race, whom they had awaited while understanding him in the Law and the Prophets. Thus it happened that the mind of that people was covered by a great cloud of its ignorance, lest, seeking him later, they should recognize the one whom previously they had been able both to announce and to refuse to love.

The name of fire, when used figuratively, sometimes designates the Holy Spirit and sometimes the wickedness of the mind. Concerning the good fire it is written: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” (Luke XII). Fire is cast upon the earth when an earthly mind, inflamed by the ardor of the Holy Spirit, is burned away from its carnal desires.

Concerning the evil fire it is said: “And now fire will consume the adversaries,” because a wicked heart wastes away through its own malice. Just as the fire of love raises the mind, so the fire of malice envelops it: the Holy Spirit elevates the heart that he fills, while the ardor of malice always bends it toward lower things.

Judea, therefore, blinded by the cloud of its ignorance, because it soon burst forth into the wickedness of persecution, was enveloped in its own fire. Through the very cruelty by which it burned, it entangled itself in the bondage of wickedness. Thus the cloud is followed by “fire enveloping it,” because the cruelty of persecution followed the blindness of their mind: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Corinthians II).

But this fire blazed in one place and shone in another. For it follows: “And brightness around it.” While persecution was being carried on in Judea, the holy preaching of the apostles was scattered throughout the whole world, as they themselves say: “The word of God had to be spoken to you, but since you judged yourselves unworthy, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles” (Acts XIII).

Because almighty God’s light was scattered among the Gentiles through the cruelty of the malice that burned Judea, and because the holy apostles were dispersed in various directions, we who were placed around Judea in darkness see the brightness of the true light through the gift of heavenly grace. Hence it is written: “To those sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death, light has arisen” (Isaiah IX).

This fire of malice, which burned from the hearts of the Jews in persecution, exercised itself first upon the very author and Redeemer of the human race, before it afflicted the holy apostles with its fury. Hence it is also added: “And from its midst there was something resembling the appearance of amber, that is, from the midst of the fire.”

(Jerome.) It must therefore be understood that in the midst of fire and the torments of God there is the likeness of amber, which is more precious than gold and silver, so that after the judgment and torments—which seem grievous and harsh to those undergoing them—the more precious brilliance of amber may appear, while all things are governed by God’s providence, and what is thought to be punishment is medicine.

(Gregory.) What is designated by the appearance of amber except Jesus Christ, the mediator between God and human beings? Amber is made from gold and silver. When gold and silver are mixed in amber, the silver increases in brightness, while the gold grows pale from its own brilliance; the one advances toward brightness, while the other is moderated in its brightness.

Since, therefore, in the only-begotten Son of God our nature has been united to the nature of divinity, in this union humanity grew in the glory of majesty, while divinity moderated the power of its own brilliance before human eyes. Insofar as the human nature was made brighter, silver grew as though through gold. And because divinity was moderated from its brilliance for our sight, gold grew pale for us as though through silver.

That immutable nature, remaining in itself while renewing all things, would have burned us with its brilliance rather than renewed us if it had wished to appear to us just as it is. But God tempered the brightness of his greatness for our eyes, so that, while his brilliance was moderated for us, our weakness might also shine through its likeness in his light and, through the grace received, so to speak, might change the color of its condition.

Thus, in the fire, “God became human” as amber, in the persecution. If anyone wishes to understand what we have said concerning the Lord’s first coming also of his second coming, he should be followed with ready agreement. For the spirit of prophecy often beholds many things at once in what it says.

The whirlwind comes from the north because the cause of sins requires that the upheaval of strict judgment disturb all the elements together. The terror of the final disturbance is said to come from the place where it is generated. Since the judgment of the final disturbance is carried out to strike the cold minds of sinners, the whirlwind is rightly said to come from the north.

This upheaval is appropriately called a whirlwind, because on that day the hearts of all who are then found in mortal flesh will be shaken by immense fear. When what is written begins to be fulfilled—“The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of heaven will be shaken” (Matthew XXIV)—what human mind will not fear the sentence of the eternal Judge?

Then all sins return together before the eyes. Then everything that was done with love is recalled with fear. Then the darkness of miserable thought arises from the punishment of imminent condemnation. Hence it is added: “And a great cloud.” For then, from the memory of sins, the darkness of blindness depresses the mind’s understanding, when the wicked are not permitted to behold the only-begotten Son of God in the form of his divinity. “For they will see him whom they pierced” (John XIX); and, “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God.”

There it is also openly added: “And fire enveloping it.” For that fire of judgment, which burns heaven, air, and earth, does not permit sinners, already lifted up in their pride, to rise again; rather, it envelops them and undoubtedly crushes them in the condemnation of their punishment.

“And brightness around it.” For “as lightning goes out from the east and appears even to the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (Matthew XXIV). Then no one will be permitted to hide safely from judgment in his mind, because he will be penetrated by the very brightness of the Judge. Concerning him it is immediately added:

“And from its midst there was something resembling the appearance of amber,” that is, from the midst of the fire. Our Redeemer, who presides over angels, archangels, and all the powers, remained one in both natures: God in the Father, and, for our redemption, he became mortal among human beings. He will then be seen in his terror, and the fire of judgment will serve him in the vengeance inflicted upon the wicked.

For this is written: “The day of the Lord will declare it, because it will be revealed in fire” (I Corinthians III). Hence the Psalmist says: “God will come openly, our God, and he will not be silent. Fire will burn before him, and around him a mighty storm” (Psalm XLIX). The apostle Peter says: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief, on which the heavens will pass away with great force, while the elements will be dissolved by the heat of fire” (II Peter III).

[Col. 0505B]

“And in the midst of it was the likeness of four living creatures. And this was their appearance: the likeness of a human being was in them.”

(Jerome.) “In the midst of it”—the word “amber” is understood, but it is better to understand this as the fire that is light for believers and punishment for unbelievers. In the midst of this fire was the likeness of four living creatures. It was a likeness, not their nature; and the four living creatures, later said to be fourfold in form, had one likeness—that of a human being—so that all things in the world might be shown to be rational: “Let us make the human being in our image and likeness” (Genesis I).

The image and likeness of God is not the form of a body but of the mind, fashioned according to the likeness of the true image of Christ, who is the image of the invisible God.

These rational natures are found in four regions: either because of the four quarters of the world by which the globe is enclosed, or because of the four regions of the celestial, terrestrial, infernal, and supercelestial realms. The apostle Paul also speaks of these: “So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Philippians II).

Paul’s testimony concerns three of them. Let us see the fourth: “Praise God, you heavens of heavens, and let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord” (Psalm CXLVIII). Again, the Apostle speaks of celestial things and of other things that are supercelestial.

Because all the saints who have perfectly abandoned the world will then come as judges on the day of judgment, it is appropriately added immediately:

“**And in the midst of it was the likeness of four living creatures.**” (Gregory.) For what are signified by the four living creatures except the four Evangelists? Nor is it without reason that through the Evangelists the number of all perfected things is expressed. For all who are now perfected in the Church have learned the uprightness of their perfection through their Gospel. “In the midst of it was the likeness of four living creatures”: for those who will then be united to his body, joined to his majesty, and seen to have become judges together with him are those who now follow perfect works according to the commandments of the Gospel. Hence it is said to the holy apostles themselves: “You who have followed me in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX). Hence Isaiah says: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people” (Isa. III). Hence Solomon speaks of the Church, saying: “Her husband is noble at the gates, when he sits with the senators of the land” (Prov. XXXI).

Who is described here as the man except him of whom it is written: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and found in appearance as a man” (Phil. II)? These living creatures, therefore, so that they may be able to rise to the power of holiness, strive toward the likeness of this man. For they would not be holy if they did not possess the likeness of this man. Whatever there is in them of the inward parts of compassion, whatever of gentleness of spirit, whatever of zeal for righteousness, whatever of the keeping of humility, whatever of the fervor of charity, this they have drawn from the very fountain of mercy, from the very root of gentleness, from the very power of justice—that is, from the Mediator between God and human beings, the Lord God.

That he possesses the likeness of this man, the distinguished preacher shows by saying: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (I Cor. IV). He urges us to rise to his likeness when he says: “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man was from heaven, heavenly. Just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of him who descended from heaven” (I Cor. XV). For every saint is led toward the likeness of this man to the extent that he imitates the life of his Redeemer. For what else is it to disagree with his commandments and works than to withdraw far from his likeness?

Holy preachers mourn the lives of sinners. But of our very Head it is written that he “wept over Jerusalem.” They rejoice in the good deeds of their subjects and love those who act rightly. But of our Redeemer it is written that, when a certain young man said, “I have kept all these things from my youth” (Matt. XIX), he loved him more. Holy preachers bear the insults inflicted upon them and return no insult in return. But when our Redeemer was told, “You have a demon” (John VIII), he did not return the insult but answered gently, saying: “I do not have a demon.”

Holy preachers burn with zeal for righteousness; but the Redeemer of all, with a whip made of cords, drove from the temple those who were selling and buying, overturned the seats of those who sold doves, and poured out the money-changers’ copper coins. In everything they do courageously, they guard humility with complete attention; but through our Redeemer it is said: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. XI). Holy preachers love even their persecutors. But the author and Redeemer of all, placed in his Passion, intercedes for his persecutors, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” They lay down their own members in suffering for their brothers, but for the life of the elect the author of life surrendered himself even unto death.

Let it therefore be said of the holy living creatures that the likeness of a man is in them. For whatever is holy and marvelous in them is there by the form of likeness—that is, by the power of imitation. Our Redeemer is the Head of us all. And through Solomon it is said: “The eyes of the wise are in his head, but the fool walks in darkness” (Eccl. II). We have eyes in our head when we behold the life of our Redeemer in silent thought, when all our intention rises toward his imitation, lest, if the eye of the mind neglects to look upon the ways of light, it should immediately close and fall into the darkness of error.

The Prophet hastened to rise toward the likeness of this man when he said: “I will exercise myself in your commandments, and I will consider your ways” (Ps. CXVIII). For whoever silently considers the ways of the Lord in his mind and hastens to exercise himself in his commandments, what else does he reform in himself except the image of the new man? Because this is constantly taking place in the hearts of the saints, it is rightly now said of the living creatures: “The likeness of a man is in them.”

After this likeness, which is now maintained in conduct, comes the time when one reaches the likeness of glory. Hence John says: “Now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be; but we know that when he appears, we shall be like him” (I John III). He immediately adds how this can happen, saying: “Because we shall see him just as he is.” For God’s being consists in remaining eternal and unchangeable. Everything that changes ceases to be what it was and begins to be what it was not. But God’s being is never to be otherwise. Hence it is said to Moses: “I am who I am. And you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. III). James also says: “With whom there is no change or shadow of alteration” (James I).

Thus John says: “We shall be like him, because we shall see him just as he is.” For by beholding the essence of his nature, we are freed from our mutability and fixed in eternity. We shall be changed in the very one whom we shall see, because by seeing life we shall be without death; by seeing the immutable, we shall transcend our mutability; by seeing the incorruptible, we shall be held by no corruption.

At that time, however, the likeness of a man will be in our bodies. Hence Paul says (Phil. III): “Our citizenship is in heaven. From there also we await the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our lowliness, conforming it to the body of his glory.” The bodies of the elect, therefore, will then be conformed to the glory of the Lord’s body. Although by nature they do not possess equality with his glory, by grace they will possess the likeness of his configuration. Since, therefore, his likeness is now acquired by the elect in their conduct, and at the resurrection the likeness of eternity follows in the mind, because we shall see him just as he is, and since our bodies also will receive his likeness in their conformity to him, it is rightly said of the holy living creatures: “The likeness of a man is in them.”

“**Each had four faces, and each had four wings, and their feet were straight feet. And the sole of their feet was like the sole of a calf’s foot. And there were sparks like the appearance of glowing bronze. And human hands were under their wings on their four sides.**” (Jerome.) Concerning the things that the prophetic utterance describes, we shall attempt to say what they seem to mean to us, after briefly summarizing the opinions of various interpreters.

Some think that the four Gospels are designated by the names of these living creatures. We too followed this interpretation in the preface to our commentaries on Matthew. Matthew is understood to have described a man: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham.” They refer the lion to Mark: “The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, Son of God, as it is written in Isaiah the prophet: ‘The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the ways of the Lord; make his paths straight.’” The calf is referred to the Gospel of Luke, since it begins with the priesthood of Zechariah. The eagle is referred to the beginning of John, who, flying aloft, began: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word.”

What we thought about this we have said in the work mentioned above, and more fully in the Apocalypse of John the forms and names of these living creatures are referred to the four Evangelists. We shall try in its proper place to explain how the description of all the living creatures can be fitted to them.

Others, following the foolish wisdom of the philosophers, suppose that the two hemispheres are represented in the two cherubim of the Temple, and that we and the Antipodes are figured as human beings lying on our backs and falling. Many, following Plato, refer the rational, spirited, and appetitive parts of the soul to the man, lion, and calf. They place reason, knowledge, understanding, judgment, virtue, and wisdom in the citadel of the brain; fierceness, anger, and violence in the lion, which they locate in the gall; and lust, luxury, and desire for every pleasure in the liver—that is, in the calf, which clings to earthly activities.

They place a fourth power above and outside these three, which the Greeks call *syntērēsis* (συντήρησις), “preservation” or “conscience.” This spark of conscience, even in Cain the sinner after he was expelled from paradise, is not extinguished. Through it, when overcome by pleasures or fury, and sometimes deceived by the very appearance of reason, we recognize that we are sinning. They properly assign it to the eagle, because it does not mingle with the three but corrects the three when they go astray. In Scripture we sometimes read that it is called the spirit: “which intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings” (Rom. VIII). “For no one knows the things that belong to a human being except the spirit that is in him”; and Paul, writing to the Thessalonians, prays that this spirit may be preserved whole together with soul and body.

Yet we see that even this conscience, in accordance with what is written in Proverbs—“When the ungodly comes into the depths of sins, he despises” (Prov. XVIII)—is cast down in some people and abandons its proper place. They do not even possess shame or modesty in their offenses, and they deserve to hear: “You have the face of a prostitute; you do not know how to blush” (Jer. III).

God therefore governs this four-horse chariot in the manner of a charioteer, restrains it when it runs with disordered steps, makes it teachable, and compels it to obey his command. We too shall touch upon this discussion of the parts of the soul—that is, of the human being, whom these same philosophers call a “small world.”

There are some who simply think that, according to the view of Hippocrates, the four elements from which all things consist are shown in the four living creatures: earth, fire, air, and water. How these are mingled with one another, and, although each is distinct, appear joined together and touch one another, and how the four forms and figures are found in one living being, is not the subject of the present work.

They also think that the four wheels rising from earthly things to lofty heights and joined to the individual fourfold living creatures signify either the mixture of these same elements or the cycle of the four seasons, which is completed in three-month periods, and the revolving year, which received its name from continually turning and returning into itself. Of these things it has been beautifully said in a single verse:

> Spring, summer, autumn, winter, the month, and the year.

And when it is said, “There was a wheel within a wheel,” they think that one year within another is signified. Concerning this another poet says (Virgil):

> The year rolls on through its own recurring tracks.

They wish the likeness of the firmament, which is compared with crystal, to be understood as the heaven that we behold. Beneath it the four living creatures revolve and pass; and they assert that the throne of sapphire color and the man seated above it in human likeness describe the rule of the one governing all things and holding everything beneath his feet—that is, the omnipotence of God. Finally, they say: “This was the vision of the likeness of the glory of the Lord.”

Through these things, as through a kind of painting and image, providence is displayed. The fact that the feet of the living creatures are said to be straight, and the sole of the foot like that of a calf or rounded, signifies that earthly things fly upward toward heavenly things and, with all corners cut away, follow roundness, which is the most beautiful of all figures. The glowing sparks indicate that all things are full of light. “And human hands were under the wings”—under the wings of the man himself, as well as of the lion, calf, and eagle—so that reason may support all things and lift them from earthly humility to heavenly heights.

We can refer these things both to the Gospels and to all that we have set forth above. I remember hearing that the four disturbances of which Cicero discusses at great length in the *Tusculan Disputations*—joy, distress, desire, and fear—are signified by the four living creatures. Two of these concern the present and two the future. Virgil briefly describes them:

> Hence they fear and desire, grieve and rejoice.

These disturbances ought to be governed by reason and the power of God, and opposed—or rather placed over them—are the four virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance, so that the disturbances may be governed by their judgment. How these virtues correspond to the faces of the man, lion, calf, and eagle, they have entirely failed to explain. (Gregory.)

The four holy living creatures, which the spirit of prophecy foresees as future realities, are described in a subtle account when it says: “Each had four faces, and each had four wings.” What is expressed by the face except knowledge, and what by the wing except flight? By the face each person is recognized; by the wing, the bodies of birds are lifted on high.

The face therefore pertains to faith, and the wing to contemplation. Through faith we are known by almighty God, just as he says of his sheep: “I am the good shepherd, and I know my sheep, and my sheep know me.” Again he says: “I know whom I have chosen.”

Through contemplation we are lifted above ourselves and raised, as it were, into the air. Each therefore had four faces. For if you ask what Matthew thinks about the Lord’s incarnation, he certainly thinks what Mark, Luke, and John think. If you ask what John thinks, beyond doubt it is what Luke, Mark, and Matthew think. If you ask what Mark thinks, it is what Matthew, John, and Luke think. If you ask what Luke thinks, he thinks what John, Matthew, and Mark think.

Each therefore had four faces, because the knowledge of faith by which they are known by the Lord God is one in each and is simultaneously present in all four. For what you find in one, you recognize at the same time in all four.

“And each had four wings.” For all of them together and in harmony preach the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of almighty God, and, lifting the eyes of their minds toward his divinity, they fly with the wing of contemplation.

The faces of the Evangelists therefore pertain to the Lord’s humanity, and the wing to his divinity. For in him whom they see as corporeal, they direct their gaze as toward a face. But while they proclaim that by his divinity he is uncircumscribed and incorporeal, they are lifted, as it were, into the air on the wing of contemplation.

Since therefore the faith of his incarnation is one in all of them, and the contemplation of his divinity is equal in each, it is rightly now said: “Each had four faces, and each had four wings.” But what virtue would it be if preachers who possessed faith in and contemplation of the Lord did not also possess holy works?

It follows: “**And their feet were straight feet.**” What is signified by feet except the steps of actions? The feet of the four living creatures are therefore described as straight, because the works of the holy Evangelists and of all the perfected are not bent back toward the pursuit of wickedness.

Those have no straight feet who turn back toward the evils of the world that they had abandoned. Of them it is written: “The dog has returned to its own vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mud” (Prov. XXVI).

But so that the seriousness, strength, and discernment of life might be displayed in these same holy preachers, it is rightly added: “**And the sole of their feet was like the sole of a calf’s foot.**” That holy preachers are designated by the name of oxen the apostle Paul teaches when he expounds the testimony of the Law: “You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain” (I Cor. IX).

Thus in holy preachers the sole of the foot is that of a calf: mature in its gait, strong, and divided. For each preacher possesses reverence in maturity, strength in action, and the divided hoof in discernment. His preaching is not readily accepted if he appears frivolous in conduct. Nor will maturity be displayed if strength in action is absent against all adversities. Yet the merit of virtue admits that very strength of action only if it is not lacking in discernment.

For behold, we read Sacred Scripture: if we take everything literally, we lose the virtue of discernment; if we direct everything to spiritual allegory, we are likewise bound by the folly of indiscretion. Holy preachers read the sacred utterances and sometimes accept the letter according to history; at other times, through the meaning of the letter, they seek the spirit. Sometimes they imitate the good deeds of the fathers who preceded them, just as they find them according to the letter; at other times they understand spiritually certain things that are not to be imitated according to the historical account, and they advance toward spiritual improvement.

What else do holy preachers do in their work except split the hoof on the foot? Of them it is further stated openly: “**And there were sparks like the appearance of glowing bronze.**”

Bronze is a very resonant metal. And rightly the voices of preachers are compared with bronze, because “their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII). Bronze is rightly called glowing, because the life of preachers both sounds and burns: it burns with desire and sounds through speech. Glowing bronze is therefore preaching set ablaze.

But sparks come forth from glowing bronze, because from their exhortations fiery words proceed to the ears of their hearers. The words of preachers are rightly called sparks, because they set aflame those whom they touch in the heart.

It should also be considered that sparks are very subtle and thin. For when holy preachers speak about the heavenly homeland, they cannot disclose as much by their words as they are able to burn with desire. From their tongue, therefore, certain sparks come to us, because of the heavenly homeland scarcely anything slight is perceived in their voice, although what they love is not loved slightly.

For they neither suffice to see the heavenly glory as much as it is, nor are they able to speak as much as they see. Glowing bronze therefore casts out sparks when a preacher can scarcely speak, even faintly, of that by which he himself burns intensely.

Divine mercy brings it about that the mind of the hearer is inflamed by these very faint sparks. For there are some who, when they hear little, are filled with greater desire, and burn perfectly with the love of God from the very source where they have received scarcely the faintest sparks of words.

The word of preaching is seed in the heart of the hearer. And the good hearer later brings forth a great harvest of knowledge from the place where he had first received a small seed of speech.

“**And human hands,**” he says, “**were under their wings on their four sides.**”

In this passage the four sides may be understood as the four regions of the world: east, west, south, and north. For the preaching of the saints, with God as its author, has gone forth into every part of the world.

We may also understand by the four sides the four principal virtues from which the remaining virtues arise: prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance. We truly receive these virtues when we preserve their order. Prudence is first, fortitude second, justice third, and temperance fourth.

For what can prudence accomplish if fortitude is absent? To know what one cannot do is punishment rather than virtue. But whoever prudently understands what must be done and courageously does what he has understood is already, beyond doubt, just.

Yet temperance must follow his justice, because justice often falls into cruelty if it has no measure. Justice is therefore truly justice when it moderates itself with the bridle of temperance, so that even in the zeal with which one burns there may be temperance. Otherwise, if one burns too fiercely and does not know how to preserve moderation, one loses justice.

There are also two lives of holy preachers: the active and the contemplative. The active is prior in time to the contemplative, because one proceeds from good works to contemplation. But the contemplative is greater in merit than the active, because the former labors in the practice of present works, whereas the latter already tastes, through inward savor, the rest that is to come.

What, then, is signified by the hands except the active life, and what by the wings except the contemplative life? “Human hands under their wings” therefore means the power of work under the flight of contemplation.

Those two women in the Gospel aptly signify this: Martha and Mary. “Martha was busy with much serving, but Mary sat at the Lord’s feet and listened to his words” (Luke X). One was therefore intent upon work, the other upon contemplation. One served the active life through outward ministry; the other served the contemplative life through the suspension of her heart upon the word.

Although the active life is good, the contemplative is better. For when the former ends with mortal life, the latter grows more fully in immortal life. Hence it is said: “Mary has chosen the better part, which will not be taken away from her.”

Since therefore the active life is lesser in merit than the contemplative, it is rightly now said: “Human hands are under their wings.” For although through the active life we do something good, through the contemplative life we nevertheless fly toward heavenly desire.

Hence among Moses’ writings the active life is called servitude, while the contemplative life is called freedom. Although both lives are gifts of grace, as long as we live among our neighbors one is necessary for us, while the other is voluntary.

For who, knowing God, enters his kingdom without first acting well? Without the contemplative life, therefore, those can enter the heavenly homeland who do not neglect the good they are able to do. Without the active life, however, they cannot enter if they neglect to do the good they are able to do.

The active life is therefore necessary, while the contemplative is voluntary. The former is servitude; the latter is freedom. Hence it is said to Moses: “If you buy a Hebrew servant, he shall serve you for six years; in the seventh he shall go out free without payment. With whatever clothing he entered, with such clothing he shall go out” (Exod. XXI).

A Hebrew servant who has been bought is commanded to serve for six years, so that in the seventh he may go out free without payment. What is signified by the number six except the perfection of the active life? What by the number seven except the contemplative life?

He served for six years and goes out free in the seventh who passes through the active life that he has perfectly displayed to the freedom of the contemplative life. For he is a servant who has resolved through the active life to serve human beings, so that after the present age he may be able to reach true freedom. Of this Paul says: “The creation itself will be freed from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. VIII).

True freedom will then be in us when our adoption reaches the glory of the children of God. Now, therefore, not only is the active life in servitude, but even the contemplation by which we are snatched above ourselves does not yet possess perfect freedom of mind; it imitates it, because that inward rest is seen only in a mystery.

Nevertheless, however narrow the contemplative life may be in its present state, it is already much broader and higher than the active life. It passes into a kind of freedom of mind by giving no thought to temporal things but to eternal things.

Since therefore the contemplative life flies toward higher things and stands far above the active life, by a certain dignity—so to speak—of its security it is aptly said: “Human hands are under their wings.”

For unless God became human, he who lifted the minds of preachers toward heavenly things, those living creatures that appear would not fly. Nor is it without reason that human hands are said to be under the wings, since it is written of this same Redeemer (Heb. I): “Though he is the radiance of glory and the form of his substance, and carries all things by the word of life” [the supplied text reads *portansque emnia*, evidently an OCR error for *portansque omnia*, “carrying all things”].

His hand therefore carries our hearts. His hand lifts us in contemplation. For unless, as has been said, the almighty Word became human for the sake of human beings, human hearts would not fly toward the contemplation of the excellence of the Word. Human minds were therefore made lofty from the point at which the humble God appeared among human beings.

Let it therefore be said of the holy living creatures—let it be said: “Human hands are under their wings.”

“**And they had faces and wings on their four sides, and their wings were joined, each to the other. They did not turn back when they moved, but each walked straight before its face,**” and so forth. (Jerome.)

The Gospels are joined to one another and adhere mutually; flying throughout the whole world, they move here and there. Their flight has no end; they are never overcome or driven back, but always proceed farther. Hence Paul says: “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead” (Phil. III).

We can also say this about the powers of the soul, about the flight of times, and about the mixture of the elements: leaving behind what is past, they always hasten toward what lies before them. That times slip away and flee is shown in a brief verse:

> But meanwhile time flees, irretrievable time flees.

(Gregory.) The living creatures have faces and wings on their four sides because in all the regions of the world the preachers show whatever they think about the humanity and whatever they think about the divinity of our Redeemer.

While they preach everywhere that God has been incarnate, they display faces in the four parts of the world; and while they proclaim that he is one with the Father and the Holy Spirit, the wings of contemplation fly everywhere.
