Their wings are joined, each to the other, because all their virtue and all their wisdom, by which they surpass other human beings through the flight of their contemplation, are mutually joined in peace and unanimity. Hence it is written: “The wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable” (James III). Hence Truth says to these same preachers: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark IX).

The wing of one living creature is therefore joined to that of another because the virtue and wisdom of holy preachers are mutually united in the peace of charity and concord. One wing would be separated from another if, in flying upward toward wisdom, each refused to have peace with the other.

It follows: “**They did not turn back when they moved, but each walked straight before its face.**”

The winged creatures—that is, the holy preachers—do not turn back at all when they move, because they pass from earthly actions to spiritual things in such a way that they never turn back again toward what they have abandoned.

For them to move along a certain path is, as it were, always to proceed in mind toward better things. By contrast, it is said of the reprobate: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke IX).

To put one’s hand to the plow is to open the soil of one’s heart, as it were, with the plowshare of compunction in order to produce fruits. But the person who looks backward after plowing is one who, after beginning a good work, returns to the evils he had abandoned.

Since this does not happen to God’s elect, it is rightly now said through the Prophet: “They did not turn back when they moved.” He indicates why they did not turn back when he adds: “Each walked straight before its face.”

Eternal things are before us, temporal things behind us. As we move toward the former, we find them; as we withdraw from the latter, we leave them behind us, as though behind our backs. Hence that great winged creature said—the one who had flown to the secrets of the third heaven: “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the prize of the heavenly calling” (Phil. III).

He had stretched forward toward what lay ahead and forgotten what was behind, because he despised temporal things and sought only eternal things. The holy living creatures therefore walk straight before their faces, because they no longer look back with any desire upon what they have abandoned, and in the eternal things they desire they place the foot of good works beneath the eye of their contemplation.

Whoever has decided to walk straight before his face must weigh with great care that one looks backward in one way through action and in another through thought.

There are some who make great resolutions and, conscious of their sins, consider distributing much of what they possess to the needy, so that they may redeem their faults before the eyes of God through compassion. They begin to carry this out, but often, while they are doing it, fear of poverty shakes their minds. Fearing that they may become needy, they become stingy toward the needy and withdraw from the good work they had begun.

These people have turned back while moving, because they refused to walk straight before their faces.

There are others who indeed perform the good works they know, and while performing them deliberate upon better things; but, reconsidering those better things, they alter what they had resolved. They do the good works they had begun, but they succumb with regard to the better works they had planned.

Such people seem to stand upright in their actions before human judgments, but before the eyes of almighty God they have fallen in their deliberation. Consequently, their good work often pleases God less, because when the foot of the mind is placed unsteadily upon a better step of deliberation, the very inconstancy of their thought accuses it.

But since all who are perfect examine themselves with great subtlety of discernment, lest they ever slip toward worse things either in action or in thought, and continually consider how much they advance each day, it is rightly said of them: “They did not turn back when they moved, but each walked straight before its face.”

“The likeness of their faces was the face of a man; and the face of a lion on the right side of all four; but the face of an ox on the left side of all four; and the face of an eagle above all four.” (Jerome)

By “faces” he means the beginnings of the Gospels. Of these, the man and the lion—that is, Christ’s birth and the prophet’s voice thundering in the wilderness—occupy the right-hand side; but the calf, that is, the sacrifices and priesthood of the Jews, is on the left, having passed away and been transferred to the spiritual priesthood, of which it is said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109). This is so, at any rate, in such a way that all things adhere to one another and are regarded as one body.

But the eagle, which is above both the birth and the prophecy—which is fulfilled by the Lord’s coming—and above the priesthood that has passed away, is outside all these things. It speaks of the spiritual birth: how the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father. Of this it is most rightly said: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isaiah 53).

These are, as we have already said, the four living creatures according to the Apocalypse, full of eyes before and behind: one living creature like a lion, the second like a calf, the third having the face of a man, and the fourth like a flying eagle (Revelation 4). There also they are said, in the manner of the Seraphim, to have six wings: with two covering their faces, with two covering their feet, and with two flying; and they do not cease day or night, saying: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God almighty, who was and who is and who is to come.” (Gregory)

But since all the elect are members of our Redeemer, while our Redeemer himself is the head of all the elect, because his members have been represented in these figures, there is no objection if he himself is also signified in all these things. For he, the only-begotten Son of God, truly became man; in the sacrifice of our redemption he graciously consented to die as a calf; by the power of his strength he rose as a lion.

The lion is also said to sleep with open eyes, because in that death in which our Redeemer was able to sleep according to his humanity, he remained immortal and watchful according to his divinity. After his resurrection, ascending into heaven, he was raised on high as an eagle. Thus he is all these things together: by being born he became man, by dying a calf, by rising a lion, and by ascending into heaven an eagle.

But since we have already said above that by these animals the four Evangelists, and under their appearance all the perfected together, are signified, it remains for us to show how each of the elect is expressed by these visions of the animals. Every elect person who is perfect in the way of the Lord is simultaneously man, calf, lion, and eagle.

Man is a rational animal. The calf, however, is customarily slaughtered in sacrifice; “but the lion, strongest of beasts, will fear no encounter” (Proverbs 30). The eagle flies up to lofty places and gazes upon the sun’s rays with unblinking eyes.

Therefore everyone who is perfect in reason is a man; and when he mortifies himself with respect to the pleasure of this world, he is a calf. Since, however, through that voluntary mortification he possesses the strength of security against every adversity, and since it is written, “But the righteous is confident as a lion and will be without fear” (Proverbs 28), he is a lion. But whoever contemplates loftily the things that are heavenly and eternal is an eagle.

Thus, just as [variant: *quoniam*, “since”] every righteous person becomes a man through reason, a calf through the sacrifice of his mortification, a lion through the strength of his security, and an eagle through contemplation, so each perfect person may rightly be signified by these holy animals. We say this for the purpose of demonstrating that what has been said about the four animals also pertains to each of the perfect.

But a great question arises for us concerning those same Evangelists and holy preachers: why is the lion and the man said to be on the right side of all four, while the calf is on the left side of all four? For it is not without cause for wonder why those two are said to be on the right and this one on the left. And again it must be asked why the eagle is remembered as being not on the right or the left, but above all four.

We have therefore proposed two questions, which it is fitting for the Lord to resolve as he opens the meaning. The man and the lion, then, are said to be on the right, but the calf on the left. For we have joyful things on the right and sorrowful things on the left. Hence we also call that “left” which we judge to be adverse.

As we have said, the incarnation is signified by the man, the passion by the calf, and the resurrection of our Author by the lion. All the elect rejoiced in the incarnation of the only-begotten Son, by which we were redeemed. But at his death the first of the elect, the holy Apostles, were saddened; then they rejoiced again at his resurrection.

Since, therefore, both his birth and his resurrection brought joy to the disciples, whom his passion had saddened, the man and the lion are described as being on their right, while the calf is on their left. For the holy Evangelists themselves rejoiced in his humanity and were strengthened by his resurrection, though they had been saddened by his passion.

The man and the lion are therefore on their right, because the incarnation of our Redeemer gave them life and his resurrection strengthened them. But the calf is on their left, because his death cast them down for a brief time into unbelief.

The place of the eagle, however, is rightly described as being not beside them but above them, whether because it signifies his ascension, or because it declares that the Father’s Word is God with the Father. Through the power of contemplation it rose above the other Evangelists. Although it speaks together with them about his divinity, it nevertheless contemplates this more subtly than all the others.

But if the eagle, joined with the other three, is remembered as making four animals, how is it described as being above all four, unless because John, by seeing the Word in the beginning, also passed beyond himself? For unless he had passed beyond himself, he would not have seen the Word in the beginning. He therefore who passed beyond himself was no longer merely above three; joined to himself, he was above four.

“And their faces and their wings were extended above. Two wings of each were joined together, and two covered their bodies.” (Jerome)

We said above that the Gospels, the ages, and all rational creatures, together with the four virtues, are joined to one another, so that whoever lacks one lacks them all. The two wings that are extended and raise themselves on high signify heavenly preaching and that all things tend toward the majesty of God. But the two by which the bodies are covered signify that human knowledge is excluded and that a perfect vision is not granted, as the Apostle says: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part will be destroyed” (1 Corinthians 13).

(Gregory)

The faces and wings are described as extended above because every intention and every contemplation of the saints is directed above themselves, so that they may attain what they desire in the heavens. Whether one is devoted to good works or to contemplation, one acts truly in a good way when one desires to please him from whom one comes.

For whoever appears to do good works but through them desires to please not God but human beings presses the face of his intention downward. And whoever contemplates the things of divinity in sacred Scripture for the purpose of being occupied with questions through what he understands, and does not desire to be satisfied by the sweetness of the blessedness he seeks but rather to appear learned—such a person does not extend the wings of his understanding above.

But when he occupies the vigilance of his mind with earthly desire, he lays down in the lowest places the wings by which he could raise himself on high and by which he himself could be lifted up. In this matter we must consider that every good work performed must always be raised by intention toward heavenly things. For whoever desires earthly glory through the good things he has done presses down both his wings and his face.

“Two,” he says, “wings of each were joined together, and two covered their bodies.” It had been said that their faces and wings were extended above, and immediately afterward this was added: “Two wings of each were joined together.” It is suitably understood that they were both extended above and joined together, while the other two covered their bodies.

But what are the wings of the animals called except wings? Here we must inquire with careful investigation what the four wings of the saints are, of which two are extended and joined above, while the other two cover their bodies.

If we look attentively, we find four virtues that lift every winged creature from earthly acts: with respect to the future, love and hope; with respect to the past, fear and repentance. The wings joined to one another are extended above because love and hope raise the minds of the saints to higher things. They are rightly called joined together because the elect unquestionably love the heavenly things they hope for, and hope for the things they love.

But the other two cover their bodies because fear and repentance conceal their past evils from the eyes of almighty God. Thus the two wings are joined above, as has been said, when love and hope raise the hearts of the elect upward and suspend them in heavenly things. The other two wings cover their bodies when fear and repentance conceal their past evils from the sight of the eternal Judge.

For when they remember that they have sinned, and fear and grieve over it, what else do they do but cover their bodies? They conceal their carnal deeds from strict judgment by placing good works over them. For whatever is covered is placed beneath, and that by which it is covered is brought over it.

When, therefore, we renounce the evils we have done and choose the good things we should do, we place, as it were, a covering over that which we are ashamed to be seen. However holy men may be in this present life, they nevertheless have something that they ought to cover before the eyes of God. For it is altogether impossible that they should never sin either in deed, speech, or thought.

Thus blessed Job, who had spoken of his perfection before human beings, nevertheless heard the voice of God and reproached himself for that very perfect speech, saying: “I will put my hand over my mouth” (Job 39). The hand signifies work, and the mouth speech. To put one’s hand over one’s mouth, therefore, is to cover the sins of speech by the power of good works.

Brothers, let us call the teacher of the Gentiles as a further witness to this matter and observe how that holy animal is supported by four wings: with two it flies upward, while with the other two it covers its body. For it conceals from judgment the past things it had done.

Let us see, then, how great a love raises him to heavenly things: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1). Let us recognize with how great a hope he is lifted to higher things: “Our citizenship is in heaven, and from there we await the Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ” (Philippians 3).

Let us see whether, placed in such great virtues, he still fears: “I discipline my body and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified” (1 Corinthians 9). Let us recognize whether he repents of having done evil: “I am the least of the Apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Corinthians 15).

What else is accused in these words but the hardness of our mind? He weeps over what he committed before baptism, while we have committed many things even after baptism and nevertheless refuse to weep.

The holy animals therefore use four wings, because through love and hope they fly toward heavenly things, and through fear and repentance they lament the unlawful deeds within themselves.

Here a question arises. If the two wings that are raised signify love and hope, while the two that cover the bodies signify fear and repentance, why are the two that are extended said to be joined together, whereas the two that cover the body are not said to be joined?

In this matter an easy explanation, granted by God, presents itself. The wings of the saints that are joined are love and hope. But the two wings that cover the bodies are not joined to one another: they are fear and repentance.

David is afflicted by fearing and repenting of the fall of the flesh. Peter bitterly wept over his fall into faithlessness. Paul mourned within himself the cruelty of his former persecution. Yet they all desire one homeland and hasten to reach one Author of all things.

Thus two wings of each are joined and two are not, because through love and hope what they desire is one, whereas through fear and repentance what they lament is different.

“And each one walked in the presence of his face; wherever the impulse of the spirit was, there they went; and they did not turn back as they walked, and so forth.” (Jerome)

He who holds the plow-handle ought not to look behind him or imitate Lot’s wife, lest he fall into the plague of Deuteronomy and perish by incurable ὀπιστοτόνος—“opisthotonos,” a backward-drawing affliction—from which Eli also fell (4 Kingdoms 3–4), because he had offended God through the fault of his sons.

How much more, then, should the four animals, which were full of light and winged, which follow the Holy Spirit going before them, and which fly throughout the world and raise themselves to high places in such a way as to protect their bodies with the wings of history, not give us a fuller view?

(Gregory)

It was said above: “Each of them walked before his face.” Now, however, it is said: “Each one walked in the presence of his face.” Thus the same statement seems to be repeated. But since *coram* means “in the presence,” a more subtle inquiry lets us distinguish walking before one’s face from walking in one’s own presence.

To walk before one’s face is to seek what lies ahead by looking toward it; but to walk in one’s own presence is not to be absent from oneself. Every righteous person who carefully observes his life and diligently considers how much he increases daily in good—or perhaps how much he decreases in good—because he places himself before himself, walks before himself. He watches attentively whether he is rising or falling away.

But whoever neglects the guardianship of his life, and either disregards or does not know how to examine what he does, says, and thinks, does not walk before himself. For he does not know what sort of person he is in his habits or actions, and he is not present to himself because he is not concerned to examine and know himself daily.

But that person truly sets himself before himself and is present to himself who observes himself in his actions as though he were another person. For we commit many sins, but they do not seem serious to us because, loving ourselves with private affection, we flatter ourselves in our self-deception with our eyes closed.

Consequently, it often happens that we judge our own serious faults lightly, but the slight faults of our neighbors severely. For it is written: “People will be lovers of themselves” (2 Timothy 3).

We know that private love strongly closes the eye of the heart. Hence what we do does not seem serious to us, while the same thing, when done by our neighbor, often appears utterly detestable. But why does what seemed trivial in ourselves appear serious in our neighbor, unless because we do not see ourselves as we see our neighbor, nor our neighbor as we see ourselves?

If we looked upon ourselves as we look upon our neighbor, we would see our own reprehensible acts strictly. And again, if we looked upon our neighbor as we look upon ourselves, his action would never appear intolerable to us, since we have often perhaps done similar things and think that we have done nothing intolerable to our neighbor.

(Jerome)

The fact that it is said a second time, “They did not turn back as they advanced,” indicates the mystery of both instruments: that in these four living creatures both the Law and the Gospel hasten toward the future and never receive a backward movement.

(Gregory)

For it is said: “Wherever the impulse of the spirit was, there they went.” In the elect and the reprobate the impulses are different: in the elect, the impulse of the spirit; in the reprobate, the impulse of the flesh.

The impulse of the flesh drives the mind toward hatred, pride, uncleanness, plunder, outward glory, cruelty, faithlessness, despair, anger, quarrels, and pleasures. But the impulse of the spirit draws the mind toward love, humility, self-restraint, generosity in mercy, inward progress, works of piety, faith in eternal things, hope of the joy to come, patience, peace, reflection upon mortal life, and tears.

We must therefore always take great care to consider, in everything we do, which impulse is leading us: whether our thought is driven by the impulse of the flesh or by the impulse of the spirit.

To love earthly things; to prefer temporal things to eternal; to seek outward goods not for necessary use but for pleasure; to seek vengeance upon an enemy; to rejoice at the downfall of a rival—this is the impulse of the flesh.

But, on the contrary, to love heavenly things; to despise transitory things; to seek things that pass away not for the enjoyment of pleasure but for necessary use; to grieve over the death of an enemy—this is the impulse of the spirit.

And because all the perfect continually exercise themselves in these virtues, it is rightly said here of the holy animals: “Wherever the impulse of the spirit was, there they went.”

But we must know that often the impulse of the flesh disguises itself beneath the appearance of a spiritual impulse, and the thought itself deceives itself about what it does carnally, imagining that it does it spiritually.

Often someone, overcome by the goads of anger, is inflamed against offenders by zeal for avenging justice more than is necessary. Passing beyond the limit of justice, he acts cruelly in his vengeance, while supposing that he is acting justly.

The impulse of the flesh is therefore veiled under the appearance of the spirit when what is believed to be done justly is not held within the restraint of discernment. And often another, devoted to excessive gentleness, observes the vices of those subject to him but refuses to correct them through the fervor of zeal. By failing to correct them, he multiplies their vices cruelly, and his laxity becomes hostile both to himself and to those under him.

Because he considers the torpor of his mind to be patience, he is drawn away from the impulse of the spirit by the impulse of the flesh.

Our first concern, therefore, in examining our heart, must be to shake ourselves awake, lest we be led toward certain things we do by an open impulse of the flesh; lest the mind, seduced by wicked pleasures, recognize that things are evil and nevertheless do them.

Our second concern must make us vigilant, lest the impulse of the flesh secretly present itself as though it were the impulse of the spirit and pretend that the faults we commit are virtues.

We must know that the faults which imitate virtues under an imposed appearance of virtue are more serious. Those faults that are recognized openly cast the mind down in shame and draw it to repentance. But these not only fail to humble it into repentance; they also lift up the mind of the person who acts, while they are thought to be virtues.

What had been said earlier about the holy animals is repeated here in order to confirm it more deeply: “They did not turn back as they walked,” because the elect press toward good in such a way that they do not return to perpetrating evil.

“For whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10). And as it is said through Solomon: “The path of the righteous is like shining light, advancing and increasing until the perfect day” (Proverbs 4).

For in their mind the good desire and understanding of inward light are already a part of the day. But because they advance in virtue until the end of life, they come to the perfect day when, having been led into the heavenly kingdoms, they will lack nothing of that light which they desire.

It follows:

“And the likeness of the animals and their appearance was like burning coals of fire and like the appearance of lamps.” (Jerome)

The burning coals and lamps running among the animals are to be interpreted from that passage of Isaiah: “And fire will devour the material like hay, and I will sanctify them in burning fire.”

Of them it is also written elsewhere: “Coals of fire will fall upon them” (Psalm 139). And against lying lips it is said in another psalm: “What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, against a deceitful tongue? The sharp arrows of the mighty one, with desolating coals” (Psalm 119).

And in another place: “You have coals of fire; you will sit upon them, and they will be your help.” Whatever creature we look upon flashes forth the knowledge of God, since the Creator is recognized from his creatures.

(Gregory)

The appearance of the animals is compared with burning coals and lamps. Whoever touches a coal is set on fire, because whoever clings to a holy man receives, through the constant sight of him, the use of his speech, and the example of his work, the means of being kindled in the love of charity, of fleeing the darkness of his sins, of burning with desire for the light, and even of burning with true love—he who previously lay dead in iniquity to the same degree that he lay cold.

Lamps, however, spread their light farther and, although they are in one place, shine in another. Whoever possesses the spirit of prophecy, the word of teaching, and the grace of miracles shines far and wide like a lamp through his reputation. Those who hear of his good works, because through them they rise toward the love of heavenly things, shine in the way they display themselves through good works, as though from the light of a lamp.

Since holy men kindle some who are placed near them, as though by touching them, to love of the heavenly homeland, they are coals. But since they shine for others who are secretly far away, becoming lamps for their journey lest they fall into the darkness of a sinful life, they are lamps.

There is this difference between coals and lamps: coals do burn, but they do not drive away the darkness of the place in which they lie. Lamps, however, because they shine with the great light of their flames, dispel the darkness spread around them.

From this we must observe that many of the saints are so simple and hidden, concealing themselves in lesser places in profound silence, that their life can scarcely be known by others. What, then, are such men but coals? Although they possess the heat of the spirit through their fervor, they do not possess the flame of example, nor do they overcome the darkness of sins in other hearts, because they altogether refuse to let others know their life. They are kindled for themselves, but they are not a light of example for others.

But those who both excel in examples of virtue and display the light of good works through life and speech to those traveling the way are rightly called lamps, because through the heat of desire and the flame of speech they drive away the darkness of error from the hearts of sinners.

Whoever, then, lives well in secret but contributes nothing to the progress of another is a coal. But whoever, established in imitation of holiness, displays to many the light of uprightness proceeding from himself is a lamp: he burns for himself and shines for others.

It follows:

“And this was the appearance running in the midst of the animals: the splendor of fire, and lightning issuing from the fire,” and so forth.

(Jerome)

The splendor of fire and lightning issue from the midst of the living creatures because, if you bring the Gospels into collision with one another, you will find the mystery of the Holy Spirit in the midst of the letter and the humble historical account.

(Gregory)

The splendor of fire and lightning issuing from the fire appears to run in the midst of the animals because, unless those winged animals received heat from the fire of truth, they would not burn in the likeness of coals and lamps.

The Holy Spirit is customarily signified by the name “fire.” Concerning him the Lord says in the Gospel: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” (Luke 12).

When a carnal mind receives the Holy Spirit, kindled by spiritual love it mourns the evil it has done. The earth burns when the conscience accuses itself, the sinner’s heart is scorched, and it is consumed in the pain of repentance.

For this reason it is written again: “Your God is a consuming fire” (Deuteronomy 4). Because he makes the mind he fills clean from the rust of sins, our Creator is called both fire and consuming.

The Holy Spirit is therefore said to run in the midst of the animals as the splendor of fire and lightning issuing from fire, because, filling the whole Church, he casts from himself flames of love into the hearts of the elect, striking them with terror like a flash of lightning and kindling their sluggish hearts to his love.

But since the Holy Spirit, God, is coeternal with the Father and the Son before the ages, we must ask why he is said to run. For everyone who runs approaches a place in which he was not and abandons the place in which he was. In what sense, then, can we say that the Spirit runs, when all things are within him and there is nowhere that he is not?

It is written: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the inhabited world” (Wisdom 1). Yet when the praise of Wisdom was being described, it was added: “For in her is a spirit intelligent, holy, unique, manifold, subtle, mobile.” A little later: “humane, steadfast.”

In these words a great question again arises for us: why is this spirit, who fills all things, called at once mobile and steadfast? But if we return to the usage of human speech, we more quickly discover the speaker’s meaning.

A person who runs everywhere in the region in which he is, undoubtedly encounters everyone everywhere and is suddenly found where he is not expected. The almighty Spirit is therefore called both mobile and steadfast in order to signify his presence everywhere.

He is steadfast because by his nature he contains all things. He is called mobile because he encounters all things everywhere, even those who do not know him. Holding all things, he is called steadfast; presenting himself as present to all, he is called mobile.

The splendor of fire and the lightning issuing from fire therefore run among the winged animals because the Holy Spirit is present both to each individually and to all together, and he sets on fire those whom he touches. He illuminates those whom he sets on fire, so that, kindled after their former coldness, they may burn and, through the fire of love they have received, return flames of example.

For lightning issuing from this fire strikes those who are sluggish, and by striking them awakens and inflames them, so that afterward, burning and shining together, they may run in his love.

Hence it is written elsewhere: “His throne was a flame of fire, and its wheels were burning fire” (Daniel 7).

Those who are guardians of souls and have undertaken the burdens of feeding the flock are not permitted to change their places. But because, placed in one location, they carry within themselves the presence of divinity and burn, the throne of God is called a flame of fire.

Those who run about in preaching out of love for the Lord are his burning wheels, because, when they run through various places from desire for him, they burn themselves and kindle others.

Nevertheless, the running and mobility of the spirit can also be understood through another consideration. In the hearts of the saints he always remains with respect to certain virtues; with respect to others, he comes when he is about to depart and departs when he is about to come.

In faith, hope, and charity, and in the other good things without which one cannot reach the heavenly homeland—such as humility, chastity, justice, and mercy—the Spirit does not abandon the hearts of the perfect.

But in the power of prophecy, eloquence of teaching, and display of miracles, he is sometimes present to his elect and sometimes withdraws himself. He is present so that they may be lifted up, and withdraws from them so that they may be humbled. He is present so that he may glorify them by the virtue he displays; he withdraws so that they may recognize themselves when his virtue has been withdrawn. He is present to show what they are through him; he withdraws to reveal who and what they remain without him.

In those virtues without which one cannot reach life, the Holy Spirit remains in the hearts of his elect. But in those through which the power of holiness is displayed, he is sometimes mercifully present and sometimes mercifully withdraws.

The spirit is therefore called running and mobile because, in signs and virtues, it is not continually possessed according to each person’s desire. It is rightly said to run among the holy animals. Running pertains to speed. The spirit runs among the perfect because, even if it withdraws from their heart for a moment, it returns quickly.

It follows:

“And the animals went and returned like the appearance of flashing lightning.” (Jerome)

Some, lest the prophet seem to speak against the two preceding statements, have thought that the apparently contradictory words—“the animals ran and returned”—should be omitted, lest they cause a stumbling block to the reader. It is better, however, to transfer into divine books what has been said, even if you do not understand why it was said, than to remove what you do not know. Otherwise many other things that are ineffable and beyond the capacity of the human mind will be erased by this license.

We, however, say that just as in Proverbs, in the same place, it is written: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you become like him” (Proverbs 26), and again a statement is set down that appears contrary to it: “Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he seem wise to himself” (ibid.), and both agree according to the diversity of times and persons—since the fool is both disregarded because he does not receive wisdom, and another foolish pride is struck down by a different folly—just as the Apostle says: “I have become foolish; you compelled me” (2 Corinthians 12), so here also we ought to inquire why above it was said for the second time, “The animals did not turn back as they advanced,” while now it is said once, “The animals ran and returned.”

The question would remain unless what follows were added: “like the appearance of flashing lightning,” which in Hebrew is called *bezeq*, and which Symmachus interpreted as “the appearance, as it were, of a ray of lightning.”

Just as the heavens flash with repeated fires, and flashes of lightning run and return in the blink of an eye and in an instant, without losing their source—or, so to speak, their fountain and substance of fire—so these animals, although they proceed with an unobstructed step, hasten toward what lies before them.

But if they see something obstructing their effort, they do not so much return as stretch themselves out against it again and offer the light that they had briefly concealed, so that they may give the servants their food at the proper time, neither giving what is holy to dogs nor throwing pearls before swine (Luke 12; Matthew 7).

Hence Paul also says: “I gave you milk to drink, not food, for you were not yet able to receive it” (1 Corinthians 3).

The election of Judas and the anointing of Saul do not prove that God was ignorant of future events; rather, they show that he is the judge of present things. Hence the Apostles are commanded (Matthew 10), if they perceive a house to be unworthy of their greeting, to shake the dust from their feet first, and the peace that they had given to the house will return to them.

(Gregory)

When it was said above, “They did not turn back as they walked,” how can it now be said, “The animals went and returned”? These statements seem quite contradictory: “They went and did not return,” and “They went and returned.”

But we recognize more quickly how it should be understood if we carefully distinguish the two lives, namely the active and the contemplative. In one we can remain fixed; in the other we cannot keep the mind intent for long.

When we leave behind our sluggishness and rouse ourselves to the pursuit of good works, where do we go except to the active life? From this we must never afterward return, because whoever returns from it to the sluggishness of negligence and the wickedness of depravity that he had abandoned clearly does not know how to be a heavenly animal.

But when we rise from the active life to the contemplative, because the mind cannot remain long in contemplation, and because everything it perceives of eternity “through a mirror and in an enigma” (1 Corinthians 13) it sees, as it were, furtively and in passing, the mind, driven back by its own weakness from the immensity of so great a height, falls back into itself.

It is therefore necessary for it to return to the active life and continually exercise itself in good works, so that, when the mind cannot rise to contemplate heavenly things, it will not refuse to do whatever good it can.

Thus, assisted by its very good works, it rises again into contemplation and receives the nourishment of love from the food of contemplated truth. Since, because of the weakness of its corruption, it cannot remain there long, it returns again to good works, is nourished by the memory of God’s sweetness, and is fed outwardly by pious actions and inwardly by holy desires.

The animals that return are rightly compared with flashing lightning. When holy men fly up to contemplate higher things and bind the first fruits of their spirit to the love of the heavenly homeland, they are weighed down by the burden of human existence and return to themselves. Then they proclaim to their brothers the heavenly things that they were at least able to contemplate through a mirror, and they kindle their minds to love of the inward brightness, which they cannot see as it is or express in speech as they saw it.

By their words they strike and set fire to the hearts of their hearers. They return like flashing lightning: when they speak of heavenly things, the light from above flashes through them, and they inflame the minds of their hearers with love of the heavenly homeland.

Thus, in the manner of flashing lightning, when they strike through their speech, they scatter the fire of spiritual desire.

In another way also the holy animals go and return. They go when they are sent out in preaching to make known the grace of the heavenly gift, and when they perform miracles before unbelievers in order to draw them to faith. But they return because, attributing these things to the power of the almighty Lord, they do not ascribe to themselves what they have done.

## BOOK TWO

[Column 0525]

## THE FIRST CHAPTER FOLLOWS

[Column 0525B]

“While I was looking at the living creatures, a single wheel appeared upon the earth beside the living creatures. It had four faces, and the appearance of the wheels and their workmanship was like the appearance of the sea [Col. 0525C]; all four had one likeness, and their appearance and workmanship were as though one wheel were within another wheel. They went in their four directions; as they went, they did not turn back. The wheels were of such size and height, and so terrible in appearance, that their entire body, all around them, was full of eyes.” (Jerome)

Up to this point, the description has been given in a pictorial manner of the four living creatures, which had four faces each, together with the spirit and the cloud that was in the midst of the spirit. Now individual wheels are assigned to the individual living creatures. These wheels were not joined to the living creatures but followed them. Alternatively, one wheel appeared upon the earth, divided into four parts and having as many faces as there were living creatures following it. So great was the likeness of the four wheels following the four living creatures that it was truly believed to be one wheel [Col. 0525D]. Their workmanship and construction were like the appearance of *tharsis*, which we render as “sea”; Aquila translated it as “hyacinth,” a stone resembling the sky. Their appearance was like a wheel within a wheel, so that one would not think it a single wheel but one wheel joined to another. They went in their four directions and were neither dragged along nor turned backward. For how could they turn back when they followed the living creatures, which were always stretching forward?

The size and height of the wheels were so great that they caused a wonder in those who saw them. Their entire body and their backs were full of light all around, so that no limb could be seen that did not have eyes of light—like the Argus whom the poets’ tales describe [Col. 0526B] as having a hundred eyes, or many eyes, and whom Juno changed into a peacock because of his negligent guardianship. Thus what in him was a marvel of the Creator God became a condemnation of an unpunished adultery.

Everything heavenly and earthly [Col. 0526C], and whatever falls within human understanding, moves by wheels alone. The sun completes its annual circle through the several months; Lucifer, who is himself the evening star, while he shines brightly at the east and west and tempers the darkness of night with a small light, completes the same course in two years. So do the other four stars called “wandering,” and whatever shines in the sky. The variations of crops, trees, and plants also run in their own wheels through the four seasons, and we see nothing that was not there before.

“Going round and round, the spirit proceeds and returns to its circuits. All the streams go to the sea, and the sea is not filled” (Eccles. 1). Why? Because they return to their springs, to the womb of the abyss.

If someone considers the wheel and course of the Gospels [Col. 0526D]—that is, of the four living creatures who breathe, live, and understand—he will see in a short time that the world has been completed through apostolic preaching. The wheel within the wheel is also the joining of the two Testaments, as signified by Jacob’s ladder, Isaiah’s tongs, and the two-edged sword; or else it signifies the Gospels joined to one another. Their height again reaches toward heaven and touches the earth slightly, while always hastening upward and pressing toward the heights.

Of these it is also said elsewhere: “The holy stones roll upon the earth” (Zech. 9), and from them the heavenly Jerusalem is built. I think that the same thing is signified by what is sung in the Psalm: “The voice of your thunder is in the wheel” (Ps. 76). And elsewhere: “Which sets the wheel of birth on fire” (Jas. 3). What meaning these testimonies have [Col. 0527A] in their own contexts is not for the present occasion.

He will approve that the whole body and the backs were full of eyes who sees that there is nothing in the Gospels that does not shine and illuminate the world with its splendor, so that even those things considered small and worthless gleam with the majesty of the Holy Spirit.

(Gregory) Therefore, when the prophet saw the living creatures, he added: “While I was looking at the living creatures, a single wheel appeared upon the earth.” Here we must ask why, since the wheels are described below, it is first said that one wheel appeared, unless because only the Old Testament was given to the ancient people, and it revolved like a wheel for the instruction of their mind.

The same wheel is rightly said to have appeared upon the earth, since it was said to sinful humanity: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3). The wheel appeared upon the earth [Col. 0527B] because almighty God placed the law upon the hearts of sinners.

But since these winged living creatures, as we have said, signify the holy evangelists, how is it that the living creatures are seen first and the single wheel afterward, when the Old Testament existed before them and the holy evangelists followed later? We can understand in this that those who in merit transcend the others were first seen by the prophet. For to the degree that the holy Gospel surpasses the Old Testament, its preachers should also have been placed first in the prophetic description.

Yet there is still something else to be considered in this description. The spirit of prophecy gathers within itself earlier and later things at once, so that the prophet’s tongue cannot utter them simultaneously; rather, what he sees in abundance flows forth through divided statements [Col. 0527C]. Sometimes he speaks of the last things after the first, and sometimes of the first after the last. Thus the prophet Ezekiel sees, under the figure of the holy universal Church, the glory of the evangelists through the likeness of the four living creatures; yet he suddenly adds things that took place in earlier times, clearly indicating that he saw together what the tongue of flesh could not say together.

But since we have said that the four living creatures also signify all the perfect, we must consider that some of the saints existed before the law, living strictly according to the natural law and pleasing almighty God. Therefore, the wheel is described after the living creatures, because many of the elect were perfect before the law in the sight of almighty God.

But if we must understand the living creatures as the evangelists alone, as we have said [Col. 0527D], there is still something else to consider. The holy prophet saw that these very words, which he uttered wrapped in obscurities, would be disclosed not to the Jewish people but to the nations. Therefore, speaking to us, he ought to describe the living creatures first and the wheel afterward, because we who, by the Lord’s gift, come to the faith learned the law through the holy Gospel, not the Gospel through the law.

Then he adds where and what sort of wheel appeared, saying: “Beside the living creatures, having four faces.” He further says: “The appearance of the wheels and their workmanship were like the appearance of the sea, and all four had one likeness; their appearance and workmanship were as though one wheel were within another wheel.”

What does it mean that, after one wheel had been mentioned [Col. 0528A], he shortly afterward adds, “as though one wheel were within another wheel,” unless that in the letter of the Old Testament the New Testament lay hidden through allegory? Hence the same wheel, which appeared beside the living creatures, is described as having four faces, because sacred Scripture is divided into four parts through both Testaments.

The Old Testament consists of the Law and the Prophets; the New consists of the Gospels and the Acts and sayings of the apostles. We know that we direct our face wherever we see what is necessary. The wheel therefore has four faces because it first saw through the Law the evils that had to be cut away among the peoples; afterward it saw them through the Prophets; more subtly, through the Gospel; and finally, through the apostles, it saw the things that had to be removed from human sins.

It may also be understood that the wheel had four faces [Col. 0528B] because sacred Scripture, extended through the grace of preaching, became known throughout the four regions of the world. Hence it is rightly described as having first appeared as one wheel beside the living creatures and afterward as having four faces, because unless the law agreed with the Gospel, it would not become known throughout the four regions of the world.

“The appearance of the wheels and their workmanship were like the appearance of the sea.” Sacred utterances are rightly said to resemble the appearance of the sea, because in them there are great rivers of sentences and heaps of meanings. Nor is sacred Scripture called like the sea without reason, because the utterances expressed in it are confirmed through the sacrament of baptism.

Or certainly we should consider that we sail upon the sea in ships when we make our way toward the lands we desire. What land do we desire except that of which it is written: “My portion is in the land of the living [Col. 0528C]” (Ps. 141)? He who crosses the sea is carried upon wood, as I have said; and we know that sacred Scripture foretells the wood of the cross to us through the Law when it says: “Cursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree” (Deut. 21). Paul bears witness to this concerning our Redeemer, saying: “He was made a curse for us” (Gal. 3).

Through the Prophets also it announces the wood when it says: “The Lord reigned from the wood” (Ps. 95). And again: “Let us cast wood into his bread.” Through the Gospel, the wood of the cross is openly shown, where the Lord’s Passion itself, which had been foretold by the prophet, is declared.

The wheel within the wheel therefore signifies that the New Testament is contained in the Old Testament. And, as we have often said, what the Old Testament promised, the New Testament displayed; what the former announces secretly [Col. 0528D], the latter openly proclaims as accomplished. The prophecy of the New Testament is therefore the Old Testament, and the exposition of the Old Testament is the New Testament.

“They went in their four directions,” he says, “and did not turn back.” Where else do the divine utterances go except to human hearts? But they went in their four directions because sacred Scripture goes to the human heart through the Law, marking out the mystery. It goes through the Prophets, prophesying the Lord somewhat more openly. It goes through the Gospel, presenting the one whom it prophesied. It goes through the apostles, preaching the one whom the Father presented for our redemption.

The wheels therefore have faces and wings, because the sacred utterances display knowledge of the commandments [Col. 0529A] together with the performance of works. They go in their four directions because they speak in distinct periods, as we have said; or certainly because they preached the incarnate Lord in all the regions of the world.

Of these he immediately adds: “And they turned back as they went.” These words were said above concerning the living creatures, but the same meaning cannot be applied to the wheels as to the living creatures. We have said that the wheels signify the Testaments. The Old Testament did indeed move when it came to human minds through preaching; but it turned back after itself, because, according to the letter, it could not be observed to the end in its commandments and sacrifices.

It did not remain unchanged, because spiritual understanding was lacking in it. But when our Redeemer came into the world [Col. 0529B], he caused what he found held carnally to be understood spiritually. Thus, while its letter is understood spiritually, all its former carnal observance gives life.

The New Testament, even through the pages of the Old Testament, has been called the eternal Testament, because its meaning is never changed. It is therefore rightly said that “the wheels went as they went, and did not turn back as they moved.” Since the New Testament is not annulled, and since the Old Testament, now understood spiritually, is retained, they do not turn back: they remain unalterable until the end of the world.

They move but do not turn back, because they come spiritually to our hearts in such a way that their commandments and teachings are never afterward changed.

It follows: “The wheels were of such size and height, and so terrible in appearance [Col. 0529C].” What does it mean that these three things are said to be present in the utterances of sacred Scripture—that they have size, height, and a terrible appearance? We must inquire earnestly what is meant by the size, height, and terrible appearance of divine Scripture.

We should know, then, that size corresponds to the life of one who acts well. Hence Paul says: “Let him who stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10). He also says to the disciples: “Stand firm in the Lord, beloved” (Phil. 4). And the prophet, who saw himself standing before the Lord in life and conduct, said: “The Lord lives, before whom I stand” (1 Kings 17).

Height is the promise of the heavenly kingdom, which is reached when all corruption of mortal life has been subdued. The terrible appearance is the terror of Gehenna, which tortures the rejected without end and preserves them forever in torment.

Thus size lies in uprightness of commandment; height in the loftiness of the promise above; and the terrible appearance in the threats and terrors of the punishment to come [Col. 0529D].

Sacred Scripture therefore has size because it directs conduct toward standing upright, so that the minds of its hearers are not bent toward earthly desire. It has height because it promises the joys of eternal life in the heavenly homeland. It also has a terrible appearance because it threatens all the rejected with the punishments of Gehenna.

It displays its size in the formation of conduct, its height in the promise of rewards, and its terrible appearance in the terrors of punishment. It is upright in its commandments, lofty in its promises, and terrible in its threats [Col. 0530A].

It has size when through the prophet it says: “Cease to act perversely; learn to do good; seek justice; assist the oppressed; judge the orphan; defend the widow” (Isa. 1). And again: “Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the poor and homeless into your house. When you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise those of your own flesh” (Isa. 58).

It has height when through the same prophet it says: “The sun shall no longer be your light by day, nor shall the brightness of the moon illuminate you; but the Lord shall be your everlasting light, and your God shall be your glory” (Isa. 60).

It has a terrible appearance when, describing hell, it says: “The day of the Lord’s vengeance, the year of retribution for the judgment of Zion [Col. 0530B]. Its streams shall be turned into pitch, its soil into sulfur, and its land shall become burning pitch; by night and by day it shall not be extinguished forever” (Isa. 34).

Therefore, when the prophet Ezekiel was speaking about the wheels, he added: “And the whole body was full of eyes all around the four.” By saying “their” in the masculine rather than “theirs” in the feminine, he clearly indicates that his speech suddenly returned from the wheels to the living creatures, through which, as has been stated, all the perfect are signified.

The bodies of the holy living creatures are therefore described as full of eyes because the conduct of the saints is watchful on every side [Col. 0530C]: it eagerly provides for good things and carefully avoids evil. This is especially difficult where the mind of the saints keeps intense watch, lest evils conceal themselves before their eyes under the appearance of good.

The life of the saints is therefore watchful on every side, lest it be free in such a way as to become proud, since pride often breaks out in words; and lest the freedom of purity, which seeks to be seen, be such that it is not humble but fearful, since fear sometimes constricts the mind so that it does not dare to speak what is right, while nevertheless pretending to be humble in that very timid thought.

Nor must it be frugal in such a way as to be grasping, since greed often seeks to be regarded as thrift, so that whatever one does not mercifully wish to spend on a needy neighbor may seem to be held justly and necessarily. Nor must it be merciful in such a way as to be wasteful, since sometimes wastefulness is thought to be mercy.

It is one thing to give those necessities to one’s neighbors from a zeal for charity, and another to scatter possessions without the intention of reward. Whatever is done [Col. 0530D] must therefore be weighed at the root of its intention, so that it may be judged according to the merit it possesses before the Creator’s judgment.

Hence the same Creator said: “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light” (Matt. 6), calling the intention the eye and the action the body. For if our intention is single before God, our action will not be dark in his judgment.

Because holy men therefore keep careful watch over themselves, examining themselves on every side and guarding themselves everywhere, lest they desire evils because of the very things themselves, or do them under the appearance of good—that is, lest vices deceive them into thinking that they are virtues—they have their whole body full of eyes all around. For all their action is both filled and surrounded by the foresight of vigilant concern.

This is why [Col. 0531A] the apostle Paul, when he saw that the Corinthians wished mercy to be shown to a certain penitent for a crime he had committed, said: “If you have forgiven anyone anything, I also have forgiven it. For whatever I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, I have done it through you in the person of Christ, so that we may not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his thoughts” (2 Cor. 2).

If forgiveness was not to be granted, why does this distinguished teacher join himself with such humility to the will of the disciples, so that neither he appeared separated from the disciples nor the disciples from him in the matter of compassion? It was because, with the watchful eye of foresight, he observed that often, while one person forgives, another becomes angry.

And what kind of sacrifice of mercy is offered to one’s neighbor together with discord? Hence he certainly says: “So that we may not be outwitted by Satan, for we are not ignorant of his thoughts.” For Satan commonly introduces the evil of quarrels [Col. 0531B] into one person’s heart from the very place where he sees another engaged in an act of charity. The good is imperfect when it is done without attention to the possibility that some evil may creep in from another side.

Unless, perhaps, failing to do what cannot be done without causing someone’s offense is itself blameworthy. We say this so that your love may know that in our good work we must sometimes avoid giving offense to our neighbor, and at other times disregard it as nothing.

We learned this from our own Author, who, when tribute was demanded from Peter, first offered an example by which he showed that he owed nothing, saying: “From whom do the kings of the earth receive tribute or tax—from their own sons or from strangers?” (Matt. 17). When he was told, “From strangers [Col. 0531C],” he immediately replied: “Then the sons are free.”

But after showing that he was free, lest he perhaps cause offense to anyone, he added: “But so that we may not offend them, go to the sea and cast a hook; take the fish that first comes up, and when you have opened its mouth you will find a stater. Take it and give it to them for me and for yourself.”

Again, when he had said: “Whatever enters the mouth does not defile a person,” the disciples came and said: “Do you know that when the Pharisees heard this saying, they were offended?” But he answered: “Every planting that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted. Leave them; they are blind guides of the blind” (Matt. 15; Mark 7).

Behold, the Truth who teaches: so that offense might not arise in certain hearts, he gave the tribute that he did not owe [Col. 0531D]; and again, because he saw offense arising in certain hearts against the truth, he allowed them to remain in their offense.

From this we must consider that, insofar as we can do so without sin, we ought to avoid giving offense to our neighbors. But if offense is taken from the truth, it is more useful to allow offense to arise than to abandon the truth.

Because the minds of the saints therefore look around themselves on every side and keep watch, directing the eye of fear and concern through all their works lest they do what is wrong, or fail to do what is right and commanded, or swell up in their thoughts after completing good deeds—and thus offend more seriously, since they appear righteous outwardly while sinning more secretly [Col. 0532A]—it is rightly said that their whole body is full of eyes.

“When the living creatures moved, the wheels also moved beside them. When the living creatures rose from the earth, the wheels rose together with them. Wherever the spirit went, the wheels also rose there, going where the spirit went and following it. For the spirit of life was in the wheels. When they went, they went; when they stood, they stood; and when they were lifted up from the earth, the wheels were lifted up together with them, following them, because the spirit of life was in the wheels.” (Jerome)

The four living creatures followed the spirit and the cloud that was in the spirit. Again, when the wheels followed the living creatures as they rose from the earth, they did not follow the living creatures but the spirit, thereby showing their own will [Col. 0532B], because the spirit of life was in the wheels.

Three things are indicated alike both in the living creatures and in the wheels: when they stood, when they moved, and when they rose. The living creatures and the wheels did all these things together. For when the living creatures stood, the wheels could not move; nor, when the living creatures moved upon the earth, could the wheels lift themselves up. Since their action was one, their rest, movement, and rising were also one.

It is said a second time that the spirit of life was in the wheels, so that we might not regard the wheels as some sort of vessels such as we see on carts, wagons, and chariots, but as living beings—or rather, as beings above living beings: “The natural person does not receive the things that belong to the Spirit” (1 Cor. 2).

These wheels, then, in which the spirit of life was present, do everything in order and measure. They have harmony with the living creatures [Col. 0532C], following them and, through them, the Holy Spirit; or rather, passing over the intermediaries, they rejoice in fellowship with the Holy Spirit. The prudent reader will be able to adapt all these things to various interpretations according to the preceding understanding.

(Gregory) “When the living creatures moved [Col. 0532D],” he says, “the wheels also moved beside them. And when the living creatures rose from the earth, the wheels rose together with them.”

The living creatures moved when holy men understand from sacred Scripture how they ought to live morally. The living creatures rise from the earth when holy men suspend themselves in contemplation.

And because, to the extent that each saint himself makes progress in sacred Scripture, that same sacred Scripture makes progress in him, it is rightly said: “When the living creatures moved, the wheels also moved together with them; and when the living creatures rose from the earth, the wheels likewise rose.” For the divine utterances grow as they are read: each person understands them more deeply in proportion to the depth of his attention to them.

Hence the wheels are not raised if the living creatures are not raised. For unless the minds of readers make progress toward higher things, the divine words lie below, as it were, not understood.

When the speech of sacred Scripture seems lukewarm to a reader, the meaning of the divine utterance does not stir his mind, and no light of understanding shines in his thoughts. The wheel is idle and remains upon the earth because the living creature is not raised from the earth.

But if the living creature moves—that is, if it seeks an ordered life of good conduct and, through the movement of the heart, discovers how to take a step in good works [Col. 0533A]—the wheels also move together with it. For you find as much progress in sacred speech as you yourself have made before it.

But if the winged living creature stretches itself upward into contemplation, the wheels are immediately raised from the earth. You understand that the things you previously believed were spoken in sacred speech according to an earthly manner are not earthly; and you perceive the words of sacred Scripture to be heavenly if, set aflame by the grace of contemplation, you suspend yourself toward heavenly things.

The marvelous and ineffable power of sacred speech is recognized when the reader’s mind is penetrated by heavenly love. Because the living creature raises itself to higher things, the wheel flies. It follows: “Wherever the spirit went, the wheels also rose there, going where the spirit went and following it.”

The wheels follow the spirit because, as has often been said, the words of sacred speech grow in understanding [Col. 0533B] according to the readers’ perceptions. In one and the same sentence of Scripture, one person is nourished by history alone; another seeks a typological meaning; another seeks, through the type, a contemplative understanding.

It sometimes happens, as we have said, that all three can be found together in one and the same sentence. Since the words of sacred speech therefore grow together with the spirit of the readers, it is rightly said here: “Wherever the spirit went, the wheels also rose there, going where the spirit went and following it.”

And it is added: “For the spirit of life was in the wheels.” The spirit of life is in the wheels because through the sacred utterances we are given life by the gift of the Spirit, so that we may drive away deadly works from ourselves.

It may also be understood that the spirit moves when God touches the mind of the reader in different ways [Col. 0533C] and according to different arrangements: sometimes arousing it through the words of sacred speech in zeal and raising it to vengeance; sometimes calming it toward patience; sometimes instructing it in preaching; and sometimes piercing it with compunction toward the lamentations of repentance.

Let us briefly return to these same words that we have discussed and see how the wheels follow the spirit, which is called the spirit of life and is said to be present in the wheels.

If the spirit of life touches the reader’s mind with the fervor of zeal, he immediately sees in the sacred utterances how Moses, returning to the camp and learning that the people had sinned through idols (Exod. 32), struck them down with the sword in the fervor of the spirit; how Phinehas, pursuing sexual immorality, appeased the Lord’s anger with the sword (Num. 25); how Peter struck and killed those who lied to him by his word (Acts 5); and how Paul [Col. 0533D] threatens negligent disciples with a rod (1 Cor. 4).

If the spirit of life touches the reader’s mind so that he practices patience, the wheels immediately follow. For in the sacred utterances he finds how Moses and Aaron, when they suffered the people’s persecution while speaking what was right, ran to the tabernacle and prayed for the very people from whom they were fleeing (Num. 20). Their holy mind endured the fear of the proud, yet did not burst forth into hatred against them.

Patience is that which loves even the one whom it bears. To tolerate while hating is not the virtue of gentleness but a covering for anger.

In the same utterances he finds how Samuel, cast down from the height of leadership [Col. 0534A], confessed that he had even prayed for those who had cast him down (1 Sam. 8); and that none of the saints reached heavenly glory except by preserving patience.

He also finds that the Author and Redeemer of the human race endured spittle, blows, a crown of thorns, the cross, and the lance, yet prayed for his persecutors (Matt. 26–27).

If the spirit of life stirs the reader’s mind toward the work of preaching, the wheels immediately follow. For in the sacred utterances he finds how Moses, at the Lord’s command, boldly rose up in preaching against the king of Egypt (Exod. 5); how Stephen said to the unbelieving Jews: “You always resist the Holy Spirit” (Acts 7), and was not afraid amid the stones; how Peter, beaten with rods so that he would not speak in the name of Jesus, answered with great boldness: “We must obey God rather than human beings” (Acts 5); and how Paul is bound with chains [Col. 0534B] (Phil. 1), yet “the word of God is not bound” (2 Tim. 2).

If the spirit of life pierces the reader’s mind with the lamentations of repentance, the wheels immediately follow, when the words of sacred Scripture set forth David’s repentance. The king, rebuked by the prophet because he had not submitted to the heavenly King, was not ashamed to confess to the one who rebuked him that he had done what he had done (2 Sam. 11).

The publican, who recognized the guilt of his wickedness (Luke 18), came to the temple unjust, yet returned from the temple justified. Peter washed away the stains of his denial with tears (Matt. 26). The thief, who recognized his guilt upon the cross, found forgiveness in death itself (Luke 23).

Concerning these wheels [Col. 0534C] the prophet continues and repeats the same words: “When they went, they went; when they stood, they stood; and when they were lifted up from the earth, the wheels were lifted up together with them, following them, because the spirit of life was in the wheels.”

These things, beloved brothers, are for the most part already known to you; but they are narrated again in a repeated description. The only new point added in these words is what is said: “When they stood, they stood.”

There are some who progress so far that they know how to distribute well the earthly things they receive. They devote themselves to mercy and come to the aid of the oppressed. Such people move in that they direct themselves toward the benefit of their neighbor.

The wheels therefore move with them, because the sacred utterances arrange the steps of their sayings along their path.

There are others who are so strong in holding to the faith they have received that they can resist every adversity. They are not only not drawn into the perversity of unbelief [Col. 0534D] but also attack those who speak perversely and draw them toward righteousness.

With these who stand, the wheels also stand, because the words of sacred speech confirm their uprightness when they hear: “Stand firm and hold to the traditions that you were taught” (2 Thess. 2). And again: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour; resist him, strong in faith” (1 Pet. 5).

There are others who despise all earthly things and do not deem any passing possession worthy of ownership. They suspend themselves in contemplation of God, as has been said. With these who are lifted up, the wheels also rise. For to the degree that each person progresses toward higher things, to that degree the sacred utterances speak to him of higher things.

The living creatures therefore move for the benefit of their neighbor; they stand for their own protection; they rise for the contemplation of God. The wheels likewise move, stand, and rise, because sacred reading, when sought, is found to be such as is the one who seeks it.

If you have progressed to the active life [Col. 0535A], it moves with you. If you have progressed to steadfastness and constancy of spirit, it stands with you. If by God’s grace you have reached the contemplative life, it flies with you.

And again it is added: “Because the spirit of life was in the wheels.” The reason it is said a second time that the spirit of life was in the wheels is that Scripture has two Testaments, and God’s Spirit willed both to be written so that it might free us from the death of the soul.

Or certainly it is because there are two commandments of charity—namely, love of God and love of neighbor—through which the words of sacred Scripture give us life [Col. 0535B].

It is therefore said a second time that the spirit of life was in the wheels, because in the divine utterances we grasp love of God and neighbor. Through the commandments of sacred Scripture, we are given life by its words, though we had been lying dead in guilt.

“‘And the likeness above the heads of the living creatures was like the appearance of a firmament, resembling terrifying crystal, spread out above their heads.’” (Jerome.) Above the four living creatures and an equal number of wheels there appeared a likeness of the firmament, which we call heaven, having the appearance of crystal. Crystal, which is most pure, is said to congeal from clean and shining waters through extreme cold, so much so that water hardened by frost is called *crystallus* in Greek. It was fitting that outstanding purity should be in the things above, which protected all things: that is, the rational and wise powers, the course of the four seasons, the regions of the world, the orders of all things, and the Gospel proclamation, which is partly understood and partly veiled.

“‘And the likeness,’ he says, ‘above the heads of the living creatures was a firmament,’ and so forth.” (Gregory.) By the Lord’s granting, we explain this [*Hanc*; variant *Haec*] in two ways, leaving it to the reader’s judgment to decide which should be preferred.

The word “firmament” may indeed be understood as referring to the heavenly powers. This firmament is rightly said to be “like the appearance of crystal,” because crystal is exceedingly hard, having been solidified from water. When the angelic nature was created, it received free choice, so that it might either persist in humility and remain in the sight of almighty God, or fall into pride and be deprived of blessedness; in this respect it was like water. But because the holy angels remained in their blessedness when the others fell, and received this as a gift—that they could no longer fall at all—their nature, since it can no longer be cast down through mutability, was hardened as though into the likeness of crystal. This crystal is said to be terrifying and spread out above the heads of the living creatures because those angelic powers who stand before the sight of almighty God are still terrifying and fearful to us, who remain in this corruption. Their joys are said to be above the heads of the living creatures because they exceed the understanding of our minds. For who, situated in corruptible flesh, could comprehend what the ineffable and endless joy of the angels is? What is that blessedness which beholds the face of the Creator without decline and remains unchangingly in his love?

The word “firmament” may also be understood figuratively as referring to our Redeemer himself: true God above all things, and perfect man made among all things, in whom our nature was confirmed before the Father. Of him the Psalmist also prophesies: “Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, and upon the son of man whom you confirmed for yourself” (Psalm 79).

Human nature, before it was assumed by the Creator of all things, was earth, for it was not yet a firmament. To sinful man it was said: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Genesis 3). But after it was assumed by the Author of all things, raised into heaven, and placed above the angels, what had been earth became a firmament.

But what likeness the firmament that is seen possesses is next explained when it is said: “Like the appearance of terrifying crystal.” Crystal, as has been said, freezes from water and becomes strong. We know, therefore, how fluid water is. The body of our Redeemer, because it was subject to suffering even unto death, was in a certain respect like water. For by being born, growing, becoming weary, hungering, thirsting, and dying, it passed through the successive moments of time in a mutable condition until his passion. Water, then, is changed into crystal when the weakness of its corruption is transformed through resurrection into the firmness of incorruption.

But it should be noted that this crystal is called terrifying—that is, fearful. Who, however, does not know how beautiful crystal is? It is astonishing how beauty and fear can meet in this crystal. Yet it is clear to all who know the truth that the Redeemer of the human race, when he appears as judge, will be beautiful to the just and terrifying to the unjust. The elect behold him as gentle; the reprobate behold this same one as fearful and terrifying. The elect will not then see him as terrifying because they do not cease now to consider his terror. And because the fear of him that they hold in their thoughts protects their minds, it is rightly added: “Spread out above their heads.”

This firmament, which appears like crystal above the heads of the living creatures, is both terrifying and spread out, because by the very thing through which it terrifies the minds of the good, it protects them. If it were not fearful in their hearts, it would neither protect them now from sins nor afterward from punishments. Since they always consider what fear threatens them from the judgment, they preserve the wings of virtue in uprightness. Hence it is appropriately added at once:

“‘Beneath the firmament their wings were straight, one toward another,’ and so forth.”

The wings of virtues are straight beneath the firmament when one person uses the good he possesses for another: when the one who has earthly wealth relieves the poverty of a needy neighbor; when the one filled with the gift of teaching illumines the darkness of an ignorant neighbor by the word of his preaching; when the one supported by temporal power raises up those oppressed by violence; when the one filled with the spirit of prophecy turns away impending evils from a neighbor’s life by persuading him toward what is good; when the one who receives the grace of healing piously and humbly attends [*intendat*; variant *impendat*, “devotes himself”], through his intercession, to the salvation of the sick; and when the one who has been freed from earthly activities and has deserved to devote himself to God alone prays for those who sin.

It often happens that the person excessively occupied with earthly wealth does not devote as much attention to prayer as he ought. It also commonly happens that the one who is free for entreating the Lord, stripped of all the burdens of the world, lacks the means of sustaining his life. But while the rich person offers food and clothing to the poor, and while the poor person offers his prayer for the soul of the rich, the wings of the living creatures are rightly extended one toward another.

It follows:

“‘Each had two wings with which it covered its body. And the other was likewise covered.’” (Gregory.) We have already said that the body signifies action and the wings signify virtues.
