Since he says, “Beneath the firmament their wings were straight, one toward another,” it must be asked how he can immediately add, “Each had two wings with which it covered its body.”

Here he plainly indicates that the wings of one were extended toward another, and yet each covered its own body with two wings. What else does this mean except that we ought to devote the virtues we receive to others in such a way that we do not cease carefully to consider the things in which we have sinned and daily to lament our guilt through fear and repentance?

We said above that the two wings with which the body was covered were fear and repentance. If, then, we grow in charity so that we extend our wings toward our neighbors, let us extend our wings toward our neighbors in such a way that we never cease to consider and lament ourselves. Let the wings be extended alongside the wings so that they may cover the bodies: let us offer examples from our good deeds, while fear and repentance conceal from judgment the evils we commit.

These wings may also be understood as the two commandments of charity, namely, the love of God and of one’s neighbor. By loving God, we pursue the evils within ourselves—that is, we cover the body. By loving our neighbor, we hasten toward whatever may benefit him—that is, we extend the wings toward one another.

One may ask why, after it has been said, “Each covered its body,” it immediately adds, “and the other was likewise covered.” If it had said “one and the other,” the manner of speaking would have been acceptable. But after saying “each,” why does it add “the other,” when all are included in “each”?

Yet if we distinguish the life of the perfect from the merits of those who are making progress, we see that “each” and “the other” have not been inserted without reason. Those who both lament their own sins and extend the wings of virtues toward their neighbor as an example are undoubtedly perfect. There are, however, many little ones who observe their tears and imitate them. They might have been naked in their depravity, but when they behold holy and vigilant men, they immediately grow angry with their own depravity and are stirred to lament. They are inflamed toward repentance, and, just as they see the holy covering their bodies with wings, so they too are covered by the wings of their tears. They strike themselves with great reproaches, asking why those who do not possess virtues scarcely lament their sins, when even those who already extend the wings of virtues toward their neighbors by their example do not cease to weep.

[Col. 0538A] “And I heard the sound of their wings, like the sound of many waters,” and so forth. (Jerome.) The voice of the flying wings is heard like the voice of many waters, which, according to John’s Apocalypse, signify peoples. Gradually progressing, it is like the voice of armies and like the voice of the Sublime God. In Hebrew he is called *Saddai*, and according to the Septuagint, “the voice of the Word,” so that we may believe that all that is preached in the world is the voice of the Son of God.

(Gregory.) In sacred language, waters commonly signify peoples. Hence it is said through John: “The waters are peoples” (Revelation 17). The people is signified by waters because in life it produces a sound through the tumult of the flesh and daily flows away through the course of mortality.

As we have often said, the wings of the living creatures are the virtues of the saints. What, then, does it mean that the prophet hears the sound of the wings like the sound of many waters, except that, through the mercy of almighty God, those wings of virtues which formerly sounded in only a few saints now resound, through the spread of preaching, in the conduct of many peoples?

When the Lord had become incarnate, suffered, and risen again, there were few winged living creatures, because very few existed who desired heavenly things and raised themselves on the wings of virtues to the heights. But after the preaching of his divinity had spread throughout the world, how many children, how many mature people, how many strong young men, how many weak persons, how many converted sinful women, how many old women and virgins now fly toward heavenly things through faith, hope, and love! Who is sufficient to tell or estimate it?

Behold, the sound of the wings that previously existed in a few living creatures now resounds among the peoples. Now the wings of virtues raise the multitude of the world toward heavenly desire. Well, therefore, is it said: “And I heard the sound of their wings, like the sound of many waters.” For, as we have said, the sound of virtues that first arose in the ear of God from a few saints was afterward multiplied through many waters—that is, through innumerable peoples.

Regarding this sound it is rightly added: “Like the sound of the Sublime God.” What does it mean that the sound of the wings in the holy living creatures is called “like the sound of the Sublime God”? Is it not that almighty God himself fills the minds of the saints with heavenly desire, and himself hears those whom he has filled? He creates love in the hearts of the saints, and he receives prayers from loving hearts. Well, therefore, is this sound of the wings called “like the sound of the Sublime God,” because whatever is done in the virtues of the saints belongs to the grace of him who bestows their merits, who is rightly called the Sublime God by the prophet.

In sacred Scripture God is sometimes called so by designation and sometimes according to his essence. He is called God by designation, as it is written: “Behold, I have appointed you as a god of Pharaoh” (Exodus 7). And as Moses says: “If anyone does this or that, bring him to the gods,” namely, to the priests (Exodus 22); and again: “You shall not revile the gods” (ibid.), that is, the priests. So also the Psalmist says: “God stood in the assembly of gods; in the midst he judges gods” (Psalm 81).

God is called according to his essence when he says to Moses: “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob” (Exodus 3). Therefore the apostle Paul, wishing to distinguish the designated name of God from God according to essence, spoke of our Redeemer, saying: “Whose are the fathers, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Romans 9).

He who is called God by designation is God among all things; but he who is God according to essence is God over all things. Thus, to show that Christ is God by nature, Paul did not merely call him God, but remembered him as God over all. For every elect person—as we have said—whether placed as an example of righteousness or for dispensing the word of preaching, may be called “god,” but only among all things, since he is god by designation. Christ, however, is God over all, because he is God by nature.

The one whom Paul calls God over all, the prophet Ezekiel calls the Sublime God. After it has been said, “I heard the sound of the wings, like the sound of many waters,” and it is further added, “like the sound of the Sublime God,” we may also understand this as referring to what we know will happen to all the elect.

The sound of the wings, as we have said, was in the holy preachers; the sound of the waters was in the peoples who were converted and followed them. But that same sound will eventually be the sound of the Sublime God, because the multitude now drawn to faith through holy teachers will one day be gathered into the heavenly homeland, where all the elect will praise without end when they see, without end, the one whom they praise.

After the prophet perceived in heaven that the sound of the wings was like the sound of the Sublime God, he returned again to earth and spoke of what the winged living creatures do here, so that there they might deserve the highest things. He says:

“‘When they walked, there was a sound like the sound of a multitude and the sound of armies.’”

When the holy preachers travel throughout the world, preaching and drawing people to faith, the living creatures also walk. And because those whom they gather rise up as soon as they believe to praise our Creator, there is a sound like the sound of a multitude. Since in preaching they also undertake warfare against the aerial powers, it is rightly added: “And the sound of armies.”

When faithful peoples are joined to the holy preachers, multitudes become armies in the formation of faith against evil spirits. As the faithful are daily filled with heavenly desires, they despise earthly things and undertake difficult struggles for the love of the eternal homeland. Armies are formed against the aerial powers because they advance armed with faith and fortified by good works. The spiritual army is addressed by Paul as though it were an army: “Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil; for our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, and against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6).

The multitudes of the saints become armies because they have undertaken warfare against the aerial powers. Concerning the holy living creatures it is further added:

“‘And when they stood, their wings were lowered.’”

(Jerome.) When the living creatures stood, their wings were lowered. They could not endure the resounding voice of almighty God in the heavens; instead, they stood and marveled, and in their silence demonstrated the power of God, who sat above the firmament.

(Gregory.) The holy living creatures stand when they consider attentively, in contemplation, the things that belong to God. But their wings are lowered because, when they behold the lofty judgments of God, the virtues they possess seem insignificant to them. This is clearly explained when it is immediately added:

“‘For when there was a voice above the firmament that was above their heads, they stood and lowered their wings.’”

We judged above that the higher firmament should be explained in two ways. As has been said, the heavenly powers may be understood by the word “firmament.” The word “firmament” may also signify the incarnate Only-Begotten, because our nature was established in him for eternity.

Let us first speak of what we understand concerning the angels, and afterward of the Lord of the angels. Behold, it is said: “When there was a voice above the firmament, they stood and lowered their wings.” Here it must be understood that “lowering” does not mean extending from below toward higher things, but lowering the wings from above toward things below, because it was previously said: “When they stood, their wings were lowered.”

We must therefore ask what the voice is that comes above the firmament. We understand this same voice better if, proceeding from the lowest things toward the higher, we ascend as though by certain steps. Just as bodily hearing is stirred by a voice, so the sense of the mind is stirred by understanding, which arises from interior things. The voice in the mind is therefore a kind of sound of understanding.

But it must be known that at times the voice of the flesh speaks to our senses, at times the voice of the soul, at times the voice of the firmament, and at times the voice that is above the firmament.

Let us place before our eyes someone who has been injured by a neighbor and who, reasoning according to human judgment, considers returning the injury and repaying evil for evil. To him the voice of the flesh speaks in his mind. For since the divine commands prescribe that we do good to those who hate us (Matthew 5), whenever anyone thinks of doing harm to those who hate him, the voice of the flesh sounds in his soul.

We perform many earthly actions each day, and afterward return to prayer. The mind is kindled toward compunction, but the images of the things we have done revolve in the mind and hinder the intention of compunction in prayer. What we willingly did outwardly, we suffer inwardly against our will, as certain phantasms of thought scatter the mind through bodily images so that it cannot gather itself wholly and intensely in prayer. This too is the voice of the flesh.

But when we also subdue these things and drive all bodily images from the eyes of the mind, seeking within ourselves the very nature of the soul—what it is that can give life to the flesh but cannot restrain itself in good thoughts as it desires—we find an intellectual spirit living through the Creator’s power and giving life to the body it sustains, yet subject to forgetfulness and exposed to mutability, often afflicted by fear and uplifted by joy.

This intellect of the soul is its voice, because it sounds forth what it is; yet this voice is still beneath the firmament. But, transcending the soul, we seek the voice from the firmament when we inquire into the nature of that innumerable multitude of the holy angels in the sight of almighty God: what their unending festival of the vision of God is; what joy without decline; what ardor of love that does not torment but delights; how great in them is the desire for the vision of God together with satisfaction, and how great their satisfaction together with desire, since desire there produces no pain and satisfaction no weariness; how, by clinging to blessedness, they are blessed; how, by always contemplating eternity, they are eternal; how, joined to the true light, they have become light; and how, always gazing upon the unchangeable one, they have been changed into unchangeableness.

But when we think about these things concerning the angels, the voice is still from the firmament, not above the firmament. Let the mind therefore pass beyond them and transcend everything created. Let it fix the eyes of faith upon the light of its Creator alone: upon God, who gives life to all things and created all things; who is everywhere and wholly present everywhere; who, though uncircumscribed and incomprehensible, can be perceived but not seen; who is absent nowhere, yet is far from the thoughts of the wicked; who is not absent even where he is far away, because where he is not present by grace, he is present by vengeance.

He touches everything, yet does not touch everything equally. He touches some things so that they may exist, but not so that they may live and perceive, as is the case with all insensible things. He touches some so that they may exist, live, and perceive, but not so that they may discern, as is the case with brute animals. He touches some so that they may live, perceive, and discern, as is the case with human and angelic nature. Although he is never unlike himself, he touches unlike things in unlike ways.

He is present everywhere and can scarcely be found. We follow him while he stands, but cannot grasp him. Let us place before the eyes of the mind that nature which holds all things, fills all things, encompasses all things, surpasses all things, and sustains all things. It does not sustain them on one side while surpassing them on another, nor fill them on one side while encompassing them on another; rather, by encompassing, it fills; by filling, it encompasses; by sustaining, it surpasses; by surpassing, it sustains.

When the mind, concentrated upon this nature, considers its power, the voice above the firmament comes to be, because it has conceived an understanding that transcends even the perception of the angels through its incomprehensibility.

When the voice above the firmament comes to be, the living creatures stand and lower their wings, because the minds of the saints, when they consider the power of their Creator in attentive contemplation, regard the virtues they possess as insignificant. They become humble in their own eyes to the degree that what resounds above the angels is exalted in their sight.

Often the good works that the saints possess flatter their thoughts, so that their minds are lifted up in confidence in themselves. But they immediately return to the hidden judgments of God: how some fall from virtues into hell through pride, while others are lifted from vices into heaven through humility. Therefore the prophet, recalling us to humility, frightens and admonishes us, saying: “Come and see the works of the Lord, how terrifying he is in his counsels concerning the sons of men” (Psalm 65).

For who could worthily consider how great is the heavenly terror of God’s counsels, when one person proceeds from virtues to vices at the end, while another brings his life from vices to its conclusion in virtues? As Solomon says: “There are righteous people upon whom what belongs to the wicked comes, as though it were the work of the wicked; and there are wicked people upon whom what belongs to the righteous comes, as though it were the work of the righteous. There are righteous and wise people, yet their works are in the hand of God. Nevertheless, no one knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred, but all things are kept uncertain for the future” (Ecclesiastes 8–9). And: “There is a way that seems right to human beings, but its end leads to death” (Proverbs 14).

To consider these hidden and profound judgments: what else is this than to lower the wings—that is, to place no confidence in any virtue, but to tremble under great fear?

“‘And above the firmament that was over the heads of the living creatures there was the likeness of a throne, like the appearance of a sapphire stone; and above the likeness of the throne there was a likeness like the appearance of a human being above it,’ and so forth.”

(Jerome.) The firmament had the likeness of crystal for those who were below; but for those who were above, it appeared like a sapphire stone. This likeness of sapphire was the throne of the one who sat in the likeness of a human being. From this we understand that the firmament, the crystal, the sapphire, and the human being are displayed in likeness, not in reality.

Many testimonies teach that the human being should be understood as God the Father. Among them is the passage in the Gospel: “A certain man planted a vineyard and leased it to farmers,” and a little later, “He sent servants, and, after them all, his son” (Matthew 21). Again: “A man made a wedding feast for his son” (Matthew 22).

This does not exclude the Son from the kingdom, of whom Isaiah wrote: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne” (Isaiah 6), and John says: “Isaiah said these things when he saw the glory of the Son of God” (John 12). Rather, it means that the Father reigns, and the Son also, for all things belonging to the Son belong to the Father, “who is the image of the invisible God the Father.”

In Daniel also, God the Father is introduced as sitting, and the Son of Man is brought before him to receive the kingdom (Daniel 7). In John’s Apocalypse the same things are written concerning the Son (Revelation 3 and 7). At the contest of the first martyr Stephen, he is seen standing at the right hand of the Father (Acts 7), of whom it is sung in the Psalms: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool” (Psalm 109).

Just as the purest and most luminous things in the heavens are indicated by crystal, illuminating our bodily eyes, so in sapphire—that is, in the throne of God—and above the firmament, which we understand as heaven, the hidden, secret, and incomprehensible mysteries of God are displayed: “He made darkness his hiding place” (Psalm 17). He is seen in cloud and darkness. Hence it is also written in Exodus: “Under his feet there was something like a work of sapphire brick [stone], and like the appearance of the purest firmament of heaven” (Exodus 24).

Therefore the bride also describes the beauty of the bridegroom in the Song: “His belly is like a tablet of ivory upon a sapphire stone” (Song of Songs 5). And in John’s Apocalypse it is written: “The first foundation was jasper, the second sapphire” (Revelation 21). And on the breastpiece of the high priest, in the row and order of the individual stones: “The second row has a carbuncle, a sapphire, and a jasper” (Exodus 28).

[Gregory.] What is signified by the throne except those angelic virtues that surpass even the angels themselves by the dignity of their position? For although angels are called messengers (Hebrews 1), and angels often come to announce something to human beings, the Thrones are never read to have been sent on a mission of announcement. This is because the Creator of all things presides over them in a far more exalted manner.

Therefore the apostle Paul, describing the orders of the heavenly hosts that he had seen when he was caught up to the third heaven, says: “Whether thrones, dominions, principalities, or powers, all things were created through him and in him” (Colossians 1). He therefore named the Thrones before the orders of the angels, because he knew that the Thrones preside over them.

The throne is aptly compared to a sapphire stone, since the sapphire stone has an azure color. The heavenly virtues, therefore, are compared to a sapphire stone because those spirits over whom almighty God presides more exaltedly hold a higher dignity of place in the heavens.

“‘And above the throne there was a likeness of a human being.’” For above those virtues that precede even the angels stands the glory of our Redeemer.

We should note the order that is observed: above the living creatures is the firmament, above the firmament the throne, and above the throne the human being. For above holy human beings who still live in the corruption of the body are the angels; above the angels are the higher angelic powers that are nearer to God; and above the powers nearest to God is “the mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2).

But if, as we said earlier, the mediator between God and human beings should be understood by the word “firmament” because of the humanity he assumed—for the spirit of prophecy often signifies many things under a single name—then the voice above the firmament was the voice that sounded from heaven over the baptized Lord, saying: “You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Mark 1).

Let us therefore ask how the living creatures hear this voice and lower their wings. Let Habakkuk answer when questioned: “Lord, I heard your report and was afraid; I considered your works and was terrified” (Habakkuk 3).

The holy living creatures hear the voice above the firmament and are afraid because, when they look upon his innocence, they see that he alone is without sin and recognize how much they themselves sin daily—sins that must be lamented without ceasing. They also consider that the Author of life himself did not depart from this life without the pain of suffering.

This, too, was the voice above the firmament, because the judgment of the almighty Father concerning the death and resurrection of the Only-Begotten proceeded from him. When the voice above the firmament comes to be, the living creatures stand and lower their wings. For the saints too, when they see the Only-Begotten scourged in this world, lay aside whatever they presume concerning their own merits.

If he did not leave this world without the scourge, will those who came into it with sin not be worthy of scourges?

The firmament itself, which is above the heads of the living creatures—that is, which transcends the minds of the righteous—has a voice above it, because our Redeemer bore in the flesh the judgment which he had appointed with [*cum*; variant *ex*, “from”] the Father in his divinity. On hearing it, the righteous are frightened and lay aside every presumption in their own strength. However strong one may be in virtues, what is the life of sinners worthy of, if even his life, which was subject to no sin, underwent scourging for us?

But behold, a difficult question arises for us when it is said that above the firmament over the heads of the living creatures there was the likeness of a throne, like the appearance of a sapphire stone. If the Lord is signified by the firmament, and those highest angelic powers by the sapphire stone and the likeness of the throne, how can they be understood to be above the firmament—that is, above the Lord—when it is immediately added: “And above the likeness of the throne there was a likeness like the appearance of a human being above it”?

For if, as has been said, the firmament represents the Lord, and the human being is again understood as the Lord, how can he himself be understood both to be above the throne and beneath the throne?

But he himself resolves the tightly bound knots of this question—the one of whom we are speaking—because, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, he opened what had been closed. The Only-Begotten of the Father, having become incarnate, was, insofar as he “became human,” below the angels, as it is written concerning him: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Psalm 8).

Rising and ascending into heaven, he presides over all the angelic powers, as it is again written concerning him: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet.” And as he himself says: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me.”

The firmament is therefore beneath the throne, and the human being is above the throne, because through the nature of the humanity he assumed he was born beneath the angels and was exalted above the angels. Before he was exalted through the glory of the resurrection, he was above the angels in divinity; nevertheless, as has been said, he was made lower than the angels in humanity, through which he was also subject to death. After he trampled down death by rising again, he placed his humanity above even the angelic majesties.

Thus the throne is first described as above the firmament, and afterward the human being as above the throne, because the Redeemer of the human race, by descending, assumed his humanity beneath the angels, and by ascending, exalted it above the angels.

We say that he was made beneath the angels in the same way that we have heard the Apostle proclaim that he was made under the law (Galatians 4). We understand the humanity he assumed as beneath the angels because of that lowering in which he deigned to appear. For as soon as the Word became flesh, God as man was already in power above the angels.

Of him it is written before his passion: “Behold, angels came and ministered to him” (Matthew 4). Yet, to show the weakness of his humanity, it is again written of him: “An angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him” (Luke 22).

In the evidence of both natures, therefore, angels ministered to him, and an angel is described as strengthening him. He is one in both natures, because the one who existed as God before the ages became human at the end of the ages. Before his passion, angels ministered to him, and an angel strengthened him. After his passion and resurrection, angels can minister to him, but they can no longer strengthen him, because, as has been said, although the firmament formerly appeared beneath the throne, the human being is now above the throne.

To show that he had seen the union [*adunationem*; variant *adjunctionem*, “joining”] of both natures in this one's person, the holy prophet immediately added:

“And I saw what appeared to be amber, like the appearance of fire within him all around, from his loins upward; and from his loins downward I saw what appeared to be gleaming fire all around, like the appearance of a rainbow when it is in a cloud on a rainy day. This was the appearance of the splendor all around; this was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the Lord.”

(Jerome.) The likeness of a man who sat upon the likeness of a throne: that throne had the likeness of sapphire stone. From the loins upward he is compared with amber. This amber had, both within and without, the appearance of fire. From the loins downward there was resplendent fire all around, to show that those things above the loins, where sense and reason reside, do not need fire or flames but the most precious and purest metal. Those things, however, which are below the loins, where intercourse, generation, and the incitements of vices are found, need the cleansing of flames, so that, when purified, they may have the likeness of the rainbow, which is commonly called *Iris*, when it appears in a cloud on a rainy day. For ἴρις (*iris*), which in Holy Scripture (Gen. IX) is called the rainbow, and in the Apocalypse of John is likewise called ἴρις (Apoc. IV and X), cannot appear except in rain and a watery cloud. It consists of diverse and most beautiful colors, which gradually pass into one another.

This rainbow is a sign of God’s mercy and covenant, which he made with human beings, so that whenever it appears in a cloud we may know, after the example of ancient times, that we shall by no means again perish by a flood. From this it is shown that after punishments and penalties, and after the purification of sins, mercy will come—at least for those who have been deemed worthy to see God reigning.

Hence it is now said: “This was the appearance of the splendor all around.” Around God, or the throne, or all the things that were seen. “And this was the vision of the likeness of the glory of God.” Not that he saw the glory of the Lord, but the likeness of his glory.

This, then, is the whole vision: the spirit lifting up, the great cloud, the four living creatures, and the same number of wheels following the living creatures and the spirit, which were deemed worthy to be beneath God’s firmament. After these had been lifted up and had heard a voice like the voice of many waters, and like the voice of God’s sublime word, and the voice of camps and an army, they lowered their wings and displayed their astonishment in silence. And there appeared one sitting upon the likeness of sapphire, like the likeness of a man who, from the loins upward, had the appearance of amber, and from the loins downward the appearance of fire all around. After this terror, the sign of mercy is given, like the appearance of a rainbow when it is in a cloud on a rainy day.

(Gregory.) What is meant by the appearance of a man being seen upon the throne, like the appearance of amber, except that in amber, as we said much earlier, gold and silver are mixed so that one substance is made from two metals? In it, the brightness of gold is tempered by the silver, and through the brightness of gold the appearance of silver becomes bright.

In our Redeemer, however, both natures—that is, divinity and humanity—are united with one another without confusion and inseparably, so that through his humanity the brightness of his divinity might be tempered to our eyes, and through his divinity that human nature might become bright and, exalted, possess a splendor beyond what it had when created.

The appearance of the man upon the throne and the appearance of amber that he saw—what it was like, and how it appeared to him—he adds by describing it:

“Like the appearance of fire within him all around, from his loins upward, and from his loins downward I saw what appeared to be gleaming fire all around.”

What does it mean that Jesus Christ, the man who is the mediator between God and human beings (I Tim. II), is described as having, from the loins upward, the appearance of fire within, all around, and from the loins downward the appearance of gleaming fire all around? We must investigate why he is said to have fire within from the loins upward, but not gleaming fire. From the loins downward, however, he is said to have the appearance of fire, but is not said to have it within, since this is also made clear by the description.

For what is expressed by the name “loins” except the succession of mortality? For this reason it is also said of Levi (Gen. XIV) that he was still in his father’s loins when Melchizedek met Abraham. From Abraham’s loins the virgin Mary came forth, in whose womb the Only-Begotten of the Father graciously consented to become incarnate through the Holy Spirit. Through this incarnation God became known to the whole world, as the Psalmist also says:

“Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty” (Ps. XLIV).

The Most Mighty took up a sword around his thigh because his word of preaching grew powerful through the incarnation.

What does this fire signify except the ardor of the Holy Spirit, who sets alight the hearts he fills? Concerning this the Truth himself says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke XII).

What, then, does it mean that in this appearance of the man shown to the prophet, fire burns within and all around above the loins, while below the loins not fire within but fire gleams all around? It means that before the incarnation of our Only-Begotten Redeemer, only Judea within itself possessed the ardor of his love; but after his incarnation, fire gleamed all around him, because throughout the world he poured forth the brightness of the Holy Spirit among the nations.

Previously, therefore, there was fire within, but no splendor, because the Holy Spirit filled many regions of Judea, but his light had not yet shone forth to the knowledge of the nations. From his loins downward, however, fire gleams all around, because after he took flesh from the virgin, he spread the gifts of the Holy Spirit far and wide throughout the human race.

It should be noted that this fire is described as being all around above the loins, not externally but internally, because, as has been said, the flame of love filled Judea throughout its boundaries among the elect and spiritual men, yet did not go outside, because it did not spread among the multitude of the nations. This flame of ardor, which was seen afterward to gleam all around, began to increase throughout all the nations at the extremities of the world, as the love of almighty God.

This may also be understood in another way. Our Redeemer, our God and Lord Jesus Christ, became known to human beings through his humanity, though through his divinity he was known to the angels even before the incarnation. Therefore, below the loins he gleams all around for us, while the fire within him above the loins burns in heaven. The heavenly spirits behold him in his divinity and are kindled by the fire of his love. We, however, who love him because of the humanity he assumed, while we are still placed in this corruptible life, have the splendor of that fire externally.

Thus there is one beneath the throne who has fire within above the loins among the angels, and fire all around below the loins among human beings, because in everything loved by angels and in everything desired by human beings there is one who burns in the hearts of those who love.

“Like the appearance,” he says, “of a rainbow when it is in a cloud on a rainy day.”

Almighty God placed the rainbow as a sign between himself and human beings, so that he would not again destroy the world by a flood, saying:

“I shall set my bow in the clouds, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth. And when I cover the sky with clouds, my bow will appear in the clouds, and I shall remember my covenant with you” (Gen. IX).

Thus in that same rainbow the color of water and of fire is shown together, since in one part it is blue and in another part red, so that it may be a witness to both judgments: one that is to be carried out, and the other that has been carried out but will not be carried out again. For the world will indeed be consumed by the fire of judgment, but it will no longer be destroyed by the water of a flood.

What does it mean that the prophet saw gleaming fire from the loins of the man seated upon the throne, like the appearance of a rainbow when it is in a cloud on a rainy day? Since, as has been said, the fire signifies the ardor of the Holy Spirit, what likeness does the rainbow have to the Spirit, so that the fire that appeared might be said to have appeared like the appearance of a rainbow? If we pay attention to the rainbow vision mentioned above, we see how the rainbow signifies the Spirit.

In the rainbow, as I have said, water and fire appear; and after the coming of the Mediator, the power of the Holy Spirit shone forth in the human race in such a way that it washed God’s elect with the water of baptism and set them ablaze with the fire of divine love. As though made from the mingled color of water and fire, a kind of rainbow is placed in the cloud for propitiation when the Truth says:

“Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John III).

This rainbow is in a cloud on a rainy day because it is shown in the Lord’s incarnation and in the outpouring of preaching, so that the hearts of believers may be recalled to forgiveness as the Lord shows mercy.

We may appropriately understand the cloud as the flesh of the Redeemer. Concerning it the Psalmist says:

“He makes the cloud his ascent.”

He made the cloud his ascent because the one who is everywhere through his divinity ascended to heavenly things in the flesh.

After the entire mystical vision has been completed, it is added:

“This was the appearance of the splendor all around, and this was the vision of the likeness of the glory of God.”

Observing what the grace of the Holy Spirit does throughout the whole world, he says: “This was the appearance of the splendor all around.” But wishing to consider what glory of that same Holy Spirit remains within, yet unable to see it as it truly is, he adds: “And this was the vision of the likeness of the glory of the Lord.” For he does not say, “the vision of the glory,” but “the likeness of the glory of the Lord.”

This shows that however intently the human mind may stretch itself—even if it already restrains from thought all bodily images and fantasies, and has removed from the eyes of the heart all circumscribed spirits—so long as it remains placed in mortal flesh, it cannot see the glory of God as it is. Whatever of that glory shines in the mind is a likeness, not the glory itself.

Hence that preacher who had been caught up to the third heaven said:

“Now we see through a mirror and in a riddle” (I Cor. XIII).

In this matter a question arises that should not be disregarded: how is it that John the Evangelist, after describing the unbelief of the Jews regarding the miracles of our Redeemer, also from the prophetic words, adds:

“Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory, and spoke of him” (John XII)?

If Ezekiel saw not the glory but the likeness of the glory, what does it mean that one is described as having seen the likeness of the glory and the other as having seen the glory?

But when John the Evangelist first narrated the miracles of our Redeemer and afterward added the unbelief of the Jews, he showed that Isaiah had seen the glory of that same Redeemer which appeared in the world. Everything miraculous that is divinely accomplished on earth is the glory of almighty God, and his glory is seen in all his works.

Isaiah therefore saw his glory on earth; Ezekiel, however, could not see his glory in heaven as it truly is. For it is one thing to see his glory in created works, and another to see it in himself. This glory of his, which exists in created things, can be seen. But that glory which is in him cannot now be seen except through a likeness. Yet if the prophet, once lifted up, was able to bear that same likeness of the glory, let us acknowledge it.

## CHAPTER II. The Prophet Is Sent to Recall the People from Their Errors

“And I saw, and I fell upon my face.”

(Jerome.) He was not lifted up by the greatness of the visions, but fell upon his face through awareness of human frailty. Hence the Apostle Paul, after his ascent to the heavenly paradise and hearing ineffable words, says that an angel of Satan was given to him to buffet him, lest he be exalted (I Cor. XII). Abraham also fell upon his face after hearing the words of God.

Yet because he had fallen not through sin but through humility, he was raised up by the Lord and commanded to hear his words.

It should also be known that falling upon one’s face is different from falling backward. After Abraham heard about the birth of Isaac, he fell upon his face and laughed (Gen. XV and XVIII). Eli, however, who had sinned, fell backward (I Kings II). And concerning Dan it is written in Genesis:

“Let Dan be a serpent on the path, biting the horse’s heel, and let the rider fall backward, awaiting the salvation of God” (Gen. XLIX).

Because he had fallen from the horse at the serpent’s bite, he therefore awaits the coming of the Savior. And in the Gospel according to John, those who had come to seize the Lord, after he answered, “I am,” fell backward upon the ground (John XVIII), unable to endure the word of the one who had said to Moses: “Go, say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. III).

“And I saw,” he says, “and I fell upon my face.”

(Gregory.) What would happen to this man if he had seen the glory itself as it is, since, seeing the likeness of that glory, he fell because he could not endure it? In this matter we should ponder and consider with great sorrow and tears into what misery and weakness we have fallen, since we cannot bear even that good for the sight of which we were created.

There is, however, another matter we should consider in the prophet’s action as it applies to us. Since we cannot see the likeness of the Lord’s glory through the prophetic spirit, we ought constantly to recognize and diligently contemplate it in sacred Scripture, in heavenly admonitions, and in spiritual commandments.

When we perceive something of God, we fall upon our face because we blush for the evils we remember having committed. A person falls there where he is ashamed. Hence Paul spoke as though to certain people lying prostrate:

“What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. VI).

After the prophet had contemplated the likeness of the Lord’s glory and fallen upon his face, he adds:

“And I heard the voice of one speaking, and he said to me, ‘Son of man, stand upon your feet, and I shall speak with you.’”

It is then added:

“And the spirit entered into me after he spoke to me, and set me upon my feet, etc.”

Behold, the divine voice commanded the fallen prophet to rise. But he could not have risen at all unless the spirit of almighty God had entered into him. For by the grace of almighty God we can indeed strive toward good works, but we cannot accomplish them if he himself does not help us—the one who commands.

Thus Paul, when admonishing the disciples, said:

“Work out your salvation with fear and trembling” (Phil. II).

Immediately he added who would work these very good things in them:

“For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure” (ibid.).

Hence the Truth himself says to the disciples:

“Without me you can do nothing” (John XV).

But in this we must consider: if our good works are so entirely gifts of almighty God that nothing in them belongs to us, why do we seek eternal recompense as though for merits? If, however, they are ours in such a way that they are not gifts of almighty God, why do we give thanks to almighty God for them?

It must be understood that only our evil deeds are ours, whereas our good deeds belong both to almighty God and to us. He himself precedes us by inspiring us to will, and follows by helping us, so that we do not will in vain but are able to accomplish what we will. Thus, when grace precedes and good will follows, what is the gift of almighty God becomes our merit.

(Jerome.) “And he said to me,” he says, “‘Son of man, stand upon your feet, and I shall speak to you.’” While lying down, he could not hear the word of God. But he hears, together with Moses: “But stand here with me.” Daniel also recalls that this happened to him.

(Gregory.) The order of speech and action must be observed. First the likeness of the Lord’s glory appears in order to cast him down; afterward he addresses him in order to raise him; then he sends the spirit of overflowing grace to lift him and set him upon his feet.

For unless we saw something of eternity in our minds, we would never fall upon our face in repentance. But once we are lying prostrate, the Lord’s voice consoles us so that we may rise to action, although we cannot do this by our own strength. His spirit therefore fills and lifts us and sets us upon our feet, so that we who lay face down in repentance for our guilt may afterward stand upright in good works.

Hence it follows:

“And the spirit entered into me,” he says, “after he spoke to me, and set me upon my feet.”

These matters having thus been explained in the present book, after the prophet stood upright at the Lord’s command, we must consider at the beginning of the following book what the divine voice commanded him.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0549]

## CHAPTER II FOLLOWS

[Col. 0549D]

“And I heard the voice of one speaking to me and saying: ‘Son of man, I am sending you to the children of Israel, to apostate nations that have departed from me,’ etc.”

(Gregory.) Thus the prophet describes his own experiences so that he may signify ours. For what does it mean that the one lying prostrate is told, “Stand upon your feet, and I shall speak with you”? The one who spoke to him while he was lying down—why does he promise to speak with him only when he is standing?

It must be understood that there are things we ought to hear while lying down and other things while standing. The one lying down is told to rise again. The one standing is commanded that he must go forth to preaching.

While we are still lying in the confusion of weakness, the authority of preaching should not yet be entrusted to us. But when we have already risen in good works, when we have begun to stand upright, it is fitting that we should be sent to preaching in order to win others.

The prophet, therefore, standing, saw a spiritual vision; and he fell. Having fallen, he received words of admonition instructing him to rise. Having risen, he heard the command to preach.

For when we still stand upon the summit of pride, but have begun to feel something of the fear of eternity, it is fitting that we should fall into repentance. And when, carefully recognizing our weakness, we have humbly lain prostrate, we are commanded through the consolation of the divine word to rise to stronger works.

When we have already persevered in the firmness of good works, it is necessary that we should now lift up others by preaching the very means through which we corrected ourselves.

The one lying prostrate is not commanded to proceed to preaching, lest a weak person destroy by his actions what he can build up by his words. Hence the Psalmist rightly says:

“He brought me out of the pit of misery and from the mire of filth. And he set my feet upon a rock and directed my steps. He put a new song into my mouth, a hymn to our God.”

First he is led out of the mire of wickedness, so that through faith his feet may be made firm upon the rock. But because right action ought to follow right faith, his steps were directed, so that after the direction of his steps—that is, after the perfection of good works—he might also receive in his mouth the new song of preaching.

Thus Paul, while proceeding proudly toward Damascus, lay prostrate after being struck down by the Redeemer’s voice. Although he was destined to become a preacher, he did not immediately hear that he should preach what he had seen. Rather, while lying prostrate, he was told:

“Enter the city, and it will be told you what you ought to do” (Acts IX).

While lying prostrate, therefore, he could hear only that, once risen, he would learn what he was to hear. Having risen, he learned that he was to preach what he had come to know.

(Jerome.) Ezekiel is frequently addressed as “Son of man,” and Daniel rarely. Both of them, in the person of the one who said, “The Son of man has nowhere to lay his head,” console the captive people and draw them back to repentance.

“I am sending you,” he says, “to the children of Israel, to apostate nations that have departed from me. They and their fathers have transgressed my covenant to this very day, etc.”

He calls them not the people of God, Israel, but apostate nations—those who have departed from the Lord. He says not only their fathers but also their sons, not so that the sons might appear liable for their fathers’ sin, but so that the impiety of both fathers and sons might be equal.

Moreover, what the Septuagint translated as “provoking me,” or “turning me into bitterness,” signifies that God, who is by nature kind and sweet, is changed into bitterness by our vices. For it is said to the saints:

“Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. XXXIII).

Sinners, however, experience him as bitter. Hence the Apostle speaks of God’s goodness and severity toward saints and sinners. And concerning sinners who lay prostrate it is written:

“The Lord raises up those who are crushed; the Lord loves the righteous; the Lord frees those who are bound” (Ps. CXLV).

To those who stand as saints he promises rewards.

(Gregory.) It should be noted that it is said:

“I am sending you to the children of Israel, to apostate nations that have departed from me.”

Just as there are two ways of departing from God, so human beings become apostates from God in two ways. Each person departs from his Creator either in faith or in action. Therefore, just as the one who departs in faith is an apostate, so the one who returns to the perverse work he had abandoned is undoubtedly counted an apostate from almighty God, even if he appears to retain the faith.

One without the other is of no benefit, because neither faith without works nor works without faith are helpful—unless perhaps they are performed in order to receive faith. Thus Cornelius first merited being heard through good works, before he became a believer.

From this it follows that he performed good works in order to receive faith. For when the angel said to him:

“Your prayers and your almsgiving have ascended as a memorial in the sight of God” (Acts X),

and immediately, on account of that ascent, commanded him to send for Simon, who was to come and preach to him, it is clear that he sought that by which he merited being heard.

“And the sons are hard of face and unyielding of heart, to whom I am sending you,” etc.

(Jerome.) This is not found in the Septuagint. It is a sign of great mercy that God sends someone to such people without despairing of their salvation, and of prophetic confidence that he does not fear going to them.

By “unyielding heart” and “hard face” we should understand what is said to the sinner:

“Your neck is an iron sinew, and your forehead bronze.”

In what follows they are reproved for their stony hearts, which God says he will remove and replace with flesh, so that in its softness it may receive God’s commandments.

“And you shall say to them: ‘Thus says the Lord God: If perhaps they themselves will hear, and if perhaps they will cease, for they are an exasperating house, and they shall know that a prophet has been among them,’ etc.”

Something similar is written in Jeremiah:

“If perhaps they will hear and repent.”

And in the Gospel:

“Perhaps they will fear my son.”

God speaks these words in the manner of one expressing uncertainty, in order to show the freedom of the human will, lest the foreknowledge of future evil or good make immutable what God knows will happen.

It is not necessary that we do something because he knows beforehand that we will do it. Rather, he knows as God what we will do by our own will.

(Gregory.) Here is one fault of pride: they have transgressed the covenant. Here is another, that of stubbornness: “to this very day.” Here, in the wickedness of the sons, is the grave fault of shamelessness: they are hard of face because they no longer feel shame for the evils they commit, and they never return to repentance after their sins because they are unyielding of heart.

But when those to whom the prophet is sent are guilty of such great wickedness and stubbornness, who would not see that the prophet’s person could also be despised by perverse people?

Yet the authority of his person is granted when it is added:

“And you shall say to them: ‘Thus says the Lord God.’”

It is as though it were plainly said: “Because you will be despised on your own account, you must speak with my voice. Do not yourself, who are sent, be despised; by proclaiming my words, show the one who sent you.”

It follows:

“If perhaps they will hear, and if perhaps they will cease, for they are an exasperating house.”

Since it is certain that almighty God knows everything, it is very surprising that he says, “If perhaps they will hear, and if perhaps they will cease.”

Therefore we must understand that this uncertainty in God’s speech does not arise from ignorance but from some symbolic meaning. For who does not know that the one who made and sees all things knows all things?

The Truth himself says in the Gospel concerning the preachers of Antichrist:

“They will give great signs and wonders, so that, if it were possible, even the elect might be led into error” (Matt. XXIV).

Why is this said with uncertainty when the Lord foreknows what will happen? There is one of two possibilities: if they are elect, it cannot happen; but if it can happen, they are not elect. Yet it is still said: “so that, if it were possible, even the elect might be led into error.”

The uncertainty in the Lord’s words therefore signified a temptation in the hearts of the elect. Those who are elect will be tempted to fall by the signs of the preachers of Antichrist, in order that they may persevere.

Through the words “if it were possible,” it is therefore expressed that the elect will be tempted in heart: they waver, but do not fall. God says “if it were possible” because they will tremble, yet they are called elect because they do not fall.

Thus the uncertainty of the Lord’s speech expresses a trembling of mind in the elect, whom he calls elect because he sees that they persist in faith and good works.

Hence here too it is said:

“If perhaps they will hear, and if perhaps they will cease.”

By the words “if perhaps” it is shown that only a few from the great multitude will hear.

What else, then, is signified by the uncertainty of God’s words except the small number of hearers?

Let us consider, I beg you, what power is contained in this effect of the Lord’s words, when he says, “If perhaps they themselves will hear.”

He says this openly to us because, afflicted, besieged, and confined, we have lost all the goods that we possessed in this world. We have seen cities torn down, camps overturned, fields laid waste, and churches dug up from their foundations. Yet even now we follow our ancestors in their iniquities and are not changed by the pride we saw in them.

They sinned amid joys; we, what is more grievous, sin even amid scourges.

But behold, almighty God, judging iniquities, has already taken away our predecessors and summoned them to judgment. He still awaits us for repentance; he bears with us so that we may return. He who has already exercised judgment upon them prolongs for us the patience of his forbearance, lest he destroy us together with our predecessors, saying:

“If perhaps they themselves will hear, and if perhaps they will cease, for they are an exasperating house.”

Every soul, even after receiving faith, is called an exasperating house if it either remains in its perversity or returns to it. For it drives away from itself by wicked behavior God, whom it had received as an inhabitant through faith.

A house is inhabited by its master. If it is a house, why is it exasperating? But if it is exasperating, why is it a house, since it will no longer be inhabited? It is a house because God had begun to dwell in it through faith. It is exasperating because, driven out by wicked behavior, he has departed from it, leaving empty the house that its heavenly inhabitant had previously filled.

Hence, as we have also learned from the voice of the Truth, the most wicked spirit, returning with seven other spirits, finds the house swept clean, because he fills a mind that has been separated from virtues.

It follows:

“And they shall know that a prophet has been among them.”

For the wicked, knowing the good often serves either to aid their salvation or to testify to their condemnation. They shall therefore know that a prophet has been among them, so that, after hearing the preaching, they may either be helped to rise or be condemned in such a way that they have no excuse.

“Therefore you, son of man, do not fear them, nor be afraid of their words, for they are unbelieving and subversive toward you, and you dwell among scorpions. Do not fear their words, and do not be terrified by their faces, for they are an embittering house,” and so forth. (Jerome.) Although they are stiff-necked and have an ungovernable heart, nevertheless my commands are stronger than they are. Do not think that you have been deceived if you are sent to people who will not listen to you as you speak. Behold, I foretell to you that they will rage, gather against you, and surround you, leaving you no means of escape. They will do this because they are [Col. 0554B] unbelieving and despise the commands of God.

(Gregory.) It is clear to what perverse people he is sent to preach, since he is warned not to fear. And because all the wicked do other evil things to those who speak good to them, and threaten still further evils, he is told, with regard to what they do: “Do not fear them.” With regard to what they threaten, it is added: “Nor be afraid of their words.” Or certainly, because the reprobate inflict evil upon the good and continually disparage their actions, the prophet who is sent is admonished not to fear either their cruelty or their words. In the command, therefore, “Do not fear,” authority for preaching is given to the prophet.

And because all who live in God are instruments of truth—so that he often speaks to me through another, and often to others through me—we ought to possess such authority in speaking a good word that the one who presides may freely speak what is right, and the one who is subject may not refuse humbly to offer what is good. [Col. 0554C] For what is said by an inferior to a superior is truly good only if it is said humbly. If uprightness of judgment loses humility in speech, it corrupts the root of its thought in the branch of the tongue. This fault is no longer merely in the branch but in the root, since the tongue would not become proud unless the heart had become swollen.

The one who is first, therefore, ought to possess humble authority in speaking; the lesser, free humility. Freedom and pride, humility and fear, must always be distinguished, lest fear pretend to be humility, or pride pretend to be freedom. Since Ezekiel was sent to speak not only to the people but also to the elders, [Col. 0554D] he is warned not to mistake careless fear for humility, when he is told: “Do not fear them.” And lest he be afraid of their disparaging words, it is added: “Nor be afraid of their words.”

The reason why he should not fear the tongues of those who disparage him is also supplied, when it immediately follows: “For they are unbelieving and subversive toward you, and you dwell among scorpions.”

(Jerome.) Each person receives a name according to his character. Thus the scribes and Pharisees are called “a brood of vipers.” Of Herod, who was changeable and cunning, it is said: “Go and tell that fox” (Luke 13). The false prophets are compared to foxes in this same prophet. Now people with an ungovernable heart are called scorpions. Hence we also read in the Gospel: [Col. 0555A] “All who came before me were thieves and robbers, and the sheep did not listen to them” (John 10). How, then, did the lost sheep of the house of Israel listen to their adversaries? It is thereby shown that those who listened to thieves and robbers lost the name of sheep and assumed other names, so that they perished not as sheep but as vipers, foxes, and scorpions.

(Gregory.) These people would have been worthy of fear by the one sent to speak to them if they had pleased almighty God in faith and conduct. But because they are unbelieving and subversive, disparaging others in their speech, they are not to be feared. It is exceedingly foolish to seek to please those whom we know do not please God.

The judgments of the righteous ought to be held in fear and reverence, because they are members of almighty God. What these people condemn on earth, the Lord will condemn from heaven. The disparagement of the wicked is therefore [Col. 0555B] an approval of our life, because it is already shown that we possess some measure of righteousness when we begin to displease those who do not please God. No one can be pleasing in one and the same matter both to the almighty Lord and to his enemies. Whoever pleases God’s enemy denies himself to be God’s friend; and whoever is subject in mind to the truth will oppose the enemies of that same truth.

Therefore holy men, inflamed with the freedom of their rebukes, do not fear to rouse against themselves the hatred of those whom they know do not love God. The prophet displayed this ardor and offered it to the Creator of all as a gift, saying: “Do I not hate those who hate you, Lord, and waste away because of your enemies? I hate them with perfect hatred; they have become enemies to me” (Psalm 138). It is as though he openly said: “Consider how greatly I love you, since I do not fear to provoke against myself the hostility of your enemies.”

Thus the righteous, just as they sometimes speak without arrogance [Col. 0555C] about the good deeds they perform, so they rebuke without a zeal for private glory the tongues of those who disparage them, because those tongues speak harmful things. When the tongues of those who disparage cannot be corrected, they must be endured in every respect with equanimity. The speech of slander must not be feared, lest, while the reproach of the wicked is feared, the path of upright conduct be abandoned.

Hence Ezekiel the prophet is now told: “Do not be afraid of their words, for they are unbelieving and subversive toward you.” These people would be less evil if those who are unbelieving were not also subversive. Because they themselves believe neither in the rewards of the heavenly kingdom nor in the punishments of Gehenna, [Col. 0555D] they have been abandoned to their wickedness and also subvert others from faith and good works, so that no one else may attain the kingdom they themselves do not wish to seek.

When such people discover that some more tender souls have begun to practice good and avoid evil, they turn them aside in various ways: sometimes by mocking what is promised in heaven, sometimes by belittling what almighty God threatens concerning the punishments of hell, and sometimes by praising temporal goods and cunningly promising the pleasures of the present age. They bend the minds of the innocent and pervert their paths. They rejoice if they can recall anyone from life and drag him to death; they delight in their own wickedness and exult in that of others. Their own punishment is not enough for them, since they act so that they will not die alone.

But if they happen to encounter someone so just and so virtuous [Col. 0556A] that they do not dare to speak against him, then, because they cannot subvert him, they immediately become scorpions. A scorpion advances by touching gently, but strikes with its tail; it does not bite from the front but harms from behind. Thus all who are flattering and malicious are scorpions: they do not resist the good to their faces, but as soon as they have withdrawn, they disparage them, stir up others whom they can, inflict whatever harm they are able, and do not cease secretly to bring about deadly injury.

They are scorpions who appear flattering and harmless to the face but carry behind their backs the means by which they may pour out poison; they strike in secret, as though secretly dragging death behind them. Hence the Psalmist also says: “They surrounded me like bees, and they burned like fire among thorns” (Psalm 118). Bees have honey in their mouths but a wound in the stinger of their tails. All who flatter with their tongues but secretly strike out of malice are bees: by speaking they offer the sweetness of honey, but by secretly striking they inflict a wound.

“You shall speak my words to them, if perhaps they will hear and fear, or desist, for they are provocateurs,” and so forth. [Col. 0556B]

(Jerome.) We must not cease speaking to the wicked, even though they are evil, but, according to the Apostle (2 Timothy 4), must preach the word of God in season and out of season. It may happen that the hard-hearted person is corrected into gentleness, and that the obedient person, having changed his will, may not listen.

(Gregory.) Let it therefore be said: “They are unbelieving and subversive toward you, and you dwell among scorpions.” They are unbelieving with regard to God; subversive with regard to their weaker neighbors; and scorpions even with regard to the strong and steadfast, whom, although they do not dare [Col. 0556C] contradict to their faces, they nevertheless secretly wound with disparagement.

The unbelieving are at the same time subversive and scorpions, because, although they hear what belongs to God, they do not believe it; they subvert from good conduct those whom they can overcome; and those whom they cannot bend they strike by hidden schemes.

In this connection we must also note that when the prophet is told, “They are unbelieving and subversive toward you, and you dwell among scorpions,” a medicine of consolation is offered to us, who are often wearied of living because we do not wish to dwell among the wicked. We complain that not all those who live with us are good. If we refuse to bear the evils of our neighbors, we decide that all ought already to be saints, since we do not wish to be what we must bear from our neighbors.

But in this matter it is as clear as daylight [Col. 0556D] that, when we refuse to bear the wicked, we ourselves still possess much less goodness than we should. Often, when we complain about the lives of our neighbors, we try to change our place and choose the privacy of a more secluded life, ignorant that, if the spirit is absent, the place does not help. Lot, of whom we speak, was holy in Sodom but sinned on the mountain (Genesis 18–19). Since places do not protect the mind, the first parent of the human race himself bears witness to this: he fell even in paradise. But all that we are saying is still drawn from earthly examples. If a place could save, Satan would not have fallen from heaven.

Therefore the Psalmist, perceiving that temptations exist everywhere in this world, sought a place to which he might flee, but could not find a secure place without God (Psalm 18). [Col. 0557A] For this reason he also asked that God himself become his place, saying: “Be for me a protecting God and a fortified place, so that you may save me” (Psalm 30).

Our neighbors must therefore be endured everywhere, since no one can become Abel unless Cain’s malice exercises him. There is, however, one reason why the company of the wicked must be avoided: lest, if they cannot be corrected, they draw us into imitation and, while they themselves are not changed from their wickedness, corrupt those who have joined themselves to them. Hence Paul says: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Corinthians 15); and as Solomon says: “Do not be a friend to an angry man, nor walk with a furious man, lest perhaps you learn his ways and take snares for your soul” (Proverbs 22).

Just as perfect men [Col. 0557B] ought not to flee from perverse neighbors, because they often draw them toward uprightness and are never themselves drawn into perversity, so the weak ought to avoid the company of the wicked, lest they take pleasure in imitating the evils they frequently see but cannot correct. We daily take into our minds the speech of our neighbors just as, by blowing and breathing, we draw air into our bodies. As foul air, drawn in continually, infects the body, so perverse speech, heard continually, infects the mind of the weak, causing it to waste away in delight in evil deeds and in the constant wickedness of speech.

It follows: “Do not fear their words, and do not be terrified by their faces, for they are an embittering house.” It is as though it were said openly: “They would be worthy of fear if they did not embitter me by their actions.” Concerning them it is further added: “Therefore you shall speak my words to them, whether perhaps they will listen and be quiet, for they are provocateurs.”

Everyone who sins—what else does he do but provoke the anger of his Creator against himself? [Col. 0557C] We know that whenever we sin in deed, in word, or in thought, we provoke God against us. Yet he bears with us and mercifully waits through his patience, while through his preachers he extends to us the word of exhortation. Every preacher who proclaims what is right, if he is heard, appeases the anger of the provoked Creator toward the transgressing people.

He must therefore take care not to do himself the evil that ordinarily provokes the Creator’s fury among the people. For this reason it is also added: “But you, son of man, hear whatever I speak to you, and do not be an embittering one, like an embittering house,” and so forth. That is: Do not yourself do the evils you see being done, lest you commit what you were sent to prohibit.

Every preacher must therefore weigh this attentively in his mind: [Col. 0557D] lest he who was sent to raise up the fallen should himself fall with them in the perversity of his conduct. Why is blessed Ezekiel, who is sent to preach, forbidden to be an embittering one? Because, unless he obeyed when he was sent to speak the words, he would have embittered almighty God by his silence, just as the people embittered him by their perverse conduct.

For just as the wicked embitter God by speaking or doing evil, so the good sometimes embitter him by withholding what is good. The guilt of the former is to do what is perverse; that of the latter is to keep silent about what is right. In this respect the good, together with the wicked, embitter God, because when they do not rebuke what is perverse, they grant the wicked, through their silence, permission to advance in evil.

It follows:

[Col. 0558A] “Open your mouth and eat whatever I give you.”

(Jerome.) “Make yourself worthy,” he says, “of my words, and receive spiritual food,” so that, just as the Gospel says, “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear,” so here it may be said: “Whoever has an open mouth for eating, let him eat.”

Hence the Lord also says to the Psalmist: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Psalm 80). And he replies: “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit” (Psalm 118). The apostle Paul, who possessed within himself “the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2), and in whom Christ the Lord was speaking, writes to the Corinthians: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians” (2 Corinthians 6). Matthew also reports concerning the Savior: “Opening his mouth, he taught them” (Matthew 5).

(Gregory.) We open our mouth when we speak what is right, [Col. 0558B] and we eat what we receive from God, because the food of life is both given and increased in our understanding when we begin to preach. Hence another prophet says: “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit.” He would not have drawn it in unless he had opened his mouth, because, unless he had devoted himself to preaching to his neighbors, the grace of spiritual teaching would not have increased in him.

It follows:

“And I saw, and behold, a hand was sent to me.”

(Jerome.) For “a hand sent,” the Septuagint translated “an outstretched hand,” which is sent and extended to those who receive the Lord’s benefits. It is withdrawn from those to whom he speaks through the prophet: “Has the hand of the Lord become shortened and contracted?” (Isaiah 50). And in the Psalm: “Why do you turn your hand away, and your right hand, from the midst of your bosom, forever?” (Psalm 73).

Finally, in his Passion he extended his wings [Col. 0558C] and received his disciples, carrying them on his shoulders. He said: “All day long I spread out my hands to a disobedient people” (Isaiah 65), so that he might gather the children of Israel as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings. Through the extension of Moses’ hands, Israel overcame Amalek.

“In it was a book rolled up, and he spread it out before me. It was written inside and outside, and written in it were lamentations, a song, and woe,” and so forth.

For “a rolled-up book,” the Septuagint translated “the beginning of the book”: [Col. 0558D] “In the hand of the Lord who sits upon the throne, which was sent and extended.” Concerning this it is also said in the Psalms: “In the beginning of the book it is written concerning me” (Psalm 39). Let us understand “beginning” as the opening.

This book, rolled up, sealed, and written inside and outside—that is, before and behind—was of such difficulty that no one could open it and read it, either in heaven, on earth, or under the earth, except the Lion from the tribe of Judah, the Root of David and Jesse, whom John in the Apocalypse said had devoured it—not the whole book, but its beginning, that is, its opening. For it is impossible for human nature to devour all the treasures of this book.

He spread it out before the prophet and offered it to him to read and understand. In Isaiah this book is said to be sealed for the unbelieving people. To this day the veil remains placed over the Jews in the Old Testament. [Col. 0559A] It was written before and behind: concerning future and past events—or, alternatively, outside in the literal letter of history, and inside in spiritual understanding.

(Gregory.) The book is rolled up when the utterance of sacred Scripture is obscure, wrapped in the depth of its meanings so that its sense is not easily penetrated. But the book is spread out before the prophet because the obscurity of sacred speech is opened before preachers.

The Lord had extended a rolled-up book when he said to the apostles: “The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field. But while the men were sleeping, his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat, and went away. When the grass had grown and produced fruit, then the weeds also appeared,” and so forth (Matthew 13).

But he spread out the book he had shown as rolled up [Col. 0559B] when he explained what he had spoken in riddles, saying: “He who sows the good seed is the Son of Man. The field is the world. The good seed—these are the children of the kingdom; the weeds are the children of the evil one. The enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the end of the age; the reapers are angels. Therefore, just as the weeds are gathered and burned with fire, so it will be at the end of the age.”

The rolled-up book is therefore spread out when what had been uttered obscurely is opened through the breadth of understanding. Truth spread out this rolled-up book when he did in the disciples what is written: “Then he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures.”

Concerning this book it is further said: “It was written [Col. 0559C] inside and outside.” The book of sacred speech is written inside through allegory, outside through history; inside through spiritual understanding, outside through the simple sense of the letter, which is suited to those who are still weak. Inside, because it promises invisible things; outside, because it orders visible things through the righteousness of its commands. Inside, because it promises heavenly things; outside, because it teaches how earthly and contemptible things are either to be used or avoided as objects of desire.

It follows:

“And written in it were lamentations, a song, and woe.”

(Rabanus.) Sacred Scripture also contains lamentations, a song, and woe. It proclaims joy concerning hope in such a way that it nevertheless indicates pressures and troubles in the present. For if we desire sweet things there, we must first endure bitter things here.

The Lord preached both song and woe to his disciples [Col. 0559D] when he said: “I have spoken these things to you so that you may have peace in me; in the world you will have tribulation” (John 16). It is as though he openly said: “Let there be within you, from me, what may restore you by consolation, since from the world there will be outside you what will oppress you grievously through its violence.”

Alternatively, Scripture contains lamentations concerning those who are summoned to repentance, just as Samuel and the apostle Paul mourned and grieved over Saul and the Corinthians, whom they desired to save. It contains a song concerning those who are worthy of God’s testimony, to whom the Psalmist commands: “Sing to the Lord a new song” (Psalm 95). Woe, moreover, is pronounced over those who are utterly without hope and, when they have entered the depths of sins, despise their condition.

(Gregory.) There is no doubt that “song” is sometimes spoken of in a good sense and sometimes in a bad sense, since we can speak both of a joyful song and of a mournful song. But following the usage of sacred Scripture, which almost always places “song” in connection with prosperity, we understand “song” in this passage in a good sense.

When almighty God had delivered his people from the Red Sea, it is written: “Then Moses and the children of Israel sang a song to the Lord” (Exodus 15). And when David had gained victory over his enemies, it is written: “David spoke to the Lord the words of this song” (2 Samuel 22).

Solomon also says: [Col. 0560A] “Vinegar on nitre, and one who sings songs with a very wicked heart” (Proverbs 25). When vinegar is poured onto nitre, the nitre immediately becomes hot and boils over. Likewise, when a perverse mind is corrected by reproof and good things are commended through the sweetness of preaching, it becomes worse through correction and is inflamed with the wickedness of murmuring by the very means through which it ought to have been restrained from evil.

In sacred Scripture, “woe” is more often [Col. 0560B] understood of eternal grief than of present grief. Hence it is written: “Woe to the wicked, it shall be ill with him; the recompense of his hands shall be given to him” (Isaiah 3). Blessed Job says: “If I am wicked, woe is me; if I am righteous, I will not lift up my head, filled with affliction and misery” (Job 10). The affliction of the righteous is temporal. Therefore the one who spoke of woe distinguished it from temporal affliction, asserting that the righteous have affliction and the wicked have woe.

Truth itself also says: “Woe to the world because of scandals” (Matthew 18); and: “Woe to you who laugh, for you shall mourn” (Luke 6); and: “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in those days” (Luke 21).

We must therefore consider how these three things are written in the sacred volume: [Col. 0560C] “Lamentations, a song, and woe.” Lamentations, because repentance for sins is written in it; a song, because the joys of the righteous are proclaimed there; and woe, because the condemnation of the reprobate is expressed there.
