If you wish to punish your sins, read the lamentation written in this volume: “Tear your hearts and not your garments” (Joel 2). Again: “Be wretched and mourn. Let your laughter be turned into mourning and your joy into sorrow” (James 4).

If you wish to rejoice over the promise of future joy, learn the reason: in this volume songs of eternal praise are written. “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; forever and ever they shall praise you” (Psalm 83). And, as a certain wise man says concerning the heavenly Jerusalem: “All its streets shall be paved with precious and pure stone, and alleluia shall be sung through all its lanes” (Tobit 13).

The citizens of the heavenly homeland had come to announce this song to us, [Col. 0560D] crying out together: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2). But if you still cling in mind to the present age, if you still take pleasure in earthly desires, you cannot love the eternal joys you hear about. Therefore recognize in this volume the woe written in it, and drive from your heart through fear what you love, so that you may be able, on the basis of judgment, to love the song you read.

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0561A] The prophet is fed with the book and sent to the children of the captivity. He saw the glory of God in the plain, and so forth.

“And he said to me: Son of man, whatever you find, eat.”

(Gregory.) Whatever is found in sacred Scripture must be eaten, because its small matters establish a simple life, while its great matters build subtle understanding.

“Eat this book and go, speak to the children of Israel.”

(Jerome.) Unless we have first eaten the opened book, we cannot teach the children of Israel. Thus David, after he himself had received mercy, says: “I will teach transgressors your ways, and the wicked shall be converted to you” (Psalm 50).

“And I opened my mouth, and he fed me with that book.”

“I opened my mouth,” he says, because I was told: [Col. 0561B] “Open your mouth and eat.” When I had opened my mouth, the Lord generously supplied food. The beginnings of willing are therefore to be in us, while the perfection of blessedness is received from the Lord: “not of him who wills or of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy.” Nevertheless, willing and running belong to our free choice.

For “I opened,” the Septuagint translated “he opened,” with God understood, because he himself both opened the prophet’s mouth and fed him.

(Gregory.) Sacred Scripture is our food and drink. Hence the Lord also threatens through another prophet, saying: “I will send a famine upon the land, not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of God” (Amos 8). By saying that, when his speech is withdrawn, he wears us down with hunger and thirst, he shows that his words are both our food and our drink.

But we must note that Scripture is sometimes food and sometimes drink. [Col. 0561C] In obscure matters, which cannot be understood unless they are explained, sacred Scripture is food, because whatever is explained so that it may be understood is, as it were, chewed so that it may be swallowed. In clearer matters it is drink, since we swallow drink without chewing. We drink the clearer commandments because we can understand them even without explanation.

Since the prophet Ezekiel was about to hear many obscure and intricate things, he is not told to drink from the sacred volume but to “eat.” It is as though he were told: “Work through it and understand it; that is, chew it first and then swallow it.”

But in dealing with the words of sacred speech, this order of our study must be preserved: [Col. 0561D] we should learn these things so that, pierced with compunction over our iniquity, we may avoid the evils we have committed and not commit others; and when, through extensive practice in tears, confidence in the forgiveness of sins has begun to arise, we should also draw others to life through the words of God that we understand.

They must be understood for our benefit and, with spiritual purpose, communicated to others. Hence it is rightly said here: “Eat this book and, going, speak to the children of Israel.” It is as though he were told concerning the sacred food: “Eat and feed others; be filled and pour forth; receive and scatter; be strengthened and labor.”

The prophet adds: “I opened my mouth, and he fed me with that book.” Another prophet testifies that the mouth is in the heart, saying: “Deceitful lips are in the heart, and they have spoken evil in the heart.” We open the mouth when we prepare our understanding for the comprehension of the sacred word.

Thus, just as the prophet opened his mouth at the voice of the Lord, [Col. 0562A] so the desires of our heart gape toward the breath of the Lord’s commandment, in order to receive something of the food of life. Yet receiving this food is not within our own strength unless he himself feeds us—the one who commanded us to eat. For the one who cannot eat by himself is fed.

Because our weakness is not fit to receive heavenly words, he himself feeds us, measuring out for us in due season our portion of wheat. Thus, while today we understand in the sacred word what we did not know yesterday, tomorrow we may also grasp what we do not know today, being nourished day by day with daily food through the grace of divine dispensation.

Almighty God stretches out his hand, as it were, to the mouth of our heart as often as he opens our understanding and places the food of sacred speech into our minds. He feeds us with the book when, distributing the understanding of his Scripture to us, [Col. 0562B] he opens our sense and fills our thoughts with its sweetness.

Hence it is added:

“And he said to me: Son of man, your belly shall eat, and your inward parts shall be filled with this book that I give you,” and so forth.

(Jerome.) The beginning of reading and of simple history is the eating of the book. But when, through constant meditation, we have stored the Lord’s book in the treasury of memory, our belly is filled spiritually and our inward parts are satisfied, so that, with the apostle Paul, we may possess “the inward parts of mercy,” and that belly may be filled of which Jeremiah speaks: “My belly, my belly—I am in pain, and the senses of my heart trouble me.”

(Gregory.) In sacred speech, “belly” is often used for “mind.” [Col. 0562C] Hence Jeremiah says: “My belly is in pain” (Jeremiah 4). Since he was speaking of a spiritual rather than a bodily belly, he added: “The senses of my heart are troubled.” It would not have pertained to the salvation of the people if the prophet had proclaimed that he was suffering pain in his bodily belly; rather, he suffered in his belly because he experienced anguish of mind.

But why should we offer the example of a prophet when we have a clearer testimony from the Lord? When Truth itself speaks, the prophet must be silent, because a lamp has no brightness in the sun. He says: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture has said, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7). Since holy preaching flows from the minds of the faithful, rivers of living water flow, as it were, from the belly of believers.

What else are the inward parts of the belly except the inner things of the mind [Col. 0562D]—that is, right intention, holy desire, humility toward God, and a loving will toward one’s neighbor? Hence it is rightly said here: “Your belly shall eat, and your inward parts shall be filled.” When our mind has received the nourishment of truth, our inner parts no longer remain empty but are satisfied with the food of life.

It belongs to the old human being to seek the present world, to love transitory things out of desire, to raise the mind in pride, to lack patience, to conceive thoughts of harming one’s neighbor out of the pain of injury, not to give one’s possessions to those in need, to seek the possessions of others in order to increase one’s own, not to love anyone purely for God’s sake, to return hostility to enemies, and to rejoice in a neighbor’s affliction. All these things belong to the old human being, which we draw from the root of corruption.

But of one who has already overcome these things and changed his mind toward kindness [Col. 0563A] in accordance with the Lord’s commandments, it is rightly said: “The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new.” New things are made in our minds when the vices of the old human being pass away from us, when the belly eats the commandment of the sacred word and the inward parts are filled to the marrow.

We have often seen certain people devote their whole mind to the study of sacred reading. As they recognized, amid the Lord’s words, how greatly they had sinned, they sacrificed themselves in tears, were continually afflicted with grief, and took pleasure in none of the prosperities of this world. The present life became a burden to them, and the light itself a weariness; they scarcely allowed their tongues to speak in conversation and found it difficult, out of love for the Creator, to relax the severity of their discipline. They rejoiced only in mourning and silence.

The belly of such people ate the sacred volume, and their inward parts were filled, [Col. 0563B] because their memory did not lose the commandments of life that their understanding had been able to grasp. Rather, the mind gathered into God preserved them continually through mourning and recollection.

It often happens that such people, through the gift of heavenly grace, also receive the word of teaching. From the nourishment of truth, which they themselves inwardly and sweetly ruminate, they gently feed their neighbors. Their preaching is all the sweeter to those who hear it because their conduct does not contradict their preaching: from their own life they draw what they communicate to their neighbors through their tongue.

Hence the prophet also rightly adds:

[Col. 0563C] “And I ate it, and it became in my mouth like sweet honey,” and so forth.

(Jerome.) David also says: “How sweet are your words to my palate, sweeter than honey to my mouth” (Psalm 118). And elsewhere: “The judgments of the Lord are true, more desirable than gold and much precious stone” (Psalm 18), and “sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.”

Samson found a honeycomb in the mouth of a lion (Judges 14). After his resurrection the Lord ate a portion of broiled fish and a honeycomb (Luke 24). In Proverbs it is also said concerning the bee, although the Hebrew copies do not contain this: [Col. 0563D] “Go to the bee and learn how industrious she is, and how she makes her work pure. From whose labors kings and the uneducated alike make use for health.”

Moses, the prophets, the evangelists, and the apostles did this, so that whoever is a king—whose heart is in the hand of God—may enjoy sweet foods. Whoever is simple and, without the serpent’s cunning, possesses the innocence of doves should believe with simple faith and be saved, because snares are everywhere. Often the devil transforms himself into an angel of light, and honey drips from the lips of the harlot, promising sweet things so that he may insert poisons.

(Gregory.) The book that filled the inward parts became sweet in the mouth, like honey. Those know how to speak sweetly about almighty God who have learned to love him truly in the inward parts of their heart. Sacred Scripture is sweet in the mouth of the person whose life is filled inwardly with his commandments, because he finds him pleasant to speak about when the commandments have been impressed within him for living.

Speech has no sweetness when a wicked life gnaws at the conscience within. Therefore whoever speaks the word of God must first strive to live rightly, so that afterward he may gather from his life what he should say and how he should say it.

[Col. 0564A] “And he said to me: Son of man, go and enter [in the Vulgate, ‘enter’ is absent] into the house of Israel, and you shall speak my words to them,” and so forth.

(Jerome.) To the one who is told, “Go and enter into the house of Israel,” it is shown that he had not been living with the sinful people, although he appeared to dwell within the same territory beside the river Chebar. For it is written: “And I was in the midst of the captivity beside the river Chebar.” The prophet’s way of life was separate, and he was offended by the sight of the wicked.

Moses did the same when he pitched the tabernacle far from the camp of the multitude. [Col. 0564B] When he had entered it, the pillar of cloud descended and stood before the door of the tabernacle.

“For you are not being sent to a people of deep and difficult speech [Vulgate: ‘unknown’ language], to the house of Israel, nor to many peoples of unknown speech, whose words you could not understand. And if I sent you to them, they would listen to you. But the house of Israel does not want to listen to you, because it does not want to listen to me. For the whole house of Israel has a worn-out forehead and a hard heart,” and so forth. Since they do not want to come to you, go to them. “For those who are healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.” Nor can you say, “I cannot speak to them, because they are of another language, and we are barbarians to one another. We cannot understand each other’s speech.” What shall I say about one people? If I were sending you to different nations, nevertheless my authority and power would overcome every difficulty.

And would that the time were already at hand when I shall send you to all nations, when I shall also give the gift of languages so that my apostles may preach, and bring the whole world under my yoke by one faith despite the diversity of languages. Those who are of deep and lofty speech, and have nothing of Jewish frivolity but proceed with a grave and solid step, would more readily listen; and although their languages are unknown, they are known in faith. Hence it follows: “And if I sent you to them, they would listen to you.” Indeed, afterward he sent him, and all alike believed. Thus Paul and Barnabas say to them: “It was necessary that the word of God should be preached to you; but since you refused to receive the message, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13). And of the centurion it is said: “I have not found such faith even in Israel” (Luke 13).

[Gregory.] At the very beginning of the command by which the prophet is sent to preach, both the calling of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Israelites are plainly indicated. For when it is said, “You are not sent to many peoples of deep speech and an unknown language, whose words you could not understand,” and immediately it is added, “And if you were sent to them, they would listen to you,” the obedience of the Gentiles is clearly declared: they would one day follow the voices of preachers without delay. When it is added, “The house of Israel does not want to listen to you, because it does not want to listen to me,” the hardness of Judea is indicated; it recognized the words of preachers but refused to follow them.

The unknown language of the Gentiles delayed obedience, although they were strangers to the eloquence of the Law. Well, then, is it said: “They do not want to listen to you, because they do not want to listen to me,” in accordance with what is written: “Whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10). The reason why they do not listen is also supplied when it is said: “For the whole house of Israel has a worn-out forehead and a hard heart.” When the house of Israel is said to have a worn-out forehead and a hard heart, what else should be understood or considered except that frequent sin wears down the forehead of the heart through shamelessness, so that the more often sin is committed, the less the sinner’s mind is ashamed of it?

Therefore the sinner eventually reaches such hardness of heart that he is not even responsive to correction. For one who has become hardened through the habit of sinning feels no word of correction—that is, no touch of the hand that probes him—just as it is said to sinful Judea: “You have acquired the forehead of a prostitute; you refused to be ashamed.”

Or certainly, the worn-out forehead is one accustomed to the pursuits of this world. For just as there are some who prefer rest to all the rewards and honors of the world, so there are others who, in order to appear to be something in this world, sweat through earthly labors, pursue lawsuits, become entangled in quarrels; and although they feel their bodies failing amid their labors, overcome by love of earthly things, they grow tired with pleasure.

“Behold, I have made your face stronger than their faces, and your forehead harder than their foreheads. I have made your face like adamant and like flint, so that you may not fear them or dread their presence, because the house is rebellious,” and so forth.

[Jerome.] The house of Israel has a worn-out forehead, shameless boldness, and a heart so hard that it may be compared with scorpions. Therefore I have given you an exceedingly hard face and a forehead that cannot be overcome by shame. From this we learn that at times it is a gift of God to resist shamelessness and, when the occasion demands it, to strike forehead against forehead. This is granted so that our modesty and human shame may not fear the plots of our adversaries.

[Gregory.] Just as shame is praiseworthy in evil, so it is blameworthy in good. To be ashamed of evil is wisdom; to be ashamed of good is folly. Hence it is written: “There is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that brings glory” (Ecclesiasticus 4). Whoever is ashamed of the evils he has committed and repents reaches the freedom of life. But whoever is ashamed to do good falls from the state of uprightness and moves toward condemnation, as the Redeemer says: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed when he comes in his majesty” (Luke 9).

There are also those who already perceive good things in their minds but do not yet openly oppose evil. Since they are good in mind, they have no authority in speech and are not suited to defend the truth. For the defender of truth must be one who neither fears nor is ashamed to speak what he rightly thinks.

Therefore the prophet is now promised this great gift: “Behold, I have made your face stronger than their faces, and your forehead harder than their foreheads.” For what is a sinner but one who is wounded, and what is a preacher but a physician? If the sinner who lies in his wound is not ashamed, why should the physician be ashamed, who provides salvation through remedies?

Often a preacher is listened to respectfully; sometimes, however, he is so despised by the perverse that it is as though he were saying nothing useful to them. Hence it is rightly said now: “I have made your face like adamant and like flint.” Both adamant and flint are hard, but one is precious and the other common. Adamant is used for ornament, while travelers trample flint beneath their feet.

It often happens that we are ashamed to say something to those whom we see listening very humbly to our correction. At other times we fear to bring a word of preaching to those whom we see setting aside and despising our rebuke. But if we judge rightly, we should take the authority to exhort or rebuke both those by whom we see ourselves honored and those by whom we see ourselves despised. We must neither be ashamed of the humility of the former nor fear the pride of the latter.

Let it therefore be said: “I have made your face like adamant”—that is, when you are honored by your hearers—and, “I have made your face like flint”—when you are trampled underfoot and despised by your hearers—so that broad honor does not restrain the tongue through shame, nor contempt silence it through weakness.

It follows: “Do not fear them, nor dread their presence, because the house is rebellious.” This has already been said above, but we should note how harsh the house is, since its harshness is repeated so frequently. The sinner must therefore be rebuked and never feared, because the house is rebellious. A person ought to have been feared if, as a human being, he had feared the author of all things. But one who has no rational sense of the fear of God is so much the less to be feared in anything, since he is not what he ought to be.

It follows:

“And he said to me: Son of man, receive into your heart all my words that I speak to you, and hear them with your ears; and go, enter among the exiles, the sons of my people,” and so forth.

[Jerome.] This is the food of the scroll, and these are the words by which, according to the differences among our hearers, we speak to people either lamentation, or a song, or a woe. Yet it must be noted that the words of God are first to be stored in our heart, heard and understood with careful attention, and only then brought forth to the people.

“Go,” he says, “enter among the exiles, or among the captives, among the sons of my people.” And our Lord came to the Jewish people, sent by the Father, to preach release to captives, so that what is written might be fulfilled in him: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men.”

[Gregory.] We must observe attentively that the Lord’s voice says to the prophet that he should first hear his words and afterward speak. We hear the words of God when we do them, and we speak them rightly to our neighbors only when we have first done them ourselves.

The evangelist Mark confirms this well when he relates the Lord’s miracle, saying: “They bring him a deaf man who could hardly speak, and they beg him to lay his hand upon him.” He indicates the order of the healing when he adds: “He put his fingers into his ears, and, spitting, touched his tongue. Then, looking up to heaven, he groaned and said to him: ‘Ephphatha,’ which means, ‘Be opened.’ And immediately his ears were opened, and the bond of his tongue was released, and he spoke correctly.”

But since the prophet is sent to admonish the exiles of the people, we must understand not only that exile which affected that people bodily, but also that which had taken place in the mind. He had come from Jerusalem to Babylon. And what is Jerusalem except “vision of peace”? What does Babylon signify except “confusion”?

Whoever falls from right actions into perverse deeds, when he slips from good conduct into vices, comes as if from Jerusalem to the city of Babylon. He has abandoned the summit of good contemplation and lies hidden in the exile of confusion. This often happens to those who, while doing good, boast of their own virtue in those deeds.

Therefore the Psalmist, praying to the Lord lest he migrate as a captive from the vision of peace—that is, from good actions—to Babylon, says: “My helper, I shall not migrate.” For if he trusted in himself, he would have migrated by falling from works of righteousness.

Yet those who have fallen from the state of uprightness into evil action are not to be despaired of, because the prophet is rightly sent to the exile of Babylon, and through another prophet the Lord says: “You shall come as far as Babylon; there you shall be delivered.” Often, after someone has fallen into the confusion of vices, he returns to repentance, ashamed of the evils he has committed, and raises himself from his falls by living well.

What, then, does this person do except come as far as Babylon and there become free? After committing deeds in a confused and perverse mind, he is ashamed of those very evils he has done, raises himself against himself, and returns to the state of uprightness by doing good.

It follows:

“And you shall speak and say to them: Thus says the Lord God: If perhaps they will hear and be still.”

Whenever the difficulty of hearing is repeated in divine utterances, so that it is said, “If perhaps they will hear,” what else is indicated than the hardness of the exiled people? These words provide us with great consolation. If almighty God, when sending a prophet to a perverse people, declares that it will be difficult to hear, why are we miserable people distressed? Why are we so often despised by our brothers when we admonish them?

We address frequent sinners, rebuke them repeatedly, and often deal with them in gentle words. Yet one listens while another refuses to listen; one receives the word of exhortation in part while another part he refuses to accept. Thus we see fulfilled daily what the Lord recounts through another prophet that he did in anger, saying: “I rained upon one city, and upon another city I did not rain. One part was watered, and the part that was not watered dried up.”

When one mind receives the words of holy exhortation and another refuses to receive them, the Lord rains upon one city and does not rain upon the other.

“And the spirit lifted me up. And I heard behind me the sound of a great commotion: ‘Blessed is the glory of the Lord from his place,’” and so forth.

[Jerome.] God, of whom it is written, “The Lord raises up the meek,” himself also raised up the prophet, who was not in the flesh but in the spirit. Walking in the spirit, he did not fulfill the works of the flesh, for the Spirit of God was in him. Therefore, despising earthly things, he was carried away by the spirit and heard behind him the sound of a great commotion, forgetting what was past and stretching toward the future, so that he might leave the plots of his enemies behind him.

We read something similar in Exodus 14, when Pharaoh and all his army were pursuing Israel. The angel in the pillar of cloud left the front of the camp, came behind it, and stood throughout the night between Israel and the Egyptians, so that, while the adversaries were terrified, Israel might hear.

“Blessed is the glory of the Lord from his place.” The Lord’s place is every place in which he finds lodging; or certainly, the Son is the place of the Father, just as the Father is the place of the Son, as the Lord and Savior says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14).

Micah also signifies this when he says: “Behold, the Lord will go forth from his place, and will descend upon the high places of the earth. The mountains will be shaken beneath him, and the valleys will melt like wax before the fire, and like water that rushes down a precipice” (Micah 1). For when the Lord and Savior descended and went forth from the Father, the high places of the earth and the mountains were shaken, and the lower places of the valleys melted.

The Lord’s place may also be the glory and inaccessible light of which the Apostle speaks: “Who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light.” When we turn over the Lord’s past judgments in our minds, we hear behind us the voice of a great commotion; when we meditate upon the future, a voice is heard from what lies before us and from the things that precede.

[Gregory.] What does it mean that, after the prophet is sent to the exile of the sons of the people, he hears behind him the voice of a great commotion saying, “Blessed is the glory of the Lord from his place”? He had been turned toward the sinners of Babylon, and he heard behind him the voice of the Lord’s glory from its place.

The Lord’s place is Jerusalem, that is, the vision of peace, because those hearts behold the things that belong to God and do not descend into the exile of Babylon—that is, into the vices of confusion. God dwells there where true peace is sought and the glory of inner contemplation is loved. For those who descend into perversity refuse to be God’s place.

The place of God’s glory is every holy soul, or each angelic spirit that remains in the heavens. The glory of the Lord is blessed from its place when eternal praise is sung to the author of all things by either chosen human beings or holy angels.

When the righteous consider the conversion of sinners, they turn the eye of their mind toward carnal actions by considering their vices, as though they were looking toward Babylon. Yet, because of the state of their uprightness, they never cease to consider the good deeds of the saints in praise of God, and although their thought is directed elsewhere, they hear behind them, as it were, the voice of the Lord’s glory from Jerusalem—that is, from its place.

What, then, does it mean that the prophet heard behind him the voice of a great commotion, except that after the sermon of preaching addressed to the hearts of sinners, the lamentations of penitents follow?

The perverse, while they act wickedly and do not hear what is right from the righteous, do not know how grave are the things they commit. Through this very ignorance they are secure in their stupor, and, lying in their sins, they rest as though softly at ease. Thus it is said of a certain sinful and secure people: “He rested upon his dregs,” because he lay secure in his sins.

But when the perverse begin to hear the word of preaching, learn what eternal punishments there are, what terror belongs to the judgment, and how subtle is the examination of each individual sin, they immediately tremble. They are filled with groans and tormented by sighs too great for them to contain. Shaken by great fear, they burst into mourning and tears.

The voice of a great commotion therefore follows the prophet, because after the word of preaching the mourning of the converted and repentant is heard. Those who previously lay quietly in their wound, later touched by the hand of healing, return to salvation with pain.

But let us hear what the voice itself says: “Blessed is the glory of the Lord from his place.” The hearts of sinners had been the place of the evil spirit; but when, angered against themselves through repentance, they return to life, they become a place of the Lord’s glory. They now rise up against themselves; with the tears of repentance they pursue the evils they have committed.

Therefore the blessing of glory is heard in praise of God from the place where the insult to the Creator had previously resounded through love of the present age. The hearts of penitents now become the Lord’s own place; previously placed in sins, they had been a place belonging to another.

Of these it is further said:

“And I heard the sound of the wings of the living creatures striking one against another,” and so forth.

The prophet heard behind him the voice of a great commotion because, as has been said, the word of preachers is followed by the mourning of penitents. He heard behind him the sound of the wings of the living creatures because from that very mourning of penitents arise the virtues of the saints. They advance all the more in holy action the more they remember that before knowing life they acted wickedly.

But these words contain a great difficulty, because the prophet does not state clearly whether each living creature strikes its own wings against itself, or whether these same holy creatures strike one another with their wings, so that one touches the wings of the other and the other touches those of the first.

Since in sacred eloquence something is often said obscurely so that, by God’s wondrous ordering, it may be expounded in several ways, we should, with the Lord’s generosity, explain both possibilities.

We have often said that the wings of the living creatures are the virtues of the saints. How, then, does each creature, shaking its wings, strike one against another, unless it is plainly made known that, if we become holy creatures, virtue awakens virtue within us, as one strikes the other toward perfection?

For example, someone possesses knowledge of the word of God, and through that same knowledge learns to possess a merciful heart. Through knowledge of God’s word he has learned: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11). Once he has begun to be merciful in giving alms, he reads the words of holy authority, and whatever is said in them about mercy he understands more fully through experience.

There it is written: “I was a father to the poor” (Job 29). Perhaps he had read this before and passed over it; but when mercy has begun to change the nature of his heart, he reads and recognizes what it means to be a father to the poor, because, returning inwardly, he understands what he hears outwardly.

For it is one thing to give alms from commandment, and another to do so from charity. To do good from commandment belongs to those who are beginning; to do good from charity belongs to the perfect. They do not act merely because they are commanded, but also love, in doing, what is commanded.

Hence the Psalmist says in praise of great virtue: “See that I have loved your commandments, Lord; in your mercy give me life” (Psalm 118).

Thus one who preserves the good of chastity in his body is inflamed with zeal against those who live luxuriously, so that they may be cleansed from the stains of impurity. Often, when he finds some people fallen, he disciplines and afflicts them and restrains them for the purity of chastity.

If perhaps his own mind is tempted by the impurity of lust, then by the very zeal with which he corrected others he admonishes and shames himself. He is ashamed to think impure thoughts, remembering that he had corrected such things in others.

Thus one wing strikes another when virtue strikes virtue and guards it from impurity.

But if, as we have said, the living creatures strike one another with their wings, so that one wing strikes another wing belonging to another creature, the meaning of this description is likewise evident, with the Lord’s generosity. What does it mean that these winged creatures strike one wing against another except that all the saints touch one another through their virtues and stir one another toward advancement by considering another’s virtue?

Not everything is given to one person, lest he fall into pride. This person receives what you do not receive, and you receive what is denied to him, so that, when he considers the good you possess and he does not, he may prefer you to himself in thought.

Again, when you see that he possesses what you do not, you may place yourself below him in your own thought. Thus what is written may be fulfilled: “Considering one another superior.”

To give a few examples from many: one person is given the virtue of remarkable abstinence, yet he does not possess the word of knowledge. Another is given the word of knowledge, yet he strives to attain the virtue of perfect abstinence and cannot. To another is given freedom of speech, so that, offering the oppressed the solace of protection, he may speak freely in defense of justice; yet, because he still possesses many things in this world, he wishes to abandon everything but cannot.

To another it has already been granted to abandon all earthly things, so that he desires to possess nothing in this world. Yet he still does not presume to exercise the authority of speech against sinners, and although he ought to speak more freely because he no longer has anything by which he is held in this world, he refuses to speak freely against others lest he lose the very quiet of his life.

To one is given the virtue of prophecy: he already foresees many things that will come, yet, seeing and sympathizing with the present distress of his neighbor, he cannot heal it. To another is given the grace of healing, and by prayers he drives away from his neighbor’s body the present illness; yet he does not know what will happen to him shortly afterward.

Almighty God therefore distributes his gifts among his elect with wondrous providence, giving to one what he denies to another, and granting one a greater gift while granting another a lesser one. Thus, when this person sees that the other possesses what he himself does not, or when the other considers that this person has received something greater and judges that he himself possesses less, each marvels at God’s gifts in the other—that is, all marvel at them in one another.

Through this very admiration each humbles himself before the other, and, seeing that another possesses what he does not, considers that person preferred to himself by divine judgment.

The living creatures therefore strike one another with their wings when holy minds touch one another through alternating virtues, and, by touching, stir one another and fly, once stirred, toward advancement.

Yet we must know that, just as each of the elect continually observes in others what they have received better from God than he himself has, so that he may prefer them to himself in knowledge and submit to them in humility, so the minds of the reprobate never consider what good another possesses more than they do. They consider only what good they themselves possess more than another.

They do not weigh what good the other spirit has received and they lack, but what good they themselves possess and what evil is present in the other. Although almighty God distributes virtues to individuals for the purpose of humbling one person before another in thought, the reprobate turn the good they have received into an occasion of pride and are ruined by it. They continually consider the good things they possess and others do not, and never strive to reflect on how many good things others possess that they themselves lack.

What divine mercy arranges for the increase of humility, depraved minds turn toward the increase of pride. Through the diversity of gifts they fall away from the good in which they ought to have grown in humility.

It follows:

“And I heard the sound of the wheels following the living creatures, and the sound of a great commotion.”

We said above that the Testaments are signified by the wheels of sacred eloquence. The voice of the wheels, therefore, is the word of the Testaments.

After the sound of the wings of the living creatures, the sound of the wheels is also heard, because, when the virtues of the saints fly toward higher deeds after receiving the word of the preachers, and stir one another toward advancement, the state of the holy Church is raised up, so that throughout the whole world the pages of the sacred Testaments may be read.

For everywhere now the holy Gospel resounds; everywhere the words of the Apostles; everywhere the Law and the Prophets. After the sound of the wings, therefore, the voice of the wheels follows, because after the miracles of the saints the words of sacred eloquence are heard freely and gladly within the holy Church.

The wheels follow the living creatures because, as was said above, after the life of the saints has come into honor, the venerable words of the Testaments likewise appear to human beings. Or certainly the wheels follow the living creatures because in the lives of the holy Fathers we learn what we ought to understand in the volume of sacred Scripture. Their actions open to us what the pages of the Testaments declare in their preaching.

But we must ask why, after it was said above, “I heard behind me the sound of a great commotion,” the sound of the wings and of the wheels is followed by the words, “and the sound of a great commotion.” If this is carefully considered, it can be seen that the repetition is not pointless.

There are two commotions by which our hearts are moved. One commotion arises from fear, the other from charity. One comes from the mourning of penitents, the other from the fervor of those who love.

After the word of preaching, therefore, comes the first commotion, when we mourn the evils we have committed. After the sound of the wings and wheels comes the second commotion, when with great tears we seek the heavenly goods we have heard about.

Behold: because within the holy Church we learn examples of virtue from many fathers, we hear the sound of the wings daily; because the sacred words resound everywhere, we are stirred, as it were, by the voices of the wheels. And because through these same sacred words we are inflamed with love for our Creator, we mourn that, still far from the face of almighty God, we burn with the fires of great fervor.

Thus the second sound of a great commotion follows the first, because when the Testaments of God begin to resound in the ear of the heart, the spirit of the hearers, pierced by love, is stirred to lamentation.

“The spirit also lifted me up, and took me, and I went away bitter, in the indignation of my spirit.”

[Jerome.] After he had been lifted up by the spirit and taken up by it, he went in the indignation and bitterness of his spirit wherever he was being carried, understanding God’s indignation and pondering in his mind what the vision signified. Or perhaps he was borne along by the impulse of his exalted spirit itself, desiring to go where the Lord commanded.

Here we should understand his spirit to mean not the Holy Spirit but the human spirit, of which it is said in many places in Isaiah: “My spirit rises to you by night, O God” (Isaiah 26). The prophet was carried away not, as some think, in the spirit, but in the body itself; we read the same concerning Habakkuk according to Theodotion (Daniel 14).

[Gregory.] Why does he who had already said that he was taken up by the spirit report again that he was lifted up and taken? The mind of preachers advances toward higher things when, through them, the minds of their hearers are moved toward desire for almighty God.

But we must ask: Since the spirit does not lift up the mind unless it has taken it, why is “lifted up” said first and “takes” afterward? In this passage, however, the word “took” is used with a settled meaning.

There are some whom the spirit lifts up but does not take. Their understanding springs toward spiritual things, yet their life remains in carnal deeds and does not correspond to their understanding. Balaam also was lifted up by the spirit of prophecy (Numbers 23), but he was not taken up, because he could truly see things far in the future and yet refused to separate his mind from earthly desires.

But because the holy prophet was lifted up in knowledge and, at the same time, taken up in life, let us now hear what sort of man he is as he proceeds to preach.

“And I went away bitter, in the indignation of my spirit.”

Since the gifts of the Holy Spirit had increased in him, why did he go away bitter? Does every heart that the same Spirit takes up become bitter in the indignation of its own spirit?

We must therefore understand that one to whom the present life is still sweet is not a preacher who has been lifted up and taken up, even if he appears to speak the word of God. The Holy Spirit moves the mind it fills to bitterness over temporal things through the delight of eternal things.

It is sweet to exist amid human affairs, but it is sweet only to one who has not yet tasted any joy of heavenly things. For the less one understands eternal things, the more delightfully one rests in temporal things.

But if someone has already tasted with the mouth of his heart that sweetness of heavenly rewards—what those angelic choirs singing hymns are like, what the incomprehensible vision of the holy Trinity is—then, the sweeter that which he sees within becomes, the more everything he endures outwardly is turned into bitterness.

He quarrels with himself over the things he remembers having done wrongly, and he displeases himself when the one who created all things has begun to please him. He reproves himself for his thoughts, pursues himself for his words, and punishes himself by weeping for his deeds.

He longs for the things above, tramples all earthly things underfoot through contempt of mind, and, so long as he does not yet possess in sight what he desires, finds it sweet to weep and afflict himself with continual lamentation. Since he does not yet see himself in the homeland for which he was created, nothing in the exile of this life pleases him more than his own bitterness.

He disdains to be subject to temporal things and sighs ardently for eternal ones.

Yet we must know that no one can do all this with his whole heart for the love of almighty God unless the Holy Spirit has taken possession of his mind. For when could a human being, by his own strength, despise earthly things, love heavenly things, seek peace with God, enter into conflict with himself, reprove himself in thought, and punish himself with groans? No one can do these things unless divine grace has strengthened him.

Hence it is added:

“The hand of the Lord was with me, strengthening me.”

We cannot rise perfectly to good things unless the spirit both lifts us up by going before us and strengthens us by following after us.

But since it was written above concerning the scroll he had received, “It became in my mouth like sweet honey,” how can it afterward be said: “I went away bitter, in the indignation of my spirit”? It is indeed very strange if sweetness and bitterness coexist.

But according to the foregoing meaning, we must understand that when the word of God begins to grow sweet in the mouth of the heart, the mind of the person becomes bitter against itself. For the more subtly he learns from it how he ought to reprove himself, the more harshly he chastises himself through the bitterness of repentance. He displeases himself all the more because, in the sacred volume, he sees more fully what he ought to love in almighty God.

But because a human being cannot advance toward these things by his own strength, it is rightly said now: “The hand of the Lord was with me, strengthening me.”

In sacred eloquence the hand of the Lord is sometimes also called the only-begotten Son, because all things were made through him. Concerning his ascension the almighty Father speaks through Moses, saying: “I will lift up my hand to heaven.”

This hand, which strengthens the hearts of the elect, said to the disciples: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15). In everything we think and everything we do, therefore, we must always pray that, with him inspiring us, we may think, and with him helping us, we may act.

“And I came to the exiles, to the heap of new grain, to those who dwelt beside the river Chobar; and I sat where they sat, and I remained there seven days mourning in their midst.”

Among the other miracles of prophecy, the books of the prophets also possess this remarkable feature: just as events are sometimes explained by words, so words are sometimes explained by events, so that not only their sayings but also their deeds are prophecies.

Hence it is now said: “I came to the exiles, to the heap of new grain, to those who dwell beside the river Chobar.”

Since the circumstances required him to indicate that he was coming to the exiles, what necessity of speech required him also to specify the place through grain by saying, “To the heap of new grain,” unless causes are often signified through things and places?

For many years of captivity had already passed while Ezekiel was prophesying, and many of those who had been led into captivity had already died in the flesh. The prophet was coming to speak to their children.

Therefore it is said to him above: “Son of man, I am sending you to the sons of Israel, to apostate nations that have withdrawn from me; their fathers transgressed my covenant even to this day, and their sons are stiff-necked and unyielding in heart. To them I am sending you.”

Since many of these would believe and, through obedience, attain the fruitfulness of good works, they are called a heap of grain. That good souls are called God’s grain is attested by another prophet, who says: “Israel is holy to the Lord, the firstfruits of his grain” (Jeremiah 2).

“And I sat where they were sitting, and I remained there seven days, mourning in the midst of them.”

It should be noted with what compassion the holy prophet joins himself to the captive people, sitting and mourning together with them in their grief, because the root of speech is the power of action, and the speech of a preacher is willingly received by the hearer when it is uttered with compassion of heart. Thus iron is joined to iron: it is first melted, so that afterward each may hold fast to the other. For if it does not first become soft, it is afterward unable to hold firmly.

[Col. 0574C] Thus the prophet sat with the captive people and remained mourning in their midst, so that, while he made himself more yielding to them by condescending through the grace of charity, he might immediately hold them fast by the strength of his word. But the Israelite people, who are called “an exasperating house,” because they did not acknowledge their faults even amid chastisements, did not humble their spirit through any mourning. The prophet endeavored to sit mourning among the nations, so that by keeping silent he might show what he had come to teach by speaking; and before he uttered words, he took on the form of speech in this very fact that he remained silent in mourning.

It follows: “And when the seven days had passed, the word of the Lord came to me, saying.”

(Gregory.) In the fact that he sat mourning for seven days and received the words of the Lord’s command after the seventh day, when he was to speak, it is plainly indicated that during those same days he had kept silent in mourning. He had been sent to preach, yet he sat silent for seven days. What does the holy prophet suggest to us by this silence, except that the person who knows how to speak truthfully is one who has first learned to keep silent well? The discipline of silence is, as it were, nourishment for speech. And rightly, through the growth produced by silence, he received an increasing grace of speech, since beforehand he kept silent in an orderly way through humility.

Hence Solomon says: “A time to be silent, and a time to speak” (Eccles. III). He does not say, “A time to speak and a time to be silent,” but places the time for silence first and afterward adds the time for speaking. For we must learn not to keep silent by speaking, but to speak by keeping silent. If, then, the holy prophet, who had been sent to speak, remained silent for a long time so that afterward he might speak rightly, we must consider how great a fault it is not to remain silent for one whom no necessity compels to speak.

It follows: “Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel.”

It should be noted that the one whom the Lord sends to preach, he declares to be a watchman. Whoever is entrusted with the care of others is called a watchman, so that he may sit in the height of his mind and derive the title of his name from the virtue of his action. For one who is below is not a watchman. A watchman always stands in a high place, so that he may see from afar whatever is coming. And whoever is appointed a watchman over the people must stand on high through his life, so that he may be of service through foresight.

Hence another prophet admonishes the watchman, saying: “Climb upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion” (Isa. XL), so that the one who has received the office of preaching may ascend to the height of good action, pass on to lofty things, and surpass the works of those entrusted to him. Thus he may see the life of his subjects more subtly, insofar as he does not subject his mind to the earthly things he despises.

(Jerome.) The hand of the Lord, however, comes upon the prophet, strengthening him so that he may be able to receive the name of watchman and teach what he says. He first spends seven days among them, observing everything they were doing, so that afterward he might know what he should rebuke. He mourns, or dwells, in their midst, seeing their crimes and God’s just sentence because of the sinners’ iniquity.

“And when the seven days had passed,” he says, “the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel.”

The one who is to be a watchman and proclaim God’s words to the people must remain at rest for a long time and grieve over what he sees, possessing nothing in his own conscience of those things that he will rebuke in others.

“And you shall hear a word from my mouth, and you shall announce it to them from me.”

(Gregory.) Behold, the prophet is again warned not to presume to speak what he has not heard, but first to open the ear of his heart to the voice of the Creator, and afterward to open the mouth of his body to the ears of the people. Hence another prophet says: “I will incline my ear to a parable; I will open my proposition on the psaltery” (Ps. XLVIII). Whoever preaches rightly first, as has been said, inclines the ear of his heart inwardly to the utterance, so that afterward he may open the mouth of his body in the proclamation of admonition.

“If, when I say to the wicked, ‘You shall surely die,’ you do not announce it to him, nor speak to him so that he may turn from his wicked way and live, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood from your hand. But if you announce it to the wicked, and he does not turn from his iniquity and from his wicked way, he himself shall indeed die in his iniquity; but you shall have delivered your soul.”

(Jerome.) There are two wicked or unrighteous persons, as the Septuagint translated it: one who hears nothing from the watchman and dies in his ungodliness, whose blood is sought from the watchman’s hands; and another to whom the watchman announces the message, but who, refusing to listen, dies through his own fault. This is so, provided that the watchman himself is free from blame.

From this we understand why the Lord threatens the wicked and says, “You shall surely die”: namely, so that he may turn from his wicked way and live. The threat is directed not against human beings as such, but against sinners; not against those who turn away from their vices, but against those who remain in sin. And there is great danger in keeping silent about God’s words for three reasons: fear, laziness, or flattery. Hence Isaiah says: “Woe is me, miserable that I am, because I have kept silent” (Isa. VI).

What follows—“But you have delivered your soul”—echoes the apostolic saying: “If anyone’s work is burned, he shall suffer loss; but he himself shall be saved, yet so as through fire” (I Cor. III). This tests whether the external watchman is free from responsibility for the death of the one who perished or is guilty of it. For the work of the teacher is the salvation of the disciple.

What, then, should we observe and consider carefully in these words, except that neither does the subject die because of the fault of the superior, nor is the superior free from guilt when the subject, refusing to hear the words of life, dies through his own fault? For death is due to the wicked person, but the way of life must be announced to him by the watchman, and his wickedness must be rebuked. If the watchman remains silent, the wicked person will die in his iniquity, because the merit of his ungodliness made him unworthy to receive the watchman’s speech. Yet the Lord requires his blood from the watchman’s hand, because the watchman himself kills him who, by keeping silent, delivers him over to death.

In both cases we must weigh how closely the sins of subjects and superiors are connected. Where the subject dies through his own fault, there the one who presides, if he has kept silent, is held guilty of death. O how free from the blood of those entrusted to him was that outstanding preacher who said: “I am pure from the blood of all. For I did not shrink from announcing to you the whole counsel of God.” If he had not announced it, he would not have been pure from their blood; but because he diligently announced the whole counsel of God to them, he was pure from their blood.

By this utterance we are convicted, constrained, and shown to be guilty: we are called priests, yet in addition to the evils that properly belong to us, we add the deaths of others, because we kill as many as we see daily proceeding toward death while we remain sluggish and silent.

When it is said, “I will require his blood from your hand,” if the word “blood” in this passage signifies bodily death, our fear of silence is greatly increased. For if the one appointed to watch over his subjects is punished so severely even for the bodily death of one who was destined to die at some time, with what guilt will he be burdened for the death of the souls of his subjects, who could have lived forever if they had heard words of correction?

But “blood” can more aptly signify sins. Hence someone, mourning over sins of the flesh, said: “Deliver me from bloodguilt, O God, God of my salvation” (Ps. L). The blood, therefore, of the dying person will be required from the watchman’s hand, because the sin of a subject is charged to the fault of the superior if he has kept silent.

There is something the watchman can do to make himself free even when the subject dies: let him rise, stay awake, and oppose evil actions, as it is written: “Run about, hasten, stir up your friend; do not give sleep to your eyes, nor slumber to your eyelids” (Prov. VI).

[Col. 0577A] Hence it is added here as well: “If you announce it to the wicked, and he does not turn from his ungodliness and from his wicked way, he too shall die in his ungodliness; but you shall have delivered your soul.”

The subject dies without you when he has found you opposing the cause of his death. For you are joined to the death that you do not oppose. We must also note what things should be proclaimed by the watchman: faith and conduct. For he says: “If you announce it to the wicked, and he does not turn from his iniquity and from his wicked way.”

“Ungodliness” pertains to unbelief; “the wicked way” pertains to evil action. Every watchman should therefore strive first to lead people to the piety of faith and afterward to the pious way, that is, to good action.

But since the subject of exhortation has arisen, we should briefly make known what order and deliberation of speech ought to be found in the mouth of a shepherd. A teacher must consider what he says, to whom he says it, when he says it, how he says it, and how much he says. If any one of these is lacking, his speech will not be fitting.

For it is written: “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned.” We offer rightly when we perform a good work with good purpose. But we do not divide rightly if we put off exercising discernment in good action.

We must consider what we say so that, in accordance with Paul’s words (Coloss. IV), “our speech may always be seasoned with salt.” We must also consider to whom we speak, because often one person accepts a word of rebuke that another does not accept; and often the same person becomes a different person according to the deed in question.

Thus the prophet Nathan (II Reg. XII) struck David after his adultery with a powerful sentence of rebuke. When Nathan spoke about the one who had stolen the sheep, saying, “The man who did this is a son of death,” Nathan immediately answered David: “You are that man.” Yet when Nathan spoke to him about the kingdom of Solomon, because David was free from that fault, he humbly prostrated himself before him in worship. In one and the same person, then, because the circumstances were different, the prophetic speech was also different.

We must likewise consider when we ought to speak. Often, although a rebuke is delayed, it is afterward received kindly; and sometimes it loses its force if it misses the time when it ought previously to have been delivered. The wise woman, seeing Nabal drunk (I Reg. XXV), did not wish to rebuke him for his fault of greed; but once the wine had passed, she profitably struck him with the words of her rebuke.

The prophet also announces that the tongues of flatterers must not be postponed to a later time, saying: “Let them be immediately confounded who say to me, ‘Well done, well done’” (Ps. LXIX). For if flattery is patiently tolerated even for a time, it grows stronger. It briefly soothes the mind, so that the person gradually abandons the rigor of uprightness in the pleasure of speech. But lest it grow, it must be rejected immediately and without delay.

We must also consider how we speak, since often words that summon one person to salvation wound another. Hence the Apostle Paul, who admonishes Titus by saying, “Rebuke with all authority” (Tit. II), exhorts Timothy in these words: “Reprove, entreat, with all patience and doctrine” (II Tim. IV). Why does he command authority for one and patience for the other, except that he saw one to possess a gentler spirit and the other a more fervent one? Severity of speech had to be enjoined upon the gentle person through the authority of command. But the one who was fervent in spirit had to be restrained by patience, lest, if he became more inflamed than was right, he should not restore the wounded person to salvation but wound one who was healthy.

We must also take care how much we say, lest, if we prolong words of exhortation or rebuke for one who cannot bear much, we bring our hearer to disgust.

“But if the righteous person turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity, I will place a stumbling-block before him; he shall die. Because you did not announce it to him, he shall die in his sin, and his righteousnesses that he performed shall not be remembered; but I will require his blood from your hand. But if you announce to the righteous person that the righteous person should not sin, and he does not sin, he shall surely live, because you announced it to him, and you shall have delivered your soul.”

(Jerome.) Just as we read of two wicked or unrighteous persons—one who did not hear and perished, and another who heard but persevered in wickedness—so there are two righteous persons: one who does not hear and perishes, and another who hears, turns to repentance, and saves his soul.

It should be noted that a righteous person can fall, even if he has a teacher to turn him toward better things. Good works, therefore, also need a constant instructor, lest the person who has grown weary on the best course draw back his foot.

The wicked or unrighteous person, if he does not turn back, will die in his ungodliness and iniquity. But the righteous person, if he commits ungodliness and sin, does not immediately die; rather, a stumbling-block, or, as others translate it, a torment, is placed before him. And, as Theodotion said, “weakness,” so that he may be tormented, find no level road, and understand that he is sick.

Of such things the Apostle also said: “For this reason many among you are weak and sick, and many sleep” (I Cor. XI). It is beneficial for the righteous person to understand his offense and the torment of his conscience, and to say with the Psalmist: “I have turned in my anguish, while the thorn is fixed in me” (Ps. XXXI).

And just as iniquities do not confront the wicked person if he turns from his wicked way and lives, so ancient righteousness does not benefit the righteous person if he is oppressed by new crimes.

When the text adds, “He shall die because you did not announce it to him,” the implication is that he could have lived if the watchman and teacher had instructed him.

“But if the righteous person,” it says, “turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity, I will place a stumbling-block before him. He shall die because you did not announce it to him; he shall die in his sin, and his righteousnesses that he performed shall not be remembered. But I will require his blood from your hand.”

(Gregory.) Because the preacher kept silent concerning the righteous person who had fallen into sin, he is held guilty of that person’s blood. And the one who did not strive to be watchful in preaching became a participant in his condemnation.

But when it is said, “He shall die in his sin, and his righteousnesses that he performed shall not be remembered,” we must consider this especially: when we commit evil, we recall our past good deeds without justification, because there should be no confidence in former good deeds when evil is being perpetrated.

It may be asked whether the righteous person should be preached to after he has fallen, or whether the preacher should keep watch beforehand so that he may not come to a fall. Without doubt, he should do so beforehand, for the text continues: “But if you announce to the righteous person that the righteous person should not sin, and he does not sin, he shall surely live, because you announced it to him; and you shall have delivered your soul.”

If, then, the preacher delivers his soul because he announced to the righteous person that he should not sin, when the righteous person falls into sin while the preacher remains silent, the preacher is held guilty because he kept silent.

But who among us, I ask, is sufficient for these things, so as not only diligently to rebuke sinners but also to watch over the righteous so that they may not fall? Conscious of our weakness, when we see righteous men, we do not presume to admonish them to hold to the way of righteousness, because we see that they already hold to it; yet it is the preacher’s duty to admonish even the righteous. Hence the outstanding preacher said: “I am debtor both to the wise and to the foolish” (Rom. I).

In all that has been said concerning the righteous person turned to iniquity, there is something difficult to speak of and greatly to be feared: the Lord says, “I will place a stumbling-block before him.” He says: “If the righteous person turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity, I will place a stumbling-block before him.”

We say that the righteous person has stumbled because he has committed iniquity. And what we say is entirely true. Why, then, does almighty God still place a stumbling-block before one whom he sees already to have stumbled and fallen through the iniquity he committed?

But the judgments of almighty God are strict. He waits a long time for the sinner to return; but when the sinner refuses to return and despises him, God places before him something at which he may stumble more grievously.

A sin that is not quickly erased through repentance is either a sin and the cause of sin, or a sin and the punishment of sin, or simultaneously a sin, the cause of sin, and the punishment of sin.

Everything committed first is a sin. But if it is not quickly wiped away by repentance, almighty God, in just judgment, permits the sinner’s bound mind to fall into another fault, so that because he was unwilling to cleanse what he had done by weeping and correction, he may begin to heap sin upon sin.

A sin that is not dissolved by the lament of repentance is therefore at once sin and the cause of sin, because from it arises that by which the sinner’s mind is bound still more deeply.

The sin that follows from sin is at once sin and the punishment of sin, because, as blindness increases, it is generated as a retribution for the earlier fault, so that the very growth of vices in the sinner may already be punishments of a kind.

Sometimes, however, one and the same sin is simultaneously sin, the punishment of sin, and the cause of sin.

Let us place before our eyes someone who desired his neighbor’s property and, because he could not obtain it openly, stole it. But when accused of theft, he denied under oath that he had stolen it.

For this person, desire was sin and the cause of sin, because through it he proceeded to robbery. The theft itself, by which he seized the desired property, became both sin and punishment of sin: it came about as a retribution for desire that had not been restrained, so that he advanced to theft and the guilt of the heart increased into action as punishment for his blindness.

But because he attempted to conceal the theft by perjury, he generated sin from sin once again. The theft, therefore, which proceeded from desire and produced perjury, became sin and the punishment of sin with respect to the preceding fault; but with respect to the subsequent fault, it became sin and the cause of sin, because it was born from the former and gave birth to the latter.

Hence the Lord now also says: “If the righteous person turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity, I will place a stumbling-block before him.” As though he said openly: Because he was unwilling to listen when he was urged to repent, when he had already stumbled, I will abandon him in just judgment and place before him something at which he may stumble elsewhere.

Yet for God to place this is by no means to force someone to sin, but to refuse to free him from sin. Thus it is said concerning Pharaoh: “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart” (Exod. VII). The Lord does not harden the heart of the sinner; he is said to harden it when he does not free it from hardness.

For the merciful God mercifully grants time for repentance. But when we turn the patience of his grace toward the increase of our guilt, he turns the very time that he mercifully arranged for pardon into something more severe for punishment. Thus, when someone refuses to return even after receiving an interval of time, he increases his evils into guilt through the very means by which he could have washed them away, had he wished to turn back.

Hence it is written: “Do you not know that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the righteous judgment of God” (Rom. II).

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0579]

## CHAPTER III FOLLOWS

[Col. 0579D]

After the Lord’s speech to the prophet had been completed—by which he appointed him watchman over the house of Israel and commanded him to announce to the wicked person that he should turn from his wicked way and live, and commanded the righteous person not to sin, lest the righteousnesses he had previously performed should perish and he himself likewise perish—the author adds what the Lord afterward instructed him to do, saying:

“And the hand of the Lord was there upon me [the Vulgate omits ‘there’], and he said to me: Rise, go out into the field, and there I will speak with you, and so forth.”

(Jerome.) Above we read: “And I came to the place of the captivity, to the heap of new grain, to those who dwelt beside the river Chobar.” And rightly the one to whom he had said, “I sat,” is now commanded to rise.

The one who had entered the place of captivity hears, “Go out,” not into rugged valleys, not onto precipitous rocks, but into the breadth of the field, which can contain the glory of the Lord. Hence it is also said to the Corinthians: “Be enlarged” (I Cor. VI), when he enters among the captives.

Because it had been said of them that they raged against him and persecuted him, he needed a strong hand in order to resist and endure the fury of his persecutors. But when he goes out into the field, the hand of the Lord does indeed come upon him, because he could not go out without the Lord’s help; yet it is not called “strong.” He goes out to see the glory of God, not to fight.

This too should be observed: while sitting among the captive people, the prophet himself did not see the glory of the Lord.

“And I rose and went out into the field, and behold, the glory of the Lord stood there, like the glory that I had seen beside the river Chobar, and so forth.”

At the Lord’s command he enters, and at the Lord’s command he goes out. He sat with those who were sitting, because the multitude of captives could not dare to approach him while he stood.

When he went out into the broad expanse of the field, he saw the glory of the Lord standing, which he had previously seen moving, lifting itself up, and at times standing. For beside the Chobar, the river of this world—which is interpreted as “very grievous”—the glory was seen. This signifies that all the glory of this world flows past and has no fixed position.

But the glory of the Lord, standing and enduring, is seen in the field together with the standing prophet; in the midst of the captives it could neither stand nor be seen.

“And I fell upon my face, and the spirit entered into me, and set me upon my feet, and spoke with me, and said to me: Enter and shut yourself up in the midst of your house.”

Unable to endure the glory of the Lord as it stood, he fell upon his face, so that the spirit entering into him might raise him up. The spirit set him upon his feet and spoke to him, saying: “Enter and shut yourself up in the midst of your house.”

The meaning is that, strengthened by the sight of the Lord’s majesty, he should fear no one and tremble before no one, but should return to his house—either, as some think, for the necessities of the body, or as a sign of the future siege.

Just as Isaiah, barefoot and naked, announced the captivity and nakedness of the people for three years, so you too, shut up in your house, will prophesy by the action itself the approaching siege of the city of Jerusalem.

(Gregory.) What does it mean that the Lord first spoke to his prophet in the midst of the Israelites, and afterward said, “Go out into the field, and there I will speak with you,” except that he first poured the grace of his prophecy into Judea and afterward deigned to display it in the breadth of the nations?

For the field appropriately signifies the Gentile world, which extends far and wide, that is, throughout the whole world. There it is also added: “Rising up, I went out into the field, and behold, the glory of the Lord stood there, like the glory that I had seen beside the river Chobar.”

In the field the prophet saw the glory of the Lord that he had seen beside the river Chobar in the midst of the Israelites, because the same majesty appeared to the nations that had earlier revealed itself to the chosen people in the Jewish community through the revelation of the Spirit.

It follows: “And I fell upon my face.”

When the prophet sees the glory of the Lord, he falls upon his face, because although a human being is raised up to understand spiritual things, nevertheless, from the contemplation of God’s majesty he understands the weakness of his condition. He is, as it were, without stability when he sees himself to be ashes and dust before the eyes of God.

It follows: “And the spirit entered into me and set me upon my feet.”

When we humbly cast ourselves down before God, when we recognize that we are ashes and dust, when, weighing the weakness of our condition, we do not possess the rigid posture of pride, almighty God raises us through his Spirit and sets us upon our feet. Thus those who have humbly lain low before themselves through recognition of their weakness may afterward stand upright in good works, as though upon their feet.

Why does this happen to the prophet in the field, except to signify specifically that the Holy Spirit would also be given to the elect among the nations? For those whom he would take up, he would first cast down from their proud position and afterward establish upon their feet—that is, upon good works.

As Paul says: “Lift up the hands that hang down and the weakened knees, and make straight paths for your feet” (cf. Heb. XII).

It follows: “And he spoke with me, and said to me: Enter and shut yourself up in the midst of your house.”

What does it mean that the prophet is led from the midst of the Israelite people into the field and afterward recalled from the field to the house, except that the grace of preaching was taken away from the Jewish people and scattered throughout the breadth of the Gentile world?

Yet at the end of the world, when the Jews return to the faith, the prophet will be brought back, as it were, to the house, so that preaching may again dwell among his own people. At present it shines in different nations as though in the field.

For it is written: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. XI). And another prophet says: “Even if the number of the children of Israel were like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved” (Isa. X).

Let the prophet therefore go out from the midst of the people into the field, and let him return from the field to the house, so that the preaching given to Judea may go out among the Gentiles; and, when the Gentiles have been filled with faith, spiritual teaching may restore to Judea the gifts it lost.

The prophet is commanded to be shut up in the midst of his house because, in the time of Antichrist, the Jewish people who have been converted will be pressed by harsh persecutions from those nations that remain in unbelief. Hence it is written: “But the court that is outside the temple gates, cast out and do not measure it, because it has been given to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months.”

“And you, son of man, behold, bonds have been placed upon you, and they will bind you with them, and you shall not go out from their midst. And I will make your tongue cling to the roof of your mouth, or to your throat, and you shall be mute, unable to act as a man who rebukes, because it is an exasperating house.”

(Jerome.) That he is shut up in the house, that he is bound with chains, that he does not go out to those among whom he dwells, but suffers the solitude of imprisonment amid the multitude of captives—as I said above—is a sign of the siege. Jerusalem, shut up and surrounded by the army of the Chaldeans, would not permit any of its inhabitants to go outside.

This is the pot of which Jeremiah speaks, and which this prophet himself mentions later, in which the flesh of the people is consumed.

As for the prophet’s tongue clinging to his palate or throat, and his becoming mute so that he has no authority as one who rebukes, the reason is clear: “Because,” he says, “it is an exasperating house.” The meaning is: Their bitterness and their contentions against God are so great that they do not deserve to hear one who rebukes them.

From this it is clear that wherever there is a multitude of sins, the sinners are unworthy to be corrected by the Lord.

“And you,” he says, “son of man, behold, bonds have been placed upon you, and they will bind you with them, and you shall not go out among them; and I will make your tongue cling to your palate, and you shall be mute, unable to act as a man who rebukes, because it is an exasperating house.”

If we follow these words according to the order of a typological interpretation, the prophet receives bonds and is bound in his house because, at the end of time, when Judea believes, it will suffer extremely severe persecutions in the time of Antichrist. The ministers of iniquity will not receive the preaching, but by resisting they will press him with the bonds of sorrow.

He will not go out among them because preaching does not reach the hearts of the wicked while the tongue of the righteous remains bound by tribulations.

For at that time there will be many unbelieving Jews who persecute those very people among the Jews who have believed. Hence it should be noted that here too it is said that the prophet will endure bonds in his own house, so that it may be signified that Judea, from its own race, will bear the tribulations of persecution when it becomes faithful.

For as long as it is not believed among them that the Only-Begotten of the supreme Father, having become incarnate, died, rose again, and ascended into heaven—as is proclaimed throughout the pages of Holy Scripture—prophecy will certainly be bound among them. If it flowed into their understanding just as it was spoken, it would possess, as it were, free steps for its preaching.

The knowledge of the preachers will therefore then be compelled to remain silent before the reprobate. Hence it adds:
