“And I will make your tongue cling to your palate, and you shall be mute, unable to act as a man who rebukes, because it is an exasperating house.”

But because, when Enoch and Elijah preach, many of those Jews who will then have remained in unbelief will return to the knowledge of the truth, as it is said concerning Elijah: “Elijah will come, and he will restore all things” (Matt. XVII), both are called the two olive trees by Zechariah (Zech. IV) and the two lampstands by John (Apoc. XI).

“When I speak with you, I will open your mouth, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Let the one who hears hear; and let the one who is at rest remain at rest, because it is an exasperating house.”

(Jerome.) What we read in Ecclesiastes—“A time to be silent, and a time to speak”—is also confirmed in prophetic speech: it belongs to the same wisdom both to keep silent and to speak at the proper time, and to give food to fellow servants at the proper time.

Hence Isaiah says to the unbelieving people: “I have been silent; shall I always be silent? says the Lord” (Isa. LXV).

The one who, because of the multitude of sins, kept his mouth closed for a long time did so because he saw that some could be converted. Concerning them it was said: “Let the one who hears hear; and let the one who refrains from evil refrain and cease” (Ezek. III).

Therefore, with his mouth opened, not by his own will but by the Lord’s command, he speaks to the people.

What we have as, “Let the one who hears hear; and let the one who is at rest remain at rest,” the Septuagint translated as, “Let the one who hears hear; and let the unbeliever be an unbeliever.”

A second edition of Aquila translated it: “The one who hears shall be heard; and the one who abandons shall be abandoned.”

The meaning is: “To the one who has, it will be given; but from the one who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away” (Matt. IV).

“When,” he says, “I have spoken to you, I will open your mouth, and you shall say to them: [Col. 0584B] Thus says the Lord God.” (Gregory)

At that time the prophet’s mouth is opened, as it were, at the end, when, through the preaching of Enoch and Elijah, the Jews returning to the faith recognize that the prophecies of sacred Scripture had been spoken concerning Christ.

But since we have discussed these matters figuratively, let us now explain the same words morally to your Charity. For what does the prophet’s being commanded to go out into the plain mean except that everyone who preaches, because he corrects those whom he sees placed outside himself and restrains them from iniquity, goes out by speaking into the plain? There he sees the glory of the Lord, because he receives the grace of teaching more abundantly in proportion as, through love of his neighbors, he extends himself in the labor of preaching.

By going out, therefore, he is led upward in vision, because from the place where, through the ministry of his speech, he illuminates the blindness of ignorance in other hearts, heavenly grace raises him to a higher understanding. But since a preacher must always return to his own mind and preserve humility and purity within, after the plain he must return to the house, so that within his conscience he may recognize what sort of person he himself is in the matters he declares.

For if he either fails entirely to observe what he says, or seeks temporal glory from the things he proclaims, he goes out into the plain by speaking, but in thought he scorns to return to the house—to himself. When we have received the Spirit, we are enclosed in the middle of the house, because through his grace we are recalled to examine the secrets of our mind, so that the soul may rest in God within itself and no longer wander, through external desires, in the pursuit of praise and glory by the restlessness of its thoughts.

Concerning this house of the heart, Truth itself says to a certain man who had been healed: “Take up your bed and go to your house.” The bed, in which there is rest for the flesh, signifies the flesh itself; the house signifies the conscience. And because, when dead in mind through vices, we lie down and rest in the pleasures of the flesh, in our weakness we are carried on a bed.

But when we have been healed in mind, so that we now resist the vices of the flesh when they assail us, it is necessary that we endure the insults of temptations from our own flesh. Therefore, when the sick man has been restored to health, he is commanded, “Take up your bed”—that is, carry the bed on which you were carried—so that, once healed, each person may carry the reproach of the flesh in which he had previously lain sick.

What, then, does it mean to say, “Take up your bed and go to your house” (John V), except: Carry the temptations of the flesh in which you have hitherto lain, and return to your conscience, so that you may see what you have done?

The prophet, therefore, is commanded to be enclosed in the house after the plain, so that a preacher, after the grace of teaching which he ministers to his neighbors, may always return to his conscience and examine himself by a careful scrutiny, lest he seek inwardly for himself any passing praise from the things he preaches outwardly.

But these matters, which we have briefly examined according to a twofold meaning, let us now lightly touch upon according to the literal sense and pass on. For what else is commended by the very words of the historical account than the virtue of obedience, when the prophet is commanded now to go into exile beside the river Chobar, now to go out into the plain, now to return from the plain to the house, so that, first going at the command, then going out shortly afterward, and again returning to the house and enclosing himself, he may always bend the judgment of his own will to the command of divine speech, in order that, suspended in heavenly vision, he may fulfill not his own will but that of his Creator?

To him it is said: “And you, son of man, behold, bonds have been placed upon you, and they shall bind you with them, and you shall not go out among them.”

Here it must be noted that the prophet foreknows the adversities, so that he may be prepared for all of them. Evils that do not come unexpectedly prevail less strongly against the mind. Yet while he foreknows the things that oppose him, the greatness of the virtue of obedience in him is shown: he knows that he will suffer adversity, and nevertheless he is not disobedient to the Lord’s voice.

The words that immediately follow require careful consideration: “And I will make your tongue cling to the roof of your mouth, and you shall be mute, unable to act like a man who reproves.” We must distinguish whether the word of preaching is withdrawn solely because of wicked hearers, or sometimes also because of a fault in the preacher.

This matter is distinguished according to four conditions. Sometimes, because of wicked hearers, speech is taken away from good teachers. Sometimes, because of good hearers, speech is given to wicked teachers. Sometimes, for the justification of both teachers and hearers, speech is given to good teachers, so that they themselves may increase in merit and their hearers may advance in understanding and life. Sometimes, however, because neither those to whom the word of teaching is offered are worthy to receive it, nor those who hold the place of teaching are worthy to utter the word of instruction, the word of preaching is withdrawn, so that both parties may be strictly judged.

Because of wicked hearers, then, speech is taken away from good teachers, as it is now said to the prophet Ezekiel: “I will make your tongue cling to the roof of your mouth, and you shall be mute, unable to act like a man who reproves, because it is a rebellious house.” Likewise it is said to Paul: “Hurry and go out quickly from Jerusalem, because they will not receive your testimony concerning me” (Acts XXII). And concerning the Apostles, when they wished to preach in Asia, it is written that “the Spirit of Jesus prevented them” (Acts XVI).

Because of good hearers, speech is also given to wicked teachers, as the Lord says concerning the Pharisees: “Whatever they tell you, observe and do; but do not act according to their works, for they say and do not do” (Matthew XXIII).

For the merit of teachers and the justification of hearers, the word of teaching is granted, as it is said to the holy Apostles: “Go now and teach all nations” (Matthew XXVIII).

Because of wicked hearers and the unworthy life of those who ought to have taught, the word of teaching is withdrawn, as Eli did not possess a word of stern rebuke with which to correct his sons. For both his negligence and the life of his sons demanded that, when the people fell with them, the ark of the Lord should pass into the hands of the Philistines (I Samuel II).

Great indeed is the grace of almighty God when, among those acting wickedly, a harsh word of rebuke is uttered by teachers. But here the opposite is said: “And you shall be mute, unable to act like a man who reproves.” He would have reproved the offenders if they had been worthy of the grace of reproof.

But since there is such diversity of merit in teaching and silence that it cannot easily be known whether the word of teaching is withdrawn because of the hearers or because of the fault of the one who appears to hold the place of teaching, what else are we commanded in doubtful matters than always to preserve humility? Thus, when we are able to speak, we are not lifted up, lest perhaps this very speech of ours has been granted not for our grace but for that of our hearers.

And again, when we are unable to speak, let those entrusted to us not judge us too hastily, lest perhaps we are unable to speak not because of our own sin but because of the sin of our hearers. In this way everything concerning our merits remains uncertain to us, so that we may hold one certain grace: humility. When we speak, let us think that this is your merit, bestowed through the gift of almighty God. And when we fall silent from the speech of teaching, even if it is our fault, let you nevertheless believe that it is especially your fault, so that, while we mutually attribute evils to ourselves and good things to others through the grace of humility, the word of teaching that had been taken away may return.

It follows: “But when I have spoken to you, you shall open your mouth, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Let the one who hears hear, and let the one who is at rest remain at rest, because it is a rebellious house.”

Often some people desire to hear the word of God, but when they see others turning away their ears, they too turn away from hearing what would bring salvation. Frequently many wish to be still and withdraw from all the activities of this world, no longer to yield to any earthly desires. But when they see others advancing through restless activity and being exalted in this world by riches and honors, because they are not yet firm in the way of righteousness, they fall into evil works through the example of others.

Hence the Psalmist, speaking figuratively of the weak, said: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps had nearly slipped, because I was jealous of sinners, seeing the peace of sinners” (Psalm LXXII). Again he says: “While the wicked man grows proud, the poor man is set aflame” (Psalm X).

## CHAPTER IV. Explanation of the brick; concerning the captivity of the ten tribes and the distress of famine

“And you, son of man, take a brick for yourself, place it before you, and draw upon it the city of Jerusalem; arrange a siege against it, build fortifications, heap up a rampart, set camps against it, and place battering rams around it,” and so forth.

(Hieronymus) As we said earlier—“Enter and enclose yourself in the middle of your house. And behold, bonds have been placed upon you, and they shall bind you, and you shall not go out”—the prophet is a type of the future siege of the city of Jerusalem. So now he is commanded by geometrical art to draw it upon a brick, and the brick itself is to be placed before the prophet, so that, after he has drawn Jerusalem, he may depict in the dust the whole siege against it: fortifications, heaps of earth carried together, the surrounding crown of the besieging army, and battering rams. Through all these means cities are customarily captured.

The fortifications are the structures by which a city is enclosed so that no one may escape the besieger. The heaps of earth are those by which the rampart and ditches are filled. The camps are the soldiers’ guards stationed all around. The battering rams are the devices by which the foundations of walls are shaken and the joining of the stones is broken apart.

This is said to signify the impending captivity of the city of Jerusalem under King Zedekiah: in his eleventh year both the king and the city were captured.

For the brick, which in Greek is feminine, ἡ πλίνθος (*hē plinthos*), Symmachus translated more plainly and more elegantly as πλίντιον (*plintion*), which we may call a small brick or a tablet. On its dust geometers customarily draw γραμμὰς (*grammas*), that is, lines and rays.

Some therefore consider it not unreasonable that the prophet should also possess knowledge of this discipline, recalling the examples that Jesus son of Nave sent spies who would map out the land—a practice properly called geometry—and that the angel in Zechariah had a geometrical measuring cord with which to measure Jerusalem.

The prophet is now commanded to draw Jerusalem in the dust, a practice that among them is properly called σκηνογραφία (*skēnographia*, “scene-drawing” or “drafting”). We may understand the brick also as a reproach against Israel, because Israel served Pharaoh in mud and brick; or because the city which they thought firm and impregnable is compared with a very fragile brick, which dissolves immediately at the touch of water.

Thus what was previously said of it—“Is it not a very hard rock or a mountain of the desert, O daughter of Zion?”—is turned into a brick that is ruined by the inundation of Babylon, in accordance with what is written: “Therefore the Lord will bring upon you many and mighty waters, the king of the Assyrians.”

“And you,” he says, “son of man, take a brick for yourself, place it before you, and draw upon it the city of Jerusalem; arrange a siege against it, build fortifications, heap up a rampart, set camps against it, and place battering rams around it. And you, take an iron pan for yourself and place it as an iron wall between yourself and the city; set your face firmly against it, and it shall be under siege. And you shall surround it. It is a sign for the house of Israel.”

(Gregory) In these words, according to the historical sense, what else is signified than the siege and destruction of the city of Jerusalem and the affliction of the sinful people? That people is called a rebellious house when it is plainly said: “You shall arrange a siege against it, build fortifications, heap up a rampart, set camps against it, and place battering rams around it.”

But because the words of prophecy generally narrate historical events in such a way that they also describe mystical realities through them, we must explain spiritually these same words that we have quoted—especially since they contain something that does not seem capable of being understood literally, namely: “And you, take an iron pan for yourself and place it as an iron wall between yourself and the city; set your face firmly against it, and it shall be under siege, and you shall surround it. It is a sign for the house of Israel.”

(Hieronymus) What we said above—that the prophet himself, together with the drawing of the brick, should go before the siege of Jerusalem as a sign, surrounding it with fortifications, a rampart, and battering rams—is now stated more clearly after the intervening material: “It is a sign for the house of Israel.” The iron pan, placed like a wall between the prophet and the city, demonstrates the great anger of God, which cannot be wearied by any prayers or bent toward mercy.

Just as iron subdues all metals and nothing is harder than it, so the unbelievable crimes of Jerusalem have made God, who is by nature gentle, exceedingly hard because of Jerusalem’s own fault. The pan is also called a wall placed between the people and God, to show that the whole multitude will shortly be broken and reduced to nothing.

The firm setting of the face against the city is the judgment of severity, in accordance with what we read written elsewhere: “The face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth” (Psalm XXXIII).

(Gregory) Why was an iron pan necessary for the prophet, so that he might place it between himself and the city and thereby separate himself from its siege? When it is said, “Take an iron pan for yourself and place it as an iron wall between yourself and the city,” it is clearly declared that by means of this iron pan he makes himself free from the siege of the city. Hence what I said earlier is added: “And you shall set your face firmly against it, and it shall be under siege.”

From this it is shown that the prophet was not within that siege, since he places an iron pan—an iron wall—between himself and the city. Yet whether in the captivity that occurred earlier or in that which later befell the Israelite people, no one was free from the danger of that captivity; the same calamity enveloped everyone alike.

What, then, can be understood literally, so that the prophet places an iron pan between himself and the city that is to be besieged? Although everything that is read in the drawing of the brick under the sign of the city of Jerusalem was literally done, you must nevertheless know that something typological is represented by the pan, while the siege of Jerusalem is described as a real event.

From this we learn that, while we know one thing to have been fulfilled according to history and recognize another as contrary to reason if understood historically, we must hold both meanings in sacred Scripture. Thus we believe that the siege of Jerusalem, which later occurred literally, was prefigured in the prophet’s words and actions, and yet through that same siege another siege—namely, an interior one—is signified.

Here we ask what is represented by the iron pan, which is called an iron wall. We know that the siege by which the city of Jerusalem was destroyed has already taken place; but let us seek another siege within, which is enacted daily. Concerning it, the following is said symbolically: “And you, son of man, take a brick for yourself, place it before you, and draw upon it the city of Jerusalem.”

But first we must ask why the prophet Ezekiel, whenever he beholds exalted realities or is commanded to perform some mystical action, is first called “son of man.” He is often raised to heavenly things, and his mind is nourished by hidden and invisible realities. Therefore, amid the mysteries he penetrates, he must be called “son of man,” so that he may always recognize what he is and never become elated because of the things to which he is led.

For what does it mean that the prophet, raised to spiritual realities, is always addressed as “son of man,” except that he is made mindful of his own weakness, so that, conscious of his frail condition, he should not be lifted up in understanding because of the greatness of his contemplation?

Since this same prophet, as we have already said above, represents preachers or teachers, it is rightly said to him now: “Take a brick for yourself and place it before you.” Every teacher, when he receives some earthly hearer for instruction in the heavenly word, takes a brick. When he begins to speak of the reward of the heavenly homeland and of the vision of supernal peace, he draws the city of Jerusalem upon the brick that he places before himself, because he considers attentively the condition of his hearer—that is, he observes his progress or failure—and moderates the words of his preaching according to the hearer’s understanding, so that the city of Jerusalem, that is, the vision of peace, may be drawn in the hearer’s mind.

Let it therefore be said: “Take a brick”—that is, the earthly heart of your neighbor—and place it before you, “so that you may carefully guard his life and understanding. And draw upon it the city of Jerusalem,” so that you may make known to him the heavenly joys that come from the vision of peace.

Jerusalem has already been drawn upon the brick, as it were, when an earthly mind begins truly to recognize the joys of inner peace, to yearn to behold the glory of the heavenly homeland. The inner vision of peace is drawn when a mind that previously savored earthly things is now raised through love to contemplate the glory of the heavenly kingdom.

But as soon as the soul begins to love heavenly things, as soon as it gathers itself with complete attention toward the vision of inward peace, that ancient adversary who fell from heaven grows envious and begins to lie in wait more intensely. He applies temptations more severe than those to which he had been accustomed, so that he often tempts a resisting soul as he had never tempted it before, when he possessed it.

Hence it is written: “Son, when you approach the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Sirach II). Hence also the demoniac who is healed by the Lord is torn by the departing demon, as it is written: “And crying out and tearing him violently, he came out of him” (Mark IX).

The teacher must therefore vigilantly make known to the advancing soul what temptations will follow, so that it may prepare itself cautiously against the snares of the evil spirit. Hence, after the city of Jerusalem has been drawn upon the brick, the prophet is rightly told: “And you shall arrange a siege against it, and build fortifications, and heap up a rampart.”

Once the vision of peace has been drawn in the soul, it is necessary that the war of temptations be announced to it. For if it is to be able to reach those eternal joys of peace, it must undoubtedly endure here the accumulated battles of tribulations.

It is rightly said concerning it: “You shall arrange a siege against it.” A preacher arranges a siege against a soul that is to be instructed when, by giving advance defenses, he shows in what ways vices oppose virtues: how lust attacks chastity; how anger disturbs the tranquility of the mind; how excessive amusement loosens the mind’s vigor; how excessive talk destroys the fortification of the heart; how envy kills charity; how pride digs up the fortress of humility; and how deceit, once it has corrupted truth in speech, also violates it in thought, so that one who refused to speak what he understood may no longer understand what he can say.

A preacher therefore arranges a siege when, through the words of holy admonition, he shows each person by what means and in what ways vices lie in wait.

Against the Jerusalem that he draws upon the brick, the preacher builds fortifications when he demonstrates how evils approach the mind in a fortified manner, so that vices conceal themselves under the appearance of virtues. Thus, as we have often said, immoderate anger seeks to appear justice; laxity in discipline wishes to appear gentleness; stinginess calls itself frugality; and the disordered dispersal of possessions names itself benevolence.

Fortifications are, as it were, built against the mind when vices grow beneath the appearance of virtues and display themselves loftily by their outward image, though in their conduct they always lie low.

The text continues: “And you shall heap up a rampart.” As soon as the mind begins to desire heavenly things, the evil spirits heap up earthly thoughts against it through their temptations. The prophet therefore heaps up a rampart when the holy preacher warns good minds how earthly desires commonly creep in.

The text further says: “And you shall set camps against it and place battering rams around it.” A teacher sets camps against the soul when he reveals the gathered and united snares of evil spirits against it, so that at times they may attack not merely through one vice but through all vices together.

Certain vices are closely related to one another, as though connected by a kind of kinship: dissipation of spirit, appetite for gluttony, and impurity of lust; or excessive talk, deceit, and perjury. For from desolation [dissipation] of spirit (*desolatione* [*dissolutione*]) the mind is dragged toward gluttony; and when the belly is distended with food, the flesh is drawn toward lust, captive through pride. Again, deceit arises from excessive talk, because it is exceedingly difficult for one who speaks much not also to lie. Often a lie is covered by perjury, so that it may be concealed from human judgments.

Pride likewise cannot exist without envy or empty glory. For every proud person envies in others the honor that he himself desires. And when he perhaps obtains it, he is lifted up in the elation of temporal glory and rejoices in empty glory that he possesses above others what he sees they have been unable to acquire.

It must also be known that often certain vices do not come to the mind simultaneously but are placed in reserve, so that one may follow another in temptation. One comes openly to the face, while another approaches from the side and inserts itself into the temptation, so that, while resistance is being offered to one, the deceived mind may be carried away by another.

The very vices mentioned above often furtively substitute themselves for one another. For sometimes, while we try to overcome anger within ourselves, leniency takes possession of the mind beyond what is necessary, so that it fails to show sinners the harshness that ought to be shown. Often, when this careless leniency displeases us as something present within ourselves, zeal draws itself toward fervor and leads the captive mind beyond the boundary of patience.

Since vices therefore come against the mind mingled and united together, camps are rightly set forth in the preacher’s mouth against the Jerusalem that has been drawn. And because at times individual vices strike the mind from different sides, battering rams are arranged around it.

The preacher places battering rams around the soul when he carefully warns how craftily lust strikes, how harshly impatience destroys, how grievously avarice inflames and kills, and how arrogantly pride extinguishes. To place battering rams around it, then, is, through preaching, to show what weapons of vices customarily strike the soul from every side.

It follows: “And you, take an iron pan for yourself and place it as an iron wall between yourself and the city.”

Because iron is a strong metal and food is fried in a pan, what is signified by the iron pan except the strong frying of spiritual zeal? Every spiritual zeal of a teacher fries his soul, because he is deeply distressed when he sees the weak abandon eternal things and take pleasure in temporal ones.

How well Paul took up the iron pan when, tormented by zeal for souls, he said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not on fire?” (II Corinthians XI). What else had he made his heart, which the zeal of souls had set aflame, than a pan in which he burned with love of virtues against vices? What was burning was a pan. It was inflamed and cooked, because it was kindled by bitterness, yet from its afflicted thought it prepared nourishment for the virtues.

But what does it mean that the prophet places this same pan as an iron wall between himself and the city, except that the same strong zeal which is now active in the teacher’s mind will be a witness on the day of the final judgment between him and the soul for which he has been zealous against vices? Even if the one who is taught refuses to listen, the teacher will nevertheless not be guilty because of the zeal he showed concerning the negligence of his hearer.

He places an iron wall between himself and the city because, at the time of punishment, the teacher is protected from the danger of condemnation by that very thing through which he now suffers the burning of zeal in guarding the heart. For no sacrifice is so acceptable to almighty God as zeal for souls. Hence the Psalmist says: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Psalm LXVIII).

Let us therefore take an iron pan and place it as an iron wall between ourselves and the city—that is, let us assume strong zeal, so that later we may find this strong defense between ourselves and the soul of our hearer. We shall find this iron wall then if we now hold it firmly: teaching, persuading, rebuking, consoling, frightening—sometimes acting gently, sometimes more severely.

The text rightly adds concerning this severity: “And you shall set your face firmly against it, and it shall be under siege.”

What does it mean to set one’s face firmly against Jerusalem drawn upon the brick except that, when the teacher announces the vision of heavenly peace to a soul and sees that it is still weak in its actions, he should show himself less yielding and lenient toward it? Hence it is written: “Do you have daughters? Preserve their bodies, and do not show them a cheerful face” (Sirach VII).

Weak souls, devoted to the desires of the world, are sometimes better preserved through severity. A firm face—that is, a face withdrawn from every hope of frivolous leniency through the guardianship of severity—terrifies the unstable soul and restrains it from love of vices by the strength of discipline.

Whenever the teacher does this, it is always necessary that sweetness and humility be retained in the heart, so that he may love greatly and never become proud through elation against the one to whom he is nevertheless unwilling to display his love and humility for that person’s benefit.

The text continues: “And you shall surround it.” A teacher surrounds the soul of his hearer when he declares that snares of temptations can be set in everything done in this life, so that, while the mind is made fearful everywhere, it may live everywhere on its guard—more watchful in proportion to its greater fear.

The text continues: “It is a sign for the house of Israel.” If this refers to the historical siege that literally took place, what the prophet did is a sign for the house of Israel. If it refers to the mystery enacted daily by the teacher concerning each person’s soul, both what he did and what he announced through his action are a sign for the house of Israel.

For just as the house of Israel endured a bodily siege, so every soul that begins to serve almighty God feels the snares of evil spirits besieging it. If it truly wishes to be rescued from them, it must know that it cannot be rescued by its own strength. Rather, it must hope for the help of the one who, while we live in corruptible flesh, can through the mystery of his redemption strengthen even the heavenly spirits who are without flesh: Jesus Christ our Lord.

“And you shall sleep on your left side, and place the iniquities of the house of Israel upon it, for the number of days during which you sleep upon it; and you shall bear their iniquity. But I have assigned you the years of their iniquity according to the number of days, three hundred and ninety days, and you shall bear the iniquity of the house of Israel. [Col. 0592D] When you have completed these, you shall sleep a second time on your right side, and you shall bear the iniquity of the house of Judah for forty days. I have assigned you a day for a year, a day, I say, for a year.”

**(Jerome.)** Let us inquire what the three hundred and ninety years are, which are reckoned as an equal number of days during which the prophet slept on his left side, bound and confined so that he could not turn to the other side, thereby signifying the captivity and miseries of the ten tribes—that is, of Israel. And what are the other forty years during which, on behalf of Judah and its iniquities, he lay on his right side—or, as Holy Scripture relates (IV Kings 15), slept?

Concerning Israel, it must be said that under King Pekah son of Remaliah, who reigned twenty years in Israel and was the nineteenth king, Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, came and captured Aijon, Abel-beth-maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, and the whole land of Naphtali, and transferred them to the Assyrians. After him Hoshea son of Elah reigned nine years in Israel, and he was captured with all Samaria by Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, and transferred to Halah and Habor, the rivers of Gozan, and to the cities of the Medes. In the sixth year of King Hezekiah, as the sacred history of Kings relates, Hoshea was captured.

If we calculate in order the number of years during which Israel was in distress and oppressed by the yoke of captivity, we can determine it as follows. From Hezekiah’s sixth year to his twenty-ninth year—for he reigned twenty-nine years altogether—there are twenty-four years. Manasseh succeeded him and reigned fifty-five years. [Col. 0593A] After him Amon reigned two years; after Amon, Josiah reigned thirty-two years. Josiah was succeeded by Jehoiakim, also called Eliakim, who reigned eleven years. After him came Jehoiachin, also called Jeconiah, who was immediately led into captivity; and Zedekiah reigned in his place for eleven years, under whom Jerusalem was captured and the Temple destroyed.

Thus, from Israel’s first captivity, which took place under King Pekah, to Zedekiah’s eleventh year, when the Temple was laid waste, there are one hundred and seventy-four years. From the second captivity, when Hoshea and all Samaria were captured and overthrown, there are one hundred and eighty-five years. The Temple’s desolation lasted seventy years; added to the first captivity, these make two hundred and thirty-four years.

For in the second year of Darius, king of the Persians, [Col. 0593C] the Temple was rebuilt by Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jehozadak, with Haggai and Zechariah prophesying. Darius reigned thirty-six years; when one year is subtracted, thirty-five years are added. After him Xerxes son of Darius reigned twenty years. After him Artabanus ruled for four months. Xerxes, who was called *Makrocheir* [Μακρόχειρ, “Long-handed”], ruled forty years. After him Xerxes ruled for two months, and Sogdianus for four months. Darius, called Nothus, succeeded him and reigned nineteen years. After him Artaxerxes, called Mnemon, son of Darius and Parysatis, reigned forty years. He is called Ahasuerus by the Hebrews; under him the history of Mordecai and Esther is related, when the entire Jewish people, delivered from the danger of death, [Col. 0593D] recovered its former liberty.

From Darius’s second year to Ahasuerus’s final year there are one hundred and fifty-five years and four months. Added to the preceding two hundred and thirty-four years, these make three hundred and eighty-nine years and four months.

The forty years represented by the sleeping on the right side are easily calculated. After Eliakim, who was called Jehoiakim, his son Jehoiachin, also called Jeconiah, reigned three months. During his reign the servants of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came against Jerusalem, and the city was surrounded with fortifications:

“Then Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came to the city with his servants to attack it. And Jehoiachin, king of Judah, went out to the king of Babylon, he himself, his mother, his servants, his princes, and his eunuchs. And the king of Babylon received him in the eighth year of his reign, and carried away from there all the treasures of the house of the Lord and the treasures of the royal house” (IV Kings 24). [Col. 0594A]

A little later:

“And he transferred all Jerusalem, all the princes, and all the mighty men of the army—ten thousand into captivity—and every craftsman and smith. Nothing was left except the poor of the people of the land” (ibid.).

After this, with the innumerable multitude of the people and all the wealth of Jerusalem, Zedekiah reigned eleven years, under whom the city was captured and the Temple destroyed. Its desolation continued until Darius’s second year, for seventy years.

In the thirtieth year of the Temple’s desolation, Cyrus reigned [Col. 0594B] in Persia, after overthrowing Astyages, king of the Medes. In accordance with Isaiah’s prophecy, he sent back to Jerusalem nearly fifty thousand people from the tribe of Judah, together with the Temple vessels that Nebuchadnezzar had carried away and the other things recorded in the history of Ezra.

Thus, just as in the case of Israel—that is, the ten tribes—we calculate three hundred and ninety years from King Pekah, under whom Shalmaneser devastated much of the Israelite people, to the fortieth year of Ahasuerus, when the persecution of the Jewish people was moderated, so from Jehoiachin’s first year, when the greater part of Jerusalem was transferred to Babylon, to the first year of Cyrus, king of the Persians—the thirtieth year of the Temple’s desolation—we calculate forty years. Under Cyrus the captivity of the Jews was relaxed and liberty was restored to the people.

Some, joining Israel’s three hundred and ninety years to Judah’s forty, make four hundred and thirty years. They wish these years to be completed from the Savior’s baptism to the consummation of the world. Others, especially the Jews, wish the four hundred and thirty years to be reckoned from Vespasian’s second year, when Jerusalem was captured by the Romans and the Temple destroyed, during the tribulation, distress, and captivity under which the people were placed. They therefore expect the people to return to their former condition, so that just as the children of Israel were in Egypt for four hundred and thirty years, so the final captivity should end after the same number of years.

It is written in Exodus:

“Now the dwelling of the children of Israel, which they dwelt in the land of Egypt, was four hundred and thirty years” (Exod. 12).

And again:

“And it came to pass after four hundred and thirty years that the whole army of the Lord went out by night.”

I am greatly astonished that the common copies have one hundred and ninety years, and that in some copies one hundred and fifty is written, when both the Hebrew text and Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion clearly retain three hundred and ninety years, and the same number is also found among the Septuagint, who nevertheless have not been corrupted through scribal error.

We believe that we have explained this most difficult question—which, not to speak arrogantly, had been explained by no one—not so much through our own knowledge as through the grace of the Lord, fulfilling what he promised:

“Seek, and you shall find; ask, and you shall receive; knock, and it shall be opened to you” (Matt. 7).

Whoever wishes to calculate from the first captivity, which took place under Menahem son of Gaddi, king of Israel, who reigned ten years in Samaria, when Pul, king of the Assyrians, came into the land of Israel and received a thousand talents of silver, and after him from the additional two years of Pekah, who reigned in Israel, will find that the three hundred and ninety years were completed in the twenty-eighth year of King Ahasuerus, when the story of Esther is said to have occurred. This is more credible, for Israel cast off the yoke of its most grievous servitude while Ahasuerus was still reigning, not after his empire had ended.

“And you shall turn your face toward the siege of Jerusalem, and your arm shall be uncovered, and you shall prophesy against it.”

Preparation of the face, strength, and the support of an extended and bared arm are required, so that the siege of the city may be demonstrated not only by the prophet’s voice but also by his gesture and appearance.

[Col. 0595B] “Behold, I have surrounded you with bonds, and you shall not turn from one side to the other until you have completed the days of your siege—or confinement.”

The left side is assigned to Israel because Samaria had been without the Temple and knowledge of God; the right side to Judah, in which the worship and religion of God existed. It must be observed that in the one case there is the punishment of sinners, and in the other the exercise of virtue. He does not turn from one side to the other, so that no respite from the torments is indicated until the complete confinement of the days mentioned above has been fulfilled.

What is a day for the prophet is a year for those who suffer. The years Laban reckoned seemed to Jacob like only a few days (Gen. 29). There is variety not only in punishments according to the diversity of merits, but also in the recompense of the good: the lambs stand on the right, and the goats on the left. [Col. 0595C] Hence it is written elsewhere:

“The heart of the wise man is at his right hand, but the heart of the fool is at his left” (Eccli. 10).

There are bonds of the Lord, with which we are bound for salvation, and there are bonds of the devil, with which he had bound the woman in the Gospel for eighteen years. Hence also:

“Each person is bound by the cords of his own sins.”

The Lord loosens these bonds in the figure of Lazarus raised from the dead, who had lain in the tomb bound with strips and bands.

“And you, take for yourself wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and vetch, and put them in one vessel; and make for yourself loaves according to the number of the days during which you sleep on your side—three hundred and ninety days—and eat them. Your food, which you shall eat, shall be by weight: twenty shekels a day. From time to time you shall eat it. [Col. 0595D] And you shall drink water by measure, a sixth part of a hin; from time to time you shall drink it. You shall eat it like a barley cake baked under ashes, and you shall cover it with human dung before their eyes.”

**(Jerome.)** The prophet is commanded to demonstrate by his actions the famine and poverty that will come upon the people of Israel. For when there is a shortage of everything, people do not seek variety or delicacies of food, but only how the belly may be filled. Thus the prophet now puts wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and oats into a single vessel; he makes three hundred and ninety loaves, to be eaten one each day, and each loaf weighs twenty shekels, that is, staters.

A shekel, or stater, contains four drachmas. Eight drachmas make a Roman ounce, so that one loaf is said to contain ten ounces—a quantity that burdens the soul more than sustains it. The barrenness of the food is increased by the barrenness of the water, for he is commanded to drink each day a sixth part of the Hebrew measure called a hin.

A hin contains two Attic *choes*, which we may call two Italian *sextarii*, so that a hin is the measure of a Jewish *sextarius* and of our military measure; its sixth part makes one-third of an Italian *sextarius*. This food and drink, according to the famous orator, does not give strength but prevents death.

When he says, “From time to time you shall eat or drink it,” he means from evening to evening, although some wrongly think it should be understood as from year to year. The loaves themselves are made like barley loaves baked under ashes. He is told to cover them with human dung—not without the knowledge of those who are to eat them. An uncertain matter can temper misery, but here they are to see it and endure the horror of the sight before the nausea of the taste.

It must also be noted that, according to the number of days of the left side, three hundred and ninety loaves baked under ashes are commanded to be made and eaten one per day, while the loaves for the forty days of the right side are entirely omitted. Thus Holy Scripture secretly indicates that the punishment of a sinful people is not the same if it possesses knowledge of God as it is for one who has completely departed from the worship of the true God.

We can also say, according to the spiritual understanding, that the Jewish people, after offending God, continue to eat loaves baked under ashes to this day, mixed with wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and oats. One of these is human food, another the food of beasts. In that they appear to believe in one God, they possess something of wheat. But because they deny the Son, they are fed with the barley of beasts, and with beans, which inflate the belly of those who eat them and are said to oppress the mind, so much so that even for Pythagoreans this food is detestable.

Because of a lentil dish Esau lost his birthright. Millet is the food of peasants, country people, and fattened animals. Oats, or vetch, and *olyra* are eaten by brute animals.

That which is written according to the Septuagint—that Elijah, fleeing from Jezebel (III Kings 19), found a loaf called ὀλγριτήν, that is, baked under ashes—is a sign of persecution and poverty. Hence he is fed by ravens: because he found no food in Israel, he was fed with the provisions of the nations, which were unclean.

[Col. 0596D] The Law itself, which they read but do not understand, is a loaf baked under ashes and covered with human dung. Therefore the Apostle Paul says that he regarded the gains of the Law and the observance of former ceremonies as dung, in order to gain Christ (Phil. 3).

“And the Lord said: Thus shall the children of Israel eat their defiled bread among the nations to which I shall drive them. And I said: Ah, ah, ah, Lord God! Behold, my soul has not been defiled, and from my childhood until now I have not eaten anything that died of itself or was torn by beasts. No unclean flesh has ever entered my mouth. And he said to me: Behold, I have given you cow dung in place of human dung, and you shall make your bread with it.”

We frequently read in many places that, according to Zechariah, prophets are portentous men who signify future events by their actions; concerning them God says:

“I have been represented through the hands of the prophets” (Hos. 12).

Just as Ezekiel ate bread in dung, so the children of Israel—or the entire Jewish people, or, as some think, the ten tribes—ate defiled bread among the nations. The threat, however, is not directed against those who have already been driven out, but against those who are to be driven from the promised land.

When the prophet learned this, according to Aquila he rejected it for the third time, saying, “Ah, ah, ah.” Finally, he obtains what he requested, and the severity of the sentence is tempered by a milder command.

It is asked why Ezekiel refused the easier alternative, whereas Hosea was immediately joined to a prostitute and did not object—or even reply that he had a chaste body and ought not to be defiled by intercourse with a harlot—when the Apostle says:

“He who joins himself to a harlot becomes one body” (I Cor. 6).

From this it is shown that the episode was a figure of the Synagogue or the Church and was not literally carried out. We have discussed this more fully in our exposition of the prophet.

That which dies of itself is called *morticinum*, because it loses its life without the shedding of blood, and in it the soul dies. What is torn by beasts is called in Greek Θηριαλώτον (*therialōton*).

When cow dung is granted in place of human dung, lesser evils are signified: although they are commanded to eat bread cooked in cow dung, they remain far from the uncleanness of human dung. This rule is observed among the Jewish people to this day: they do not eat their bread in human dung. For they do not serve idols [Col. 0597C] or venerate the various portents of demons, but eat it baked in cow dung, since they perform everything for the sake of the flesh, the belly, and the goods of this earth, according to what is said:

“He who does these things shall live in them.”

We, however, despise earthly things. We not only tread underfoot the food of human dung and consider earthly delights worthless, but we eat the bread that came down from heaven and enjoy that food of which the Psalmist sings:

“Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 77),

living not on Egyptian flesh but on the thinness of manna.

“And he said to me: Son of man, behold, I shall break the staff of bread in Jerusalem, and they shall eat bread by weight and with anxiety, and they shall drink water by measure and in distress, so that, when bread and water fail, each person may fall upon his brother, and they may waste away in their iniquities.”

The entire sleeping on the left and right sides, and the bread baked under ashes mixed from six different kinds of grain, signify the evils of the world. The purpose is to proclaim the incredible famine of food and scarcity of water in Jerusalem.

“So that each person may fall upon his brother”—hoping for help from another, which he does not foresee existing within himself. Human nature is such that, when evils press upon people and the weight of distress bears down on them, they place their confidence more in someone near them than in themselves.

“And they shall waste away in their iniquities”—while suffering everything on account of their iniquities.

I fear that this breaking of the bread may already be found in our Jerusalem, in which the vision of peace is seen. The Lord breaks it when he is angry and judges us unworthy of his bread. Would that we might at least deserve to receive it by weight and with anxiety, and that the extreme dryness of our parched tongue might be moistened by the fingertip of Lazarus (Luke 16).

When the bread and water of the Church fail, one person falls against another, and everywhere there is discord, as we split the tunic of Christ, which even the soldiers did not dare to tear during the Savior’s Passion. We waste away in our iniquities because we do not possess the righteousness of God.

It is written in Jeremiah that “the little ones”—that is, the common people of the Church—“asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them” (Lam. 4). [Col. 0598A]

But Paul, who was a man and knew that Christ had broken the legal loaves and given them to the disciples for distribution, speaks confidently:

“The bread which we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ?” (I Cor. 10).

Those who need the milk of infancy and cannot receive solid food are unable to eat the staff—or strength—of bread. Nothing so strengthens the soul of the one who eats as the bread of life, concerning which it is written:

“Bread strengthens the human heart.”

## CHAPTER V. Different judgments upon the people are signified by the hair of the head and beard; and concerning future evils upon Jerusalem.

“And you, son of man, take for yourself a sharp sword that shaves the hair, and draw it over your head and your beard. Then take scales for weighing, divide the hair into three parts: burn one-third in the middle of the city, when the days of your confinement are completed; cut one-third with the sword all around it; and scatter the remaining third to the wind. I shall unsheathe the sword after them. Then take a small number from them and bind them at the edge of your cloak. From these again take some, throw them into the midst of the fire, and burn them in the fire; and from it fire shall go out into the whole house of Israel.”

**(Jerome.)** In what follows, the Lord himself explains through the prophet the riddle of the hair divided into three parts, saying:

“One-third of you shall die by pestilence and be consumed by famine in your midst,”

signifying that famine and pestilence are represented by fire.

“And one-third of you shall fall by the sword around you,”

describing slaughter and wars outside.

“And the remaining third I shall scatter to every wind,”

showing that these are the people who will be led into captivity. After them he says that he will unsheathe or pour out his sword, so that captivity will not be the final evil. He then takes from the scattered captives and binds at the edge of his cloak those who will return from captivity to Jerusalem. From these also he takes a portion and consumes it with fire and flame, signifying the Macedonians, under whom the inhabitants of Judah, and especially Jerusalem, suffered severe hardships.

When he says that “from it”—that is, from the Jewish people—fire will go out into the whole house of Israel, or, according to the Septuagint, “from her,” with the city of Jerusalem understood, [Col. 0599A] the history of the Maccabees relates (I Macc. 2–4) that some Jews surrendered themselves to Antiochus Epiphanes and incited him to persecute the people. It also records many other events, as does the same history and, above all, the works of Josephus concerning the conflict between Hyrcanus and Alexander. Through the opportunity created by these conflicts, the consul Pompey captured Jerusalem and subjected it to Roman rule. Later, under Titus and Vespasian, the city was captured and the Temple overthrown. After fifty years, under Aelius Hadrian, the city was burned and destroyed to its foundations, so that it even lost its former name.

Just as the hair of the head and beard is a sign of beauty and manliness, and when shaved exposes an ugly nakedness, and just as the hair is the outermost and, so to speak, lifeless part of the body, so Jerusalem and its people—lifeless and separated from the living body of God—are handed over to famine and pestilence, slaughter and the sword, captivity and dispersion.

From this dispersion, under the figure of the hair, a portion is bound at the edge of the cloak, so that a small remnant may again be handed over to the fire. From it an immense flame, almost laying everything waste, goes out into the whole house of Israel.

This may be understood differently according to the mystical sense. For it is also written in Job:

“And, having shaved his head, he fell upon the earth and worshiped” (Job 1; Gregory, *Moral Commentary*, book 2, chapters 29–30).

What is signified by the cut hair, except the subtlety of the mysteries? What by the head, except the summit of the priesthood? Hence also the prophet Ezekiel is told:

“You, son of man, take for yourself a sharp sword that shaves the hair, take it, and draw it over your head and your beard.”

Thus the judgment of the Redeemer is expressed through the prophet’s action. When he appeared in the flesh, he shaved the head, because, abandoning the kingdom of the Israelites, he cut off its beauty of virtue.

What, however, is signified here by the earth except the sinner? To the first sinful human being it was said:

“You are earth, and to earth you shall go.”

By the name “earth,” therefore, sinful gentile humanity is designated. For while Judea considered itself righteous, it is clear how reprobate it regarded the gentiles, as Paul testifies:

“We are Jews by nature, and not sinners from the gentiles” (Gal. 2).

Our Mediator fell to the earth as though with his head shaved, because, abandoning Judea, he came to the knowledge of the gentiles after withdrawing his mysteries from its priesthood. He shaved the hair from his head because he removed the mysteries of the Law from that first priesthood of his. He fell to the earth because he gave himself to sinful people who were to be saved; and while he abandoned those who seemed righteous to themselves, he took up those who both knew and confessed themselves to be unrighteous.

It follows:

“Thus says the Lord God: This is Jerusalem. I have placed her in the midst of the nations, and lands around her, but she despised my judgments, so that she was more impious than the nations, and my commandments more than the lands that surround her. For they rejected my judgments and did not walk in my commandments.”

**(Jerome.)** The same prophet testifies here that Jerusalem is situated in the middle of the world, demonstrating that it is the navel of the earth. Expressing the Lord’s nativity, the Psalmist says:

“Truth has arisen from the earth” (Ps. 48).

And afterward, speaking of his Passion:

“He has worked salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. 73).

On the eastern side it is surrounded by the region called Asia; on the western side by the region called Europe; to the south and southwest by Libya and Africa; to the north by the Scythians, Armenia, Persia, and all the peoples of Pontus.

It is therefore placed in the midst of the nations so that, since “God was known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. 75), all the surrounding nations might follow its example. Yet Jerusalem followed the impiety of the nations around it and surpassed them even in its wickedness.

“Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because you have surpassed the nations that are around you, you have not walked in my commandments, you have not carried out my judgments, and you have not acted according to the judgments of the nations that are around you. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, and I myself shall execute judgments in your midst in the sight of the nations. I shall do in you what I have not done and what I shall never again do, because of all your abominations.”

Why, he says, should I complain that you have not walked in my commandments and have not carried out my judgments, when by your wickedness you have surpassed all the nations around you and have not done what they have often done by the natural law written in their hearts?

Therefore I myself—not through angels or other ministers—shall execute my judgments against you in the sight of all, judgments such as I have never before executed and shall never execute again. By saying “judgments,” he demonstrates the truth of the sentence, so that anger may not seem to exceed the measure of punishment.

He did not do such things to any nation as he did to Jerusalem:

“For the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it shall be beaten with many blows” (Luke 12); “and the mighty shall suffer mighty torments” (Wis. 6).

“And I shall never again do the like,” he says.

He beautifully says, “I shall not do the like.” For long after the killing of Christ he will do things more severe. It is one thing sometimes to have worshiped idols, for which they were previously punished; it is another to have slaughtered the Son of God.

“Therefore fathers shall eat their sons in your midst, and sons shall eat their fathers, and I shall execute judgments against you. And I shall scatter all your remnant to every wind.”

With reference to what he had said above—“Because you have surpassed the nations around you, you have not walked in my commandments, and you have not carried out my judgments”—he repeated “therefore” three times.

First:

“Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you; I myself shall execute judgments in your midst.”

Second:

“Therefore fathers shall eat their sons in your midst.”

Third:

“Therefore, as I live, says the Lord God, because you have profaned my sanctuary in all your offenses,”

and so forth.

Nevertheless, it must be noted that wherever the matter is honorable and good and suited to the merit of those who endure it, God declares that he himself does it. But where the matter is grievous and unworthy of God, he says that it happens, but not that he himself causes it. Thus here:

“Therefore fathers shall eat their sons in your midst, and sons shall eat their fathers.”

He did not say, “I shall cause fathers to eat their sons in your midst, and sons to eat their fathers.” But what was honorable and did not appear unworthy of the majesty of God, he says that he himself does. For it follows:

“And I shall execute judgments against you, and I shall scatter all your remnant to every wind.”

We can find something similar in the curses of Deuteronomy, especially in this passage:

“I shall glorify those who glorify me; but those who despise me shall be brought to nothing” (Deut. 28).

He himself glorifies those who glorify him. But those who despise him will not be despised by the Lord or brought to nothing by him—for this is what would follow if that were stated—but they will simply be brought to nothing, not by God, but according to their merits and sins.

We read in the Book of Kings (IV Kings 6) that, when famine compelled it, a mother devoured her son. Josephus also records that many such things occurred during the siege of Jerusalem. But no history relates that fathers ate their sons or sons their fathers, unless perhaps we should believe that even these things happened amid the many evils of necessity.

This may also be referred to our Jerusalem, when teachers rise against disciples—that is, fathers against sons—and disciples against teachers—that is, sons against fathers—in mutual sedition. Then what the Apostle says is fulfilled:

“But if you bite and accuse one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another” (Gal. 5).

Hence the prophet also sang in mystical language:

“When those who afflict me approached against me, to eat my flesh” (Ps. 26).

Job says something similar:

“If my maidservants said, ‘Who will grant us that we may eat of his flesh?’” (Job 31).

And concerning teachers who pursue profit from their disciples and have no concern for their salvation, it is said:

“Those who devour my people as though they were eating bread” (Ps. 52).

Of them the Apostle also says:

“And they devour widows’ houses” (Luke 20).

We may understand the fathers who ate their sons and the sons who ate their fathers not only in the Babylonian siege but also in the Roman siege. What is said—“I shall scatter all your remnant to every wind”—belongs more particularly to the Roman captivity, when they were dispersed throughout the whole world. This is the scattering of the hair and beard to every wind.

“Therefore, as I live, says the Lord God, because you have profaned my sanctuary in all your offenses and in all your abominations, I too shall break you, and my eye shall not spare, and I shall not have pity.”

This is said specifically to Jerusalem: “Because you have profaned my sanctuary by abandoning me and worshiping idols in my Temple, I too shall break all your idols, crush them, cut them apart, or cast them away, because you first cast me away. My eye shall not spare you when I see you submitting your neck to famine, the sword, and slavery, nor shall I have pity, because you do not deserve my mercy.”

For it is written:

“Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5).

The same must be understood of the Church. God can say daily to teachers and priests who act negligently:

“Because you have profaned my sanctuary in all your offenses and in all your abominations that you have committed, I too shall crush and break you.”

I shall repay through myself what you have perpetrated against my people. Concerning them this same prophet speaks more fully: they cover themselves with the wool of the sheep, feed on their milk and cheese, and do not seek the broken or diseased sheep.

“One-third of you shall die by pestilence and be consumed by famine in your midst. One-third of you shall fall by the sword around you. I shall scatter the remaining third to every wind, and I shall unsheathe the sword after them. I shall fulfill my fury and cause my indignation to rest upon them, and I shall be comforted; and they shall know that I am the Lord who has spoken in my zeal, when I have fulfilled my indignation against them.”

Since we discussed this chapter above, it seems that it should now be omitted. But I shall add what is necessary concerning the words:

“I shall fulfill my fury and cause my indignation to rest upon them, and I shall be comforted; and they shall know that I am the Lord who has spoken in my zeal, when I have fulfilled my indignation against them.”

We have often explained how the fury, indignation, and zeal of God are to be understood: God speaks in terms of human emotions, not because he himself becomes angry, but because through punishments and torments we perceive God as angry.

His zeal must be understood metaphorically in terms of a husband and wife. As long as a man loves his wife, he is jealous; but if he neglects her, he says what we shall say later:

“My zeal shall depart from you, and I shall no longer be angry with you.”

The statement, “They shall know that I am the Lord who has spoken in my zeal,” does not refer to those who were consumed by famine and pestilence, nor to those who fell by the sword around the city, but to those who are scattered to every wind. Through the deaths of others and their own miseries, they will perceive the anger of the God whom they refused to perceive as merciful.

“And I shall make you a desert in the sight of everyone who passes by.”

It is beneficial for all the vices in Jerusalem to be laid waste and reduced to a desert, and for it to recognize its own sins, so that the city which ought to have been an example of virtues to the other nations may become an example of miseries.

We may understand its daughters as cities or villages, or as churches dispersed throughout the world. Thus whoever is a pilgrim of this world and says with the Psalmist,

“I am a sojourner and a pilgrim, like all my fathers” (Ps. 38),

and concerning whom it is said,

“Those who passed by did not say, ‘The blessing of the Lord be upon you’” (Ps. 128),

may see its disgrace and grieve.

[Col. 0602D] “And you shall be a reproach and a blasphemy, an example and an astonishment among the nations that are around you, when I execute judgments against you in fury, indignation, and rebukes of wrath, because I am the Lord who has spoken.”

That Jerusalem is worthy of lamentation when it has offended God, so that he might execute judgments against it in fury and indignation, Paul testifies when he says:

“We were by nature children of wrath, as also the others” (Eph. 2).

And again:

“We who are in this tabernacle groan, being burdened” (II Cor. 5).

We speak together with Jerusalem:

“I shall bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him.”

“When I send against you the most grievous arrows of famine, which shall be deadly, and which I shall send to destroy you; and I shall gather famine against you, and I shall break the staff of bread among you.”

**(Jerome.)** It is clear that famine, pestilence, the most savage beasts, and whatever other evils we endure in this world come upon us because of our sins. Hence that famine which is recorded in Ruth (Ruth 1) and in the Book of Kings (III Kings 17), under Elijah, when heaven was shut for three years and six months, and under Elisha (IV Kings 6), whose incredible scarcity was compensated by sudden abundance, was sent by the judgment of God.

This happened not only then in Jerusalem but also happens in our Jerusalem, where, because of the greatness of our sins, famine is first sent upon us so that we cannot hear the word of God. Then death follows famine, so that those who did not hear, “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33), may afterward experience:

“The death of sinners is most grievous” (ibid.).

We have spoken above about the firmament and the staff of bread.

“‘And I will send famine and the most savage beasts against you, until they destroy you. Pestilence and bloodshed will pass through you, and I will bring the sword against you. I, the Lord, have spoken.’ The fact that the most savage beasts are brought upon a land of desolation, which has been devastated by famine, sword, and plague, is also demonstrated by present circumstances, when a familiar animal, a dog, is driven by madness against its masters’ flesh, and the land is filled with bears, wolves, and every other kind of beast. That pestilence and bloodshed pass through it signifies disease and the sword. But the most savage beasts are also sent against our Jerusalem when we are handed over to shameful passions, to a depraved mind, and to a conscience of sins [Col. 0603C] that torture and tear our soul apart. Dissensions, heresies, schisms, rivalries, envies, sorrows, slanders, many desires, and greed—which is the root of all evils—are the most savage beasts. When they are within us, we deserve to hear: ‘Your apostasy shall correct you.’ And we pray and say: ‘Do not hand over to the beasts the souls confessing you.’”

## CHAPTER VI

The prophet shows that the people were struck by plagues because of the sin of idolatry.

“‘And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set your face toward the mountains of Israel, and you shall prophesy against them and say: Mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord: Thus says the Lord God to the mountains [Col. 0603D] and the hills, the crags, and the valleys,’ etc.” What is often said in this prophet—“Adonai the Lord”—seems to require a brief explanation for Greeks and Latins who do not know the Hebrew language. *Adonai* is one of the ten names of God, and it means “Lord,” a word that we often use also of human beings. Thus Sarah, calling Abraham her lord (Genesis XVIII), called him by this name. And where it says, “My lord the king,” *Adonai* is written. Therefore, when the two names “Lord” and “Lord” are joined, the first name is common, while the second properly belongs to God: it is, as it were, ineffable, and the name that was written on the golden plate which was on the forehead of the high priest.

The mountains of Israel, however, which had been occupied by the images of demons, hear and understand their Creator not with their ears, but through the command and power of the Creator. In the same way: “The sea saw and fled; the Jordan turned back” (Psalm CXIII). Certainly this was not with the eyes of the flesh, with which it did not see. And to the sea it is said: “Be silent, be still” (Mark IV); the blasts of the winds are commanded, and the worm that struck Jonah’s shelter is ordered (Jonah IV). And of the same earth it is written: “He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble” (Psalm CIII).

The prophet speaks to these mountains, indicating that the idols, the altars, and all the ceremonies by which they had previously served idols must be destroyed. We may understand the mountains as those who excelled in power, wisdom, knowledge, and riches. We should also observe that he is commanded to make his face firm, and it is set against the mountains; yet he speaks not only to the mountains, but also to the hills, crags, and valleys, in which a lower rank and degree of prudence and knowledge are recognized. It seems to me, tropologically, that the mountains are those who have attained perfect knowledge; the hills, those who are somewhat lower; and the crags, those who possess no knowledge but, trusting merely in their manner of life, presume to themselves that they understand something of the interpretation of the Scriptures, “having,” as the Apostle says, “a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Romans X). The valleys, however, may be called the newest members of the Church, inferior in both life and knowledge, yet not withdrawing from the Lord’s assembly. All of them are commanded to hear the word of God, so that each may understand, according to his capacity and judgment, what the Lord commands.

[Col. 0604C] “‘Behold, I will bring a sword upon you, and I will destroy your high places, demolish your altars, and your images shall be broken. I will cast your slain before your idols, and I will place the corpses of the children of Israel before the face of your images, and I will scatter your bones around your altars in all your settlements.’”

He tells the mountains of Israel that the Lord will destroy their high places, where they worshiped men whom they had fashioned as gods; that he will break their altars and images; and that he will cause their worshipers to be killed in the sight of their shrines, so that the corpses of the dead may lie where sacrifices had previously lain. He will scatter the bones—not of the mountains, but of those who had lain upon the mountains—around the altars and throughout all the cities and villages of Israel.

This is the literal sense. Otherwise, it also applies to those who are lifted up in pride, of whom the Apostle says (I Corinthians VIII): “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.” The sword is brought against them so that all the images they have fashioned from their own minds may be shattered; they may lie as slain men and recognize themselves as dead, seeing that their images and inventions are of no benefit to them. And when he says that he will scatter the bones of the mountains around the altars, he indicates that the strongest among them will be separated from one another. It is beneficial for the wicked of a perverse knowledge to be divided from the wicked. Just as those who, in their evil agreement, built a tower for their own advantage were scattered, and their languages were divided lest their most wicked agreement make them worse (Genesis XI), so the bones of the mountains should be scattered, that they may understand their vain endeavors. The reading that we have included—“And I will place the corpses of the children of Israel before the face of your images”—is not found in the Septuagint.

“‘The cities shall be deserted, the high places shall be demolished, your altars shall be devastated and shall perish, they shall be broken, and your idols shall cease; your shrines shall be crushed, your works shall be blotted out, and the slain man shall fall in your midst, and you shall know that I am the Lord.’” (Jerome.) The reason why the cities of the mountains must be deserted is clear: the high places are to be demolished, the altars and idols destroyed, the shrines brought to ruin, and all worship of images brought to an end. The slain shall fall in the midst of the mountains, and they shall know that he is the Lord.

Through this we are given an opportunity to pursue a more spiritual understanding: the cities of the heretics—which are interpreted as churches—their high places of pride, and the altars of their perverse doctrines are to be broken; their idols are to perish, which they had fashioned for themselves from their own hearts; and their shrines are to be crushed—not temples, but those structures that had risen against the temple of the Lord. In Greek they are called *τεμένη* (*temenē*), that is, sanctuaries and shrines. All the works of the mountains are to be crushed, because they are not works of God but of teachers of false knowledge.

When they have fallen in the midst of the mountains—whether those whom the mountains themselves had killed, or ecclesiastical men who had killed them, while they lived wickedly, for their salvation—then the end of the proud mountains will come, so that they may know that he is the Lord. It may also be that, from one people of the mountains of Israel, when some have been killed, the others come to recognize him: “When the pestilent man is scourged, the fool will be wiser.”

[Col. 0605C] “‘And I will leave among you those who escape the sword among the nations, when I scatter you among the lands. And your survivors shall remember me among the nations to which they were led captive.’”

The words that the Lord spoke to Elijah—“I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal”—and what the Apostle Paul writes—“So too at the present time there is a remnant according to the election of grace, and they have been saved” (Romans XI)—can be applied to this chapter. The apostles too, who were from the seed of Israel and had escaped the sword, were therefore preserved so that they might be scattered among the nations, preach the Gospel throughout the lands, and remember God among the nations in which they were living during the time of their captivity.

It may also be said that some were preserved from the Jewish captivity for this reason: that among the nations they might remember his name and proclaim his power. Likewise, from the peoples of the heretics, those who were able to escape the sword of their destruction and the most wicked faction that had risen up against God will be scattered here and there. They will remember the name of God, doing penance, and will rejoice that they have been captured by ecclesiastical men.

“‘Because I have broken their adulterous heart, which departed from me, and their adulterous eyes, which followed their idols; and they shall be displeased with themselves because of the evils that they had committed in all their abominations. And they shall know that I am the Lord; I have not spoken in vain when I determined to do this evil to them.’” (Jerome.) According to the Septuagint, the Lord swore and determined to do the things that he demonstrated by his deeds [Col. 0606A], whether he “broke” the adulterous heart that had departed from God—of those concerning whom he speaks through Hosea: “They were seduced by the spirit of prostitution” (Hosea IV)—and the adulterous eyes that followed idols.

Through their windows death is said to have entered; for this reason, in Daniel also (Daniel XIII), the two elders ordered Susanna to be exposed, so that they might enjoy the beauty of her naked body. The Lord did not speak in vain when he determined to do evil or evils, since those who were subject to the sentence do penance when threatened by him. But if the heart is hard and unyielding, and does not perceive even through punishments the benefits of the one who corrects it, it is said to them: “I struck your children without cause; you did not accept discipline.”

It is also beneficial for heretics that their heart—the most wicked treasury of perverse doctrines—be crushed, because it has departed from the Lord. Their eyes have prostituted themselves after their inventions; when they remember the Lord, they will be displeased with themselves because of all their abominations, and, understanding the truth of the true faith, they will know that he is the Lord. For this reason he often brings tribulation, which seems harmful and most grievous to those who endure it, so that they may turn to repentance.

“‘Thus says the Lord God: Strike your hand and stamp your foot, and say: Alas! because of all the abominations of the evils of the house of Israel.’”

The prophet is commanded to display the magnitude of the sins with his hands, feet, and speech, so that through bodily gesture and the inflection of his voice he may show the demeanor of one who is astonished, amazed, and mourning. For just as, when we see something new and wondrous, we shudder in both body and mind, so that we clap our hands, stamp our feet upon the ground, and bend our voice toward weeping, so now the prophet, seeing with the eyes of his mind the future punishments, speaks against all the abominations of the wicked of Israel, which follow.

Spiritually, we strike our hand when we separate ourselves from evil works. We stamp our foot when we do not walk along the paths of sins. We lament and weep when the things being done displease us. The reason for mourning is that the inhabitants of the mountains and the altars, and the worshipers of idols, are about to fall by sword, famine, and pestilence. They are led by various errors, changing their faith daily and being carried about by every wind of doctrine. These are struck by the sword and [Col. 0606D] divided into parts, abandoning the unity of ecclesiastical faith. Whoever has no spiritual food dies of famine, not knowing the one who said: “I am life” (John XIV). Moreover, whoever is devoted to one or several vices and cannot be separated from them falls, as though by some womb-born pestilence.

“‘He who is far away shall die of pestilence; he who is near shall fall by the sword; and he who is left and surrounded shall die of famine, and I will pour out my indignation upon them.’”
