Whoever escapes the siege of the city and migrates to the wilderness will die of pestilence; whoever is nearby will fall by the sword of the enemy; and whoever is surrounded by the hostile army will perish through famine and want. In all these things the indignation [Col. 0607A] of God will be fulfilled, so that those who remain may know that he is the Lord.

Whoever has also withdrawn from the Church will immediately die of pestilence. Whoever seems to himself knowledgeable and diligent, unless he takes care, will be struck by the sword of the enemy. Whoever is content with a simple faith and lives in the Church like the irrational animals, yet makes no progress in any good work and is not an imitator of the ant, which prepares and gathers food for itself at harvest, will die of famine. In all these things the wrath of the Lord will be fulfilled.

“‘And you shall know that I am the Lord, when your slain lie in the midst of your idols, around your altars, on every high hill and on all the summits of the mountains, beneath every leafy tree and beneath every spreading oak, the place where they burned fragrant incense [Col. 0607B] to all their idols.’”

The literal sense is clear and requires no interpretation: on the mountains of Israel and on the high hills, among the very altars of the idols and the sacred groves—which are called leafy trees—the Israelite army was slain, so that they might be punished where they had sinned.

According to the anagogical sense, let us follow the order we have begun. When the teachers of the heretics have been crushed and overcome by ecclesiastical men who are instructed in knowledge of the Scriptures, we see the slain of perverse doctrines lying among the images they had fashioned. Those who had raised themselves against the knowledge of God lie prostrate on the mountains and hills beneath every leafy tree: they had pompous words and the shadow of leaves, but no fruits of good works. They were beneath every spreading oak, which produces not the fruit of human beings but of pigs. There they burned fragrant incense, not to God but to their idols.

They could not say what is written of Noah: “The Lord smelled the odor of a good fragrance” (Genesis VIII). Nor could they say what Paul declares: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place.” Just as the holy man delights God by his fragrance, so the sinner—of whose person that psalm is sung—“My wounds have become foul and festering because of my foolishness” (Psalm XXXVII)—burns foul-smelling incense to his idols.

[Col. 0608A] “‘And I will stretch out my hand against them, and I will make the land desolate and abandoned, from the wilderness of Deblatha throughout all their settlements. And they shall know that I am the Lord.’” (Jerome.) “O mountains of Israel, when your slain have fallen in the midst of your altars and idols, on every high hill and on all the summits of the mountains, and when I have filled your sacred groves with the corpses of the dead, in which they once burned fragrant incense to their idols, then I will stretch out my hand for vengeance, which until now had been held back, and I will reduce the whole land of Israel to a wilderness, from the wilderness of Deblatha, which is in the land of Hamath and is today called Ἐπιφάνεια [Epiphaneia] of Syria, throughout all their settlements.”

Thus it will be clear to everyone that there is nothing between the wilderness and the Great Sea [Col. 0608B] that the hostile sword has not consumed. Many think that this is the same place concerning which it is written in Jeremiah: “They seized Zedekiah in the wilderness that is near Jericho, and all his companions fled from him. When they had captured the king, they brought him to the king of Babylon at Reblatha, which is in the land of Hamath.” Because of the closeness—or rather the similarity—of the Hebrew letters *daleth* and *resh*, which are distinguished by a small stroke, the place may be called either Deblatha or Reblatha.

According to the mystical interpretations, the Lord stretches out his hand over all who have been deceived by heretical error, so that he may make their land—which is interpreted as the Church—desolate, like the wilderness of Deblatha. In our language, this name means a mass of figs, or dried figs, compacted together. After they have found, beneath a feigned sweetness that did not belong to cultivated land but to the bitterness of the wilderness, that “honey drips from the lips of the prostitute woman; for a time she fattens the throats of those who eat, but afterward it is found to be more bitter than gall,” they will then know that he is the Lord.

This is also signified by the two baskets of figs placed in Jeremiah opposite the temple (Jeremiah XXIV): one contained very good figs and the other very bad figs. One of these refers to the Church of Christ, the other to the congregation of the wicked.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0607]

[Col. 0607D] Near the end of the preceding book, the prophet foretold from the word of the Lord the deserved punishment of those who served on the mountains of Israel and at the high places of idols; and, according to the mystical sense, he struck the heretics with a righteous judgment, since they worshiped images on the mountains of the pride of their errors. Now a likeness threatens them with destruction, foretells affliction, and announces the appointed end, so that they may endure the vengeance of the Lord’s wrath and receive a fitting reward for their work. Hence what follows.

## CHAPTER VII

Concerning the imminent and prolonged captivity and its cause; and how the people, not rebelling, cast their riches far away because of their flight.

“‘And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: And you, son of man, thus says the Lord God concerning the land of Israel: The end has come, the end upon the four wings of the earth, etc.’” (Jerome.) We have interpreted these as the regions of the world: east, west, south, and north. Isaiah also speaks of these wings: “Lord, from the wings—or boundaries—of the earth we have heard wonders,” things that were being accomplished throughout the whole world through the apostles.

And concerning the saints it is written: “If you sleep among the midst of the lots, you shall be like the wings of a dove covered with silver, and her hind parts with the pallor of gold” (Psalm LXVII). Hence, when the Lord drew near and saw Jerusalem, he wept and said: “How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you were unwilling” (Matthew XXIII). He is the one who, in the song of Deuteronomy (Deuteronomy XXXII), spreading his wings, received and took them up upon his shoulders.

One of the spiritual interpreters places four kinds of believers in the four wings of the earth by which we fly upward to heavenly things: the house of Aaron, the house of Levi, the house of Israel, and those who fear the Lord. Of these the Psalmist sings: “House of Israel, bless the Lord; house of Aaron, bless the Lord; house of Levi, bless the Lord; you who fear the Lord, bless the Lord” (Psalm CXXXIV). By Aaron he understands the priesthood; by Levi, the temple attendants and ministers; by Israel, the entire people; and by those who fear the Lord, proselytes.

We, however, think that the passage should be explained simply: after the threat against the mountains of Israel, the prophetic word is directed against the whole land of Israel, whether the ten or the twelve tribes. The prophet is not predicting things that are still to come, but sees the captivity already rushing upon them. Ezekiel began to prophesy to the captives in Babylon in the fifth year of Zedekiah. In the ninth year Nebuchadnezzar came and besieged Jerusalem, and captured it in the eleventh year of Zedekiah. From this it is clear that the end had come and was drawing near—not upon mountains, hills, crags, and valleys, but upon the four regions of the land, from every side of Israel, not upon the whole earth. If he had said “of the whole world,” it could have been understood universally; but “of the land” simply signifies the land of Israel. Thus he had begun: “Thus says the Lord God concerning the land of Israel: The end has come, the end upon the four regions of the land.”

[Col. 0609C] “‘Now the end is upon you, and I will send my fury against you, and I will judge you according to your ways, and I will set all your abominations against you. My eye shall not spare you, and your abominations shall be in your midst; and you shall know that I am the Lord.’”

The word is therefore directed to the land of Israel: the end, the consummation, has come upon it, and the Lord sends his fury against it—not unjustly, nor proceeding merely from indignation, but full of equity and reason—so that he may judge it according to its ways and show it all its abominations, that it may remember its deeds and understand what evil it has done.

When he says, “My eye shall not spare you, and I will not have pity,” he is like a most compassionate physician who wishes to cut away putrid flesh and burn diseased wounds with a cautery. He does not spare in order to spare; he does not have pity in order to show greater pity, lest anything putrid remain in the body and corrupt the healthy flesh by its proximity [Col. 0609D]: “The Lord strikes the one whom he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives” (Hebrews XII). To the same understanding belongs: “I strike, and I heal” (Deuteronomy XXXII). Every medicine has bitterness for a time, but afterward the fruit of the pain is shown by health.

God says something similar through Amos: “Because I have known you from all the tribes of the earth, therefore I will punish you for all your sins” (Amos III). “For the Lord knows those who are his.” He speaks of its ways, of the course of its entire life, and of its abominations; he will place its stains in its midst, so that before the eyes of the sinful woman who is being punished for the sake of health her former sins may be set. When the Lord has done this, those who have been afflicted will know that he is the Lord. The same is expressed by the testimony: “I will punish Jacob according to his ways, and according to his inventions I will repay him” (Hosea XII).

“‘Thus says the Lord God: One affliction, behold, an affliction has come; the end has come, the end has come. It has awakened against you; behold, it has come. Contraction has come upon you, you who dwell in the land.’”

[Col. 0610A] He says that the final stage of the sins of the land of Israel has arrived, so that it can no longer escape the sentence of God, which it had long deserved. Because it had not yet completed its sins, the punishment was delayed, according to what is written: “For the sins of the Amorites have not yet been completed” (Genesis XV). Hence the Lord also says to the Jews: “And you, fill up the measure of your fathers” (Matthew XXIII). [Col. 0610B]

Misery has therefore come upon you; affliction and captivity have come. And lest you think that I am again threatening future events, I point them out and demonstrate them with my finger: “Behold, the end has come; the end has come.” What had seemed to you until now to be asleep and at rest has suddenly awakened against you and risen up: “Contraction has come,” which in Hebrew is called *sephphira*—the order and sequence of all evils whose coming you had always feared with apprehension.

As for the words “upon you who dwell in the land,” we should understand them according to the Apocalypse of John: “Woe to all who dwell upon the earth” (Apocalypse VIII). For the saint is not an inhabitant of the earth, but a newcomer and pilgrim. He says: “I am a newcomer and a pilgrim, as all my fathers were.” For this reason Abraham is also called a Hebrew, that is, a pilgrim [Col. 0610C] and passerby, hastening to pass from the present age to the things that are to come.

We may also interpret this passage spiritually against the Jewish people, upon whom the end and consummation came, “from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom they killed between the temple and the altar” (Matthew XXIII). As long as they had not laid hands on the Son of God, the Lord’s sentence seemed to sleep for them and was delayed. But when they killed the heir, so that the inheritance might perish, then it awoke against them and rose up: the whole order of miseries and perplexity, because they did not seek heavenly things but wished to cling to earthly things.

“‘The time has come; the day of slaughter is near, and not the glory of the mountains.’”

[Col. 0610D] The time of slaughter and famine is now also demonstrated among the Jewish people, since they have neither prophets nor the word of God by which the souls of believers are nourished. Understand the mountains as the teachers who possess knowledge of the Scriptures. Of these it is also said elsewhere: “You shine wondrously from the everlasting mountains” (Psalm LXXV).

The Septuagint, however, which reads “not with disturbance and not with pains,” signifies that they possessed such great ignorance of God and blindness of mind that they were neither troubled by their crimes nor tormented by the pain of repentance.

“‘Now I will shortly pour out my wrath upon you, and I will repeat my fury, and I will judge you according to your ways. And now I will place—or give—you all [Col. 0611A] your abominations.’”

If we calculate from the fifth year of the deportation of the kingdom of Jeconiah to the ninth year of the reign of Zedekiah, when Nebuchadnezzar came and besieged Jerusalem, there will be three intervening years. Hence it is rightly said: “Now I will shortly pour out my wrath upon you—or against you.” I will no longer announce or threaten things that will happen far in the future. Now I will complete my fury against you. This fury and wrath are not without judgment, but he will repay their ways upon their own heads and make them experience all their abominations.

We may also speak of the final captivity: after the killing of Christ, when the end came upon them and sin awoke against them, what is written was fulfilled: “Now the wrath of God has come upon them to the end.” [Col. 0611B] When Jerusalem was surrounded by Titus and Vespasian, its desolation arrived, and this was fulfilled: “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matthew XXIII). Then they were judged according to their ways and the blasphemies by which they denied the Lord; they experienced the fury of God, and all his indignation was poured out upon them. They received the consequences of their crimes, so that the desolation of the temple might remain until the consummation.

“‘And my eye shall not spare, nor will I have pity; but I will lay your ways upon you, and your abominations shall be in your midst, and you shall know that I am the Lord who strikes.’”

He added the reasons for the severity and austerity—or, as the heretics think, the cruelty—of God, explaining why his eye does not spare and he does not have pity: [Col. 0611C] “‘I will give you your ways, and your abominations shall be in your midst.’” Thus you may feel what you have done, and, seeing your abominations either before your eyes or placed in the midst of all, may correct your error through repentance. When you turn away from your former deeds and hate what you have done, then you will know that he is the Lord, who strikes for the purpose of correcting and chastises every son whom he receives (Hebrews XII).

“‘Behold the day; behold, it has come. Contraction has gone forth; the rod has blossomed; pride has germinated; iniquity has risen up as the rod of wickedness—not from them, not from the people, nor from their noise—and there shall be no rest for them. The time has come; the day has drawn near. Let not the buyer rejoice, and let not the seller mourn, because wrath is upon all its people. For he who sells shall not return to what he has sold, and yet their life is among the living. For the vision concerning all its multitude shall not return. And a man shall not be strengthened in the iniquity of his life.’” (Jerome.)

[Col. 0611D] He says that the day has contracted and been shortened, and that the captivity is imminent and near. The rod, which had threatened you for a long time, has blossomed, and from its flower it gives birth to the fruit of punishments. Your pride has germinated, as you deserved, so that upon the rod of your wickedness—the rod with which you impiously beat those subject to you—iniquity might arise. This is not from the pitiable people, nor from those who are described by their teachers as being like irrational animals, nor from their cry and noise by which they vainly shout, misled by the priests and Pharisees into crying with one voice [Col. 0612A]: “Crucify! Crucify such a man!” Therefore there will be no rest for them, but eternal captivity.

The Septuagint, however, according to the sense in which it is written, “For you do not know what the coming day will bring forth,” says: “Behold, the day gives birth to what it had conceived long before; the end has come, and the encompassing has gone forth,” encompassing and holding all your evils.

In the fact that they too translated “the rod has blossomed,” we may use the testimony: “Do not take the rod away from your son” (Proverbs XIII). And the Apostle says: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love and a spirit of gentleness?” (I Corinthians IV). God also resounds through the mouth of the Psalmist: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with scourges; but I will not remove my mercy from them” (Psalm [Col. 0612B] LXXXVIII).

Therefore the Lord visits and strikes so that all the pride that had long lain enclosed may die and be exposed; that injury may be aroused against the pride that has arisen and germinated; and that the strength of the wicked may be crushed, not with disturbance or haste. For the end of the flowering rod is health and correction, which comes not through the merit of those being corrected, nor through any beauty they possess—for they do not possess it—but through the mercy of the Lord.

This is a difficult passage, with great disagreement between the Hebrew and the Septuagint; much has been added to the latter from the edition of Theodotion so that it might appear to have some coherence: “The time has come; the day has drawn near.” This is said not only to Jerusalem, that the time of its captivity has come and the day has drawn near when it will be surrounded by the Babylonian [Col. 0612C] army, but the Lord also speaks to the man who rejoiced in his constructed and enlarged barns: “Fool, this night your soul will be taken from you. And the things you have prepared—whose will they be?” (Luke XI).

Hence the Apostle also says: “The time is shortened.” And elsewhere: “For the form of this world is passing away” (I Corinthians VII). It should be noted that he did not defer it to the future, but said of the present: “It is passing away.” Every day the form of the world slips away. It never remains in the same condition, but the form of things that grow and decline is always passing by and changing. Hence the Lord says: “Heaven and earth will pass away.”

If these things, through which everything in the world continually passes and goes away, are so, what can be permanent in human affairs? “Let not the buyer rejoice, and let not the seller mourn.” [Col. 0612D] It is natural to rejoice in the purchase of possessions and to mourn in their sale. But when servitude and captivity are imminent, both joy and sadness are vain in either case. Hence the Apostle says: “The time is shortened. From now on, let those who have wives live as though they had none; those who weep as though they did not weep; those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice; those who buy as though they did not possess; and those who use this world as though they did not use it” (I Corinthians VII).

The flood also overwhelmed buyers and sellers, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Because wrath is upon all its people.” This is not found in the Septuagint. In place of “people,” according to the Hebrew, “multitude” and “crowd” may be understood. This is what *amona* signifies. [Col. 0613A] The reason is clear: the buyer should not rejoice and the seller should cease mourning because the wrath of God will shortly come upon the whole multitude of the land of Judea, or of Jerusalem. This is understood from what precedes, where it is written:

“‘Thus says the Lord God of Israel: He who sells, and shall not return to what he has sold.’”

He speaks according to Hebrew custom. Every purchase returned to the seller in the fiftieth year of release, which among them is called the jubilee. Therefore, before the year of remission arrives, when possessions return to their former owners, captivity will come upon them and remove the entire custom [Col. 0613C] of the city.

[Col. 0613B] As for what the Septuagint translated—“he who buys shall not return to the seller”—although it does not accord at all with the historical sense, according to the anagogical sense it may have this meaning: the person who had been deceived by heretical error, when he understands the teacher’s fraud, will by no means return to the seller, that is, to the teacher, but will despise and reject him.

“‘And yet their life is among the living, because the vision concerning all its multitude shall not return.’” Just as possession will not return to its former owner when the overthrow of the city is imminent, so the prophetic vision and threat directed against the whole multitude of the city will not return and become void, but will be fulfilled in events while those to whom the prophetic word is directed are still alive. He says this to show the imminence of the captivity, lest they say according to their custom: “This vision is for distant days, and it will be fulfilled after many times.”

We may also say that, after the prophetic vision departed from the Jews—“For the Law and the prophets were until John the Baptist” (Matthew XI)—after the killing of the Savior it did not return to them, nor did they deserve to have prophets any longer. He says significantly: “The vision shall not return to all its multitude.” Therefore it will return to those among them who believed in the Lord: namely, the apostles and the remnant of the Jewish people who were saved from Israel.

[Col. 0613D] These two verses are also not found in the Septuagint: “And a man shall not be strengthened in the iniquity of his life.” The Septuagint reads: “And a man shall not possess in the eyes of his life.” According to the Hebrew, the sense is: his iniquity will not benefit a man, nor will it provide him with any strength. According to the Septuagint: a man will not obtain what he desired, what he thought precious in the world; when freedom perishes, everything beautiful will be lost. The ambiguity of the Hebrew letters *yod* and *waw*, which are distinguished only by size, caused some to interpret the word as “iniquity” and others as “eyes.”

“‘Blow the trumpet; let everyone prepare.’”

We read in many places about the blast and sound of trumpets, as in: “Like a trumpet, raise your voice” (Isaiah LVIII); and elsewhere: “Blow the trumpet at the new moon, on the distinguished day of your solemn feast” (Psalm LXXX); and in the Apostle: “For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, [Col. 0614A] and with the trumpet of God” (I Thessalonians IV). And in the Gospel: “Do not sound the trumpet before you” (Matthew VI).

The history in Numbers also relates the making of hammered and silver trumpets (Numbers X), which are compared with prophetic speech and apostolic teaching. Now it is commanded that everyone, at the signal of the blast and trumpet, prepare for battle. According to the present sense, however, those who have been assigned to this duty are commanded ironically to blow the trumpet, so that everyone may prepare against the Babylonian army.

“And there is no one who goes into battle. For my wrath is upon all its multitude.” These words are not found in the Septuagint. God had commanded that they should sound the trumpet to prepare an army capable of resisting the strength of the Babylonians, but the command was useless, since there is no one among the people who dares to go to war. The people have therefore been weakened and lack the strength to fight, because all God’s wrath is upon its entire multitude—namely, upon the city of Jerusalem or the land of Judah. Likewise, in our own land and Jerusalem, when either public persecution or the incitements of various vices strive to overcome us, teachers sound the trumpet in vain and hasten to prepare us for battle, since there is no strength among the people. That strength has been withdrawn because their sins have earned the Lord’s wrath.

“‘The sword outside, pestilence and famine within. He who is in the field shall die by the sword; and those who are in the city shall be devoured by pestilence and famine. And those who flee from them shall be saved. They shall be in the mountains, all of them trembling like doves of the valleys, each one trembling because of his iniquity.’” We read above about the three groups: those who die in the city from pestilence and famine; those whom the sword kills outside; and those who escape captivity by flight. Whoever among them is saved will go to the mountains and, trembling like murmuring doves, will mourn his sins.

In the tropological sense, however, this should be understood as follows: whoever is in the field and countryside, outside the boundaries of the Lord’s city—which is interpreted as the Church—will be struck by the adversary’s sword. But whoever conducts himself negligently in the city and does not prepare food for himself, of which it is written in Proverbs, “He who tills his land shall be satisfied with bread,” will die of hunger and pestilence. These few who have escaped either the sword of the heretics or the hunger and death of their own sloth will not be saved except in the mountains, and unless they take up the wings of a dove, fly away, and find rest. These doves tremble as long as they remain in the valleys and are afraid of everything; we are commanded to imitate their innocence. Concerning them it is written in the Psalm: “If you sleep among the midst of the lots, the wings of a dove are silvered, and the hindparts of its back are in the pallor of gold” (Ps. LXVII). In the form of this dove the Holy Spirit descended and remained upon the Lord the Savior.

“‘All hands shall be loosened, and all knees shall flow with waters; they shall gird themselves with sackcloth, and dread shall cover them.’” Instead of “knees flowing with waters,” the Septuagint translated: “the thighs shall be polluted with moisture” [Col. 0615A]. When all have trembled and fled to the mountains, everyone’s hands will be loosened, and no one will be able to resist the enemies. Through the enormity of their fear, urine will pollute their knees, and the bladder will be unable to restrain the flowing waters. They will gird themselves with sackcloth, and trembling will possess everything.

This happened to that people not only under the Babylonians but also under the Romans, when God’s wrath reached its full measure against them. Likewise, in our Judea, in which there is confession of the Lord, when iniquities have multiplied and the charity of many has grown cold, the hands of all good works will be loosened. All the knees—or thighs—of those who sought unlawful intercourse will flow with water, those whom Scripture calls unclean because they suffer an issue of semen under the Law. Therefore those who are such ought to gird themselves with the sackcloth of repentance and fear the coming judgment. Whoever does so will deserve to hear Isaiah saying: “Strengthen the hands that are slack, and make firm the feeble knees” (Isa. XXXV).

“‘On every face there shall be confusion, and on every head baldness.’” The redness of the face is an indication of shame; consciousness of sins shines upon the face, and the hope of salvation is present when wrongdoing is followed by embarrassment. Therefore it was said to the woman who gloried in her sins with a hard heart: “You have the face of a prostitute; you do not know how to blush” (Jer. III).

Baldness of the head likewise signifies mourning, when we lose the beauty of our hair and the loveliness of our locks. Accordingly, it is said to Jerusalem: “For your head’s adornment you shall have baldness because of your deeds” (Isa. III). The same prophet says: “On every head they shall shave the crown, and every beard shall be cut off” (Isa. XV). Micah likewise says to the same Jerusalem: “Make yourself bald and shave yourself for the children of your delights; enlarge your baldness like an eagle” (Mic. I).

Baldness is also commanded to be made over the dead. Only the holy—namely, the Nazirites and those who deserve to attain the Lord’s priesthood—do not shave their heads. For they do not have the works of death, nor are they unclean, since Nazirites are, that is, holy ones of the Lord. But if someone should die beside one of them, all the preceding days will not be counted as part of his consecration.

Samuel was holy to God, and therefore he possessed the everlasting adornment of his head and heard the words from the Song of Songs: “Your locks are black like a raven.” Samson, however, because he lost his hair, lost his strength (Judg. XVI); when his hair gradually grew back, his former strength returned, so that at his death he killed more people than he had killed while alive. Elisha, although he had baldness of the body, nevertheless, because he was a Nazirite of the Lord, enjoyed the locks of his head (IV Kings II). Therefore the boys, because they were children and had not yet reached manhood, mocked his baldness, saying, “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead”; and they were torn apart by the bites of wild beasts, whose dwelling place is in the hills and forests.

“‘Their silver shall be thrown outside, and their gold shall be as refuse.’” The Septuagint has: “Their silver shall be thrown into the streets, and their gold shall be treated with contempt.” Compelled by flight and captivity, they will throw the weights of their gold and silver into the streets, wishing only to preserve their lives, so that what had previously been an instrument of luxury may not become a burden.

Otherwise, in the anagogical sense, this concerns those who are captives and flee from Jerusalem. All silver will be thrown into the streets, into the broad and spacious way that leads to death, because they abandoned the narrow path of salvation. All gold, too, will be treated with contempt, or will be reckoned as refuse and filth; for that which is outside the Lord’s Church cannot possess purity.

“‘Their silver and their gold shall not be able to deliver them on the day of the Lord’s wrath.’” No one doubts that in a time of siege and famine, gold and silver cannot save the hungry; striking their teeth against the most precious metal, they will blunt them like the hardest stone. Accordingly, what follows is:

“‘They shall not satisfy their soul, and their bellies shall not be filled.’” From the evils of the present time we have learned that many rich people, surrounded by silk, jewels, and quantities of gold and silver, have been consumed by poverty and ended as beggars.

That the silver and gold of those who are outside the Church do not deliver the souls of their possessors on the day of the Lord’s wrath, but leave them in eternal hunger and torment them with an empty belly, is shown by the testimony that says: “A man’s own riches are the ransom of his soul” (Prov. XIII). These are “one’s own riches,” which the truth of Christ has taught us to possess. He commanded us to make friends for ourselves from unrighteous mammon (Luke XVI), so that they may receive us into eternal dwellings.

“‘Because it became the stumbling-block of their iniquity.’” (Jerome.) Therefore, he says, the souls of those who possess gold and silver will not be satisfied, nor will their bellies be filled, because this very gold and silver has become the stumbling-block of their crimes. He signifies idols, which, made of gold and silver, despise their own makers. For this the Septuagint translated: “Because it was the torment of their iniquities,” so that they may be tormented in their own wicked error and understand that they have wrongly turned God’s gifts into blasphemy.

“‘And they placed the ornament of their necklaces in pride. And they made from it the images of their abominations and their idols.’” What I had given, he says, as an ornament to those who possessed wealth, they turned into pride, so that what could have enabled them to free their souls through almsgiving and good works became for them material for arrogance [Col. 0616D]. Finally, from their gold and silver they made idols and turned my gifts into images of demons.

The tropological interpretation is easy: the gold and silver signify the meanings and words of Scripture, which are the choice things of the world and are given to us as adornment. The heretics have turned them into fuel and material for pride, and from them have made images of their various doctrines, abominations, and offenses, so that by means of what could have enabled them to worship and adore God, they have offended God.

“‘Therefore I gave them over to uncleanness, and I shall give them into the hands of strangers, for plunder, and to the impious of the earth as spoil, and they shall defile it.’” Because from the gold, silver, and ornaments of necklaces that I had given them they made images of their abominations and idols, therefore I gave these things over to uncleanness and filth. For these things Symmachus translated “nausea,” wishing to express the foulness of idols.

“And I shall hand them over,” he says, “into the hands of enemies, so that they may plunder everything.” I will not so much defile them as show that they have been defiled, though previously they seemed most holy. We too are handed over into the hands of enemies and of those who are alienated from God when we make our ornaments into images of demons, and all our glory is possessed by the impious, or by the pestilences of the earth, so that they may subject us to their power.

“‘And I shall turn my face away from them, and they shall violate my secret place; emissaries shall enter it and defile it.’” When, he says, because of the people’s former abominations, I have turned my face away from them and judged them altogether unworthy of my sight, then they shall violate my secret place, which signifies the Holy of Holies. For this the Septuagint has: “And the impious and the pestilences of the earth shall break into it.” Apart from the priests and the high priest alone, no one dared to enter there. We know that this was done by the Babylonians, by King Antiochus, by Gnaeus Pompey, and finally under Vespasian and Titus, when the temple was captured and overthrown, and all the events described in the prophet’s following discourse were perpetrated.

God also turns his face away from our evil works. And because his face has been turned away, God’s secret place is violated, so that instead of priests and holy men, pestilences enter and defile everything. Thus the place that ought to have been a place of holiness becomes a place of uncleanness, according to the Gospel saying: “My Father’s house shall be called a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of robbers.”

“‘Make a conclusion, because the land is full of the judgment of bloodshed, and the city is full of iniquity.’” Therefore, O prophet, briefly conclude my wrath against the land of Judah and the city of Jerusalem, so that, just as the land is full of the judgment of bloodshed—for all are judged because they shed innocent blood, which Scripture records the Jews also did in the case of Naboth—so their own blood may likewise be shed, and the city may be shown to be full of iniquity [Col. 0617D].

Under Manasseh also, the city of Jerusalem was filled with the blood of prophets from gate to gate. A conclusion, disturbance, and crushing will come upon them, so that no one will be able to escape the impending miseries.

“‘And I shall bring the worst of the nations, and they shall possess their houses.’” In place of the priests and prophets I shall bring the worst of all the nations—the Babylonians—so that they may possess your houses and subject you to servitude. Likewise, the worst demons will possess our houses, that is, our souls—for we are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwells in us—if our land is full of bloodshed and our dwelling is full of iniquity.

[Col. 0618A] “‘And I shall cause the pride of the mighty to cease, and they shall possess their sanctuaries.’” Therefore the worst of the nations will possess the houses of the mighty and proud and will obtain their sanctuaries, because an unclean being enters the place of holiness and pollutes it with its uncleanness. Significantly, since God’s holy things had been polluted and the secret place violated, he did not say, “They shall possess my sanctuaries,” but “their sanctuaries,” because after the pollution they ceased to be mine.

“‘When distress comes, they shall seek peace, and there shall be none.’” He will seek peace but will not find it—the one who heard from the apostles, “Peace to this house” (Matt. X), but did not preserve it or make it rest in his mind. Having driven it away by evil works, he cannot find it. For this is the peace “which surpasses all understanding,” and which the Savior, ascending victoriously to the Father, left to the apostles (John XIV).

“‘Disturbance shall come upon disturbance, and report upon report.’” Just as it is said to the saints, “Rejoice; again I say, rejoice,” and it is written of them, “They shall go from strength to strength,” so that present blessings may be heaped upon future blessings, so for those upon whom distress has come, who sought peace and did not find it, “disturbance shall come upon disturbance,” or woe upon woe, according to what is written in the Apocalypse: “One woe has gone, and another woe is coming” (Apoc. IX).

“‘And report shall come upon report, and messenger upon messenger,’” according to blessed Job: “While he was still speaking, another messenger came,” increasing evils with evils. Describing the roar and tumult of Babylon as it approached, he adds:

“‘And they shall seek a vision from the prophet, and the law shall perish from the priest, and counsel from the elders.’” Properly, each thing is sought from its proper person: prophecy of future events is sought from the prophet; interpretation of the Law is the priest’s office; mature age seeks prudent counsel, according to what is written: “In the counsel of the righteous and in the great assembly are the works of the Lord” (Ps. CX).

These things occurred not only at the time when the Babylonian army was coming against Jerusalem and visions were sought from prophets, priests, and elders; they are also sought daily in the churches. If the churches have lost vision, law, and counsel, they boast in vain of possessing prophets, priests, and elders.

[Col. 0618D] “‘The king shall mourn, and the princes shall be clothed in mourning.’” Holy Scripture records that Zedekiah mourned and that all the princes of the Jewish people were consumed with grief. Although at first sight this may seem blasphemous, we can say that Christ is the mourning king, mourning our vices and sins; he speaks in the Psalms: “What profit is there in my blood, when I go down into corruption?” (Ps. XXIX). As he approached Jerusalem, he wept over it and said: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which kills the prophets and stones those sent to you, how often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling!” (Matt. XXIII).

The princes may likewise be the apostles in the good sense, mourning sinners; or, in the contrary sense, those to whom it is said: “Hear the word of the Lord, princes of Sodom” (Isa. I). “And he shall be clothed,” according to the Septuagint, “with destruction”—the one who does not have the armor of God and has not put on Christ. “For as many as have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. III).

“‘And the hands of the people of the land shall be disturbed.’” Or, according to the Septuagint, “shall be loosened.” When there is no vision in the prophet, knowledge of the Law in the priest, or counsel in the elders; when the king mourns and the prince is in grief or destruction, then consequently the hands of the people will also be disturbed, losing their proper order, or will be loosened, no longer possessing their former strength.

And fittingly it does not say “the people of God,” whose hands will be disturbed and whose citizenship is not in heaven, but “the people of the land,” concerning whom it is written: “Those who depart from you shall be written upon the earth.”

“‘According to their ways I shall deal with them, and according to their judgments I shall judge them’”—or, as the Septuagint translated, “I shall avenge them.” God repays sinners according to their ways, so that the truth of judgment may be maintained. In the case of the saints, however, he exceeds the measure of mercy: “For the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII). “For the wages of sin is death,” which the sinner receives according to his ways and works. The virtue of the righteous, however, enjoys the Lord’s generosity, concerning which Paul says: “The gift of God is eternal life.”

What he adds—“And according to their judgments I shall judge them”—echoes the Gospel saying: “With what judgment you judge, you shall be judged.” It also echoes the apostolic saying: “In whatever judgment you judge another, you condemn yourself; for you do the same things that you judge.”

“‘And they shall know that I am the Lord.’” This verse occurs frequently in this prophet: punishment and suffering are followed by knowledge of God, so that those who did not understand him through his benefits may know him through torments.

## CHAPTER VIII. The vision of the likeness of God; concerning the wall that was dug through, the men holding censers, those worshiping toward the rising sun, and those applying a branch to their nostrils

“‘And it came to pass in the sixth year, in the sixth month, on the fifth day of the month, that I was sitting in my house, and the elders of Judah were sitting before me,’” etc. (Jerome.) We read that the earlier vision was made to the prophet in the fifth year of Jehoiachin’s exile, in the fourth month, on the fifth day of the month [Col. 0619D]. The vision that we now wish to explain is said to have occurred in the sixth year of the same king, in the sixth month, on the fifth day of the month. It is therefore clear that these events took place after a year and two months, and either that the prophecy was interrupted for a year and two months, or that the events related in the earlier discourse occurred throughout the full fourteen months.

The sixth year, the sixth month, and the fifth day of the month—numbers that refer to the making of the world—signify the fleshly senses that behold earthly things and do not yet contemplate heavenly realities. Whoever understands that the discourse was addressed to the elders of Judah will not be surprised that the prophecy occurred at this time. Seventy of them held censers, and twenty-five worshiped in the temple toward the sun. The prophet sat in his house, avoiding the crowds, while the elders of Judah sat before him, either wishing to hear the prophet’s words or lying in wait for his statements.

They are significantly called “the elders of Judah,” so that we may understand that this was said not concerning Israel—that is, the ten tribes that had previously been taken captive—but concerning those who had been carried into captivity with Jehoiachin from the tribe of Judah.

“‘And the hand of the Lord God fell upon me there, and I saw, and behold, a likeness resembling the appearance of fire: from the appearance of his loins downward, fire; and from his loins upward, something resembling the appearance of splendor, like the vision of amber.’”

The hand signifies ἐνέργεια, that is, “activity” or “operation,” so that he may understand the mysteries of the vision. It should also be considered that he does not see the realities themselves, but a likeness of fire, since fire appeared from the loins downward. From the loins upward there appeared something resembling the appearance of splendor, like the vision of amber.

In place of “splendor,” which in Hebrew is called *zor*, Theodotion translated “a gentle breeze,” so as to indicate God’s refreshment in the higher regions. Thus, in the Book of Kings (III Kings XIX), blessed Elijah does not contemplate the Lord’s arrival in storm or whirlwind, nor in the heat of fire, but in the appearance of a slight and most gentle breeze, thereby demonstrating the gentleness of almighty God.

The works of intercourse, which are signified in the loins and downward, are purified by fire; the works of virtue that rise from the loins toward the upper parts possess splendor and radiance. Yet it is not said that the fire reaches to the feet, nor that the splendor of amber reaches to the head, but “downward” and “upward,” so that among sinners as well as saints, according to the diversity of their merits, one may reach to this limb or that, and another to those limbs or others. Just as those who possess the perfection of holiness reach all the way to the crown of the head, so those who are in the depths of sins must be believed to possess the soles of fiery feet.

“‘And the likeness of a hand was sent forth and grasped me by the lock of my head.’” Here also the likeness of a hand is not an actual hand extended; for there is nothing bodily in God. A hand is seen as a member of the human body, familiar and customary, so that it does not terrify the one who is taken up and grasped. If the prophet had been touched by the likeness of a serpent or any other beast, the dissimilarity of the members would itself have terrified the one being taken up.

Only part of the hair is grasped, because human nature cannot endure the grasping of the entire head. In place of “lock,” the Septuagint translated κράσπεδον, that is, “fringe.” One of these is ordinarily understood of the hair, the other of garments.

“‘And the spirit lifted me up between earth and heaven.’” First he is grasped by the likeness of a hand; afterward he is lifted by the spirit. The spirit does not immediately raise him to heaven, but between earth and heaven, so that, leaving earthly things meanwhile, he may hasten toward heaven. We may also say that because of his good works the prophet was grasped by the likeness of God’s hand, and because of his knowledge of spiritual things he was lifted by the spirit.

“‘And he brought me to Jerusalem in a vision of God, to the inner gate that faced north, where the statue of the idol of jealousy was set up to provoke jealousy. And behold, there was the glory of the God of Israel, according to the vision that I had seen in the plain.’”

When he says, “He brought me to Jerusalem in a vision of God,” he shows that he was transported not in the body but in the spirit. By such a vision we can behold the heavens, the depths of the sea, and the underworld, while comprehending the principles of each thing in thought.

First he came to the vestibule that faced north, so that there he might see the statue of the idol of jealousy, set up to provoke jealousy; from that place he could penetrate into the interior and behold the other things that are described afterward. History relates that a statue of the idol Baal was set up in the temple. It is aptly called the idol of jealousy because it provokes the Lord to jealousy and rivalry, according to what is said in Deuteronomy: “They provoked me to jealousy with what was not God, and I shall provoke them to jealousy with a people that is not a people” (Deut. XXXII).

“‘The likeness of a hand sent forth,’ he says, ‘grasped me by the lock of my head. And the spirit lifted me between earth and heaven, and brought me to Jerusalem in a vision of God, to the inner gate that faced north, where the idol of jealousy was set up to provoke jealousy.’” (Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XXXI, chapter 39.)

For what is the lock of the head except the gathered thoughts of the mind, so that they do not flow away dispersed but remain held together by discipline? A hand is therefore sent down from above, and the prophet is lifted by the lock of his head, because when our mind gathers itself through watchfulness, heavenly power draws us upward from the depths [Col. 0621C].

He rightly says that he was lifted between earth and heaven, because every saint placed in mortal flesh has not yet fully reached heavenly things, but has nevertheless already abandoned the depths. He is led in a vision of God to Jerusalem, because each person who advances contemplates, through the zeal of charity, what the Church ought to be.

It is also rightly added that “he was led to the inner gate that faced north.” For holy men, when they look through the entrance of inward contemplation, discover that more evil than good is done within the Church. They turn their eyes, as it were, toward the northern side—that is, toward the left of the sun—because against the coldness of vices they kindle themselves with the goads of charity.

There it is rightly added: “For there also the idol of jealousy was set up to provoke jealousy.” When they observe that within the holy Church some people, while bearing only the outward appearance of believers, commit acts of robbery and vice, what else do they see in Jerusalem but an idol? It is called an idol of jealousy because by this means heavenly rivalry is provoked against us, and it strikes sinners with greater severity in proportion to the greater love with which the Redeemer loves us.

Hypocrites, therefore, because they do not gather the thoughts of their minds, are not held at all by the lock of the head. And when they discover the sins entrusted to their charge, what do they know of their own? Thus they are sluggish toward heavenly things, toward which they ought to burn, while they burn anxiously for earthly matters, toward which they ought laudably to have been sluggish.

Indeed, after neglecting the care of their children, you often see them gird themselves against dangers with immense labor: crossing seas, entering lawsuits, knocking at the doors of magistrates, breaking into palaces, taking part amid the quarrels of crowds, and defending earthly inheritances with laborious vigilance. If someone should perhaps say to them, “Why do you do these things, since you have abandoned the world?” they immediately reply that they fear God, and for that reason they toil with such zeal to defend their inheritances.

“‘And he said to me: Son of man, lift your eyes toward the way of the north. And I lifted my eyes toward the way of the north. And behold, from the north gate of the altar was the idol of jealousy at the very entrance.’” (Jerome.) He said to me, he says, either the glory of God that I had seen in the plain, or the spirit that had lifted me between heaven and earth. He spoke to me after he had transported me to Jerusalem and made me see either the city or the temple. And he commanded me to lift my eyes toward the way of the north. There stood the statue of Baal, which he calls the idol of jealousy at the very entrance of the gate.

Those who refer the idol of jealousy—or the possessor—to the glory of God or to the spirit act impiously, changing the person of the idol into the majesty of God.

“‘And he said to me: Son of man, do you think that you see what these people are doing—the great abominations that the house of Israel commits here—and that I should go far away from my sanctuary? And still turning, you shall see greater abominations.’” Do not suppose, he says, that I am abandoning the temple unjustly and leaving the city to be destroyed. Look at what they are doing in the temple. When you have seen these things, do not think that the crimes have reached their end; you will see still greater things.

This can also be understood of our Jerusalem and our temple, when, following the example of Hophni and Phinehas, we commit the crimes of idols in the tabernacle of God and fornicate with those who have vowed themselves to the army and service of God [Col. 0622C]. We tear away the firstfruits of his sacrifices and give them for the use of dependents and servants, and we do everything for the sake of profit. But if the things we see are so great, how much greater must those things be judged which escape human consciousness?

“‘And he brought me to the entrance of the court, and I saw, and behold, one opening in the wall. And he said to me: Son of man, dig through the wall. And when I had dug through the wall, one doorway appeared. And he said to me: Enter and see the most wicked abominations that these people commit here,’” etc.

What I translated as, “And I saw, and behold, one opening in the wall,” is not found in the Septuagint. Since everything is shown as though in an image and painting, he says that he saw one opening in the wall and was ordered to dig through it and enlarge it, so that, once the opening had been made wider, he might enter more freely and see what he could not see while standing outside.

This shows that both in churches and in each of us, greater vices are revealed through small ones, and that through certain openings one reaches the greatest abominations. “For a tree is known by its fruit” (Matt. XII); “For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Luke VI). Words that burst forth are signs of the inner person. Thus a shameful utterance sometimes reveals a lustful person who cunningly conceals his vices. A desire for some small object signifies hidden avarice within.

Greater things are shown through lesser ones [Col. 0623A], and consciousness cannot be disguised by the face and eyes, when a luxurious and wanton mind shines in the face and the secrets of the heart are revealed through bodily movement and gestures.

“‘And I entered and saw, and behold, every likeness of creeping things and animals, an abomination, and all the idols of the house of Israel were painted on the wall all around.’” Not only did the idol of jealousy stand at the entrance of the north gate, but all parts of the temple were painted with various images of idols, so that there was no kind of beast that the painting on the wall did not display.

To this day we observe the same thing in the shrines and temples of the pagans: foolish religion worships every kind of beast. Hence Virgil also [Note: *Aeneid*, Book VIII, in the description of Aeneas’ shield]:

> “And monsters of gods of every kind,” he says, “and the barking Anubis,”

as though those too were not monsters whom he praises,

> “against Neptune, and Venus, and against Minerva.”

We can also show idols depicted on the walls of our temples, when we are subject to every vice and paint in our hearts the consciousness of sins, together with various images. Concerning these it is said in the Psalms: “Lord, in your city you will destroy their image” (Ps. 72). And elsewhere: “Nevertheless man walks about in an image” (Ps. 38). That is to say, there is no human being who does not bear some image, whether of holiness or of sin.

Therefore it is said to the furious and wrathful: “Their fury is like that of a serpent, like a deaf asp that stops its ears and will not hear the voice of charmers” (Ps. 57). And concerning wicked men: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matt. 3). And concerning the deceitful and fraudulent: “Go, tell that fox” (Luke 13). And concerning lovers of women: “They became raging stallions toward women for me; each one neighed for his neighbor’s wife” (Jer. 5). And concerning the brutish and senseless: “Do not become like horse and mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. 31). (Gregory, *Moralia*, book 26, chapter 6.)

Truly holy men, when they recognize that someone is being scourged for his fault, even if they correct certain disordered things in him, nevertheless sympathize with certain things that cause him grief. Thus they know how to press down what is swollen, while also knowing how to cherish what is wounded, so that, while they soften what is hard in such people, they may strengthen what is weak.

But arrogant men, because they do not possess the inward organs of charity, not only fail to sympathize with the righteous when they grieve, but even afflict them under the appearance of a just rebuke. Or, if there are small faults in them, they magnify them; or they distort things that are truly good so as to interpret them badly in their own minds.

Although chaste teachers also often make the vices of offenders appear greater and investigate hidden things from certain public signs, so that they may recognize greater matters from the smallest ones. Hence it is said to Ezekiel: “Son of man, dig through the wall.” Immediately afterward he added: “When I had dug through the wall, a single doorway appeared. And he said to me: Enter and see the most detestable abominations that these people commit here. And I entered and saw, and behold, every likeness of reptiles and animals, an abomination; and behold, all the idols of the house of Israel were depicted on the wall.”

By Ezekiel, then, the person of rulers is signified; by the wall, the hardness of subjects. And what is it to dig through the wall except to open the hardness of the heart by harsh corrections? When he had dug through it, a doorway appeared. For when the hardness of the heart is split open either by diligent questioning or by timely correction, a kind of door is revealed, through which the inner thoughts of the one being corrected may all be seen.

Hence it is rightly added there: “And he said to me: Enter and see the most detestable abominations that these people commit here.” One enters, as it were, in order to see abominations when, after certain outwardly appearing signs have been examined, one penetrates the hearts of subjects so that everything illicit that is being thought there becomes known.

Thus he added: “And I entered and saw, and behold, every likeness of reptiles and animals, an abomination.” In reptiles, wholly earthly thoughts are signified; in animals, thoughts that have already been lifted somewhat above the earth, but still seek the rewards of earthly payment. Reptiles cling to the earth with their entire bodies, whereas animals are suspended above the earth by their bellies, yet are always inclined toward the earth by their appetite for food.

Reptiles, therefore, are within the wall when thoughts revolve in the mind that are never lifted from earthly desires. Animals are also within the wall when, even if certain just and honorable things are already being contemplated, such thoughts nevertheless serve the pursuit of temporal profits and honors. By themselves they are already lifted, as it were, from the earth, but through ambition, like an appetite for food, they lower themselves toward the depths.

Hence it is rightly added: “And all the idols of the house of Israel were depicted on the wall.” For it is written: “Avarice, which is the service of idols” (Col. 3). Therefore idols are rightly described after the animals, because although some people raise themselves from the earth through honorable action, they nevertheless lower themselves to the earth through dishonorable ambition.

It is also rightly said, “They were depicted,” because when the outward appearance of external things is drawn inward, whatever is contemplated through deceptive images is, as it were, painted in the heart.

It must therefore be noted that first a hole in the wall is seen, then a doorway, and finally the hidden abomination is revealed. For the sins of each person are first shown by outward signs, then by the door of open iniquity. Only afterward is all the evil hidden within disclosed. Teachers therefore customarily examine small matters with great care, so that from the outermost things they may reach greater hidden matters. They stir up words of harsh rebuke in order to uproot the thorns of deadly thought.

When they do these things, they act with the wisdom of charitable love; they do not swell with the inflation of pride. They are prepared to die for those whom they afflict as though raging against them even to death. In their thoughts they preserve what they love; in outward appearance they adopt what they pursue. By preaching good things they implant them, while warning against evil things. They do not, like Elihu, offer prayers that arise from desire; toward those entrusted to them they are sometimes fervent in correction, as though no fervor were kindling them.

They greatly fear that, if they cease correcting the wicked, they themselves will be punished for the latter’s condemnation. And when they inflame themselves toward words of denunciation, they come to this unwillingly, yet nevertheless prepare this defense for themselves before the strict Judge.

“And there were seventy men of the elders of the house of Israel, and Jaazaniah son of Shaphan was standing in the midst of those who stood before the paintings, and each had a censer in his hand, and a vaporous cloud rose from the incense.” (Jerome.)

When he says that there were seventy men of the elders of the house of Israel holding censers in their hands, he shows that there were also many other elders who did not do this, but were perhaps held by other sins. He singles out one, Jaazaniah son of Shaphan, standing in their midst as the leader of their crime and sacrilege. They had abandoned the worship of God and worshiped idols; in the temple they did not adore God, whose temple it was, but the paintings on the walls.

It is beautifully said: “Jaazaniah son of Shaphan stood,” that is, in the midst of his own “judgment” and condemnation, “among the elders who stood,” because both he, their leader, and those over whom he was leader stood firmly in their crimes. They did not waver in evil but persisted in it with the greatest strength.

The vapor of cloud, confusion, and storm that rose from the incense of those offering sacrilege demonstrated their conduct.

This happened at that time according to the literal sense. But we too must pray that the elders of the house of Israel, multiplying the sacred number seven by seven decades, may not stand in their errors and worship painted idols, and that the vapor of sacrilege may not rise or ascend in resistance to God.

When we see a most wicked people gathered together, concerning whom it is written, “I hate the assembly of the wicked” (Ps. 25), and elders worse than the people, with an even more wicked leader placed over both people and elders, let us say that Jaazaniah is standing before the paintings and that each has a censer in his hands—not worshiping the majesty of God, but their own opinions—and that not the fragrance of a good odor reaches God, but a stench reaches the idols.

“And he said to me: Surely you see, son of man, what the elders of the house of Israel do in darkness, each one in the hidden place of his chamber. For they say: The Lord does not see us; the Lord has abandoned the earth,” and so forth.

He says that what they do gathered together in the temple shows what each one does in his own chamber. But according to the allegorical sense, it may better be understood that certain leaders of the churches do in darkness things that are shameful to speak of.

This is the hidden man of the heart concerning whom it is said: “Enter into your chamber” (Matt. 6). And again: “He who sees in secret will repay you.” Let each person recall his own conscience and remember in darkness the works of darkness, knowing what is written: “Everyone who does evil hates the light, lest he be reproved by the light” [Col. 0626A] (John 3).

In himself he will understand the fulfillment of this saying: “He who is drunk is drunk at night” (1 Thess. 5). This cannot stand according to the literal sense. For how many become drunk at daytime banquets and feasts? But because drunkenness of the heart, which offends God, belongs to darkness and not to light, whoever becomes drunk is drunk at night.

When the elders of the house of Israel did evil in darkness and in the hidden places of their chambers, and thought that they could conceal themselves from God, they consequently said: “The Lord does not see us; the Lord has abandoned the earth.” There are many sinners who walk according to their own thoughts and do not think that God cares about mortal affairs or that our vices concern him.

Certainly, when we sin, if we thought that God saw us and was present, we would never do what displeases him. Moreover, what follows—“The Lord has abandoned the earth”—is also the opinion of certain philosophers. From the courses and regularity of the stars they suppose that providence exists in heavenly things but disregards earthly matters, since nothing on earth is conducted rightly or according to order.

Because they either thought that providence did not exist, or that providence which had previously been among the peoples had at that time abandoned its own people, therefore the eye of God will not spare, nor will he have mercy, so that, raging against their vices, he may be appeased toward virtues and repay their ways and sins upon their heads—either upon the ruling part of the heart or upon the rulers of the people, according to the book of Numbers, in which the leaders are called the heads of the peoples.

“And he said to me: Turning again, you will see still greater abominations than these. And he led me through the doorway of the gate of the house of the Lord that faced north, and behold, women were sitting there mourning Adonis.”

What we have translated as Adonis is called *Tammuz* in the Hebrew and Syriac language. Since, according to the pagan story, the lover of Venus and a most beautiful young man was killed in the month of June and was thereafter said to have come back to life, they call that same month of June by his name and celebrate an annual festival for him. In it he is mourned by women as though dead, and afterward he is sung and praised as one who returns to life.

Consequently, after it has been shown what the leaders and elders of the house of Israel did in the temple, in darkness, and in their chambers, the vices of the women are also described. They mourn when deprived of the company of their lovers, and rejoice if they are able to possess them.

Since the same pagan religion subtly interprets such shameful stories of the poets, it accompanies the death and resurrection of Adonis with lamentation and rejoicing. It thinks that the one is represented in seeds that die in the earth, and the other in crops in which the dead seeds are reborn.

Let us likewise call those who are distressed or rejoice over the evils or goods of the world “women,” because of their soft and effeminate spirit. Let us say that they mourn Tammuz—that is, those things which in the affairs of the world are thought to be most beautiful.

“And he said to me: Surely you have seen, son of man; you will see still greater abominations than these. And he brought me into the inner court of the house of the Lord. And behold, at the doorway of the temple of the Lord, between the vestibule and the altar, were about twenty-five men, with their backs toward the temple of the Lord and their faces toward the east. And they worshiped the rising sun.”

Since we read above, after the idol of jealousy that appeared at the northern gate, “You will see still greater abominations,” and since the paintings of all the beasts that they worshiped had been displayed on the wall—paintings before which the seventy elders and Jaazaniah son of Shaphan stood holding censers in their hands—the statement “You will see still greater abominations than these” is repeated a second time.

What, then, is the greater abomination than the three crimes described above? It is clearly the fourth that follows: “Behold, at the doorway of the temple of the Lord, between the vestibule and the altar, were about twenty-five men, with their backs toward the temple of the Lord and their faces toward the east, and they worshiped the rising sun.” They had despised the Lord, that is, the Creator, and worshiped the sun, that is, a creature of the Lord.

The Lord himself had commanded through Moses that they should not worship God, in the manner of the Gentiles, facing east, but should worship toward the temple, wherever it might be in relation to them—whether east, west, south, or north. The Lord was believed to dwell in the Holy of Holies. We read that Daniel also did this in Babylon (Dan. 6): opening the windows of his upper room, he worshiped the Lord toward the temple that was in Jerusalem. No one doubts that this was sacrilege according to the literal sense.

According to the allegorical sense, all heretics are worse than those who came before them: worse than the idol of jealousy, the painted figures of animals on the wall, and the mourning for Adonis, through which idolatry and pleasure are signified. Anyone who understands the prophet when he says, “But you hate discipline and cast my words behind you” (Ps. 49), will recognize this.

And elsewhere: “They turned their back to me and went away” (Jer. 2).

Do we not know Marcion and the other heretics who tear apart the Old Testament? Despising the Creator, that is, the just God, they worship and adore some other supposedly good God whom they have fashioned from their own heart. And what of all the heretics of our own time who preach that the Son of God is a creature, yet adore him after abandoning the temple of divinity and turning their backs upon it? By their own confession they declare that they worship a creature.

We, however, worship the Sun of righteousness in such a way that we worship God in the temple of the Old Testament, where the Law and the Prophets are, where the cherubim and the mercy seat are.

“And he said to me: Surely you have seen, son of man. Is it a light thing to the house of Judah that they should commit these abominations which they have committed here? For they have filled the land with iniquity and have turned to provoke me. And behold, they apply the branch to their noses,” and so forth.

For what we translated as, “And behold, they themselves are as those who apply the branch to their noses,” the Septuagint translated, “And behold, they themselves are as those who mock.” The addition from Theodotion is, “They stretch out the branch,” so that the whole reads: “And behold, they stretch out the branch as those who mock.”

This signifies the twenty-five men, who are firmly established in a square formation and form the figure of a square through the five senses multiplied by five. They not only have the temple behind them but, like idolaters, apply a branch to their noses—undoubtedly a palm branch, which in Greek is called *baia*—thereby signifying that they worship idols.

Indeed, Job says that among his other virtues he also possessed this one: that he never, when looking at the sky, the sun, the moon, and the shining stars, kissed his hand, that is, worshiped creatures.

“Therefore I too will act in fury; my eye will not spare, nor will I have mercy. And when they cry out to my ears with a loud voice, I will not hear them.”

He says: Because of all these things that they have done, I too will act in fury, and my eye will not spare, nor will I have mercy.

Hearing this, the ancient heretics slander the Creator as though he were cruel and bloodthirsty. They do not consider the apostle Paul, who certainly is, as they wish to claim, an apostle of the good God, writing to the Corinthians: “When I come again, I will not spare” (2 Cor. 13), so that he may correct offenders with a rod and draw the erring back to salvation.

For those who do not understand what is beneficial to them and frequently pray for the opposite, it is advantageous for them not to be heard by the Lord. Hence in the Lord’s Prayer we say: “Your will be done”—not our will, which is accustomed to err, but your will, which knows what is to come. Sometimes it is a great blessing not to deserve mercy in the present.

The Lord, therefore, will not spare those who belong to the house of Judah and have withdrawn from the confession of the Church. And when they cry out with a loud voice, of which the Lord said, “Their cry has reached me,” nevertheless the Lord will not hear them, so that, compelled by their evils, they may understand what they have done.

## CHAPTER IX. On the six men sent for the devastation of the people; and on the man clothed in linen, with the inkhorn

“And he cried in my ears with a loud voice, saying: The visitations of the city have drawn near,” and so forth.

For “visitations,” the Septuagint translated “vengeance”: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord” (Rom. 12). Every vengeance is also a visitation, as of someone sick, as of someone bearing wounds, as of someone awaiting the hands of physicians, according to what is said elsewhere: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with scourges; but I will not remove my mercy from them” (Ps. 88).

And rightly, as we said above, visitation or vengeance is said to be approaching when captivity is near.

“And each had a vessel of slaughter in his hand.” He did not say, “had,” as the Septuagint translated, for he is not narrating past events but displaying present and future ones. Whoever strikes the wicked because they are wicked, and possesses vessels of slaughter in order to kill the worst offenders, is a minister of the Lord.

“And behold, six men were coming from the way of the upper gate that faces north. Each had a vessel of destruction in his hand. And there was also one man in their midst, clothed in linen, with a writer’s inkhorn at his loins. They entered and stood beside the bronze altar. And the glory of the God of Israel was taken up from the cherub that was above him to the threshold of the house. And he called the man who was clothed in linen and who had the writer’s inkhorn at his loins.” (Gregory, *Moralia*, book 22, chapter 19.)

What else, then, are the six men who come except the six ages of the human race? They come from the way of the upper gate, because from the creation of paradise, as from the entrance of the world, they unfold from the earlier generations. The gate faces north because, clearly, if the mind of the human race, opened to vices, had not abandoned the warmth of charity and sought the torpor of the mind, it would not have emerged into this breadth of mortality.

“And each had a vessel of destruction in his hand.” Each generation, unfolding through its successive ages, possessed before the Redeemer’s coming, in its own conduct, the means by which it incurred the punishment of condemnation.

“And there was one man in their midst, clothed in linen.” Our Redeemer was willing to have, according to the flesh, parents from the priestly tribe. He is said to come clothed in linen, or certainly because linen comes from the earth, whereas wool is born from corruptible flesh. He receives the clothing of his body from a virgin mother, not from the corruption of sexual union. Certainly he came to us clothed in linen.

“And he had the writer’s inkhorn at his loins.” The loins are the rear part of the body. Because the Lord himself died for us, rose again, and ascended into heaven, the New Testament was then written through the apostles. This man had the inkhorn at his loins. For the one who composed the writing of the New Testament after departing carried the inkhorn, as it were, behind him.

He considers this inkhorn attached to the man clothed in linen who says: “Let him who judges write the book himself” (Job 31). But why, blessed Job, do you desire a book to be written by the one who is judge? The passage continues: “So that I may carry it on my shoulder and bind it around me like a crown” (ibid.).

To carry the book on one’s shoulder is to fulfill Sacred Scripture through action. Notice how orderly the description is: first it is carried on the shoulder, and afterward it is placed around one like a crown. For if the commandments of sacred speech are now carried out in practice, afterward they present us with a crown of victory in the reward.

(Jerome.) Six men come to erase the sins of human beings, who were made on the sixth day of the world’s creation, and descend from the upper gate—or, as the Septuagint translated it, “the lofty gate toward the north.” Each had an axe in his hands, concerning which John says: “The axe has already been placed at the root of the trees. Every tree that does not bear fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. 3).

There was in the midst of the six men one man, that is, a seventh, in the garb of a high priest, clothed in linen garments. He had a writer’s inkhorn at his loins, with which he would record all sins and separate the number of the saints from that of sinners; or else he had a sapphire-colored belt, the color of the sapphire stone that forms part of the high priest’s ornaments.

“And the six men entered and stood beside the bronze altar.” For there were two altars: one, the golden altar of incense inside, and the other, the bronze altar of burnt offerings before the temple. They are said to stand beside the altar prepared to obey the command of the one who orders them, so that they may know that anyone whom they see there whose sins have not been forgiven is subject to the Lord’s sentence and to slaughter.

The glory of the God of Israel also rose—or was taken up—from one cherub and went to the threshold, or to the open space of the court of the house and vestibule. This place is not covered by a roof but enjoys the freedom of the air. That glory of the Lord itself called the man who was in the high-priestly garb and “had the inkhorn at his loins,” and spoke the words that Scripture records.

Some interpret the six men as six angels who obey God’s will, and understand the one who had the high-priestly garment as the Savior, in accordance with the fact that he is priest and the angel of great counsel, and with the statement: “You are a priest according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109).

The *podērē* (ποδήρη), which the Septuagint translated, is one of the eight garments of the high priest. In Latin it is called *talaris*, because it descends as far as the feet, and from this it received its name.

When I asked a Hebrew what this meant, he replied that in Greek it is called *kalamárion* (καλαμάριον), because pens are kept in it. We call it an *atramentarium*, an inkhorn, because it contains ink. Many more accurately call them *thecae*, cases, because they are cases for the pens of writers.

One cherub from among the four cherubim is sent by the glory of the Lord’s majesty to speak to the one who was clothed in the high-priestly garments. Although many think that *cherubim* (τὰ χερουβεὶμ) is neuter in gender and plural in number, we must know that *cherub* is masculine singular, and *cherubim* is masculine plural. This is not because there is sex among God’s ministers, but because each is called by different genders according to the character of its own language.
