Angels are called in the plural *malachim*, *cherubim*, and *seraphim*, all of the same gender and number. But *Sabaoth*, which is interpreted as “of armies,” “of hosts,” or “of powers,” is feminine plural and ends in the final syllable *-oth*.

Those who wish the Savior to be understood under the figure of the high priest use the example from John’s Apocalypse. It is written there: “And I turned and saw the voice that was speaking with me; and when I had turned, I saw seven golden lampstands, and in the midst of the lampstands one like the Son of Man” (Rev. 1).

“And the Lord said to him: Pass through the midst of the city, through the midst of Jerusalem, and mark a Tau upon the foreheads of the men who groan and grieve over all the abominations that are committed in its midst. And he said to them in my hearing: Pass through the city after him and strike. Let your eye not spare, nor have pity. Kill old man, young man, virgin, little child, and women, unto destruction. But do not kill anyone upon whom you see the Tau, and begin from my sanctuary,” and so forth.

The one who was clothed in a linen or ankle-length garment and bore the appearance of a priestly habit is commanded to place a sign upon the foreheads of those who groan and grieve over all the abominations committed in the midst of Jerusalem.

For the sign that the Septuagint, Aquila, and Symmachus translated, Theodotion put the Hebrew word itself, *Tau*, which is the last of the twenty-two letters among the Hebrews, so that it might signify perfect knowledge among the men who groan and grieve.

Or, as the Hebrews suppose, it is because their law is called *thora* or *Torah*, which begins its name with this letter. Those received this seal who had fulfilled the precepts of the Law.

And, to come to our own matter, in the ancient Hebrew letters still used by the Samaritans, the final letter Tau has the likeness of a cross, which is painted upon the foreheads of Christians and frequently marked by the inscription of the hand.

Some think that, because this is the final letter according to the Hebrew alphabet, it indicates that remnants of the saints remain among the multitude of sinners.

Those who groan and grieve are therefore saved: they not only did not consent to evil deeds but also mourned the sins of others, just as Samuel mourned over Saul and the apostle Paul (1 Cor. 5) over those who did not repent after sinning.

Hence he himself said: “We who are in the tent groan” (2 Cor. 5); and elsewhere: “I have great sorrow and unceasing pain in my heart” (ibid.).

The six men are commanded to kill everyone except those who can say: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Ps. 4). They are not to spare the old man, the young man, the virgin, the little child, or the woman.

According to the mystical interpretations, the old are those in the Church concerning whom it is said: “The gray hair of a person is his wisdom” (Wis. 4). The young are those most ready for the battles of faith. Virgins are those who preserve chastity with their whole mind. Little children are those nourished with the milk of infancy and who have not yet received solid food. Women are those who, through the weakness of their sex, testify to the feebleness of the soul.

None of these are spared if, without the seal of Christ, they think themselves to be something.

What follows—“And begin from my sanctuary”—or, as the Septuagint translated, “And begin from my holy ones”—signifies either the priests who were active in the temple and who had been the cause of sin among the peoples, and who therefore deserved to suffer punishment first. For it is time for judgment to begin from the house of God.

“So they began with the elders who were before the face of the house. And he said to them: Defile the house and fill the courts with the slain.”

For “courts,” which are called *aseroth* in Hebrew, the Septuagint put “streets.” The elders who are killed are those of whom we read above that they had censers and burned incense to idols.

There is no longer any worship of the temple, because, with God offended, everything has been defiled, so that from the place where the sin occurred, judgment may also begin. The courts are filled with corpses in the temple, not the streets, which were certainly outside—unless perhaps we may understand “streets” as the city’s public squares.

The angels could not have dared to defile the temple with the blood of the dead, in which the glory of God had previously dwelt, unless the Lord of glory had commanded this.

Everyone who is dead through sin defiles the courts of the temple and the streets of the Lord’s city. In those streets lives the person who, rising with Christ, ceases to be dead.

“And they went out and struck those who were in the city.” Or, as others translated it, “They struck the city,” calling the city itself by the name of those who were in it.

“And when the slaughter was complete, I remained, and I fell upon my face and cried out: Alas, Lord God, will you then destroy all the remnant of Israel, pouring out your fury upon Jerusalem?”

When all who did not bear the seal had been struck down in the slaughter, the prophet fell upon his face because of the multitude of the slain, thinking that no one except himself remained.

Because this appeared contrary to the sentence by which the Lord had commanded that those with marked foreheads should not be killed, the wording was drawn out in the Vulgate edition. But following the Hebrew truth, we have written, “I remained.”

It should be noted that he did not say “I alone.” If he had said this, it would have seemed contradictory. Instead he said, “I remained,” with the others who had their foreheads marked understood.

So that we may know that “I remained” is spoken figuratively, in the book of Kings, when Elijah speaks to the Lord—“They have demolished your altars, and I alone am left, and they seek to take away my life” (1 Kings 19)—he added “alone,” because he did not know that others had remained.

Some think that this may also be understood as spoken from the person of the Lord, in whose type Ezekiel came beforehand, concerning the people of the Jews, when all had turned aside and together become useless. The Prophet testifies: “Save me, O Lord, for the holy one has failed” (Ps. 11). The Lord alone was found to be the one “who committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2).

When he added, “pouring out your fury upon Jerusalem,” the word “pouring out” shows the magnitude of the punishments, as we read elsewhere: “Contempt was poured out upon princes” (Ps. 106); and again: “My steps almost poured forth” (Ps. 72).

In a good sense: “The love of God has been poured out in our hearts” (Rom. 5); and: “Grace has been poured upon your lips” (Ps. 44).

In the contrary sense: “Pour out your fury upon the nations that have not known you, and upon the kingdoms that have not called upon your name” (Jer. 10); and: “Draw out the sword and shut it against those who persecute me” (Ps. 34).

“And the Lord said to me: The iniquity of the house of Israel and of the house of Judah is exceedingly great, and the land is filled with blood. The city is filled with apostasy. For they said: The Lord has abandoned the earth, and the Lord does not see. Therefore my eye will not spare, nor will I have mercy; I will repay their ways upon their heads,” and so forth.

When the Lord saw his prophet weeping for the people and wondering at the greatness of the indignation, he gave the reasons—not, as the prophet supposed, for an unjust punishment or one exceeding the proper measure, but for a deserved and righteous sentence.

“The iniquity,” he says, “of the ten tribes of Israel and of the two tribes of Judah is great”—and not merely great, but exceedingly great. Nor was it enough to say this once; he repeats “exceedingly,” so that the magnitude of the punishment may correspond to the magnitude of the iniquity.

From this we learn that, contrary to what many think, especially the Stoics, sins are not all equal, but are either great or small; and that the judgment of the one who punishes differs according to the quality and measure of those who sin.

“The land is filled,” he says, “with blood,” or, as the Septuagint translated it, “with peoples.” “And the city is filled with apostasy.” Or, as the Vulgate edition has it, “with iniquity and uncleanness.”

It was not a little blood that was poured out, but blood from gate to gate; and the entire city turned away from the worship of God. It is therefore full of uncleanness, namely, the filth of idolatry.

The cause of such great crimes is that they thought there was no providence over the earth and that God did not care about mortal affairs. As we read elsewhere:

> Surely such is the labor of the gods above,  
> such the concern that troubles their repose.

Because they either thought there was no providence, or that the providence which had previously been among the peoples had at that time abandoned its own people, therefore God’s eye will not spare, nor will he have mercy. He will rage against their vices, be gracious toward virtues, and repay their ways and sins upon their heads—either upon the ruling part of the heart or upon the rulers of the people, according to the book of Numbers, in which the leaders are called the heads of the peoples.

“And behold, the man who was clothed in linen, who had the inkhorn at his loins, answered and said: I have done as you commanded me.”

The Septuagint: “And behold, the man who was clothed in the *poderes*, that is, the ankle-length garment, and who was girded about the loins with a belt. And he answered with a word, saying: I have done as you commanded me.”

He is the man who was commanded to pass through Jerusalem and place a sign upon the foreheads of those who groan and grieve over all their iniquities. He says that he has fulfilled the Lord’s commands and armed the foreheads of the mourners with the seal of the letter Tau.

But the six men whom the Lord had commanded—“Pass through the city after him and strike, and have no mercy even unto destruction”—report nothing of the kind. For they fulfilled a sentence not of joy but of mourning, a sentence demonstrated not in speech but in action.

## CHAPTER X. On the man who took coals from the midst of the wheels; and on the cherubim, and the repetition of the vision and of the wheels
“Then I looked, and behold, upon the firmament that was above the head of the cherubim there appeared something like a sapphire stone, like the appearance of the likeness of a throne above it. And he said to the man who was clothed in linen, and said: ‘Enter into the midst of the wheels that are beneath the cherubim, and fill your hands with burning coals of fire that are between the cherubim, and scatter them over the city,’” etc.

Concerning the firmament that was above the cherubim, the sapphire stone that had the likeness of a throne, and the wheels that followed the living creatures, what was said above should suffice. Let the reader also be content with their explanation. But now, regarding the command given to the one clothed in linen—for which the Septuagint here translated *stola* [“robe”]—to take coals from the midst of the cherubim and pour or scatter them over the city, it seems to me to show that after the slaughter and killing of many, and with corpses of the dead lying in the streets, burning coals are taken up to punish or cleanse Jerusalem. In accordance with what is written in Isaiah: “He sanctified him in burning fire, and it shall devour the material like hay.” These are the coals which, as a remedy for the tongue and for falsehood, by laying waste to vices and sins, the prophet, when questioned, desires:

“What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, for a deceitful tongue? The sharp arrows of the mighty one, with destructive coals” (Psalm 119).

We shall be able to find many things of this kind in the holy Scriptures, about which we have often spoken. This alone should be noted: in Isaiah, where he had sinned only in speech and said that he had unclean lips, one coal is grasped with tongs for his cleansing (Isaiah 6); here, however, because the city was full of iniquity and, after the punishments, of corpses of the dead, more coals of fire are taken, and not with one hand but with both, so that all Jerusalem may be cleansed.

“And he entered in before my sight. Now the cherubim were standing on the right side of the house when the man entered, and the cloud filled the inner court. And the glory of the Lord was lifted up from above the cherub to the threshold of the house; and the house was filled with the cloud, and the court was filled with the brightness of the glory of the Lord. And the sound of the wings of the cherubim was heard as far as the outer court, like the voice of God Almighty speaking. And when he commanded the man who was clothed in linen, saying: ‘Take fire from the midst of the wheels that are between the cherubim,’ he entered and stood beside the wheel. And the cherub stretched out his hand from the midst of the cherubim toward the fire that was between the cherubim, and took it and placed it in the hand of the one clothed in linen. And he took it and went out, and there appeared in the cherubim the likeness of a human hand beneath their wings.”

While the prophet watched, the man clothed in a long or linen garment entered. He entered, as is said a second time, into the midst of the wheels beneath the cherubim, in order to fill his hands with fiery coals. After entering, he merely stood beside the wheel. Whether because of grief over the punishment of Jerusalem or because he was overwhelmed by the greatness of the glory, he himself did not put his hand into the fire. Rather, one of the cherubim—that is, a cherub—extended his hand, took the fire that was in the midst of the cherubim, and placed it in the hand of the man clothed in linen garments. He took it and went out; yet Scripture does not say what he did after going out, leaving the narration of a sorrowful matter to our understanding rather than presenting it to our eyes.

When the man clothed in linen garments entered, the cherubim were standing on the right side of the house, so that the holy and heavenly powers may be understood to hold the right side of the house of God, while those who are sent for punishments, of whom it is written, “He sent among them the sending of evil angels” (Psalm 77), may be believed to occupy the left side. When the glory of the Lord was lifted up from the cherub who was about to hand the coals of fire to the man, and had passed to the threshold of the house, immediately the inner court was filled with cloud, darkness, and gloom. For punishments are not carried out in the presence of the majesty of the Lord. And the glory of the Lord is seen in the court, concerning which it is written: “The sound of the wings of the cherubim was heard as far as the outer court.” In place of “sound,” the Hebrew has the word *qol* [“voice”], and that voice had the likeness of the voice of God Almighty speaking.

Note, reader, in what respects the earlier vision and this one agree or differ, so that from the comparison of the two you may understand the divine mysteries without our prompting. Recall also what I mentioned earlier: if in the firmament, in the throne, and in the hand of a man the term used is not “reality” but “likeness”—for we do not contemplate the glory of the Lord face to face with unveiled countenance, but see everything in likeness and image so long as we are enclosed in a fragile, mortal, and corruptible body.

# BOOK SIX

[Column 0635]

## CHAPTER X CONTINUED

[Column 0635A]

Although reason would require that one and the same vision be included together in a single volume, perhaps some wonder why I separated it from the others in the division of the books. The reason for this division must therefore also be made clear. Just as I separated the second book, concerning the manifestation of the wheels, from the first book, where the description of the four living creatures occurred—not because of any difference in meaning, but to avoid making the work too long, lest the book’s length weary the reader—so now, to avoid the same weariness, after the vision of the glory of the Lord and the simultaneous manifestation of the cherubim, I judged that the sixth book should begin with the account of the four wheels. Concerning these the prophet narrates as follows:

“And I looked, and behold, four wheels beside the cherubim: one wheel beside one cherub, and another wheel beside another cherub. The appearance of the wheels was like the appearance of a chrysolite stone. Their appearance was one likeness in all four, as though one wheel were within another wheel. And when they moved in the four directions, they went forward and did not turn back as they went; but toward the place to which the first one inclined to go, the others followed, and they did not turn. And their entire body, and their necks, and their hands, and their wings, and their rims, were full of eyes all around the four wheels. And he called these wheels ‘whirling ones,’ while I heard him. Now one had four faces: one face was the face of a cherub, the second face was the face of a man, the third was the face of a lion, and the fourth was the face of an eagle; and the cherubim were lifted up,” and the rest. (Jerome.)

Observe what the appearance of the wheels was at first. According to the Septuagint, it was “like the appearance of *tharsis*.” But now, according to the same translators, it is “like the appearance of a carbuncle,” so that the likeness of the wings through the fire handed over by the Cherub may be indicated. Although in Hebrew both above and here *tharsis* is written, Aquila translated it as “chrysolite,” and Symmachus as “hyacinth.”

Again, where we have translated “their entire body”—with “wheels” understood—the Hebrew reads: “All their flesh,” as well as their necks, hands, wings, and rims. The term “flesh” is applied to the heavenly powers so that, when we read, “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God, nor will corruption possess incorruption” (1 Corinthians 15), we may understand that it is not the substance of flesh but its works that are condemned. For *Bostar*, which is written in this passage, signifies not “body” but “flesh.” He called the rims of the wheels “iron *canthoi*,” by which the roundness of wooden wheels is enclosed and tightened.

Earlier, therefore, he said: “The bodies of the living creatures are full of eyes”; now he says of the wheels: “Their bodies, and their necks, and their hands, and their wings, and their rims were full of eyes all around the four wheels.” (Gregory, in his exposition of the Gospel.)

But we should know that often, while we attend to one matter, it happens that we neglect another; and where we neglect, there beyond doubt we have no eye. For we know what that Pharisee who had gone up into the temple to pray said, as the Gospel testifies. He said: “God, I give you thanks.” He rightly gave thanks to God, from whom he had received the good deeds he had performed; and he adds: “Because I am not like other men: robbers, unjust, adulterers, or even like this tax collector. I fast twice on the Sabbath, I give tithes of all that I possess” (Luke 18).

Behold: the Pharisee had an eye for displaying abstinence, showing mercy, and offering thanks to God, but he had no eye for preserving humility. What good is it if almost the entire city is carefully guarded against the enemy’s ambushes, if one opening is left exposed through which the enemies may enter? What benefit is there in a guard established almost everywhere, when through the neglect of one place the whole city is opened to its enemies? The Pharisee fasted, gave tithes, and returned thanks to God; he kept watch, as it were, almost all around the perimeter of his city. But because he did not attend to one opening in himself—pride—he admitted the enemy precisely where, through negligence, he had closed his eye. (H.)

These wheels, however, possess not only flesh, or a body or limbs, but also necks, hands, and wings, so that we may understand individual operations rather than images of limbs. The wheels themselves are called in Hebrew *gelgel*, which Symmachus translated as “whirling ones,” and Aquila as “wheel.”

Furthermore, what follows—from “while I heard him” to the place where it is written, “the cherubim were lifted up”—is not found in the Septuagint but was added from the Hebrew. In this we must observe that it is not said, as above, “the face of a man and the face of a lion on the right of the four, and the face of a calf on the left of the four, and the face of an eagle on the right of the four,” so that some might be thought to be on the left and others on the right. Rather, the order of all alike is described, when Scripture says: “One had four faces: one face was the face of a cherub, the second face was the face of a man, the third was the face of a lion, and the fourth was the face of an eagle.” Thus the first, second, third, and fourth faces are described not by a difference of location, right and left, but in a single order progressing by degrees.

He called the one face—that is, the first—the face of a cherub, whereas above he had said “the face of a calf.” From this it is understood that the face of a cherub is the face of a calf; the explanation of the preceding vision contains the meaning of all these things.

“This is the living creature that I saw beside the river Chebar. And when the cherubim moved, the wheels also went alongside them. And when the cherubim lifted their wings in order to rise from the earth, the wheels did not remain behind but were also beside them. When they stood, they stood; and when they were lifted up, they were lifted up with them. For the spirit of life was in them,” etc.

All things live for God and perceive their own Creator. For he is not the God of the dead but of the living; hence the bodies of all the wheels are full of eyes. And in the psalm it is said: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands. Day pours forth the word to day, and night announces knowledge to night” (Psalm 18). The sun and moon, the sea and rivers, the mountains and hills also praise him. The elements revolve in their own circuit year by year, and we discern the order of the heavens on earth, so that, preserving the order of the ancient law, they may revolve and run, and we may see nothing new upon the earth.

When it says, “This is the living creature that I saw beside the river Chebar,” Scripture shows that in explaining the living creature we must understand the same things that we understood above. It is well said: “When they went, they went; when they stood, they stood; when they were lifted up from the earth, they were lifted up together; and the wheels followed them. For the spirit of life was in the wheels.” (Gregory.)

For the most part these matters have already been said, but they are narrated again in a repeated description. Let us therefore not be troubled to repeat briefly in our exposition what the Spirit graciously narrated again through the prophet. The only new point added in these words is the statement: “When they stood, they stood.” There are some who progress far enough to know how to administer well the earthly things they have received. They devote themselves to works of mercy and assist the oppressed. Such people go forward, in that they direct themselves toward the benefit of their neighbor. With them, therefore, the wheels move, because the sacred words arrange the steps of their sayings along their path.

There are others who are so strong in holding the faith they have received that they are able to resist every adversity. They are not in the least drawn into the perversity of unbelief; rather, they oppose those who speak perversely and lead them toward righteousness. With these who stand, the wheels also stand, because the words of sacred speech confirm their uprightness when they hear: “Stand firm and hold fast to the traditions that you have learned”; and again: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls about, seeking someone to devour; resist him, strong in faith” (1 Peter 5).

There are others who despise all earthly things and do not consider themselves worthy to possess anything that passes away; they suspend themselves, as has been said, in contemplation of God. With these who have been lifted up, therefore, the wheels are also lifted up. For to the degree that each person has progressed toward higher things, to that same degree the sacred words speak to him about higher matters.

The living creatures therefore go forward for the benefit of their neighbor, stand for the guarding of themselves, and are lifted up for the contemplation of God. The wheels also go forward, stand, and are lifted up with them. For sacred reading, when sought, is found to be of the same character as the one who seeks it. It walks with you toward the active life. When you have progressed toward immobility and steadfastness of spirit, it stands with you. When by God’s grace you have reached the contemplative life, it flies with you.

And again it adds: “For the spirit of life was in the wheels.” The spirit of life is said a second time to be in the wheels because there are two Testaments of Scripture, and God’s Spirit willed both to be written in order to free us from the death of the soul. Or certainly because there are two commandments of charity—namely, love of God and love of neighbor—through both of which the sayings of holy Scripture give us life.

Thus it is said a second time, “For the spirit of life was in the wheels,” because in the divine utterances we grasp love of God and love of neighbor, and through the commandments expressed in sacred Scripture we, who lay dead, live. Hence through the Psalmist it is said to almighty God: “I will never forget your ordinances, because by them you have given me life” (Psalm 118). The ordinances are called God’s commandments, by which he justifies us as he corrects us. Concerning them the Psalmist says more plainly: “I will meditate on your ordinances; I will not forget your words” (ibid.).

In them, therefore, he justifies us, because through them he reveals spiritual life to us and, through the breathing of the Spirit, pours it into our minds. Since this is accomplished daily through the gift of grace in the minds of the elect, it is rightly said: “The spirit of life was in the wheels.”

This Scripture has become for us a light on the path through the darkness of the present life. Hence Peter says: “You do well to attend to it, as to a shining lamp in a dark place” (2 Peter 1). Hence the Psalmist says: “Your word is a lamp to my feet, Lord, and a light to my paths” (Psalm 118).

Yet we know that our own lamp is obscure to us unless truth illumines it in our minds. Hence again the Psalmist says: “For you illumine my lamp, Lord; my God, illumine my darkness” (Psalm 17). For what is a burning lamp except light? But created light does not shine for us unless it is illumined by uncreated light. Therefore, since almighty God both created the words of the holy Testaments for our salvation and himself opens them to us, “the spirit of life was in the wheels.”

“And the glory of the Lord went out from the threshold of the temple and stood above the cherubim. And when the cherubim lifted their wings, they were lifted up from the earth before my eyes. And as they went out, the wheels also followed. And it stood at the entrance of the eastern gate of the house of the Lord, and the glory of the God of Israel was above them. This was the living creature that I saw beneath the God of Israel beside the river Chebar. And I understood that they were cherubim, four in number, with four faces each and four wings each. And there was the likeness of a human hand beneath their wings. And the likeness of their faces was the same faces that I had seen beside the river Chebar. And each went forward with its appearance and its movement before its face,” etc. (Jerome.)

The glory or majesty of the Lord, which had stood at the threshold of the temple, stood above the cherubim. When they lifted their wings, the prophet saw them rise, with the wheels following alongside them, and stand at the entrance of the eastern gate of the house of the Lord. Thus the protection of God gradually departed from Israel. At first it was in the temple; then it stood in the court of the temple, or at the threshold. When it withdrew from the temple, cloud and darkness filled the inner chambers of the temple.

Again the glory itself sat upon the cherubim; and when they immediately flew away and went out toward the exterior, the wheels followed, and the glory stood at the eastern gate of the house of the Lord—not at the door of the temple, but beyond the court and threshold, at the entrance of the eastern gate of the house of the Lord.

When the prophet saw this, he said: “This is the living creature that I saw beneath the God of Israel beside the river Chebar, and I understood that they were cherubim.” For what new thing had he seen that enabled him to understand that they were cherubim, when previously he had not understood this?

In our language, “cherubim” means “a multitude of knowledge,” the knowledge of God’s mysteries, and his throne and resting place. Hence it is said in the Psalmist: “You who sit upon the cherubim, reveal yourself.” For the glory of the Lord always sits in a multitude of knowledge, and it is revealed when all things are shown to be governed by providence. Nothing happens by chance, nor can anyone say, “The Lord has abandoned the earth,” and “the Lord did not see.”

Hence the cherubim’s gaze and their desire signify forgetting what lies behind and stretching toward what is ahead. Therefore, since the contemplative life is signified in the cherubim and the active life in the hand, as we showed above, it is rightly repeated here: “And there was the likeness of a human hand beneath their wings.”

The hand of a human beneath their wings is therefore the power of action beneath the flight of contemplation. For who can enter the kingdom of God while knowing him unless he first acts well? Without the contemplative life, those who do not neglect the good they are able to perform can enter the heavenly homeland. Without the active life, however, they cannot enter if they neglect to perform the good they can do.

The former, then, belongs to necessity, the latter to willingness; the former to servitude, the latter to freedom. Hence it is said to Moses: “If you buy a Hebrew servant, he shall serve you for six years; in the seventh he shall go out free without payment. With whatever garment he entered, with such shall he go out,” etc. (Exodus 21.)

A Hebrew servant who has been bought is commanded to serve for six years, so that in the seventh he may go out free without payment. What is signified by the number six except the perfection of the active life? What by the number seven except the contemplative life? He serves for six years and goes out free in the seventh who, through the active life that he has perfectly displayed, passes into the freedom of the contemplative life.

It should also be noted that he goes out free without payment, because those who, after doing everything, call themselves unworthy servants are doubtless saying that just as the active life came by gift, so the contemplative life will also come by grace.

“With whatever garment he entered, with such shall he go out.” For it is entirely necessary that each of us persevere in what he begins and continue to the end of the work in the intention with which he began. He passes well into the contemplative life who, in the active life, has not changed the garment of his intention for something worse.

He is a servant who has resolved, through the active life, to serve human beings, so that after the present age he may be able to attain true freedom. Concerning this Paul says: “For creation itself will be set free from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Romans 8).

Then true freedom will exist in us, when our adoption reaches the glory of the children of God. But now not only is the active life in servitude; even in contemplation itself, by which we are carried above ourselves, it does not yet possess freedom of mind perfectly, but imitates it, because what is most inward is seen in an enigma. Yet however narrow contemplation may be, it is already far broader and higher than the active life, which passes into a certain freedom of mind, no longer thinking about temporal things but about eternal things.

# CHAPTER XI

Concerning the twenty-five men; concerning the captivity, that they themselves were the flesh and Israel the cooking pot; concerning the dispersion of the people, etc.

[Column 0640B]

“And the Spirit lifted me up and brought me to the eastern gate of the house of the Lord, which looks toward the rising of the sun.” (Jerome.)

Because the glory of the Lord had gone out from the threshold of the temple and stood upon the cherubim, and after the cherubim flew away the glory itself stood at the entrance of the eastern gate of the house of the Lord, the prophet, who could not go there by himself, was lifted up by the Spirit and brought to that same eastern gate of the house of the Lord, which looks toward the sun of righteousness. Concerning him it is written: “Behold, a man whose name is Orient” [“Rising”]. Thus he would not remain in the temple, which was shrouded in a cloud of ignorance, but, standing at the eastern gate of the house of the Lord, would recognize the mysteries that follow.

[Column 0640C]

“And behold, at the entrance of the gate were twenty-five men. And I saw in their midst Jezonias son of Azur and Pheltias son of Banaiah, princes of the people. And he said to me: ‘Son of man, these men devise iniquity and deliberate an evil plan in this city, saying: “Were not houses built long ago? This is the cooking pot, and we are the meat.” Therefore prophesy against them, prophesy, son of man.’ And the Spirit of the Lord fell upon me. And he said to me: ‘Speak: Thus says the Lord: So you have spoken, house of Israel, and I know the thoughts of your heart. You have killed many in this city and filled its streets with the slain. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Your slain whom you placed in its midst are the meat, and it is the cooking pot. But I shall lead you out from its midst. You feared the sword, and I shall bring the sword upon you, says the Lord God. And I shall cast you out from its midst and deliver you into the hand of enemies, and I shall execute judgments upon you. By the sword you shall fall; in the borders of Israel I shall judge you. And you shall know that I am the Lord. It shall not be a cooking pot for you, and you shall not be meat in its midst. In the borders of Israel I shall judge you, and you shall know that I am the Lord.’”

What follows is not found in the Septuagint but was added from the Hebrew: “Because you have not walked in my commandments, and you have not carried out my judgments, and you have acted according to the judgments of the nations that surround you,” and the rest.

The prophet is taken up, in accordance with what is written: “The Lord lifts up the meek” (Psalm 146). Or he is lifted from the earth and brought to the eastern gate of the house of the Lord, so that he may understand the mysteries of the twenty-five men who were around the gate, and of Jezonias son of Azur and Pheltias son of Banaiah, the princes of the people.

These men, then, who stood at the entrance of the eastern gate of the house of the Lord, despairing of salvation and, conscious of their crimes, prepared for destruction, unwilling to correct their sins through repentance, say that although the houses that had previously fallen were recently rebuilt after the first captivity, nevertheless they know that this city is like a cooking pot and that they are the meat, to be consumed and burned in it, in accordance with what is written in Isaiah: “Though the storm pass through, it shall not carry us away.”

When they had said these things, the Spirit of the Lord fell upon the prophet and commanded him a second time to prophesy and say: Because you have said these things, and the secrets of your hearts do not escape me, I shall interpret for you how the city is a cooking pot and how you are counted as meat—not according to the meaning you have expressed, but according to another meaning that you do not fear.

The city is indeed like a cooking pot, but it shall not be filled with your flesh; rather, it shall be filled with the flesh of those whom you have killed. But you, who think that you will die in this city, I shall lead out from the midst of the city and deliver into the hands of enemies. I shall execute judgments upon you, so that when you have fallen by the sword, not in the city or outside the borders of Israel, but within the borders of your own province, then you will know that I am the Lord.

You shall suffer all these things because you have not walked in my commandments and have not carried out my judgments, but have committed the crimes of the other nations around you.

Although what is said is clear according to the literal sense, and although for a little while we set aside the names of Jezonias and Azur, Pheltias and Banaiah, which we reserve for another time, this should nevertheless be said: even today, in the Church, which is the house of God, before the gate and at the entrance—or on the way of the gate, which signifies the Savior, through whom we enter to the Father—there are twenty-five men who refer everything to the senses.

As far as my memory does not fail me, I have never been able to find this number in a favorable sense, although in Leviticus men are chosen for the priestly ministry from the age of twenty-five years. In the Hebrew, however, it does not have this number, which is given in the Septuagint, but thirty, which is included at the beginning of this prophet and in the age of the Lord, when he came to the waters of the Jordan and was baptized by John.

But if in the Gospel (Matthew 23) five wise virgins and five foolish virgins are found, we should know that this number, being placed in the middle, may, according to the character of those who use it, be applied either to a good or to a bad meaning.

These men, therefore, who refer everything to the senses and have two princes, about whom we spoke above, are contained in the number two, which divides unity and, in the number of the second day, does not appear before the Lord according to the Hebrew truth. Hence in Noah’s ark unclean animals are brought in two by two (Genesis 7).

The Lord, compressing division into unity, made both one and destroyed the dividing wall, condemning enmity in his flesh (Ephesians 2). Hence he speaks in a more august and sublime way: “I and the Father are one” (John 10), calling us back from Jewish duality into the unity of Christian faith.

Finally, after the Jewish priesthood had been lost, the Lord suffered not under one prince but under two, Annas and Caiaphas, in order to expose the false error of their religion.

There are many at the entrance of this gate before the eastern house of the Lord who are compared through their vices to the nations, despair of salvation because of the consciousness of their sins, and say: “The city in which we dwell is a cooking pot, and we are all the meat; we shall be consumed by the heat of Babylon, whose idols are fiery.”

Because they refuse to repent and despair of salvation, they therefore hear that they are not the flesh of the former and ruined city, but those whom they have scandalized and killed. Therefore the sword is brought upon them, so that after they have been judged at the borders of Israel—not among the nations but among Christians—they may then know that he is the Lord, according to what is read in the Psalms: “When he slew them, they sought him” (Psalm 77), so that they may recognize through torments the one whom they had not perceived through benefits.

“And it came to pass, when I was prophesying, that Pheltias son of Banaiah died; and I fell upon my face and cried out with a loud voice, and said: ‘Alas, alas, alas, Lord God, are you making an end of the remnant of Israel?’”

While the prophet was prophesying, one of the two princes, Pheltias son of Banaiah, died. His name is interpreted as “declining ruin,” and he is the son of a builder or mason. The other prince, Jezonias son of Azur, was preserved unharmed. Jezonias signifies “his ears sound,” with “of the soul” understood. Azur, however, is interpreted as “support” or “helper.”

Therefore, the one who had declined from the Lord by falling and who was of an exceedingly evil building rightly falls while the one whom the Lord strengthened is prophesying; but the one who obeyed God’s commandments and was sustained and supported by his help rightly remains in authority over the people.

We read in Exodus (Exodus 2) that when Pharaoh, king of Egypt, died, the children of Israel groaned because of their work with straw and bricks and cried out to the Lord, whom they had been unable to invoke while he was alive. Isaiah likewise, when the leprous king Uzziah had died, said: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and lofty throne, and the seraphim were standing around him” (Isaiah 6). Understanding that he had unclean lips and dwelt among a people with unclean lips, he deserved that a coal be sent from the altar and cleanse his unclean lips.

Here, however, while the strength of God was prophesying, the prince who had declined from the service of the Lord falls so that he may be raised up by Christ. For if the Lord is resurrection and the devil is ruin, how is it said of the Savior: “Behold, this one is appointed for the ruin and resurrection of many in Israel” (Luke 2)? He is appointed for the ruin of those who stood wickedly and for the resurrection of those who had fallen.

When the prophet saw this, he fell upon his face—not because of the merit of one who was sinning, but out of the affection of one who was mourning. With a loud voice, which came from the great ardor of faith, he cried out three times and said: “Alas, alas, alas, Lord God, are you making an end of the remnant of Israel?” The meaning is: Are even those remnants who seemed to remain among the people being destroyed because you are angry?

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘Son of man, your brothers, your brothers, your close kinsmen, and all the house of Israel, all of them, to whom the inhabitants of Jerusalem said: “You have gone far away from the Lord; to us the land has been given as a possession.” Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because I have driven them far away among the nations, and because I have scattered them throughout the lands, I shall be for them a little sanctuary in the lands to which they have come.’”

The word of the Lord therefore came to Ezekiel, who had said, “Alas, alas, alas, Lord God, are you making an end of the remnant of Israel?”—with reference to the death of Pheltias and of those who were killed with him. The remnant was not, in fact, those whom the prophet thought were in Jerusalem, but those who appeared to be captives in Babylon.

The meaning is: O son of man, your brothers, born from the same stock as you, your brothers, I say, to whom the inhabitants of Jerusalem said: “You have gone away from the Lord because you are captives, and you surrendered yourselves with Jeconiah, whereas the land of Israel has been given to us as an eternal possession”—tell them that although I have driven them far from the land of Israel, scattered them among the nations, and commanded them to live in foreign lands, because they have obeyed my command I shall also be with them in foreign and hostile places as a little sanctuary.

Some among them will be found who do not in any way submit their necks to idolatry but remember the commandments of God, as Daniel and the three boys did; and we must believe that there were others like them, in the likeness of such great leaders, whom Scripture now recalls.

From all these things we learn that we must not insult those who have been handed over to punishment by God’s judgment, nor reproach a person who has turned away from his sins, nor ever say to penitents and to those who have gone out from the Church, “You have gone far away from the Lord; to us the land has been given as a possession.” For thus says the Lord: Although I have separated them for a little while from my Church and scattered them among the nations, nevertheless I shall be for them a little sanctuary while they remember their sins.

And those who because of their vices have departed from their own land should hasten, through repentance, to return to their former dwellings.

“Therefore speak: Thus says the Lord: ‘I shall gather you from the peoples and bring you back from the lands in which you have been scattered, and I shall give you the soil of Israel. And they shall enter there and remove from it all its offenses and all its abominations. And I shall give them one heart, and I shall put a new spirit within them, and I shall take away the heart of stone from their flesh and give them a heart of flesh, so that they may walk in my commandments and keep my judgments and perform them; and they shall be my people, and I shall be their God. But as for those whose heart walks after their offenses and abominations, I shall place their way upon their own head,’ says the Lord God,” etc.

The divine word speaks to those who were captives in the land of Babylon, to the brothers of the prophet Ezekiel and to his relatives, to whom the inhabitants of Israel said: “You have gone far away from the Lord; the land has been given to us as a possession.” But he speaks as follows: “I will gather you from the peoples and restore to you the land of Israel.” When you have entered it, you will remove all the idols by which you had offended God. And I will give you one heart of fear and service of God, so that you may no longer serve different idols, or another one than the one you previously had; and I will give a new spirit within you, in accordance with what is written: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit [Col. 0644B] within me” (Psalm 50 [51]). And I will take away from you the heart of stone—that is, a hard heart—in accordance with what Stephen, the first martyr in Christ, says: “You stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart” (Acts 7). Pharaoh’s heart also was hardened, so that he would not release the people of Israel. “And I will give you,” he says, “a heart of flesh” (Exodus 8), soft and tender, capable of receiving God’s commandments, so that they may be written on tablets of fleshy hearts. A soft heart is therefore given and a hard heart removed, so that they may walk in my commandments, keep my judgments, and be among God’s people; and the Lord, who had previously been their adversary, may be their God.

But those who do not correct their former sins through repentance, and instead walk after their abominations, I will repay, he says, with what they deserve, so that their ways will be placed upon their heads [Col. 0644C]. Many think that these things happened to the tribe of Judah, and to those who returned with them, under Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, Jeshua son of Jehozadak the high priest, Ezra, and Nehemiah. The inhabitants of Jerusalem who were taken captive under Zedekiah, king of Judah, or those who fled with Jeremiah to Egypt, are also understood to have been scattered throughout all the lands and never to have returned to the city of Jerusalem. But their complete conversion—the conversion of those who were captives and of the remnant of Israel—is understood in Christ, when the remnant was saved, and three thousand believed in one day, then again five thousand, and others, about whom James says to the apostle Paul: “You see, brother, how many thousands of believing Jews there are? They are all zealous for the Law” (Acts 21). Yet even today the proud inhabitants of the city of Jerusalem [Col. 0644D], whose heart walks after its offenses and abominations, deserve God’s displeasure; while those who were outside, after their heart of stone has been removed and they have received a very tender heart, return through repentance to the Church, walk in the Lord’s commandments, keep his judgments, become the Lord’s people, and have as their God the Lord whom they had previously offended. [Col. 0646C]

“And the cherubim lifted up their wings, and the wheels with them. And the glory of the God of Israel was above them. And the glory of the Lord went up from the midst of the city and stood upon the mountain that is east of the city.” Gradually the glory of the Lord withdraws from Jerusalem. First, abandoning the Temple, it stands in the court or on the threshold of the house [Col. 0645A]; afterward at the entrance of the eastern gate. Finally, when the wings and the wheels following them have been lifted up, it stands upon the mountain that is east of the city. There can be no doubt that this signifies the Mount of Olives, from which the Savior ascended to the Father. The glory of the Lord, which had departed from the city of Jerusalem, stood upon the Mount of Olives as a sign of resurrection and light, so that from there it might behold Jerusalem, destined to perish and burn. And when it says, “The glory went up from the midst of the city,” the Lord expresses the same thing in other words to the disciples: “Rise, let us go from here” (John 14); and to the Jews: “Your house will be left to you desolate” (Matthew 23). Josephus likewise reports that a voice of angels and the power of the heavenly beings, who had previously been stationed as the city’s protection, were heard in the Temple saying, “Let us depart from these dwellings.” And, remarkably [Col. 0645B], to the present day the glory of the Lord, which abandoned the Temple, stands upon the Mount of Olives; shining in the sign of the cross, it looks upon the formerly Jewish Temple, reduced to ashes and embers.

“And the spirit lifted me up and brought me into Chaldea, to the exiles, in a vision, by the spirit of God. And the vision that I had seen was taken away from me. And I spoke to the exiles all the words of the Lord that he had shown me.” For what we have translated from the Hebrew truth as “and the vision that I had seen was taken away from me,” the Septuagint translated, “and I went up from the vision that I had seen.” Both expressions mean that the prophet was not transported bodily from Babylon to Jerusalem, but in spirit; and when the vision that had led him in spirit to Jerusalem and shown him everything [Col. 0645C] narrated by the preceding passage had been taken away, he returned to himself and spoke to the exiles everything that had been shown to him—namely, to those of whom it was written above: “I was sitting in my house, and the elders of Judah were sitting beside me. And the hand of the Lord God fell upon me there, and I saw.”

In a remarkable way, while those who had come to visit him were sitting there, the Prophet perceived mystical visions; he was absent from those sitting before him—absent in spirit, present in body. Everything happened so that the captives might receive consolation: they would be brought back to the land of Israel, walk in the Lord’s commandments, become his people, and have him as their God. But those who would not be converted to repentance and would walk after their abominations [Col. 0645D] would receive what they had done. We have often pointed out that in the Holy Scriptures words are frequently spoken for realities.

## CHAPTER XII

The prophet demonstrates by an enacted sign the distress and imminence of the siege of Jerusalem.

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, you dwell in the midst of an exasperating house, which has eyes to see but does not see, and ears to hear but does not hear, because it is an exasperating house, etc.” We have also often taught that “exasperation” is used to mean bitterness, so that the sense is: “You dwell in the midst of a house that turns sweetness into bitterness,” which makes the Lord, by the bitterness of its vices [Col. 0646A], bitter and cruel, though by nature he is sweet and merciful. Otherwise, we read concerning God: “Taste and see that the Lord is good, or sweet” (Psalm 33 [34]). The Prophet dwells among a people who provoke God to bitterness, a people that has eyes but does not see and ears but does not hear—not because of any defect in its senses, but because of the obstinacy of its perversity. Hence the Lord also says to the Jews: “If you were blind, you would have no sin” (John 9), condemning and exposing their deliberate blindness. Since, therefore, they have eyes to see and do not see, and ears to hear and do not hear, and they despise your words, teach them through an image and a picture; display the matter through bodily enactments, so that they may recognize the coming captivity not only by hearing but also with their eyes.

[Col. 0646B] “Therefore, son of man, prepare for yourself vessels for exile, and you shall depart by day before their eyes. You shall depart from your place to another place in their sight, if perhaps they will look, because they are an exasperating house,” etc. There is no doubt that the whole content of this passage indicates the future captivity of King Zedekiah and the tribe of Judah, who was captured together with Jerusalem. But since some wish Zedekiah’s captivity—Zedekiah means “the Lord is righteous”—to precede as a type of the Savior, who, descending from heavenly things to earthly things, assumed a human body, and they take these to be the vessels of captivity, I think it necessary to warn the prudent and cautious reader that we include these interpretations so that we may not appear to omit anything, but that we do not approve them. For an impious king cannot precede as a figure of the one who is the example of all piety. That Zedekiah was captured by the Babylonians and Chaldeans is related both by the prophet Jeremiah and by the history of the Kings; it also relates that he was led from place to place—that is, from Jerusalem to Babylon—and the other events that Ezekiel recounts in what follows. Those who refer his captivity and migration from place to place to the Lord Jesus Christ understand this as signifying his descent from heavenly things to earthly things.

“And you shall bring out your vessels by day before their eyes, as the vessels of one migrating. But you shall go out in the evening before them, as one who departs goes out before their eyes. Dig through the wall for yourself, and go out through it before their eyes. You shall carry upon your shoulders; you shall flee in darkness; you shall cover your face [Col. 0646D] and shall not see the land, because I have made you a portent for the house of Israel,” etc. The Prophet is commanded to perform symbolically what Zedekiah will do in reality. Gather your bundles, then, for these are the vessels of one migrating, in their sight. After they have seen what you are going to do, you shall go out in the evening like one who is migrating. For we read that Zedekiah fled by night, after a breach had been made in the wall, toward the desert regions of the Jordan, and that there he was seized by the Babylonians; this is signified by the wall being pierced. When it says, “You shall carry upon your shoulders,” your bundles are understood, together with whatever fleeing people customarily carry for the necessities of the journey. “You shall bring them out in darkness,” so that no one may see you. “You shall cover your face”—either because blindness came upon him when Nebuchadnezzar tore out his eyes [Col. 0647A], or so that he would not be recognized as the king himself and the vigilance of his guards would be increased. What follows, “And you shall not see the land,” signifies that he was led blind to Babylon and did not see it. “Because I have made you a portent,” he says, “for the house of Israel.” For both the words and deeds of the prophets were given as signs and figures. Hence in Zechariah men are called portentous, because they portend future events. And in Hosea God says: “In the hands of the prophets I have been represented” (Hosea 12).

Those who wish Christ to be understood in the person of Ezekiel take the vessels of captivity as the human body, and the wall that was pierced as the barrier of hell, which he broke through; when he rose, he was seen only by believers; and he was carried upon shoulders when he ascended victoriously to heaven with the angelic powers [Col. 0647B]. That he goes out hidden and covers his face signifies that the divine majesty was not to be seen in mortal flesh. And that he does not see the land signifies that it is not illumined by his eyes, since it does not deserve his gaze. “For the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Psalm 33 [34]), and he turns his face away from the impious. They say that he did all these things so that, through the likeness of a man, he might turn the hard hearts of the Israelite people toward faith; and he is given as a portent to the house of Israel, in accordance with what is written: “Behold, this one is appointed for the resurrection and downfall of many, and as a sign that will be opposed.”

“Therefore I did as he had commanded me: I brought out my vessels as the vessels of one migrating by day, and in the evening I pierced the wall for myself with my hand. In darkness I went out [Col. 0647C], and I carried them upon my shoulders in their sight.” He testifies that he fulfilled by his action what he had previously been commanded to do. According to either interpretation, what was explained above requires no further interpretation. But this should be noted: at one and the same time Jeremiah was prophesying in Jerusalem, while Ezekiel was prophesying in Babylon; Jeremiah’s prophecy was sent to the captives, and Ezekiel’s to those who lived in Jerusalem. Thus God’s providence was shown through one person in different regions, and those who heard might understand that whatever happened to the people did not depend on the power of idols but occurred by the Lord’s command.

[Col. 0647D] “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, surely the house of Israel, the exasperating house, has said to you, ‘What are you doing?’ Thus says the Lord God: If the exasperating house asks you, ‘Why are you doing these things?’ say to them: Thus says the Lord God: This burden is upon the prince who is in Jerusalem and upon the whole house of Israel that is in their midst. Say: I am your portent. As I have done, so it shall be done to them; they shall go into exile and captivity. The prince who is in their midst shall be carried upon shoulders. He shall go out in darkness; they shall pierce the wall to bring him out; his face shall be covered so that he will not see the land with his eyes. And I will spread my net over him, and he shall be caught in my snare; I will bring him to Babylon, to the land of the Chaldeans, but he shall not see it, and there he shall die. And all who are around him, his guard and his troops [Col. 0648A], I will scatter to every wind, and I will draw the sword after them. And they shall know that I am the Lord when I scatter them among the nations and disperse them throughout the lands. And I will leave a few men among them, escaping sword, famine, and pestilence, so that they may recount all their crimes among the nations to which they will enter. And they shall know that I am the Lord” (Jerome).

First let us explain the historical sense. “Say,” he says, “to them, son of man”—whether they ask or do not ask, “What are you doing?” The burden and vision that are upon the ruler who is in Jerusalem signify the ruler Zedekiah. And say: “I am your portent,” or, as the Septuagint translated it, “I am the one who makes portents,” so that future events may be known from present ones. “As I have done, so it shall be done to them”—to the ruler and to all who are in the ruler’s company: they will be led captive into Babylonian exile. “And the ruler who is in their midst shall be carried upon shoulders” [Col. 0648B], either on those of beasts or of those who had fled with him, “in darkness” and in the darkness of night. “He shall go out, and his companions shall pierce the wall to bring him out.” “His face shall be covered,” either because of the fear of one fleeing or because of the injury of blindness, “so that, being blind, he will not see the land of Babylon.” “And I will spread my net over him, and he shall be caught in my snare.” For he was captured by the Babylonians with the Lord’s permission. What he suffered at the hands of his enemies, he testifies that the Lord himself caused to happen. Led to Babylon, he will not see the land of the Chaldeans, and there he will die in captivity.

When he has been captured, I will scatter all his associates, assistants, and companions in flight here and there [Col. 0648C]. I will not permit them to depart in safety, but I will draw my sword against them into the hands of their enemies. Thus, when they have been scattered among the nations, they will understand that I am the Lord and that everything happened by my will. “And I will leave,” he says, “a few of his associates”—those who fled with him and were able to escape—who survived sword, famine, and pestilence. When they reach various regions, whether through flight or captivity, they will recount all their crimes, in word and by example, because of which they deserved such great evils; and they will understand that I myself am God.

[Col. 0648D] “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, eat your bread in agitation, and drink your water in haste and sorrow; and say to the people of the land: Thus says the Lord God to those who dwell in Jerusalem, in the land of Israel: They shall eat their bread in anxiety and drink their water in desolation, so that the land may be desolated of its multitude, because of the iniquity of all who dwell in it. And the cities that are now inhabited shall be desolated, and the land shall be deserted. And you shall know that I am the Lord,” etc.

After the prophecy concerning the ruler and his companions, which had been displayed through a bodily image, he turns to the people. Whatever is said to the Prophet is conveyed through the Prophet to the inhabitants of Jerusalem: in the calamity of the siege they will eat their bread in poverty and distress, and they will drink their water not in abundance but with torment and tribulation. “These things,” he says [Col. 0649A], “are spoken to you, O prophet, so that you may speak to the people of your land and say: Thus says the Lord to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, which is in the land of Israel: Besieged by Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans, you will endure the evil of hunger and thirst, so that the whole land and its multitude may be destroyed.” He signifies the inhabitants by the land that is inhabited. And lest they think this is happening to them without cause, say to them, he says, that because of their crimes and iniquity all the cities of Judea must be reduced to solitude, and the cultivation of the entire land must perish, so that they may recognize the God who is raging, whom they did not wish to recognize as merciful.

According to the allegorical interpretation, we can say that the inhabitants of Jerusalem are believers in Christ who dwell in the Church. Even if through their sins they have deserved his displeasure, let them eat bread with poverty and drink water with sorrow [Col. 0649B] and distress—not enduring the food of bread or the drink of water, but hunger for the word and teaching of God. For whenever, whether through the fault of rulers who are to be captured and handed over to the Babylonians or through our own hardness, we lose the word of God and are no longer worthy to possess useful waters, then we will take our food in pain and poverty. The land will lose the multitude of believers; the cities, understood as the churches throughout the whole world, will be desolated; and the land will be deserted, so that all may know that this is the Lord’s displeasure. We can also understand this in the time of persecution.

[Col. 0649C] “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, what is this proverb that you have in the land of Israel, saying, ‘The days will be prolonged, and every vision will perish’? Therefore say to them: Thus says the Lord God: I will bring this proverb to an end, and it shall no longer be spoken as a common saying in Israel. And speak to them: The days have drawn near, and the fulfillment of every vision. For no vision will any longer be empty, nor any divination ambiguous in the midst of the children of Israel, because I am the Lord. I will speak whatever word I speak, and it shall happen. It shall no longer be delayed; but in your days, exasperating house, I will speak the word and perform it, says the Lord God” (Jerome).

The whole sense of this chapter is as follows. Above, he had prophesied against the ruler who was in Jerusalem; afterward he announced to the people that famine and the burning torment of thirst were coming. The multitude, not believing this, used an old and familiar proverb [Col. 0649D]: “The threat of the prophets is postponed for a long time, and every vision will perish.” Therefore say to them, he says, that my threat will not be delayed, nor will a false and ambiguous prophecy be delivered to the peoples—one whose fulfillment is uncertain, or which is spoken at one time and fulfilled at another. Rather, while you are still alive, you will speak, and the word I have spoken will be fulfilled in those who hear.

[Col. 0650A] “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, behold, the house of Israel says, ‘The vision that this man sees concerns many days, and he prophesies for distant times.’ Therefore say to them: Thus says the Lord God: No word of his will be delayed any longer. The word that I speak will be fulfilled, says the Lord God.”

This signifies the impending captivity of the city of Jerusalem and the imminent capture of Zedekiah together with the people of Judah. But not only at that time: even to this day the unbelieving populace and the hard hearts of mortals do not accept God’s prophecy. Everything that the Prophets threaten, and everything that the Gospel proclaims, they suppose is to be postponed to another time. We should know that the parable placed here by the Septuagint is understood as a proverb, in accordance with what we read in the Psalm: “And I became a proverb to them” (Psalm 68 [69]). And in this same prophet: “What is this proverb among you, in the people of Israel, saying, ‘The fathers ate sour grapes, and the children’s teeth were set on edge’?” We touch briefly upon obvious matters so that we may dwell on the more obscure ones.

## CHAPTER XIII

The word of the Lord against the false prophets who deceive the people of God, and against women who prophesy falsely.

[Col. 0650B]

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, prophesy against the prophets of Israel who prophesy, and say to those who prophesy from their own heart: Hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God,” etc.

This is a discourse against the false prophets who deceived the people and prophesied something contrary to God’s commandments. No one should be troubled by the fact that they are called prophets. Holy Scripture has this custom: it calls each person a prophet of his own prediction and speech. Thus the prophets of Baal are called prophets, as are the prophets of idols and the prophets of confusion. Hence the apostle Paul calls a Greek poet a prophet [Col. 0650C]: “One of their own prophets said, ‘Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies’” (Titus 1). And in Hosea we read: “The prophet is a madman, the bearer of the spirit” (Hosea 9). Whatever was said to the Israelite people at that time is now referred to the Church: the holy prophets are the apostles and apostolic men, while the lying and mad prophets are all heretics, whose leaders fabricate things from their own hearts. Those who have been led astray by them submit to the lies of others.

“Woe to the foolish prophets who follow their own spirit and see nothing.” Since, according to the rule of Scripture, the name “prophets” is common to good and wicked alike, they differ in this: good prophets are called wise, while evil ones are foolish and senseless [Col. 0650D]. The former refers to ecclesiastical men, the latter to all heretics who abandon the Spirit of God and follow their own spirit, because they prophesy not through divine inspiration but from their own heart; hence they see nothing. The wise person follows not the thoughts of his own heart but the Spirit of God.

This accords with what was said above, where the living creatures and the wheels followed the Spirit of God. And the prophet says: “You shall walk after the Lord your God” (Hosea 11). Elsewhere: “Lead me in the right path” (Psalm 118 [119]); and again: “Your good Spirit will lead me into a level land” (Psalm 142 [143]). For the people of God, the pillar of fire and the cloud were guides in the wilderness (Exodus 13). Jeremiah says [Col. 0651A]: “I have not grown weary in following you” (Jeremiah 17). Which of the heretics who follows his own spirit does not stumble into darkness and, being blind, lead the blind into a pit? Indeed, although in their mysteries—even in their orgies—they may seem to see more than the teachers of the Church, nevertheless they see absolutely nothing, because they have lost the sun of righteousness. In vain they imitate those who were formerly called “seers,” to whom it is said: “You who see, go away; withdraw to the land of Judah, and do not prophesy in Bethel” (Amos 7). Therefore the visions of Isaiah and Obadiah are placed in titles. And the Lord commanded the Apostles: “Lift up your eyes and see” (John 4). The Prophet entreats prayerfully: “Open my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your law” (Psalm 118 [119]).

“Your prophets, Israel, are like foxes in the deserts [Col. 0651B]. You have not gone up in opposition, nor built a wall for the house of Israel, to stand in battle on the day of the Lord. They see empty things and prophesy lies, saying, ‘Thus says the Lord,’ although the Lord has not sent them, and they persist in confirming the word. Surely you have seen an empty vision and spoken a lying divination, saying, ‘Thus says the Lord,’ although I have not spoken,” etc.

Let us first speak according to the Hebrew: the prophets of Israel are like foxes, stealing domestic birds every day. According to Aquila and the Septuagint, they dwell “in the deserts”; according to Symmachus and Theodotion, “in ruins and dilapidated places.” They are unable to go up in opposition or to set up a wall for the house of Israel. We read [Col. 0651C] that Aaron confronted the fire devouring the people of Israel, met it, stood in the midst, and placed himself as a wall for the people’s salvation (Numbers 16). Jeremiah, too, is told not to confront the Lord or persist in prayer against his anger. For just as a wall is set against an enemy, and one customarily confronts an adversary who is advancing, so God’s sentence is broken by the prayers of the saints. Hence Moses is told: “Leave me, and I will destroy this people” (Exodus 32). For when someone is told, “Leave me,” it is shown that he has the power to hold back the one speaking.

These prophets cannot stand in battle on the day of the Lord, to fight for the people through prayers and resist God’s sentence through supplication. Because they see empty things and prophesy lies, claiming to have been sent by the Lord when they have not been sent by God, and because they persist in error and wish to establish their own word, they are rebuked [Col. 0651D]: everything they proclaim is empty, though they call their own lie the word of the Lord.

“Prophesy,” he says, “against the prophets of Israel who prophesy, and say to the prophets” (Origen). Just as the Prophets’ work consisted in saying what they were commanded to say, so by the same Spirit it is necessary for anyone who wishes to explain what has been secretly signified, so that he may show that the prophecy is now directed against those who teach contrary to God’s will, who prophesy from their own heart.

[Col. 0652A] According to the simple interpretation, some of the prophets, speaking from the divine Spirit, did not speak from their own heart but from God’s understanding. Others, pretending to be prophets and saying, “Thus says the Lord,” though the Lord was not speaking in them, became false prophets. The present discourse can also apply to those who teach in the churches if they teach otherwise than truth requires. If someone takes what the Lord Jesus Christ said and understands it in the sense in which the one who taught it himself understood it, he speaks the words of God’s Son not from his own heart but from the Holy Spirit, if the Holy Spirit agrees with the will of the one who spoke in the apostles. But if someone reads the Gospel and imposes his own meaning upon it, not understanding it as the Lord spoke, that person is a false prophet, speaking from his own heart within the Gospel.

“Like foxes in the desert, your prophets, Israel.” The fox is a wicked, cunning, untamable, and wild animal. “Say,” the Savior says, “to that fox: Behold, I cast out demons and perform healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am perfected” (Luke 13). Samson needed such foxes against the foreigners [Col. 0652B] (Judges 15). He captured three hundred of them, tied their tails together with a cord, and sent them to destroy the enemies’ crops. Such are false teachers: cunning, malicious, and like beasts. If I am such a one, I am a fox. But not simply a fox: a fox in the deserts, a fox in ruins, a fox in the rocks. These cunning creatures are contained in various disturbances.

Such cunning and wicked creatures always dwell in deserts and solitudes. Wherever the soul is inhabited by God and filled with the Holy Spirit, the teaching of heretics cannot penetrate there, nor can their word break forth. But where there is Christ’s solitude, where there is the desert of righteousness, there the poisons of the most wicked discipline are found [Col. 0652C]. Therefore, as he says, “like foxes in the deserts,” your prophets, Israel, did not stand in a firm place. If you wish to examine false teachers, you will see that they are weak and unstable, unable to say: “He set my feet upon a rock and directed my steps” (Psalm 39 [40]). Because they are not the kind who stand, founded upon a strong root, they did not stand in a firm place; instead, they set about moving their feet.

[Col. 0652D] All heretics are like foxes because of their deceit and wickedness. The Savior speaks of them: “Foxes have dens, and the birds of heaven have nests.” And concerning Herod it is written: “Say to that fox.” Concerning these same foxes, which deceive the simple and little ones and ravage Christ’s vineyard, Solomon says: “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards” (Song of Songs 2). And in the Psalm, concerning those who are overthrown by their deceit, it is sung: “They will enter into the lower parts of the earth; they will be given over to the power of the sword; they will become portions for foxes” (Psalm 62 [63]).

These prophets, who are like foxes, did not stand in a firm place, nor did they deserve to hear with Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16). “You have not gone up,” he says [Col. 0653A], “in opposition, nor built a wall for the house of Israel, to stand in battle on the day of the Lord” (Gregory). To go up in opposition is to confront the powers of this world with a free voice in defense of the flock. And to stand on the day of the Lord is to resist in the battle, out of love for righteousness, those who fight wickedly. For what else is it for a shepherd to fear to speak what is right than to turn his back through silence? If he exposes himself on behalf of the flock, he sets up a wall for the house of Israel against its enemies.

Again, it is said to the sinful people: “Your prophets saw false and foolish things for you, and they did not expose your iniquity, so as to provoke you to repentance.” In sacred speech, prophets are sometimes called teachers. While they judge present things to be fleeting, they reveal what is to come; yet the divine word rebukes them for seeing falsely. Because they fear to rebuke sins, they flatter sinners with an empty promise of security. They do not expose the iniquity of sinners because they fall silent instead of speaking words of reproof. The key of opening is the word of correction, which reveals the fault that often remains unknown even to the one who committed it.

According to the Septuagint, the false prophets gathered flocks over the house of Israel—that is, a multitude of foolish people against the house of God [Col. 0653B]. They themselves did not rise, nor could they raise up others; whatever they did and do is full of lies. What follows, “And they began to raise up the word,” signifies that they indeed wish to rise and lift themselves to lofty things, but they cannot accomplish what they desire. They are told: “Have you not seen a false vision and spoken empty divinations?”

Therefore they did not rise; that is, the false prophets and false teachers have not yet attained the baptism of the resurrection. The things they claim to see from the Lord are false, and they can never behold the truth. [Col. 0653C] Take an example: whoever reads Scripture and receives it otherwise than it is written sees Scripture falsely. But whoever hears Scripture and interprets it according to the understanding of truth sees the truth.

The saints do not practice divination: “There is no divination in Jacob” (Numbers 23). But sinners divine false things, saying: “Thus says the Lord,” although the Lord did not send them. Listen to heretics and how they claim to possess the tradition of the apostles; listen to false teachers and how they assert that their doctrine is the Lord’s doctrine, and that their understanding agrees with the understanding of the prophets. They say: “Thus says the Lord,” although the Lord did not send them.

“And they began to raise up the word; have you not seen a false vision?” For they too wish to raise up some word in their own defense. But the Lord rebukes them and says [Col. 0653D]: “Have you not seen a false vision and spoken empty divinations? And you said, ‘The Lord says,’ although I have not spoken.”

“Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because you have spoken empty things and seen lies, therefore, behold, I am against you, says the Lord God. And my hand shall be against the prophets who see empty things and prophesy lies. They shall not be in the council of my people, they shall not be written in the writing of the house of Israel, and they shall not enter the land of Israel. And you shall know that I am the Lord God” (Jerome).

Under the persona of the prophets, this is a discourse against heretics who speak empty things and see lies. They persist in affirming their doctrine, but the Lord himself comes against them [Col. 0654A], rises up against them, and stretches out his hand over them to strike, not withdrawing it to spare.
