He threatens that they will not be in the future council of God’s people, nor in his Church, but in the synagogue of the devil; nor will they be written in the house of Israel. Concerning them it is said elsewhere: “They shall be written upon the earth,” not in the land of Israel, which is the land of the living. And of that land it is now said: “They shall not enter the land of Israel,” but rather the land of the dead and the shadow of death. After they have suffered these things, separated from the assembly of God’s people, they will understand that he is the Lord.

“Because they have deceived my people, saying, ‘Peace,’ when there is no peace. And he was building a wall; but they were coating it with mud without straw. Say to those who coat it without proper mixture that it will fall. For there will be a flooding rain, and I shall send very large stones crashing down, and a storm-wind that scatters. And behold, the wall has fallen. Will it not be said to you, ‘Where is the coating that you applied?’ Therefore thus says God: I shall make the spirits of storms break forth in my indignation. And there shall be flooding rain in my fury, and great stones of wrath for destruction. And I shall destroy the wall that you coated without proper mixture, and level it to the ground. Its foundation will be exposed. It will fall and be consumed in its midst, and you shall know that I am the Lord. And I shall complete my indignation against the wall and against those who coat it without proper mixture, and I shall say to you: ‘There is no wall, and there are none who coat it—the prophets of Israel, who prophesy to Jerusalem [Col. 0654C] and see for it a vision of peace. And there is no peace,’ says the Lord God, etc.”

The prophets of Israel who will not be in the council of God’s people, nor be written in the record of the house of Israel, nor enter the promised land, will suffer these things because they deceived my people. Instead of the strictness of repentance and the hardship of conversion, they announced peace and prosperity to them, according to what is said elsewhere: “Peace, peace, and there is no peace” (Jer. VIII). Thus God, metaphorically, was building a wall for them through the commands of the Law, the utterances of the holy prophets, and threats, so that he might remove from them every incursion of wild beasts and hostile attack, while, converted to God, they were enclosed by this as by a very strong wall. [Col. 0654D] But the false prophets repeatedly promised them peace. This repetition of the word “peace” signifies this: “Say,” he says, “to those who promise them empty things and offer them futile assistance, that this wall and this rampart will fall. And I shall send a most violent rain”—namely, he signifies the fiercest enemies, the Babylonians and Chaldeans—“and hailstones rushing down from above.” Everything is expressed metaphorically, so that a sudden whirlwind may overturn and demolish the unstable rampart. Afterwards it will be said to them, that is, to the false prophets: “Where is the coating that you applied, and where is what you promised as assistance?”

Whatever we have said about the false prophets can also be referred to heretics: all their fabrications are dissolved by God’s wrath; [Col. 0655A] and the construction of their wicked doctrines, which does not possess the seasoning of the Holy Spirit, collapses and crumbles down to its foundations and dust. The rampart itself is leveled to the ground; it falls, and the prophets who made the promises are consumed, together with the people to whom the promises were made, in its midst. After he has completed his indignation and said to them, “This is not a wall”—that is, “your defense does not exist”—and “there are none who coat it,” but everything is empty and comes to nothing: “Then by your deeds you shall know that I am the Lord.”

So that we may know who those are who coat the wall, what follows says: “The prophets of Israel”—that is, the false prophets—“who prophesy to Jerusalem and see for it a vision of peace.” These are the cause of sin, ruin, and foolish security. “For there will be no peace, says the Lord.” For the Lord did not send them, nor did he speak to them.

What the Septuagint translated, “And upon their joints,” is not found in the Hebrew. It signifies either the joints of stones in a wall or the wooden supports by which walls are strengthened. Likewise, what we read above—“he was building,” or “he builds, a wall”—many refer to the people of Israel, who promised themselves the empty assistance either of the Egyptians or of peace.

“And you, son of man, set your face against the daughters of your people, who prophesy from their own heart, and prophesy against them, and say: Thus says the Lord God: Woe to those who sew cushions under every elbow of the hand and make pillows beneath the head of persons of every age, to capture souls. And when they captured the souls [Col. 0655C] of my people, they gave life to their souls. And they violated me before my people for a handful of barley and a fragment of bread, to kill souls that do not die and to give life to souls that do not live, lying to my people who believe lies. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against your cushions, with which you capture the flying souls, and I shall tear them from your arms. And I shall release the souls whom you capture, souls for flight. And I shall tear your pillows apart, and I shall free my people from your hand; nor will they any longer be in your hands for plunder. And you shall know that I am the Lord, because you made the heart of the righteous grieve deceitfully, though I did not cause him grief, and strengthened the hands of the wicked, so that he would not return from his evil way and live. Therefore you shall no longer see empty visions, nor practice divinations any longer, and I shall rescue my people from your hand, and you shall know that I am the Lord,” etc.

(Hieronymus.) Above, the divine speech was directed against the prophets who coated the wall with mud that had no straw and could provide no strength to the wall or rampart. Now he is commanded to set or direct his face against the daughters of the people, the prophetesses; and, as the Septuagint translated it, to “make it firm.” Just as against the prophets other false prophets were inspired by a diabolical spirit to overturn God’s commands, so against the prophetesses—such as Deborah (Judg. V), Huldah (IV Kings XVII), and the four prophesying daughters of Philip the evangelist in the Acts of the Apostles [Col. 0656A] (Acts XXI)—other women of this sex were inspired by a demonic spirit. Among these were Prisca and Maximilla, who by lying prophecy overturned faith in the truth.

The Hebrews say that these women were trained in magical arts through necromancy and the Pythian spirit, like the woman who appeared to have raised the soul of Samuel (I Kings XXVIII); and like the woman in the Acts of the Apostles whose divination obtained much profit for her masters. From her an unclean spirit was expelled by the command of the apostle Paul (Acts XVI).

We, however, shall say that other heretics, through the falsehood of their doctrines, proclaim their own virtue. Among these were Pythagoras and Zeno, from whom came the Stoics, as well as the Brahmins of India and the Gymnosophists of Ethiopia, who, because of their abstinence in food, attribute a wonder-working power to themselves before the gentiles. They are rightly said to coat a wall and promise it some strength; but because they do not have Christ as its seasoning, their labor is empty, “and the building is destined to perish. For unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have labored in vain” (Ps. CXXVI).

Others, teachers of pleasure and lust, are said to sew cushions and place them beneath every elbow of the hand: the Epicureans and Pyrrhonians, and among us Jovinianus and Eunomius, who say: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (Isa. XXII).

Therefore the prophet is commanded to set, or make firm, his face against the daughters of his people. First it must be explained what is meant by a face that is set, directed, and made firm: namely, what is written concerning the Lord: “The face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth” (Ps. XXXIII). “For as wax melts before the face of fire, so sinners perish before the face of God” (Ps. LXVII).

Woe, therefore, to these heresies and doctrines which, while promising repose, deceive every age and sex in order to capture the souls of the wretched and defile all my people, as though I were thought to love pleasure—not for a homer and half a kor of barley, as we read in Hosea, but for a handful of barley, which brute animals eat, and fragments of bread: not a whole loaf, that is, the solid testimonies of the Scriptures, but testimonies broken, cut short, and diminished by heretical perversity, so that they may deceive even the holy and drag them to death, while attempting to give life to sinners through empty promises.

Therefore the merciful and compassionate God does not kill the prophetesses themselves, but tears apart their cushions, which, flying like nets, capture souls, so that once they have been torn, the souls may have the freedom to fly. He also tears apart the veils, or pillows, upon which the principal part of the soul reclined and with which the heads of the deceived were covered. The Apostle teaches that men’s heads are not to be veiled, but that with unveiled face they are to contemplate the glory of the Lord.

“For,” he says, “you were breaking the spirits of those who serve God with false terrors, and by fraudulent promises you were keeping the wicked enclosed, so that, if they repented, they might receive back the life they had lost. Therefore you shall by no means see empty visions, nor shall I call your lies prophecies, but divinations.” Of these it is written: “There is no augury in Jacob, nor divination in Israel” (Num. XXIII). “That I may rescue my people from your hands, so that by your deeds you may know that I am the Lord, who have freed the lost” [Gregory, *Pastoral Care*, part II, chap. 8].

For plainly, when self-love has seized the mind of a ruler, it sometimes drives that mind disorderly toward softness, and sometimes toward harshness. Through his own love, the ruler’s mind is turned toward softness, because when he sees subjects committing sins, he does not dare to correct them, lest his affection toward them grow cold. At other times he soothes the errors of his subjects—errors which he ought to rebuke—with flatteries. Hence it is said through the Prophet: “Woe to those who sew cushions under every elbow of the hand and make pillows beneath the head of persons of every age, to capture souls.”

To place cushions beneath every elbow of the hand is to support with flattering praise souls falling away from their uprightness and reclining in love of this world. The elbow of one lying down is, as it were, received by a cushion, and the head by pillows, when the harshness of correction is withdrawn from the sinner and the softness of favor is applied to him, so that he may lie comfortably in error, struck by no harshness of contradiction. Rulers who love themselves certainly offer this to those from whom they fear they may be harmed in their pursuit of temporal glory. For those whom they see as unable to do anything against them they always oppress with the harshness of rigid denunciation; they never admonish them mercifully, but, forgetting pastoral gentleness, terrify by the right of domination.

The divine voice rightly rebukes such rulers through the Prophet, saying: “But you ruled over them with severity and with power” (Ezek. XXXIV). Loving themselves more than their author, they raise themselves boastfully over their subjects and attend not to what they ought to do, but to what they are able to do. They fear nothing of the coming judgment; they shamelessly glory in temporal power; they delight in doing unlawful things freely and in ensuring that no subject contradicts them.

Therefore whoever strives to do what is wrong and yet wants others to remain silent about it is himself a witness against himself: he desires to be loved more than the truth, since he does not want the truth defended against him. No one lives in such a way as not to sin to some extent. Therefore he desires the truth to be loved more than himself who wants no one to spare him against the truth.

For this reason Peter willingly accepted Paul’s rebuke. For this reason David humbly heard the rebuke of a subject. Good rulers, because they do not know how to love themselves with private affection, regard a word of free and pure truth from their subjects as an act of humble obedience.

Yet amid these things, care of governance must be tempered with such great skill in moderation that, when the minds of subjects are able to judge certain matters rightly, they may come forward with freedom of speech, while that freedom does not burst into pride. Otherwise, if freedom of tongue is perhaps granted to them without measure, humility of life may be lost by them.

It must also be known that good rulers ought to seek to please people, but so that, through the sweetness of their reputation, they may draw those nearest to them toward love of the truth—not so that they may desire to be loved for themselves, but so that they may make their own affection, as it were, a road by which they may lead the hearts of their hearers to love of the Creator.

It is difficult for even a preacher who proclaims entirely correct things, if he is not loved, to be heard willingly. Therefore the person in authority ought to strive to be loved, so that he may be heard. Yet he must not seek affection for his own sake, lest he be found to resist by a hidden tyranny of thought the one whom he is seen to serve through his office.

Paul expresses this well when he reveals to us the hidden purpose of his effort, saying: “Just as I also please everyone in all things” (I Cor. X). Yet he says again: “If I were still pleasing people, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. I). Paul therefore pleases and does not please: in seeking to please, he seeks not to please himself through people, but the truth through himself.

## CHAPTER XIV. Because of the uncleanness of men he does not preach to them, nor are they freed from the prophets or from the plagues

“And certain elders of Israel came to me and sat before me. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, these men have placed their uncleannesses in their hearts and set the stumbling-block of their iniquity before their faces. Shall I answer them when they inquire of me? Therefore speak to them, and say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Every man, every man of the house of Israel, who places his uncleannesses in his heart and sets the stumbling-block of his iniquity before his face, and comes to the prophet, asking him to inquire of me, I, the Lord, shall answer him according to the multitude of his uncleannesses, so that the house of Israel may be caught in its own heart, by which they have departed from me in all their idols.

Therefore say to the house of Israel: Thus says the Lord God: Turn and depart from your idols, and turn your faces away from all your contaminations. For every man, every man of the house of Israel, and of the resident foreigners who dwell as immigrants in Israel, if he has become alienated from me in Israel, and has placed his idols in his heart and set the stumbling-block of his iniquity before his face, and comes to the prophet to inquire of me through him, I, the Lord, shall answer him through myself. I shall set my face against that man and make him an example and a proverb, and destroy him from the midst of my people, and you shall know that I am the Lord.

And if the prophet has gone astray and spoken a word, I, the Lord, have deceived that prophet. I shall stretch out my hand against him and wipe him out from the midst of my people Israel, and they shall bear their iniquity. According to the iniquity of the one who inquires, so shall be the iniquity of the prophet, so that the house of Israel may no longer go astray from me and may no longer be polluted by all its transgressions, but may be my people, and I may be their God, says the Lord of hosts,” etc.

(Hieronymus.) After he had spoken to the prophets who prophesied from their own heart and coated the wall without proper mixture, and to the prophetesses who sewed pillows and placed them beneath every [Col. 0659A] elbow of the hand, and made veils and covered the heads of persons of every age—through which the doctrine of perverse teachings is indicated—not all the elders came to the prophet, lest all should appear to be in error, but certain elders of Israel came. They sat before the prophet, meanwhile delaying in silence the explanation of why they had come. Immediately the word of God came to the prophet, indicating why they were present.

For it is not natural for a human being, even one of holy heart, to know the secrets of another person. Hence this is said of the Savior alone: “But Jesus, seeing their thoughts, said: Why are you thinking evil in your hearts?” (Matt. IX). The sense is this: “Son of man, these men who sit before you have placed their uncleannesses, or thoughts, in their hearts.” According to Symmachus and Theodotion, they have placed “idols and a stumbling-block”—that is, the ruin and torment of their iniquity—before their face, and in this state they have come to inquire of the Lord’s word.

“Shall I answer such men?” They come to me with their former thoughts, not even at this time abandoning the crimes of their impiety, but believing in idols and fraudulent divinations, having the ruin and torment of iniquity before their face, while they despair of better things and are prepared for punishment, and yet seek through you to learn my words.

Therefore, because they have come to you with a perverse heart, answer them—not in your own person, lest the authority of the response be slight—but by my command. And you shall say to them: “Thus says the Lord God.”

The meaning of the entire passage, if I were to compress its broad explanation into a brief statement, is this: “Every man”—not of other nations, whose error may be forgiven, but of the house of Israel—who comes to the prophet to inquire while still carrying the former vices about which we spoke above, I shall answer according to his heart and his uncleannesses, so that he may hear according to what he wants and believes. For one who asks not with the intention of learning but of testing does not deserve correction.

They have departed from me and followed idols. This is a brief threat: let them depart from idols and perverse thoughts, and turn to me, abandoning their own crimes. For one who inquires deceitfully does not deserve to hear the truth; rather, he must be caught by his own heart, just as the scribes and Pharisees, when they questioned—or rather, tested—the Lord, heard: “Why do you test me?” (Matt. XXI). And again: “Nor shall I tell you by what authority I do these things” (ibid.).

But when such a man is found and inquires in such a way, God sets his face against him, or confirms it, so that the hardness of his forehead may be softened by the severity of his countenance. He becomes an example and a proverb—or an object of concern and destruction—so that, when he has been destroyed from God’s people, the rest may know that he is the Lord who knows the secrets of the heart and understands the perversity of the mind, and who considers not the words of speakers but their hearts.

What follows seems to raise a question: “When the prophet goes astray and speaks a word, I, the Lord, have deceived that prophet.” This must not, I think, be understood of a true prophet, but of a false prophet, who is called a prophet by homonymy. This can also be resolved from the passage of Scripture in which King Ahab of Israel, going to battle, does not wish to hear the prophet Micaiah but submits to the counsels of the false prophets. Micaiah says that he saw the Lord sitting on his throne and the spirit of error voluntarily offering itself to deceive the king.

The Devil also is said in the book of Job to wander around the earth and stand in the presence of God, and to receive from the Lord power first over Job’s possessions and then over his body. Balaam, too, the diviner, is sent by the Lord to deceive Balaak son of Beor.

All this is said so that it may not be attributed to the strength of the false prophets that the people are deceived. Rather, the people prefer to hear falsehood than to lend an ear to the truth, and it is an act of God’s wrath that a perverse and unbelieving people listen to false prophets more than to true prophets.

Finally, he stretches out his hand against him—the prophet is understood—and he is erased from the midst of his people, so that he may bear his iniquity. For the error is similar and the punishment alike, so that both the one who inquires and the one who is questioned bear their iniquity. Thus the house of Israel—those who wish to hear God’s words—will no longer be deceived by perverse prophecies, but will be God’s people and will deserve to have the Lord as their God.

In what he said, “I, the Lord, have deceived him,” Solomon’s words agree when, speaking about God, he says: “He mocks the mockers” (Prov. III). There is also this testimony: “If they walk against me perversely, I too shall walk against them in perverse fury” (Lev. XXVI).

What is said a second time—“Every man, of the sons of Israel and of the resident foreigners who are joined to them”—shows in us, according to the Apostle, a twofold human being: the inner and the outer. For many, while possessing the bodily appearance of a human being, assume the images of various beasts, which the Prophet prays may be scattered: “Lord, in your city you shall scatter their image” (Ps. LXXII).

Those of whom it is written, “When a human being was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. XLVIII), are not human beings who are truly human, but human beings who are beasts. Again, those who hear in the Gospel, “Serpents, brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matt. XXIII), are not human beings who are truly human, but human beings who are serpents.

And those of whom it is written, “Foxes have dens and the birds of heaven nests” (Matt. VIII), and concerning Herod, “Tell that fox” (Luke XIII), are not human beings who are truly human, but human beings who are foxes. Those who possess both uses of the name “human being,” however, if they go astray, are corrected by punishments so that they may understand that he is the Lord.

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, when a land sins against me by committing repeated transgression, I shall stretch out my hand against it, break its staff of bread, send famine upon it, and cut off from it human being and beast. And if these three men—Noah, Daniel, and Job—were in its midst, they would deliver their own souls by their righteousness, says the Lord of hosts.

And if I were to bring the most evil beasts upon the land to devastate it, and it became impassable because no one could pass through it on account of the beasts, if these three men were in it, as I live, says the Lord, they would deliver neither sons nor daughters, but they alone would be delivered, while the land would be desolated.

Or if I were to bring a sword upon that land and say to the sword, ‘Pass through the land,’ and cut off from it human being and beast, and these three men were in its midst, as I live, says the Lord God, they would deliver neither sons nor daughters, but they alone would be delivered.

But if I were also to send pestilence upon that land and pour out my indignation upon it in blood, to cut off from it human being and beast, and Noah, Daniel, and Job were in its midst, as I live, says the Lord God, they would deliver neither son nor daughter, but by their righteousness they alone would deliver their souls.

For thus says the Lord God: Even if I send these four most evil judgments—sword, famine, pestilence, and evil beasts—against Jerusalem, to cut off from it human being and cattle, nevertheless a remnant shall be left in it of those who bring out sons and daughters. Behold, they shall come out to you, and you shall see their way and their deeds, and you shall be comforted concerning the evil that I brought upon Jerusalem, concerning all that I inflicted upon it. They shall comfort you when you see their way and their deeds, and you shall know that I did not do without cause all that I did in it, says the Lord God.”

Four plagues are brought upon the transgressing—or, as the Septuagint translated it, sinful—land: famine, beasts, sword, and pestilence. If these are brought separately upon separate regions, and if these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, whose righteousness is proclaimed by the words of Scripture, intercede for the sinful land, they will be able neither to save it nor even to save their sons and daughters if they have committed the works of the sinful land; they will be able to save only themselves.

It is asked: Since Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and Moses and the other patriarchs and righteous prophets were also just, why are only these three mentioned? The matter is easily resolved. Noah could not delay the impending flood over the whole world, because the entire earth had corrupted the ways of the Lord; but he preserved his sons, who perhaps possessed the same virtue, for the propagation of the human race.

Daniel likewise did not mitigate the impending captivity of the Jewish people by any tears. Job, too, not because of sins but for the sake of testing, delivered neither his household nor his children.

Others say that these three men alone saw prosperity and adversity and then prosperity again; therefore they are named together. This secretly signifies that just as they saw good things and bad things and then joyful things again, so the people of Israel, who had first enjoyed good things and afterwards endured the yoke of captivity, may, if they repent, return to their former salvation.

But if Noah, Daniel, and Job, gathered together and placed in one location, cannot withdraw the sinful land—that is, those who dwell on the land—from God’s wrath, what shall be said of those who think that sinful children can be freed from the fires of Gehenna by the merits and virtues of their parents? Thus neither can a martyr-father free a transgressing son, nor will a mother of holy conduct give the rewards of chastity to an immodest daughter.

Conversely, “the sins of parents will not harm their children, but the soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. XVII). Lot, living in Sodom but a stranger in spirit and flesh, did not free his wife, who had looked behind her, but only his daughters, who perhaps had not sinned.

And the holy man Josiah not only did not save the sinful people by his virtues, but he himself also died in their sins. If at times the Lord promises mercy to the descendants of Abraham and David on account of them, it must be noted that he does not spare those who persist in crimes; rather, those who repent are spared, so that the conversion of the children may be aided by the merits of their fathers.

Since these things are so—since the prayer of such great men does not save the sinful land from individual plagues—the Lord says: Because Jerusalem has sinned wickedly, I shall bring four plagues upon it at once: the sword, by which it is slaughtered by enemies; the famine that it endures during the siege; the beasts by which fugitives are devoured in deserts and wooded places; and the pestilence that always follows famine and scarcity, for which the Vulgate translated “death.”

“These things,” he says, “I shall bring upon it so that neither human beings nor beasts may remain in it. Nevertheless, in my clemency, while four plagues are threatening at once and laying everything waste, I shall leave some in it who will bring out their sons and daughters, and they shall come here as captives”—that is, to Babylon and Chaldea.

When you see them and examine their deeds, then you shall understand that they were justly captured and that my judgment was just. Your captivity will have consolation when you understand that I freed them from the sword, famine, beasts, and pestilence for this reason: so that through their perversity you may learn that Jerusalem was overthrown, the temple burned, and the people led captive, except those whom the sword, famine, beasts, and pestilence consumed.

These things have been said about that Jerusalem whose captivity, while Ezekiel was prophesying among the Chaldeans, drew near. But also upon our land, to which it is said, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III), and upon our Jerusalem and each of the believers, if they despise God’s commands and deserve to be called transgressors, famine will be brought—not famine of bread or thirst for water, but famine of hearing the word of God.

A sword will also be brought, concerning which we read: “They shall be delivered into the hands of the sword; they shall be portions for foxes.” And to Mary: “A sword will also pierce your soul” (Luke II). Beasts will also be brought, to which the righteous asks that he not be handed over: “Do not hand over to beasts the soul that confesses you” (Ps. LXXIII).

Pestilence will also be brought, for which the Septuagint interpreted “death,” concerning which it is written: “The death of sinners is most evil” (Ps. XXXIII), and: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. XVIII).

From all these things neither spiritual parents, whom we understand as teachers of doctrine, nor rulers will be able to deliver anyone unless there is the assent of the children and they aid the entreaties of those parents by their own efforts. For “the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the iniquity of the wicked shall remain upon him.” “Each one shall die by his own sin, and by his own righteousness he shall be saved.”

The Jews say in vain, “Abraham is our father” (John VIII), since they do not possess Abraham’s works. If there is confidence in anyone, let us trust in the Lord alone. For “cursed is every person who places hope in a human being,” however holy they may be and however much they may be prophets. We read: “Do not trust in human beings” (Ps. CXLV). And again: “It is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in rulers” (Ps. CVII)—not only in the rulers of this age, but also in the rulers of the churches, who, if they are righteous, will save only their own souls. They will not be able to save the sons and daughters whom they have begotten in the Church if they have been negligent.

And yet the Apostle says: “If anyone’s work is burned up, he himself will be saved, but only as through fire” (I Cor. III).

The hand is stretched out over the transgressing land so that the staff, or strength, of bread may be broken. Its extension threatens plagues, although the one who extends it and raises it does not wish to strike sinners, but to terrify them by its extension and preserve those who have been terrified.

## BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 0663]

[Col. 0663B] The seventh book begins with the comparison in which the Lord compares Jerusalem to a fruitless vine. Rebuking it for the abominations of its idols, he says that it derives its origin from the land of Canaan and has an Amorite as father and a Hittite as mother. The nourishment of its cradle does it no good, because it has been polluted by incomparable fornication with various lovers. He says that their crime is greater than the sin of Sodom and Samaria, calling them to repentance so that through repentance they may receive remission of sins.

## CHAPTER XV. The Lord’s speech against Jerusalem, the fruitless vine
«And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, what will become of the wood of the vine, among all the woodland trees that are among the trees of the forest? Will wood be taken from it to make something, or will a peg be fashioned from it on which to hang any vessel? Behold, it has been given to the fire as fuel. The fire has consumed both its ends, and its middle has been reduced to ashes. Will it be useful for any work? Even when it was whole, it was not suitable for any work. How much less, when the fire has devoured and burned it, will anything made from it be useful? Therefore thus says the Lord God: As the wood of the vine among the trees of the forest, which I gave to the fire to devour, so will I hand over the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and I will set my face against them. They will go out from the fire, and the fire will consume them. And you will know that I am the Lord, when I set my face against them and give the land desolate and deserted, because they have acted treacherously, says the Lord God.»

(Hieron.) The overthrow of the city of Jerusalem is foretold through various comparisons, which the Greeks call *parables*. Just as above, in the frying pan in which the flesh of the people was fried, and on the brick on which the fortifications, siege-mounds, battering rams, and siege-tower engines were depicted, the possession and famine of the same city were described—and just as later in this same work we shall read the same thing, while in Jeremiah too it is written that the pot kindled from the face of the North signifies the city of Jerusalem, and that the felled forests of the Negeb, Teman, and Darom predict this very event—so in the present passage that same Jerusalem is compared with a vineyard and a fruitful vine.

Of this it is written elsewhere: «I planted you as a fruitful vine, wholly true seed; how have you been changed into the bitterness of a foreign vine? (Jer. II).» And in Isaiah: «I planted,» he says, «a vineyard of Sorech (Isa. V),» which means something chosen and beautiful. And in the Psalm we read: «You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it; you were its guide on its journey before it (Ps. LXXIX).» And we learn more plainly when Scripture says: «The vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is the house of Israel (Isa. V).»

As long as this vineyard bears fruit, among all the trees of the forest nothing is more precious than it. But if it ceases to have grapes, it will be useful for nothing except to be handed over to the fire, together with its root and branches. Other trees of the forest—to say nothing of fruit-bearing trees, which Scripture also does not mention here—when they have no fruit, provide very great usefulness once cut down: they serve every agricultural purpose and the uses of weapons; they are thinned into shields, shaved into spear shafts, fitted into doors, and used for chests, boxes, and small containers, supplying the entire household with furnishings.

But if the vine once ceases to bear grapes, it is so useless that not even a peg can be made from it on which anything might hang. When you cut off its branches, the fire first seizes both ends of them, and afterward the flame consumes them; and once reduced to ashes they are so completely useless that even while whole and without fruit they provide no benefit.

The Hebrew word *sene*, written with three letters—sin, nun, and yod—is ambiguous. If it is read *sene*, it signifies “two”; if *sane*, “years.” Hence it happened that, instead of “both its ends,” as we have translated it, the Septuagint rendered it “its annual pruning,” while Aquila said “its two extremities,” and Symmachus and Theodotion, “its two ends.”

The order is as follows: Just as a fruitless vine is handed over to the fire for no useful purpose, so Jerusalem—and indeed its inhabitants—will be handed over to the flames, so that they may go out from the fire. «And the fire will consume them»: that is, even if they escape from the city, they will be consumed outside by the enemy’s sword. Those who remain, crushed by the very weight of their miseries, will recognize that I am the Lord. «When I set—or make firm—my face against them, and give them over to everlasting desolation.» For they did not merely neglect God like the other nations; they acted treacherously. It is one thing to neglect what one does not know, and another to despise what one has worshiped.

We may understand the vine and Jerusalem, according to the spiritual sense, as the multitude of believers. If it becomes negligent, loses the cultivation of its former religion, bears no fruits of virtue, and produces no wine that gladdens the human heart, it will be handed over to everlasting fires and counted as nothing. «For the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it will be beaten with many blows (Luke XII).»

The Lord teaches something similar in the Gospel according to John: «I am the true vine, and my Father is the cultivator. Every branch that remains in me and does not bear fruit, the Father will remove; and every one that bears fruit, he will cleanse, so that it may bear more fruit (John XV).» If the Savior is the vine, we are the branches, and the Father is called the cultivator, then as long as we keep God’s commandments we are continually cultivated, and our cultivation is purification. «For it depends neither on the one who wills nor on the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy (Rom. IX).»

If those who bear fruit are cleansed by the Father so that they may bear greater fruit, it is shown that all our effort reaches its goal through God’s help and produces the fruit of fullness. But the branch that has produced no fruit will be removed by the Father; and once it has been removed, Scripture does not say what the Father does with it—unless perhaps separation from Christ’s body is everlasting punishment and destruction.

What we have understood in the vineyard and the vine, the Savior teaches under another figure in the Gospel: «Salt is good. But if salt has become tasteless, it is useful for nothing except to be thrown outside and trampled underfoot by people (Mark IX).» And the eye that illumines the whole body, if it has been blinded, hears from the Lord: «If the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness itself be? (Matt. VI.)»

By comparison with the treacherous person, and with the one who first confessed God and afterward denied him, the punishment of those who have never possessed knowledge of God is lighter. The trees of the forests, or woodlands, according to the variety of believers, have some usefulness in the great house, in which there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also wooden and earthen ones—some for honor, others for dishonor.

## CHAPTER XVI. Catalogue of the uncleannesses and iniquities of Jerusalem, and the correction that calls her back to salvation: the Lord justifies Sodom and Samaria by comparison with Jerusalem.

«And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, make known to Jerusalem her abominations, and say: Thus says the Lord God to Jerusalem,» and so forth.

(Hieron.) Under the figure of a prostitute, with whom Jerusalem was first joined in the companionship of a husband, her origin, upbringing, puberty, marriage, adultery, rejection, and subsequent restoration are woven together, so that the husband’s clemency and judgment, as well as the crimes of the adulteress and prostitute, may be recognized.

After all her punishments, he establishes with her an everlasting covenant, so that she may remember her iniquity and be ashamed, and may no longer dare to open her mouth because of her shame, when he has been reconciled to her concerning all that she had done. For it is of great benefit to sinners to know what they have done. Hence the penitent says: «For I know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me (Ps. L).»

Jerusalem can be understood in four ways: either as that Jerusalem which was burned by Babylonian and Roman fire; or as the heavenly Jerusalem of the firstborn; or as the Church, whose name means “vision of peace”; or as the souls of individuals, who behold the Lord through faith. The interpretation that many apply to the heavenly Jerusalem, however, the Church does not accept, lest we be compelled to refer everything woven together in this prophecy to the downfall, sufferings, and restoration of the heavenly powers to their former state.

«Your root and your origin are from the land of Canaan; your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite.» Great faith, and the prophets’ great boldness, for one man to accuse an entire city of low birth. Daniel is remarkable, who dared, while still a boy, to say to the offending elder who joined adultery to murder: «Seed of Canaan and not of Judah, appearance deceived you (Dan. XIII).»

Isaiah too is great, crying out to the rulers and people of the Jews: «Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; give ear to the word of the Lord, people of Gomorrah (Isa. I).» But Ezekiel is no less great, speaking confidently to the whole city: «Your root and your origin are from the land of Canaan; your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite (Ezek. XVI).»

Stephen also, the first martyr of the Gospel, spoke to the raging people: «You stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart, you have always resisted the Holy Spirit (Acts VII).»

Although we may understand Jerusalem’s root and origin—the land of Canaan—in accordance with the fact that the people were called in Egypt and lived there for a long time—for Ham, the father of Canaan, was the founder of the Egyptian nation—nevertheless, in keeping with the likeness of their crimes, we shall say that Egypt is the root of Jerusalem.

Hence her father is called an Amorite, which means “celebrated in much speech.” «And your mother a Hittite,» that is, *ἐξιστῶσα*—“one who drives out of one’s mind”—who is either herself mad or sends others into madness. «For everyone who commits sin is born from the devil.» Hence throughout the world this ancient father bears a famous name, and he turns many toward madness.

Jerusalem is commanded, whether according to the letter or according to the spirit, to abandon her ancient father, and it is said to her: «Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house. And the king will desire your beauty (Ps. XLIV).» And it is promised to her that, if after sin she wishes to return to her true father, «I will restore you as you were when you were born.»

What great nobility was hers, that the city of Jerusalem, descended from the stock of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, had God as her father! Yet because she sinned and abandoned her true parent, she deserved to hear: «Your root and your origin are from the land of Canaan; your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite.»

If she heard this, what will become of us, who were called from the filth of the nations and lost every stain in the Savior’s baptismal washing, if we defile Christ’s garment and do not have a wedding garment at the banquet? Surely we shall be handed over, with hands and feet bound, to everlasting fires, where there is weeping of the eyes and gnashing of teeth (Matt. XXII).

«And when you were born, on the day of your birth your navel was not cut, and you were not washed in water for salvation, nor salted with salt, nor wrapped in swaddling clothes. No eye pitied you, to do any one of these things for you, taking pity on you; but you were thrown upon the face of the earth in the rejection of your soul, on the day when you were born,» and so forth.

(Hieron.) Let us discuss each point according to the order of the reading. When Jerusalem was born from an Amorite father and a Hittite mother, and poured forth from the womb, her navel was not cut—the navel by which fetuses are nourished in the womb, like trees and shrubs nourished through their roots by the hidden moisture of the earth.

Just as the seed-bearing power of men is signified by the loins, so the female sexual organs are called the navel in the modest language of Scripture, as Job testifies, when under the figure of the dragon he speaks to the devil: «His strength is in his loins, and his power in the navel of his belly (Job XL).»

This dragon, the ancient serpent called the devil and Satan, who deceived the whole world, has power against men in the loins and against women in the navel. This signifies concerning Jerusalem that she did not immediately receive the law, nor were the beginnings of her shameful birth cut away, but that she first lived a Gentile life.

(Greg., Book XIII of the *Moralia*, chapter XI.) To cut off the navel on the day of birth is, at the time of conversion, to cut off the lust of the flesh. Because it is difficult to correct what has been badly begun and to reform what has once been misshapen into something better, Judah is reproved for her birth: although she was born in God, she retained an uncut navel because she did not sever her flowing luxury.

(Hieron.) For this the Septuagint translated: «On the day when you were born they did not bind your breasts.» Holy Scripture has the custom of naming the heart “the breast,” or “the chest,” or “the breasts,” according to what seems appropriate to each passage. Priests, in whom doctrine ought to reside, require the breastpiece, and receive the law from their mouths. «John reclines upon the breast of the Lord, so that he may draw streams of wisdom from the most abundant fountain (John XIII).»

In the *Song of Songs* the Virgin’s breasts are described: «Your two breasts are like two young fawns, twins of a gazelle, feeding among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows are removed (Song IV).»

An attentive mother, as soon as a baby girl is born, binds her breasts, so that they may resist swelling from infancy and preserve virginal beauty. When she has reached the age of puberty, it will be said of her: «Will a bride forget her adornment, or a virgin her breast-band? (Jer. II.)»

It follows:

«And you were not washed in water for salvation.» The bloody bodies of infants are customarily washed as soon as they are brought forth from the womb; so spiritual birth too requires a saving washing (*lavacrum*). For no one is clean from uncleanness, not even if his life is but a single day. And we read in the Psalms: «I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me (Ps. L).»

The second birth dissolves the first birth, for it is written: «Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God (John III).» There are many washings that the pagans promise in their mysteries, and the heretics as well; they all wash, but they do not wash for salvation. Therefore it is added: «And you were not washed in water for salvation.»

This may be understood not only of heretics but also of members of the Church who do not receive saving baptism with full faith. Of them it must be said that they received water but did not receive the Spirit. So too Simon Magus, who wished to buy the grace of God with money, was indeed baptized in water, but was by no means baptized for salvation.

Third it is said: «Nor were you salted with salt.» The tender bodies of infants, while they still retain the warmth of the womb and bear witness through their first cry to the beginnings of laborious life, are customarily touched by midwives with salt, so that they may be drier and contracted. Jerusalem, however, born from evil parents, acquired neither flavor nor care.

But those who are reborn in Christ hear: «You are the salt of the earth (Matt. V),» and the Apostle commands them: «Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt (Col. IV).» Hence in common speech the wise are called “salty,” and the foolish “insipid.”

In Leviticus the law also decrees: «Every sacrifice of yours shall be salted with salt. The salt of the covenant of the Lord shall not be absent from your sacrifices. With all your offerings you shall offer salt (Lev. II).» Whoever is seasoned with this salt, and through its admixture has dried every harmful decay and moisture, will no longer say: «My wounds have festered and become corrupt because of my foolishness.»

Fourth: «Nor were you wrapped in swaddling clothes.» The Savior too was wrapped in the swaddling clothes of infancy. Everyone who is born needs the protection of God through the wrapping of swaddling clothes.

It is natural—provided that the parents’ care is not lacking—that, once infants are born, their navel is first cut; then they are washed with water to cleanse away the blood; third, the moisture of their bodies is dried by the addition of salt; fourth, their tender bodies are wrapped in swaddling clothes. This is for two reasons: so that the body may be dried by the salt, preserved and constricted by the swaddling clothes lest it flow away, and so that the most delicate limbs may not easily become deformed.

Hence the bodies of barbarians are straighter than Roman bodies. For they are continually wrapped in swaddling clothes until the second or third year. But Jerusalem was not like this: her navel was not cut, her breasts were not bound, she was not washed in water for salvation, was not salted with salt, and was not wrapped and constricted in the swaddling clothes of infancy.

Why she deserved none of these things, the following Scripture testifies: «No eye pitied you, to do any one of these things for you, taking pity on you.» For this the Septuagint rendered: «Your eye did not always pity you, to do one of all these things for you.»

It is necessary that the two editions have two interpretations. The first signifies: «No eye pitied you, to do any one of these things for you, taking pity on you.» The sense is: No one pitied you; with God offended, no one’s inward compassion was stirred over you so as to do at least one of the four things mentioned above for you, because you did not deserve to receive them all together.

In the other version it says: «Your eye did not pity you, to do one of all these things for you.» Its meaning is: You acted in such a way, and were born in sins—your mother conceived you in transgressions—that you did not even pity yourself. Since you acted so that through evil deeds you became cruel toward yourself, what could I do for you, when you did not deserve to receive even one of the things mentioned above?

Therefore, because none of the things customarily done for infants was done for you—and this was not without cause or judgment, but through your own vice and sin, since you did not even pity yourself—you were thrown upon the face of the earth, or the plain: «And you were thrown out because of the perversity of your soul, on the day when you were born.»

Let us pray that through the perversity of our soul we may not be thrown upon the face of the plain, where the road is broad and spacious, leading to death, and where the cavalry of the Chaldeans rages. At the same time, it must be considered that no one can commit anything perverse on the day when he is born, except at the time of the washing, when the wise generation of the believer is received through faith.

«But as I passed by you, I saw you trampled in your blood. And I said to you, when you were in your blood: Live, I said to you, in your blood; live. I made you numerous like the growth of a field, and you multiplied, and became great, and entered in, and reached the adornment of a woman. Your breasts swelled, and your hair grew, and you were naked and full of shame,» and so forth.

(Hieron.) After you had been thrown upon the face of the plain, or upon the face of the earth, because of the perversity of your soul, you no longer deserved my help. Nevertheless, as I passed by you I saw you trampled, or mixed, in your blood—that is, guilty of mortal crimes—and I summoned you to repentance.

I said to you: Although you are in your blood, nevertheless live, having been converted. Such abundance of every good thing was in you that you resembled a most fertile field, and possessed the blessing of Jacob with which his father blessed him, saying: «Behold, the scent of my son is like the scent of a full field, which the Lord has blessed (Gen. XXVII).»

You entered the inner chambers of the Lord and said with the bride: «The king brought me into his chamber (Song I).» And you reached the adornment of a woman.

For this the Septuagint translated: «And you entered into cities of cities,» so that just as the *Song of Songs* and the age are called “of ages,” so cities may be called “of cities.” Concerning these it is said in the Gospel: «Have authority over ten cities, or over five cities (Luke XIX),» so that you may be called not merely a city but a metropolitan city, in accordance with what is said in Isaiah: «Faithful Zion, mother of cities (Isa. I).»

Symmachus interpreted this as «and you reached the adornment of women,» or, as Theodotion has it, «and you entered into the adornment of adornments.» We, following the Hebrew sense, have said: «And you reached the adornment of a woman.» This indicates the time of puberty, when girls are called marriageable and can be joined to the embraces of husbands.

Accordingly, it follows: «Your breasts swelled, and your hair grew.» The maturity of young women is indicated modestly, when their breasts swell or rise and their hair grows.

When she was prepared for marriage and possessed bodily beauty, she had no covering of garments and was not protected by God’s help. Whoever does not have Christ’s garment is naked. Whoever is not clothed with compassion, goodness, humility, chastity, gentleness, and patience lies upon the face of the earth, and his beauty is marred by shame and nakedness.

«And I passed by you and saw you. And behold, your time was the time of lovers. And I spread my garment over you and covered your shame.»

What clemency! It had not been enough to see her once, trampled in her blood, and summon her to repentance; but when she was sinning, he visited her again. Because she was naked and full of shame, he came again and visited her, and behold, her time was the time of lovers.

That was the time when women can be joined to men and endure marital intercourse. Yet the merciful God spread his wings, received them, and carried them on his shoulders, in accordance with what is said in the Gospel: «How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling (Luke XII).»

Or he spread his garment in place of wings. For this is what *πτερύγιον* means—the covering with which Ruth too was covered when she slept at the feet of Boaz; and at the edge—that is, the *πτερυγίον*—of our garment we are commanded to attach hyacinth-colored tassels.

He did this to cover Jerusalem’s shame, indicating by this name the female genital body. For according to the Apostle, «we surround the dishonorable parts of our body with greater honor (I Cor. XII).» Hence the Psalmist sings: «Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered (Ps. XXXI).»

Because Ham did not cover his father, he is marked by an everlasting curse. What we have said about Jerusalem, let us refer to our own soul, which, as long as it remains in infancy, is free from sin. But when the time of its maturity arrives, there are many lovers of demons, heretics, and perverse doctrines who desire to turn toward it. They are driven away by God’s protection, so that the soul may receive not the devil’s agents but the Savior’s ministers.

For the love of those who turn aside and for “breasts,” the Hebrew has *dodim*, which according to the character of that language signifies all the things translated above. The time of love, and of breasts or lovers of God, may be understood as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, when the Lord promised them that after the Egyptian slavery he would free his people.

«And I swore to you and entered into a covenant with you, says the Lord God.»

Because I spread my garment, or my wings, over you and covered your shame, therefore I swore to you and entered into a covenant, or testament, with you, so that you might be joined to me rather than to the others who wished to turn toward you, in accordance with the words: «The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek (Ps. CIX).»

For an oath is the end of every dispute. «As I live, says the Lord, I desire the repentance of the sinner rather than his death (Ezek. XVIII).» At the time of the wedding, therefore, Israel receives God’s oath as the gift of a complete dowry.

And because David had said of himself: «Remember, Lord, David and all his meekness, who swore to the Lord and vowed a vow to the God of Jacob (Ps. CXXXI),» the Lord himself also swears to him, as Scripture says: «The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not disappoint him.»

«And you became mine, and I washed you with water, and cleansed your blood from you, and anointed you with oil.»

Because I spread my wings over you and covered your shame, and swore to you and entered into a covenant with you, you therefore became my possession: though you had been alien, when you appeared unclean, you began to be mine when I confirmed my covenant with you by an oath.

Or, according to the customary language of the prophets, “you became mine,” he says, because you were joined to my marriage. «And I washed you,» he says, «with the water of saving baptism.» «For unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God (John III).»

And elsewhere we read: «He himself will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire (Mark I).» Isaiah also speaks of this baptism, saying: «The Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion and cleanse the blood from their midst, by the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning (Isa. IV).»

When he has washed and cleansed the blood—as he healed the woman with the hemorrhage who had been bleeding for twelve years when she touched his fringe (Mark V)—it is not enough for him to wash with water and cleanse the blood unless he also anoints with oil.

Thus the Samaritan, whose name means “guardian,” first treated the wounds of the half-dead man with an infusion of oil, and afterward restrained them with the austerity of wine. Our Lord, however, was anointed with another oil—not one that would mitigate the pain of wounds, but one that would grant joy, as the Holy Spirit says to him: «Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions (Ps. XLIV).»

The opposing powers too possess a counterfeit gentleness of oil, promising sweet things through heretics that are turned into bitterness. The Prophet condemns and recalls them: «May the oil of the sinner not make my head fat (Ps. CXL).»

But if from anointing comes the name “Anointed,” that is, Christ, consider how greatly Jerusalem has advanced: she too, anointed with spiritual oil, has received the name of Christ. Accordingly, we read of Abraham in the Psalms: «Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act wickedly against my prophets (Ps. CIV).»

«And I clothed you in garments of many colors.»

The Septuagint: «And I clothed you in various garments,» that is, in the ceremonies of the law, so that, occupied with their observance, you would abandon idols.

These are the various garments in which Joseph was clothed. His brothers could not sell him until they had first stripped him of the varied tunic. And of the bride it is said in the forty-fourth Psalm: «The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in gilded apparel, surrounded by variety.»

This is the garment of which the Apostle also speaks: «Put on the new man, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of the Creator (Eph. IV).» Do we wish to know what the various garments are? The same Apostle teaches us, writing to believers: «Put on therefore compassion, goodness, humility, gentleness, and patience (Col. III).»

What is more beautiful than this variety, of which Job too spoke: «Who gave women wisdom in weaving, or skill in varied work? (Job XXXVIII.)»

The high priest too, once each year, when he burned incense for the people and entered the Holy of Holies, used various garments. Certainly, if wealth rather than holiness, and diversity of virtues, produced variety in clothing, Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar would be said to have possessed these garments, and not Joseph, who, with a foreigner and shepherd as his father, could not have had varied and royal garments.

«And I shod you with hyacinth-colored footwear.»

Accordingly, those preparing the Passover are commanded to have their loins girded and their feet shod, without any variation of color. These are the shoes of which the Apostle also writes: «With your feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace (Eph. VI).»

Jerusalem is not shod with hyacinth-colored footwear until she has been washed with water. Hence the feet of the Apostles, whom the Lord had first commanded to shake the dust from their feet, are washed by the Savior. And the bride says in the *Song of Songs*: «I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them? (Song V.)»

The divine word also testifies concerning Moses and Jesus that they should loosen the strap of their footwear, because the place where they stood was holy. Once the feet have been washed and cleansed of every impurity, they are shod with hyacinth-colored or violet-colored footwear. Both colors are sky-blue, *κυάνεος*—“deep blue”—so that they may be snatched up to meet the Lord in the air and hasten toward the heavenly kingdoms.

«And I girded you with fine linen.»

Jerusalem is not only clothed in garments of many colors and shod with hyacinth-colored footwear; she is also girded with fine linen. From this exceedingly fine material the threads of the high priest’s garment are woven.

The wife in Proverbs, who wove two cloaks for her husband—one for the present age and one for the future—is said to have made garments for herself from fine linen and purple. With this fine linen the loins are girded whenever the fat incentives of lust must be weakened, leaving none of the coarseness of sensual desire.

Thus we fulfill the Apostle’s command: «Stand therefore, with your loins girded in truth (Eph. VI),» as though he were saying in other words, “with fine linen.” And the Lord speaks to the Apostles: «Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands (Luke XII).»

For unless we bind the flowing discharges of the loins, we cannot have lamps in our hands. Hence God also says to Job: «Gird your loins like a man (Job XXXVIII).»

Those who eat the lamb with shod feet, holding a staff, standing in the truth of the Gospel, and prepared for the blood of Christ, are said to have their loins girded. Elijah and John the Baptist too are girded with this belt that mortifies the loins. Concerning these the penitent groans mournfully, saying: «For my loins are filled with mockeries (Ps. XXXVII).»

«And I clothed you in fine garments.»

Appropriately, to those of whom he had rebukingly said, «The heart of this people has grown fat; Jacob ate and drank, was filled, grew fat, kicked, and abandoned God his Maker,» the thinness of garments is then granted.

In the Book of Wisdom too, which some title as Solomon’s, the spirit of wisdom is called “only-begotten and manifold, subtle and changeable.” The manna of which it is written, «Man ate the bread of angels (Ps. LXXVII),» is also said to have been exceedingly fine, resembling frost and coriander seed.

According to the interpretation of Aquila’s second edition, which rendered the term as “flowery garment,” we may understand metaphorically either the abundance of the land of Judah or the beauty of divine worship.

«And I adorned you with an ornament.»

Here he gives a general designation of the ornaments that he later enumerates individually: bracelets, a necklace, earrings, a crown, and the rest of the ornaments he bestowed upon Jerusalem.

Isaiah says that through her fault she lost all these things. For it is written: «Because the daughters of Jerusalem were lifted up—that is, became proud—and walked with an elevated neck (Isa. III),» and so forth: instead of a girdle they were given ropes; instead of head ornaments they were disfigured with baldness; and instead of beautiful and soft garments they were surrounded with the harshness of sackcloth.

«And I gave bracelets upon your hands.»

When God gives us good works, he surrounds our hands with a bracelet. Hence he also says that he has been likened to the hands of the prophets. We frequently read that the word came to the hand of Haggai, or Jeremiah, and the others (Hos. XII).

In Job too (Job XL), the dragon’s lip is pierced by a bracelet, and all his poisonous hisses—which are understood as perverse doctrines—are pierced by the circle of good works.

«And a necklace around your neck.»

It is also written in Isaiah: «The Lord will remove the glory of their clothing, and the little chains, the clusters, the circlets, and the *kathema* (Isa. III).»

I think that by *kathema* they mean a necklace descending onto a woman’s breast, made of various gems; it too is a most beautiful ornament of women.

«And I gave an earring upon your mouth,» or «your nose.»

Apart from Symmachus, who translated it as *ἐπιρρίνιον*—“a nose ornament”—all have rendered the Hebrew word *nezem* as “earring.” It does not mean that earrings are placed upon the hands, and they are called earrings because they hang from the ears; rather, it means that a circle made in the likeness of earrings is designated by the same word.

Even to this day, among women’s other ornaments, golden circles are accustomed to hang from the forehead over the mouth and to extend toward the nostrils. We understand these mystically when, with the Apostle, we can say: «We are the good fragrance of Christ among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing: to some an odor of death unto death, but to others an odor of life unto life (II Cor. II).»

When we live, and it can be said of us: «The dead will not praise you, Lord, but we who are living (Ps. CXIII),» then God smells the fragrance of our sacrifice, a good odor, and we have a golden circle of divine perceptions and doctrines in our ears.

But when we are dead and wallow in filth and the sordidness of shameful things, we have that earring in our nostrils of which Solomon writes: «As a golden earring in a pig’s snout, so is beauty in a woman of bad character (Prov. XXI).»
[Col. 0674B] “And earrings in your ears.” The Septuagint has: “And little wheels upon your ears.” Whoever closes his ears so as not to hear a sentence of bloodshed, and fences them with thorns so as not to become partner to the envious and slanderers—of whom it is written, “Do not associate with slanderers, for their destruction will come suddenly, and who knows the ruin of both?” (Prov. XXIV)—both that of the slanderer and of the one who willingly listens, has earrings and little wheels in his ears. These are not the wheels that follow the Cherubim—for that belongs to the angelic powers—but little wheels, diminutively, which correspond to human frailty.

Therefore it is also said to God: “The voice of your thunder is in the wheel” (Ps. LXXVI). In those who pass beyond earthly things and scarcely touch the earth with slight traces—of whom it is written, “Stones that roll upon the earth”—the voice of the Lord’s thunder and of lofty doctrines resounds. But those who are led by human errors and have no firm footprints, “but are carried about by every wind of doctrine” (Eph. II), and, expelled from the paradise of steadfastness, dwell in the region of Naid—which is interpreted as “fluctuation”—deserve to bear the sentence of the lying tongue, which sets the wheel of our birth on fire.

“And a crown of beauty upon your head.” The other ornaments belong to the individual limbs. The adornment of the head is the dignity of the whole body. By “crown” he means the women’s diadem, by which the luxuriance of their hair is bound and adorned. If we wish to know what the crown of beauty is upon the head of Jerusalem, let us read Exodus, in which it is written: “And he made a golden plate, and wrote upon it letters formed by the seal of the Lord’s holiness, and placed it upon Aaron’s head” (Exod. XXXIX).

The sign of the Lord’s holiness is the name of the omnipotent God, which is written with four Hebrew letters. Among them it is called ineffable, since his name cannot be pronounced; yet even the Gentiles are not ignorant of his majesty, as the altar of the Athenians bears witness: “To the unknown God.” Hence the Apostle also says: “The one whom you worship as unknown, him I proclaim to you” (Acts XVII).

I think this is the crown of which the Psalmist also says: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Ps. IV). And the Apostle said: “I have finished my course, I have kept the faith. From now on the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the righteous Judge will give me” (II Tim. IV). And elsewhere, addressing believers: “My joy and my crown” (Phil. IV), for children are the glory of their fathers. And in Solomon it is written: “Old age is a crown of glory” (Prov. XII)—that is, the old age of those who have destroyed the things belonging to children and, after reaching the age of the mature man, have come to old age and to the names of the Fathers. John writes to these after children and young men, who can say: “When I was a child, I spoke as a child and thought as a child; when I became a man, I put away the things of a child” (I Cor. XIII).

“And you were adorned with gold and silver.” We have often said that gold pertains to the mind and silver to eloquence. May the Lord grant that we may deserve to receive divine understanding and wisdom, and to express with the beauty of eloquence what we conceive in our minds, and never make idols out of these things, as the heretics do, of whom it is written: “I gave them silver and gold, but they made Baal from the silver and gold” (Hos. II). This is even more appropriate according to the spiritual interpretation of the adornment of women. Otherwise, silver, a cheaper material, is the ornament of country women, the poor, and maidservants; it is not fitting for Jerusalem, which is said to have advanced to the rank of queen.

“And you were clothed in fine linen, embroidered cloth, and garments of many colors.” All the adornment of women is described so that she may be washed, cleansed, anointed with oil, and clothed in garments of varied colors. We shall apply all these things, according to the foregoing explanation, to spiritual understanding: she is to be covered with fine linen and with delicate fabrics, so that the tender limbs of the wife are not weighed down by the heavy burden of cloaks, but that the clothing may at once provide both use and beauty.

“You ate fine flour, honey, and oil, and you became exceedingly beautiful.” After clothing, he takes care of food, so that Jerusalem may eat fine flour, honey, and oil—either separately, as most think, or mixed together into a sweeter bread, the bread that descended from heaven. Under these three names, some believe, the mystery of the Trinity is indicated—not that there is one substance and another, but that through the different names of fine flour, honey, and oil, the one sweetness of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is displayed.

It should also be observed that in many sacrifices fine flour is offered—that is, the marrow and purest part of grain—of which it is written: “He satisfied them with the fat of wheat” (Ps. LXXX); not barley or meal, which is offered only when a husband is stirred by the spirit of jealousy. In the Book of Judges we read of Deborah, whose name means “bee,” whose prophecies are most sweet honey; she is referred to the Holy Spirit, who among the Hebrews is called *rua* in the feminine gender. In the Gospel according to the Hebrews, which the Nazarenes read, the Savior is also introduced as saying: “Just now my mother, the Holy Spirit, seized me.”

Fine flour, moreover, which is made from wheat, is referred to the Lord, who says of himself: “Unless a grain of wheat falls and dies in the earth, it remains alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John XII). Oil, however, which sustains and refreshes the limbs of the weary, which nourishes the light, and by which the continual light of the lamps is kindled in God’s tabernacle, is said to correspond to the Father.

All these things bestow grace upon believers, as the Apostle says: “There are divisions of graces, but one Spirit; and divisions of ministries, but one Lord; and divisions of operations, but one and the same God” (I Cor. XII). Whoever has eaten such food, and has been fed and nourished by this sweetest and most pleasant bread, shining with the splendor of oil, will be transformed into beauty and become exceedingly beautiful—not merely once, but repeatedly, “exceedingly.” For the doubled adverb gives weight to the sentence, so that nothing further can be added to the greatness of the beauty.

“And you advanced to royalty.” This is not found in the Septuagint, who perhaps, when at Alexandria they translated the Scriptures from the Hebrew truth into the Greek language, feared saying it lest they should seem to offend the king of Egypt by recalling that the kingship owed to Jerusalem by God belonged to her. Although learned men judge that the Septuagint translated only the five books of Moses.

After her manifold adornment, therefore; after the crown; after the abundance of gold and silver; after the garments and most beautiful cloaks; after her incredible beauty, she advances to become a queen, because she is the city of the great King. Of him it is written: “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Ps. XVII). And in the Apocalypse of John, Jerusalem is described “as a bride adorned and prepared for her husband” (Rev. XXI). In the Psalms also it is said of her: “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in gold, surrounded with variety” (Ps. XLIV).

Whatever we say about Jerusalem, so that we do not linger over each detail and make the length of the books burdensome to readers, let us refer it to the Church. For if Jerusalem, according to the Apostle, is our mother, and our mother is the Church, then Jerusalem is consequently the Church, the mother of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven.

“And your name went out among the nations because of your beauty, for you were perfect in my beauty, which I placed upon you, says the Lord God.” The meaning is this: By my benefits and my astonishing generosity you attained the name of queen, so that the speech of all nations concerned you, and you were made perfect not by your own merits and virtues but by my liberality.

“For unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it keep watch in vain” (Ps. CXXVI). The one who plants and the one who waters is nothing unless the Lord gives the increase, because “it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX). Thus, after we have done everything, we should say: “We are useless servants; we have done what we were obliged to do” (Luke XVII). This does not mean that human free will is taken away by God’s beneficence, but that freedom itself ought to have the Lord as its helper.

“And trusting in your beauty, you committed fornication in your own name, and you displayed your fornication to every passerby, so that you might become his,” and so forth.

[Col. 0677A] It is a great danger to trust not in God’s mercy but in one’s own beauty. The higher someone is, the more he ought to fear lest he fall and commit fornication in his own name. For hostile powers despise ordinary foods and desire strange nourishment. Hence it is said of the devil: “His foods are choice” (Hab. I). He does not wish to deceive just anyone. He hastens to overthrow King Saul, who was chosen by the Lord, and the Apostle Judas. Let us therefore not trust in our own beauty, nor think that God’s generosity is our own virtue; rather, let us hear: “Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what the coming day will bring” (Prov. XXVII); and elsewhere: “Brothers, if a person is overtaken in any sin, you who are spiritual restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Gal. VI).

Nor should we display or pour out our fornication to every passerby, so that we become not the possession of the God in whom we believe but of him by whom we are polluted—of him who receives every vice and takes into his bosom the spirit of passing sins of various kinds, spreading his legs for every passerby. Such a person pours out his fornication and begins to endure the dominion of the one whose guest he has become.

“And taking some of your garments, you made for yourself high places sewn together here and there, and you committed fornication upon them, such as has neither been done nor shall be.” With regard to Jerusalem according to the literal sense, this may be understood as meaning that she devoted all the precepts of the Law, her riches, and the abundance of all things to idols—something no other nation had done or would do. For all the nations that served idols from the beginning are not guilty of so great a crime.

Our Jerusalem, however, which is interpreted as “vision of peace,” is torn apart by heretics when they pluck one or another testimony of the Scriptures from its proper place and attempt to sew it onto passages to which it cannot be fitted. Of such people we read above in this same prophet: “Woe to those who sew pillows under every elbow and make coverings over the head of persons of every age” (Ezek. XIII).

The Lord forbids this when he says in the Gospel: “No one puts a patch of new cloth on an old garment; otherwise it takes away from its fullness, and a worse tear will result. Nor do they put new wine into old wineskins” (Matt. IX). Such are the Nazarenes, who try to adapt observance of the old Law to evangelical grace. So too are all heretics who attempt to sew a testimony, fitting in its own place to one meaning, onto another meaning, when the Lord’s tunic, woven from above throughout, cannot be divided at all, but, woven by the Holy Spirit, admits no tear.

As for what is said according to the Septuagint, “and you shall not enter, nor shall it be,” this signifies that when you have made idols for yourself out of perverse doctrines—things that you consider high places—and have committed fornication upon them, believing in what you yourself have fabricated, you will not be able to enter the temple of God, and your images will have no substance and will not exist forever, as the Apostle says: “We know that an idol is nothing in the world” (I Cor. VIII).

[Col. 0678A] “And you took the vessels of your adornment, made from my gold and my silver, which I gave you, and you made for yourself images of males, and committed fornication with them.” According to the literal sense, the Lord commanded in the Law that censers, bowls, the lampstand, the ark of the covenant, and everything else be made either of gold or overlaid with gold, while other things were to be made of silver. Jerusalem melted all these things down and turned them into idols of Bel, or Baal, Chemosh, Astaroth, and Milcom.
