According to the spiritual interpretation, we make idols from the gold and silver of the Holy Scriptures when we corrupt, through heretical perversity, the grace of understanding and eloquence, and “set our mouth in heaven, while our tongue traverses the earth.” The images are called masculine because every heresy commits fornication with them, since each person thinks that he worships and possesses the strongest things, which he himself has fabricated and which cannot be overthrown by any attack.

These are the images that we have fashioned from our own hearts, and which must be destroyed in the heavenly Jerusalem. Concerning them the Prophet declares: “Lord, in your city you will shatter their images” (Ps. LXXII). For anyone who is a human being and has lost the name of God is described as follows: “Nevertheless, a person walks in an image; nevertheless, he is troubled in vain” (Ps. XXXVIII). We, however, have one man and venerate one image, which is the image of the invisible and omnipotent God.

“And you took your garments of many colors and covered them.” “Them” means the masculine images, so that she turned all the worship she had received for use into blasphemy. We do this whenever we surround heretical perversity with prudence, temperance, courage, justice, and all the virtues, and under their pretext deceive the simple, so that, seeing the honey of the virtues, they do not beware of the poisons of the vices.

“And you placed my oil and my incense before them. And my bread”—or, as the Septuagint translated, “my breads”—which I gave you, fine flour, oil, and honey, with which I nourished you, you placed before them as a fragrant odor.”

The oil of which we spoke above, and the incense, of which the Psalmist cries: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight” (Ps. CXL), and the loaves of the Presence which we are commanded to offer to the Lord; also the fine flour, the purest understanding of the Scriptures; and the honey which Jonathan tasted, after which his eyes were opened and he was strengthened—all these things wretched Jerusalem placed before idols, or before masculine images, so that they might be a fragrant odor to them, although by nature they are sweet and most pleasant. But when they are offered to idols and false doctrines, they are turned into bitterness.

“And it happened,” says the Lord God, “that you took your sons and daughters, whom you bore for me, and sacrificed them to them for consumption. Is your fornication a small matter, that you slaughter my sons and give them over, consecrating them to them? And after all your abominations and fornications, you did not remember the days of your youth, when you were naked and full of confusion, trampled in your blood.”

That Jerusalem sacrificed her sons and daughters to idols—those of whom it is written, “I begot sons and raised them up, but they despised me” (Isa. I)—Holy Scripture recalls: “They sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons” (Ps. CVI). And again: “Whom they sacrificed to the carved images of Canaan.” He calls them “his own” according to the Hebrew. For he himself had spoken of them: “my sons,” or, according to the Septuagint, “your sons,” whom you had begotten through fornication.

When you did these things, he says, you did not remember your infancy, when I took you covered in blood and washed you, and, after the many things narrated by the prophetic utterance, joined you to myself.

Our Jerusalem also, if it is overthrown by heretical deceit, takes away her sons—those who are more advanced in faith—and her daughters, who do not possess such strength of faith; or, certainly, sons who understand spiritual matters and daughters who follow the simple historical sense. She hands them over to demons to be devoured, and while killing them she believes that she is giving life to and placating the images, which are glutted by their slaughter.

What is said according to the Septuagint—“above all your fornication and your abominations”—signifies that the doctrine of heretics is worse than all sins and fornications: it makes the sons of God sons of demons, or rather kills those whom it had either begotten for God with great labor or made its own sons, whom it had begotten in fornication.

“And it happened after all your wickedness—woe, woe to you, says the Lord God. You built yourself a brothel and made yourself a place of prostitution in every street; at every head of a road you built a sign of your prostitution, and you made your beauty abominable. You spread your legs for every passerby, multiplied your fornications, and committed fornication with the sons of Egypt, your neighbors, who have great flesh. You multiplied your fornications in order to provoke me.”

What we have said once, twice, and repeatedly, let it suffice to have said forever: under the figure of a woman committing fornication after receiving her husband’s benefits, the fornication of Jerusalem is described—how she departed from God and was joined to idols, and was not content with secret fornication, but built herself a brothel and placed a sign on every road for passersby, so that they would come to the prostitute and satisfy their lust—not so much hers as that of the woman who spread her legs for every passerby and disfigured the greatness of her beauty by the greatness of her fornication.

Among other things, she also prostituted herself through love of great flesh to the Egyptians, her neighbors. And to display every kind of shame, she was disfigured by manifold impurity. No one doubts that Palestine is near Egypt, since the Lord says to Abraham: “I will give you all the land from the river of Egypt to the great river, the Euphrates” (Gen. XV), so that on one side she has the Egyptians and on the other the Assyrians, with whom she is also said to have committed fornication later.

The fornication of Jerusalem with the Egyptians is the imitation of their idolatry. And to our Jerusalem—whether the Church or the souls of believers—if they are negligent and open to every vice, a double sentence of cursing is directed, so that they may hear: “Woe, woe to you, says the Lord God,” according to what is written in the Apocalypse of John: “Woe upon all the inhabitants of the earth” (Rev. VIII).

For if the holy person says: “I am a sojourner and a stranger, like all my fathers” (Ps. XXXVIII), why should the sinner not be called an inhabitant of the earth? He builds himself a brothel who sins with complete brazenness, according to what is written: “When the sinner has come into the depths of sin, he despises” (Prov. XVIII).

And he builds a very high place in every street. “For broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction” (Matt. VII). At every head of a road he builds, so that he may leave no kind of sin untouched, but, imitating the prostitute of Proverbs, openly in the streets and in the corners of the streets invites foolish young men passing by to her embraces and pollutes the beauty of the soul, which she received as a benefit from God the Creator.

All her paths are full of shame, and she opens her heart and spreads her legs to every thought that supplies fuel for the vices. She commits fornication with the Egyptians, her neighbors, whose examples she follows—namely, the Gentiles, who glory in their own shame—and she is so wicked that she surpasses even them in depravity. She does all these things in order to provoke God to anger.

The Egyptians are said to have “great flesh,” either because of the greatness of their shame or because of the deformity of their sins. Hence the holy person is said to have little flesh, which diminishes in him daily and is made thin through the virtues, so that it is no longer called flesh but spirit; and he says in the psalm: “My soul thirsted for you, O God; how greatly my flesh thirsted for you in a dry and waterless land. Thus I appeared to you in the sanctuary” (Ps. LXII).

Therefore the Corinthian fornicator is handed over to the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved. Concerning this flesh it is written: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field. The grass withered, and its flower fell; but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isa. XL). Concerning it the Apostle also said: “Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. XV). And in Genesis God says: “My spirit will not remain in these human beings, because they are flesh” (Gen. VI). And to believers it is said: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh, but in the spirit” (Rom. VIII).

There is, however, another flesh, that of the saints, concerning which it is written: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Isa. XL).

“Behold, I will stretch out my hand over you, and I will remove your statutes, and I will give you over to the souls of those who hate you, the daughters of the Philistines, who burn”—or, alternatively, “are ashamed”—at your wicked way.”

The Lord stretches out his hand over Jerusalem in order to correct her in her sin and remove her statutes. As long as she kept God’s commandments, they were called the statutes of the Lord. But when she worshiped idols and exchanged religion for impiety, they were no longer called her statutes. This should be understood not only of the Law and its ceremonies, but also of Sabbaths, feast days, and new moons.

For when he gives the Law, he says: “My Sabbaths and my feast days” (Lev. XIX). But when they departed from God, it is said to them: “I will not accept your new moons, Sabbaths, or great day. Your fasting, rest, and festivals my soul hates” (Isa. I).

The same is written concerning the people. For the one who was previously called the people of God, after departing from God, is described to Moses in these words: “Your people whom you brought out of the land of Egypt have sinned” (Exod. XXXII).

This stretching out of the hand is elsewhere called lifting up or visitation. For when God does not correct the sinner, he contracts his hand. But if someone sins and begins to languish under God’s law, visitation is sent to him, according to what is sung in the Psalms: “If his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments, I will visit their iniquities with the rod” (Ps. LXXXVIII).

And in this prophet it is written: “If the land sins against me by committing a transgression, I will stretch out my hand over it and break the support of its bread” (Ps. CIV), and so forth. Here we ask what difference there is between stretching out the hand and sending it forth. The devil says to the Lord: “Send out your hand and touch all that he has; otherwise he will bless you to your face” (Job II). It seems to me that the hand is sent out for the testing of those to whom it is sent. It is stretched out for the punishments of those who deserve penalties.

Not only is the stretching out and sending forth of God’s hand spoken of, but also its spreading out, as Isaiah proclaims in the person of the Lord: “All day long I spread out my hands to a disobedient and contradictory people” (Isa. LXV). The holy person is also said to raise his hands, as Scripture says: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Ps. CXL).

Now that God’s statutes have been removed from the Jewish people, let us ask them what observance of the Law they possess. They cannot offer sacrifices, since the Temple has been taken away and destroyed; nor can they practice the stoning of adulteresses or carry out the punishments for other crimes permitted by the Law; nor can they observe the rest of the land in the year of remission, or other things of this kind.

She is given over to the souls of the daughters of Palestine who hate her, when she is handed over to the Philistines, whom the Septuagint indiscriminately call “foreigners.” By these we may understand the cities or towns of Palestine. Our Jerusalem also, if we pass over God’s ceremonies, and his hand is stretched out over us and all observance of the Law is removed, will be handed over to the daughters of Palestine, not to their sons.

For we will not first be handed over to stronger punishments, but, according to the quality of our sins, to lesser ones, so that, corrected by the lesser, we may avoid greater torments of suffering. *Philisthiim*, that is, “Philistines,” with the first part of the word altered, is interpreted as “falling,” “by a cup,” or “by a deed”—perhaps “by an action.” This signifies that we will be handed over to hostile powers that have drunk from the cup of Babylon and fallen, and whose works are perverse.

The correction and disgrace of wretched Jerusalem will be so great that even the hostile powers themselves will be ashamed at the magnitude of our sins. Once God’s ceremonies have been removed from the Jewish people, the priesthood and the giving of the Law also pass over to us, as Scripture says: “Appoint, O Lord, a lawgiver over them” (Ps. IX). And elsewhere: “Set a law for me, O Lord, in your way” (Ps. XXVI).

“And you committed fornication with the sons of the Assyrians, because you were not yet satisfied. And after you had committed fornication, you were still not satisfied. And you multiplied your fornication in the land of Canaan with the Chaldeans, and still you were not satisfied.”

Above it was written that Jerusalem committed fornication with the sons of Egypt, her neighbors, who have great flesh. Here another neighboring people, the Assyrians, is indicated. Therefore she is handed over to both nations, because she worshiped the images of both. Entering Chaldea, which is the land of Canaan, she imitated the errors of those whose power ruled over her.

According to the tropological interpretation, we often pass from one sin to another. When we have not repented of our former crimes, we add offenses to offenses and are satisfied by no error. Rather, like a long rope and the strap of a stubborn heifer, we drag our sins along and multiply our covenant—or our fornication—in the land of Canaan, which is interpreted as something like “fluctuation,” and with the Chaldeans, whose name also sounds among us as though it meant “demons.” We always have our footprints in sand and can never say, “He set my feet upon a rock.”

We are subjected to the perversities of heretics, who have the likeness of demons, or to the demons themselves, concerning whom Paul writes: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. VI).

[Col. 0682C] “With what shall I cleanse your heart, says the Lord God, when you do all these works of a prostitute and a shameless woman, because you built your brothel at the head of every road and made your high place in every street, and you did not become like a prostitute who increases the price through disdain?”

God says all these things to Jerusalem because he cannot find a remedy by which he might cure her, sick and half-dead, according to what Isaiah writes: “What more was there to do for my vineyard that I have not done for it?” (Isa. V). And Hosea says: “What shall I do for you, Ephraim? What shall I do for you, Judah? Your mercy is like a morning cloud and like the dew that passes away in the morning” (Hos. VI).

Your idolatry was not committed secretly but with complete brazenness, so that you placed altars and bases—or your high place, of which we spoke above—at all the beginnings of roads and crossroads, and made your high place in every street. You did not imitate the clever prostitutes, who are accustomed to increase the price of lust through difficulty and thereby provoke their lovers to greater madness.

Or, according to the Septuagint, you were not like a prostitute who gathers payments, but you gave what you ought to have received, so that, even though you committed fornication and followed demons, you were not protected by their help; rather, oppressed by various captivities, you experienced your calamities.

This may also be referred to every Christian soul that, having abandoned the worship of God, allows itself to be polluted by the vices of luxury and, following a worldly life, does not prosper even in that life: it loses the riches of religion and does not receive the riches of the world. There was no difficulty in violating her; she thrust herself upon her lovers.

There is also another spiritual fornication, when we abandon the Church and join ourselves to heretics, building our brothel at the head of every road. The divine word commands us concerning these roads: “Stand in the ways and seek the everlasting paths of the Lord, and see which is the good way, and walk in it” (Jer. VI)—namely, in the books of Moses, Joshua, Judges, and Kings, and in Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the other prophets.

She builds her brothel at all the beginnings of the roads because, on account of the perversity of her doctrine, she misuses testimonies from the Scriptures. She says: “This is what Isaiah said; this is what Hosea says; this is what Moses spoke; this is what Daniel said.” It is fitting that she does not place her brothel in the middle of the roads or at their end, but at the beginning. For if she came to knowledge and to the depths of the divine books, she could not err.

She also makes her high place, or her base, in every street, allowing herself to be given over to the licentiousness and vices of the Gentiles and the impious. Even among the heretics themselves, after she has been disfigured by them, she has no favor but lies open to contempt, because she has so easily lost the chastity of her former faith.

This statement—which, as we said above, is not found in the Hebrew—“you committed fornication threefold in your daughters,” may be understood according to the literal sense of Jerusalem, as meaning that she committed fornication in every kind of place, in her towns and villages, and that no corner or street remained where she had not erected signs of idolatry.

Or it may refer to the Church and to believers who were deceived because they did not heed the Apostle: “May the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, and may your spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (I Thess. V). They committed fornication in every respect—in body, soul, and spirit.

We read in Proverbs: “Describe it for yourself threefold, that you may answer the words of truth that are proposed to you” (Prov. XXII). We are commanded to understand the utterances of truth, that is, the Holy Scriptures, in three ways: first according to the letter; second, at an intermediate level, through tropology; third, at a higher level, so that we may recognize spiritual mysteries.

According to the letter, there is this: “Let us not commit fornication, as some of them committed fornication and fell in one day twenty-three thousand” (I Cor. X). And: “Do not grumble, as some of them grumbled and perished by the destroyer” (ibid.).

At the intermediate level, according to tropology, we move away from the letter for a little while and ascend to higher things, as the Apostle says: “It is written: You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain” (I Cor. IX). And immediately he continues: “Is it for oxen that God is concerned? Or does he certainly speak for our sake?” (ibid.).

The final level, that is, the third, higher, and sacred understanding, is according to the same Apostle: “For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife; this is a great mystery, but I speak of Christ and the Church” (Eph. V).

The daughters of the fornicating Church are the souls of believers who were at first faithful and afterward deceived in heresy, whose guilt is referred back to their mother.

“But like an adulterous woman who brings strangers in upon her husband. Payments are given to all prostitutes, but you gave payment to all your lovers and gave them gifts so that they might come to you from every side to commit fornication with you. And what happened in you was contrary to the custom of women in your fornications. And after you there will be no fornication. For in that you gave payments and did not receive payments, what happened in you was contrary.”

Jerusalem therefore took the abundance of all things that had been bestowed upon her by her husband’s generosity and gave it to strangers—to demons and idols—according to what is written in Hosea: “She did not know that I gave her grain, wine, and oil, and multiplied silver for her. But she made silver and gold into Baals” (Hos. II).

Therefore, in anger, he immediately adds: “For this reason I will return and take away my grain in its season and my wine in its season. I will take away my garments and my linen, so that I may no longer cover her shame. And now I will reveal her uncleanness in the sight of her lovers, and no one will rescue her from my hand” (ibid.).

Although all fornicated women customarily receive payments from their lovers, Jerusalem did the opposite, giving rather than receiving, in order to display the greatness of her payment. “She honored them,” he says, “so that they would come to her from every side,” lest there be any neighbor who did not share in her disgrace.

Jerusalem surpassed other prostitutes in this as well: she not only gave her own possessions, which she had acquired through the labor appropriate to her shameful practice, but also gave her lovers and adulterers the gifts belonging to a husband. Her adulterous openness to every kind of depravity was so great that she was preferred not only to those who were prostitutes in the present but also to those who would be prostitutes in the future.

Therefore, following Symmachus, we translated: “And after you there will be no fornication.” In comparison with yours, every subsequent fornication will be considered lighter.

Whatever we have said about Jerusalem may also be referred to the Church and to the souls of believers, who give their lovers the gifts belonging to a husband—gold, namely understanding; silver, namely eloquence; and garments, by which our ugliness and shame are covered. They give these gifts either to hostile powers or to teachers of perverse doctrines when they assert that luxury does no harm; that promiscuous desire, according to the genital organs of the body, demands intercourse by natural law; that all foods should be used indiscriminately because they were made to be consumed; and that prudence is necessary only insofar as it benefits oneself.

They assert also that justice has no place, since if one practiced it one would have to beg. With such teachings, wretched Jerusalem—who ought to be the vision of peace—takes the sharpness of her intellect and the beauty of her eloquence and turns them into depravity. She goes forth adorned against her husband on behalf of her lovers with the ornaments in which she had been adorned by her husband for the good use of those gifts.

What follows is:

“And you gave them gifts so that they might come to you from every side to commit fornication with you.”

This signifies every kind of sin: she is not content with a single offense, but endures a hunger for sinning and, polluted in every member according to the laws of nature, is defiled even to the crown of her head.

“Therefore, prostitute, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God: Because your bronze was poured out, and your shame was exposed in your fornication, with your lovers and with all the detestable idols, in the blood of your sons whom you gave to them, behold, I shall gather all your lovers with whom you have mingled, and all whom you loved, together with all whom you hated. I shall gather them against you from every side, and I shall uncover your shame before them, and they shall see all your disgrace; and I shall judge you with the judgments of adulteresses and of those who shed blood. I shall give you into the blood of fury and jealousy, and I shall hand you over to them; and they shall destroy your brothel and demolish your place of prostitution. They shall strip you of your garments and take away your vessels of adornment. They shall leave you naked and filled with shame, and they shall bring a multitude against you; they shall stone you with stones and cut you down with their swords. They shall burn your houses with fire, and they shall execute judgments upon you in the sight of many women. You shall cease from fornication, and you shall no longer give payments; my indignation against you shall rest, and my jealousy shall be taken away from you. I shall rest and no longer be angry, because you did not remember the days of your youth, but provoked me in all these things. Therefore I also have placed your ways upon your head, says the Lord God, and I have not acted according to your crimes, in all your abominations.”

First, we lay the foundations of the history, because you did these things and those things that the preceding discourse has included. Therefore hear, prostitute, what you have done and what you are to suffer. You poured out your bronze, which you had received from me, and gave payment to your lovers, though you ought to have received it. And you killed your sons when you offered them to idols, so that you proved to be not only an adulteress but also a murderer of your own children.

“Therefore I shall gather against you all your lovers with whom you have fornicated”—both those whom you loved and those whom you hated. I shall strip you according to the law concerning adulteresses, so that all may see your disgrace and your sexual organs, on account of which they had previously been carried away by the madness of love. All this is said about Jerusalem by means of the metaphor of an adulterous and murderous woman who has not only fornicated against her husband but has also killed her children.

The statement that all the nations whose idols she worshiped would be gathered against her, that she converted all God’s gifts into their worship, and that the temple of Baal would be destroyed and all the city’s altars overturned by fire, with nothing remaining in her, is likewise expressed through this metaphor. [Col. 0685D] And just as people customarily throw stones at an adulteress and slaughter a prostitute, so that she may be killed by the wounds inflicted by each person, and so that all the women may see the punishment of the fornicator, so Jerusalem is to be abandoned in the sight of the neighboring cities and all the nations around her. This is to happen so that she may cease from fornication, no longer give payments to her lovers, and so that God’s indignation may rest and he may no longer be angry with her, having ceased to love her.

From this we understand that it is a great offense for God not to care at all, but to permit a person to his own crimes and sins. “My jealousy shall be taken away from you, and I shall rest and no longer be angry,” as though she were another’s, had departed from me, and I had handed her over to eternal nakedness. But if this happened to Jerusalem because she fornicated with idols, what do we suppose she will suffer when she has slaughtered the Son of God? And, he says, you did all these things, forgetting your former benefits, and provoked me to anger—or grieved me, whom you ought by good works to have provoked to joy. Therefore I also repaid your deeds upon your head. And when I overthrow you, adulteress, I shall nevertheless exercise less of my anger against you than you deserved, so that divine clemency may also be demonstrated in this: that the sins are greater than the punishments.

According to the tropological interpretation, every soul receives spiritual money from God, in accordance with what is said in the Gospel (Matt. XXV; Luke XIX) in the parables of the five, two, and one talents, and of the ten servants who each received a mina. When they have acted negligently, they become debtors of ten denarii and of five hundred; and for this reason, in the presence of the lovers whom we understand as demons and opposing powers, the shame of Jerusalem is revealed, either on the day of judgment or at the time of repentance, when sinners are rebuked.

At first, only God Almighty sees what is hidden, as the Gospel discourse says: “And your Father who sees in secret” (Matt. VI). And elsewhere: “God, who searches hearts and kidneys” (Ps. VII). And in the Book of Kings: “You alone know the hearts of the children of men” (II Chron. VI). But when the matter has been brought to completion, “there is nothing hidden that shall not be revealed, nor covered that shall not be made known” (Matt. X). And elsewhere: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and disclose the purposes of hearts; and then each person’s praise will come from God” (I Cor. IV).

And when the time of correction arrives, what is written in Hosea will be fulfilled: “Now their thoughts have surrounded them” (Hos. VII). And elsewhere: “Their thoughts accusing or defending one another on the day when God judges the hidden things of human beings” (Rom. II). And again: “Behold, the human being and his works are before his face.” And all those who had previously fornicated with her shall see her disgrace. God will give her into the blood of fury and jealousy, for a husband’s fury against an adulterous wife is great, and she cannot be redeemed at any price.

The blood of the sons may be understood in this way: let us call the good thoughts implanted by God in human beings the sons of Jerusalem. The adulteress kills them when she turns toward evil deeds. It is also beneficial for Jerusalem that her brothel be dug up and the whole seedbed of her fornication destroyed. When this has happened, she will no longer give payments, God’s indignation will rest, and he will no longer be jealous of her, secure in her chastity—namely, according to those who interpret these statements in a favorable sense.

Others, however, as we said above, refer them to the opposite sense, so that it is a sign of God’s great anger when he is no longer angry: once he has despised the fornicator, he despairs of her salvation. But if heretics who do not accept the Old Testament reproach, according to the Septuagint edition, what is said here—“And you grieved me in all these things”—on the ground that God not only receives anger but is also subject to grief and sorrow, let us ask them how they accept what is certainly a command of the good God: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Eph. IV). Whatever they say in defense of that testimony, we shall apply in explanation of the present passage.

“And behold, everyone who speaks a proverb among the people will take up this proverb concerning you, saying: ‘As the mother, so also her daughter; you are the daughter of your mother, who rejected her husband and her children; and you are the sister of your sisters, who rejected their husbands and their children.’”

After the catalogue [Greek: κατάλογος] of vices and the correction of Jerusalem, by which she is recalled to salvation, a familiar proverb is applied to her: or, as the Septuagint translated it, a “parable”: “As the mother, so also the daughter.” Jerusalem’s mother, as it is written above and in what follows, is called Cethaea, interpreted as “raving” or “turning into madness.” Through her are signified the provocations of this age, which lead the captive soul to destruction and separate it from its husband. There is no doubt that the husband is the Word of God and his teaching.

“And the sister of your sisters.” A little later we shall read of Sodom and Samaria. One signifies the life and luxury of the Gentiles; the other, the traps of heretics.

Moreover, what is read in the Septuagint—“the sisters of your sisters,” who rejected their husbands and their children—has no intelligible sense. For what other sisters did Sodom and Samaria have, since they are the sisters of Jerusalem? We must also ask what husbands Sodom and Samaria abandoned and what children they cast away. Unless perhaps we can say that the feet of those who are always in error are unsteady, and that they have no firm footsteps, as belong properly to the truth; rather, they run here and there and are carried about by every wind of doctrine, passing from one falsehood to another. When they realize that they have labored in vain at the first, they move on to a second and a third.

“Your mother is Cethaea, and your father is the Amorite; your elder sister is Samaria, she and her daughters, who dwell on your left. And your younger sister, who dwells on your right, is Sodom and her daughters. Yet you did not walk in their ways, nor did you act according to their crimes; you did almost—indeed, nearly—worse things than they in all your ways.”

Above he had said: “Your father is the Amorite and your mother is Cethaea”; here, with the order and number changed: “Your mother is Cethaea and your father is the Amorite.” For when crimes increase, they are divided into parts; once unity has been abandoned, they grow into a crowd and multitude, which cannot ascend to the heights with Jesus.

That Samaria and Sodom are sisters of Jerusalem, one on the left and the other on the right, you will approve even according to the bodily sense if, looking eastward from the temple of Jerusalem, you observe that Samaria, which is said to be the elder, is larger, because she sinned first and was led captive by the Assyrians, while Sodom is younger and smaller, referring to the multitude of the nations. Otherwise, at that time Sodom no longer existed, since before we read in Scripture of Jerusalem, Sodom together with Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim had been destroyed by divine fire. Jerusalem, called Judah by another name, stands between the two sisters and was led by the Chaldeans into Babylon.

Jerusalem sinned far more wickedly than Samaria and Sodom, worshiping the idol of jealousy in the temple and afterward killing the Son of God. According to the tropological interpretation, however, Samaria and Sodom—that is, heretics and pagans—often commit lighter sins than those who are regarded as Jerusalem, that is, church members. Hence it is said to the Corinthians, who indeed believed in Christ but were oppressed by evil works: “It is commonly reported that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not even found among the Gentiles” (I Cor. V), and so forth.

Heretics who nevertheless accept the Old Testament customarily understand from this passage three natures: spiritual, soulish, and earthly. They refer the spiritual nature to Jerusalem, the soulish to Samaria, and the earthly to Sodom. Let us briefly ask them how the three natures—spiritual, soulish, and earthly—which are certainly different from one another, can be said to have one mother and one father, since that does not agree with their fiction. And how, according to this same prophet, the soulish and earthly nature are restored to their former state, as is the spiritual nature—a view that is likewise contrary to their own arguments.

That Samaria is understood as heresy is confirmed in the prophet Hosea and in many other places, especially by this testimony: “Woe to those who despise Zion and trust in Mount Samaria; they have harvested the first fruits of the nations” (Amos VI). For all heretics despise Zion, which is interpreted as “watchtower” and refers to the Church. They place their confidence in the mountain of Samaria, namely, in the pride of perverse doctrines, which they regard as lofty; and through these fraudulent proclamations they harvest and plunder the first fruits of the nations, drawing the powerful among the Gentiles into heretical error by the wonder of their teachings.

“As I live, says the Lord, Sodom your sister herself and her daughters have not done as you and your daughters have done. Behold, this was the iniquity of Sodom your sister: pride, fullness of bread, abundance, and ease for herself and her daughters. They did not extend their hand to the needy and poor. They were exalted and committed abominations before me. Therefore I removed them, as you have seen. And Samaria did not commit half your sins; but you surpassed her in crimes and justified your sisters in all your abominations that you committed.”

In the Old Testament, God’s oath is: “As I live, says the Lord.” In the New Testament: “Amen, amen, I say to you.” But if this designation is also common to others—“The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob is not the God of the dead but of the living” (Mark XII)—and elsewhere: “I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. CXIV), we ask in what sense God uniquely claims for himself the common designation.

But just as we speak of a good tree, a good man, a good shepherd, and a good servant, while no one is absolutely good except God alone, so although angels and the other powers, as well as the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles, are living, they are called dead in comparison with God Almighty: “For who is the human being who lives and shall not see death?” (Ps. LXXXVIII). Hence the Apostle Paul also says of God: “Who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light” (I Tim. VI). And concerning the fountain of the living, he says: “Our life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. III).

This one, then, who swears and says, “As I live, says the Lord,” describes the crimes of Sodom and her daughters and places pride first—the devil’s own and original sin. Hence the same apostle says: “Lest, being puffed up with pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil,” on account of which the devil fell from heaven. For he had said: “By strength I shall act, and by the wisdom of my understanding I shall remove the boundaries of the nations; I shall devastate their strength, shake inhabited cities, and grasp the whole world in my hand like a nest; and like broken eggs I shall take them away.”

And: “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. IV). We also read elsewhere: “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?” (Ecclus. X). And the Gospel recounts how the pride of the Pharisee was overcome by the humility of the tax collector (Luke XVIII).

The seedbed of pride is fullness of bread, abundance of all things, and ease; or, as the Septuagint translated it, “the abundance of luxury and indulgence.” The rich man in the Gospel, clothed in purple, is said to have committed no other crime than that, overflowing with wealth and delights, he had burst into such pride that he did not extend his hand to the needy and poor Lazarus. He so forgot his condition that he did not even give the wretched man what was to be thrown away (Luke XVI). For this reason it is written elsewhere: “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled,” and so forth (Matt. XXIII).

Pride, fullness, abundance of all things, ease, and delights constitute the sin of Sodom. From this follows forgetfulness of God, which regards present goods as permanent and never expects to lack what it needs. Therefore the Law also commands: “Take care lest, when you eat and drink and are filled, build excellent houses, possess sheep and cattle, silver and gold, you forget the Lord your God.”

(Greg.) When it is said to Jerusalem, “This was the iniquity of Sodom your sister: pride, fullness of bread, and abundance,” it is plainly shown that she lost salvation because, through the fault of pride, her mind exceeded the measure of moderate nourishment.

(Hieron.) Elsewhere it is written concerning Israel: “He ate and drank and was filled, grew fat, and kicked—the beloved one” (Deut. XXXII). Knowing this, the wisest of all, Solomon, asks in the Proverbs: “Give me what is necessary and sufficient, lest, when filled, I become a liar and say, ‘Who sees me?’ Or, having become poor, I steal and swear falsely by the name of my God” (Prov. XXX).

As for what follows—“And you justified your sisters in all your abominations that you committed”—it does not simply declare Sodom and Samaria righteous, but righteous by comparison with those who are worse. In the same way, the tax collector mentioned above is not said to be absolutely righteous, but righteous by comparison with one who is worse. [Col. 0690A] Yet although Sodom and Samaria are such, they did not commit even half as much sin in comparison with Jerusalem: “The servant who knows the will of his master and does not do it shall be beaten with many stripes” (Luke XII). And: “The powerful shall suffer powerful torments” (Wis. VI).

Moreover, because the Hebrew text contains “ease” in place of “riches,” one should understand it in relation to the saying: “Every idle soul is in desires”—that is, something must always be done, lest, when the hand ceases working, the field of our breast be occupied by the thorns of evil thoughts.

“Therefore you also bear your disgrace, for you surpassed your sisters in your sins, acting more wickedly than they; for they have been justified by you.”

(Hieron.) After shipwreck, the second plank is to blush when you have sinned and not to submit to that rebuke which is directed against Jerusalem: “You have acquired the face of a prostitute; you do not know how to blush.” One bears one’s torment when one is tortured by one’s own conscience and, in this age, willingly endures punishment so as not to endure eternal torments.

We corrupt our brothers or sisters by our sins when, through our sin, they are provoked to greater crimes. I shall make what I am saying clearer by an example: imagine someone established at the summit of priestly office who does not live well and disgraces his dignity by his deeds. Is not a lay brother corrupted by imitating his vices? For whoever causes one of the least to stumble is thrown into the depths with a millstone tied around his neck.

The sisters of Jerusalem, Sodom and Samaria, are likewise justified—not because they are righteous in themselves, but, as we have said, by comparison with one who is worse.

[Col. 0690C] “Therefore be ashamed also and bear your disgrace, you who justified your sisters.” Shame is followed by disgrace, disgrace by correction, correction by consolation, and consolation by salvation, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Tribulation produces endurance, endurance proof, proof hope; and hope does not disappoint” (Rom. V). There is no doubt that this refers to the future, because in the present she has blotted out her sins through shame.

Something similar is expressed by the Gospel saying: “There is a shame that leads to death, and there is a shame that leads to life” (Ecclus. IV). The Holy Spirit also urges sinners in the Psalms: “Let all my enemies be ashamed and put to shame; let them turn back and be very quickly ashamed” (Ps. XXXIX). It is also written elsewhere: “You first declare your sins, so that you may be justified” (Isa. XLIII). And again: “The righteous person is an accuser of himself at the beginning of his speech” (Prov. XVIII).

It is therefore not surprising that Jerusalem is summoned to shame and disgrace, since she sinned so greatly that she justified her sisters. To her it is next said: “You and your daughters, return to your former state.”

“And I shall turn them back, restoring them with the restoration of Sodom and her daughters, and with the restoration of Samaria and her daughters. And I shall turn your restoration among them, so that you may bear your disgrace and be ashamed of all that you have done while consoling them.”

Jerusalem makes great progress when, after the shame and disgrace imposed upon her by God’s judgment—which she willingly accepted and bore, saying, “I shall endure the anger of the Lord, because I have sinned against him”—she is promised restoration to her former state. Yet because she was justified by comparison with her crimes, Sodom and Samaria, one of which is on the right and the other on the left, are restored first.

First comes the restoration—or, as Aquila translated it, the captivity—of Sodom. Second comes the captivity of Samaria, as Aquila and Symmachus likewise translated it. Finally Jerusalem is restored, since she had been weighed down by greater iniquity and had shown her sinful sisters to be righteous by comparison with herself.

Who could doubt that among three sinners—or rather, impious persons—a Gentile, a heretic, and a church member, the one who possessed the greater dignity deserves far greater punishments? “For the powerful shall suffer powerful torments,” as we have said. The one who is least, however, is worthy of mercy. “The servant who knows the will of his master and does not do it shall be beaten with many stripes.” Hence Peter also says: “It is time for judgment to begin from the household of God” (I Pet. IV). And in this same prophet the command is given to those holding axes: “Begin from my sanctuaries.”

Thus, after the sisters of Jerusalem have first been converted and restored to their former state, Jerusalem, as the last, is to bear her disgrace, be ashamed, and blush over the sins she committed, and console all her sisters by enduring more severe things. Or certainly she is to be ashamed and blush because she provoked God to anger. From this it is clear that God’s anger is not natural to him; rather, our vices provoke the most merciful and gentle God to anger, as the Apostle says: “Do you despise the riches of his goodness, forbearance, and patience, not knowing that God’s goodness leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself” (Rom. II)—wrath that God does not possess by nature.

Hence it is also written elsewhere: “You sent forth your wrath, which devoured them like stubble” (Exod. XV). For what is joined and united in one body cannot be sent forth; rather, what is outside the body is sent forth, such as a spear, missile, arrow, or sword. We also read in the Gospel that it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment than for the one that did not receive the apostles.

“And your sister Sodom and her daughters shall return to their former state, and Samaria and her daughters shall return to their former state. And you and your daughters shall return to your former state.”

Among their other fables, including endless genealogies and delusions, the Jews also dream of this: at the advent of their Christ, whom we know to be the Antichrist, Sodom will be restored to its former state during the thousand-year reign, so that it will be like the paradise of God and like the land of Egypt. Samaria, too, will recover her former happiness, so that the ten tribes may return from the Assyrians to the land of Judah.

For we read that the ten tribes were captured by Pul, Shalmaneser, and Tiglath-pileser, kings of the Assyrians, and remain captives there to this day. Jerusalem also, they say, will then be rebuilt, together with all her daughters—that is, the cities, villages, and fortresses that will flourish under her power as they flourished before. Jerusalem herself will be built with gold, silver, and precious stones. Concerning her Isaiah prophesies: “I shall appoint your judges as at the first and your counselors as at the beginning. After this you shall be called the city of righteousness, the mother of cities, faithful Zion” (Isa. I). Our Apocalypse also speaks of her (Apoc. XXI). David sings: “Do good, Lord, in your good pleasure toward Zion, and let the walls of Jerusalem be built” (Ps. L). And elsewhere: “The cities of Judah shall be built; they shall inhabit them and dwell there, and their offspring shall be established forever” (Ps. LXVIII).

But leaving the perfect knowledge of these matters to God’s judgment—indeed, trusting with complete confidence that after the second coming of the Lord and Savior nothing humble or earthly will exist, but only the heavenly kingdoms first promised in the Gospel—we say that all these things have been fulfilled, and are fulfilled daily, in the state of the Church.

Sodom returns to its former state when the soul that was formerly Gentile, restored to its own nature and made righteous, understands the Creator. Samaria receives her ancient blessedness when, rejecting heretical error, she is joined to Christian teaching and faith. And when they have returned, Jerusalem—the vision of peace, which is interpreted as the Church—will return to her former state. Concerning her it is written: “His place has been made in peace” (Ps. LXXV). And: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose fellowship is altogether one” (Ps. CXXI). And the Apostle says: “But the Jerusalem above is free, which is our mother” (Gal. IV). And again: “You have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and countless thousands of angels gathered together” (Heb. XII).

And she will return with her daughters, who are scattered throughout the whole world. We have discussed this more fully in our explanations of Isaiah. [Note: Hear Jerome speaking, whom Rabanus describes.]

“Now your sister Sodom was not heard of from your mouth in the day of your pride, before your wickedness was revealed, as at this time, to the reproach of the daughters of Syria and of all the Palestinian daughters around you, who surround you on every side. You have borne your crime and your disgrace, says the Lord God.”

Because you surpassed your sister in crime and were not terrified by her example so as to avoid suffering similar things and restrain your foot, now your disgrace has been revealed. Hear God’s sentence—or, according to the Septuagint, bear; or, according to Aquila and Theodotion, you have borne; or, according to Symmachus, you will bear—your crime and your disgrace. After you have suffered punishments for sacrilege, you shall receive forgiveness not by virtue of your own covenant but through my clemency.

In Hebrew, Syria is called Aram, which is interpreted as “loftiness.” According to the explanation of that passage in the prophet Isaiah in which Aram and Ephraim agree against Judah and Jerusalem, the clever wisdom of the Gentiles, which promises itself the loftiness of knowledge, joined with the wickedness of heretics, attacks Judah, in whom there is true confession, but cannot prevail.

Here too, the same arrogance of Syria—that is, of the philosophers—together with the daughters of foreigners, in whom the manifold error of different peoples is displayed, mocks Jerusalem and makes her an object of reproach, though Jerusalem’s vices have surpassed its own.

“For thus says the Lord God: I shall deal with you as you have despised the oath, in order to annul the covenant. But I shall remember my covenant with you in the days of your youth, and I shall raise up for you an everlasting covenant. You shall remember your ways and be ashamed when you receive your sisters, your elder ones together with your younger ones. I shall give them to you as daughters, but not according to your covenant. I shall raise up my covenant with you, and you shall know that I am the Lord, so that you may remember and be ashamed, and may no longer open your mouth because of your shame, when I have been reconciled to you concerning all that you have done, says the Lord God.”

For this reason I told you: bear your crime and your disgrace—or you have borne them, or you will bear them—so that you may receive what you deserve, because you despised my oath and annulled my covenant. But when this has been fulfilled—“I kill and I make alive; I strike and I heal” (Deut. XXXII)—then I shall remember the covenant that I formerly made with you, and I shall raise up for you not the covenant of the Law, which has passed away, but the everlasting covenant of the Gospel.

When you remember your ways and receive your sisters, elder or younger—Samaria and Sodom and their companions—I shall give them to you as daughters, or as a testing. “For there must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest” (I Cor. XI). I shall do this not because of your merit but because of my mercy. Then you shall know that I am the Lord, remember my benefits, be ashamed, and say with the Apostle: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle,” and so forth (I Cor. XV).

“And you shall no longer open your mouth because of your shame.” It belongs to the saints to open the mouth, according to Paul: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians” (II Cor. VI); and to the Lord and Savior, who “opened his mouth and taught them, saying” (Matt. V). In the Psalms he says: “I shall open my mouth in parables” (Ps. LXXVII).

But to the sinner it is said: “You have sinned; be silent” (Ecclus. XXI). And: “Why do you recite my covenant with your mouth?” (Ps. XLIX). And: “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. XV). The holy person, however, deserves to hear: “Open your mouth, and I shall fill it” (Ps. LXXX).

From this we understand that, even when by the Lord’s mercy we have received our former glory—indeed, when we have received the everlasting covenant of the Gospel—after the Lord has been reconciled to us concerning all that we have done, we must retain the memory of our past sin and always keep our mouth closed, because we have been saved not by our works but by God’s grace.

## BOOK EIGHT

[Col. 0693]

[Col. 0693C] “The Lord is faithful in his words and holy in all his works.”

This prophetic statement is plainly shown to have been fulfilled in the fact that the Lord reminds the Israelite people of the benefits with which he nourished them from the beginning, and reproaches them for the hardness of their mind, because they were always ungrateful for all his benefits and repaid his good deeds with the evils of distrust and disobedience.

Most of these matters were recalled in the preceding book. Now, however, through an enigma and a parable, he foretells the evils that will come upon the people and its prince because of their unfaithfulness. Thus those who are guilty, persist in their wickedness, and refuse to repent will in no way be able to escape the vengeance of just retribution; rather, they will receive the punishment deserved by their deeds.

Hence it follows:

### CHAPTER XVII. Jehoiachin in Babylon as a captive; Zedekiah and Jerusalem are given into the hands of Nebuchadnezzar; and a prophecy concerning Christ is set forth

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, propose an enigma, tell a parable to the house of Israel, and say: Thus says the Lord God: A great eagle, with great wings, long stretches of limbs, full of feathers and varied plumage, came to Lebanon and took the marrow of the cedar. He tore off the top of its branches and carried it to the land of Canaan; he placed it in the city of merchants. Then he took some of the seed of the land and placed it in the ground as seed, to establish its root over many waters. He placed it on the surface. When it had sprouted, it grew into a spreading vine of low stature, with its branches turned toward the eagle. Its roots were beneath it. Thus the vine became and produced branches, and sent out shoots, and so forth.”

When the prophet is told, “Propose an enigma, tell a parable,” or, as the Septuagint translated it, “Tell a narrative and speak a parable,” it is shown that what is said is obscure. For there is no doubt that an enigma and a parable present one thing in words but hold another in their meaning. The Savior also spoke to the people in parables, which he explained privately to the apostles.

Therefore we must understand “enigma” and “parable” as truly an enigma and a parable. Two eagles are proposed in the present prophecy of Ezekiel. We must now speak of the first and discuss the second later; for the moment, we shall follow the simple historical interpretation.

“A great eagle, with great wings, long stretches of limbs, full of feathers and varied plumage”—or, as the Septuagint translated it, “full of talons”—is Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Chaldeans. Concerning him Hosea also speaks: “Like an eagle over the house of God” (Hos. VIII). He, ruling many nations and surrounded by an innumerable army, came against the house of God—there is no doubt that this signifies the temple—or, as Scripture now says, “to Lebanon,” concerning which Zechariah speaks: “Open your doors, Lebanon, and let fire consume your cedars; howl, fir tree, because the cedar has fallen, for the magnificent have been devastated.”

Frequently in the Holy Scriptures the temple, which was renowned and exalted, is called Lebanon (Zech. XI).

“He took the marrow of the cedar and tore off the top of its branches. And he carried it to the land of Canaan and placed it in the city of merchants.” Instead of “merchants,” or “commerce,” the Septuagint translated it as “walled city.” This indicates King Jehoiachin of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar captured with his mother, the princes of the people, all the wealth of Jerusalem, and the vessels of the temple, and carried away [Col. 0695B] to Babylon, which is in the land of Canaan, where he grew old.

As the writing of Matthew the evangelist later testifies, our Lord and Savior was born from his line through Shealtiel and Zerubbabel. Nebuchadnezzar then took from the seed of that same land—that is, from the royal stock—Mattaniah, the uncle of Jehoiachin, changed his name, called him Zedekiah, and appointed him king in Jerusalem. He placed him over many peoples, yet he set him on the surface and did not establish his authority with the deep root of imperial power. Rather, he placed him there so that he would be looked upon and remain under Babylonian control, or with his stature humbled and his branches turned toward Babylon.

For this is what Scripture says: “of low stature, with its branches turned toward it,” the eagle being understood. The Septuagint translated it more explicitly: “And what had been planted grew. It became a weak and small vine, so that only its branches were visible.” Thus he seemed indeed to possess a kingdom, but his humble and weak kingdom was governed according to the will of the Babylonian ruler.

For the present, this is sufficient concerning the chapter; to it we shall append what follows.

“Then another great eagle appeared, with large wings and many feathers. And behold, this vine, as though sending its roots toward it, extended its branches toward it, so that it might water it from the beds of its shoots. It was planted in good soil beside abundant waters, so that it might produce foliage and bear fruit and become a great vine. Say: Thus says the Lord God: Will it prosper? Will He not tear out its roots and strip away its fruit, and dry up all the branches of its shoots, so that it will wither—and not by a great arm or by many peoples—to uproot it entirely? Behold, it has been planted: will it prosper? When the scorching wind touches it, will it not dry up, and will it not wither in the beds of its shoots?” etc.

The second eagle, that is, the other one, itself also great and full of feathers and many talons, because of its rapacity and the devastation of very many nations, is Pharaoh, king of Egypt. And behold, this vine—understand: King Zedekiah—had been established in Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar. “It began,” he says, “to send its shoots toward it,” that is, to send ambassadors to the king of Egypt and to seek from him assistance against the king to whom it was subject. For this is what Scripture now says: “so that it might water it from the beds of its shoots.” It had been planted in good soil by Nebuchadnezzar, so that it might produce foliage, bear fruit, and grow into a broader vine.

Therefore the prophet is commanded to speak to the vine that had been planted by Nebuchadnezzar and had sent its branches toward the Egyptian eagle: “Will it prosper, because it has attempted to do this, or will all its shoots and branches not immediately wither?” “And not,” he says, “by a great arm or by a numerous people.” For Zedekiah, having fled and been deprived of the assistance of the king of Egypt, was captured by the commanders of Nebuchadnezzar in the deserts of Jericho, and all his companions were scattered here and there. Thus it is written in the Book of Kings, in Chronicles, and in Jeremiah.

(Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XXXI, chapter 47.)

In Sacred Scripture, the word “eagle” sometimes designates evil spirits, who seize souls; sometimes the powers of the present age; and sometimes either the most subtle understanding of the saints or the incarnate Lord, who swiftly traverses the depths and soon returns to the heights.

By the name of eagles, plotting spirits are expressed, as Jeremiah bears witness when he says: “Our persecutors were swifter than the eagles of heaven.” Our persecutors are swifter than the eagles of heaven when wicked men do such things against us that, by the inventions of their malice, they seem to outstrip even the aerial powers.

By the word “eagle,” earthly power is represented. Hence through the prophet Ezekiel it is said: “A great eagle, with great wings, long-limbed, full of feathers and variegated, came to Lebanon and took the marrow of the cedar and tore away the top of its foliage.” By this eagle, who other than Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, is represented? He is described as having great wings because of the vastness of his army; as long-limbed because of the length of time; as full of feathers because of his many riches; and as full of variegation because of the countless forms of earthly glory.

“He came to Lebanon and took the marrow of the cedar and tore away the top of its foliage,” because, attacking the grandeur of Judea, he removed the nobility of its kingdom as though it were the marrow of a cedar. And when, by taking captive, he removed the tender offspring of the kings from the summit of their kingdom, he tore away, as it were, the top of its foliage.

By the word “eagle,” either the subtle understanding of the saints or the flight of the Lord’s ascension is signified. Thus the same prophet, describing the four evangelists whom he had seen under the form of living creatures, testifies that the faces of a man, a lion, an ox, and an eagle appeared to him. Without doubt, by the eagle he signifies John, who in flight left the earth, because through subtle understanding he penetrated the inner mysteries by contemplating the Word.

John himself, in his Revelation, does not disagree with this prophetic statement concerning himself, saying: “The first living creature was like a lion, the second like a calf, the third living creature had a face like a man, and the fourth living creature was like a flying eagle” (Rev. IV).

Although each figure appropriately corresponds to one of the evangelists—one indicating the order of Christ’s human birth, another, through the sacrifice slaughtered for the world, the death of a calf, another the strength of his power, like the roar of a lion, and another, contemplating the birth of the Word, gazing upon it as an eagle gazes upon the rising sun—these four living creatures can nevertheless signify their single head, of whom they are members.

For he is man, because he truly assumed our nature; he is a calf, because he patiently died for us; and he is a lion, because through the strength of his divinity he broke the bond of the death he had assumed. Finally, he is an eagle, because he returned to heaven, from which he had come. Thus he is called man in being born, calf in dying, lion in rising again, and eagle in ascending into heaven.

In Job also we read: “Does the eagle rise at your command and place its nest in lofty places?” (Job XXXIX.) But in this passage the name “eagle” represents the subtle understanding of the saints and their sublime contemplation.

The sharpness of the eagle’s sight surpasses that of all birds, so that no radiance of its light, striking its eyes fixed upon the sun's ray, causes them to close. Thus the eagle is raised at the command of God when the life of the faithful, obeying divine commands, is suspended in heavenly things. It is also said to place its nest in lofty places because, scorning earthly desires, it is already nourished by hope of heavenly things.

It places its nest in lofty places because it does not construct the dwelling of its mind in a low and inferior manner of life. Beholding the eagle building the nest of hope in lofty places, Paul says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III). And again: “He raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places” (Eph. II).

It has its nest in lofty places because it surely fixes its purpose on things above; it does not wish to cast its mind down to the depths, nor to dwell in low places through the degradation of human conduct. Perhaps Paul was being held in prison when he testified that he was seated with Christ in the heavenly places. He was where he had already fixed his burning mind, not where his still sluggish flesh necessarily held him.

This is commonly a distinctive mark of the elect: they know how to travel the road of the present life in such a way that, through the height of hope, they know themselves already to have reached the heights. Thus they see everything that passes away beneath them and trample upon everything that stands prominent in this world out of love for eternity.

“Then the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Say to the rebellious house: Do you not know what these things signify? Say: Behold, the king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and took its king and its princes and brought them to himself in Babylon. And he took one of the royal offspring, struck a covenant with him, and received an oath from him. He also took the mighty men of the land, so that the kingdom might be humble and not rise up, but might keep his covenant and observe it.

“But that man, withdrawing from him, sent messengers to Egypt, so that it might give him horses and a numerous people. Will he prosper, or will he obtain deliverance, who has done these things? And will he who broke the covenant escape? As I live, says the Lord God, he will die in the place of the king who made him king, whose oath he annulled and whose covenant with him he broke, in the midst of Babylon.

“And Pharaoh will not make war against him with a great army or a numerous people, by casting up a rampart and building siegeworks, to destroy many lives. For he had despised the oath in order to break the covenant; and behold, he gave his hand. After doing all these things, he will not escape.”

This is the riddle; this is the parable: under the two eagles, Scripture reveals the two kings, of Babylon and Egypt, and King Zedekiah, who, abandoning his sworn agreement with Nebuchadnezzar, transferred himself to the king of Egypt.

“He will strike a covenant with him,” it says, “and receive an oath from him, so that he may keep his covenant and observe it.” He who breaks the covenant, it says—will he escape? From this we learn that faith must be kept even among enemies, and that one must not consider to whom one has sworn, but through whom one has sworn.

For the man who trusted you because of the name of God and was deceived was found to be much more faithful than you, who, under the pretext of divine majesty, plotted against your enemy—or rather, against one who had already become your friend.

“For he will die,” it says, “in the place of the king who made him king, whose oath he annulled and whose covenant with him he broke, in the midst of Babylon.” We read that Zedekiah was captured and brought to Riblah; there, after his sons had been killed, he was blinded and transported to Babylon, shut up like a wild beast in a cage.

Thus, although Scripture may appear to contradict itself, it is nevertheless entirely true in both passages. For it had been said to Zedekiah: “You shall enter Babylon, and you shall not see it.” He entered, because he was led to Babylon; and he did not see it, because he had been blinded.

What follows—“And Pharaoh will not make war against him with a great army or a numerous people, by casting up a rampart and building siegeworks, to destroy many lives”—is understood in two ways: either the king of Egypt, coming against Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, would be unable in battle, even with a small army, to resist so great a multitude; or Zedekiah himself would be attacked by Pharaoh, from whom he had hoped for assistance.

This does not mean that Pharaoh actually attacked him, or that Scripture testifies to this anywhere. Rather, the attack by Nebuchadnezzar occurred on the occasion of the king of Egypt; and the one who was seen to attack Jerusalem, which he was besieging, was not the king in whom Zedekiah had placed his vain hope.

“Behold,” it says, “he gave his hand to the king of Egypt,” and surrendered himself, committing sacrilege through perjury against God. “Will it benefit him?” And after doing all these things, he will not escape.

“Therefore thus says the Lord God: As I live, I will place upon his head the oath that he despised and the covenant that he violated. I will spread my net over him, and he will be caught in my snare. I will bring him to Babylon, and there I will judge him for the violation by which he despised me. And all his fugitives, together with his entire host, shall fall by the sword, and the survivors shall be scattered to every wind. And you shall know that I, the Lord, have spoken,” etc.

The secular saying is:

> “Fraud or valor—which would one seek in an enemy?”

Those who say that enemies should be deceived commonly bring this objection against us. Even if we were to agree with them, Zedekiah acted much worse. He did not deceive an enemy, but a friend, to whom he had been bound by the covenant of the Lord.

Therefore, so long as you [do not, added in some manuscripts] swear or [do not, added in some manuscripts] enter into a covenant in the name of God, it is a matter of prudence and courage either to deceive or to overcome your adversary by whatever means you can. But once you have bound yourself by an oath, the person who trusted you is no longer an adversary but a friend, deceived under the pretext of the oath—that is, by the invocation of God.

Therefore Scripture now says: “The oath that he despised and the covenant that he violated, I will place upon his head.” And lest we think that “oath,” “covenant,” and “agreement” refer to the king of Babylon or to Zedekiah, who had made it, the passage continues: “for the violation by which he despised me.”

Therefore, whoever despises an oath despises the one through whom he swore. He wrongs the one whose name his adversary trusted. For this reason He says: “I will spread my net over him, and he will be caught in my snare. I will bring him to Babylon, and there I will judge him.”

Whatever, therefore, Nebuchadnezzar did against Zedekiah, he did not do by his own strength, but through the wrath of God, in whose name Zedekiah had committed perjury.

According to the allegorical interpretation, although the interpretation may appear forced, we should understand that just as other living creatures are accustomed to be referred both to the good and to the evil, so too with the eagle and the lion.

With reference to the good it is said: “A lion’s cub is Judah.” With reference to the opposite it is said: “Our adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls around” (1 Pet. V). And in the psalm: “He lies in wait in secret like a lion in his lair,” etc. (Ps. X).

With reference to the good, Scripture says of the eagle that the righteous man, having become rich, makes wings for himself like an eagle so that he may return to the house of his predecessor. And in Isaiah it is written (Isa. XL) that the righteous receive wings like eagles; they run and are not wearied, they walk and do not hunger.

Appropriately, then, the one who had said, “By strength I shall act, and by the wisdom of my understanding I shall remove the boundaries of the nations and plunder their resources. I shall shake inhabited cities and seize the whole world in my hand like a nest, and like broken eggs”—is now described under the figure of an eagle. He does not wish merely to touch the small and lowly shrubs of Lebanon, which is interpreted as “brightness” and is related to incense, but the tops of the cedars.

And he does this concerning princes and the royal stock, in accordance with the saying of Habakkuk: “His chosen food” (Hab. I). He establishes a covenant with those whom he has captured, so that they may submit their necks to the king of Babylon and fulfill what the Apostle says: “Whom I handed over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Tim. I). And elsewhere: “Whom I handed over for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved” (1 Cor. V).

Therefore, if perhaps we are expelled from the congregation of the brethren and from the house of God because of some sin, we ought not to resist, but should accept the sentence pronounced against us with an even temper and say with the Prophet: “I will endure the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him, until he justifies my cause,” etc.

It frequently happens that, having been subject to one person, we pass over to another who promises us his assistance. He will not allow us to remain in our former state, and this must be avoided by every means, lest our branches be dried up and our shoots wither, and we be judged to have acted against the covenant of God.

“Thus says the Lord: I myself will take from the marrow of the lofty cedar and place it from the top of its branches; I will pluck off the tender shoot. And I will plant it upon a high and elevated mountain; upon the lofty mountain of Israel I will plant it. It will produce a shoot and bear fruit, and become a great cedar. And all the birds will dwell beneath it; every winged creature will nest in the shade of its foliage.

“And all the trees of the region shall know that I am the Lord: I have humbled the lofty tree and raised up the lowly tree; I have dried up the green tree and made the dry tree put forth foliage. I, the Lord, have spoken and acted.”

The true Nebuchadnezzar therefore takes from the marrow of the lofty cedar, from the top of its branches, so that the kingdom may be humble and not rise up.

But the Lord God, the almighty Father, who spoke to Ezekiel, takes from the royal stock and from the line of David and plants it upon a high and elevated mountain. He speaks of this in the psalm: “But I have been established as king by him upon Zion, his holy mountain” (Ps. II).

For the prince had failed from Judah and the ruler from Israel until the one came to whom it had been promised: “And he shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX).

He produced a shoot, bore fruit, and surpassed all cedars by his loftiness, so that all the birds of heaven might dwell beneath him and all the winged creatures be protected by his shade. Of him Habakkuk says: “Horns are in his hands; there his strength is hidden.” And he who desires to gather them says, “like a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings” (Matt. XXIII).

Thus all the trees of the region may know that he is the Lord—speaking figuratively (*tropikōs*, τροπικῶς) of believers.

He is the one who once humbled Israel, the lofty tree, and exalted the lowly people of the nations; who dried up the green tree of the Jews, flourishing and sprouting in the Law and the Prophets; and who made the dry tree of the nations put forth foliage, so that he might fulfill in deed what he had always spoken.

The words of Simeon in the Gospel signify the same thing when he says: “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and rising of many” (Luke II). So too the mustard seed, which is the smallest of all seeds, becomes, once it has grown, a dwelling place for birds.

Some interpret the lofty tree that was humbled and the lowly tree that was exalted differently, referring them to the passion of the Lord and Savior: “Who, although he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” After the resurrection, this tree was later exalted: first green, it was dried up by death, and afterward, coming back to life, it recovered its former greenness.

Others, interpreting both passages in a Jewish sense, refer them to Israel: Israel was humbled and dried up at the first coming, and at the second it will be restored to its former condition, when what the Apostle Paul says has been fulfilled: “When the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. XI).

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the sour grape: that neither a father is held liable for his son nor a son for his father in sins, but each person will bear his own burden; and wherever he is found, there he will be judged; and sinners are recalled to repentance

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: What is this that you turn into a proverb among yourselves in the land of Israel, saying: ‘The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the children’s teeth have been set on edge?’” etc.

(Hieronymus.)

Divine Scripture calls attention to what was said in Exodus: “I am the Lord your God, a jealous God, who repay the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, and show mercy to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments” (Exod. XX).

And again:

“The Lord descended in a cloud and stood beside Moses. And Moses invoked the name of the Lord, and the Lord passed before his face. And he invoked him, saying: ‘Lord God, merciful and compassionate, patient and of great mercy and true, preserving justice and mercy for thousands, removing iniquities and injustices and sins, yet not clearing the guilty, repaying the iniquities of the fathers upon the children and upon the children’s children, to the third and fourth generation’” (Num. XXXIV).

These passages must be understood as a parable and proverb, so that one thing sounds in the words while another is held in the meaning—just as we said above concerning the parable of the two eagles.

Thus the Lord also says in Psalm LXXVII: “I will open my mouth in a parable; I will utter propositions from the beginning.” And in the Gospel (Matt. XIII) he presents the parable of the seed, the weeds, and the mustard seed—which, although it is the smallest of all seeds, grows into a great tree—in such a way that one thing is displayed in the words while another is contained in the meanings.

Even until the present day we thought that the two testimonies from Exodus quoted above were not parables but simply expressed a straightforward meaning. And although we did not dare to say anything, or for the earthen vessel to speak against the potter, asking, “Why have you made me thus or thus?”, we nevertheless suffered a hidden scandal: it seemed unjust for God that one person should sin and another should pay the penalty for his sins.

For if he repays the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation, it would appear unjust that one person should sin and another be punished. But from what follows—“of those who hate me”—the difficulty concerning the threat or command is resolved.

They are not punished in the third and fourth generation because their fathers sinned, as though the fathers, who were sinners, ought rather to have been punished; they are punished because they became imitators of their fathers and hated God, as hereditary evil and impiety grow from the root into the branches as well.

Heretics who do not accept the Old Testament and oppose the Creator commonly say at this point: How good and just is the God of the Law and the Prophets, who, remaining quiet and silent, repays the sins of the fathers upon those who have not sinned! How great, indeed, is his cruelty, that he extends his wrath to the third and fourth generation!
