We shall answer them, and show that here too the clemency of the Creator God is demonstrated. It is not a sign of cruelty and severity to retain wrath until the third and fourth generation, but a sign of mercy to defer the punishment of sin.

For when he says, “Lord God, merciful and compassionate, patient and of great mercy,” and adds, “repaying the iniquity of the fathers upon the children and the children’s children,” this indicates that he possesses such great mercy that he does not punish immediately, but postpones the sentence of punishment.

But if vengeance against sinners is deferred until the third and fourth generation, what more does he do for the righteous and the holy? The passage continues: “And preserving justice and mercy for many thousands, for those who keep his commandments and perform his precepts.”

It is written in Proverbs: “As a sour grape is harmful to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so is iniquity to those who practice it” (Prov. X). From this it is evident that it is not the teeth of others that suffer and are set on edge, but the teeth of those who have eaten the sour grape.

The meaning of this passage is as follows: Just as it would be ridiculous and incoherent for someone to say, “The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the children’s teeth have been set on edge,” so it is unjust and perverse for the fathers to sin while their children and grandchildren are tormented.

There are some who explain what is written in Exodus—“repaying the iniquities of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation”—by referring the statement to the human soul. They say that the father in us is the gentle impulse, the point of the senses, and the incitements of vices; the son is the thought, if the thought conceives sin; the grandson is what one has thought and conceived, if one has carried it out in deed.

The great-grandson, that is, the fourth generation, is reached when one not only does what is evil and wicked but also glories in one’s crimes, according to what is written: “When the wicked comes into the depths of evil, he will despise it” (Prov. XVIII).

God therefore does not punish the first and second impulses of thoughts, which the Greeks call *propatheiai* (προπαθείαι), “preliminary impulses”—without which no human being can exist—but only when someone resolves to carry out what he has thought, or refuses to correct through repentance what he has done.

Hence it is written: “No human being is without sin, not even if his life should last a single day; and the years of his life are countable.” And elsewhere: “Who will boast that he has a pure heart?” (Job XXV.) And again: “Even the stars are not clean in his sight, and against his angels he devised something perverse.”

But if that sublime nature is not without sin, what should be said of human beings, who are surrounded by fragile flesh and ought to say with the Apostle: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. VII.)

And also: “When we have done everything, we ought to say, ‘We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we were obliged to do’” (Luke XVII). And: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain; unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it keep watch in vain” (Ps. CXXVI).

As proof of this point—that the first impulse of thought, or rather the small movement of the mind, is not punished by God, but only when one consumes in deed what one has conceived in the mind—we should bring forward the passage in Genesis concerning Ham. Ham sinned by mocking his father’s nakedness, but the sentence was received not by the one who laughed, but by his son Canaan: “Cursed be Canaan; he shall be the servant of his brothers” (Gen. IX).

For what justice is there in the father’s sin being followed by a sentence against the son? Likewise, what the Apostle states in the opposite direction—that a woman will be saved if her children remain in faith, holiness, and chastity—seems to lack justice if good sons and grandsons should save their parents.

For how many holy parents have bad children? And, conversely, how many sinful parents have begotten righteous and holy children?

Therefore, everything we have said above must be understood according to this meaning: the sins of parents and of those who beget are punished in the branches, not in the root.

For the present, let what we have said concerning the proverb or parable suffice. Thus the Law and the Prophets—that is, Exodus and Ezekiel—or rather God himself, who spoke both here and there, do not appear to differ in their judgments, nor does one passage correct what the other had cursed.

But if anyone is able to discover either a better or another interpretation that removes the difficulty caused by these seemingly contradictory testimonies, we should rather accept that person’s judgment.

“‘As I live,’ says the Lord God, ‘this parable shall no longer serve as a proverb for you in Israel. Behold, all souls are mine: as the soul of the father is mine, so also the soul of the son is mine. The soul that sins shall itself die.’”

What is signified by “As I live, says the Lord,” and by “parable” or “proverb,” we have explained more fully above. It will by no means be called a parable in Israel, but among those who do not possess knowledge of God and cannot perceive the truth.

“All souls,” he says, “are mine”—according to creation, not according to merit. Thus Moses is called “a man of God,” concerning whom it is written: “The prayer of Moses, the man of God.” And Elijah said to the commander of fifty soldiers: “If I am a man of God, let fire descend from heaven upon you and upon your fifty men” (2 Kings I).

But a man of sin and a son of iniquity is not called a man of God. Likewise, those are called servants and attendants of God of whom it cannot be said: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John VIII). And again: “By whatever a person is overcome, by that he is enslaved” (Rom. VI).

Just as the sins of children do not harm their fathers, so the sins of fathers do not flow over onto their children: “But the soul that sins shall itself die”—not through the abolition of its substance, but through exclusion from the fellowship of the one who says: “I am life” (John XIV).

Elsewhere he says: “Everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die” (John XI). And: “Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever keeps my word shall never see death” (John VIII).

“For our life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. III). We shall live by it when Christ, our life, appears in glory, and what is written will be fulfilled: “Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death into life” (John V).

The statement made by Balaam—“May my soul die among the souls of the righteous” (Num. XXIII)—has this meaning: he desires to die to the world and to sin and to live with the souls of the righteous, whose life is Christ. They can sing: “I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. CXIV), for he is not the God of the dead but of the living.

And if Balaam, as is entirely true, when translated into our language means “a vain people,” it is clear that the formerly vain people of the nations desires to have fellowship with the souls of the righteous—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—who are called upright and righteous. Hence the Book of Genesis also received its name from them.

“And if a man is righteous and does what is just and right, does not eat upon the mountains, does not lift his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel, does not violate his neighbor’s wife, does not approach a menstruating woman, does not grieve anyone, restores the pledge to the debtor, takes nothing by force, gives his bread to the hungry, covers the naked with clothing, does not lend at interest and does not take more, turns his hand away from wrongdoing, renders true judgment between one man and another, walks in my commandments, and keeps my judgments so as to do what is true—he is righteous; he shall surely live, says the Lord God.”

“Do you wish,” he says, “to know that what was said—‘I will repay the sins of the fathers to the third and fourth generation’—does not mean what most people suppose, nor is it like this statement: ‘The fathers ate sour grapes, and the children’s teeth were set on edge’ (Ezek. 18)? Listen to what I am about to say. If the father is righteous, doing these things and not doing those things, but has a very wicked son who, abandoning his father’s virtues, gives himself over to crimes, will not that father live, because he is righteous, while that son will surely die because he has committed everything which the father avoided in becoming righteous?”

Let us examine the father’s catalogue of virtues, which seems to me to be divided into seventeen parts. The first is that he has done what is just. The second, similar to this, is that he has joined righteousness to justice. The third is that he has not eaten upon the mountains. The fourth is that he has not lifted his eyes to idols—or, as the Septuagint translated it, “to the thoughts of the house of Israel.” The fifth is that he has not violated his neighbor’s wife. The sixth is that he has avoided intercourse with a menstruating wife. The seventh is that he has not grieved anyone—or, as the Septuagint translated it, “oppressed anyone by force.” The eighth is that he has restored the pledge to the debtor. The ninth is that he has taken nothing by force—or, according to the Septuagint, “has not committed robbery.” The tenth is that he has given his bread to the hungry. The eleventh is that he has covered the naked with clothing. The twelfth is that he has not lent money at interest. The thirteenth is that he has taken nothing more from what he had given. The fourteenth is that he has turned his hand away from wrongdoing. The fifteenth, which seems similar to the first but differs from it in some respect, is that he has rendered true judgment between one man and another, or between himself and his neighbor. The sixteenth is that he has walked in God’s commandments. The seventeenth is that he has kept his judgments and ordinances.

We shall explain what each of these means in what follows: “If a man is righteous,” he says, “and does what is just.” It is written in Proverbs: “The thoughts of the righteous are judgments” (Prov. 12). Whoever possesses this virtue, so that he does nothing without reason and judgment, can say the prophetic words: “The judgments of God are true, justified in themselves” (Ps. 18). And when he has rightly judged everything, so that he does not show partiality to the poor in judgment, he will fulfill the Lord’s command: “You shall judge the lesser as well as the greater,” confidently saying: “My soul has desired to desire your judgments at all times.” And again: “I have chosen the way of truth; I have not forgotten your judgments” (Ps. 118). And in the same Psalm: “I have known that your judgments are righteous.” He will advance to such great blessedness that he understands the Lord’s judgments, which are “a great abyss,” and says with the Apostle: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and how inscrutable his ways!” (Rom. 11.) In prayer he will also remember: “For your judgments are delightful.”

After judgment comes righteousness. Whoever possesses it will clearly possess Christ, who, according to the Apostle (1 Cor. 1), “has become for us righteousness, sanctification, and redemption.” He is to practice true righteousness and show no partiality in judgment, knowing that, in judging others, he must judge according to his own righteousness.

The third is not eating upon the mountains. The Jews consider this to belong to the sin of idolatry, for we often read in the books of Kings and Chronicles: “Nevertheless he did not remove the high places; the people still sacrificed upon the high places and burned incense on the heights” (3 Kings 22; 4 Kings 12, 15; 2 Chron. 20, 33). Scripture thereby indicates that upon mountains and in groves they sacrificed victims to idols and burned incense.

We, however, shall say that the man who eats upon the mountains is the one who says with the Pharisee: “I thank you, God, that I am not like this tax collector; I fast twice a week, I give tithes of all that I possess,” and so forth (Luke 18). By contrast, the tax collector, hearing the one who had said, “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11), was striking his breast with his hand—that is, the treasury of his worst thoughts—and “did not dare to lift his eyes toward heaven.” Likewise, the statement made elsewhere, “Do not seek what is too great for you, and do not search out what is stronger than you” (Sir. 3), condemns all heretics who eat upon the mountains of pride, despise ecclesiastical simplicity, and do not know what is written: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (1 Pet. 5).

In the fourth place comes: “And he has not lifted his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel.” For “idols,” the Septuagint translated “thoughts.” All heretics make idols—that is, images—which they fashion from their own hearts, and toward which they lift the eyes of their hearts, considering their falsehood and lie to be truth. The images of the house of Israel are those which are found in the Church and, under the pretext of falsely named knowledge, lead simple people astray, introducing the doctrines of philosophers into the house of Israel—those, namely, who behold God with the mind.

In the fifth place comes: “And he has not violated,” or “defiled,” his neighbor’s wife. This plainly prohibits adultery; but because “his neighbor” is added, unless every human being is understood as one’s neighbor, the command seems to mean that we should abstain from our friends’ wives but may freely defile the wives of enemies and strangers. Every human being, however, must be understood as one’s neighbor, according to the Gospel parable (Luke 10) proposed by the Savior concerning a man who, going down to Jericho, was wounded by robbers. When the Pharisee asks who his neighbor was, the Savior teaches that the neighbor is the one who showed him kindness.

According to mystical interpretation, a wife can be understood as the wisdom of a holy man, as Solomon says: “Love her, and she will embrace you; cherish her, and she will guard you” (Prov. 4). He desires to defile this wisdom who criticizes the blessings of others and, inflamed by the torches of envy, violates holy things, corrupts what is chaste, and defiles what is pure.

The sixth is: “And he has not approached a menstruating woman,” or wife. Each month women’s heavy and sluggish bodies are relieved by the discharge of unclean blood. If a man has intercourse with a woman during this time, the fetuses are said to contract a defect from the seed, so that lepers and elephantiasis sufferers are born from such conception, and diseased corruption produces ugly bodies in either sex, whether through the smallness or the disproportion of their limbs.

Men are therefore commanded to know definite times for intercourse—not only with other men’s wives but also with their own wives, to whom they appear to be joined by the law, since Scripture says: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1): when intercourse is appropriate and when they should abstain from their wives. This is also expressed by the Apostle and Ecclesiastes: “A time for embracing, and a time to be far from embraces” (Eccl. 3). Let the wife therefore beware lest, overcome by the desire for intercourse, she entice her husband; and let the husband beware lest he use force against his wife, thinking that the pleasure of marriage must at all times be subject to him. Hence Paul also says: “Let each one know how to possess his own vessel in holiness and chastity” (1 Thess. 4).

Beautifully, among the brief maxims of Xystus the Pythagorean, it is said: “The man who is an excessively ardent lover of his own wife is an adulterer.” When a certain person translated this book into Latin, he wished to honor it with the name of the martyr Sixtus, without considering that throughout the entire volume—which he foolishly divided into two parts—the name of Christ and of the apostles is wholly absent. Nor is it surprising that he transformed a gentile philosopher into a martyr and bishop of the city of Rome, since he also changed Eusebius of Caesarea’s first book in defense of Origen by giving it the name of the martyr Pamphilus, so that, with such a praiser, he might more easily commend to Roman ears the utterly impious books *On First Principles* (*περὶ Ἀρχῶν*).

The seventh place follows: “And he has not grieved a person,” or, as the Septuagint translated it, “has not oppressed him by force.” I do not know who is free from this vice and sin. The Egyptians oppressed the Hebrews by force. Hence Habakkuk also complains: “Why does the impious oppress the righteous?” (Hab. 1). Would that this were said only of those who are outside, and not also of those who are within. For the leaders of churches are accustomed to oppress the people through pride. Of them it is written: “They have appointed you ruler; do not exalt yourself; be among them as one of themselves” (Sir. 32). The Savior also commanded: “Whoever wishes to be first among you must be last of all” (Mark 9).

What is said according to the Hebrew: “And he has not grieved a person,” agrees with the apostolic testimony: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit, who dwells in you” (Eph. 4). And in the Gospel which the Nazarenes read according to the Hebrews, the one who has grieved his brother’s spirit is counted among the greatest crimes. But if the grief of another kills the one who causes the grief, what must be said of wickedness and a tyrannical mind? To such a person belongs the saying: “What does earth and ashes boast of?” (Sir. 10.) Forgetting his condition—how he is full of phlegm, bile, and excrement, and will shortly be ploughed by worms—he sets his mouth against heaven, and his tongue passes through the earth, saying with the true Nebuchadnezzar: “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will set my throne; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14).

The eighth is: “He has restored the pledge to the debtor.” Not to every debtor; otherwise many would find in the recovery of pledges an opportunity for acquiring wealth. Rather, he must restore it to the debtor of whom the law says that he is poor, has given his own garment as a pledge, and must receive back his covering before sunset, lest, tortured by the cold, he cry out to the Lord, who avenges his injury. If, according to what follows, we must give bread to the hungry and cover the naked with clothing, how much more must we return what belongs to him, provided that the debtor’s poverty is beyond doubt?

We may also understand “return the pledge to the debtor” in the sense that, when we are joined to someone by love and he is indebted to us, we return his pledge to him by giving mutual love, retaining no part of his debt with us any longer.

The ninth place belongs to: “He has taken nothing by force,” or, according to the Septuagint, “has not committed robbery.” The Apostle also speaks of robbers, saying that, among other sinners, one must not even eat with such a person. Every robbery involves violence; unless force has been applied, robbery achieves nothing.

There is, however, also a holy violence and an admirable robbery, of which the Gospel writes: “From the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11). Jude, the brother of James, also speaks of this: “Save some by snatching them from the fire; on others have mercy with fear” (Jude 23). By contrast, hostile powers hasten to seize prey for the destruction of those whom they carry off.

Jacob signifies this too when he says: “An evil beast has devoured him; an evil beast has carried off Joseph” (Gen. 37). Hence the Lord’s sheep, which follow him, are not snatched from his hands. He himself says: “What the Father has given me is greater than all, and no one can snatch it from my hand [elsewhere: ‘from my Father’s hand’]” (John 10). From this it is clear that the Father and the Son have one power, might, and substance. For if no one can snatch from the Son’s hand what the Father has given him, and the same things are in the Father’s hand and are not snatched from him, it is plainly demonstrated that everything belonging to the Father and the Son is shared in common: the Father holds in the Son’s hand just as what belongs to the Son is held in the Father’s hand.

The tenth is: “He has given his bread to the hungry.” By this we are taught that almsgiving is not to be given to those who are full, but to the hungry; nor should bread be given to those who belch from fullness, but to those who are tormented by emptiness. All food is included in bread. Significantly, it says “his own,” lest we turn into an act of mercy bread acquired through robberies, usury, or another person’s misfortune. “A man’s own riches are the ransom of his soul” (Prov. 13).

We see many clients, poor people, and farmers doing this—not to mention the violence of soldiers and judges, who oppress by force or commit theft, so that they may give a little to the poor out of much and glory in their crimes. Publicly the deacon even recites in the Church the names of those who make offerings: “So much has this person offered; so much has that person promised.” They take pleasure in themselves to the applause of the people, while their conscience torments them. We provide the wretched with an occasion to rejoice over what they give and not grieve over what they have stolen.

It is better, however, to understand the righteous man’s bread as the one who says: “I am the bread that came down from heaven” (John 6), and the bread which we ask to be given to us in prayer, “our substantial bread,” or “our bread for the coming day”: “Give us this,” so that, although we shall always receive it afterward, we may deserve to receive it daily in the present age. The righteous man gives this bread to the hungry, of whom it is written: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matt. 5). Because he is righteous, he makes the common bread of all his own bread—the bread which had failed in Judea, as the prophet says: “I will remove from them strength,” or “the staff of bread” (Ezek. 4).

Yet what we are saying, if we belong to Christ—or rather, what the prophet recalls—is the bread of believers and of the hungry. It must absolutely not be given to those who have eaten and drunk, have been filled, and, having grown fat, have kicked (Ps. 77). Of them it is said: “Woe to you who are full now, for you shall hunger” (Luke 6), lest they vomit it up, as Solomon says: “For he will vomit and defile your good words” (Prov. 23). The Savior expresses the same thing in other words: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine.”

The eleventh place belongs to: “And he has covered the naked with clothing.” This statement, in accordance with the explanation of the preceding verse, must be interpreted in two ways: we are to provide covering for the physically naked, as the Savior says, “I was naked and you clothed me” (Matt. 25); and we are to give Christ’s garment to those who are naked in faith and virtues. Of this garment it is written: “As many of you as were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3). The man who had no wedding garment was naked in this respect and was cast out of the banquet. Concerning this nakedness the Lord also says to Jerusalem: “You were naked and full of shame” (Ezek. 16).

The twelfth place is held by: “And he has not lent at interest,” or, as the Septuagint translated it, “has not given his money at interest.” In the Hebrew, interest of every kind is prohibited; in the Septuagint, only monetary interest, in accordance with what is written in the fourteenth Psalm: “He who has not given his money at interest.” How then is it said, “You shall not lend at interest to your brother, but to a foreigner you shall lend at interest” (Deut. 23)? Observe the progress at the beginning of the law: interest is taken away only from brothers; in the Prophet, interest is prohibited from everyone, as Ezekiel says, “He has not given his money at interest.” In the Gospel, moreover, there is an increase of virtue, when the Lord commands: “Lend to those from whom you do not hope to receive.”

The thirteenth place follows: “And he has not taken more.” Some think that interest exists only in money. Divine Scripture, anticipating this, removes the excess from every kind of thing, so that you may not receive more than you gave. In the fields, interest is commonly demanded in grain, millet, wine, oil, and other products—or, as the divine word calls it, “abundance.” For example, in winter we give ten measures and at harvest receive fifteen: that is, an additional half. The man who considers himself most just will take an additional quarter of the portion.

They commonly argue as follows: “I gave one measure, which produced ten measures when sown. Is it not just that I receive an additional half-measure of my own, since by my generosity he has nine and a half measures of my property?” “Do not be deceived,” the Apostle says (Gal. 6); “God is not mocked.”

Let the merciful moneylender answer us briefly: did he give to someone who had, or to someone who did not have? If he gave to someone who had, he ought not to have given; but he gave as though to someone who did not have. Why, then, does he demand more as though from one who had? Others commonly accept little gifts of various kinds in place of money lent at interest and do not understand that whatever it may be is called interest and excess, if they receive more from the person to whom they gave than they had given.

The fourteenth step is: “He has turned his hand away from wrongdoing,” so that he flees wrongdoing in every act. Wrongdoing is committed not only with the hands but also with other members, as Solomon says: “Put far from you crooked lips” (Prov. 4). And in the Psalms: “They have spoken iniquity on high” (Ps. 72). The foot also runs toward wrongdoing, and so does the eye if it lusts after another man’s wife. Such a person is not an imitator of him of whom it is said: “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2). Hence we are commanded to make friends for ourselves from unrighteous mammon, so that they may receive us into eternal dwellings (Luke 16).

The fifteenth is: “He has rendered true judgment between one man and another,” or between himself and his neighbor. This seems to mean the same as the first statement, where it was written: “If a man is righteous and does what is just.” But the addition of “true” judgment, which he renders between one man and another, or between himself and his neighbor, is seen to intensify the virtues—*epitasin* (*ἐπίτασιν*). Hence, at the beginning of Proverbs, after many commandments, a correction concerning judgment is introduced: “To know wisdom and discipline, to understand the words of prudence, to receive the subtleties of discourse, and to know true justice, and after all to correct judgment” (Prov. 1).

For this reason the Apostle also reproves those who are established in the Church (1 Cor. 6), because they have lawsuits among themselves and choose the least and most despised person. According to the Gospel, the one who judges between one man and another is first: he has destroyed the things that belong to little ones and has reached the mature man; yet he still needs the judgment of someone greater in order to attain the truth of judgment.

Next, in the sixteenth place: “He has walked in my commandments”; and in the seventeenth: “He has kept my judgments, or ordinances, so as to do them and preserve what he has done.” Both statements have many possible meanings, if we wish to rehearse all the commandments of the law, in which the Lord’s commandments and ordinances are said to reside. The 118th Psalm is full of commandments and ordinances, as is, in part, the eighteenth, in which it is written: “The ordinances of the Lord are right, rejoicing the heart,” and: “The commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes.”

Here one asks how, in this same prophet, God could have said: “I gave them ordinances that were not good, by which they would not live” (Ezek. 20). The answer is easy, and will be fuller in what follows: the Jews do not live when they follow the letter that kills, whereas Christians live when they understand the life-giving Spirit. It would take too long, if we wished to establish by testimonies where the Lord’s commandments and where his ordinances are said to be, and by what differences or obscurities each of them is surrounded.

Hence in the present passage it is added: “He is righteous; he shall surely live, says the Lord God.” Whoever does these things and does not do those things will by no means be punished for his father’s offenses, but will live by his own virtues.

“But if he begets a son who is a robber and sheds blood, and does one of these things, does not walk in the way of his righteous father, but does not do all these things, rather eating upon the mountains, defiling his neighbor’s wife, grieving the needy and the poor, committing robberies, not returning a pledge, lifting his eyes to idols, committing abomination, lending at interest and taking more—will he live? He shall not live. Since he has done all these detestable things, he shall surely die. His blood shall be upon him.”

Let us first speak according to the historical meaning, so that you may know that the iniquities of fathers do not overflow upon their children. If the righteous man has done the things which the preceding passage set out in order, he shall live. But if he has begotten a son who departs from the service of the Lord and exchanges his father’s virtues for vices, doing what his father did not do and not doing what his father did, will he be able to live? Certainly he will not live, but will be guilty of his own blood.

According to the spiritual understanding, however, the righteous ecclesiastical man, if he has preached the faith of the Gospel and his son and disciple has been deceived by heretical error, will be called “pestilent.” Of him it is also written in the first Psalm: “He did not sit in the seat of pestilence.” In Proverbs, the self-confident, shameless, and proud man is likewise called pestilent.

This man pours out the blood of those whom he has deceived and heaps all sins upon himself: he eats upon the mountains of pride, pollutes his neighbor’s church, grieves the needy and the poor in knowledge of the Scriptures, oppresses and overthrows them, and commits robbery by carrying off those whom he has led astray from the Church. He does not return the pledge he received from his teacher, so as to fulfill what is written: “You received without payment; give without payment” (Matt. 10). He lifts his eyes toward the idols and images which he fashioned from his own heart, commits every abomination, and lends money at interest so that the disciple’s diligence may increase the teacher’s error; then he demands from those to whom he gave more than he had given. Certainly he will not be able to live, but will die in his own blood.

“But if he begets a son who, seeing all the sins of his father which he committed, fears and does not commit them; who likewise does not eat upon the mountains, does not lift his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel, does not violate his neighbor’s wife, does not grieve a man, does not retain a pledge, does not commit robbery, gives his bread to the hungry, covers the naked with clothing, turns his hand away from injury to the poor, does not take interest or excess, does my judgments, walks in my commandments, he shall not die in the iniquity of his father, but shall surely live. His father, because he slandered, used force against his brother, and did evil in the midst of his people, is dead in his own iniquity.” (Jerome.)

“Do not be surprised,” he says, “if the son of a righteous man, turning toward vices and sins, dies by death, when, conversely, the son of a sinner and an impious man, if he sees the perversity of his father’s ways and turns away so as not to do evil but to do good, is not held guilty of his father’s crimes.” This can also be understood of us, concerning whom it is said in the Psalms: “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house; and the king will desire your beauty” (Ps. 44). We who have been born from the stock of the nations are to leave behind our parents’ crimes, do what is just and right, and live in it.

He therefore repeats what we have discussed more fully above, and so we pass over everything briefly, wishing to move on to what is more obscure and new.

“And you say, ‘Why will the son not bear the iniquity of the father?’ Clearly because the son has done what is just and right, has kept all my commandments, and has done them; he shall surely live. The soul that sins shall itself die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor the father the iniquity of the son. The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the impiety of the impious shall be upon him.”

He answers the question which the hearer could have raised in opposition. “You are accustomed,” he says, “to ask: Why will the righteous son not bear the iniquity of his father?” He himself answers: “Clearly because the son has acted well and has not committed his father’s offenses.” It is just that, just as the sinner dies in his own crime, so the righteous should live in his own virtues. Let the soul that has sinned die, and let the soul that has kept God’s commandments live.

“But if the impious man repents of all his sins which he has committed, keeps all my commandments, and does what is just and right, he shall surely live and shall not die. None of all his iniquities which he committed shall be remembered against him; in the righteousness which he has practiced he shall live.” (Jerome.)

“To such an extent,” he says, “the sins of fathers do not overflow upon their children, and a wicked father does not burden a righteous son, nor are some punished for the crimes of others, that the very same person who was previously impious and sinful, if afterward he repents and, turning toward better things, wipes away his former sins, is not judged according to the oldness of his sin but is received into my flock through the renewal of virtue.”

At the same time, we must consider what kind of impious and sinful person he receives in repentance. “If he turns away,” he says, “from all his sins which he has committed and keeps all the Lord’s commandments”—that is, if he abandons every crime and pursues every virtue. If he does every good thing and abandons every evil thing, I too will forget all his iniquities which he committed, and “in the righteousness which he has practiced he shall live.” He will live not so much by my righteousness as by his own, although it belongs to my righteousness to repay good to the good and evil to the wicked.

“Is it my will that the death of the impious should occur, says the Lord God, and not rather that he should turn from his ways and live?” (Jerome.)

Therefore, it is the Lord’s will that all be saved and come to knowledge of the truth. Wherever God’s judgment appears severe and fierce, it condemns not human beings but sins.

“But if the righteous man turns away from his righteousness and does iniquity according to all the abominations which the impious is accustomed to commit, will he live? None of all his righteous deeds which he performed shall be remembered; in the transgression by which he transgressed and in the sin by which he sinned, in those he shall die.” (Jerome.)

Just as former sins do not weigh down the righteous man who was previously a sinner, so former acts of righteousness do not help the sinner who had previously been righteous. For each person will be judged in the condition in which he is found.

“And you said: ‘The way of the Lord is not fair.’ Hear, O house of Israel: Is my way not fair, and are not your ways rather perverse?” (Jerome.)

He gives the reasons why the Lord’s judgment is just. “You think,” he says, “that I am unjust, so that I repay the sins of fathers to their children, and that while some eat sour grapes the teeth of others are set on edge? Behold, each person dies in his own sin and is made alive in his own righteousness; in both cases it is not the past but the present that is judged. Rather, your judgment is unjust, because you think that the parable is not a parable but accept it as though it were historical fact, so that the crimes of some are punished in others.”

“For when the righteous man turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity, he shall die in them. In the iniquity which he committed he shall die.” (Jerome.)

This can also be understood in the following way: the formerly righteous people of Israel turned away from their righteousness because they abandoned the author of righteousness, and they committed iniquity by denying the Son of God. They shall die in the sin and crime which they committed—not in many sins, but in one, killing the heir in order to destroy the inheritance.

“And when the impious man turns away from his impiety which he committed and does what is just and right, he will preserve his soul alive. For, considering his situation, he turns away from all his iniquities which he committed; he shall surely live and shall not die.”

Conversely, he says, the people of the nations, who did not possess knowledge of God, if the impious man turns away from his impiety—which he previously practiced in idolatry—and does what was commanded by the law to Israel, will first make alive his soul, which had been dead. Seeing that he had perished in the iniquities which he committed, he will believe in the one who says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14); he shall surely live and shall not die.

“And the children of Israel say: ‘The way of the Lord is not fair.’ Are my ways not fair, O house of Israel, and are not your ways rather perverse?”

To this day Israel blasphemes God, asking why he abandoned his own people and accepted the multitude of the nations. The Lord rebukes this, declaring that their ways are perverse, while the Lord’s judgment is just: when the former tenants have been destroyed, he sends other cultivators into his vineyard. Understanding this, the Jews said in the Gospel parable: “This shall not happen.”

“Therefore I will judge each person according to his ways, O house of Israel, says the Lord God.”

Whether they are from the multitude of the nations or from the people of Israel, those who are judged are judged in this way: “There is no partiality with God”; each person will be crowned for his own faith and condemned for his own impiety and unbelief.

“Turn and repent of all your iniquities, and iniquity shall not be your ruin. Cast away from you all your transgressions by which you have transgressed.”

This speech is directed specifically to Israel, so that they may repent and abandon their iniquities, or transgressions, by which they have transgressed against God. It can also be understood of both peoples, so that Israel and the multitude of the nations alike may abandon their vices and turn to him who can heal their brokenness.

“And make for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit.”

Abandoning the oldness of the letter, live in the newness of the spirit. The new heart of Israel is to believe in the one whom it had previously denied. The new heart of the nations is to abandon idols and, having rejected the worship of the dead, to believe in the one who is the life of the living.

“And why will you die, O house of Israel?”

As we said above, it is better to understand this exhortation—“Turn and repent”—as referring to the Jews, whom he does not wish to die and to whom he now says: “Why will you die, O house of Israel?” You have Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as fathers, concerning whom it is written: “The God of the living and not of the dead.” Why will you die through your own fault, when by the merit of your fathers and by my mercy you ought to live?

“For I do not desire the death of the sinner, says the Lord God. Return, and you shall live.”

“I do not wish you to die,” he says, “you whom I brought forth for salvation. I brought forth children and exalted them, but they rejected me. Return, therefore, and live.” The command “Return” is spoken only to those who were previously with God and afterward abandoned his company. Live through repentance, you who died through sin. Therefore Israel, because it does not return to its former state, must be believed to be dead.

**CHAPTER XIX. Concerning Joachim and Jechoniah, and Joachim’s captive son; concerning the remnant of Judah, which had no king.**
[Col. 0714B] “And you, take up a lamentation over the princes of Israel, and say: Why did your mother, a lioness, lie down among lions? In the midst of young lions she raised her cubs, and brought forth one of her cubs. He became a lion and learned to seize prey and devour human beings. The nations heard of him, and they seized him, not without wounds. And they brought him in chains to the land of Egypt. When she saw that she had grown weak and that her hope had perished, she took one of her cubs. She made him a lion, and he walked among lions. He became a lion, learned to seize prey, and devour human beings. He learned to make widows and to turn their cities into a desert; the land and its fullness were desolated by the sound of his roaring. Nations gathered against him from all around, from the provinces. They spread their net over him, and he was captured by their wounds; they put him into a cage, brought him in chains to the king of Babylon, and put him in prison, so that his voice would no longer be heard over the mountains of Israel, etc.”

(H.) We shall say that, since the captivity was near, the prophet is not so much foretelling the future as recounting the past. For after the sixth year of King Zedekiah, as we immediately read in what follows: “And it came to pass, in the seventh year, in the fifth month, on the tenth day of the month, that a lamentation was taken up over the princes, or prince, of Israel.” And it is said: “Why did your mother, a lioness, lie down among lions?” The lamentation over the princes therefore concerns all those, namely, who were born from the stock of Josiah. The mother of the princes, Jerusalem, is called a lioness; she bore and nourished cubs, and brought forth one of her cubs.

“And he made him a lion”: this signifies Jehoahaz, the son of Josiah, whom Pharaoh Neco brought to Egypt and set Joachim in his place. When Joachim died, his son Jeconiah was made king; together with his mother and the nobles of the city, he was brought by Nebuchadnezzar to Babylon. From him was born Shealtiel, the father of Zerubbabel, who received his name from having been born in Babylon.

It is therefore clear that, under the metaphor [μεταφορά] of the lioness, the cubs, the lion, and again another lion, the events are being described that had already occurred at the time when the prophet spoke these words. For after Jerusalem brought forth from the royal line Jehoahaz, the son of Josiah, and made him king, he became so cruel within a short time that, figuratively, he is said to have seized prey and devoured human beings.

When the Egyptian came against him, he seized him, “not without wounds,” or “in a pit,” as the Hebrew properly contains it, so as to preserve the figurative image of the capture of lions, which are always caught in pits. “And he brought him in a bridle,” or “in chains,” to the land of Egypt, where he died.

When his mother Jerusalem saw this—she who had given birth to him, nourished him, and established him as king—and saw that her hope had perished, she took Jeconiah, the son of Joachim, from among the other kings and made him king. He too, imitating the cruelty of his predecessor, is described under the ferocity of a lion: he devoured human beings, made many widows, turned cities into a desert, and terrified the whole province by the sound of his roaring. Thus, when the nations came against him, spread their net over him, caught him in a pit, and put him into a cage and chains, this did not in fact happen to Jeconiah. He himself surrendered to the king of Babylon and was carried away to Chaldea; rather, the imagery of the lion is preserved—the lion that is caught in pits, bound in chains, and kept in cages.

Otherwise, according to the historical interpretation, we read this of Zedekiah, who was made king of Jerusalem after Jeconiah. This circumstance has led many to understand Zedekiah rather than Jeconiah, because chains are mentioned, as well as a cage and a prison. Jeconiah, however, was kept in prison and was not killed; he was merely removed from the kingdom. But history tells us that Zedekiah was led blind to Babylon and immediately killed there.

[Col. 0715C] “Your mother was like a vine in your blood, planted beside water; its fruit and its branches grew from abundant waters. It produced strong rods for ruling scepters, and its height was exalted among the foliage. It saw its height in the multitude of its branches, but it was uprooted in anger and thrown to the ground. A scorching wind dried up its fruit; its strong rods withered and dried out; fire consumed them. And now it has been transplanted into the desert, into a dry and pathless land. Fire went out from the rod of its branches and consumed its fruit. It had no strong rod, no scepter for ruling; it was a lamentation, and it shall be a lamentation, etc.”

One reality is expressed in different words. Just as in the preceding passage we read that Jerusalem was compared to a beautiful woman and again to a lioness that had nourished lions in her lair, so now she is compared to a very beautiful vine planted beside abundant waters. Because its branches were nourished by moisture, they grew so greatly that one branch—which Scripture calls a very solid or very strong rod—developed into scepters for rulers.

How, then, has that vine, so rich in fertility, fruit, and beauty, now been transplanted into the desert, into a dry and pathless land? This signifies the land of Babylon, to which they were carried; or Egypt, to which they fled; or the land of Judah itself, in which a few poor people remained, with Gotholias [Gedaliah] appointed over them to gather and govern the remnant of the people.

Against him rose Ishmael, from the royal line and from the rod of the vine’s branches. He killed him at Mizpah and consumed all the fruit of the vine. From that time there was no strong rod or scepter of rule in the vine itself. For no king remained to govern the people; instead, together with Johanan the son of Kareah, they fled to Egypt. Therefore it is a lamentation, a parable of mourning, so that the royal stock may be mourned, since kingship ceased in Judah thereafter, until he should come “to whom it has been reserved”: “And he himself was the expectation of the nations.”

From this it is evident that both the preceding passage, where it says, “Why did your mother, a lioness, lie down among lions?” and this passage, where it is written, “Your mother was like a vine in your blood, planted beside water,” refer to Jerusalem. She lost her lions and her branches, and no rod remained in her that might rise up as a tribe or as a scepter of rulers.

For it begins with a lamentation and ends in a lamentation. “Take up a lamentation over the princes of Israel”: that is, at the beginning and now at the end there is mourning, and the royal stock must be followed in a lament and a parable of mourning.

Moreover, according to the anagoge [ἀναγωγή], which others refer to the heavenly Jerusalem, saying that many fell from it into this valley of tears, ceased to be kings, and that a once most beautiful vine was dried by a scorching wind, so that no living branch remained in it, we understand Jeremiah’s lament under the figure of the city to refer to the Church. For at the end of time, because iniquity has multiplied, the love of many will grow cold, so that even God’s elect will be tested, if that is possible, and its princes will be caught in the devil’s nets. He will not be content with capturing one king but will hasten daily to capture kings and princes, according to what is written: “His choice morsels.”

The branches of the Church too, which formerly equaled flowers and the redness of blood, will later be dried by a scorching wind. The parable of the Gospel also expresses this interpretation (Luke 8), where, after the sun had risen, the plants that had sprouted were scorched and suddenly dried up, so that scarcely one of the branches remained to grow into a rod and become a worthy ruler of the people.

Amos expresses the same thing in other words: “I will bring famine and thirst upon the land, not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the words of God” (Amos 8). Therefore we ought to mourn and lament over the princes of Israel, through whose fault and pride Judah was laid waste and Jerusalem captured.

[Col. 0716D]

## CHAPTER XX

The Lord does not answer those who question him because of their sins, but reproves their crimes and blasphemies; also, concerning the rejection of the law and sacrifices, and the return of the captives to their own land.

“And it came to pass in the seventh year, in the fifth month, on the tenth day of the month, that men from the elders of Israel came to inquire of the Lord, and they sat before me, etc.” (Hieron.)

After eleven full months and five days from the preceding vision, the word again comes to the prophet, after men from the elders of the house of Israel came to inquire of God and sat before him.

Many examples testify that it was the custom of the people of Israel to ask the Lord through the prophets whatever they wished to know. When Saul was seeking the donkeys, he went to Samuel and received advice from his servant that he should offer the prophet a quarter of a shekel (1 Kings 9). When Jeroboam’s son was sick, his wife was sent to Shiloh to Ahijah [Abijah] the prophet, carrying gifts—loaves, cakes, grapes, and a jar of honey—in order to learn about her son’s illness (1 Kings 14). David also asks the prophet Nathan, another prophet, whether he ought to build a temple for the Lord (2 Samuel 7). Ahab inquires whether he should go up to Ramoth-gilead or not (1 Kings 22). In Isaiah and in the Book of Kings, what is to come upon Sennacherib is announced (2 Kings 19; Isaiah 37).

Nor is it surprising that in the Old Testament the prophets announce to individuals the things that are to come, since we read that Agabus prophesied what was going to happen to Paul (Acts 21). For it is written in Deuteronomy: “The nations whom the Lord your God is destroying before you will listen to dreamers and diviners, but the Lord your God has not given you such a thing” (Deuteronomy 18).

It belongs to the nations to approach Chaldeans, soothsayers, haruspices, diviners, lot-casters, and the oracles of demons, by which their error is mocked. Thus now also the elders of Israel approach the prophet in order to inquire of the Lord through him; yet the text says nothing about their question, since the one who was to be questioned knew what they were asking. In this there is a miracle: he knows why they have come and answers the things that their silent speech held within their hearts.

[Col. 0717C] “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, speak to the elders of Israel and say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Have you come to inquire of me? As I live, says the Lord God, I will not answer you.”

To the holy, when they ask appropriately, a promise is given: “While you are still speaking, I will say, ‘Here I am.’” But to sinners, such as the elders of Israel were, whose crimes the prophet describes below, no answer is given, but a rebuke for their sins. He adds an oath: “As I live,” so that the sentence of refusal may be firmer.

“If you judge them, if you judge them, son of man.” They had indeed come to inquire, wishing to learn the future concerning matters about which they were uncertain. “But you, son of man, judge them,” so that there may be not a prophet’s answer but the sentence of a judge on account of the iniquities they had committed and the crimes of their fathers they had followed.

Or certainly: “If I have avenged them with vengeance.” The meaning is that they were so covered with iniquity that they were not even worthy of correction and reproof, according to what is said in the prophet: “I will no longer punish your daughters when they commit adultery, nor your daughters-in-law” (Hosea 4). Thus sinners who have entered into the depths of sin are abandoned to do the desires of their hearts.

“Show them the abominations of their fathers, and say to them.” If the sins of fathers do not pass over to their children, why are the abominations and iniquities of the fathers now charged against the elders? For this reason: to show that they are doing things like their parents and drawing out the longest possible cord of sin through inherited evil, so that those whose vices they imitate may fear their punishments.

[Col. 0718A] “Thus says the Lord God: On the day when I chose Israel and lifted up my hand over the offspring of the house of Jacob, and appeared to them in the land of Egypt, I lifted up my hand over them, saying: I am the Lord your God. On that day I lifted up my hand over them to bring them out of the land of Egypt into a land that I had provided for them, flowing with milk and honey, which is glorious among all lands, etc.”

In Egypt, therefore, he became known to the people and to the offspring of the house of Jacob, when he lifted up his hand over them against the Egyptians and said, “I am the Lord your God.” He chose them in order to bring them out of the land of Egypt into a land flowing with milk and honey. For they were not yet able to take solid food; like little children and infants, they needed honey and milk appropriate to infancy.

According to the literal sense, no one who has considered the entire land from Rhinocorura to Mount Taurus and to the River Euphrates, together with the power of its cities and the pleasantness of its regions—Palestine, Phoenicia, Arabia, Syria, Coele-Syria, Cilicia, and the other territories that the Lord promised to Israel if it kept God’s commandments—can doubt that the land of Judah was renowned and more fertile than all other lands. Because Israel did not receive these territories, the fault lay in its unbelief.

Even in Palestine and the province of Judah many peoples remained who were not expelled. For the promisor is not guilty if the one to whom the promise is made makes himself unworthy of it, especially when the promisor offers a choice: “If you are willing and obey me, you shall eat the good things of the land; but if you refuse, the sword shall devour you” (Isaiah 1).

Those who are chosen are therefore chosen for the present; the one who is chosen is not thereby immediately incapable of being tested or of perishing. Saul was chosen as king, and Judas as an apostle, yet afterward they fell through their own fault.

The lifting up or extension of the hand indicates the posture of one striking, so that he might strike the Egyptians on their behalf and liberate the people of Israel from Egypt.

“And I said to them: Let each one cast away the offenses of his eyes, and do not defile yourselves with the idols of Egypt. I am the Lord your God.”

He commands those leaving Egypt first to forget the idols to which they had long been enslaved—or rather, to cast them away from their eyes, so that they might not consider them worthy even of being seen, and no longer submit to the things by which they had long been defiled. “I,” he says, “am the Lord your God,” not the monstrous objects of Egypt, nor the images of various creatures.

But for us too, when we leave Egypt, we are commanded to cast away the offenses of our eyes, so that we may not delight in the things in which we formerly delighted in the world, and may not be defiled by the images of Egypt—namely, by the inventions of philosophers and heretics, which are rightly called idols.

From spectacles also—or rather, from the offenses of Egypt—we must remove our eyes: from the arena, the circus, the theaters, and everything that contaminates the purity of the soul and enters the mind through the senses. Thus what is written is fulfilled: “Death entered through your windows.”

“And they provoked me.” The Septuagint has: “And they departed from me”; or, as Symmachus translated it, “They did not obey me.” Immediately after being called, they depart from God, so that there is no interval between the calling and the departure. This too must be noted: no one departs from God unless he has previously been with him. Hence in the Book of Job the dragon is called an apostate, a transgressor, and one who has departed.

“They would not listen to me. Each one did not cast away the abominations of his eyes, and they did not abandon the idols of Egypt” (Job 34). Therefore, he says, they provoked me and departed from me because they would not listen to me, while human free will is preserved. They did everything that I had commanded by the law that they should not do, immediately despairing of salvation, murmuring against Moses, and distrusting God’s restraints. Hence what follows:

“And I said that I would pour out my indignation upon them and fulfill my anger against them in the midst of the land of Egypt.”

As soon as I commanded them to abandon or cast away the offenses of their eyes and not to defile themselves at all with the idols of Egypt, they provoked me and refused to listen to what I said. On the contrary, they did what I had commanded them not to do. Therefore I had resolved to pour out my fury and indignation upon them and fulfill the anger that I had conceived in my mind in the midst of the land of Egypt, because they had not yet gone out of Egypt.

For what follows says: “So I cast them out of the land of Egypt and brought them into the wilderness.” This shows that they had not yet left Egypt when he wished to pour out his indignation upon them, fulfill his anger against them, and strike them in the midst of the land of Egypt.

“And I acted for the sake of my name, so that it would not be profaned before the nations among whom they were, and among whom I had appeared to them in order to bring them out of the land of Egypt.”

What I had planned to do as an act of justice I did not do, because of the greatness of my mercy, lest my name be profaned and I appear unable to complete what I had promised to Israel. I therefore spared my name, lest the nations among whom I had become known in the land of Egypt have an occasion for blasphemy.

Up to this point the prophet describes what he promised them while they were in the land of Egypt, how they immediately offended him, and what the Lord planned against them but did not do. What follows he spoke to those who had left Egypt:

[Col. 0719D] “So I cast them out of the land of Egypt and brought them into the wilderness, and I gave them my statutes and showed them my judgments, which, if a person does them, he shall live by them. Moreover, I gave them my Sabbaths, so that they might be a sign between me and them, and might know that I am the Lord who sanctifies them. But the house of Israel provoked me in the wilderness; they did not walk in my statutes, and they rejected my judgments, which, if a person does them, he shall live by them. They greatly profaned my Sabbaths. So I said that I would pour out my fury upon them in the wilderness and consume them, but I acted for the sake of my name, so that it would not be profaned before the nations from whom I had cast them out in their sight.”

These words are addressed to those who were brought out of Egypt into the wilderness, so that, freed from the vices of the Egyptians, they might more easily fulfill God’s commandments in solitude, carry out his judgments, and keep his Sabbaths. These were given as a sign between the one who gave them and those to whom they were given, as Scripture says:

“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Command the children of Israel and say to them: See that you keep my Sabbaths, for this is a sign between me and you throughout your generations, so that you may know that I am the Lord who sanctifies you. Keep the Sabbath, because it is holy for you; whoever profanes it shall surely die. Whoever does any work on it, that person shall be cut off from the midst of his people” (Exodus 31).

The Sabbath and circumcision were therefore given as signs of the true Sabbath and true circumcision, so that we might know that in the perfect and eternal Sabbath we must rest from the works of the world, and circumcise not the foreskin but the heart.

Thus, working for six days, we rest on the seventh, so that day and night we may do nothing other than recognize that all our life belongs to the Lord. When the week returns, we consecrate ourselves entirely to his name, so that through the sanctification of the day we may remember the Lord who sanctifies us.

The Lord gave these commandments, statutes, and observance of the Sabbath in the wilderness so that those who performed them might live by them, not pass from them to greater things, as was promised in the Gospel. They violated them not once or slightly, but greatly, so that the intensification [ἐπίτασις] of the violation might be shown.

Therefore he said and resolved in his mind to pour out his fury upon them in the wilderness and consume them, when he spoke to Moses: “Leave me, and, angered with fury against them, I will destroy them” (Exodus 32). But he did not do so, sparing the Egyptians and the other nations lest they be scandalized, and also sparing those whom he had pitied while awaiting the repentance of the converted.

It must be noted that when he spoke after their offense while they were still in Egypt, he said: “I acted for the sake of my name, so that it would not be profaned before the nations from whom I cast them out in their sight.” At that time they were still in the midst of those nations, because they had not yet left. But now, after they have gone out, it is said: “From whom I cast them out in their sight.”

[Col. 0720D] “Therefore I lifted up my hand over them in the wilderness, so that I would not bring them into the land that I had given them, flowing with milk and honey, the preeminent land among all lands, because they had rejected my judgments, had not walked in my statutes, and had profaned my Sabbaths; for their heart followed the idols. But my eye spared them, so that I would not kill them; I did not consume them in the wilderness.”

I had resolved to pour out all my fury upon them, destroy them, and consume them. But I acted for the sake of my name, so that it would not be profaned among the nations—namely, the Amalekites and the others who fought against them in the wilderness—and so I would not bring them into the land that I promised them, flowing with milk and honey, the preeminent land among all lands, or, possibly, “a honeycomb.” For the cause of this punishment and sentence is stated: “Because they had rejected my judgments, had not walked in my statutes, and had profaned my Sabbaths.”

The cause behind that cause was that they should not do these things, because their heart followed the idols of Egypt. Yet, he says, my eye spared them, so that I would not kill, destroy, or utterly consume them.

Here it is asked how he spared those whose corpses fell in the wilderness, since, except for Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb the son of Jephunneh, no one entered the promised land. From this we understand that they are alive, not reserved for eternal punishments, not erased from the book of the living, and not consumed before the face of the Lord.

For if they are to be considered to have perished because they were not brought into the promised land, then Moses too perished, since he saw the promised land but did not enter it. Concerning him the Lord speaks in the Book of Joshua: “Moses my servant is dead” (Joshua 1:2). And in Malachi: “Remember the law of Moses my servant” (Malachi 4). In Jeremiah the Lord speaks of him as of a friend and intimate companion: “Though Moses and Samuel stood before me” (Jeremiah 15).

Otherwise, we must believe that Moses’ prayers were heard when, interceding for the people, he said: “If you forgive their sin, forgive it; but if you will not, erase me from your book, which you have written” (Exodus 32).

To show that God’s sentence upon sons and servants is not for destruction but for correction, let us hear the testimonies of Scripture: “My son, do not reject the discipline of the Lord, nor lose heart when you are reproved by him; for whom the Lord loves he disciplines, and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12). And elsewhere: “When he was killing them, then they sought him” (Psalm 77). And in the song of Deuteronomy: “I kill and I make alive” (Deuteronomy 32).

We can also say according to the literal sense that he did not erase or consume them together with their stock and descendants, but, after killing the fathers, spared the sons whom he brought into the promised land.

“I also said to their sons in the wilderness: Do not fall into the statutes of your fathers, nor keep their judgments, nor defile yourselves with their idols. I am the Lord your God. Walk in my statutes, keep my judgments, and perform them. Sanctify my Sabbaths, so that they may be a sign between me and you, and so that it may be known that I am the Lord your God.”

After the killing of the fathers who fell in the wilderness, he gives commandments to their sons, whose salvation was the occasion of mercy toward the fathers. The Lord’s eye, he says, spared them so that he would not kill or destroy them entirely, but would preserve the fathers in the sons.

He attests the same things that he had spoken to the fathers: after they have walked in his statutes, kept his judgments, and preserved the sanctification of the Sabbath, which was given as a sign, then they will know that he is their Lord God.

The statutes and ordinances of the fathers, and their judgments, signify an ingrained error, so that they may not imitate the sins of those whose punishments they behold.

[Col. 0722A] “But the sons provoked me: they did not walk in my statutes, nor keep my judgments, to perform the things which, if a person does them, he shall live by them. They profaned my Sabbaths, and I threatened to pour out my fury upon them and fulfill my anger against them in the wilderness. But I withdrew my hand and acted for the sake of my name, so that it would not be profaned before the nations from whom I had cast them out in their sight.”

But the sons too, he says, followed the crimes of their parents and did everything they had done. Therefore they deserved a similar sentence. Yet they were preserved by the same greatness of my mercy by which their fathers were preserved, and for the same reasons for which I had shown mercy to their fathers, so that, as the one and same Creator of both, I might mitigate my anger by similar patience.

We pass quickly over what is clear and move on to more obscure matters.

[Col. 0722B] “Again I lifted up my hand against them in the wilderness, to scatter them among the nations and disperse them throughout the lands, because they had not performed my judgments, had rejected my statutes, had profaned my Sabbaths, and their eyes had followed the idols of their fathers. Therefore I also gave them statutes that were not good and judgments by which they would not live, and I defiled them through their gifts when they offered every firstborn that opens the womb because of their transgressions. And they shall know that I am the Lord.”

The Scripture does not say where, in the Old Testament, the Lord lifted up his hand against the sons of those who had fallen in the wilderness, intending to scatter them among the nations. But from what is reported here, we must believe that it happened.

Or this signifies that, after they entered the promised land, at various times, on account of many sins, they were handed over to different nations and kings. At that time the Lord’s statutes, which by nature were good, and the judgments by which believers could live, became for them “not good,” since in captivity they were entirely unable to keep the precepts of the law and perform what the divine word had commanded.

He did not say, “I gave them bad statutes,” but “not good” ones. For it does not immediately follow that what is not good is bad, just as the Apostle teaches (1 Corinthians 7) that it is good for a man not to touch a woman, but that, because of sexual immorality, it is good for each person to have his own wife and for each to possess his own vessel in sanctification and purity. If he does not do this, it is neither good nor bad.

God therefore gave those dispersed among the nations statutes that were not good—that is, he abandoned them to their own thoughts and desires, so that they would do what is unfitting. And he defiled them through their gifts, like a priest separating lepers from the people and demonstrating that they were defiled, since they offered to idols what they ought to have offered to God and passed through the fire of Baal every firstborn that opens the womb—that is, their firstborn children.

After they had been abandoned by God and handed over to the worship of idols, they would then understand that he was the Lord whom, through their own fault, they had provoked to anger.

Symmachus interpreted this passage more clearly, using the future instead of the past: “Therefore I too will give them statutes that are not good and judgments because of which they will not live, and I will defile them because of their gifts, because they consecrate and pass through fire every firstborn that opens the womb, so that I may destroy them, and they shall know that I am the Lord.”

The meaning is this: Because I saw that the sons equaled their fathers in crimes and did the same things by which their fathers had offended God, I wished to divide them among the nations and scatter them throughout the whole world. I intended to give them statutes that were not good and judgments by which they would not live, so that I might defile them through their gifts, since they consecrated all their firstborn to idols, destroy them forever, and make them know that I was God.

By this he shows that he did not give statutes that were not good to those who remained in the wilderness, but that he planned to give what he did not give to those whom he wished to scatter among the nations and make strangers throughout the world, so that there, through their own fault, they would make God’s good commandments “not good,” while offering to idols what God had commanded them to offer to him.

It may also be said that before their offense they received only the Decalogue; after idolatry and blasphemy, however, they received the many ceremonies of the law, so that they might offer to God the sacrifices they had been offering to demons, and so that, by comparison with sacrilege, what was not good in itself and yet not actually evil—because it was offered to God—might become lighter. It was nevertheless not good because they had offended the author of goodness (Gregory, *Moralia*, book 28, chapter 17).

For when the weak people unwillingly bore the rags of the commandments, they reached a firmer condition through that very bondage. Because fear had first restrained them from sin, they afterward appropriately passed into the freedom of the spirit.

The Lord himself reproves through the prophet these rags that he gave to beginners, saying: “I gave them statutes that were not good.” Things that are bad cease to seem bad in comparison with worse things, and things that are good do not appear good in comparison with better things.

Thus, just as Judah, which sinned more grievously than Sodom and Samaria, is told: “You justified your sisters in all your abominations that you committed” (Ezekiel 16), so, in comparison with the commandments of the better New Testament that followed, the good commandments given to the inexperienced are said to be “not good.” For minds clinging to the practices of bodily life could not be torn away from lower things unless they advanced gradually through a progressive form of preaching.

[Col. 0723C] “Therefore speak to the house of Israel, son of man, and say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Moreover, in this also your fathers blasphemed me, when they had despised me, treating me with contempt, and I had brought them into the land over which I had lifted up my hand to give it to them. They saw every high hill and every leafy tree, and there they sacrificed their victims; there they presented the provocation of their offering; there they placed the fragrance of their offering, and there they poured out their libations. And I said to them: What is this high place to which you are going? And its name was called ‘high place’ to this day.”

(Hieron.) I wished, he says, to scatter among all nations those who were sinning in the wilderness, and to give them statutes that were not good, so that they might sacrifice to idols what they ought to have offered to me and consecrate every firstborn to them through fire, in order that I might kill and destroy them.

But when he says, “I wished,” he shows that he did not do what he wished. The clause that follows—“And they shall know that I am the Lord”—is not found in the Septuagint. For it did not seem fitting to them that, after their killing, they should know that he was the Lord.

“But you, son of man, speak to them again,” that is, to the elders of the house of Israel who came to question you. Your fathers, from whose stock you descended, blasphemed me in this also and treated me as nothing. After I had brought them into the land that they possessed by my strength, the land that I had given them to possess, they turned it into an occasion for provoking me.

When they saw every high hill and leafy tree, they sacrificed on the mountains, in groves, and in wooded places; they sacrificed victims to idols and poured out libations.

“When I saw this, I said to them: What is Bamah?” For this is what *bamah* means: “high place.” Or, “Why are you entering such a place,” which you have chosen for yourselves among all the hills, so that even to this day such places are called *bamoth*, and the ancient error retains its former name?

[Col. 0724B] “Therefore say to the house of Israel: Thus says the Lord: You defile yourselves in the way of your fathers, and you commit fornication after their offenses. In the offering of your gifts, when you pass your sons through fire, you defile yourselves with all your idols to this day. And I will answer you, house of Israel: As I live, says the Lord God, I will not answer you.”

You imitate the vices of your fathers and walk along the same paths, so that similar offenses may deserve a similar punishment. You have advanced so far in wickedness that you consecrate your sons to demons by passing them through fire.

Nor is this sufficient if done only once; even to the present day you continue to do the same—not that the elders in captivity are doing this, but that those who were living in Jerusalem, and over whom captivity was impending, did not cease to do all these things.

And although you are bound by such great crimes, you seek, he says, an answer from me. “As I live, says the Lord God,” and I swear by myself that I will not answer you. And what follows says:

[Col. 0724C] “Nor shall the thought of your mind be fulfilled when you say: ‘We shall be like the nations and like the families of the earth, to worship wood and stone.’ As I live, says the Lord God, I who will reign over you with a strong hand, an outstretched arm, and poured-out fury.”

The meaning is this: Do not think that the thoughts with which you blaspheme against me can be fulfilled. You say: “We do not want to be under the Lord or to be called his people. Rather, just as all the nations throughout the world live according to their own will, worship wood and stones, and serve idols, so we too shall be one nation among the many.”

God answers this and swears by himself, saying: “I will not abandon or despise you, as negligent masters customarily despise runaway servants, but I will draw you back under my rule. With an outstretched and striking arm and with fury poured out, I will restore you to your former servitude. I will reign over you, so that, whether you wish it or not, you will have me as king and will experience an angry king whose mercy you have neglected.”

[Col. 0725A]

“And I will bring you out from the peoples, and gather you from the lands in which you have been scattered; with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, and with wrath poured out, I will reign over you.”

“Nor,” he says, “will I allow you to remain among the nations or to be held in everlasting captivity; rather, I will bring you out from the peoples and gather you from the lands into which hostile necessity scattered you here and there for service.” I will do this not to destroy and obliterate you, but to be your King. From this we understand that even what heretics call the Creator’s cruelty sounds forth clemency, since he becomes angry and rages for this purpose, pouring out all his wrath so as to draw back to his kingdom those who chose the tyranny of demons for their service.

[Col. 0725B] “And I will bring you into the wilderness of the peoples, and there I will enter into judgment with you face to face. Just as I entered into judgment against your fathers in the wilderness of the land of Egypt, so I will judge you, says the Lord, and subject you to my scepter; and I will bring you into the bonds of the covenant. And I will select from among you the transgressors and the impious; I will bring them out from the land of their sojourn, but they shall not enter the land of Israel, and you shall know that I am the Lord.”

“I will do,” says the Lord, “for you who are in Babylon and now serve idols what I did for your fathers in Egypt: I will bring you into the wilderness of the peoples, and there I will enter into judgment with you face to face, just as I entered into judgment against them when they came out of Egypt. And after I have judged you, I will subject you to my scepter and authority, and I will make a covenant with you; I will bring you into your land in the bonds of love, so that, bound by my love, you may in no way depart from me. But the transgressors and the impious, who in hardness of heart persist in evil deeds, I will select from among you—not for possession, but for rejection. I will indeed bring them out from the land of their sojourn, but, once brought out, they shall not enter the land of Israel; rather, they shall perish in various regions. By distinguishing between the good and the evil, you shall know that I am the Lord, who does all things with judgment.”

The discourse hastens on to what follows, and we run briefly through each point so as to provide readers with the meaning alone.

[Col. 0725D] “And you, house of Israel, thus says the Lord God: Let each of you go after your idols and serve them.
