But if even in this you will not listen to me and will profane my holy name further through your gifts and your idols, on my holy mountain, on the high mountain of Israel, says the Lord God, there the whole house of Israel shall serve me—all of them, I say, in the land in which they shall please me. There I will seek your firstfruits and the beginning of your tithes, in all your holy offerings. I will receive you as a pleasing fragrance when I bring you out from the peoples and gather you from the lands into which you were scattered; and I will be sanctified in you before the eyes of the nations, and you shall know that I am the Lord.”

Concerning this mountain on which the whole house of Israel will serve God, Isaiah and Micah sang with one voice:

[Col. 0726A] “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be manifest on the summit of the mountains, and it shall be raised above the hills; all the nations shall flow to it, and many peoples shall go and say: ‘Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the mountain of the God of Jacob. He will teach us his ways, and we shall walk in his paths.’ For from Zion the law shall go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. II; Mic. IV).

And again Isaiah says:

“Go up onto a high mountain, you who announce good news to Zion; raise and exalt your voice, you who evangelize Jerusalem” (Isa. XL).

We understand this mountain to be either Zion or the Church—which is interpreted as “watchtower” and is established in the height of holy doctrines—or the Lord and Savior himself, in whom both the firstfruits and the tithes and every act of worship are transformed into a pleasing fragrance. Thus all the surrounding nations, seeing that the Lord’s people have been saved, may glorify God and those who have been saved may know that he himself is the Lord.

[Col. 0726B] “When I bring you into the land of Israel, into the land over which I raised my hand, swearing that I would give it to your fathers, then you shall know that I am the Lord.”

“When I bring you,” he says, “into the land of Israel, over which I raised my hand, swearing that I would bring your fathers into it—a land which they lost through their own fault, and which you received not so much through your own merit as through my clemency—then you shall know that I am the Lord.”

[Col. 0726C] “And you shall remember your ways and all your crimes by which you were defiled in them, and you shall be displeased with yourselves in your own sight, because of all your wicked deeds that you committed. And you shall know that I am the Lord, when I do good to you for the sake of my name, not according to your evil ways or according to the worst crimes of the house of Israel, says the Lord God.”

We cannot remember our crimes and faults unless we have been brought into the land of Israel and, once placed there, say with the Apostle: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Cor. XV).

“And you shall be displeased,” he says, “with yourselves in your own sight, because of all your wicked deeds that you committed”; or, as Symmachus translated it: “And you shall seem small to yourselves because of all your wicked deeds that you have done,” so that, after they have been exalted, they may believe themselves humble, because the Lord gives grace to the humble. And elsewhere it is written: “Before destruction a man’s heart is exalted, and before exaltation it is humbled” (Prov. XIII). Destruction follows pride, and exaltation follows humility.

“And you shall know that I am the Lord, when I do good to you.” We know the Lord and Savior more fully when he did good to us, suffered for our sins, and bore our iniquities and grieved for us—not because of any merit in those who are saved, but for the sake of his name. Otherwise, our life and our worst crimes deserved not mercy but punishment.

Whatever we have said about the people of Israel—who, after being freed from Egypt, committed many sins in the wilderness and offended God, and afterward, when brought into the promised land, revered idols and worshiped pieces of wood and stones, yet were later preserved by God’s clemency—let us apply to those who were freed from the Egypt of this age by the Lord’s uplifted hand and brought into the wilderness of vices, who again longed for Egypt and did things for which they ought to have been punished, but nevertheless were preserved through repentance, not by their own merit but by the Lord’s clemency.

BOOK NINE.

[Col. 0727]

PREFACE.

When blessed Jerome had reached this point in expounding the prophetic book, he began the opening of the seventh book as follows:

“Long ago, when we were boys, we read: ‘Nothing is so easy that it does not become difficult when you do it unwillingly.’”

I have placed this saying here so that you may know, most learned Emperor, how difficult it is for me—after the excuse by which I wished to free myself from this work—to do what may perhaps be easy for others more skilled than I: to expound a prophetic book wrapped in the most obscure mysteries. I cannot accomplish this from my own understanding; moreover, because the dimming eyes of old age suffer something of blessed Isaac’s affliction, I am quite unable to reread the statements of others by night-light; even in the brightness of sun and day they scarcely become fit for me to read. Therefore I ask your reverence kindly to receive what I have excerpted from the judgments of the holy Fathers and arranged in an order for reading. And, as I have already said, if the books prove unequal to one another in brevity or length, attribute this to the brevity or length of the visions, since wherever we can, we do not wish to separate things joined together or fit discordant material into a single collection.

[Col. 0727C] THE TWENTIETH CHAPTER FOLLOWS.

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set your face toward the way of the south, and let your drops fall toward the south-west, and prophesy against the forest of the field of the south, and say to the southern forest: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will kindle a fire in you, and it shall consume every green tree and every dry tree in you. The flame of the burning shall not be extinguished, and every face from the south to the north shall be burned in it. And all flesh shall see that I, the Lord, have kindled it, and it shall not be extinguished. And I said: ‘Ah, ah, ah, Lord God! They say of me: “Does he not speak in parables?”’” and so forth.

The divine word speaks through the metaphor (μεταφορά) of the forest against Jerusalem, which is a dwelling place of beasts and savage men: it will kindle it, and all its trees will be consumed. He does not call them trees that needed fruit, but wood prepared for burning. First he burns the green wood in it, according to what we read in this same Prophet: “Begin with my holy ones.” Afterwards he burns the dry wood, which could contain nothing green—namely, the saints and sinners together—so that some may escape the evils of captivity by death, while others may be handed over to eternal punishments.

When it adds, “from the south to the north,” this indicates from Jerusalem to Babylon, so that the whole route of those going into captivity, falling by sword, famine, and pestilence, may be filled with destruction. For those who are in Babylon, Jerusalem lies to the south. Conversely, Jeremiah’s pot, which signifies Jerusalem, is kindled from the face of the north—that is, from Babylon.

Beautifully, at the beginning he says, “Let your drops fall toward the south-west,” so that God’s entire anger may not appear to have been poured out, but only a certain drop and portion. But if there is such savagery in a drop, what must be imagined in the full rains, so that all flesh—which is to see the salvation of God—may recognize through the burning of the forests and the flame that no aid can extinguish that he himself is the Lord?

Understanding this, the prophet replied: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God!” Or, as the Septuagint translated it: “By no means, Lord.” And it adds: “They say to me: ‘Does he not speak in parables?’” Or, “Is this a parable?” The sense is: “Speak more plainly; we do not understand through the parable what you are saying. Reveal your meaning to us in God’s open speech.”

Tropologically, however, Theman, Nageb, and Darom—which the Septuagint rendered as Egypt—can be understood as Egypt. For we frequently read in Daniel that “south” is taken for Egypt, while Egypt refers to the straits of this present world.

Ezekiel therefore prophesies what evils are to come upon the world. He calls it a forest that lacks fruit-bearing trees and is instead a habitation of beasts. Concerning it Psalm XXVIII also says: “The voice of the Lord brings the deer to birth, and he will uncover the dense thickets of the forests.” These are the forests and wooded places that devoured more of Absalom’s army in battle than the sword killed.

The green wood is first kindled in the forests, and then the dry wood: those who live in evil and those who are dead to righteousness. When it says, “And all faces from the south to the north shall be burned in it,” it means from those who appeared to be fervent in spirit to those who, as iniquity increased and the love of many grew cold, lost their former warmth. Thus all flesh may perceive that the Lord’s flame is not extinguished.

The Prophet prays that what the Lord threatened may not take place—namely, that the forest be kindled and all the wood consumed—so that they may either still receive an opportunity for repentance, or he may not be forced to announce grievous things, especially since the people do not understand them and, through the obscurity of the words, are driven still further toward madness.

CHAPTER XXI. The word of the Lord against Jerusalem concerning the misery of the doubled or tripled sword. The word of the Lord against the sons of Ammon concerning the drawn sword.

[Col. 0729A] “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set your face toward Jerusalem, and let your drops fall upon the sanctuaries, and prophesy against the land of Israel. And you shall say to the land of Israel: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, and I will draw my sword from its sheath, and I will kill in you the righteous and the wicked. But because I have killed in you the righteous and the wicked, my sword shall go out from its sheath against all flesh, from the south to the north. And all flesh shall know that I, the Lord, have drawn my sword from its sheath, irrevocably,” and so forth.

Because above he had said, “They say of me, ‘Does this man not speak in parables?’” and the people were demanding an open statement, the Lord now speaks more plainly what he had expressed through metaphor—or, as others translated it, through a proverb. The southern forest, Nageb, Darom, and Theman, means Jerusalem; its temple means the Holy of Holies; and the whole land of Judea, together with the flame that is to consume the forest, is understood as the devouring sword drawn from its sheath to kill the wicked and the righteous. This is the green and dry wood.

Thus the Lord also says: “If they do these things in the green wood, what will they do in the dry?” (Luke XXIII). What he had said there—“And all flesh shall see that I, the Lord, have kindled it,” namely, the forest or flame, “and it shall not be extinguished”—he now expresses in other words: “So that all flesh may know that I, the Lord, have drawn my sword from its sheath irrevocably.”

Indeed, against Jerusalem the flame was not lulled, the fire was not extinguished, and the sword was not recalled, because only a short time intervened before Jerusalem, together with its temple, was set ablaze by Babylonian fire.

[Col. 0729C] “And you, son of man, groan in the breaking of your loins, and groan in bitterness before them. And when they say to you, ‘Why are you groaning?’ you shall say: ‘Because of the report; for it is coming, and every heart shall melt, and all hands shall be weakened, and every spirit shall faint, and water shall flow down all knees. Behold, it is coming and shall happen, says the Lord God.’”

At first he had said: “Prophesy, or let your drops fall, toward the south, the south-west, and the south; and toward the southern forest.” Because this seemed obscure and the people did not understand the prophet’s words, the matter is presented a second time more plainly: the southern forest means Jerusalem, all the fruitless trees at whose roots the axe has been placed mean its inhabitants, and the sword is interpreted in place of the fire.

Third, the prophet is commanded, when they are silent and do not ask why he has prophesied these things, to perform actions that will make them ask, and then to answer what the Lord has spoken.

“Groan,” he says, “and howl,” not with a light voice or restrained grief, but “in the breaking of your loins,” so that your groaning may come forth from your inmost entrails and from the bitterness of your soul. Do this before them, so that when they ask why you are being crushed by such groaning and what evil has happened to you that you should lament in this way, you may answer them in my words:

“For this reason I weep, and I cannot conceal the pain of my heart, because the report that had continually sounded in my ears is being fulfilled in action. What is coming is the approaching army of the raging Babylonians. When it comes and besieges Jerusalem, then every heart will melt and all hands will be weakened, so that, when terror seizes human minds, no one will dare resist.

“For the spirit of all the warriors will faint, and such trembling and fear will seize everyone that, compelled by terror, their limbs and entrails will dissolve, and the bladder will be unable to retain its fluid, so that urine will soil the knees. It is natural that when fear compels it, the bladder is relaxed and fluid flows against a person’s will. This also tends to happen in severe illness, so that after the strength of the sick has failed, not only their knees but also their beds are soiled.”

“Behold,” he says, “what I have often foretold is coming; it is being fulfilled in action, and what has been spoken—not by me, but by the Lord—will happen.”

I know that someone, in connection with “the breaking of the loins” and “water flowing,” repeated many testimonies, so that the chastity of the Prophet might be preserved, and interpreted the bitterness of the soul and the inward pain of the mind as meaning that the waters of semen soil the knees; but this interpretation does not apply to the present passage.

[Col. 0730B] “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, prophesy and say: Thus says the Lord God: Speak: ‘A sword, a sword has been sharpened and polished, sharpened to slaughter victims; it has been sharpened, and it has been polished to shine. You who move the scepter of my son, you have cut down every tree. And I gave it to be polished, so that it might be held in the hand.’ This is the sharpened sword, and this is the polished sword, so that it may be in the hand of the killer. Cry out and howl, son of man, because this has come upon my people. This is against all the rulers of Israel; those who had fled have been delivered to the sword together with my people. Therefore slap your thigh, because it has been tested, and do this when it has overthrown the scepter and it shall be no more, says the Lord God.

“‘You, therefore, son of man, prophesy, and strike hand against hand; let the sword be doubled and tripled—the sword of those who are slain. This is the sword of the great slaughter, which makes them stupefied and causes their hearts to melt, and multiplies the ruins. At all their gates I have given the confusion of the sharpened sword, polished to shine, equipped for slaughter. Sharpen yourself; go to the right or to the left, wherever the desire of your face directs you. Indeed, I too will strike hand against hand and will fulfill my indignation; I, the Lord, have spoken,’” and so forth.

It would be excessive to set down both editions, and the length of the books would be increased, especially where there is either no difference or only a small one. Therefore I will present a few points that differ from what we have said.

Where we have: “You who move the scepter of my son, you have cut down every tree,” they translated: “Kill, despise, reject every tree.”

Again, where we have: “Those who had fled were delivered to the sword,” both they and the others translated: “My guests,” or “the inhabitants.”

Where we have: “Slap your thigh,” they put: “Strike with your hand.”

Where we translated: “And do this when he has overthrown the scepter,” their edition has: “The tribe has been rejected.”

He is speaking to the sword of Nebuchadnezzar, so that it may come against Jerusalem and be sharpened and polished, since many are to be slaughtered. He addresses the sword itself:

“You are the one who moves and overthrows the scepter of my son”—that is, the rule of the people of Israel—“and you cut down every tree,” the entire multitude of the people.

“I gave this sword,” he says, “so that it might be held in the hand of Nebuchadnezzar and be in the hand of a most powerful man.”

[Col. 0731A] Therefore, O prophet, cry out and howl, and testify to the evils that are pressing upon them with the lamentation of your voice. This sword spared no one and left no one untouched by the impending evils. It came upon the people; it came upon the rulers of Israel; it came upon my guests and priests who dwelt in my temple.

Therefore, “strike your thigh or your hand, and assume the posture of one who mourns.” For this sword has been tested by me. And this will happen when it has overthrown my scepter and kingdom, which will no longer exist and will come to an end in King Zedekiah.

Again, Prophet, I command you: you who had struck your thigh, strike your hands in astonishment and wonder, so that the sword may come not only once but a second and a third time to kill. First Nebuchadnezzar had come when he carried away Jehoiakim. Second, when Jehoiakim was reigning. Third, when Zedekiah was reigning.

And this is the tripled sword, when a great slaughter took place and it multiplied the ruins to such an extent that they were stupefied in mind and melted in heart, and it brought confusion at all their gates.

The sharpened and polished sword, made bright, equipped and prepared for slaughter, is therefore commanded to go either to the right or, if it wishes, to the left: “Wherever,” he says, “the desire of your face pleases you, enter boldly, with me as your leader and helper. ‘I will strike hand against hand,’ so that, as your supporter and encourager, I may urge you on while you rage against my adversaries. Do not hesitate, do not fear, and do not be afraid to suffer what Sennacherib suffered. I am the Lord who has spoken. You are the minister of my will; fulfill my sentence.”

According to the Ἀναγωγή—that is, the spiritual interpretation—we can understand the sharp sword prepared for slaughter as the devil. Concerning him the Apostle says: “To hand such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved” (1 Cor. V). And elsewhere: “Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I handed over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Tim. I).

And it is written in the Psalms: “He sent forth fury, anger, and distress, an assault through evil angels” (Ps. LXXVII). Some think that this is the sword that was also in the hand of the angel when Jerusalem was struck under David.

Others suspect that this refers to the sword of which it is written in the Gospel: “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword” (Matt. X)—a sword that divides every bond of kinship among them, so that the evil may fall and the saints rise again.

But it is impious to understand this of the Savior’s sword rather than of the devil, who overthrows the Lord’s scepters in the Church, who killed all among the people, both leaders and guests of God. The Lord approves this sword when it has overthrown Judas the traitor and those like him, of whom it is written that, after he had eaten the morsel, “Satan entered into him” (John XIII).

The sword of those who are slain is doubled and tripled so that Jerusalem’s sin may be expiated, because she received double for her sins from the hand of the Lord.

But the Lord rejoices and exults and encourages the raging sword to go either to the right or to the left, and wherever the desire of its face carries it, so that when the evil have been killed, the good may remain, and what is written may be fulfilled: “What has straw in common with grain? says the Lord.”

[Col. 0732A] “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: And you, son of man, mark out for yourself two ways by which the sword of the king of Babylon may come. From one land both shall go forth, and by hand he shall cast a lot; at the head of the road to the city he shall cast the lot. You shall mark out the way by which the sword may come to Rabbath of the sons of Ammon and to Judah, toward fortified Jerusalem.

“For the king of Babylon stood at the fork of the road, at the beginning of the two ways, seeking an omen, mixing arrows; he questioned idols and consulted entrails. At his right hand the divination was made concerning Jerusalem: to set up battering rams, to open his mouth for slaughter, to raise his voice in howling, to set battering rams against the gates, to heap up a rampart, to build fortifications.

“And it will be like consulting an oracle in vain in their eyes and imitating the rest of the Sabbath; but he himself will remember iniquity in order to seize them. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because you have brought your iniquities to remembrance, exposed your transgressions, and made your sins appear in all your thoughts—because, I say, you have brought them to remembrance, you shall be seized by the hand.” (Jerome.)

I know that in this passage, according to the Septuagint interpreters, I have read a multifaceted exposition that relates Rabbath of the sons of Ammon to the people of the nations, but Judah and Jerusalem to those who are gathered under Christ’s name and give dignity to the name by their deeds. It understands the king of confusion—the devil—to stand at the head of every road and lie in wait secretly, fulfilling the verse: “Beside the path they placed a stumbling block for me” (Ps. CXXXIX).

It understands him to stand at the fork of the road, either wishing to hold fast those who belong to him or desiring to acquire a new service for himself, and always to proceed toward the right—that is, toward those who have been placed on the right—so as to attack them, rejoice in slaughter, and capture wretched Jerusalem through battering rams and a mass of earthly works.

At first, indeed, it seems to him that he is accomplishing nothing and laboring in vain. But when he remembers the iniquities of those who dwell in the Church—or rather, when through evil deeds they recall to hostile powers the memory of their former crimes—all the sins and thoughts of the people are revealed. They are therefore captured because they have heaped old offenses upon new ones.

Another person may have offered this interpretation to us; we must continue with the truth of the history that we began.

When the divine word had said to me: “Prophesy, son of man, and speak to the sword, and say: ‘Sword, sword,’” and the other things contained in the prophecy of the sword, “the word of the Lord came to me a second time, saying”:

“Do you wish, son of man, to know what this sword is and to learn more openly the identity of the raging sword? Listen to what I say: Mark out two ways, so that by them the sword of the king of Babylon may come. It will indeed depart by one road from the land of the Chaldeans, but when it comes through the wilderness and desert to the fork of the land of Arabia, which is called the land of the sons of Ammon, one road leads to Jerusalem on the right, while the left leads to Rabbath of the sons of Ammon, a metropolitan city that is today called Philadelphia.

“Remembering the destruction that befell the king of Assyria, when one hundred and eighty-five thousand were killed in a single night, he will fear turning to the right and going against fortified Jerusalem. He will stand at the very crossroads and, according to the custom of his people, consult an oracle: he will put arrows into a quiver and mix them—arrows inscribed or marked with the names of individuals—so that he may see whose arrow comes out and which city he ought to attack first.

“The Greeks call this βελομαντεία, ‘divination by arrows,’ or ῥαβδομαντεία, ‘divination by rods.’ Therefore he questioned idols and consulted entrails.

“His divination was made to the right, so that he should proceed against Jerusalem and attack it, carry up earthworks, set up battering rams, build fortifications, and enclose the city. He would open his mouth for slaughter and stir up the roar of an exulting and howling army.

“By doing this he will seem to the inhabitants of Jerusalem to be consulting an oracle in vain and, as it were, observing the rest of the Sabbath—namely, playing and accomplishing no work. But the king of Babylon will rely not on his own strength but on the iniquity of the people. He knows that they have offended God, heaped the sins of their fathers upon new offenses, and exposed their transgressions to all; therefore he did not doubt victory, because he trusted in Jerusalem’s iniquity.”

This is according to the Hebrew text, from which the Septuagint differ in many places, not so much in meaning as in wording.

[Col. 0733C] “But you, profane and wicked ruler of Israel, whose day has come at the appointed time of iniquity, thus says the Lord God: Remove the turban; take off the crown. Is this not the thing that will exalt the humble and humble the exalted? Iniquity, iniquity, iniquity—I will make it so; and this shall not happen until he comes to whom judgment belongs, and I give it to him.”

After the overthrow of Jerusalem and the captivity of the people, the word is directed to the ruler of Israel. There is no doubt that Zedekiah is signified in him; in Zedekiah the rule of the kings of Israel from the line of David came to an end.

“Your day has come,” he says, “a day long predetermined for you; because of you the priesthood and kingdom of the Jewish people have perished.”

The turban is the insignia of the high priest; the crown, that is, the diadem, is the sign of the king. Is this not the turban and the crown that did nothing according to judgment, but, imitating the king of Babylon, exalted those whom it wished and humbled those whom it wished?

Therefore, not once, nor—as the Septuagint have it—twice, but a third time I will place iniquity upon you forever. It was not immediately reckoned against you, but it will remain until Christ comes, to whom judgment belongs, and the Father gives him the kingdom and priesthood—or the Church gathered from the nations:

“For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V).

And elsewhere: “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Ps. LXXI).

He is the one to whom everlasting rule and priesthood have been entrusted. Concerning him Jacob also spoke:

“The ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor the leader from his loins, until he comes to whom it has been entrusted; and he shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX).

In the place where we translated, “Is this not the thing?”, Symmachus beautifully translated, “Neither this nor that.” Because he had said, “Remove the turban; take off the crown,” he added, “Neither this nor that exists”—that is, both the kingdom and the priesthood shall cease.

Hence those who afterward, until the coming of Christ, were kings and priests alike—one of whom, Hyrcanus the high priest, placed a diadem upon his head—vainly wished to claim both this and that for himself. The kingdom was not due to him after Zedekiah, but to the one to whom it had been entrusted and who was the expectation of the nations.

Malachi also speaks concerning them:

“You priests who profane my name” (Mal. I).

And shortly afterward:

“I have no pleasure in you, and I will not accept sacrifices from your hands. For from the rising of the sun even to its setting, my name is great among the nations, and in every place sacrifice is made and a pure offering is presented to my name.”

[Col. 0734B] This pure offering, without the blood of goats, rams, and bulls, is fulfilled at Christ’s coming, because the one desired by the nations has come and the sun of righteousness has risen, in whose wings there is healing.

[Col. 0734B] “And you, son of man, prophesy and say: Thus says the Lord God to the sons of Ammon and concerning their disgrace. And you shall say: ‘Sword, sword, draw yourself for slaughter; polish yourself, so that you may kill and shine. When they saw vain things concerning you and divined lies, so that you might be placed upon the necks of the wounded wicked, whose day has come at the appointed time of iniquity, return to your sheath, to the place in which you were created. In the land of your birth I will judge you and pour out my indignation upon you. In the fire of my fury I will blow upon you, and I will deliver you into the hands of foolish men and craftsmen of corruption. You shall be food for fire; your blood shall be in the midst of the land. You shall be handed over to oblivion, because I, the Lord, have spoken.’”

We have read above that the sword of the king of Babylon stood at the head of two roads, at the fork between the right and the left, one leading to Jerusalem and the other to Rabbath of the sons of Ammon. The lot came out so that it should proceed first against Jerusalem; once Jerusalem had been attacked and captured, the kingdom and priesthood were also foretold to have perished forever.

What remained was for the sons of Ammon, and the order of the division itself demanded that we learn what happened on the left-hand road. Therefore the prophet is commanded to speak to the sons of Ammon and concerning their disgrace, since they too are to be captured, and the word is directed to the same sword:

“O sword, sword, prepared for slaughter, polished so that you may shine and kill! Although idols answered you and everything answered by demons is vain—namely, that you should threaten the necks of the wounded and that through you what the Lord had long threatened should be fulfilled—nevertheless, once you have completed your work against the sons of Ammon, return to your sheath, that is, to Babylon, to the place where you were made and created. There, in the land of your birth, I will judge you and pour out my indignation upon you, and you will be captured by the power of the Medes and Persians.”

This is stated more fully in Isaiah’s book, in the vision against Babylon:

“Behold, I will raise up the Medes against them.”

And shortly afterward:

“And that Babylon, glorious among kingdoms, renowned in the pride of the Chaldeans, shall be as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah; it shall not be inhabited forever” (Isa. XIII).

And because he had once begun speaking under the figure of the sword about the king—or rather the kingdom—of Babylon, he preserves the μεταφορά, the metaphor.

“In the fire,” he says, “of my fury I will blow upon you, so that I may cause you to be consumed by fire, and deliver you into the hands of foolish and ignorant men who have no skill in forging or sharpening swords. Thus you shall no longer be sharpened, polished, or made bright for slaughter; rather, you shall be food for fire, and your blood, which you shed while all looked on, shall flow back upon you. You shall be delivered to eternal oblivion and perish forever, because I, the Lord, have spoken”—and for him to speak is to accomplish.

CHAPTER XXII. The word of God against Jerusalem because of the shedding of blood and its other evils: concerning the people being melted like metal; concerning the one who might interpose a hedge; concerning the roaring lion; and so forth.

«And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: And you, son of man, will you not judge the city of bloodshed? And will you not show her all her abominations? And you shall say: Thus says the Lord God: A city that sheds blood in her midst, so that her time may come, and that has made idols against herself, so that she might be defiled. By your blood, which you have shed, you have become guilty; and by your idols, which you have made, you have been polluted. You have brought your days near and have caused the time of your years to arrive. Therefore I have made you a reproach to the nations and a mockery to all lands, those near you and those far from you; they will triumph over you, filthy, noble, great in destruction.

Behold, the princes of Israel, each relying on his own arm, were in you to shed blood. They dishonored father and mother in you; they oppressed the stranger in your midst; they saddened the orphan and the widow among you. You despised my sanctuaries; you profaned my sabbaths. Slanderous men were in you to shed blood, and upon the mountains they ate in you. They committed wickedness in your midst. They uncovered the nakedness of their father in you, and they humbled the woman unclean through menstruation in you. Each man committed an abomination with his neighbor’s wife; the father-in-law polluted his daughter-in-law; the brother wickedly violated his sister, the daughter of his father, in you.

They accepted gifts among you in order to shed blood. You accepted interest and increase, and you greedily oppressed your neighbors; and you forgot me, says the Lord God. Behold, I have clapped my hands over your greed, which you have practiced, and over the blood that has been shed in your midst. Will your heart endure, or will your hands prevail, in the days that I shall bring upon you? I, the Lord, have spoken, and I shall act. I shall scatter you among the nations and disperse you throughout the lands. I shall make your uncleanness cease from you, and I shall possess you in the sight of the nations; and you shall know that I am the Lord,” and so forth. (Jerome.)

“And you,” he says, “son of man”—for I shall use the customary form of address to you—“judge the city of bloodshed and show her all her abominations,” so that she may know that she deserves to suffer the captivity approaching her, and that through the shedding of much blood she has brought near the time of her ruin. First among all her crimes, she worshiped idols instead of God, and adored the works of her hands. You brought near the time of your years, which had long been announced and deferred so that you might do penance: “But according to your impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath” (Rom. II).

Therefore I made you a reproach to the nations and a derision to all the lands around you, both near and far, which will triumph over you or mock you. “Filthy, noble, great in destruction”: filthy, because you ceased to be clean; “noble” in evil, since formerly you surpassed all cities in noble excellence; “great in destruction,” so that the higher you were, the more forcefully you might fall.

Meanwhile, to pass over the rest, I shall enumerate a few things that were found in you. Your princes, judging not by justice but by the strength of power and the arm, shed innocent blood in you. Others dishonored their father and mother, or cursed their parents, as Scripture says: “Whoever curses his father and mother shall die the death.” They oppressed the stranger and sojourner in your midst, as though the hardship of sojourning and exile from his homeland were not enough for him. They saddened or oppressed the orphan and widow among you, so that those whose entire protection rests in the justice of the laws were not merely saddened but oppressed by you.

You despised my sanctuaries, or holy places, and profaned my sabbaths, so that you did not distinguish between holy and polluted, between the day appointed for religious observance and the rest of the sabbath, devoted to the worship of God, and the other days on which the law permits one to work and serve the needs of the flesh.

“Slanderous men,” or, according to Symmachus and Theodotion, “deceitful men”—the Hebrew says *rachil*—were in you, and they were murderers, whether because they blasphemed God or because they did everything through deceit or violence. And they ate upon the mountains, those who are wise in high things, and, lifted up against God in pride, they committed wickedness or incest in your midst. What is ordinarily done rarely, even in corners and secrecy, when evil people avoid the consciousness of others, you did openly.

What incest means is indicated by the following statement: “They uncovered their father’s nakedness in you,” having joined themselves to their stepmother against right and law; “they humbled the uncleanness of the menstruating woman,” neither sparing nature nor granting an interval to shame; and they neighed after the wife of their neighbor. And what is more criminal than this, the father-in-law burned with desire for his daughter-in-law, and the brother did not recognize the rights of his sister, violating not a uterine sister but one born of the same father.

They accepted gifts in order to shed innocent blood. They turned the necessities of the poor into profit, accepting interest and increase, and through greed they oppressed their friends. “But you did this,” he says, “O Jerusalem, because you forgot me”; for remembrance of God excludes every disgraceful act.

Therefore I assumed the appearance of an angry Lord, and I clapped my hands against your greed and against the blood that was shed in your midst, so that you might understand and recognize in your mind whether you could endure my anger either in spirit or with your hands. “For I, the Lord, have spoken, and I shall act,” so that after Jerusalem has been captured, I may scatter you among the nations and winnow you into the air like useless chaff to be carried here and there. And I am so merciful that my severity is turned into mercy. I shall do everything so that your uncleanness may cease from you and you may recover your former purity; and when you have recovered it, I shall possess you in the sight of all the nations, so that when you have been possessed by me, you may then understand that I am the Lord.

«And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, the house of Israel has become dross to me. All these are bronze and tin and iron and lead within the midst of the furnace; they have become silver dross. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because you have all become dross, behold, I shall gather you in the midst of Jerusalem, as silver, bronze, iron, tin, and lead are gathered into the midst of the furnace, so that I may kindle a fire in it for melting. Thus I shall gather you in my fury and in my anger; I shall rest and melt you, and I shall kindle you in the fire of my fury, and you shall be melted in its midst, as silver is melted in the midst of the furnace. So shall you be in its midst. And you shall know that I, the Lord, have poured out my indignation upon you.”

Now *dross* signifies the filth and refuse of metals. Accordingly, when captivity is near—indeed, when the city’s destruction is imminent—fire is applied, so that under the image of smelting pure silver may remain, which had been mixed with and corrupted by bronze, tin, iron, and lead. Three of these—bronze, tin, and lead—are materials that can be cast and are dissolved by fire. Iron, however, softens and is thinned between an anvil and a hammer, and receives various forms according to the craftsman’s will.

Therefore, just as silver, which the metals mentioned above have corrupted, will be cast into the furnace so that, once the impurities and adulterating materials have been removed, it may remain pure, so, he says, I shall gather you into the midst of Jerusalem and surround you with the siege of Babylon, so that I may kindle in you a fire for melting. What the immense heat of flames accomplishes there, hunger and pestilence will accomplish here, so that after I have gathered you and kindled you in the fire of my fury, I shall then rest, and, satisfied with the vengeance of your punishments, restrain my grief. I shall do all this so that, after I have poured out my indignation upon you, the end of your torment may be the knowledge of me. And you shall know that I am the Lord, judge and recompenser of all.

That God is called a smelter we read in many other places, but especially in Malachi and Isaiah. One of them says: “Behold, the Lord comes forth like the fire of a smelter and like the cleansing herb, and he shall sit smelting as gold and silver, and he shall smelt the sons of Levi.” The other says: “And the Lord shall wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion, and shall cleanse the blood from their midst by the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning.”

And I think that this also signifies what is said in the Psalms: “Test me, Lord, and try me,” followed by: “Burn my kidneys and my heart,” so that every harmful humor of phlegm in my loins may be dried up.

What we have understood concerning Jerusalem, let us also understand concerning the state of souls, which were created pure by God and received gold in understanding and wisdom, and silver in speech and eloquence, so that they might express in words what they have conceived in the mind. Concerning silver we read: “The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested by fire, proved upon the earth, purified sevenfold.” Concerning gold and silver likewise, the sixty-seventh Psalm contains this passage: “If you sleep among the middle boundaries, the wings of a dove are silvered, and the hinder parts, or inner parts, of its back are in the green or pale color of gold.”

For all the glory of the king’s daughter is within, as she says in the Song of Songs: “The king brought me into his chamber.” Whoever sleeps and rests between the two Testaments immediately takes up the wings of the dove, silvered, and will shine with the radiance of gold in the treasure of his heart.

I think that the following passages should also be referred to this meaning: for sinners and for those who have deserved God’s offense, heaven is bronze and earth iron, and especially the land of Egypt, from which the Lord leads Israel out as from an iron furnace. In Zechariah, too, wickedness sits upon a talent of lead. And in the song of Exodus it is said: “They sank like lead in mighty waters.” For they were pressed down by the heavy weight of sins and could say: “Like a heavy burden they have weighed heavily upon me.”

And just as the appearance of gold is falsely imitated by the likeness of bronze, so the whiteness of silver is imitated by tin, which a simple and uneducated person does not easily distinguish. It often happens that gold and silver mixed together through heretical perversity are separated by the fire of the Holy Spirit and by the judgment of the Lord, so that pure gold remains, and silver, concerning which the prophet says: “I gave them gold and silver, but they made Baal from them.” To this is similar: “I led them out with silver and gold, and there was no feeble one among their tribes.”

And let the end of all punishments be the knowledge that he is the Lord. (Gregory, *Pastoral Care*, chapter 14.)

“All these,” he says, “are to me bronze, tin, iron, and lead in the midst of the furnace.” As though he were saying openly: I wished to purify them through the fire of tribulation, and I sought to make them silver or gold; but in the furnace they became bronze, tin, iron, and lead to me, because even in tribulation they broke out not into virtue but into vices.

For bronze, when struck, gives off a louder sound than the other metals. Therefore whoever, placed under blows, bursts forth into the sound of murmuring has become bronze in the midst of the furnace. Tin, when it is fashioned by art, imitates the appearance of silver. Therefore whoever does not lack the vice of pretense in tribulation has become tin in the furnace.

He uses iron who lies in wait for the life of his neighbor. Iron, therefore, is in the furnace when a person does not abandon the malice of harming others in tribulation. Lead is heavier than the other metals. Lead, therefore, is found in the furnace in one who is so weighed down by the burden of his sin that, even while placed in tribulation, he is not lifted from earthly desires.

Hence it is written again: “Much labor has been spent, and its excessive rust has not come out of it, nor through the fire.” He applies to us the fire of tribulation so that he may cleanse the rust of vices in us; but we do not lose our rust through the fire when, even amid chastisements, we do not cease from vice. Hence the prophet says: “The smelter has smelted in vain; their wickednesses have not been consumed.”

«And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, say to her: You are a land unclean and not rained upon in the day of fury. The conspiracy of the prophets is in her midst, like a roaring lion tearing prey; they have devoured souls, they have taken wealth and payment, and they have multiplied her widows in her midst. Her priests have despised my law and polluted my sanctuaries. They have made no distinction between holy and profane; they have not understood between polluted and clean; they have turned their eyes away from my sabbaths, and I was profaned in their midst.

Her princes in her midst are like wolves tearing prey, to shed blood, to destroy souls, and greedily to pursue profits. But her prophets plastered them without tempering, seeing empty visions and divining lies for them, saying, ‘Thus says the Lord God,’ when the Lord had not spoken. They slandered the people of the land with slander, and they seized them violently; they afflicted the needy and the poor, and oppressed the stranger with slander, without judgment.

And I sought among them a man who would set up a hedge and stand opposed before me on behalf of the land, so that I would not destroy it; but I found none. And I poured out my indignation upon them; I consumed them in the fire of my anger. I returned their way upon their own heads, says the Lord God.» (Jerome.)

A careful listener might inquire what the dross was that corrupted the purity of the silver and mixed it with bronze, lead, tin, and iron. What is expressed there under the figure of the city and the furnace is proclaimed here under the image of land that has not been watered and has not received rain.

We should understand those rains as the ones concerning which it is written: “I shall command the clouds not to rain upon it” (Isa. V), which we await when the early and latter rain is given to us, concerning which it is written: “You will set apart a voluntary rain, O God, for your inheritance” (Ps. LXVII).

[Gregory.] Let us consider what the Lord says through another prophet that he did in anger: “I rained upon one city, and upon another city I did not rain; one part was rained upon, and the part that was not rained upon dried up” (Amos IV). When one mind receives the words of holy exhortation and another refuses to receive them, the Lord rains upon one city and does not rain upon another. But when the same neighbor who hears corrects himself from some vices while refusing to amend himself from others, the same city is partly watered and partly remains dry, because in one part it repels from itself the rain of preaching.

There are some who do not hear the words of exhortation at all; these entirely refuse to receive the rain. And there are some who hear but nevertheless do not follow them from the depths of their being, because they cut away some vices in themselves but persist gravely in others.

For often we see certain people who, through the word of preaching, drive away from themselves the heat of greed, so that they not only no longer seize what belongs to others but also distribute their own possessions to the needy; yet they do not tame the impulses of anger, nor preserve the restraints of patience through peace of mind.

Often others receive the word of exhortation within themselves, overcome the uncleanness of the flesh, and preserve their bodies in chastity; yet they still do not incline their minds toward their neighbors as they should, but raise themselves in thought through the rigidity of pride.

In these people one part is watered and produces fruit, while the part that is not watered dries up, because, not fully receiving the word of exhortation, it remains barren of good works. (Jerome.)

The day of fury is the day that each person brings upon himself through the multitude of his sins. We wish to know what the dross of the city is, what the harshness of the land is—land full of thorns and briars and covered with filth.

“The conspiracy,” he says, “of the prophets,” or, according to the Septuagint, “of the leaders,” is in her midst; they have the likeness of a lion, concerning which Peter also wrote: “Our adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion” (I Peter V). This lion and all his companions do not seek to devour bodies but souls. They accept payments and judge everything by money; and no one doubts that this happened to the Jewish people at that time. For because of the priests, princes, and prophets, the Lord brought evil upon them.

But in our Jerusalem we often see those who, according to the Septuagint, devour souls through their power and accept payment so that they may make many widows—women who have lost the Lord as their bridegroom. The faction and conspiracy of these prophets is that they support one another and do everything for the sake of disgraceful profit.

The priests, who ought to be the overseers of the temple and from whose mouth knowledge of the law is sought, violate the sanctuaries. They recognize no distinction between holy and profane except that of money. They turn their eyes away from the sabbaths and do not recall the rest of God, which consists in knowledge of the Scriptures, nor do they say with the prophet: “Open my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law” (Ps. CXVIII). Nor do they heed the Apostle’s words: “But we all, with unveiled face, contemplate the glory of the Lord” (I Cor. III).

Among such prophets and priests the Lord in their midst is defiled, concerning whom it is written: “There stands among you one whom you do not know” (John I).

The prophets, or leaders, are compared to lions, but the princes—by whom we understand men of lower rank—imitate the rapacity of wolves, so that they shed not the blood of bodies but of souls, and greedily pursue profits. They are by no means content with the saying, “Those who serve the altar live from the altar”; after approaching the service of God, they gather the wealth of Croesus.

Those prophets who foretell future events also plastered them without tempering. We spoke above of prophets who, without mixing in straw, plastered a wall that is destroyed by rains. Such men see empty visions and do not so much prophesy as divine lies, saying to the miserable land, “Thus says the Lord; this he promises,” when the Lord has not spoken to them.

The people of the land, being not truly God’s people but imitators of earthly works, princes, and priests, did everything through slander and power, oppressing not the rich but the poor. Concerning these it is written: “Poverty does not endure threats, and the redemption of a man is his own wealth” (Prov. XIII).

They also oppressed the stranger and sojourner, who had not yet become a citizen of his church but was merely a hearer and possessed only the beginnings of faith. After they had crossed sea and land, they made one proselyte and made him a son of Gehenna.

Amid such great vices and such a multitude of crimes, I sought from among them a man who could resist my anger and, like Moses, Aaron, and Samuel, oppose himself to my fire and conflagration, but I could not find one.

Therefore I poured out my entire indignation upon them and consumed them—not without measure and judgment, but so that I might return their ways upon their heads, either assigning to the leaders their own sins, or, certainly, upon the heads of the people, the leader, the prince, and the prophets, none of whom dared resist the angry Lord. Because of them, the land became filthy and desolate and did not deserve to receive the rain of the Lord.

CHAPTER XXIII. The word of the Lord against the harlot sisters Oholah and Oholibah, concerning their uncleannesses and God’s vengeance upon them for their idols.

«And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, there were two women, daughters of one mother; and they committed fornication in Egypt, in their youth they committed fornication. There their breasts were handled, and the bosoms of their virginity were crushed. Their names were Oholah, the elder, and Oholibah, her sister. And I possessed them, and they bore sons and daughters; and their names were Samaria, Oholah, and Jerusalem, Oholibah.

Oholah therefore committed fornication against me, and lusted after her lovers, the Assyrians, who came near her clothed in hyacinth-blue, governors and magistrates, desirable young men, all horsemen riding horses. And she bestowed her fornications upon them, upon all the chosen sons of Assyria; and with all those after whom she lusted she was defiled by their uncleannesses. Moreover, she did not abandon the fornications which she had had in Egypt. For they had slept with her in her youth, crushed the breasts of her virginity, and poured out their fornication upon her. Therefore I delivered her into the hands of her lovers, into the hands of the sons of Asshur, after whom she lusted. They uncovered her shame, took away her sons and daughters, and killed her with the sword. Thus she became notorious among women, and they executed judgments upon her,» etc. (Jerome.)

Scripture in Kings and Paralipomena testifies that the twelve tribes of Israel, which had been united in Egypt, were afterwards divided into two, and that ten tribes were called Judah and Israel. Over Judah, from the stock of David, reigned Rehoboam son of Solomon in Jerusalem, where were the Temple, the priests, and a great part of the tribe of Levi. But over the ten tribes in Samaria reigned Jeroboam son of Nebat, of the tribe of Ephraim and Joseph. Their Samaria is now called Oholah, which in our language means “tabernacle.” Jerusalem, however, is Oholibah, that is, “my tabernacle is in her”; for among the ten tribes there was likewise a tabernacle, not of God but of idols. For Jeroboam, in order to turn the people away from the worship of God, had set up golden calves in Dan and Bethel.

Let us therefore speak of each separately. These two women, Samaria and Jerusalem, were daughters of one mother, begotten from the stock of Israel, and committed fornication in Egypt in their youth. For, when brought out of Egypt on Mount Sinai, they would not have received a law forbidding them to worship idols unless they had worshiped the Egyptian monstrosities in Egypt. Their mother may also be the Hittite woman, of whom we read above: “Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite” (Ezek. XVI). And when it is said, “Let each put away the abominations of Egypt from before his eyes,” this signifies that Israel served idols in Egypt and that there the breasts of her virginity fell, or were broken.

Samaria is called the greater and elder, either because of the multitude of the ten tribes, or because, after Moses’ death, Joshua son of Nun, of the tribe of Ephraim, governed the people. Hence we read that Jeroboam, who tore them away from the house of David, was of that tribe. And God possessed them, or they became his when they groaned because of the works of Egypt, having first been enslaved to mud and brick; afterwards they bore him sons and daughters, whether in the wilderness or in the land of promise.

Oholah, that is Samaria, first committed fornication against God when she lusted after the Assyrians, clothed in hyacinth-blue—not merely some from among the people, but rulers and magistrates, not men worn out by age but all young men, chosen horsemen—whose idols she followed and from whom, contrary to God’s command, she sought help. They came and defiled her, so that she did not abandon what she had done in Egypt in her youth. For the Egyptians had lain with her in her youth; she worshiped their images, and there she was deflowered and her breasts were crushed. Such was the abundance of her fornication that they are said not to have committed fornication with her but to have poured out their fornication upon her.

Therefore she was delivered to those very lovers of hers—Pul, Tiglath-pileser, and Shalmaneser—after whose desire she lusted; and they uncovered her shame, allegorically, as that of a harlot. The exposure of the city is its captivity: they led away her sons and daughters captive and slaughtered her herself with the sword, so that, destroyed as an example to all women, she is everywhere spoken of to her discredit. They executed judgments and vengeance upon her, leaving in her nothing of salvation; and to this day the ten tribes remain held captive in the mountains and cities of the Medes, to which they were transported.

In the higher sense we have discussed more fully in the prophet Hosea what Joseph, Ephraim, Samaria, Jezreel, and Israel signify, and how they are opposed to the house of David and Jerusalem, which signifies the Church. Of them also the seventy-seventh Psalm speaks: “The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, turned back on the day of battle”; and again: “He rejected the tabernacle of Joseph and chose the tribe of Judah.” For God chose the Church, the house of confession, and rejected the tabernacle of Joseph, whose name means “increase”; for, setting aside God’s law, they added golden calves to their worship. They are called Oholah—that is, a tabernacle not of God but of error and demons—and the greater and elder sister, because of the multitude and because, having committed fornication against God, they were carried captive by the Assyrians.

For she abandoned the truth of faith and lusted after the rulers of the heretics, her lovers, who were clothed in hyacinth-blue, promising themselves lofty and heavenly things, and who are riders, concerning whom it is said: “These in chariots and those on horses” (Ps. XIX): chosen sons of Assyria, rulers and magistrates, who promise themselves knowledge and eloquence. She did this because she practiced in heresy the same fornications which she had had in Egypt—that is, before she believed, while she was still living in the world. She was deflowered by Assyrian men, who persist in wickedness, or by avengers; for our adversary the devil himself is both enemy and avenger. They crushed Samaria’s breasts and destroyed the virginity which she had possessed in the Church.

Therefore, according to the Apostle who writes, “I delivered them to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme” (I Tim. I), and, “I delivered them to the destruction of the flesh” (I Cor. V), that the spirit may be saved, she was delivered to her lovers. They uncovered wretched Samaria’s shame and displayed all her foulness. They led captive her sons and daughters, those endowed with knowledge and those simple and unlearned, and killed her herself with the spiritual sword. Throughout the world they are spoken of to their discredit and become notorious among all the doctrines of the age, so that her shame may be punished as an example to all women.

«When her sister Oholibah saw this, she lusted more madly than she, and impudently yielded her fornication, surpassing her sister’s fornication, to the sons of Assyria: to rulers and magistrates coming to her, clothed in varied garments, horsemen riding horses, and young men, all exceedingly handsome. And I saw that she was defiled: both followed one way. Yet she increased her fornications. When she saw men painted on a wall, images of Chaldeans portrayed in colors, with their loins girded with belts and dyed tiaras upon their heads, all having the appearance of rulers, in the likeness of the sons of Babylon and of the land of the Chaldeans in which they were born, she lusted after them at the sight of her eyes and sent messengers to them in Chaldea. When the sons of Babylon came to her, to the bed of the breasts, they defiled her by their prostitutions; and she was defiled by them, and her soul was sated with them. She displayed her fornications and uncovered her shame. Then my soul withdrew from her, as my soul had withdrawn from her sister. For she multiplied her fornications, remembering the days of her youth in which she committed fornication in the land of Egypt, and she lusted after their intercourse, whose flesh is like the flesh of asses and whose issue is like the issue of horses. And you revisited the wickedness of your youth, when your breasts were handled in Egypt and the bosoms of your virginity were crushed,» etc.

According to the letter the interpretation is easy. Oholibah, that is Jerusalem, in which was God’s tabernacle, saw her sister’s punishments but was not warned by the example to withdraw her foot from error; instead she increased her sister’s fornication. For Samaria once made idols outside, in Dan and Bethel; but Jerusalem repeatedly worshiped, in high places and in God’s Temple, the image of Baal, and committed fornication with the Assyrians. Baal, or Bel—or, to speak more plainly, Belus—is the religion of the Assyrians, consecrated in honor of his father by Ninus, son of Belus. She shamelessly yielded her fornication to the Assyrians, rulers and magistrates clothed in varied and multicolored dress, horsemen, and handsome young men, so that the fornication of the two sisters became one.

Jerusalem increased her fornications in this respect: when she saw images of Chaldeans on walls, she lusted madly, and, deceived by their appearance and clothing, sent messengers to seek their aid. They came and defiled her. Since pleasure is not lasting but soon produces satiety, defiled by them and sated with them she withdrew from their alliance. Therefore I too, seeing her turpitudes and fornications made public to all, withdrew from her, so that she who had surpassed her sister’s crimes might also surpass her sister in the magnitude of her punishments. Such was her shamelessness that, now at a more serious age, she committed all the errors of her youth and pursued Egyptian vices also in desire for the Chaldeans.

For once she lusted after intercourse with the Egyptians, whose flesh resembles that of asses and whose issue of seed—or whose genitals—is so abundant and so great as to surpass the deformity of horses. Nor did the wickedness of her youth cease; rather, after she had become mine, she returned, so that both in the wilderness and in the land of promise she longed for the old lust in which she had been deflowered, her breasts crushed, and all virginal beauty lost. (Gregory.) Since the wantonness of the lustful is expressed aptly by comparison under the name of asses, it is fittingly declared when the Prophet says: “whose flesh is like the flesh of asses.”

(Jerome.) But according to the moral sense it is difficult to understand how the Church can surpass the lust of heresy, unless perhaps we can say this: “The servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it will be beaten with many stripes” (Luke XII); heretics commit abominations outside and perish by shipwreck outside Noah’s ark. But members of the Church, if, while following the true faith, they imitate the vices of Assyria and Chaldea and follow the variegated images of sins, deserve greater punishments. Do we not send messengers to the Chaldeans, who are interpreted as “like demons,” when we lay open and offer them breasts in our hearts to be broken—the heart being the dwelling-place of the mind? Sated with pleasures, do we not pass from one woman to another and desire not so much fornication as a number of harlots? And do we not come to such madness that, after many years of the Lord’s service, we return to Egypt and do what we did in the world before receiving the name of faith?

“Therefore, Oholibah, thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am going to stir up against you all your lovers, of whom your soul was satiated, and I will gather them against you on every side: the sons of Babylon and all the Chaldeans, nobles, tyrants, and princes; all the sons of Assyria, handsome young men, commanders and magistrates, all the chiefs of chiefs, and renowned horsemen. They will come against you equipped with chariots, and the whole multitude of peoples will arm themselves against you on every side with breastplate, shield, and helmet. I will set judgment before them, and they will judge you by their judgments. I will set my jealousy against you, which they will exercise against you in fury. They will cut off your nose and your ears, and what remains of you they will strike down with the sword. They themselves will seize your sons and your daughters, and your remnant will be devoured by fire. They will strip you of your garments and take away the vessels of your glory. I will cause your wickedness to cease from you, and your fornication from the land of Egypt. You will not lift your eyes toward them, and you will no longer remember Egypt.”

Because you remembered the flesh of the Egyptians and imitated the disgracefulness of that unclean nation, which worships images of all animals, therefore I will bring against you your lovers, whose embraces had satisfied you, but from whose covenant you withdrew, so that as great as their love had formerly been, so great would their hatred become: the sons, I say, of Babylon, and all the Chaldeans, nobles, tyrants, and princes [Note: [Col. 0745D] Much is missing here; consult Jerome for what you seek.]. “All,” he says, “the Assyrian horsemen, and handsome young men, commanders and magistrates,” or *tristatae*, whom we have interpreted as “chiefs of chiefs,” concerning whom we also read in Exodus (chapter XV): “Chosen *tristatae* [τριστάτας],” for which the unadorned Latin rendered “three standers” (*ternos statores*). Among the Hebrews, *tristata* is the name of the second rank after royal dignity. Concerning them it is written: “Yet he did not attain to the three” (2 Kings XXIII); they were commanders of cavalry and infantry and of the tribunes, whom we call magistrates of both branches of military service and prefects of the commissariat.

“All,” he says, “in chariots and on horses, armed with breastplate, helmet, and shield, besieged you on every side; and I will give them judgment, so that you may be judged by those whom you had abandoned and whose covenant you had made void. ‘And they will judge you by their judgments,’ as an adulteress. ‘And I will set,’ he says, ‘my jealousy against you, which they will exercise against you in fury.’” For my jealousy exists even among enemies of the faith that has not been preserved.

“‘They will cut off,’ he says, ‘your nose and your ears,’ as though you were an adulteress caught in adultery, so that, disfigured, you may cease to please.” For just as all the beauty of the face consists in the beauty of the nose, and in the ears from which, among women, rings and pearls hang, so the dignity of the king and of the judges, signified by the mouth and ears, will be cut off by their sword.

“‘They themselves will seize your sons and your daughters.’” “Your sons,” he says, “and your daughters,” not “my sons” and “my daughters,” because they were begotten in adultery; and the rest will be devoured by fire. “And they will strip you,” he says, “of your garments with which I had adorned you, and of the vessels of your glory, which I had granted you—golden and silver vessels—for the rites of the temple; concerning them it is written: ‘I gave them gold and silver, and they made them for Baal’ (Hos. II).”

I will do all this so that, after your beauty has been destroyed and your sorcerous face disfigured, your wickedness may at last cease, and the fornication that you learned and practiced in Egypt may end. After you have lost your nose and ears, you will no longer dare to lift your eyes toward the Chaldeans and display your ugliness to your former lovers, nor will you remember any longer the lust of the Egyptians, whose great flesh delighted you.

All these things are spoken under the figure of an adulteress and one disfigured because of adultery, so that she may no longer glory in her beauty, but may be ashamed of the ugliness that she deserved through the greatness of her pleasures. Whatever is said figuratively (*τροπικῶς*) about Jerusalem can also be referred to the soul, which, joined to God’s virtues in an embrace, afterward committed adultery with vices and withdrew from him. When all its crimes have been exposed, it has been stripped and disgraced and displayed to everyone, so that it may at last cease from its wickedness and not glory in the dignity of its name, but, because of the consciousness of evil and the memory of Egypt, no longer dare to raise its eyes toward heaven.

Hence its nose is cut off and its ears are amputated, because it had turned the fragrance of good perfume into stench and had heard the judgment of blood. We understand this not only with respect to smell and hearing, but also sight, of which Samson and Zedekiah were deprived because they had abused it (Judg. XVI). God also made them deaf and mute, lest their tongue should pass over into the land; and every sense of touch will be taken away from those who have utterly lost life. All these things will happen so that everything may be purified by fire, the fornication of Egypt may perish, and it may no longer be able to raise its eyes toward evil.

“‘Because thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will deliver you into the hands of those whom you hate, into the hands of those of whom your soul was satiated. They will act against you in hatred, take away all your labors, and leave you naked and full of disgrace. The disgrace of your fornications will be exposed. Your wickedness and your fornications have done this to you, because you fornicated after the nations, among whom you were polluted by their idols. You walked in the way of your sister. I will give her cup into your hand. Thus says the Lord God: You will drink the cup of your sister, deep and wide. You will be made a laughingstock and a mockery, though you are most capacious for drunkenness; you will be filled with pain, with a cup of grief in sorrow, the cup of your sister Samaria. You will drink it and drain it to the dregs; you will devour its fragments, and you will tear your breasts, because I have spoken,’ says the Lord. ‘Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because you have forgotten me and cast me behind your back, you too must bear your wickedness and your fornications.’”

It benefits Jerusalem to have hostility toward the Assyrians and Chaldeans and in no way remember Egypt, but to be delivered into their hands for punishment—into the hands of those who hated her. She is not delivered to them until her soul has been satiated with them, so that, after she has repented of her former sins, she may then be cleansed through punishments, lose all the labors she acquired by the art of prostitution, and see her nakedness and disgrace. She may then know that the Lord did not do all these things to her, but that her fornications did so—those by which she fornicated after the nations listed above, so that she might worship their images.

“‘You walked in the ways of your sister Samaria,’” he says; therefore you must drink her cup, whose sins you followed. The cup, which is often understood as punishments and torments, has many examples, among them this: “A cup of unmixed wine full of mixture is in the hand of the Lord, and he poured from this into that; nevertheless its dregs were not emptied: all the sinners of the earth will drink from it” (Ps. LXXIV). And in Isaiah it is called “the cup of ruin and the goblet of wrath” (Isa. LI). God also speaks to Jeremiah: “Take from my hand the cup of unmixed wine, and you shall give all the nations to which I send you to drink; they will drink, vomit, and go mad” (Jer. XXV).

Just as certain purgatives are administered so that the harmful humor present in bodies may be expelled, so the Lord gives a very pure cup of torments, in order to remove from sinners whatever gall and bitterness there is and restore them to their former health. That cup will be deep and wide: deep in the magnitude of its punishments, wide in the duration of captivity.

But when, he says, you have become drunk, have been overcome by pain, and have drunk the cup to the dregs—when you have drained it so completely that you even devour the fragments of the cup—then you will become weary of your former fornication and tear your breasts, which had been broken in Egypt and subdued and battered by your lovers. Or else: I will remove all your festivals and new moons, so that instead of solemnity and joy you may have perpetual lamentation and grief.

Therefore, because you did these things, forgot me, and cast me behind your back—either behind you because of the vices of the body, or behind the genitals, by which the ugliness of shame is indicated—therefore bear your wickedness and impiety, that is, the punishments which you deserved because of your impiety and crimes.

What is said—“you will drain it to the dregs, and devour its fragments”—can be understood meaningfully of Jerusalem, which drank last the cup of her sister Samaria and, as it were, drained to the bottom the dregs of her torments.

“‘And the Lord said to me: Son of man, will you judge Oholah and Oholibah, and declare to them their crimes, because they are adulteresses and blood is on their hands, and they fornicated with their idols? Moreover, they offered to them for devouring their sons, whom they had borne to me. They did this also to me. They polluted my sanctuary on that day and profaned my Sabbaths. When they sacrificed their sons to their idols and entered my sanctuary on that day to pollute it, they did these things also in the midst of my house. They sent messengers to men coming from afar, to whom they had sent a messenger. And behold, they came—the men for whom you washed yourself, painted your eyes, and adorned yourself with feminine ornaments. You sat upon a very beautiful couch, and a table was prepared before you. You placed my incense and my perfume upon it, and the sound of an exultant multitude was heard there. And among the men who were brought from the multitude of peoples and came from the wilderness, they placed bracelets on their hands and beautiful crowns on their heads. And I said to her who was worn out by adulteries: Now she will commit fornication in her fornication also. They entered into her as they enter a prostitute; so they entered into Oholah and Oholibah, those wicked women. The men, therefore, are righteous. They will judge them with the judgment of adulteresses and with the judgment of those who shed blood, because they are adulteresses and blood is on their hands. For thus says the Lord God: Bring against them multitudes, and hand them over to tumult and plunder; let them be stoned with the stones of the peoples and pierced with their swords. They will kill their sons and daughters, and burn their houses with fire. I will remove wickedness from the land. All women will learn not to act according to their wickedness. They will lay your wickedness upon you, and you will bear the sins of your idols. And you will know that I am the Lord God.’”

It was fitting that the one who had described the adulteries of Samaria and Jerusalem separately should announce their punishments together. Everything is spoken as though to adulteresses, and, with a recapitulation (*ἀνακεφαλέωσις*) having been made, their crimes are briefly set forth, so that, rightly and in accordance with the command of the law, the people’s stoning of the adulteresses may follow.

Therefore, because they are adulteresses, pronounce a just sentence. They committed adultery with idols, and blood is on their hands—namely, the blood of those whom they sacrificed to idols, so that they might consecrate to demons the sons whom they had borne to me. Nor did they do this outside, in the mountains and sacred groves, as they had often been accustomed to do; at last they polluted my temple, setting up the statue of Baal in it, and profaned my Sabbaths, so that reverence for neither place nor time was preserved among them.

Nor were they content with their present adulteries, nor was it enough for them to sacrifice my sons to their idols or demons. They also lusted after foreign pleasures and worshiped the images of the Assyrians and Chaldeans. When these men came, you, Oholibah—that is, Jerusalem—assumed toward them every adornment of an adulteress: you washed your body, painted your eyes with antimony, adopted feminine dress, sat upon a couch prepared for lust, and set out banquets by which you might restore the strength of your lovers, exhausted by desire.

You offered to idols my incense and the perfume which I had specifically commanded to be made—and had commanded that the person who wished to make it for private use should be exterminated from the people. You did this to gather crowds of people; or else you sang with every kind of music, so that you might please your lovers not only by sight, but also by hearing, smell, and all the senses. They came to you drunk—not displaying any urban refinement, but bearing the appearance of rustic men and brigands from the wilderness and solitude.

And you, worst of sisters, burned with such madness for pleasures that you placed your bracelets and hair ornaments upon your own arms—or upon the arms of your lovers—and crowns upon their heads, or upon your own, so that you might be disfigured by being covered with adornment.

Therefore I said to her—whether Jerusalem, Samaria, or both: You have so worn out your forehead that you no longer pollute yourselves in secret, nor avoid the gaze of husbands or men, but publicly prostitute yourselves like harlots. They entered into you as into prostitutes, eagerly desiring to pollute you. Therefore I will hand you over for punishment to those to whom you willingly handed yourselves over for disfigurement.

For they are righteous men insofar as, at my command, they torture the adulteress and murderess. For thus says the Lord God: At the prompting of your voice, gather against them, O prophet, a multitude of peoples. First let all their substance be plundered; then let them be stoned and pierced with swords, and let their sons and daughters be slaughtered and their houses burned.

All this will happen so that impiety may be removed from the land, and all women and all provinces may learn to avoid similar things through fear of their punishments. After you have received what you deserve and borne the crimes of your idols, then you will know that I am the Lord.

All these things are spoken figuratively (*τροπικῶς*) and under the type of adulteresses against Samaria and Jerusalem: they were handed over to the Assyrians and Chaldeans, led into captivity, and their cities were burned. The peoples who had worshiped images of demons instead of God were killed.
