These things can also be understood as referring to the time after Christ’s coming: righteous men from the peoples themselves judge Samaritans and Jews by comparison with themselves and hand them over for devouring, concerning whom the Lord had said: “Your house will be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII). And: “When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army, know that its desolation is near.”

For to this day they are adulteresses, and they are crushed by the stones of the whole world. They sent messengers to those who were far away, and they could not say: “I am God who draws near, and not from far away, says the Lord.” They prepared themselves for their lovers, the demons, and turned all the worship and adornment that they had received from God as a natural good into the worship of demons. They offered their works and beauty—what we understand by bracelets and diadems—to their adulterous lovers.

Their punishment is a warning to the nations, indeed to those from the nations who have believed, lest they suffer similar things if they do what Samaria and Jerusalem did. Their impieties will then be removed when they have received their crimes and taken away from their eyes the veil placed before the face of Moses (Exod. XXXIV), so that they may know that it is the Lord Jesus Christ himself whom they denied to be the Son of God (2 Cor. III).

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### By the liquefied pot the burning of Jerusalem is proved; he also foretells that the people will be killed and taken captive by Nebuchadnezzar.

“And the word of the Lord came to me in the ninth year, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, saying: Son of man, write down for yourself the name of this day, on which the king of Babylon established himself against Jerusalem today; and speak by way of a proverb to the house of provocation a parable, and say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Set up a pot—set it up, I say—and pour water into it. Gather its pieces into it, every good part, the thigh and the shoulder, the choice pieces full of bones. Take the fattest animal, and also arrange a pile of bones beneath it. Let its cooking boil, and let its bones be thoroughly cooked in its midst.

Therefore thus says the Lord God: Woe to the city of blood, the pot whose rust is in it and whose rust has not gone out of it. Piece by piece, cast it out. No lot fell upon it. For its blood is in its midst; it poured it out upon the clearest rock. It did not pour it upon the ground so that it could be covered with dust, so that I might bring up my indignation and take vengeance in retaliation. I set its blood upon the clearest rock, so that it would not be covered.

Therefore thus says the Lord God: Woe to the city of blood, whose great fire I will make. Gather the bones which I will kindle with fire. The flesh will be consumed, the whole composition will be cooked, and the bones will waste away. Set it also empty upon the coals, so that its bronze may grow hot and melt, its uncleanness may be smelted in its midst, and its rust may be consumed. It has been sweated over with much labor, yet its excessive rust has not gone out of it, not even through fire.

Your impurity is abominable, because I wished to cleanse you, but you were not cleansed from your filth. Nor will you be cleansed beforehand, until I cause my indignation to rest upon you. I, the Lord, have spoken. It has come, and I will act; I will not pass over it, nor spare, nor be appeased. According to your ways and according to your devices I have judged you, says the Lord,” and so forth.

Let us therefore speak of each point. In the ninth year of the captivity of King Joachim—for he began to prophesy in the fifth year—and in the tenth month of that same ninth year, on the tenth day of the tenth month, the word of the Lord came to the prophet Ezekiel, who was settled in the regions of Babylon.

And he said to him: Son of man, write down for yourself this very day, and know that today the king of Babylon has taken Jerusalem in the region of Judea under siege and is fortifying it with an army. Describe this siege by means of a parable and proverb, which in the present passage signifies a metaphor and transference.

“Set up,” he says, “a bronze pot,” that is, a cauldron, “and pour water into it. Cut the whole body of the fattest animals into pieces, both thigh and leg and shoulder, and carefully separate the flesh from the bones. After putting the flesh in the cauldron, place the bones beneath it—or arrange them under the cauldron—and make piles and heaps of bones, so that the cooking of the cauldron may boil not once but repeatedly, the flesh may be thoroughly cooked within, and the bones below may be burned by the fire.

But do you wish, prophet, to know what this cauldron is, or what the flesh and bones are? Say: “Thus says the Lord: Woe to the city of blood”—that is, to Jerusalem, the cauldron whose rust—that is, whose excessive wickedness—remains in it. Although fire has been placed beneath it, its rust has not departed from it. Even when captured and tortured, they persisted in their former crime.

“Piece by piece and individually consume it”; let no one remain for safety. “No lot fell upon it,” so that some might perish and others be saved; rather, destruction came upon all alike. “For its blood”—that is, murders and the slaughter of its children—“is in its midst.” This blood “it poured upon the clearest rock,” so that it might be evident to everyone and not be covered by earth or dust, lest my indignation pass over it; rather, vengeance might hasten upon the blood exposed in the open.

It is natural that if blood is poured upon the ground, the earth absorbs the moisture of the blood, or gradually covers it with earth and dust. But when blood has been poured upon the clearest rock, which has no hollow, it flows away and occupies a broad surface. This indicates that they committed not secret but public murders, in accordance with what is said to Cain: “The blood of your brother cries out to me” (Gen. IV).

Therefore say to the city of blood—not of one blood but of many: “Behold, I will make a great fire in you,” or “I will bring out a log,” which the common people call a firebrand. I will kindle not only the soft and tender flesh in you, but also the bones beneath it with such force that nothing will remain in you that is not burned by fire.

When both flesh and bones have been consumed and burned, set the empty cauldron itself upon the coals, so that its bronze too may waste away and be consumed. When the bronze has been consumed, let its rust also perish—that is, when the city has been consumed by fire, let wickedness perish with the city.

But what benefit is there in having done what was commanded, when not even through fire could the rust and wickedness of the cauldron and city be removed, and when criminal and abominable impurity remains in it? This is what *Zemma* signifies, and he turns by apostrophe to the cauldron itself, that is, to the city itself: “I wished to cleanse you, but you were not cleansed from your filth.” Nor will you be able to be cleansed any longer until I complete my indignation in you.

I, the Lord, have spoken, and my sentence cannot pass away. The siege of the city has now arrived; I will do what I threatened. I will not pass over your crimes, as I often did; I will no longer spare you, nor be appeased by you, even if you multiply your prayers. I will repay you your ways and your devices—rather, I will judge you according to your works and thoughts—in order to show my mercy in this also, like a physician who does not spare rotten flesh so that healthy limbs may be saved. He does not spare in order to spare; he is cruel in order to show mercy, and he considers not the patient’s pain but the wound’s healing, in accordance with the Gospel saying that he would rather have one limb perish than the whole body be destroyed.

It should also be noted how, from the beginning of the prophecy up to the present day, when Jerusalem began to be besieged, the captivity proceeds in sequence. First the sword is provoked. Then two roads are set forth, Ammon and Jerusalem, and the lot falls to Nebuchadnezzar on the right-hand side. Silver, bronze, tin, lead, and iron are smelted in the city. The land also receives no rain but is occupied by thorns.

Afterward, under the name of the two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah—Samaria and Jerusalem—their sins are recounted: how the former has been captured and the latter is to be captured. Finally, in the ninth year, the tenth month, and the tenth day of the month, while Ezekiel was in captivity together with those who were with him and had surrendered with King Jehoiachin, the day on which the city began to be besieged is shown. The likeness of the cauldron is set forth, so that just as flesh and bones heaped into a cauldron are consumed by fire, so the entire city with its inhabitants may perish. None of those who are besieged will remain: some will be consumed by famine, sword, and pestilence, and the rest will be led captive to Babylon.

This same prophecy can also refer to the time of the Lord’s passion, because of which Jerusalem was surrounded by an army and her children were killed. When Titus, son of Vespasian, besieged it, no one escaped to safety, the temple was overturned, and after fifty years, under Hadrian, the city was consumed by everlasting fire.

Jeremiah also sets forth the present captivity, which Ezekiel was witnessing in Babylon, at the beginning of his book: “What do you see, Jeremiah?” He answered: “A burning pot, with its face from the face of the north.”

Some, following the allegorical interpretation, transfer this whole passage to the consummation of the age. They temper the number nine—which in the Holy Scriptures signifies punishments and sorrows and always follows justice—with the mercy of the tenth month and the tenth day. For punishments are imposed upon the sick for this reason: so that health may follow pain.

The world, therefore, which lies in the evil one, is kindled by divine fire on the day of judgment, and the city of blood is placed upon burning coals, so that what is written in Isaiah may be fulfilled: “You have coals of fire; you will sit upon them, and they will be your help” (Isa. XLIV).

The difficult question is how, when the coals and bones are consumed—even though the Pharisees too are full of such things, to whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who are like whitewashed tombs, which within are full of filth and the bones of the dead” (Matt. XXIII)—the rust and filth of the world are not consumed, but wickedness remains even after the severity of judgment.

This is easily resolved if we understand the Apostle’s statement: “God has enclosed all things under sin, so that he may have mercy on all; for the creation has been subjected to vanity” (Rom. XI; Col. III; Rom. VIII). The blood that has been poured out in the open is set forth so that the crimes of all creation may be exposed.

We can understand the clearest rock as the Lord Savior—the rock that followed the people of Israel in the wilderness. Concerning it is written: “They drank from the rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. X). In him all things are revealed, and what is written is fulfilled: “Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed” (Matt. X).

The Lord says that he will not have mercy, will not pass over the sins of the world, will not spare the impious, and will not be appeased, so that the ways of the impious may perish, in accordance with what is written at the end of the first psalm: “And the way of the impious will perish” (Ps. I).

*(Greg.)* What is there now, I ask, that can delight us in this world? Everywhere we see mourning; from every side we hear groaning. Cities have been destroyed, camps overturned, fields devastated, and the earth reduced to solitude. No inhabitant remains in the fields, scarcely any dweller in the cities. Yet those few remnants of the human race are still struck daily and without cease, and the scourges of heavenly justice have no end, because the guilt of their actions has not been corrected even amid the scourges. We see some led into captivity, others mutilated, others killed.

What, then, is there in this life that can delight us? If we still love such a world, we no longer love joys but wounds. And Rome herself, who once seemed to be mistress of the world—what state do you see her in now? Worn down by immense sufferings in many ways, by the desolation of her citizens, the pressure of enemies, and the frequency of her ruins, so that we see fulfilled in her what is said against the city of Samaria through this same prophet:

“Set up the pot—set it up, I say—and pour water into it; gather its pieces into it.” And shortly afterward: “Its cooking boiled, and its bones were thoroughly cooked in its midst.” And again: “Gather the bones which I will kindle with fire; the flesh will be consumed, the whole composition will be cooked, and the bones will waste away. Set it also empty upon the coals, so that its bronze may grow hot and melt.”

The pot was set before us when this city was established; water was poured into it and its pieces were heaped up when peoples flowed toward it from every direction. Like hot water, they seethed with the activities of the world, and like pieces of flesh they melted in the very heat of their fervor. It is rightly said of it: “Its cooking boiled, and its bones were thoroughly cooked in its midst,” because at first the activity of worldly glory grew intensely hot in it, but afterward that glory itself, together with its followers, failed.

By the bones the powerful of the world are signified; by the flesh, the peoples. For just as flesh is carried by bones, so the weakness of peoples is governed through the powerful of the world. But behold, all the powerful of this age have now been taken away from it. The bones, therefore, have been cooked through; behold, the peoples have failed, and its flesh has melted.

Let it therefore be said: “Gather the bones which I will kindle with fire. The flesh will be consumed, and the whole composition will be cooked, and the bones will waste away.” Where now is the senate? Where is the people? The bones have withered, the flesh has been consumed, and every order of worldly dignitaries in it has been extinguished; its whole composition has been cooked through.

Yet we few who remain are still pressed daily by swords and daily by countless tribulations. Therefore let it be said: “Set it also empty upon the coals,” because the senate is absent, the people have perished, and yet pains and groans multiply daily among the few who remain. Now empty Rome burns.

Why speak of these things concerning human beings, when, as the ruins increase, we also see its buildings themselves being destroyed? Hence it is appropriately added concerning the now-empty city: “Let its bronze grow hot and melt.” For now the pot itself is also being consumed—the pot in which flesh and bones were formerly consumed—because after the people have failed, even the walls fall.

Where are those who once rejoiced in its glory? Where is their pomp, their pride, their frequent and immoderate joy? Fulfilled in it is what the prophet says against destroyed Nineveh: “Where is the dwelling place of the lions and the pasture of the lion cubs?” (Nahum II).

Were its commanders and princes not lions, who ran through the various provinces of the world, seizing booty by raging and killing? Here the lion cubs found pasture, because boys, adolescents, young men of the world, and the sons of worldly people flocked here from every side when they wished to advance in this world.

But behold, it is now desolate; behold, crushed; behold, oppressed by groans. No one now runs to it in order to advance in this world. No powerful or violent man remains who might seize booty by oppression. Let us say, therefore: “Where is the dwelling place of the lions and the pasture of the lion cubs?”

What happened to Judea, we know was said by the prophet also concerning it: “Enlarge your baldness like an eagle” (Mic. I). Human baldness ordinarily occurs only on the head; the baldness of an eagle, however, occurs over its whole body, because when it has grown very old, its feathers and wings fall from all its limbs.

It enlarges its baldness like an eagle because it has lost the feathers that represented its people. The feathers of its wings also fell, with which it had been accustomed to fly after prey, because all its powerful men have been extinguished, through whom it seized what belonged to others.

We know that what we say about the ruin of the Roman city has happened in all the cities of the world. Some places have been desolated by calamity, others consumed by the sword, others tormented by famine, and others swallowed up by openings in the earth.

Let us therefore despise with our whole soul this present age, or regard it as already extinguished. Let us end our worldly desires at least with the end of the world, and imitate as far as we can the deeds of the good, so that we may deserve to reach the eternal and stable kingdom.

“Then the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, behold, I am taking from you the desire of your eyes by a stroke; yet you shall not mourn, nor weep, nor shall your tears flow. Sigh in silence; you shall not perform the mourning of the dead. Let your crown be bound upon you, and your sandals shall be on [Col. 0754D] your feet; you shall not cover your face with a garment, nor eat the food of mourners.” So I spoke to the people in the morning, and my wife died in the evening; and I did in the morning as he had commanded me. And the people said to me, “Why do you not tell us what these things mean that you are doing?” And I said to them: “The word of the Lord came to me, saying: Speak to the house of Israel: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am profaning my sanctuary, the pride of your power, the desire of your eyes, and that upon which your soul trembles; and your sons and daughters whom you have left shall fall by the sword. And you shall do as I have done. You shall not cover your faces with a garment, and you shall not eat the food of mourners. You shall have crowns upon your heads, and [Col. 0755A] sandals on your feet. You shall not mourn or weep, but you shall waste away in your iniquities, and each one shall groan toward his brother. And Ezekiel shall be a portent for you. According to all that he has done, you shall do when this comes to pass; and you shall know that I am the Lord God.

“And you, son of man, behold, on the day when I take away from them their strength, and the joy of their dignity, and the desire of their eyes upon which their souls rest, and their sons and daughters—on that day when the fugitive comes to you to announce it to you—on that day, I say, your mouth shall be opened together with that of the fugitive, and you shall speak and shall no longer be silent. And you shall be a portent for them, and you shall know that I am the Lord.”

**(Jerome.)** Above, the burning of the pot and cauldron had shown the siege of the city; now the prophetic word testifies that it has been captured and destroyed, and that the whole people has either been killed by the sword or [Col. 0755B] led into captivity. And first, according to our custom, let us lay the foundations of the historical interpretation.

“Son,” he says, “behold, I shall take away from before your eyes whatever is desirable to you, and I shall take it away by a stroke”—or, as the Septuagint translated it, “in preparation”—so that you may prepare yourself not to do the things that are customarily done in mourning. “You shall not mourn, nor weep, nor shall flowing tears” show the grief of your heart. But if perhaps you are overcome by excessive sorrow, keep your groan silent and do not burst into words. “You shall not perform the mourning of the dead”; or, as the Septuagint translated it, “the groan of the blood of the loins is mourning.” By this he indicates that his wife is going to die. For immediately it follows: “And my wife died in the evening,” [Col. 0755C] which properly pertains to the joining of the loins.

Nothing is more precious to a man than a good and beloved wife, who is provided for a man by God, joined to him by the Lord’s law, and made one body with him. And what follows—“Let your crown be bound upon you, and your sandals shall be on your feet”—means this: You shall retain the hair which mourners cut in mourning, and sandals on your feet, which mourners customarily cast off. Hence David also, fleeing from his son Absalom (2 Kings 15), and repenting over the death of Uriah, walked barefoot.

The Hebrews say that, even to this day, the Babylonian teachers of the Law, observing the commandments, wrap around their heads the Decalogue written on little parchments, and that these are the things commanded to be before their eyes and hanging on their foreheads, so that they may always see what has been commanded. And because Ezekiel was a priest, they say that he ought by no means to [Col. 0755D] remove the crown of glory, but should keep it bound upon his head. Let them say this; but we, following the Septuagint, should understand “crown of hair,” namely, the head of hair, although their interpretation too has by no means expressed the force of the Hebrew language.

“Nor shall you cover your face with a garment,” he says, “nor take the food of mourners,” things that are customarily done in mourning, so that they may cover the face. “I spoke,” he says, “to the people what the Lord commanded me.” “And in the evening my wife died”: the desire of the eyes, of the loins, and the mourning of blood. Immediately, on the following morning, I did everything that had been commanded me.

And the people asked me why I had acted contrary to the custom of everyone. To those who were seeking the reasons for such great patience I replied: The word of the Lord that came to me [Col. 0756A] commanded me to speak these things to the people of Israel:

“Behold—I mean, now—I shall profane my sanctuary,” so that the temple may be burned and lie open to all foreigners and profane persons; and that in which you took pride—that is, your confidence, hope, and desire of salvation—and at whose siege your souls trembled, I shall also consume with the sword your sons and daughters whom famine and pestilence had left to you. Whatever I have done, you shall do.

When custom is observed in mourning, the grief is divided; but when such a necessity of evils presses upon people that each person is anxious about his own death, and the suffering is greater than all weeping, he does not groan over the misery of others, however close they may be. “You shall do nothing,” he says, “of what is customary in mourning. Rather, when the city and temple have been burned, you shall be stunned [Col. 0756B] by the magnitude of your evils. You shall not cut your hair, nor walk barefoot; you shall not mourn, nor cover your faces with a garment, nor accept food from those who console you. Instead, you shall waste away and be consumed in your iniquities. And you shall scarcely have a free groan, lest you offend the pride of the victors if you are seen to weep publicly. Thus the prophet Ezekiel shall be a portent for you, and everything that he did not do at the death of his wife, you shall not do at the overthrow of the city and temple.”

And still more openly, he says: “O son of man, at the [Col. 0756C] time when I take away from them their strength”—the strength of the temple, as we have said, their confidence—“and the joy of their dignity, and that in which alone they had hope and desire, in which their souls rested”—and, moreover, I shall take away their sons and daughters, as is understood from what precedes—“at that time, when a fugitive comes to you from Jerusalem,” or one who has escaped, saying that the city has been overthrown, then you, who had previously been silent and had no freedom to groan, and who possessed such patience that at the death of your wife and in the pain of your loins you shed no tear, shall open your mouth and speak—not to the one who has come, but together with him—so that whatever you had foretold was going to happen, he may announce as having now been accomplished. You shall no longer be silent, but shall rebuke them and say that all these things have rightly come upon them.

Thus you shall be a portent for them, in accordance with what is written in Zechariah (Zech. 3), that prophets are men who signify what is to come. And the Lord says elsewhere: “In the hands of the prophets I have been represented.”

Let this suffice according to the historical interpretation.

**(Maurus.)** Let us come to the anagogical interpretation, if the prudence of a cautious reader does not find it [Col. 0756D] forced. No one doubts that “son of man” refers to the Lord and Savior, who at the final hour—that is, toward the evening of this world—lost his former wife, and neither wept for her, nor covered his face with a garment, nor accepted any human consolation. In the morning he foretold these things that were fulfilled in the evening. And again, in the morning of his second advent, he will prove that the things he had foretold were going to happen have taken place: that the sanctuary of the Jews, and that which they had held desirable in their eyes and over which their souls trembled, has been polluted; and that their sons and daughters have been cut down by the Roman sword.

As for what is said—“You shall have crowns upon your heads, and sandals shall be on your feet”—we shall refer it to the point that they must by no means [Col. 0757A] mourn or assume the signs of mourning after they have received reality in place of the shadow, and after some of them have become Nazarenes.

And each one shall be consoled over his brother, so that Ezekiel, whom God the Father strengthened, may be a portent for them, announcing what is to come. And after Jerusalem has been overthrown, the temple burned, and the whole world has heard of it, and the dispersion of Israel, which inhabits the ends of the earth, has occurred, then, with the words [Col. 0758A] of the Lord completed in deed, they shall have freedom. When his sanctuary has been polluted, and the Law has been fulfilled or destroyed according to the outward letter, the glory of the Gospel shall be opened toward the West; and Israel shall know that he is the Lord and God who foretold these things in the morning and proved by his advent that they had been fulfilled in the evening and at the consummation of the world.

# BOOK TEN

[Col. 0757]

After the end of the ninth book of this work, which [Col. 0757B] we recently completed, we wish to place at the beginning of the tenth the preface of blessed Jerome, which begins as follows:

“What benefit our writing on the prophets may bring to others is a matter for God’s judgment and for the conscience of those who, setting aside declamations, applause, and verbal ornamentation, desire to know what their discourse either recounts as past, censures as present, or foretells as future. For the moment, it benefits us first: while we do this and think of nothing else, we undertake explanations as though by stealth, and we compensate for the miseries of the days by the labor of the nights. The mind is nourished and forgets the calamities of the age, which, already placed at its final end, groans and labors until he who restrains it is removed from the midst, and the feet of the statue once made of iron are crushed by the fragility of clay toes.

“The world is falling, [Col. 0757C] yet the stiff neck is not bent. Riches are perishing, yet greed does not cease. People hasten to gather what will again be seized by others. Tears have dried up; all compassion has been removed. Many ask, few give. Nor are we ashamed to lie upon the riches of Croesus, while preferring poverty in a cheap little cloak, and to preserve hunger and the destruction of multitudes in our own treasures, after the example of that purple-clad rich man who, even if he did nothing else—for Scripture does not testify to his robberies and injustices (Luke 16)—nevertheless had no limit to his cruelty and pride: to Lazarus, lying before his doors and half-dead, he did not order even those things to be given which are thrown to dogs. How many Lazaruses now lie about, and how many people are covered by purple garments in various colors, though they do not even turn to their own use the things they preserve only to perish!

“These words, virgin of Christ Eustochium, [Col. 0757D] may have been spoken by the abundance of the heart, and we may have said them somewhat more freely than befits our humility. We have said these things, therefore, grieving at the inflamed greed of many near the end of the age. They do not consider how much they have, but how much they lack, wishing to possess everything alone. Hence it seems good to me that the character of Christ’s worshipers should be free from greed, content with what is present. It is indeed a good bargain if, from perishable and present things, we purchase for ourselves eternal rewards and the kingdoms of heaven.

“Otherwise, the book on Ezekiel, which contains the rebuke of the sons of Ammon and of the other nations, together with prophecies of future things, shall have this beginning.”

## CHAPTER 25

The word of the Lord against the sons of Ammon, Moab, and Seir, and against the Philistines, who rejoiced over the ruin of Jerusalem and afflicted the daughters of Judah.

[Col. 0758B]

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set your face against the sons of Ammon, and you shall prophesy concerning them, and you shall say to the sons of Ammon: Hear the word of the Lord God. Thus says the Lord God: Because you said, ‘Aha, aha!’ over my sanctuary, because it has been polluted, and over the land of Israel, because it has been desolated, and over the house of Judah, because they have been led into captivity—therefore, behold, I shall hand you over to the sons of the East. They shall establish their sheepfolds in you as an inheritance, and they shall pitch their tents in you. They themselves shall eat your crops, and they themselves shall drink your milk. And I shall make Rabbah a dwelling-place for camels, and the sons of Ammon [Col. 0758C] a resting-place for flocks; and you shall know that I am the Lord.

“For thus says the Lord God: Because you clapped your hands, stamped your feet, and rejoiced with all your heart over the land of Israel, therefore I shall stretch out my hand over you, and I shall hand you over as plunder to the nations. I shall cut you off from among the peoples, destroy you from the lands, and crush you. And you shall know that I am the Lord.”

When Jerusalem had been captured or besieged, and after the one who had been able to escape came to Babylon and announced that the city was on the point of being captured, or that it had been overthrown together with the temple, the prophetic word, following the custom of all the prophets, turns against the surrounding nations that had insulted the ruin of Jerusalem and the burning of the temple. First it turns against the sons of Ammon, whose capital was called [Col. 0758D] Rabbath. Today, because of Ptolemy, king of Egypt, surnamed Philadelphus, who ruled Arabia together with Judea, it is called Philadelphia.

“Son,” he says, “set”—or “make firm”—“your face against the sons of Ammon,” who were descended from the stock of Lot, “and say to them: Thus says the Lord God.” These are not the prophet’s words but the Lord’s. We have discussed more fully elsewhere in this same prophet the firming of the face.

“Because you said, ‘Aha, aha!’”—or because you insulted and rejoiced—“because my temple and sanctuary have been polluted by the entrance of enemies, and over the land of Israel, because it has been desolated,” and specifically over the house of Judah, the two tribes that have now been led into captivity, “therefore I shall also hand you over to the sons of Edom,” whom we have interpreted as the Easterners.

There is no doubt that the Midianites [Col. 0759A] and the whole wilderness lie adjacent to the land of Arabia, since they have herds of camels and multitudes of sheep and goats, and live from these resources. The historical account also relates that this happened to the land of Israel in the Book of Judges, when the Midianites came and devoured all their regions as far as Gaza.

**Μεταφορικῶς**—metaphorically—through the Midianites, the Ishmaelites and Hagarenes, who are now called Saracens, are signified. They falsely assume the name of Sarah, so that they may seem to have been born of a free woman and mistress. Scripture indicates that Nebuchadnezzar and his entire army would come and capture the city of Rabbah, whether it is called by this name properly or because of its greatness; for *Rabbath* means “greatest.”

And lest we doubt that Nebuchadnezzar [Col. 0759B] overthrew Arabia after Jerusalem had been captured, Scripture testifies above: “And you, son of man, set before yourself two roads, one for Ammon and one for Jerusalem, and let the sword of the king of Babylon come.” And again: “At the head of the road of the city he shall cast the road, setting it so that the sword may come to Rabbah of the sons of Ammon and to Judah, to fortified Jerusalem.” And again: “Thus says the Lord God to the sons of Ammon, and concerning their reproach.”

The sons of Eden will therefore come and establish their sheepfolds as shepherds, and pitch their tents. They will ravage your crops and drink milk and the richness of the land, sending in herds of camels and all kinds of peoples, so that the sons of Ammon become a resting-place for flocks. Through the necessity of these evils they will understand that he is the Lord who both foretold future events and commanded that they come to pass.

Nor [Col. 0759C] is this enough for the sons of Ammon: they insulted and said, “Aha, aha!” over the temple and sanctuary of the Lord, which had been polluted by the entrance of different nations. Their insolence in insulting was so great that the entire people clapped with hands and feet together and shouted with all the affection of their hearts, because the land of Israel had been desolated. Therefore the Lord himself, not through angels or other ministers, stretching out his hand to strike, will hand them over as plunder—not to camels and flocks of sheep, but more openly to the nations—so that they may be utterly uprooted from the number of peoples, perish, and be reduced to nothing. And after they have been crushed, then they shall understand that he is the Lord who judges all things and has power over every land.

According to the tropological interpretation, we can understand the sons of Ammon [Col. 0759D], generated from the seed of Lot in a cave, and generated in drunkenness and incest, as all heretics. The apostle John says of them: “They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2).

They arose from inclination, for this is how *Lot* is rendered in our language: “For all have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. 13:3). Against these the prophetic face is set or made firm, so that by its severity it may crush them. And it says to them:

“Because you insulted my Church during the time of persecution, and because of the fault of various persons, so that my sanctuary was polluted”—whether through the fault of those who served me or through the cruelty [Col. 0760A] of enemies who persecuted my people—“and because you considered the land of Israel, the senses that see God, to be desolate of its choir of virtues; and because the sons of the house of Judah”—that is, of the one who confesses the Lord, in whom there is true faith and right confession—“have been led into captivity and have ceased to serve the Lord, therefore every insulter shall be handed over to the sons of the East, who have proceeded from the true light; and you shall be handed over as an inheritance, so that you too may learn to confess the Lord.”

By way of metaphor it is said that the sons of the East shall place their sheepfolds over them, pitch their tents, drink their milk, and eat their crops; and that a city once characterized by pride shall become a dwelling-place for camels that, having laid down the burden of sins, can enter through the eye of a needle. It shall become a resting-place for flocks governed by the good shepherd, so that, when they have done this and have been mingled with and handed over to the shepherds of the East, they may understand that he is the Lord.

Again [Col. 0760B] he reproaches them for insulting with excessive affection of heart the ruins of God’s people and for considering the land of Israel completely deserted, thereby deserving the hand of the avenging God. Those who had exceeded the proper measure of exultation and joy over the ruin of the house of Judah shall not be handed over to the sons of the East; rather, they shall be plunder for all the nations, be cut off from the peoples, perish, and be crushed. They must be believed to belong not to the stock of Abraham but to all the nations. Then, through the magnitude and crushing of their evils and through the destruction of the people, they shall know that he is the Lord.

What we have understood generally of the Church [Col. 0760C] can be understood of each of the saints. Worldly people and hostile powers rejoice at their ruin if they have lost their chastity over a long period, while evil persons consider it a consolation for their crimes if they have more companions in guilt and punishment. And no one does this unless he is a son of Ammon—that is, a son of the people generated in deviation.

“Thus says the Lord God: Because Moab and Seir said, ‘Behold, the house of Judah is like all the nations,’ therefore, behold, I shall open the shoulder of Moab from the cities—from its cities, I say, the renowned cities of the land, Beth-ieshimoth, Beel-meon, and Kiriathaim—to the sons of the East together with the sons of Ammon. And I shall give it as an inheritance, so that there may no longer be any memory of the sons of Ammon among the nations. And in Moab I shall execute judgments, and they shall know [Col. 0760D] that I am the Lord.”

**(Jerome.)** The Hebrews tell a ridiculous story in this passage. After the city had been opened and the temple unlocked, when the sons of Ammon, Moab, and Seir entered the temple and saw the cherubim protecting the mercy seat, they said: “Just as all the nations worship images, so Judah too has idols belonging to its religion.” And for this reason, they say, the Lord became angry and handed them over to captivity.

We, however, shall say that they too insulted the house of Judah when it was captured by the Chaldeans, thinking that, as among the other nations, there was no help of God there, and that the kingdom of Judah and Jerusalem, deprived of God’s protection, had lain open to Babylonian power. Therefore, not after a long time but immediately, the Lord threatens that he will dissolve—or open—the shoulder of Moab, that is, its strength and power, from its cities, so that the Babylonian victor may enter among them also; so that cities cease to exist in Moab; and so that the famous cities within its borders and territories may be destroyed. He names Beth-ieshimoth, Beel-meon, and Kiriathaim.

For these names, the Septuagint, wishing I know not what, translated “the house of Beth Iasimuth,” although this word means “a deserted village.” Beel-meon even to this day is a very large village in Moab; they translated it “upon the fountain.” And Kiriathaim they rendered “a maritime city.” It too is handed over, together with the sons of Ammon, to the sons of the East—that is, to the Babylonians—according to the interpretation that we gave concerning the sons of Ammon.

“And I shall give Moab,” he says, “as an inheritance,” so that, just as there is no longer any memory [Col. 0761B] of the sons of Ammon among the nations, so also in Moab I may execute acts of vengeance and judgments, so that they may know that I am the Lord, who handed Judah over because of its sin and will appear as avenger against the sons of Ammon and Moab.

Even to this day Moab, which is interpreted as “from the father,” and Seir, which is rendered “hairy” or “shaggy,” despise and scorn the house of Judah, in which there is true confession. It thinks that this house can be overthrown as easily as the fortifications of other cities are overthrown. Therefore the Lord threatens that he will open or dissolve [Col. 0761A] all the strength of the Moabites, so that they cease to possess cities and so that all the boundaries which, because of the striking of the waves, they call promontories may be destroyed.

And the renowned and chosen land [Col. 0761C] of Beth-ieshimoth, which is interpreted as “house of solitude” and “deserted,” and Beel-meon, which is likewise rendered “having a fountain” or “upon a fountain,” and Kiriathaim, which the Septuagint translated “a maritime city,” shall perish. Although they may have the strength of warriors, although they may go forth renowned for their skill in battle, and although they may march surrounded and fortified on every side, nevertheless their renowned land is not a house of habitation but a house of solitude.

And although they think they possess a fountain of knowledge and a maritime city capable of withstanding all the storms of the world, promising themselves patience and strength, nevertheless they will return to the point where they are handed over to the sons of the true light of the East in Christ, just as the sons of Ammon were handed over, who trusted in themselves amid a heretical multitude.

Let us consider the progress and, within this very [Col. 0761D] threat, the mercy of God: they are handed over with the sons of Ammon to the sons of the East as an inheritance, so that no heresy may any longer be named among the nations. When judgments and acts of vengeance have been carried out against Moab for its arrogance concerning worldly matters, they may finally know that the Lord is the one who orders all things.

To establish that Moab in the present passage is understood as the pride of philosophers, concerning whom it is said, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the understanding of the intelligent,” a few examples from the prophets should be recalled.

Amos says: “Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Moab, and for four, I will not turn him aside, because he burned the bones of the king of Edom to ashes” (Amos 2). Truly, whatever there is in the world of perverse doctrines, whatever pertains to earthly knowledge and is considered strong, is overturned by dialectical skill and dissolved, like something burned, into ashes and cinders, so that what was thought to be strongest may be shown to be nothing.

Isaiah also [Col. 0762A] rebukes the pride of Moab, saying: “We have heard of the insolence of Moab; he is exceedingly insolent. I have taken away his pride” (Isa. 16). Jeremiah too, prophesying against all the nations, speaks specifically to Moab: “Because you trusted in your fortifications” (Jer. 48). And shortly afterward: “You will have confidence in your glory.” And again: “How do you say, ‘We are strong?’” And then: “The day of Moab is near, when it will come, and its evil is exceedingly swift.” And more plainly: “Say, ‘How has the glorious staff been crushed, the rod of magnificence?’” And again: “The horn of Moab has been crushed.”

These things are said so that, under the name of Moab, the foolish pride of the world, lifting itself up to heaven, may be crushed.

[Col. 0762B]

“Thus says the Lord God: Because Edom carried out vengeance, to avenge itself upon the sons of Judah, and sinned by transgressing, and sought vengeance against them, therefore thus says the Lord God: I shall stretch out my hand over Edom, and remove from it man and beast. And I shall make it desolate from the south. And those who are in Dedan shall fall by the sword. And I shall execute my vengeance upon Edom by the hand of my people Israel. And I shall act against Edom according to my anger and my fury, and they shall know my indignation, says the Lord God.”

Earlier, Moab and Seir made two statements: “Because Moab and Seir said.” Later, however, [Col. 0762C] he was silent concerning Seir and spoke only against Moab. Now he takes up again the question he had begun: what did Seir—that is, Edom—do?

No one who possesses knowledge of the Scriptures will doubt that Esau, Seir, Edom, Idumea, and Duma are called one nation. And to say nothing of the other prophets—Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Amos—who prophesied against Idumea, Duma, and Edom, the prophet Obadiah directs his entire prophecy against this nation; we discussed him formerly as best we could.

Seir is therefore accused, because, being hairy, he received the name “hairy.” Edom means “bloody,” because he lost his birthright over the cooking of red lentils and received his name from the food. Esau, too, is interpreted as “made.” And this should be known: in Hebrew, *Idumea* is never written, but always *Edom*, which the Greek translation rendered as *Idumea*.

Idumea therefore [Col. 0762D] did not speak as Moab did; rather, it carried out vengeance upon the sons of Judah and sinned—or it retained the memory of its former pain in order to take vengeance on those by whom it had been supplanted in the womb. Therefore the Lord himself, not through angels or anyone else, stretching out his hand over Idumea, removed from it man and beast and reduced its cities to a desert—that is, Theman, which we translate as “the south.” From it and from another city, Dedan, they will fall slain by the sword.

And when they have taken vengeance on Judah, I shall execute vengeance upon the Idumeans by the hand—or in the hand—of my people Israel, so that they may be oppressed by those against whom they exercised vengeance. They will act against Edom, or Idumea, according to my anger and fury, so that they may fulfill my indignation. And by the hands [Col. 0763A] of my people Israel my anger will rage against the hostile nation, and they shall understand that my vengeance was just against the unjust vengeance of Idumea, says Adonai the Lord.

According to the tropological interpretation, this seems to me to be the meaning: Idumea is called earthly and carnal. It rises up against the spirit so that we may not do the things that belong to the spirit. It hastens to draw back to itself the soul placed in the middle, and wishes to exact vengeance upon the sons of Judah, to whom it had previously been subject. It remembers the ancient pain that it had not possessed power of its own.

Therefore the Lord himself, being the avenger of the sons of Judah, stretches out his hand over Idumea and [Col. 0763B] removes from it man and beast—whatever appears to possess reason or simple faith—so that he may reduce it to solitude. From Theman, which is interpreted as “failing,” and Dedan, which likewise signifies kinship, he kills all by the sword. He placed the sword in the hand of his people Israel, so that Edom might be overthrown, feel the anger and fury of the Lord, and understand that his vengeance had achieved this end: that it should serve the house of Judah.

This is what the Apostle also discusses when he writes: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Rom. 9). He loves Jacob because Jacob supplants and overcomes what is carnal and earthly and deserves to receive its blessings. For first we live according to the flesh, and afterward according to the spirit; first there are vices, then the virtues by which vices are overthrown. The heart of man is inclined to evil from childhood, while mature age condemns the errors of adolescence. Hence David also says: “Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorances” (Ps. 24).

Nevertheless, [Col. 0763C] it must be understood that Jacob received the first blessing and Esau the second. And finally it is said of him: “You shall be the servant of your brother” (Gen. 27). After the flesh has been subjected to the spirit and joined to it, it ceases to be flesh, and Idumea passes into Judah.

“Thus says the Lord God: Because the Philistines carried out vengeance and avenged themselves with all their heart, killing and fulfilling their ancient enmities, therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I shall stretch out my hand over the Philistines, and destroy [Col. 0763D] the destroyers, and annihilate the remnants of the maritime region. I shall execute great acts of vengeance against them, reproving them in fury. And they shall know that I am the Lord when I execute my vengeance upon them.”

After the sons of Ammon, Moab, and Seir, who are themselves Idumeans and who are related by kinship to the people of Israel and the house of Judah through Lot and Esau, he comes to the Philistines. The Septuagint translated them as *allophuli*, that is, “foreigners”—not by the general name for all nations that are not of the Jewish race, but by the specific name of their own nation, which is now called Palestine. The letter *phē* was changed according to Greek usage into π, just as among us the Hebrew *pasḥa* is celebrated as the Greek and Latin *Pascha*.

*Philistines* is interpreted as “those falling by the cup.” They too were made drunk from Babylon’s golden cup. They rage and insult with all their heart, remembering the ancient enmities by which they were divided from the people of God. Although the Lord says, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord,” they themselves take revenge, killing and fulfilling their ancient hatreds. For this they will feel the hand of the Lord extended against them, and he will destroy the destroyers.

For this reason the Septuagint, [Col. 0764A] I do not know with what intention, translated the word as “Cretans,” although Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated the Hebrew word *chorethim* as either “destroyers” or “destruction,” not only in the present passage but also in Zephaniah, where these things are said against the Philistines (Zeph. 2):

“Gaza shall be plundered, and Ashkelon shall be for destruction; Ashdod and Ekron shall be uprooted. Woe to the inhabitants of the maritime region, [Col. 0764B] the dwellers of Crete. The word of the Lord is against you, Canaan, land of the foreigners. And I shall destroy you from your habitation. And Crete shall become pasture for shepherds and a resting-place for sheep.”

Here too, although the Septuagint translated the word as “Crete,” the other translators rendered κάῤῥον—that is, “destruction” or “perdition.” With God’s help, we have discussed what seemed appropriate to us concerning this in the prophet mentioned above.

Hence, of the two legions of David, one of which was called *Phelethi* and the other *Cerethi*, the latter received from its work of killing and slaughtering the name *Chorethim*, that is, “destroyers.”

The Lord destroys [Col. 0764C] all the remnants of the maritime region, which is beaten by salt waves, and he will execute not minor but great acts of vengeance in fury, so that his fury may have its end in mercy. And after he has executed vengeance, reproving them in fury, then the Philistines shall know that he is the Lord.

## CHAPTER 26

Tyre, because it exulted over the sufferings of Jerusalem, is foretold to be destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar.

“‘And it came to pass in the eleventh year, on the first day of the month, that the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, because Tyre said concerning Jerusalem, “Aha! The gates of the peoples are broken; she has turned toward me; I shall be filled. She has been laid waste”—therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, Tyre, and I shall bring up against you many nations, as the sea brings up its waves; and they shall destroy the walls of Tyre and demolish its towers. And I shall scrape away its dust from it and make it a polished rock. It shall be a place for drying fishing nets in the midst of the sea, for I have spoken, says the Lord God; and it shall become plunder for the nations. And her daughters who are in the countryside shall be killed by the sword. And they shall know that I am the Lord.’”

The order of the prophecy is connected as follows. He had spoken against the sons of Ammon and Moab and Seir, who are the Edomites, and against the Philistines, who dwell along the coast and occupy the same boundary in the coastal region. After the Philistines comes the region of Phoenicia, whose capital is the city of Tyre, called *Sor* in Hebrew and Syriac.

And because Tyre too rejoiced and uttered insults, saying, “The gates of the peoples are broken; I have the safest harbor, and when she has been overthrown the whole multitude that was ruled by her authority has turned toward me”—and because she has been laid waste, therefore I shall be filled, or rather, she that was previously full shall be reduced to desolation.

You have therefore spoken these things and insulted the ruins of Jerusalem, which was overthrown by God’s judgment because of its sins. Therefore it is not through messengers, nor through any others, but I myself shall be against you, Tyre. Like the waves of the sea, I shall bring up against you the Babylonians, together with many nations. By their assault your walls and towers shall be destroyed, so completely that they will fall to the ground; its dust shall be scraped away, or scattered in various directions by the wind. Thus it shall be humbled until it resembles a most polished rock. Such will be the desolation in the city that was once most crowded that fishermen’s nets will be spread out and dried in its midst. For I, the Lord, have spoken, and my words cannot be made void.

“And I shall deliver it as plunder to the nations.” Her daughters also, who are in the countryside, or in the field—that is, the cities, towns, villages, and fortresses along the Phoenician coast—shall be killed by the sword. Μεταφορικῶς—“metaphorically”—he who called them daughters introduces the killing by the sword, so that by the end of these events they may know that I am the Lord, who commanded them to occur.

According to tropological interpretation, since the Hebrew name *Sor* is translated as “distress,” every soul occupied by disturbances may be called *Sor*. When such a soul sees Jerusalem overthrown by God’s judgment because of its vices and sins—Jerusalem in which there was a temple and the vision of peace—it rejoices and thinks that the rule of the once-famous city is to be transferred to itself. This may also be understood of contrary doctrines and of worldly people: when they see a holy person fall through negligence, they rejoice and exult, as though another’s ruin were their resurrection.

Therefore the Lord threatens that he himself will fight against such people and bring up against them, like the waves of the sea, many nations that will destroy within them whatever appears most fortified and firm. He will overthrow all their arguments so completely that they will be reduced to dust. He will also cause the nets and fishing gear with which they previously fished for the deceived multitude to cease, and he will have them spread out and dried on the ground of the deserted city, so that other fishermen may take their place—those whom the Lord sent out to fish.

He will also have her daughters, who were previously kept as though in a bridal chamber and who, because of their mystical and more secret teachings, were not easily believed likely to come forth and be brought into public view, brought out and cut down by the ecclesiastical sword. Then they will understand that he is the Lord, who for a time abandoned Jerusalem because of its sins and destroyed Tyre’s defenses because of its insult and rejoicing.

“‘For thus says the Lord God: Behold, I shall bring against Tyre Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, from the north, the king of kings, with horses and chariots and horsemen, and with an assembled people and a great multitude. He shall kill your daughters who are in the countryside with the sword. And he shall surround you with fortifications and pile up a rampart around you. He shall raise a shield against you; he shall set lances and battering rams against your walls, and he shall destroy your towers with his armor. The inundation of his horses shall cover you; their dust shall cover you, and at the sound of the horsemen, wheels, and chariots your walls shall shake. When he has entered your gates as one enters the entrances of a destroyed city, he shall trample all your streets with the hooves of his horses. He shall strike your people with the sword, and your noble statues shall fall to the ground. They shall ravage your wealth and plunder your merchandise; they shall destroy your walls and overthrow your splendid houses; and they shall cast your stones, timber, and dust into the midst of the waters. I shall put an end to the multitude of your songs, and the sound of your lyres shall no longer be heard. And I shall make you a most polished rock; you shall be a place for drying fishing nets, and you shall never again be rebuilt, for I have spoken, says the Lord God.’”

Thus, after saying, “I shall bring up against you many nations, as the sea brings up its waves,” and, “Tyre shall become plunder for the nations,” he states more explicitly that the Lord will bring Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, from the north—the king of kings—with horses and chariots and an immeasurable multitude of soldiers. First he will overthrow the cities and fortresses subject to Tyre along the coast; afterward he will have Tyre besieged and surround it with an army, a rampart, fortifications, shields, and battering rams. He will attack and destroy its walls.

His cavalry will be so numerous that the dust raised by the riders, the noise of the shouting army, the clatter of the wheels, and the neighing of the horses will shake the foundations of the city. He will enter the city through its shattered walls as though entering safely from the open field. Such confidence will the victorious army possess that the hooves of the horses will trample the streets of Tyre, and the entire population will fall in the midst of the city. Its once-noble statues, together with all its substance, will fall to the ground. None of its former wealth will remain in the conquered city; its noble houses too will be destroyed along with the walls.

The savagery of the victors will be so great that the timber and stones left after the burning will be thrown into the middle of the sea. Either Nebuchadnezzar or the Lord himself will bring to an end the entire joy of the city, which previously resounded with songs and psalteries. It will be overturned down to the ground and become a place for drying fishing nets.

But the following statement, “You shall never again be rebuilt,” appears to raise a question: how can Tyre not have been rebuilt, when today we see it as the most distinguished and beautiful city of Phoenicia? For this reason some wish these things to be understood as something Tyre will suffer at the end of time, after which it will not be rebuilt.

But how will they be able to preserve the person of Nebuchadnezzar, especially since we read later that Nebuchadnezzar attacked Tyre but did not receive the reward for his labor, and that Egypt was therefore given to him because he had fulfilled God’s judgment in attacking Tyre? They say that they have read Greek and Phoenician histories—especially those of Nicolaus of Damascus—and other histories of foreign peoples that contradict this passage, and that they found nothing concerning the Chaldeans’ attack on the city of Tyre. Yet we can prove that many events are said in Scripture to have occurred which are not found in the Greek books. Nor should we submit to the authority of those whose faithlessness and lies we detest.

Therefore the statement, “You shall never again be rebuilt,” may be understood to mean that Tyre will never again be queen of the peoples or possess its own empire as it did under Hiram and the other kings. Instead, it will serve either the Chaldeans, the Macedonians, the Ptolemies, or, finally, the Roman kings.

No one, according to the anagogical interpretation, doubts that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, who comes from the north, signifies the devil. Although he is an exceedingly harsh and sinister wind, he is called “right” in name, arrogating to himself the dignity of that name. He is the king of kings and of all the kingdoms that he showed to the Lord and said to him, “All these things have been given to me, and I shall give them to you if you fall down and worship me” (Matt. IV).

He possesses horses and chariots, concerning which it is written: “A horse is deceptive for salvation” (Ps. XXXII); and, “All those who mount horses have fallen asleep” (Ps. LXXV); and elsewhere, “Horse and rider he cast into the sea” (Exod. XV).

He kills Tyre’s daughters—that is, souls in distress and placed in a certain prison of sins—in the broadest field and countryside. He surrounds Tyre with his fortifications, keeping it enclosed so that no one can escape from it the rule of the king of Babylon. He destroys its walls and overturns its towers. Whatever strength it possessed in its doctrines will tremble at the inundation of his horses, the sound of the horsemen, and the clatter of wheels and chariots. He will enter its gates without anyone preventing him and enter the streets of the city, for “broad and spacious is the way that leads to death” (Matt. VII).

The hooves of his horses will trample, and he will cast down to earth its entire substance, or its noble statues by which they had fixed images of falsehood for themselves. Concerning these it is written: “Lord, in your city you will destroy their image” (Ps. LXXII). When the walls have been destroyed, the noble houses that it had prepared for itself and in which it rejoiced will also be overthrown. It will come into such desolation that its stones and timber, with which it had built its walls and constructed its foundations, will be thrown into the abyss.

Its songs and music, in which it trusted through the wisdom of this age, will cease; the sound of all its lyres will no longer be heard. Its fishing will end, and it will become so humbled that it will be a place for drying fishing nets. It will not be rebuilt, because, delivered over to the sentence of the Lord, it has been utterly overthrown by Nebuchadnezzar, in accordance with what the Apostle also says: “Whom I delivered to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Tim. I).

These are difficult passages, and the prudent and diligent reader ought to pardon my labor; or, if he can find something better, I too shall adopt his opinion, provided he understands that the pardon he grants me he will receive from others.

“‘Thus says the Lord God to Tyre: Will not the islands be shaken at the sound of your downfall and the groaning of your slain, when those killed have been slain in your midst? And all the princes of the sea shall descend from their seats, strip off their garments, and cast away their richly varied clothing, and clothe themselves with astonishment. They shall sit on the ground and, stunned at your sudden fall, marvel over you. Taking up a lament over you, they shall say to you: How have you perished, you who dwell in the sea, renowned city, which was strong in the sea with its inhabitants, whom all feared? Now the ships shall be stunned on the day of your terror, and the islands shall be troubled in the sea, because no one is coming out from you.’”

First let us set forth the very brief words of the historical account, disclosing metaphorically the meaning of what has been said.

“Thus says Adonai the Lord to Tyre,” which is called *Sor*. “On the day of your downfall, when you fall while Nebuchadnezzar attacks you, and amid the groaning of the wounded or slain who have been killed in your midst, will not the islands be shaken? Will not all the kings descend from their seats or thrones, and the princes of the sea, who rule over various islands? Will they not remove their diadems from their heads, laying aside all the glory of kingship? Will they not cast away their most precious garments, shining with extraordinary variety, and be turned by the magnitude of their astonishment into madness? Cast down in humility, will they not sit on the ground? And when they see you fallen, will they not fear a similar fate for themselves, realizing that nothing among the goods of earth is permanent?”

But, on the other hand, they will take up a lament over you and recall a mournful song, saying: “How have you perished, you who dwelt in the sea, renowned or celebrated city?”

We read in Greek, Latin, and foreign histories that Tyre was an island and had no entrance from the mainland. Later, however, either Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Chaldeans, or, as some maintain, Alexander, king of the Macedonians, threw up ramparts and prepared a place for attack with siege works, covered approaches, and battering rams; thus the island was made a peninsula.

Therefore you, O Sor—that is, O Tyre—which were once the strongest of all islands, or, in everyone’s judgment, the most celebrated of cities, together with your inhabitants whom all feared: how have you suddenly fallen?

“Now the islands shall be astonished,” or “shall fear,” because of you. And, as it is better expressed in Hebrew: “The ships on the day of your terror and downfall, and the islands shall be troubled in the sea.” Hence it is more coherent to read “ships” above, so that “islands” not be repeated a second time. The reason is that no one comes out from you, or, as the Septuagint translated it, “on the day of your departure,” when you have been led away captive.

Let these things meanwhile serve as foundations of a kind of historical account. Now let us endeavor to place a spiritual summit upon them.

Imagine someone who, having preserved chastity for a long time, flourished in many virtues but afterward fell into some grave and deadly sin. At the sound of his downfall, and of the slaughter of his virtues, will not all the islands be shaken—that is, those who are beaten by the salty and bitter waves of this age?

Will not all who appeared as princes amid the saltiness of this world descend from the throne of their pride? Cast down in humility, will they not remove from their heads the diadems that they seemed to possess through good works? Will they not cast off garments distinguished by the varied colors of the virtues, and clothe themselves with astonishment, appearing somehow insane through the magnitude of their fear?

They will sit on the ground and, stunned at his sudden fall, marvel over him, to such an extent that all will take up lamentation and mourning for him who has fallen, saying: “How have you perished, you who were previously safe? How have you fallen, you who had stood for so long, who in the sea of this age were thought to be renowned among all distinguished people, who in everyone’s judgment were strong?”

And your inhabitants—that is, the strongest kindred resisting all the fiery darts of the devil, who had previously been a terror to all adversaries—have been turned into astonishment.

The ships also—that is, all the saints who pass through the waves of this age—are stunned when they see you fallen, on the day of your terror and downfall. And the islands will be troubled, lest they themselves suffer something similar. The falls of others serve as examples for the righteous, since we all remain in this world in a weak, feeble, and fluctuating condition. Our victory is never certain and secure.

When those who previously stood go out from you, or at your departure, at your end and consummation—for we are judged not by past events but by present ones. We must be cautious and always fearful lest the storm of a single hour overthrow our ancient glory and solid firmness.

“‘For thus says the Lord God: When I make you a desolate city, like cities that are not inhabited, and bring the abyss up over you, and many waters cover you, and drag you down with those who descend into the pit, to the people of eternity, and place you in the farthest land, like ancient deserts, with those who are led down into the pit, so that you may not be inhabited—when I give glory in the land of the living, I shall reduce you to nothing, and you shall not be; and when you are sought, you shall no longer be found forever, says the Lord God.’”

Join these words with what was said above: “When I make you, O Tyre, a city desolate forever, like other cities that are entirely uninhabited; when I bring the abyss up over you and many waters cover you”—whether hostile multitudes without number, or, certainly, because he is addressing an island and a city situated on an island, metaphorically comparing the multitude of adversaries with the waves of the abyss.

“And when I drag you down with those who descend into the pit,” or into the ditch, to those who are in hell, concerning whom we also read in the Psalms: “They shall enter into the lower parts of the earth; they shall be delivered into the hands of the sword; they shall be portions for foxes” (Ps. LXII)—to the everlasting people, “where there is weeping of the eyes and gnashing of teeth.”

And I shall place you in the farthest land, where the ancient dragon has been established. As in ancient deserts and wastelands, where there is no remembrance of good deeds but eternal punishments, so I shall not cause you to rise again in the land of the living, concerning which it is written: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. V); and elsewhere, “I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. CXIV).

Then you shall be reduced to nothing, or perish forever. “You shall no longer be,” according to what is written elsewhere: “Leave me, that I may be refreshed before I depart, and I shall be no more” (Ps. XXXVIII).

This does not mean that the one who is in everlasting punishment ceases to exist, but that in the holy Scriptures one who does not live for God is said not to subsist. Hence Esther too, speaking against idols, says: “Do not deliver your scepter, she says, to those who are not” (Esth. IV). Certainly those for whom she begs existed, but they did not exist for God, because they had ceased to exist in the virtues and for the living God.

It should also be noted that Tyre is sought by him who came to seek and save what was lost. Leaving the ninety-nine sheep on the mountains, he seeks the one wandering sheep. The woman who had lost one drachma also searches for it and finds it, then calls her neighbors to share her joy (Luke XV, XIX).

But if Tyre, when sought, is not found, the fault lies not with the one who seeks but with the one who has fled the hand of the good shepherd. “And you shall no longer be,” he says, “forever.” Or, as *lōlām* is written in Hebrew and *aiōn* in Greek, it signifies one age, in accordance with Isaiah, who says that after seventy years Tyre will be restored to its former condition.

They say that one age—that is, the duration of human life—is reckoned as seventy years, according to the Psalmist: “The days of our years are seventy years; and if in strength, eighty years; and what is beyond this is labor and sorrow” (Ps. LXXXIX).

In this brief metaphorical account we have spoken about Tyre. It may also be applied to those who, situated in the distress of this age, are led down to hell, covered by abysses and waves of punishments, dragged down to the lower parts of the earth, joined to those who are in the ancient wasteland, and led into the everlasting pit or ditch, so that they may no longer be inhabited by the Holy Spirit. Concerning them it is written: “When the wicked falls into the depths, he despises.”

They will no longer be in the land of the living, but will perish and be reduced to nothing, and will cease to exist for God. Those who say that the punishments of the wicked—but not of sinners—are everlasting abuse these testimonies. They say that the wicked, when sought by God, were not found and ceased to exist eternally, because through their own fault they lost him who says: “I am life” (John XI, XIV).

## CHAPTER XXVII  
### The mourning and downfall of Tyre, which is compared with a ship. The commerce of the lands is described.

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Therefore you, son of man, take up a lament over Tyre and say to Tyre, which dwells at the entrance of the sea, the marketplace of the peoples for many islands: Thus says the Lord God,” and so forth.

If I wished to encompass the whole prophecy against Tyre, or concerning the lamentation over Tyre, in a single discourse, I would make it too long and obscure the reader’s understanding, since he cannot hold everything in his mind at once—especially because in this passage the edition of the Septuagint differs from the Hebrew, that is, in what they have added or subtracted.

Therefore we shall be content with our interpretation, and wherever they differ we shall place the alternatives alongside one another, leaving the complete judgment concerning all things to God. We shall briefly indicate what seems to us correct in each case.

One who is mourned is still cared for by the one who mourns him. Hence Samuel wept and mourned over Saul (1 Sam. XV). The Apostle Paul too (1 Cor. XII) laments and grieves over those who have committed fornication and have not repented. Jeremiah wrote four alphabetical lamentations over the overthrow of Jerusalem.

According to the literal sense, therefore, Tyre, or Sor, dwells at the entrance of the sea, either because it was formerly an island or because, with its very safe harbor, it receives ships coming from the open sea. It is the marketplace of the peoples for many islands, or from many islands. This remains the case even today, since the commerce of almost all nations is conducted there.

Following the interpretation we have begun, let us refer everything said about Tyre to the distress of this world, which lies in wickedness and is narrowed and struck by various disturbances like waves. Of such merchants the mystical psalm also speaks: “Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing business upon many waters; they have seen the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep” (Ps. CVI).

“O Tyre, you said: ‘I am perfect in beauty, and I am situated in the heart of the sea.’”

Tyre’s first crime is that, if it appears to possess anything good, it does not attribute it to God but to itself, and reckons every beauty that comes to it from different regions as the result of its own care and virtue. For it said, “I am perfect in beauty,” or, “I have surrounded myself with beauty,” although it is situated in the heart—that is, in the midst—of the sea, and, like an island, is moved and tossed and shattered by the blows of the waves.

That the heart of the sea signifies the middle is also shown by that prophetic saying: “Therefore we shall not fear when the earth is shaken and the mountains are moved into the heart of the sea; its waters roared and were troubled” (Ps. XLV). Our Lord too is said to have descended into the heart of the earth—that is, into its middle—and to the underworld.

True and perfect beauty is found in no human being except in the body of Christ, which is interpreted as the Church, and in the virtues gathered together in many saints. Hence he himself speaks to the bride: “You are altogether beautiful, my companion, and there is no blemish in you” (Song IV).

“Your neighbors who built you filled your beauty. With fir trees from Senir they built you, with all the boards of the sea. They took cedar from Lebanon to make a mast for you.”

O Tyre, then, which in your pride said, “I am perfect in beauty,” or, “I have surrounded myself with beauty,” although you are situated in the midst of the sea, hear how much has been bestowed upon you by God’s generosity.

Your neighbors and those sharing your borders—not those from distant regions but those from nearby lands—filled your beauty. And you think that what belongs to another is yours?

He speaks metaphorically as though to a ship, signifying the beauty of the city and the abundance of all its possessions. After describing all its equipment—the mast, antennae, oars, sails, prow, keel, ropes, coverings, skins, and the other things required by well-equipped ships—he then announces that a storm and a south wind will come upon it, stirring up enormous waves, and that it will suffer shipwreck. By these things he signifies the overthrow of the city of Tyre by King Nebuchadnezzar or, as many think, by Alexander, king of the Macedonians, who is said to have besieged and captured the city after defeating Darius in Lycia, maintaining the siege for six months.

According to the mystical meanings, the boards of the Tyrian ship are cut from fir trees or cedars of Senir, with which it is covered and joined together; and its mast is made from cedar or cypress of Lebanon. Fir trees are used because of the lightness of their wood and the fact that the joined boards hold and grip one another more gently; or cedars are used because the wood is imperishable.

Senir is said to mean “the way of the lamp,” or, as we more accurately think, “the God of watchfulness,” because all the prosperity and illumination of the ship comes from the true light. According to the literal sense, Senir is the same mountain as Hermon, which others call Sanior; read the historical account. Lebanon is interpreted as “brightness” or “whitening,” which likewise pertains to grace coming from elsewhere.

“‘They hewed oaks from Bashan for your oars; they made your benches for you from Indian ivory, and your cabins from the islands of Italy.’”

What beauty the ship and its equipment possess: it has cedar oars, not from just anywhere but from Bashan; ivory benches; and cabins or storage chambers in which the most precious merchandise is kept, from the islands of Kittim, which we translate as Italy, understanding by this all the regions of the western islands nearest to Greece.

Accordingly, let us say according to ἀναγωγήν—“anagogical interpretation”—that the oars of the Tyrian ship are made from Bashan, concerning which it is also written in the Psalms: “The Lord said, From Bashan I shall turn them; I shall turn them from the depths of the sea” (Ps. LXVII). The Lord turns the shame of sinners and converts it into oars, so that, sailing with the apostles, they may reach the land and the shores.

Benches are made from ivory when they mortify their bodies, or when they devote the use of their teeth to the praises of God. Cabins or storage chambers are made from the islands of Kittim, which, according to the etymology of the Hebrew language, is translated as “the stricken one,” so that it is not so much killed by the devil’s blows as tested by them.

We may also understand the ivory to signify the woodland houses from the islands of Kittim, which heretics attempt to build not in the house of God but in the Tyrian ship. Possessing their own ivory of speech, they use their tongues to build temples contrary to the temple of God, and woodland houses—habitations of beasts—although Scripture says that groves, forests, and sacred woods are not to be planted in the house of God.

“‘Variegated linen woven in Egypt was made for you as a sail, to be placed on the mast; blue and purple from the islands of Elishah were made into your covering.’”
