Because Tyre had said, “I am perfect in beauty,” or, “I myself have surrounded myself with beauty,” she is reproved for what she received from each region, in accordance with the Scripture: “What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. IV).

It is therefore described what each province sends, in accordance with Virgil’s words:

> India sends ivory, and the gentle Sabaeans their fragrant incense;  
> but the harsh Chalybes send iron, and Pontus its poisonous  
> castoreum, and so forth.

Linen grows especially abundantly in Egypt. From it the sail of the Tyrian ship is woven, the sail that hangs from the mast, and its covering, which in the heat of the sun provides shade for sailors and passengers. It is made from blue and purple, which come from the islands—Elishah being the name given to the islands of the Ionian Sea.

According to the Septuagint, however, coverings for the Tyrian ship are woven from linen for bedding and rest, so that, covered with them, it may be more glorious and have a more beautiful garment around it.

We have often pointed out that linen should be referred to earth, because it arises from the earth; blue to the air; and purple to the sea, from which it is made. When scarlet, dyed twice, is added—the colors from which the high priest’s garments are woven—they signify the four elements: earth, fire, air, and water, from which everything consists. Tyre has taken these for itself so that it may not use God’s creatures with gratitude but say, “I am perfect in beauty,” or, “I myself have surrounded myself with beauty.”

“‘The inhabitants of Sidon and Arvad were your rowers. Your wise men, Tyre, became your pilots. The elders of Gebal and its wise men provided sailors for you, for the service of your varied equipment. All the ships of the sea and their sailors were among your people of commerce.’”

Above he had said, “Your neighbors who built you filled your beauty.” Before coming to those who live far away, he describes the assistance of the neighboring provinces.

“Your inhabitants,” he says, or the rulers of Sidon and Arvad, the neighboring island, were your rowers. Your wise men, O Tyre, became your pilots. Governance properly belongs to the wise, as Scripture says: “Where there is no guidance, they fall like leaves.”

The elders or senior men of Gebal and its wise men provided sailors for service, or strengthened Tyre’s counsel and supplied its varied equipment. All the ships of the sea and their sailors belonged to the people of Tyrian commerce, or “in the west of the west.”

This is the literal interpretation. According to the mystical meanings, however, since the Sidonians are interpreted as “hunters,” and the Aradians as “those who cast down,” we shall say that the glorious and exceedingly proud city of Tyre—which, once the wind blows, must afterward be crushed—has citizens or rulers who are hunters. Concerning them it is written: “Our soul has escaped like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters” (Ps. CXXIII).

Where we read “hunters,” the Hebrew has “Sidonians.” These people hunt unwary souls, draw down those established in high places to earthly things, and become rowers in order to lead them to shipwreck.

The wise men of Tyre, understood in the evil sense—by whose wisdom the children of darkness are wiser than the children of light—pilot Tyre, which has been prepared for shipwreck.

The elders of Gebal and its wise men provided sailors for Tyre’s service, or strengthened its counsel. Sacred history relates that many elders were rejected by the Lord and younger men chosen, as a type of the Synagogue and the Church.

The elder Cain is cast away, and the younger Abel is chosen. Ishmael, Abraham’s son, is alienated from his father, while the younger Isaac receives the inheritance. Of Isaac’s sons, the elder Esau is a hunter and wanders in the forests; the younger Jacob dwells simply at home. Hence it is also written in Malachi: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. I).

Certainly, according to the Apostle (Rom. IX), they had done neither good nor evil while in their mother’s womb; they had neither merit nor offense, so that one should be chosen and the other rejected, except that, as we said, in the type of the Synagogue and the Church, the elder is rejected and the younger assumed.

“All the ships of the sea and their sailors were among the people of Tyrian commerce,” or “in the west of the west.” This is like the expressions “Song of songs,” “ages of ages,” and “works of works,” so that the song is greater than other songs, the age longer than other ages, and the work more useful than other works. Thus “west of the west” signifies the greatness of the western regions.

The beautiful ships of the sea, their sailors, and their rowers, who serve the Tyrian ship, do not proceed toward the east or toward the rising of the light, where the Sun of righteousness is born, but toward the west of the west, where the light sets and from which darkness begins.

“‘Persians, Lydians, and Libyans were in your army; your warriors hung shield and helmet upon you for your adornment.’”

The Persians were exceedingly strong; sacred and secular history relate that their king Cyrus, celebrated in Isaiah’s prophecy, overthrew Astyages, king of the Medes, and captured Babylon. Xenophon writes at length that the Lydians too were at that time counted among the strongest nations, and that their king Croesus was captured by the same Cyrus. We read in the book of Chronicles that the Libyans, together with the Troglodytes and Ethiopians, came against Jerusalem.

Because these peoples were then flourishing and famous as warriors, they are remembered as defenders of the city of Tyre. To terrify the enemy, they hung shields and helmets on the battlements of its walls.

The spiritual interpretation, however, says that the Persians—whose name is interpreted as “those who test” or “those who are tested”—and the Lydians, whom we understand as “those who have been begotten,” and the Libyans, who in Hebrew are called *Phut* and are translated as “mouth,” from the mouth and not from bone, vainly attempt to defend Tyre. They are overcome by temptation and serve generation and lust; they multiply only empty words, having neither the helmet of salvation nor the shield of faith, but displaying merely the glory and clamor of speech as Tyre’s adornment.

“‘The sons of Arvad, with their army, were upon your walls all around. The Pygmies, who were in your towers, also hung their quivers on your walls all around; they filled your beauty.’”

The word *gamadim* was interpreted by the first edition of Aquila as “Pygmies,” by Symmachus as “Medes,” by the Septuagint as “guards,” and by Theodotion as “gomadim,” retaining the Hebrew word itself.

We see to this day the island of Arvad, which is entirely a city, with the town of Antaradus situated opposite it, close to Tyre and extending along the Phoenician coast of the mainland.

These people are in the army of the city of Tyre and guard its towers. They hung their quivers all around and fill its beauty, showing that they are archers; or perhaps they are pygmies—that is, warriors and men very ready for battle.

But if *Aradii* means “those who cast down,” everyone who displays knowledge under a false name and carries in the quiver of his breast the fiery darts of the devil, with which he wounds and inflames the hearts of the deceived, should be called an Aradian. He desires to cast down those who strive to climb to high places, and he fills the beauty of Tyre, concerning which it is also written in Proverbs: “Let not the desire for beauty deceive you, lest you be caught by your eyes.” And again: “Like a gold ring in a pig’s snout, so is beauty in a woman of bad character.”

“Your Carthaginian merchants, from the abundance of every kind of wealth—silver, iron, tin, and lead—filled your markets.” Not only in the present passage, but also in Isaiah it is written: “Howl, ships of Carthage” (Isa. 23). The other translators rendered the Hebrew word as *Tharsis*, which everyone agrees was a colony of the Tyrians. From the regions of the West they filled Tyre’s markets with silver, iron, tin, and lead. *Tharsis* in our language means “exploration of joy.” But here we must understand “explorers” not in a good sense, such as those whom Moses sent to explore the promised land, but in the opposite sense, like those whom the Apostle says he avoids, “because of the false brothers secretly brought in, who came in to spy out our freedom, which we have in Christ” (Gal. 2). He also speaks of those concerning whom Joseph says: “You are spies; you have come to observe the tracks of the land” (Gen. 42). His brothers, understanding that it was no small crime to spy out another’s affairs by treachery, replied: “Your servants are not spies.”

These, therefore, multiply Tyre’s markets not with gold or precious stone, but with silver, iron, tin, and lead: possessing verbal elegance and weapons for assault; tin representing the likeness of eloquence, since it imitates silver; and lead representing the gravest impiety, according to Zechariah (Zech. 5), in which a woman sat upon a talent of lead, and the Egyptians were submerged in the depths like lead. A discussion of each metal separately would be lengthy, but we must attend to brevity.

“Greece, Tubal, and Meshech were your merchants; they brought slaves and bronze vessels for your people. From the house of Togarmah they brought horses, horsemen, and mules to your marketplace.” “Ionians,” he says, are called in Hebrew *Javan*; and *Tubal* means the eastern Iberians, or the Spaniards of the West, who are called by this name from the river Iberus. And by Meshech we understand the Cappadocians, whose metropolis, later called Caesarea by Caesar Augustus, is still called Mazaca in their own language. These people made Tyre’s commerce valuable by bringing slaves and bronze vessels from Corinth to Tyre, and from the house of Togarmah—that is, from Phrygia—horses, horsemen, and mules, of which that province once possessed a very great abundance.

The Hebrews say that they interpret Greece, that is, *Javan*, as “It is” and “it is not,” which properly refers to secular wisdom. When its adherents discover something correct, it is called “is”; when it points in the opposite direction, “is not.” For they too discuss many natural goods, and matters of duty, self-restraint, and contempt for wealth—claims which the Stoics especially appropriate to themselves. They appear to enrich the souls of those whom they have deceived, and they have bronze vessels with which they counterfeit the appearance of gold, thrusting these upon the peoples of Tyre in order to overthrow them through belief in false doctrine.

From the house of Togarmah, moreover—whose name means “foreigner” and “newcomer”—horses, horsemen, and mules will be brought to Tyre’s marketplace and markets. Concerning these it is written: “A horse is a deceitful thing for salvation” (Ps. 32). And elsewhere: “All those who mounted horses slumbered” (Ps. 75). And in another psalm: “Do not become like a horse and a mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. 31). For this reason Doeg, the accuser and slayer of the priests, was also superintendent over many; and such are those from the house of the foreigner and newcomer who do not eat the flesh of the lamb, concerning whom it is written: “The foreigner and the hired servant shall not eat of it.” Thus all Tyre’s markets are filled with these people.

“The sons of Dedan were your merchants.” In place of this, I do not know what the Septuagint intended when it translated “sons of the Rhodians,” unless perhaps, through the similarity of the first letter, they read *Radan* instead of *Dedan*. Radan itself is the largest of the Cyclades, lies in the Ionian Sea, was once a very powerful city renowned for naval warfare, and because of its exceptionally safe harbor was a refuge for all merchants.

Since “Rhodians” translates into our language as “those who see judgment,” this is now said tropologically of those who perceive the truth of judgment but do not practice it. The Apostle says (Rom. 2): “Therefore you are inexcusable, O every human being who judges. For in judging another, you condemn yourself; for you do the same things that you judge.” But it is better to take Dedan as the name of another place, as it is found in Hebrew and among the other translators.

“Many islands were the commerce of your hand. They exchanged ivory tusks and ebony for your price. The Syrian merchant was your merchant; because of the abundance of your works they offered in your market stacte, purple, embroidered cloth, fine linen, silk, and *Chodchod*.”

Even to this day the inborn passion for commerce remains among the Syrians. They roam throughout the world in their desire for profit, and possess such a madness for trading that, although the Roman world is now occupied, amid swords and the slaughter of the underworld they seek wealth and flee poverty through dangers. Such people are Tyre’s merchants: they buy and sell embroidered cloth, purple, and patterned fabrics. They also offer fine linen, silk, and *Chodchod* in her market. In place of purple, which all interpreted as *stacte*, that is, “a drop,” the Septuagint translated it as such. But what *Chodchod* signifies I have not yet been able to discover. The Hebrews say that all the most precious merchandise is signified by this name, or that it is a certain kind of precious merchandise whose name is not reproduced in Roman speech, or that it is the common word used by sellers of miscellaneous wares.

To pass from the many islands to the *anagogy* (ἀναγωγή), the merchants of Dedan, battered by the salty and bitter waves of this age, abandon ivory tusks, promising the whiteness of eloquence. Concerning these it is written: “From ivory houses, from which the daughters of kings delighted you in your honor” (Ps. 44). Yet they are not white, nor do they imitate the bride of whom it is said: “Who is this woman who comes up whitened, leaning upon her beloved?” (Song 8). Rather, they are ebony, black in color, unable to change their blackness, as Jeremiah says: “Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots?” (Jer. 13).

The Syrian, that is, *Aram*, which means “exalted,” and swells with pride, is also Tyre’s merchant. Amid the abundance of Tyre’s works he carries false-named knowledge, promising many varieties, stacte of excellent fragrance, and purple representing royal dignity; patterned cloth representing the art of dialectic; fine linen, for which the Septuagint translated *Tharsis*, devoted to earthly works; and silk, for which the Hebrew has *ramoth*, meaning “vision of death.” For all earthly works hasten toward destruction.

And whatever *Chodchod* may be, the one who offers it in Tyre’s markets—while Dedan is understood from these wares, which are said to be brought to its merchants and islands, either as the region of India or, as some think, the land of the Idumeans and the vast wilderness—it sounds like “kinship,” so that we may recognize among heretics a likeness to divine doctrines.

“Judah and the land of Israel were your merchants. They offered wheat from the first harvest, balsam, honey, oil, and resin in your markets.” It is said what resources the land of Judah, now called Palestine, abounds in: wheat, balsam, honey, oil, and resin, which are brought by Judah and Israel to Tyre’s markets.

Since the literal meaning is clear, in accordance with the spiritual sense we shall say that the land of confession and the understanding that beholds God—by which the Church is signified—ought not to bring Tyre the first wheat, which, falling into the earth, multiplies and is understood as the word of God: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Matt. 4).

Then there is balsam, which grows in the vineyards of Engedi, or the ointment of which it is written: “Like ointment on the head, which descends upon the beard of Aaron” (Ps. 132). And honey, concerning which Solomon also speaks: “You have found honey; eat as much as is sufficient. For if you eat more, you will vomit it up,” when excessive fullness turns honey into wormwood.

There is also the oil by which the lamp is lit in the tabernacle of God—unless we apply to ourselves the prophetic saying: “You were selling oil in Egypt” (Hos. 12). If it occurs in Egypt and in Tyre, it will be turned to the opposite meaning, and of it will be said: “But do not let the oil of the sinner fatten my head.” Resin too is light and suitable for bodies, and is taken as medicine. Hence it is written in Jeremiah: “Is there no resin in Gilead, or is there no physician there? Why has healing not risen for the daughter of my people?” (Jer. 8).

Jacob also had this resin (Gen. 43), which he sent to his son Joseph together with honey, terebinth, nuts, incense, and stacte. The Ishmaelites who bought Joseph from the land of Israel (Gen. 37) likewise carried these goods into Egypt: spices, resin from Gilead, and stacte.

And so that we may know more clearly what wheat, balsam, honey, oil, and resin mean when they are brought to Tyre’s market, let us hear the words of the Lord: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine” (Matt. 7). To the Canaanite woman, who pleaded for her daughter, saying, “My daughter is severely tormented by a demon” (Matt. 15), the Lord replied: “It is not right to take the children’s bread and give it to dogs.” But because she had come out from the borders of Tyre and Sidon and was approaching the land of Israel, she obtained what she had requested.

“Damascus was your merchant, amid the abundance of your works, in the wealth of various goods, in rich wine and wool of the finest color.” This signifies that, among Tyre’s other commerce, the richest wine and especially wool were brought to its markets from Damascus—something we still observe today.

But if Damascus is interpreted as “drinking blood,” and the true tradition of the Hebrews says that the field in which Abel was killed by the parricide Cain was in Damascus, and that the place was therefore marked by this name, it was rightly there that Paul (Acts 9), after the killing of Stephen, the first martyr in Christ, went to Damascus in order to lead believers in Christ bound to Jerusalem.

By the mercy of God—who makes people seeing and blind—Paul lost the eyes of the flesh so that he might receive those of the mind. The scales of the dragon fell from his eyes, by which he had lost the light of truth, so that he might go to the street called Straight and find Ananias, whose name in our language means “obedient.”

From this land, then, concerning which it was said, “Cursed is the earth that opened its mouth and drank the blood of your brother” (Gen. 4), Tyre’s markets are supplied with rich wine and shining wool, or “wine of Chelbon,” which means “milky.” In place of “wool of the finest color,” the Septuagint understood “wool from Miletus,” or *Soor*. Miletus is not found in the Hebrew, but because the finest wool is brought from there, they translated Miletus for *Soor*. From this it is evident that Tyre feeds on the milk of infancy and possesses no clothing of its own, but gathers it from elsewhere and from various provinces.

But the interpretation of Damascus as “blood of sackcloth” and “blood of the kiss” does not suit the present passage. Hebrew names are frequently interpreted in various ways according to differences of accent, changes of letters, and especially changes of vowels, which among the Hebrews possess their own particular properties.

“Dan, Greece, and Mozel placed worked iron in your markets; stacte and reed were in your commerce.” The Septuagint has: “Dan, Javan, and Mozel in your markets,” words which were added to their edition from Theodotion. “Worked iron and a wheel are in your mixture.”

From the name of the patriarch Dan, the tribe, and the place where the tribe dwelt, received its name. Today that place is Paneas, formerly called Caesarea Philippi. Hence the river Jordan also received its name: *Jor*, namely, the stream of Dan that flows from Lebanon. *Javan* means Greece, which, as we have said, is interpreted as “It is and it is not.”

In place of *Mozel*, Symmachus translated “bringing,” so that the sense is: “Dan and Greece brought worked iron to your markets,” and so forth. Aquila, however, rendered it “from Uzal.” We should understand these as regions from which iron, stacte, and reed were transported to Tyre’s markets.

Let us say that Greece, that is, Javan, possesses worked iron, ready for war, constructed by the art of dialectic, boasting that it brings everything forward by judgment and reason; and that it offers a vocal sound—represented by the reed—and stacte of excellent fragrance. Or else the worked iron and wheel signify a composition of words that rolls onward and possesses the flow of speech.

“Dedan, your merchants, dealt in carpets for sitting.” The Septuagint has: “Dedan’s merchants, with chosen beasts for chariots.” The Hebrew and the Septuagint differ greatly in the present passage, apart from the name of the region, which is close in form to *Dedan* and *Dadan*: there is an immeasurable difference between “in carpets for sitting” and “with chosen beasts for chariots.”

There is no doubt that four-horse chariots, chariots, and horses are understood in a bad sense if they are earthly; otherwise they refer to heavenly things. Elijah is carried away in a chariot, and Elisha calls him: “My father, my father, the chariot and horsemen of Israel” (2 Kings 2). And the eyes of Gehazi are opened (2 Kings 6), so that he sees chariots on the mountain and horses without riders, prepared for the Lord’s session.

In carpets, however, the beauty of words is displayed. Upon these the merchants of Dedan ride and rest, coming in ordered repose to Tyre’s markets.

“Arabia and all the princes of Kedar were your merchants; they came to you with lambs and rams.” In place of “lambs, rams, and goats,” the Septuagint translated “camels, rams, and lambs.”

Arabia and the princes of Kedar—which is now the region of the Saracens, as was fully demonstrated in Jeremiah’s speech written against Kedar—abound in these animals, namely lambs, rams, and goats, and by bringing them multiply Tyre’s markets. It is also an exceptionally fertile region for camels because of the breadth of its desert pastures and the mildness of the climate, which this animal enjoys.

Arabia means “evening,” and Kedar means “darkness.” Concerning this it is also said in the Psalms: “I dwelt with those who dwell in Kedar” (Ps. 119). These regions bring to Tyre camels weighed down by the heaviest burdens of sins, or lambs, rams, and goats which they sacrifice on their altars, having fashioned them from an unrighteous and rebellious heart.

In this same prophet’s vision of the shepherds, we also read of rams disturbing the purest waters, pushing against the sheep with their sides and fighting with their horns. We read also of goats, which habitually stand on the left, and of lambs that falsely claim to be the Lamb of whom it is written: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1).

In a good sense Isaiah writes that camels come to Jerusalem from Midian—which means “judgment of the Lord”—and from Ephah, and that rams come from Nebaioth and Sheba, bearing gold and frankincense; the latter two gifts are also offered to the Lord by the Magi. These camels, having laid down the burden of sins, can enter the narrow and constricted way that leads to life.

[Col. 0780A] “The merchants of Sheba and Raamah were your merchants; with all the finest spices, precious stone, and gold, which they offered in your market.”

In the Psalms, where it is written, “The kings of Arabia and Sheba will offer you gifts” (Ps. 71), the Hebrew has: “The kings of Sheba and Sheba will offer you gifts.” One *Sheba* is written with the letter *sin*, the other with *samekh*, which resembles our letter.

Since *Sheba* means “conversion,” it must be said that in the present passage it signifies not conversion but turning away, from which gifts are brought to Tyre, together with all spices and the finest fragrances, precious stone, and gold—things all displayed in Tyre’s markets.

These people too falsely promise the finest fragrance and precious stone, with which they strive to build churches of their perversity, and gold, which they promise in understanding; everything is perverse. They receive nothing freely and give nothing freely, but buy and sell everything, whereas the kings of Arabia and Sheba offer gifts freely to Christ. These are the people who do everything for the sake of shameful profit and have received these gifts from the one who says in the Gospel (Matt. 4): “All these things have been handed over to me; if you fall down and worship, I will give them to you.”

I have not been able to find *Raamah*, or, according to the Septuagint, *Rhegma*, in any other place in Scripture, nor have I discovered what region it is or what it signifies, except that it is clear from its association with Sheba that it is a region near that province.

“Aram, Channe, and Eden were your merchants. Sheba, Asshur, and Chelmad were your sellers; they were your merchants in every kind of article, in coverings of hyacinth and embroidered cloth, and in precious treasures, which were wrapped and bound with cords.”

Aram, or, as the Septuagint says, Charran, means “holes” in our language; Channe means “preparation”; Eden means “delights.” Thus in Tyre’s commerce, through the bodily senses—which are indicated by the holes—is the entire preparation of the people of this age, who think that their only delights consist in increasing the trade of the city of Tyre.

We have spoken above about Sheba. Asshur means “directing.” Chelmad, or, as some copies have it, Cherma, is translated “into vineyards.” There is no doubt that this refers to the vineyards of Sodom, which come into Tyre’s market to direct what is perverse—or rather, to condemn it through punishments and correct what had been corrupted—in accordance with what is said in the Psalms: “That you may destroy the enemy and the avenger.”

They possess furniture of many kinds and distinguished by incredible variety, bound in coverings of hyacinth; or their treasures are fastened with cords, which they have stored up for themselves on earth, according to what is written: “Everyone is bound by the cords of his sins” (Prov. 5). They did not conduct free commerce, but tied everything in the bonds of sins.

Because of the similarity of color, let us refer the hyacinth coverings to the powers of the air, which distribute their treasures in the markets of the world.

“They also had cedars in your commerce. The ships of the sea were your princes in your commerce.” In place of cedars, the Septuagint translated “cypresses.” Since we have spoken above about both, it would be superfluous to increase the reader’s weariness.

[Col. 0781A] “You were filled and glorified—or burdened—exceedingly in the heart of the sea.” Nothing, he says, was lacking to you that pertains to the wealth of the islands. Yet this glory was a burden to its possessor, since he could not bear wealth moderately. Poverty too is often a temptation. Hence Solomon (Prov. 30) asks only for necessities and equally detests wealth and poverty, lest in the one case pride and in the other impatience and falsehood creep in.

“Your rowers brought you into many waters.” Above we read that the rowers of the city of Tyre were Sidonians and Aradians, one group interpreted as “hunters,” the other as “those who set down.” For they hunt the souls of those whom they lead according to their own will amid the waves of this age, and they do not raise them to lofty things but plunge them into the depths.

Nor do they imitate those who sailed until the morning watch, broke the insane waves of the sea, and were worthy to receive the Lord and Savior. Immediately, with such a passenger and companion, they reached the harbor of rest, concerning which the Gospel gives a fuller account.

“The south wind shattered you in the heart of the sea.” All Tyre’s wealth perishes when the south wind blows. In Hebrew this wind is more significantly called *Cadim*, which we can translate as “the burning wind.” Concerning it the saint also said: “The sun shall not burn you by day, nor the moon by night” (Ps. 120).

Jacob was scorched by this wind, yet not shattered, when he said: “By day I was scorched by heat, and by night by frost” (Gen. 31). Those also who were hired at the first hour endured the heat and burning of the entire day (Matt. 20), yet they receive the denarius, because they were scorched but not shattered.

Hence the bride also says in the Song: “I am black and beautiful, because the sun has looked upon me,” or, as it is better contained in the Hebrew: “The sun has discolored me” (Song 1).

“Your riches, your treasures, and your varied equipment.” Many read: “In the heart of the sea are your riches, your treasures, and your varied equipment,” so that all Tyre’s wealth and entire substance are placed in the heart of the sea and are overwhelmed by the waves of the world. Its inhabitants have nothing stable or lasting, in fulfillment of the Gospel saying: “Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke 12), and the Apostle’s saying: “Those who desire to become rich fall into temptation and many snares, and are dragged down into the depths” (1 Tim. 6).

The historical meaning is clear, and for that reason we attach brief observations to nearly every verse. For the discourse is already hastening toward the end of the book.

“Your sailors and your pilots, who maintained your equipment and presided over your people, and your warriors who were in you, together with your whole multitude that is in your midst, will fall in the heart of the sea on the day of your ruin.”

We read that the rowers, or sailors, of the city of Tyre were Sidonians and Aradians, concerning whom we have already spoken; and, according to the Septuagint edition, the counselors were from Byblos, which in Hebrew is called Gebal. Its warriors were Persians, Lydians, and Libyans. All of these will fall and be shown to be worthless when Tyre falls and all her glory comes to an end in ruins.

The multitude, which the Septuagint translated as “mixture,” signifies the common people, apart from the leaders; they too will be crushed by the same judgment, without the distinction of titles. The prophecy is interwoven between a city and a ship: from one you may understand the other, yet both refer to the consummation of the age and to shipwreck.

“At the sound of the cry of your pilots the fleets will be shaken, and all who held the oar will descend from their ships. The sailors, all the pilots of the sea, the passengers, and the lookouts will stand on land; they will wail over you with a loud voice and cry bitterly. They will throw dust upon their heads and sprinkle themselves with ashes; they will shave themselves bald on account of you and gird themselves with sackcloth; they will weep for you in the bitterness of their souls with a most bitter lamentation; they will take up a mournful song over you and lament you.”

When Tyre has fallen, her pilots will be thrown into confusion. They will descend from the fleets, and the rowers, passengers, lookouts—or sailors—and all the pilots of the sea, tossed by the waves, will at last stand on steady ground. They will wail over her with a loud voice—her whom they had previously enriched with their merchandise—and they will express the bitterness of their minds by their cries.

They will also throw dust, or earth, upon their heads, doing penance for earthly works. They will be sprinkled with ashes, either like the heifer according to the Law, so that they may be purified, or certainly they will spread ashes beneath themselves, according to the saying addressed to Jerusalem: “Scatter earth upon your head, spread ashes beneath you, and make lamentation.”

It is also written in the Gospel: “If these signs had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes” (Matt. 11). And the Psalmist says: “I ate ashes like bread” (Ps. 101).

They will shave their heads over Tyre, as is customary in mourning, at the time when the magnitude of their grief has excluded all joy. The Apostles’ hairs were numbered, because they had consecrated their hair to the Lord like Nazirites. And Samson, as long as he had his hair, possessed strength; once his hair had been cut, he was captured by the Philistines (Judg. 16).

When it is said, “They will gird themselves with sackcloth,” the former lust of the loins is condemned, so that those who had lived in luxury may afterward repent and live in austerity and hardship. The Ninevites wore sackcloth (Jonah 3). And again it is said to Jerusalem: “Lament before me like a bride, girded with sackcloth for her virginal husband” (Joel 1).

“And they will weep for you,” he says, “in the bitterness of their souls, with a most bitter lamentation.” “For it is better to enter the house of mourning than the house of feasting” (Eccl. 7). Thus they will lament Tyre and repeat a mournful song, which the following Scripture adds.

To make us understand the progress of those who lament the one who is falling—and who previously lived in the heart and midst of the sea—the example of the prophet teaches us. He too is commanded to lament Tyre, so that when the time of repentance has been fulfilled, she may be restored to her former state and, taking up the lyre, sound forth to the Lord. Read Isaiah.

Some people, foolishly—but it must nevertheless be mentioned because we have read it—interpret the pilots as the bishops of the heretics, the counselors as the presbyters, the lookouts as archdeacons, and the rowers and sailors as deacons; they refer the passengers to the entire people. If they had added the helmsman as the devil, they would have completed the tragedy.

All these will wail together and weep most bitterly. After they have perceived the shipwreck of their vessel and stood on land, they will repent; they will have lost all the beauty of their false-named knowledge, and in place of joy and gladness they will mark their repentance with sorrow in the bitterness of their hearts.

“What city is like Tyre, which has become silent in the midst of the sea? At the departure of your merchandise from the sea you filled many peoples, and by the abundance of your riches and your peoples you enriched many kings. Now you have been shattered by the sea; your wealth and all your multitude, which was in your midst, have fallen into the depths of the waters. All the inhabitants of the islands were astonished at you, and all their kings, struck by the storm, changed their faces. The merchants of the nations hissed over you. You have been brought to nothing, and you shall be no more forever.”

In their lamentation over Tyre, the pilots, rowers, lookouts, and passengers will remember these things. What other city has become so silent that it has no confidence to speak and hears the Gospel saying: “Be silent and be still” (Mark 4)? And from the Psalms: “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteous deeds and take my covenant upon your lips?” (Ps. 49).

With how many goods, O Tyre, have you been enriched, and what did you seek with such labor, so that day and night you might gather what would perish in shipwreck? You filled many peoples and enriched kings with your wealth, concerning whom it is written: “The kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Ps. 2).

But now you have been shattered in the sea and in the depths of the waters, according to what is written about Pharaoh: “He cast Pharaoh’s chariots and his army into the sea; they sank into the depths like a stone” (Exod. 15). And he could have said: “I have come into the depths of the sea, and the storm has overwhelmed me” (Ps. 68).

All the islands—or the inhabitants of the islands—that are beaten by the waves of this age will be astonished at you. Their kings, struck by the storm, will perceive their own destruction. Imitating the voice of the serpent, they will hiss and say: “You have been brought to nothing,” or, “You have become a ruin,” so that you did not possess the nature of perdition but its will—and you will not exist.

If he had said this much, a great question would arise: how can she not exist when we now see her built up? But from what follows—“forever”—he indicates the duration of a single age, which is reckoned, according to the lifespan of a human being, as a cycle of seventy years; or else “you will not exist” means “you will not exist for God,” as the Apostle says: “He calls into being the things that do not exist” (Rom. 4).

And the prophet Isaiah says: “Behold, all your adversaries will be ashamed and confounded. They will be as though they did not exist” (Isa. 41). And Esther, according to the Septuagint translators, says: “Do not hand over your scepter to those who do not exist” (Esth. 14). And in the Psalms: “Let me recover strength before I depart and exist no more.” We have explained above in what sense these testimonies are to be understood.

All these things can be referred to the person of the heretics. In Tyre’s destruction and shipwreck they will recognize their error. Placed in the midst of the sea, they will desire to save their souls, and they will lament the wealth wrongly gathered, by which they had enriched many kings—namely, their patriarchs and the ignoble multitude—in whose midst their wealth will collapse into the sea.

The inhabitants of all the islands too, if we wish to refer what has been said to a good interpretation, will be astonished at Tyre’s destruction. And all the kings of the islands, either themselves struck as though by a storm, will change their faces, or certainly they will reveal the grief of their hearts by weeping and tears, and will testify to the magnitude of their astonishment by wonder and hissing: how she has been reduced to nothing and perished, though she promised salvation to many nations.

And she will be no more—not merely for a definite period, if we interpret *aion* (αἰών) as “an age,” but forever, because the same word signifies both.

## BOOK ELEVEN

[Col. 0783]

[Col. 0783D] It would have been appropriate for me to include the prophecy concerning Tyre and the prince of Tyre in a single volume, and not to separate them in the order of the books, since they are joined both in subject and in prophecy. But because there is much that is said, exceeding the limits of length, the explanation has therefore been postponed to the eleventh book. We believe that, by the mercy of God and also through the prayers of all the saints, it will reach its conclusion, so that we may discuss as well what is written in Ezekiel against Pharaoh and all Egypt.

## CHAPTER TWENTY-EIGHT

The word of the Lord against the prince of Tyre and concerning his pride. The word of the Lord against Sidon, and the Lord’s promise concerning the gathering of the children of Israel.

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, say to the prince of Tyre: Thus says the Lord God: Because your heart has been lifted up and you have said, ‘I am God, and I have sat in the seat of God, in the heart of the sea,’ though you are a man and not God, and you have made your heart like the heart of God—behold, you are wiser than Daniel? No secret is hidden from you. By your wisdom and understanding you have made strength for yourself and acquired gold and silver in your treasuries. By the abundance of your wisdom and in your commerce you have multiplied your strength for yourself, and your heart has been lifted up in your strength. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because your heart has been lifted up like the heart of God, therefore behold, I will bring foreigners against you, the strongest of the nations; and they will bare their swords against the beauty of your wisdom, and profane your splendor. They will kill you and hand you over, and you will die the death of the slain in the heart of the sea. Will you still say, ‘I am God,’ in the presence of those killing you, though you are a man and not God, in the hand of those who kill you? You will die the death of the uncircumcised at the hand of foreigners, because I have spoken, says the Lord God.” (Jerome.)

Just as the wealth, and then the ruin and lamentation, of the city of Tyre are first described under the figure of a ship, so now a prophetic word is first spoken to the prince of Tyre: he has been raised up through pride and has not used well the riches that he possessed. Then comes mourning and lamentation over how he has fallen from such great blessings to such great evils. First, therefore, the first matters must be discussed.

It is written in Isaiah concerning the king of Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar, that he made himself equal to God’s power and was lifted up to such arrogance that he dared to say: “I will ascend above the stars of heaven, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV). When he had been cast down from his throne, he deserved to hear: “How has Lucifer fallen, who used to rise in the morning?” And concerning Pharaoh, in this same prophet: “The rivers are mine, and I made them.” And concerning the prince of Tyre, that with a lifted heart he arrogantly said: “I am God, and I have sat in the seat of God,” or, “I have dwelt in the dwelling-place of God,” although he is a man and not God.

Although these statements seem to exceed the powers of human frailty, and to be not so much the words of human beings as of raging demons, nevertheless, according to *hyperbole* (ὑπερβολή), we must understand that they became so swollen and failed to know their own measure that, lifted up by worldly prosperity and royal power, and supposing present blessings to be everlasting, they ceased to know themselves as human beings and claimed eternal dominion for themselves. This is so even though, under the type of princes, kings, individual cities, or provinces, hostile powers are being indicated.

The apostle Paul also writes concerning them: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers and the rulers of the darkness of this age, and against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. VI). And elsewhere: “We speak wisdom among the mature, yet a wisdom not of this age nor of the rulers of this age, who are being destroyed” (I Cor. II). Again, arguing about wisdom, he says: “None of the rulers of this age understood it; for if they had understood it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (ibid.).

In Daniel’s prophecy also it is plainly read that there is a prince of the people of Israel, Michael, and a prince of Greece and a prince of Persia (Dan. X). And Moses writes more openly in the Song of Deuteronomy: “When the Most High divided the nations, when he scattered the sons of Adam, he established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God,” or, as it is better found in Hebrew, “according to the number of the sons of Israel. And the Lord’s portion became his people Jacob, and Israel the lot of his inheritance” (Deut. XXXII).

Nor will we be surprised that, on the opposing side, the worst kings are presented as types of transgressing princes, when we teach that the best kings—David, Solomon, and Josiah—and the patriarchs and prophets preceded as figures of the Lord and Savior. Let us therefore discuss what has been written according to both interpretations: of equally proud kings and apostate princes.

“Since you are,” he says, “in the midst of the sea,” and are held in the narrow confines of an island—indeed, since you are a human being and surrounded by the frailty of human flesh—you have been lifted up by swelling of heart and have imagined that you dwell on God’s throne, in heaven. And because you boast of such great wisdom that the people of your kingdom challenged Solomon with riddles, are you wiser than Daniel, who by God’s grace overcame all the magicians and diviners and is now the wisest man in Babylon?

Or it may also be understood in this way: even if you are wiser than Daniel, who by everyone’s confession is the wisest, and by the greatness of your riches and power you desire to make yourself equal to God’s power, nevertheless you will be seized by your adversaries; and when your city has been destroyed, you will be pierced by many wounds. You will no longer say, “I am God,” but, instructed by destruction, you will recognize that you are a human being, not God.

But if we wish to say that the prince of Tyre signifies the same power to which the city or province itself was entrusted by God, let us take up this testimony: “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.’ But you shall die like human beings, and fall like one of the princes.” Provinces were handed over to them for governing, as to judges by an emperor. They forgot that their honor depended upon another’s command, as happened recently with Heradianus in Africa. They were raised up in tyrannical spirit against their king and lord, so that, scattered throughout the world under the names of idolatry, they assumed for themselves the names of gods. Inflated with pride, they fell into the judgment and snare of the devil.

The Savior also spoke of him in the Gospel: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke X).

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, raise a lamentation over the king of Tyre and say to him: Thus says the Lord God: You are the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God. Every precious stone was your covering: sardius, topaz, and jasper, chrysolite, onyx, beryl, sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald. Gold was the work of your adornment, and your settings were prepared on the day when you were created. You were a cherub, extended and protecting, and I placed you on God’s holy mountain. You walked in the midst of fiery stones, perfect in your ways from the day of your creation, until iniquity was found in you. In the abundance of your commerce your inner parts were filled with iniquity, and you sinned. I cast you out from God’s mountain and destroyed you, O cherub who protected, from the midst of the fiery stones. Your heart was lifted up in your beauty; you corrupted your wisdom because of your splendor. I cast you to the ground; I placed you before the faces of kings, so that they might look upon you. In the abundance of your iniquities and in the iniquity of your commerce you profaned your sanctuary. Therefore I will bring forth fire from your midst; it shall consume you, and I will reduce you to ashes upon the earth in the sight of all who see you. All who see you among the nations shall be astonished at you. You have become nothing, and you shall not exist forever.” (Jerome.)

Since we have explained who the prince of Tyre is and how he fell through pride, let us now understand his lamentation over his former glory. First, he is reminded of what he had been, so that he may grieve that he has lost what he possessed.

“You,” he says, “are the seal of likeness,” in accordance with what the Evangelist John says properly concerning the Savior: “For God the Father has sealed him” (John VI); and concerning human beings: “He has sealed, because God is true.” And in the Psalms: “The light of your face has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Ps. IV). And elsewhere: “Beloved, we are now children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him” (I John III).

Hence it is also said to God: “Who shall be like you?” For likeness is one thing, and equality another. Therefore that is a most savage heresy which confesses in Christ only a likeness to the Father and takes away his nature. We, however, say that in the Son there is not merely likeness but equality. For this reason the Jews persecuted him: not only because he was breaking the Sabbath, but because he was making himself equal to God. Where there is equality, there is the same nature and one substance.

This is what the Apostle says concerning likeness: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. IV), so that you may receive his likeness, which you lost through your own fault. And because in Latin manuscripts *resignaculum* is read in place of *signaculum*, some understand the passage in this way: the king of Tyre annulled and destroyed the seal and figure of God, which had been impressed as though in very soft wax, so that instead of being a seal he became an erasure, no longer possessing the image and likeness of God, according to which the first human being was created, when God said: “Let us make humanity in our image and likeness.”

It should be noted that the image was made at that time alone, whereas the likeness is completed in Christ’s baptism. Accordingly, the words “full of wisdom and perfect in beauty” are joined to the one who is called “the seal of likeness,” as though he were a crown adorned and composed from different flowers of virtue. The diligent person increases this crown through personal effort, nourishing the good of nature by industry, while the negligent person diminishes it. In accordance with what is said in Proverbs under the figure of a beautiful but ill-mannered woman: “Like a gold ring in a pig’s snout, so is beauty in an ill-mannered woman” (Prov. XI).

It follows: “You were in the delights of the paradise of God.” In Hebrew, instead of this, it has *in Eden*, as the history of Genesis also relates. *Eden* is translated as “delights.” He beautifully calls it “the paradise of God” by way of distinction, to show that there is also a contrary paradise, not God’s, among those who exchange truth for falsehood and boast that they possess paradise.

By this language he demonstrates that the one of whom these things are written is not a human being at all, but an opposing power that once dwelt in God’s paradise, although the Jews judge that this is prophetically spoken, by the figure called *hyperbole* (ὑπερβολή), concerning Hiram, king of Tyre. When it is said to him, “You were in the delights of the paradise of God,” or “you were made so,” it shows what he possessed and what he lost.

(Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXXIII, chapters 24 and 25.) With the first words, “You are the seal of likeness,” he has embraced everything. For what good did he not possess who was the seal of God’s likeness? The likeness of such a seal is expressed figuratively from the seal of a ring, as that which is essentially present in the seal itself.

Although the human being was created according to the likeness of God, he attributes something greater to the angel when he says that the angel was not created according to the likeness of God, but was himself the seal of God’s likeness. Thus, the more subtle the angel is in nature, the more fully the likeness of God is believed to have been expressed in him.

For this reason, still indicating his primacy of power, the same prophet adds: “Every precious stone was your covering: sardius, topaz, jasper, chrysolite, onyx, beryl, sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald.” He named nine kinds of stones, because there are nine orders of angels. For when angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, virtues, principalities, powers, cherubim, and seraphim are openly mentioned in the sacred writings, the various distinctions of the heavenly citizens are shown. This Behemoth is described as having been covered with them, because he had them as a garment for his adornment; and when he surpassed their brightness, he was brighter by comparison with them.

Concerning him the prophet further says: “Gold was the work of your adornment, and your settings were prepared on the day when you were created.” Gold was the work of his adornment because he shone with the brightness of wisdom, which he received when he was well created. Settings are made in stones so that, bound with gold, they may be joined in the composition of an ornament and may not be separated from one another. The gold poured between them binds them by filling the settings.

Thus the settings of this stone were prepared on the day of his creation, because he was created capable of charity. If he had wished to be filled with it, he could have clung to the steadfast angels, as stones placed in a royal ornament. If he had allowed himself to be penetrated by the gold of charity, he would have remained fixed in the royal ornament, joined to the holy angels.

This stone therefore had settings, but through the vice of pride they were not filled with the gold of charity. For stones are bound with gold so that they do not fall; and this one fell because, though pierced by the craftsman’s hand, he scorned being bound by the ties of love. Now the other stones, which had likewise been pierced for him, have been bound together as charity penetrates each of them. When he fell, they received the gift of no longer being loosened by falling from the royal ornament.

(Jerome.) Furthermore, concerning the fact that this is joined to the dwelling-place of paradise—“Every precious stone was your covering,” or “your binding and enclosure: sardius, topaz, jasper, chrysolite, onyx, beryl, sapphire, carbuncle, emerald”—this must be observed: the king of Tyre was not surrounded, covered, or, as Symmachus translated it, bound and constrained by every precious stone. Rather, every stone that he possessed was precious, not the prince of Tyre himself.

Otherwise, there are many precious stones that Scripture names in the present passage: chalcedony, sardonyx, chrysoprase, hyacinth, crystal, and the most precious pearl. Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion also differ greatly among themselves and from the translators of the Septuagint in this passage—not only in the order but also in the number and names of the stones.

In the Apocalypse of John (Rev. XXI), where Jerusalem is described as constructed from living stones, the same stones are placed in its foundations, with their order slightly changed at the end. Its gates are said to have been built with the brightness of crystal. The same stones are also described on the breast of the high priest in four rows, on the breastplate (Exod. XXVIII). On his shoulders are two onyx stones, on which the names of the twelve patriarchs are written.

The true high priest—of whom it is written, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CXIX)—carries them on his breast and carries them on his shoulders. Thus, in the twelve stones, he displays the number of the apostles, and in the two stones, the mysteries of both Testaments.

One of these, John the Evangelist, reclined on his breast so that he might draw up the streams of wisdom and be able to say: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God” (John I).

These are the living stones from which the Church is built, concerning which the apostle Peter writes: “If you have tasted that the Lord is gracious, and coming to him as to a living stone, rejected indeed by human beings but chosen and honored by God, you yourselves, as living stones, are being built into a spiritual house, into a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ” (I Pet. II).

For Scripture says: “Behold, I am laying in Zion a cornerstone, chosen and precious; and whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame” (Isa. XXVIII). Concerning this the Chosen Vessel also agrees in the same words, saying: “You have been built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus our Lord himself being the cornerstone, in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple of God” (Eph. II).

These are the stones concerning which we also read elsewhere: “Holy stones roll upon the earth like wheels” (Zech. IX)—touching the ground only slightly and hastening toward heavenly things through their rolling motion.

Concerning them Scripture also says: “Behold, I will prepare your carbuncle stone, and your foundations of sapphire; I will make your battlements of jasper, your gates of crystal stone, and your entire wall of chosen stones. All your children shall be taught by God, and great shall be the peace of your children; you shall be built in righteousness” (Isa. LIV). We have said what seemed to us concerning this in our explanations of the same prophet.

The twentieth Psalm also sings of such stones: “O Lord, the king shall rejoice in your strength, and he shall exult greatly in your salvation. You have granted him the desire of his soul, and you have not deprived him of the request of his lips. For you came before him with the blessings of sweetness; you placed upon his head a crown of precious stone.”

These are the pearls of the prophets and apostles. In comparison with Christ, all of them are sold in the Gospel so that the most precious pearl may be purchased. This is the stone concerning which Zechariah writes that it has seven eyes—that is, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit (Zech. III). Read Isaiah.

The apostle Paul also places gold, silver, and precious stones in the foundation of the Church, upon which they are to build (I Cor. III). It is not appropriate to discuss at this time the colors, natures, and effects of each of them; they require a volume of their own. Thus, in Ezekiel, Exodus, the Apocalypse, and Isaiah, when all the stones and their orders are compared with one another, they pose a great question both to the reader and to the interpreter.

“You were a cherub,” he says, “extended and protecting, on God’s holy mountain; you walked perfect in the midst of fiery stones.”

(Gregory, in the cited chapter and XXVI.) For *cherub* is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge.” This one is therefore called a cherub because there is no doubt that he surpassed all others in knowledge. He walked perfect in the midst of fiery stones because he stood glorious in the splendor of his creation among the hearts of angels kindled with the fire of charity.

He aptly calls him “extended and protecting.” Everything that we protect by stretching over it, we shade. Because he is believed to have overshadowed the brightness of the others by comparison with his own brightness, he is said to have been extended and protecting. He covered the others, as it were, by overshadowing them, because he surpassed their greatness by a greater excellence.

What is there called beautiful among many branches, what is there called the seal of likeness, what is there called the cherub, and what is there called protecting, is in Job, in the voice of the Lord, called “the beginning of the ways of God” (Job XL). His former greatness and what he lost are indicated in such remarkable terms so that, by terrifying the human being, he may show that the human being himself, if he grows proud, will suffer because of the fault of arrogance. If God did not spare the one whom he raised, by creating him, to such glory and brightness, when striking him down, what will become of us?

Let the human being therefore consider what he deserves when lifted up on earth, if an angel, even though exalted above the other angels, is cast down in heaven. Hence the prophet rightly says: “My sword has become drunk in heaven” (Isa. XXXIV), as though he were openly saying: Consider with what anger I will strike the proud of the earth, if I did not spare even those whom I created beside me in heaven when they were struck down because of the vice of arrogance.

(Jerome.) Moreover, where the Hebrew text says, “You were a cherub, extended and protecting,” the object understood is the ark of God and the mercy seat; or, according to the Septuagint, that he was anointed and created with the cherub. From this it is shown that the passage cannot apply to a human prince of the city of Tyre, but to a holy and preeminent power that was appointed prince of the city of Tyre.

“And I placed you,” he says, “on God’s holy mountain”—without doubt signifying paradise, to which Paul says that he was caught up after the third heaven (II Cor. XII). *Cherub* is masculine singular, while the plural is *cherubim*. They are interpreted as “a multitude of knowledge.” Upon them God rests and sits, and he uses them as his chariot, as the prophet says to him: “You who sit upon the cherubim, reveal yourself” (Ps. LXXIX). And elsewhere: “He mounted upon the cherubim and flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds” (Ps. XVII).

This cherub, whether created with the cherub or himself the cherub, extended and protecting the mysteries, was placed on God’s holy mountain. We have spoken of this frequently. The apostle Paul also says—if one accepts the Epistle to the Hebrews: “You have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and thousands of angels” (Heb. XII).

Or certainly, as we have said, God’s holy mountain is to be understood as paradise. He also walked in the midst of fiery stones, concerning which it is written: “He makes his angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire” (Ps. CIII).

It is not only God, who is called a consuming fire, who consumes hay, wood, and stubble, but also the angels, who are called fiery stones and burning in spirit. Hence the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke XII).

What follows—“Perfect in your ways from the day of your creation”—for which the Septuagint has, “You were blameless in your days, from the day when you were created, until iniquity was found in you”—shows that every creature was created good by God and possessed perfect virtue. Thus the prince of Tyre also was blameless, so that thereafter the fault might belong not to nature but to the will: “Until iniquity was found in you.”

It was found by God; it had been held enclosed in the treasuries of your heart through pride and the abuse of the power that you had received.

“In the abundance of your commerce,” he says, “your inner parts were filled with iniquity, and you sinned. And I cast you out from God’s mountain; I destroyed you, O cherub who protected, from the midst of the fiery stones. Your heart was lifted up in your beauty; you corrupted your wisdom because of your splendor. I cast you to the ground; I placed you before the faces of kings, so that they might look upon you. In the abundance of your iniquities and in the iniquity of your commerce you profaned your sanctuary. Therefore I will bring forth fire from your midst; it shall consume you.”

His inner parts—or his storehouses—were likewise filled with iniquity in the abundance of his commerce. For while he acquired many things and was not content with the knowledge he had received, nor with the power over which he had been placed, he filled the storehouses and innermost places of his heart, so that, saturated and fattened, he might kick against his Creator.

“For Jacob ate and was satisfied, and the beloved kicked; he grew fat and thick and broad, and abandoned God who had made him” (Deut. XXXII). And: “From the heart proceed evil thoughts” (Matt. XV). On account of these God says: “You sinned, and I cast you out from God’s mountain”—or, “you were wounded by God’s mountain.” Reading this, we are compelled to fear.

If the cherub, extended and protecting, placed on God’s holy mountain and perfect and blameless in the midst of fiery stones, filled his inner parts with iniquity through the abundance of his commerce, sinned, and was cast out from God’s mountain—that is, from the dwelling-place of paradise—or was wounded by God’s mountain, which is plainly understood as Christ; or, again, if he was established and dwelling on God’s mountain and was wounded by himself, pierced by the evil of conscience when he understood himself to be unworthy of dwelling on the mountain, what must we think about ourselves?

Therefore it is said to him: “I destroyed you, O cherub who protected, from the midst of the fiery stones,” so that you might no longer remain among the fiery stones, but perish. O cherub—or cherubim—you who protected, I brought you out from the midst of the fiery stones, in accordance with what is written concerning Adam: “He cast out Adam and placed the cherubim” (Gen. III), opposite the paradise of delights.

He gives the reasons why he was led out or cast from the midst of the fiery stones: “Your heart was lifted up in your beauty,” while you thought that what belongs to God was your own. Hence the apostle says that he received a thorn in the flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet him, so that he would not grow proud because of the abundance of revelations and fall into the judgment of the devil (II Cor. XII).

“And therefore,” he says, “your teaching was corrupted along with your beauty,” or, “you corrupted your wisdom in your beauty.” Because you wished to be more than you had been created to be and to know more than you had received from God, you lost even what you possessed; and in place of beauty and instruction, ugliness and foolishness took possession of you. Therefore you were cast to the earth, although previously you dwelt on God’s mountain.

Isaiah writes concerning this: “How has Lucifer fallen, who used to rise in the morning?” (Isa. XIV). And the Savior says in the Gospel: “I was watching Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke X). Jeremiah also says to Jerusalem: “How has the Lord in his anger obscured the daughter of Zion? He has cast the glory of Israel from heaven to earth” (Lam. II).

He was cast before the sight of all kings, so that they might be terrified by his example—whether these are good kings, whose heart is in the hand of God, or evil ones, whose kingdoms the devil showed to the Savior. Those kings met the king of Babylon and said: “You too have been captured like us and counted among us.”

Therefore he also profaned his sanctuary, which he had possessed when he dwelt on the mountain and lived in the midst of fiery stones.

It follows: “I will bring forth fire from your midst; it shall devour you.” That fire had been kindled in the heart of the king of Tyre by the one whose arrows are fiery and concerning whom it is written: “All adulterers are like an oven; their hearts are burning” (Hos. VII).

Isaiah also speaks of this fire: “Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame that you have kindled” (Isa. L), so that, going out from within, it may devour its possessor, in accordance with what is written in the same Isaiah: “It devoured its substance like hay” (Isa. V). “On that day the mountains, hills, and forests shall be extinguished, and it shall devour from soul to flesh.”

Nadab and Abihu had offered this fire, which is called foreign, upon the altar of the Lord (Lev. X), and therefore they were consumed by divine fire. Hence Moses says: “This is the word that the Lord has spoken: ‘I will be sanctified in those who approach me.’” God’s sanctification is the punishment of sinners.

After this it is said: “And I will reduce you to ashes,” so that the fire may consume everything that you built upon your evil conscience. When you ought to have been at rest and, on the Sabbath, should have done no servile work, you gathered wood on the Sabbath, so that the fire within your breast might have something to devour.

It is also beneficial for all evil works to be reduced to ashes, so that the destructive fire may be utterly extinguished and all may see and be astonished that the king of Tyre has perished and become nothing—not over many ages, but in one age, or certainly forever—so that what is written may be fulfilled: “I will not spare you, and I will not have pity.”

The Hebrews, among their other fables, genealogies (γενεαλογίαι), and interminable questions, commonly understand these words as spoken against Hiram, king of Tyre. Yet from Solomon to Ezekiel there are many years, and it is plainly evident that such a person could not have lived throughout that period. They therefore pronounce the passage as though the prophet were speaking to him ironically: “Are you the seal of God’s likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty? Are you adorned with every stone? Are you a cherub, or created with a cherub, when, on the contrary, you have sinned and are to be reduced to ashes?”

They add a marvel to their fable, saying, contrary to Scripture—or rather without the authority of Scripture—that Hiram lived for a thousand years. But how violent this interpretation is, the prudent reader understands without our judgment.

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set your face against Sidon and prophesy against her, and say: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, Sidon, and I will be glorified in your midst. And they shall know that I am the Lord when I execute judgments in her, and when I am sanctified in her, and when I send pestilence and blood into her streets. And the slain shall fall in her midst, by the sword on every side, and they shall know that I am the Lord.

“And there shall no longer be for the house of Israel a stumbling-block of bitterness or a thorn causing pain, from all those surrounding them who oppose them; and they shall know that I am the Lord God.

“Thus says the Lord God: When I gather the house of Israel from the peoples among whom they have been scattered, I will be sanctified in them before the nations. And they shall dwell in their own land, which I gave to my servant Jacob. They shall dwell there securely, and they shall build houses and plant vineyards; they shall dwell confidently when I have executed judgments upon all those around them who oppose them. And they shall know that I am the Lord their God.” (Jerome.)

Consequently, after Tyre, the word is spoken to Sidon, for both cities belong to one province. In the Gospel, Tyre and Sidon are likewise named together: “If the miracles that were performed in you had been performed in Tyre and Sidon…” (Matt. XI; Luke X). Hence the Canaanite woman, whose daughter was tormented by a demon and who came out from the borders of Tyre and Sidon, obtained what she requested.

The divine word foretells that Sidon also will be captured by the Babylonians, and that through the weight of her evils she will learn that he is the Lord when he judges her and is sanctified in her, and when he consumes her with famine, pestilence, and the sword, so that the slain fall in her streets. She will no longer be a stumbling-block to God’s people, nor will her inhabitants frequently attack them.

When this has happened, the people of Israel—whom he had scattered among various nations—will return to their own land, and he will be sanctified in them: not, as in the case of Sidon, in an evil sense, but in a good one, when he has shown them mercy. They will dwell in the land that he gave to their father Jacob. They will dwell securely and trust in the Lord; they will build houses and plant vineyards when he has fulfilled his promises. Then they will know that he is the Lord, whose promises are utterly firm.

Many refer this to the time of Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Nehemiah, when the people of Israel returned and dwelt in the land of Judea. Others hope that it will be fulfilled at the end of time and in the thousand years.

According to the spiritual interpretation, however, this seems to us to be the meaning. The Sidonians are interpreted as “hunters.” Concerning them it is written in the Psalms: “Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters and from the harsh word” (Ps. CXXIII); and in Proverbs: “The eye of the adulteress is the sinner’s snare” (Eccl. VII).

There are also hunters opposed to these, in a good sense, concerning whom Jeremiah writes: “Behold, I will send fishers and hunters, and they shall hunt you from every hill and mountain” (Jer. XVI). The Lord also sends such men to fish, and makes them, from fishers of fish, fishers of human beings (Matt. IV). Hence the village of Peter and Andrew is called by this name; for Bethsaida is interpreted in our language as “house of hunters.”

Against these exceedingly wicked hunters, therefore, the word of God is directed, and the prophet is commanded to set, or firmly establish, his face against Sidon. He must not be tossed about by every wind of doctrine, but, standing in the truth, must kill his hunters.

What, then, are the things that the Lord threatens Sidon? “Behold, I myself will come against you, and I will be glorified in you when I have killed you. And all who remain shall know that I am the Lord when I repay you what you deserve. I will send pestilence and blood into your streets.”

Sidon’s streets are rightly called streets. “For broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction” (Matt. VII). “And the slain shall fall, those who had stood wrongly, by the sword on every side.” By that sword which the Lord came to bring upon the earth (Matt. X), so that it might separate what was wrongly joined. Those who remain shall know that he is the Lord.

When those adversaries have ceased, there will no longer be a stumbling-block of bitterness, nor a thorn of pain piercing and wounding God’s people. All these things are spoken against the opposing powers: they will be destroyed at the end of time, and there will be eternal security when the Lord gathers the house of Israel—that is, those who behold God with understanding.

He will be sanctified in them, and what is written will be fulfilled: “Be holy, because I am holy” (Lev. XIX). They will dwell in their own land, concerning which we read elsewhere: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. XXVI). He had given it to Jacob, who had previously supplanted his brother and had deserved to receive his birthright.

“And they shall dwell in it securely,” or “in hope.” “They shall build houses and plant vineyards, and they shall dwell” again “in hope,” in accordance with what is read in Isaiah: “You who have been weaned from milk, you who have been taken away from the breast, await tribulation upon tribulation, and hope upon hope” (Isa. XXVIII).

“They shall build houses”—and in the Gospel the one builds a house who establishes its foundations not upon sand but upon rock. Concerning these houses it is written: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Ps. CXXVI).

## CHAPTER XXIX

The word of the Lord against Pharaoh and Egypt, in which the desolation of Egypt is foretold and its restoration after forty years is promised, and Nebuchadnezzar is promised as a reward for his labor against Tyre.

[Col. 0795A]

“In the tenth year, in the twelfth month, on the first day of the month, the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘Son of man, set your face against Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and prophesy concerning him; speak concerning all Egypt, and say: Thus says the Lord God,’ etc.”

After Sidon, which itself is situated on the Phoenician coast, the word is addressed to the prophet in the tenth year of the captivity of King Joachim, and in the twelfth month and on the first day of the month, so that he may set his face—or harden it—against Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and speak concerning him and concerning all Egypt, or against all Egypt. For Egypt is a province situated on the opposite side of Judea along the same coast; and he is to prophesy what is going to happen to it.

If, however, it is necessary to say something about the numbers, what place does one have among ten? Hence, too, at the beginning of Genesis it is not said, “there was evening and morning, the first day,” but “one day,” so that it may teach that the same day is continually rolled onward, and that the same order among ten decades—that is, the number one hundred—will be held by the tenth number. It is on the tenth day that the lamb is taken for sacrifice, so that it may be slaughtered on the fourteenth day. In this way the order of numbers proceeds through ten hundreds, a thousand, ten thousand, one hundred thousand, and beyond, by its successive decades.

After the tenth year, the twelfth month is mentioned, so that the complete number of the twelve apostles and prophets, who are contained in one volume, may be indicated.

Moreover, according to the Septuagint, the tenth month—called *Thebeth* in Hebrew, *Tybi* among the Egyptians, and January among the Romans, because among them it is the gate (*janua*) of the year—after all heat has been removed, holds the primacy of winter’s cold. Let this suffice concerning the numbers.

But above all, we must inquire whether this is the same Pharaoh who is named in Exodus, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and many other places, and in the Song:

> “I have compared you, my beloved, to my cavalry  
> in Pharaoh’s chariots” (Song of Songs 1),

or whether he is one Pharaoh and another a different one. It seems to me that there was not a single Pharaoh; rather, among the Egyptians this name designated royal dignity, just as among the Romans their kings are called Caesars and Augustuses, after the first Gaius Caesar and his second, adopted son Octavian, who was later called Augustus; among the Syrians they are called Antiochi, among the Persians Arsacids, among the Philistines Abimelech, and after Alexander the Ptolemies ruled Egypt down to Cleopatra, after whose defeat at Actium Egypt became a Roman province. [Col. 0795B–D]

Therefore, in the present passage the word of the Lord is directed against any one king of Egypt, whose name is interpreted as *διασκεδαστής* (*diaskedastēs*), that is, “destroyer,” “slaughterer,” and one who cuts and divides everything with the sword. According to the mystical meanings, this must be referred to the power to which Egypt is subject. For no human being would dare to say, “The rivers are mine, and I made them”; nor would he be called a great dragon, sitting in the midst of his rivers.

Egypt, however, is called *Mesraim* in Hebrew, and is translated into our language as “one who constricts,” namely, one who oppresses those subject to him and does not allow them to raise their eyes toward heaven, but, in accordance with the Gospel (Luke 13) and the example of that woman whom the devil had bent down for eighteen years, continually thrusts them toward earthly things.

Let us therefore see what threat is made against Pharaoh and all Egypt.

> “Behold, I am against you, Pharaoh, king of Egypt,  
> the great dragon who lies in the midst of your rivers  
> and says: ‘The river is mine, and I made myself.’  
> I will put a bridle in your jaws,  
> and I will make the fish of your rivers cling to your scales.  
> I will draw you out from the midst of your rivers,  
> and all the fish of your rivers will cling to your scales.  
> I will throw you into the wilderness,  
> and all the fish of your river with you.  
> You will fall upon the face of the earth.  
> You will not be gathered up or collected.  
> I have given you to the beasts of the earth  
> and to the birds of the sky as food.  
> And all the inhabitants of Egypt shall know that I am the Lord,  
> because you became a staff of reed to the house of Israel.  
> When they grasped you with their hand,  
> you broke and tore their whole shoulder;  
> and when they leaned upon you,  
> you were crushed and dislocated all their loins.”
