He speaks against Pharaoh, the prince of Egypt, and under his figure addresses the great power to which Egypt has been entrusted for rule. Yet it is also proud against its Creator, claiming dominion over the earth for itself and offering itself to the Egyptian peoples to be worshiped.

He speaks according to the situation of the province, as though to a king who trusts in the inundation of the Nile, does not greatly desire rains from heaven, and thinks himself the creator of the river—or boasts that the rivers, that is, the *διώρυκες* (*diōrykes*, “canals”) and channels of the Nile, were made by him.

“I will not send an angel,” he says, “but, O great dragon, who lie and sit in the midst of your rivers, I myself will come to you to punish you.” For you dared to say, “The river Nile is mine, and I am my own creator,” or, “I myself made the river by which all Egypt is irrigated.”

And when I come, “I will put a bridle in your jaws,” or constrain with nooses the mouth with which you spoke boastfully. I will make all your companions and commanders, whom he calls “fish,” cling to your fins or scales, so that, when you are drawn out of the river, you may be thrown down or laid aside.

For you had lifted yourself up excessively in the wilderness, and you will fall upon the face of your plain or land, since Egypt is a flat province. Your corpse will not be gathered up or collected—that is, you will by no means be buried—but “I will give you to the beasts and birds of the sky to be devoured.” When the inhabitants of Egypt see these things carried out against you by my judgment, they will recognize that I myself am the Lord. [Col. 0796A–D]

These things will happen to you because you deceived my people Israel by your aid, so that they trusted not in God their Creator but in you. You were for them a staff of reed, according to Isaiah (Isaiah 36), an empty rod and an exceedingly fragile reed. Those who leaned upon you discovered that their support was futile, so that you broke under those who relied upon you and tore their shoulder and the hand by which you were held.

While they felt secure in you, all their loins were crushed, and they fell to the ground, receiving wounds instead of assistance.

These things are said metaphorically, as though against the king of Egypt, because that province itself was not Israel’s enemy; rather, while it made great promises, it separated them from God’s help.

According to the *ἀναγωγή* (*anagōgē*, the spiritual or higher interpretation), we often read of the dragon as the opposing power. Hence Pharaoh is called *διασκεδαστής* (*diaskedastēs*), because he separates people from God and joins them to himself; and Egypt is translated as “those who trouble and afflict,” namely, those whom it can subjugate.

This is the transgressor of whom Job speaks at length (Job 40). It is written in the Psalm:

> “You crushed the heads of the dragon;  
> you gave him as food to the peoples of Ethiopia” (Psalm 73).

He is called the great dragon in comparison with lesser dragons, concerning which it is sung:

> “You crushed the heads of the dragons in the waters.”

And elsewhere:

> “This is the great and spacious sea;  
> there are creeping things without number,  
> small animals with great ones.  
> There the ships travel.  
> This dragon, which you formed to mock it” (Psalm 103).

Of him it is also said elsewhere:

> “He is king over all that are in the waters,  
> and the beginning of the Lord’s formation,  
> made so that he might be mocked by his angels.”

He sits, or lies, in the midst of his rivers—not in one river but in many, which we understand as the various heresies through which he has flowed into the Egypt of this age and irrigated the souls of the deceived, not with rains coming from heaven but with muddy waters from the earth. Jeremiah forbids us to drink them, saying:

> “What have you to do with the way of Egypt,  
> to drink the water of the Gihon?” (Jeremiah 2)

Instead of *Gihon*, the Hebrew has *sior*, a word translated as “turbid and muddy waters.” [Col. 0797A–C]

To understand what the rivers of the Egyptian dragon are, we can learn from their opposites. The Lord speaks of his rivers:

> “Whoever believes in me,  
> rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7).

And to the Samaritan woman:

> “Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him  
> will never thirst,  
> but the water that I shall give him  
> will become in him a fountain of water  
> leaping up into eternal life” (John 4).

These are the rivers that come from heaven, of which David sings:

> “The rushing of the river makes glad the city of God” (Psalm 45),

with no doubt that he means the Church.

Let us therefore consider what punishment and penalty belong to the dragon. The text continues:

> “I will put a bridle, or a snare, in your jaws.”

To this is similar what Job says:

> “You will draw out the dragon with a hook  
> and put a halter around his nostrils.  
> He trusts that the Jordan will enter his mouth;  
> in his eyes he will receive it.  
> You will pierce his nostrils with a stake  
> and his lip with a ring” (Job 40).

(Gregory, *Moralia* 33.8.) What else are we to understand by the stakes—that is, the poles—which are sharpened in order to be driven in, except the sharp counsels of the saints? These pierce the nostrils of this Behemoth, as they watchfully discern his most cunning snares and transfix them by overcoming them.

Through the nostrils scent is drawn, and by drawing in breath one comes to know even a thing that is far away. By the nostrils of Behemoth, therefore, his crafty snares are signified, by which he attempts with great cunning both to discover the hidden goods of our hearts and to scatter them through his evil persuasion.

Thus the Lord pierces his nostrils with stakes, because he penetrates and weakens his crafty snares through the sharp perceptions of the saints.

(Jerome.) The Lord places a bridle in the jaws of this dragon, pierces his lips, and constrains them with the circle of a ring when, through ecclesiastical men instructed in the holy Scriptures, he imposes silence upon him and all the doctrines of perversity are dissolved.

He makes the fish of his rivers cling to his fins or scales. These are the heretics who, through pride, hasten to high places, so that, bound with the dragon, they may form one body with him and be joined to him either in fellowship of error or in likeness of punishment, just as one who clings to the Lord is one spirit with him.

The Egyptian dragon does not have one river but many rivers, by which he irrigates Egypt, lowly and cast down, possessing no mountains within itself and not having the waters of Siloam, which flow quietly, but turbid and muddy waters.

Hence the Lord draws him out from the midst of his rivers, so that he may no longer lie or sit in them; and he makes all the fish cling to his scales according to the quality of their vices, attached throughout the dragon’s body—to his head, belly, tail, and extremities—so that when the dragon is drawn out, the fish clinging to him may also be drawn out with him.

“And I will throw you,” he says, “into the wilderness,” so that you may no longer find anyone to deceive. Or certainly, “I will cast you down from the summit of your pride,” and I will cast you down quickly.

In accordance with the Apostle’s words:

> “But may the God of peace crush Satan under your feet quickly” (Romans 16),

when the dragon has been crushed and cast down, the fish of that river will also be cast down, and the author of crimes, who previously thought himself standing and ranging throughout the whole world, will fall.

He will fall upon the face of his own land, from which he was hurled down from heaven, so that he may no longer be gathered in the churches of heretics. Nor will he be collected or buried among those who believed him, once they have been freed from him. Instead, he will be given to the beasts of the earth and the birds of the sky to be devoured.

These are the beasts concerning which it is written:

> “Do not hand over to the beasts the soul that confesses you” (Psalm 73).

And the birds of the sky are those which, along the road, eat the seed. According to the Savior’s interpretation, they are the devils. For not only is the prince of wickedness called the devil, but his disciples also bear the name devils. Thus it is said concerning Judas:

> “Did I not choose you twelve? And one of you is a devil” (John 6).

The birds are called “of the sky” because they promise themselves exalted things. After the dragon with his fish has been cast down and thrown away, and delivered to the beasts of the earth for devouring—beasts possessing no gentleness within themselves—and to those who are carried about by every wind of doctrine, then the inhabitants of this age will understand that he himself is the Lord. [Col. 0797D–0798D]

The entire cause of the punishments is that he had falsely promised help to the house of Israel and had been for it a reed or a staff of reed, empty and vain, possessing no fullness within itself, because he could not say:

> “But we have all received from his fullness” (John 1),

while Scripture commands:

> “You shall not appear before the Lord your God empty or vacant” (Exodus 23).

That we ought not to seek help from Egypt is also attested elsewhere in Scripture:

> “Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help” (Isaiah 31).

Concerning this staff of reed, Rabshakeh vainly reproaches King Hezekiah of Judah, saying:

> “Behold, you trust in this broken staff of reed, in Egypt;  
> whoever leans upon it, it enters his hand.  
> Such is Pharaoh, king of Egypt,  
> and all who trust in him” (Isaiah 36).

Rabshakeh was indeed lying when he said these things about the just king; Rabshakeh’s own name is interpreted as “abounding in the cup.” For he was drunk from Babylon’s golden cup, and therefore poured out upon the people who confessed the Lord the things that belonged to himself.

Here, however, Pharaoh is reproached because he was for the house of Israel a staff or rod of reed, promising them a vain and fragile support that would quickly be crushed.

To understand what this staff of reed is, upon which the house of Israel must not rely, we can learn from the opposite staff and rod of the Lord, concerning which it is said to the Lord:

> “Your rod and your staff,  
> they themselves have comforted me” (Psalm 22).

Aaron also possessed this rod. With it he devoured the Egyptian dragons (Exodus 8, 10), struck the banks of the Nile, and brought forth gnats throughout all Egypt.

Moses also, according to the Septuagint, stretched out this rod and raised it toward heaven; and the Lord brought a south wind over the land throughout that day and night. In the morning the wind lifted up and brought locusts over all the land of Egypt.

I think it is of this rod that it is written in the Book of Numbers (Numbers 17) that it blossomed and produced nuts, or almonds.

The Apostle also possessed it when he said:

> “What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod?” (1 Corinthians 4).

And those who celebrated the Passover held staffs in their hands (Exodus 12). Without these staffs, which supported the weakness of the human body, they could not eat the flesh of the lamb.

This is the rod from the root of Jesse, upon which the seven spirits rested.

But Pharaoh is not such a one, nor is the Egyptian staff a rod of this kind. Rather, it is a reed that deceives those who grasp it and tears their shoulders—that is, their strength. Whoever leans upon it has his loins dislocated; he will not be able to stand or, girded about the loins, celebrate the Passover. This applies to those whose hearts and loins God searches (Psalm 7). [Col. 0798A–0799C]

> “Therefore thus says the Lord God:  
> Behold, I will bring a sword against you,  
> and I will destroy man and beast from you.  
> The land of Egypt shall become a wilderness and a desolation,  
> and they shall know that I am the Lord.  
> Because he said, ‘The river is mine, and I made it,’  
> therefore, behold, I am against you and your rivers.  
> I will make the land of Egypt a desolation,  
> ravaged by the sword,  
> from the tower of Syene to the borders of Ethiopia.  
> No human foot shall pass through it,  
> nor shall the foot of an animal pass through it;  
> it shall not be inhabited for forty years.  
> I will make the land of Egypt desolate  
> in the midst of desolated lands,  
> and its cities shall be desolate  
> in the midst of overthrown cities;  
> they shall be desolate for forty years.  
> I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations  
> and disperse them through the lands.

> “For thus says the Lord God:  
> At the end of forty years  
> I will gather Egypt from the peoples  
> among whom they had been scattered.  
> I will restore the captivity of Egypt  
> and settle them in the land of Pathros,  
> in the land of their origin,  
> in the land from which they were taken.  
> There they shall be a humble kingdom;  
> among the other kingdoms it shall be the humblest.  
> It shall no longer exalt itself over the nations,  
> and I will diminish them,  
> so that they may not rule over the nations.  
> Nor shall they any longer be a source of confidence to the house of Israel,  
> teaching iniquity, so that they flee and follow them.  
> And they shall know that I am the Lord God.”

(Jerome.) Join what follows to the preceding words: Because you were a staff of reed to the house of Israel, and not only were you broken in its hand, but, according to Isaiah, you pierced its hand; now you have torn its shoulder, and you yourself have been crushed and have dislocated the loins of those who leaned upon you. Therefore I will bring against you the sword of the enemy, and with men I will destroy the beasts. The land of Egypt will be turned into desolations, and a second time the Egyptians will know that I am the Lord.

Nor will I be content with this alone. Because it burst into such great blasphemy as to say that its rivers and all the abundance of Egypt belonged to it, I will therefore remove the one who had called himself its creator, together with the rivers he had boasted were made by him, and the rest of the land of Egypt. I will turn it into the longest desolation, ravaged by the sword from the tower of Syene to the borders of Ethiopia.

Instead of “tower,” which is called *magdal* in Hebrew, the Septuagint placed the name of the place and wrote *Magdolon*. The tower of Syene still exists today as a fortress subject to Roman rule. There are the cataracts of the Nile, and to that point the Nile is navigable from our sea.

He therefore says that all Egypt will be devastated as far as the borders of Ethiopia, to which the farthest region of Egypt is joined. Thus no human foot will pass through Egypt, no animals will be found there, and it will not be inhabited for forty years.

Egypt is spared because the Egyptians were once hospitable to Israel; therefore their condemnation is shorter in duration. Tyre kept its sabbaths for seventy years and was then restored to its former condition. The captivity of Judea and the destruction of the Temple likewise completed seventy years, up to Cyrus, king of the Persians:

> “The mighty will suffer mighty torments.”

When he says, “I will make the land of Egypt desolate in the midst of desolated lands,” he signifies the Philistines, Idumeans, Moabites, and all the other regions against which the prophet’s earlier prophecy was directed.

Then he will scatter, or sow, the Egyptians among the nations and disperse them through the lands. And because the Lord is merciful and compassionate, patient and rich in mercy, after forty years Egypt will be restored. All its captivity will be brought back to its ancient soil and settled in the metropolitan city called Pathros, where it arose and from which it proceeded—yet only so far as to lose its former pride for its own benefit, and to be a humble kingdom, indeed the humblest of all the nations.

It will no longer exalt itself against the nations or exercise power over them. Reduced to a small number, it will no longer deceive the house of Israel through reliance upon itself, nor teach them iniquity, or bring back to their memory the iniquity by which, having abandoned God’s help, they sought Egypt as a support.

All these things will happen so that the Egyptians may recognize a third time that he himself is the Lord. [Col. 0799D–0800D]

We have touched on these matters briefly, laying the foundations of the historical account. Now the cloud of allegory must be discussed, and it will attempt, with the same brevity, to avoid prolonging this explanation.

The word is addressed to the dragon who had said, “The rivers are mine, and I made them”: the Lord himself will bring a sword against him. Of this sword it is written in Isaiah:

> “My sword is drunk in heaven.”

Now it will descend upon the earth to destroy from it man and beast, whatever appears to possess either reason or simplicity. It will destroy them absolutely—but for the dragon, or so that they may perish to the dragon and live to God.

Let the land of Egypt become destruction according to the preceding sense, so that it may perish to the dragon and, after its destruction, be reduced to a wilderness, ceasing to have such an evil inhabitant.

Then men and beasts, and the devastated land, will know that he himself is the Lord—in the sense in which it is written in Psalm 77:

> “When he killed them, then they sought him.”

For everyone who seeks will find.

It is an act of God’s mercy that the abundance of this world should perish and the streams of Egypt dry up; indeed, that their land should become desolations. And let the judgment of the Lord be scattered from the tower of Syene, which is interpreted as “a circuit,” so that it may have nothing upright within itself, as far as the land of the Ethiopians, who are called “humble.” Thus all pride that had raised itself against the knowledge of God may be destroyed and humbled for its salvation.

Nor should the foot of man—that is, anything possessing reason—pass through Egypt. Nor should the foot of a beast walk there, so that it may not hold even the simple, whom Pharaoh wished to keep in Egypt after the human beings had been released, while Moses resisted and desired that the animals also be freed from Egypt’s captivity.

“And it shall not be inhabited for forty years.” This number is always associated with affliction and punishment. Thus Moses (Exodus 34), Elijah (1 Kings 19), and the Savior himself (Matthew 4) fasted for forty days and nights.

For forty years the people were in the wilderness, so that afterward, circumcised at Gilgal (Numbers 14), they might be freed from the reproach and disgrace of Egypt.

In the sacramental meaning of this number, the same prophet also sleeps for forty days on his right side on behalf of the tribe of Judah. And the people who were to serve in Egypt are announced as doing so for four hundred years—forty decades, or four *ἑκατοντάδες* (*hekatontades*, “hundreds”).

The rains of the Flood likewise bring shipwreck upon the world for forty days. For it was just that one who offended God by loving and cherishing the four elements of the world, by which all things are said to consist, should be punished by that same number; and that Israel, which had sinned against the Sabbath, should endure a punishment of seven decades—that is, seventy years.

The land of Egypt is given over to desolation, and its cities are placed in the midst of desolated lands and overthrown cities. These cities were not built of stones but of brick and straw. Thus Egypt, which had been wrongly joined to itself, is scattered and dispersed through the lands, so that the grain may be separated from the straw.

When the forty years have been completed, Egypt is restored; its captivity is brought back and settled in the land of Pathros, which is interpreted as “trampled bread.” There is the bread that said, “I am the bread that came down from heaven,” trampled down by heretical perversity, so that when such people come to the Church, they dwell in trampled bread.

They must by no means lift themselves up in pride, but must be a humble kingdom. Once restored to their former condition, they should humble themselves through humility because they lived in Egypt and built cities of brick.

Among the many kingdoms of the Church, let them be humble and know against whom they sinned. Egypt must no longer exalt itself over the churches divided throughout the world, but must be reduced to a small number; few must remain in it among the nations. They must no longer deceive the house of Israel—that is, the Church—nor promise it a vain hope and confidence, teaching iniquity so that people flee ecclesiastical discipline and follow Egyptian pleasures.

These things will happen so that the Egyptians may recognize a third time that he himself is the Lord.

It seems to me that this is said because the first knowledge of the Egyptians is in the flesh, the second in the soul, and the third in the spirit: first upon the earth, second after the life of this world has ended, and third after the resurrection.

> “And it came to pass in the twenty-seventh year,  
> in the first month and on the first day of the month,  
> that the word of the Lord came to me, saying:  
> ‘Son of man, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon,  
> made his army perform a great service against Tyre.  
> Every head was bald,  
> and every shoulder was rubbed bare;  
> yet no payment was made to him or to his army from Tyre  
> for the service by which he served me against it.

> “Therefore thus says the Lord God:  
> Behold, I will give Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon,  
> the land of Egypt.  
> He will carry off its multitude,  
> plunder its booty,  
> and seize its spoils.  
> It will be payment for his army  
> and for the work by which he served me against it.  
> I have given him the land of Egypt  
> because he labored for me,  
> says the Lord God.

> “On that day a horn will sprout for the house of Israel,  
> and I will give you an open mouth among them.  
> And they shall know that I am the Lord.”

The question is raised how, immediately after the tenth year of the preceding discourse, the twenty-seventh year is now placed, while in what follows the tenth and twelfth years occur, and in the final description of the Temple the twenty-fifth year is mentioned. The solution, however, is easy.

Because both the preceding prophecy and this one concern Egypt, although they were given at different times, they have nevertheless been joined together because they prophesy concerning one province. We read the same thing frequently in Jeremiah, where the times are described in reversed order. Events concerning Zedekiah are first related in some passages, and afterward those concerning Jehoiakim (Joachim), who preceded him.

In the Psalms, however, since the work is lyric poetry, no historical order is required.

Let us therefore speak first according to the literal sense. When Nebuchadnezzar was attacking Tyre, he could not bring up battering rams, siege engines, and covered ways against its walls because the city was surrounded by the sea. He ordered the immense multitude of his army to carry stones and earth. When the sea—or rather the very narrow strait—had been filled in, he made the neighboring shore contiguous with the island.

When the Tyrians saw that this was now almost completed and that the foundations of the walls were being shaken by the blows of the battering rams, the nobility placed whatever precious things it possessed in gold, silver, clothing, and varied furnishings upon ships and carried them off to the islands. Thus, when the city was captured, Nebuchadnezzar found nothing worthy of his labor.

And because in this matter he had obeyed God’s will, after several years of Tyrian captivity Egypt was given to him. Tyre was much more savage than Egypt. Tyre attacked Jerusalem, whereas Egypt promised vain assistance. It is one thing to deceive through the weakness of hope and another to fight against God’s people.

This, then, is what is said concerning Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, in his attack upon Tyre: “He made his army serve me, so that it might fulfill my will.”

“Every head,” he says, “was made bald, and every shoulder was rubbed bare”—namely, the shoulders of those carrying baskets of earth and stones, by which their shoulders were scraped and their heads made bald.

Yet neither he nor his army found anything worthy in Tyre. And because he served me in this way and fulfilled my will against Tyre, I will therefore give him the land of Egypt.

Some say that this was fulfilled under Nebuchadnezzar. Others say it occurred under Cambyses, son of Cyrus, who devastated Egypt as far as Ethiopia, killing Apis and destroying all their images. For this reason, they think he was driven insane, being thrown from a horse and pierced by his own dagger.

Herodotus recounts this history at great length. He describes all Egypt by its districts, villages, and fortresses; the origin of the Nile and of that people; and the measurement of the land around its circuit, extending to the Ethiopian desert, the shores of the Great Sea, and the borders of Libya and Arabia.

The reason for the Lord’s anger against Egypt is that it deceived God’s people with its assistance, preventing them from hoping in the Lord, and provoked him to anger.

“On that day,” he says, “when Egypt is captured, a horn will sprout for the house of Israel.” There is no doubt that this signifies the royal line.

Some refer this to Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel, who was descended from the line of David through Jeconiah. Others refer it to the final time, when they think Elijah will also come.

But, understanding the Lord’s horn as Christ, we apply the present history to the present time. “When,” he says, “this has first been fulfilled, then your mouth will be opened, and your prophecy will no longer declare itself with uncertain promise; rather, it will be seen accomplished in deed, so that those who hear may know that I am the Lord, whose saying is doing.”

Let these things be said according to the literal sense, or rather according to the truth, of the prophecy.

Moreover, from the fact that Nebuchadnezzar received payment for a good work, we understand that even the deeds of gentiles, if they have done anything good, do not pass without reward in God’s judgment.

Hence Nebuchadnezzar is called through Jeremiah “God’s dove,” because he served God’s will against a sinful people. “I will bring,” he says, “my servant Nebuchadnezzar.”

From this it is clear that we are condemned by comparison with the gentiles if they act according to the natural law while we neglect even the written law. The Apostle Paul discusses this fully in his Epistle to the Romans.

And lest we seem to pass over anything, let us inquire, according to the spiritual understanding, where we have read this number—that is, twenty-seven.

In the Book of Genesis (Genesis 7), Scripture testifies that in the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, in the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the second month, the waters of the Flood were brought upon the face of the earth. Later, in the seventh month of the same year, which is near the Sabbath, on the twenty-seventh day of that seventh month, the waters of the Flood ceased and Noah’s ark rested upon the mountains of Ararat, which are interpreted as the mountains of Armenia.

From this we understand that the number is intermediate and can be applied in both directions: in it God’s anger begins with the Flood, while in the seventh month his mercy is shown by the same number of days.

Because among the Hebrews the month—which among us proceeds through the Kalends, Nones, and Ides—is calculated according to the course of the moon, and because the Greek word *μήνη* (*mēnē*), meaning “moon,” gave the month its name, this is said to have occurred on the twenty-seventh day of the moon, when a small amount of light remained, so that his anger might not be entirely without mercy.

When the whole orb of the moon is full, Passover and all the principal solemnities are celebrated. We have mentioned this briefly so that we may understand that both good and evil are contained together in this number: good in the case of Nebuchadnezzar, whose labor receives payment, and evil in the case of the Egyptians, whose devastation is announced. [Col. 0802A–0804B]

## CHAPTER XXX. The destruction of Egypt and its cities, together with the provinces allied with it, is lamented.

«And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, prophesy and say: Thus says the Lord God: Howl, “Alas, alas for the day,” because the day is near, and the day of the Lord is approaching; it will be a day of cloud, a time of the nations. A sword will come upon Egypt, and there will be terror in Ethiopia when the slain fall in Egypt, its multitude is taken away, and its foundations are destroyed. Ethiopia, Libya, and Lydia, and all the remaining populace, and Cub, and the sons of the land of the covenant with them, shall fall by the sword.

Thus says the Lord God: Those who support Egypt shall fall, and the pride of its power shall be destroyed. From the tower of Syene they shall fall by the sword within it, says the Lord of hosts. They shall be scattered in the midst of desolated lands, and its cities shall be in the midst of deserted cities. And they shall know that I am the Lord, when I have set fire to Egypt and all its helpers have been crushed.

On that day messengers shall go forth from my presence in triremes to crush Ethiopia’s confidence, and there shall be terror among them on the day of Egypt, for it will surely come. Thus says the Lord God. I will bring an end to the multitude of Egypt by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. He and his people, the mightiest of the nations, shall be brought to destroy the land; they shall draw their swords against Egypt and fill the land with the slain. I will dry up the channels of the rivers, and I will deliver the land into the hand of the worst of men; I will lay waste the land and its fullness by the hand of foreigners. I, the Lord, have spoken.

Thus says the Lord God: I will destroy the idols, and I will bring an end to the images from Memphis; and there shall no longer be a ruler in the land of Egypt. I will bring terror upon the land of Egypt; I will destroy the land of Pathros, set fire to Tahpanhes, and execute judgments in Alexandria. I will pour out my indignation upon Pelusium, the stronghold of Egypt, and I will kill the multitude of Alexandria.

I will set fire to Egypt: Pelusium shall suffer like a woman in labor; Alexandria shall be laid waste; and in Memphis there shall be daily anguish. The young men of Heliopolis and Bubastis shall fall by the sword, and the cities themselves shall be led captive. In Tahpanhes the day shall grow dark, when I have shattered the scepters of Egypt there and its proud strength has failed within it; a cloud shall cover it. Its daughters, too, shall be led into captivity. And I will execute judgments in Egypt, and they shall know that I am the Lord.»

After the twenty-seventh year of King Jehoiachin’s captivity, he returns to the present occasion, when he had begun to prophesy against Egypt—that is, to the tenth year, the tenth month, and the eleventh day of the month. He says that he was commanded by the Lord to speak to all nations, and especially, together with them all, to Egypt.

What, then, are the things he says? “Howl, ‘Alas, alas for the day,’ because the day is near, and the day of the Lord is approaching”—not shining with a bright sun, but covered with clouds and bringing Babylonian storm. When the sword begins to devastate Egypt, there will be terror in Ethiopia, which is near Egypt, lest the Babylonian blade reach even to it. For the wounded shall fall in Egypt, and its multitude shall be removed; everything shall be destroyed down to its foundations, so that if anyone from Ethiopia, Libya, Lydia, or, generally, from the various peoples, and Cub—which Symmachus translated as “Arabia”—or from the sons of the land of the covenant, that is, from the Jewish people, is found in Egypt, he too shall fall by the sword.

For these peoples the Septuagint has: “Persians and Cretans and Lydians and Libyans and all the mixed peoples; and the sons of my Covenant shall fall by the sword with it.” And so that we might know that all these nations had been assisting Egypt, the following statement makes it clear: “Those who support Egypt shall fall,” or “the supports of Egypt,” that is, its allies. All the pride of its empire, or the insult of its strength, shall be destroyed and brought low.

From the tower of Syene, which we have said is situated at the farthest boundaries of Egypt—or “from Magdalo to Syene,” as the Septuagint translated it—all the cities of Egypt shall be deserted, so that they may know the Lord, when the fire of the Chaldeans has devastated everything, its helpers have been crushed, and messengers have come forth, according to Aquila and Theodotion, in *siim*, which Symmachus translated as “those who hasten,” while we have rendered it “in triremes.” For thus we have received it from the Hebrews: that all Ethiopia’s confidence may be crushed; and when the neighboring province has been laid waste, terror may seize the one nearby.

But so that we might know what this sword is that would devastate Egypt and terrify Ethiopia, what follows makes it clearer: “I will bring an end to the multitude of Egypt by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon.” He will not come alone, but accompanied by many nations, so that all Egypt will be filled with the blood of the slain. [Col. 0806A]

So great will be the Lord’s anger that the channels of the rivers—that is, the Nile’s *διώρυχες* (“canals” or “channels”)—will be dried up to the ground, and the fullness of Egypt will be laid waste by the hand of pestilent or utterly wicked men; for my words cannot be rendered void.

His indignation will proceed to the point that Egypt’s images will be destroyed, and the idols of Memphis will cease—Memphis, which to this day is the metropolis of Egyptian superstition—or, alternatively, the nobles and rulers of Memphis and of the land of Egypt. Such terror will seize all Egypt that the whole land of Pathros will perish, and fire will devastate Tahpanhes—or, as the Septuagint translated it, Tanis.

“And I will execute judgments,” he says, “in Alexandria,” which is so called today. Its former name, however, was No, which Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated as it stands in the Hebrew. In its place, the Septuagint, for reasons I do not know, said Diospolis, which is a small city of Egypt. We have put “Alexandria” for No by anticipation, which in Greek is called *prolepsis*, following Virgil’s line, “And Lavinian shores came”—not because they were called Lavinian at the time when Aeneas came into Latium, but because they were afterward called Lavinian, so that the passage might be clearer to the reader’s understanding.

“And I will pour out,” he says, “my indignation upon Sain,” which we have translated as Pelusium. It is called the stronghold of Egypt because it has an exceptionally secure harbor, and maritime commerce is conducted there to a very great extent. Hence the poet also calls a lentil “Pelusian,” not because that variety of legume grows there especially, but because it is brought there in great quantities from the Thebaid and all Egypt by a branch of the Nile.

“And I will kill,” he says, “the multitude of Alexandria,” which again is given as No in the Hebrew; for it the Septuagint translated not Diospolis, as above, but Memphis. And to show that the city was already populous at that time, he says, “I will destroy the multitude of No,” and “I will set fire”—that is, the king of Babylon in Egypt, who will ravage everything like fire.

“Pelusium shall suffer like a woman in labor,” that is, it shall be distressed by turmoil; and in Alexandria, that is, in No, there shall be a breach. “And the waters shall spread,” for which the Septuagint again translated “Diospolis.” It is customary among the Egyptians, because of the Nile’s flooding, to build elevated embankments and the banks of the Nile. If these are breached through the negligence of their keepers or through the excessive volume of the waters, the waters do not merely irrigate the fields below but overwhelm and ravage them. This signifies that Egypt will be occupied by the army of the Chaldeans just as it is accustomed to be covered and ruined when the waters of the Nile overflow and rise beyond measure.

For the flooding of the waters and the bursting and breaching of the embankments, the Hebrew has: “And in Memphis there shall be daily anguish”—there, where the Nile is divided, where the temple of Apis is, and where oracles give their responses; there daily anguish shall arise.

The young men of Heliopolis, which in Hebrew is called *On*, and of Bubastis, another city, shall also fall by the sword, so that the cities themselves—that is, their inhabitants, or their women—shall be led into captivity, a sex exposed to such abuse. In Tahpanhes, which is the royal city, the scepters of Egypt shall be shattered—that is, the entire royal stock. [Col. 0807A]

When its power has failed after the princes have been killed, then the day shall grow dark, and everything shall be filled with gloom and darkness, so that the city itself shall be covered by a cloud of grief and mourning. And its daughters—that is, the remaining towns—shall be led into captivity, so that, after I have executed judgment in Egypt and shown myself judge in all things, then the Egyptians may know that I am the Lord.

We have described these matters as though for children learning their first elements, so that through letters, syllables, names, and the joining of words they may proceed to the reading of prose or poetry. Now let us undertake the tropological interpretation and display the vast sea of discussion on a small, almost pictorial tablet.

The word of the Lord, which was always in the Father, came to the prophet, and he calls him not by his own name but “son of man.” In the Holy Scriptures this expression is always understood in a favorable sense when it is singular, as in this same prophet, in Daniel, and in the Gospel. Otherwise, in the plural, it is read in the opposite sense, as in: “The sons of men, their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword.” And again: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” (Psalm 4.)

“For the lion will roar, and who will not fear? The Lord has spoken, and who will not prophesy?” (Amos 3.) “Howl,” he says, “alas, alas for the day, because the day is near and approaching,” says the Lord; “it will be a day of cloud, a time or end of the nations.”

There is a twofold consummation: either the consummation of all things generally, when the end of the world arrives, or the consummation of individuals particularly, when the time of death draws near. It is called “near” because, compared with eternity, all time is short. Thus Jacob says of the hundred and thirty years he had lived: “Few and evil are the days of my life” (Genesis 47). And the Psalmist, discussing the frailty of the entire human race, says: “Our days pass like a shadow” (Psalm 101).

Considering this, we shall neither exalt ourselves through power, nor recline upon riches, nor rejoice in prosperity, knowing that everything will soon be taken away. Beautifully, then, it is called “the day of the Lord,” when the whole conduct of the world shall be destroyed, and, error having been removed, the one truth shall appear. It is also called a day of cloud and mist, for no one who is both fearless and uncertain about the sentence awaits the Judge without terror.

“And it will be a time,” or “an end of the nations,” not merely of the single Egyptian nation but of all nations, so that it may be clear that the prophecy concerns every nation.

It follows: “A sword will come upon Egypt.” The turning and flaming sword is the divine word, which will divide the good from the evil and consume the utterly wicked with its fire. It will come upon the Egypt of this world, so that there will be terror in Ethiopia, where those who dwell beyond Egypt in the night and darkness of error reside, and whose blackness is either converted with difficulty into whiteness or not converted at all.

The wounded who stood wrongly in wickedness shall fall in Egypt. “Its multitude shall be taken away.” For broad and spacious is the way that leads to death. Its foundations shall be destroyed, so that nothing of Egypt’s former stability may remain; and, its evil foundations having been abandoned, the foundation of Christ shall be laid, upon which the Church may be built. “For every planting that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted” (Matthew 15).

Hence Jeremiah is also commanded to destroy what had been built, so that he may build better things. The Ethiopians, Libyans, and Lydians shall perish in Egypt—or, according to the Septuagint, the Persians, Cretans, Lydians, Libyans, and Cub, that is, the Arabs—and all the remaining populace, whom the Septuagint translated as “hybrids and mixed peoples.” Through the interpretation of the names, which we set out in the vision of Tyre, we can understand all of these as different nations, according to the diversity of their vices.

Hence the Apostle says: “You Gentiles in the flesh,” who are called uncircumcision (Ephesians 2); for he would never have said “Gentiles in the flesh” unless there were others in the spirit. As he says elsewhere: “Consider Israel according to the flesh” (1 Corinthians 10).

Therefore we must take the greatest care that we do not return in our hearts to Egypt, from which we once departed, and are found among the other nations and perish by the sword. Concerning this it is subsequently said: “The young men of Heliopolis and Bubastis shall fall by the sword,” especially since it is added: “And the sons of the land of the covenant,” or “of my Testament,” “shall be struck down together by the sword.”

Of these it is written: “Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help, relying on horses and chariots” (Isaiah 31). But if the people of the other nations are slaughtered in Egypt, how much more the sons of the covenant and Testament of God, who, despising the bread of angels, remembered Egypt’s melons, onions, garlic, and cucumbers.

Then the supports and buttresses of Egypt shall fall—those that supported it in wickedness: the subtleties of dialecticians and the tricks of philosophers. Its insulting and arrogant empire shall also be destroyed, for it speaks everything through arrogance and regards ecclesiastical simplicity as worthless.

“For from the tower of Syene they shall fall within it.” Syene lies at the remotest boundaries of Egypt, bordering Ethiopia and the land of the Blemmyes, where the Nile is unnavigable, the roar of the cataracts is heard, and everything is impassable and filled with snakes and venomous creatures.

But if, as we said above, *Magdalus* signifies magnificence and *Syene* signifies a circuit, it is clear that Egypt’s wealth, its insulting strength and magnificence—that is, its boasting and exaltation—are being condemned, things that belong to Egypt’s circuit, where nothing is stable but everything rolls on in uncertain motion and reaches ruin.

Then the cities of Egypt shall be scattered, and the land shall be deserted; no congregation possessing any stability shall remain, so that at the end of things they may know that he is the Lord, when he sends fire upon Egypt—the fire that the Lord desires to burn, so that the hay, wood, and straw built upon the foundation of Christ may be consumed and all the helpers of perverse doctrines may be crushed.

From this we should understand that those possessing knowledge falsely so called, and those of whom it is written, “Disperse all the nations that desire wars” (Psalm 67), are called the companions and helpers of Egypt.

“On that day,” he says, “messengers shall go forth from my presence.” Of them it is written in the Gospel: “Their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18). And in the parable of the sowing, angelic reapers—that is, those who are messengers—are sent to gather all scandals and throw them into the furnace of fire, “where there is weeping of the eyes and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 13).

They will hasten to fulfill the command, to frighten—or crush—the confidence of Ethiopia, which has reached the summit of wickedness, so that, in Egypt’s overthrow, Ethiopia may be crushed and terrified, because the day of the Lord is a day of vengeance and retribution, in which the darkness of sins is driven away and the light of virtues remains.

“And I will bring an end,” he says, “to the multitude of Egypt by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon,” to whom they have been delivered for punishment. He is the enemy and avenger, who also received his reward because he had served in the conquest of Tyre, so that the multitude of Egypt might cease to be many, though there are always many in it.

But if someone objects, asking how that statement in Deuteronomy is to be understood—“Our fathers went down into Egypt with seventy souls, but now you have become like the stars of heaven in multitude” (Deuteronomy 10)—the answer is easy. He did not give the example of an earthly multitude but of a heavenly one, which shines with virtues and is full of lights.

Over this multitude of Egypt “the mightiest of the nations shall be brought,” so that they may destroy the land. For these the Septuagint translated “pestilent ones,” which I do not know how to reconcile with those who are brought by the Lord, unless perhaps in accordance with the example: “A sending through evil angels” (Psalm 77).

They shall draw their swords against Egypt and fill the land with the slain, or with the wounded, so that those who have been killed and wounded may recognize themselves as such. Egypt will be so destroyed and reduced to nothing that all the rivers of eloquence, by which Egyptian errors were watered like reed and papyrus, will dry up. They will be delivered into the hand of the worst men, who will torture them, and the fullness of the land of Egypt, which had grown in evil, will be destroyed by the hand of those alienated from God.

For it is not good angels but evil ones who are appointed over punishments. They must know these things, because the Lord has spoken. This statement is frequently repeated so that those who hear may know that the words are not the prophet’s but the Lord’s, whose commands cannot be rendered void.

It follows: “And I will destroy the images,” which the Septuagint translated as “abominations.” “And I will bring an end to the idols,” or the nobles, “of Memphis; and there shall no longer be a ruler,” or rulers, “in the land of Egypt.”

For it belongs to the most merciful Lord to overthrow magical practices, so that no likeness that falsely represents the image of truth may remain in Egypt. Let the nobles of Memphis also perish. Memphis is interpreted as “from the mouth,” from which they fashioned all the idols. When the heads and teachers of idols have been cut off, there will be no prince in Egypt, and all Egypt will be filled with terror and destruction.

Concerning its cities it is said: “I will destroy the land of Pathros, and I will set fire to Tahpanhes,” or Tanis. “And I will execute judgments in No [Alexandria]”; the Septuagint translated it as Diospolis. “And I will pour out my indignation upon Sain [Pelusium], the stronghold of Egypt.”

Pathros is interpreted as “the trampling of bread”; Tanis as “a humble command”; Diospolis, in place of which the Hebrew has No, as “rest”; and Sain as “temptation.” By these names the various assemblies of heretics and every gathering of lies are indicated. They trample and despise ecclesiastical bread; they follow a humble command that does not lead to heavenly things; they devote themselves to pleasures and are in a kind of rest such as we read that the rich man in the Gospel possessed; and they serve temptations, one of whom asked the Lord for power to tempt Job (Job 1).

The Lord will destroy and burn all these things, pour out his indignation upon them, and shatter Egypt’s strength, so that, reduced to nothing, they may no longer trouble God’s people or make them place their hope in their assistance. Having abandoned the truth, they may seek falsehood and, like someone wounded by a reed instead of a staff, be wounded by their own support.

After this it is said: “And I will kill,” or “destroy,” “the multitude of Memphis.” [Col. 0810B] In the Hebrew it has *No*. Above, the same Septuagint translated this as Diospolis, which is interpreted as “rest.” For there are many who seek rest and wish to lie upon ivory couches and eat suckling lambs.

Or, according to the Septuagint, who translated it as Memphis, there are many who say to others, “Let me remove the speck from your eye” (Matthew 7), while they themselves have beams in their own.

And fire is given to Egypt, which consumes verbosity and pleasures with its heat. “All temptation shall suffer,” and in Diospolis—which in the Hebrew above is called No—“there shall be a breach,” so that the waters may be poured out, every evil congregation may be scattered, and it may perish here and there.

Or, according to the Hebrew: “In Memphis there shall be daily anguish,” so that they may give an account for every idle word and understand that nothing they have said escapes the Lord’s judgment.

“The young men of Heliopolis and Bubastis shall also fall by the sword.” Heliopolis is called *On* in Hebrew, which is interpreted as “pain.” Bubastis, according to the Egyptian language, means “experience of the mouth.”

All those who could not bear the world’s pain but pursued the pleasures of Diospolis and trusted in the volatility of words, and who, arguing against other doctrines, had experiences of victory, shall be cut down by the sword of the Lord’s word. Those who are not truly young but are called women because of their weakness of mind shall be led captive; or the cities themselves shall be led captive through pain and the boasting of the mouth.

“And in Tahpanhes,” he says, “the day shall grow dark.” Tahpanhes is interpreted as “yielding to the mouth,” implicitly the mouth of the devil. Those who yield to him will lose the light of truth and change day into night.

The scepters of Egypt and all its empire shall feel themselves shattered in Tahpanhes, so that its insulting strength—or the pride of its power—may fail there; the rays of the Sun of Justice may be darkened by cloud; and not women but daughters may be led into captivity. The Lord will execute not one judgment but many judgments in Egypt.

For just as there are different dwellings of the righteous with the Father, so there are different judgments of punishment for Egypt, so that when all these things have taken place, the Egyptians may know that he is the Lord, whose judgments are true and justified in themselves.

«And it came to pass in the eleventh year, in the first month, on the seventh day of the month, that the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, I have broken the arm of Pharaoh, king of Egypt. And behold, it has not been wrapped so that it might be restored, nor treated, nor bound with bandages, nor stitched with linen, so that, after receiving strength, it might be able to hold a sword.

Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and I will crush his strong arm, though it is already broken, and I will make the sword fall from his hand. I will scatter Egypt among the nations and disperse them throughout the lands.

And I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, and I will place my sword in his hand. I will break Pharaoh’s arms, and they shall groan with the groaning of the slain before his face. I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, and Pharaoh’s arms shall fall. And they shall know that I am the Lord, when I have given my sword into the hand of the king of Babylon and he has stretched it out over the land of Egypt.

I will scatter Egypt among the nations and disperse them throughout the lands. And they shall know that I am the Lord.»

(Hieronymus.) He returns to the sequence of the prophecy. For after the twenty-seventh year he now gives the eleventh, a question that is also contained in the preceding material. Although the word of the Lord against Tyre occurred in the eleventh year, which was given earlier, in what follows he speaks to Pharaoh in the tenth year. Again he gives the twenty-seventh year, as we said, and now the eleventh.

To omit the other matters contained in the order of the Psalms: it is asked how the third psalm is placed before those psalms in which David “changed his face” before Abimelech, and those concerning Doeg the Edomite, and when he was found in the cave, and the fiftieth, the psalm of repentance, whose title shows that he went in to Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, when these psalms are earlier than Psalm 3, in which he is noted as fleeing from the face of his son Absalom.

In the Psalms the answer is easy: the work is lyric poetry, and in such a work the historical order is not sought, but the poems of individual events. In history, however, this must be said: things spoken about one matter at different times ought not to be divided in the narration but enclosed within a single account of the same subject. For example, matters spoken about Egypt at one time and another should be learned in one continuous order of reading.

Even after saying this, the question nonetheless remains why, in this same place, the word of the Lord was first given to Pharaoh in the eleventh year, then in the twenty-seventh, and afterward in the tenth, when, according to the sequence, the tenth year should have been given first, the eleventh second, and the twenty-seventh third, with each prophecy marked accordingly.

To this we can reply: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and inscrutable his ways!” (Romans 11). And elsewhere: “Who can investigate the abyss and wisdom?”

We can also say that in the prophets the historical order is not always preserved—only in certain passages, not in all. For they do not recount past events but announce future ones, according as the will of the Holy Spirit directs.

In historical works, however—such as Moses’ five books, Joshua, the books of Judges, Ruth, and Esther, Samuel and Kings, the book of Chronicles, and Ezra, with Nehemiah joined to it—an inverted narrative is nowhere found.

Let what we have said about the order of the years suffice. Now let us see what prophecy there is against Pharaoh or concerning Pharaoh.

He says that he has broken Pharaoh’s arm, and that it has not been wrapped, bound, stitched with linen, or treated with a poultice. In accordance with what is written: “There is no balm to apply, nor oil, nor bandages.” If this had been done, then, after recovering its strength, it could indeed have held a sword and gone out to war.

Therefore the merciful and compassionate God again crushes his arm, or arms, so that the sword may fall completely from his hand, and Egypt may be scattered among the nations and dispersed throughout the lands.

The arm can signify strength and power, as Scripture says: “Break the arm of the sinner and the wicked” (Psalm 10). It is broken in our adversaries when they persecute us but cannot overwhelm us. And for the salvation of God’s servants, the king of Babylon often rises against Pharaoh, so that the stronger may crush the powerful and the wicked may be handed over to those worse than themselves. God strengthens the arms of the worst men so that the one who has been delivered may know that he is the Lord; and the completion of virtue consists in knowing that he is the Lord.

Conversely, we can say: “The sons of Eli, sons of pestilence, not knowing God.” And in a favorable sense, it is written concerning kings who did what was right in the sight of God that they knew the Lord.

# BOOK TWELVE

[Col. 0811]

[Col. 0811D] I wanted to join the prophetic history concerning Egypt and its king into a single book. But because the length of the account does not permit this, just as we divided the history of Tyre and its prince into two books, so now also we shall divide the material concerning Egypt and Pharaoh between two books.

## CHAPTER XXXI. The word of the Lord against Pharaoh, that he will be delivered into the hands of Nebuchadnezzar; and concerning Assyria, delivered to him under the name of a tree
“**And it came to pass in the eleventh year, in the third month, on the first day of the month, that the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, speak to Pharaoh king of Egypt and to his people: Whom are you like in your greatness? Behold, Assyria was like a cedar in Lebanon, beautiful in its branches and thick with foliage, lofty in height, and its crown rose up among the dense branches. The waters nourished it; the deep raised it up; its rivers flowed around its roots, and it sent out its channels to all the trees of the region. Therefore its height was exalted above all the trees of the region, its branches multiplied, and its boughs grew tall because of the abundant waters. When it extended its shade among its branches, all the birds of the sky made their nests in it; beneath its foliage all the beasts of the forest gave birth, and beneath its shelter dwelt the assembly of all the nations. It was exceedingly beautiful in its greatness and in the spreading of its branches, for its roots were beside abundant waters.

“‘The cedars in the paradise of God were not taller than it. The fir trees did not equal its crown, and the plane trees were not equal to its foliage. No tree in the paradise of God was its equal or comparable in beauty, because I made it beautiful, with many dense branches. All the trees of delight that were in the paradise of God envied it.

“‘Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because it was exalted in height and lifted up its crown, green and dense, and its heart was exalted in its height, I delivered it into the hand of the mightiest of the nations. He shall deal with it as its wickedness deserves. I cast it out, and foreigners, the most cruel of the nations, cut it down. They shall throw it upon the mountains, and its branches shall fall in all the valleys. Its boughs shall be broken on all the rocks of the land. All the peoples of the earth shall withdraw from its shelter and abandon it. All the birds of the sky shall dwell upon its ruin, and all the beasts of the region shall be among its branches.

“‘Therefore all the trees by the waters shall no longer exalt themselves in their height, nor set their loftiness among the dense and leafy trees; nor shall all those watered by the waters stand in their height, because they have all been handed over to death, to the farthest land, in the midst of the sons of men, among those who descend into the pit.

“‘Thus says the Lord God: On the day when it descended to the underworld, I proclaimed mourning; I covered it with the deep, I restrained its rivers, and I checked the abundant waters. Lebanon mourned over it, and all the trees of the field were shaken. At the sound of its fall I caused the nations to tremble, when they led it down to the underworld with those who descended into the pit. And all the trees of delight, the finest and most excellent in Lebanon, all that were watered by the waters, were comforted in the land below.

“‘For they too shall descend with it to the underworld, to those slain by the sword; and the arm of each one shall rest beneath its shelter, in the midst of its nations. Whom are you like, O glorious and exalted one, among the trees of delight? Behold, you have been brought down with the trees of delight to the farthest land. In the midst of the uncircumcised you shall sleep, with those who were slain by the sword. This is Pharaoh and all his multitude, says the Lord God.’” (Jerome.)

First, it must be understood that everything said concerning the king of Assyria in the future tense is remembered by the Septuagint as though it had already happened. Thus he speaks either of the tree or of the ruler of the Assyrians, so that one person is understood in both the masculine and feminine gender: the tree refers to the Assyrian, and the Assyrian is named in the tree.

Nor is there any mention in the present passage of the king of Babylon, lest he appear, while placed among a captive people in Chaldaea, to provoke the anger of his masters and rulers. Instead, the passage speaks of the king of Assyria, who had already been captured by the Chaldaeans at that time, and all the strength of Assyria was subject to Babylonian rule. Hence the Assyrians captured the ten tribes—that is, Israel. The Chaldaeans conquered the two tribes, Judah and Benjamin, and destroyed the city of Jerusalem.

Therefore, when the divine word is about to speak against Pharaoh king of Egypt and his people, it uses this opening against him: “Whom are you like in your greatness? Behold, Assyria was like a cedar in Lebanon,” and so forth.

The meaning is: Do not be surprised that you are to be defeated and destroyed by the Babylonians, and that you are to lose your empire and all the wealth of Egypt is to be destroyed, since Assyria, much stronger than you, was itself destroyed when the same Chaldaean conquered it.

He describes the power of the king of Assyria under the figure of a cedar tree, according to the Hebrew text, or of a cypress, according to the Septuagint, standing on Mount Lebanon. It was beautiful in its branches, dense with foliage, raised up to the clouds, and grew to such a height because it was watered not by ordinary waters but by the deep—that is, by waters in the greatest abundance. For “the deep” means a multitude of roaring waters.

Thus all the birds made nests in its branches, and beneath its foliage all the beasts of the forest gave birth. And so that we would not doubt which birds of the sky and beasts of the forest were meant, he states it more openly: “And beneath its shelter dwelt the assembly of very many nations.”

The cedars, he says, and the cypresses, firs or pines, and plane trees—or cypresses—were not equal to its branches. And lest he speak individually of all the trees, he says: “And no tree in the paradise of God was its equal or comparable in its beauty,” and so forth.

From this some understand that the passage is not speaking of the king of Assyria but of the opposing power which, in the oracle against Tyre, is said to have been created among the cherubim and adorned with precious stones, and afterward, through its own fault, fell to earthly things. This is the one who is called Lucifer when falling in Isaiah (Isa. XIV), and whom the Lord indicates in the Gospel: “I was watching Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke X).

(Gregory.) For whom can the cedars and plane trees signify, except those hosts of the heavenly virtues, of lofty height, planted in eternal joy and verdure? Although they were created exalted, they were nevertheless neither superior nor equal to this one, who is said to have been made beautiful with many dense branches. The beauty that made him superior to the other legions rendered him so much more splendid, as the multitude of angels placed beneath him adorned him.

This tree had as many dense branches in the paradise of God as it beheld legions of heavenly spirits placed beneath it. He was condemned for sin without pardon because he had been created great beyond comparison.

(Jerome.) But for the present let us follow the historical account and understand that these things are said hyperbolically—ὑπερβολικῶς—that the Assyrian possessed such great power and so oppressed all the nations that he compared himself with the strength of the angels. Everything, however, is said metaphorically—μεταφορικῶς—under the loftiest cedar or cypress with reference to the Assyrian, and his killing is called a cutting down.

As for what follows—“I delivered it into the hand of the mightiest of the nations”—he calls the king of Babylon by this name, so that the one who conquered Assyria may be understood to have done so not through his own strength but through divine power.

“According to its wickedness,” he says, “I cast it out,” secretly warning Babylon that he ought not to be cruel or oppress the people of God who had been delivered into his hands, lest he suffer the same things as the Assyrian, who had been cruel and wicked.

“And foreigners, the most cruel of the nations, shall cut it down,” or, according to the Septuagint, “the pestilential ones”—a phrase he never wished to utter while situated in Chaldaea, lest it stir him against his own nation.

It is also thrown upon the mountains; its branches fall in all the valleys; they are broken on the rocks; and it is abandoned by all the peoples—that is, by the birds of the sky and the beasts of the field. It will come to such destruction that all the trees which had seemed lofty in comparison with the tree of Assyria will cease, following its example, to exalt themselves and raise themselves on high. They will no longer stand in their height; once that tree has been cut down, all will likewise be cut down through fear.

What had been spoken figuratively is made clearer: “All,” he says—meaning the kings—“have been handed over to death, to the farthest land,” that is, to the underworld; “in the midst of the sons of men,” no longer among trees, “among those who descend into the pit”—there can be no doubt that this signifies the regions below.

After the cutting down of the Assyrian tree—or India [variant: “in the day”]—when the Assyrian descended to the underworld, the Lord proclaimed mourning. Again he speaks of him figuratively: he was covered by the deep, in accordance with what is written: “I came into the depth of the sea, and the storm overwhelmed me” (Ps. LXVIII); and all the rivers—that is, all the nations—ceased to water him any longer. Lebanon was crushed over him, or was darkened over it, meaning either the tree or the Assyrian.

And lest we think that the passage concerns a tree, it follows: “At the sound of its fall I caused the nations to tremble.” For what fall of a single tree could be so great that all the nations would be shaken at its sound?

“When I led it down,” he says, “to the underworld.” Literally, a tree cannot be led down to the underworld. “With others who descended into the pit,” that is, into the regions below.

“And all the trees of delight were comforted in the land below,” that is, in the heart of the earth. The Hebrew term for “delight” is *Eden*, and here it signifies beautiful and excellent wooded groves and forests that had been in Lebanon: “and they were watered by the waters.”

“For they too,” the trees, “shall descend with it”—that is, with the Assyrian—“to the underworld, to those slain or wounded by the sword.” Trees are not wounded by swords but cut down, nor do they descend to the underworld.

“And the arm,” he says, “or the seed,” since among the Hebrews the word *zeraʿ* signifies both—“shall rest beneath its shelter, in the midst of the nations,” not of forests but of peoples.

Finally, there is an apostrophe addressed to the Assyrian himself, or to Pharaoh:

“Whom are you like, O glorious and exalted one, among the trees of delight?” No one, he says, was your equal, but you surpassed all kings in power. Yet with the other kings who were in your company you have been led down to the lower lands—that is, to the underworld—as Scripture says: “They shall enter the farthest parts of the earth; they shall be handed over to the power of the sword; they shall become portions for foxes” (Ps. LXII).

“In the midst,” he says, “of the uncircumcised you shall sleep, with those who were slain by the sword.” He shows which trees were meant: the cedar or cypress wounded by swords and lying among the uncircumcised.

And in order to join the conclusion to what came before—for above he had said, “Whom are you like in your greatness? Behold, Assyria was like a cedar in Lebanon, beautiful in its branches and foliage,” and so forth—he now adds: “So is Pharaoh and all his multitude, says the Lord.”

As the Assyrian cedar and cypress were overthrown when the Babylonian cut them down, so Pharaoh and his people—that is, the tree itself and its branches—will be cut down by the Babylonian.

Let these things meanwhile be understood historically, although many interpret them as events that will occur at the consummation of the world. They compare Pharaoh, that is, the power to which Egypt is subject, with the most powerful king of Assyria, namely, the Antichrist. If that one falls, then the other rulers of these darknesses and the princes of the world will fall more easily as well.

Let us therefore speak of each point, touching on everything briefly, so that we may seem not so much to discuss and explain obscure matters as to provide material for those who desire to explain them.

First we must examine why, in the eleventh year, the third month, and the first day of the month, the word of the Lord came to Ezekiel, saying: “Son of man, speak to Pharaoh king of Egypt and to his multitude.”

The word of the Lord is spoken to Pharaoh in the eleventh year, for he had not yet reached the twelfth, a number signifying complete and perfected power. Hence Jacob had twelve sons (Gen. XXXV), from whom the twelve names of the prophets were later contained in one volume. There were also twelve apostles; because Judas the betrayer was one of them, Matthias was chosen in his place (Acts I). The daughter of the ruler of the synagogue was also raised by the Lord when she was twelve years old. The woman with the hemorrhage received healing in her twelfth year (Matt. IX).

But because Pharaoh is rebuked and afterward lamented, the third month and the first day are added to the number eleven years. Hence, in what follows, in the twelfth year, the twelfth month, and the first day of the month, the word of the Lord comes to Ezekiel, saying: “Son of man, take up a lamentation over Pharaoh king of Egypt, and say to him” (Ezek. XXXII).

The one who is lamented is lamented so that he may understand how many good things he has lost. Yet because he was Pharaoh, and his arm had not yet been bound nor his former strength restored, twenty-nine days still remained in the twelfth year and twelfth month, so that the number of twelve years might be completed.

Therefore, on the first day of the month, the word of the Lord comes to the prophet, and he is commanded to speak to the king of Egypt and to his multitude. It is remarkable that the four interpreters did not say “people” but “multitude”: “For many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XXII). And in the Law it is written: “You shall not be with the multitude for evil.”

The king of Egypt is told: “Whom are you like in greatness,” or “in your height?” He had exalted himself and was subject to the sentence: “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled” (Matt. XXIII). Yet his height is not to be compared with that of the one who, like a cedar or cypress in Lebanon, was beautiful in branches, dense in foliage, lofty in height, and raised his head to the clouds.

According to David, the truth of God reaches to those clouds, and they are commanded not to rain upon Israel. His beauty is also praised, a beauty changed by perverse will into ugliness, so that it is said of him: “The Lord shall break the cedars of Lebanon” (Ps. XXVIII). He himself, exalted and established on the highest mountain of Lebanon, fell all the more violently because he had been so much higher.

Holy Scripture, wishing to demonstrate his height, calls him a great cedar nourished by waters. These were not the waters of Shiloah, which go quietly, but the waters of Rezin and the waters of Egypt, concerning which it is written: “What have you to do with drinking the water of Gihon?” (Jer. II)—or Sior, a name that signifies turbid waters.

The deep also exalted him, over which darknesses were borne at the beginning of the world, and to which the demons in the Gospel begged not to be sent. The rivers of that deep were around his roots, concerning which it is said: “What have you to do with the way of the Assyrians, to drink the waters of the rivers?” And elsewhere: “Behold, the Lord will bring upon you the mighty and abundant water of the river: the king of the Assyrians and all his glory” (Isa. VIII).

The deep also sent out its channels to all the trees of the region, so that it might water not only the prince of this world but also his companions. Therefore he was exalted and grew above all the loftiest trees: “His branches multiplied,” and he possessed the empire of the whole world, saying: “All these things have been delivered to me.” “And his branches grew tall,” branches that had been watered by the waters of the deep. He extended or spread his shelter so that he might subject all things to his dominion.

“All the birds of the sky made their nests in his branches.” Everyone who commits sin is born of the devil and is counted among the number of his branches. Those birds made nests in his branches that, according to the Gospel parable, devour the seed beside the road. Or, because “all have sinned and lack the mercy of God” (Rom. III), and because it was said: “All have turned aside; together they have become worthless” (Ps. LII), for this reason they made their nests in his branches.

It follows: “Beneath his foliage all the beasts of the forest gave birth”—those who have lost the gentleness of Christ.

“And beneath his shelter dwelt the assembly of very many nations,” so that there was no one who was not covered by his shelter, except the one who said: “Behold, the prince of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me.”

“Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and thus death passed to all men” (Rom. V); in him all sinned, and in Adam all die. We have all sinned and lack the glory of God, yet even in that dwelling there are different conditions.

Some dwell in his branches like birds, promising themselves knowledge through philosophy and the doctrines of heretics. Others are like wild beasts, savage and cruel. Others are like a multitude of very many nations, signifying the mingling of different people in vices and sins.

“Assyria was exceedingly beautiful in its greatness and in the spreading of its branches,” because its root had been watered by abundant waters, so much so that in the paradise of God no cedar or cypress was taller than it; nor did the firs and pines equal its height, nor were the plane trees equal to its foliage.

Therefore no tree in the paradise of God was its equal, “because no tree in the paradise of God was its equal or comparable in its beauty.” For they were not raised up through pride, but knew their own humility and did not attempt, with sacrilegious intent, to claim the likeness of God for themselves.

As for what follows—“And all the trees of delights that were in the paradise envied it”—we explain it in this way: the trees of paradise envied the multitude of its branches. “For many are called, but few are chosen,” and “broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction” (Matt. XX; VII). It desires to have as many for salvation as Assyria had for destruction.

Therefore Assyria was exalted in height and lifted up its height, green and dense. Or it raised its crown as far as the clouds, and its heart was exalted, so that it might say: “I shall be like the Most High.”

Therefore it was “delivered into the hand of the mightiest of the nations.” We should understand this as another detestable power to which it is handed over for punishment; for he is the enemy and avenger.

Assyria is to be understood as the Antichrist, and the mightiest of the nations to whom it was delivered as Satan, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “Those whom I delivered to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Tim. I).

He “shall deal with it” in whatever way the Lord commands him. This cypress was cast out of the paradise of God because of its wickedness. “Foreigners and the cruel shall cut it down,” or “the pestilential ones among the nations,” so that what is written may be fulfilled: “When the pestilent man is scourged, the fool will become wiser” (Prov. XIX). And again: “Now the axe is laid to the root of the trees” (Matt. III).

They shall cut it down upon the mountains, so that it may fall in its pride. “In all the valleys its branches shall fall,” so that all who were in its company may be led down to Tartarus.

“And they shall withdraw from its shelter and abandon it,” so that the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth, which had previously been beneath it and covered by its shelter, may afterward share in its punishment.

When the other trees of the forests or of paradise see that the cypress Assyria has fallen by the sentence of the Lord, they will not exalt themselves in pride, nor esteem themselves as anything, nor regard the waters that nourish them as their own riches. For all the branches, birds of the sky, and beasts of the earth that had been under the rule of Assyria will be led to death, to the farthest land. Concerning them it is written: “At his presence all who descend into the earth shall fall” (Ps. XXI). And elsewhere: “They shall enter the farthest parts of the earth” (Ps. LXII). They will be not with the angels but with the sons of men who descend into the pit, or into the eternal grave.

When he has descended to the farthest parts of the earth and has become a portion of foxes, by which he is to be torn apart, then there will be mourning either by all his companions or by the holy powers, who will grieve that he has descended to the underworld.

Therefore the Lord says: “I covered him with the deep,” whose waters had previously nourished him. “I restrained his rivers,” that is, those of the deep, “and checked the abundant waters,” so that they would not water him but rather overwhelm him.

“Lebanon was saddened over him,” the place in which he had been exalted. “All the trees of the field were shaken,” fearing a similar cutting down. “At the sound of his fall I caused the nations to tremble,” so that no one would remain ignorant of his destruction and his descent to the underworld with his other companions.

All the trees of delight—that is, of paradise—received consolation, seeing evil repaid with evil and good with good. These trees of Lebanon were watered by the rivers of the Lord, by which the fallen tree had also been watered. Or they signify all the trees that had once been good and were watered by the waters and dwelt in the height of Lebanon. They will receive consolation when they see their prince undergoing torments like theirs: “For they too shall descend to the underworld, to those slain by the sword of the Lord.”

And all the strength of the trees shall dwell beneath its shelter—that is, in punishment, in the midst of all the nations that will be held within the prisons of the underworld.

After this the word is turned toward Pharaoh himself, to whom it had been said at the beginning, “Whom are you like in your greatness?” It is said to him: “Whom are you like, O glorious and exalted one, among the trees of delight?” Surely, to the Assyrian, who fell.
