You also were glorious and exalted among the trees of Eden—that is, of delight and paradise. And behold, you have been led down like the Assyrian, with all the trees that once flourished in delight, to the farthest land and to the underworld.

You shall sleep not in rest but in punishments, in the midst of the uncircumcised—that is, of the unclean—and with those who fell by the sword of the Lord.

And so that we may know who is meant by the one to whom he says, “O glorious and exalted one among the trees of delight,” he makes it clearer: “This is Pharaoh and all his multitude,” or, according to the Septuagint, “So is Pharaoh and all his multitude.” As the Assyrian above was cut down and fell, so shall the Egyptian be overthrown.

## CHAPTER XXXII

**A lamentation over Pharaoh, who will be handed over to Nebuchadnezzar to be killed; giants are described “per mures” [through mice; reading uncertain], with whom he descends to the underworld**

**[Col. 0819D]**

“‘And it came to pass in the twelfth year, in the twelfth month—or the tenth month—on the first day of the month, that the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, take up a lamentation over Pharaoh king of Egypt, and say to him:

“‘You are compared to a lion among the nations and to a dragon that is in the sea. You tossed your horn in your rivers, troubled the waters with your feet, and trampled their rivers. Therefore thus says the Lord God: I will spread my net over you in the assembly of many peoples, and I will draw you out in my net, and cast you upon the land. I will throw you upon the face of the field, and I will make all the birds of the sky dwell upon you, and I will satisfy the beasts of the whole earth with you. I will place your flesh upon the mountains and fill the hills with your corruption. I will water the land with the stench of your blood upon the mountains, and the valleys will be filled with you.

“‘When you have been extinguished, I will cover the sky, and I will make its stars dark. I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon shall not give its light. I will cause all the lights of heaven to mourn over you, and I will bring darkness over your land, says the Lord God.

“‘I will trouble the hearts of many peoples when I bring your destruction among the nations, into lands that you do not know. I will cause many peoples or nations to be astonished at you, and their kings will fear you with great terror when my sword begins to fly over their faces. Each one will suddenly be stupefied for his own life on the day of his destruction, because thus says the Lord God:

“‘The sword of the king of Babylon shall come upon you. With the swords of the mighty I will cast down your multitude. All these are unconquerable nations. They shall destroy the pride of Egypt, and its multitude shall be scattered. I will destroy all its cattle that are over many waters, and no longer shall the foot of man trouble them, nor the hoof of cattle disturb them.

“‘Then I will make their waters exceedingly pure, and I will bring their rivers like oil, says the Lord God, when I have made the land of Egypt desolate. The land shall be deserted from its fullness when I strike all its inhabitants, and they shall know that I am the Lord.

“‘It is a lamentation, and the daughters of the nations shall lament him. They shall lament him over Egypt and over all its multitude, says the Lord God,’” and so forth. (Jerome.)

In many copies, according to the Septuagint, the twelfth year and the tenth month are given. According to the other interpreters, however, it is the tenth year and the twelfth month. This is understood either because Jerusalem had already been captured and Pharaoh’s joy was removed by the evils threatening him, or because it was about to be captured and he was to grieve over his own great miseries, rather than rejoice in the captivity of others.

Meanwhile, laying down briefly certain foundations of the historical interpretation, let us examine what the Hebrews understand in this passage.

Pharaoh is compared to a lion, not of one nation but of many nations, or to a dragon in the sea, so that he may possess both land and waters. He was raised up in pride by the irrigation of rivers, which he calls his horn, since, through the multitude of his army, he was able to cross all the waters and trouble them.

Therefore he says that he will spread his net over his multitude and draw him out with his net or hook, cast him—or stretch him—upon the land. He had been like a serpent coiled in many spirals, so that he might be devoured by all the birds of the sky.

When not only the birds but all the beasts of the earth have torn him apart, the remains of his flesh will fill the mountains, valleys, and fields, so that everything will swarm with worms. He speaks metaphorically: after the birds of the sky and beasts have been satisfied with his flesh—that is, with his army and entire multitude—the remaining portion will be changed into worms and corruption.

“Then,” he says, “the heavens will be wrapped in darkness; the sun, moon, and other lights will not give their light, but everything will grow dark over you, and nothing joyful will remain for you.”

At your destruction all peoples and all their kings will fear with great terror, seeing my sword flying here and there, sparing no one, and fearing a similar destruction in your ruin.

But so that you may know what this sword is, hear more clearly: “The sword of the king of Babylon shall come upon you. With the swords of the mighty”—or of giants—“I will cast down your entire multitude.” These giants are unconquerable nations, held by the army of the king of Babylon.

“These shall destroy,” or disperse, “the pride of Egypt” and all its multitude. Nothing will remain in Egypt; human beings, cattle, and brute animals alike will be taken away.

Such will be the solitude in Egypt that neither the foot of man nor the hoof of cattle will trouble its waters. Everything will be quiet, and its rivers will flow like oil, exceedingly pure and shining, with no one passing through them or disturbing their currents.

This is because of the desolation of Egypt, which will be reduced to a wilderness and deprived of all its multitude when the Lord strikes its inhabitants, so that those who remain may understand that he is the Lord.

Therefore this is a lamentation over Pharaoh, and the daughters of the surrounding nations shall lament him—not only him but also his multitude, which will be destroyed when the Lord lays waste to it.

Let what has been said briefly concerning the simple letter suffice. Let us come to the spiritual interpretation.

I do not think we need labor greatly to discover who Pharaoh king of Egypt is, since we have explained above that he is the power to which Egypt is entrusted—whether a single province or Egypt as the whole world. It was not created a lion but, through its own fault, was made like a lion among the nations: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. XLVIII).

Peter also speaks of this lion: “Our adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about” (1 Pet. V). And in the ninth psalm it is written: “He lies in wait in secret, like a lion in his den; he lies in wait to seize the poor.”

Jeremiah also says by the Holy Spirit: “The lion from the forest has struck them” (Jer. V).

That the devil is called a dragon, for whom Aquila translated *Leviathan*, explaining the name as “dragon,” I have demonstrated above through many testimonies. He said: “The rivers are mine, and I made them.”

This dragon, with his rivers as though with horns, tossed many nations. We may understand these as those gathered around Marcion, Valentinus, Arius, Eunomius, and the other leaders of heresies, who imitate ecclesiastical men when they say to the Lord Savior: “In you we shall toss our enemies with the horn” (Ps. XLIII).

But they do not toss them toward salvation, so as to lift them from earth to heaven; they toss them down into the depths.

Hence it follows: “You troubled the waters with your feet,” in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “He who troubles you shall bear judgment” (Gal. V).

For he does not wish to drink the waters of Shiloah, which go quietly, but the turbid and muddy waters of Egypt. Before they were trampled by the dragon’s feet, they were pure and flowed in their proper order. But after they were troubled by his feet, they lost the order of their course.

For heretics do not use the testimonies of Scripture in a coherent manner; rather, they trouble everything.

And because he is the enemy and avenger, the Egyptian dragon not only troubles foreign waters with his feet but tramples his own rivers, so that he may not spare those whom he has once brought under his power.

Seeking to avoid this, the righteous pray: “Let not the foot of pride come against me” (Ps. XXXV). And elsewhere, having been trampled, he asks not to be trampled again: “Have mercy on me, O Lord, for man has trampled me” (Ps. LV).

The hostile man is the devil. Another psalm also speaks of him: “So that man may no longer magnify himself upon the earth” (Ps. IX).

Therefore: “Thus says the Lord God: I will spread my net over you in the assembly of many peoples.”

The Lord’s net, woven from the teaching of the Old and New Testaments, is cast over the dragon, who dwells amid the multitude of peoples and always delights in crowds and numbers.

He will draw him out in his net or on his hook. This is the net spoken of in the Gospel (Matt. XIII), which is cast into the sea of this world in order to draw out many fish—some to be chosen and others to be cast away.

Or it is the hook concerning which it is written in Job: “Can you draw out the dragon with a hook and put a bridle around his nostrils?” (Job XL). Aquila translated this: “You shall draw out Leviathan with a hook and bind his tongue with ropes.”

The dragon, or Leviathan, is drawn out of the sea by the Lord’s hook or net so that he may be cast—or stretched—upon the earth. All his coils, with which he concealed his ambushes, are opened and brought into public view. He is thrown down and lies upon the earth, although he had placed his mouth in heaven and boasted that he was like the Most High.

Hence it follows: “I will make all the birds of the sky dwell or sit upon you, and I will satisfy the beasts of the whole earth with you.”

This accords with what is written: “You gave him as food to the peoples of Ethiopia” (Ps. LXXIII)—those who are called either birds or beasts of the earth.

The birds are those which, as we have said, snatch away the seed beside the road. The beasts of the earth are those made savage by vices, which may be referred to heretics and Gentiles.

As for what follows: “I will place your flesh upon the mountains and fill your hills with your corruption,” or “I will fill the valleys with your blood,” its meaning is that we should understand the birds of the sky and beasts of the earth as the peoples deceived by him and the cruelty of the Gentiles.

Let us refer the mountains to the leaders of heresies, such as Valentinus and Marcion, and the hills to their successors, who are filled with the dragon’s corruption. Or let the valleys, which are filled with the dragon’s blood, signify the lower classes of believers.

Alternatively, the mountains may signify the opposing powers that move through the air, and the valleys the powers that penetrate the regions below and have been given over to eternal punishments.

Moreover, when it says: “I will water the land with the stench of your blood upon the mountains,” or “the land shall be watered from your dung upon the mountains,” and “the valleys shall be filled from you,” it signifies that all the pride and arrogant swelling of heretics is filled not with living and pure blood but with blood that is rotten and foul, in accordance with what is written: “Set them like dung upon the earth” (Ps. LXXXII).

From this the holy man is delivered, the one who is “raised from the dust and lifted from the dung heap, to set him with princes, with the princes of his people” (Ps. CXII).

The valleys, being deeply depressed, signify either the underworld, as we said above, or the humble understanding of heretics, who do everything for pleasure and earthly riches.

As for what is joined to this—“When you have been extinguished, I will cover the sky, and I will make its stars dark; I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon shall not give its light; I will make all the lights of heaven mourn or grow dark over you, and I will bring darkness over your land, says the Lord God”—if we follow the literal sense, it cannot be understood at all.

For when Pharaoh or the dragon was killed, when did the sun, moon, and stars not give their light, and when was the sky covered with darkness, in accordance with that poetic line:

> And the impious ages feared eternal night.

Therefore, this must be said: when Pharaoh, who transformed himself into an angel of light, has been extinguished—for it is written elsewhere of him, “The light of the wicked will be extinguished” (Prov. XXIV)—the heaven, or the heavens, will be covered with darkness, concerning which Paul also speaks: “the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. VI). And the Lord caused his stars—or those of the dragon, or of heaven—to become black. Concerning this the apostle Jude also writes: “wandering stars” (Jude v. 13), for whom the gloom of darkness is reserved forever.

The sun also will be covered with a cloud: the sun of iniquity, which is opposed to the sun of righteousness. By the cloud we may understand either the Lord and Savior himself, who descended into Egypt upon a light cloud, unburdened by any weight of sins, or the prophets and apostles, concerning whom we read: “I will command the clouds not to rain upon it rain” (Isa. V). And in the Psalms: “Your truth reaches to the clouds” (Ps. XXXV).

When the sun of iniquity has been darkened, the moon—which we understand as the church of the heretics, and which was thought to receive its light from the sun of iniquity—will not give its light, nor will it deceive believers with knowledge falsely so called. All the luminaries also, and whatever teaching appears to exist among the heretics, will be blinded when the dragon has been extinguished; or they will mourn their prince, who has been lost, so that the Lord himself will cover the land of the heretics with darkness: namely, with ignorance of the truth, so that the blind lead the blind into the pit, and the inhabitants of the earth are sent into the outer darkness, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth.

[Col. 0823C]

After this it is said: “And I will provoke the heart of many peoples, when I bring about your ruin—or your captivity—among the nations, upon a land that you do not know,” so that those who had previously served Pharaoh may become angry against him, seeing that his captivity has been brought to another land unknown to the dragon. Nor should we doubt that the lands unknown to Pharaoh are good lands—namely, when Pharaoh’s captivity is exchanged for another captivity, concerning which it is said to the Savior: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he received” (Ps. LXVII), or, according to the Apostle, “he gave gifts to men.”

“And I will astonish,” he says, “many peoples because of you,” so that those who had previously admired Pharaoh’s power may afterward be astonished that he had fallen from his height.

[Col. 0824A]

The kings of the peoples also will fear him with great terror—those whose kingdoms the devil showed to the Lord—and concerning whom the Psalm says: “The kings of the earth stood forth, and the princes gathered together” (Ps. II).

This will happen “when the sword of the Lord begins to fly over their faces,” that is, the faces of the kings or the peoples. The sword of the Lord is to be understood as the living and effective word of God, sharper than every two-edged sword. It flies, moves swiftly, and flashes before the eyes of those who see it, terrifying their faces. In their astonishment at Pharaoh’s ruin, they will see themselves cast down in him.

The sword of the Lord, concerning which it is written, “Behold, this one is appointed for the falling and rising of many” (Luke II), raises up those who lie prostrate and changes those who have risen wrongly through humility. But the sword of the king of Babylon will come upon the Egyptian dragon, so that the Lord may cast down his multitude by the swords of the mighty, or of giants—the multitude that followed the king of Egypt.

“The unconquerable,” he says, or “the pestilential ones from the nations,” “all these,” so that the wicked may be handed over for punishment to worse beings, concerning whom it is written: “sending forth through evil angels” (Ps. LXXVII); and the Apostle says: “Whom I handed over to Satan,” he says, “so that they may learn not to blaspheme; or for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved” (I Tim. I).

When the pride of Egypt has been cast down through such ministers, and its multitude has been scattered, all its cattle, which were over many waters, will perish.

[Col. 0824C]

“And no longer will the foot of man disturb them.” For if blessed is the one who sows upon the waters where ox and ass tread, then, conversely, unhappy is the one who can retain the simple in his error any longer, so that the foot of man does not tread upon them, and the waters of Egypt appear to contain not even the sign of wisdom and reason. “Nor will the hoof of cattle disturb them,” so that he may make turbid and muddy what had been limpid and shining.

Then the Lord himself, not others, will restore the purest waters which had been troubled by the dragon’s dominion, so that their rivers may flow like oil and become nourishment for the true light. These things will happen when the Lord makes the land of Egypt desolate, destroys its multitude, and strikes all its inhabitants, so that by this achievement they may know that he himself is the Lord.

[Col. 0824D]

As for what follows—“There is lamentation, and the daughters of the nations will lament him over Egypt, and over its multitude they will lament him, says the Lord God”—the meaning is clear: the souls of all the nations that had previously been oppressed, or of those nations that did not dwell in Egypt at all but in the land of the living, will lament the slain dragon and all his multitude, not in hope of salvation, but because through his own fault and pride he has been cast down from such power into eternal punishments.

“And it came to pass in the twelfth year, on the fifteenth day of the month: the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, sing a lamentation over the multitude of Egypt. And drag it down, itself and the daughters of mighty nations, to the furthest land, with those who descend into the pit. Whom do you surpass in beauty? Descend and sleep with the uncircumcised. In the midst of the slain they will fall. The sword has been given. And they dragged it down, with all its peoples. The most powerful of the mighty will speak to it from the midst of hell, those who descended with its helpers and slept uncircumcised, slain by the sword.

“There is Asshur and all its multitude around it; its graves are all the slain and those who have fallen by the sword, whose graves were assigned in the remotest parts of the pit. And its multitude was around its grave, all slain and fallen by the sword, who had once spread terror in the land of the living.

“There is Elam and all its multitude around its grave. All these were slain and fell by the sword; they descended uncircumcised to the furthest land. They placed their terror in the land of the living, and they bore their disgrace with those who descend into the pit. In the midst of the slain they placed its resting-place, among all its peoples around it, its grave. All these were uncircumcised and slain by the sword. For they had spread terror in the land of the living, and they bore their disgrace with those who descend into the pit. In the midst of the slain they were placed.

“There are Meshech and Tubal and all its multitude around it; its graves. All these were uncircumcised and slain, and fell by the sword—those who spread their terror in the land of the living. They will not sleep with the mighty who have fallen and are uncircumcised, who descended to hell with their weapons. They placed their swords under their heads, and their iniquities were upon their bones, because they became the terror of the mighty in the land of the living.

“And you, therefore, will be crushed in the midst of the uncircumcised, and you will sleep with those slain by the sword. There is Edom and its kings, and all its princes, who have been placed with their army among those slain by the sword, and who slept with the uncircumcised and with those who descend into the pit.

“There are all the princes of the north and all the hunters, who were led away with the slain, trembling and confounded in their strength, because they slept uncircumcised with those slain by the sword, and they bore their confusion with those who descend into the pit.

“Pharaoh saw them and was comforted over all his multitude, which had been slain by the sword: Pharaoh and all his army, says the Lord God, because he had spread his terror in the land of the living; and he slept in the midst of the uncircumcised with those slain by the sword—Pharaoh and all his multitude, says the Lord God.”

In the meantime, according to the historical sense, the meaning is evident. For in the same twelfth year, and, as we suppose, in the same month—but not on the same day of the month as above—rather, on the fifteenth day, a lamentation is taken up not over Pharaoh but over the strength, or multitude, of Egypt. It is dragged down from its pride, together with all its daughters, or the mighty nations, to the furthest land, that is, into the depths of hell.

[Col. 0825A]

And it is said to the king of Egypt: “Whom do you surpass, that you should deserve to escape death?” For since Asshur and Elam—that is, the Persians—and Meshech, which is interpreted as “Cappadocians,” and Tubal, whom some wish to understand as Iberians and others as Italians, as well as the Edomites, the princes of the north, and the Sidonians, with all their armies, through whose aid they had brought terror upon all the nations, have died and been slain by the sword, and have placed their swords under their heads—a statement to be understood more emphatically [ἐμφατικώτερον]—will you alone be able not to suffer the same things? Rather, when you see so great a multitude of sleepers with you in the underworld, and your grave surrounded by the memorials of once very powerful princes, you will have consolation, considering the torments lighter because of the company of so many.

[Col. 0826B]

For the present, it is enough to have spoken briefly according to the simple sense. Now, with the same brevity, insofar as the difficulty of the explanation permits, let us gather the chief points of the spiritual interpretation.

Above, the word of the Lord came to the prophet on the first day of the month; here, on the fifteenth. The first day—that is, the beginning of the month—is the day of the new moon; the fifteenth is when the entire orb of the moon is full. And if it was the first month, it was the first day of Unleavened Bread; but if the seventh, it was the feast of Booths, when the tabernacles are erected—festivals that are among the greatest observances of the Hebrews.

A lamentation is made over the strength of Egypt so that it may cease to be strong in evil and receive weakness; and when it has become weaker, then it may be stronger. In place of “the strength of Egypt,” the Hebrew has “the multitude.” “For broad and spacious is the way that leads to death, and many enter through it” (Matt. VII). Conversely, it is said to Israel: “But you are few among all the nations” (Deut. XXVIII), for virtue is always rare, “and narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life, and few are those who enter through it.”

As for the mourning over Egypt and the leading down of its dead daughters, according to the Septuagint, or of the mighty daughters of the nations, to the furthest land, into the pit or deepest ditch, this signifies the souls dwelling in the Egypt of this age, who have lost the one who says: “I am life” (John XIV). Dead through sins, they are dragged down to the underworld by the weight of those sins, as the sinner says: “For my iniquities have gone over my head, and like a heavy burden they have been made heavy upon me” (Ps. XXXVII).

These are the ones concerning whom it is written elsewhere: “They will enter into the lower parts of the earth; they will be handed over to the power of the sword; they will become portions for foxes” (Ps. LXII); for “whoever digs a pit will fall into it” (Ecclus. XXVII). Hence we also read: “He opened a pit and dug it, and he fell into the pit that he made” (Ps. VII).

And what follows—“Whom do you surpass in beauty? Descend and sleep with the uncircumcised”—is addressed specifically to Pharaoh, king of Egypt; or, as in the Septuagint, with the addition from Theodotion, to Egypt itself: “Descend from the most beautiful water, and sleep with the uncircumcised.”

This applies especially to the one who, reborn in the baptism of Christ and hearing with the Church, “Who is this who ascends, made white, leaning upon her little brother?” (Song VIII), is afterward stained either by fornication or by other vices, is expelled from the Church, and is told: “Descend from the most beautiful water and sleep with the uncircumcised”—that is, with the unclean—according to the sense expressed by the Apostle: “We are the circumcision, who serve God in the spirit and glory in the Lord, and do not put confidence in the flesh” (Phil. III).

All these will fall in the midst of the wounded, or the slain, together with that Pharaoh, by the sword which the Lord came to bring upon the earth. For just as Christ’s sword separates the good from the evil, saying, “I did not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword” (Matt. X), so the sword of the heretics slaughters all peoples and leads the wounded down to the underworld.

[Col. 0827B]

These are the most powerful and rebellious giants, who set their mouths on high. And the higher they raise themselves through pride, the more deeply they are dragged down to the bottom of the pit and to the farthest depths of hell.

(Gregory.) According to the tropological sense, however, whoever exalts himself above himself is weighed down by the burden of his own elation, and sinks into the depths all the more by how much, rushing into the vice of pride, he has withdrawn from the one who is truly exalted. From there he desires the lowest things all the more, from where he imagined himself joined to the highest. Thus the Prophet says to the soul that exalts itself: “Whom do you surpass in beauty? Descend and sleep with the uncircumcised.”

For everyone who neglects to consider the foulness of his weakness but, through the arrogance of pride, attends to the glory of his virtue, descends from the very place in which he is more beautiful: by exalting himself over his merits, he falls into the depths of destruction from the very place where he judged himself glorious. Descending, he slept with the uncircumcised, because he perished in eternal death together with the other sinners.

(Jerome.) “All of whom were slain by the sword.” And so that Pharaoh, or all the strength of Egypt dragged down to the underworld, might know whom it had as companions in punishment, the following passage makes clear. “There is Asshur and all his multitude,” or “his synagogue.” For the princes of the heretics are the devil’s synagogue, since it is truly his congregation, concerning which it is said in the Apocalypse: “Those who are the synagogue of Satan” (Rev. II).

I think that the following verses, which are marked beforehand with an obelus according to the Septuagint, should be passed over, and that what is found in the Hebrew should be said: “Around it are their graves,” namely, the graves of those deceived by him, all of whom were wounded or slain by the sword, and therefore fell: “whose graves were assigned in the remotest parts of the pit.”

That the pit is called hell is clearly demonstrated by that psalm in which the penitent says: “I have been made like those who descend into the pit” (Ps. XXVII). We must not understand it according to the proper meaning of the Latin word as the place called in Greek λίμνη [limnē], such as the Lake of Tiberias, Lake Larius, Lake Benacus, and many others. Rather, these are what we customarily call cisterns. They are called pits because they cool the waters and remove all the heat from them; sinners and all heretics dig them.

And, as far as my memory goes, Scripture testifies that no saint dug a pit—that is, a cistern—but that all who did so were sinners, among them King Uzziah, who was struck with leprosy (2 Chron. XXVI) and who fell through his pride. It is written of him that he was a man devoted to the works of the earth, that he built many towers of pride at the corners, and that he dug pits.

Conversely, it is said to the righteous: “Drink waters from your vessels and from the springs of your wells” (Prov. V). And again: “Let the spring of your water be your own.” Hence the Lord also says: “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves pits”—that is, cisterns—“which cannot hold water” (Jer. II).

It follows: “And its multitude was around its grave.” All these surround the Assyrian, and they are a very great multitude; all were wounded and slain, falling by the sword. None of them can stand with Moses, nor hear the words, “You who stand in the house of the Lord” (Ps. CXXXIII); but all were wounded, slain, and falling—those who once spread terror in the land of the living.

[Col. 0828B]

They spread terror among those who had been placed over the churches, lest they make peoples of the dead in the land of the living and deceive the simple. Hence Paul also said: “But I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve in his malice, your minds may somehow be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ” (2 Cor. XI). But this fear is mitigated by hope in the Lord, as the Psalmist says: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life; from whom shall I tremble?” (Ps. XXVI).

After this it is said: “There is also Elam [There is Asshur] and all its multitude around its grave.” There can be no doubt that these are the Assyrians. Elam is translated into our language as “their ascent.” For all who, despising Christ’s humility, have ascended into the devil’s pride and have thought themselves to be something in knowledge falsely so called are to be called Elamites.

They surround the grave of the Assyrian king and are slain and wounded by the sword. And although they set their mouths on high, nevertheless they descended unclean and uncircumcised to the furthest land, so that the higher they had been raised, the more forcefully they might fall.

These “placed their terror”—not once but a second time—“in the land of the living.” For what member of the churches is safe from the terror of such Elamites, and has not lost someone from his flock? Beautifully, the Church of Christ is called “the land of the living,” so that, conversely, the assemblies of the heretics may be believed to be lands of the dead.

“And they bore,” he says, “their disgrace, or their torment, with those whom they dragged down with them into the pit,” and into the depths of hell, whose resting-place was among the slain. These were the ones whom they slaughtered with their own sword, and such peoples surround them. These peoples are the peoples of the Assyrian king. Although they boast that they are circumcised, they are nevertheless uncircumcised and slain by the sword.

And for the third time they spread terror and fear in the land of the living; therefore they bore their torment and punishment in the midst of those whom they had deceived by their frauds.

“There also is,” that is, beside the Assyrian, “Meshech and Tubal and all its multitude around its grave: all uncircumcised, slain and fallen by the sword, who had spread their terror in the land of the living.”

(Jerome.) For Meshech and Tubal, Symmachus and Theodotion translated “their resting-place,” in order to show that the resting-places of the heretics—or rather, the everlasting pits—are the punishments of the Assyrian king. Meshech means “madness,” Tubal “turning,” not from evil to good, but from good to evil; or “the whole,” to show that all heretics are mad and with equal zeal turn toward worse things. Nor is it surprising that, being mad and heaped together for evil, they have a multitude, since they are companions of the king of Egypt, who delights in a multitude. “All these were slain by the sword, who spread their terror,” not once, nor twice, nor three times, “in the land of the living,” concerning whom we have spoken more fully above.

It follows: “And they will not sleep with the mighty,” or giants, “who have fallen and are uncircumcised, who descended to hell with their weapons, and placed their swords beneath their heads; and their iniquities were in their bones, because they became the terror of the mighty in the land of the living.” These, he says, who had been leaders of the heretics, reached so great a height of wickedness and punishments that they do not deserve to bear sufferings like those of the mighty and giants who fell from the beginning. Without performing repentance for their error, they descended to hell with their weapons, rebellious against God and his Church, carrying their weapons with them. Of these it is written: “The teeth of the sons of men are weapons and arrows” (Ps. LVI). “And they placed,” he says, “their swords beneath their heads,” resting in a hostile mind and embracing the missiles of their opinions as their highest victory—so much so that their iniquities were in their bones; that is, they possessed the strongest contrivances and doctrines of their error, because in their life, or in the land of the living, they became the terror of the mighty. This is said a fourth time: that by their perversity they might terrify the strongest, those who possessed knowledge of the Scriptures and were from the region of the living, while they descend to hell with their weapons, place their swords beneath their heads, and their iniquity reaches even to their bones.

(Gregory, Moral. IX.46.) Rightly, therefore, it is said through the prophet: “They descended into hell with their weapons.” The weapons of sinners are the members of the body, by which they pursue the various desires that they behold. Hence the Apostle rightly says: “Do not present your members as weapons of iniquity to sin” (Rom. VI).

To descend into hell with weapons, therefore, is to endure the torments of eternal judgment with those very members by which they fulfilled the desires of their will, so that pain may then consume them on every side—those who now, subjected to their own pleasures, fight on every side against the justice of the one who judges justly.

(Jerome.) After this it is written: “And you, therefore, will be crushed in the midst of the uncircumcised.” This is said either to Pharaoh or to the strength, or multitude, of Egypt, which itself also is crushed, according to what is written: “But God will crush Satan under your feet swiftly” (Rom. XVI).

“And you will sleep,” he says, “with those slain by the sword.” There, in perpetual sleep, Edom and all its kings will be with the Assyrian and with the multitude of Egypt—all who served earthly works or delighted in blood. For Edom signifies both “earthly” and “bloodthirsty.”

[Col. 0830B]

All the kings and all the princes of whom the Apostle frequently speaks—those occupied with earthly works and daily shedding the blood of those whom they have deceived by their fraud—slept with the uncircumcised and the unclean, and with those who descended into the pit. Concerning them we spoke above; they will be in that same company.

So also will be the princes of the north, from which evils blaze forth over the earth, and from which, both in Jeremiah and in this same prophet, that pot full of flesh and bones is kindled. And not only the princes of the north, but all the rulers of Asshur.

In place of this, the Hebrew has “all the Sidonians,” whom we translate as “hunters,” according to what is written: “Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters” (Ps. CXXIII). In the Hebrew, “of the Sidonians” is found instead. These Sidonians, or hunters, will be led trembling into the underworld, having once trusted in their own strength.

They will sleep unclean, and they will bear their confusion, or torment, having the eternal remorse of an evil conscience, so that their fire will not be extinguished and their worm will not die (Isa. LXVI; Mark IX).

When Pharaoh sees all these, he will be comforted—either because he still possesses his former malice and sees that he has many companions in punishment, or because he was indeed comforted when he saw them also confounded in their punishments and terrors.

[Col. 0830D]

He will be comforted “over all his multitude, which was slain by the sword”—namely, Pharaoh’s multitude and that of all his companions, especially the king of Assyria, Meshech and Tubal, the Edomites, the princes of the north, and the Sidonians. For these had spread their terror in the land of the living.

This is said a fifth time so that we may beware of and flee from all such nations, which have deceived us through all our senses, and know that they are dreadful and cannot easily be avoided unless we guard our heart with all vigilance.

“He also slept,” he says, “with his companions slain by the sword.” His companions are his multitude, proceeding along the broad and spacious way toward eternal punishments.

# CHAPTER XXXIII

Concerning the watchman who sounds the trumpet so that sinners may return to repentance; and how each person will be judged wherever he is found; the word of the Lord against those who wish to possess an inheritance from the multitude without holiness, and against those who have turned the words of prophecy into a song.

[Col. 0831A]

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, speak to the children of your people, and say to them: When I bring a sword upon a land, and the people of the land take one man from among their lowliest members and appoint him over themselves as a watchman, and he sees the sword coming upon the land and blows the trumpet and gives warning to the people—if, on hearing the sound of the trumpet, whoever he may be does not take heed, and the sword comes and takes him away, his blood shall be upon his own head. He heard the sound of the trumpet and did not take heed; his blood shall be upon him. But if he takes heed, he shall save his life. But if the watchman sees the sword coming and does not sound the trumpet, and the people do not take heed, and the sword comes and takes a life from among them, he indeed has been seized in his iniquity, but I shall require his blood from the hand of the watchman. And you, son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel. Therefore, hearing the word from my mouth, you shall announce it to them from me. When I say to the wicked man, ‘Wicked man, you shall surely die,’ and you have not spoken so that the wicked man may guard himself from his way, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but I shall require his blood from your hand. But if, when you warn the wicked man to turn back from his ways, he does not turn back from his way, he himself shall die in his iniquity, but you shall have delivered your life.”  

(Jerome.) Once again the word of the Lord comes to the prophet, who had been silent for some time, because a prophet—and human frailty—cannot sustain a constant and uninterrupted prophecy addressed to him. He speaks the same things that are contained above:

“Son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel. You shall hear the word from my mouth, and you shall threaten them from me. When I say to the wicked man, ‘You shall surely die,’ and you have not announced it to him, nor spoken so as to warn the wicked man, that he might turn from his ways and live, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity, and I shall require his blood from your hand. But if you warn the wicked man and he does not turn back from his iniquity and from his way, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity, but you shall deliver your life.”

If you examine these carefully, you understand that they are indeed similar, but not identical, since they differ in many respects. We must observe this throughout all the Holy Scriptures: wherever there appears to be some similarity of meaning, the same things are not said in every detail; rather, many things are either omitted or added, and the difference between individual words has its own significance.

Meanwhile, before we come to higher matters, a brief explanation of the meaning must be given. If a watchman has been appointed among the peoples to announce the sword of the Lord and the coming wrath, and, when he gives warning, the people refuse to listen, the watchman will be free, while the one overwhelmed by the sword will bear the guilt of his own blood. But if he listens, he will save his life. If, however, the watchman does not sound the trumpet, and the people, unaware that the sword is coming, do not take heed, the people will indeed die in their own iniquity; nevertheless, I shall require the blood of the dying man from the watchman’s hand.

And so that the prophet Ezekiel might know that this general discussion applies especially to him, he says: “And you, son of man”—you have not been appointed watchman for the house of Israel by the land and by the people of the land, as I said above, but by me. “Therefore, when I say to the wicked man, ‘You shall surely die,’ and you have not spoken to him so that he may guard himself and be delivered from destruction, he indeed will die in his own iniquity, which he had previously committed and from which he could have been delivered if you had warned him; but I shall require his blood from your hand.”

But if you warn the wicked man and command him to turn back from his worst ways, and he refuses to do so, he will indeed die in his own iniquity, but you will have delivered your life from the destruction caused by negligence.

From this we learn that a person, however unjust and wicked, can be saved from his wickedness if he listens to the teacher’s words and performs repentance. Likewise, the teacher is exposed to danger if he refuses to teach, whether through fear of danger or through despair concerning the sinner, since he is held guilty of the blood of one who could have been delivered and rescued from death had he not fallen through the teacher’s silence. In both cases free choice is preserved: it lies with the teacher either to be silent or to speak, and with the hearer either to listen, act, and be saved, or to despise and perish through his own contempt.

Nor does it immediately follow that, because the prophet foretells something, what he has foretold must come to pass. He does not foretell it in order that it may come, but so that it may not come. Nor, because God speaks, is what he threatens necessarily bound to happen; rather, he threatens so that the one threatened may turn to repentance and what would happen if the Lord’s words were despised may not occur.

We can interpret this passage in three ways. The land that appointed a watchman for itself may, according to the literal sense, be the land of Judea; or, according to the spiritual understanding, it may be the Church, which often chooses a watchman from among the lowliest members of its people—that is, the one whom the Apostle also appoints as judge when writing to the Corinthians; or certainly it may be the soul of the believer, which places mind and reason over the people and crowd of its thoughts, so that it does not accept every impulse of its thoughts, but judges and distinguishes which things it ought to follow and which it ought to avoid.

The watchman of the land of Judea may be understood as either a king or a prophet. The watchman of the Church may be a bishop or a presbyter, who, elected by the people, recognizes through reading the Scriptures and foresees what is to come, announces it to the people, and corrects the delinquent.

Therefore we must greatly fear lest we approach this office unworthily and, having been chosen by the people, give ourselves over to negligence and sloth—and, worse than these, serving pleasures, the belly, and leisure, think that we have received an honor rather than a ministry. For “the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve” (Matt. XX). And he washed the feet of his disciples, to show that all dirt and vice must be washed away and cleansed by the teacher in his disciples.

Nor should we immediately reply: “What benefit is there in teaching if the hearer does not wish to do what you teach?” Each person is judged according to his own mind and duty: you, if you have not spoken; he, if he has scorned to listen.

(Gregory.) For this reason also, in another place, he commanded a frying pan to be placed between himself and the city:

“And you, take for yourself an iron frying pan, and place it as an iron wall between yourself and the city; and you shall set your face firmly against it, and it shall be under siege, and you shall surround it” (Ezek. IV).

Paul had placed this frying pan as a wall between himself and the disciples when he said:

“I am clean from the blood of all of you. For I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God” (Acts XX).

Therefore, teachers must now desire to burn with the ardors of zeal, lest afterward they be forced to be tormented by the fire of Gehenna because of the coldness of their negligence.

But one thing is owed to the unjust and subject, and another to the just and not subject. Fear ought to kindle us toward correcting and guarding the former, since we must give an account for them; toward reverencing the latter, the very equity that we have considered ought to incline us.

But arrogant men, because they do not understand the form of this discernment, display toward the just and those not subject what they see being done by good preachers toward the unjust and subject. When they rush unjustly into the heat of correction, they also go beyond the limits in words of cursing. Because they do not love their neighbors as themselves, they do not cease wishing for their neighbors what they fear will happen to themselves.

(Jerome.) Solomon speaks about negligent teachers:

“Hidden wisdom and concealed treasure—what benefit is there in either?” (Eccli. XLI.)

Something similar is signified in the Gospel (Matt. XVIII): whoever causes one of the least of the Church to stumble, it would be better for him to have a millstone tied around his neck and to be cast into the depths than, having been placed as a watchman, to harm many.

“Therefore you, son of man, say to the house of Israel: Thus you have spoken, saying, ‘Our iniquities and our sins are upon us, and in them we waste away; how, then, can we live?’ Say to them: ‘As I live,’ says the Lord God, ‘I do not desire the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn back from his way and live. Turn back from your worst ways; why will you die, house of Israel?’”

(Gregory.) Since he has no desire that even one of the little ones should perish, how can he be thought, without grave sacrilege, to wish not all people universally but only some to be saved? Therefore, all who perish perish against his will. Thus he cries out daily to each one of them:

“Turn back from your worst ways.”

And:

“Why will you die, house of Israel?”

And again:

“How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling?” (Matt. XXIII.)

And:

“Why,” he says, “has this people in Jerusalem turned away with a contentious turning? They have hardened their necks; they refused to return.”

Therefore the grace of God is present every day. Since it desires all people to be saved, it calls them without exception, saying:

“Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI).

But if he calls not everyone universally but only some, it follows that not everyone is burdened either by original or by actual sin. Nor would that saying be true:

“For all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. III),

nor would it be believed that death has passed through all human beings.

And so completely do all who perish perish against the will of God that God is not even believed to have made death, as Scripture testifies:

“For God did not make death” (Wis. I),

nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living.

Hence it often happens that, when we ask for harmful things as though they were good, our prayer is heard either more slowly or not at all. Conversely, what we believe to be contrary, the Lord, like a most merciful physician, deigns to inflict even against our will for our benefit. Sometimes he restrains and turns back our harmful plans and deadly efforts from their destructive outcome; he draws those hastening toward death back from the jaws of hell to salvation and extracts them from danger while they remain unaware.

“Therefore you, son of man, say to the children of your people: The righteousness of the righteous will not deliver him on whatever day he sins. And the wickedness of the wicked will not harm him on whatever day he turns back from his wickedness. And the righteous will not be able to live by his righteousness on whatever day he sins. Even if I say to the righteous, ‘He shall surely live,’ and, trusting in his righteousness, he commits iniquity, all his righteousnesses shall be consigned to oblivion, and in the iniquity that he has committed, in that he shall die.

“But if I say to the wicked, ‘You shall surely die,’ and he performs repentance for his sin, and does judgment and righteousness, restores the pledge, returns what he has stolen, walks in the commandments of life, and does nothing unjust, he shall surely live and shall not die. None of his sins that he has committed shall be counted against him. He has done judgment and righteousness; he shall surely live.

“And the children of your people said: ‘The way of the Lord is not equally measured, and their own way is unjust.’ For when the righteous turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity, he shall die in them. And when the wicked turns away from his wickedness and does judgment and righteousness, he shall live in them. And you say, ‘The way of the Lord is not right.’ I shall judge each one of you according to his ways, house of Israel.”

(Jerome.) If we read carelessly, this prophecy appears to us to be the same as the one above, in which it is said:

“Do I desire the death of the wicked,” says the Lord, “rather than that he turn from his evil way and live?”

And at the end of that same prophecy:

“Turn back and return from all your wickednesses, and they will not become a torment of iniquity for you.”

There the word is addressed to those who wish to perform repentance and erase their sins by righteousness, so that they may turn with confidence and perform repentance with a full heart.

Here, however, he speaks to those who, because of the magnitude of their sins—or rather, of their wickedness—despair of salvation and say:

“Our iniquities and our sins are upon us, and in them we waste away; how, then, can we live?”

The meaning is this: Since death has once been set before us, and no medicine can restore health to our wounds, why should we labor and be consumed in vain? Why should we spend the present life in despair, so that at least we may enjoy it, since we have lost the future life?

God answers them that he does not desire the death of the wicked, but that he turn back and live. And he turns his speech toward the wicked who are in despair:

“Turn back from your worst ways.”

And so that we may know who the wicked are to whom he speaks, the following statement makes it clear:

“Why will you die, house of Israel?”

Life and death in this passage do not signify that life by which we all live under the common law of nature together with the beasts, or by which we are dissolved in death. Rather, they signify the life and death of which it is written:

“I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. CXIV).

And:

“The soul that sins shall itself die.”

From the particular exhortation with which he addressed the house of Israel, he passes to a general discussion: neither does past righteousness save the righteous if he has become occupied with new crimes, nor do former sins destroy the sinner or wicked man if he has corrected his old errors through works of righteousness. God judges neither by the past in either case, but by the present.

“If I say,” he says, “to the righteous, ‘You shall live,’” and promise him the rewards of righteousness, but he, trusting in them, sins, all his former righteousnesses shall be consigned to oblivion, and he shall die in his present iniquity. My judgment has not changed, since I cannot give to the same man, when he is a sinner, what I promised when he was righteous.

Conversely, if I threaten a sinner and wicked man and say, “Yet three days and Nineveh shall be overthrown,” but he performs repentance and corrects his old error through good works, so that he does judgment and righteousness, restores the pledge, returns what he has stolen, walks in the commandments of life, and does nothing unjust, ought he not to live the life that is Christ and by no means die, since the threat ought not to punish a sinner who has become righteous?

The divine word says something similar to Jeremiah when he went down to the potter’s house (Jer. XVIII) and heard either the promises or the threats of God. These are given in order either to summon people to salvation or to deter them from sin.

Therefore those who say, “The way of the Lord is not equal,” are convicted, because their own judgment is unjust: they have an evil eye and judge not the new but the old.

All these things demonstrate that neither should a sinner despair of salvation if he performs repentance, nor should a righteous person trust in his righteousness if through negligence he loses what he had acquired with great labor.

We pass quickly over what is clear, so that we may linger on what is more obscure. The comparison of the two prophecies will be able to show in what respects the present prophecy differs from the earlier one and in what respects it speaks similarly. As for what it means to do judgment and righteousness, restore the pledge, return what was stolen, walk in the commandments of life, and the rest, we have spoken above in this same prophet.

“And it came to pass in the twelfth year, in the tenth month, on the fifth day of the month of our captivity, that one who had escaped from Jerusalem came to me, saying: ‘The city has been devastated.’ But the hand of the Lord had come upon me in the evening, before the one who had escaped arrived, and it opened my mouth until he came to me in the morning; and when my mouth had been opened, I was no longer silent.”

In the eleventh year of the reign of Zedekiah, in the fifth month, the city of Jerusalem was captured. This prophecy, however, belongs to the twelfth year, the tenth month, and the fifth day of the month of the captivity or transmigration, when Jeconiah was taken captive.

From this it is shown that, after one year, four months, and twenty-five days, a citizen of Jerusalem came to Babylon and announced that the city had been captured and devastated. One day before the arrival of the man who was to report these things, the hand of the Lord came upon the prophet Ezekiel in the evening and opened his mouth, which had long been closed. Ezekiel had here previously related all that the man was about to report; and he was no longer silent, seeing his prophecy fulfilled in reality and the people who were in Babylon—or those who had been taken captive—no longer able to doubt the prophetic prediction.

The prophet’s mouth is opened when what he had previously announced has been shown to have taken place, and he proclaims with complete freedom what he demonstrates to be not future, but either present or past.

This is according to the literal sense. But according to the *anagogy*—that is, the higher spiritual interpretation—if Ezekiel is interpreted as “strength of God,” while Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God, this is to be understood: when Jerusalem had been captured and overthrown, whoever was able to escape the unbelief of the Jews—such as the apostles and the remnant that was saved—announces to Christ that all the ceremonies of the Jews have been overthrown, although some people still today think that they must be observed, refusing to hear the Apostle:

“You have fallen away from grace, you who are justified in the law” (Gal. V).

I marvel at the stubbornness of people who wish to defend in words what they do not dare to fulfill in practice—unless perhaps, under the clothing of sheep, that is, of Christians, Jewish wolves are concealed, who sound forth as defenders of the synagogue in the churches of Christ.

Therefore, when Jerusalem has been captured and overthrown, the mouth of the Lord is opened through the apostles and apostolic men, who can say:

“Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians, and a great and effective door has been opened to me” (1 Cor. XVI).

And:

“I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit” (Ps. CXVIII).

This mouth will never be able to keep silent, nor will it hear with Israel, “Hear, Israel, and be silent”; rather, it will resound throughout the whole world, and the Gospel of Christ will be opened to the nations.

According to this interpretation, therefore, the twelfth year is referred to the twelve tribes; the tenth month to the time of Jewish atonement, which in Greek is called *hilasmos* (ἱλασμός), “propitiation”; and the fifth day of the month to the bodily senses. We have shown that all these things were destroyed and passed away when Jerusalem was captured and the Gospel took their place.

And “in the evening”—that is, at the consummation of the world—the hand of the Lord came upon the true Ezekiel, who had sung through the prophets of the future ruins of the city and showed them fulfilled in the morning.

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, those who dwell in these ruins upon the soil of Israel speak, saying: ‘Abraham was one, and he inherited the land. But we are many; the land has been given to us as a possession.’

“Therefore say to them: Thus says the Lord God: ‘You eat with blood, you lift up your eyes to your abominations, and you shed blood; shall you ever possess the land as an inheritance? You have stood upon your swords, you have committed abominations, and each one of you has defiled his neighbor’s wife; and shall you possess the land as an inheritance?’

“Say this to them: Thus says the Lord God: ‘As I live, those who dwell in the ruins shall fall by the sword; whoever is in the open country shall be handed over to the beasts for devouring; and those who are in the strongholds and caves shall die by pestilence. I shall make the land a desolation and a wilderness, and its proud strength shall fail, and the mountains of Israel shall be desolated, because there will be no one who passes through them. And they shall know that I am the Lord, when I make the land desolate and deserted because of all their abominations that they have committed.’

“And you, son of man, the children of your people who speak about you beside the walls and at the doors of their houses, each man to his neighbor, saying: ‘Come, let us hear what word proceeds from the Lord’—they come to you as though the people were entering, and they sit before you, my people, and hear my words, but they do not do them, because they turn them into a song for their mouths, and their heart follows their greed. You are to them like a musical song, sung with a sweet and pleasant sound. They hear your words and do not do them. But when what was foretold comes—for behold, it is coming—then they shall know that a prophet has been among them.”

After Jerusalem had been captured and the temple overthrown, the poor of the land, about whom Jeremiah writes, had been left alone in Jerusalem. They cultivated vineyards and fields and lived amid the ruins of the burned city.

Although they ought to have performed repentance for the things because of which the captivity had come, they deceived themselves with empty hope and said:

“Our father Abraham was one, and yet he possessed this land as an inheritance.”

They did not mean that Abraham himself had possessed it, but that his seed had received the land of promise. If that one man multiplied into so many peoples, then we, who are much more numerous and have been left in the land of Judea and dwell in deserted and ruined cities, will certainly multiply much more, so that we may possess more than that one man possessed.

The Lord answered them that Abraham possessed the land of promise through the one thing that is faith:

“For Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Rom. IV).

But these people, occupied with unbelief and crimes, even if they are more numerous, cannot possess it.

At the same time he lists the things by which they offend God. There are six kinds of sins:

“You who eat with blood”;

“who lift up your eyes to your abominations”—that is, to your idols;

“and shed blood”—that is, commit murder.

“Can you, while doing these things, retain possession of the land as an inheritance?”

Nor are you content with this as the limit of your crimes, but “you stand upon your swords,” daily ready to kill and imitating Esau, who stood and lived by his sword. “You commit abominations,” namely, incredible shamefulnesses of lust. “And each one of you defiles his neighbor’s wife,” making his crime more serious by defiling the wife of a friend and neighbor.

“And when you do these things,” he says, “do you imagine that you will possess the land as an inheritance?”

Therefore answer them, O prophet, and pronounce this sentence against them from my word:

“I swear by myself that those who dwell in ruins and crumbling walls shall fall by the sword. Those who are in the fields, or in the open country, shall be devoured by beasts; and those who are in walled places, in strongholds and caves, shall not be able to avoid God’s wrath, but shall die of famine and pestilence.”

“And I shall make,” he says, “the land of Judea a desolation, and its proud strength shall fail”—the strength that it once possessed.

“God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James IV).

The mountains also and everything else shall be abandoned, and they shall come into such a desolation that no one will pass through them. Then the few who remain must not trust in their own multitude, but must recognize from the magnitude of the desolation that I am the Lord who made the land a wilderness because of all the abominations they committed.

Let this be said against those who, after Jerusalem had been captured and the whole region of the Jews laid waste, dwelt in small numbers amid ruins, deserted cities, and villages.

Now let us come to the tropological sense, and, according to our custom, let us compress a lengthy discussion rather than expound it at length.

Every heretic dwells among ruins and in deserted places, and thinks that he possesses the land of Israel. He says:

“If Abraham, one man, came through his faith to such blessedness that his seed was multiplied like the sand of the sea and like the stars of heaven, how much more shall we, who are more numerous, possess the land of Israel—that is, of those who see God—and Judea, the confession of the Lord?”

The Lord answers them:

“He possessed the land through the merit of faith, but your unbelief—or rather, your blasphemy—will not be able to possess the land of Israel, that is, the Church.”

First, you eat with blood, pouring out the blood of those whom you cause to stumble. Then you lift your eyes toward your own impurities and abominations, which you have fashioned from your own mind, although you ought to imitate the ecclesiastical man and say:

“To you I have lifted my eyes, who dwell in heaven” (Ps. CXXII).

Third, you shed blood, not giving life to those whom you have led astray, but killing them.

Nor is it enough for you to have done these three things, but “you stand upon your swords”—that is, you persist in the perversity of your doctrine and are ready for slaughter. You commit abominations, doing in your chambers things that are shameful to speak of. And you have defiled your neighbor’s wife, namely, ecclesiastical conduct, hastening every day to snatch away from Christ’s embrace those whom you have deceived.

And when you have done these things, do you think that you will possess the land of Israel as an inheritance?

God declares to them that whoever dwells in the ruined meeting places of the heretics will fall by an ecclesiastical sword. Concerning this it is written:

“Double-edged swords are in their hands” (Ps. CXLIX).

And in the Gospel:

“I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. X).

And the servant who gives himself over to luxury and leisure will be divided—that is, struck by the blade—and his portion will be placed with the unbelievers.

Whoever is in the field or in the open country will be handed over to beasts for devouring. Wishing to avoid them, the prophet prays:

“Do not hand over to the beasts the soul that confesses you” (Ps. LXXIII).

But whoever is in strongholds and fortified places, concerning which it is written:

“The righteous ascends fortified cities and destroys their defenses” (Prov. XXI),

places in which the wicked trusted, and whoever dwells in caves, concerning which it is said:

“It is written: ‘My Father’s house shall be called a house of prayer,’ but you have made it a den of robbers” (Matt. XXI),

such a person will die from hunger for the word of the Lord and from pestilence.

And the whole land of the heretics will be made a wilderness, so that their pride will be broken and the mountains will be reduced to desolation—those who promised themselves the heights of knowledge and are called the mountains of Israel because they overthrow those whom they have deceived under the name of Christ.

No one will pass through them, nor will anyone be able to say what Moses said:

“While I pass by, I shall see this great vision” (Exod. III).

For they are inhabitants of perverse mountains, not travelers and resident aliens. When they have suffered these things, then they will know that he is the Lord who made their land a wilderness because of the abominations they committed.

On that same day and at that same time—that is, in the twelfth year, the tenth month, and the fifth day of the month—when the one who had escaped from Jerusalem arrived, and when the prophet spoke to those who were in the land of Judea and promised themselves hope of an eternal possession, he commanded the prophet to speak to the people who were in Babylon and living there with him, and to rebuke them for the flattering ambushes of those who desired to hear the prophet’s words not for the salvation of their souls but for the pleasure of their ears.

They sat beside the walls and at the doors of their houses, not wishing to enter into the prophet’s meaning, but encouraging one another and saying:

“Come, let us hear what word proceeds from the Lord.”

And so they came as a people entering the Church of God.

“And they sit before you, my people”—those who say that they are my people—but they do not wish to do what they have heard.

Such people seem to me to resemble those who are entertained by theatrical songs, whether they listen to tragedians or comedians, and are there flattered with pleasure. Thus, when they have gone away from you, they repeat and sing the things they heard and deceive themselves with sweet sounds.

“They shall hear your words,” he says, “and shall not do them.”

Many such people exist in the churches even today. They say:

“Come, let us hear this man or that man as he rolls out the words of his preaching with marvelous eloquence.”

They arouse applause, shout aloud, and wave their hands. What they had neglected in their actions, once they recognize that it has come—for what the prophet declares by the word of God must necessarily come—then they will begin to approve and understand that everything they had heard was not the word of a human being, but of the Lord, who spoke through the prophet and the ecclesiastical man.

## CHAPTER XXXIV  
The word of the Lord against negligent shepherds who oppress the flock and seek their own interests; and the promise of a new shepherd and of many blessings.

[Col. 0840A]

“Then the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel. Prophesy and say to the shepherds: Thus says the Lord God: Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who were feeding themselves! Are not flocks fed by shepherds? You ate the milk, clothed yourselves with the wool, and slaughtered what was fat, but you did not feed my flock. You did not strengthen the weak, heal the sick, bind up the injured, bring back the strayed, or seek the lost. [Col. 0840B] Instead, you ruled them harshly and with force. My sheep were scattered because there was no shepherd; they became food for every beast of the field, and they were scattered. My flocks wandered over every mountain and every high hill; my flocks were scattered over the whole face of the earth, and there was no one to search for them—no one, I say, to search for them.

“Therefore, shepherds, hear the word of the Lord: As I live, says the Lord God, because my flocks have become plunder and my sheep food for every beast of the field, because there was no shepherd—for the shepherds did not seek my flock, but the shepherds fed themselves and did not feed my flocks—therefore, shepherds, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I myself will come against the shepherds and require my flock from their hand. I will make them cease from feeding my flock, so that the shepherds will no longer feed themselves; and I will rescue my flock from their mouths, so that it will no longer be food for them.

“For thus says the Lord God: Behold, I myself will seek my sheep and visit them, as a shepherd visits his flock on the day when he is among his scattered sheep. So I will visit my sheep and rescue them from all the places where they were scattered on the day of cloud and darkness. I will bring them out from the peoples, gather them from the lands, and lead them into their own land. I will feed them on the mountains of Israel, beside the streams and in all the inhabited places of the land. [Col. 0840D] I will feed them in the richest pastures, and their grazing places will be on the high mountains of Israel. There they will lie down in green grass and feed in rich pastures upon the mountains of Israel. I myself will feed my sheep and I myself will make them lie down, says the Lord God. I will seek what was lost, bring back what was cast away, bind up what was broken, strengthen what was weak; and I will guard what is fat and strong, and feed them with judgment.

“As for you, my flocks, thus says the Lord God: Behold, I judge between sheep and sheep, between rams and goats. Was it not enough for you to feed on the good pasture, but you also trampled the remnants of your pastures with your feet? And while you drank the purest water, you muddied what remained with your feet. My sheep fed on what your feet had trampled, and they drank what your feet had muddied. Therefore, thus says the Lord God to them: Behold, I myself judge between the fat sheep and the lean sheep. Because you pushed with flank and shoulder and tossed about all the weak animals with your horns until you scattered them outside, I will save my flock, and it will no longer be plunder; and I will judge between sheep and sheep.

“I will raise up over them one shepherd who will feed them: my servant David; he will feed them, and he will be their shepherd. I, the Lord, will be their God, and my servant David will be prince in their midst. I, the Lord, have spoken. [Col. 0841B] I will make with them a covenant of peace, and I will remove the evil beasts from the land. Those who dwell in the wilderness will sleep safely in the forests. I will make them a blessing around my hill, and I will send rain in its season; they will be rains of blessing. The tree of the field will yield its fruit, and the land will yield its produce, and they will be secure in their land without fear.

“They will know that I am the Lord, when I have broken the chains of their yoke and rescued them from the hand of those who ruled over them. They will no longer be plunder for the nations, nor will the beasts of the earth devour them; they will dwell securely, without any terror. I will raise up for them a renowned shoot, and they will no longer be diminished by hunger in the land, nor will they any longer bear the reproach of the nations. They will know that I am the Lord [Col. 0841C] their God, with them, and that they are my people, the house of Israel, says the Lord God. You, my flocks, the flocks of my pasture, are human beings; and I am the Lord your God, says the Lord God.”

*(Jerome.)* After the capture of Jerusalem had been announced in Babylon by the one who had escaped, he spoke about those who were living in the ruins of Jerusalem, and afterward about those who remained in captivity but nevertheless persisted in wickedness, refusing to hear the Prophet’s words. Now he directs his discourse against the shepherds—that is, against the rulers—through whose fault the sheep, that is, the peoples, have been scattered.

It should be noted that from the twelfth year, the tenth month, and the fifth day of the month of Jeconiah’s deportation or captivity, together with those who had been taken captive with him, up to the twenty-fifth year, when the Temple was built upon the mountain of the constructed city and the incredible mysteries of the Church were disclosed, no intervening year or period is inserted. It is simply said: “The word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, speak to them and to those others.” We must therefore understand that all the matters read in these thirteen years were spoken at different times, yet that no definite intervals of time are given between them.

The discourse is directed against the shepherds of Israel, whom we should understand either as the kings and rulers, scribes and Pharisees, and teachers of the Jewish people, or, in the Christian people, as bishops, presbyters, and deacons. According to mystical interpretations, they may also be the angels of the individual churches, to whom John writes in his Apocalypse (Rev. I, II, III), and whose angels see the face of God daily.

The first statement is: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel.” Although they ought to feed the Lord’s flock and care for its salvation, they hasten after their own indulgence. Hence one must take the greatest care to observe those admonitions: “Do not seek to become a judge, lest perhaps you be unable to remove iniquities” (Sir. VII); and again: “The greater you are, the more humble yourself, and you will find grace in the sight of the Lord” (Sir. III); and again: “They have appointed you leader; do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them” (Sir. XXXII).

For this reason the Apostle says that he was like a little child, even an infant, among the disciples. What follows—“You ate the milk and clothed yourselves with the wool”—he speaks, through the metaphor (*per metaphoram*) of shepherds, to the rulers. Of such people it is also written elsewhere: “They devour my people as though they were eating bread” (Ps. XIII). By “milk,” understand every kind of food; by “wool,” the many varieties of clothing.

When it says, “You slaughtered what was fat,” it speaks of the wealthy among the people, whom wicked rulers are said to slaughter in the churches when they preach to them but dare not rebuke their vices. Of them the prophet also says: “My people, those who call you blessed, deceive you and confuse the path of your feet” (Isa. III). James also speaks of them (James II): When people enter their assemblies dressed in splendid clothing and wearing a gold ring, they are honored by them. But to the holy poor man it is said: “You sit on a footstool, or on the ground, or stand.”

These rulers do not strengthen or consolidate what is weak. Paul says: “Receive the weak” (1 Thess. V), and: “Receive the one who is weak in faith” (Rom. XIV). Again: “Many among you are weak and sick” (1 Cor. XI). To such people the divine word is sent, of which it is written in the Psalms: “He sent his word and healed them, and rescued them from their destructions” (Ps. CVI).

“And what was broken,” he says, “they did not bind up,” because they do not consider the deadly wounds among the people—such as an adulterer, murderer, or sacrilegious person. What was cast away, or what they saw going astray, they did not bring back, allowing such people to be deceived by heretics. What had perished they did not seek. They did not desire so much to save the lost as to devour those who were in the churches, ruling them harshly and with force.

This applies especially to the arrogance of bishops: to those who disgrace the dignity of their name by their conduct and assume pride instead of humility, thinking that they have obtained honor rather than a burden. Whenever they see anyone in the Church taking precedence and possessing the word of God, they strive to crush him. Hence, according to the Septuagint, it is written: “What was strong you afflicted with labor.”

The people of God were scattered either by vices or by heretical error, because there was no good shepherd who would lay down his life for the sheep (John X), but all were hirelings who considered only the profits they might obtain from the flocks. When they saw the wolf, they fled; through their negligence the Lord’s flock was devoured by the beasts of the field. Of these it is written: “You appointed darkness, and it became night; in it all the beasts of the field pass through: the young lions roaring to seize and seek food for themselves from God” (Ps. CIII).

“You ruled them,” he says, “with harshness and with force.”

*(Gregory.)* They rule with harshness and force when they hasten to correct their subjects not by reasoning calmly with them but by bending them severely through domination. True teaching, on the contrary, flees this fault of pride all the more vehemently in thought, the more ardently it pursues the teacher of pride himself with the arrows of its words. It is careful not to preach with more elevated manners the one whom it attacks with sacred words in the hearts of its hearers.

They strive both to speak of humility—which is the teacher and mother of all virtues—and to show it in their lives, so that they may express it to their disciples of truth more by their conduct than by their words. Hence Paul, speaking to the Thessalonians and almost forgetting the dignity of his own apostleship, says: “We became little ones among you” (1 Thess. II).
