Likewise the apostle Peter, when he said, “Always ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you for a reason concerning the hope that is in you” (1 Pet. III), asserted that a particular manner of teaching must be maintained in the knowledge of doctrine, adding: “But with gentleness and fear, keeping a good conscience.”

When Paul says to his disciple, “Command these things and teach with all authority” (Tit. II), he does not recommend domination by force but the authority of a good life. What is taught “with authority” is first practiced and only afterward spoken; for teaching loses confidence when conscience hinders the tongue. He therefore suggested not the power of exalted speech but the confidence of good action.

Hence it is also written of the Lord: “He was teaching as one having authority, and not as the scribes and Pharisees” (Matt. VII). He alone spoke uniquely and supremely with the authority of goodness, because he committed no evil through weakness. From the power of his divinity he possessed what he supplied to us through the innocence of his humanity.

We, who are weak human beings, when we speak to human beings about God, must first remember what we are, so that from our own weakness we may consider how we ought to teach and care for our weak brothers. Let us therefore consider whether we are now as some of those whom we correct, or whether we were once such people and are no longer so through the working of divine grace. We should correct with a humble heart all the more gently as we recognize ourselves more truly in those whom we amend.

But if we are neither now nor ever were like those whom we wish to correct, let us beware lest our heart become proud and, because of that very innocence, fall into a worse condition. When we rebuke their vices, let us bring their other virtues before our eyes. If they possess no virtues at all, let us take refuge in the hidden judgments of God. For just as we received the good that we have without any merits of our own, so grace from above may also be poured into them, so that, once awakened, they may eventually surpass even the good things that we previously received.

Who would have believed that Saul would surpass the stoned Stephen in apostolic merit, when at Stephen’s death he guarded the garments of those who were stoning him? The heart must first be humbled by these reflections, and only then should the iniquities of sinners be rebuked.

*(Jerome.)* “They are scattered and wander over all the mountains”—those mountains that are raised up against the knowledge of God—and over every high hill: through heretical pride they despise the simplicity of the Church. “They are scattered over the whole face of the earth,” seeking earthly things rather than heavenly ones. “There was no one to seek or bring them back,” because, occupied with pleasures, they do not care about the losses of the Lord’s flock.

Therefore the word of the Lord is addressed to the wicked shepherds: “You have done this and that,” the things explained above and those which he enumerates a second time. It follows: “Behold, I myself will come to the shepherds and require my flock from their hand.” It would be better for them to have a millstone tied around their neck than to scandalize even the least of my people (Matt. XVIII).

This will be their greatest punishment: “that they will no longer feed my flock,” lest under the pretext of caring for the sheep they feed themselves and gather wealth. “And I will rescue my people from their mouth.” “I will require them,” he says, “from their hand and rescue them from their mouth,” from which they are devoured by greedy jaws.

When he has sought out the sheep, he visits them as sick, emaciated, and scattered through the negligence of the shepherds. He will rescue them from every place, “on the day of cloud and darkness,” of which Joel also speaks: “The day of the Lord is at hand, and the day of darkness and gloom is near, a day of cloud and mist” (Joel II).

Then they are led out from the lands so that they may be brought into their own land, which is the land of the living. He himself feeds them upon the mountains of Israel. Of these David says: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which help will come to me” (Ps. CXX). And not only on the mountains but beside the streams and in all the inhabited places of the land, in the richest pastures and on the high mountain.

Of this Isaiah and Micah prophesy more fully. Or, on the high mountains of Israel, they will rest in green grass and say: “The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing; he has placed me in a place of pasture; he has led me beside waters of refreshment” (Ps. XXII). They will feed in the richest pastures upon the mountains of Israel.

This is an infinite promise and hope of blessedness, when the Lord himself promises, saying: “I will feed my sheep,” and will by no means entrust them to evil shepherds. “And I will make them lie down, says the Lord God,” so that they may rest in the bosom of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Then what had perished among the nations will be sought, what had gone astray through the persuasion of heretics will be brought back, what had been broken will be bound up, and what had been crushed and weakened will be strengthened, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “He heals their infirmities and binds up their bruises” (Ps. CXLVI).

“What is fat,” he says, “and strong I will guard,” so that it will not be devoured by beasts; “and I will feed my sheep with judgment,” knowing which pasture is due to each sheep. For there are different dwelling places with the Father. “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V).

He has spoken these things against the shepherds. Now he speaks to the sheep—that is, to the people—and to the flock of both kinds of animals, namely, sheep and goats. And not only to sheep and goats but to rams and he-goats, who are rulers among the flocks. To them he says: Was it not enough for you to feed on the good pastures of the Scriptures? Yet you also trampled the remnants of your pastures with your feet.

When you drank the purest water of the utterances of God, you muddied the remaining waters with your feet, so that my people might eat the pastures trampled by you and drink the muddied waters, and through your fault receive as corrupted and violated what was good in itself.

All heretics do this: they attack the utterances of the Scriptures and, as far as they can, defile them. But ecclesiastical men also who do not preserve the truth of doctrines, instead fabricating things from their own hearts and making their own presumption their teacher, are held by a similar error.

When they have persuaded the people that the things they invent are true, and have aroused applause and shouting in theatrical fashion, they forget their own ignorance. With raised brows and carefully weighed and measured words, they assume for themselves the authority of teachers.

*(Gregory.)* Shepherds drink the clearest water when, rightly understanding, they draw up the streams of truth. But to disturb that same water with their feet is to corrupt the pursuits of holy meditation by evil living.

Their sheep drink the water muddied by their feet when their subjects do not follow the words they hear, but imitate only the evil examples they see. When they thirst for teachings that are overturned by deeds, they take mud into their cups as though from corrupted springs.

*(Jerome.)* Let us therefore see what the judgment is between sheep and sheep, and by what judgment the good and true shepherd judges them, he who received all judgment from the Father.

“Behold,” he says, “I myself judge between the fat sheep and the lean,” or between the strong and the weak. The strong push and collide with the weak animals with their flanks and shoulders, and toss them about with their horns, not knowing that in the Law a goring bull is to be punished.

They pushed with their flanks and gored with their horns until they scattered and drove the sheep outside. Through the pride of the great and the injustice of rulers, people are often expelled from the Church, so that those whom the Lord himself saved may be scattered.

But the Lord will no longer abandon them as plunder. He will judge between sheep and sheep—not between the names of dignities with which rulers swell, but between one human being and another, according to the fact that each is a servant of the Lord.

Then he will raise up one shepherd who says in the Gospel, “I am the good shepherd” (John X): his servant David, according to the fact that he deigned to assume the form of a servant. David is interpreted as “strong of hand.” He himself will feed them, and the Lord will be their God—whether Son and Father, or certainly shepherd according to the flesh he assumed; but Lord and God according to the Word who was in the beginning with God.

As the sheep advance toward rational life, this David will no longer be called shepherd but prince in their midst. Of him it is written: “There stands among you one whom you do not know” (John I).

Then he will establish with them a covenant of peace, not of wars and discord, because “his place has been made in peace” (Ps. LXXV), but the peace of Christ, which surpasses all understanding, and of which he says: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John XIV).

“And he will make the evil beasts cease from the land,” whether vices and disturbances by which human souls are harassed, or hostile powers by which they are attacked.

“Those who dwell in the wilderness will sleep securely in the forests.” For the Lord will reveal the dense places of the forests, and in his temple all will say glory. Once the beasts have been expelled and the land reduced to solitude by creatures of this kind, they will sleep securely and say: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” (Ps. XXVI).

He will place those who sleep securely around his mountain or hill, and they will be a blessing. Then he will give rain in its season, and the rains will be rains of blessing, which he promises in the blessings of Deuteronomy.

“And he will give,” he says, “the tree of life,” of which it is written in Genesis (Gen. III), and the tree of wisdom, of which it is said: “She is a tree of life to all who take hold of her” (Prov. III). He will give its fruit, when the earth also gives its fruit—or the trees of the regions, meaning the great multitude of the saints.

“And the land will yield its shoot,” for “truth has sprung up from the earth.” “And they will be in their land without fear,” or in the hope of peace, in the land of the living, the land of the meek. Of it it is written: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. V).

Thus, in the happiness of all things, they will know that he is the Lord, when he has broken the chains—or iron band—of their yoke, by which they were oppressed as by an exceedingly heavy rule. When he rescues them from the hand of those who rule over them, or from the slavery of those who afflict them—for everyone is the servant of the one by whom he is conquered—

“they will no longer be plunder for demonic nations, nor will the beasts of the earth devour them,” concerning whom we have spoken. “They will dwell securely, without any terror,” according to the earlier interpretation.

“And I will raise up for them,” he says, “a renowned shoot,” or a planting of peace, which says in the Gospel: “I am the true vine” (John XV). “And they will no longer be diminished by hunger in the land.” Hunger therefore exists in earthly things; but the hunger to hear the word of God will no longer exist in the land under the good shepherd, the renowned shoot, celebrated in everyone’s speech, and the planting of peace.

Nor will they any longer be subject to the reproaches of the nations, so that they may say: “Where is their Lord God?” [Col. 0846D] After all these things they will know that he is not only the Lord, as he had also said above, but—by the addition—that the Lord of all is especially their God, who says in the Gospel to the apostles: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII).

When the Lord himself is their God, then they too will be his people—not just any people, but those who have deserved to be called the house of Israel.

And lest we think that all these things refer only to shepherds, sheep, goats, and rams, he solves the riddle—or rather the metaphor (*metaphora*)—and states it more plainly: “You, my sheep, the sheep of my pasture, are human beings.” Therefore the whole divine discourse concerns human beings. To them he says: “I am the Lord your God, says the Lord God.”

*(Gregory.)* Sometimes, then, he calls human beings those whom he distinguishes from beasts by reason—that is, those whom he shows not to be worn down by the bestial movement of the passions. Through the prophet the Lord says to them: “You are human beings, the flocks of my pasture” (Ezek. XXXIV). The Lord feeds those whom the pleasure of the flesh does not affect in the manner of beasts.

On the other hand, those who succumb to carnal affection are no longer called human beings but animals. Thus, concerning certain people who die in their sin, the prophet says: “The animals have rotted in their dung” (Joel I). For animals to rot in their dung is for carnal people to end their lives in the stench of lust.

They are shown not to be human beings but animals. Of them the prophet says: “Each man neighed after his neighbor’s wife” (Jer. V); and another prophet said: “Their flesh is the flesh of asses, and their discharge is the discharge of horses” (Ezek. XIII).

## BOOK THIRTEEN

[Col. 0847]

At the end of the preceding book, the Lord, through the Prophet, rebuked the shepherds of the Israelites because they were insufficiently diligent in guarding God’s flock. Through the same admonition he censures the shepherds and rulers of the Church because, devoted to the pleasures of the world and the concerns of this life, they are insufficiently attentive to the care of Christ’s sheep and to the governance of the faithful souls entrusted to them.

Now, at the beginning of the present book, he commands the prophet to deliver a speech of rebuke against Mount Seir—that is, Idumea—because, thinking arrogantly, it despised the Israelite people. He threatens it with future destruction because of the evil it had committed against its neighbors; and afterward the Lord promises his people restoration and liberation from all their enemies.

All these matters can be transferred not only, according to the historical sense, to the former people and the times of the Law, but much more, according to allegory, to the time of the New Testament and to the Christian people, where God’s manifest power shines forth in the liberation of the elect and his just judgment (the text reads *juste*, “justly,” [for *justum*, “just”]) is revealed in the confusion of his enemies.

## CHAPTER THIRTY-FIVE

Discourse concerning Mount Seir and its condition, because it afflicted the people of the Lord.

«And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set your face against Mount Seir, and you shall prophesy against it, and say to it: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, Mount Seir, and I shall stretch out my hand against you, and I shall make you desolate and deserted. I shall demolish your cities, and you shall be desolate, and you shall know that I am the Lord, because you have been an everlasting enemy and have delivered the children of Israel into the hands of the sword in the time of their affliction, in the time of their final iniquity. Therefore, as I live, says the Lord God, I shall hand you over to blood, and blood shall pursue you. And since you hated blood, blood shall pursue you. And I shall make Mount Seir desolate and deserted, and I shall remove from it the one who goes and the one who returns, and I shall fill its mountains with its slain. On your hills and in your valleys and in your torrents, those slain by the sword shall fall. I shall hand you over to everlasting desolations, and your cities shall not be inhabited. And you shall know that I am the Lord God, because you have said, “The two nations and the two lands shall be mine, and I shall possess them as an inheritance,” although the Lord was there. Therefore, as I live, says the Lord God, I shall act according to your anger and according to your jealousy, which you showed while hating them, and I shall make myself known to you when I judge you, and you shall know that I am the Lord. I have heard all your insults, which you uttered against the mountains of Israel, saying, “They have been given to us as desolate places, for us to devour.” And you rose up against me with your mouth and reviled me; I heard your words. Thus says the Lord God: While the whole earth rejoices, I shall reduce you to desolation, just as you rejoiced over the inheritance of the house of Israel because it had been laid waste; so shall I do to you. You shall be laid waste, Mount Seir, and all Idumea. And they shall know that I am the Lord.» (Jerome.)

But the words added in the Septuagint, «And they shall be consumed,» are not found in the Hebrew. If the word of God were always in the prophets, and if it continually had a dwelling-place in their hearts, Ezekiel would never so frequently write, «And the word of the Lord came to me, saying.» But because, on account of human frailty and the necessities of this life, it sometimes withdrew from them, John the Baptist therefore says: «The one who sent me to baptize, he said to me, “Upon whomever you see the Holy Spirit descending in the form of a dove and remaining upon him, he is the one”» (John 1). For «and remaining upon him» would never properly be said of Christ unless it sometimes withdrew from others; otherwise God also says to Moses: «I shall take away from the spirit that is in you» (Numbers 11). He would certainly not have it unless it had descended upon him from the Lord.

The whole prophecy of this chapter is against Mount Seir, that is, against the descendants of Esau and Edom, who in Greek and in our language are called Idumaeans. For, at the time of necessity and distress, when Judah was being captured by the Babylonians, they insulted them and, after the Jewish people had been expelled, thought that the land had been handed over to them for possession. They not only did not receive their brothers, namely, the children of Jacob their brother, but also persecuted them and delivered them into the hands of the sword. Hence Symmachus translated more explicitly: «You hated your blood, and blood shall pursue you.»

It is prophesied that he too shall be captured and reduced to everlasting desolations, and that, at the end of things, he shall recognize God as judge, because he said, «The two nations and the two regions are mine»: either the Idumaeans and the Jews, or certainly Judah and Israel, namely, the two and the ten tribes. And you spoke of the mountains of Israel, saying: «They have been given to us as desolate places, for us to devour,» without considering that this blasphemy would rebound against God. Hence what follows: «While the whole earth rejoices, I shall reduce you to desolation.» The meaning is: when the whole land of Judea has recovered its former condition, you shall remain in everlasting desolation.

As for what follows, «Just as you rejoiced over the inheritance of the house of Israel because it had been laid waste, so shall I do to you,» it is not found in the Septuagint, but was added under asterisks from Theodotion’s version. All the anger of God against Mount Seir advances toward this end: when he and all Idumea have been laid waste, they shall know that he is the Lord.

I have said these things rapidly according to the history and the sense rather than the words. I shall pass on to the *anagogy*—the spiritual or higher interpretation—and, for the sake of brevity, touch on a few points. «Set,» he says, or «turn,» «your face against Mount Seir.» Significantly, he says «turn» from one prophecy to another prophecy. But the face is not that of the body, but of the mind, of which the Apostle also says: «But we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord.»

Mount Seir, which is interpreted as «rough» and «hairy,» is to be understood as the contrary power that presided over the nation of the children of Esau and raised itself against the people of Judah, that is, against confession and true faith. If a prudent reader objects how Seir, that is, «rough» and «hairy,» is understood here in a negative sense, since Elijah too is called a hairy man, I shall answer briefly: It is written of Esau (Genesis 25) that he was red and like a hairy skin; but of Elijah, that he was merely a hairy man. In Esau, who was bloodthirsty and murderous and is compared to a hairy skin, this is an indication of mortal deeds and of death itself; in Elijah, it signifies an increase of manliness (2 Kings 1). Therefore his dwelling in the wilderness and the austerity of his way of life demonstrated not merely a man but a very strong man.

Jacob, moreover, who had supplanted Esau and received his birthright, because he lived simply at home and was not a hunter like the giant Nimrod, is for that reason called light and bright. Let us therefore see what God commands to be said to or against Mount Seir: «Behold, I am against you, Mount Seir.» I shall not send angels, nor shall I employ other ministers, but I myself shall come against you: «And I shall stretch out my hand against you,» so that I may assume the posture of one striking.

«And I shall make you desolate and deserted»: you who were badly inhabited and had very many partners in your impiety, so many that you even built cities and claimed a kingdom of your own, shall now be desolate together with your cities, which Jeremiah too is commanded to destroy and dig up, so that he may build good cities in their place. You shall advance to the point of knowing that I am the Lord, whom, before your desolation, you could not know.

The whole cause of the sin is that you have been an everlasting enemy. Hence the Psalm also says: «Be angry and do not sin» (Psalm 4), so that we may quickly be reconciled with our enemies and change hatred into love. But such was not Mount Seir, which, because of everlasting enmity, shut up or besieged the children of Israel through treachery in the hands of the sword.

From this we understand that whoever takes up the sword against the children of God, acts deceitfully in any matter, and besieges them, shall be delivered into the hands of the sword like Mount Seir, in the time of final iniquity, when the days are evil, the world lies in the power of wickedness, and, because iniquity has multiplied, the love of many grows cold (1 John 5).

There is also another sin of Mount Seir: because he hated the blood of the righteous, which he desired to have poured out in each persecution, he shall suffer persecution from that very blood. Hence beneath the altar the souls of the saints cry out and implore the Lord for vengeance for their blood (Revelation 6).

Those who go and return are removed from Mount Seir—that is, every inhabitant, whether human beings or animals, who are saved in the Church. Of them it is written: «You will save humans and animals, Lord» (Psalm 35). In Mount Seir both are destroyed, so that those who seem to possess some rational understanding and those who are content with simple faith alike perish at God’s command.

«And its mountains shall be filled with the wounded and the slain.» Not only the mountains that have reached the summit of impiety, but also the hills—that is, the lesser disciples of Mount Seir—and the valleys, which are sunk in the lowest places, or the torrents, which have turbid waters gathered from here and there and flowing down from pride; or, according to the Septuagint, the plains, which lie between the hills and the valleys. All these shall fall slain by the sword of the Lord and by the outstretched hand of the one who strikes, so that they may be reduced to everlasting desolations.

And if there were any cities—that is, assemblies of evil habitation—they too shall perish, and shall cease to maintain an evil agreement. Their tongues shall be divided, so that they cannot build a tower of blasphemy against God; and, reduced to desolation and desert, they shall know that he is the Lord.

Nor is it enough for Mount Seir to have said all that the preceding discourse related. In his pride he also said: «The two nations and the two lands or regions are mine.» Namely, Idumea and Judea: «I shall possess heretics and members of the Church alike.» And this, he says, you said «when the Lord was there,» presiding over his own people.

Therefore the Lord swears and says: «As I live, says the Lord God,» that, according to your anger with which you raged against the people of God, and your jealousy with which you persecuted the household of Christ, hating those whom you desired to possess, when I strike and judge you, then I shall become known to you. And you shall know that I learned your insults and blasphemies not from another reporter, but that I myself heard what you spoke against the mountains of Israel, saying: «They have been given to us as desolate places, for us to devour.»

We ought to understand the mountains of Israel as Moses, the prophets, and the apostles, whom heretics and the devil, the prince of heretics, think have been delivered to them for devouring, whenever no one is found in the Church who can fight for the mountains of the Lord and defend their dismemberment with his voice.

«And you rose up,» he says, «against me with your mouth»: either you spoke grandly, not, as you suppose, against the mountains, but through them against me; «and you reviled—or cried out—against me.» For all your prayers, O Mount Seir and companions of Mount Seir, of whom it was said above, «I shall fill its mountains and hills, valleys and plains,» or torrents, were against me—not prayers and supplications, as you suppose, addressed to God, but cries, outcries, and blasphemies.

Hence the Lord also threatens and says: «Just as you rejoiced over the inheritance of the house of Israel,» when through your persecutions it was scattered, torn apart, and dispersed throughout the whole world, «so shall I do to you.» For while the whole earth rejoices—the land of the living and the land of the saints—and all have been converted to the service of God, you «shall be laid waste, rough mountain, hairy mountain. And all Idumea,» that is, works devoted to earthly things, gore, and blood. Then you shall know that I am the Lord, who elsewhere have spoken: «I am the Lord your God.»

## CHAPTER XXXVI

That the Lord will avenge Israel against its enemies, restore it, and multiply it in its land; and that he afflicted Israel because of the sin of idolatry. On the grace and power of baptism: the people are called to repentance, and complete restoration and multiplication are promised.

«But you, son of man, prophesy concerning the mountains of Israel and say: Mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God: Because the enemy has said concerning you, “Hurrah! The everlasting heights have been given to us as an inheritance,” therefore prophesy and say: Thus says the Lord God: Because you have been desolate and trampled on every side and have become an inheritance for the remaining nations, and you have ascended upon the lips of the tongue and become the reproach of the people, therefore, mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord.

Thus says the Lord God to the mountains and hills, to the torrents, valleys, and deserted ruins, and to the abandoned cities that have been depopulated and mocked by the remaining nations all around. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because I have spoken in the fire of my jealousy against the remaining nations and against all Idumea, who gave my land to themselves as an inheritance with the sword, with all their heart and from their whole soul, and expelled its inhabitants in order to lay it waste, therefore prophesy concerning the soil of Israel and say to the mountains and hills, ridges and valleys: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I have spoken in my jealousy and in my fury because you have borne the disgrace of the nations.

Therefore thus says the Lord God: I have raised my hand that the nations around you themselves may bear their own disgrace. But you, mountains of Israel, shall put forth your branches and yield your fruit for my people Israel, for it is near: it is about to come. For behold, I am coming to you, and I shall turn toward you, and you shall be plowed and receive seed, and I shall multiply human beings upon you, the whole house of Israel. The cities shall be inhabited, and the ruins shall be restored, and I shall fill you with human beings and animals, and they shall multiply and increase.

And I shall make you inhabited as at the beginning, and I shall bestow greater blessings upon you than you had at the outset, and you shall know that I am the Lord. And I shall bring human beings upon you, my people Israel, and they shall possess you as an inheritance. You shall be their possession, and you shall no longer continue to be without them.

Thus says the Lord God: Because they have said concerning you, “You devour human beings and choke your people,” therefore you shall no longer devour human beings, and you shall no longer slay your people, says the Lord God. Nor shall I make you hear the disgrace of the nations any longer, and you shall no longer bear the reproaches of the peoples. And you shall no longer lose your people, says the Lord God.»

(Jerome.) Above, the prophet’s face is set, or turned, against Mount Seir; here the son of man speaks to or concerning the mountains of Israel, which are commanded to hear the word of God. To set aside for a little while the tropological interpretation of the whole prophecy concerning the mountains of Israel, its brief sense here is this:

Because the enemy, that is, Mount Seir, insulted you and thought that he himself would possess you forever, and that the once lofty places of the Lord, now desolate, had passed to him as an inheritance—and because he not only said this but also possessed you for some time, to such an extent that he spoke arrogantly against you, saying that you were a reproach to all the nations—therefore thus says the Lord God, not only to Mount Seir but also to its mountains, hills, torrents, valleys, deserts, devastated places, and abandoned cities, because he spoke in the fire of his jealousy against all the nations, but especially against Idumea.

When, he says, Idumea held my land as a possession together with the other nations, it possessed it by the sword and with all its heart, in order to expel its inhabitants and lay the land waste. Therefore speak, he says, prophet, concerning the land of Israel, and say to the mountains, hills, and ridges, for which the Septuagint translated «the wooded places» (*tais napais*), which we understand as forested regions. And to the valleys, he says, the Lord God speaks: in my jealousy and fury I shall become the avenger of your reproach, and I shall raise my hand so that the nations around you may bear their disgrace and shame.

But you, O mountains of Israel, according to your former condition, shall put forth shoots and send out branches, or, according to the Septuagint, produce grapes with which my people Israel may be satisfied. Do not think that this will happen after a long time: it is near, it is imminent, and the time will come. And lest this be difficult for you, I myself shall come to you; and I, who had withdrawn from you, shall turn toward you, so that you may recover your former cultivation and everything may be filled with seed.

Thus there shall be many human beings among you, and the cities that had previously been destroyed shall be inhabited. And I shall multiply not only human beings, but animals also shall likewise multiply and increase. And I shall make you inhabited as at the beginning, when, under Moses as leader, the two and a half tribes received their possession beyond the Jordan, and under Joshua son of Nun the other nine and a half tribes possessed the land of Judea.

I shall bestow upon you blessings much greater than those you had at the beginning, before you experienced various captivities. And when I have done this for you, then you shall know that I am the Lord. And you shall be filled, he says, O land of Israel, with my people, who shall hold you as an inheritance. You shall be their possession, and you shall no longer remain without children.

When your inhabitants have multiplied, O mountains of Israel, your enemies shall certainly no longer say against you that you devour human beings and that your possession is without children. On the contrary, you shall multiply human beings, and your posterity shall put forth a very abundant offspring. Nor shall you hear or bear the disgrace of the nations any longer, and you shall not lose your people, so that you might ever again suffer captivity, because the Lord has spoken these things.

In a paraphrase, according to Jewish usage, we might say that these are the things they expect in the thousand-year kingdom, when they claim that the city of Jerusalem will be built, together with the temple described at the end of this volume, and that all things will enjoy prosperity. Some of them think that these things were fulfilled under Zerubbabel. But how could the statement stand: «I shall make you inhabited as at the beginning, and I shall bestow greater blessings upon you than you had at the outset»?

Under Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Nehemiah, only a few of the people were brought back, and they were subject first to the Medes and Persians, and afterward served Macedonian, Egyptian, and Roman kings of various nations, down to Titus and Vespasian. They continue to serve them even to this day, so that what is said in the final part of the prophecy cannot stand at all: «You shall no longer bear the reproach of the peoples, and you shall no longer lose your people.»

And because it would take too long now to speak against the Jewish doctrine and the blessedness that serves the Jewish belly and throat—for they desire everything earthly and say, «Let us eat and drink»—and because the Apostle also speaks of them: «Food is for the belly, and the belly for food; but God will destroy both it and them» (1 Corinthians 5), let us pass in brief explanation now to the spiritual understanding, according to which we have also interpreted the final portions.

For we do not expect, according to the Jewish fables that they call *deuterōseis*—«secondary interpretations»—a jeweled and golden Jerusalem from heaven. Nor do we expect again to suffer the injury of circumcision, nor to offer sacrifices of bulls and rams, nor shall we sleep in the leisure of the Sabbath. This is promised by many of our own writers, especially Tertullian’s book entitled *On the Hope of the Faithful*, the seventh book of Lactantius’s *Institutes*, the frequent interpretations of Victorinus, Bishop of Petau, and recently our Severus in the dialogue he entitled *Gallus*. And, to name Greeks and join the first with the last, Irenaeus and Apollinaris.

We therefore shall say that the mountains of Israel are the prophets and apostles, who hear the word of God and whom the enemy, the devil, insulted, saying: «Hurrah! The once lofty mountains, of which it is written, “Mountains surround him, and the Lord surrounds his people” (Psalm 124), have been given to me as a possession when they were desolated by the constraints of persecution, trampled on every side, made an inheritance for the remaining nations, and blasphemed by all.»

Therefore the Lord speaks to the trampled and desolated mountains—not only to the mountains but also to those lower down, established at each level in the land of Judea, that is, on the mountain of the Church, of which it is written: «A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden» (Matthew 5). He speaks also to the hills and torrents, whose faith is increased by the winter of persecutions and the storm of affliction; and to the valleys, which are pressed down by humility; and to the deserted churches, ruins, and abandoned assemblies of churches throughout the world, such as the persecution was under Diocletian and Maximian throughout the whole world, when the churches were proscribed and devastated, and when the nations of the Gentiles and of the heretics all around mocked the Church.

He says that he spoke in the fire of his jealousy and fury, specifically against Idumea, which, devoted to earthly works, wanted everyone to bear the image of the earthly after laying aside the image of the heavenly. For they gave God’s land to themselves as an inheritance, persecuted the Church of the Lord with all their heart and soul, expelled it from its dwelling-places, and devastated it.

But what did it profit the nations, what did it help the heretical peoples to insult the land of the Lord, when he speaks to it and to its mountains, hills, and ridges—or wooded places, which flourished with the beauty of paradise—and when, as we said above, he speaks to the hills in his jealousy and fury and raises his hand in reproach against the adversaries who persecuted the Church, so that they may bear their own disgrace and shame?

Then, after the persecutors have been killed and peace has been restored to the Church, the mountains of Israel—namely, the apostles and apostolic men—shall make their trees sprout, extend their branches, and produce grapes to be pressed in the Lord’s winepress. From them must is poured out to intoxicate the peoples of believers, and wine is pressed that gladdens the human heart, so that all the fruit of the mountains, from which the bread descending from heaven is prepared, may be eaten by God’s people Israel.

And lest we perhaps despair in persecutions, it is added: «The time is near when it shall come. It shall surely come and shall not delay» (Habakkuk 2). Hence he promises his coming to the mountains and to those who have endured through tribulations, and declares that the land, first broken up by Christ’s plowshare and receiving every seed of the virtues, shall be cultivated by the heat of persecution, from which human beings and the whole house of Israel shall be born and multiplied.

And when the cities—that is, the churches of believers—have been inhabited by the returning crowds, then not only human beings, who shall abound in knowledge of the Scriptures, but also the animals, namely, the simple believers, shall multiply and grow. And the churches shall be inhabited as at the beginning, that is, before persecution existed. They shall flourish with greater blessings than they possessed at the outset, crowned with the victories of the martyrs.

Then they shall know that he is the Lord, who restored his people to its former condition, so that it may possess the churches and itself be the inheritance of the churches. And it shall no longer be without children whom it had lost in persecution.

Therefore the prophet is commanded to speak to the land of the meek and the land of the living, or to the mountains of Israel, and to say: «You shall no longer suffer the reproach of persecutors, nor shall they insult your slaughtered people like sheep destined for slaughter.» For when peace has been restored, all reproaches shall cease.

Nor shall you bear disgrace and shame among the various nations around you any longer; rather, you shall have your own nation and people, because the truth of the promise has been confirmed by the Lord’s word.

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:

“Son of man, the house of Israel dwelt in its own land and polluted it by their ways and by their practices. Their way before me became like the uncleanness of a menstruating woman, and I poured out my indignation upon them because of the blood which they had shed upon the land. They polluted it with their idols, and I scattered them among the nations; they were dispersed throughout the lands. According to their ways and their inventions I judged them. And when they entered among the nations to which they went, they profaned my holy name, when it was said of them, ‘This is the people of the Lord, yet they have gone out from his land.’ And I spared my holy name, which the house of Israel had profaned among the nations to which they went.

“Therefore say to the house of Israel: Thus says the Lord God: It is not for your sake that I shall act, O house of Israel, but for the sake of my holy name, which you profaned among the nations to which you entered. And I shall sanctify my great name, which has been profaned among the nations, which you profaned in their midst, so that the nations may know that I am the Lord, says the Lord of hosts, when I have been sanctified in you before their eyes.

“For I shall take you from among the nations, gather you from all the lands, and bring you into your own land. I shall pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your impurities; from all your idols I shall cleanse you. And I shall give you a new heart, and I shall place a new spirit within you. I shall remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh, and I shall place my spirit within you. I shall make you walk in my commandments, observe my judgments, and carry them out. And you shall dwell in the land which I gave to your fathers, and you shall be my people, and I shall be your God. And I shall save you from all your impurities. I shall summon the grain and multiply it, and I shall not bring famine upon you. I shall multiply the fruit of the tree and the produce of the field, and you shall no longer bear among the nations the reproach of famine. You shall remember your evil ways and your practices that were not good, and your iniquities and crimes shall become displeasing to you.

“Not for your sake shall I act, says the Lord God; let this be known to you. Be ashamed and confounded because of your ways, O house of Israel. Thus says the Lord God: On the day when I cleanse you from all your iniquities, make the cities inhabited, and restore the ruins, and when the deserted land has been cultivated—what was formerly desolate—then, in the sight of every passer-by, they shall say: ‘That land, which was barren, has become like a garden of delight, and the deserted, abandoned, and ruined cities have been fortified and inhabited.’ And the nations that have been left all around you shall know that I am the Lord: I have built up the ruined places and planted the uncultivated land; I, the Lord, have spoken and acted. Thus says the Lord God:

“‘Moreover, the house of Israel shall seek me, so that I may do this for them. I shall multiply them like a human flock, like a holy flock, like the flock of Jerusalem during its festivals. Thus the deserted cities shall be filled with human flocks, and they shall know that I am the Lord.’”

(Hieronymus.) What is said is clear, and the whole meaning concerning the mountains of Israel, which had first been deserted and afterward restored, is now set forth more plainly. God gives the reasons why he handed the people of Israel over to captivity, and, because of his own clemency, promises that he will bring them back into the land of Judea and grant them much greater things than he had taken away.

Some Jews refer this to the time of Zerubbabel, when, after the Persian king released them from captivity, many from the tribes of Judah and Benjamin were brought back to Judea. Others refer it to the thousand-year reign, when, under Christ—whom they think is still to come—a city of Jerusalem will be built and a temple constructed, concerning which we shall speak in the final part of this prophecy.

Meanwhile, to leave aside Jewish fables and interminable genealogies, let us briefly run through the *pericope*—περικοπή—of this chapter according to our customary practice and explain what seems to us appropriate according to ecclesiastical understanding.

The house of Israel—that is, the Jewish people—once dwelt in its own land, that is, in the land of Judea, when it had been brought out of Egypt. But they polluted it by their ways, their practices, or their idols. They became so polluted that they were compared with the uncleanness of a menstruating woman. Therefore God poured out his indignation upon them because of the blood of the prophets and righteous men which they had shed upon the land, as the Savior says in the Gospel (Matthew 23): “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you.”

And again: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the blood shed from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, son of Barachiah, whom they killed between the altar and the temple, shall be required of this generation.”

They not only shed blood, but also polluted the land with their crimes. Therefore he scattered them, either in the Babylonian captivity or under the Romans, when they truly shed the blood of Christ and were dispersed throughout the lands, as chaff is scattered, and judged according to their ways and their most wicked inventions. Thus, even among the nations to which they had been led as captives, they polluted the holy name of God, since all the nations mockingly said of them: “This is the people of God, who boasted that they alone knew the worship of God.”

“When I saw this,” he says, “I spared them, not for their sake but for the sake of my holy name—for I am the Creator of all—and I sanctified them and restored them to their former glory.” Thus he poured clean water, the water of saving baptism, upon believers and those converted from error; he cleansed them from their abominations and from all the errors with which they had been occupied; and he gave them a new heart, so that they might believe in the Son of God, and a new spirit, concerning which David says: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me” (Psalm 50).

It should be observed that the new heart and the new spirit are given through the pouring and sprinkling of water. When the new heart and the new spirit have been given, all hardness—which is compared to stone—will be removed from the Jewish heart. In place of the heart of stone there will be a heart of flesh, soft and tender, able to receive the Spirit of God within itself and to have the saving letters inscribed upon it.

(Gregory.) He removes the heart of stone when he takes away from us the hardness of pride; and he gives a heart of flesh when he immediately turns that same hardness of ours into feeling.

(Hieronymus.) Then they shall walk in the commandments of the Lord and observe his judgments. They shall dwell in the land of confession which he gave to their fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and to all the saints and prophets; they shall become God’s people, and the Lord shall be their God. This is proved in the present time.

And when they have been saved, the Lord will summon the grain and multiply it: “Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone” (John 12). They will no longer suffer hunger—not hunger for bread or thirst for water, but hunger for hearing the words of God (Amos 8). This hunger was suffered by the one who departed from his father and squandered all the substance he had received, and who, compelled by the necessity of famine, fed upon the pods of pigs (Luke 15).

Then the fruit of the tree will be multiplied—that is, of wisdom, concerning which it is written: “She is a tree of life to all who lay hold of her”—and the produce of the field will be multiplied, in the likeness of Jacob, whose fragrance was like the fragrance of a full field which the Lord had blessed (Genesis 27).

They will no longer bear among the nations the reproach of famine, which the unbelief of the Jews suffers even today. But after they have attained blessedness, they will imitate the Apostle, who says: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God” (1 Corinthians 15).

They will remember their most wicked ways and their practices that were not good, by which they had offended God. Their iniquities and crimes, in which they had previously gone astray, will become displeasing to them.

The Lord will grant all these things, not for the sake of those who perished through their own error, but for the sake of his holy name. Therefore he urges the house of Israel to be confounded and ashamed because of its former vices and to recognize its Creator.

After he has cleansed the people of Jewish believers from their iniquities, caused the cities of the Church to be inhabited, restored the ruins that had fallen in the synagogues, and cultivated the land of confession with the rites of God—land that once seemed desolate to all the saints who pass beyond the works of earthly conduct—then all will say:

“How has the land of Judea, which was once uncultivated, now become like God’s paradise? And how have the cities of Judah, which were once deserted and abandoned and had been undermined by their unbelief, now been raised up and fortified in the confession and name of the Lord Savior?”

Thus every creature, and the multitudes of angels that surround the land of Israel, will know that the Lord has rebuilt the scattered cities, planted the uncultivated regions, and fulfilled in deed what he had promised through the prophets.

Nor will he be content to show his generosity toward the people he has saved by this gift alone; he will grant much greater things. He will be found by the house of Israel, though he had long been sought and not found. And after it has found him, he will multiply them like sheep—not irrational animals, but human sheep, filled with reason and confession, like the sheep of the saints and the flocks of Jerusalem, in which the worship of God and the vision of peace are found in a particular way during its festivals.

At those festivals we eat the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth and feed upon the flesh of the Lamb and drink his blood; and during the seven weeks and in the tabernacles of this age we celebrate the Lord’s feasts (1 Corinthians 5). Thus the cities that were once deserted will become full of human flocks, and by this they will know that he is the Lord who has provided all things.

With respect to the historical truth—or rather, the faithfulness of the prophecy—how the people of Israel will be restored to their complete condition, and how the remnant of the Jewish people, according to the teaching of the Apostle Paul, is saved in the apostles and in all those who believed from among the Jews at the beginning and who continue to return to the Church even to this day, it is enough to have said this briefly. Now the meaning must be disclosed with equal brevity according to the allegorical interpretation.

Whoever belongs to the house of Israel and perceives the peace of Christ, which surpasses all understanding, dwells in his own land—that is, the Church—or in the lodging of the flesh which has been given to him by the Lord.

But if he pollutes either land by his most wicked ways and is compared with the uncleanness of a menstruating woman, God pours out his indignation upon him because of the blood—whether his own blood or that of those whom he has caused to stumble—which he has shed upon the earth, and because of the perverse thoughts by which he pollutes it.

Then he will be scattered among the nations, made like unbelievers, and dispersed throughout the earth like chaff, so that he may be separated from the grain of the Church and judged according to his ways.

But if even then he does not recognize his sin and instead pollutes his holy name, all among whom he dwells will say: “Behold the people of God; behold the one who has gone out from his land”—or rather, who has been cast out.

But if they repent, and I am sanctified in their midst, then every multitude of the nations will know that I shall take them from the lands into which they had been scattered and bring them back into the land of the Church.

I shall pour upon them not the waters of saving baptism, but the waters of teaching and of the word of God. I shall cleanse them from all their impurities and from all the idols and errors which they had fashioned in their hearts.

“And I shall give them,” he says, “the new heart which they had lost through sin, and I shall renew a right spirit within their hearts” (Psalm 50). I shall remove the heart of stone, that is, the unbelieving heart, and give them a heart of flesh, soft and tender, which receives the commandments of God, so that they may walk in my commandments and carry out the judgments which they had previously neglected.

They shall dwell in the land which I had given to their fathers—that is, to their teachers and instructors. And they shall again be God’s people, and the Lord shall become their God, whom they had previously offended.

Then they shall be saved from all their impurities, and the grain by which heavenly bread is made shall be multiplied for them, and they shall no longer suffer hunger for the word of God. The tree of wisdom shall be multiplied among them, and its shoots shall fill their hearts.

They shall no longer be a reproach among the nations. After God has had mercy on them, they shall remember their most wicked ways and know where they had been. Their iniquities will become displeasing to them; and, as the Lord says, he will do this not for their sake but because of his own clemency.

Therefore he exhorts those who have gone astray to be confounded and ashamed because of their ways, to be restored to the cities of the Church and to inhabit them again, and to rebuild everything that had collapsed in them and return to their former rites.

The land that was once deserted, which had seemed desolate to inhabitants, strangers, and those passing beyond the conduct of this world, will return to its former condition. Everyone will marvel and say:

“That uncultivated land, that deserted land in which all virtues once perished, has now become like a garden of delight and the paradise of God.”

And the cities that were once deserted, which did not have God as their guest, were abandoned by the Holy Spirit, and had been undermined by unbelief, have been united by the faith of Christ, so that all around may know that the Lord has rebuilt scattered souls, planted and sown in them the trees of every virtue, and himself brought about in reality what he had promised in words.

Again the prophetic word exhorts the repentant that, even after they have returned to the churches, they should continually seek the Lord and find him. Thus the Lord’s flocks will be multiplied by the crowds of those who return—not flocks of beasts and irrational animals, but flocks of human beings filled with faith and reason; holy flocks, the flocks of the city of Jerusalem, in all the festivals which God’s mercy has restored to them.

After the cities of the Lord have been filled with a multitude of such flocks, then all will know that he is the Lord.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

### On the General Resurrection; on Christ; and on the fact that in the last days Judah and Jerusalem will receive him and there will be one people

[Col. 0859C] “The hand of the Lord came upon me, and he brought me out in the spirit of the Lord and set me down in the midst of a plain that was full of bones, and he led me around among them in a circle. There were very many upon the face of the plain, and they were exceedingly dry.

“And he said to me: ‘Son of man, do you think that these bones will live?’ And I said: ‘Lord God, you know.’ And he said to me: ‘Prophesy concerning these bones, and say to them: Dry bones, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God to these bones: Behold, I shall send spirit into you, and you shall live. I shall place sinews upon you, cause flesh to grow over you, stretch skin over you, and give you spirit, and you shall live; and you shall know that I am the Lord.’

“And I prophesied as he had commanded me. And as I prophesied, there was a sound, and behold, a commotion; and the bones came together, each bone to its joint. And I saw, and behold, sinews and flesh rose upon them, and skin was stretched over them from above; but they had no spirit.

“And he said to me: ‘Prophesy to the spirit; prophesy, son of man, and say to the spirit: Thus says the Lord God: Come from the four winds, O spirit, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live.’

“And I prophesied as he had commanded me, and the spirit entered them, and they lived and stood upon their feet, an exceedingly great army. And he said to me: ‘Son of man, all these bones are the whole house of Israel. They themselves say: Our bones are dried up, our hope has perished, and we are cut off.’

“Therefore prophesy and say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I shall open your tombs and bring you up from your graves, O my people, and I shall bring you into the land of Israel. And you shall know that I am the Lord when I have opened your graves, brought you up from your tombs, O my people, and given my spirit within you, and you have lived. And I shall cause you to rest upon your own soil, and you shall know that I am the Lord; I have spoken and acted, says the Lord God.”

(Hieronymus.) This is a famous vision, celebrated in the reading of all the Churches of Christ.

Those who think that this passage concerns the resurrection—which both Jews and Christians universally believe to be God’s word—customarily say the following: “The hand of the Lord came upon the prophet,” that is, the Lord and Savior, upon whom the Father worked all things: “For all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that has been made” (John 1).

“And he brought me,” he says, “in the spirit of the Lord”—the hand of the Lord being understood. He brought him in the spirit, not in the body but outside the body. And he placed him, or set him down, in the midst of a plain full of human bones.

He did not allow him to rest, but made him walk all around the bones, which were not covered by earth but lay upon the plain. They were not merely numerous, but exceedingly numerous; and because of the antiquity of time they were extremely dry and withered, containing no moisture at all.

When the divine word asked him whether he thought these bones could live, he replied: “Lord God, you know,” for you possess complete knowledge of future things.

The Lord said to him: “Prophesy concerning these bones,” or “over these bones,” “and say to them: Dry bones, hear the word of the Lord.”

Here one may wonder how he spoke to dry bones, which could hear the word of God before they possessed sinews, flesh, skin, and life-giving spirit. First the bones are joined to other bones by the bonds of sinews; then they are filled with flesh. Above them, for the sake of beauty, skin is stretched out to cover the ugliness of the exposed flesh. Then they receive spirit, which makes them live; and after they have lived, they know that he is the Lord.

When the prophet said what he had been commanded, a commotion immediately occurred, and the bones were joined to their own structure, bound by sinews, filled with flesh, and covered with skin. Human bodies lay there, but they had no spirit.

Therefore the prophet prophesies to the spirit and says: “Thus says the Lord God: Come from the four winds, O spirit”—that is, from the four regions of the world. Just as in the first creation of humanity God breathed into his face and “he became a living soul” (Genesis 2), so in the second creation—that is, the resurrection of the dead—the dead are to be made alive by the breathing of the spirit.

The spirit entered the human bodies, and immediately they lived and “stood upon their feet.” Hence the resurrection is called a gathering or a great assembly of the dead, and, as the Hebrew has it, a great army. At that time the following is fulfilled: “Send forth your spirit, and they shall be created, and you shall renew the face of the earth” (Psalm 103).

But what follows—“And he said to me: Son of man, all these bones are the whole house of Israel”—appears to raise a question, since the passage seems to speak not of the general resurrection but specifically of the resurrection of the house of Israel, which says: “Our bones are dried up, our hope has perished, and we are cut off from our land,” or, more generally, “we have completely despaired.”

When they say this, Ezekiel is compelled for the third time to prophesy and say to the dry bones: “Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I shall open your tombs.”

Here it is asked: if he opens the tombs, how could he earlier have said: “There were very many upon the face of the plain, and they were exceedingly dry”?

“And I shall bring you,” he says, “out of your tombs, O my people,” according to what is written in the Gospel (John 5): “The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who have done good will come out to the resurrection of life.” And again: “Those who hear will live.”

But if, as some think, the divine word speaks here of the general resurrection, why was it necessary to say specifically: “And I shall bring you into the land of Israel”? The dead must rise throughout the whole world, from the places in which they were buried.

And when he says: “When I have brought you out of your tombs and given my spirit within you, and you have lived, then I shall cause you to rest upon your own soil,” the meaning is that, after you have rested in the land of Israel, you will know that I am the Lord who has fulfilled my promises in deed.

Those who understand these words as referring to the general resurrection refer the statement that appears to cause difficulty—“These bones are the whole house of Israel”—to the resurrection of the saints. Concerning this the Apostle John also speaks in the Apocalypse: “Blessed and holy is the one who has a share in the first resurrection; over such the second death has no power” (Revelation 20). That is, there is one resurrection of the saints and another of sinners.

Hence Psalm 1 also says: “The ungodly shall not rise in the judgment, nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous.”

They affirm that the land of Israel which the Lord promises to those who rise is the land concerning which it is written: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land” (Matthew 5); and: “I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm 114).

This is the view of those who, as we have said, maintain that Ezekiel wrote concerning the general resurrection.

Those who interpret these matters differently should not reproach us because, by explaining this passage otherwise, we may seem to deny the resurrection. For we know that much stronger testimonies, about which there is no doubt, are found in the holy Scriptures.

Such is the passage in Job: “You shall raise up my skin” (Job 19), which supports this interpretation; and in Daniel: “Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall rise, some to eternal life and some to eternal reproach and confusion” (Daniel 12).

And in the Gospel: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Luke 12).

And in the Apostle Paul: “He will give life to your mortal bodies because of his Spirit dwelling in you” (Romans 8), along with many other passages.

It is therefore evident that we do not deny the resurrection; rather, we contend that these words are not written about the resurrection, but that, through the parable of the resurrection, the restoration of Israel is prophesied—the Israel that at that time was captive in Babylon.

Nor will we immediately provide the heretics with an opportunity by refusing to understand these words as referring to the common resurrection. The likeness of resurrection would never have been used to signify the restoration of the people of Israel unless the resurrection itself stood firm and was believed to be future. For no one confirms uncertain matters by uncertain matters.

Our entire argument tends toward this point: just as it seems incredible that a future resurrection should be promised to dry bones consumed by great antiquity, yet what is promised will nevertheless come to pass, so too the resurrection of the people of Israel, who were led into captivity and scattered throughout the whole world, seems incredible to those who do not know God’s power. Yet it will come to pass, because the Lord says: “I have spoken, and I shall act as I have promised.”

Finally, in the preceding prophecy, in which the ancient condition of the mountains of Israel is promised again, the Lord says to them: “I shall turn toward you, you shall be cultivated, you shall receive seed, and I shall multiply human beings among you, the whole house of Israel.”

And again, the statement that the house of Israel will dwell in its own land—which was once uncultivated and afterward will become like a garden of delight—and that the deserted and abandoned cities will be fortified, and that the house of Israel will be multiplied in them like a flock of sheep, along with the other things that follow, belongs to the same meaning.

That meaning is now expressed under the form of allegory and parable by the image of dry bones, entirely without the moisture of life. Thus is fulfilled what is written in the Gospel: “Things that seem impossible among human beings are possible with God” (Luke 18).

They were brought out of their tombs—that is, from the tombs of captivity and from the bonds by which they had been held fast in Babylonian servitude.

The Jews affirm that all these things were fulfilled either under Zerubbabel, as I said earlier, when a great commotion occurred and the kingdom of the Chaldeans was transferred to the Medes and Persians, or in the presence of their Christ, whom they think is still to come.

We, however, understand them spiritually as having been fulfilled after the cross of the Lord Savior. We remember that they occur daily, especially in those who, like Lazarus, are bound by the wrappings of their sins and are raised at the voice of the Lord. They truly are the house of Israel, once dry and without any hope of salvation, but when the spirit of grace enters them and the Lord extends his hand, they are freed from the depths of hell.

And those who had earlier said, “Lord God, you know,” afterward hear, once they have been delivered: “You of little faith, why did you doubt?”

---

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:

“‘And you, son of man, take one piece of wood and write upon it: “For Judah and for the children of Israel, his companions.” Then take another piece of wood and write upon it: “For Joseph, the wood of Ephraim and for the whole house of Israel, his companions.” Join them one to the other as a single piece of wood, and they shall become one in your hand.

“‘When the children of your people speak to you, saying, “Will you not explain to us what you intend by these things?” you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I shall take the wood of Joseph, which is in the hand of Ephraim, and the tribes of Israel that are joined to him, and I shall place them together with the wood of Judah. I shall make them one piece of wood, and they shall be one in his hand.

“‘The pieces of wood upon which you have written shall be in your hand before their eyes, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I shall take the children of Israel from among the nations to which they have gone; I shall gather them from every side and bring them to their own soil. I shall make them one nation in the land, upon the mountains of Israel, and one king shall rule over all of them. They shall no longer be two nations, nor shall they ever again be divided into two kingdoms.

“‘They shall no longer defile themselves with their idols, their abominations, or any of their iniquities. I shall save them from all their dwelling places in which they sinned, and I shall cleanse them. They shall be my people, and I shall be their God. And my servant David shall be king over them, and there shall be one shepherd over all of them.

“‘They shall walk in my judgments, observe my commandments, and carry them out. They shall dwell upon the land which I gave to my servant Jacob, in which your fathers dwelt. They shall dwell upon it, they and their children and their children’s children, forever; and my servant David shall be their prince forever.

“‘I shall make a covenant of peace with them; it shall be an everlasting covenant with them. I shall establish them, multiply them, and place my sanctuary in their midst forever. My tabernacle shall be among them; I shall be their God, and they shall be my people. And the nations shall know that I am the Lord who sanctifies Israel, when my sanctification is in their midst forever.’”

(Hieronymus.) The historical account of the kingdoms relates that under Rehoboam, the son of Solomon, the twelve tribes were divided (1 Kings 12). Two tribes—that is, Judah and Benjamin—together with the Levites and priests, followed Rehoboam, who reigned in Jerusalem, and his kingdom was called Judah.

The other ten tribes, who said, “We have no portion in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse,” submitted their necks to Jeroboam, son of Nebat, from the tribe of Ephraim, who was descended from Joseph, and served him. They were called, for the most part, by their ancient name, Israel.

For a long time the kingdoms of Judah and Israel fought against each other and obeyed their own kings. The first ten tribes were captured by the Assyrians; after some time, those called Judah were led captive by the Chaldeans into Babylon. The tribe of Judah was restored to its ancient land after seventy years. But the ten tribes called Israel remain to this day in captivity in the mountains and cities of the Medes.

The present prophecy therefore promises from the mouth of the Lord that the two kingdoms will be joined together: the kingdom of Judah and the kingdom of Israel. The staff of Ephraim, who was descended from the stock of Joseph, together with the remaining tribes associated with him, will be taken up and joined to the staff of Judah, so that they will no longer be called Judah and Israel but will be called Judah by one name. Under the figure of the prophet who precedes in a type of the Lord Savior, they will be held not in two hands but in the one hand of Christ.

For he says that he will take the children of Israel from among the nations to which they were led captive and bring them back into the land and onto the mountains of Israel, concerning which we read above. He says that they will be called one nation and ruled under the authority of one king, “so that they will no longer defile themselves with their idols and abominations. Once they have been freed from the dwelling places of captivity in which they sinned, they will be cleansed from every vice and become God’s people, so that the Lord will be their God.

“And my servant David,” he says, “shall be king over them.” Concerning him the angel also speaks in the Gospel (Luke 1), saying that he will reign over the house of Jacob and that there will be no end to his kingdom.

His clemency will be so great that he will be called not only king but also shepherd, because he softens the proud title of imperial rule by the name of shepherd. After they have become one nation and have dwelt in the land and upon the mountains of Israel, they will walk in all the judgments of the Lord and observe his commandments.

They will dwell not in another land but in the land which he gave to his servant Jacob, in which their fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and the other saints dwelt. And not only will they dwell there, but also their children and grandchildren, according to that line of Virgil:

> And the children of their children, and those who shall be born from them.

And let them dwell, not for a short time, but forever. But do you wish, he says, to know who this king and shepherd is? He is the one of whom I said above, “My servant David”—“who, though he was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. II).

And when they are under such a king, I will make a covenant of peace with them—not, as in the Old Testament, a covenant of conflicts and wars, but a pact of peace that surpasses all understanding. Concerning this the Savior says to the apostles (John XIV): “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you.” And the Prophet says: “His place has been established in peace” (Ps. LXXV). When he has founded and established them in the Church, so that they can say, “He set my feet upon a rock” (Ps. XXXIX), then they will multiply, either in the number of believers or in the increase of virtues.

“And I will give,” he says, “my sanctification—or sanctuary—in their midst forever.” The Jews interpret this as referring to the temple that was built under Zerubbabel. But how can what is said to be “forever” stand, when that temple, built by Zerubbabel and later restored by many, was burned by Roman fire? All these things must be referred to the Church and to the times of the Savior, when his tabernacle was set up in the Church, where our God was made present and we became his people. The purpose of all this is that they may know that he is the Lord, and that he himself sanctifies Israel—not according to the flesh, but according to the spirit—when his sanctification has been established forever in the midst of believers.

As for the fact that the Lord rejected the tribe of Ephraim and chose the tribe of Judah, we also read it in the Psalms, where it is written: “And he rejected the tabernacle of Joseph, and did not choose the tribe of Ephraim, but chose the tribe of Judah” (Ps. LXXVII). Concerning Judah it is written: “The ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor the leader from his thighs, until he comes to whom it has been reserved, and he will be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX).

For truly, at the coming of the Lord and Savior, the two rods—or, as it is written in Hebrew, the two pieces of wood—were joined into one scepter; and in the baptism of Christ, things formerly separated are united, so that they may become one new person and one nation. They will no longer defile themselves with idols and abominations, but will be the people of God through a cleansing bath; Christ will rule over them, and they will dwell upon the land—the land of the living—which he had given to his servant Jacob, who supplanted the people of Israel in his mother’s womb.

But if we wish to understand this according to the prophecy of Hosea, most of which is directed toward the ten tribes—that is, toward Joseph, Ephraim, Samaria, and Israel—as knowledge falsely so called and the various crowds of heretics, we shall say the following. At the final time, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered and all Israel has been saved, then also the hostile peoples who fought against the house of Judah and against the confession of the Church will surrender themselves to the ecclesiastical faith. Abandoning every error, the rulers of this world who are to be destroyed, and their patriarchs who led them into the abyss of blasphemies, they will arise and leave behind their idols and abominations, which they had fashioned from their own hearts. From all their dwelling places in which they sinned, they will pass over to the ecclesiastical faith, be cleansed, become the people of Christ, and have him as their God. I know that I have discussed this more fully in the prophet Hosea.

But if Jews and Christians who judaize wish to refer these things to a thousand-year reign, they are forced to accept that all who are saved will dwell in the land of Israel; that Jerusalem will be rebuilt; that the temple will be constructed; that all the ceremonies of the Law will be performed; that the Sabbath will be observed; that the injury—or burden—of circumcision will be undertaken; that people will eat and drink; and that abundance of riches will be regarded as the highest blessedness and the sum of all prosperity. Yet the Apostle says: “Food is for the stomach and the stomach for food; but God will destroy both it and them” (1 Cor. VI).

Just as the preceding prophetic passage, in the figure of the resurrection, demonstrated the restoration of the Jewish people—not a carnal restoration but a spiritual one—so this prophecy also pertains not to the happiness of the flesh but to that of the soul, and to the faith of Christ, through which we are cleansed in baptism. His kingdom is eternal, so that we need not await things that we know have already happened and are happening every day.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Lord’s discourse against Gog and Magog; concerning their destruction and the sin of the people

> “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set your face against Gog and the land of Magog, the prince of the chief of Mosoch and Thubal, and prophesy against him, and say to him: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, Gog, prince of the chief of Mosoch and Thubal. And I will turn you around and put a bridle in your jaws, and I will bring you out, and all your army, horses and horsemen clothed in breastplates, all of them, a great multitude, grasping spear and shield and sword. Persians, Ethiopians, and Libyans with them, all shield-bearing and helmeted. Gomer and all his armies; the house of Thogorma, the sides of the north, and all his strength, and many peoples with you. Prepare and equip yourself, and all your multitude that has been gathered to you, and be a command for them. After many days you will be visited. In the last of the years you will come to a land that has returned from the sword, that has been gathered from many peoples to the mountains of Israel, which had been continually desolate. This land was brought out from the peoples, and all of them dwelt in it securely. Rising up like a storm, you will come, and like a cloud to cover the land—you and all your armies, and many peoples with you.
>
> “Thus says the Lord God: On that day words will rise into your heart, and you will conceive a most evil plan, and you will say: I will go up to a land without a wall; I will come to those who rest and dwell securely. All of them dwell without a wall; they have neither bars nor gates, so that you may seize spoil and take plunder, to lay your hand upon those who had been desolate and afterward restored, and upon the people gathered from the nations, who have begun to possess and to dwell at the center of the earth. Sheba and Dedan, and the merchants of Tarshish, and all its lions, will say to you: Are you coming to take spoil? Behold, you have gathered your multitude to seize plunder, to take silver and gold, to carry away goods and possessions, and to plunder innumerable spoils.
>
> “Therefore prophesy, son of man, and say to Gog: Thus says the Lord God: Will you not know on that day, when my people Israel dwell securely, that you will come from your place, from the sides of the north—you and many peoples with you, all riding horses, a great assembly and a mighty army? You will rise up against my people Israel like a cloud, to cover the land. In the last days you will be; and I will bring you against my land, so that the nations may know me when I am sanctified in you before their eyes, O Gog.
>
