> “Thus says the Lord God: Are you that one of whom I spoke in ancient days through the hand of my servants, the prophets of Israel, who prophesied in those days and those times that I would bring you against them? And it shall be on that day, on the day of Gog’s coming against the land of Israel, says the Lord God, that my indignation will rise in my wrath and in my jealousy. In the fire of my anger I have spoken: for on that day there shall be a great shaking upon the land of Israel, and the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, the beasts of the field, and every creeping thing that moves upon the ground, and all the human beings who are upon the face of the earth, will be shaken before my presence. The mountains will be overturned, the hedges will fall, and every wall will collapse to the ground. And I will summon the sword against him on all my mountains, says the Lord God; each one’s sword will be directed against his brother. And I will judge him with pestilence and blood, with a violent rain and immense stones. I will rain fire and sulfur upon him, and upon his army, and upon the many peoples who are with him. And I will magnify myself and sanctify myself, and I will be known in the eyes of many nations, and they will know that I am the Lord.”

*(Jerome.)* First, the foundations of the historical account must be laid, and it must be understood that this is the final word of the Lord to the prophet Ezekiel. For after this we cannot find anything similar, except for what is written in the twenty-fifth year of Jeconiah’s captivity: “The hand of the Lord was upon me, and he brought me there”—that is, into the land of Israel—when the construction of the temple is described and the order of its rites is narrated.

Next, we must observe that the prophet’s face is said to be set—or fixed—against Gog and the land, or against the land of Magog. For firmness and much reflection of countenance are necessary if we are to understand what is said, according to the apostolic passage: “But we all, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as from the Spirit of the Lord” (1 Cor. III).

Accordingly, the Jews and our judaizers believe that Gog consists of the savage and innumerable Scythian nations that extend beyond the Caucasus Mountains and Lake Maeotis, and by way of the Caspian Sea as far as India. They think that after the thousand-year reign these nations will be stirred up by the devil and will come into the land of Israel to fight against the saints, gathering many nations with them.

First comes Mosoch, whom Josephus interprets as the Cappadocians; then Thubal, whom he likewise identifies as the Iberians or Spaniards, while the Hebrews suspect them to be Italians. They have with them in their army Persians, Ethiopians, and Libyans. They also include Gomer and Thogorma, whom they interpret as Galatians and Phrygians; likewise the Sabaeans and Dedan, and the Carthaginians or Tarshish. This is also what John records in his Apocalypse:

> “And when the thousand years have been completed, Satan will be released from his prison, and he will go out to deceive the nations at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, to gather them for battle; their number is like the sand of the sea. And they went up over the breadth of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city. And fire came down from God out of heaven and consumed them. And the devil, who deceived them, was cast into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast and the false prophets were; and they will be tormented day and night forever and ever.”

They do not understand that John’s entire book, which is prefaced by the title “Revelation,” is mystical, and that we need revelation in order to be able to say with the Prophet: “Open my eyes, and I shall contemplate the wonders of your law” (Ps. CXVIII).

Others, however, abandoning the earthly sense and the Jewish and old-womanish tales that are harmful, and by accommodating themselves to their own opinions plunging into the depths, climb excessively to the heights and invent far worse nonsense. They describe wars against the devil and his entire army in the heavenly Jerusalem, and under the etymologies of the individual nations they interpret the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.

We leave all these matters to the judgment of the reader. We shall attempt not so much to condemn what is foreign as to affirm an ecclesiastical explanation. In Greek, Gog is δῶμα, which in Latin means “roof” or “house-covering.” Magog, moreover, is interpreted as “from the roof.” Therefore, all pride and falsely named knowledge that raises itself against knowledge of the truth are signified by these names.

These are the roofs of which Isaiah also speaks in his vision against the valley of Zion: “What has happened to you now, that you have all climbed upon vain roofs?” We shall interpret the roof as the leaders of the heretics, and those “from the roof” as the people who have accepted their doctrines.

It is fitting that, after the many mystical prophecies in this book, the final prophecy is against Gog and Magog. For if, according to Peter, the time of judgment is “that it should begin with the household of God” (1 Pet. IV), and according to this same Ezekiel, who says, “Begin with my saints” (Ezek. IX), and if death, the last enemy, is to be destroyed, then in Isaiah also the first discourse is against Judah, in which there is confession of the Lord, and the last against the four-footed creatures that are in the desert.

Rightly, then, this last discourse is also against Gog and Magog, who attack the city of God, which the river’s rushing waters gladden, and which says in Isaiah, “I am a fortified city that is attacked.” Concerning it, it is written in the Gospel (Matt. V): “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden.” And more fully in the Psalm: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose fellowship is in unity; mountains surround it, and the Lord surrounds his people” (Ps. CXXIV).

As for the army of Gog or Magog, who, according to the Septuagint, Symmachus, and Theodotion, is the prince of Ros, Mosoch, and Thubal: Aquila interprets the first nation, Ros, as “chief,” and we have followed him, so that the meaning is “prince of the chief of Mosoch and Thubal.” Indeed, we have been able to find this nation neither elsewhere in Scripture nor even in Josephus, who explains the names of all the Hebrew nations in the first book of his Antiquities. From this it is clear that Ros signifies not a nation but a chief.

This too should briefly be noted: in Ezekiel Gog is said to be prince of the land of Magog; but the Apocalypse mentions Gog and Magog as nations that go out from the four corners of the earth. Just as from Jacob, who was afterward called Israel, the entire Hebrew people received the name Israel; and just as from Aram came Syria, and from Mesraim Egypt, whose names are written in Genesis; so also, from the prince Gog, all who are subject to him are called Magog. Mosoch, moreover, is interpreted as “madness,” and Thubal as “all” or “everything.”

Thus the prince and chief of proud madness and of all evils, according to what is written, “The world is set in wickedness” (1 John V), are called Gog and Magog. These hostile and adversarial nations of the saints go out from the corners of the earth, abandoning the straight line and the arrangement of God’s camp that is described in Numbers.

They do not know this testimony: “Many will come from the east and the west and from the north and the south, and will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of God” (Matt. VIII). And elsewhere: “I will say to the north, ‘Give up,’ and to the south, ‘Do not hinder.’ Bring my sons from a distant land and my daughters from the end of the earth, all who are called by my name” (Isa. XLIII).

But these are not the sort of corners of the earth from which Gog and Magog go out. Near such corners stands the harlot in Proverbs (Prov. VII), who hastens to deceive foolish young men passing through the streets, that is, along the broad and spacious way that leads to death (Matt. VI). The scribes and Pharisees also pray in the corners of the streets so that they may be seen by human beings; they have received their reward.

What, then, is the threat against Gog? “I will turn you around, or convert you, and I will put a bridle in your jaws.” First, I will make you waver from your own decision and turn you around. “And I will put a bridle in your jaws.” Concerning this it is written: “With bit and bridle restrain their jaws, who do not draw near to you” (Ps. XXXI), so that the untamed, wanton horse, falling headlong over precipices, may be subdued by the Lord’s bridle.

To him the Prophet says: “Mount upon your horses, and your riding is salvation” (Hab. III). And to Job, through the clouds and the whirlwind, it is said: “You have clothed the horse with strength” (Job XXXIX). Such were the horses and horsemen whose multitude John saw in heaven.

He therefore says to Gog: “I will bring you out,” or “I will gather you,” and all your army or strength. One who is brought out and gathered from dispersion is drawn back to salvation, according to what is promised in the Law: “If your dispersion should be from the summit of heaven to its summit, from there I will gather you” (Deut. XXX).

His horses and horsemen, clothed in breastplates, imitate the armor of the Apostle (Eph. VI), and boast that they possess breastplates of righteousness. Their multitude is enormous, and they all seize shield and sword against the Church. They are extremely savage nations hostile to Israel: Persians, Ethiopians, and Libyans, whose wars against the people of God are recounted.

Gomer also and the house of Thogorma, who come from the sides of the north—which is the coldest wind and is called by the name “Right”—and all the strength of Magog and all the peoples subject to him will come with him to battle.

He is addressed ironically: “Prepare yourself and equip yourself, and gather to yourself your entire multitude, which obeys your commands. But know that after many days you will be visited,” according to what is written: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with blows” (Ps. LXXXVIII).

“In the last of the years,” he says, “you will come.” Hence John also says: “Little children, it is the last hour” (1 John II). And the people of the Gentiles, in the eleventh hour, are brought in to work in the vineyard.

Gog comes to conquer their land—that is, the land of the meek and the land of the saints, which bears fruit a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold. It is a land that has returned, or turned away, from the sword. For he knows what is written: “Scatter, Lord, the nations that desire wars” (Ps. LXVII). And it stands in peace.

“And it has been gathered from many peoples and nations,” so that, having despised the error of the nations, it might come to the mountains of Israel—that is, to the patriarchs and prophets, who were once continually desolate, without the law and commandments of God. Later it is said to it: “The children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Gal. IV).

These are the deserts and waterless places in which the devil could not find a dwelling, because they had been called to salvation. Later, having taken with him seven other demons more wicked than himself, he returned to his own house (Matt. XII), that is, to the people of Israel.

“This land,” he says, “was brought out from the peoples”—the land being understood; or, he was brought out from the Gentiles, so that the people of believers may be understood, who dwelt in peace and trusted in the Lord.

But Gog, rising up with his entire army, will come like a storm and like a cloud to cover the land of believers. For what heretic, whose prince is the devil, does not come against the Church like a storm and hasten to oppress and cover the simple among believers with the cloud of his words?

Hence it is said to him: “As far as it lies within you, you will cover everything—you and all your armies, and many peoples with you.” Fittingly, Gog, when he rises, has no willing rain, no timely or late shower to gladden parched fields, but storm and darkness, so that he may confuse everything with darkness and error.

Therefore the Lord God speaks to him: “At that time”—that is, in the last days—“words will rise into your heart, and you will conceive a most evil plan,” as Scripture says: “If the spirit of one who has authority should rise against you, do not leave your place” (Eccl. X).

By contrast, God rises in the heart of the saint, concerning whom it is written: “He has arranged ascents in his heart” (Ps. LXXXIII).

Gog says: “I will go up to a land without a wall,” or “a land cast down”—that is, one deprived of God’s help and not fortified by the arguments of the dialecticians. “I will come to those who rest and dwell securely,” or “in peace,” for our king is peaceable, and his place is in peace.

“All of them,” he says, “dwell without a wall; they have neither bars nor gates.” This is what the devil, the prince of the heretics, says: that the Church has no defenses and no secular wisdom—which is foolishness with God—so that he may seize the spoils, invade the Church’s plunder, and lay his hand upon those who had been desolate when they did not know God, but were afterward restored through Christ and came to the Father, to whom Christ says in the Gospel (John XVII): “Father, reveal your name to human beings.”

And so that we may know that the people who had been desolate and were afterward restored signify the Christian people, the passage continues: “And upon the people gathered from the nations, who began to possess the inheritance of Christ and to dwell at the center of the earth.” Concerning this it is written: “He worked salvation in the midst of the earth, for truth has sprung up from the earth” (Ps. LXXXIV); and truth says in the Gospel: “I am the way, and the life, and the truth” (John XIV).

While Gog is thinking and saying these things and hastening to seize the Church’s possession, the nations that had been converted from their former error to salvation—Sheba and Dedan, and the merchants of Tarshish, of Carthage or of the sea, who amid the waves of this world seek the profits of commerce through good works—and all their villages, or “lion-cubs,” as the Hebrew contains, will speak to him as follows.

Sheba and Dedan, the merchants of Tarshish, and all the saints who are called lion-cubs—or, certainly, the villages and dwellings of believers—will say:

“O Gog, are you coming for this reason, to seize the spoils of the Church? Have you gathered your multitude for this reason, so that Christ’s possession may become your inheritance? Or do you think that you will possess the silver and gold of the Church—which are understood as eloquence and understanding—so that you may carry away all its goods and possessions and plunder the innumerable spoils gathered through Christ’s victories?”

Therefore, O prophet Ezekiel, who in the figure of Christ are called “son of man,” speak to Gog and say to him: “Thus says the Lord God.” When all the error of the world has been removed, my people Israel—those who see God with the mind—will dwell securely in the Church, or in peace. Then you will know, or rise up, and come from your place.

What the place of heretical perversity is, the following passage shows: “From the sides of the north,” which attempts to cool all the warmth of believers.

Many peoples will come with him, “all riding horses,” concerning whom it is written: “He cast horse and rider into the sea” (Exod. XV). A great assembly and a mighty army will come with him. “And rising up,” he says, “against my people Israel like a cloud and darkness, to cover” my land, of which we spoke above.

“In the last days you will be,” when the Gospel preaching is present. “And I will bring you against my land. For there must also be heresies” (1 Cor. XI), so that those who are approved may become manifest, and so that, by the will of God, the devil and all the doctrines of perversity may be [text uncertain: Greek Ἀναγώνιστος, apparently an epithet or corrupt reading] abandoned.

“So that all the nations may know and understand me, when I am sanctified in you before their eyes, O Gog”—that is, when through your punishments they understand that I am the judge.

And he turns in apostrophe to Gog himself: “Are you not that one of whom I spoke in ancient days through the hands of my servants, the prophets of Israel?” Namely, Moses, who says in the book of Numbers, at least according to the Septuagint: “A man will come forth from his seed, and will rule many nations; Gog will be exalted, his kingdom, and his kingdom will increase” (Num. XXIV).

But according to the Hebrew, I found it written this way: “Therefore let Gog [Agag], its king, be removed, and his kingdom will be taken away,” because the kingdom of Israel was destroyed under Saul on account of Agag, king of Amalek.

And elsewhere: “He will cleanse the land of his people.” Joel also describes the nations that are to be gathered in the valley of Jehoshaphat—that is, in the judgment of God (Joel III). Isaiah and all the prophets likewise describe them, in whose hands and good works the word of the Lord is spoken.

When, therefore, you come against the land of Israel, “my indignation will rise against you in my fury, and in my jealousy for my people. In the fire of my anger I have spoken,” a fire that consumes all the wood of your vices.

“At that time,” he says, “there will be a great shaking upon the land of Israel.” For when the devil sends frequent persecution against the Church, and when that persecution has been quieted and overcome by God’s protection, then the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, the beasts of the field, every creeping thing that moves upon the earth, and all the human beings upon the face of the earth will be shaken before him.

This is clearly demonstrated concerning the inhabitants of the Church. Some dwell as fish of the sea, others as birds of heaven, others as beasts of the field, and others as the various creeping things that move upon the earth; still others dwell upon the face of the earth while retaining the dignity of human beings.

That the diversity of their ways is marked by various names is also written by the Apostle to the Corinthians (1 Cor. XV). He says that after the resurrection there are different bodies: some heavenly, some earthly; one body of a fish, another of a bird, another of beasts, another of creeping things, and another of human beings who have retained their former name.

In the Acts of the Apostles also, the sheet shown to the apostle Peter three times by its four corners (Acts X) signifies the diversity of believers, a diversity that is also contained in the ark of the flood.

Then, before the face of the Lord and at the sight of his majesty, the mountains that raised themselves against the knowledge of God will be overturned. The hedges—or valleys—will fall, whether those sunk down to the depths through humility of understanding, or the fortifications that promise something in imitation of the Church of God.

Concerning these hedges it is said: “Whoever destroys a hedge will be bitten by a serpent” (Eccli. X). And all the walls will collapse to the ground. For when the strength of ecclesiastical discourse appears, all the defenses of the heretics will fall.

“And I will summon,” he says, “against him”—that is, against Gog, the prince of the heretics—“the sword on all his mountains,” and the leaders of his army will be destroyed by the sword of the Lord. Then heresy will fight against heresy, and their mutual conflict will be our victory.

“And I will judge him,” he says, “with death or pestilence, with blood, with violent rain, and with immense stones,” or hailstones. Gog is judged by his own death and by the blood he shed; by the violent rain, that is, by the words of an educated and perfected man; and by immense stones that overwhelm him with testimonies of Scripture, or by hailstones that make his heat grow cold: “For all adulterers, their hearts are like an oven” (Hos. VII).

“I will rain fire and sulfur upon him.” Through these are demonstrated the punishment and judgment of eternity. And not only upon him, who was the author of perversity, but also “upon all his army and multitude, and upon the many peoples who are with him.” For heretics have many companions—indeed, the devil, their prince, is surrounded by an innumerable multitude.

When all error has been removed, and the leaders of the heretics have been punished and destroyed, the Lord is magnified and sanctified in believers, and becomes known in the eyes of the many nations that have believed his faith. They will know and recognize, both from their own blessedness and from the punishments of their adversaries, that he is the Lord.

We have interpreted these things as best we could, obeying the command: “You shall not turn aside to the right or to the left, but you shall walk by the royal road.” If anyone criticizes what we have written, let him either bring forward better interpretations for us to follow, or, if he wishes to say nothing, let him leave perfect knowledge to God. Let him know, however, that it is not our abilities but our intention that must be judged.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. In the last days Gog and Magog will rise up; concerning the gathering of birds and beasts to eat their corpses

> “But you, son of man, prophesy against Gog and say: Thus says the Lord God: I am against you, Gog, prince of the chief of Mosoch and Thubal. And I will turn you around and bring you back, and I will make you rise from the sides of the north, and I will bring you against the mountains of Israel. And I will strike your bow from your left hand, and I will cast down your arrows from your right hand. You shall fall upon the mountains of Israel—you, and all your armies, and your peoples who are with you. I have given you to the wild beasts, to the birds, to every winged creature, and to the beasts of the earth for devouring. Upon the face of the field you shall fall, for I have spoken, says the Lord God. And I will send fire upon Magog and upon those who dwell securely in the islands, and they shall know that I am the Lord.
>
> “And I will make my holy name known in the midst of my people Israel, and I will no longer profane my holy name. And the nations shall know that I am the Lord, the Holy One of Israel. Behold, it is coming and it has happened, says the Lord God. This is the day of which I spoke.
>
> “And the inhabitants will go out from the cities of Israel, and they will kindle and burn the weapons, the shield and spears, the bow and arrows, the staffs of the hands, and the lances; and they will burn them in the fire for seven years. They will not carry wood from the regions, nor cut it from the forests, because they will burn the weapons in the fire. And they will plunder those by whom they had been plundered, and they will strip those who had despoiled them, says the Lord God.
>
> “And it shall be on that day that I will give Gog a named place as a tomb in Israel, the valley of travelers east of the sea, which will cause passersby to be astonished. And they will bury Gog there and all his multitude, and it will be called the Valley of Gog’s Multitude. And the house of Israel will bury them for seven months, so that they may cleanse the land.
>
> “All the people of the land will bury him, and the day on which I was glorified will be named for them, says the Lord God. And they will continually appoint men to survey the land, who will bury and search for those who had remained upon the face of the earth, in order to cleanse it. After seven months they will begin the search, and they will travel throughout the land.
>
> “And when they see a human bone, they will set up a marker beside it until the buriers bury it in the Valley of Gog’s Multitude. The name of the city will be Amona, and they will cleanse the land.”

*(Jerome.)* The heirs and disciples of Jewish tradition and of endless fables insist that these things will take place after the thousand-year reign: Gog, the prince of Rosmosoch and Thubal, will be killed in the territory of Israel and devoured by all the birds and beasts; and the inhabitants of the cities of Israel will have no need for wood obtained by cutting down forests for seven years, but will use the weapons of Gog—namely, shields, spears, arrows, staffs, or lances.

They say that Gog himself will be buried in a valley called in Hebrew *Ge*, and that his tomb will be called ποαγανάριον [Jerome: πολυάνδριον], that is, “a place where a multitude of people has been buried.” He is to be buried by the house of Israel for seven months, so that the land may be cleansed. They also say that the day on which Gog was killed will be glorious and renowned, and that men will be appointed to search carefully for and bury the bones, so that nothing unburied remains in the land.

After seven months—or during the seven months—they are to traverse the land, and wherever they see a human bone lying, they are to indicate it by placing a marker nearby, so that afterward those appointed to this work may bury it. The name of the city is to be Amona, which in Greek is called ποαγανάριον—that is, “a multitude of buried people”—and thus the land is cleansed.

Let them have said these things. We, however, maintaining the meaning of the explanation we have begun, shall discuss each of the points we have set forth.

Gog himself has his own trinity: Ros, Mosoch, and Thubal—namely, head, madness, and all things—so that there is no vice which does not reside in Gog’s possession. He will be led forth, or driven about, and fondled and coaxed, so that, hoping for victory, he may be led to battle to be killed. He will ascend from the sides, or from the remotest regions, of the north, from which evils blaze forth over the whole earth; and by him he will be brought against the mountains of Israel, whom we ought to understand as the apostles and apostolic and ecclesiastical men. When he has been brought to the mountains of Israel, then the bow in his left hand will be struck down, together with the arrows held in his right hand. For he too imitates those whom he has deceived by pretending to have weapons on the left and on the right, through a good and an evil reputation. These are the arrows and missiles of which the Psalmist also speaks:

> “For behold, sinners have bent the bow, they have prepared their arrows in the quiver, to shoot in the darkness at the upright in heart” (Psalm 10).

These burning missiles of the devil must be extinguished by the shield of faith.

Gog, who had ascended upon the mountains of Israel, is cast down, or falls, upon those very mountains, with his whole army and all his forces. He will become food for wild beasts, birds, every winged creature, and the beasts of the earth—that is, for adversaries and powers which would eat the seed beside the way, and for bloodthirsty beasts. For just as it is written of the dragon, “You gave him as food to the peoples of Ethiopia” (Psalm 73), so all who have been deceived by heretics are food for demons.

Gog will fall either in the breadth of the plain or in the cultivated field tilled by God’s farmers; for it cannot happen that the Lord’s words should prove void. Then fire will be sent into Magog—that is, against those who have received Gog’s teaching, and against those who, like islands beaten by the waves of the world, suppose that they ought to be secure. It is that fire of which the Lord speaks: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke 12).

“So that all may know and understand that I am the Lord, and that my holy name may become known in the midst of my people,” who was in no way led astray by Gog’s authority, “and my name may no longer be polluted among the heretics through the pretext of a false name of knowledge, so that the nations which are round about may know that I am the Lord.”

What follows—“Behold, it comes, and it has happened”—is said of the judgment of Christ, who, when he comes, will come and will not delay. That is the day of punishments and vengeance of which the Lord has spoken through all the prophets.

“And the inhabitants of the cities” of Israel: the peoples who believe. By the cities of Israel we understand the churches of right faith. “And they shall kindle and burn the weapons,” of which it is written elsewhere:

> “He will break the bow and shatter the weapons, and burn the shields with fire” (Psalm 45),

namely, shields and spears, bow and arrows, staffs in their hands with which they celebrated a perverse Passover; lances or pikes with which they inflicted broad and incurable wounds of doctrine; and the shields, bows, and arrows mentioned above.

What follows—“And they shall burn them with fire for seven years”—must be explained from Exodus and Leviticus, in which the law commands that in the seventh year, the year of remission, when freedom is restored to Hebrew slaves, all debts are cancelled, the ancient possession returns to its owners, rest is granted to the land, and all crops are given to the poor, the armor of the heretics may perish within the sacred and perfect number of seven years. Ecclesiastical men will not cut wood from the fields and regions, forests and thickets of the nations, whom they desire rather to save than to destroy, but from the shields, spears, arrows, staffs, pikes, and lances of the heretics whom they have conquered.

For they too possess various weapons with which to attack the Church of Christ. These must be set alight by learned men with the fire of the Holy Spirit, namely, with ecclesiastical speech; whoever possesses it will be able to say:

> “Was not our heart burning within us on the way, when he opened the Scriptures to us?”  

Nor can we have complete peace and confidence of habitation unless we plunder all the adversaries’ equipment, so that everything may perish and be consumed into ashes; and unless we plunder those who had previously plundered us, and lay waste those who formerly laid waste the Church.

“On that day,” in the clear light of preaching, “I will give Gog a named place for a tomb in Israel,” he says. According to the Hebrew, it is “the valley of those who travel,” east of the sea, “which causes passers-by to be astonished.” The meaning of this statement is as follows: Gog’s tomb will not be in the mountains, but in sunken valleys and rugged places, which in Hebrew are called *Ge*. The heretics, although situated in the west, falsely represent these as places of the east in order to deceive travelers—that is, those who pass through this present world and are not inhabitants but pilgrims, saying the prophetic words:

> “I am a stranger and a sojourner, like all my fathers” (Psalm 38).

For who among those passing by, of whom it is written, “And those who passed by did not say, ‘The blessing of the Lord be upon you’” (Psalm 128), does not marvel and stand astonished when he sees the valley of travelers—which appears to travelers as a valley, but to its inhabitants as a mountain? This is according to the Hebrew.

The Seventy, however, translated it as “the polyandrion of those who have come to the sea, and they will build around the entrance of the valley.” For the labor of those who go out from the cities of Israel is to close off and build around every entrance and exit of heretical perversity—those who had come from the sea and delighted in its bitterness, in the masses of its waves and the cruelty of shipwreck—and to bury them in the earth’s abysses, so that they may no longer be able to emerge and deceive anyone by their fraud.

There, then, they would bury Gog and all his multitude, in which the heretics have always delighted. “And the name of that valley in which Gog is buried will be called ‘the multitude of Ge,’ or ‘polyandrion,’ that is, ‘the tomb of a very great multitude.’” And just as above we said that the adversaries’ weapons are to be burned for seven years, so the earth will be cleansed of the filth of the heretics for seven months.

From the first month, when we celebrate the Lord’s Passover and by the blood of the lamb avoid the destroyer of Egypt on our doorposts, until the end of the year—that is, until the seventh month, when we set up tents and shelter ourselves among the other foliage also beneath branches of palm trees, so that perfect victory over our enemies may be displayed—we complete all the festivals among the peoples.

Not only the teachers but the whole people will eagerly do this: they will bury Gog and cover the earth, and will not allow the free air to reach him. After the slaughter and death—or burial—of Gog, ecclesiastical men will be chosen who will devote themselves to ensuring that no remnant of the former filth, nothing dead, remains in the land of Israel. They will cleanse the land, seek out the dead, and bury them, so that the land of the Church may be purified.

But if, during the seven months, when everything ought to have been cleansed, those who traverse and go around the land should see that some bone of a man—that is, some hardness of heretical perversity—or some dead remnant of former doctrine has remained, they will place a marker beside it, or build one there. Then, after those of this kind have been marked, they will either be cleansed or buried with Gog and shut away in the multitude of his burial.

The name of the city where the Lord’s servants have achieved victory, where the adversaries lie, and where the whole multitude of his enemies has been struck down, is called Amona or *Polyandrion*, so that the end of all things may be the restoration of purity. Finally, it follows: “And they will cleanse the land.”

There can be no doubt that these are the men of whom it was written above: “They will begin to search and will go around traversing the land.”

(MAURUS.) In the Apocalypse of John (Apocalypse 20), when the descent of the angel from heaven was mentioned—the angel who captured the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years—the Scripture subsequently says:

> “And when the thousand years have been completed, Satan will be released from his prison, and he will go out and deceive the nations which are at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, and will gather them for battle; their number is like the sand of the sea. And they went up over the breadth of the earth, and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city; and fire came down from God out of heaven and devoured them. And the devil, who deceived them, was cast into the lake of fire and sulphur, where the beast and the false prophets are; and they will be tormented day and night for ever and ever.”

(Bede on the Apocalypse.) “Devil” is interpreted as “flowing downward,” while in Greek he is called the accuser. “Satan” means adversary or transgressor. Thus he is called “dragon” on account of his malicious capacity to harm, “serpent” on account of his cunning in deceiving, “devil” on account of the fall of his status, and “Satan” on account of his obstinacy in opposing the Lord.

“And he bound him for a thousand years.” That is, restraining his power to seduce human beings who were destined to be liberated, he curbed and held it back; if he had been permitted to exercise it fully by force or fraud over so long a period, he would have deceived very many of the weak.

He said “a thousand years” while referring to a part, that is, to the remainder of the thousand years of the sixth day, on which the Lord was born and suffered. “And when the thousand years have been completed, Satan will be released from his prison.” He said “completed” of the whole while referring to a part. For he will be released in such a way that three years and six months of the final contest remain.

Apart from this figure of speech, however, the time is rightly said to have been completed. Those very small remnants ought not to be counted together with seven hundred years and the additional years which God has willed, which by the Apostle are called an hour.

“And he will go out and deceive the nations which are over the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, and will gather them for battle.” He will then deceive them for this purpose, in order to gather them for this battle; for previously also he deceived them in whatever ways he could, through many and various evils.

“He will go out” means that he will enter into open persecution: he will burst forth from the hiding places of hatred. Moreover, Gog and Magog either signify the whole by a part, or, according to the interpretation of their names—which are said to mean “roof” and “from the roof”—they designate hidden and open enemies. They themselves are “the roof,” because in them the enemy is now enclosed and concealed; and they themselves will be “from the roof” when they burst forth into open hatred.

“And they went up over the breadth of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city.” They are not said to have come, or to be going to come, to one particular place, as though the beloved city—that is, the Church—were to be confined to some single location. Rather, by the expression “the breadth of the earth,” he wished to indicate that it would then be persecuted among all nations, and, under the name “camp,” that it would not abandon its military service.

“And fire came down from God out of heaven and devoured them.” This should not be understood as the final punishment. Rather, it is the fire of envy by which the opposition will be tormented because of the steadfastness of the saints. For heaven is the firmament; this is the fire which went out from the mouth of God’s witnesses and will devour their enemies.

On the last day he will not rain fire down upon them; instead, he will send those gathered before him and judged into the eternal fire, about which it is added here:

> “And the devil, who deceived them, was cast into the lake of fire and sulphur, where the beast and the false prophet are.”

That is, at the final judgment the devil will be cast into eternal fire, where also all those whom he sent ahead will be—the greater part, namely, of the impious city. The beast must be understood according to its various contexts: sometimes as the devil, sometimes as the Antichrist, and sometimes as the impious city itself. The sudden destruction of the impious may also be signified by the name of the fire descending from heaven.

> “Therefore you, son of man, thus says the Lord God. Say to every winged creature and to every bird, and to all the beasts of the field: Assemble, hasten, gather from every side to my sacrifice, which I sacrifice for you, a great sacrifice upon the mountains of Israel, so that you may eat flesh and drink blood. You shall eat the flesh of the mighty and drink the blood of the princes of the earth—of rams, lambs, and goats, and of bulls, all fattened and fat. You shall eat fat until you are satisfied and drink blood until you are drunk, from the sacrifice which I shall sacrifice for you. You shall be satisfied at my table with horse and mighty rider, and with every warrior, says the Lord God. And I will set my glory among the nations, and all the nations will see my judgment which I have executed and my hand which I have laid upon them. And the house of Israel will know that I am the Lord their God, from that day and thereafter. And the nations will know that the house of Israel was taken captive because of its iniquity, because they abandoned me, and I hid my face from them and delivered them into the hand of their enemies, and they all fell by the sword. According to their uncleanness and their crime I dealt with them, and I hid my face from them.

> “Therefore thus says the Lord God: Now I will restore the captivity of Jacob and have mercy upon the whole house of Israel. And I will be zealous for my holy name, and they will bear their shame and all their transgressions by which they transgressed against me, when they dwell confidently in their land, fearing no one, and when I bring them back from the peoples and gather them from the lands of their enemies, and I am sanctified in them before the eyes of many nations. And they will know that I am the Lord their God, because I transferred them among the nations and gathered them upon their own land, and did not leave any of them there. And I will no longer hide my face from them, because I have poured out my spirit upon the whole house of Israel, says the Lord God.”

(Hieronymus.) Those whom we mentioned above—Jews and our Judaizers—refer everything up to the point where the building of the temple follows to the final time. They interpret the flesh of Gog and his entire army as though birds and beasts were to be filled with the flesh of the fattest sacrificial victims; Israel is to be restored to its former condition, and no longer attacked by the nations, while God pours out his spirit upon them, so that they may dwell in their own land—not all the nations, but specifically the house of Israel.

Following the tropological interpretation we have begun, however, we shall say that the Lord summons all the birds and all the beasts in order to hand over the leaders of the heretics to them for devouring, as though they were the fattest sacrificial victims. They are called birds and beasts either because they swiftly range everywhere, or because of their wildness and cruelty. They are handed over to the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved and they may learn not to blaspheme.

They will eat a great and very fat sacrifice—not elsewhere, but upon the mountains of Israel, whom we ought to understand as the prophets, apostles, and holy men. For in them the teachers of opposing doctrines fall, and they perish, wounded by those very men. Upon these mountains the Church is built—or, to speak more truly, upon the mountain of mountains. Isaiah and Micah speak of it:

> “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will announce his way to us” (Isaiah 2; Micah 4).

These swift and savage birds and beasts will eat flesh and drink blood—those who cannot possess the kingdom of God. “The flesh of the mighty,” or of the giants who rebelled against the knowledge of God; and the blood of princes—not of heaven, but of the earth—they will drink, those who have savored all earthly things.

“The blood of rams, lambs, and goats,” or, according to the Seventy, “of rams, calves, and goats,” so that three animals are signified which are sacrificed in God’s victims. For heretics imitate ecclesiastical gentleness, but their offering advances not toward the worship of God but toward the food of demons. It is their very fat sacrifice: they are filled as with fat and drink the blood of the deceived to drunkenness.

God sacrifices this victim through ecclesiastical men, so that the worst banqueters may be filled with the multitude of the deceived and drink to vomiting and drunkenness. When you see holy men, instructed in the divine Scriptures, cutting down the horses and riders of the heretics, of whom it is written, “He cast horse and rider into the sea” (Exodus 15), and striking down all the rebels and giants with their sword, and pouring out the blood of all the warriors of false-name knowledge, then know that the Lord’s table has been prepared, so that he may set his glory among all the nations which believe in his name.

Then they will understand the judgment which he has executed upon the adversaries of the holy churches, and the strong hand with which he has struck them. The house of Israel will know and recognize that he is their Lord God, who said, “I am the Lord your God,” from the day of the Lord’s victory and forever.

They will also reflect that for this reason the house of Israel was once taken captive by the heretics and scattered throughout the entire world of perverse doctrines: because they abandoned him who for a time hid or turned his face away from them, delivered them into the hand of the heretics, and they fell, pierced by their sword, on account of their uncleannesses and iniquities—the reason why he hid and turned his face away from them.

Having set forth the explanations according to what is written, “There must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest” (1 Corinthians 11), he speaks of the captivity of Israel—that is, of the Church, in which those who see God dwell. Now he promises that he will restore the captivity of Jacob to the Church. Jacob had supplanted the Jewish people and was afterward himself supplanted by the frauds of the heretics. He will have mercy upon the whole house of Israel—not according to the flesh but according to the spirit.

“And I will take up,” he says, “my zeal for my holy name,” by which he is blasphemed among the nations because of the heretics, so that, after I have liberated them, they may be ashamed and confounded that they transgressed against me after abandoning the ecclesiastical faith.

They will be very quickly confounded and ashamed when they dwell in their land, the land of the meek and the land of the saints: “And they will dwell confidently,” or “in peace,” fearing no longer the snares of the heretics. Then they will be brought back from the peoples and gathered from the lands of their enemies into their own land. And the Lord will be sanctified in them before the sight of many nations, which will themselves believe in the Lord.

The end and perfection of blessedness will be to know and recognize that he is their Lord God, because he appeared to them among the nations, or transferred them out of the nations, gathered them upon their own land—the land of Judea, the land of confession, the land of the meek, and the land of the living—and left not even one of them to heretical perversity.

He will no longer hide his face from them or turn away from them, because he has poured out his spirit of grace. The prophet Joel also speaks of this:

> “In the last days I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh” (Joel 2).

He will pour it out upon the house of Israel. But if, following the Seventy, we read “fury” instead of “spirit”—a reading not found in the Hebrew—the meaning is that he will no longer hide his face from those upon whom he had previously poured out his fury.

Up to this point in the prophet Ezekiel, with God assisting and, as we hope and believe, opening our mouth, we have spoken without destroying the opinions of others who have written, or of those who may write hereafter, but asserting our own opinions, whatever their worth.

In the building of the temple, however, the order of the priests, the division of the holy land, the river flowing from the temple, the trees ever green on both banks, bearing fruit in each month, and the remaining matters contained in the prophetic book up to its end, we openly confess our ignorance. For the present, we judge it better to say nothing than to say too little.

# BOOK FOURTEEN

[Column 0879]

## PREFACE TO THE KING OF FRANCE

[Column 0879D]

We concluded the preceding book with the words of blessed Jerome, who refused a mystical explanation of the prophet Ezekiel’s final vision. Following the sense of that explanation in his response to the virgin Eustochium, at the beginning of the present book we think that we must respond to you, most noble Emperor, who compel us beyond our strength to expound the aforesaid vision to its end in a moral sense.

I already replied to you when you suggested this to me that, because of the ignorance of my mind and the weakness of my body, I did not dare undertake so great a work—one which the wisest teachers were at least fearful to touch, much less to explain fully in its entirety. But you rejected this reply of mine and pressed more insistently, asking me to begin what you had urged and to strive to bring it to completion, in whatever way I could.

I shall therefore obey your will. As I did in the preceding books, following the footsteps of the holy teachers, I shall briefly and concisely set down what I have found already explained. Whatever divine grace may further inspire me with for completing this work, I shall likewise insert, so that the reader, learning the sayings of the earlier authorities and rereading our own, may follow whatever he judges to be wholesome and useful for himself.

## CHAPTER 40

On the building of the city and the man who stood at the gate and measured the outer wall with his reeds; on the places assigned for the guarding of the temple and altar; on the table of the court and the altar of burnt offerings; and on the measurement of the vestibule of the temple.

> “In the twenty-fifth year of our captivity, at the beginning of the year, on the tenth day of the month, fourteen years after the city was struck down, on that very day the hand of the Lord came upon me, and he brought me there.” (Gregory, in the Commentary, here and thereafter.)

About to speak of mystical matters, he first sets forth the historical narrative, so that what is believed in the revelation may be fixed by its date. It should be noted that at the beginning of this book he indicated the year in which he began to prophesy. At the end, however, he inserted the time when he saw the final vision, so that it may be known over how many years he delivered the book of his prophecy.

For he placed the time when he began to prophesy at the beginning of his discourse, saying:

> “The heavens were opened, and I saw visions of the Lord on the fifth day of the month; that was the fifth year of the captivity of King Jehoiachin.”

Now he says:

> “In the twenty-fifth year of our captivity.”

The same prophet had been taken to Babylon in the first captivity with King Jehoiachin. Concerning the second captivity of Jerusalem he adds:

> “Fourteen years after the city was struck down.”

For Zedekiah had reigned in the city of Jerusalem for eleven years after the first captivity, in which the prophet Ezekiel was led away with King Jehoiachin. After the captivity of that same Zedekiah—which was the city’s second captivity—the prophet saw his final vision in the fourteenth year.

Thus eleven and fourteen joined together make twenty-five. If, therefore, he spoke of the first vision in the fifth year of the earlier captivity, and describes this final vision as having occurred in the twenty-fifth year, it is entirely clear that his discourse continued for twenty years, up to the words of the final vision.

No one should be troubled by the fact that in the middle of his prophetic book, when he was speaking about the Babylonian king, he mentions the twenty-seventh year. Since in that passage he inserts nothing about the time of his own captivity, he plainly demonstrates that he is describing the years of that king, concerning whom he had begun to prophesy.

(Hieronymus.) But if, following Theodotion, in the place where we have read “at the beginning of the year” we read “in the ninth year, on the tenth day of the month,” the ninth year among the Hebrews is called the seventh month. Among them this month has the name *Tishri*, so that on the first day of the seventh month there is the blowing of trumpets, and on the tenth day of that same month there is the day of fasting and expiation.

The fifteenth day, when the whole orb of the moon is complete, is understood as the day of the Feast of Booths. Thus, on the tenth day of the expiation of the Lord, the building of the city was shown to Ezekiel; and just as he demonstrated the restoration—or rather the revivification—of the people in the bones of the plain under the image of the resurrection, so now the Lord promises the restoration of the city, which had been consumed by Babylonian fire fourteen years earlier, under the description of its structure.

Just as the type had shown the captivity and destruction of the burning pot from the face of the north, and the truth of the prophecy had been confirmed by the event, so the truth of the future building might be proved by the prophecy, through faith in what had already occurred.

Nor is this said of the time which certain ignorant Jews propose, when the temple was built under Zerubbabel and under Jesus son of Jozadak the high priest, while Haggai and Zechariah were prophesying. For this temple now being described, together with its priestly order, the division of the land, and its fertility, is much more magnificent than the one Solomon had built.

The temple built under Zerubbabel was so small and so insignificant in comparison with the former one that those who had seen the first temple and afterward looked upon this one lamented and attested their grief with tears. The cry of those who wailed was much louder than the sound of the trumpets. Read the Book of Ezra.

Moreover, what is added—“fourteen years after the city was struck down,” or captured—signifies, according to mystical interpretations, fourteen generations. When these had been completed, from David to the birth of Christ, the restoration of the city is promised by him of whom it is written:

> “He himself will build my city and bring back the captivity of my people” (Isaiah 45:13).

And again:

> “He came to preach release to captives and sight to the blind, saying to those who were in chains, ‘Come out,’ and to those who were in darkness, ‘Be revealed’” (Isaiah 61).

(Gregory.) What is it, then, that through this final vision almighty God deigned to show the mercy of his promise on that very day on which, in the stricken city, he fulfilled the wrath of justice, except that the power of divinity—which is not said to be diverse, moved, or changeable—by that same light of justice gives life to those afflicted and repentant, while it strikes down the proud and obstinate?

Having first stated the time of his vision, he adds:

> “The hand of the Lord came upon me, and he brought me there. In the visions of the Lord he brought me into the land of Israel.”

What he had said, “He brought me there,” he repeats by adding, “He brought me into the land of Israel.” He says:

> “The hand of the Lord came upon me, and he brought me there in the visions of the Lord.”

For the hand signifies the power of authority, while the visions signify the revelation itself which he had received. The hand, therefore, is in the vision, and power is in contemplation. What does he plainly indicate by these words except that he says nothing literally about the city which he had seen? For he speaks spiritually about a city which he contemplates spiritually.

> “And he set me upon a very high mountain.”

Whom, then, does the very high mountain signify except the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2), who is indeed from the earth but is above the earth? His flesh, that is, has its material from the depths, but by his power he rises above the heights. It would have been insufficient to call him “high” unless he had added “very high”: for he was made not only man, but, through the conception of that humanity which was assumed by him, God-man; not merely man above human beings, but man also made higher than the angels.

(Hieronymus.) The hand of the Lord comes upon him so that, although situated in Babylon according to the flesh, he may come in spirit to the land of Israel; and he is placed, not merely in a vision but in the visions of God, upon a very high mountain, concerning which Isaiah and Micah prophesy:

> “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob” (Isaiah 2; Micah 4).

This mountain is very high in comparison with the other mountains, of which the Prophet bears witness, saying:

> “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains; from there will my help come” (Psalm 120).

> “And upon it there was something like the structure of a city, facing toward the south.”

(Gregory.) It should be noted that it does not say, “Upon it there was a structure,” but “something like a structure,” so that it might be shown that everything was being said not about the structure of a bodily city but of a spiritual city. For he who declares that he saw not a structure but something like a structure directs the heart of the hearers toward a spiritual construction, as it is said through the Psalmist:

> “Jerusalem, which is built as a city” (Psalm 121).

Because in it the vision of earthly peace is constructed from the gathering of holy citizens, heavenly Jerusalem is built as a city. Yet, because in this land of pilgrimage it is struck by scourges and beaten by tribulations, its stones are daily squared. It is itself the city, namely, the holy Church, which is destined to reign in heaven but still labors on earth, in which “the Lord is great and exceedingly worthy of praise, in the city of our God, on his holy mountain” (Psalm 45).

(Hieronymus.) God is known in the towers of this city when he receives it. Of it another passage says:

> “The force of the river gladdens the city of God” (Psalm 45).

And again:

> “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matthew 5),

which says in Isaiah:

> “I am a fortified city, a city under attack” (Isaiah 26).

He did not say “a city that is conquered,” but “a city that is attacked”: a city built upon a rock and shaken by no storm.

(Gregory.) This city already possesses here a great building in the conduct of the saints. In a building, one stone supports another: one stone is placed upon another, and the one who supports is supported by the other. Thus in the holy Church each person both supports another and is supported by another. For neighbors mutually endure one another, so that through them the building of charity may rise.

Hence Paul admonishes us, saying:

> “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6).

Declaring the power of this law, he says:

> “The fullness of the law is charity” (Romans 13).

For if I neglect to bear with you in your conduct, and you disdain to tolerate me in mine, from where does the building of charity arise among us, when mutual love does not join us through patience?

The stones placed at the summit and outermost edge of the structure are themselves carried by others, but they do not carry others. For those who are to be born at the end of the Church—that is, at the end of the world—are indeed tolerated by their predecessors so that their conduct may be shaped toward good merits; but since they are not followed by those who might advance through them, no faithful person already carries upon himself the stones of the building.

Now, therefore, others are carried by us, while we have been carried by others. The foundation bears the entire weight of the structure, because our one Redeemer bears the conduct of all alike. Concerning him Paul says:

> “No one can lay another foundation except that which has been laid” (1 Corinthians 3).

It should also be noted that the city which the Prophet saw was facing toward the south. Those who are attentive to sacred language recognize that the south wind is customarily understood as a figure of the Holy Spirit. Conversely, the north often signifies the devil, because it slackens in heat and constricts in cold. Truth says:

> “When iniquity has abounded, the charity of many will grow cold” (Matthew 24).

This city, therefore, is said to face toward the south, as though it were plainly said: That former city, the synagogue, stood toward the north in its unbelieving members and endured in the cold of faithlessness. But the holy Church, which has conceived the warmth of faith’s charity, faces toward the south through heat and is, as it were, fanned by a warm wind; it rejoices not in its own confidence but in the gift of spiritual grace.

“And he brought me there.”

(Hieronymus.) The hand of God is understood. “There” means, as it were, to the structure of the city, so that he might show him there everything that was within.

(Gregory.) The one who enters the building of the heavenly city is the one who considers, by imitating them, the ways of the good in the holy Church. To enter the building means to observe lovingly how the elect of the holy Church advance in the Lord.

Whoever therefore diligently strives to observe life in the holy Church, so that he may advance either in the life of the good married, or in the fortress of those who practice continence and abandon everything belonging to this world, or even in the eminence of preachers, has already entered the building of the city set upon the mountain.

But whoever neglects to consider the life of those who are better in order to advance still stands outside the structure. If he admires the honor which the holy Church already possesses in the world, he sees and marvels at the building from outside; and because he is intent only upon external things, he has not entered within.

“And behold, a man whose appearance was like the appearance of bronze.” [Col. 0884D] He who is prefigured by the mountain is signified in the man; and this man is said to measure the building. Rightly, the Lord is signified both by the man and by the mountain, because he himself orders everything within the holy Church by judging, and he himself carries that same holy Church and, by carrying it, raises it to heavenly things.

Thus also in the holy Gospel our Redeemer himself speaks, saying: “He who enters through the door is the shepherd of the sheep” (John 10). And shortly afterward: “I am the door.” Then again, after a little, he adds: “I am the good shepherd.” If, therefore, he is himself both shepherd and door, and the shepherd enters through the door, why should he not here also be understood as both the mountain and the man who measures the building on the mountain—that man, namely, of whom it is written: “Behold, the man whose name is Orient” (Zech. 6)?

(Jerome.) He did not have the appearance of electrum, as is said at the beginning of this book, nor was he girded with a golden belt, as is related in John’s Apocalypse (Rev. 1), but according to the Hebrew he had the appearance of bronze. This material is more resonant than all metals and carries its ringing sound far. Hence also in Daniel (Dan. 2), in the image composed of gold, silver, bronze, and iron, the kingdom of Alexander and the Greeks is represented by the likeness of bronze, so that the eloquence of the Greek language might be signified. From this it is clear that those who do not yet fully know the mysteries of the spiritually built temple still require instruction. We all know, moreover, that bronze is a very durable metal and thoroughly resonant.

(Gregory.) What, then, does it mean that the appearance of the mediator between God and human beings is compared with the appearance of bronze, except what we plainly know: that the only-begotten Son, taking the form of a servant, changed the frailty of human flesh into eternity through the glory of his resurrection? For in him the flesh has now become enduring without end: “Rising from the dead, he dies no more, and death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6). What does it mean, moreover, that his incarnation itself is compared with the sound of metal, except that through this assumption of our humanity the glory of his majesty resounded to all?

“And a linen cord was in his hand.”

(Jerome.) The linen cord is not found in the Septuagint translators, but rather “a builder’s cord.” The cord in his hand was either a linen cord or a builder’s cord; concerning it, it is written in Zechariah (Zech. 2) that he had a measuring cord, in order to measure the breadth and length of the city. The builders may signify either the angels who minister at God’s command, or Moses and all the prophets and apostles who build the city of God and are helpers or ministers of the Lord’s will.

(Gregory.) Whom else should we understand by builders than the holy teachers who, by speaking spiritual things, fit living stones—that is, the souls of the elect—together for the heavenly building? Whatever the ancient Fathers, whatever the prophets, whatever the apostles, whatever the successors of the apostles have said: what else was it but the fitting together of stones in this structure of the saints, which is built each day? With a builder’s cord it is customary to determine the equality or straightness of a rising wall: if a stone is inward, it is said to be outward; if it projects outward, it is drawn back inward. The preaching of teachers certainly does this each day: whatever soul perhaps ought not to assume the burdens of governance, even if it desires to appear outwardly, is recalled inward; and again, one that wishes to remain hidden and care only for itself, if it can be useful to itself and to many, is brought outward so that it may appear, even when it desires to remain hidden. Thus the order of the holy stones is maintained, when the one who willingly seeks honor is often rejected, while the one who flees honor is raised to the summit of the sacred order.

But since, as we have learned through our translator, the Hebrew history does not have “a builder’s cord,” but rather “a linen cord in his hand,” we should explain what is more certainly found in our text. We know that a linen cord is finer than cords made from other materials. And what should we understand by the linen cord except a finer preaching, that is, spiritual preaching?

The severity of the Law was indeed a cord, but it was not linen, because it restrained a crude people without subtle preaching. Through penance it cut away not the sins of thought but those of deed. But after the Lord himself, by preaching, had also bound human thoughts, and it became known that sin is perfected even in the heart, he held a linen cord in his hand. For he says: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you: Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.” The linen cord, therefore, is subtle preaching, which binds the mind of the hearer so that it may not loosen itself even in wretched thought.

And what follows:

“And a measuring reed was in his hand.”

(Jerome.) This signifies prophetic grace, concerning which it is written in the forty-fourth Psalm: “My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe.”

(Gregory.) Concerning the holy Church, the Lord promises through another prophet, saying: “The greenness of reed and rush shall arise in it” (Isa. 35). I remember having explained elsewhere that writers should be understood by the reed, and hearers by the rush. But since both the rush and the reed usually grow in the moisture of water, and both draw their growth from the same water, while the reed is taken up for writing but writing cannot be done with the rush, what should we understand by rush and reed except that there is one teaching of truth that irrigates many hearers? Yet, once irrigated, some progress so far in the word of God that they even become writers, like reeds; others hear the word of life and retain the truth of good hope and upright works, but are nevertheless entirely unable to write. What are these in the water of God except, so to speak, certain rushes? Such men do progress by learning, but they are in no way able to form letters.

Our Redeemer, therefore, because he granted that the words he spoke should also be written through the labor of teachers, held a reed in his hand. It is called a measuring reed because the labors of teachers are held under the dispensation of a hidden judgment, so that they may benefit some who read and be unable to benefit others who read. Hence, when the holy apostles asked for a teacher who would speak the truth more openly, why he spoke to the crowds in parables, they heard: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not” (Luke 8).

Or certainly the reed is a measuring reed because, in his sacred speech itself, we recognize that what has been written for us contains hidden dispensations. For by his incomprehensible judgment one person is brought within the measure of the elect, while another is left outside, so that he may in no way deserve to belong to the number of the elect.

He therefore has a cord; he has a measuring reed in his hand. For one who measures a place with a cord draws the cord in one place, pulls it back from another, brings it here, and withdraws it elsewhere. In precisely this way our Redeemer acts in the gathering of human beings: he leads some out of their sins, while he leaves others in their sin. In those whom he has deigned to gather, he has drawn the cord of hidden measure; and from those whom he judged should be left behind, what else has he done but withdraw the cord? Thus the good are held within the measure of the heavenly structure, while the wicked remain outside the structure, in whom there are no good things deemed worthy of esteem, as though without measure.

Our Redeemer held this cord and measuring reed in his hand when he deigned to admonish the apostle Paul through the appearance of a Macedonian man (Acts 16), so that the same Macedonian man said: “Cross over and help us.” Yet, when the apostles wished to go to preach in Asia, the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them. Why is it that the holy apostles are called to go where they perhaps had not been thinking of going, and are forbidden to go where they desired? Is it not because the cord of hidden judgment and the measuring reed are held in his hand, so that some may hear the words of life while others may in no way deserve to hear them?

The measuring reed may also be understood as Holy Scripture, because whoever reads it measures himself in it: how much he progresses in spiritual virtue, how far he has remained separated from the good things commanded, how much he is already rising to do good, and how much he still lies prostrate in evil deeds.

It follows:

“But he stood at the gate.”

(Jerome.) He stood at the gate because through him we enter to the Father, and without him we cannot enter the city of God: so that he may receive the worthy and cast out the unworthy. Judgment is also at the gate; hence the Prophet says: “They hated those who rebuked at the gate” (Ps. 29); and elsewhere: “They shall not be confounded when they speak with their enemies at the gate.”

This man spoke to the prophet. In his hand was the cord, and his appearance was like bronze; he held the reed in his hand. He spoke to Ezekiel as the true architect whom the apostle Paul imitated when he said: “As a wise architect I laid the foundation” (1 Cor. 3). He calls the architect wise in distinction from one who is foolish. In Zechariah (Zech. 11) he is called a foolish shepherd.

(Gregory.) Whoever stands at the gate is, in one respect, inside and, in another, outside, because one aspect of him is seen outwardly while another is hidden within. Our Redeemer, therefore, incarnate for our sake, mercifully stood before human eyes as though at a gate: he appeared visible through his humanity and preserved himself invisible in his divinity.

For this reason the Jews, who had awaited him according to the promise of the prophets, were thrown into confusion by the shame of their unbelief: the one whom they believed would come for their deliverance, they saw as mortal. Whoever stands at the gate, as was said above, is seen in one respect outside and in another inside. Thus the unbelief of the Jews was not entirely abandoned by the manifestation of divine power. For, seeing his miracles, they were drawn to believe; but, considering his passion, they disdained to believe that the one they saw as mortal was God. Hence it happened that they doubted concerning his identity.

They saw him hungry, thirsty, eating, drinking, growing weary, and sleeping, and they judged him to be a mere human being. They saw him raising the dead, cleansing lepers, giving sight to the blind, and casting out demons, and they perceived that he was more than human. Yet the humanity they considered in his very miracles disturbed their hearts. Therefore the holy Church, already desiring to see him openly in the voice of the bride, says: “Behold, he stands behind our wall” (Song 2).

He who displayed to human eyes what he had assumed from mortal nature, while remaining invisible in himself, stood, as it were, behind a wall for one seeking to see him openly: he did not present himself to be seen in the majesty that had been revealed. For he stood, as it were, behind a wall: he displayed the nature of humanity that he had assumed and concealed the nature of divinity from human eyes.

But since this man is said to stand at the gate, we must ask whether he stood with his face toward the inside and his back toward the outside. He therefore stood inside, with his face toward the outside. If we examine what has been said before and what follows, we quickly discover how he stood.

First it is said: “It was like a structure of a city facing toward the south, and he brought me in there”; and shortly afterward it is added concerning the same man: “But he stood at the gate,” and immediately thereafter: “The same man spoke to me.”

(Gregory.) Since, after bringing the prophet into the building, he stood at the gate and spoke, it is surely evident that he stood with his face toward the inside and his back toward the outside. But when the prophet had been brought in, and the man standing at the gate spoke, he undoubtedly had his face turned toward the gate, from which the prophet heard the speaker’s words.

What does it mean that the man looks inward while the prophet is outside? What does it mean that the man’s face is turned toward the building while the prophet’s eyes are toward the gate, except that the only-begotten Son of the Father was incarnate for this reason: to bring us into the spiritual building, that is, into the faith of the holy Church? Those whose eyes he continually directs toward his building are the ones who constantly observe how much each person progresses in the virtues.

The prophet looks from gate to gate because whoever hears the words of God ought always to place the eyes of his heart upon his departure and meditate without ceasing on when he will leave the present life and reach eternal joys. For this reason God was incarnate: to bring us into faith and lead us out into the vision of himself. Hence also he speaks in the holy Gospel, saying: “If anyone enters through me, he will be saved; and he will enter and go out and find pasture” (John 10). He will enter, that is, into faith; he will go out into vision; and he will find pasture in eternal satisfaction.

The Psalmist also says: “May the Lord guard your entrance and your departure” (Ps. 120). The Lord guards each soul’s entrance, by which it enters into faith, and its departure, by which it goes out into vision, so that neither, while entering the Church, may it be overthrown by errors, nor, while still leaving temporal things for the eternal, may it be snatched away by the ancient enemy.

The man, therefore, who appeared stood at the gate and spoke in this way, because Christ Jesus, the mediator between God and human beings, gave the disciples the commandments of life even at the very time of his passion: so that those who believe in him might always look toward the gate and, weighing his passion with attentive consideration, might not turn the eyes of their hearts away from their own departure.

When we, too, have begun to despise the barriers of the flesh, to pass through the narrowness of our mortality by the desire for immortality, to strive toward the freedom of the heavenly light, and to long for the joys of our heavenly homeland, we keep our eyes toward the gate. For while we desire to pass from temporal sacraments to eternal things, we have, so to speak, already turned our backs on the present life and keep the face of our hearts fixed upon the desire for our departure.

[Col. 0889B] “Son of man, see with your eyes and hear with your ears.” After he has been led to a testimony of spiritual things, why is he told, “See with your eyes,” with “your” being added? And when it says, “Hear with your ears,” why is “your” likewise added?

It should be understood that bodily eyes and ears are also present in carnal people and are used by them for things perceived bodily. But the eyes and ears of the heart belong only to spiritual things: they see invisible things through understanding and hear the praise of God without sound. The almighty Lord was seeking these ears when he said: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8).

Why, whenever the prophet is led to see spiritual things, is he called “son of man,” except because by this designation he is always reminded of what derives from weakness, lest he be exalted by the greatness of his contemplation?

It should also be noted that the expressions are different: “See with your eyes,” “hear with your ears,” and yet he is called “son of man.” But what else is plainly said to him through these words except: Look upon spiritual things spiritually—and yet remember the weakness of your flesh?

This is also why it often happens that one who is more deeply caught up in contemplation is more heavily wearied in temptation. Thus it frequently happens to those who are making good progress: when their mind is either affected by compunction or carried above itself by contemplation, temptation immediately follows, lest they become exalted over the things to which they have been carried. For through compunction or contemplation the mind is raised to God, but, struck back by the weight of temptation, it returns to itself; thus temptation weighs it down, lest contemplation inflate it, while contemplation raises it up, lest temptation overwhelm it.

“See,” he says, “with your eyes and hear with your ears.”

(Jerome.) Not with the eyes of the flesh, but of the spirit; not with the ears of the body, but of the soul. “Lift up,” he says, “your eyes and see, for the fields are already white for harvest” (John 4). And: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8).

The construction of the city is seen, and the order of the ceremonies, and the description of the priests and of the land, is heard. It was not enough to command him to see with his eyes and hear with his ears; he also added: “And set your heart on everything,” or, “Set in your heart everything that I shall show you.” For it is of no benefit to have seen and heard unless you place what you see and hear in the treasury of memory.

When he says, “Everything that I shall show you,” he makes the hearer attentive. He also prepares the eyes of the heart, so that he may retain in memory what is to be shown him, because you have been brought here so that everything may be shown to you.

By this statement he shows in particular that nothing is sweeter than the contemplation and knowledge for which the prophet longs, saying: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to behold the delight of the Lord and to visit his temple” (Ps. 26). Hence he adds and says: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where the glory of your dwelling resides” (Ps. 25).

“Announce,” he says, “everything that you see to the house of Israel,” so that those who cannot see for themselves may learn through you what is shown to you by the Lord.

The house of Israel means those who perceive God with the mind.
