Among them was Nathanael, who sought Christ with the greatest devotion and deserved to hear: “Behold, a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John 1). He sees in order to announce who, in proportion as he himself has progressed, also takes care through preaching that his neighbor may progress. Hence it is written elsewhere: “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come.’” For whoever already has the voice of the calling God in his heart must necessarily burst forth in the voice with the ministry of preaching to his neighbor, and therefore call another who has himself already been called.

“And behold, an outer wall all around the house on every side.”

(Gregory.) Often in sacred speech the incarnate Lord himself is called a wall because of the protection he provides, as it is said concerning the holy Church through the Prophet: “A wall and a rampart shall be placed in it.” He himself is our wall, surrounding us on every side by his protection.

The prophets, however, were the rampart before our wall, because before the Lord appeared in the flesh they were sent to construct faith by prophesying. It should be noted that this wall of the spiritual building is said to be outside. A wall built for the fortification of a building is ordinarily placed not inside but outside.

Why, then, was it necessary to say “outside,” when a wall is never ordinarily placed inside and must necessarily be placed outside in order to defend what is within? But what else is plainly demonstrated by this word except the Lord’s incarnation? God is a wall for us within; the wall outside is God made human.

Hence it is said to him through a certain prophet: “You went forth for the salvation of your people, to save your anointed ones” (Hab. 3). This wall—that is, the incarnate Lord—would not be a wall for us if he had not been outside, because he would not protect us within if he had not appeared outwardly.

Nor should we pass over carelessly the fact that this wall is said to be placed all around the house, on every side. The house of God is not only the holy angels, concerning whom the Psalmist says: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place of the dwelling of your glory” (Ps. 25); we too are his house, since he deigns to dwell in our minds.

The wall is all around the house on every side because the only-begotten Son of the Father, who is above and is the strength of the angels, himself became below the redemption of human beings: for them, strength lest they fall; for us, help so that we may rise after falling.

If, however, by the house of God in this passage only the multitude of redeemed human beings is signified, the Lord is our wall on every side and all around. To guard us perfectly, he showed us everything that he taught. As it is written: “What Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1).

Because he came to call us to the heavenly homeland, he taught us to despise transitory goods and not to fear temporal evils. Hence he despised insults, endured injuries, did not fear death, and did not shrink from the gallows of the cross. When they wished to seize him and make him king, he immediately fled, indicating to us by these examples that we ought both not to fear the adversities of this world and to avoid its prosperities, since its goods more often occupy the mind than its evils disturb it.

Before his passion he heard insults, yet did not return insults. He silently endured his betrayer for a long time and did not refuse to give a kiss to the one who greeted him falsely. He accepted death so that we would not fear dying. He showed the resurrection so that we might believe that we can rise again. After his passion, he also called those who had crucified him to the grace of faith and returned a gift in place of their iniquity.

He therefore became a wall for us all around and on every side, since he instructed us in everything by his example.

It follows:

“And in the man’s hand was a measuring reed of six cubits and a palm.”

(Jerome.) The measuring reed, which had six cubits and a palm, signifies that our conduct is known to God, since it is contained within the six days in which the world was made; and that the reckoning of our individual works is known to him, so that one aspect pertains to works and another to the mind. Hence the breadth is equal to the height: breadth refers, as we have said, to works, while height refers to the mind that hastens toward high things.

It is enough to have warned once that I know *cubitus* and *cubita* to be neuter in gender. But for simplicity, ease of understanding, and common usage, I use the masculine gender. For we are not concerned to avoid faults of speech, but to explain the obscurity of Holy Scripture in whatever words may serve.

(Gregory.) Since the reed signifies Holy Scripture, we have already said in the preceding exposition that it is called a measuring reed because we measure all the activity of our life by it, so that we may see either how much we progress or how far we remain from progress.

For often, when doing something, we already think that we possess a certain merit. But when we return to the words of God and hear the sublime commandments, we recognize how far we still fall short of progress. The measuring reed, therefore, is that by which the life of hearers is measured through the hands of those who write.

This reed is said to be in the hand of the man either because sacred speech is in the power of the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, or certainly because he completed by his works what he wished to be written.

The same reed is described as six cubits long. There are two lives in which almighty God instructs us through sacred speech: the active and the contemplative. What else is expressed by the six cubits except the active life, since on the sixth day God completed all his works?

The palm, however, which is said to be above the six cubits, belongs already to the seventh, yet it is not a cubit. Thus the active life is signified by the six cubits and the contemplative life by the palm, because we complete the former through work, while in the latter, even when we stretch out our heart toward it, we can scarcely touch a small part.

The active life is to give bread to the hungry, to teach the ignorant by the word of wisdom, to correct the erring, to recall a proud neighbor to the way of humility, to care for the weak, to dispense to each person what is useful, and to provide for those entrusted to us how they may be able to persevere.

The contemplative life, however, is to retain the love of God and neighbor with the whole mind, while resting from external action and clinging to the desire for the Creator alone, so that one no longer wishes to do anything, but, having trampled down all cares, the mind burns to see the face of its Creator. It already knows how to bear with sorrow the burden of corruptible flesh, while longing with all its desires to be present among the hymn-singing choirs of angels, to be joined to the heavenly citizens, and to rejoice in incorruption eternal in the presence of God.

In the palm, therefore, the hand and fingers are extended, but only a small portion of the cubit’s measure is reached by the palm. For however greatly the mind may burn with love, and however much it may stretch itself toward God in virtue and thought, it does not yet see perfectly what it loves; rather, it is only beginning to see what it will love. For, as the most powerful preacher says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13). And: “Now I know in part, but then I shall know even as I am known” (ibid.).

“And he measured the breadth of the building with one reed, and its height also with one reed.”

(Gregory.) Almighty God, who is neither extended by great things nor confined by small ones, speaks of the whole Church together as though he were speaking of one soul. And often nothing prevents what he says of one soul from being understood of the whole Church at once.

The breadth of the building pertains to charity, concerning which the Psalmist says: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. 118). Nothing is broader than to receive everyone into the bosom of love and to endure no narrowness of hatred. Charity is so broad that in the expansiveness of its love it can contain even enemies. Hence it is commanded: “Love your enemies and do good to those who hate you” (Matt. 5).

We should also consider that breadth extends toward equality, while height extends toward sublimity. Breadth therefore pertains to love of neighbor, and height to the understanding of the contemplative. But the breadth and height of the building are measured by one reed, because each soul, to the extent that it is broad in love of neighbor, is also lofty in the knowledge of God. For as it enlarges itself beside itself through love, it is exalted above itself through knowledge; and it becomes as lofty above itself as it extends itself beside itself in love of neighbor.

The building inhabited by God is completed from both angelic and human nature: the angelic creature is above, while the human creature is still below. These two creatures may also be signified by the breadth and height of the building, since one remains still in lowliness while the other abides in the heights. Yet both are measured by one reed, because human humility will one day be brought to equality with the angels. Hence it is written: “They neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels in heaven.” And through John it is said: “The measure of a human being, which is that of an angel” (Rev. 21).

Humanity is brought to that height of glory at which the angels rejoice that they are established. The breadth of the building, therefore, is as great as its height, because all the elect who now labor in lowliness will one day not be unequal to those most blessed spirits.

[Col. 0893B] “And he came to the gate that faced the eastern road, and he went up its steps, and he measured the threshold of the gate with one reed in breadth—that is, one threshold with one reed in breadth.” (Jerome) A man whose name is “Orient” enters through the eastern gate, so that he may illuminate those whom he finds at the front of the vestibule, or at the very entrance of the gate. He does not enter by one step but by several, whose number is not stated, so that the difficulty of the ascent may be apparent; and however many steps you may imagine, know that they are fewer than the number left uncertain.

I think this is the gate of which the Psalmist also sings: “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it” (Psalm 117). (Gregory) But who else is signified by the name of this gate except the Lord himself and our Redeemer, who became for us the door of the heavenly kingdom, as he himself says: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14)?

But since we have said that the same man clothed in linen bears the figure of the Lord, we must ask how it can be appropriate for the same Lord to be signified both by the man and by the gate. When the man comes to the gate, does he perhaps come to himself? Or is it rather so because in the Gospel he himself testifies, saying: “He who does not enter the sheepfold through the door, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber; but he who enters through the door is the shepherd of the sheep” (John 10). And a little later it is said: “I am the door.” Then he adds: “I am the good shepherd.” If, therefore, the shepherd enters through the door, and he himself is the door and himself the shepherd, then without doubt he enters through himself.

Behold, as we seek to unravel the meaning of Ezekiel, let us also read a question from the Gospel. We must therefore ask how he both enters and enters through himself. For the Lord and our Redeemer is one substance with the holy Church, which he redeemed according to the flesh, as Paul bears witness, saying: “I complete what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ in my flesh, for the sake of his body, which is the Church” (Colossians 1). The Church is the body of that Head, and Christ is the Head of this body.

Of this Head he exalted the body, that is, the holy Church, when through the Psalmist he says: “But now he has exalted my head above my enemies.” Since the Church herself too is to be exalted one day, she already rejoices in heaven that her Head has been exalted above her enemies. Therefore, when all the elect attain life, because they are his members and through him enter to him, he enters through himself to himself: for it is he who enters in his members; he is the Head to whom the entering members come.

The prophet Ezekiel also indicates this in many ways. He says that a man came to the gate and shows which gate it is by saying: “the one that faced the eastern road.” For he himself is also the way, who said: “I am the way and the truth” (John 14). He is also the eastern way, of whom it is written: “Behold, a man whose name is Orient” (Zechariah 6). Therefore the gate faces the eastern way because it signifies him who made for us a path to the rising of the light.

[Col. 0894B] The name “gate” may also signify each preacher, because whoever opens the door of the heavenly kingdom for us with his mouth is a gate. Hence twelve gates are described either in John’s Apocalypse (Revelation 21) or in the final vision of this prophet.

The name “gate” may also appropriately signify knowledge of the sacred Scriptures, which, when it opens understanding for us, throws open the door of the heavenly kingdom. By the name “gate” we may also understand faith, which we first touch in order to enter the structure of the virtues.

“He went up,” it says, “by its steps.” For what are the steps of this gate except the merits of the virtues? Unless, in the knowledge of Christ Jesus, the mediator of God and human beings, or in the knowledge of divine speech, or in the faith that we have received concerning him, we advance by certain steps toward higher attainments, no one suddenly becomes supreme. In a good way of life each person begins with small things in order to reach great ones.

The Lord describes these steps under the figure of the harvest, saying (Mark 4): “The kingdom of God is as if a man should cast seed upon the ground, and sleep and rise night and day, and the seed should sprout and grow, while he does not know how. For the earth bears fruit of itself: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. And when the fruit has appeared, immediately he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come.”

A person casts seed upon the earth when he implants a good intention in his heart. After he has cast the seed, he sleeps, because he already rests in the hope of a good work. He rises by night and by day—that is, he advances amid adversity and prosperity. The seed sprouts and grows while he does not know how, because he is still unable to measure his own progress; once conceived, virtue is led onward toward growth.

The earth bears fruit of itself because, when grace goes before it, the human mind rises spontaneously toward the fruit of good works. But this same earth first produces the blade, then the ear, and then full grain in the ear. To produce the blade is to possess the still-tender beginnings of goodness. The blade reaches the ear when virtue conceived in the soul draws it onward toward the progress of good works. It produces full grain in the ear when virtue has advanced so far that it can become the substance of a strong and perfected work.

“When the fruit has appeared, immediately he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come.” [Col. 0895A] For almighty God puts in the sickle when the fruit has appeared and cuts down his harvest: when he has led each person to perfected works, he cuts short that person’s temporal life by a sentence sent forth, so that he may bring his grain to the heavenly storehouses.

The man clothed in linen therefore comes to the gate because the Lord and our Redeemer is brought to himself when his members enter; and he goes up its steps because, as we make progress, he is exalted for us all the more, insofar as he is recognized as lofty and incomprehensible. He is said to ascend in the steps of our virtues because he appears to us so much higher as our mind is separated from lowly things.

“And he measured,” it says, “the threshold of the gate with one reed in breadth—that is, one threshold with one reed in breadth.”

[Col. 0895B] (Jerome) He measured the threshold of the gate so that we might know that everything is open to the knowledge of God. The threshold is said to be one reed in breadth, while its height and length are not stated. For it is a way and an entrance; through it one must proceed toward the interior.

(Gregory) Why, after “the threshold of the gate” has been said, is “one threshold” immediately added, unless it openly indicates that another threshold is still to be mentioned below? The gate rises from the threshold so that it may be a gate. If, therefore, the gate is the Lord, who is the threshold of this gate except the ancient fathers, from whose lineage the Lord deigned to become incarnate, as Paul says: “To them belong the fathers, and from them, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Romans 9)?

It should be noted in this statement of Paul that gods and other human beings are also called gods, as it is said to Moses: “I will appoint you as a god to Pharaoh” (Exodus 7). And through the Psalmist the Lord says: “I said, You are gods” (Psalm 81). Again: “God has taken his stand in the assembly of gods” (Psalm 81). But it is one thing to be called God by designation, and another to be called God by nature. Although Moses was appointed as a god to Pharaoh, he is said to be a god within all things, not God over all things. But he who was made incarnate in the womb of the Virgin is called God over all things.

Thus the threshold of the gate is the fathers from whom he was born who opened for us access to the heavenly kingdom. The threshold of the gate is measured with one reed: those ancient fathers who were able to proclaim our Redeemer both by prophecy and by living well possessed, as it were, six cubits in perfection of works and a palm in the beginning of contemplation. Their life, made noble by unity of faith, perfected action, and incipient contemplation, constituted the measure of the threshold in one reed.

It follows:

“And the chamber was one reed in length and one reed in breadth.”

[Col. 0895D] (Jerome) Although in this passage the Septuagint, as is found in many copies, superfluously mentions length and breadth, and calls the chambers *thalamos* and the side-posts *parasades* [παρασάδες], each has one reed both in length and height; but there are five cubits between chamber and chamber, so that the inner parts of the chambers may have the full measure of a reed—that is, six cubits and one palm—when works and reason agree together.

[Col. 0896A] But the things that are outside, namely the five cubits between chamber and chamber, have not yet penetrated the secrets of Christ and cannot say: “The king brought me into his chamber” (Song of Songs 1). And elsewhere: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Psalm 45). Rather, while the disciples who remain at home with Christ hear his mysteries, these cannot; they desire God’s word to go out to them. Therefore a measure of five cubits is assigned to them, so that they may be taught to refer everything to the five senses.

(Gregory) Let us consider what ordinarily takes place in a chamber, and from this gather what takes place in the holy Church. In a chamber the bridegroom and bride are joined in covenant and united to one another in love. What, then, are the chambers in the holy Church except the hearts in which the soul is joined by love to the invisible Bridegroom, so that it burns with desire for him, desires nothing that is in the world, regards the length of the present life as punishment, hastens to depart, and rests in the embrace of love in the vision of the heavenly Bridegroom?

A mind that has already become such receives no consolation from the present life, but sighs from its depths for him whom it loves; it burns, breathes after him, and is troubled. Even the health of its body becomes worthless to it, because it has been pierced by the wound of love. Hence in the Song of Songs it says: “I am wounded by love” (Song of Songs 2). A heart that knows nothing of the pain of this wound possesses an unhealthy well-being.

But when the soul begins to breathe after heavenly desire and to feel the wound of love, it becomes healthier through the wound, whereas previously it was sick through its health. For a mind that loves its Bridegroom strongly, the one consolation concerning the delay of the present life is this: that, because it is kept from his vision, other souls may advance through his word and burn with the flames of love for the heavenly Bridegroom.

Let us consider, I beg, what kind of chamber the mind of Paul had, when he said: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1). With how great a love had he united himself to almighty God, who reckoned life to be Christ alone and death to be gain? Hence he says again: “Having the desire to depart and to be with Christ, which is much better.”

But behold: we see how deeply you languish in love, you who desire to depart. Since you see yourself meanwhile being delayed, why do you not seek to be supported by flowers? He does seek this, plainly, for he continues: “But to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake.” And to disciples who were making progress he says: “For what is our hope or joy or crown of glory? Is it not you before our Lord Jesus?”

Hence the same chamber is said to have been measured with one reed in length and one reed in breadth. Length pertains to the long-suffering of expectation, and breadth to the expansiveness of love. Therefore each chamber has as much length as it is able to have breadth, because a mind kindled by heavenly desire shows as much long-suffering in waiting for God as it possesses love for gathering in its neighbor, and it patiently bears the delays of time while expanding itself for the neighbor’s progress through the breadth of charity.

The length itself may also signify the long-suffering of patience shown toward the neighbor. And because breadth signifies charity, which opens the bosom of the mind and receives both friends and enemies into love, the chamber has as much length as breadth: for the wider the mind is through love, the more patient it is through long-suffering. Each person bears with the neighbor to the extent that he loves.

It follows:

“And between the chambers, five cubits.”

[Col. 0897A] (Gregory) He had spoken above of one chamber, and afterward says that there are five cubits between the chambers, for the reason that many chambers make one, just as many churches are called one Church. Hence in John’s Apocalypse (Revelation 12) it is written to seven churches, through which the one catholic Church is signified.

Those who, as we have said, thirst in the holy Church to see God with fervent love and are already joined to him through desire are called chambers. Yet there are some within it who, unable to penetrate subtle things and still weighed down by the five bodily senses, love him who made all things so much less as they are more tightly bound to things that have been made.

They do indeed strive to exercise themselves in the fear of the Lord and to extend themselves in love of their neighbor; they perform good works bodily and redeem sins by almsgiving. But because they do not know how to burn inwardly with love for heavenly desire, they are still held, as it were, bound by the bodily senses.

These, therefore, are not chambers, but they are contained among the chambers. Through the guidance of those who love the vision of God perfectly, they too are led toward progress of mind. There are therefore five cubits between the chambers, because those who have not yet risen from the external five senses to mystical understanding, while they are among those who burn with the spirit of love, make progress in the construction of faith as though dwelling among the chambers, and are not separated from the measure of the heavenly building.

For they withdraw themselves somewhat from the appetite of bodily senses and, enlarging the space of the mind, imitate the charity they see; extending themselves here and there, they reach toward the chambers. The fact that they are described not by six cubits but by five signifies their still-existing imperfection. Yet they are remembered as being within the measure of the spiritual building through good desire, because the voice of the holy Church says through the Psalmist: “Your eyes saw my imperfect state, and in your book they are all written” (Psalm 139). Again the Psalmist says: “The Lord has blessed all who fear him, the small together with the great.”

They are therefore imperfect and small. Yet insofar as they are able, they love God and their neighbor, and for that reason they do not neglect to perform the good things they can. Even if they have not yet advanced to spiritual gifts, so as to be able to take hold of the mind for perfected action or kindled contemplation, they do not depart. Thus they too, although in a lower place, are placed in the building of the holy Church.

Even if they are perhaps lesser in teaching, prophecy, the grace of miracles, or the fuller practice of contempt for the world, they nevertheless stand upon the foundation of fear and love, on which they are made firm. Although they do not burn with the fire of heavenly desire, they are animated by the warmth of charity in those external things they are capable of practicing, and they are contained among the buildings of their more excellent neighbors.

It follows:

“And the threshold of the gate beside the vestibule of the gate, inwardly, was one reed.”

[Col. 0898A] (Jerome) The threshold of the other gate—or, as it appears in the Septuagint, of the second vestibule—and that of the third had the same measure, one reed. After this vestibule, that is, after the threshold of the gate, eight cubits are placed at the entrance, so that the inner parts of the vestibule might possess not the number seven, nor six cubits and one palm, but the number eight, which pertains to the mystery of the resurrection and of the Lord’s Day.

(Gregory) Since the threshold now being described is said to be inward, beside the vestibule of the gate, it is clearly shown that the threshold described earlier was outward. But if the gate is the Lord, let us inquire what is the inward and outward threshold of the gate.

Through a threshold one enters the gate. What, then, are these two thresholds except the fathers of the Old Testament and the fathers of the New Testament? Not only those from whom the Lord deigned to become incarnate, but all the fathers of the Old Testament were the threshold of this gate, because those who were worthy to proclaim him and hope in him opened the access of faith to all who came to him, so that everyone who believed in the Lord entered, as it were, through the threshold of this gate.

But why is the outer threshold mentioned first, and the inner threshold afterward? It is because first came the fathers of the Old Testament, and afterward the teachers of the New Testament. The outer threshold rightly signifies the fathers of the Old Testament, because through their preaching sinful works were condemned. Through the preaching of the new fathers, however, each person’s mind is restrained even from unlawful thoughts, since guilt is shown to exist fully even in the deliberation of the heart.

The former took care to restrain the souls of their hearers from crimes, cruelties, and robberies. The latter, cutting away not only perverse works but also unlawful thoughts, have become for us nothing other than the inner threshold. Hence the Truth himself says: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not kill’; and whoever kills shall be liable to judgment. But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother without cause shall be liable to judgment” (Matthew 5).

The outer threshold also rightly signifies those fathers who were established farther away in the intervals of time from the incarnation of our Redeemer. The Church began already with Abel’s blood and is one Church of the elect who preceded and followed. Yet because it is said to the disciples, “Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it,” it was as though the ancient fathers stood outside, since they did not see the bodily presence of our Redeemer.

[Col. 0899A] They were therefore outside, but they were not separated from the holy Church, because in mind, action, and preaching they already held these mysteries of faith. They saw the lofty character of the holy Church, which we see not while awaiting it but already possessing it. Just as we were saved through faith in the past passion of our Redeemer, so they were saved through faith in that passion which was to come. They were therefore outside, not outside the mystery, but outside the time.

But if in this passage we understand the gate as sacred Scripture, it too has two thresholds, an outer and an inner, because it is divided into the letter and allegory. The outer threshold of sacred Scripture is the letter; its inner threshold is allegory. Since through the letter we proceed toward allegory, we come, as it were, from the threshold that is outside.

There are many things in Scripture that build up the mind according to the letter, so that through what is done outwardly the mind of the hearer is drawn inward. There we find commandments concerning action and examples of virtue. There we are commanded what we must do even bodily. There what is prescribed for practice is displayed in the actions of holy and courageous men.

After the clearer commandments and examples of the virtues have instructed us in good action, then, if we are able, let us direct the foot of the mind toward the inner threshold—that is, toward the mystical understanding of inward contemplation.

It should be noted that the threshold of the gate is measured by one reed. The reed extends to six cubits and a palm, because in sacred Scripture are found both the teaching of perfected action and the beginning of heavenly contemplation.

But if in this passage the gate is understood as each preacher, the outer threshold in the gate is the active life, while the inner threshold is the contemplative life. Through the former one walks in faith; through the latter one hastens toward the vision. The former leads outwardly, so that each person may live well; the latter leads inwardly, so that from a good life one may reach eternal joys.

“And he measured the vestibule of the gate, eight cubits, and its front, two cubits. The vestibule of the gate was inward.”

(Gregory) The man whose appearance was like the appearance of bronze measured the vestibule of the gate as eight cubits, and its front as two cubits. And lest we should think that this vestibule was outside the gate, it is added: “The vestibule of the gate was inward.”

(Jerome) “And on its front,” he says, “there were two cubits,” belonging either to the two Testaments, or to the letter and the spirit, or to the mystery of the tongs by which, in Isaiah (Isaiah 6), a coal is taken from the altar and brought to cleanse the prophet’s lips.

And so that we may know what this vestibule is, which is bounded by eight and two cubits, he states it more clearly: “The vestibule of the gate was inward,” through which we arrive at the temple of God.

(Gregory) What, then, is signified by the inner vestibule except the breadth of eternal life, which is already conceived in the mind through hope within the narrow confines of the present life? Of this the Psalmist says: “Enter his gates with confession, his courts with hymns of confession” (Psalm 100).

When we confess our sins with tears, we enter the gate of the narrow way. But when afterward we are led to eternal life, we enter the courts of our gate in praise of confession. For there there will no longer be narrowness when the joy of eternal solemnity has received us.

Because of the narrowness of our confession, the Truth says: “Enter through the narrow gate.” And when the Psalmist presumed that he would be received into the breadth of eternal joy, he said: “You have set my feet in a spacious place” (Psalm 31).

Thus one proceeds to the court through the gate, because one reaches the breadth of solemnity from the narrowness of confession. Those joys that David calls courts are called by Ezekiel the inner vestibule.

Therefore this vestibule is said to be measured by eight cubits, for there all those will be received who now labor in the exercise of works and sigh for eternal joys through the grace of contemplation. Nor is it without reason that the measure of the vestibule is given as eight cubits, because the whole of time unfolds in seven days. The eternal day that follows when the succession of seven days has been completed is, of course, the eighth.

Hence the Psalmist, considering the day of the resurrection and about to speak of the severity of the final judgment, prefaced the title: “For the end: a psalm of David, for the eighth” (Psalm 6). To show which “eighth” he meant, he followed at the beginning of the psalm with these words concerning that day of terrifying dread: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your fury.”

For now, whoever is chastised by scourges and corrected by reproofs is chastised in gentleness, not in anger. But in that strict examination every rebuke and correction will be fury and anger, because after correction there will be no pardon.

The reason for this number eight is that after the Sabbath the Lord chose to rise from the dead. The Lord’s Day, which is the third from the Lord’s death, is counted from the creation of the days as the eighth, because it follows the seventh.

Thus the true passion and true resurrection of our Redeemer also signified something concerning his body in the days of his passion. He suffered on the sixth day; on the Sabbath he rested in the tomb; on the Lord’s Day he rose from the dead.

The present life is still our sixth day, because it is spent in pain and tormented in distress. But on the Sabbath we rest, as though in a tomb, because after the body we find rest for the soul. On the Lord’s Day, which is the third from the passion and, as we have said, the eighth from creation, we rise bodily from death and rejoice in the glory of the soul together with the flesh.

What our Savior wonderfully accomplished in himself, he truly signified in us, so that pain might receive us on the sixth day, rest on the seventh, and glory on the eighth.

Hence Solomon says: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight, because you do not know what evil may come upon the earth” (Ecclesiastes 11). We give a portion to both seven and eight when we order the things that unfold in seven days in such a way that through them we may come to eternal goods, so that by acting cautiously now we may afterward avoid the anger of the fearful judgment.

[Col. 0901A] The vestibule is therefore measured inwardly by eight cubits, because through the light that follows the seven days the breadth of eternity is opened to us. But no one comes to it unless he has held the love of God and neighbor with a devoted mind in this life.

Hence it is added: “And its front, two cubits.” The front of the gate is the good merit of the present life. Just as the inner vestibule should be understood as eternal rest, so the front of the gate must signify the quality of visible life.

The front of the gate is measured by two cubits because whoever strives here to preserve love of God and neighbor reaches the court of eternity. Therefore, for our life to be measured by two cubits, it must daily be stretched through charity toward love of God and neighbor together. Charity is not true if it has less than two cubits.

[Col. 0901B] “Now the chambers of the gate toward the eastern road were three on this side and three on that side, and the measure of the three was one.”

(Jerome) The chambers and rooms that were toward the road of the eastern gate, for which the Septuagint writes *elau* [αἰλάμ, “vestibules”], were three on this side and three on that side, of one measure—that is, one reed, which had six cubits and one palm. There was one reed in length, one reed in breadth, and five cubits between the chambers.

Therefore, lest we think that there were only two reeds, he placed three on each side of the gate in order to indicate the number six. This number is also indicated in the Gospel by the water jars in which water was changed into wine; and every day Jewish waters are changed, and the wine that gladdens the human heart is made sweeter by the blood of Christ.

(Gregory) We have already said above what the chambers and the eastern road signify, and we do not think it necessary to repeat it at greater length. But we must ask what is meant by the words: “three on this side and three on that side.”

The chambers beside the eastern road are the hearts of those who burn with love of God, whether they were elect under the Old Testament or followed under the New. It is clear that all were kindled by love of the Trinity. For they would not truly love God if they had not received the grace of that Trinity which is God.

Thus beside the eastern road there are three chambers on this side and three on that side. Since the Lord deigned to become incarnate between the ancient and the new fathers, the eastern road appeared, as it were, in the middle of the chambers, because the chambers are adorned for the true vision through knowledge of the Trinity.

But if we refer the same number to the virtues of the elect, there are three virtues without which one who is already able to perform anything cannot be saved: faith, hope, and charity. And because the same hope, faith, and charity existed in the ancient fathers as in the new teachers, three chambers on this side and three on that side are described beside the eastern road.

Or certainly, there were three divisions among the ancient fathers, and three among the new follow under grace. The ancient people had fathers before the Law, then those under the Law, and afterward the prophets. In the new people, first the firstfruits of the Hebrews believed; afterward the fullness of the Gentiles followed in faith; and at the end of the age the remnant of the Hebrews is saved (Romans 11).

[Col. 0902A] Since, therefore, the incarnation of the Lord had on the earlier side fathers before the Law, fathers under the Law, and finally prophets, while on the later side it gathered the faithful from the Hebrews, the faithful from the Gentiles, and afterward the entire remnant of the Hebrews, the eastern road is said to have three chambers on this side and three on that side.

We may also understand this appropriately if we say that there are three orders of the faithful, whether in the Old or in the New Testament: one order of preachers, another of the continent, and another of good married people (Ezekiel 14).

Hence the same prophet earlier saw three men delivered: Noah, Daniel, and Job. In these three, preachers, the continent, and married people are signified. Noah governed the ark amid the waters and therefore bore the figure of rulers. Daniel lived devoted to abstinence in the royal court and thus signified the life of the continent. Job, living in marriage and managing his household, pleased God; through him the order of good married people is rightly represented.

Since, therefore, even before the coming of the mediator there were preachers, continent persons, and good married people who awaited that coming and greatly thirsted to see it, and afterward we see preachers, continent persons, and good married people who no longer desire our Redeemer to become incarnate but to be contemplated in the glory of his majesty, the eastern road has three chambers on this side and three on that side, in accordance with the Psalmist’s words concerning this same road, namely our Redeemer: “Around him were his tabernacles” (Psalm 18).

But we must weigh carefully what is said: “the measure of the three was one.” For although the excellence of preachers is far above that of the continent, and the eminence of the continent greatly exceeds that of married people, what does it mean that the measure of the three is said to be one?

Married people, although they may act well and desire to see almighty God, are nevertheless occupied with domestic concerns and, compelled by necessity, divide their minds between the two. The continent, however, are removed from such activity and restrain the pleasure of the flesh even from licit marriage; they are entangled neither in concern for a spouse or children nor in harmful and difficult thoughts about household affairs.

Preachers, meanwhile, not only restrain themselves from vices but also prevent others from sinning, lead them to faith, and instruct them in the pursuit of a good way of life. How, then, is their measure one, when the quality of their lives is not one? The measure of the three is one because, although there is great diversity of merits among them, there is no difference in the faith in which they are stretched out.

The same faith that makes these firm in the greatest things contains the weakness of the others in small things. Truly the measure of the three is one because, in the final recompense, although the dignity of all will not be the same, the life of blessedness will nevertheless be one for all.

Hence the Lord himself says: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14). Yet because they were brought into the vineyard, although they came at different hours, they received one denarius. How, then, can many dwelling places agree with one denarius except because the dignities of the blessed citizens will indeed be different, but the rest of eternal recompense will be one?

For although the merit of individuals will be unequal, there will be no diversity of joys. One may rejoice less and another more, but one joy will nevertheless gladden them all: the vision of their Creator.

This must also be understood of the ancient and new fathers. Although the eastern road has three chambers on this side and three on that side, the measure of the three is one, because the same faith and the same merit that possessed the hearts of those who came before filled the hearts of those who followed under the New Testament, as Paul also says: “Having the same spirit of faith, according to what is written: ‘I believed, and therefore I spoke’; and we also believe, and therefore we speak” (2 Corinthians 4).

Those spiritual fathers believed that almighty God is the Trinity, just as the new fathers openly proclaimed the same Trinity. Isaiah heard the angelic hosts in heaven crying: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts” (Isaiah 6). To show the Trinity of persons, “holy” is said three times; but to show that the Trinity is one substance, it is not “Lord of hosts” in the plural but “Lord of hosts” in the singular.

David, likewise understanding this, says: “May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us” (Psalm 67). Having named God three times, he then adds, to show that this God is one: “and may all the ends of the earth fear him.”

Paul also says: “From him and through him and in him are all things” (Romans 11): “from him,” namely from the Father; “through him,” that is, through the Son; “in him,” that is, in the Holy Spirit. Having named this third person, he adds: “To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.”

For by not saying “to them” but “to him,” he distinguished the persons by saying “him” three times, while by adding “to him be glory” he did not divide the substance.

Since, therefore, the faith of the ancient and new fathers is one, the chambers are rightly described as having one measure for the three. This is repeated in other words when it is added:

“And one measure for the fronts on both sides.”

(Gregory) There is one measure for the fronts on both sides because our fathers, whether they came earlier from the Old Testament or now from the New Testament, meet in the one faith of the mediator. Because they are full of charity, they subdue the flesh through abstinence, enlighten the hearts of their hearers with the light of preaching, perform signs, and work mighty deeds.

Because their good works are made known outwardly to us, they are not inappropriately called the fronts of this heavenly building. Everything that is now displayed openly is a front, so that the vestibule of the building may be what is reserved for us inwardly.

It follows:

“Then he measured the width of the threshold of the gate, ten cubits, and the length of the gate, thirteen cubits.”

(Hieronymus.) He also measured the width of the threshold of the gate as ten cubits—the number of perfection—which is contained either in the Decalogue or in the mystery of the four Gospels, which, beginning from one, reaches four in such a way as to complete the number ten. [Col. 0904A] Its length, however, was thirteen cubits.

The threshold of the gate, in which the sacred number of the Old and New Testament is contained, may be understood as the Lord himself, who says: “I am the door” (John 10). Or certainly all the saints, through whom we enter into knowledge of God, may be understood, concerning whom the apostle Paul spoke: “My mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; widen your hearts also” (2 Cor. 6).

The thirteen cubits, following the number eight of the books of Moses, contain a mystery that is also shown in the five loaves and in the Samaritan woman of the Gospel (John 4), who is reproved for having had five husbands and for not having the sixth, whom she thought she had. Yet both the number eight and the number five are brought to completion in the one cubit—that is, in the thirteenth—in which all things are recapitulated in Christ. [Col. 0904B] Hence it is said: “One cubit is the end of both,” since one measure of Christ embraces both the Old and the New Testament.

(Gregory.) We have already said much above concerning the meaning of the gate, but we must retain one point that may enable the reader’s prudence to penetrate the rest. It has been said that the sacred Scripture can be represented by the gate. But we must now laboriously examine why the width of the threshold of the gate is measured at ten cubits and its length at thirteen.

In this passage, “length” means the height of the gate, just as we call someone “tall” whom we see to be high in stature. For the length of the gate cannot mean its transverse dimension, since its width is shown by ten cubits. What, then, is the width of the threshold of the gate except the law of the Old Testament? And what is the length of the gate except the grace of the New Testament? Sacred Scripture, while through the Old Testament it restrained crimes of action and commanded the giving of tithes, lay, as it were, through humble commandments in the width of the threshold. But while through the New Testament it restrained wicked thoughts, commanded that all things be abandoned for God, and ordered that bodily life be despised together with the present age, our gate rose, as it were, to the height of length.

For lesser commandments were given to the Israelite people through the Law; therefore Moses spoke to that people on the plain. Higher commandments the Lord gave to the holy apostles; therefore he taught them the commandments of life on the mountain (Matt. 5). When, however, our Redeemer says through the Gospel: “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish but to fulfill” [Col. 0904D] (ibid.), he came to fulfill the Law by adding the grace of justice to the Law: so that what the Law commanded in lesser matters, he might assist in perfecting in higher matters; and what the Law restrained from action, he might cut away from the heart.

Thus the Law, which lay in width, understood, rose in height. For the knowledge of God that existed among the spiritual fathers was not known to the whole Hebrew people. Although the prophets proclaimed almighty God—namely, the holy Trinity—the people did not understand. They held only the Decalogue as law, without knowing the faith of the Trinity.

Let the width of the threshold of the gate therefore be measured by ten cubits, because that stubborn people, ignorant of the subtlety of faith, served the commandments of the Decalogue. But let the length of the gate be measured by thirteen cubits, because through the New Testament the knowledge of the Trinity grew in the heart of the faithful people beyond the commandments of the Decalogue—which it more truly observes—and it perfected the commandments of the Law precisely by believing that the Lord almighty is the Trinity.

Here it may reasonably be asked why, after saying above that the width of the threshold of the gate was measured by one reed, he subsequently adds that it is measured by ten cubits, and then says that the length of the gate is measured by thirteen cubits. For, as has often been said, one reed has six cubits and a handbreadth. Ten cubits already contain their measure beyond the reed, while thirteen exceed ten.

What, then, does it mean that first the threshold of the gate is measured by one reed, then its width by ten cubits, and finally [Col. 0905B] the length of the gate by thirteen, except that the holy fathers whom we know to have existed before the Law knew that there is one almighty God, namely, the holy Trinity? Yet they did not openly proclaim the Trinity that they knew. Obeying its commands and preserving purity of life, they possessed, as it were, the perfection of action in the six cubits of the reed, and, often seeing angels, they possessed the handbreadth of contemplation.

But once that uncultivated Hebrew people had been given the commandments of the Decalogue, it tried to keep them; nevertheless, it was not instructed in knowledge of the holy Trinity. Although the spiritual fathers had known this perfectly, the great multitude of the synagogue could neither discover the mystery of the Trinity nor knew how to seek it. [Col. 0905C]

When grace came through the New Testament, however, the whole faithful people recognized that the one God is the Trinity and completed the power of the Decalogue in knowledge of him. First, then, let the threshold of the gate be measured by one reed; afterward, its width by ten cubits; and finally, the length of the gate by thirteen cubits. For before the Law the holy fathers possessed both active and contemplative life; under the Decalogue of the Law the people, ignorant of the mystery of the divine substance, served within the width of the commandments; and now, while more truly keeping the precepts of the Decalogue, everyone who comes to faith recognizes the mysteries of the holy Trinity.

In this connection we must also know that through the progression of time the knowledge of the spiritual fathers increased. Moses was more instructed in the knowledge of almighty God than Abraham; the prophets more than Moses; the apostles more than the prophets. I am mistaken if Scripture itself does not say this: “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. 12).

But let us show, if we can, from the words of that same Scripture the things we have said concerning Abraham, the prophets, and the apostles. Who does not know that Abraham spoke with God? Yet the Lord says to Moses: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, and I did not reveal my name Adonai to them” (Exod. 6). Behold, more had been made known to Moses than to Abraham, since he revealed to Moses that he said he had not revealed to Abraham.

Let us see whether the prophets were able to grasp more of divine knowledge than Moses. Certainly the Psalmist says: “How I have loved your law, O Lord; all day long it is my meditation” (Ps. 118); and he adds: “I have understood more than all my teachers, because your testimonies are my meditation,” and again: “I have understood more than the elders.” Thus, when he recalls that he meditates on the Law and testifies that he has understood more than all teachers and elders, he makes clear that he had received more divine knowledge than Moses.

But how are we shown more clearly that the holy apostles were taught more than the prophets? Certainly the Truth says: “Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke 10). Therefore they knew more of divine knowledge than the prophets, because what those men saw only in spirit, the apostles also saw bodily.

Thus the statement of Daniel mentioned above has been fulfilled: “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied.” Let the measure of the reed, which is six cubits and a handbreadth, be extended to ten cubits, and let the measure of ten cubits finally rise to thirteen: for the farther the world is led toward its end, the more generously the entrance to eternity is opened to us.

It follows:

“And a border before the chambers, one cubit.”

(Gregory.) As we have often said, the chambers are the hearts of the elect, burning with love for almighty God. What is expressed by the border before the chambers except faith? Unless faith is held first, one can in no way attain spiritual love. For charity does not precede faith; faith precedes charity. No one can love what he has not believed.

The border, then, is before the chambers: faith is before the ardor of charity. As it has been said, unless you believe what you hear, you cannot in any way be inflamed with love for what you have heard. But the border before the chambers is one cubit, because faith joins the hearts of hearers to God in love when it is not divided by errors and schisms but perseveres in unity. Thus the border of one cubit leads the mind of the hearer to the chamber, because the form of the heavenly Bridegroom whom it proclaims here it will later display in heaven.

Hence it is rightly added:

“And one cubit is the end of both.”

“Both” is said as though it were “of both sides.” By the width of the threshold and the length of the gate, we said, the Old and New Testament are signified. Finally it is added that one cubit is the end of both, because the Old Testament announced to us one mediator between God and human beings, and the New Testament announces that the same mediator will come in eternal glory—the one whom we have already come to know as incarnate for us.

One cubit, then, is the end of both, because the one whom the Law foretold appeared in the flesh, and the one of whom the New Testament now speaks will appear in the glory of his majesty. The end of both will come when, seen in the power of his divinity, he fulfills everything that has been foretold.

For it is written: “Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10)—an end not that destroys, but that perfects. He perfected the Law when he appeared incarnate, just as the Law had foretold. But the New Testament still speaks much about his judgment. It still relates much about his kingdom, which we do not yet see fulfilled. Behold, the Gospel is read daily, and the life to come is proclaimed. The end of the New Testament, therefore, will also come when he fulfills what he promised concerning himself.

The New Testament is brought to an end precisely by being fulfilled: for when the one of whom it speaks has been seen, the words of that Testament will cease. Let it therefore be said of the threshold and the gate: “One cubit is the end of both.” For when “the one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2), appears in his majesty, he will fulfill everything foretold and promised in both Testaments.

But if in this passage he mentions both the border and the chambers, this too does not depart from the meaning just given. When the great majesty of our Redeemer has been revealed to us, faith comes to an end. When human beings begin to see what they believed, the chambers also reach their end, because the hearts of the faithful are perfected in his love incomparably more fully than they are now. One cubit, then, is the end of both, because the vision of the one Lord and Savior brings faith to an end in his elect and perfects charity.

It is fitting to consider who we are, since we discuss these things. Certainly we come from the Gentiles; certainly our ancestors were worshipers of wood and stone. How, then, has it come about that we examine the profound mysteries of the prophet Ezekiel—things that the Hebrews themselves still do not know? Let us therefore give thanks to the One who fulfilled in deed everything written about him in sacred discourse, so that what could not be understood when heard might be disclosed when seen. There are contained in it his incarnation, his passion, his death, his resurrection, and his ascension. But who among us would have believed these things when heard, unless we had known them as accomplished?

Thus the sealed book, as we read in the Apocalypse of John (Rev. 5), which no one could open and read, was opened by the Lion of the tribe of Judah. In his resurrection and passion he disclosed all its mysteries to us. By enduring the evils of our weakness, he showed us the blessings of his power and glory.

He became flesh in order to make us spiritual. He bent down graciously in order to raise us up. He went out in order to bring us in. He appeared visibly in order to show the invisible. He endured scourging in order to heal. He bore insults and mockery [Col. 0907D] in order to free us from eternal disgrace. He died in order to give life.

Let us therefore give thanks to him who gives life and who died—and for this reason give even greater thanks to him who gives life, because he died. Hence Isaiah, contemplating our salvation and his passion, rightly says: “That he may do his work, his strange work; that he may perform his work, his work foreign to him” (Isa. 28).

The work of God is to gather the souls he created and restore them to the joys of eternal light. But to be scourged, smeared with spittle, crucified, to die and be buried—this is not the work of God in his own substance, but the work of sinful humanity, which deserved all these things because of sin. Yet “he himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree.” Though he remains in his own nature forever incomprehensible, he deigned to become comprehensible in our nature and to be scourged. For unless he who was almighty had assumed the nature of our weakness, he would never have raised us to the power of his strength.

Thus, “that he may do his work, his strange work,” and “that he may perform his work, his work foreign to him,” because God, having become incarnate in order to gather us to his righteousness, deigned to be beaten for us like a sinful human being. He performed a strange work in order to perform his own: by enduring the evils of our weakness, he brought us, his creatures, to the glory of his strength.

“But the chambers were six cubits on this side and on that.”

(Hieronymus.) The statement “on this side and on that” means that they were six cubits on both sides. They had neither a handbreadth nor the proportion added above that would summon the present way of life to future blessedness, but only six cubits. Hence it follows:

“And he measured the gate from the roof of the chamber to its roof, or wall.”

He found the width to be twenty-five cubits. Although this number is itself square, it nevertheless refers to the senses. If you arrange five cubits opposite one another five times, you produce the number twenty-five, which lies between the roof of one chamber and the roof of the other. Yet each, placed opposite the other, has a doorway opposite a doorway at its upper ends.

Let these things not seem frivolous to the reader, although I myself dislike what I have said, feeling that I am knocking at a closed door. They should nevertheless be read with indulgence. Otherwise I could simply have confessed my ignorance and cut off every desire for study. For since we are far from perfect knowledge, we consider it a lesser fault at least to say a little rather than nothing at all. [Col. 0908C]

(Gregory.) After mentioning the chambers above, the prophet adds: “The chambers were six cubits on this side and on that.” This raises a great question for us: why did he say above that the chamber was measured by one reed, which he declared to have six cubits and a handbreadth, while below he says that the chamber was measured by six cubits alone? If it is measured not by a reed but by six cubits, the handbreadth that was said above to be present is missing.

But if the chambers are the understandings and thoughts of the faithful, in which chaste souls are joined to their Creator in love, and if perfect action is expressed by the six cubits while the handbreadth expresses the beginning of contemplation, we must observe the members of the holy universal Church. We quickly discover that in it there are chambers measured by one reed, and others measured by six cubits alone.

Some of the faithful love almighty God in such a way that they are perfect in action and elevated in contemplation. These certainly possess the reed in their measure, because they have both the six cubits of action and the handbreadth of contemplation. Others indeed love almighty God and exercise themselves in perfect good works, but they do not know how to contemplate his greatness with more subtle understanding. They love, but do not know how to investigate the joys of his glory.

These therefore have six cubits but do not have the handbreadth, because they are already joined to him through love but are separated from him in contemplation. Yet these chambers are said, after the mention of one cubit, to be on this side and on that, because faithful souls from the Jewish people and from the Gentiles have come together in love of our Creator and Redeemer.

Therefore, when our Redeemer was riding on a colt and going toward Jerusalem, as the Evangelist testifies: “Many spread their garments on the road; others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road; and those who went before and those who followed cried out, saying: Hosanna, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. 21).

Our Savior goes toward Jerusalem seated on a colt when, ruling the soul of each faithful person—that is, his own beast—he leads that beast to the vision of inner peace. He also sits when he presides universally over the holy Church and kindles it with desire for heavenly peace.

Many spread their garments on the road because they subdue their bodies through abstinence, preparing a path for him to the mind or offering good examples to those who follow. Others cut branches or leaves from the trees and spread them on the road because they gather words and teachings of the Fathers from their speech and, in humble preaching, lay them along the road of God before the soul of the hearer who is approaching. This is what we too, unworthy as we are, do now. When we take up the teachings of the Fathers in exhortation, we cut leaves from the trees in order to spread them on the road of almighty God.

But those who went before and those who followed cried out, “Hosanna.” The Jewish people went before; the Gentiles followed. And because all the elect—whether those who were able to exist in Judea or those who now exist in the Church—believed and believe in the mediator between God and human beings, both those who went before and those who followed cried out.

They cried “Hosanna.” In Latin, Hosanna means “save us.” From him the earlier generations sought salvation, and those living now seek it; and they confess that he who comes in the name of the Lord is blessed.

His chambers, therefore, are on this side and on that, because the hearts of those who love him embrace the faith that is in him both from the earlier part of the world and from its last part.

“And he measured,” it says, “the part from the roof of the chamber to its roof, with a width of twenty-five cubits.”

We have often said that the gate signifies faith, and through that same faith our Creator, the mediator between God and human beings, Jesus Christ, can be signified, because through the faith that is in him the entrance to life is open. But we have also rightly understood the sacred Scripture, which opens this same faith to us in the understanding of our Redeemer, as the gate. For when it is known as it ought to be, we enter through it into the understanding of visible things.

The gate—that is, sacred discourse—also has a roof, because we cannot yet penetrate everything we hear concerning heavenly things. It remains, therefore, that in what we understand we should advance daily in charity. Although our neighbors do not see how greatly we are loved by us, and although in sacred discourse we humbly revere what we do not yet understand, nevertheless in those matters to which we have attained through understanding we ought to expand ourselves through good action. Concerning this we shall speak more fully in the following book.

## BOOK FIFTEEN

[Col. 0909]

## CHAPTER XL FOLLOWS

[Col. 0909C]

“And he measured the gate from the roof of the chamber to its roof, its width being twenty-five cubits.”

(Gregory.) We are endowed with five bodily senses: sight, taste, smell, hearing, and touch. This number five, multiplied by itself, rises to the number twenty-five. Yet we cannot perform any external action concerning the heavenly commandments through these five bodily senses alone. The judging mind presides inwardly over their functions and recognizes what it can do externally justly or mercifully, as though those functions were reporting to it and serving it.

When, therefore, the mind is filled with fear of almighty God, it is necessary that our five senses, like subordinate functions, serve us in good action. Through them, when we begin to do something merciful, mercy itself opens more widely each day and expands, as it were, the bosom of good work.

The five senses are therefore multiplied in themselves when what is done through them is multiplied daily by progress in good works. Hence the width is said to be twenty-five cubits, because fear, greed, and sluggishness are narrow.

Whoever is afraid to give bread to the needy lest he himself lack it is still in the narrowness of fear. Whoever does not offer clothing to one who is cold because he desires to possess it alone is still confined by the narrowness of his greed. Whoever does not do good because the sluggishness of his spirit makes him idle has his own torpor as a narrowness.

But to look upon the needy, hear a prayer, give alms, offer protection, and, for the sake of protecting the poor person, not fear the hostility of anyone who opposes him—this is great breadth of mind.

Let the width between the chamber and the gate therefore be measured at twenty-five cubits, because through the external activity of the senses it is tested and made known what invisible realities instruct us.

If, then, as we have said, the gate in this passage is understood as sacred Scripture, we must ask what is signified by the roof of the chamber and by the roof of the gate. The chamber has a roof, because the mind of those who love is concealed, and the fervor of love is hidden. The gate also has a roof, because sacred Scripture was indeed written entirely for our sake, but is not entirely understood by us.

Much in it is so open that it feeds the little ones. Some things are expressed in more obscure sayings, so that they may exercise the strong, in order that, when understood with labor, they may be more pleasing. Other things in it are so closed that, when we recognize that we do not understand them, acknowledging the weakness of our blindness, we may advance more toward humility than toward understanding.

There are matters that speak of heavenly things in such a way that they are open only to those heavenly citizens who remain in their homeland, while they are not yet disclosed to us who are on pilgrimage. If someone traveling toward an unknown city hears many things about it on the road, he gathers some from reasoning, but others, because he does not yet see them, he cannot know in any way. The citizens who are in the city, however, both see what is left unspoken about it and understand what is said about it.

We, then, are still on the road. We hear many things about that heavenly homeland; some we already understand through spirit and reason, while some, not understood, we revere. Hence it is written concerning the same sacred discourse: “Stretching out heaven like a skin, who covers its higher parts with waters” (Ps. 103).

Heaven is stretched out like a skin because sacred Scripture is explained to us through the mouths of mortals by means of interpretations. But there are waters in heaven—namely, the higher multitudes, that is, the ranks of angels—in which the higher parts of that heaven are covered. For what is higher and more obscure in sacred discourse is open only to angelic spirits and remains unknown to us.

The chamber therefore has a roof, because one’s neighbor does not yet know how much he is loved by another. The gate, that is, sacred discourse, also has a roof, because we cannot yet penetrate intellectually everything that the abundance of goodness contains within.

For whatever you have already learned from sacred Scripture, and whatever neighbor you silently love, you display in the breadth of good work. Let the width between the chamber and the gate therefore be twenty-five cubits, because good action bears witness between charity and knowledge.

If good action should be absent, it is certain that you have neither come to know God nor loved your neighbor—that is, you possess neither the gate of sacred discourse nor the chamber of love.

It should also be noted that the measurement is said to extend from the roof of the chamber to the roof of the gate. For our humility is tested by those things that are covered from us in sacred Scripture. Whatever we do not understand in it, we ought not arrogantly criticize but humbly revere.

Let there therefore be great breadth from the roof of the chamber to the roof of the gate; and from the hidden things of our charity toward our neighbor to the humility of knowledge directed toward God, let us always perform good works insofar as we understand and are able.

The gate itself may also be understood as the entrance to the heavenly kingdom. It now has a roof, and the chamber has a roof, because neither how great our charity toward God and neighbor is nor when we shall be brought from this world into the rest of eternal life is known.

For our Creator always willed the day of our death to be unknown to us, so that, while it is always unknown, it might always be believed to be near, and each person might be more fervent in action because he is uncertain of his summons.

Hence the width of twenty-five cubits extends from the chamber to the gate, because the charity that we once desire in God and neighbor we must practice, to the entrance of the kingdom, in every way we can, with manifold and unceasing effort.

From the roof of the chamber to the roof of the gate, therefore, there is great breadth, because from the grace by which we begin to love God until that love itself opens the entrance to the heavenly kingdom, we must expand ourselves in the great activity of good works: patiently enduring adversity; willingly and kindly giving what we have; loving even those by whom we suffer; giving what we possess and not coveting what we do not possess; loving our neighbors as ourselves; considering their goods our own and mourning their evils as though they were our own.

There is great breadth in such a mind, in which there is no narrowness of hatred. We have learned this breadth, conceived from love of God and neighbor, through the sacred commandments.

We may also understand the twenty-five cubits themselves without incongruity if we examine them according to sacred discourse. He had said that the chambers were measured by six cubits; and on the sixth day humanity was created, and on that day the Lord is described as having completed his works. Therefore six is also customarily used to signify perfection.

Since we have learned every good work through the four books of the holy Gospel, if we multiply six by four, we reach twenty-four. To this is added the monad, because there is one through whom all act rightly. Thus this breadth had to be expressed by twenty-five cubits, because every good action is learned, as we have said, through the four books of the holy Gospel and is completed in the knowledge and confession of the one God.

It follows:

“And a door opposite a door.”

In this passage, “opposite” does not indicate hostility but directness. A door is opposite a door when one reaches the inner entrance by a straight route from the outer one.

In the knowledge of almighty God, our first door is faith. The second is his appearance, toward which we arrive by walking through faith. In this life we enter through the first so that afterward we may be brought to the second. A door is therefore opposite a door, because through the entrance of faith the entrance to the vision of God is opened.

If someone wishes to understand both these doors as existing in this life, that too does not depart from a sound interpretation. We often wish to contemplate the invisible nature of almighty God, but we are in no way able to do so. The soul, wearied by these difficulties, withdraws into itself and makes for itself steps of ascent, so that it may first consider itself, if it is able, and then investigate, as far as it can, the nature that is above it.

But if our mind is scattered among bodily images, it is not sufficient to consider either itself or the nature of the soul, because, by however many thoughts it is led, it is blinded, as it were, by that many obstacles.

The first step, then, is to gather itself to itself. The second is to see what sort of thing it is that it gathers. The third is to rise above itself and subject itself, by directing its attention to contemplation, to the invisible Creator.

But it does not gather itself to itself at all unless it has learned to restrain from the eye of the mind the phantasms of earthly and heavenly images: whatever arises in its thought from sight, hearing, smell, touch, or bodily taste, it must reject and trample down, so that it may seek within itself what it is like without these things.

For when it thinks about these matters, it turns, as it were, certain shadows of bodies inwardly. Everything must therefore be driven away from the eyes of the mind by the hand of discernment, so that the soul may consider itself as it was created under God and above the body: made alive by what is above, it may give life to what is below and under its governance.

It is infused throughout in such a way that it is not divided into parts according to the parts of the members. For if any part of the body is struck in any place, the whole soul suffers. Yet in a marvelous way, while presiding over the members by one and the same act of giving life, and while it is not diverse in itself by nature, it performs diverse actions through the body.

It is the soul that sees through the eyes, hears through the ears, smells through the nostrils, tastes through the mouth, and touches through all the limbs. By touching, it distinguishes the smooth from the rough. Although it performs such diverse operations through the senses, it arranges them not as diverse things but by one and the same reason in which it was created.

When, therefore, the soul thinks of itself either through bodily images, it has already entered the first door. But from this door it proceeds toward another, so that it may contemplate something of the nature of almighty God.

The soul is life for the flesh within the body. God, however, who gives life to all things, is life for souls. If life that has been given life is of such great magnitude that it cannot be comprehended, who can comprehend intellectually how great is the majesty of the life that gives life?

Yet to consider and distinguish this very matter is already, to some extent, to enter. For from its own estimation the soul gathers what it should think about the unbounded Spirit, who governs incomprehensibly and created incomprehensibly.

Our Creator presides over his creature by a distance that is incomparably great. He has made some things so that they may exist but not live; others so that they may exist and live but not possess any discernment of life; others so that they may exist, live, and discern.

One has made all things, yet he is not divided among them. For he is truly supreme and never unlike himself. The soul, although not diverse from itself by nature, is nevertheless diverse in thought. In the very instant in which it thinks about sight, it forgets to think about hearing; and in the instant in which it thinks about hearing or taste, it cannot think about smell or touch.

Through attention and forgetfulness it is therefore always unlike itself, holding now one thing and now another in thought. Almighty God, however, because he is not unlike himself, sees everything by the same power by which he hears it all; he creates by the same power by which he judges his creature.

To see everything simultaneously is therefore also to govern, and to govern is to see. He assists the righteous with one thought and condemns the unrighteous with another. Yet one and the same nature, always unlike itself in nothing, arranges unlike things.

Why should we marvel at this concerning the power of the Creator, when we see traces of his power even in creation? The nature of mud and wax is different, but the ray of the sun is not different. Yet although it is not different, it works differently in mud and wax: by the one and the same heat of its fire it hardens mud and melts wax.

Perhaps this lies in the nature of mud or wax and not in the substance of the sun itself, which seems to operate differently in different natures. Almighty God, however, possesses within himself the power to arrange changing things without change. Far otherwise, he performs unlike things without diversity in himself or succession of thoughts: God, who is never unlike himself, performs unlike things and is everywhere and wholly everywhere.

For he says: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. 66). And it is written of him: “He measures heaven with a handbreadth and encloses the earth in a span” (Isa. 40).

From this it is necessary to consider that he who presides over heaven as over a throne is above and within; and he who measures heaven with a handbreadth and encloses the earth in a span is outside, above, and below.

Thus, to indicate that almighty God is within and above all things, he declared that heaven is his throne. To show that he surrounds all things, he says that he measures heaven with a handbreadth and encloses the earth in a span.

He is therefore within and outside; below and above. He is above by governing and below by bearing; within by filling and outside by surrounding.
