Thus he is inside in such a way that he is outside; he surrounds in such a way that he penetrates; he presides in such a way that he bears; he bears in such a way that he presides.

When the soul, lifted up toward itself, both understands its own measure and recognizes that it transcends all bodily things, and then stretches from its own understanding toward the understanding of its Creator, what does it now behold except a door opposite a door?

Hence the Prophet says to the Creator of all things: “Your knowledge has become wonderful from me” (Ps. 138). For however intently the soul may strive, it is not fully sufficient to penetrate even itself. How much less can it penetrate the greatness of him who was able to create the soul?

And when it labors over understanding the knowledge of God, becoming weary and failing, it adds: “It was strengthened, and I shall not be able to reach it.” But when, striving and reaching out, we grow weary of seeing something of the invisible nature, we are struck back and driven away. Although we cannot penetrate the inner regions, we nevertheless already see the inner door from the outer door.

For the very labor of contemplation is a door that shows something of what is within, even though we still lack the power to enter.

«And he made façades for sixty cubits, and in front of the gate an atrium all around, on every side; and before the face of the gate that extended as far as the face of the vestibule of the inner gate, fifty cubits; and slanting windows in the chambers, and in the façades of those that were within the gate, all around. Likewise, in the vestibules there were windows all around on the inside, and before the façades, representations of palms.» (Jerome)

I think that between the outer wall of the temple, all around, and the building itself in the atrium—that is, in the middle—there were certain structures placed for ornament, which Symmachus interprets as *circumstantiae*, that is, things standing around: structures raised from the ground up into the air, occupying a space of sixty cubits. Again, as one went out from the inner gate toward the face of the vestibule that looked toward the outer gate, there was a space of fifty cubits, in which there were slanting windows. The Septuagint calls these “hidden,” while Symmachus calls them *toxika*—“arrow-windows.”

These windows were in the chambers, that is, in the individual rooms and porticoes extending before the rooms, occupying fifty cubits. These slanting windows, or *toxika*, received their name from arrows because, like arrows, they admit a narrow light into the buildings, while widening inward; and everything all around was filled with windows of this kind. “And before the façades,” he says, “of the porticoes there was a representation or carving of palms.” This shows that at the entrance of the gate, immediately upon entering, a wall sixty cubits long confronts them, with various ornaments that refer to the structure of the world, so that the Creator may be understood from his creatures. All things proceeding in order and according to reason display the variety of the world, which among the Greeks is called *kósmos* (κόσμος), taking its name from ornament, and which was made in six days, so that ten units may be reckoned for each day: the perfect number, as we have said above.

After this, as we enter the inner atrium, chambers with slanting windows confront us before the very vestibule of the inner gate. They occupy a space of fifty cubits, and this too is a sacred number. After the seven complete weeks of festivity and joy, the first day of the octave begins, which is the day of resurrection, and it brings us into the vicinity of the temple. For when we have done everything, repenting of our former error, we then become neighbors and intimates of God: in the outer atrium, the order and stability of creatures teach us knowledge of the Creator; in the inner atrium, the true Jubilee, in which all our debts are forgiven, instructs us in *theology* (θεολογία) and leads us into the Holy of Holies.

It should also be noted that the inner atrium has many windows—not straight and even, but slanting and narrow on the outside, widening inward—so that through certain small openings we may penetrate to the interior and reach the fullness of the exceedingly bright light that is present in the temple. Finally, after the seventy and fifty cubits, the chambers, the porticoes, the façades of the porticoes, and the many windows, a carving or representation of palms is shown to us all around, so that, possessing victory over the world, we may become worthy to see the palms of the virtues.

It follows: “And he made,” he says, “façades for sixty cubits, and in front of the gate an atrium all around, on every side.” (Gregory)

We have often said that the number six signifies the perfection of a good work. We do not follow the view that the wise men of this world have tried to establish, saying that the number six is perfect because, when counted in its proper order—one, two, three—the number six is completed; or because it is divided into three parts, namely a sixth, a third, and a half, that is, into one, two, and three. Rather, we say that the number six is perfect because, as was said shortly before, on the sixth day God completed all his works.

Since he gave the sinful human being the Law, which is written in ten commandments, and since six multiplied by ten rises to the number sixty, the perfection of good works is rightly signified by sixty cubits. The Lord also plainly indicates this in the Gospel. When explaining the parable of the sower, he said: “Another fell on good soil and produced fruit, growing and increasing; and it yielded one thirtyfold, one sixtyfold, and one a hundredfold.” The good soil yields thirtyfold when the mind conceives the perfection of faith, which is in the Trinity. It yields sixtyfold when it brings forth perfected works of a good life. It yields a hundredfold when it advances to the contemplation of eternal life.

Our left hand is the present life; the right hand, the life to come. The contemplation of eternal life is rightly signified by the number one hundred, because when, after thirty and sixty, we arrive by counting at the number one hundred, that same hundred passes over to the right. Faith and works are still on the left, because while we remain here, we believe what we do not see and work so that we may see. But when the mind has lifted itself into contemplation of eternal life, its reckoning reaches, as it were, the right hand.

Thus he made façades for sixty cubits. Since the number sixty signifies perfection, what else are signified by the façades of the building but the works themselves, which are seen outwardly? To give the word of preaching to one’s neighbors, to provide food for the hungry and clothing for the cold, and patiently to endure adversity for the sake of good works—what else are these but façades of the heavenly building? For the beauty of outward works adorns the dwelling of God, which is still hidden within.

But these façades have an atrium all around them, because works are great when the breadth of charity enlarges them in the mind. Of charity it is written: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad.” The atrium before the façade is therefore the breadth of love within the perfection of the work. And it should be noted that he says, “all around,” so that a person may continually enlarge himself in the breadth of charity in everything he does, lest fear or hatred constrict him.

If someone speaks the word of God but does not preserve in his mind the charity he preaches, he has the façade of the building, but no atrium before the façade. If someone gives alms generously to the needy but perhaps becomes proud in his heart because of it, and does not assist his neighbor’s poverty out of charity but silently exalts himself through vanity, he displays a façade in the building but has not made an atrium beside the façade.

If someone tolerates insults inflicted by a neighbor and silently bears the evil accusations made against him, he demonstrates great patience. But he has the atrium before the façade if he has no pain in his heart and seeks to win even the person who acted wrongly over to the tranquility of gentleness. For if, while practicing patience outwardly, he retains pain within and does not love the person whom he endures, he has a façade in the building but no atrium before the façade. The person who has subjected himself to the narrowness of hatred has plainly lost the breadth of charity. For, as we already said in the preceding section, true patience is that which also loves the person whom it bears. To tolerate someone while hating him is not the virtue of gentleness but a veil for rage.

It should also be noted that this very atrium is called the atrium of the gate. Our gate is the entrance to the kingdom; and to love God and one’s neighbor is already to strive toward entry into the kingdom. To the extent that someone loves, to that extent he approaches the entrance. To the extent that he neglects to love, to that extent he refuses to enter, because he does not strive to see what he desires.

We therefore have the atrium of the gate when, through the breadth of charity, we already enter by desire into the heavenly life, which we are still entirely unable to reach. Thus, when a good work is performed toward one’s neighbor, what remains is to discern the intention of that good work: whether the mind seeks no recompense of present favor, but directs its hope toward the promise of the future, hoping for eternal things from temporal things and heavenly things from earthly things.

Hope of heavenly realities strengthens the mind, so that it is not shaken by the waves of earthly turmoil. Concerning this hope Paul also says: “Which we have as a sure and firm anchor of the soul, and entering even into the interior of the veil.” Concerning this interior place it is likewise added here: “And before the face of the gate, which extended as far as the face of the vestibule of the inner gate, fifty cubits.”

What is said here, “before the face of the gate,” describes not an outer location but a place before the inner gate, since it is said to extend as far as the face of the vestibule of the inner gate. Hence this same place is said to have been measured as fifty cubits. For the number fifty signifies eternal rest.

The number seven possesses its own perfection, because on that day the number of the days was completed, and through the Law the Sabbath was given for rest. The number seven, multiplied by itself, reaches forty-nine. When one is added to it, it arrives at the number fifty, because all our perfection will consist in the contemplation of that One in whose vision nothing of salvation or joy will then be lacking for us.

For this reason also the Jubilee—that is, fifty years—was given over to rest, because whoever reaches the eternal joys of almighty God will have neither labor nor groaning.

It should be noted, however, that the place described as extending for fifty cubits is said to reach the face of the vestibule of the inner gate. The prophet therefore does not at this point describe the vestibule of the inner gate itself, but the place farther within that extends toward the vestibule of the inner gate. Through this place, as we have said, our hope is signified: while it seeks eternal rest, it leads the mind toward the vestibule of the inner gate.

The very fact that we desire heavenly things, that we sigh for the promised joys, and that we seek the rest of eternal life means that we are already approaching the face of the inner vestibule. Let faith, then, be signified by the gate; charity by the atrium; and hope by the place that approaches the face of the vestibule of the inner gate. Without these three virtues, no one who is capable of using reason can enter the heavenly building.

Let faith therefore be held in the gate, because it introduces us to understanding; charity in the atrium, because it enlarges the mind in love; and let hope be described by fifty cubits, because through desires and sighs it introduces the soul to the hidden joys of rest. Although we do not yet see the light of truth as it truly is in that rest, we already see something of it through the cracks of understanding.

Hence it is added here: “And slanting windows in the chambers.” In slanting windows, the part through which the light enters is narrow, but the interior part that receives the light is broad. So too the minds of contemplatives, although they see something of the true light only faintly, are nevertheless enlarged within themselves with great breadth. Yet they can scarcely contain even the small things that they behold.

Very little is what the contemplative sees of eternity, but from that very little the bosom of the mind is loosened and enlarged for an increase of fervor and love. From the very point at which they admit the light of truth into themselves, as it were through narrow passages, they become spacious within themselves.

This greatness of contemplation, since it can be granted only to those who love, is said to be present in the chambers—in those that are said to be beside the chambers, no longer outwardly but inwardly. For concerning these same windows it is added: “And in the façades of those that were within the gate, all around.”

They were in the chambers, and they were also in the façades of those structures that had been built within the gate, all around. For whoever has a heart turned inward also receives the light of contemplation. Those who still think excessively about outward things do not know what the cracks of contemplation drawn from the eternal light are. The infusion of incorporeal light cannot be grasped while the images of bodily things occupy the mind: when only visible things are contemplated, invisible light is not admitted into the mind.

But whoever directs his attention to the light of contemplation must take great care to keep his mind always in humility, never exalting himself because of the grace poured into him. He should also consider what the slanting windows are like that signify the minds of contemplatives.

Through slanting windows light enters, but a thief does not enter, because those who are true watchers always press their understanding down into humility. The understanding of contemplation enters their minds, but the boastfulness of pride does not. The windows are therefore open and fortified: the grace by which they are filled is open in their minds, yet they do not allow the adversary to enter them through pride.

It should also be noted that slanting windows are said to be within the gate, all around. The grace of contemplation is not given only to the highest and withheld from the least. Often the highest receive it, often the lowest; more often those who are withdrawn from the world, and sometimes even married people. If, then, no state of the faithful is excluded from the grace of contemplation, whoever has a heart turned inward can also be illumined by the light of contemplation. For slanting windows have been constructed within the gate, all around, so that no one may boast of this grace as though it were his unique possession.

Let no one think that he alone possesses the gift of true light. In the very matter in which someone thinks himself preeminent, another may often be richer, though he does not think that the other possesses anything good.

Hence this too is appropriately added: “Likewise, there were also windows in the vestibules, all around on the inside.” After saying “windows in the façades,” he adds, “windows in the vestibules, all around on the inside.” For not only the higher members of holy Church, who stand out prominently, possess the grace of contemplation; often this gift is received also by those members who, although they already soar toward the heights through desire, still lie below through their service.

If almighty God did not pour the light of contemplation even into those who appear despised, there would not have been windows in the vestibules.

We therefore see some people established in the highest places of holy Church, speaking lofty things about heavenly realities and, with wondrous zeal, searching out the secrets of the heavenly homeland as far as their illumined mind can manage. These are windows in the façades.

Others, however, are contained within the bosom of holy Church and appear despised in human eyes, but devote themselves privately to the pursuits of wisdom. They long for heavenly things and, as far as they are able, contemplate what the eternal joys are. These too are slanting windows, though the sun is not in them.

It is rightly said, “all around,” because every investigation of hidden things has a circuit, when the mind says in its thought: “Could this be it? Could that be it?” It circles around, as it were, in order to find what it seeks. When the unbounded light begins to break forth into recognition, a ray of truth comes as if through a slanting window.

Thus, in our contemplation, we accomplish many things by circling through our thoughts, just as we often seek examples of good people in order to advance in conduct. When the mind begins to consider passing over to better things, it searches out whatever better example it may hear from others; now it examines the life of one person, now that of another saint.

Hence a certain chosen one, who had sent the eyes of his mind throughout the whole world, within the expanded bosom of holy Church, seeking the lives of good people for imitation, said: “I will go around and sacrifice in his tabernacle a sacrifice of jubilation” (Psalm 26). Behold, he went around in order to offer a sacrifice of jubilation: for unless he sent his mind here and there to search out the lives of good people, he would not have reached the sacrifice of jubilation.

But when holy men are brought within the Church to the highest places, their life is set up like a mirror, so that all may see the good things they ought to imitate. Hence this too is appropriately added: “And before the façades, representations of palms.”

What else is signified by palms but the rewards of victory? Palms themselves are customarily given to the victorious. Thus it is written concerning those who had conquered the ancient enemy in the contest of martyrdom and were already rejoicing as victors in their homeland: “Palms were in their hands, and they cried out with a loud voice, saying: Salvation belongs to our God, who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb” (Revelation 7).

To have palms in one’s hands is to have held victories in one’s works. The palm of that work will be bestowed where one already rejoices without a contest.

Here, therefore, it does not say “palms before the façades,” but “before the façades, representations of palms.” For the victory will be seen there, where joy will already be without end.

We often see holy men performing wondrous deeds: doing many mighty works, cleansing lepers, driving out demons, dispelling bodily illnesses by their touch, and proclaiming future events through the spirit of prophecy. Yet none of these things is a palm as yet, but only a representation of palms. For such things are sometimes given even to the reprobate. Thus Truth says in the Gospel (Luke 13): “Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?’ And then I will declare to them, ‘I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of iniquity.’”

There is, however, one sure sign of election: steadfastness in charity, as it is written: “By this it will be known that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13). When the elect perform these miracles, they perform them in a manner very different from that of the reprobate. What the elect strive to do out of charity, the reprobate strive to do through pride. Yet even for the elect, the very miracles they perform through charity are not yet palms but still representations of palms, because outwardly they show what sort of people they are held to be inwardly by almighty God.

There will be a palm for them there, where the struggle with death will no longer exist. For the outstanding preacher then saw that the true palm would be given to those who conquer, when he foresaw the resurrection of the dead, saying: “For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality. Then the saying that is written will come to pass: ‘Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?’” (1 Corinthians 15). Then, therefore, victory will be perfect, when death has been completely swallowed up.

“Then he led me out to the outer court. And behold, there were storerooms and a pavement laid with stone around the court: thirty storerooms around the pavement, and the pavement in front of the gates was lower. And he measured the breadth from the front of the lower gate to the front of the inner court on the outside, one hundred cubits toward the east and toward the north.” (Jerome)

That man, then, who had a builder’s cord in his hand and a measuring reed, and who stood at the gate, after showing the prophet, among other things, the outer court of sixty cubits and another vestibule of the inner gate extending fifty cubits, led the prophet out to the outer court—or, as it is contained in the Septuagint, brought him into the inner court. And I am sufficiently astonished, according to the literal sense and the Septuagint, how, after the outer parts of the court extending seventy and fifty cubits, there can be an inner court stretching across a breadth of one hundred cubits, unless perhaps, according to mystical interpretations, the inner things in doctrine are broader in proportion to the progress of those entering.

When he had been brought into the inner court—or led to the outer court, as it is contained in the Hebrew—he immediately saw thirty chambers or storerooms. As Symmachus translated it, these were side chambers prepared for the dwelling of Levites and priests, and a pavement laid with living stones; or else they were intercolumnar spaces, so that it might be shown that the inner or outer court had, before its doors, a row of columns. And [Col. 0921A] the pavement in front of the gates—or porticoes behind the gates. In these porticoes, I think, columns had been arranged in order, so that porticoes were in front of the storerooms, and at the fronts of the porticoes were columns supporting the porticoes.

The pavement, then, which was laid with stones and extended before the porticoes of the court, was lower than the ascent of the porticoes, and had the same length as the building of the chambers. The same man, in whose hand were the cord and the reed, measured from the front of the lower gate—or, as the Septuagint has it, the outer gate—to the front of the court or inner gate, one hundred cubits toward the east and, as it is said in the Hebrew, also toward the north.

From this we understand that the evangelical saying narrated by the Savior concerning seed sown in a field, in good soil that produces crops according to the variety of virtues—thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold—agrees with the prophecy of this passage. Here too the thirtieth, sixtieth, and hundredth numbers are set forth, so that by these stages we may be able to reach perfect knowledge, provided that the number fifty leads us to the inner building: for, when the Sabbath of seven weeks has ended, it breaks forth into the day of resurrection.

Storerooms are so called because they are filled with spiritual riches, concerning which it is written: “The redemption of a man’s soul is his own riches” (Prov. XIII). The Apostle Paul also rejoices over his disciples because they are filled with every word and all knowledge. In the Persian language, *gaza* means “riches.”

Or else the chambers, which in Greek are called παστοφορία (*pastophoria*), show rooms prepared for the bridegroom’s coming. They were thirty in number, to indicate the perfect age of their inhabitants. The pavement was laid with stone, so that the footsteps of the inhabitants might not be polluted with mud, earth, or the dust of sins, but that they might walk upon living stones from which God’s temple is built. Or there were intercolumnar spaces before the doors of the chambers, supporting the building placed above them. These are the columns about which the Apostle Paul writes (Gal. II): “Peter and John, who were reputed to be pillars, gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship.” And elsewhere (I Tim. III): “The pillar and foundation of the truth.” In John’s Apocalypse we read (Apoc. III): “The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go out no more.”

The pavement, therefore, which was in front of the gates, of which we have already spoken—or the porticoes behind the gates, which protected the inhabitants of the chambers from the rains—was lower. For the things that are lower are always placed in higher positions, so that by ascent and steps we may reach mystical and secret things filled with spiritual riches.

Often the complete number is found in the number ten multiplied by ten, which also multiplies Isaac’s seed into a hundredfold harvest. But because he was on earth and could still say, “I am a sojourner and a pilgrim, like all my fathers” (Gen. XXIII), he is said to have sown barley and reaped a hundredfold harvest. For the grain of wheat had not yet died in the earth so as to produce much fruit and satisfy the hunger of the Jewish people for hearing God’s word with the bread that came down from heaven.

**Gregory.** After the prophet has said much about the grace of contemplation, introducing the oblique windows, he says that he was led outside and records that he saw storerooms. What else is signified by these storerooms except the knowledge of teachers? Yet in this matter one may ask: since holy teachers teach both spiritual and earthly things, why does the prophet say that he was led outside and saw the storerooms outside?

It must be understood that there is one contemplation that sees as much as it cannot express, and another knowledge and teaching that sees as much as it can express through the tongue. In comparison with that light which cannot be expressed by speech, everything that can be expressed by speech is, as it were, outside.

He therefore says: “And he led me out to the outer court, and behold, there were storerooms and a pavement laid with stone around the court.” Since in Greek *phylaxe* means “to preserve,” while *gaza* in the Persian language means “riches,” a storeroom is ordinarily called a place in which riches are kept. What, then, is signified by storerooms except, as we said before, the hearts of teachers filled with the riches of wisdom and knowledge?

For, according to Paul’s words: “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge in the same Spirit” (I Cor. XXII). Some, through the gift of grace, understand even those things which they have not heard expounded by teachers; these, clearly, have received words of wisdom. Others cannot understand by themselves what they have heard, but retain what they have read in commentators and set it forth intelligently, having learned what they read. From what source, then, are these people filled, except with a word of knowledge?

This may also be understood in another way: wisdom pertains to life, whereas knowledge pertains to teaching. Therefore, one who lives well and preaches prudently is rightly called a storeroom of the spiritual building, because riches are distributed from his mouth. The same teacher of the nations saw his disciples abounding in these riches when he said: “You have been enriched in him, in every word and in all knowledge” (I Cor. I).

Moreover, spiritual riches lead to the eternal homeland and differ greatly from earthly riches, because spiritual riches increase when distributed, whereas earthly riches either are distributed and diminish, or are kept and become useless. Therefore those who contain these true riches within themselves are rightly called storerooms.

These storerooms also have a pavement around them, because the humility of their hearers clings to them and lies beneath them. That pavement is rightly said to be laid with stone in the court, because faithful souls joined to one another in the breadth of charity are called stones on account of the firmness of their faith, and are laid in the pavement through the structure of humility.

The Apostle Peter had seen these minds of the faithful, strong in faith, when he said: “You also, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house” (I Pet. II). Concerning these stones of the holy Church the Lord says through Isaiah (Isa. LIV): “I will set jasper for your battlements, and your gates in carved stones, all your boundaries in precious stones, all your children taught by the Lord.”

What Isaiah saw as all the boundaries of the Church—precious stones—Ezekiel declared to be a pavement laid with stone around the court, since he goes on to say concerning the storerooms: “Thirty storerooms around the pavement.”

The number ten is always understood as perfection, because the keeping of the law is contained in the ten commandments. The active and contemplative life are joined together in the commandments of the Decalogue, because in them both the love of God and the love of neighbor are commanded. The love of God pertains to the contemplative life, while the love of neighbor pertains to the active life.

But each teacher, in order to expand fully into the active life and rise vigilantly into the contemplative life, must be perfected in faith in the holy Trinity. Hence these same storerooms are said to be thirty in number, so that, when ten is multiplied three times, the life and speech of the teacher may be established in the Trinity.

Yet in this matter we must observe attentively that, after the prophet had described the storerooms, he added that there was a pavement around them, and then below he says that the storerooms were around the pavement, so that the storerooms appear to be around the pavement and the pavement around the storerooms. The pavement and the storerooms were distinguished in such an arrangement that the storerooms were within the pavement and the pavement was laid between the storerooms.

This is not without a great mystery: the pavement is said to be around the storerooms, and the storerooms are said to be around the pavement. The pavement has storerooms around it because the life of hearers is daily instructed and guarded by the speech of teachers. Good teachers watch over the life of their hearers through words of holy instruction—sometimes with the consolations of sweetness, sometimes with the severity of rebuke—in order to defend their hearers’ lives from vices.

But the storerooms themselves have pavement around them because often the heart of teachers is also touched by temptations of vices: sometimes it is lifted up by the boasting of pride, and sometimes inflamed by the goads of anger. Yet when they consider the lives of good hearers, and weigh how those hearers have progressed through their exhortations, they are ashamed not to be such as, by God’s authorship, they see others have become. Before they fall fully into guilt, they establish themselves firmly in their minds.

For when their own words return to their memory, they are ashamed not to observe what they say. Hence it is also said through Solomon: “The soul of one who labors labors for himself, because his mouth has compelled him” (Prov. XVI). Our mouth compels us to labor when, through what we have said, we are restrained from vices. It is exceedingly shameful to fall through negligence precisely where, by preaching, we have tried to raise others.

Therefore the storerooms have pavement around them because the venerable life of hearers is a great protection for teachers, and the teachers’ own speech becomes their aid. They are ashamed not to resist the vices that assail them when they have armed others against vices.

For, as long as we live in this life, what else are we doing against evil spirits except standing in battle formation? As we said before, the teacher’s mind may be struck by some form of pride. But, whether so that he himself may not perish or so that he may not draw others to destruction by his example, he carefully and quickly examines himself. In his thoughts, with his hearers brought to mind, he reproaches and humbles himself, and in whatever ways he prevails, acts so that pride may not rule his mind or dominate his conduct.

For it is written: “The beginning of every sin is pride” (Eccl. X). What fruit of a good work, then, will remain before God if its root has rotted through pride?

Often, as has been said, his mind is tempted by anger. But by quickly examining himself he gathers himself together, and by weighing himself down with discipline he ensures that the movement of his spirit does not pass into speech or break out in his voice. Thus the anger of a troubled mind, wherever it arises through negligence, dies suffocated there through judgment.

As a result, the mind gives birth to virtue from a conceived fault. For although it did not wish to guard itself firmly enough to prevent rising into agitation, it nevertheless conquered itself firmly in the midst of agitation. Hence Solomon rightly says: “The patient man is better than the strong, and one who rules his spirit than one who captures a city” (Prov. XVI).

“And the pavement in front of the gates, according to the length of the gates, was lower.” If we refer the length of the gates to the place in which the gates were constructed, the pavement was lower according to the length of the gates: it extended as far as the place of the gates could hold, and so did the lower pavement.

The length of the pavement, therefore, was not unlike that of the gates, but the pavement was nevertheless not equal to the gates. What does it mean that the pavement was equally long with the gates but not equal to them, except that the life of peoples is far removed from the life of teachers? Although those who strive toward the heavenly kingdoms have the same perseverance of hope, they do not have the same devotion to living.

Let the pavement, therefore, extend equally in length, because hearers retain within themselves the same faith and hope that preachers certainly possess. But let the pavement lie lower, so that all hearers may recognize that their preachers greatly surpass their own merits.

But if by the length of the gates we should understand their height, as we said above, then, since one ascended to the gates by steps, the pavement lies lower in proportion as each gate rises in height. For the holier the life of the teacher, the humbler becomes the understanding of the hearer, who despises himself when he perceives the life of his preacher rising to great heights.

A hearer may perhaps imitate some of the teacher’s good qualities but not others. In those things in which he succeeds, he progresses; in those in which he does not succeed, he grows in humility. Thus what he cannot imitate for advancement itself becomes advancement for him.

For if we weigh the deeds and words of our preachers that we read, we recognize how high the gates have risen. To say nothing of the display of signs, let us speak of the virtues of their hearts.

Certainly Paul, who says that through the law he died to the law, and that the law itself preached this to him so that he might believe in Christ, was inflamed with great fervor of faith. He refused to observe the precepts of the law carnally and forbade circumcision to be practiced among the Gentiles. And when the Apostle Peter still wished the custom of the law concerning circumcision to be observed, Paul opposed him to his face and says that Peter was blameworthy in this matter. Speaking to the disciples about his conduct, he calls it not only fault but, what is more, hypocrisy—that is, pretense—saying: “When Peter came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he was blameworthy” (Gal. II). And shortly afterward: “The other Jews joined him in his pretense” (ibid.).

But that first of the apostles, when he admonished the disciples about many things and learned that some were disparaging Paul’s writings, says: “Our beloved brother Paul, according to the wisdom given him, wrote to you, speaking in them about these matters, in which there are some things difficult to understand, which the ignorant and unstable distort, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own destruction” (II Pet. III).

Behold, Paul writes in his Epistles that Peter was blameworthy; behold, Peter asserts in his Epistles that Paul is admirable in what he wrote. Certainly, if Peter had not read Paul’s Epistles, he would not have praised them. But if he read them, he found there that he himself was called blameworthy.

Therefore, as a friend of truth, he praised even the fact that he had been rebuked. He was pleased by this very thing: that in matters where he had not held the right opinion, he had yielded to a younger brother and had become the follower of one junior to him, so that he might take precedence even in this respect. Although he was first in the height of the apostolate, he would also be first in humility.

Let us therefore consider on what mountain peak he stood who praised the Epistles in which he found himself written as deserving blame. What such great gentleness could there have been, what peace of soul, what firmness of mind and untroubledness of thought?

Behold, he is both rebuked by his junior and does not disdain being rebuked. He does not recall that he was called first among the apostles; nor that whatever he loosed on earth would be loosed also in heaven; nor that he had walked on the sea; nor that he had raised paralytics by commanding them in Jesus’ name; nor that he had healed the sick by the shadow of his body; nor that he had killed liars by a word; nor that he had raised the dead by prayer.

So that he might not disdain hearing words of rebuke, he thrust from his memory, as it were, all the gifts he had received, in order to hold firmly to the one gift of humility.

Let us consider, if we can, the Apostle Paul, who was as patient among persecutors as he was gentle among disciples. Certainly, when he came to Corinth, he withdrew the Corinthians from the service of idols, made known to them who the true God was, and preached to them the joys of eternal life.

And when he had gathered a great multitude of people into the faith, he endured such great poverty there that he suffered severe need for food. He did not receive earthly bread from the disciples to whom he preached heavenly bread. He devoted himself in speech to the life of his hearers and devoted himself to the labor of his hands for the life of his body.

From other lands, too, support was sent to him by disciples so that he could continue preaching to the Corinthians. He himself says to those same Corinthians in an Epistle: “When I was with you and was in need, I was a burden to no one. For the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied what I lacked” (II Cor. XI).

Let us therefore consider how lofty are the gates of this spiritual building, which even spiritual fathers admire. How much humility, then, is necessary for us in admiring them, since we are the pavement?

But since we have understood the height of the gates under the name of length, let us now learn something about their breadth.

“And he measured,” it says, “the breadth from the front of the lower gate to the front of the inner court on the outside, one hundred cubits toward the east and toward the north.”

If we understand the gate as the entrance through which we enter into knowledge of the Lord, the lower gate is faith, while the inner court is contemplation. The lower gate has breadth at its front because faith, through the amplitude of its charity, possesses an operation visible to one’s neighbors.

When we see this practiced vigorously by the more perfect, we who are constricted in good works receive from them examples of great action. Each holy action becomes for us a kind of breadth of the way, which previously had been the narrowness of difficulty.

The inner court also has a front because the contemplative life, through certain signs of desires and sighs, shows how much it sees within, since it loves so greatly.

The number ten, multiplied by itself, rises to one hundred. Hence perfection is rightly signified by the number one hundred, as is said concerning the elect: “Everyone who leaves house or brothers or sisters, or father or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name’s sake, will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life” (Matt. XIX).

No holy person, after all, abandons earthly things so that he may possess more of them in this world. Whoever leaves the earth through earthly desire does not leave the earth but desires it. Nor will one who leaves a single wife receive a hundred wives. Rather, perfection is signified by the number one hundred, after which eternal life is also promised: whoever despises temporal and earthly things for God’s name receives perfection of mind even here, so that he no longer desires what he has despised, and in the age to come reaches the glory of eternal life.

Therefore the man measured the breadth from the front of the lower gate to the front of the inner court on the outside, one hundred cubits, because our Redeemer daily measures the life of the faithful, through teachers and instructors, according to the measure of perfection—either in the appearance of good works through faith or in holy desires through contemplation.

Who, then, is measured by one hundred cubits except one whose good action is governed by right intention, so that in what he does he does not turn toward the pursuit of earthly profit or passing praise?

Behold, showing mercy to one’s neighbors, giving away what one possesses, and giving promptly to the needy is breadth at the front of the lower gate. But if, while giving what is yours, you do not desire what belongs to another, and if you do not seek earthly glory from the good work itself, then you are rightly measured by the number one hundred, that is, by perfection.

For one who appears to give his own possessions mercifully but perhaps violently seizes those belonging to others still does not know what the way of perfection is, nor has he understood from what point one proceeds toward perfection, because he has not even found its beginning. First he ought to have torn desire from his mind, and afterward to have distributed what he possessed in material goods.

Hence it is written: “Turn away from evil and do good.” For what good can there be in what one does if one has not yet turned away from evil?

There are also some who, as has been said, abstain from food and afflict their flesh, but when they are tested, are found to pant after the glory of the world. These show the front of the inner court, but they are not measured by one hundred cubits.

These, then, are among the number of perfection, concerning whom Paul says: “Those who have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. V).

It must also be noted that it is not said that these things are measured inwardly but outwardly. For our Redeemer, when he approves or judges human deeds, does not measure inwardly. Hence it is also said through the Gospel: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. VII).

When we see some people giving alms, hastening to those afflicted, helping the oppressed, seeking no glory in this world and longing for none of this world’s advantages, while we see others subduing their flesh, persevering in tears, occupying themselves with heavenly words, and desiring no passing honor, what ought we to do except believe them perfect and judge them holy?

Because by what we see we perceive them to be perfect, we measure their life by one hundred cubits.

And because many among the Jews, and very many among the Gentiles, have reached this summit of perfection, it is rightly added: “Toward the east and toward the north.”

The Jewish people is rightly called the east, because from its flesh was born the one who is called the sun of righteousness, concerning whom the prophet says: “But for you who fear the Lord, the sun of righteousness shall rise” (Mal. IV).

The Gentiles are represented by the north, which for a long time languished in the cold of its unbelief, and in whose heart reigned the one who, as the prophet testifies, said of himself: “I will set my throne in the north.”

Therefore, because the incarnate almighty Lord made some perfect within the holy Church from the Jews and others perfect from the Gentiles, he measured one hundred cubits not only toward the east but also toward the north.

**Jerome.** But how one hundred cubits extended not only to the eastern gate but also to the northern gate, the following testimony will show.

“And he measured the gate that faced the way of the north of the outer court, both in length and in breadth, with its chambers three on this side and three on that, and its front and its vestibule according to the measure of the first gate, its length being fifty cubits and its breadth twenty-five cubits. Its windows, vestibule, and sculptured work were according to the measure of the gate that faced east, and its ascent was by seven steps. And its vestibule was in front of it, and the gate of the inner court was opposite the northern and eastern gate. And he measured from gate to gate one hundred cubits.”

The man whose cord was in his hand measured also the gate of the outer court that faced north—or brought the prophet in through the northern gate.

Second, through the southern gate.

Third, through the eastern gate.

“For from the north evils will be kindled against the inhabitants of the earth.” And fittingly, one who is an inhabitant of the earth, not a sojourner and pilgrim, lies open to the arrows of the one who comes from the north, whose fiery arrows, according to the Apostle, are extinguished by the shield of faith.

The outer court is situated toward the north, but toward the south, that is, toward the south wind, the court is not outer but inner. For Scripture says: “And he brought me into the inner court, to the southern gate,” and the same is similarly found concerning the eastern court.

The first entrance into virtue is to trample the north beneath one’s feet and to reach the summit of the number one hundred through the numbers fifty and twenty-five. Then one is brought into the southern region and drives away the cold of the north. At that point one comes to perfect virtue, that is, to the eastern gate, where the sun of righteousness rises and through which the high priest alone enters.

It must also be observed that, although there are four regions, the western gate is passed over. Concerning it, at the beginning of the sixty-seventh Psalm, it is written: “Make a way for him who ascends over the west; the Lord is his name” (Ps. LXVII).

Thus, after we have prepared a way for the Lord and fulfilled what John the Baptist cries in the wilderness—“Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight” (Matt. XI)—we may hear what is said at the end of the same psalm: “Sing to God, sing praise to the Lord, who ascends above the heaven of heaven toward the east.”

The statement that there were three chambers on this side and three on that teaches that both letter and spirit, and both forms of understanding—the historical and the tropological—pertain to the mysteries of the Trinity.

The addition, “And its front and its vestibule were according to the measure of the first gate,” signifies the eastern gate, which is called “first” not in order but in merit.

“And it had,” he says, “fifty cubits in length and twenty-five in breadth,” so that in the fiftieth year, after seven weeks, eternal rest might be shown, extending through the day of resurrection toward the kingdoms of heaven, in which true rest exists.

Regarding the number twenty-five, about which we have already spoken, the measure of the five senses is maintained through five rows of a square, one of which corresponds to length and the other to breadth. In length, the rest and delight of more sacred knowledge are signified; in breadth, the order of present things pertaining to the senses is represented.

What follows—“Its windows, vestibules, and sculptured work”—or, as the Septuagint added, “its palms were according to the measure of the gate that faced east”—subtly indicates that whoever, placed at the entrance of virtues, has entered three chambers on each side and recognized the front and vestibule according to the measure of the first gate, reaches and beholds those things which he will also receive in full at the eastern gate.

Furthermore, what follows—“Its ascent was by seven steps, and its vestibule was before it,” or “within”—has this meaning: through the seven steps of the week, through the pot kindled on the north side, and through the Jewish ceremonies, to which God gave commandments that were not good and statutes by which they should not live, we ascend to higher things.

And we ascend to its vestibule, that is, the vestibule of the gate, for which the Septuagint rendered *elamoth*. This vestibule is before the gate, or within it.

There is not only one northern gate, which above is called the outer gate, but also another inner gate resembling the eastern gate, as the Septuagint states more clearly: “And the gate of the inner court facing the northern gate, just as there was a gate facing east.”

“And he measured from the outer northern gate to the inner gate of the same north one hundred cubits,” so that by these stages and measurements, withdrawing from the outer gate, we may be able to reach the inner gate. The mystery of this number has been discussed above.

**Gregory.** The gate faces the way of the north when any preacher recognizes the life of a sinner and opens to him the inner things of life through the word of preaching. This gate is called the gate of the outer court.

The outer court is the present life, in which everything done bodily is also seen bodily. It is measured both in length and in breadth because, when a sinner is led to faith, his teacher must consider how far he progresses through the preacher’s admonition in the length of hope and in the breadth of charity.

If one who is converted to God still hopes for the good things of the present life, he does not have length, because the life in which he has placed his hope is brief. If, through desire for earthly things and hatred of his neighbor, he remains constricted, he does not have breadth, because he does not know either how to despise transitory things or how to expand himself in love of his neighbor.

But when a convert patiently hopes for the joys of eternal life, bears the troubles of his neighbors with charity, and disdains desiring what he does not possess, the gate has length and breadth. For the progress of the hearer is the glory of the preacher. Hence the great preacher says to certain people: “You are my joy and my crown” (Phil. IV). And again: “Now I live, if you stand firm in the Lord” (I Thess. III). And once more: “For what is our hope or joy? Is it not you before our Lord?” (I Thess. II).

The length and breadth of the gate that faces north are present because, when a preacher converts an unbeliever languishing in the cold of his sin to faith, he makes that person’s glory his own by extending him in the length of hope and expanding him in the breadth of charity. And because, through the word of preaching, each hearer progresses in the knowledge of the holy Trinity and in love of that same Trinity, the gate has three chambers on this side and three on that.

Everything the Creator says about the Trinity through the New Testament is shown by him from the Old Testament, and he perfects the hearts of hearers in love of the heavenly homeland. Thus the soul clinging to God, like a bride with her bridegroom, already sits in a kind of chamber and turns itself completely away from earthly desires.

Or, as was said much earlier, there are three orders of those who live well: the good married, the continent, and the preachers. Since the Church has these three orders of good people not only from the Gentiles but at times also from the synagogue, when a great multitude of spiritual people ardently awaited the grace of the Redeemer, the gate of the heavenly building has three chambers on this side and three on that.

For whenever a preacher urges a hearer toward the heavenly homeland, he shows that both the new fathers and the ancient fathers longed for it with heavenly desire. Examples usually move the heart more deeply than words of preaching. When a preacher says what sort of people in marriage, continence, or preaching existed in the New Testament in relation to the love of almighty God, or what sort existed in the Old Testament, the gate that speaks shows that it has three chambers on each side.

This gate also has a front, because there are open works in the preacher’s life that can be seen. It also has a vestibule before its front, because before he reveals good works, he preaches faith, through which the soul, coming humbly, is lifted to the height of good actions. All these things are according to the measure of the first gate, as is added: “For he measured its length as fifty cubits and its breadth as twenty-five cubits.”

You remember that I have already discussed these matters more fully above. We said that the number fifty represents rest, because the fiftieth year was also given to the ancient people as a year of rest and was called the jubilee. The number seven, by which all this time unfolds, multiplied seven times reaches forty-nine; one is added to it because eternal rest is perfected in the contemplation of the One.

This number fifty is therefore length for us, because no one can reach that rest unless he can now extend his hope toward it with patient perseverance. Hence, immediately after the length of fifty cubits, the breadth of twenty-five cubits is added. This breadth pertains to love of neighbor. For charity expands itself in love of the brethren and exercises toward them every good work it can.

All good works that are performed bodily are displayed through the five bodily senses: sight, hearing, touch, taste, and smell. The number five, multiplied by itself, reaches twenty-five, because when good works begin to be performed, they arouse the soul through fervor to increase, and multiply through themselves. Thus they create breadth for the mind, so that it may not be constricted through lukewarmness but expanded in good works through charity.

Every sluggishness is a constriction of lukewarmness; every kindness of charity is a great breadth. Even if one lacks material things that could perhaps be offered to a needy neighbor, the substance of good will is broad enough, and it suffices for the reward of the kingdom, as it is written: “Peace on earth to people of good will” (Luke II).

> “Its windows,” he says, “and its vestibule and its sculptured work were according to the measurement of the gate that faced east.”

All these matters have already been discussed more fully above, and therefore the exposition should not be delayed by a laborious treatment. This, however, must be noted with particular care: the gate to the north is said to possess all the features that the gate to the east possesses—namely, windows of contemplation, a vestibule of humility, and sculptured work of good action.

For all who, through having been born to God in their way of life, have remained in innocence possess the gate to the east, because the entrance to the heavenly kingdom lies open to them through the light they have received. And all who afterward have fallen into sins and been weighed down by the cold of their sluggishness, but return through repentance and grow warm again toward the love of their heavenly homeland, possess the gate to the north, because even after the cold of their sin the entrance to the kingdom is opened to them by mercy.

Thus the gate to the north is said to possess what the gate to the east possesses, because converted sinners are enriched with virtues just as are those who avoided falling into sin. Hence, through the voice of the Psalmist, the Lord says: “I ate ashes like bread” (Psalm 101), because he received penitents as he received the righteous. For it is written concerning sinners: “Long ago they would have repented in sackcloth and ashes.” Ashes, therefore, are eaten like bread when the sinner is recalled through repentance to the grace of his Maker as though he were innocent.

The gate to the north, then, has windows, a vestibule, and sculptured work, because when the sinner is restored to life after his transgressions, he often receives the light of contemplation; and from the very remembrance of his iniquity he draws the grace of great humility and the effectiveness of good action, so that everything commanded to be done may appear to be sculpted in his life.

> “There were seven steps to ascend to it, and a vestibule before it.”

One ascends to the gate by seven steps because, through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, the entrance to heavenly life is opened to us. Isaiah, enumerating this sevenfold grace in our Head himself, or in his body, which we are, says:

> “The spirit of wisdom and understanding shall rest upon him, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isaiah 11).

When speaking of heavenly things, he counted these steps by descending rather than ascending: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear. And since it is written, “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm 110), there is no doubt that one ascends from fear to wisdom, but does not return from wisdom to fear, since wisdom evidently possesses perfect love. It is also written: “Perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4).

The prophet, therefore, because he was speaking from heavenly things down to those below, began with wisdom and descended to fear. But we, who strive from earthly things toward heavenly things, should count those same steps in ascending, so that we may be able to reach wisdom from fear. In our mind, then, the first step of ascent is the fear of the Lord; the second, piety; the third, knowledge; the fourth, fortitude; the fifth, counsel; the sixth, understanding; and the seventh, wisdom.

There is indeed fear of the Lord in the mind; but what sort of fear is it if piety is not joined to it? Whoever does not know how to show mercy to his neighbor, whoever pretends not to share in his neighbor’s affliction—such a person’s fear is nothing before the eyes of almighty God, because it is not raised up to piety.

Yet piety often tends to err through disordered mercy, if it happens to spare what should not be spared. Sins that can be struck by the fires of Gehenna must be corrected by the rod of discipline. But disordered piety, when it spares temporarily, drags a person toward eternal punishment.

Therefore, in order that piety may be true and rightly ordered, it must be raised to another step, namely, to knowledge, so that it may know what to punish according to judgment and what to forgive according to mercy. But what if someone knows what ought to be done, yet lacks the strength to do it?

Our knowledge must therefore grow into fortitude, so that, when it sees what ought to be done, it may be able to do it through strength of mind, lest it tremble through fear and, collapsing through dread, be unable to defend the good that it perceives. Yet fortitude often falls uselessly through its own presumption if it is improvident and insufficiently watchful against vices.

Let it therefore ascend to counsel, so that by foresight it may advance everything that it can courageously do. But counsel cannot exist if understanding is absent. For if one does not understand the evil that burdens the one who does it, how can one solidify the good that gives assistance? Let us therefore ascend from counsel to understanding.

But what if understanding keeps watch with great acuity and does not know how to govern itself through maturity? Let us therefore ascend from understanding to wisdom, so that wisdom may arrange maturely what understanding has discovered with sharpness.

Since, then, through fear we rise to piety, through piety we are led to knowledge, through knowledge we are strengthened into fortitude, through fortitude we strive toward counsel, and through counsel we advance in understanding, we ascend by seven steps to the gate through which the entrance to spiritual life is opened to us.

It is rightly said that there was a vestibule before it, because unless someone first possesses humility, he will not ascend these steps of spiritual gifts, as it is written:

> “Upon whom shall my spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?”

The vestibule may also be understood as faith. It is itself before the steps and the gate, because we first come to faith so that afterward, through the steps of spiritual gifts, we may enter the entrance to heavenly life. We do not come to faith through virtues; rather, through faith we attain virtues. Through faith, therefore, one comes to works, but through works one is made firm in faith.

The vestibule, then, is before the steps, because the one who has first believed ascends afterward by the steps of virtues to the entrance of the gate.

It follows:

> “And the gate of the inner court was opposite the gate of the north and the eastern one.”

In this passage, “opposite” does not signify opposition but alignment. The gate of the inner court was positioned so that the gate of the north and the gate of the east extended toward it by a straight approach.

What, then, does it mean that the inner gate is shown as positioned in a straight course opposite the gate of the east and the gate of the north, except that it is plainly made known that, whether for the Jewish and Gentile peoples, or for the righteous and sinners who have returned after their sins, the entrance to the heavenly kingdom is opened equally?

The mercy of our Creator is broad. The inner gate faces not only the gate of the east but also the gate of the north, because the joys of the inner court are opened not only to those who remain in innocence but also to sinners who condemn their sins through repentance, so that they may recognize the ineffable mysteries of their heavenly homeland; recognizing them, thirst for them; thirsting, run toward them; running, arrive.

What remains, then, except that all who recognize those joys of the heavenly homeland should direct themselves toward the course of a more perfect life? Hence it is plainly added here:

> “And he measured from gate to gate one hundred cubits.”

We have already said above that the number one hundred is perfect because ten is multiplied by ten. Therefore, whoever sees the entrance of the inner court must necessarily run through a life of perfection, so that from the gate of beginning he may arrive at the entrance of consummation.

Let the inner court, which extends from the exterior gates to the inner gate, therefore be measured at one hundred cubits, so that the one who began to enter through love may possess in his mind the breadth of perfection. Thus prosperity may not exalt him, nor adversity constrict him; rather, despising all transient things, he may run through the court of perfection until he reaches the hidden joys.

There are indeed many who have already entered through the seven steps to the entrance of the exterior gate: humble through the fear of God, merciful through devotion to piety, discerning through knowledge, free through strength of mind, cautious through counsel, provident through understanding, and mature through wisdom. Yet they remain bound by certain necessities and serve the cares of this world. In the very things from which they have already shaken their minds to a great extent, they are still held unwillingly.

While they carry the burdens imposed by earthly occupation, they practice the heavenly commandments less fully. They have no leisure to yearn from the depths of their being for the eternal homeland, and their desires for it languish in them in some fashion, because a mind impeded by temporal cares is not permitted to love the true joys it has come to know as much as it wishes.

Often such people shake the yoke of the world from their necks, abandon everything, and lay down the burdens of earthly care. In order to widen the heart’s capacity for heavenly desire, they seek a withdrawn life. In it, intent upon holy prayers and devoted to sacred meditations, they afflict themselves with daily weeping, melt the oldness of their heart in the fire of love, and renew themselves by kindling their desire for heavenly joy.

When such people are carried from the exterior gates to the inner gate through the court of good endeavor, this court is measured in them at one hundred cubits, because through delay and exercise they advance daily in holy perfection. To be perfected in the mind through daily desires is, as it were, for the inner court to be measured at one hundred cubits.

For this reason, then, there are one hundred cubits from gate to gate: so that the delay itself may be like a period of progress, through which one grows daily in virtues and arrives more perfectly at the inner entrance.

It follows.

> “And he led me to the southern way, and behold, a gate that faced south. And he measured its front and its vestibule according to the preceding measurements, and its windows and the vestibules around it, like the other windows: fifty cubits in length and twenty-five cubits in width. And one ascended to it by seven steps. And there was a vestibule before its doors.” (Gregory)

All these matters have already been discussed concerning the gate of the east and the gate of the north. It is not appropriate for us repeatedly to recite what we have explained once and twice. We must nevertheless note that in the spiritual building one entrance lies open toward the east, another toward the north, and another toward the south.

Just as sinners are signified by the cold of the north, so those who burn in spirit are signified by the southern way, because, kindled by the heat of the Holy Spirit, they increase in virtues like the light of midday.

Let the gate toward the east therefore stand open, so that those who have begun the sacraments of faith and have not afterward been submerged in any depth of vices may arrive at the hidden joys.

Let the gate toward the north stand open, so that those who, after beginning in heat and light, have fallen into the cold and darkness of their sins may return through the compunction of repentance to forgiveness and learn what true joy of the inner reward is.

Let the gate toward the south stand open, so that those who burn with holy desires in virtues may daily penetrate, through spiritual understanding, the mysteries of inner joy.

At this point, however, one may ask: since there are four such regions, why are there said to be not four but three gates in this building of the exterior court? The question would rightly arise if the prophet had seen not a spiritual but a bodily building.

Holy Church, that is, the spiritual building, has only three gates by which it reaches the hidden joys: faith, hope, and charity—one toward the east, another toward the north, and a third toward the south.

The gate in the east is faith, because through it the true light is born in the mind. The gate toward the north is hope, because anyone placed in sins perishes utterly if he despairs of forgiveness. Therefore, the one who has been extinguished by his own iniquity must be revived through hope in mercy.

The gate toward the south is charity, because it burns in the fire of love. At the southern gate the sun is raised high, because through charity the light of faith is lifted up in love of God and neighbor.

Thus one proceeds by three gates to the inner court, because through faith, hope, and charity one arrives at the hidden joys.

Another question also arises: why is the gate of the inner court said to be positioned opposite the gate of the east and the gate of the north, while it is left unspoken to whom the southern gate is open?

But because we have said that the east signifies beginning and the north signifies falling, it was fitting that it should be stated openly both concerning those who are beginning, for whom the sun is still in its warmth, and concerning those who have fallen but return through conversion, that the gate of the inner court is open to them. In this way he assures us through those cases about which doubt might have arisen.

This did not need to be said concerning the southern gate, because no one is unaware that those who remain in virtues through the fervor of the spirit reach the inner joys.

It follows.

> “And there were sculpted palms, one on this side and another on that, on its front.” (Jerome)

The two sculpted palms of which we spoke concerning the northern region of the gate are also mentioned here. It is sufficient to point out that whatever is placed there, according to the lower understanding—that is, according to the letter—we understand in the southern gate according to the spiritual sense. History and allegory run along the same lines, but the former is lower and the latter higher. The former clings to earth; the latter flies up to heaven.

> “And all around, through the windows, everything was full of light.”

For each πρόβατα (*probata*, “sheep”) has its own boundaries, and through these a proper light enters the soul of the believer, especially if the length of his life has been extended to the year of the jubilee—that is, through the mystery of the Jubilee—and he has been able to reach the breadth of a more divine understanding.

Within this breadth, Wisdom moves confidently through the streets, and cries out with a sublime voice. She enters by seven steps in order to reach the vestibule, and through the palms she holds the eternal victory of her purpose and endeavor.

And lest we should suppose that there was only one court on the southern side, a second court is mentioned, together with the gate of the inner court on the southern way; and he measured from gate to gate on the southern way one hundred cubits, so that after the mysteries of the heptad and of the Old Instrument he might arrive at the good land and the grace of the Gospel.

(Gregory) What does it mean that earlier paintings of palms were mentioned on the fronts, while now sculpted palms are said to be on the front? In sculpture, works appear to have been expressed in stone. But, as we said above, the painting of palms is the display of signs.

Now the sculpting of palms is mentioned so that the manifestation of good works may be signified. To the chief preachers themselves it is said:

> “Let your good works be seen, and let them glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5).

Those, therefore, who show that holy works are impressed upon their life have sculpted palms on their front, because they already demonstrate in their holy works how great a victory will follow them in the future.

Or certainly, because we said that faith is signified by the east, hope by the north, and charity by the southern gate, we must note that the gate of the east is said to have a painting of palms, while the north and the south have sculpting. It often happens that those who are still beginners have not yet exercised themselves in solid and great works.

But those who return to virtue after their iniquities generally exercise themselves in great works, so that they may conceal their sins before the eyes of almighty God. And those who have already grown through the fervor of the spirit in virtues burn, as it were, like midday in holy actions.

Thus there is painting in the gate of the east, but sculpting in the gates of the north and south, because the sign of victory that is shown in beginners is held more solidly and firmly by those who return and those who burn with zeal.

It must also be noted with great care that it says, “on this side and on that.” For all who strive toward the entrance of life must have a palm on both the right and the left side. The words “on this side and on that” signify both sides.

The one whom prosperity does not exalt therefore has a palm on the right; the one whom adversity does not cast down has a palm on the left. Paul carried a palm, as it were, on both sides when he said:

> “By the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, through glory and dishonor, through evil report and good report, as deceivers and yet truthful” (2 Corinthians 6).

Adversity did not break him, nor did prosperity lift him up into the swelling of his mind. He therefore carried the palm on both sides, because he remained strong in adversity and humble in prosperity.

Whoever is exalted by prosperity does not know how to have a palm on the right; whoever is broken by adversity does not know how to carry a palm on the left.

Therefore, in order that a palm may be carried on the forehead on both sides, both confidence in adversity and fear in prosperity must always be present to our minds, lest adversity drag us into despair or prosperity exalt our spirit through confidence in itself.

Hence the same outstanding preacher said:

> “I know how to be brought low, and I know how to abound” (Philippians 4); “in every place and in all things I have been instructed, both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need. I can do all things in him who strengthens me” (ibid.).

Is it some sort of skill to be brought low and to abound, to be filled and to be hungry, to abound and to suffer need, so that so great a preacher presents himself as knowing these things as something extraordinary? It is indeed a great art and an astonishing knowledge of discipline, which must be learned with the full effort of the heart.

The person whom poverty does not break, whom it does not withdraw from thanksgiving, and whom it does not kindle with desire for temporal things knows how to be brought low. For in this passage the Apostle means by being brought low to endure poverty. Immediately, by contrast, he added: “I know how to abound.”

The one who is not exalted by the things he has received, who does not twist them toward the use of empty glory, who does not possess alone what he has received but mercifully distributes it among the needy—he knows how to abound.

He also knows how to abound who uses the food he has received not for stuffing his belly but for restoring strength, and does not give the flesh more than necessity demands.

He knows how to be filled who endures the lack of food without murmuring and, for the sake of the necessity of nourishment, does nothing by which the soul may fall into the snare of sin. He knows how to be hungry.

The one whom neither pride raises up in abundance nor greed provokes in need knows how to abound and how to suffer need.

When he immediately added, “I can do all things,” lest we should think these words arose from self-exaltation, he added in whom: “in him who strengthens me.”

Behold, a branch rises high; but because it remained attached to its root, it remained green. Rising high, it would wither if it separated itself from the root. He attributes nothing to himself who confesses that he can do all things not in himself but in him who strengthens him.

The outstanding preacher therefore has a palm on both sides: abundance does not lead him to pride, nor poverty to greed.

Let us therefore learn how to abound, so that we may share with the needy everything we have received from him; so that abundance may not exalt the mind; so that it may not perhaps rejoice because it possesses what another lacks, and rejoice no longer in the common good but in what belongs to itself.

Truth recalls the disciples from private joy to common joy when, as they returned from preaching and rejoiced in the subjection of demons, he warned them, saying:

> “Do not rejoice in this, but rather rejoice and exult because your names are written in heaven.”

Not all the elect cast out demons, but the names of all the elect are nevertheless recorded in heaven. The disciples are therefore warned to lay aside private joy and rejoice in a common and everlasting happiness.

Whoever rejoices in possessing what another does not have possesses, because of that very abundance, a private joy that has made him worse.

Against this desire for abundance John warns us, saying:

> “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world” (1 John 2).

He immediately supplied the reason why:

> “If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him” (ibid.).

> “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6),

because one cannot love transient and eternal things simultaneously.

If we love eternity, we possess all temporal things for use, not for affection, because he immediately supplies the same reasoning, saying:

> “For everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, and the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life.”

People desire to possess things, and more than is necessary, so that they may become proud through possessing them and, because another does not possess them, exalt themselves in their thoughts.

Let us learn to suffer poverty, lest we seek with guilt to possess what we do not have. Let us not consider happy those whom we see weighed down with possessions.

The things that people prepare for themselves as though for the expenses of the present life are exceedingly numerous. They carry much, but along a brief road. Poverty is a great companion for us on this journey: when earthly substance is lacking, it does not constrict the mind with the account we must render concerning it to the eternal Judge.

We travel toward our homeland more freely because, as on a road, we are free from a burden.

Let us learn to be filled, lest in taking bodily nourishment we serve gluttony more than necessity. Desire asks for more than necessity, and often, while we strive to satisfy the body’s lack, pleasure steals in and exceeds the proper measure of refreshment.

The result is that one sin passes into another, because often another temptation of the flesh arises from the very point at which the flesh is served too immoderately in refreshment. For through the sin of the first human being, nature was weakened, and we are born into this world with our temptations. At times the flesh is our helper in good work; at times it is our seducer into evil.

If, therefore, we give it more than we owe, we nourish an enemy; and if we do not give back to its necessity what we owe, we kill a fellow citizen.

The flesh must therefore be satisfied, but only to the point at which it is able to serve us in good work. Whoever gives it so much that it becomes proud plainly does not know how to be satisfied.

It is therefore a great art to be satisfied, lest anyone, through satiety of the flesh, break out into the wickedness of shameful conduct.
