Let us learn to hunger, so that, because of the abundance that follows, our present poverty may please us; lest the necessity of the belly draw us into guilt; lest want suggest sin to the mind itself; lest, while the flesh is afflicted by hunger, the spirit be provoked to greed and seek, with guilt, to provide what might satisfy the flesh in its need; lest the heart leap up in indignation and kindle the tongue into the bitterness of murmuring.

The person who, in the poverty of his flesh, looks around on every side and guards himself from the snare of sin knows how to hunger.

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us flee anger and greed in adversity and avoid exaltation and immoderate joys in prosperity. Since we desire to enter the court of inner life through its three gates—faith, hope, and charity—let us hold palms on both sides.

> “And he introduced me,” he says, “into the inner court at the southern gate, and he measured the gate according to the preceding measurements, etc.” (Jerome)

Each court has its own measurements and arrangements, and within the same measurements there is a different grace, since we recognize the same things differently at the beginning, in progress, and at the end.

This detail, however, which is not found in the Septuagint—“and a vestibule around it, twenty-five cubits in length and five cubits in width”—appears to create a question. Since it is not present in the old translation, how are twenty-five cubits and five cubits placed after the progress of the third step?

The ambiguity is removed by what follows:

> “And its vestibule toward the exterior court, and its palms on the front.”

This means that the court which had twenty-five cubits in length and five in width was not the inner but the exterior court, so that the length possessed the breadth of the former court—that is, twenty-five cubits—of the exterior court, while in width it held five cubits.

We shall refer these measurements, twenty-five and five, to the same senses: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch.

If we ascend to higher things, we multiply them fivefold and transform bodily senses into spiritual ones, as in the words:

> “Lift up your eyes and see that the fields are already white for harvesting” (John 4);

> “Let the one who has ears to hear, hear” (Luke 8);

> “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Psalm 33);

> “We are the good fragrance of Christ among those who believe” (2 Corinthians 2);

and in John’s Epistle:

> “What we have heard and seen, and our hands have touched, concerning the Word of life” (1 John 1).

Finally, not merely seven steps, as in the northern region, but the number eight is placed after the seven, so that we may pass from the Synagogue to the Church, from the Old Instrument to the New, and from earthly things to heavenly things.

> “And he introduced me into the inner court by the eastern way, and he measured the gate according to the preceding measurements: its chamber, its front, and its vestibules, as above, and its windows, and the vestibule around it, fifty cubits in length and twenty-five cubits in width, and its vestibule, that is, of the exterior court.” (For this the Septuagint and Symmachus have “inner.”)

> “And there were sculpted palms on its front, on this side and on that, and there were eight steps by which it was ascended.”

From the northern region, in whose court one ascended by only seven steps, he passes to the southern gate and the court of that region, to which one ascends not only by seven steps, as above, but also by eight—namely, so that we may pass through the old things to the new.

To speak more plainly, we pass through the patriarchs and prophets to the apostles, so that in one case there may be a hebdomad and in the other an ogdoad.

Now he comes to the final, or rather the highest, point, and introduces the prophet through the way of the inner gate—or through the court—to which one proceeds by the eastern way.

The word “way,” according to the Septuagint, occurs only in this passage; in the northern and southern regions it is entirely omitted. We may therefore understand that in the eastern gate alone that way is intended which says:

> “I am the way, and the life, and the truth” (John 14).

Through him we come to the Father. And concerning him it is written:

> “Blessed are the undefiled in the way” (Psalm 118),

those who perceive nothing sinister concerning Christ, whose faith is pure and in no way polluted by the filth of heretics.

The same number of chambers, fronts, vestibules, windows, and their light is preserved, as well as the same measurement of length and width—fifty and twenty-five cubits—preserving their mysteries.

And his vestibule, of the gate or of the inner court, which according to the Hebrew is placed outward, is so placed that everything may be enclosed by eastern light, according to what is written:

> “There is no one who can hide himself from his heat.”

But if we take “exterior” and “interior” together, understanding the court in this way, we should understand that God is both surrounding and indwelling, as the prophet says:

> “He who holds heaven in his palm and the earth in his fist” (Isaiah 40),

so that all things are understood to be enclosed by him.

And again:

> “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Acts 7),

so that he should be believed to be within all things, in accordance with that passage of Virgil (*Aeneid* 6.723):

> *Principio coelum ac terras, camposque liquentes,*  
> *Lucentemque globum lunae Titaniaque astra*  
> *Spiritus intus alit; totamque infusa per artus*  
> *Mens agitat molem, et magno se corpore miscet.*

> “In the beginning, a spirit within nourishes heaven and earth, the liquid fields, the shining sphere of the moon, and the Titanian stars; infused through all its members, Mind moves the whole mass and mingles with the great body.”

When, through the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, through glory and dishonor, through good and evil report, through praise and blame, we have gained victory over this age, then palms are given to us on both sides. Neither joys have changed us, nor sorrow, nor will prosperity or adversity overcome us.

We do not ascend to the heights by eight steps, as in the northern region, nor by seven and eight, as is contained in the southern region, but by seven steps alone, since the number eight—that is, the mystery of the Gospel—is sufficient for us, so that we may say with the Apostle:

> “Even if we knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him so” (2 Corinthians 5),

with “according to the flesh” understood.

# BOOK SIXTEEN

[Column 0939]

If anyone is troubled by the fact that in explaining the prophecy we have composed some books longer and others shorter, and have not divided the prophecy itself into equal portions, so that one part has more verses and another fewer, let him know that this results from the difficulty of the explanation and the depth of the mysteries.

For our predecessors, whose authority we follow and whose style we imitate, were accustomed to proceed in this way: they lingered longer in treating obscure passages, and in clearer ones they completed the measure of their exposition more quickly.

Therefore, having now completed two books on the structure of the Temple—the fourteenth and fifteenth in the order of the entire work—we decide to begin the third, which is sixteenth in order. In it, the man who showed all these things to the prophet introduced the prophet himself to the gate that faced north. We shall begin as follows.

## CHAPTER FORTY

> “And he introduced me to the gate that faced north. And he measured, according to the preceding measurements, its chamber, its front, its vestibule, and its windows around it, fifty cubits in length and twenty-five cubits in width; and its vestibule faced the exterior court; and there was sculpted palm work on its front, on this side and on that, and it was ascended by seven steps,” etc. (Jerome)

He is therefore introduced again to the gate that faced north, but not, as above, to the exterior court; rather, he is introduced to the inner court.

For when it is said in what follows that “its vestibule faced the exterior court,” it is shown that this court was situated within. Through this, the progress of the one entering is indicated: each place has its own names and measurements; the windows around it are full of the light of knowledge, displaying all things; and through the fifty and twenty-five cubits are placed the mysteries of remission and of the divine senses.

Thus, when placed in the vestibule of the inner court, we see exterior things and, contemplating knowledge of past and present things, proceed toward the double palms and victories. We come to know the mysteries of the eight steps, having entered the treasuries in which the riches of the Temple are contained, and in which our prayers are washed from every stain of sin.

Two tables are also placed on each side, so that first the whole burnt offering may be sacrificed, which the sacred fire entirely consumes; then an offering for sin; and finally one for ignorance, whether we committed it knowingly or unknowingly.

On the exterior side as well, according to the Septuagint, there was a constructed channel that carried outside the ashes of the burnt offerings and the broths of the meat. Alternatively, there were two tables, and on the other side of the vestibule of the same gate two tables—that is, four on each side, four here and four there.

Behind them, or at their side, were another eight tables, making sixteen tables altogether. By this number the mysteries of the prophets are indicated, so that whatever we offer may be shown to have been foretold by their prophecies through the gracious dispensation of the Gospel.

The fact that four tables are brought in, constructed of squared stones, and that these same tables are for the sacrifice of burnt offerings, signifies the living stones that roll upon the earth and possess with them the cornerstone by which the walls of the Old and New Instrument are held together.

The number four demonstrates the mysteries of the Gospel. In length and width each table has one and a half cubits, squared, which together make three cubits. These three cubits have a height of one cubit, so that the mysteries of the one Trinity may preserve the measure of one cubit—that is, of divine majesty—for the Lord says to the disciples:

> “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28).

The name of God is like one cubit of height, embracing three distinct properties and always consuming the burnt offerings of our oblations.

Upon the four tables of burnt offerings, constructed of living stones and described as to length, height, and width, vessels are placed in which the burnt offering of the martyrs is sacrificed. Of them it is said:

> “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his holy ones” (Psalm 115),

as well as the offerings of those who sacrifice their souls to the Lord through continence and purity of body.

I think that the names of these tables are contained in the apostles Matthew and Luke, Mark and John. A crown bent over from above surrounded the inner edges around them, so that it might hold the burnt offerings within and not allow them to flow about indiscriminately, and might retain the flesh of the offering.

Alternatively, as the Septuagint translated it:

> “And the tables themselves were covered above,”

because of the violence of the rains and the excessive dryness of the summer sun, so that the flesh placed upon them might say with the prophet:

> “By day the sun shall not burn us, nor the moon by night” (Psalm 120).

The one of these—excessive rains and storms of tribulations—dissolves our offerings; the other, the fierce heat of persecutions, causes whatever has been offered to wither.

(Gregory.) These words of prophecy require reading more than exposition. For they are repeated in three gates, having already been spoken a second or third time concerning the exterior gates, though a few details are altered in their description. We must now ask what these three interior gates are; what is meant by the fact that the vestibules of those same gates measure twenty-five cubits in length and five cubits in width; and why one ascends to them by eight steps rather than seven, as was said of the exterior gates.

The gate of the inner court mentioned above is not one of these three interior gates, because it is said to face the eastern and northern gate. These, however, are separately said to be situated inside, toward the south, the east, and the north. Thus, rightly, access to the interior is designated through that gate, since—as has already been said in the preceding discussion—it is open either to Jews and Gentiles, or to those beginning and persevering in the good, or to those who fall from the good but rise again through repentance after their sins.

Now, after the gates have separately been described in the east, north, and south, why are the gates of the inner court again described separately in the south, east, and north? If God grants us the ability, great concentration is needed to investigate the depth of so great a matter.

For if by the name “gates” we understand holy preachers, we must know that there is one Church in the preachers of the Old and New Testaments. The gates have seven or eight steps because they unanimously preach the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. They announce the eighth step as the reward of eternity. Hence it is written: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight” (Ecclesiasticus 11).

What, then, can we understand the exterior gates to be except the ancient fathers, who through the precepts of the Law knew how to guard the people’s actions more than their hearts? The interior gates, therefore, should be understood as the preachers of the holy Church, who by spiritual admonitions guard the hearts of their disciples, lest they take pleasure even in their thoughts in the evils they do not commit.

Of the former, it is said that one ascends by seven steps; of the latter, the ascent is said to be by eight steps. For in the reverence paid to the Law there was a seventh day, while in the New Testament there is an eighth day with its sacramental meaning: namely, the day called the Lord’s Day, which is the third from the Passion but the eighth from creation, since it follows the seventh.

But if by the name “gates” we understand only the holy apostles, who were the first preachers of the holy Church and taught us above all to hold fast to faith, hope, and charity, then they are gates for us in these virtues, leading us through those same virtues to the inner understanding of eternal wisdom. Yet if they are the exterior gates, whom do we understand as the interior ones? And if they are the interior ones, whom do we understand as the exterior ones?

In this matter it may usefully be understood that they are both exterior and interior gates for us. When they preach to beginners not lofty and mystical matters but things they are capable of grasping, they are exterior gates. But when they speak to the perfect of profound and mystical things, they are interior gates.

Let us see how the exterior gate is opened: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Corinthians 3). Let us see how the interior gate is opened: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Corinthians 2). Let us see whether the same gate is both interior and exterior: “I am a debtor both to the wise and to the foolish” (Romans 1). He says again: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober, it is for you” (2 Corinthians 5).

In that, by contemplating and speaking, he is beside himself for the wise, he is an interior gate. But in that he restrains himself soberly in preaching to the little ones, and does not show how great is the intoxication of the spirit poured into the mind when he preaches, he makes clear that he is an exterior gate.

Thus they are both exterior and interior gates for us: they establish us at the first entrance in faith, hope, and charity, and, when they preach the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom to those who are already advancing, they lead us inward through a subtler understanding.

Hence their ascent is first described by seven steps and afterward by eight. For through the eighth step the mysteries of that life are signified, which the perfect understand in their secret places—those who have learned already to transcend all temporal things in their minds; who wholly despise the present life, which unfolds in the course of seven days; and who are nourished by intimate contemplation.

The gates of the spiritual building therefore have seven steps, because they preach to their hearers the fear of the Lord, piety and knowledge, fortitude and counsel, understanding and wisdom. But when they command that everything be abandoned, when they admonish that nothing in this world be loved or held fast through attachment, and when they urge their hearers to devote themselves to contemplation of their heavenly homeland and to delight in its mysteries, they add a step and pass into the interior.

Truth showed this step to a certain man. When the precepts of the Law were recited to him, he replied: “All these things I have kept from my youth” (Matthew 19; Luke 18). He was, as it were, standing on seven steps when he said that he had kept everything from his youth. But he is immediately told: “One thing is still lacking to you: if you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come and follow me.”

In these words he saw the eighth step, but did not wish to ascend it, because he went away sad. Whoever, then, after despising temporal possessions, is nourished by contemplation of eternity, searches out the joys of the heavenly kingdom, and, after the seven steps that he has held through fear, action, and growth in the understanding of wisdom, enters through the eighth step into the interior gate.

Through the number eight, moreover, both the day of eternal judgment and the resurrection of the flesh are signified. Hence the psalm written “for the eighth” begins with fear of judgment, when it says: “Lord, rebuke me not in your anger, nor correct me in your wrath” (Psalm 6).

Now is the time of mercy; but in that judgment there will be a day of wrath. On that day all this present time will end, the time that unfolds through seven days. What follows the seven days is rightly called the eighth, in which our flesh will also rise from the dust, so that it may receive from the Truth what it has done, whether good or evil.

Therefore circumcision is also commanded to take place on the eighth day according to the Law. For through the member that is circumcised mortal propagation is generated, and the number of those departing and succeeding increases. But at the resurrection of the dead there will be no further propagation of the flesh, nor any departure or succession, because “they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of God in heaven” (Matthew 22). Thus on the eighth day the foreskin is commanded to be cut off: there propagation of the flesh has no place, where the risen flesh possesses the permanence of eternity.

Through this member the Virgin Mother descended, she who conceived God in the womb without the admixture of male flesh. He first showed us the glory of the eternal homeland in his resurrection: rising from the dead, he dies no more, and death will no longer have dominion over him. He gave us an example, so that we might believe that at the last day the same things will happen to our flesh that we have recognized as having happened to his flesh on the day of resurrection.

But since our discourse has brought us to the resurrection of the flesh, it is exceedingly sad and most grievous that we know some people in the Church to stand and doubt the resurrection of the flesh. The ancient fathers most certainly believed that it would come, even when they had no example of that resurrection.

By what condemnation, then, are those worthy who have already received the example of the Lord’s resurrection and yet distrust their own resurrection? They hold the pledge but have no faith. They fill the churches, but because they doubt their own resurrection, they stand there empty in mind.

The interior gates have vestibules that measure twenty-five cubits in length. For if we multiply eight by three, we arrive at twenty-four; one is added to it so that we may have twenty-five. Good hearers, who are, as it were, certain vestibules of the gates, possess the longsuffering of eternal hope and sustain the eighth day in faith in the Trinity.

Because the Trinity is one God, they multiply eight by three, but are made firm in the confession of the one God. The vestibules are level because the hearts of good hearers are humble. They have length because they persevere patiently in hope. Their length is measured by twenty-five cubits because they believe in the resurrection of the flesh through the Trinity on the eighth day and confess that the same holy Trinity is one God.

They also have five cubits in width because, through the simple life conducted by the five senses, they are enlarged in love of neighbor.

It should also be noted that, after other vestibules of the gates have previously been mentioned, the vestibule that is five cubits wide is afterward said to face outward. For there are certain hearers who penetrate more deeply into the understanding of the interior life by advancing in virtues. There are also some simple people who live well, but according to the bodily senses. Hence they are said to face outward: they look, as it were, toward the outside because they live according to the bodily senses.

Nevertheless, although they face outward, they are within, because, even though they do not know how to transcend the bodily senses through understanding, they humbly hold fast to faith and charity. Thus they are within the spiritual building through love, and look, as it were, outside through simplicity.

The outward-facing vestibule may signify the faith of beginners, and the inward vestibule the faith of the perfect, who already shine through it in virtues. The inward vestibule may also signify the higher precepts, while the vestibule facing outward may represent the still lesser precepts.

Through the vestibule one goes to the steps and the gate, because through the precepts of preaching one reaches virtues and access to heavenly grace. But when some are commanded to meditate on eternal things in their thoughts, to savor heavenly things, and are told in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs to live in these realities, an inward vestibule is, as it were, shown—one measured by fifty cubits in length and twenty-five in breadth. We now remain silent about these numbers, because we have already said much about them above.

But when others are commanded that a husband should render the marital debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband, the vestibule that faces outward is, as it were, represented. Although it faces outside, it is nevertheless within, because the inexperienced hearer still does what belongs to the flesh, yet is not excluded from the number of the good.

The Lord may be signified by the eastern gate; Judea by the southern gate; and converted Gentile peoples by the northern gate.

But in this matter a question presses upon the mind: why, in the earlier account, the prophet first described the eastern gate, then the northern, and afterward the southern, whereas, when he narrated these same gates in the outer court, he described first the southern gate, then the eastern, and third the northern?

Why did he not preserve the same order with which he had begun, but change it in describing the gates—first mentioning the eastern, northern, and southern gate, and afterward the southern, eastern, and northern?

But if the Gentiles are signified by the name “north,” it is clear to all who read attentively that the Gentiles existed before the synagogue. For Heber himself, from whom the Hebrews received their name, was chosen from among the Gentiles.

Let the eastern gate, then, be mentioned before the northern and southern gates, because in his divinity the Lord was born before the Gentiles and Judea, since he existed before all ages.

But in the subsequent account let the southern, eastern, and northern gates be mentioned, because our Redeemer deigned to be born in human nature between Judea and the Gentiles. He came at the end of the synagogue and before the beginning of the Church, which he gathered from the Gentiles.

Thus in the first description the eastern gate should stand before the northern and southern gates. In the second, the eastern gate should be named between the southern and northern gates. For in his divinity he preceded all things, while in his humanity he came among all things. He became both the end of departing Judea and the beginning of the Gentiles that followed.

Since, therefore, we have investigated, as far as the Lord granted us, the matters that had not yet been discussed, and have passed over those that had been repeated many times, we now come to matters that are stated in order, with almost none of what has already been said repeated in them.

> “And through each treasury there was a doorway in the fronts of the gates; there they washed the burnt offering.” (Gregory.)

Above we said that the treasuries are the hearts of teachers, which preserve the riches of knowledge. The fronts of the gates are the words and deeds of preachers, in which we recognize outwardly what sort of people they live as inwardly before themselves.

There is a doorway through each treasury in the fronts of the gates because each teacher opens understanding in the heart of the hearer through the sayings and deeds of the Fathers.

When we examine the preaching of the apostle Peter, search through the words of Paul, investigate the Gospel of John, and meanwhile draw our hearers through words toward a better understanding, what else are we doing except opening a doorway in the fronts of the gates?

Thus it is said that through each treasury there is a doorway in the fronts of the gates, because if a teacher does not confirm what he says by the words of the apostles, he has no doorway in the fronts of the gates. If he has no doorway, he cannot be called a treasury of the spiritual building, because if he does not open understanding through these things, he is not a teacher.

But when good hearers come to know the words and deeds of the apostles through the mouths of teachers, they silently reprove their own faults within themselves and pursue with tears everything they remember having done wickedly.

Hence it is also added here concerning the doorway that is in the fronts of the gates: “There they washed the burnt offering.” Those who have devoted themselves to the Lord through faith in holy conduct have become a burnt offering to the Lord.

But because they still suffer many things in themselves from their corruptible flesh, and because the purity of their hearts is still polluted by sordid thoughts, they return daily to tears and afflict themselves with continual weeping. For they consider the words and deeds of the holy Fathers, and, when they judge themselves unworthy, they wash the burnt offering in the doorway of the gates.

Consider, for example, someone who has vowed, out of fear of the almighty Lord, to be patient: to return no insult for an insult and to endure everything with equanimity. Yet when an insult suddenly delivered by the mouth of his neighbor strikes him, he is perhaps disturbed and says something he ought not to have said.

Certainly this person is already a burnt offering, but still polluted. Perhaps he displayed patience in response to the insults inflicted upon him and remained silent, yet is still touched by grief because of those same insults that he bears, and his spirit is wounded by them in charity.

True patience is that which also loves the person whom it bears. To endure while hating is not the virtue of gentleness but a covering for rage. Such a person often judges himself in his thoughts and reproves himself because he grieves, yet cannot prevail over himself to cease grieving.

He is therefore already a burnt offering through good devotion, but is still polluted by the grief with which he is touched.

Another person has resolved within himself to give everything he possesses to the needy, to reserve nothing for himself, and to entrust his life solely to divine providence. But while he gives to the poor what he has, a thought may steal into his mind saying, “How will you live if you give everything away?”

Yet he does not cease giving. What he began to give joyfully he afterward gives sadly. What is this person’s mind except a burnt offering of mercy, yet polluted by the sadness of thought? Either he ought not to have deliberated so gravely, or after deliberation he ought in no way to have doubted.

Another person, having despised the proud honors and dignities of the world, has resolved to avoid them. He seeks to occupy the lowest place among human beings, so that he may be found all the higher in enduring glory the humbler he is seen to be in passing life.

Perhaps, when he suddenly realizes that he is despised by his neighbor, he disdains the reason for which he is despised. He does wish to be in a lowly place, but does not wish to be regarded as contemptible.

Devotion already lifts this person up, but weakness still weighs him down. He is therefore already a burnt offering through devotion, but still polluted by weakness.

Those, then, who are touched by some fault of weakness in the things they have most excellently vowed, when through the words of teachers they understand the sayings of the Fathers, recognize in what great fault they lie, and afflict themselves with the lamentations of repentance—these wash the burnt offering in the doorway of the gates.

It must be understood that there is this difference between a sacrifice and a burnt offering: every burnt offering is a sacrifice, but not every sacrifice is a burnt offering. In a sacrifice, part of the animal was offered; in a burnt offering, the whole animal was customarily offered. Hence in Latin the word *holocaustum* means “wholly burned.”

Let us therefore consider what a sacrifice is and what a burnt offering is. When someone vows something of his own to God but does not vow something else, it is a sacrifice. But when he vows to almighty God everything he has, everything he has vowed, and everything he understands, it is a burnt offering.

For there are some who are still held in this world in their minds, yet from the possessions they have they provide assistance to the needy and hasten to defend the oppressed. These offer a sacrifice in the good things they do, because they immolate part of their activity to God while reserving part of it for themselves.

There are others who reserve nothing for themselves, but immolate to almighty God their understanding, tongue, life, and substance—all that they have received. What do such people offer except a burnt offering—or rather, what do they become except a burnt offering?

The Israelite people first offered a sacrifice in Egypt, and a second in the wilderness. Whoever still has his mind in the world but has already begun to do some good has offered a sacrifice to God in Egypt.

But whoever abandons the present world and does whatever good he can, as though Egypt had already been left behind, offers a sacrifice in the wilderness. For, having driven away the tumult of carnal desires, he immolates to God in the quiet and solitude of his mind whatever he does.

Although, as has been said, a burnt offering is a sacrifice, a burnt offering is greater than a sacrifice, because when the mind is not weighed down by love of this world, everything that one possesses is consumed in the sacrifice of almighty God.

We must know, however, that there are some who, even while abandoning the world, offer everything they possess, yet are not at all contrite over the good things they do. The good they perform is a burnt offering, but because they do not know how to weep and judge themselves, and do not kindle themselves to tears out of love, their burnt offering is not perfect.

Hence the Psalmist says: “May the Lord remember your sacrifice, and may your burnt offering grow rich” (Psalm 19). A dry burnt offering is a good work that the tears of prayer do not moisten. A rich burnt offering, however, is produced when what is done well is watered by tears together with a humble heart.

Thus it is said again: “I will offer you marrow-filled burnt offerings” (Psalm 65). Whoever performs a good work but does not know how to weep out of love and longing for almighty God has a burnt offering, but does not have marrow in his burnt offering.

But whoever does good works, longs already for the vision of his Creator, hastens to reach the joys of eternal contemplation, and, inflamed by the love with which he burns, slays himself in tears—such a person has offered to the Lord marrow-filled burnt offerings.

We must therefore strive both to abandon evil completely and to perform the good that we are able to perform, and, so that we may be pierced with love of eternal light in the very good things we do, we must remember that love itself scatters the darkness of the heart’s ignorance, enabling us to see more subtly and preventing anything crooked from being mingled with the good things we do.

We must consider what our work is like, what thought is present in the work, and what intention is present in the thought. When we recognize that something malicious or wrongly directed has been mingled with our good work, let us return to tears and wash the burnt offering.

There are some who have devoted themselves to the Lord in great actions and have reached such perfection that no difficulty ever bends them. Thus, in their resolve regarding chastity, the flesh does not lay the mind low through the pleasure of an evil thought. It strikes through suggestion, but is not permitted to rise, because it is crushed by the strength of judgment.

In their resolve regarding patience, no disordered word proceeds from their mouth, nor does silent grief weigh upon their mind. In their generosity in almsgiving, no suspicion of poverty produces sadness. In their resolve regarding humility, no contempt wounds their spirit.

Yet, although they already show themselves strong in the things they have rightly vowed, they recall and lament their earlier sins, committed before their good resolution, and they mourn whatever they remember having done unlawfully.

These people are a burnt offering through the life they now lead, but through the life they formerly led they are polluted. They therefore wash the burnt offering in the doorway of the gates, because in the understanding they receive from the sayings of the Fathers they afflict themselves with daily lamentation and cleanse with tears the life they once polluted by wicked deeds.

Let us, then, amid these things, turn the eyes of our minds back to our past life. Let us remember who we were when we followed the desires of this world. And if we serve the Lord with our whole heart, let us, because we remember that we sinned, dissolve in tears and wash the burnt offering.

Behold, we have devoted our chastity to almighty God; but if an impure thought still pollutes the mind, let us return to tears and wash the burnt offering.

Behold, we have resolved to preserve patience; but if anger still disturbs us, if silent grief torments the mind, let us return to tears and wash the burnt offering.

Behold, we have already vowed to distribute what we possess and to occupy a humble place in this world; but if suspicion of poverty still depresses the mind, or if the contempt of our neighbor confounds us with some indignation, let us return to tears and wash the burnt offering.

Great indeed is the merciful bosom of our Creator for receiving the tears of the humble. Where the tears of countless human beings have been received, there our tears too will find their place.

> “And in the vestibule of the gate were two tables on this side and two tables on that side, so that the burnt offering and the sacrifice for sin and for guilt might be slaughtered upon them. And on the outer side that ascends to the doorway of the gate that leads toward the north were two tables; and on the other side, before the vestibule of the gate, were two tables. Four tables on this side and four tables on that side, along the sides of the gate. There were eight tables upon which they slaughtered.” (Gregory.)

In these words a great obscurity of uncertainty arises: whether this is said of one particular gate, or of two, or of each of the gates. But since four tables are described along the sides, and afterward, in the concluding statement, it is said, “There were eight tables upon which they slaughtered,” it is clear that the Spirit is not speaking of each of the gates described above.

For if the six gates previously narrated had four tables along their sides, all of them together would be said to have not eight but forty-eight tables.

Again, if this is said of one gate, our understanding is struck by a great difficulty. For after the vestibule of the gate has been described, where two tables on this side and two on that side were said to be located, two more tables are still mentioned on the outer side that ascends to the doorway of the gate leading toward the north. Then it is added: “And on the other side, before the vestibule of the gate, were two tables.”

If there were two tables on each side within the vestibule of the gate, then, when it is added, “And on the outer side were two tables, and on the other side before the vestibule were two tables,” and the gate facing the northern road is mentioned as lying between them, it is plainly evident that there was one vestibule inside and another outside. For first the interior gate was described, and afterward, in this passage, the exterior northern gate.

When he previously described three gates, he also mentioned three others belonging to the inner court, of which he had narrated the northern gate as the outermost—but, as was said, the northern gate of the inner court.

Now, therefore, when two tables on this side in the vestibule of the gate and two tables on that side are described, the discourse still concerns the same interior gate, especially since it immediately adds that on the outer side that ascends to the doorway of the gate reaching toward the north there were two tables, and on the other side before the vestibule of the gate there were two tables.

The interior gate is therefore described as having two tables along each side in its vestibule, and the exterior gate likewise as having two tables. Thus four tables on this side and four on that side are formed: two on each side in the vestibule of the interior gate, and two on each side outside, in the northern gate. Together they are eight, upon which the sacrifices are offered.

As was said above, the gates may be understood as the holy preachers, so that the vestibule of the gate is the people. When the people receive the words of preaching with a humble mind, tables for sacrifice are constructed in them from the virtues.

There is likewise no obstacle to understanding the gate as that through which the understanding of sacred discourse is opened to us by the mouths of preachers. The words of that same preaching are then the vestibule of the gate: we first receive them humbly, and afterward come to the understanding of sacred discourse.

Let the interior gate, therefore, be the New Testament, and the exterior gate the Old Testament, because the former opens spiritual understanding, while the latter preserved the literal sense of sacred discourse for minds that were still inexperienced.

The interior gate has, among the great multitude of the faithful, two sides: love of God and love of neighbor. There are two tables on each side because in love of God faith and life must necessarily be maintained. In love of neighbor, the goodness of patience must be guarded above all.

Faith and life are necessary in love of God, for it is written: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews 11). It is written again: “Faith without works is dead” (James 2).

In love of neighbor, patience and kindness must be preserved, because it is written of that same love: “Charity is patient, charity is kind” (1 Corinthians 13). Patient, namely, so that it bears with equanimity the evils inflicted by neighbors; kind, so that it generously bestows its own good things upon neighbors.

The exterior gate, namely the Law, also has two sides: the spiritual Fathers and the carnal people. In each of these there are two tables. Among the spiritual Fathers it has teaching and prophecy; among the carnal people it has circumcision and sacrifice.

Upon these eight tables the sacrifice is offered, because whatever faith believes, whatever life displays in the example of good works, whatever patience humbly endures, whatever kindness generously supplies, whatever teaching beneficially teaches, whatever prophecy foretells for the future, whatever circumcision bound by an external commandment, and whatever sacrifice the devotion of the one offering accomplished—all this is shown to be a victim in the eyes of almighty God.

For under the Law also, through the carnal sacrifice, what else was the people offering except the devotion of their heart?

It should be noted, however, that only four tables are mentioned as having been for the burnt offering. These we understand to belong to the vestibule of the interior gate, so that we may conclude concerning the remaining four that they were constructed for sacrifice, not for a burnt offering.

For, as I declared in the preceding discussion, a burnt offering means “wholly burned.” The Law indeed commands that God and neighbor be loved, that the divine commandments be kept, and that one be restrained from coveting another’s possessions; but it does not command that everything be abandoned.

In the New Testament, however, Truth declares to us: “Unless someone renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14; Matthew 16). And again he says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Luke 9).

The tables of the interior gate therefore have a burnt offering, because in the virtues of the New Testament we burn everything, as it were, through a burnt offering when we renounce all such things.

But the tables of the exterior gate have a sacrifice, not a burnt offering, because the legal precepts command tithes to be offered but do not command that everything be abandoned.

Of the four tables of the interior vestibule it is said that the burnt offering and the sacrifice for sin and for guilt are to be offered upon them. There is this difference between sin and guilt: sin is doing evil, whereas guilt is abandoning the good things that ought especially to be held fast. Or, certainly, sin is in action, while guilt is in thought.

Rightly, therefore, in the four tables of the interior gate a burnt offering is offered for sin and for guilt. For whoever is able completely to despise the present world and, abandoning everything, to give himself as a burnt offering to the Lord, knows perfectly how to lament both the sins of his actions and the sins of his thoughts—whether the evil he has done or the good he ought to have done but did not.

Whoever has abandoned everything sees his faults more freely in tears. And when earthly care no longer obstructs his mind, what else has he given to almighty God as a burnt offering, together with his actions, except his own mind?

Nor does it seem foreign to reason that, when the Prophet spoke of the outer side and mentioned the doorway of the gate, he added, “which leads toward the north.”

In the exterior gate, the Law was held in the guardianship of the letter. The doorway of the gate is the historical understanding of the Law itself, which leads to fear of the Lord.

That gate is said to lead toward the north because the same Law bound the cold hearts of the Jewish people under fear of threats. That people would have run, as it were, through warmth if they had kept the Lord’s commandments out of love. But because they guarded the letter under fear of the threatened death, they remained, as it were, in the numbness of cold.

Hence it is said to the new peoples who love eternal rewards rather than fear temporal punishments, and who are already warmed: “You have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear, but the spirit of adoption, in which we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8).

Let it therefore be said: “Four tables on this side and four tables on that side, along the sides of the gate.” When faith and life, teaching and prophecy are guarded in the minds of the good, our gate—that is, the understanding of sacred discourse—has four tables along one side.

And when holy preaching preserves patience and kindness among peoples who are advancing, whereas it formerly preserved circumcision and sacrifice among carnal people, four tables are also shown on the other side, as it were. Together all eight are made for sacrifice: four interior ones for a burnt offering, and four exterior ones for sacrifice.

For those who preserve faith, life, patience, and kindness in the holy Church undoubtedly already excel in the highest virtues. And those who in the synagogue knew teaching and prophecy, circumcision and sacrifice, offered some things while retaining others for themselves, and gave the victim of their devotion to almighty God.

But because it was said above that the four tables of the interior vestibule were constructed so that a burnt offering might be offered upon them both for sin and for guilt, where these tables were constructed is revealed below, when it is added:

“Now four tables for the burnt offering were constructed of squared stones.” But whom shall we understand by the squared stones in this passage [Col. 0951D], except certain saints whose life knows how to stand firmly in prosperity and adversity? For a squared stone stands equally on whichever side it is turned. Whoever, therefore, is not lifted up in prosperity, is not broken in adversity, is not drawn toward evil by enticements, and is not recalled from good work by reproaches is a squared stone; and, as though standing on every side, he has a stable position and does not fall in any change of circumstance.

Certainly, when the Prophet knew that the Jewish people were perishing from the faith and foresaw the holy apostles rising within the Church, through whom many from the nations were established in the strength of faith and life, he spoke in great consolation, saying: “The stones have fallen, but we shall build with squared stones [Col. 0952A] [Bricks]” (Isa. IX). Seeing, then, the apostles, martyrs, and teachers arising in the holy Church from the fall of stones—that is, from the destruction of the Jews—he grieved less, because he saw the building of almighty God, that is, the holy Church, being constructed from squared stones.

The four tables, therefore, are built from squared stones, because faith and life, patience and kindness, were given from the lives of the saints as an example to succeeding peoples, so that the vestibule might now have tables—that is, so that the people might possess the virtues of life on which they may kindle the sacrifice of prayer to almighty God upon the altar of their heart. For whatever good the faithful peoples of the holy Church either did or do, they received it as an example from the life of their preachers. How, then, would this vestibule have tables unless it had found squared stones? When the life of the holy preachers is recognized by the faithful people for the imitation of the saints’ virtues, tables are surely constructed in the vestibule from squared stones.

The Synagogue, too, had spiritual fathers in teaching and prophecy, from whom it could draw an example of life in the virtues. But its unformed people served more through fear than through love; although they saw the life of their fathers, they refused to imitate it. Therefore the outer gate, which reaches toward the north, has neither tables nor a burnt offering.

But because we have spoken of these things morally, it remains that we should examine the same tables according to their typological meaning. Our gate, then, in the inner vestibule has four tables [Col. 0952C], because the holy Church received four governing orders for the instruction of the faithful peoples, which Paul enumerates as gifts of almighty God, saying: “He himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, and others as shepherds and teachers” (Eph. IV). He names shepherds and teachers as one governing order, because the one who teaches is truly the one who feeds the flock of God.

The outer gate, too, had four tables, because the Synagogue itself maintained an external observance through the chief priests, the elders of the people, the scribes, and the Pharisees; the Pharisees, in fact, were also called teachers of the law. Whether in the outer gate or in the inner gate, there are two tables on this side and two on that, because at its beginnings the holy Church had apostles and prophets [Col. 0952D]. By “prophets,” however, we do not mean those who had existed among the earlier people, but those who arose in the holy Church after the apostles. In the later period, which is the present one, it has evangelists and teachers.

Because “gospel” means good news, we call evangelists those who announce the good things of the heavenly homeland to unformed peoples. These evangelists and teachers certainly existed in the earlier period as well, but by the Lord’s generosity they continue to the present day, since even now we know that unbelieving peoples are daily being drawn to faith and that the faithful are instructed by teachers in good conduct.

The apostles and prophets, however, have been taken away from the present age. Therefore we say that our gate—that is, the holy Church—has these tables, as it were, on another side, and that the gate proceeding toward the north has two tables on this side and two on that: namely, those chief priests and elders of the people whom we have mentioned, in the greater authority of governance; and the scribes and Pharisees, who presided over that unformed people in a lesser position.

But these tables are beside the gate proceeding toward the north because, when these four orders presided over the people, the Synagogue, raging in persecution of our Redeemer, broke out into the torpor of unbelief. Nevertheless, these tables had a sacrifice, which they held according to the letter alone. Thus they fell into the torpor of coldness, because they were not kindled with the flame of the Spirit.

The inner tables, however, have a burnt offering, because whether in the hearts of the apostles and prophets or in the minds of evangelists and teachers, the fire of the Spirit both burned and burns. Since it consumes all their thought in good work, the flame of God’s love kindles everything it finds, as one complete burnt offering.

Those offer a burnt offering who are kindled to the marrow either in good work or in holy thought. These tables, then, were made from squared stones, because, while they meditate daily in their hearts on the words of sacred speech, the words of prayer are brought together for offering to the Lord as a burnt offering, as though from squared stones. For the words of sacred Scripture are squared stones, because they stand firm everywhere and are found blameworthy on no side: in everything they narrate as past, in everything they announce as future, in everything they proclaim morally, and in everything they utter spiritually, they have a stable position, as though on different sides, because they contain no reproach.

The hearts of the saints, therefore, are God’s tables, constructed for a burnt offering from squared stones, because those who always think upon God slay themselves to the Lord in thought, turning away from carnal life. Hence it is written: “His God’s law is in his heart, and his steps shall not be shaken” (Ps. XXXVI). And hence it is written: “In my heart I have hidden your words, that I might not sin against you” (Ps. CXVIII).

But we have learned from what these tables are constructed; let us also hear what their measurements are. It follows:

“Length, one cubit and a half; width, one cubit and a half; and height, one cubit.”

We have often said that length refers to the long endurance of hope, while width refers to the breadth of charity. The tables, therefore, which are constructed for the burnt offering are measured in length at one and a half cubits, because the holy fathers and teachers, who extend themselves patiently toward the innermost secrets of hope, are, insofar as human measure is concerned, very perfect through the fact that they live in the virtues. But insofar as those divine mysteries are concerned which cannot be fully grasped by human beings, they are not perfect as long as they remain in this mortal flesh.

In themselves, therefore, they already have one cubit, but in God they do not yet have the cubit: for they already advance fully in the virtues, yet they still know something of God only in part.

Here again Paul comes forward as a testimony in the measurement of the table. Let us see whether his life is measured by a complete cubit. He says: “Let all of us who are perfect think this” (Phil. III). Let us see whether, in what he understands concerning God, he has already fully reached the mysteries that must be attained. He said: “I do not consider myself to have grasped it” (ibid.); and again: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part; but when the perfect comes, the partial will be brought to an end” (I Cor. XIII). Again he says: “Now I know in part, but then I shall know fully, just as I have been fully known” (ibid.).

If, therefore, he is perfect and knows in part, he has the cubit with respect to himself, but still has a half-cubit above himself. Let the hearts of the saints, then, be extended toward the long endurance of hope; let them be extended toward the perfection they possess in one cubit. But because they cannot yet see fully where they direct the eye of hope, let what they have beyond one cubit be cut down to a half-cubit, so that in this life they may always regard themselves as imperfect and run more ardently toward perfection.

The tables also have a width of one and a half cubits, because the hearts of the saints, enlarged in the breadth of charity, possess one cubit with regard to the neighbor whom they love and see. They can love perfectly those whom they are able perfectly to know in some respect. They love and follow almighty God to the marrow, yet they cannot love him as much as they ought, because they cannot yet see the one whom they love; and the measure of love is smaller where the measure of knowledge is still smaller.

They therefore have one cubit and a half above it, because what is already complete in them in love—that which is much lesser, namely, charity toward the neighbor—is one thing, while what is much greater, namely, love of God, whom they do not see, is not yet complete in them.

The height of the measurements, however, is one cubit. For what is the height of the saints except the invisible things? What is not seen is believed through faith. Therefore, through this height, the mind of the righteous is led upward so that it may despise all visible things on earth and follow in heaven the invisible things it hears.

But the height of the measurements has one cubit, because the unity of faith exists in the heart of all the saints. The fathers of the Old Testament and the preachers of the New have professed that the Trinity is one God. The height of the measurements, therefore, has neither more nor less than one cubit, because the faith of all the fathers agrees with itself in great unity.

But those who, already advancing in the highest virtues through the long endurance of hope, have one and a half cubits, and who are measured in the breadth of charity by one and a half cubits, while in the height of faith they exceed by one cubit, are great and worthy of the highest admiration. They ought, therefore, to receive the souls of the little ones into the bosom of their way of life and offer them before the Lord as a kind of burnt offering and sacrifice. Hence it appropriately follows:

“Upon them they place vessels in which the burnt offering and the victim are sacrificed.”

For what are the souls of the faithful except holy vessels that receive the word of piety, so that from their minds a burnt offering of life and prayer may be sacrificed? Hence it is that Paul, while he was still unformed in the calling of faith—for he had already received the Lord’s words and was full of heavenly grace—is called a vessel, when it is said: “He is a vessel of election for me.” Hence the Prophet admonishes shepherds and teachers, saying: “Be clean, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. LII). For those carry the vessels of the Lord like tables who, by instructing the faithful, bear their life, so that at some time they may lead it to the Lord as a burnt offering and sacrifice.

Nor should we carelessly overlook the fact that in these same vessels both a burnt offering and a victim are said to be sacrificed. A burnt offering, as we said above, is a victim. Yet a victim is not always a burnt offering, because when something is offered in part and retained in part, it is indeed a sacrifice, but it is not a burnt offering.

Among the great multitude of the faithful, there are some who abandon everything that belongs to the world, give away all that they possess, reserve nothing for themselves, yearn with their whole being for the eternal homeland, and slay themselves in tears with their whole heart. These are vessels upon the table in which a burnt offering is sacrificed.

There are others who care for their own household, think about their children, and preserve an inheritance for them, yet, mindful of eternal judgment, extend mercy to the poor and give them food and clothing to the extent they have determined. These, certainly, are vessels upon the table in which a victim has been sacrificed, but not a burnt offering.

For the patience and teaching of the saints, by admonishing and enduring, persuading and frightening, instruct the hearts of others to the point that they abandon everything and kindle their whole selves in the love of the Lord. They instruct others only to the point that, since they cannot abandon everything, they at least become merciful to the extent that they are able, and divide their care between the flesh and the soul.

The tables of the Lord, furnished from squared stones, carry vessels in which a burnt offering and a victim are sacrificed, because the perfect, as has been said, when they abandon everything, kindle their whole heart in the love of the Lord, while the imperfect offer a sacrifice which they have devoted in part. It follows:

“And their rims were one palm wide, turned inward all around.”

What does it mean that the rims of the tables are measured by a palm, except that the hand is extended in the palm, and that the holy fathers and teachers proclaim those things in which the works of their hearers may be extended? For we extend the hand, as it were, when we enlarge our works.

Let every teacher, then, speak; let him exercise the heart of the hearer and shake off the torpor of the idle. When he stretches them toward works, let him show that he has a palm on his rims.

It should also be considered that the greater and the smallest finger are extended in the palm. What is signified by the greater and the smallest finger except a great and an extreme action? Let the table, therefore, have a palm on its rim, so that people may remain vigilant in the preaching of their teachers and, by their admonition, perform great works without neglecting even the smallest. Let them attend to the smallest things in such a way that they are not sluggish in doing the greater.

Hence Truth says through the Gospel: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and leave aside the weightier matters of the law: judgment and mercy and faith. These you ought to have done, and not to have omitted those others” (Matt. XXIII).

Through judgment, mercy, and faith, the greater finger of action is shown. Through mint, dill, and cumin, without doubt the smallest finger is represented. “These you ought to have done, and not to have omitted those others,” because, if we wish to measure our work by a palm, it is necessary that the smallest finger be extended in such a way that the greater finger is not drawn back.

It is fitting that, when the rims of the tables are measured and the measure of a palm is mentioned, “one” is added, so that, just as unity is maintained in faith through the preaching of teachers, so also unity of minds may be preserved in action. Thus one person should not burst into the evil of discord because of the good work performed by another.

We ought to do good works in such a way that through them we also preserve, insofar as we rightly can, harmony with those with whom we live: not by abandoning what we are doing, but by forestalling through good persuasion the evil of discord that we fear.

It must be carefully considered that it is said that “the rims of these same tables are turned inward.” The rims of the tables are turned inward when teachers recall to their conscience by silent reflection what they say, when they examine themselves carefully to see whether they do what they teach.

Therefore, the teacher who must speak about the proper measure of discipline should know that he is God’s table, with a rim turned inward, so that what he says in teaching he may vigilantly practice under the spirit of discernment. Nor, if he considers that certain things are lacking in himself, ought he to keep silent about that preaching. His position requires him to speak.

Let him therefore confront himself with his own words. If he does not speak because he does not practice, let him practice because he is compelled to speak. Wherever he sees that he fulfills in action what he says, there let him admonish his hearers and kindle their minds to zeal for good action. But wherever he does not yet see himself fulfilling what he says, let him kindle himself likewise toward the good about which he admonishes his hearers, so that he too may learn in action what Truth speaks through him in preaching.

Often we learn by speaking, compelled by the teaching of our speech, what we do not know through living. When the guilt of our laziness arises in the mind from reflection, sudden compunction pierces that same mind, and, awakened by its own voice, it becomes alert in action—although previously it had been sluggish in idleness and without a voice.

For behold, when the rim of the table is extended by a palm—that is, when the teacher’s mouth argues against vices and the hearts of the hearers are kindled toward good works—many who hear his words recognize how great or what sort of evils they have committed. They come to him in confession and ask with tears that he become an intercessor for their sins, so that by praying he may erase the faults which he reveals by preaching. Hence it is added:

“Upon the tables, however, were the flesh of the offering.”

The holy teachers, when they pour out prayers to almighty God for the repentant, the sinful, and the confessing, carry upon the tables of the Lord the flesh of the offering by requesting pardon for their carnal life.

In order that there may be people for whom they can pray after conversion and weeping, they ought first to preach to those same people while they remain in sin. When they have begun to abandon their sins and hasten toward innocence, the growth of preaching must increase in the teacher’s mouth toward them. He must press the words of his teaching upon some of them with greater force in proportion as he considers that they have fallen more grievously, knowing that he receives a greater reward for himself in proportion as he raises others from deeper sins through his words.

The meaning of sacred speech is mystical, as the Prophet, understanding wisely through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, said: “Your testimonies are wonderful, O Lord; therefore my soul has searched them out, etc.” (Ps. CXVIII).

To what, then, should I compare the word of sacred speech except to a stone in which fire lies hidden? It is held cold in the hand, but when struck by iron it flashes forth in sparks. That which the hand previously held cold emits fire, which later burns.

So it is with the words of sacred speech: through the narrative of the letter they are held, as it were, cold. But if someone strikes them with attentive understanding, with the Lord inspiring him, he draws fire from their mystical meanings, so that the mind may afterward burn spiritually in those words which previously, through the letter, he too heard coldly.

For behold, the Prophet says:

“And outside the inner gate were the chambers of the singers, in the inner court which was at the side of the gate looking toward the north, and their fronts were toward the southern road, one at the side of the eastern gate, which looked toward the northern road.”

In these words of the letter, whose mind could be kindled to the love of God? Rather, who would not grow lukewarm merely from reading them? But if the spiritual marrow hidden in the letter is examined, sparks of understanding emerge from it and kindle what previously sounded cold to the ears of the heart.

Nevertheless, in order that the inner meaning may be opened to us with the Lord inspiring us, the narrative must first be laid out according to the letter. He says that there was an inner gate, and outside it a court called inner; then other gates—the northern, southern, and eastern—are described, so that he may show that the very court which he had said was outside the inner gate was inner in relation to the outer gates.

This court, then, is both outside and inside: outside because it is beyond the inner gate, but inside because it is within the outer gates. The chambers of the singers are also said to be in this same court. They are described as being placed beside the gate that looks toward the north, but these same chambers look toward the southern road.

Then it is added: “At the side of the eastern gate, which looked toward the northern road.” From these words it is clearly understood that all the chambers of the treasury were placed between the side of the gate looking toward the north and the side of the eastern gate; that gate, in turn, looked toward the northern road.

The fronts of the chambers, therefore, were toward the southern road, but their position was between the eastern and northern gates. The inner gate thus had the northern gate on one side and the southern gate on the other, while the eastern gate rose at the front of the vestibule. In this way the court was outside the inner gate, yet it was also inner, since the outer gates surrounded it.

We have briefly passed over these matters from the words of the letter. Let us now briefly seek their mystical meaning.

In the earlier section three gates were described: the eastern, northern, and southern. Immediately afterward three other gates of the inner court were related: the southern, eastern, and northern. Then the gate of the inner court was mentioned, in which the tables constructed from squared stones are remembered, and the gate looking toward the north, in which there were tables for sacrifice but not for a burnt offering.

For this reason we said that the inner gate signifies the Church and the outer gate the Synagogue. Yet, after these things have been completed, the Prophet again begins to describe the inner gate and three others—the northern, southern, and eastern—and says that in their inner court, which was outside the inner gate, there were chambers of singers, priests, the temple, the altar, and sacrifices.

Since in these words he begins to narrate matters concerning the foundation of the holy Church different from those he had previously stated, it is evident that he has changed the meaning of the inner gate. For if he were saying everything according to one meaning, he would not repeat the same things in a new order and in another form.

How, indeed, can we say that outside the inner gate there are a court, chambers, singers, priests, a temple, an altar, and sacrifices, if the holy Church is signified by the same inner gate in this passage? Since all these things are within it, how can they be outside the inner gate if they are not outside the Church?

The inner gate can therefore be understood as the one of which we spoke much earlier, which is said to be situated opposite the northern and eastern gates. We said that it signifies the entrance through which the way to the inner joys of the heavenly homeland is opened to us. Thus here also the gates narrated around the vestibule signify the holy Church, while the inner gate signifies the entrance to the heavenly kingdom.

But lest anyone think that I am forcibly bending the words of the Holy Spirit toward my own understanding, and say that I ought not to have changed the meaning of the inner gate as signifying the holy Church, let us, with the grace of almighty God shining upon us, retain what we have begun: let the inner gate signify the Church, which leads people to inner joys; and let the chambers, singers, priests, temple, altar, and sacrifices be in the court outside the gate, yet not outside the Church.

If we investigate carefully, nothing prevents us from understanding the inner gate, as has been said, to signify the holy Church, concerning which it is now said: “And outside the inner gate were the chambers of the singers in the inner court.”

For two things are mentioned: the inner gate and the inner court outside it, so that this same court may be both outer and inner—outer in relation to the gate, but inner, as we said earlier, in relation to the gates which he subsequently introduced in his narrative.

The holy Church has two lives: one which it leads in time and another which it receives eternally; one in which it labors on earth and another in which it is rewarded in heaven; one in which it gathers rewards and another in which it already rejoices in the rewards it has received.

In both lives it offers sacrifice: here, the sacrifice of compunction; there, the sacrifice of praise. Of the former sacrifice it is said: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God” (Ps. L). Of the latter it is written: “Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness, offerings and burnt offerings” (ibid.). Again he says of it: “That my glory may sing to you and I may not be pierced with compunction” (Ps. XXIX).

In both sacrifices flesh is offered. Here, the offering of flesh is the mortification of the body; there, the offering of flesh is, in the praise of God, the glory of resurrection. For then flesh is offered there as a burnt offering, when, changed into eternal incorruption, it has nothing resistant and nothing mortal, because, kindled wholly at once by the fires of his love, it will remain forever in praise.

Let this inner gate, therefore—that is, the holy Church—have its inner things, namely, that life which is still hidden from our eyes. Let it have outside itself an outer court, that is, the present life in which every good thing is done so that one may reach the good without end.

Let the chambers of the singers, then, be in the inner court, which nevertheless is outside the gate. For all the elect and perfect who still subsist in mortal flesh are both within the bosom of the holy Church and still outside the secret joys of the inner life.

What, then, are the chambers of the singers except the holy desires of those who love, who guard the divine commandments in their minds as certain riches and preserve them by singing, because they fulfill God’s commandments not from fear but from love? The precepts of sacred speech themselves become songs for them, which they continually practice not from sorrow but from desire.

In the preceding discussion we said that the eastern gate signifies faith, the northern gate hope, and the southern gate charity.

These chambers, then, are said to be between the eastern and northern gates and to look toward the southern road, because the hearts of the saints, placed between faith and hope, look toward the southern road and burn with the fires of holy charity.

The eastern gate itself is also said to look toward the northern road, because through faith all sins are indeed forgiven for us in baptism. Yet, while we still live here, even after faith we frequently incline toward sins, and the eastern gate looks toward the northern road when our life, after receiving faith, still grows torpid to some extent in the coldness of guilt.

For who in this life can live without sin after faith, when John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I)? James, agreeing with his words, says: “For we all offend in many things” (James III).

If past sins have been forgiven upon the reception of faith, yet after faith we still incline toward sins, what confidence in righteousness or hope of lasting life can we have, except that, while we are still between the eastern and northern gates, we lift our eyes toward the southern road? Thus, burning with holy charity, the warmth of love may free us from the guilt of lukewarmness and coldness.

Let the chambers, then, be between the eastern and northern gates, but, as was said, let them turn their fronts toward the southern road, so that, between the fact that we were born in faith and the fact that, having afterward fallen into sins, we presume upon the hope of mercy, we may exercise ourselves in the fervor of charity and direct the eyes of our hearts toward the place where we are kindled by the fire of love.

The northern gate, however, can signify the Gentiles; the southern road, Judea; and the eastern gate, the Lord himself. For the Gentiles are not unreasonably represented by the north, which was possessed in the coldness of torpor by the one who said: “I shall sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north” (Isa. XIV).

Judea is rightly understood through the southern gate, in which the spiritual fathers burned with heavenly love. One of them says: “Turn, O Lord, our captivity, like a torrent in the south” (Ps. CXXV). Although it had a carnal people, in whom it bore the coldness of the north, in its holy teachers and prophets it burned toward God and the neighbor with the warmth of charity.

The eastern gate, however, not unreasonably signifies the one of whom it is written: “Behold, the man whose name is Orient.” Concerning him Zechariah says: “The Orient from on high has visited us” (Zech. VI; Luke I).

Let the chambers of the singers, then, be at the side of the northern gate, because the hearts of the saints were not spiritually kindled only in Judea. Rather, among the multitude of the Gentiles converted to the mysteries of the holy faith, the hearts of the saints burn with love, long for the joys of the eternal homeland, and breathe after fellowship with their fellow citizens in heaven.

Yet they receive examples of this fervor, which they have received as a gift of the Holy Spirit, from the spiritual fathers of the Synagogue. Hence these same chambers, although placed at the side of the north, extend their eyes toward the southern road.

For behold, we come from the Gentiles, but in the fact that we burn through holy love, we look to the fathers of Judea, who daily offer us examples of holy desire in their words.

Did he not burn as though with the heat of midday fervor who was consumed with longing and said: “As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God. My soul thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. XLI). Again he says: “I shall sing and understand in the immaculate way: when will you come to me?” (Ps. C).

He too had been kindled by this same fervor who said: “Now dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke II).

Therefore, because we come from the Gentiles but set before ourselves the holy fathers of Judea for imitation of divine love, we are, as it were, certain chambers of singers at the side of the gate that looks toward the northern road, but we turn our fronts toward the southern road.

It should also be noted that these same chambers are said to be between the northern and eastern gates. For after the Lord’s incarnation, a multitude of Gentiles came to the faith, and among these faithful peoples, between them and the mysteries of the Lord’s incarnation, which they love to the marrow, the hearts of those who love rise up.

Let the holy chambers, then, have the eastern gate on one side and the northern gate on the other, because between the mysteries of their redemption, which they follow, and certain carnal people whom they tolerate even within the holy Church, many advance toward God with strong love, grow in virtues, seek the coming of the eternal Judge, and, between what they love and what they endure, preserve in their minds, as it were, certain chambers containing the riches of the Spirit.

They do not fail between the mysteries they love and the things contrary to them which they now bear, because they turn their fronts toward the southern road. For what do we endure that our fathers did not previously endure for the love of the Lord?

It should also be noted that the eastern gate is described as being between the southern and northern gates, because our Lord and Redeemer was born from Judea and immediately built the Church from the Gentiles in his faith.

He appeared, as it were, between the southern and northern gates, because he came from the one and converted the other to his service. Hence it is fittingly said that this same eastern gate looks toward the northern road, because the Lord, once born, destroys the Synagogue and gathers the multitude of the Gentiles.

It should also be noted that when the chambers were mentioned and their fronts were said to be toward the southern road, “one” was added, so that we might clearly understand that there is not one road to the heavenly homeland for us who come from the Gentiles and another for those fathers who were in Judea. Rather, this same one road belongs both to us and to them, the road that leads us to eternal joys, which says to us through the Gospel: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV).

Concerning him the Psalmist says: “That we may know your way upon earth, and your salvation among all nations.” What is *Jesus* in Hebrew is called *Savior* in Latin. The Savior’s way, therefore, is known on earth, because Jesus, God before the ages and made man at the end of the ages, was manifested to the nations.
