There is therefore one way both for those who are from the south and for those who look from the northern side, because to the elect Jews and Gentiles our Lord and Redeemer, having driven away the punishment of fear, became the way of love to the Father and the help by which they arrive. It follows:

“He said to me: ‘This is the treasury that faces the southern way, belonging to the priests who keep watch in the temple guardrooms.’” And immediately it is added: “Moreover, the treasury that faces the northern way shall belong to the priests who keep watch over the altar’s ministry.”

In these words of the prophet we must first inquire who the priests of the higher order are: whether those who keep watch in the temple guardrooms, or those who serve in the ministry of the altar. But since a little later it is added, “[Col. 0961D] The altar was before the face of the temple,” it is plainly shown that those who keep watch in the temple guardrooms are the priests of the higher order, since they certainly minister at the altar that is farther within. Those, however, who keep watch at the altar that is before the face of the temple are inferior in proportion as they minister in the outer areas.

We must therefore now inquire which priests are said to guard the temple, and which are said to keep watch over the altar’s ministry. For the teacher of the nations, writing to the faithful, says: “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. 3). Who, then, are the priests who guard God’s temple, except those who, by praying, preaching, and keeping watch through spiritual actions, defend the holy Church from the assaults of evil spirits, [Col. 0962A] the persuasions of the wicked, and the errors of heretics?

Was he not a guardian of the temple who, enumerating the labors of his suffering, says: “In labor and hardship, in many watchings, in hunger and thirst, in many fasts, in cold and nakedness” (2 Cor. 11)? And he immediately adds: “Besides those things which are external, my daily pressure, the concern for all the churches” (ibid.). Consider, I ask, with how great concern the guardian of the temple keeps watch. Behold, he himself suffers immeasurable things, yet shares the concern of his heart with others. What virtue, I ask, is it to think more about the welfare of one’s neighbors than about one’s own affliction? Who could estimate this worthily, who could weigh it worthily? He labors, mourns, hungers, thirsts, suffers cold, fasts, and keeps watch; yet, while keeping watch, he thinks about the concern of all the churches. Behold, the most vigilant guardian of the temple has been set before us as an example. Let whoever is able imitate him.

To suffer adversity for the truth, to expend one’s goods for one’s neighbors, to remain vigilant concerning the care of souls; to seek out and restrain anyone who might slip into unbelief, pride, plunder, or impurity: this is to guard the temple of God, that is, the holy Church.

There are, however, priests of the lower order who keep watch over the altar’s ministry. These, namely, with the assistance of the greater priests, carefully investigate the sins of those who offend, correct the life of carnal people, and lead them to the point where, through the lamentations of repentance, they burn the flesh in sacrifice—the flesh that they had previously allowed to live in sin.

For those who preside over the holy churches are not able to do everything by themselves. While they are occupied with spiritual matters, if anything wicked or carnal is committed, they entrust such matters to others for examination and correction. Through these men, while the carnal life is corrected and progress is made toward the practice of abstinence and prayer, the flesh is, as it were, already burned upon the altar, so that before the sight of the almighty Lord a sacrifice may arise with a pleasing fragrance from the very place where guilt had previously been displeasing.

But a question arises here. Since it was said above that the treasuries had their faces toward the southern way, why is it now said that the treasury facing the southern way belongs to the priests who keep watch in the temple guardrooms, while the treasury facing the northern way belongs to the priests who keep watch over the altar’s ministry? If both faces extended toward the southern way, how can one now be said to face the southern way and the other the northern way?

But from these words we understand that the treasury of the priests who keep watch in the temple guardrooms had been placed so that it faced only the southern way. The treasury of the priests who keep watch over the altar’s ministry, however, was situated in the court in such a way that it faced both the southern and the northern ways. Thus, together with the treasury of the priests who keep watch in the temple guardrooms, it looked toward the southern way; yet, without the treasury of those same priests, the treasury of the priests who keep watch over the altar’s ministry could see the northern way.

But what is this, dearest brothers? What mystical meaning can we discern in these words, except what follows from the matters already set forth? The spiritual helper of the higher order can now be understood: the priests of the higher order who keep watch in the temple guardrooms look only toward the southern way, because they are occupied solely with spiritual pursuits and are always attentively devoted to the things that belong to the love of God.

The priests of the lower order, however, who preside over the examination of sinners’ offenses, also turn their eyes toward the northern way, so that they may see in the minds of sinners what chills of sluggishness are present. Bringing these, through words of correction, all the way to the groans of repentance, they burn them like flesh upon the Lord’s altar.

They also look with the greater priests toward the southern way, because, insofar as concerns themselves, they burn with the fire of charity and are kindled with the flames of love for God. But because they frequently correct the sins of offenders, they also turn their eyes toward the northern way.

(Hieronymus.) Both, serving the Lord according to their offices, are called the sons of Zadok. Hence it follows:

“These are the sons of Zadok, who from the sons of Levi approach the Lord in order to minister to him.”

Zadok, therefore, who is interpreted as “just” or “justifying,” signifies the almighty God. Of him it is written: “The Lord is just, and he has loved justice; his face has looked upon uprightness” (Ps. 10). These sons of Zadok are from the sons of Levi, whose name is interpreted as “taken up”; and they too are taken up by the Lord so that they may approach him. Thus it is no longer said only of Moses, “Moses approached the Lord,” as though others did not approach; rather, all who serve him and minister to the Lord are said to draw near.

(Gregorius.) All who steadfastly devote themselves to spiritual actions are sons of the Just One, and from the sons of the people who have been taken up they approach the Lord in order to minister to him. For from among the faithful themselves those are chosen who come to the service of the almighty One and devote themselves to heavenly pursuits for the instruction of the people.

But we must diligently inquire who those are who minister to the Lord. For not all who read, nor all who preach, nor all who give away their possessions, nor all who chastise their bodies through abstinence, minister to the Lord. Those who seek their own glory by reading and preaching, who desire to receive praise from people by giving away what they possess and by mortifying their bodies through abstinence, minister to themselves, not to the Lord.

In contrast, the Lord says through the Psalmist: “He who walks in the spotless way, he ministered to me” (Ps. 100). A person has a stain in his way when, in the good work he performs, he sets before himself the reward of earthly glory, because he seeks to receive his payment in this world. Thus the appearance of a good work is defiled in the sight of God by the stain of a wicked intention.

Perhaps someone, devoted to the study of discipline, burns with zeal and cuts away the faults of offenders, but if he is moved to do these things not by love of the almighty One but by his own motives, he ministers in them to himself, not to the Lord. Another, not wishing to appear harsh, tolerates many offenses gently. Since he does not wish to seem strict for the Lord’s sake, through his pursuit of gentleness he ministers to himself, not to the Lord.

It remains, therefore, that whether we grow weary in the ministry of the word, or give our possessions to the needy, or subdue the flesh through abstinence, or are moved by zeal, or at times tolerate wrongdoing gently through patience, we must examine our intention with the greatest care, so that everything we do may be done not from zeal for ourselves but from zeal for the Lord, lest in what we do we minister rather to ourselves than to the Lord.

“And he measured the court, one hundred cubits in length and one hundred cubits in width, forming a square.”

(Hieronymus.) This man who introduced Ezekiel into the outer court—and, so to speak, measured the court itself as far as the Holy of Holies—measured the court in which there were two chambers, or treasuries, assigned as dwellings to the guardians of the temple or of the altar. He found it to be one hundred cubits in length and one hundred cubits in width, forming a square, so that the priests serving in the ministry of God, who had entered by the narrow and constricted way, might have very broad walkways and dwell in the complete and consummate number of virtues.

(Gregorius.) We have often said that length signifies the longsuffering of hope, while breadth signifies the expansiveness of charity. It has already been fully explained above that the number one hundred, in which ten is multiplied ten times, signifies the summit of perfection.

What, then, is the court of the spiritual building except the breadth of the faithful peoples? The longsuffering of hope and the breadth of charity are not empty in the hearts of the faithful, for through faith everything that has power is brought into operation. Hence Paul says: “In Christ Jesus neither circumcision has any power, nor uncircumcision, but faith which works through love.”

If, then, in the life of the faithful, according to a certain manner, longsuffering of hope is perfect in each person, breadth of charity is perfect, certainty of faith is perfect, and zeal for action is perfect, the court of the temple has one hundred cubits in a square. In the measure of a square, one side is not larger and another smaller; rather, all four sides together extend with equal dimensions. So too the same virtues we have mentioned—faith, hope, charity, and action—are found to be equal within us for as long as we live in this life.

Charity is therefore said to be greater than hope and faith because, after we reach the vision of our Creator, hope and faith pass away, but charity remains. For now, as much as we believe, so much do we love; and as much as we love, so much do we presume to hope. The apostle John also bears witness concerning faith and action, saying: “Whoever says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John 2). Knowledge of God belongs to faith, while keeping his commandments belongs to action. When virtue seeks the time and place for acting, a person acts in proportion to his knowledge of God, and he shows how much he knows God in proportion to how much he acts through good works.

Let the faithful peoples therefore measure their virtues in a square. Each person believes as much as he hopes, loves, and acts; hopes as much as he believes, acts, and loves; loves as much as he believes, hopes, and acts; and acts as much as he believes, loves, and hopes. Since there are many peoples in the holy Church—strong through faith, longsuffering through hope, expansive through charity, and effective through action—the court of the temple is measured as one hundred cubits in a square.

To speak also in another way about their virtues: often some among them are prudent through understanding, strong in adversity, just in action, temperate in pleasures, and moderate in every zeal through discernment. While they possess prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance—or, as some prefer to enumerate them, prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice—they possess the measure of the spiritual court in a square.

For these virtues themselves, which we have said that good and faithful people possess, are in a square, so that one does not exceed another. Prudence is great, but if a person is less temperate from pleasures, less strong in dangers, or less just in actions, he is plainly less prudent.

Temperance is great, but if a person understands less clearly what he ought to moderate; if he is less capable of enduring adversity through fortitude and therefore sinks in spirit through fear; or if he sometimes rushes precipitately into works of justice, he is less temperate.

Fortitude is great, but if a person understands less clearly which good things he should preserve and which evils he should resist; if he restrains himself less from the desire for pleasure and is overcome by delight; or if he maintains works of justice less firmly and is sometimes conquered by the domination of injustice, he is less strong.

Justice is great, but if a person distinguishes less than he ought between just and unjust actions; if he moderates his care for the world less through detachment from pleasure; or if he strengthens himself less against adversity, he is less just.

Let the life of perfect believers therefore be measured in a square, and let one side of the spiritual court be as great as each of the others. Each person is as prudent as he is temperate, strong, and just; as temperate as he is prudent, strong, and just; as strong as he is prudent, temperate, and just; and as just as he is prudent, temperate, and strong.

There are nevertheless many among them who still live carnally. Even if they perhaps do not know letters and cannot read the commandments of God, they certainly see good things in the conduct of many faithful people, things that they may imitate. Behold, the voices of the holy Gospel and of the apostles resound in the Church. Behold, the examples of those who live well are set before human eyes every day. They will not be able to say in excuse for themselves, “We did not see what we ought to imitate.” Hence it follows:

“And the altar was before the face of the temple.”

What is the temple except the faithful people? Thus the apostle Paul says to the disciples: “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. 3). And what is the altar of God except the mind of those who live well? Such people rightly remember their sins, wash away their stains with tears, mortify the flesh through abstinence, do not entangle themselves in the activities of this world, give to the needy what they possess, and do not desire to possess what they do not have.

Their heart is therefore rightly called the altar of God, [Col. 0966A] where the fire of compunction burns from sorrow and the heart is consumed. The altar is before the face of the temple when many are set before the sight of the holy Church who, mindful of eternal judgment, daily slay themselves as a sacrifice to God in the lamentations of compunction.

As has been said, they chastise their bodies so that they may fulfill what is said by the teacher of the nations: “that you may present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God.” A victim is killed in order to be offered; but a living victim is a body afflicted for the Lord. It is both called a victim and living, because it lives in virtues and has been slain to vices. It is a victim because it is now dead to this world and to wicked actions; it is living because it performs every good work of which it is capable.

But since the discussion has introduced the flame of compunction under the name of the altar, I think it necessary to show what distinction exists within this same compunction. There is one compunction that arises through fear, and another that arises through love. For it is one thing to flee punishments and another to desire rewards.

Hence the Law commands two altars to be made in the tabernacle: one outside and the other inside; one in the court and the other before the ark; one covered with bronze and the other clothed in gold. On the bronze altar flesh is burned, while on the golden altar spices are burned.

What is this, dearest brothers—that flesh is burned outside and spices within—except what we see every day, namely, that there are two kinds of compunction? Some still mourn through fear, while others already afflict themselves with lamentation through love.

Many, remembering their sins and fearing eternal punishments, afflict themselves with daily tears. They mourn the evils they have committed and burn their vices with the fire of compunction, although they still suffer their suggestions in the heart. What are such people except the bronze altar, on which flesh burns, because they are still mourning carnal deeds?

Others, freed from carnal vices or already made secure through prolonged weeping, burn with the flame of love in tears of compunction. They set the rewards of the heavenly homeland before the eyes of their heart and long to be among the citizens above. The servitude and the length of their pilgrimage appear burdensome to them. They desire to see the King in his beauty and do not cease to weep daily out of love for him.

What are such people except the golden altar, in whose heart spices have been burned, because virtues are aflame? It is rightly said of this same altar that it is placed before the veil of the ark in the Holy of Holies.

For he himself has become for us the ark of the covenant—our Redeemer, of whom we read that “in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.” The ark within the veil is our Redeemer in heaven. The golden altar on which incense is burned before the veil signifies the hearts of the saints, which, kindled with great virtues in the love of God, burn through holy desire for him whom they cannot yet see with unveiled face.

There is a veil between the ark and the altar, because the obstacle of our corruption, which still separates us from the vision of God, has not been removed. But as long as we remain before the veil, we ought to burn like incense with the flame of love. Through tears of compunction we ought to seek nothing earthly, nothing transitory. Let he alone suffice for us who made all things. Let us transcend everything through desire, so that we may gather the mind into the One.

Kindled no longer by fear of punishments or by the memory of vices, but by the flame of love, let us burn in tears with the fragrance of virtues.

“And he brought me into the vestibule of the temple, and measured the vestibule: five cubits on this side and five cubits on that side. The width of the doorway was three cubits on this side and three cubits on that side. The length of the vestibule was twenty cubits, its width eleven cubits, and it was ascended by eight steps.”

(Hieronymus.) The man mentioned above also brought Ezekiel into the vestibule—or πρόπυλον, “forecourt”—of the temple. He measured it at five cubits on this side and five cubits on that, because the one who was brought in had been instructed in divine understandings. He knew neither right nor left, but entered by the royal way.

The width of the doorway through which the entrance to the vestibule of the temple was made had three cubits on this side and three on that. Here we should observe the elegance of Holy Scripture: it did not say “on the right and on the left,” lest it seem to name anything left-handed in the Holy of Holies, but “on this side and on that,” that is, on either side.

At once the prudent reader understands that the number three pertains to the mystery of the Trinity, which is the door of those who enter to God: the Father is in the Son, the Son is in the Father, and the Holy Spirit is in both. This threefold number is one door for those who, after the baptism of the Trinity, arrive at salvation.

But what follows—“the length of the vestibule was twenty cubits, and its width eleven cubits”—seems to raise the question how the number twenty, which refers to two decades, and the eleventh, which needs one more in order to complete the sacred number twelve, can be said to exist in the vestibule of the temple. Many resolve this as follows.

Although the priests are holy, established in the ministries of the temple, and daily offer sacrifices to Christ, nevertheless, because they dwell in this mortal and fragile body, subject to illnesses and vices, they possess the number twenty and the number eleven. Hence the Apostle also said: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7).

This does not mean that, in accordance with the most savage heresy, we believe bodies ought to be abolished. Rather, our desire is to be clothed over, not stripped; to receive immortality in place of mortality; and to put on incorruption in place of corruption.

“And it was ascended by eight steps.” By eight steps—or by ten, which is the perfect number—or by eleven, about which we have already spoken—one ascends to the gate of the saints. On its façades were columns, one on this side and another on that. He did not say “two,” lest he fall into the dual number, but “one and one,” which is a perfect number and, through its unity, imitates God.

These were the two columns of which it is also said in the Apocalypse: “Whoever conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall never go out.” Peter and John too are called columns of the Church, through whom we enter the Holy of Holies, and whose teaching is our entrance to Christ.

“And there were columns on the façades, one on this side and another on that.”

Concerning these columns it is read in the Book of Kings and in Chronicles, where the structure of Solomon’s temple is described: in the vestibule of the temple he placed one on the right and another on the left beside the temple’s doorway.

These are the columns of which Paul says (Gal. 2): “James, Cephas, and John, who were regarded as columns, gave the right hand of fellowship to me and Barnabas, so that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcision.”

By these words he seems, as it were, to explain the mystery of the material columns: what they signified and why two were made. The apostle and the spiritual teachers signify all who are strong in faith and action and chosen for contemplation of the things above. They are two so that, by preaching, they may bring both the Gentiles and the circumcision into the Church.

They stood in the portico before the doors of the temple and wonderfully adorned its entrance on both sides with their dignity and beauty. The door of the temple is the Lord, “because no one comes to the Father except through him” (John 14). And as he says elsewhere: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John 10).

The columns placed on both sides stand around this door when the ministers of the word show both peoples the entrance to the kingdom of heaven, so that whether someone comes to the faith of the Gospel from the light of knowledge of the Law or from the severity of paganism, he may have ministers prepared who show him the way of salvation both by word and by example.

Or certainly, because the following is written concerning these same columns in the Book of Chronicles: “He placed the columns in the vestibule, one on the right and the other on the left” (2 Chron. 3), the columns were made two and arranged in this way so that they might teach us to keep the entrance to the heavenly homeland before the eyes of our mind both in prosperity and in adversity.

(Maurus.) We believe that these things, which we have said according to the teaching of our predecessors concerning the measurement and arrangement of the temple, the vestibule, and the other things described there, are sufficient for the sober reader. Now we shall explain how the prophet himself was brought into the temple and what he did there.

# BOOK SEVENTEEN

[Col. 0969]

## CHAPTER XLI. The temple and the Holy of Holies are measured; the spiral staircase is also discussed; and the sacrifices of the temple and sanctuary, together with the doorkeepers of the sanctuary.

[Col. 0969A]

“And he brought me into the temple, and measured the doorposts: six cubits in width on this side and six cubits in width on that side, the width of the tabernacle. The width of the doorway was ten cubits, and the sides of the doorway were five cubits on this side and five cubits on that side. And he measured its length, forty cubits, and its width, twenty cubits.”

(Hieronymus.) After many mysteries, various entrances, and the particular properties of the individual places, at last the man who had the builders’ cord and the measuring reed in his hand brings the prophet Ezekiel into the temple [Col. 0969B] and measures the doorposts of the temple. In place of this word, the Septuagint translated *aelam*, Theodotion *aelim*, and Symmachus “all around.”

On either side the width of the tabernacle was six cubits, containing the mystery of all creatures, since the world was completed in six days. Through knowledge of these things, and through the causes and order of creation, we enter the temple of God; from the order and stability of created things we recognize the Creator.

The width of the temple doorway was ten cubits, the sacred and perfect number, in which, on the tenth day of the seventh month, there is a fast and propitiation. On the tenth day of the first month, which is called Nisan, the lamb is taken for the sacrifice and preparation of Passover. Therefore, in the seventh month, tithes are offered into the storehouses of God—or, as Scripture commonly calls them, the winepresses.

Hence the Apostle says: “Be enlarged yourselves” (2 Cor. 6). After someone has entered the temple through the ten-cubit doorway, the sides of that doorway on either side—or, as it is more properly said in Hebrew, its “shoulders”—are to be measured, for shoulders always refer to works.

Thus Issachar “desired what was good, resting between the boundaries; and seeing that rest was good, and that the land was fertile, he placed his shoulder under labor and became a husbandman” (Gen. 49). In the high priest’s vestment, the shoulder-piece is also fastened together with the breastpiece, so that works may be joined to reason, and the ecclesiastical man may say: “From your commandments I have gained understanding” (Ps. 118).

The shoulders of the doorway had five porticoes on either side, so that through earthly and divine senses—concerning whose distinction we have often written—we might enter the inner parts of the temple. The man who was the prophet’s guide measured it at forty cubits in length and twenty cubits in width—or, more properly, the length and width of the doorway, since above he had spoken only of its width and shoulders.

There is no doubt that twenty times forty makes eight hundred, a number close to eight. Hence Ecclesiastes commands: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight” (Eccles. 11). I know that I have often discussed the mystery of this number.

Or, because we enter the Lord’s holy court through the tribulations and narrow passages of this age, the doorway had a length of forty cubits, for this number is always associated with labor. Thus Moses (Exod. 34) and Elijah (1 Kings 19) neither ate bread nor drank water for forty days. For forty years the people of Israel were afflicted and tested in the wilderness, and through many labors entered the promised land (Num. 14; Deut. 2). The Lord and Savior too, according to the weakness of the body he assumed, was tempted in the wilderness for forty days (Matt. 4), so that after his victory the angels might come and minister to him.

When, through tribulations and narrow passages, we are able to say the apostolic words, “In everything afflicted, but not hemmed in” (2 Cor. 4), and the prophetic words, “In tribulation you enlarged me” (Ps. 4), then an extremely broad entrance is opened for us, having a width of twenty cubits. Having overcome the struggles and earthly things of the world—for twenty is itself a dual number—we enter the inner sanctuary of the temple and hear the Lord commanding his disciples: “Take courage; I have conquered the world.”

“And entering farther within, he measured at the front of the doorway two cubits, and the doorway ten cubits, and the width of the doorway seven cubits. And he measured its length, twenty cubits, and its width, twenty cubits before the face of the temple. And he said to me: ‘This is the Holy of Holies.’”

(Hieronymus.) However far we advance, a greater progress is always opened to us. Thus, after entering the temple, we enter again farther within, or, as the Septuagint translated, “the inner court.” At its front there were two cubits, so that, according to the sense given above, through the dual number we might enter the place where the Holy of Holies is.

The doorway itself was six cubits, through which, once we have entered, we possess eternal rest, signified by the number seven. For this the Septuagint translated: “And the width of the doorway was seven cubits on this side and seven cubits on that side.” In the Hebrew and in the other editions, however, only seven cubits are given once for the width of the doorway.

What follows—“And he measured its length, twenty cubits, and its width, twenty cubits before the face of the temple, and he said to me: ‘This is the Holy of Holies’”—signifies that before the face of the temple and at its entrance, the measure of our past labor and struggle always confronts us.

Whatever meaning a dual number possesses in individual numbers is possessed by two decades. We should also consider that, after entering farther within through a doorway having two cubits at its front, six cubits, seven cubits in width on either side, twenty cubits in length, and the same number at the very doors of the temple, the prophet is taught what that place is and by what name it is called.

For he said to me: “This is the Holy of Holies.” But if the Holy of Holies is before the temple—or, as Scripture calls it, before the face of the temple—how great a blessedness ought we to estimate in the entrances and inner parts of the temple? Concerning this the prophet says: “This labor was before me until I enter the sanctuary of God and understand their final destiny” (Ps. 72).

It should also be noted that in the description of the tabernacle the phrase “holy of holies” is expressed in the plural; here, however, it is “the Holy of Holies” in the singular, so that after the Holy of Holies we may come to the Holy Place, just as after many songs we come to the Song of Songs, which is the song of all songs and through which, as we sing, we are joined to the bridegroom’s embraces.

“And he measured the wall of the house, six cubits, and the width of the side-chamber, four cubits all around the house. The side-chambers, side by side, were twice thirty-three. And there were projections that entered through the wall of the house into the side-chambers all around, to support them without touching the wall of the temple. And there was a circular pavement ascending upward by a spiral staircase, and it led by a circuit to the upper chamber of the temple. Therefore the temple was wider in its upper parts, and so one ascended from the lower parts to the upper ones toward the middle.”

But where the Septuagint has, “and from the middle to the third story,” that is, “to the three upper chambers”—and *thrael*—this is not found in the Hebrew.

«And I saw in the house a height all around, with side chambers founded to the measure of a reed, six cubits of space, and the width along the outer wall of the side chamber five cubits. And the interior of the house was in the side chambers of the house. And between the storerooms was a width of twenty cubits all around the house on every side. And there was a side-chamber door toward the place of prayer (which is not found in the Septuagint), one door toward the northern way and one door toward the southern way; and the width of the place of prayer was five cubits all around. And the building that was separated and faced toward the way looking toward the sea was seventy cubits wide; but the wall of the building was five cubits wide all around, and its length was ninety cubits.»

After he had reached the Holy of Holies, of which we spoke above, that venerable man measured the wall of the Holy of Holies. It had six cubits because of the structure of the world and of every visible creature, which was created in six days; and the width of one side was four cubits, not on one side only, but all around. The width of four cubits extended around the house, to indicate the four elements from which all things are composed, and especially human bodies. Against these the saints fight, submitting themselves to the power of the soul; thus they deserve to enter the interior places and to know the Lord’s mysteries.

The side chambers themselves, which were around the house and were separated from the wall of the temple by a space of four cubits, were joined to one another, so that one side chamber touched another and had in length not thirty-three cubits but twice thirty-three—that is, sixty-six. The Old Testament speaks in Leviticus (Lev. XII) of the birth of a male child: after one week, the woman who gave birth and the one who was born are to complete thirty-three days before coming for purification. But if she has given birth to a female, the number is to be doubled, that is, sixty-six.

And because, in order to come to the Holy of Holies, we need not only a first birth but also a second, so that, born in the flesh, we may be reborn in the spirit, therefore the number given is not sixty-six but twice thirty-three: so that both births may be owed to God their author and to his mercy, and so that the side chambers supporting the structure of the temple may surround the house with a double wall.

What follows according to the Hebrew—“And there were certain projections that came out through the wall of the house, along the side chambers all around, to support them and not touch the wall of the temple”—signifies that holy men, in the multitude of believers, break out through the wall of the temple, that is, through all the side chambers around it; they support the foundations of the Church, yet do not touch the wall of the temple, content merely to have seen it from afar and to have worshiped its unspeakable mysteries. For now we see through a mirror in an enigma, and we cannot touch or comprehend the truth in its fullness.

But as for the fact that the passageway rose upward in a circle by a spiral and led around to the upper chamber of the temple, and that therefore the temple was broader in its upper parts, so that one ascended from the lower parts to the upper and to the middle, I think it is clear to the reader that the things below are always narrower—in fasts, in sleeping on the ground (*χαμευνίαις*, literally “ground-sleepings”), and in restraint of food—and that, as we gradually climb toward the heights, a broader way is opened before us and what is written is fulfilled: “In tribulation you have enlarged me” (Ps. IV).

By a circle and a spiral we ascend to the upper chamber of the temple. Among all figures, this form is also judged by the philosophers of this age to be the more beautiful, since the heavens, the sun, the moon, and the other stars, as well as the point of the earth; and even in human bodies the eyes, like other stars, the shape of the head, which is the receptacle of all the senses, the rounded fingers, the thighs, and the arms all display this circular form.

The upper chamber of the temple, to which we climb from narrower places to higher ones, I think is what Elijah and Elisha had in the Book of Kings (III Kings VI; IV Kings IV), and what Tabitha possessed in the Acts of the Apostles—that is, Δορκάς, “Gazelle”—our little doe, who had climbed to the heights through good works (Acts IX; Acts X). The apostle Peter, upon whom the Lord solidified the foundations of the Church, went beyond the upper chamber and came to the roof, which is more significantly called in Greek δῶμα, that is, the roof-terrace; and there he learned the mysteries of the Church, previously unknown to the world.

The Savior of the human race also celebrates Passover in an upper chamber, a great and spacious upper chamber, cleansed of every defilement, furnished and prepared for a spiritual banquet. There he handed on to his disciples the mystery of his body and blood and left us the everlasting festival of the spotless Lamb. (Bede.)

What is written about the structure of the temple in the Book of Kings—“The door of the middle side chamber was on the part of the right side of the house, and by a spiral they ascended to the middle upper chamber, and from the middle to the third”—can suitably be applied to this passage according to its mystical meaning. For this passage can properly be referred to the Lord’s body.

The door of the middle side chamber was on the part of the right side of the house because, when the Lord had died on the cross, one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance. And appropriately it was on the part of the right side of the house, because the holy Church believes that his right side was opened by the soldier. Here too the evangelist used a fitting word: he did not say “he struck the side” or “he wounded it,” but “he opened it,” as though it were the door of the middle side chamber through which a way to heavenly things was opened for us.

Finally, he added: “And immediately blood and water came out” (John XIX)—water, by which we are washed in baptism, and blood, by which we are consecrated in the holy chalice. Through this door we ascend to the middle upper chamber, and from the middle to the third, because through faith and the mysteries of our Redeemer we ascend from our present life in the Church to the rest of souls after death. Then, when the day of judgment comes, we shall pass again from the rest of souls to the immortality of our bodies, as though into a third upper chamber, through a more exalted progress; and from there we shall live in the great blessedness of both, body and soul.

This journey took place invisibly, so that only those who had entered knew it, although those standing outside could also see the door itself. For the deeds of the faithful in this world and the celebrations of the sacraments can also be observed by the reprobate; but the inner mysteries of faith and the grace of love are recognized by no one except the one who, with the Lord as guide, ascends through them to heavenly things: “For whoever says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John II).

“And I saw,” he says, “in the house a height all around, with side chambers founded to the measure of a reed, six cubits of space, and the width along the outer wall of the side chamber five cubits. And between the storerooms”—which Symmachus calls *exedras*—“was a width of twenty cubits all around the house.” (Jerome.)

By these numbers it is shown that, after rising above this world and earthly perceptions, and beyond the dual number of two tens, which is represented by twenty, we may deserve to ascend not only into the Holy of Holies but also into its upper chambers. We must always remember that through the six days of our creation, through the five senses, and through the twenty cubits of width, we have ascended to the upper chamber of the temple; leaving behind earthly lowliness and the sense of the letter, we have passed to the summit of the Church and rejoiced in fellowship with the Holy Spirit.

“And there was,” he says, “a side-chamber door toward the place of prayer, opposite the northern way.” From the north evils blaze out over the whole earth, and the Lord promises that he will drive it away from us, saying: “And I will drive away from you the one who is from the north.” It is beautifully arranged that the place of prayer should be at the door opposite the north, so that, according to the Apostle, we may pray without ceasing (1 Thess. V) and say with Jeremiah: “Let not the pupil of my eye be silent” (Lam. II), whether we desire to avoid present evils or give thanks for those of the past.

For as long as we are in the tabernacle of this body, we groan and say:

“Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. VII.)

There was also a door toward the southern way, likewise having, according to the Hebrew, a place of prayer and extending five cubits all around. Through the cold of the north we pass to the warmth of the south, yet again we seek a place of prayer at the northern door, so that we may escape dangers, and at the southern one, so that we may give thanks for the past and possess the victory in security.

The five cubits here too indicate the divine senses, through which we climb from earthly things to higher realities.

“And the building,” he says, “that was separated and faced toward the way looking toward the sea was seventy cubits wide.” Thus, after labors, dangers, and the waves and shipwrecks of this age, and after the seventy years about which Jeremiah, Daniel, and Zechariah write (Jer. XXV; Dan. IX; Zech. VII), we may attain the true and legitimate sabbath of seven decades, so that eternal rest may be ours. And through the width of five cubits we may come to a length of ninety cubits, the age at which Sarah bore the son promised to her. She, being ninety years old—that is, possessing nine decades—gave birth to Isaac, while Abraham, having reached one hundred years, that is, ten decades, was joined with her in the mystery (Gen. XXI). What this number signifies, the following Scripture will show.

“And he measured the length of the house, one hundred cubits, and that of the separated building and its walls, one hundred cubits in length. The width in front of the house and of the building that was separated, toward the east, was one hundred cubits. And he measured the length of the building opposite the front of the separated building, toward the rear, the *hecthecas*—that is, the projections—on both sides, one hundred cubits; and the inner temple and the vestibules of the court, the thresholds, and the slanting windows, *hecthecas* all around, opposite each threshold on three sides, and covered with wood all around. The ground extended up to the windows, and the windows were closed above the doors, and up to the inner house and outside along every wall, within and without, according to its measure; and cherubim and palm trees were carved. There was a palm tree between cherub and cherub. Each cherub had two faces: the face of a man beside the palm tree on one side and the face of a lion beside the palm tree on the other side, represented throughout the whole house all around. From the ground to the upper part of the gate, cherubim and palm trees were carved on the wall of the temple. The threshold was square. And the appearance of the sanctuary was opposite the appearance of the wooden altar; its height was three cubits, its length two cubits, and its corners, length, and walls were wooden.” (Jerome.)

The Holy of Holies and the inner temple are described here as having, after the ninety cubits, one hundred cubits on three sides. This is the perfect number of ten decades, so that we may serve the Lord in mind, speech, and deeds, remembering the apostolic example in which he says “that we may be able to know what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height.”

What the Hebrew calls the separated building and its walls, the Septuagint interprets as “the separating structures,” which do not adhere to the walls of the temple but have their own neighboring walls. The temple itself, its corners, and its *aelam*, that is, its πρόπυλον or vestibule, were also covered externally with wood, signifying, of course, the wisdom that Scripture records the tree of life as having been placed in paradise.

According to the Septuagint, the windows too were made in the form of a net, like latticework, so that they were closed not with transparent stone or glass but with finely incised and patterned wood. In the Hebrew, however, they are called slanting windows, and they existed on only three sides of the temple: on the right and left sides and at the rear—that is, toward the south, north, and west. The eastern side had no windows, because the entrance itself admitted bright light inside, and the entire interior of the temple was filled with the light of the doors, so that through each window and opening of the lattice one could look inside.

(Bede.) The interlacing of the net signifies the unity of faith, which exists in the bond of peace. But when he says that the windows were slanting, he indicates the abundance of the inner light. The windows of the temple are the holy and spiritual teachers in the Church, to whom, as their minds are carried beyond themselves toward God, it is granted to see more distinctly than others the heavenly secrets of mysteries.

Some publicly disclose to the faithful what they see in secret, just as windows, having received the sun’s light, fill all the inner chambers of the temple. Hence the same windows are rightly said to have been slanting—that is, broader on the inside—because whoever has received even for a moment the radiance of heavenly contemplation must immediately enlarge the bosom of his heart through greater self-discipline and prepare himself by diligent practice to undertake greater things.

Likewise, when the Prophet says that the ground extended up to the windows and that the windows were closed, this signifies the scarcity of spiritual teaching among teachers. For the Apostle Paul says: “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Cor. XIII).

(Gregory.) In this temple the windows are priests and watchmen who pour the light of holy preaching into the people of the faithful. But when the ground extends up to the windows, the windows are closed, because when earthly thought grows in the hearts of priests, the windows do not pour forth light: the priests become silent in the office of preaching.

(Jerome.) Not only were the exterior surfaces covered with wood, but there was such an abundance of wood all around that both the pavement and everything from the pavement up to the windows were joined with wood. According to the Septuagint, these windows opened in three ways, so that, when opened, a threefold understanding might be shown in the temple of God, according to what is said elsewhere: “But you, describe them in three ways” (Prov. XXII).

Through these windows one looks not only inward but also outward, so that we may know what is invisible in the interior and what is visible in the exterior; that one thing may show the mind and another the flesh, one thing spiritual understanding and another a simple historical account.

Throughout all the walls around, both within and without, there were their proper measurements. For nothing was made by God in the temple, and especially in the Holy of Holies, without reason and measure.

Cherubim too were carved, unquestionably in the wood extending from the pavement up to the windows. The carvings were so skillfully fashioned that they seemed not carved but attached. “Cherubim” is interpreted as “a multitude of knowledge.” Thus, within the interior places of the temple, after the multitude of knowledge, palm trees are carved for it, in which there is a sign of victory, as the Apostle says: “But I pursue toward the appointed prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus” (Phil. III). These palm trees were between cherub and cherub, so that one cherub was enclosed on both sides by two palm trees.

(Bede.) Hence it is also written in the Book of Kings: “And he made in them cherubim and palm trees and various figures, as though projecting from the wall and coming out.” Solomon makes cherubim on the walls of the temple when the Lord grants his elect to direct their life according to the rule of the holy Scriptures, in which there is a multitude of knowledge.

He makes cherubim when he teaches them in this world to imitate, according to their measure, the chastity of an angelic way of life. This is accomplished especially through vigils and divine praises, through sincere love of the Creator and of one’s neighbor.

He makes palm trees when he fixes the memory of eternal reward in their minds, so that they are less able to fall from the citadel of righteousness because they always have the reward of righteousness before the eyes of their hearts.

He makes various figures, as though projecting from the wall and coming out, when he bestows on the faithful the manifold works of the virtues—for example, compassion, kindness, humility, patience, bearing with one another, and forgiving one another; and above all, having charity, which is the bond of perfection.

When these virtues have become so habitual in the elect that they seem naturally implanted in them, what else are they but the projecting figures of the Lord’s house, as though coming out from the wall? For they no longer learn from others externally the words and works of truth; rather, as though rooted and ready within themselves, they always bring forth from the depths of the heart what ought to be done or said.

(Jerome.) The cherub did not have four faces, as we read at the beginning of this prophet—namely, those of a man, a lion, a calf, and an eagle—but only two, that is, those of a man and a lion. The first of these pertains to reason, the second to fury. By “fury” we do not mean what is close to disturbance and vice, but what strengthens the softness of the mind and makes the spirit of the combatant more courageous.

At the beginning we are subject also to desire, which is represented by the calf because of the works of the earth; some things are carnal and others spiritual, the latter being assigned to the eagle. But when we have entered the Holy of Holies and possessed the interior places of the temple, we need nothing except reason and strength: the one refers to understanding and prudence, the other to perseverance of spirit.

Thus every wall around the temple, from the pavement to the ceiling, had cherubim and palm trees carved with marvelous art. After these, the sanctuary and the temple were opened with four corners opposite the front of the holy places. First we have the multitude of knowledge, through which we gain victory over the enemy; afterward the sanctuary and temple are opened to us. The temple has four corners, a most firm standing, and no slope toward any side. For such is the nature of a quadrangular measure: it stands upon a stable base.

And, in the mystical number that is clear to the prudent reader, it possesses the four elements from which all solid and enduring things consist. Everything looked toward the front of the sanctuary. Before that sanctuary—or within that sanctuary—was the form of a wooden altar, three cubits high, two cubits long, and two cubits wide; these joined together make seven cubits.

That altar had horns, and both its bases and its walls—that is, its sides—were wooden. Human speech can explain the mysteries of the holy Scriptures in this way: how is it that the altar on which fire was to be kindled, namely, the table of incense, suffers nothing from the fire but, so to speak, becomes purer through fire? Just as the works of the saints, of which the Apostle writes, “The fire will test what sort of work each one has done,” do not perish but are shown to be purer through fire, so the wood of the altar, which comes from the wood of paradise, is not burned by the nearby fire but is made purer.

Nor is it surprising to believe this of the sanctuary, the inner parts of the temple, and the altar of incense, since even *ἀμίαντος*—a kind of wood, or a material resembling flax—becomes cleaner the more it is burned.

(Maurus.) Nevertheless, the height of the altar, which is three cubits, may mystically signify the hearts of the elect, who strive toward heavenly things through faith, hope, and charity. Its length, which was two cubits, may signify their long-suffering and patience: they await the future kingdom and exercise themselves in good works through the two commandments of charity until they reach everlasting joys.

Appropriately, in the construction of God’s tabernacle, both altars—the altar of burnt offering and the altar of incense—are commanded to be made from acacia wood, which is said to resemble white thorn and to be incorruptible. This is because there is one firmness of sincere faith. The hearts of all the elect must be fortified and prepared to receive the fire of love and to offer libations of virtues to God, because the Apostle speaks generally to the lowly together with the great: “Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God” (1 Cor. VII).

Appropriately, the fire was one and not different: in one altar it burned the victims, and in the other the incense. For there is one Spirit who gives life to the minds of all the faithful through the varied grace of his gifts.

(Jerome.) Forgive me, reader, for the difficulty, and grant pardon to my poor understanding. Through the slanting windows, made in the form of a net and always closed, we can scarcely introduce the eye into the inner house of our heart, so that we see everything we perceive in shadow and image, and with the Apostle cry out: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and inscrutable his ways!” (Rom. XI.) And: “Who has known the mind of the Lord?” (ibid.)—except the one who is the angel of the great counsel and can open his mysteries to the worthy.

The Romans call *ἐκθέται* the terraces projecting from the walls of upper chambers, or balconies; some Greeks call them *ἐξώστρας*, “projecting balconies.”

«And he said to me: This is the table before the Lord. And there were two doors in the temple and in the sanctuary, and in the two doors, on each side, there were two little doors folding inward upon one another; for there were two doors on each side of the doors. And cherubim were carved on those doors of the temple, and figures of palm trees, just as they were also represented on the walls. Therefore the wood was thicker on the exterior front of the vestibule, above which were slanting windows, and the likeness of palm trees on either side, on the shoulders of the vestibule, along the sides of the house and the width of the walls.»

The man, then, who had led the prophet into the hidden places of the temple and, among other things, had shown him the wooden altar, which according to the Septuagint had corners, horns, and wooden walls, said to him: “This altar that you see is itself the table before the Lord,” which burns in the likeness of the bush yet is not consumed. Of this the holy man speaks to God: “You have prepared a table before me, against those who afflict me” (Ps. XXII).

There were also two doors in the temple and in the sanctuary itself, through which the mysteries of both instruments are revealed. And in the two doors, on each side, there were two little doors folding inward upon one another, so that in the historical account you may possess spiritual understanding, and in the tropological interpretation the truth of the history; each of these requires the other, and if one is lacking, knowledge is incomplete.

What follows—“There were two doors on each side of the doors”—is clear according to the literal sense. In larger dining rooms, two doors are commonly attached and joined to one another, so that the greater entrance is not closed or opened by two huge doors but by four smaller ones.

(Bede.) These doors can be understood figuratively in many ways. Most suitably, they signify the angelic spirits through whose ministry we are brought into the dwelling of our heavenly homeland. They also represent the apostles and apostolic men, to whom the keys of the kingdom of heaven have been given. Having received from the Lord the power to bind and loose (Matt. XVI), they admit the worthy within the gate of the kingdom and, by excommunicating or anathematizing the stubborn, impure, and proud, drive them from entrance into eternal life.

The works of righteousness, by whose merit one reaches the heavenly kingdom, can also rightly be signified typologically by the doors through which one entered the Holy of Holies, according to what is written in the Book of Wisdom: “The keeping of the laws is the consummation of incorruption; and incorruption makes one near to God” (Wis. VI). Thus the desire for wisdom leads to the everlasting kingdom.

All these interpretations fit appropriately. There are two little doors either because angels and holy men love God and their neighbors, and no one can enter the gate of life except through this twofold love; or because the same gate of life is opened to the faithful of both peoples, namely Jews and Gentiles.

The doorposts have five corners, because the court of heaven receives not only the souls of the elect but also opens its gates at the judgment to bodies endowed with immortal glory.

(Jerome.) On these doors of the temple, or of the Holy of Holies, cherubim were carved, about which we spoke above, and figures of palm trees, so that, after the multitude of knowledge, victory might be provided to those entering. The figure of palm trees was also on all the walls of the temple.

He gives the reasons why cherubim were carved on the doors themselves and why figures of palm trees were represented there. Hence the wood at the exterior of the vestibule gate was thicker, so that it might possess strength and be able to receive the carving. Beautifully, according to the spiritual understanding, the doors are both stronger and carved, so that they may possess both firmness and beauty, lest anyone like Uzziah should burst into the Holy of Holies and claim the priesthood for himself.

(Bede.) Especially those entrusted with the care of the faithful and given the keys of the kingdom of heaven must devote themselves with every diligence to ensuring that, to the degree that they excel others in rank, they also surpass them in the merit of good action.

They have the image of cherubim carved in them when, as far as is possible for mortals, they imitate an angelic life on earth both in mind and in deed. They have the forms of palm trees when, with steadfast attention, they meditate on the gifts of heavenly reward. For the palm is the ornament of a victorious hand.

(Jerome.) Above these doors were slanting or hidden windows, so that even the light supplied from within would not possess perfect knowledge, nor be bright and open to all, but would be hidden for the most part. For now we see in an enigma and do not yet know as we ought to know. But when what is perfect comes, then what was partial will be destroyed.

“And there was a likeness of palm trees on either side.” Elegantly, in the interior of the temple and in the Holy of Holies, he did not say “right” and “left,” lest anything left-handed should seem to be intended in matters that are great and mysterious. Instead he said “on either side,” in accordance with what is written in the Gospel: “If anyone strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also” (Matt.). Could he not have said “the left” as well? But when the right is struck, another right is offered, because in a holy man both sides are right, and both are perfect.

“And on the shoulders of the vestibule, along the sides of the house and the width of the walls.” For this the Septuagint translated “on the ceiling beams of the *aelam*,” that is, of the προπύλον, and “the sides of the house,” of equal weight or measure. Through this it is subtly shown that the doorposts of the lintel or vestibule—for this is what the “shoulders” seem to signify—and the sides of the house and the width of the walls are all full of reason and measure; nothing is found in the temple of the Lord that has been established without measure and wisdom.

## CHAPTER XLII

On the storerooms of the southern and northern building and the description of those buildings; on the places where the priests ate, who were not to go out to the people until they had removed the garments of their ministry; and so forth.

“Then he led me out into the outer court by the way leading north, and brought me into the treasury that was opposite the detached building and opposite the structure facing north, having on the side facing the length one hundred cubits, at the northern entrance, and a width of fifty cubits, opposite the twenty cubits of the inner court and opposite the stone-paved pavement of the outer court, where there was a portico joined to a threefold portico. And before the treasuries was a passageway ten cubits wide, looking toward the interior, with a way of one cubit. And their doors were toward the north, where the treasuries on the upper levels were lower, because they supported the porticoes that projected from them over the lower and middle parts of the building. For they were three-storied and had no columns, as the columns of the courts did; therefore they projected over the lower and middle courts, fifty cubits from the ground. And the outer wall was alongside the treasuries that were on the way of the outer court, in front of the treasuries. Its length was fifty cubits, because the length of the treasuries of the outer court was fifty cubits, while the length before the front of the temple was one hundred cubits. And beneath these treasuries was an entrance from the east for those entering them from the outer court, in the width of the wall of the court that was opposite the eastern way, in front of the detached building. And before the building were treasuries, and a way before them, like the treasuries that were on the northern way. Their length and their width were alike, and all their entrances, their likenesses, and their doors were like the doors of the treasuries that were on the way facing south. There was a door at the head of the way that was before the detached vestibule, for those entering by the eastern way.” (Jerome.)

I had intended, out of despair at the magnitude of the subject, to pass over the present testimony in silence; but I judged it better to say something than to say nothing at all. I adopt that Socratic saying: “I know that I do not know.” For it is part of knowledge to know what one does not know.

After the prophet had carefully contemplated the things that were within, the man whose hand held the measuring cord and the reed led him out to the outer court by the way leading north—the court that he had already seen above, before he penetrated into the interior. But we see things differently when we possess complete knowledge and when we are at the beginning of instruction. It is necessary that one who has seen the interior should, according to the same form and measurements and according to the hidden mysteries, also see what is exterior.

He was led into a treasury—or, as Symmachus and the Septuagint translated it, an *exedra*—and, according to Theodotion, a παστοφόριον, which is rendered “chamber.” This was opposite the detached building. As for the fact that the Septuagint added five *exedrae* in place of “treasury,” that is not found in the Hebrew. The treasury was opposite the detached building about which we spoke above, *gazera*; it was detached because it received those who came from the north.

It was opposite the structure facing north—that is, one looking toward the northern regions but not situated in the north—so that passage might be easier for those leaving behind the cold of the north, from which evils blaze forth upon the earth. We read in the Book of Numbers (Num. XXXII) that the tribes of Dan, Naphtali, and Asher, the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, the maidservants of Rachel and Leah, encamped in the northern regions.

Now, on the side facing the length of the northern entrance, there were one hundred cubits, and its width was fifty, so that by ten tens the quadrangular and perfect number might be displayed, and by seven weeks—the number of remission—which breaks forth into the beginning of unity, that is, into the ogdoad, the priestly spaces in the temple of God might be signified.

The clause that is joined according to the Hebrew, “opposite the twenty cubits of the inner court,” for which the Septuagint translated, “which had been marked out like the gates of the inner court,” has this meaning: the hundred and fiftyfold number of the outer court possesses the same force as the twentyfold number of the inner court. For if you count four times five in the number twenty, you will find both Testaments: the Law held within the Gospel, and the Gospel arising from the root of the Law. In place of this number, the Septuagint interpreted “the likeness of the inner court,” perhaps fearing to place the number twenty in the inner court, where Esau’s gifts are offered.

It follows: “And opposite the stone-paved pavement of the outer court, where there was a portico joined to a threefold portico.” In its place the Septuagint translated: “And like the columns of the outer court, set in order opposite the front of the threefold porticoes.”

This signifies that the pavement of the outer court was laid with living stone, so that neither the dust of summer nor the mud of winter might soil the footsteps of the priests. Hence also the Lord, about to ascend to the Father, washes the apostles’ feet (John XIII), so that, with their footsteps cleansed and purified, they may ascend the kingdoms of heaven. He also commands the apostles (Matt. X; Mark VI), whenever they enter a city and the inhabitants do not receive them, to shake the dust from their feet, so that they may not allow any earthly gifts to remain with them.

The pavement was not only laid with stone, but a portico was also joined to a threefold portico. One portico, protecting the priests from rain and heat and joined to a threefold portico, demonstrates the mystery of the Trinity: although it is divided by the names of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, it is nevertheless joined together in one divinity.

There was also before the treasuries—or *exedrae*, or chambers—a passageway ten cubits wide, looking toward the interior, with a way of one cubit. The addition made by the Septuagint, “one hundred cubits in length,” is superfluous, because it is not found in the Hebrew. By inserting it, they removed what is found in the Hebrew: “looking toward the interior, with a way of one cubit,” which we translated from the Hebrew truth.

This signifies that before all the doors of the treasuries, or *exedrae* and chambers, there was a passageway ten cubits wide. Ten is itself a perfect number, either because of the Decalogue or because of the mystery of the Gospel. For if one proceeds from one through two and three to the fourth number, the number ten of the Gospels is produced. In its breadth the priests walk, proceeding before each treasury, provided always that they look toward the interior of its way, which leads to one cubit—namely, to the worship of the one divinity. The Son says to the Father: “I have revealed your name to the human beings” (John XVII). This is the way looking toward the interior, of which he says in the Gospel: “I am the way, and the life, and the truth” (John XIV), because no one comes to knowledge of the Father except through the Son.

“And their doors were toward the north, where the treasuries on the upper levels were lower, because they supported the porticoes that projected from them over the lower and middle parts of the building. For they were three-storied and had no columns, as the columns of the courts did. Therefore they projected over the lower and middle parts, fifty cubits from the ground.”

The phrase “their doors” is understood to mean the doors of the *exedrae* or treasuries, about which the preceding discussion was concerned. These treasuries were lower on the upper levels—that is, in the upper chambers. Elijah and Elisha ascended such upper chambers (1 Kings VI; 2 Kings IV), as did the Lord with his disciples when he was about to celebrate the Passover (Mark XIV; Luke XXII), and Tabitha, who was raised because of the faith of the apostle and the merit of her virtues (Acts IX).

These are the upper chambers about which it is written in the Psalm: “He waters the mountains from his upper chambers” [or, “from his heights”] (Ps. CIII). Unless someone becomes a fountain and rises to higher things, he will not be watered by the Lord’s rains; and according to the diversity of merits, one is watered from the first, second, and third upper chamber.

The treasuries themselves, that is, the Lord’s storehouses of riches, are lower on the upper levels. For the higher someone is, the more he is humbled with the Apostle, saying: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Cor. XV).

The treasuries themselves were lower in the upper chambers because they supported the porticoes that projected from them over the lower and middle parts of the building. He gives the reasons why the treasuries placed in the upper chambers were lower: because, he says, they supported the porticoes that enjoyed the open air. They projected over the lower and middle parts of the building, so that the second chamber might be higher than the pavement of the lower house, and the third chamber higher than the second. The higher one ascended, therefore, the higher was the chamber one occupied; and the more one grew in humility, the higher one became, as the Lord says: “Whoever wishes to be greater among you must become the least of all” (Matt. XXIII).

For they were not supported by other columns, as we read of the columns of the courts; rather, they projected over the lower and middle parts, fifty cubits from the ground—the number of remission of all debts. These, then, are the three-storied structures concerning which it is commanded: “Describe them threefold, with counsel and knowledge, so that you may answer the words of truth concerning what is proposed to you” (Prov. XXII).

The lower and exterior structures therefore need columns. But those that are higher and interior have no need of columns—that is, of external assistance.

After this it is said: “And the outer wall was alongside the treasuries that were on the way of the outer court, in front of the treasuries. Its length was fifty cubits, because the length of the treasuries of the outer court was fifty cubits, while the length before the front of the temple was one hundred cubits.”

The outer wall (*peribolus*) signifies the wall that was external and enclosed the treasuries on the way of the outer court. It was fifty cubits long, concerning the mystery of which number we have often spoken. But the length before the front of the temple was not fifty cubits, as it was before the treasuries; it was one hundred cubits, so that after the remission of all sins we might await perfect rewards in the number one hundred.

In place of *peribolus*, or wall—which in Hebrew is called *gader*—the Septuagint interpreted “light,” which comes from outside and illuminates the eyes of our heart. The natural light within us is insufficient to possess the full radiance of knowledge in the realm of perception unless that light enters from outside through the grace of God, first illuminating the eyes of our heart. It also makes clear the entire outer court, which extends fifty cubits in width. But afterward, when we come before the front of the temple, we receive perfect rewards in the number one hundred.

There was beneath the treasuries an entrance from the east for those entering them from the outer court. We must possess the riches of God and find, from the outer court beneath the treasuries, an eastern entrance. Through the width of the outer wall, which faces the eastern way, we must come to the building that is set apart for the holy; before it are treasuries, and along that way is a likeness of the treasuries that were on the northern way.

Although we reach the eastern entrance, the likeness of greater things is present in lesser things. We cannot reach the light of the east except by the northern way—that is, we must proceed through lesser and lower things to greater and higher ones.

At this entrance the length was like the width, that is, the same measure in a square. All the entrances, likenesses, and doors had the same measure and likeness as the treasuries that were on the way facing south. For through the east, extinguishing the cold of the north, we reach the south, in which the bridegroom reclines at midday and dwells in full light.

At the head of that same way—the eastern way, which is open to those entering—there is a door. Unless it is opened by the one who says, “I am the door,” and who possesses the key of David, leading to the vestibule of the saints set apart by virtues, and receiving those who come from the north, we cannot enter.

“And he said to me: The treasuries of the north and the treasuries of the south, which are before the detached building, are holy treasuries. In them the priests who draw near to the Lord in the Holy of Holies eat. There they shall place the holy things, the offering for sin, and the offering for guilt. For the place is holy. When the priests enter, they shall not go out from the holy places into the outer court; there they shall lay aside their garments in which they minister, because they are holy, and they shall put on other garments; thus they shall go out to the people.” (Jerome.)

The man who guided the prophet, after leading him into the outer court and showing him everything narrated in the preceding passage, including the treasuries—or *exedrae*—in which he had remained for a considerable time, said to him: These are the treasuries, or *exedrae* and chambers, toward the north and south, which are before the detached building. They are called holy treasuries, in which the priests eat who draw near to the Lord in the Holy of Holies.

From this we learn that there are many kinds of food which priests may or may not eat; and even among those foods which may be eaten, they are not all consumed in every place, by everyone, or at every time.

I think that the treasuries of the north and south signify either the simplicity contained in the historical sense or the mysteries of spiritual understanding, so that through the north we may come to the south. The letter and the foundations of history must not be read in such a way that we never reach the heights; nor should the roof be placed upon a most beautiful building in such a way that its foundations are not solid.

The priests who eat in the storerooms in which many riches are contained are those who draw near to the Lord. Scripture testifies of them (Exod. XXIV) that Moses drew near to the Lord, while the others could not approach.

In the construction of the mystical temple and in the mystery of the Church there are many priests and apostolic men who draw near to the Lord—not in just any place, but in the Holy of Holies.

The words “the sons of Zadok,” which the Septuagint includes, are not found in the Hebrew. “There,” he says, “the priests shall place the holy things and the offering”—that is, the victim of the burnt offering—and the offering for sin and for ignorance. Thus they will know how to offer not only the continual sacrifice, but also, according to the variety of times and the character of sin and ignorance, how to appease the Lord, because the place is holy and priestly dignity dwells there, able to plead for the others.

When it is necessary to go out to those who cannot penetrate the entrances of the temple or know the secrets of divine knowledge, the priests, he says, should go outside to them, into the outer court. They should by no means go out wearing the garments in which they had been clothed within—namely, the mercies of compassion and the Lord Savior, concerning which it is written: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. XIII). Nor should they use those words of which God says: “My mystery is for me and for my own,” lest they fall under what the Savior forbids when he says: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not cast your pearls before swine” (Matt. VII).

Rather, they shall lay aside within the garments in which they are clothed when they minister in the inner rooms of the temple. For these garments are holy, and they ought not to be brought before those who do not possess perfect holiness. They shall put on other garments and thus go out to the people.

This is how, he says, they should speak to the people: in a way that the people can hear. Hence the Apostle also spoke to the Corinthians, among whom “fornication was heard of, and such fornication as does not occur even among the Gentiles” (1 Cor. V): “I gave you milk to drink, not food—that is, solid food—for you were not yet able to receive it” (1 Cor. III). Again he says to them: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. IV).

For solid food not only does not benefit little ones and nursing infants; it kills them, although it is suitable for people of mature age.

This may also be understood in another way. (Gregory.)

Priests, even after contrition and tears, are compelled to learn about the necessities of their children and patiently to hear what they shrink from hearing in their minds. After sighing over heavenly things, they must bear the burdens of whatever carnal people bring, and often transform their heart according to the differing condition of those who arrive.

Sometimes a priest rejoices in spiritual gains. But when someone grieving comes to him, unless he takes that grief upon himself and sympathizes with the person’s tribulation, he does not truly share the person’s sorrow. At another time he mourns the losses of souls, and suddenly people arrive who rejoice in certain successes of their own. If the priest does not rejoice with their joy, he is thought to love his children less because he does not exult in their happiness, especially since Paul says: “Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep” (Rom. XII).

I see nothing so burdensome to the priestly order as bending the rigor of the mind through compassion and changing one’s spirit according to the persons who arrive; yet this is exceedingly necessary. For how is a sinner brought by the priest’s preaching to the grace of good works if the preacher himself appears ungrateful?

Hence it is later said through this same prophet that when the priests minister within, they are to wear linen garments. Concerning these garments it follows: “When they go out to the outer court, to the people, they shall remove the garments in which they ministered and shall place them in the treasury of the sanctuary.”

Woolen garments are, of course, coarser. But when a priest approaches the holy ministry, when he enters inwardly through contrition, he must, in a subtle understanding, be clothed as though in a linen garment. But when he goes out to the people, he ought to put away the garments in which he ministered within and appear before the people clothed in other garments.
