For if he remains fixed in the rigor of his contrition, if he persists in the grief he possessed at the time of prayer, he will not admit the words of exterior matters. And what will the flock do about necessities if the shepherd refuses to hear and consider what the present time requires? Therefore, when going out before the people, the priest should put on coarser garments, so that, for the benefit of his children, he may adapt the disposition of his mind even to bearing earthly things.

“And when he had completed the measurements of the inner house, he led me out by the way of the gate that faced the eastern way, and measured it all around. He measured against the eastern wind with the measuring reed, all around, five hundred reeds by the measuring reed. He measured against the northern wind five hundred reeds by the measuring reed, all around. And toward the southern wind he measured five hundred reeds by the measuring reed, all around. And toward the western wind he measured five hundred reeds by the measuring reed. By the four winds he measured its wall all around: its length was five hundred cubits and its width five hundred cubits, separating between the sanctuary and the place of the common people.” (Jerome.)

It should be known that after the eastern and northern winds, the order of the southern and western winds is reversed in the Septuagint. For they first placed the western wind—that is, the sea—and afterward the southern, whereas in the Hebrew the southern wind is placed first and the western afterward.

When Scripture now says, “And when he had completed the measurements of the inner house, he led me out by the way of the gate that faced the eastern way,” it shows that everything mentioned above, both outside and inside, and in the inner parts of the temple—that is, the Holy of Holies—properly belongs to the construction of the temple and to the inner temple.

Hence it now follows: “He led me out by the way of the gate that faced the eastern way, and measured it all around,” or, “the likeness of the house.” This demonstrates that what is seen is not the house itself but the likeness of the house, because “now we see through a mirror in an enigma; but when what is perfect has come, then what is partial will be destroyed” (1 Cor. XIII).

Thus Moses in the tabernacle and Solomon in the building made not the reality of the tent and temple, but their likeness and figure, so that through those things that are lesser and earthly we might understand the things that are heavenly and belong to the spiritual building.

The man who had led out the prophet did not first measure in the outer court, but by the way of the gate that faced the eastern way. First he measured toward the eastern wind, that is, toward the eastern region, five hundred reeds around; second, toward the north; third, toward the south; fourth, toward the sea, that is, toward the west.

By the four winds he measured the wall around, both in length and in width—that is, as a square. The wall contained two thousand reeds altogether. But if a reed was six cubits and a palm (*palaestē*)—and the *palaestē* is one-sixth of a cubit—it is clear that the outer wall had a circumference of two thousand reeds, which make twelve thousand three hundred thirty-three and one-third cubits.

Let the prudent and diligent reader read the Book of Joshua, and he will find how this measure is preserved in the surrounding lands. Hence the legion of demons also chose this number when drowning the swine (Luke VIII), so that what had been separated by the Lord’s command from those who serve God might be turned in the opposite direction for the destruction of those who pursue a life worthy of mire and filth.

The entire outer wall, which possesses an extremely spacious length and width in a square, contains the number of the apostles, namely twelve thousand, so that one thousand might be assigned to each apostle. Yet it does not reach the measure of the fullness of Christ and of the perfect man unless the *palaestē* is added to it—three hundred thirty-three cubits and one-third of a cubit—through which the mystery of the holy and venerable Trinity is demonstrated. It surrounds and fortifies everything and makes the inhabitants of its temple completely secure.

Hence Noah’s ark has a length of three hundred cubits and a height of thirty cubits, which is completed in one cubit. The fifty cubits added there in its width, as we have often said, signify the mystery of remission. Hence also the Lord came to baptism at the age of thirty (Luke III).

This same prophet, at the beginning of his book, gives the thirtieth year; and this number, three hundred and thirty, is completed by adding three and one-third. But what, through the simplicity of the translation, we have in the Septuagint and in our translation—because we paid little attention amid the speed of dictation—“its wall all around, five hundred cubits in length and five hundred cubits in width,” the Hebrew does not contain. It simply has “five hundred in length and five hundred in width,” with “reeds” understood, just as it was said above regarding the eastern wind, the northern, the southern, and the sea: the wall of each side was measured by the one holding the reed at five hundred reeds.

The number five hundred, which is close to fifty, and which pertains to the remission of all sins, is demonstrated not only by the Old Scripture but also by the Savior’s words in the Gospel, when he says: “Two debtors owed money to a certain moneylender: one owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty” (Luke VII).

“And the wall separates between the sanctuary and the place of the common people.” From this we understand that the entire description of the temple above had been assigned to the ministries of the priests, who are the sons of Zadok; but this wall, extended over so great a space and surrounding everything, separates the sanctuary from the place of the common people.

## CHAPTER XLIII

The prophet saw the glory of God; he rebukes the Jews for their idols; he is commanded to show the form and description of the house; concerning the measure of the altar of burnt offerings, and its rite and sacrifices.

“Then he brought me to the gate that faced the eastern way. And behold, the glory of the God of Israel entered by the eastern way; and his voice was like the sound of many waters, and the earth shone from his majesty. And I saw a vision according to the appearance which I had seen when he came to destroy the city, and appearances according to the sight which I had seen beside the river Chebar. And I fell upon my face; and the majesty of the Lord entered the temple by way of the gate that faced east. And the spirit lifted me up and brought me into the outer court; and behold, the house was filled with the glory of the Lord. And I heard one speaking to me from the house. And the man standing beside me said to me: [Col. 0988A] Son of man, this is the place of my throne and the place for the soles of my feet, where I dwell among the children of Israel for ever. And the house of Israel, they and their kings, shall no longer defile my holy name by their fornications, by the ruins of their kings, and by their high places. They built their threshold beside my threshold and their doorposts beside my doorposts, with only a wall between me and them. They defiled my holy name by the abominations which they committed; therefore I consumed them in my wrath. Now then let them put away from me their fornication and the ruins of their kings, and I will dwell among them always.” (Jerome.)

Let us speak briefly of each point, as far as the difficulty permits explanation, lest, while we strive for brevity, the veil not only of Moses but also of the prophet Ezekiel should remain upon us, though we desire with unveiled face to contemplate the truth of the Lord.

Therefore the glory of the God of Israel enters by the eastern way, by which it had also departed when the city of the Lord was struck in wrath. It enters—indeed, returns—to it, because he had shown that the temple of the Lord was built on the mountain. Yet what follows is much greater: “The Spirit lifted me up and brought me into the outer court; and behold, the house was filled with the glory of the Lord.” Here only the glory of the God of Israel enters; there it is said that the fullness of the glory of the Lord was in the temple. Isaiah also writes of this: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne” (Isa. VI). And the house is full [Col. 0988C] of his glory when, contemplating the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, we are transformed into the image of the Creator (2 Cor. II).

The voice of God was also like the sound of many waters: that is, of all the peoples throughout the world, as John the Evangelist interprets it (Rev. I); or like the sound of armies and like the voice of many who sing in harmony, so that the army of God might know the mysteries. Understanding this, Jacob called the name of that place “Camps” (Gen. XXXII), concerning which it is also written elsewhere: “The chariots of God are ten thousandfold, thousands of those rejoicing” (Ps. LXVII). But one voice is called the voice of camps and of a multitude because of their single agreement in praise of God; and the voice of those singing to Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is threefold: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth; [Col. 0988D] the whole earth is full of his glory” (Isa. VI).

It follows: “And the earth shone from his majesty.” This was properly accomplished at the coming of Christ, when “the sound of the apostles went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII). It is fulfilled daily in believers, and will be fulfilled perfectly when this corruptible thing puts on incorruption and this mortal thing is clothed with immortality.

But the words that follow, “And I saw a vision according to the appearance which I had seen when he came to destroy the city,” are translated by the Septuagint: “when I entered to anoint the city.” Although the Hebrew is clear, the Septuagint contains great obscurity: how Ezekiel entered to anoint the city, though it fell at his prophecy and threat. Unless perhaps we say that the prophet’s rebuke is the city’s anointing, the anointing with the oil of priestly and royal exultation. Those who willingly receive and desire to hear it become the Lord’s anointed, concerning whom it is written: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act maliciously against my prophets” (Ps. CIV).

But he can, in an anagogical sense (*ἀναγωγή*, spiritual ascent), anoint the city concerning which it is written, “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. LXXXVI), who has seen the vision of the chariot and of God’s mysteries which Ezekiel beheld beside the river Chebar, a name signifying burden and weight. For what is heavier than the rivers of Babylon, beside which David sat and wept when he remembered Zion? Of these it is written: “For the form of this world passes away” (1 Cor. VII). I think that nothing in the confusion of this age is lasting, but that all things pass away and flow on. Whoever considers this will fall upon his face, understanding how far he is from the majesty of God, and will bend his knees to the Father in the name of Jesus Christ.

“And when I had fallen,” he says, “the majesty of the Lord entered the temple by way of the gate that faced east, and immediately the Spirit raised me up—for while lying down I could not go on—and brought me into the outer court.” For I had fallen outside. And behold, having first seen the glory of the God of Israel coming by the eastern way, I saw his house filled with the glory of the Lord, and heard from the inner house a voice speaking to me. [Col. 0989C] Scripture does not report what it said, unless perhaps it was that of the Apostle: “And I heard unspeakable words which it is not permitted for a human being to utter” (2 Cor. XII).

But that man, he says, who stood beside the prophet, said to him words which we plainly understand to be the Lord’s. To whom else could what follows apply: “Son of man, this is the place of my throne and the place for the soles of my feet, where I dwell among the children of Israel for ever,” except to him who dwells in the Church, among the children of Israel who see the Lord, and dwells for ever, not temporarily as in Solomon’s temple? His place is that concerning which it is written: “And his place was made in peace” (Ps. LXXV), a peace which surpasses all understanding. And the place for the soles of his feet is that of which the apostles say: “Let us worship in the place where his feet stood” (Ps. CXXXI). He beautifully said “stood,” for the Lord’s feet stand in the Church; in the Synagogue they walk and pass on.

To show that this is said of the Church, it is added: “And the house of Israel shall no longer defile my holy name.” This properly concerns those who live in the Church in holy conduct. He makes clearer who formerly defiled God’s holy name: “They and their kings”—both people and priests—“by their fornications,” by which they committed fornication against God, “and by the ruins of their kings,” who vainly assume for themselves through pride the royal name. Then follows: “and by their high places”; for an arrogant mind offends God, while a humble one calls forth mercy.

After pride—or rather through pride—they built their threshold beside God’s threshold and their doorposts beside his doorposts. Let those little women burdened with sins hear this according to the letter, those who are carried about by every wind of doctrine (Eph. IV), always learning and never arriving at knowledge of the truth: a mind joined to God, not the proximity of churches or dwelling near God, calls his mercy down upon itself; indeed, the Lord’s indignation is stirred when an unworthy inhabitant is in a place consecrated to God. “They built,” he says, “their threshold beside my threshold,” so that there was no difference between sacred and profane. “And their doorposts beside my doorposts,” so that laity and priests had one entrance. Therefore the Apostle says: “Let a person test himself, and so approach the body [Col. 0990B] and blood of the Lord” (1 Cor. XI).

To make his statement more grave, he adds the following verse: “And there was a wall between me and them,” so that a very short wall divided the priestly sacrifices and the places of the mysteries of Christ’s body and blood. “And they defiled,” he says, “my holy name by the abominations which they committed.” What benefit is proximity of dwelling, or a wall between our cell and the altar of the Lord, when the Lord’s name is contaminated and defiled by things which we do in secret and which it is shameful even to mention?

I think that no one defiles God’s name except one who has appeared to believe in his name and to be enrolled under his title; just as the person who first believed in Christ takes Christ’s members and makes them members of a prostitute, so the person who first received faith in God’s name defiles that name. Otherwise, although the Gentile and the Jew are defiled and polluted—indeed, are pollution and defilement itself—they cannot defile and pollute God’s name in the way that those persons do, to whom it is said: “Through you my name is blasphemed among the Gentiles” (Isa. LII).

“Therefore I consumed them in my wrath,” because they did the things we have mentioned. Yet the merciful Lord again commands the prophet to order them to remove their former fornications far from himself, and to abandon and put away the ruins of their kings and princes, not so much from themselves as from God. He immediately promises the reward of good work: “And I will dwell among them.” Of him the Gospel also says: “One stands in your midst whom you do not know” [Col. 0990D] (John I). And he will dwell not for a short time, as in the Synagogue, but for ever; this is proved in the Church of Christ.

“‘But you, son of man, show the house of Israel the temple, so that they may be ashamed of their iniquities and examine the structure, and blush for all that they have done. Show them the form of the house and its structure, its exits and entrances, its entire design, all its ordinances, its whole arrangement, and all its laws; and write them before their eyes, so that they may observe all its designs and ordinances and carry them out. This is the law of the house: on the summit of the mountain, all its boundaries round about; it shall be the holy of holies. This, then, is the law of the house.’”

(Hieron.) It is no small task to demonstrate to one’s hearers what one has seen with bodily eyes or perceived with the mind, so that they too may seem to have seen it with you. Hence Josephus writes that those who were sent by Jesus son of Nave to survey the land were γεωμέτραι—“geometers”—and possessed the art that now belongs properly to philosophers, namely geometry.

The house—that is, the temple—which Ezekiel saw situated on the mountain is shown to the house of Israel, those who contemplate God in spirit. It is shown not merely on the mountain, but, as the text now says, on the summit of the mountain. We must by no means suppose that this is the temple which is described as having been built by Solomon in the books of Kings and Chronicles (3 Kings 6; 1 Chronicles 3). That temple belongs to another order and has different measurements in each of its parts. It is so much inferior to the temple now shown to Ezekiel that not only its worshipers and custodians, but even its builder Solomon himself, sinned and offended God—although afterward he did penance, writing the Proverbs in which he says: “At the end I repented, and looked around to choose instruction.”

But the temple shown to Ezekiel, and through Ezekiel to the house of Israel, is such that whoever beholds it with the mind ceases from his iniquities—not from some of them, but from all. Or, as it is contained in the Hebrew: “Let him be ashamed and bear his punishment for all that he has done.” He bears the punishment of his iniquities who ceases to commit his former sins.

It greatly benefits the one who has sinned previously to see the house of God and to know the principles of its entire structure, so that he may cease from sinning and, possessing that desire, say to the Lord: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the dwelling-place of your glory” (Psalm 25). And again: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Psalm 26)—when I shall have begun to live and to be with Christ, who is the life of believers.

(Greg.) In the tropological sense, the temple of God is shown to the children of Israel for their confusion when the soul of each righteous person—whom God inhabits by breathing into him—is displayed to sinners in all the splendor of its holiness, for their shame. Thus they may see in that soul the good they neglect and blush within themselves at the evil they practice.

To measure the structure is to weigh carefully the life of the righteous. But while we measure the structure, it is necessary for us to blush for everything we have done. For the more carefully we examine the lives of the good, the more severely we condemn in ourselves all our wrongful deeds.

The prophet is rightly told to show the temple, because when the sinner refuses to consider the uprightness of the righteous, he should at least recognize it through the voice of the preacher. To show the temple to sinners is to recount the works of the upright to those who are unwilling to consider them of their own accord.

Those who desire, as we have said, to be led to the heights must always attend to the progress of those who are better, so that they may judge their own faults more strictly in proportion as they see more clearly in others what they ought to admire. But why speak of sinners in this regard, when we see even those who practice righteousness carried forward by such a dispensation?

One person receives the gift of knowledge, yet does not attain the virtue of remarkable abstinence. Another girds himself with the great virtue of abstinence, yet does not expand into the highest contemplation of conscience. Another is able through the spirit of prophecy to know all future things, yet through the grace of healing cannot relieve the evils of present affliction. Another relieves the evils of present affliction through the grace of healing, yet, because he does not possess the spirit of prophecy, does not know what will follow.

Another can already give much of his own possessions to the needy, yet cannot freely oppose those who act unjustly. Another boldly resists those who act unjustly for God’s sake, yet refuses to give the needy everything that he possesses. Another, restraining himself even from idle speech, has overcome the wantonness of the tongue, yet still does not perfectly trample down the goads of rising anger. Another has already completely subdued rising anger, yet still loosens his tongue in merriment.

What is this, that one person lacks the good in which another excels, while the one who excels and abounds in many things sees goodness present in others that he laments is lacking in himself? It is because, by a wondrous dispensation toward us, one is shown to be better than another through the fact that one possesses what the other does not. Thus each person advances all the more ardently in humility as he considers himself inferior to those who possess the goods he lacks.

And so, while one person looks at something admirable in another, and the other at something admirable in the first, their distinct virtues both restrain them from the height of pride and kindle them to pursue progress. We apply ourselves to improving ourselves with great concern when we see in others a virtue that we do not possess.

(Hieron.) It follows: “Its exits and entrances”—the house is understood. The exits are those of people who go out to those who are outside, and the entrances are those of people who penetrate into the interior through the discipline of teachers.

“And all its design,” he says—or “its substance,” as the Septuagint translated it. This refers not so much to the nature of the house as to its furnishings and riches. “And all its ordinances, its whole arrangement, and all the laws of the temple you shall show them”—to those who have borne the punishment of their iniquities and have ceased, or have been ashamed, of the things they previously did.

He shows these things to them so that they may observe everything that has been commanded. For it is of no benefit to know the design of the house and all its divisions, concerning which it is written, “There are many dwelling-places with my Father” (John 14), and again, “He established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the children of Israel” (Deuteronomy 32)—or according to the number of God’s angels—unless you do what has been commanded.

The house and the law of all God’s commandments, and the city established on the summit of the mountain, must be understood as that of which it is written: “A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden.” And again: “The river’s stream makes glad the city of God.” This clearly refers to the Church, which is situated on that mountain that is at the summit of all mountains, and from which the prince of Tyre was wounded.

All the boundaries and limits of this house are the holy of holies. In that house—that is, in the tabernacle constructed by Moses, and in the temple built by Solomon—only the innermost places, where the cherubim, the mercy-seat, the ark of the covenant, and the altar of incense were located, were called the holy of holies.

But in this house shown to Ezekiel, which has been established on the summit of the mountain, all its boundaries are reckoned as the holy of holies. The statement that follows, “This is the law of the house,” either refers to what has already been said, or to what will be said afterward.

“Now these are the measurements of the altar, in the truest cubit, which contained a cubit and a palm. In its hollow was a cubit, and a cubit in breadth, and a border extended to its lip, one palm all around. This too was the trench of the altar. From the hollow of the ground to the lowest ledge were two cubits, and its breadth was one cubit; and from the lower ledge to the greater ledge were four cubits, and its breadth was one cubit. Ariel itself was four cubits, and from Ariel upward to the horns were four. Ariel was twelve cubits long by twelve cubits wide, a square with equal sides. The ledge was fourteen cubits long by fourteen cubits wide, at its four corners; and there was a rim around it of half a cubit, and its hollow was one cubit all around. Its steps faced east.”

It is written: “Who can search out the abyss and wisdom?” (Ecclesiasticus 1). And: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Romans 11)—its depth is immeasurable, and who will discover it?

It would be a considerable undertaking if we wished to compare Solomon’s temple with this temple, and all its parts and chambers with those of the present temple. Since this is extremely difficult, for the moment let us compare, however briefly, the altar shown to Ezekiel with the altar that we read about in Exodus (Exodus 27).

There the altar is described as five cubits long and five cubits wide—that is, a square—and three cubits high. Here, however, departing from the five senses, it tends toward unity, in which the perfect or truest cubit is placed. To it is joined the palm, that is, the παλαιστή, which, as we said above, contains a sixth part of a cubit.

In its hollow—that is, in the hollow of the altar—there was a cubit, which received what was consumed by fire; and in its breadth there was another cubit, so that the interior parts—that is, the hidden spaces and areas of the altar indicated by its breadth—might be bounded by one cubit.

As for what follows, “And its rim extended to its edge,” Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion rendered the word as “boundary”; the Septuagint again translated it as *gisum*, a term whose meaning, as I said earlier, I cannot ascertain, nor can I confidently say to what language it belongs. I can only point out to the reader that where I have now translated it as “rim,” above I rendered it as “crown.”

It is briefly shown that around the altar itself—that is, at its margin and circumference—there was a projecting edge, like a crown in the form of a lily, presenting great beauty to the eye. This rim, or γισός, extended around it with a breadth of one palm, or παλαιστή.

The trench of the altar—or its depth and height, for which the Hebrew has *gab*—was two cubits from the hollow of the ground to the lowest ledge, or to the highest mercy-seat. Its breadth was one cubit.

The lower, deeper parts, joined to the earth, are contained in the dual number, which is also used of unclean animals. But the higher parts, reaching to the ledge or mercy-seat—which Theodotion called by the Hebrew name *azara*—have a breadth of one cubit, so that the dual number may pass into the singular, and the good of marriage that is below may advance toward the blessedness of unity.

[Col. 0994B]

(Greg.) The virtue of patience, which is better than arrogance, can therefore be understood in the trench of the altar. Hence it is written: “The patient person is better than the arrogant” (Ecclesiasticus 7). The patient person chooses to endure any evils rather than have his good deeds recognized through the vice of ostentation. The arrogant, on the other hand, chooses that good things about him—even false ones—be boasted of, lest he be able to endure even the smallest evils.

Since, therefore, when patience is abandoned, the other good deeds already accomplished are also destroyed, it is rightly commanded that a trench be made in the altar of God shown to Ezekiel, so that the burnt offerings placed upon it may be preserved there. For if there were no trench in the altar, any sacrifice found upon it would be scattered by a breeze that came upon it.

What, then, do we understand by the altar of the Lord except the soul of the righteous? Whatever good deeds it has performed, it places upon itself as sacrifices before his eyes. And what is the trench of the altar except patience? While it humbles the mind to endure adversity, it displays it as though placed at the bottom, in the manner of a trench.

Let a trench therefore be made in the altar, lest the sacrifice placed upon it be scattered by the breeze: that is, let the mind of the elect preserve patience, lest, stirred by the wind of impatience, it lose even what it has done well.

This same trench is rightly said to be one cubit, because if patience is not abandoned, the measure of unity is preserved. Hence Paul also says to the Galatians: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ.” The law of Christ is the charity of unity, which is fulfilled only by those who, even when burdened, do not go beyond the bounds.

(Hieron.) What follows—“And from the lower ledge to the greater ledge, four cubits, and its breadth one cubit”—for which the Septuagint has, “And from the smaller mercy-seat to the greater mercy-seat,” while Theodotion translated *azara* in both places—must be understood as follows.

The smaller mercy-seat is the stone cut from the mountain without hands; the greater mercy-seat is the same stone that grew into a great mountain and filled the whole world. Or, according to another interpretation, the smaller mercy-seat is when he “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2); the greater mercy-seat is when he received the glory that he had with the Father before the world existed (John 17).

First we recognize the humbler things concerning Christ, and thus arrive at the height of his divinity. Yet the mercy-seat of both natures—the lesser and the greater—belongs to the mystery of one altar.

Between the two mercy-seats, the lesser and the greater, there were four cubits, signifying the four elements of the world, which themselves also reach the height of one cubit. It must also be observed that, in the measurement of the altar, the first cubit in breadth is joined to nothing else but is perfect in its own unity. The second cubit of breadth, however, rises to the summit after two cubits. The third cubit, after the smaller and greater mercy-seats, advances through the four elements toward the mystery of one cubit.

Thus the first, second, and third cubit in the altar of the Lord should in no way be called first, second, and third, but one, one, and one.

Ariel itself was four cubits, and from Ariel upward there were four horns—or, as the Septuagint says, from Ariel to the upper parts of the horns there was one cubit. Ariel, as many think, is interpreted “God is my light.” Concerning this we have spoken more fully in the prophet Isaiah, where it is written: “Woe to you, city of Ariel, which David besieged” (or “surrounded”) (Isaiah 29).

But in my opinion it means “lion” or “strong one of God.” This name properly refers to the altar, in which there is either the illumination of God or his lion and strength, as Jacob says to Judah: “Judah is a lion’s cub; you have gone up to the prey, my son. You have lain down and rested like a lion and like a lioness; who will rouse him?” (Genesis 49).

It is four cubits, and it has four horns—or the upper parts of its four horns are completed in one cubit—so that the measure of the Gospels and the strength spreading throughout the whole world may be displayed under the illumination of God and the strength of the lion, and may reach the one cubit of divine confession.

To make the obscurity of the present passage gradually clearer, it follows: “And Ariel was twelve cubits long by twelve cubits wide, a square with equal sides.” No one doubts that this refers to the twelve tribes written of in the Apocalypse of John, and to the number of the apostles, concerning whose mystery I remember having spoken above.

Through the four sides of the world, the twelve cubits together make forty-eight cubits, corresponding to the priestly cities, so that the strength of the Church may be firmly established upon these foundations spread throughout the whole world.

The ledge—which the Septuagint called the mercy-seat, Theodotion, as above, *azara*, and Symmachus translated as περίδρομή, that is, “circuit”—was fourteen cubits long by fourteen cubits wide at its four corners. “And there was a crown around it of half a cubit,” for which the Septuagint again used *gison*.

Its hollow—or, according to Symmachus, “its completion and perfection,” one cubit all around—quietly indicates that our Lord, who is truly called the mercy-seat, came not only for our sins but for the whole world. He descended to earthly things through the fourteen generations from Abraham to David, and again through another fourteen to the captivity of Jeconiah, and through the mystery of the same number; so that in the third τεσσαρακαιδεκάς (group of fourteen), and through the mystery of the divine gift, he might save the four corners of the world, concerning which it is written: “Many will come from east and west and north and south, and will recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 8).

What follows—“And the crown, or *gison*, around it”—the mercy-seat is understood—“had half a cubit, and the hollow of the mercy-seat,” or its completion and perfection, which Symmachus translated as περίδρομή, had one cubit. This signifies that both sinners and the righteous are saved through the Lord’s mercy, as the apostle Paul says: “We have been reconciled to God through the blood of his Son” (Romans 5).

Of sinners it is said that they possess the measure of half a cubit around them, yet are saved by the mercy of the Creator, according to what is written in the Psalm: “You will save them for nothing.” Of the righteous, it is said that they are saved in the singular and perfect number of one, and imitate the one divinity, as the same apostle says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5).

The final statement in this testimony, “And its steps faced east,” means that we must understand the steps of this mercy-seat as the seventy-four books of the Old Testament, which had harps in the Apocalypse of John (Revelation 5) and crowns on their heads; or as the mystery of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, in which true mercy is granted to us.

To put it more plainly: the number of the steps is left uncertain so that, however diligently we may be able to climb toward higher things, we may think ourselves placed among the lower, and consider the statement of the Psalm: “They will go from strength to strength” (Psalm 83).

“And he said to me: Son of man, thus says the Lord God: These are the rites of the altar on whatever day it is made, so that a burnt offering may be offered upon it and blood poured out. You shall give them to the priests and Levites who are of the seed of Zadok, who approach me, says the Lord God, to offer me a bull from the herd as a sin offering. Taking some of its blood, you shall place it on the four horns, on the four corners of the ledge, and on the crown around it; and you shall cleanse it and make atonement for it. You shall take the bull that was offered for sin and burn it in a separate place of the house, outside the sanctuary. On the second day you shall offer an unblemished male goat for sin, and they shall make atonement for the altar as they made atonement with the bull.”

(Hieron.) After showing the prophet the altar, its cubit, its two cubits, then another cubit, four cubits, and a third cubit, as well as twelve cubits by twelve cubits, its four horns, Ariel twelve cubits by twelve cubits, and the ledge—that is, the mercy-seat—fourteen cubits by fourteen cubits, together with its crown and its hollow of half a cubit all around, and its steps facing east, whose number is uncertain, the man whose reed and cord were in his hand spoke and taught him how, once the altar had been completed, it ought to be purified or consecrated.

First a victim is offered and given to the priests from the tribe of Levi, who are of the family of Zadok. A bull is offered. The bull that was sacrificed for us is mentioned in many passages of Scripture, especially in the Epistle of Barnabas, which is counted among the apocryphal writings.

On the second day a male goat is offered. Hence, when they are about to celebrate Passover, they take a lamb and a kid from the flock; and those who were unable to celebrate the first Passover celebrate it in the second month. One of these refers to the righteous, and the other to the penitent.

(Isid.) Since Christ, according to the flesh, arose from the Jews who lived under the yoke of the law, the sacrifice of a bull is rightly named. But because, in his incarnation, he was made from the common mass of humanity, he is again called a goat. This animal wears a rough covering of hair—rough, as it were, like the whole race of living beings filled with sin, since nothing is rougher than sin.

Therefore, wishing to demonstrate this openly, the lawgiver says: “When he has slaughtered the goat for the sin of the people,” understanding here the whole human race, which once was not a people but now is a people, since Jesus took firstfruits from us.

Thus, to show that Christ is principally from the Jews because of his kinship with Abraham, yet also bears the firstfruits of our whole nature, which is in sin—for which reason he was also called Adam—the law took both a bull and a goat as figures of his sacrifice.

Although the sacrifice is one, whether it is called a bull or a goat, and although the result is the same in both—for through it the remission of sins is brought about—the things done with the goat and the bull are necessarily common.

You see the one who kills the goat before the Lord—that is, before the Father—and brings its blood into the interior of the veil, that is, to the Father. He makes atonement for the sanctuary from the uncleannesses of the children of Israel, from their transgressions, and from all their sins.

He seems indeed to be speaking about the tabernacle. But he is not speaking about that which is subject to the senses—for what expiation or propitiation could the tabernacle accomplish, or what could the skins and other materials accomplish from which the Jewish tabernacle, which was perceptible to the senses, was made? Rather, he speaks of the human race as a whole.

Our human stock was holy from the beginning, so that the spirit of God dwelt in it. This is shown by the fact that God threatened to remove it in anger when those who descended from Seth, although righteous and called sons of God, desired the women who were called daughters of men and became one kind with the wicked and unjust.

For he said: “When the sons of God saw the daughters of men, that they were beautiful, they took wives for themselves from all whom they chose. And the Lord God said: My spirit shall not remain in human beings forever, because they are flesh” (Genesis 6).

Therefore, if the spirit of God dwelt in human beings before they began more readily to follow every passion, the human race was rightly holy. For the Holy of Holies would not have taken firstfruits from it. But because it was defiled, he purified it from the uncleannesses of the children of Israel.

According to the interpretation concerning perceptible Israel, Jesus was sacrificed and offered a sacrifice for the whole human race for the purification of our uncleannesses. What uncleannesses? “From their transgressions,” he says, “and from all their sins.” For uncleanness of soul is not harmed by the pollution of a dead body, by pork, or by anything else of that kind, but by harming one’s neighbor, sinning against God, or despising God’s commandments.

(Hieron.) But if we prefer the translation of the Septuagint, who said, “On the second day they shall take two unblemished kids for sin,” what we are about to say is bold; nevertheless, the opinion of others must be stated simply. They say that two unblemished kids were offered on the altar of the Lord on account of the Lord’s passion: James and Stephen. One of them was chief among the number of the apostles, the other chief among the seven chosen for the Lord’s ministry.

This is the James who saw the Savior transfigured on the mountain, who, with the Lord, Peter, and John, beheld the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue raised to life, and who, in the catalogue of the apostles—in which the names are joined in pairs—is placed before his brother.

Herod killed him, and like an unblemished kid he was sacrificed on the second day after the Savior’s passion. The Jews also overwhelmed Stephen with stones. No one could resist his wisdom and teaching, and he saw the Son standing at the right hand of the Father and said: “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Acts 6–7).

Just as the Apostle calls certain believers the firstfruits of Achaia and Asia (1 Corinthians 16), so these two were the firstfruits of the martyrs whom the later confession of Christ crowned.

It should also be noted that the bull is offered whole as a burnt offering, and the fat of its body is consumed by divine fire. For although we once knew Christ, now we no longer know him according to the flesh.

But James and Stephen, who were offered on the second day—or the goat which, according to the Hebrew, is mentioned—are indeed offered as a victim, but the burnt offering is reserved for the presence of the Lord.

The blood that is taken signifies what Peter speaks of: “You were redeemed from your futile way of life handed down by your fathers with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1). The apostle Paul also teaches: “You were bought at a price” (1 Corinthians 7). And elsewhere: “Making peace through the blood of his cross, whether on earth or in heaven” (Colossians 1).

This signifies that the four horns of the altar are purified by the Savior’s blood—that is, the four regions of the world. The crown of the mercy-seat, or its bases, is sprinkled around it, so that everything may be purified and the propitiation may be firm.

A goat, or the two kids about whom we spoke above, is taken on the second day because this animal is always hastening toward high places and suffers no danger on precipices; it finds a path where other living creatures meet destruction. Hence in Greek speech the herd of goats and kids is called the conduct of those who dwell on high.

Moreover, the altar of Christ is purified by blood, and the prayers of the saints remain pure before God.

It should also be noted that, according to the Hebrew, Ezekiel himself, as though a priest, is commanded to take the bull, make it a burnt offering, and sprinkle its blood around both the altar and its corners and crown, or base. But the Septuagint translators show that other priests do this, concerning whom it is said: “You shall give them to the priests of Levi who are of the seed of Zadok and who approach me.”

“When you have finished making atonement for it, you shall offer an unblemished bull from the herd and an unblemished ram from the flock, and you shall offer them before the Lord. The priests shall throw salt upon them, and they shall offer them as a burnt offering to the Lord. For seven days you shall prepare a male goat for sin each day, and they shall offer a bull from the herd and a ram from the flock, unblemished. For seven days they shall make atonement for the altar and cleanse it and fill its hand. When the days are completed, on the eighth day and thereafter the priests shall make your burnt offerings upon the altar, and the offerings that are made for peace; and I shall be reconciled to you, says the Lord God.”

(Hieron.) After the altar and its measurements have been shown at the summit of the mountain, and its purification and consecration have again been revealed to the prophet through one unblemished bull and a goat—or two kids, of which we referred the first to the Lord Savior and the other two to the apostles and ministers—so that the law and the prophets might not seem to have been excluded from the consecration of the spiritual altar belonging properly to the Church, an unblemished bull and a ram are taken after the altar has been consecrated and offered before the Lord.

The sons of Zadok—that is, the righteous priests—sprinkle salt upon their heads, so that both the law and the prophets may be seasoned with the savor of the Gospel. There is no sacrifice, according to the command of the law and the interpretation of the Apostle, who says, “Let your speech be seasoned with salt” (Colossians 4), that lacks salt.

(Isid.) That salt is to be understood as apostolic wisdom the Lord clearly shows us when he says to the apostles: “You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt has lost its savor, it is good for nothing from then on except to be thrown outside and trampled by people” (Matthew 5).

For this reason he called salt apostolic wisdom. Just as ordinary food, suitable for nourishment, is thoroughly seasoned with salt, so every useful word that is spoken for the sake of helping necessarily requires the seasoning of apostolic wisdom.

Therefore he commanded that salt should not be absent from sacrifices, but that salt should be offered with every gift, so that whatever you teach, whatever you correct, and whatever virtue you practice, you may carry out the zeal and imitation of the apostles. Remember Paul’s saying: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 1).

And again: “Therefore you are no longer strangers and sojourners” (Ephesians 2), but citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the chief cornerstone.

Here he did not simply say “salt,” but indicated the intelligible meaning intended by the lawgiver: “You shall not remove the salt of the covenant of your God,” he says (Leviticus 2). And if the covenant, or testament, is rational, then the salt too is rational.

Both offerings are presented as burnt offerings to the Lord, so that the fattier body of the letter, signified in the law, and the obscurity of prophecy may be transformed by the fire of the Lord—that is, by the Holy Spirit, of whom Paul says, “fervent in spirit” (Romans 12)—into a spiritual and subtle substance.

If we wish to know more clearly who the unblemished bull from the herd and the ram from the sheep are, let us understand them as Moses and Elijah. The former was the gentlest of all the people who lived on earth (Numbers 12); the latter, equal to Moses in the ardor of faith, dared to say, “I alone have been left” (3 Kings 19).

Where the Hebrew has “you shall offer the bull,” the Septuagint has “the priests shall offer it.” There should be no dispute about this, for Ezekiel himself, to whom these things are spoken, belongs to the number of priests, being of full and perfect age, and he increased the priestly rank through the grace of prophecy.

Moses and Elijah are seen with the Lord on the mountain (Matthew 17)—that is, the law and the prophets, who announced to him what he would suffer in Jerusalem.

After the altar has been purified, a goat or kid is offered for sin each day for seven days, together with an unblemished bull from the herd and an unblemished ram from the flock, so that through these sacrifices the altar may be perfectly purified over seven days.

The seven days signify the Sabbath rest that, according to the Apostle, is reserved for the people of the Lord. In them we hope for eternal and true rest, and we shall by no means perform the servile work of sins.

In the goat, bull, and ram three general kinds of sin are shown, to which the whole human race is subject. We sin either in thought, in speech, or in deed.

Thought is referred to the ram, because it is the first of all sins and the source from which the other two sins arise. The kid or goat refers to language and speech, which is always discussing higher things. Deeds are properly assigned to the bull, which is devoted to the plow, labor, and earthly works.

These unblemished offerings, therefore, we must present to God for the seven days of the true and perfect Sabbath, and we must purify the altar so that our prayer may reach God pure.

What follows—“They shall cleanse it and fill its hand”—which both the Hebrew and the other translators rendered in this way, signifies that the gifts of the altar itself, for whose purification the sacrifice is offered, must also be completed, just as an offering is made for the priests, the people, and the high priest, so that nothing may appear to have stood empty before the Lord.

For this the Septuagint translators wrote, “They shall cleanse it and fill their hands,” with the priests understood. When their hands have been filled with good works—for this is what “hands” fully signifies—after the Sabbath has passed, they shall come to the eighth day of resurrection and say with the Apostle, “We have risen with Christ.” From the eighth day onward they shall reach toward heavenly things and offer on our behalf burnt offerings, or offerings for peace, for our sins and for our salvation, so that through the fire of the Holy Spirit everything that we think, say, and do may be transformed into a spiritual substance, and the Lord, pleased by such sacrifices, may become reconciled to us.

## CHAPTER XLIV  
### Concerning the closed gate; that the uncircumcised must not enter the sanctuary; and concerning the holiness and inheritance of the Levites

[Col. 1001A]

“Then he turned me toward the way of the outer sanctuary gate that faced east, and it was closed. And the Lord said to me: ‘This gate shall be closed and shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it, because the Lord God of Israel has entered—or shall enter—through it; and it shall remain closed to the prince. The prince himself shall sit in it to eat bread before the Lord. He shall enter by way of the vestibule of the gate, that is, through the Church, and he shall go out by way of it.’”

**(Jerome.)** In place of what is written in Hebrew, “It was closed for the prince,” the Septuagint translated, “It shall be closed; the ruler himself shall sit in it.”

[Col. 1001B] Scripture mentions many gates in Ezekiel’s description of the temple, both inside and outside. The preceding discussion has also treated the form and consecration of the altar and the sacrifices. When that is finished, it comes to the outer sanctuary gate that faced east and was closed. At once the man who was guiding the prophet and showing him everything spoke to him:

“This gate which you see closed shall always be closed and shall not be opened.”

He then gives the reasons why it is to remain closed:

“Because the Lord God of Israel has entered,” or shall enter, “through it.”

According to the Hebrew, it shall be closed for the prince, whom the Septuagint translated as the ruler:

“The prince and ruler himself—that is, the *Nasi*—shall sit in it to eat bread before the Lord. He shall enter by way of the vestibule of the gate, and [Col. 1001C] he shall go out by way of it.”

What is this gate that is always closed, through which the Lord God of Israel alone enters? Surely it is the one of which the Savior speaks in the Gospel:

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, and woe to you teachers of the law, who take away the key of knowledge: you yourselves do not enter, and you prevent those who are entering” (Luke 11).

Isaiah also writes about this gate under the name of a book:

“The words of this book shall be like sealed words. When you give it to a man who does not know letters and say to him, ‘Read,’ he will answer you, ‘I do not know letters.’ And they will give it to a man who knows letters, saying, ‘Read.’ And he will say, ‘I cannot read, because it is sealed’” (Isaiah 29).

This is the book whose seals no one can break and open, neither in heaven nor on earth nor beneath the earth, except the one of whom it is said in John’s Apocalypse:

“Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root and Offspring of David, has conquered, so that he may open the book and break its seals” (Revelation 5).

[Col. 1001D] Before the Savior assumed a human body and humbled himself, taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2), the Law and the Prophets, and all knowledge of the Scriptures, were closed; paradise was closed. But after he hung upon the cross and said to the thief, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23), immediately the veil of the temple was torn, and everything was opened. Once the veil had been removed, we say:

“But we all, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory” (2 Corinthians 3).

But if everything has been unveiled—for in Christ, according to Paul’s words, everything is revealed—[Col. 1002A] how will the gate be closed and not be opened, and no man pass through it?

From this we learn that, although in comparison with divine knowledge we have attained the highest understanding, we now know in part and understand in part. But when perfection comes, then what is partial will be destroyed. Thus, in another passage, the Apostle speaks of himself as imperfect and again as perfect (1 Corinthians 13). If this is not interpreted, it appears contradictory. He says:

“Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect, brothers; I do not consider myself to have grasped it. But forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the goal toward the prize of God’s heavenly calling” (Philippians 3).

When we might have thought that, according to his own confession, he was not perfect and was seeking rather than having found the truth, he says that not only he but others also are perfect:

“Let all of us who are perfect think this way” (ibid.).

The meaning of this passage is that, in comparison with other people who do not care about knowledge of the Scriptures or the mysteries of God, I confess myself to be perfect. But with respect to knowledge of the divine majesty, I now see in a riddle, through cloud and darkness, and I say with the Prophet:

“Your knowledge has become wondrous beyond me; it is strengthened, and I cannot attain it” (Psalm 138).

[Col. 1002B] Therefore this gate, which is closed to all—for no man shall pass through it—shall be closed to the prince or ruler, and shall be opened for the coming of the one who “shall sit in it to eat bread before the Lord.”

Of him he himself professes in the Gospel:

“My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to complete his work” (John 4).

He is the prince and high priest according to the order of Melchizedek (Psalm 110), both sacrifice and priest. In the presence of the Father he eats heavenly bread with us and drinks the wine of which he says in the Gospel:

“I shall not drink from the fruit of this vine until I drink it new in the kingdom of my Father” (Matthew 26);

that is, in the kingdom of which the Apostle writes:

“The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17).

The gate shall remain closed, for no one can understand, in view of its majesty, the mysteries of the Lord’s passion and of his body and blood.

[Col. 1002C] Yet our prince is of such goodness and mercy that, although he alone sits in the closed gate and eats bread before the Lord, he wishes to have many as companions at his table and banquet, and says:

“Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone opens, I will enter to him, and I will dine with him, and he with me” (Revelation 3).

He alone eats bread before the Lord because his substance and divine nature are separated from all created substances.

He enters and leaves by the same vestibule gate because he is both within and outside—that is, infused into and surrounding all things. He enters through the gate so that he may bring in with him those who cannot enter without his teaching and help; and he goes out so that he may bring in others again and speak to those who do not grasp more difficult things.

[Col. 1002D] That the eastern gate is always closed beyond the boundaries of the world and is in no way open to human sight is proved by John’s Gospel, which says:

“No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has himself declared him” (John 1).

It is as though he had said in other words:

“It shall remain closed to the prince; the prince alone shall sit in it to eat bread”—the bread of perfect and consummate knowledge.

“For no one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Matthew 11).

Beautifully, some understand the closed gate through which the Lord God of Israel alone enters, and for which the ruler is the one to whom the gate is closed, as the Virgin Mary, who remained a virgin both before and after childbirth.

For when the angel was speaking, he said:

“The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1).

And when he was born, she remained eternally a virgin, confounding those who suppose that after the Savior’s birth she had sons by Joseph, on the basis of the brothers who are mentioned in the Gospel. Jerome says that in Rome, during his youth, he wrote a not very large book against Helvidius, the heretic of that time, concerning this little question.

# BOOK EIGHTEEN

[Col. 1003]

## CHAPTER FORTY-FOUR FOLLOWS

[Col. 1003B]

After the description of the holy house, its adornment, and the manifestation of the glory of the Lord that entered the temple by the eastern way, as well as the Lord’s commands to the prophet, he now instructs him concerning all the ceremonies of the house of the Lord and all its laws. The mystery of these matters is to be explained in the present book, the eighteenth book of this work.

“And he led me by the way of the north gate into the presence of the house. And I saw, and behold, the glory of the Lord had filled the house of the Lord, and I fell upon my face. And the Lord said to me: ‘Son of man, set your heart, see with your eyes, and hear with your ears everything that I speak to you concerning all the ceremonies of the house of the Lord and all its laws. And set your heart upon the ways of the temple, at every exit of the sanctuary.’”

**(Jerome.)** The man who guides the prophet and by whose showing he comes to know everything in the temple, after showing him the gate that was closed and would never be reopened, yet open to the one who entered through closed doors, leads the prophet to the way of the north gate. Since this gate too was in the presence of the house, there can be no doubt that it signifies the temple.

When the prophet saw, directly opposite him, the house of the Lord filled with the glory of the Lord—the same glory that he was facing while positioned on the northern side—he immediately fell upon his face, unable to bear the majesty of the Lord’s glory.

[Col. 1003C] Therefore, because he had been cast down in humility, the Lord—not a man—said to him:

“Son of man, set your heart,” and so forth.

At the completion of the tabernacle and of the temple building constructed by Solomon, the glory of the Lord appeared. It was later surpassed, in comparison with the glory of the Gospel, as the Apostle says:

“For what was glorified in that case had no glory, because of the glory that surpasses it. For if what was being destroyed came through glory, much more will what remains be in glory” (2 Corinthians 3).

We must be careful not to think that the destruction of the former glory means its abolition. Rather, we should understand that when perfection comes, what had been partial will be destroyed. It is like comparing the rays of the sun with a lamp, or the light of a lamp with that of a small lantern.

[Col. 1003D] For this reason it is also said of John the Baptist:

“He was a lamp burning in the house” (John 5).

But after the sun of righteousness came, the lamp’s light was hidden, as the same prophet and Baptist said:

“He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3).

The prophet fell upon his face lest, while wishing to see more than human frailty could behold, he should lose even the light of his eyes. Therefore the Lord addresses him familiarly as “son of man” and commands him to set his heart, see with his eyes, and hear with his ears.

First, the mind must be opened to understand what is said. Second, the eyes of the heart must be opened for understanding; of these it is said to Abraham:

“Lift up your eyes and see the stars of heaven” (Genesis 15).

Third, one must hear with those ears of which the Savior says:

“Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8).

Thus he may understand all the ceremonies and ordinances of the temple, and finally set his heart upon the ways of the temple, because there are various entrances to God. Or “the ways of the temple” signifies the order of the ceremonies, and “the exits of the sanctuary.”

[Col. 1004A] This is therefore a preface and preparation of the prophet for understanding what he will subsequently learn concerning the order of the temple. It should also be noted that in the region of this world, which lies in the evil one and is established in the cold of the north, the heavenly order of ceremonies is shown to us.

“And you shall say to the house of Israel that provokes me: Thus says the Lord God: Let all your crimes be enough for you, house of Israel, because you bring in foreigners—strangers uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh—to be in my sanctuary and to profane my house. You offer my bread, the fat and the blood; you have broken my covenant through all your crimes, and you have not kept the ordinances of my sanctuary. You have appointed for yourselves, in my sanctuary, guardians of my observances.”

[Col. 1004B] When he says, “Let all your crimes be enough for you,” or “your iniquities,” he urges repentance for former sins, lest we add sins to sins and prepare fuel for a future fire.

But let us hear what Isaiah says:

“Woe to those who draw sins along as with a long rope, and iniquity as with a cart-rope” (Isaiah 5).

The first sin is that they bring in foreign sons or strangers, uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh, to be in God’s sanctuary and profane the house of the Lord.

“A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (1 Corinthians 5).

In some copies of Proverbs the following is also found:

“Do not bring the impious into the tents of the righteous.”

At this point the Jews and Ebionites press us, since they accept circumcision of the flesh. How can we explain the present passage, “uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh,” unless, after spiritual circumcision, we must also receive circumcision of the flesh?

[Col. 1004C] But we read Paul saying:

“I testify again to every man who receives circumcision that, if you receive circumcision, Christ will be of no benefit to you” (Galatians 5).

And Jeremiah says:

“Behold, your ears are uncircumcised, and you were unwilling to listen” (Jeremiah 6).

Moses also spoke in the presence of the Lord in Exodus, saying:

“Behold, the children of Israel have not listened to you; how then will Pharaoh listen to me? I am slow of speech.”

The Hebrew has this more appropriately:

“I am uncircumcised in lips.”

Let us question them—or rather, compel them—to circumcise their ears and cut away their lips, so that they may appear to fulfill Scripture.

But if they begin to interpret circumcision of the ears as meaning that we tolerate nothing shameful or dishonorable in what we hear, and circumcision of the lips as meaning that we say nothing indecent, let us tell them that they must preserve the same interpretation in the heart and in the flesh.

We circumcise the heart with God’s knife, and the foreskin is removed from our heart when shameful thoughts no longer come out of it. Nor is it said of us:

“The heart of this people has become fat, and they have heard heavily with their ears” (Acts 28; Isaiah 6).

[Col. 1004D] The flesh, likewise, is circumcised so that we no longer perform earthly works that we are compelled to perform for the body’s needs—taking food and drink, sleeping, and using clothing—unless we do all these things not for pleasure, luxury, and idleness, but for the necessity of nature and the support of this body.

Whoever drinks a little wine for the sake of his stomach and his frequent illnesses (1 Timothy 5), and hates drunkenness, circumcises his flesh.

Whoever sleeps as much as nature allows will hear Solomon say:

“If you sit down, you will be without fear; if you sleep, you will sleep sweetly, and you will not fear the terror that comes upon you, nor the attacks of the impious that come upon you” (Proverbs 3).

Whoever flees fornication and renders the debt to his wife, returning again to the same relationship lest Satan tempt him, will hear, together with the people of Israel:

“On this day I have taken away the reproach of Egypt from you.”

[Col. 1005A] He will also use clothing that repels the cold, not clothing whose thinness displays naked bodies. The flesh weakened by fasts and circumcised by continence flees the reproach of the Egyptians, who are men of great flesh. It can say what is read in many copies according to the Septuagint edition:

“As my flesh wasted away in a desert land, pathless and waterless, so I appeared to you in the sanctuary” (Psalm 63).

Whenever, therefore, we wish to bring foreigners into God’s temple, let us circumcise their ears, lips, heart, and all their flesh, as well as their eyes, taste, and sense of smell, so that we may do everything with the fear of God and with reason.

Let bishops and presbyters hear this, and the entire ecclesiastical order, so that they do not bring in foreign sons, uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh, to be in God’s sanctuary and profane his house.

[Col. 1005B] If they do this, what follows will apply to them:

“You offer my breads”—that is, the loaves of the Presence, in all the churches and throughout the world, springing from one bread.

And not only bread, but also fat, of which it is written:

“He satisfied them with the fat of grain” (Psalm 81),

and the blood poured out in Christ’s passion.

The passage should be read in this way, restoring the order of the reading:

“When you bring foreign sons, uncircumcised in heart and body, into my sanctuary, and profane my house, do you dare to offer bread and fat and blood, the mystical sacraments? Do you not understand that you have broken and transgressed my covenant through all your crimes and impieties, and that you have not kept the ordinances of my sanctuary, nor appointed guardians of my ceremonies in my sanctuary?”

[Col. 1005C] The whole threat is directed against those who have not listened to the Apostle’s warning:

“Do not be hasty in laying hands on anyone, and do not share in the sins of others” (1 Timothy 5).

Or it may certainly be understood in this way:

“You have broken my covenant through all your crimes, and you have not kept the ordinances of my sanctuary; yet you dare to appoint the unworthy and the foreign as guardians of my sanctuary’s observances for yourselves”—with the implication, “not for me.”

The meaning is: those who serve and minister to you in carnal matters, and who profane my sanctuary for the sake of your comforts.

“Thus says the Lord God: No foreigner, uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh, shall enter my sanctuary—no foreign son who is among the children of Israel.

“But the Levites who went far away from me in the error of the children of Israel and wandered from me after their idols shall bear their iniquity. They were in my sanctuary as attendants and gatekeepers of the gates of the house, and as ministers of the house. They slaughtered the burnt offerings and sacrifices of the people, and they stood before them to minister for them.

[Col. 1005D] “Because they ministered for them before their idols, they became a stumbling block of iniquity to the house of Israel. Therefore I lifted my hand against them, says the Lord God, and they bore their iniquity. They shall not approach me to exercise the priesthood for me, nor shall they draw near to any of my sanctuaries, near the holy of holies. Rather, they shall bear their shame and the crimes they committed.

“I shall appoint them as gatekeepers of the house, for all its service and for everything done in it.

“But the Levitical priests, the sons of Zadok, who kept the observances of my sanctuary when the children of Israel wandered from me, they shall approach me to minister to me, and they shall stand in my presence to offer me fat and blood, says the Lord God. They shall enter my sanctuary, and they shall approach my table to minister to me and to keep my observances.”

The Hebrew has this meaning:

“No foreigner, uncircumcised in heart and flesh, shall enter my sanctuary,” even if he appears to be among the people of Israel.

But the Levites—that is, the priestly order—who went far from me in the error of the children of Israel and followed idols shall bear their iniquity, because they were in my sanctuary ministering in the office of the gates of the house and as its ministers.

[Col. 1006A] They offered the burnt offering and the sacrifices of the people, and they stood in their presence to minister for them.

Because they ministered for them before their idols and became a stumbling block of iniquity to the house of Israel, therefore I lifted my hand against them, says the Lord God, and they bore their iniquity. They shall not approach me to exercise the priesthood for me, nor shall they draw near to any of my sanctuaries near the holy of holies. Instead, they shall bear their shame and the crimes they committed.

In place of the priestly office in which they had been accustomed to offer the burnt offering, sacrifices, and every kind of offering, they shall be reduced to the lowest rank. They shall be gatekeepers of the house, to everlasting disgrace, so that they may be seen by the whole people as they enter and leave, and so that their fall from that lofty dignity to the lowest rank may be evident.

“But the priests,” he says—that is, the Levites—“who are the sons of Zadok,” that is, of the righteous one or of the righteous God, and who, during the time of the error of all Israel, “kept the observances of my sanctuary, they shall approach me to minister to me and stand in my presence” [Col. 1006B] and offer me fat, that is, the richest sacrifice, and blood, namely, a living and pleasing sacrifice to God.

“They shall enter my sanctuary and approach my table,” to burn incense to me and observe the entire rite of sacrifice.

But if this is so—if those who, during a time of error and persecution, followed idols that they had fashioned from their own hearts, and who not only by word but also by a signed document asserted that the Son of God was a creature, and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever—how do they assume for themselves the priestly and episcopal dignity, and dare to offer sacrifices to God, though they were once worshipers of idols?

But, as the most ardent poet testifies:

> Whatever is committed by many goes unpunished.

The multitude of sinners has made pardon easier to obtain for the impious. Those who, after being reduced to the lay state, ought to have lamented their former sacrilege now sit reclining on episcopal thrones and belch forth upon us the nausea of feigned faith—or rather, the openly displayed shortcuts of manifest perfidy.

[Col. 1006C] Let them at least hear this late and observe the commands of almighty God:

“No foreigner, uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh, shall enter my sanctuary.”

Even if he is a son, even if he is joined to us by kinship, even if an ancient relationship binds him to us, if he is uncircumcised in heart or flesh, let him not be brought into God’s sanctuary, lest we make ministers of Christ into our own ministers and profane the Lord’s altars for the sake of carnal comforts.

In place of our reading,

“I shall appoint them as gatekeepers of the house in its service and in everything done in it,”

referring to those Levites who went far from God in the error of the children of Israel and followed the idols to which they sacrificed, Symmachus, considering the order and meaning of the passage, translated more correctly:

“I had appointed them as guardians of the doors of the house, of all its service, and of everything done in it.”

Thus it does not refer to those who are in the temple, but to those who had been there.

[Col. 1006D]

“When they enter the gates of the inner court, they shall be clothed in linen garments or robes, and no woolen garment shall come upon them when they minister at the gates of the inner court and within. They shall have linen bands on their heads, or linen turbans upon their heads; linen undergarments shall be on their loins, and they shall not gird themselves violently or tightly. When they go out to the outer court, to the people, they shall remove the garments in which they ministered and place them in the storerooms of the sanctuary. They shall put on other garments, and they shall not sanctify the people with their garments.

“They shall not shave their heads, nor let their hair grow long, but they shall cut their heads by trimming the hair. No priest shall drink wine when he is about to enter the inner court.”

**(Jerome.)** First the historical meaning of the words must be explained. Among the other things that the divine speech commands priests to observe, it also orders this: at the very gates of the inner court they are to be clothed in garments—that is, linen robes—and they are not to use woolen clothing either at the gates of the inner court or within, that is, in the inner chambers and the holy of holies.

[Col. 1007A] Their headbands or turbans are to be of linen, and their undergarments of linen are to be on their loins.

What follows according to the Septuagint is:

“They shall not gird themselves violently.”

Aquila and Symmachus translated this as “in sweat.” Theodotion, expressing the Hebrew word itself, wrote *in Jeze*; Aquila’s second edition has *Buza*.

This signifies that they are not to be forcibly girded tightly and constrictively, like prisoners, lest they become incapable of performing priestly and Levitical duties, of holding and cutting up the victims, or of dragging them and moving about.

Since he had once prescribed which garments the priests were to use when they were within, engaged in their ministry, he commands again that, when they go out, they remove their former garments in the storerooms—or chambers—of the holy things and put on others.

[Col. 1007B] Otherwise, if they retained the holy garments, they would sanctify the people outside, who had not yet been sanctified or prepared for the sanctification of the temple, to become a Nazirite of the Lord.

From this we learn that we must not enter the holy of holies in ordinary garments polluted by daily use, but with a clean conscience and clean clothing, to hold the mysteries of the Lord.

The priests of Egypt use linen clothing not only within but also outside. Divine religion, however, has one form of dress for ministry and another for ordinary life and common use.

Underclothing is rightly worn so that decency and propriety may be preserved, lest, when they ascend the steps of the altar and move about in their ministry, they expose their nakedness.

What all these things signify according to the spiritual meaning will be shown by the words that follow.

[Col. 1007C] The Apostle teaches that there are holy and spiritual garments when he says:

“Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 13).

And elsewhere:

“Put on compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience” (Colossians 3).

Again:

“Having put off the old man with his deeds, and having put on the new, which is renewed in knowledge according to the image of its Creator” (ibid.).

I think the same is signified by this:

“For this corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality. When this corruptible body has put on incorruption and this mortal body has put on immortality, then the word that is written will come to pass,” and so forth (1 Corinthians 15).

**(Maurus.)** Concerning priestly garments, more is written in Exodus. Priests are therefore commanded to put on linen or fine-linen garments when they minister to the Lord at the gates of the inner court and within—that is, to possess purity of body and mind—and not to display anything woolen, that is, soft and sluggish, in their conduct.

[Col. 1007D] Fine linen, *byssus*, grows from the earth, but after being extracted from the earth and subjected to prolonged labor—drying, pounding, cleansing, boiling, and spinning—it normally loses its grassy color and takes on a whiteness of its own. It signifies bodies shining with the beauty of chastity.

These bodies are born amid the allurements of the flesh, but through the great labor of continence they sweat out their native moisture, as it were, and attain the beauty of purity worthy of God through diligent fasting and vigils, prayer and reading, perseverance and humility.

The Apostle’s words can rightly be applied to them:

“Do you not know that your members are a temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you?” (2 Corinthians 6).

Priests have linen tunics when they dedicate their entire bodies to the whiteness of chastity.

They gird their tunics with belts when they surround that same chastity with vigilant guardianship of the mind, lest their conscience remain sluggish in the practice of good works, and lest, through boasting of chastity, they diminish even the merit of chastity itself.

[Col. 1008A] The linen band, or tiara, also called a turban or mitre, covered their heads, so that they might guard in the beauty of chastity the bodily senses that are especially active in the head—sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—and hope, for this same guardianship, to receive the crown of life that God promised to those who love him.

They are commanded to have linen undergarments on their loins, that is, to preserve continence.

These undergarments, which are commanded to be made for covering the shame of the flesh, specifically signify that aspect of chastity which restrains the desire for sexual union. Without it, no one can receive the priesthood or be consecrated to the ministry of the altar—that is, unless he remains a virgin or has not dissolved the bonds of marital union.

[Col. 1008B] This virtue is not imposed by God’s law as necessary for everyone, but is to be offered to the Lord through voluntary devotion. He says concerning it:

“Not everyone can receive this word” (Matthew 19).

Yet immediately, with kindly exhortation, he invites those who are able, saying:

“Let the one who is able to receive it receive it.”

A little later he promises a hundredfold reward in this life and eternal life in the age to come to those who for his sake have left a wife or other relatives and the entanglements of this world.

Therefore, with a clear distinction, Moses is not commanded to clothe Aaron and his sons in this garment in the same way as in the earlier passage:

“You shall clothe Aaron your brother and his sons with all these things”; but he says, “You shall make linen undergarments for them, to cover the flesh” (Exodus 28).
