He says: Let them cover the shame of their own flesh; you shall make the undergarments for the high priest and his sons; you shall teach the rule of chastity; you shall tell those who are to exercise the priesthood that they must abstain from marital embrace.

[Col. 1008C] Yet you shall impose no violent yoke of this kind of continence upon anyone. Rather, whoever wishes to become a priest and serve in the ministry of the altar must, of his own accord, cease to be the servant of a wife.

When they have done this, and, having undertaken the purpose of continence, agree to be ministers of the sanctuary and altar, the divine law will be present, imposing upon them—as though it were another garment suited to priests—and abundantly instructing them how they ought to live and teach.

**(Jerome.)** We make these garments through our own labor; they are woven from above, like the tunic that the Lord had, which cannot be torn. We put them on when we come to know the Lord’s secrets and mysteries.

We possess the Spirit who searches even the heights [Col. 1008D] and depths of God. These things are not to be shown to the common people or proclaimed to a populace that has not been sanctified or prepared for the holiness of the Lord, lest, if they hear greater things, they be unable to bear the majesty of knowledge and be choked, as it were, by solid food, when they still need to be nourished with the milk of infancy.

Scripture, on the other hand, teaches that there are very evil garments, as in what is sung in the Psalms about Judas the betrayer:

“He clothed himself with cursing as with a garment” (Psalm 109).

And shortly afterward:

“Let it be for him as the garment with which he covers himself, and as the belt with which he always girds himself.”

Therefore the Lord, who suffered for us and bore our sins, is said in Zechariah to have filthy garments (Zechariah 3). It is written of them:

“Jesus was clothed in filthy garments.”

Later he removes them, as Scripture says:

“Take the filthy garments away from him and clothe him with the long robe,” and so forth.

[Col. 1009A] What follows—“There shall be linen bands or turbans upon their heads”—I think points to the crown of graces, of which it is written:

“For your head shall receive a crown of graces” (Proverbs 4).

Nor should the question of a covered or uncovered head trouble us because the Apostle says:

“A woman ought to have a veil on her head, because of the angels” (1 Corinthians 11).

“For if a woman is not veiled, let her also be shorn. But if it is shameful for a woman to be shorn or shaved, let her be veiled. A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but woman is the glory of man.”

If men are not to cover their heads, this appears contrary to the command that priests now cover their heads with bands or turbans.

[Col. 1009B] But if we read the earlier passages more carefully, the present difficulty will be resolved. Above it says:

“When they minister at the gates of the inner court and within.”

If we enter the holy places and stand in the presence of the Lord, we ought to cover our heads, because no living person will be justified in the sight of God, and from infancy the human heart has been inclined toward evil.

For the same reason we use undergarments within, lest any shame of a polluted conscience or of marital activity appear in the sight of God.

The Savior also wishes the Apostles to be girded with these undergarments when he says:

“Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12).

The Apostle says to believers:

“Stand therefore, with your loins girded in truth” (Ephesians 6).

And the imitators of Christ hear what is written of him:

“Righteousness shall be the belt around his loins, and truth the band around his sides” (Isaiah 11).

[Col. 1009C] Whoever is girded with this belt and has risen to the summit of the virtues is not to be bound violently, lest he appear to observe the good of continence unwillingly and to eat bread in the sweat of his face, rather than perform the Lord’s command willingly.

Finally, when he goes outside and mingles with the people, the priest removes the priestly garments in the storeroom in which the Lord’s riches are preserved. Priests use other garments and teach the common crowd differently, lest the people be sanctified by their robes.

It is burdensome for the multitude to undertake a load beyond its strength, as Solomon says:

“The one who hastily sanctifies something from his own possessions is a snare to a man.”

[Col. 1009D] What follows concerning the priests—

“They shall not shave their heads, nor let their hair grow long, but they shall trim their heads by cutting the hair”—

clearly shows that we must be neither like the priests and worshipers of Isis and Serapis, with shaved heads, nor let our hair grow long, which is characteristic of the luxurious, barbarians, and soldiers. Rather, the respectable appearance of priests is to be shown in their faces.

For this reason the Septuagint translated:

“They shall not shave their heads, and they shall not cut their hair close, but they shall thoroughly cover their heads.”

From this we learn that the head is neither to be made bald with a razor nor cut so close that we appear like shaven men. Rather, the hair should be left long enough for the skin to be covered.

Or perhaps priests are always to cover their heads, according to Virgil’s line:

> Cover your hair with purple, wrapped in the mantle.

But this is a forced interpretation. Indeed, Nazirite men also offer themselves voluntarily, and whoever makes a vow and does not fulfill it is guilty of violating his vow. Hence it is said of widows: “When they have become wanton against Christ, they wish to marry, having condemnation because they have annulled their first faith” (1 Tim. 5). For it is better not to promise than to promise and not to perform. Hannah offered Samuel (1 Sam. 1), who remained in perpetual holiness; and Manoah offered his son Samson (Judg. 13), but the sanctification of his hair was disgraced by Delilah’s lust. Finally, the Lord departed from him, and he was condemned to blindness [Col. 1012A], except that later, when his hair grew, he recovered his former strength; and, as a type of Christ, he killed far more foreigners in his death than in his life.

The Lord wishes his priests to possess perpetually the hair of sanctification, and their heads to be covered—not by some covering from outside, but by their own natural hair—not for adornment and luxury, but for propriety. Hence even the hairs of the apostles’ heads are numbered, as the Savior says: “But even the hairs of your head are numbered” (Matt. 10)—of that head concerning which it is written in Ecclesiastes: “The eyes of the wise man are in his head” (Eccl. 2); “but the head of the man is Christ” (1 Cor. 11). The sinner tramples and despises that head and, so to speak, shaves it with a razor, removing its beauty [Col. 1012B]—which the Ammonites also did to those whom David had sent as ambassadors (2 Sam. 10).

But if transgression of the law dishonors God, then, conversely, the one who preserves the commandments of the law honors him, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “That all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.” “The priests,” he says, “shall not shave their heads, nor let their hair grow long, but they shall carefully trim their heads.”

(Gregory.) Priests are rightly so called because they preside over the faithful in order to provide sacred leadership. The hair on the head, however, signifies outward thoughts in the mind. Since it grows imperceptibly above the brain, it expresses the cares of the present life, which arise from a negligent faculty of perception and, because they sometimes emerge inopportunely, proceed as though without our noticing. Since, therefore, all who preside ought indeed to have external concerns, but ought not to devote themselves excessively to them, priests are rightly forbidden both to shave their heads and to let their hair grow long: so that they neither cut off the thoughts of the flesh completely, despite the care owed to their subjects, nor again allow them excessive freedom to grow. Hence it is well said: “They shall carefully trim their heads,” so that temporal cares and anxieties may emerge as far as necessary, yet be cut back promptly lest they grow beyond measure.

Thus, while life in the body is protected through the outward administration of providence, and while the heart is not again expended upon it through excessive preoccupation, the hair on the priest’s head is both preserved so that it covers the skin and cut back lest it cover the eyes.

(Hieronymus.) Furthermore, what follows—“Every priest, when he is about to enter the inner court, shall not drink wine” [Col. 1012D]—clearly shows that drunkenness and strong drink overthrow the state of the mind, and that we do not possess full understanding when the soul is occupied by wine and satiety. Drunkenness, however, is manifested not only in drinking wine but in all things by which the mind is made drunk and tossed about: in contracts and worldly business, in losses and profits, in love and hatred. It cannot maintain its proper state.

And because we are surrounded by fragile flesh, and are compelled, for food and clothing and the necessities pertaining to the body, to do certain things that we ought not to do, at least this is required of us: when we return to ourselves, and know why we were born, and enter the inner parts and inner sanctuaries of the temple, we must withdraw from the vices of the world and commit not even the smallest sins [Col. 1013A]. From this it is shown both that we must not commit even minor sins on account of the necessities of the flesh, and that there is a time when, entering the inner court, we must be free from every drunkenness of the world and from everything alien to us.

The priests and Levites therefore abstain from wine not only during their ministry, but even when they are about to enter the holy of holies, lest the mind be oppressed and the understanding become dull. Hence the Apostle says: “It is good not to drink wine” (Rom. 14). And elsewhere: “And wine, in which is debauchery” (Eph. 5). “The people ate and drank, and rose up to play” (Exod. 32). The fact that he permits Timothy to drink a little wine (1 Tim. 5) clearly demonstrates why he permitted it: “For your stomach,” he says, “and your frequent illnesses.”

(Isidore.) To this day you find this law observed in the churches. For he did not command complete abstinence from wine, but only that, when we ascend to the tabernacle of testimony or to the altar—that is, when we undertake any ministry of heavenly teaching—we abstain. The altar is a figure of ministry; the tabernacle of testimony signifies contact with heavenly things. Hence Paul also wrote to Timothy: “Use a little wine for your stomach and your frequent illnesses.” Whoever uses it sparingly—that is, during the time of ministry and teaching—abstains from all drunkenness and intoxication.

Likewise, those priests who devote themselves to study will observe the law. For this reason the command is given not only to Aaron but also to his sons, who had attained a higher office. Paul likewise wrote similar words to the Ephesians [Col. 1013C]: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which is debauchery, but be filled rather with the Spirit” (Eph. 5). Drunkenness makes the mind dull and turns its sobriety to what is worse, so that what is being done is not understood.

Isaiah testifies to this when he says: “Woe to those who rise early to pursue drunkenness and drink until evening, so that they burn with wine. Harp and lyre, tambourine and flute and wine are in your feasts, but you do not regard the work of the Lord, nor consider the works of his hands” (Isa. 5). But those who do not see the works of the Lord—how can they distinguish between sacred and profane, or clean and unclean? How can they exhort and enlighten the people from the Scriptures?

Desiring to show that this command is of higher dignity, he says that the Lord himself declared it. But observe how he says that the Lord spoke to Moses not through the tongue but through the hand—or perhaps he wished altogether to display the dignity of the law, since God explained it, Moses wrote it down, and received from God what had been set forth at his command [Col. 1013D].

“ They shall not take a widow or a divorced woman, whether repudiated or dismissed, as wives, but a virgin from the seed of the house of Israel. They shall also take as a wife the widow who has been widowed by a priest, and they shall teach my people what is between the holy and the polluted, and show them what is between the clean and the unclean. And when there is a dispute—what the Septuagint adds, ‘of blood,’ that is, concerning a capital crime—they shall stand in my judgments and judge my laws. And they shall observe my commandments at all my solemnities.”

(Hieronymus.) This entire passage contains commandments concerning priests. After the many matters we have explained above, they are ordered not to take as wives a widow or a divorced woman, whether repudiated or dismissed. The widow and the repudiated woman signify the Synagogue—that is, the assembly of the Jews—which did not receive the Lord. Hence she is rightly called dismissed, or the widowed Synagogue.

(Isidore.) Concerning her it is written in the Law (Lev. 13): “He shall not take as wife a prostitute or a degraded harlot, nor one who has been repudiated by her husband, because he is consecrated to his God and offers the bread of presentation. Let him therefore be holy, because I, the Lord who sanctify you, am holy.”

If, then, we priests preserve the sanctification given to us by God, we sanctify through our sanctification the one who is holy by nature—and this only for us, because he wished to be sanctified in those who are conformed to him and participate in his glory. He has employed this transformation figuratively and spoken typologically.

Nevertheless, he does not wish those who are sanctified by him to take as wife a prostitute or a degraded harlot, clearly directing his words against the synagogue of the Jews. Since she is a harlot, hear the Lord speaking through Isaiah: “How the faithful city, Zion, full of judgment, has become a harlot! Righteousness dwelt in her, but now murderers” (Isa. 1). Likewise in Hosea: “I will remove her fornication from her midst, and her adultery from between her breasts” (Hos. 2).

David also proclaims her profanation. He says to God: “You profaned her sanctity on the earth; you destroyed all her walls” (Ps. 88). The sanctification of the Jews was unquestionably their synagogue. In it was the sacrifice of the tabernacle, and in it their lawful observances were completed. She is also repudiated by God as by her husband, who had become her husband through election; but when he later found her blameworthy, he repudiated her.

Since she has been completely dismissed, hear the voice uttered by Hosea (Hos. 2): “Judge your mother, judge her, because she is not my wife, and I am not her husband.” Hear also what the prophet Isaiah delivered: “Thus says the Lord: What is this bill of repudiation of your mother that I sent to her?” (Isa. 50). Where there is repudiation and dismissal, it is clear that she was a wife, concerning whom these words were spoken.

He therefore does not wish the priest to take her as a wife, so that they may not proclaim any of the lawful observances pertaining to her, nor use those things which she used according to the letter—that is, so that they may neither perform sacrifices of irrational creatures nor undertake physical purifications in which spiritual realities were believed to be signified.

(Hieronymus.) Again, “dismissed” may be understood as the multitude of heretics who went out from us because they were not of us. “But a virgin,” he says, “from the seed of the house of Israel, who was nourished in the house of God, in the Law and the Prophets” (Prov. 4). Concerning her the Apostle also speaks: “I wish to present you all as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11).

She is the virgin of whom the divine word says elsewhere: “Love her, and she will preserve you; embrace her, and she will exalt you; honor her, so that she may embrace you” (Prov. 4). Who this virgin is whom one ought to love, and who preserves her lover, will be known by the one who reads: “I loved and sought her from my youth, and I sought to take her as my bride, and I became a lover of her beauty” (Wis. 8). And again: “The Lord of all loved her.”

The priest ought to take not only a virgin but also a widow as wife, provided that she was previously the wife of another priest: namely, the knowledge that another worshiper of God discovered. For we ought not to be satisfied only with new teaching, but also cultivate the old and join it to our company, provided that she has been instructed in sacred worship.

It is also the priest’s duty to teach the people what is between the holy and the polluted, and between the clean and the unclean—referring the first, in one sense, to doctrines, and the second to works accomplished through the flesh. “For who understands his sins?” (Ps. 18.) And when there is a dispute concerning every matter—or, as the Septuagint translated it, concerning blood, that is, concerning what pertains to a mortal crime—the priests shall stand in God’s judgments, so that they may not judge according to rank or show partiality to the poor or the rich in judgment, but stand in the judgments of God and remember that psalm: “God stood in the assembly of gods; in the midst he judges gods” (Ps. 81). He calls those who possess the power to judge human beings “gods”; and according to the judgment by which they judge, judgment will be passed upon them (Matt. 7).

“They shall observe my laws and my commandments at all my solemnities,” so that they may know how Christ was sacrificed for us as the Passover; how we ought to complete seven weeks in joy and gladness; how to humble our souls in fasting; how to understand the sound of trumpets; and how to understand the spiritual Feast of Booths, in which we say: “I am a sojourner and a pilgrim, like all my fathers” (Gen. 27; Ps. 38).

These are the true solemnities, which one will interpret more appropriately when explaining the Pentateuch. The priest’s first virtue is not merely to teach what he knows, but to observe all God’s festivals, so that he may command others to observe what he himself has observed. We also learn in Malachi that it is the priest’s duty to possess knowledge of the law: “The lips of the priest will guard knowledge, and they will seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.”

“And they shall sanctify my Sabbaths. They shall not enter a place where there is a dead man, lest they be polluted, except in the case of a father or mother, son or daughter, brother or sister who has not had a husband; in these they may be defiled. After he has been cleansed, seven days shall be counted for him. On the day when he enters my sanctuary, and the inner court, to minister to me in the sanctuary, he shall offer for his sin to the Lord God, or he shall offer an atonement. They shall have no inheritance. I am their inheritance, and you shall give them no possession in Israel. I am their possession.”

The command is still being given to priests. Here one must observe that he did not say simply, “They shall sanctify the Sabbaths,” or, according to Isaiah, “My soul hates your new moons and Sabbaths” (Isa. 1), but, with a distinction, “my Sabbaths.”

Hence it is also written in the Gospel [Col. 1016A]: “The priests in the temple violate the Sabbath and are without guilt”—not the Sabbath of God, but the Sabbath of the letter, the Sabbath of the Jews, which those who are a chosen, royal, priestly race rightly violate. But by the Sabbath that has been sanctified let us understand what the Apostle also teaches was left for the people of God, concerning which it is said: “If they shall enter into my rest” (Ps. 94)—which in Hebrew is called *sabbath*.

The one who does not carry the burden of sin on the Sabbath sanctifies God’s Sabbath; nor does he say: “Like a heavy burden they have weighed heavily upon me” (Ps. 37). Such a person does not gather wood on the Sabbath, nor build upon the foundation of Jesus Christ—wood, hay, and stubble (1 Cor. 3). He does not kindle a fire that consumes useless material, and on the Sabbath he remains in one place [Col. 1016B]. He does not go outside, but, placed like a pillar in the temple of God, remains there. Concerning him John writes in the Apocalypse: “The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall never go outside again” (Rev. 3).

What follows—“They shall not enter a place where there is a dead man, lest they be polluted”—properly concerns priestly duty: not to touch corpses, so that the one who intercedes for the sins of others may himself approach the altar clean. Concerning such dead people the Savior also speaks in the Gospel: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matt. 8).

These people are defiled in a dead father when they abandon their Creator, and in a dead mother when they depart from the Church. In a son and daughter one thing pertains to thoughts and another to works. This is expressed more significantly in Greek: *τὰ νοητὰ καὶ αἰσθητά*—“the intelligible and the perceptible.”

A brother and sister, too, who have been reborn in the same Spirit: if one regards such a person as dead, one is defiled through him—provided only that the sister has remained a virgin and has not been stained by the embrace of any man. From this we understand the privilege of virginity: contact with any man removes perfect purity. Whether this has been said rightly or wrongly we leave to the reader’s judgment.

Nature’s affection is also demonstrated in this matter, so that, according to the order of love, as it is written, “Set love in order within me” (Song 2), after God, the parent of all things, one should love one’s father according to the flesh, and one’s mother, son, daughter, brother, and sister—provided only that she has not left the household and passed into another’s authority.

After the priest has been cleansed according to the order of purification prescribed in the Mosaic Law [Col. 1016D], seven days shall be counted for him—either the perfect number of repentance, or, after the consummation of the world, when we pass into the true *ὀκτώαδι* [octad], so that he may enter the holy of holies. This is the inner court: there he may minister in the sanctuary and always offer a sacrifice for the sin of his conscience, with no time in which he does not remember that he had been defiled through father and mother, son and daughter, brother and sister.

We are compelled to do many things while situated amid the straits of this world, either by the condition of the flesh or by the weakness of nature. But whoever is such that he ministers in the sanctuary, enters the inner court, and always offers sacrifice to God—so that he is a true priest, or rather an imitator of the one concerning whom it is written, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109)—will have no inheritance except God, who is his inheritance.

Nor will he receive a possession in Israel—that is, among the undistinguished multitude—but a priestly one, so that the Lord may say of him: “I am the inheritance”; and, “I am their possession.” When they have found him, they will speak and say: “I will hold him and not let him go” (Song 3), and they will sing with the prophet: “The Lord is my portion” (Ps. 77).

(Adamantius.) Moses gave no inheritance to the Levites, nor did Jesus. What else, then, should be understood except that there are in the Church of the Lord certain people who surpass the rest of humanity in strength of soul and the grace of their merits, to whom the Lord himself is said to be an inheritance?

And if it is permitted to hear something of what is hidden in such matters and to disclose something of the concealed mystery, let us see whether this may perhaps be what secretly displays the figure of priests or Levites. In the whole people—I mean those who are saved—the greater and far more numerous part consists unquestionably of those who, believing simply, please the Lord through fear of God, good works, honorable conduct, and commendable actions.

But there are few, and very rare, who devote themselves to wisdom, preserve their minds pure and clean, and cultivate their souls in every distinguished virtue. Through the grace of teaching they enlighten the simpler among the rest concerning the path by which they should walk and arrive at salvation. Perhaps these are designated under the name of Levites and priests, whose inheritance is the Lord himself, who is wisdom, which they are said to have proclaimed above all others [Col. 1017C].

Nevertheless, I find some difference between what Moses distributed and what Jesus distributed.

When Moses distributed the land beyond the Jordan to two and a half tribes (Num. 35), he did not give the Levites the portion of land that fell to them. Jesus, however, gave them dwellings not only among the tribes over which he himself presides, but also among those that Moses had settled beyond the Jordan. Dwellings for the Levites are assigned within each tribe, so that we might understand an even more magnificent mystery.

For this Levitical or priestly order, which devotes itself to the wisdom and knowledge of God, could not receive a share of dwelling from Moses, because Moses was not the truth but the minister of the exemplary shadow. Jesus our Lord [Col. 1017D], however, who was the wisdom of God, himself provides dwellings for the wise.

Moses could not say: “Go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19). This is to give a portion to the Levites. Moses could not say: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14). Moses could not say: “For everyone who does not hate his father or mother, brothers and sisters, and even his own life, cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14).

Moses could not do this; for that reason he could not distribute the dwellings of priests or Levites. Blessed, therefore, is the one who shows himself to be such and is found perfect in all those things that Jesus commands, so that he may receive from Jesus a share in the heavenly dwelling in the future. Concerning this the Lord Jesus himself says: “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me; and just as I am in you and you are in me, so we are one, and they may be one in us” (John 17).

If, hearing that the Lord is called the inheritance of the perfect and the eminent, you do not understand or inquire what is signified by this name, hear that the Lord is wisdom. To the one, then, to whom the Lord is said to be an inheritance, that person receives an inheritance of wisdom. The Lord is called righteousness; therefore, the one for whom the Lord is an inheritance obtains an inheritance of righteousness. The Lord is peace; the Lord is redemption; the Lord is salvation; “in the Lord are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. 2). Whoever has the Lord as his inheritance will receive all these things as an inheritance.

Nevertheless, even those for whom the wisdom of God, the Word of God, the truth, and righteousness are said to be an inheritance receive for the present a dwelling together with those whose inheritance is held on earth, so that through their association those who are not yet able by themselves to become participants in the wisdom and knowledge of God, his truth and Word, may do so.

Thus divine administration extends even to the least. Those who are not principally able to become capable of divine grace may deserve to be enlightened through the fellowship of the saints, and what the Apostle says to the Corinthians concerning the saints of Jerusalem may be fulfilled: “That your abundance may become a provision for their need, so that their abundance may become a provision for your need” (2 Cor. 8).

Thus now, too, Levites and priests who possess no land are commanded to dwell together, so that the priest and Levite may receive from the Israelite the earthly things they do not possess, and, in turn, the Israelite may receive from the priest and Levite the heavenly and divine things he does not possess.

For the law of God has been entrusted to priests and Levites, so that they may devote themselves to this alone and be free from every concern for the Word of God. But, so that they may be free for this, they must use the services of the laity.

If the layperson does not provide the priests and Levites with what is necessary, they, occupied with such matters—that is, with bodily concerns—will devote less time to the law of God. If they do not have leisure and do not attend to the law of God, you will be in danger. For the light of knowledge that is in them will be darkened because you did not supply oil for the lamp, and through your fault what the Lord said will come about: “The blind leading the blind, both will fall into a pit.”

The further saying of the Lord will also be fulfilled: “If the light that is in you is darkness, how great is that darkness!” Therefore, so that the light of knowledge may shine in priests, let their lamp always be lit. Perform your duty; fulfill God’s command concerning service to the priests.

But if, after receiving from you what is necessary, they nevertheless neglect to devote themselves to learning, to being free for the Word of God, and to meditating on the law of God day and night—though they received these things not as avarice but as a blessing—they themselves will see how they must render an account to the Lord for your souls.

“They shall eat the sacrifice for sin and for guilt, or for ignorance, and every vow or separated offering [Col. 1019A] in Israel shall belong to them. The firstfruits of all the firstborn, and all the libations from everything that is offered, shall belong to the priests. And you shall give the firstfruits of your foods to the priest, so that he may store up a blessing for his house—or, alternatively, so that he may place blessings upon your houses.”

(Hieronymus.) One must consider that everything the Lord now speaks through the prophet he had already spoken through Moses, and one must ask why he repeats the same things that had been said. It is so that what has been erased from human minds through negligence in reading, contempt in hearing, or forgetfulness may be renewed by the living voice—not written with pen and ink, but with the Spirit and Word of God.

Hence the Savior left no volume of his teaching of his own, although the ravings of many apocryphal writings fabricate such a thing. Rather, through his own Spirit and that of the Father, he speaks daily in the hearts of believers. This will be the answer to those who criticize the prophets, asking why they repeat in their books matters contained in the Pentateuch.

(Isidore.) The legislator omitted nothing that was necessary. He indicated differences in ways of life and showed us, in the offering of sacrifices, the paths by which we ought to conduct ourselves. After this he necessarily explains the sacrifice of Christ, through which the remission and redemption of sins have been granted to us.

(Hieronymus.) The priests, therefore, shall eat the sacrifice for sin, for guilt, or for ignorance, concerning whom it is said: “They shall eat the sins of my people” (Hos. 4). One should not rejoice so much at the offering of gifts as fear condemnation in relation to one’s dignity, if one abuses it unworthily.

In the literal sense, the firstborn and firstfruits are the first creatures, both animate and inanimate, to be born, and the first things that the earth produces. The firstfruits of our foods are also offered to the priests, so that we taste none of the new harvest except what the priest has tasted first.

We do this so that the priest may store our blessing and offering in his house, or so that, in response to his prayer, the Lord may bless our houses. Great is the dignity of priests, but great also is their ruin if they sin. We rejoice at ascent, but let us fear the fall. It is not as great a joy to have held lofty things as it is a sorrow to have fallen from higher ones.

For we shall render an account not only for our own sins but also for those whose gifts we misuse and for whose salvation we are not at all concerned.

(Adamantius.) From all sanctified fruits, therefore, holy firstfruits must be offered to the spiritual high priest. From what fruits, then, shall we offer spiritual firstfruits? Hear which fruits the Apostle enumerates: “The fruit of the Spirit,” he says, “is love, joy, peace, patience,” and so forth (Gal. 5).

What firstfruits, then, shall I offer to the true high priest from the fruit of love, which is the first fruit of the Spirit? I think that the firstfruits of love are these: that I love the Lord my God with all my heart, and with all my soul, and with all my mind (Matt. 22). These are the firstfruits.

What is the second thing I ought to have from this fruit of love? That I love my neighbor as myself. These [Col. 1020A] firstfruits of love are offered to God through the High Priest; those that come second are left for my own use.

I think there is still something from the fruit that ought to be held in third place: that I love even my enemies. See whether you can similarly find corresponding firstfruits among the other fruits of the Spirit.

Joy is written as the second fruit of the Spirit. If, then, I rejoice in the Lord, rejoice in hope, and rejoice when I suffer insults for the name of the Lord, in all these things and in others like them I have offered the firstfruits of joy to God through the true High Priest.

Likewise, if I endure with joy the plundering of my possessions, and if I tolerate with joy tribulations, poverty, or any kind of insult, this too is a fruit of joy, second among the fruits of the Spirit [Col. 1020B]. For if I rejoice in worldly matters, honors, and riches, these joys are false, arising from vanities of vanities. But if I rejoice in evils, and exult in the downfall of others, these are not only empty but also diabolical joys; indeed, they should not be called joys at all: “There is no rejoicing for the impious, says the Lord” (Isa. 48).

Thus, in both the Old and New Testaments, the ministers of the altar and the servants of the Lord’s temple are commanded to obtain nourishment from the abundance of offerings and the giving of tithes; nor are they permitted in any way to covet the acquisition of earthly possessions.

Hence, in the Gospel, the Lord commanded the apostles and preachers of the Gospel, saying: “Go and preach, saying that the kingdom of heaven is near. Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons [Col. 1020C]. You received freely; give freely. Do not possess gold, silver, or money in your belts; no bag for the journey, nor two tunics, nor sandals, nor a staff. For the laborer is worthy of his food” (Matt. 10).

Hence Paul also says to the Corinthians: “Do you not know that those who work in the sanctuary eat what comes from the sanctuary, and those who serve the altar share with the altar?” (1 Cor. 9). Thus the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel.

Hence, writing to Timothy, he says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself. And the one who competes in the contest is not crowned unless he competes lawfully” (2 Tim. 2). “The farmer who labors ought first to receive from the fruits” [Col. 1020D].

For it is not fitting that one who ought always to stand at the divine office should occupy himself with acquiring earthly profit. If someone asks what the tithes signify mystically, let him know that in them one may understand observance of the law, or the integrity of Catholic faith, or the perfection of good works. This is especially appropriate for those who ought to offer God a special service according to the election by which they have been chosen for divine ministry.

For in the number ten the knowledge of creature and Creator is comprehended, since the number seven refers to human nature, with the three showing the powers of the soul. Hence it is written in Deuteronomy: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Deut. 6). The body, however, consists of the four well-known elements. If to this number seven you add the number three, expressing faith in and confession of the holy Trinity, you will properly complete the number ten.

“The priests shall not eat any carcass or anything torn by beasts, whether of birds or cattle.”

(Hieronymus.) In the literal sense these commandments apply to the whole chosen, royal, and priestly race, which properly refers to Christians who have been anointed with spiritual oil, concerning which it is written: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44). They are commanded not to eat a carcass, whether of birds or cattle, whose blood has not been poured out—what is called “strangled” in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 15), and what the letter of the apostles from Jerusalem commands us necessarily to observe.

“And anything torn by beasts,” because this too has likewise been strangled. The command condemns priests who, through greed of the appetite, do not observe this rule concerning thrushes, fig-peckers, dormice, and other such creatures.

According to the allegorical sense (*anagoge*), however, we can call “a carcass” one in whom the blood of the soul has died, one who imitates Nabal of Carmel—whose name is interpreted as “fool”—who, after hearing of David’s anger, trembled with fear, and whose heart died within him (1 Sam. 25).

But “one torn by beasts,” concerning whom the Prophet sighs lest he be torn by their bites, saying, “Do not hand over to the beasts the soul that confesses you” (Ps. 73), is the one devoured by the bites of the adversary, the lion, and of the leopard, which does not change its spots, and of the bear raging over its stolen cubs, and by the fury of wolves and the other beasts whom we understand as a variety of demons.

We shall call “birds” those “who set their mouth against heaven”; and “cattle” those that bend down toward the earth and serve only the belly and the things beneath the belly.

(Isidore.) Again, we can understand “a carcass” as a sinner, since he endures the cruel death of sin; and “one torn by beasts” as not merely an ordinary sinner but a very great sinner, to such an extent that evil demons work in him. Such was Judas, who, when the devil entered his heart, handed Christ over, as we said previously when the legislator explained sacrifices of pollution.

There he says that the one who touched carcasses or things torn by beasts—that is, the one who shared or participated with those mentioned above—must wash his garments and his body. Here, however, he speaks of the one who eats, namely, the one who has made the whole of another’s sin his own and fulfilled his own evil intention through the evil that the other committed.

Such were Annas and Caiaphas, who did not merely become participants in Judas’s betrayal. They themselves bought him and gave him money for the betrayal; and, being hungry for or desiring the Lord’s death in order to feed and nourish their own intention and satisfy their desire, they prevailed through Judas.

Those who eat carcasses or things torn by beasts of this kind are said to have to wash their garments and their body. One washes one’s garment and body when one cleanses oneself entirely, both the inner and the outer person, because the body is inside the garment just as the inner person is inside the outer person.

How does one wash? Either through baptism or through an abundance of tears resembling the waters of baptism. Whoever does not do this will bear his own iniquity—that is, the recompense for his injustice. For you will find divine Scripture threatening to repay sins with punishments. Hence Ezekiel introduces God saying: “My eye will not spare you, and I will not have mercy; but I will place your ways upon you, and your abominations shall be in your midst” (Ezek. 6).

## CHAPTER XLV. Concerning the sanctified place in which are the Holy of Holies and the dwelling of the saints; concerning justice in weights and measures; concerning the quantity of the firstfruits; concerning the two first solemnities of the first month, which are not in the Law; concerning the offerings of Passover, Pentecost, and the Feast of Booths.

“‘And when you begin to divide the land as a possession, set apart for the Lord a sacred portion of the land, twenty-five thousand in length and ten thousand in width. It shall be sacred throughout all its boundaries on every side. And from this sacred portion there shall be a square, five hundred by five hundred, on all four sides, with fifty cubits of open land around it. And from this measure you shall measure a length of twenty-five thousand and a width of ten thousand. In it shall be the temple and the holy of holies: the sacred portion of the land shall belong to the priests, the ministers of the sanctuary who approach the Lord’s ministry. And it shall be their place for houses and for the sanctuary of holiness, twenty-five thousand in length [Col. 1022C] and ten thousand in width. The Levites who minister in the house shall themselves possess twenty chambers. And you shall give the city as a possession five thousand in width and twenty-five thousand in length, corresponding to the sacred portion, for the whole house of Israel. And for the prince likewise, on both sides, from the separation or firstfruits of the sanctuary and from the city’s possession, opposite the face of the sanctuary’s separation and opposite the face of the city’s possession, from the seaward side as far as the sea and from the eastern side as far as the east, there shall be for him a possession in Israel, its length alongside each portion extending from the western boundary to the eastern boundary of the land. And my princes shall no longer oppress my people, but they shall give the land [Col. 1022D] to Israel according to their tribes.’”

(Jerome.) After the ceremonies of the priests, their worship, and the food which they ought to eat or avoid, he now gives a description of the holy land. Before dividing it entirely among the tribes, he commands that a place be selected from all the tribes having a length of twenty-five thousand and a width of ten thousand. Since it is not stated whether these measures are cubits, feet, or ells, it is understood to signify the measuring reed that was in the man’s hand and was six cubits and a sixth part of a cubit long—that is, a παλαιστήν [palastēn, a handbreadth]. Let the diligent reader calculate how many thousand paces these reeds make, and how many thousands there were in length and width.

After this description [Col. 1023A] he again commands that, from the sacred land selected from all the tribes of Israel—that is, twenty-five thousand reeds in length and ten thousand in width—another area be selected for building the sanctuary, that is, the temple of the Lord: an inner tract of land measuring five hundred reeds on every side, or two thousand in total. And lest other buildings perhaps be joined to the temple’s construction, he commands that the land be left vacant for fifty cubits around it, in the suburbs—or, as Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and the Septuagint translated it, “as a boundary, separation, and open space.”

When this description has been completed, another measure of sacred separation is commanded: a length of twenty-five thousand reeds and a width of ten thousand. Beyond the former measure, another tract of land [Col. 1023B] is to be measured, in which there is by no means a temple—that is, a holy place—but what is holy and the holy of holies: “And the priests who approach the Lord’s ministry shall dwell in it.” They shall dwell there during the time when they are performing their priestly office. It shall be, as we have said, a possession twenty-five thousand reeds in length and ten thousand in width.

The Levites, moreover, who serve the priests and have their own ministries, shall receive a place in which to build twenty chambers: according to Aquila, exedras; according to Symmachus, bedrooms; according to Theodotion, gazeras; or, as the Septuagint translated it, a city. By this we understand that a certain separate place for the habitation of the Levites is called by the name “city”; this place shall have five thousand reeds in width and twenty-five [Col. 1023C] thousand in length.

All these things—that is, the sanctuary and the other sanctuary, the holy place and the holy of holies, the dwellings of the priests, and the houses of the Levites who minister to the priests—are called separated and consecrated places, for ministry and sanctification, for the house of Israel.

After the fourfold description of the holy land, a fifth division is introduced. The prince or leader of the people shall receive on both sides—that is, on either side of the sanctuary—a possession for himself, and he shall reside in the city. His possession shall face the place separated for the temple and the face of the city; it shall extend from the side of the sea, that is, from the west, to the other side of the sea, having the width which the Prophet later describes in the account of the individual tribes.

Then it follows: “In length, alongside each portion which the individual tribes receive, from the western boundary,” that is, from the sea, “to the eastern boundary,” whose endpoint we shall learn from the description of the tribes. This shall be the possession of the leader or prince in the land of Israel.

For the present, let these remarks suffice, so that the plain historical meaning may be understood. But if we wish to compare spiritual things with spiritual things and, following certain interpreters, ascend to higher realities—those who assert that present things are a figure of future things and that everything spoken of pertains to the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the mother of us all, and to the church of the firstborn—it will not indeed be difficult to repeat what others have said, but we fear that a prudent reader may not accept such an interpretation. Therefore [Col. 1024A] everything must for the present be referred to the present time, to the Church which now labors in the world and hastens toward heavenly things. From the whole world, some are to be chosen as God’s possession, those who possess the holy place; others, who have advanced to greater things, are to hold the holy of holies.

Among the ministers also there is a different order of priests and Levites. Some offer sacrifices to God daily through their prayers and virtues; others occupy a second and lower rank, serving these and serving through those who have climbed to the summit of virtues.

Finally, there is to be a leader or prince so capable that he receives a possession opposite one tribe and that the merit of one compensates for the merits of many. At first, while he remains in the world, he is to possess a width extending from sea to sea. Then, from the west [Col. 1024B] or sea to the east, he is to abandon present things and hasten toward the future, possessing his own definite inheritance.

Let the princes by no means desire what belongs to others, and let each tribe retain its own portion. This can properly be applied to bishops and presbyters, to whom it is said that they must not further ravage or plunder God’s people, nor possess the land of Israel as an inheritance. Let each one have his own possession, established according to his rank.

The twenty-five thousand refer to the senses, since this number is set down four times. The ten thousand refer to perfect knowledge, so that in one case only the simple history is retained, while in the other there is also discussion of θεολογία [theologia, theology] and heavenly virtues, because ten is a perfect number.

This too must be considered: the priests, [Col. 1024C] who have been established in the higher rank, possess twenty-five thousand in length and ten thousand in width. The Levites, however—that is, the lower rank—have the same number in length, namely twenty-five thousand, but their width ends with the number five. Hence they possess only twenty chambers, the number in which Esau’s gifts are offered.

The prince who is truly prince among the people and deserves to receive the name of leader takes his possession on both sides of the sanctuary, namely from all those who are subject to him by their will. He is an inhabitant of the city and makes the salvation of many his own reward.

In the first temple, which is called the sanctuary, five hundred reeds are described on each side, and again fifty cubits, by which the whole possession of the priests is separated. In the second sanctuary, where the holy of holies is located, the width and extent of the temple are not described, but the number is uncertain. We find the same in the prince’s possession: he has a possession among the people of Israel without any stated number, since the progress of all redounds to the prince, and the salvation of the disciples is the teachers’ reward.

“‘Thus says the Lord God: Let it be enough for you, princes of Israel; cease from iniquity and robbery, and practice judgment and righteousness. Separate your boundaries from my people,’ says the Lord God.”

(Jerome.) Instead of “robbery,” the Septuagint translated “misery”; instead of “boundaries,” “oppression.”

The meaning is this: You who have received your portion, O princes—since Scripture says that the prince shall also receive a possession on both sides, in the sacred separation of the sanctuary and in the city—you shall give it, as is understood. Your power is so great that your possession has taken a portion belonging to one tribe. Therefore I command and admonish you: let it be enough that you have committed iniquity and robbery up to this point, while you invade and plunder what belongs to others.

And because it is written, “Turn away from evil and do good” (1 Pet. III), conversely: “Practice judgment and righteousness,” judging orphans and justifying widows. “Separate your boundaries from my people,” so that you do not move the landmarks, and because mere proximity injures the weaker person, who cannot withstand the arrogance of the greater and more powerful.

Hence Isaiah says: “Woe to you who join house to house and unite field to field, even to the boundary of the place. Will you alone inhabit the earth?” (Isa. V.) What madness it is, when houses are needed to keep out the rain and fields to sow crops, to desire to possess so much that you cannot inhabit it all, cannot cultivate it all, and turn another person’s need into your pleasure.

According to the tropological interpretation, some think that this was said against heretics. When they have moved their feet from the east, they come to the plain of Shinar, which is interpreted as “shaking of teeth,” and build a city of confusion and a tower of pride. These people join houses to houses—that is, doctrines to doctrines. Through Micah they are told: “Do not build in the house of derision” (Mic. VII), lest upon the foundation of Christ, which the apostle Paul laid (1 Cor. III), [Col. 1025C] and upon which they ought to build gold, silver, and precious stones, they instead build wood, hay, and straw, whose end is burning.

Concerning such houses the Savior speaks in the Gospel: “Everyone who hears my words and does not do them will be like a foolish man who builds his house upon sand. The rain descended, the rivers came, the winds blew, and struck that house, and it fell; and great was the ruin of that house.”

The heretics continue joining new things to old and changing the same things into newer ones until both human understanding and speech fail. Let this suffice for the present concerning the people of that time and concerning heretics.

Moreover, this command can also be applied to our own princes, who, after the manner of Pharaoh and the Egyptians, oppress the sons of Israel through their power (Exod. II), and do not remember what is written: “They have appointed you leader; do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them” (Ecclus. XXXII).

And there is also what the Lord says in the Gospel: “But if that servant says in his heart, ‘My master is delaying his coming,’ and begins to strike the servants and maidservants, to eat and drink and become drunk, the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know; and he will divide him and appoint his portion with the unbelievers” (Matt. XXIV; Luke XII).

He also teaches his disciples these commandments in the Gospel: “You know that the rulers of the nations lord it over them, and those who are greater exercise authority over them. It shall not be so among you. But whoever wishes to become great among you [Col. 1026A] shall be your servant” (Matt. X; Luke XXII). And whoever wishes to be first shall be the servant of all. Just as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.

There is much more that I could recall from the sacred Scriptures, where the pride of the great is restrained and all masters are summoned to humility by him who says, “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart.”

“‘A just balance, a just ephah, and a just bath shall be yours. The ephah and the bath shall be equal and of one measure, so that the bath contains a tenth part of a kor, and the ephah a tenth part of a kor; their proportion shall correspond to the measure of the kor. The shekel contains twenty obols. Moreover, twenty shekels, twenty-five shekels, and fifteen shekels make a mina.’”

(Jerome.) Let us speak according to the Hebrew text and the literal meaning, and explain more clearly what seems to us to be intended in each detail.

The balance, called in Hebrew mozene, is understood in relation to things that are weighed. The ephah, which in Greek is corruptly called ephi, refers to the measure of various grains—for example, wheat, barley, and legumes. The bath, called in Hebrew bati, is the same measure as the ephah, but applies specifically to liquids such as wine, oil, and similar substances.

The kor contains thirty modii and is the basic measure in both categories, that is, for both dry and liquid substances. A tenth of a kor, for things measured by the modius, is called an ephah, that is, three modii; and a tenth of a kor for liquids is called a bath, or vadus, so that the ephah and the bath are the same measure.

(Maurus.) Hence in the Law it is commanded (Lev. VI; Exod. XXIX): “A tenth part of an ephah mixed with oil,” which will measure a quarter of a hin, “and a libation of wine of the same measure” is to be offered as a burnt offering.

The measure of the ephah, which contains three of these other measures, signifies faith in the Holy Trinity. We are commanded to offer a tenth of it—that is, belief in Christ’s incarnation, which the Law commends to us in the fullest manner—or observance of the Decalogue itself. We are likewise commanded to offer oil, that is, charity and mercy. We are also commanded to offer wine for a libation, that is, spiritual grace or participation in Christ’s passion; and all this according to the division of the measure of the hin, that is, according to the distribution of perfect devotion.

(Jerome.) The shekel, called in Greek a stater, contains twenty obols. The mina, called mna, contains sixty shekels, which make twelve hundred obols.

What is said—that twenty shekels, twenty-five shekels, and fifteen shekels make a mina—should not disturb the reader. The difficulty is introduced into the numbers precisely to engage the hearer’s attentive mind. Hence many things are said in parables and riddles, “so that whoever has ears to hear may hear” (Matt. XI). Every prophecy contains the truth under obscurity, so that the disciples may hear inwardly, while the ignoble crowd outside does not know what is being said.

Therefore divine Scripture commands that weights be just, saying: “There shall not be in your purse a greater and a lesser measure; a true and just balance shall be yours, and a true [Col. 1027A] and just measure shall be yours” (Lev. XIX). And in Proverbs it says: “A greater and a lesser balance, both are abominable in the sight of God” (Prov. XI).

This must be observed not only in commerce and in the ordinary affairs of daily life, but justice must be maintained in everything. Scripture says: “You shall make a balance and a counterweight for your words,” so that in our speech, actions, and thoughts we may do everything with weight and reason.

We read elsewhere that an obol—that is, a twentieth part of a shekel or stater—is the smallest portion: “The whole world is the wealth of the faithful; for the unbeliever, not even an obol,” as though he had said in other words: the unbeliever possesses nothing in speech and lacks even the smallest portion.

Concerning this another saying occurs in the Gospel: “He will not come out from there until he has repaid the last quadrans” (Matt. V), that is, even the final and smallest coin.

We read that ten minas were entrusted to individual servants for trading. In another parable talents were divided among servants; there is also the debtor of five hundred denarii and of fifty, the laborers in the vineyard who each receive a denarius, and the widow who lost a drachma and scarcely found it after lighting a lamp (Luke XIV; Matt. XXV; Luke VII; Matt. XX; Luke XV). It is not for the present occasion to discuss what meaning all these things have.

“‘And these are the firstfruits which you shall take: a sixth part of an ephah from a kor of wheat, and a sixth part of an ephah from a kor of barley. The measure of oil also: a bath of oil is a tenth part of a kor, and ten baths make a kor, because ten baths fill a kor.’”

(Jerome.) Let us first speak according to the literal meaning. The people owed the Levitical tribe the δέκαδες [dekades], that is, the tenth part of all produce, by the commandment of the Law. Again, from these tithes the Levites—that is, the lower rank of ministers—gave tithes to the priests; this was called the Δευτεροδέκαδη [Deuterodekadē, second tithe].

There were also other tithes which each person among the people of Israel set apart in his storehouses, so that he might eat them when he went to the temple in the city of Jerusalem and, in the temple vestibule, invite priests and Levites to banquets. There were still other tithes which they stored for the poor.

The firstfruits, however, which they offered from their crops, were not fixed by any specific number but were left to the discretion of those making the offering. We have received the tradition of the Hebrews—not commanded by the Law, but established by the judgment of the teachers—that the person giving most offered a fortieth part to the priests, while the person giving least offered a sixtieth; between a fortieth and a sixtieth, they were permitted to offer whatever they wished.

What was therefore left uncertain in the Pentateuch is here specifically defined because of the priests’ avarice, so that they may not demand more from the people when firstfruits are brought: namely, that they offer a sixtieth part of what the earth produces.

For if the kor, called in Hebrew omer and by the Septuagint κόρος [koros], contains thirty modii both for dry substances and for liquids, and if the ephah and the bath, as we said above, are a tenth part of a kor, and if a sixth of both the ephah and the bath is commanded to be given to the priests [Col. 1028A] as firstfruits, then it is clearly calculated that the priests should receive one sixtieth as firstfruits, since this amounts to half a modius from three modii.

For the present, let it suffice that we have both understood and heard these things according to the literal meaning and according to the Hebrew truth. Let us now return to the spiritual understanding.

First, we must ask how it is said: “Honor the Lord from your just labors, and give him from the fruits of your righteousness, so that your storehouses may be filled with grain and your winepresses overflow with wine” (Prov. III). After you have offered the firstfruits of your labors and virtues and have said, “Behold, now I have brought you the firstfruits of the land, which you gave me, Lord,” may you deserve to hear: “Blessed are you in the city, and blessed are you in the field; blessed are the fruit of your womb, and the produce of your land, and the offspring of your cattle,” and so forth (Deut. XXVIII).

According to the Apostle (Eph. I), may you possess every blessing of spiritual things in the heavenly places in Christ, since whatever you have you do not consider to be your own virtue but the mercy of him who gave the crops.

If we have such knowledge of the Scriptures that we can disclose and teach people—meaning the rational creature—mystical things, we give the firstfruits of our wheat. But if, after a pure anagoge, we follow only the history, which can nourish the simple, according to what is written, “You will save humans and beasts, O Lord,” we give the firstfruits of our barley.

Isaac too sowed barley, but in the land of foreigners, and it produced a hundredfold. Whoever gives the firstfruits of barley can say: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing; he has settled me in a place of pasture; he has led me beside waters of refreshment” (Ps. XXII).

But whoever feeds rational animals changes the statement and says: “You have prepared a table before me against those who trouble me” (Ps. XXII).

After offering the firstfruits of oil and wine, he adds and says: “You have anointed my head with oil, and how excellent is your inebriating cup!” (ibid.), with that oil which, without sediment and exceedingly pure, is prepared for the Lord’s lamp.

Whoever prepares it has his face brightened with oil, with the oil of gladness with which Christ was anointed above his companions (Ps. XLIV). Having become an olive tree, he will sing with the prophet: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord” (Ps. LI).

And he will offer that wine which overflows from the winepresses of the Savior, as the Lord says: “I am the vine, you are the branches, and my Father is the farmer” (John XV).

We read three psalms concerning these winepresses: the eighth, the eightieth, and the eighty-third; all of them refer to the mysteries of the Church.

In the ancient Law, the firstfruits were without measure or number: “For God did not give the Spirit by measure” (John III). In the second building of the temple, which the prophecy of Ezekiel contains, there is a fixed measure, namely the number sixty, by which the world is completed, as it is said to us: “With whatever measure you measure, it shall be measured back to you” (Matt. VII).

“‘And one ram from a flock of two hundred, from those which Israel has nourished, for a sacrifice, and for a burnt offering, and for a peace offering, to make atonement for them, says the Lord God. All the people of the land shall be obliged to offer these firstfruits to the prince in Israel. And upon the prince shall fall the burnt offerings, the sacrifice, and the libations on the solemnities, on the New Moons, and on the Sabbaths, at all the solemnities of the house of Israel. He shall offer for sin the sacrifice, the burnt offering, and the peace offerings, to make atonement for the house of Israel.’”

Above he said what proportion of weighed things, and what measure of both dry and liquid substances, ought to be offered to the prince. Now he applies the same order of firstfruits to animals, commanding that one ram from a flock of two hundred be offered—animals which Israel nourishes—for a sacrifice, a burnt offering, and a peace offering, to make atonement for the people, says the Lord God.

What we translated as “from those which Israel has nourished” is written in Hebrew as memmasce. Aquila and Symmachus interpret it as ἀπὸ τῶν ὑδάτων [apo tōn hydatōn, “from the waters”]; the Septuagint and Theodotion as ἀπὸ τῶν ποτιστηρίων [apo tōn potistēriōn, “from the watering places”]. The first expression refers to irrigated places, the second to channels or pools, so that the prince’s firstfruits are nourished nowhere except in irrigated places.

Just as above we read that a sixtieth part should be offered to the prince from things that are weighed and measured, so now a two-hundredth part of the animals is commanded to be offered. The whole people are subject to such legal commands, so that they offer to the leader or prince what is offered through him as burnt offerings, sacrifices, and libations at each solemnity on behalf of the people, and so that the house of God may be expiated.

From this we should observe that just as the people are obligated to offer firstfruits to the prince, so the prince is obligated to offer victims on behalf of the people. According to the tropological interpretation, we can understand this prince as none other than the Lord Savior.

He receives a ram from two hundred animals—or, as the Hebrew expression more significantly indicates, βόκκημα [bokkēma], which can refer to every kind of animal and not specifically to a ram. He receives an animal or ram that has been nourished in irrigated places, namely in the sacred Scriptures, and he can say: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing; he has settled me in a place of pasture; he has led me beside waters of refreshment” (Ps. XXII).

These were irrigated places, indeed channels, to which Jacob led his flocks so that they might drink and conceive there and produce offspring marked according to the colors of the rods for the Lord (Gen. XXX).

For a sacrifice, Aquila and Symmachus interpret the term as “gift.” In Hebrew it is called Manaa, and it properly does not refer to a victim but to things offered in sacrifice from fine flour, meal, and oil. A burnt offering is what is offered wholly to God and consumed by sacred fire.

Peace offerings are offered when we are reconciled to God, and the Apostle speaks on our behalf: “We entreat you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God” (2 Cor. V). And elsewhere: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (ibid.).

This prince, to whom the firstfruits from the animals are offered, is also the king, as is shown even in the title of the cross, written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin letters. When the Jews insisted that the triumphal title be removed, the throng of the nations, in Pilate, answered, “What I have written, I have written.”

“‘They shall be under the prince,’” he says (John XIX).

The priestly dignity is fittingly reminded to what office it is subject, so that it may know that at all solemnities it ought to offer on behalf of the people the sacrifice and libations offered from the earth, both on the New Moons—that is, the neomeniae—and on the Sabbaths, when, with darkness covering all things, the beginning of lunar light appears.

And during the rest of the Sabbaths, it is to offer for sin, to make atonement for the house of Israel, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of truth. This is the house of the living God and the house of Israel, which needs expiation for its sins.

Since, therefore, we have the laws of the festivals in our hands and our discussion now concerns them, let us examine more carefully what the order of the festivals is, so that from their order and the rite of the sacrifices we may gather how each person can prepare a festival for holy God through his own actions and conduct.

The first festival of God is the one called unceasing. For commands are given concerning sacrifices that are to be offered unceasingly and without any interruption at all, in the morning and in the evening.

In prescribing the rites of the festivals, he does not immediately come first to the festival of Passover, or to Unleavened Bread, or to the Feast of Booths, or to the other festivals concerning which commands are given. Instead, he places first the festival in which he commands an unceasing sacrifice to be offered, so that whoever wishes to be perfect and holy may understand that a festival is not to be observed for God at one time and not observed at another, but that the righteous person must always and unceasingly keep the festival.

The sacrifice which is commanded to be offered continually, both in the morning and in the evening, indicates that one must persist with unceasing devotion both in the Law and the Prophets, which signify the morning time, and in evangelical teaching, which signifies the evening—that is, the Savior’s advent at the evening of the world.

Thus the Lord says concerning such festivals: “And you shall observe my festival days.” The Lord’s festival day, therefore, is present if we offer him an unceasing sacrifice and pray without interruption, so that our prayer may rise before him like incense in the morning and the lifting of our hands may become an evening sacrifice for him (Ps. CXL).

The first solemnity, then, is that of perpetual or unceasing sacrifice. Those who worship the Gospel ought to fulfill it in the manner explained above.

But since, as the prophetic word thoroughly teaches (Amos VII), the festival days of sinners are turned into mourning and their songs into lamentation, it is certain that one who belongs to sin and observes the day of sin cannot observe a festival day. Therefore, on the days when he sins, he cannot offer an unceasing sacrifice to God.

The person who can offer it is the one who unceasingly guards righteousness and preserves himself from sin. On whatever day he interrupts this and sins, it is certain that on that day he does not offer an unceasing sacrifice to God.

What is the festival of the Sabbath except that of which the Apostle says: “Therefore a sabbatism remains, that is, an observance of the Sabbath, for the people of God” (Heb. IV)?

Let us therefore leave behind the Jewish observances of the Sabbath and see what the Christian observance of the Sabbath ought to be.

On the Sabbath day one ought to perform none of the ordinary works of the world. If, therefore, you cease from all secular works and do nothing worldly, but devote yourself to spiritual works; if you assemble in church, lend your ear to divine readings and teachings, think of heavenly things, concern yourself with the future hope, keep the coming judgment before your eyes, and look not to present and visible things but to invisible and future things—this is the observance of the Sabbath for the Christian.

But the Jews too ought to observe these things. Indeed, even among them, if someone is a smith, a builder, or engaged in any such craft, he rests on the Sabbath day. But the reader of the divine Law or the teacher does not cease from good work, and yet he does not profane the Sabbath. For he says to them: “Have you not read that the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath and are without guilt?” (Matt. XII.)’”

Therefore, the one who has ceased from worldly works and devotes himself to spiritual activities is the one who celebrates the sabbath sacrifice and the festal day of the sabbaths. Nor does he carry burdens on the way. For every sin is a burden, as the Prophet also says: “Like a heavy burden, they have become too heavy for me” (Ps. 38). Nor does he kindle that fire—namely, the fire of which it is said: “Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame that you have kindled; each one of you” (Isa. 50). But he also remains in his own place and does not go out from it. What, then, is his place? The spiritual soul, surely. Righteousness is his place, truth, wisdom, sanctification, and everything that Christ is: Christ is the place of the soul. From this place it must not depart, if it is to keep the true sabbaths and celebrate the festal day in the sacrifices of the sabbaths, as the Lord also said: “The one who remains in me, and I in him” (John 15).

But when we speak of true sabbaths, if we inquire more deeply into what the true sabbaths are, the true observance of the sabbath lies beyond this world. For what is written in Genesis (Gen. 2)—that God rested on the sabbath day from his works—we do not see as having happened then, on the seventh day, or as happening even now. We always see God at work, and there is no sabbath on which God does not work, on which he does not make his sun rise over good and evil and rain upon the just and the unjust (Matt. 5); “on which he does not produce grass on the mountains and plants for the service of human beings” (Ps. 146); on which he does not strike and heal, bring down to the underworld and bring back; on which he does not kill and make alive.

Hence, when the Jews objected to him concerning work and healing on the sabbath, the Lord also replied to them in the Gospels: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5). By this he showed that God rests on no sabbath of this present age, either from the administration of the world or from his providential care for the human race. For at the beginning he created the creatures and brought forth as many substances as he knew, as the creator of all things, would suffice for the perfection of the world; but until the consummation of the age he does not cease providing for and ordering them.

There will therefore be a true sabbath on which God will rest from all his works: the age to come, when pain, sorrow, and groaning will flee away, and God will be all things in all. On that sabbath may God grant us also to celebrate a festal day with him and to keep the festivals with his holy angels, offering the sacrifice of praise and rendering our vows to the Most High. Then perhaps the unceasing sacrifice, which we explained above, will be offered more perfectly; for then the soul will be better able to stand continually before God and offer the sacrifice of praise through the great High Priest, who is a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.

The third festival is designated as the day of the New Moon, on which a sacrifice is offered, as it is written: “On the kalends”—that is, at the beginnings of the months—“you shall offer a burnt offering to the Lord,” and so forth. New Moon means the new moon. This, then, is also a festival, when the moon is renewed. It is called “new” when it has drawn near to the sun and become very closely joined to it, so that it lies hidden beneath the sun’s brightness.

But it may perhaps seem strange, indeed superfluous, that divine law should command this. For what religious observance is appropriate to the new moon—that is, when it is joined to and clings to the sun? If these matters are considered according to the letter, they will appear not so much religious as superstitious. But the Apostle Paul knew that the law does not speak about such things, and that the Holy Spirit does not command any rite that appears to be observed by Jews as holy. Therefore he said to those who had received the faith of God: “Let no one judge you in food or drink, or in respect of a festival, or of a new moon, or of a sabbath, which are shadows of things to come” (Col. 2).

If the sabbath, which we have explained above as best we could, is a shadow of things to come, and the New Moon is a shadow of things to come, it is certain that the other festivals likewise are shadows of things to come. But now let us consider the New Moon.

We have said that the festival of the New Moon is called so when the moon begins to be renewed, draws very near to the sun, and becomes completely joined to it. Christ is the Sun of righteousness. If the moon—that is, his Church, which is filled with his light—is joined to him and clings to him completely, so that, according to the Apostle’s saying, “the one who joins himself to the Lord becomes one spirit with him” (1 Cor. 6), then it celebrates the festival of the New Moon. For it becomes new when it has cast off the old human being and put on the new, “who was created according to God” (Eph. 4); and thus, by reason of its renewal, it rightly celebrates the solemnity that is the festival of the New Moon.

It is finally new when it can neither be seen nor apprehended by human eyes. For when the soul has joined itself wholly to the Lord and has wholly entered into the splendor of his light, when it thinks of nothing earthly at all, seeks nothing worldly, and does not strive to please human beings, but has wholly given itself to the light of wisdom and wholly surrendered itself to the warmth of the Holy Spirit, having become subtle and spiritual, how can it be seen by human beings or apprehended by human sight? For the merely natural person cannot understand or discern the spiritual person. Therefore it most worthily celebrates the festival and slaughters the New Moon offering to the Lord, having been renewed by him.

Fourth among the festivals of God is placed the solemnity of Passover, at which festival the lamb is slain. But you should behold the true Lamb, the Lamb of God, the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, and say: “Our Passover, Christ, has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5). Let the Jews, with their carnal understanding, eat the flesh of the lamb; let us eat the flesh of the Word of God. For he himself said: “Unless you eat my flesh, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6).

What we are saying now is the flesh of the Word of God—provided that I do not offer vegetables to you as to the weak, or nourishment of milk as to children; provided that we speak of what is complete, strong, and powerful: we set before you the flesh of the Word of God to eat. For wherever mystical discourse is brought forth, wherever there is doctrinal teaching filled with faith in the Trinity and possessing solidity, wherever the mysteries of the spiritual law are disclosed after the veil of the letter has been removed, wherever the soul’s hope is lifted from the earth and cast into the heavens, and placed among those things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor entered into the human heart” (1 Cor. 2)—all these are the flesh of the Word of God. Whoever can feed upon it with perfect understanding and a purified heart truly sacrifices the sacrifice of the Passover festivals, and celebrates the festal day with God and with his angels.

After this—or rather, as a festival joined to it—comes the festival of Unleavened Bread. You will celebrate it rightly if you drive out from your soul every leaven of malice and wickedness and keep the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Cor. 5). For we must not suppose that almighty God writes laws for human beings about leaven and commands that a soul be exterminated from the people if they should happen to be found to have a little of this leaven, mixed from flour, in their house, or that the divine majesty should have been so greatly concerned about this leaven that it declares itself offended to such an extent that it commands the soul—which he himself made in his image and likeness—to be exterminated and destroyed because of it.

This does not seem to me a fitting interpretation of the divine laws. Rather, what God rightly abhors is this: that the soul should be weakened and swollen toward wicked deeds by a spirit of malice, anger, or evil.
