God does not want such things to be in the soul, and unless we cast out such leaven from the house of our soul, we shall rightly be exterminated.

But do not despise it even if you see only a little malice fermenting within you, because “a little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (1 Cor. 5). Therefore do not neglect even a small sin, since from one sin another is generated. For just as righteousness is generated from righteousness, and chastity from chastity—for if someone first begins to be chaste in a small way, then, having received the leaven of chastity, becomes daily more chaste—so also the one who has once stored within himself, even if only a little, the leaven of malice becomes daily more wicked and worse than himself. Therefore, if you wish to celebrate the festival of Unleavened Bread with God, do not allow even a small leaven of malice to remain within you.

After this comes the sixth festival, which is called the festival of New Things, that is, the firstfruits are offered from the new produce. When a field has been sown, carefully cultivated, and the crop has reached maturity, then the festival of the Lord is celebrated in the perfection of the fruits. If you therefore wish to celebrate the day of New Things with the Lord, see how and where you sow, so that you may be able to reap such fruits as will make God rejoice and enable you to celebrate the festal day. You will not be able to fulfill this in any other way than by hearing the Apostle say: “The one who sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit” (Gal. 6).

If you sow and reap in this way, you truly celebrate the day of New Things. Therefore the Prophet also admonishes us, saying: “Renew new fields for yourselves, and do not sow upon thorns” (Hos. 10). The one who renews his heart and his inner self from day to day renews new fields for himself; he does not sow upon thorns, but upon good soil, which returns to him fruit a hundredfold, sixtyfold, or thirtyfold (Luke 8). This, then, is the one who sows in the Spirit and gathers the fruits of the Spirit. The first of all the fruits of the Spirit is joy (Gal. 5). Rightly, therefore, the one who reaps joy celebrates the festival of new fruits; especially the one who reaps peace and patience together with it, and goodness and gentleness, and gathers other fruits like these. He will most worthily celebrate the festival of new fruits before the Lord.

Then follows the festival of Weeks. For just as among the days every seventh day is observed as a sabbath and is a festival, so among the months every seventh month is a sabbath of the months. In it, therefore, the festival called the Sabbath of Sabbaths is celebrated, and on the first day of the month there is a memorial of trumpets. But who is the one who celebrates the festival of the memorial of trumpets, except the one who is able to commit to memory and store up in the treasury of his heart the prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic Scriptures, which sound as though with a certain heavenly trumpet?

The one who does this and meditates on the law of the Lord day and night (Ps. 1) celebrates the festival of the memorial of trumpets. If anyone is able to obtain those gifts of the Holy Spirit by which the prophets were inspired, and to sing: “Blow the trumpet at the beginning of the month, on the day of his notable solemnity” (Ps. 80), and knows how to exult in the Psalms, he worthily celebrates the solemnity of the trumpets before God.

There is still another festival, when they afflict their souls and humble them, though they are not celebrating festive rejoicing. O wondrous festival! A day of festivity is called the affliction of the soul. “For this,” he says, “is the day of propitiation, the tenth day of the seventh month.” You see, then, that if you wish to celebrate a festal day, if you wish God to rejoice over you, afflict your soul and humble it. Do not allow it to fulfill its desires, nor permit it to wander about wantonly; rather, as far as possible, afflict and humble it.

Finally, the festival of Passover is also said to have the bread of affliction, as does the festival of Unleavened Bread. No one can celebrate a festal day unless he has eaten the bread of affliction and eaten the Passover with bitterness. “For you shall eat unleavened bread,” he says, “with bitterness.”

You see, then, what the festivals of God are like. They do not admit bodily sweetness; they desire nothing relaxed, pleasurable, or luxurious, but demand affliction of the soul, bitterness, and humility, because “the one who humbles himself will be exalted” (Matt. 23) before God. This, therefore, is also what the day of propitiation demands. For when the soul has been afflicted and humbled before the Lord, then God will be propitious toward it; and then there comes to it the one whom God set forth as a propitiatory offering through faith in his blood: Christ Jesus, its Lord and Redeemer (1 John 2).

Now let us see what the final festal day of God is, by which God rejoices in a human being. “The Feast of Tabernacles,” he says. He rejoices over you when he sees you dwelling in tabernacles in this world; when he sees that you do not have your mind and purpose fixed and founded upon earthly things, nor desire what is earthly, nor regard the shadow of this life as your own permanent and lasting possession, but consider yourself to be placed here as in transit and hastening toward that true homeland from which you came, saying: “I am a sojourner and a pilgrim, as all my fathers were” (Ps. 38).

For the fathers also dwelt in tabernacles, and Abraham lived in huts—that is, in tabernacles—with Isaac and Jacob, heirs with him of the same promise. Therefore, when you are a sojourner and pilgrim on earth, when your mind is not fixed and rooted in earthly desires, but you are ready to pass on quickly and are always ready to stretch forward to what lies ahead, until you reach the land flowing with milk and honey (Phil. 3) and receive the inheritance of things to come—if, I say, God sees you placed in this condition, he rejoices in you and celebrates a festal day over you.

These things concern the present. But in the future, if you wish to consider how festal days are celebrated, raise your understanding a little from the earth, if you can, and for a while forget the things that appear before us. Picture for yourself how heaven and earth will pass away, and the entire present form of the world will pass away. But let a new heaven and a new earth be founded.

Remove from your sight even the light of this sun, and give to that world which is to come sevenfold the light of this sun—or rather, according to the authority of Scripture, give it the Lord himself. Set in place the light of the attending angels of glory. Set in place the Powers, Authorities, Thrones, Dominions, and every name of the most glorious heavenly powers—not only those named in the present age, but also those named in the age to come.

Among all these, consider and imagine how the festal days of the Lord can be celebrated there: what festival, what joys, what greatness of gladness there will be. For even those spiritual festivals mentioned above, although they are great and truly pre-eminent when celebrated spiritually in the soul, are nevertheless partial, not complete. The saints therefore celebrate a festal day in this world only in part, because they know in part and prophesy in part. But when what is perfect has come, these partial things will be abolished (1 Cor. 13).

For just as this partial knowledge yields to perfect knowledge, and this partial prophecy yields to perfect prophecy, so this partial festival yields to the perfect festival. For this world cannot contain what is perfect. Here, as we have said, the necessity of the body supplies now food, now drink, now sleep, and now also arouses whatever concern for the necessities of the present life may be required; all these things undoubtedly interrupt the uninterrupted continuity of God’s festival.

But when what has been spoken concerning those who will be restored among the holy ones has come—provided that we also may deserve to be among those who are restored—when they will neither hunger nor thirst nor sleep nor labor, but will be ever-watchful, as the life of the angels is said to be ever-watchful; when they deserve to be restored to that order, then there will be a true and incorruptible festival. Its prince, bridegroom, and Lord will be Jesus Christ himself, our Savior.

But having thus given a preliminary account of the individual festivals, the following book demonstrates what offerings ought to be presented and sets forth their mystical observance in a brief discourse.

# BOOK NINETEEN

[Col. 1035]

## CHAPTER XLV FOLLOWS

[Col. 1035C]

“Thus says the Lord God: In the first month, on the first day of the month, you shall take an unblemished bull from the herd, and you shall make atonement for the sanctuary. The priest shall take some of the blood of the sin offering and place it on the doorposts of the house, on the four corners of the ledge of the altar, and on the doorposts of the gate of the inner court. Thus you shall do on the seventh day of the month for everyone who sinned through ignorance and was deceived by error, and you shall make atonement for the house.

“In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, you shall have the solemnity of Passover. Unleavened bread shall be eaten for seven days. On that day the prince shall offer for himself and for all the people of the land a bull as a sin offering. During the seven-day solemnity he shall offer a burnt offering to the Lord: seven unblemished bulls and seven unblemished rams each day for seven days, and a male goat as a sin offering each day. He shall offer an ephah for each bull and an ephah for each ram, and a hin of oil for each ephah.

“In the seventh month, on the fifteenth day of the month, at the solemnity he shall do as was stated above for seven days, both for the sin offering and for the burnt offering, and with the offering and the oil.” (Jerome.)

I have set down the entire chapter, so that, if divided into separate sections, it would not disturb the reader’s mind. First, we must speak about the variety of interpretations. Where we translated “on the four corners of the ledge of the altar,” the Septuagint translated, “and upon the four corners of the temple and upon the altar.” Where we said, “for everyone who sinned through ignorance and was deceived by error,” they placed, “for the ignorant person and for the child.”

Also, where we said, “and he shall offer an ephah for the bull and an ephah for the ram, and a hin of oil for each ephah,” their edition reads: “You shall give an offering and a cooked portion for the bull, and a cooked portion for the ram, and a hin of oil for the cooked portion.” In the final verse, where we said, “with the offering and the oil,” they said, “as with the *manaa*, as with the oil.”

“In the first month,” he says, “and on the first day of the month”—there is no doubt that Nisan is signified—“you shall take a bull from the herd,” not one that has been raised at home, but one that is in the herd, that is, from the flock and the number of the many. “Also on the seventh day of that same month.” These two solemnities—the first day of the first month and the seventh day of that same month—are not found in the Mosaic Law.

But the fourteenth day of the month, on which Passover is celebrated and which Moses commands to be observed, is the time when we eat unleavened bread for seven days. The fourth solemnity, of which he says, “In the seventh month, on the fifteenth day of the month, at the solemnity,” and so forth, seems to me to signify the Feast of Tabernacles, which he has placed here without naming it.

Let us therefore proceed through each point and briefly explain what seems to us to be its meaning. The Apostle also teaches that there are spiritual solemnities: “Therefore let no one judge you in food or drink, or in respect of a solemnity, or of a new moon, or of sabbaths, which are shadows of things to come” (Col. 2). And through Isaiah God says: “I do not accept your new moons, your sabbaths, and your great day; my soul hates fasting and holidays, and your new moons and solemnities” (Isa. 1).

It is clear that the one who hates the solemnities of the Jews loves his own solemnities—namely, the sabbath that has been left for the people of God—so that we may see what has been given to us by God and speak not in words taught by human wisdom, but in the teaching of the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual things.

In the present age, which lies in wickedness, we cannot see good days, but we shall see them in the new age. Concerning these days the Holy Spirit sings in the Mosaic song: “Remember the days of old; understand the years of generation upon generation” (Deut. 32). Concerning them the holy man also spoke in the Psalm: “At night I meditated in my heart” (Ps. 76). And again: “I remembered the eternal years and meditated.”

Let the one who does not accept this understanding answer how he can explain what Isaiah prophesies about the future and new age: “There shall be month after month, and sabbath after sabbath, and all flesh shall come to worship before the Lord” (Isa. 66). Then true worshipers will worship neither on Mount Garizim nor in Jerusalem, but in spirit and truth; then there will be a new heaven and a new earth, and every creature will be freed from slavery to corruption into the freedom of the children of God, and the sun will receive seven times as much light, while the moon will be made equal to the sun.

For we have drawn near to Mount Zion, which is interpreted as “watchtower,” and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem (Heb. 12), and to thousands of angels and solemn assemblies. Concerning this solemnity another prophet also speaks: “What will you do on the days of assembly and on the days of the solemnity of the Lord?” (Hos. 9). This is what is also said elsewhere: “Celebrate your festivals, Judah; fulfill your vows” (Nahum 1).

If, then, we have learned about spiritual solemnities, we shall consequently also be taught about spiritual victims. A young bull (*vitulus*) is taken from the herd—or a bull (*taurus*), as Symmachus translated it—free and not pressed under any yoke, that is, unburdened by the weight of sins, and unblemished: “he who committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2). It is a young bull, bearing horns and hoofs, so that the sanctuary may be cleansed and atoned for in it.

“And the priest,” he says, “shall take some of its blood, which will be for the sin of all.” In other words, it is called a lamb in Exodus and in the Gospel, when John the Baptist says: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1).

The blood itself is precious—the blood in which we are redeemed through the passion of the Lord and Savior, whose flesh nourishes us and whose blood we drink. With this blood the four corners of the ledge of the altar are touched. Theodotion renders the Hebrew word itself as *azara*, or “of the temple,” as the Septuagint translated it, “so that the house and altar may be sanctified.”

For all the elements of the world are sanctified by this blood, so that when someone has been atoned for and cleansed, he may enter the gate of the inner court, become able to know the Lord’s mysteries, and then come to the seventh day of the first month, attain rest, and offer sacrifice to the Lord both for ignorance, concerning which David says, “Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorance” (Ps. 24), and for the child, who, when he reaches the measure of a mature person, will destroy the things that belong to childhood.

He speaks confidently: “When I was a child, I spoke as a child; I understood as a child” (1 Cor. 13). Or this refers to the one who has been deceived by error and sinned not so much deliberately as through a mistaken view of what was good.

When the two solemnities of the first month have been completed—that is, those of its first and seventh days—we come to the fourteenth day of the month, on which the solemnity of Passover occurs, concerning which it is written: “For our Passover, Christ, has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5). Then we eat unleavened bread for seven days in rest and security from all things, destroying the leaven of malice and wickedness and eating the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, while our prince offers all these things on our behalf, and first for himself.

For he assumed a human body and, through sin, destroyed sin—he who suffers for us and bears our infirmities. Therefore he offers for his own house, which is written in the Septuagint but is not found in the Hebrew text: that is, for the Church and for all the people of the land, namely, for the entire human race. For he is the Savior of all human beings, and especially of believers; he himself is the propitiation for our sins, and not only for ours but for those of the whole world.

After the bull has been offered for all the people of the land, during the remaining seven days of the Lord’s passion, seven bulls and seven unblemished rams are offered each day, so that they may be consumed as a burnt offering by the Lord’s fire. The seven bulls and seven rams are those who are conformed to the Lord’s passion, imitating the true bull and the true ram, so that through the blood of the martyrs the sins of the whole world may be cleansed throughout the seven days. (Adamantius.)

A male goat is also offered daily as a sin offering, for seven days, that is. But if someone is found who can remove the veil placed over the reading of the Old Testament and seek from it what the true sacrifices are that purify the people on the festival days, then he will see how wondrous and magnificent are the things signified through what ignorant people regard as superfluous and superstitious.

Paul—and those like him—will have understood these matters more fully and perfectly from wisdom itself and from the Word of God. But, insofar as we can gather from their writings, in which they have given us, as it were, through a shadow and image, certain indications for our common edification, we shall attempt to examine briefly some matters concerning the rite of sacrifices.

At the festival of Passover, a lamb is written to be the one who purifies the people; in other cases, a bull, a male goat, a ram, a she-goat, or a heifer, as you have learned from what has been read. One of these animals taken for the purification of the people is the lamb, and that lamb is said to be our Lord and Savior. For John, who is greater than all the prophets, understood it in this way and marked him out, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1). (Gregory Nazianzen.)

If the lamb given for the purification of the people refers to the person of our Lord and Savior, it seems to follow that the other animals assigned to the same purposes of purification must likewise refer to certain persons who contribute something toward the purification of the human race.

Consider, therefore, whether, just as our Lord and Savior was “led like a lamb to the slaughter” (Isa. 53) and offered as a sacrifice on the altar, granting remission of sins to the whole world, so perhaps the blood of the other saints and righteous persons—“from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah the prophet, who was killed between the temple and the altar” (Matt. 23)—was poured out, one person’s blood like that of a heifer, another’s like that of a male goat or she-goat, or like that of some other such animal, to make atonement for the people in some measure.

Whether these things should be referred to the persons of the righteous and prophets who were slain in this world, or to those who say, “For your sake we are put to death all day long; we have been regarded as sheep for slaughter” (Ps. 42), who would readily dare to affirm? For these animals must not be understood as referring to one person or another according to their species, but according to figure.

The Lord Jesus Christ is not called a lamb because he was changed and transformed into the form of a lamb. Nevertheless, he is called a lamb because his will and goodness, by which he reconciled God and granted human beings forgiveness of sins, proved to be for the human race like an unblemished and innocent lamb offered in sacrifice, by which God is believed to be appeased toward human beings.

Thus, if one of the righteous here was offered for divine reconciliation like a ram, a bull, or a male goat, his sacrifice can be understood as obtaining purification for the people. Or does Paul not appear to have offered himself as a burnt offering for the people of Israel when he said: “I myself wished to be accursed from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh” (Rom. 9)?

Do you wish to know that Paul also offers himself as a victim to be slaughtered? Hear him say elsewhere: “For I am already being poured out as a sacrifice, and the time of my departure” (2 Tim. 4)—or, as we read in the Greek manuscripts, “of my return”—“is at hand.”

Thus, figuratively, it can be understood that one person is offered for the festival of New Things, another for the festival of the sabbath, and another for the festival of Tabernacles: a male goat, a bull, or a ram is offered to reconcile God to human beings. For as long as there are sins, sacrifices for sins must necessarily be sought.

Suppose, for example, that there had been no sin. If there had been no sin, it would not have been necessary for the Son of God to become a lamb, nor would it have been necessary for him, placed in the flesh, to be slaughtered; he would have remained what he was in the beginning, God the Word.

But since sin entered this world, and the necessity of sin requires propitiation, and propitiation does not occur except through a sacrifice, it was necessary that sacrifices for sin be provided. And since sin itself had different and various qualities, sacrifices of different animals were commanded—without doubt, sacrifices corresponding to the varieties of sins.

Thus one of the saints—or, as we have said, of the angels or of human beings—becomes a bull who intervenes at one festival for the offenses of the people; another becomes a ram at another festival, and through their intercession purification from sins takes place. If human beings can be purified from sins and become purer, the sacrifices also become fewer. For if sacrifices are offered for sins, and if they are multiplied in proportion to the multitude of sins, then without doubt they are also reduced in proportion to their smallness.

(Hieronymus.) We must also attend more carefully to the fact that an ephah for the bull, an ephah for the ram, and a hin of oil are offered, as the law commands. But in the offering of the male goat neither an ephah nor—according to the Septuagint translation—a cooked portion is mentioned. They translated *πέμμα* (*pemma*), that is, “cooked portion,” for “ephah.” The hin, which is a fixed measure of oil, about which we have already spoken, is included in the sacrifice of the bull and the ram, so that, after the appeasement of sins, we may receive the nourishment of everlasting light, rest from labor, and healing from weariness.

In the seventh month also, on the fifteenth day of the month—that is, at the Feast of Tabernacles—the same order of offerings and sacrifices is to be observed, both for sin and for the burnt offering, and with the offering and the oil, so that, when the darkness has been driven away and the light of oil has arisen, we may attain the festival of the Lord and have brighter solemnities, in which all our sins are forgiven.

## CHAPTER XLVI

Concerning the sacrifices of the Sabbath and the New Moon; through which gates the princes and the people must enter and leave in order to pray to God; concerning the prince’s voluntary burnt offering, which the prince may give; and concerning the destruction of the kitchens.

[Col. 1040D]

“Thus says the Lord God: The gate of the inner court that faces east shall be closed for the six days on which work is done; but on the sabbath day it shall be opened, and on the day of the Kalends it shall be opened. And the prince shall enter by way of the vestibule of the outer gate and shall stand on the threshold of the gate. And the priests shall offer his burnt offering and his peace offerings, and he shall worship upon the threshold of the gate, and he shall go out. But the gate shall not be closed until evening. And the people of the land shall worship at the doorway of that gate on sabbaths and on the Kalends before the Lord. The burnt offering that the prince shall offer to the Lord on the sabbath day shall be six unblemished lambs and one unblemished ram, and the grain offering shall be an ephah for the ram. For the lambs, the grain offering shall be whatever his hand can provide, and a hin of oil for each ephah. On the day of the Kalends, there shall be an unblemished bull from the herd, and six lambs and rams shall be unblemished; and he shall make a grain offering of an ephah for the bull and also an ephah for the ram. For the lambs, it shall be according to what his hand finds possible, and a hin of oil for each ephah.”

Before we explain what these things signify, the very words of Scripture must be unfolded paraphrastically. “The gate,” he says, “of the inner court for six days” (of which it is written, “For six days you shall labor and do all your work”) [Col. 1041B] “shall be closed”; and not just any gate, but the one “that faces east,” from which the sun of righteousness rises. On the sabbath day, however—that is, the seventh day, on which there is rest—it shall be opened each week; and again, when thirty days have been completed, when one month ends and another begins, that is, at the new moon, on the day of the Kalends, it shall be opened, so that what privilege the seventh day has in the week, the beginning of the month may also have.

Why the gate of the inner court that faces east is opened on the seventh day and on the day of the Kalends, the following passage will show. “And the prince,” he says, “shall enter by way of the vestibule of the outer gate,” namely, of the outer court, “and shall stand on the threshold of the gate,” that is, of the inner court that faces east. He shall not enter the inner court; rather, while he stands there, the other [Col. 1041C] priests shall offer the burnt offering for him—which Symmachus translated as “offering”—and the peace offerings, or “those things pertaining to salvation.” After the prince’s victim has been consumed by the sacred fire and the leader has been reconciled to God, he may then worship upon the threshold of the inner-court gate, where he had stood, and go out.

What, then? Will the gate immediately be closed after the prince’s departure? Certainly not. It shall remain open until evening, so that after the prince all the people of the land may worship opposite the doorway of that gate. They shall worship on the sabbaths and on the Kalends, when the gate is opened.

And because he had said above, “The priests shall offer his burnt offering and his peace offerings,” without indicating the number of the burnt offerings, he now adds: “This burnt offering the prince shall offer to the Lord [Col. 1041D] on the sabbath day.” He shall offer it not personally but through the priests, concerning whom it is written: “And the priests shall offer his burnt offering and his peace offerings.” “Six,” he says, “unblemished lambs and one unblemished ram,” so that the grain offering of the ram is an ephah, which in Hebrew is called *ephah*. For the six lambs, the offering shall be whatever the hand of the one making the offering is able to provide; and for each ephah there shall be a measure of oil called a *hin*.

On the day of the Kalends—that is, the days of the new moons—the privilege over the sabbath day shall be this additional one: a bull, or an unblemished young bull, shall be sacrificed from the herd. The remaining offerings—that is, the six unblemished lambs, the unblemished ram, and their offerings—shall retain the sabbath ritual. Only this provision is added: just as an ephah of offering [Col. 1042A]—that is, of fine flour—and a hin of oil are offered with the ram, so they shall also be offered with the bull.

Let these things have been set forth for clarity; now, with the Lord granting it, let us disclose the spiritual meaning.

For the six days on which we labor in the world, the eastern gate of the inner court is closed to us. But when we have come to the seventh day—that is, to the sabbath day, on which there is eternal rest—or to the day of the Kalends, when, after blind night and dreadful darkness, the beginning of light appears, the eastern gate is opened to us. And if one of us has attained, through the merits of virtues, the name and dignity of a leader, he shall enter by way of the vestibule of the outer gate—that is, through the labors of this world—and through the gate of the Church, which is still established within earthly boundaries. He shall not enter the inner court—for this is what is written in the present passage—but [Col. 1042B] shall come to the threshold of the inner gate and stand there.

But if in the present Scripture the prince does not enter the inner court but stands on its threshold, no one doubts that we now see in part and know in part, and that we do not yet behold the glory of the Lord with unveiled face. Accordingly, while the prince stands on the threshold of the gate of the inner court, the other priests entrusted with this office—whom we may understand as angelic powers—shall offer the burnt offering and the peace offerings for him.

For we need the mercy of God, and every creature is unclean in comparison with the Creator and must be purified by divine fire, by which the lips of the prophet Isaiah were also purified (Isa. VI). After he has received peace through the sacrifice, then, standing on the threshold, he may worship the omnipotence of God and confess himself [Col. 1042C] unworthy to enter the inner court—and immediately enter it.

After the one who is first has gone out, the gate of the inner court of this age shall not be closed until evening; rather, it shall remain open so that the people of the land may also be at the doorway and worship him—not at all times, but when they have rested from sins and, once the darkness has been driven away, have received the light of faith and knowledge.

This very burnt offering, which the prince offers through the priests on the sabbath day, is completed by the number six, corresponding to the six lambs: namely, to the six days on which we labor in the world. And there is an unblemished ram, the leader of the flock, so that for each ram an ephah is offered as the grain offering—that is, a tenth part of a *cor*.

For the sacrifice of the six lambs no fixed measure is prescribed, “but whatever his hand shall provide,” [Col. 1042D] that is, according to the quality and measure of his works. For each ephah he shall offer a hin of oil—that is, the oil which the five virgins prepared for themselves—so that it may anoint or mix the fine flour, and every offering of God may be full of the light of truth, and the face of the one making the offering may be gladdened by the oil.

On the day of the Kalends—that is, the thirtieth day, when the firstborn and the Levites are counted in the Law—there is offered, in addition to all Israel, about whom we spoke above, an unblemished bull from the herd. We discussed this more fully in the preceding chapter. There are also six unblemished lambs and unblemished rams, and the other offerings made on the sabbaths, so that we may attain eternal rest and deserve to hear: “Well done, good servant, because you were faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things; enter into the rest of your lord” (Matt. XXV) [Col. 1043A]. Thus we may not only reach the gate of the inner court but also enter its inner chambers and possess it by our deeds: “Those planted in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God” (Ps. IX), shall flourish.

“When the prince is about to enter, he shall enter by way of the vestibule of the gate, and by the same way he shall go out. And when the people of the land enter into the presence of the Lord at the appointed festivals, the one who enters by the north gate to worship shall go out by way of the south gate. And the one who enters by way of the south gate shall go out by way of the north gate. He shall not return by way of the gate through which he entered, but shall go out opposite it. The prince shall be in their midst: he shall enter with those entering and go out with those [Col. 1043B] going out. And at the market festivals and at the appointed festivals there shall be an ephah of offering for the bull and an ephah for the ram. For the lambs there shall be an offering according to what his hand finds possible, and a hin of oil for each ephah.”

That prince of whom it was said above, “The prince shall enter by way of the vestibule of the outer gate,” shall enter by the same gate and go out by the same gate. For he is endowed with free will and has the power to lay down his life (John X) and again to take it up; and whether he comes to us or ascends to the heavenly realms, he exercises the same liberty of his majesty. Accordingly, he does not seek market festivals, appointed festivals, or any distinction of days, because every time is a festival for him.

The people, however, enter and go out only at market festivals and appointed festivals, and not by the same way but by one way and then another. For it is written: “When the people of the land enter into the presence of the Lord at the appointed festivals, the one who enters by the north gate to worship shall go out by way of the south gate”; and the one who enters by way of the south gate shall go out by way of the north gate. He shall not return by way of the gate through which he entered, but shall go out opposite it.

This command is given not only to those who come out of Sodom, to whom it is said, “Do not look back” (Gen. XIX), nor only to those who put their hand to the plow, that they should not look back at what is behind them, but also to those established in the house of the Lord: they are commanded not to look behind them and return to the weak and beggarly elements, and, having begun in the spirit, to be consumed in the flesh. Rather, they should proceed from spiritual things to greater things and say with the Apostle: “Forgetting the things that are behind and stretching forward to those that are ahead” (Phil. III), so that they may no longer know in part and prophesy in part (1 Cor. XIII), but may come to perfection—yet according to that perfection which human nature can contain. Thus we may understand the Gospel saying: “When you have done all things, say, ‘We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we were obliged to do’” (Luke XVII).

Therefore the Apostle, in the same Epistle, speaks of two kinds of perfection. As one imperfect he writes: “Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect; but I pursue it, if I may apprehend that for which I have also been apprehended by Christ [Col. 1044A]” (Phil. III). Immediately he speaks as one perfect: “But one thing I do: forgetting what is behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, according to my purpose I pursue the prize of the heavenly calling. Let as many, therefore, as are perfect, be of this mind” (ibid.).

How can the statement stand, that the one who had said, “Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect,” should dare to say, “Let as many as are perfect be of this mind”? From this it is clear that every human being and the whole creation, even when it has attained perfection, nevertheless needs the mercy of God and possesses complete perfection by grace, not by merit.

The people of the land are therefore commanded “that if they enter by the north gate to worship, they shall go out by way of the south gate.” Who are these people to whom this command is given? The Gentiles, surely: those who, having abandoned the north gate—from which evils blaze forth upon the earth—enter the temple shall not leave except by way of the south gate, toward the gate of light, the gate of warmth, the gate at which the bridegroom lies at midday.

Accordingly, in the same Song of Songs it is said: “Arise, O North Wind, and come, O South Wind” (Song IV).

But the one who enters by way of the south gate shall go out by way of the north gate. Who is this people? The Jews, certainly, who, abandoning the gate of the way of light, go to the north gate, concerning which it is said: “The north wind is a most harsh wind” (Sir. XLIII). For Jeremiah’s pot is also kindled from the face of the north (Jer. I).

Let us interpret it in another way. The one who leaves sins enters by the north gate and goes out by the south gate who follows virtues. Conversely, if a righteous person falls into sins, he enters by the south gate but goes out by way of the north gate.

“But the prince,” he says, “shall be in their midst,” namely, in the midst of those entering and going out, according to what is written: “One stands among you whom you do not know” (John I). And the Apostle says: “Do you not know that Christ is in you?” (2 Cor. XIII). But if Christ is said to have stood among those who did not know him, how much more among those who do know him!

When Christ stands among those who know him, then the body becomes dead because of sin, but the spirit becomes alive because of righteousness. The prince enters with those who enter and goes out with those who go out, standing as witness to the virtue and sin of both groups.

At the market festivals, therefore, and at the appointed festivals—namely, the sabbaths and the Kalends—and at every festival of which we spoke earlier, an ephah is offered as the grain offering both for the bull and for the ram. For the lambs there shall be no fixed measure, nor is the matter left to arbitrary choice; rather, one shall use one’s strength and the goodness of one’s conscience, offering as much as one can, not as much as one wishes. And above all, there shall be a hin of oil for each ephah, so that the fine flour may be anointed and the lamp kindled in the sight of the Lord, and the one who uses it may say: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God” (Ps. LI).

“When he makes a voluntary burnt offering or voluntary peace offerings to the Lord, the gate that faces east shall be opened for him, and he shall make his burnt offering and his peace offerings as is customarily done on the sabbath day; and he shall go out, and the gate shall be closed after he has gone out. And he shall make a year-old unblemished lamb a burnt offering to the Lord every day. He shall make it continually, morning by morning. And he shall make a grain offering over it, morning by morning, a sixth part of an ephah, and a third part of a hin of oil, to mix with the fine flour. A grain offering to the Lord, a lawful, continual, perpetual offering. He shall make the lamb, the grain offering, and the oil, morning by morning, a perpetual burnt offering” (Jerome).

Where our text reads “unblemished,” the Hebrew has *thamin*. Aquila translates it as “perfect.” Where the Septuagint has *manaa*, Theodotion translates “offering,” while Aquila and Symmachus render it “gift.” For what we translated “voluntary,” the Septuagint has *homologia* (ὁμολογία), that is, “confession,” and for “prince” it has “leader”; for this is what *nasi* signifies.

The passage still concerns the prince, of whom Isaiah speaks: “Behold, I have given him as a witness to the nations, as a leader and instructor to the nations” (Isa. LV). And Ezekiel says: “And I, the Lord, will be their God” (Ezek. XXXIV). David says: “A prince in their midst” (Ps. XLV).

When this prince therefore makes a voluntary offering and says, “Make pleasing the voluntary, or spontaneous, offerings of my mouth, O Lord” (Ps. CXVIII), the voluntary burnt offering signifies that he offers his whole self to God; and the voluntary burnt offering and the voluntary peace offerings are not found in the preceding passage. For it is written: “The priests shall offer his burnt offering and his peace offerings,” whereas the voluntary offerings and freewill offerings mentioned here are entirely omitted there. Thus he does not act from necessity but from will: after the burnt offering, he offers peace offerings and is reconciled to God.

Hence virginity is greater than marriage, because it is neither demanded nor paid back, but offered. For the peace offerings, called *selamim* in Hebrew, the Septuagint uses the term “salutary,” so that the reconciliation effected by the peace offerings may itself be the offerer’s salvation.

When the prince has done this, the gate facing east shall be opened for him—or, according to the Septuagint, “he shall open for himself the gate that faces east”—that very gate of which it is written: “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it” (Ps. CXVII), and from which the sun of righteousness rises.

“And he shall make,” he says, “his burnt offering and his peace offerings,” of which we have just spoken. He shall make them because the sacrifice is voluntary; the priests shall not make them for him, as is customary on the sabbath day.

Therefore at all times the gate of the Lord stands open for a voluntary burnt offering and peace offering. He does not observe the sabbath; rather, all days are reckoned to him as rest. Accordingly, after he has offered the burnt offering and the peace offerings, he immediately goes out, and the gate is closed behind him—or he closes the gate—so that the prince’s privilege may be preserved and his sacrifice may not be mingled with the people.

And because he had spoken generally of “a voluntary burnt offering or voluntary peace offerings to the Lord,” without specifying a bull or young bull, a ram or sheep, or a goat for sin, he teaches what the burnt offering itself is. “He shall make,” he says, “a year-old unblemished lamb a burnt offering,” and not on particular days but every day; not at any hour, but in the morning: “morning by morning [Col. 1046A] he shall make it,” each morning, when the sun has risen and the beginning of light appears. David speaks of this morning in the Psalm: “In the morning you shall hear my voice; in the morning I shall stand before you and see” (Ps. V).

The one who is recognized as living in a life of light prays in the morning. We call it morning when, after the darkness has been dispelled, the coming of bright light has shone forth. The Church knows that it had been in the darkness of sins and gathered out of the night of this world; it therefore rightly believes that it is heard when it has burst forth into the light of heavenly conduct. It repeats the morning because it continually experienced, through the Lord’s favor, the necessity of standing before him in prayer with a lucid mind.

Observe why “morning” is said: namely, when the mind, having been enlightened, begins at the very beginning of good works to recognize the truth. You should not think that after sin there is a delay during which one could not be heard, as the prophet Ezekiel says: “On whatever day the impious person turns away from his impiety, none of his iniquities shall be remembered” (Ezek. XVIII).

To stand before someone means always to be present before him. Through this expression the continuity of religious devotion is indicated. For the one is rightly said to stand before God who can worthily appear in his sight, as Elijah said of himself: “The Lord lives, before whom I stand.”

Above he said, “You shall hear”; here he adds, “and I shall see,” because in that resurrection he will behold the one to whom here he entreated in holy prayers.

But who this unblemished—or perfect—and year-old lamb is, Isaiah teaches more fully, saying: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, and he did not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII). Jeremiah says: “But I was like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter, and I did not know” (Jer. XI). John the Baptist says: “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John I).

This is the lamb sacrificed in Egypt, by whose blood the doorposts are armed with faith and the destroyer is shut out. He is year-old because he proclaimed the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of retribution.

Let the reader not be surprised that he is at once prince, priest, bull, ram, and lamb, since in the Holy Scriptures, according to the variety of circumstances, we read of him as Lord, God, man, prophet, rod, flower, root, prince, judge, king, righteous one and righteousness, apostle and bishop, arm, servant, only-begotten Son, shepherd, son and child, only-begotten and firstborn, door, way, angel, arrow, wisdom, and many other things. If I wished to cite testimonies for all of them, they would require a book of their own.

In the burnt offering of this unblemished and year-old lamb, which is always offered in the morning, the prince himself shall make the offering—*manaa*, that is, fine flour or a gift—morning by morning, a sixth part of an ephah, “fine flour” being understood. A sixth part of an ephah is half a *modius*. For if an ephah is a tenth part of a *cor*, that is, three *modii*, there is no doubt that a sixth part of an ephah makes half a *modius*.

Of the measure of oil called a hin, a third part is likewise offered, so that it may be mixed with or poured over the fine flour. This is a lawful, continual, perpetual offering to the Lord, which is interrupted on no day but is always offered at sunrise, so that what is stated at the end of this chapter may be fulfilled: “He shall make the lamb, the grain offering, and the oil, morning by morning, a perpetual burnt offering.”

“Thus says the Lord God: If the prince or leader gives a gift to one of his sons, it shall be his sons’ inheritance; they shall possess it as an inheritance. But if he gives a bequest from his inheritance to one of his servants, it shall belong to him until the year of remission”—for which Theodotion inserted the Hebrew word itself, *deror*—“and it shall return to the prince. His inheritance, however, shall belong to his sons. And the prince shall not take from the people’s inheritance by force or from their possession, but from his own possession he shall give an inheritance to his sons, so that my people may not be scattered, each one from his possession” (Jerome).

Thus far the passage has concerned the prince; now instructions are given concerning his heirs—or rather, concerning the gifts, inheritance, and bequests that he ought to give and concerning whose possession they are, whether temporarily or permanently.

“If,” he says, “he gives his sons either a gift or an inheritance, they shall possess it,” because it is owed to them by right of succession, and possession cannot pass from one person to another. But if he gives it to one of his servants as a bequest, he shall possess it only until either the seventh year of remission, called *deror*, or the Jubilee, that is, the fiftieth year, arrives. Then every purchase and gift returns to its former owners, so that the servant has the use of the possession for a time, while ownership belongs to the prince’s sons.

What follows—“And the prince shall not take from the people’s inheritance by force,” or, as the Septuagint translated it, “so as to oppress them,” or, as Aquila and Symmachus translated it, “so as to afflict and grieve them”—but shall give an inheritance to his sons from his own possession, censures not only the priests and princes of that time but also our own. These become richer through the dignity of the priesthood and, beyond what is owed to them by the Lord’s arrangement, seize things from the poor by force or strip the wealthy under the pretext of honor, so that they leave nothing even to their own sons, to whom the paternal inheritance is owed, except what was left to them by their parents.

Therefore, a priest who is richer when he leaves the priesthood than when he came to it ought to give whatever he has acquired beyond that to the poor, to the holy brethren, and to the members of the household of faith [Col. 1047D], whose merits surpass those of children. Thus he may return to his Lord the things that belong to the Lord, who says in the Gospel: “Whatever you have done for one of the righteous, you have done for me” (Matt. XXV).

For he himself is received as a guest in the poor, visited in prison, clothed when naked, given drink when thirsty, and fed when hungry, so that “my people may not be scattered from their possession.” For if the prince has permission to receive, seize, or hold under the appearance of honor things that are not his, and to leave them to his children, the people gathered in the name of God will be scattered into parts and torn apart—or, according to the Law, so that gradually one person’s inheritance may pass to another and the boundary cord of the division may perish, by which the inheritance perhaps came to each person.

Therefore, the one who leaves to his sons, brothers, and relatives other people’s gifts or goods, acquired by robbery, adulation, blandishments, or the precept of religion, scatters the people of God and takes away from them the possession of everlasting faith.

“And he brought me in through the entrance beside the gate, into the priests’ storerooms of the sanctuary, which faced north; and behold, there was a place extending toward the west. And he said to me: ‘This is the place where the priests shall cook the guilt offering, where they shall cook the sacrifice, so that they may not carry it out into the outer court and sanctify the people.’ And he brought me out into the outer court and led me around the four corners of the court. And behold, there was a small court in the corner of the court; there were small courts at each corner of the court. In the four corners of the court [Col. 1048B] there were small courts, forty cubits long and thirty cubits wide. All four had one measure, and a wall surrounded the four small courts all around; kitchens had been constructed beneath the porticoes around the circuit. And he said to me: ‘This is the house of the kitchens in which the ministers of the house of the Lord cook the sacrifices of the people or the sacrifice’” (Jerome).

For *zeba* means “sacrifice” in Hebrew. The man who held the reed in his hand and the builder’s cord with which he measured the building “brought me,” he says, “through the entrance beside the gate,” or behind the gate. He did not specify which gate—whether the eastern, southern, or another quarter—but left it uncertain, so that I might go to the place of the sanctuary, “and into the storerooms,” or chambers, of the priests, which faced north and west, that is, toward the north and the west. Holy Scripture has the custom, according to the situation of the land of Judea, of always calling the west “the sea.”

It must also be considered that the place of the priests, where sacrifices are cooked for guilt, ignorance, and sin, so that they may not be offered raw in the outer court, is situated toward the north and west, from which the coldest wind arises and where the light of the sun sets. From this it is shown that whatever pertains to food is either for error or for sin. But if a sacrifice is offered even for ignorance, how much more for the consciousness of guilt! Hence Job offered a victim every morning for his sons, fearing that they might have sinned through ignorance (Job I).

What follows—“so that they may not offer it in the outer court and the people may be sanctified,” who had not been prepared for sanctification—signifies that we must not readily give holy things to those who are not holy, nor cast pearls before swine according to the Gospel, nor give what is holy to dogs.

Accordingly, Moses wants the people to be sanctified for three days from every impurity and from intercourse with their wives (Exod. XIX), so that they may approach Mount Sinai and, having been sanctified, receive holy things. If those who were about to approach in order to hear and receive the words of God are commanded to be sanctified by abstaining from their wives, it is clear that the apostolic saying is contained in the Law: “Do not defraud one another, unless perhaps by mutual consent for a time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (1 Cor. VII). They are to abstain from their wives by mutual consent in order to devote themselves to prayer.

After this it is written: “And he brought me out into the outer court and led me around the four corners of the court. And behold, there was a small court in the corner of the court, small courts at each corner of the court.” Small courts had been arranged in the four corners of the court. The man whom he often mentions brought him out from the place of the priests, which extended toward the north—or which was set apart—where they cook for guilt, sin, or ignorance. He brought him into the outer court.

From this we understand that the court from which he had come out was the inner court, and that there are many courts in the Holy Scriptures, of which we read: “You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God” (Ps. CXXXVI). And in John: “I have other sheep that are not of this court; I must bring them also, and they shall hear my voice, and there shall be one court and one shepherd” (John X). For the Greek word is *aulē* (αὐλή), which Latin simplicity has rendered *ovile*, “sheepfold.”

When he said, “of this court,” he showed that there is another one, either among the multitude of the Gentiles, in contrast with Israel, or in heaven, in distinction from the earthly court. A court is assigned to each according to the quality of his merits and his function; I discussed this more fully above.

This court of which the present passage speaks had, at each of its four corners, small courts, which the Septuagint calls smaller ones; for ease of understanding we have called them *atriola*, “small courts,” using the diminutive Greek form, *hypokoristikōs* (ὑποκοριστικῶς).

It was forty cubits long and thirty cubits wide. I remember having discussed these numbers in this same prophet, explaining that one refers to tribulations and narrow places, the other to the age of perfection. Thus Moses, Elijah, the Lord, and the Savior fasted for forty days in the wilderness. And men do not approach the priestly office after their twenty-fifth year but after their thirtieth. For this reason the Lord was also thirty years old when he came to baptism. In this same prophet the thirtieth year is likewise placed at the beginning.

Where, then, there is food, there are also distress and temptation by which food is prepared. But when we have come to the age of mature men, there we must trample all things underfoot and say: “Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content” (1 Tim. VI); and: “If the Lord gives me food to eat and clothing to put on” (Gen. XXVIII); or certainly: “Food is for the stomach and the stomach for food, but God will destroy both it and them” (1 Cor. VI).

In the future we shall neither eat nor drink, but shall feed upon that bread which came down from heaven (John VI). Of it the Psalter sings: “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. LXXVII); and: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” (John IV).

The fact that the measure of the small courts was one measure in all four, and that they occupied the corners of the greater court, signifies the four regions of the world. In the sweat of our face we eat bread (Gen. III), and every labor serves the belly and the dung heap. These four small courts, or one wall, surrounded them.

Kitchens had been constructed beneath the porticoes around the circuit, or they had nearby dining couches, so that where there is food, there is also the preparation of tables.

And lest the Prophet be unaware of what the things he saw were, he said to him: “This is the house of the kitchens in which the ministers of the Lord cook the sacrifices of the people.” The sacrifices of the people, which are offered for guilt, sin, and ignorance, are the nourishment and refreshment of the priests, so that they may remember that they ought to desire nothing else, since even in the temple meat has been prepared for their refreshment.

(MAUR.) It is indeed read in Leviticus, where the consecration of Aaron and his sons to the priesthood is recounted, that Moses gave this command concerning the cooking of the consecrated meat for the use of those same priests:

“Cook the meat before the entrance of the tabernacle and eat it there; eat also the bread of consecration that has been placed in the basket, as the Lord commanded me, saying: ‘Aaron and his sons shall eat them.’ But whatever remains of the meat and the bread, fire shall consume. You shall not go out from the entrance of the tabernacle for seven days, until the day on which the time of your consecration is completed; for your consecration shall last seven days” (Lev. VIII).

(Isidore.) This also pertains, not incongruously, to the significance of such kitchens. The Lawgiver has now made special provision and distinguished the mysteries, and through the things he contemplated has figuratively taught that they are to be fulfilled within the Church and in no way made public to the eyes and ears of the profane, nor given to just anyone as an opportunity for profanation.

Since the tabernacle of the testimony of God signifies heaven, while the court of this tabernacle signifies the Church, because it has been placed before the entrance to heaven—the Church itself bearing the image of the heavenly Jerusalem, as we said earlier—he commanded that the sacrificial meats be cooked in it.

For he says: “He commanded them, saying: ‘Cook the meat before the entrance of the tabernacle [Col. 1050C] and eat it there.’”

How, then, can the wisdom of the Spirit in these matters fail to be astonishing? He left no doubt concerning this interpretation. By commanding that the meat be eaten together with the bread, he intended us to understand that this mystery is called by him both bread and flesh, like the body of Christ, “the living bread that came down from heaven.” This was so that the mystical banquet should properly be celebrated there.

Aaron and his sons rightly eat it. For unless Christ himself comes at the request of the priests’ mouths and sanctifies and renders the banquet propitious, the things that are done do not become the Lord’s sacrifice in any way.

But he commanded that whatever remained of the meat and bread be burned in the fire. We now see this also taking place visibly in the Church, and whatever happens to remain uneaten is committed to the fire.

Therefore, from what is carried out visibly there arises for attentive persons the meaning of an intelligible reality. When we fall short in eating the sacrifice and cannot consume it whole—perhaps because the mind has grown weary or failed—the question arises whether what is seen should be understood as the Lord’s body, into which not even angels can look with their eyes; it must not be left over, but must also be committed to the fire of the Spirit, so that it may consume what is inedible to us through weakness. How it consumes it is understood when we consider that what appears impossible to us is possible for the power of the Spirit.

## CHAPTER XLVII  
### Concerning the many waters that proceed from the temple, the grace of baptism, the division of the land inherited by Israel, and the gate of the city whose name is “House of Judah”

[Col. 1051A]

“Then he turned me toward the gate of the temple, and behold, waters were flowing out from beneath the threshold of the temple toward the east—for the front of the temple faced east. The waters were descending along the right side of the temple, to the south, beside the altar. And he led me out by way of the gate of the north and turned me toward the outer road outside the gate, the road that faced east. And behold, waters overflowing from the right side, as the man went out toward the east; he had a measuring cord in his hand. He measured a thousand cubits and led me through the water as far as the ankles. Again he measured a thousand and led me through the water as far as the knees. He measured a thousand and led me through the water as far as the loins. And he measured a thousand: a torrent which I could not cross, because the waters of the deep torrent had swelled and it could not be forded.” (Jerome.) In place of this, the Septuagint translated: “And he measured a thousand, and he could not cross,” because the water was being carried along like a precipitous torrent which cannot be crossed.

These waters, which were flowing out from beneath the threshold of the temple, were not carried toward the north or the west, but toward the east. And they were on the right side of the temple, that is, toward the south—and toward the south not of just any place, but of the altar. From this it is clear that the waters are sacred and signify the teaching of our Savior, in accordance with what is written: “The law shall go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isaiah 2). And in another place: “Everything shall be filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as abundant waters cover the sea” (Isaiah 11).

The prophet Zechariah also prophesied concerning these waters, saying: “On that day living water shall go out from Jerusalem, half of it toward the eastern sea, and half of it toward the western sea” (Zechariah 14). Concerning these waters the Lord also spoke to the Samaritan woman: “If you knew who it is that says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you perhaps would have asked him, and he would have given you living water” (John 4). And again: “Everyone who drinks of this water shall thirst again; but whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst” (ibid.).

And in the temple he cried out and said: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly.” He said this concerning the Spirit whom those who believed in him were to receive (John 7).

These are the waters of which the Prophet spoke in the psalm: “He led me beside waters of refreshment” (Psalm 22). And Ezekiel: “I will take you from among the nations and from the lands, and I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your uncleannesses”; for fountains of water have appeared (Ezekiel 36). And in the ninety-second psalm it is sung: “The rivers of the Lord have lifted up; the rivers have lifted up their voices above the voices of many waters; marvelous are the swellings of the sea” (Psalm 92; Psalm 29).

These are the waters of Siloam, “which go quietly” (Isaiah 8), concerning which Isaiah says: “You shall draw waters from the fountains of the Savior” (Isaiah 12). And the Psalmist: “Bless the Lord from the fountains of Israel” (Psalm 67). And the same Isaiah says concerning the Lord the Savior: “This one,” he says, “shall dwell in a lofty cavern of the strongest rock; bread shall be given him, and his water shall be faithful. For water has burst forth in the wilderness, and a valley in thirsty land” (Isaiah 33).

And it is said to believers: “Do not fear, for I have redeemed you; you are mine, and if you pass through water, I am with you” (Isaiah 43). And again: “You who thirst, go to the water” (Isaiah 55). And through Jeremiah God says: “My people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves cisterns that cannot hold water” (Jeremiah 1).

Just as we read in a positive sense of the waters that go out from the threshold of the temple and are referred to the teaching of the Church, so there are bitter and very bad waters, to which the prophet Jeremiah forbids us to approach, saying: “What have you to do with the way of Egypt, to drink the waters of Geon?” (Jeremiah 2). In Hebrew these are called *sior*, that is, turbid and muddy waters.

Concerning these God speaks in anger against heretics: “Behold, I will feed them with distress, and I will give them a drink of gall” (Jeremiah 9). In these waters the Egyptian dragon reigns, who says: “The rivers are mine, and I made myself” (Ezekiel 29), who sees every lofty thing and is himself king of those who are in the waters.

Therefore the ecclesiastical man entreats the Lord and says: “Save me, O Lord, for the waters have come in as far as my soul. I am stuck in the mud of the deep, and there is no foothold; I have come into the depths of the sea, and the storm has overwhelmed me” (Psalm 67). And again: “Let me be delivered from those who hate me and from the depth of the waters. Let not the storm of water overwhelm me, nor let the deep swallow me, nor let the pit close its mouth over me” (ibid. 15).

And in another psalm: “Unless the Lord had been with us, let Israel now say, unless the Lord had been with us: when men rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive. When their fury was enraged against us, perhaps the water would have swallowed us” (Psalm 123).

And the bride in the Song of Songs: “Many waters cannot extinguish love, nor can rivers overwhelm it” (Song of Songs 8).

This is the water of which Hosea says: “Gilead, a city that has despised me, works vanities, troubling the water; and its strength is the strength of pirate men” (Hosea 6). This water is also called by another name *Mara*, that is, bitterness; into it the wood of the cross is cast, and the bitter things are turned into sweet.

Consider the law of Moses, if it is understood according to the carnal sense of the Jews, how bitter it is: digging out an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth; Judah in his fornication with Tamar; Hosea joined to a prostitute; Jeremiah’s *περίζωμα* (*perizoma*, “girdle”); Moses’ Ethiopian wife and the killing of the Egyptian; and a thousand other matters which, if we understand them according to the letter that kills, and not according to the life-giving Spirit, are bitter, and build up their reader less than they destroy him.

These waters, then, which go out from the temple of the Lord, proceed toward the east and descend along the right side of the temple, toward the south of the altar, where the bridegroom feeds and reclines with his guests. But what follows—“And he led me by the way of the gate of the north and turned me toward the road outside the outer gate, the road that faced east”—quietly indicates that we cannot immediately reach the eastern gate unless we come to it by a long circuit through the way of the northern gate.

For unless we overcome the coldest wind by the warmth of faith and tread upon its regions, so that the apostolic saying may be fulfilled in us, “But God will crush Satan under your feet swiftly” (Romans 16), we shall not be able to enter through the gate by which the waters go out and are on the right side.

And note that these waters, which go out through the eastern gate, flee the left-hand parts so completely that they are described as proceeding from the right side of the altar toward the south:

“The man,” he says, “who had the cord in his hand, after he had led me through the northern gate from outside to the road that faced east—and he too was in the same place—measured a thousand cubits of that same water and led me through the water as far as the ankles.” Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated “ankles” as *ἀστράγαλοι* (*astragaloi*); in place of this the Septuagint translated: “but he shall pass through into the water of remission.”

We can understand this as signifying the first sins of human beings, which are forgiven when we enter the waters of the Lord; they display the saving grace of baptism and are the beginnings of progress. Indeed, they reach only as far as the ankles, which are near the sole and heel and are exposed to the serpent’s bites, as the Lord says: “You shall watch his head, and he shall watch your heel” (Genesis 3).

And in the Psalter it is said concerning Judas the betrayer: “He who ate my bread magnified his supplanting against me” (Psalm 40), or “his heel.” For this is what the Greek *πτέρνα* (*pterna*) signifies.

After the thousand cubits that reach as far as the ankle, he measured another thousand cubits in the water, “and led me through the water as far as the knees.” After the remission of sins, when we make some effort to ascend from earthly things to higher realities, we bend our knees before the Lord, as the Apostle says: “That every knee should bow, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2).

A third time he measured another thousand cubits, “and led me,” he says, “through the water as far as the loins.”

By these steps we reach lofty things, yet these very heights extend only as far as the hips and loins, so that every ignoble lust may be cut away from us and we may possess bodily sanctification, without which no one sees God.

Hence in this same prophet God is seen as fiery from the feet to the loins. The works of the loins require fire and purification, as the righteous man says: “For my loins are filled with illusions” (Psalm 37), by which the enemy deceives us by fantasies both by day and by night.

But from the loins to the head and crown he shines with the splendor of the most precious metal, electrum, so that there may be nothing dirty or useless in him.

Therefore now, for the fourth time, it is said: “And he measured a thousand”—the word “cubits” being understood—“a torrent which I could not cross.” This is much better than the Septuagint, who said, “which he could not cross.” The prophet, and every human nature, cannot cross beyond the loins the torrent of thoughts and the incitements of vices in the heart.

But the man who was clothed in *baddim* and was the prophet’s guide crossed through clearly, “who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 11).

He gives the reason why the prophet could not cross the fourth thousand cubits: “Because,” he says, “the waters of the deep torrent had swollen, and it could not be forded.”

But how is it written, with the prophet boasting, “Our soul has crossed the torrent”? This is easily resolved if we know that the Hebrew reads: “The torrent has crossed my soul.”

Isaiah also speaks of this torrent: “Behold, I will incline over them as a river of peace, and as an overflowing torrent of glory.” And in the thirty-fifth psalm it is said concerning the saints: “They shall hope in the protection of your wings; they shall be intoxicated with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delights, for with you is the fountain of life.” And in the hundred and twenty-fifth: “Turn again, O Lord, our captivity, like a torrent in the south.” And concerning the Savior: “He shall drink from the torrent on the way” (Psalm 109).

For what human being can boast that he has a pure heart? Or into whose mind has the death of desire not entered through the windows of the eyes—or, to say little, the tickling of the soul? “The world is placed in evil” (1 John 5), and from childhood the human heart has been inclined toward evil, so that from the beginning of birth not even a single day of the human condition is without sin.

Hence David also confesses in the psalm: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Psalm 50)—not in the iniquities of my mother, nor precisely in my own, but in the iniquities of the human condition.

Therefore the Apostle also says: “Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Romans 5).

(Gregory.) What, then, is signified by the number one thousand except the fullness of the number assigned? Thus the man who appeared measures a thousand cubits, and the Prophet is led through the waters as far as the ankles. For when our Redeemer, as we turn toward him, grants us the fullness of a good beginning, he pours into us, by the gift of spiritual wisdom, the first traces of our work.

For the water’s reaching as far as the ankles means that, through the wisdom we have received, we already hold the footprints of the righteousness we desire. Again he measures a thousand, and the Prophet is led through the water as far as the knees. For when the fullness of good work is granted, our wisdom is increased to this point: that it is no longer bent even in small actions.

Hence Isaiah says: “Strengthen the slack hands and make firm the feeble knees, and make straight paths for your feet” (Isaiah 35). The water reaches the knees when the wisdom we have received firmly binds us to the righteousness of good work.

Again he measures a thousand, and the Prophet is led through the water as far as the loins, because then the fullness of work grows within us when the wisdom we have received has extinguished, as far as possible, every pleasure of the flesh.

For unless pleasure of the flesh were in the loins, the Psalmist would not have said: “Burn my loins and my heart” (Psalm 25). Thus the water reaches the loins when the sweetness of wisdom also destroys the incitements of the flesh, so that the fires of pleasure which could burn the mind grow cold.

He then measured another thousand, namely the torrent which the Prophet could not cross. Concerning it he also says: “Because the waters of the deep torrent have swollen, and it cannot be forded.”

Once the perfection of work has been received, one comes to contemplation. In that contemplation, while the mind is lifted on high, it sees in God that it cannot penetrate what it sees. It is as though it touches the water of the torrent which it cannot cross: it beholds through contemplation what it desires, yet cannot perfectly behold even that which it desires to behold.

The Prophet therefore eventually reaches the water which he does not cross, because when he is finally led to the contemplation of wisdom, its very immensity—which raises the human being toward itself—deprives the human mind of full knowledge, so that he loves it by touching it, yet cannot penetrate it by crossing through.

Blessed Job, seeing that these increases of virtue are distinctly granted to human beings by heavenly gift, called them steps, because by them one ascends in order to arrive at the possession of heavenly things. Thus, making mention of the sacred books, that is, of the divine utterance, he says: “I shall declare him by each of my steps” (Job 31). For truly the person ascends to the teaching of God who breaks through to obtain it by the steps of holy action; and, as though by each of his steps, he declares the book who demonstrates that he has received its knowledge not by words alone but also by works.

(Jerome.) We say *cubitos* in the masculine gender and not the neuter *cubita*, according to the rule of the grammarians, as I also taught above. The ignorant do this through ignorance of the rule, but we use the customary form for the sake of the simple and unlearned, whose number is greater in the congregation of the Church.

“And he said to me: ‘Surely you have seen, son of man.’ And he led me out and turned me toward the bank of the torrent. When I had turned, behold, there were very many trees on both banks of the torrent. And he said to me: ‘These waters that go out toward the eastern sand-hills and descend to the plains of the desert shall enter the sea and flow out, and the waters shall be healed. And every living creature that creeps, wherever the torrent comes, shall live; and there shall be very many fish after these waters have come there. They shall be healed, and everything shall live wherever the torrent comes, and fishermen shall stand beside it. From Engaddi to Engallim there shall be a drying-place for nets. Its fish shall be of very many kinds, like the fish of the great sea, in exceedingly great number. But in the places where the waters go beyond the banks and are marshy, they shall not be healed, but shall be given over to salt-pits. And upon the torrent, along its banks on both sides, every fruit-bearing tree shall grow. Its leaf shall not fall, and its fruit shall not fail. Each month it shall produce first-fruits, because its waters shall go out from the sanctuary. Its fruit shall be for food, and its leaves for medicine.’”

I wished to set down the whole chapter, although it is long, all at once, so that I would not interrupt the reader’s meaning and so that the order of the reading, divided into sections, would not disturb the hearer’s understanding. Let us therefore say what seems to us concerning each point.

The man who was Ezekiel’s guide admonishes the prophet to look more attentively and to see, and to turn the eyes of his mind toward hidden mysteries. He calls him “son of man,” either in the figure of the Lord the Savior—for Ezekiel is interpreted as “strength” or “command of God”—or certainly as a reminder of human frailty, lest he forget his condition while great things are being shown to him.

He leads and turns the admonished prophet toward the bank of the torrent, so that, since he could not cross its middle depth, he might at least recognize the things that are on the banks.

“And when I had turned,” he says—or, “when he who was the guide and instructor had turned me”—“behold, on the bank of the torrent or river there were exceedingly many trees, or very many trees, on both sides.”

This torrent, which because of the abundance of its waters flows in the manner of a torrent and receives rains from heaven, concerning which we spoke in the preceding reading, is called by the Septuagint a river, because it has perpetual waters, not waters collected here and there from rains, but waters flowing from a living and perpetual spring.

We read much about this river in the Holy Scriptures, but for the present only a few passages should be mentioned, beginning with this: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Psalm 45). And in another place: “The river of God is filled with waters; you have prepared their food, for thus is your preparation” (Psalm 64).

And again in the plural: “The rivers have lifted up, O Lord; the rivers have lifted up their voices above the voices of many waters; marvelous are the swellings of the sea” (Psalm 92). And in Isaiah: “I will make a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert” (Isaiah 43). And in another passage of the same prophet, more clearly: “A glorious river flowing in a thirsty land shall appear in Zion” (Isaiah 33).

Above this river there were very many trees on both sides of the bank, so that, as it were, between the two instruments—the Old and the New—the river might run enclosed. The many trees, or very many and exceedingly numerous trees, I think are those which Scripture says abound in various fruits in paradise.

(Maurus.) For it is written in the psalm concerning the blessed man who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night that he becomes “like a tree planted beside the courses of waters, which shall give its fruit in its season, and its leaf shall not fall, and all that he does shall prosper” (Psalm 1).
