This tree is principally understood as the Lord Christ, because of the cross which he accepted for the salvation of humankind; it is rightly called the tree of life, since the Lord Christ, who is our life, was hung upon it, and to the thief who confessed on that same cross it was said: “Amen, I say to you, today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23).

This is also the tree planted beside the courses of waters, that is, beside the saving teaching of the Lord himself, who says to the Samaritan woman in the Gospel: “If you knew who it is who asks you for water, you would have asked him to give you living water,” and so forth (John 4).

It gave its fruit in its season when he established churches at the proper time, in which there exists spiritual refreshment for the souls of the faithful. Its leaves remain on this tree because the words of life abide there, fixed in truth, as it is said in the Gospel: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Luke 12).

And observe that the Lord’s words are compared with the leaves of a tree: for just as leaves cover the fruits, so they guard his promises. These are the spiritual waters; these are the healing leaves.

Concerning them blessed John says in the Apocalypse: “And he showed me the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb. In the middle of its street, and on both sides of the river, was the tree of life, bearing fruit twelve times, yielding its fruit each month; and the leaves of that tree were appointed for the healing of the nations” (Revelation 22).

(Bede.) By the twelve months he indicates the whole duration of life—that life concerning which it is said: “And your years shall not fail” (Psalm 101). And again: “Month after month and sabbath after sabbath” (Isaiah 66). There the present face of the Lord is eternal health and the eternal food of life.

It can also be understood simply that through the teaching of the twelve Apostles the cross of Christ bears fruit: “And the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations.” If the fruit is understood as the reward of blessed immortality, the leaves are rightly understood as perpetual song, falling to the healing of those who sing by a blessed destiny. For there are the true healing of the nations, full redemption, and everlasting happiness.

(Jerome.) The guide who goes before and is the teacher instructs the prophet and says: “These waters which go out”—either “into Galilee of the nations,” according to the Septuagint, or, as is more accurately contained in the Hebrew, “toward the eastern sand-hills”—“and descend to the plains of the desert,” or “to Arabia,” “shall enter the sea,” or “to the outlets of the sea,” “and the waters shall be healed.”

We said earlier that the waters signify either the grace of baptism or evangelical teaching. If they go out from the threshold of the temple and hold to apostolic discipline, they make the previously barren and infertile sand-hills fruitful; and all the plains and deserts are so irrigated that they express within themselves the mystery of the fountain of Jericho, which Elisha healed with evangelical and apostolic salt (2 Kings 2), so that where previously there had been barrenness and death, there might be abundance and life.

Nor did they heal only the deserts; they enter the eastern sea, that is, the Dead Sea, in which nothing living could exist, the exceedingly bitter sea which in Greek they call *τὴν λίμνην ἄσφαλτον*—that is, “the lake of bitumen.” And in a wondrous manner the evangelical waters heal the dead waters, which received the name of death because they contain nothing living.

For they did not know him who says: “I am life” (John 15). And in truth, according to the literal sense, up to the present nothing that breathes and can move can be found in this sea because of its excessive bitterness—not even little snails, small worms, eels, or the other kinds of animals or reptiles, whose tiny bodies we can know better than their names.

Indeed, if the Jordan, swollen by rains, should carry fish into it as it flows, they immediately die and float upon the thick waters. Since these waters, as the simple statement testifies, have no usefulness, when they have been healed by the torrent of the Lord according to the spiritual understanding—as the foolish superstition of the Jews believes will happen—they will have very many fish, and everything wherever this torrent reaches will live.

Thus fishermen will stand on the banks from Engaddi to Engallim. The first name means “the fountain” or “eye of the kid”; the second means “the fountain” or “eye of the calves.” Engallim is at the beginning of the Dead Sea, where the Jordan enters it; Engaddi is where it ends and is consumed.

I think that the Dead Sea is the one of which Zechariah speaks: “On that day living water shall go out from Jerusalem” (Zechariah 14), half of it toward the eastern sea. Daniel also agrees with this in these words: “I saw, and behold, the four winds of heaven were striving upon the great sea” (Daniel 7). And David: “Marvelous are the swellings of the sea” (Psalm 92). And in the person of the Savior in the psalm: “I have come into the depth of the sea, and the storm has overwhelmed me” (Psalm 68).

The king of Egypt, likewise, is called a dragon by the same Ezekiel (Ezekiel 32), who dwells in the sea and agitates the rivers as though with his horns. And again: “This sea is great and spacious” (Psalm 103).

As long as it does not receive into itself the waters of the river or torrent, it kills everything that it contains. But the Lord, of whom it is said, “He will strike and heal after two days,” and on the third day, “We shall rise and live in his sight” (Hosea 6), speaks in the same prophet Hosea:

“I bound Ephraim; I took him in my arm, and they did not know that I healed them, in the corruption of humanity; he was wounded for our sins and weakened for our iniquities; the discipline of our peace was upon him, and by his bruise we were healed” (Hosea 11; Isaiah 53).

He healed this sea, which is extremely salty and dead through excessive bitterness, by his death. Through Isaiah he says: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to evangelize the poor, to heal the brokenhearted” (Isaiah 61).

Hence through Jeremiah he cries out: “Turn back, children; turn back, and I will heal your wounds” (Jeremiah 3). For the impatient people had said, unable to bear the pain of their wounds any longer: “The summer has passed, the harvest is over, and we have not been saved” (Jeremiah 8).

Therefore the Lord answered them: “Is there no balm in Gilead, or are there no physicians there? Why, then, has the healing of the daughter of my people not arisen?” And Jeremiah himself cries out and says: “Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved” (Jeremiah 17).

Finally, the angels who presided over the Jewish people at the time when the foolish multitude cried out, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27), and when the veil of the temple was torn and all the mysteries of the Hebrews were disclosed, answered the commanding Lord and said: “We have healed Babylon, and she is not healed; let us leave her” (Jeremiah 51)—that is, the city of confusion and of vices.

Josephus also relates in his History that after the Lord had been crucified, and the veil of the temple—or the lintel of the temple—had been torn and collapsed, a voice was heard in the inner shrine from the heavenly powers: “Let us depart from these dwellings.”

All this has not been said superfluously but necessarily, because the Dead Sea is said to have been healed when the river of the Lord flowed into it.

Over this sea, from Engaddi—the eye and fountain of the kid, which is always offered for sins—to Engallim, the fountain of the calves, which are slaughtered for the Lord and imitate the calf offering horns and hooves, which is slaughtered at the altar as a type of the Savior, there will be fishermen to whom Jesus says: “Come to me; I will make you fishers of men” (Matthew 4).

Concerning them Jeremiah also says: “Behold, I will send fishermen” (Jeremiah 16). And there will be very many kinds—indeed, species—of fish in the sea that was once dead. These are the fish that Peter draws out on the right side at the Lord’s command (John 21), and they were one hundred and fifty-three, so numerous that the nets were breaking because of them.

For those who have written about the nature and properties of animals say—those who have learned *ἀλιευτικά* (*alieutiká*, matters concerning fishing) in both Latin and Greek, among whom Appianicus the Cilician [Al., “Cilix”] is a highly learned poet—that there are one hundred and fifty-three species of fish, all of which were caught by the Apostles. Nothing remained uncaught, since the noble and the ignoble, the rich and the poor, and every kind of human being is drawn from the sea of this world to salvation.

But what follows—“On its shores and in the marshy places,” or “in those places which go beyond the shores, the waters shall not be healed”—quietly indicates that whoever was not in Noah’s ark perished while the flood reigned, and that those whom this river has not reached do not receive healing.

“But they shall be given over to salt-pits,” he says, in accordance with what is written:

“When the pestilent man is scourged, the fool becomes wiser” (Proverbs 19),

for the examples of the worse instruct the good.

Or they shall be given over to salt-pits in accordance with what is written in the Gospel: “Salt is good; but if salt has become tasteless, it is useful for nothing” (Matthew 5), so that they may forever lack crops and greenery, as the city, sprinkled with salt after its ruin, also demonstrates.

But over the torrent or river, on its banks on both sides, every fruit-bearing tree shall grow—or, as all translators unanimously rendered it, *βρῶμα* (*brōma*), which means food and nourishment, something that can be eaten; in Hebrew it is called *Machal*.

“And nothing,” according to the Septuagint, “shall grow old in it,” but its fruits shall be renewed daily; or, “Its leaf shall not fall, and its fruit shall not fail,” according to what is written in the first psalm: “And he shall be like a tree planted beside the courses of waters, which shall give its fruit in its season, and its leaf shall not fall.”

“Each month,” he says, “it shall produce first-fruits,” or, as it is written in the Septuagint: “In the renewal of its fruit it shall produce first-fruits,” so that all the fruit of believers may be first-fruits, and each month may be assigned to one of the Apostles.

This shall happen “because its waters shall go out from the sanctuary.” Lest we think that such abundance of fruit belongs to the banks, trees, or months, he gives the reason for the fruitfulness and adds that its waters shall go out from the sanctuary. “Therefore it depends not on the one who wills or runs, but on God who has mercy” (Romans 9).

The tree of life holds the primacy among all these trees. It is understood as wisdom, concerning which it is written: “She is a tree of life to all who believe in her” (Proverbs 3).

And what is said—“Its fruit shall be for food, and its leaves for medicine”—demonstrates the mysteries of the divine books. One of these belongs to the letter, the other to the spirit, so that we understand simple words in the leaves, but a hidden meaning in the fruits.

For just as knowledge of the Scriptures leads to the kingdoms of heaven and supplies us with the bread of him who says, “I am the bread that came down from heaven” (John 6), so its leaves contain moral teaching and grant healing, curing the wounds of sinners.

In place of “leaves,” which in Hebrew are called *Ale*, because of the similarity of word and sound, the Septuagint translated “ascension.” This too can be explained in such a way that, after the food of the fruits, we ascend to heavenly things by the admonitions of the words.

## BOOK TWENTY

[Col. 1059]

[Col. 1059D] Since in the preceding book the prophet had recalled the offerings of the individual festivals and the offering of the prince, as well as the duties of the priests, and had related the abundance of the waters and the fruitfulness of the trees on their banks, he now turns from this to set out, according to the Lord’s command, the boundaries of the land of the twelve tribes and of the spiritual possession, the first-fruits of the sanctuary, and to describe the possession of the Levites. Finally, by marking the gates of the city in the four quarters, he shows at the end of the book that the Lord is the inhabitant of that temple—he who is the beginning and author of every good thing and the consummation of perfected work.

## CHAPTER FORTY-SEVEN FOLLOWS
“Thus says the Lord God: This is the boundary within which you shall possess the land among the twelve tribes of Israel, because Joseph has a double measuring-cord. You shall possess it individually, each equally with his brother, over which I raised my hand to give it to your fathers; and this land shall fall to you as a possession.” (Adamant.)

Just as the shadows and copies of heavenly things serve those who receive the Law, which is the shadow of that true Law, so, correspondingly, the copy and shadow of the heavenly division serve those who divide the inheritance of the land in Judaea. There was therefore truth in heaven, but the shadow and copy of truth on earth. As long as this shadow stood on earth, there was an earthly Jerusalem, there was a temple, there was an altar and visible worship, there were high priests and priests; there also remained [Col. 1061A] the cities and villages of Judah, and all those things which are now reported as described in this book.

But when, at the coming of the Savior our God, salvation descended from heaven—“Truth has sprung up from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven” (Ps. LXXXIV)—the shadows and copies fell. Jerusalem fell, the temple fell, and the altar was taken away, so that there is no place either on Mount Gerizim or in Jerusalem where one must worship, but “true worshipers, who worship the Father, shall worship in spirit and truth” (John IV). Thus, when the truth was present, the type and shadow ceased.

And when that temple was present which was fashioned by the Spirit of God and the power of the Most High in the Virgin’s womb (John I), the temple constructed of stones was destroyed. The high priest of the coming good things was present, [Col. 1061B] and the high priests of bulls and goats ceased. The Lamb of God came, who takes away the sins of the world; the lamb taken from the sheep ceased, slaughtered for so many ages to no purpose and in vain.

Therefore the first and second divisions of the inheritance are reported as having taken place. The first was made through Moses; the second, which is also the more powerful, is described as having been made through Jesus. (Nazian.)

Moses assigns a possession beyond the Jordan to the tribe of Reuben, to the tribe of Gad, and to half the tribe of Manasseh, while all the others receive their inheritance through Jesus (Num. XXXII). We have already explained how those who preceded in time pleased God through the Law before those who reach the promises through faith in Jesus; yet they do not attain what is perfect, awaiting those who come later, who will please God at a different time but with one faith, [Col. 1061C] as the Apostle said (Heb. XI): “So that they should not attain perfection without us.”

We may infer this from the following example. For if “when God scattered the sons of Adam, he established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God”—or, as we read in other copies, “according to the number of the sons of Israel”—at the beginning of the world, and the sons of that Adam were scattered according as either their merits or the consideration of Adam himself required, what shall we say will happen when the last Adam, who was made not into a living soul but into a life-giving spirit, begins not to scatter but to administer and order his children by divine favor, not at the beginning but at the end of the world—not to those who all died in Adam, but to those who are all made alive in Christ?

Without doubt there will then be a certain division and distribution, one that must be assessed not only according to the merits of those who administer it, but also according to the consideration of the last Adam, in whom all are said to be made alive. For by the grace of God we have been saved, and not from ourselves; and “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII).

By God’s gift he bestows the glory of the heavenly kingdom upon his saints and elect, he himself granting it, who says to his disciples: “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations, and I appoint for you, just as my Father appointed for me, a kingdom, so that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and sit upon twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Luke XXII).

For what we said, “because Joseph has a double measuring-cord,” the Septuagint translated, “an increase of cord.” For Joseph is interpreted as “increase”; they understood the thing instead of the name and confused the reader’s mind.

For after the tribe of Levi had been removed and assigned to the temple sacrifices, two tribes remained, into which Joseph was divided: Ephraim and Manasseh. They said to Joshua the son of Nun: “Why have you given me the possession of one lot and one measuring-cord, although I am such a multitude and the Lord has blessed me?” (Josh. XVII). Joshua answered them: “If you are a numerous people, go up into the forest and cut out spaces for yourself in the land of the Perizzites and Rephaim, because the possession of Mount Ephraim is too narrow for you.”

And again: “Joshua said to the house of Ephraim and Manasseh: You are a numerous people and of great strength. You shall not have one lot, but you shall go up to the mountain and cut down and clear spaces for yourself in order to dwell there, and you will be able to go farther when you have overthrown the Canaanite, whom you say has iron chariots and is exceedingly strong.”

I have said this because Scripture now mentions that Joseph—that is, Ephraim and Manasseh—has a double measuring-cord, while each tribe receives spaces of land equal to its numbers, not according to the discretion of the one dividing but by lot, which remains in the power of the Lord.

In human custom, when something is divided by lot, it appears that one lot happens to fall to one person and another to another. In Holy Scripture, however, it is not so. I often asked myself whether the holy Fathers had entrusted judgment in so great and important a matter to lots. If this had indeed been done among the saints, then there would be nothing surprising about other men or nations; there would be nothing exceptional in the things said to have been divided by lot by the saints.

Let us see, then, whether we can find something in Scripture that reveals to us what power is contained in lots. Let us begin with Leviticus, where it is written: “And they shall receive,” it says, “two lots: one lot for the Lord, and one lot for Apopompaeus, that is, for the one who sends away. And upon whichever one the lot falls, they shall take that goat belonging to Apopompaeus and lead it alive into a deserted place, and release it for its dismissal; but they shall sacrifice the other goat to the Lord,” and the rest that is there, which those who read it certainly know.

And again: when Moses divided by lot the land for the tribe of Reuben, the tribe of Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh, who had requested beyond the Jordan that they receive the land requested by the children of Israel. Jesus himself, in accordance with the Lord’s command, gave Caleb the son of Jephunneh and the tribe of Judah their lot. He gave Ephraim and the remaining half of the tribe of Manasseh theirs. After this he gathered the children of Israel in the assembly and said:

“I will cast the lot and bring it forth before the Lord, provided that you first describe the land and bring me its description.”

And so, after the lots had been cast, the inheritance was distributed to the people of God. This lot was not moved by chance but according to what had been predestined by God.

Indeed, the tribe of Benjamin first received its lot, where Jerusalem was located. After this the tribe of Simeon received the second; then Issachar; afterward Zebulun; then Asher; after this also Naphtali; then Dan (Josh. XVI–XIX). At the end came those three tribes who had descended from Jacob’s concubines.

I therefore asked myself what the principle of lots might be, so that from the many testimonies of Scripture we might recognize what was hidden. I found, moreover, that gentile men also used lots, at the time when Jonah was sailing and the storm was raging. For those who were sailing said: “Let us cast lots and learn on whose account this great evil has come upon us” (Jonah VII), as though the lot had such power that it could reveal on whose account danger threatened those at sea.

Although they were gentiles and strangers to the knowledge of God, they were not deceived in this belief; rather, the lot disclosed to them the truth concerning Jonah. Inquiring further about these matters, I find Solomon also saying in Proverbs: “The lot restrains disputes and decides between the powerful” (Prov. XVIII), as though showing that disputes cease where the lot is cast.

But when I found that many passages in the Old Testament mention lots, I turned also to the New Testament, to see whether lots were perhaps despised there, or whether their use was mentioned somewhere there as well. I find that, when one of the number of the apostles was lacking and it was necessary to appoint another in Judas’s place (Acts I), the apostles assembled. They were certainly much wiser than those who now ordain bishops, presbyters, or deacons. They chose two and placed them in the midst, yet they did not allow themselves to decide which one should be appointed according to their own preference.

Rather, “after praying,” it says, “they cast lots,” so that from the two whom they had placed before the Lord—Joseph, who was called Barnabas and surnamed Justus, and Matthias—“the lot fell upon Matthias, and he was numbered with Christ’s apostles.” Since the proper procedure had preceded, the lot no longer conveyed chance but divine judgment through wisdom.

I continued to ask whether the New Testament names the lot in Christ or in the Church, or in mystical matters that appear to pertain to the soul. I find Paul writing to the Ephesians about Christ: “In him,” he says, “we were called by lot, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will, so that we might be for the praise of his glory, we who previously hoped in Christ” (Eph. I).

And he writes similarly to the Colossians: “Giving thanks to God the Father, who made us worthy to share in the portion of the lot of the saints in light” (Col. I).

After gathering so many testimonies from the Holy Scriptures concerning the mention of lots, in order that by considering many passages we might more diligently grasp their power, I myself have not yet been able either to see a clear meaning fully disclosed by all these things or to overcome the fear that has settled upon my mind about declaring and stating something concerning so great a matter.

Let this much suffice, insofar as the matter permits: the lot drawn by the apostles indicates this to us. When the lot is drawn with complete faith and after prayer has preceded it, the lot declares openly to human beings what the will of God contains secretly.

According to the interior understanding, Paul seems to judge likewise when he says, “in the portion of the lot of the saints in light,” and, “called by lot in Christ.” We must consider whether perhaps not only among human beings but also among the heavenly powers a lot is conducted [Agassur; perhaps agatur, “is conducted”], and some power presides over this duty, which, for example, when Jesus the son of Nun was distributing the inheritance by lot, might provide not some grace but guidance in the lot according to what it is to please God.

It may cause the first things to happen to the one whom it knows to hold the first place with God, so that what is held secretly with God may also be shown to human beings through the governance of the lot; it may make another occupy the second place and another the third. I believe that this is found not only on earth but also in heaven, and that a division of this kind, distinguished before the Lord by consideration of merits, exists even at that time: “When the Most High sees the nations and scatters the sons of Adam, and establishes the sons of the nations according to the number of the angels of God” (Deut. XXXII).

“And the Lord’s portion became Jacob, the allotment of his inheritance, Israel.” You see, then, that here too it says that Israel is the Lord’s portion and inheritance by lot. The lot must not therefore be thought to have come by chance.

One angel, for example, received the nation of the Egyptians; another, that of the Idumaeans and Moabites; another, India or each of the nations that exist upon the earth. Even there, although these nations are said to have been divided by lot according to the number of the angels of God, that lot must nevertheless be understood to have operated as we said among human beings: the lot reveals publicly the judgment of God that is hidden.

Thus, there also, each angel must be believed to have received that nation in the division according to his merit and virtue. There are ineffable mysteries of the divine administration in each of these things, so that all may be ordered appropriately according to their proper rank through the service of each power.

For the Apostle says: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?” In imitation of these things, therefore, we must believe that Scripture also reports lots, that the inheritance is distributed through Jesus, that it is assigned to each tribe by divine administration, and that, through the ineffable providence of God, the portion of the future inheritance is foreshadowed in the present things by these lots [Col. 1064D] and brought to completion.

For the Law is said to possess a shadow of future good things. And, as the Apostle says concerning those who have come to the Lord Jesus Christ: “You have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem.”

There is a city in heaven called Jerusalem, and there is Mount Zion. It is certainly not without reason that Benjamin received Jerusalem and Mount Zion in his lot, because the order of that heavenly Jerusalem undoubtedly required that Benjamin should already receive some earthly Jerusalem, which preserves the figure and form of the heavenly one.

Likewise, it must be said concerning Benjamin that, for a definite reason, Hebron was assigned to the lot of Judah, or that the individual cities were recorded for the several tribes: unless it is because those heavenly places in which Jerusalem and Zion are said to exist—and undoubtedly the other places that are near or joined to them—contained in themselves in heaven the cause and rationale of what was represented on earth by distribution through lot.

This, then, is why divine wisdom arranged for certain names of places to be written in Scripture, names that contain a kind of mystical interpretation. Through them it is indicated to you who observe these things by what principles, and not by chance or accident, they have been arranged.

For if it must not be thought that it happened by chance, for example, that one angel was called Michael, another Raphael; and, to descend to human matters, that it was not by chance that one patriarch was called Abraham, another Isaac, and another Israel; nor even among women did it happen by accident, but by a definite divine rationale, that one was called Sarah instead of Sarai, and that Israel came from Jacob, or Abraham from his former name; and if it is certain that each angel or human being also receives names from the duties and actions entrusted to him, then it follows that certain heavenly places and cities also exist—just as the heavenly Jerusalem and Zion are said to exist—and others whose type and image are contained by these earthly places, which are now mystically signified for us in this Scripture through Jesus the son of Nun.

I think it was of these cities that it was said: “The cities of Judah shall be built, and they shall dwell there, and they shall inherit it” (Ps. LXVIII). Of these also our Lord and Savior says: “There are many dwelling places with my Father” (John XIV).

And it must be believed that it is of these cities that the Lord says to the servant who has done good business: “I have authority over ten cities” (Luke XIX), and to another, over five.

We have dared to present these things to you concerning the division by lot of the land of Judah, insofar as it was permitted, prompted by Scripture, which says that Jerusalem is heavenly Zion and that the other things similarly written exist in heaven. These have given us occasion to understand from all these matters that heavenly mysteries are described in them.

“But this is the boundary of the land on the northern side: from the Great Sea, by the road of Ethalon, as one comes, Sedada, Emath, Berotha, Sabarim, which lies between Damascus and the border of Emath; the middle court of Thicon, which is near the boundaries of Auran or Auranitis, [Col. 1065D] and the boundary shall be from the sea as far as the court of Enon or Serenan, the boundary of Damascus; and from the north toward the north, the boundary of Emath, the northern side.”

“(Jerome.) Between the description of the Holy Land of the twelve tribes by Joshua the son of Nun and what is now commanded to be done through Ezekiel, there is this difference: there the land is divided by lot among the tribes; here it is assigned by the command of the Lord who orders it.

“Thus, in the Book of Numbers (Num. XXXIV), in which the whole Promised Land is divided in a brief account by its four sides, this description is given from the north, that is, from the northern side. The boundaries will begin on the northern side from the Great Sea and proceed as far as the highest mountain; from there one will come to Emath, [Col. 1066A] as far as the boundaries of Sedada. The borders will continue as far as Zephrona and the village of Enan or Aserenan.

“The Hebrews say that the northern side begins from the Great Sea, which extends along the shores of Palestine, Phoenicia, and Syria—the region called Coele-Syria—and Cilicia, and stretches through Egypt toward Libya. When it says that the boundaries proceed as far as the highest mountain, the Hebrews believe that either Mount Amanus or Taurus is meant; Taurus seems more likely to us.

“‘From there,’ it says, ‘you shall come to Emath,’ which is now called Epiphania, its name having been changed after Antiochus, the most cruel of tyrants. For he bore the title Ἐπιφανής, ‘Epiphanes.’ ‘As far as the boundaries,’ it says, ‘of Sedada,’ a place that also occurs in the present reading of Ezekiel.

“‘The borders shall proceed as far as Zephrona,’ the city that today they call the town of Zephirium in Cilicia. But what follows, ‘and the village of Enan,’ for which Aserenan or Enan is written in Hebrew, is also contained in the present passage.

“For the present, it is enough to have briefly summarized the historical account and to have placed the descriptions of Numbers and Ezekiel alongside one another, so that the prudent reader may understand where they mention the same, neighboring, or different things.

“Now let us interpret the names individually and, with the Lord supplying what is needed in each case, discuss the anagogy—ἀναγωγή, the spiritual interpretation—that they seem to offer us.

“Ethalon is interpreted as ‘the cradle of sorrow’; Sadada, ‘his side’—understand ‘from the side,’ not ‘from breadth’; Emath, ‘fury’; Berotha, ‘wells’; Sabarim, ‘the circuit of mountains’; Damascus, ‘blood of sackcloth’ and ‘kiss’ or ‘cup.’

“Symmachus interprets the house or court of Thicon as: ‘the middle court that proceeds to the boundaries of Auran.’ Thicon therefore means ‘middle.’ Auran, which the Septuagint rendered in Greek as Auranitis, means ‘anger.’ Aser Enon, which is the boundary of Damascus, is called in our language ‘the court of the fountain.’

“Thus the northern side extends from the Great Sea by the road of Ethalon, which is interpreted as ‘the cradle of sorrow’; through repentance it comes to Sadada, where there is a turning aside from the side. For we understand Emath, which threatens us, as the indignation of the Lord; or Emath, once the truth has been discovered, opens for us the wells of Berotha, which the princes Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob dug.

“By a long circuit we reach the mountains of Sabarim, which are situated between Damascus—that is, the blood of sackcloth—and the boundary of Emath, as we said above, ‘of truth.’ Just as through sorrow we turn aside from impending evils and avoid them by turning aside, so after blood and sackcloth, that is, after a bloodstained life, before we come to the boundaries of Emath, we go around and reach the mountains of which it is written: ‘The mountains are round about him, and the Lord is round about his people.’

“This place is called the court of Thicon, that is, the middle court, as Symmachus interpreted it, near the boundaries of Auran, which signifies anger. With the prophet we say: ‘I shall bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him’ (Mic. VII).

“And from the sea as far as the boundaries of Damascus: in this region the Apostle Paul also, from the Jewish fury and the shedding of ecclesiastical blood, saw the light in blindness. Having taken up the sackcloth of the former persecution, he preached the Gospel, so that he might reach the court of the eternal fountain and, once placed in the north, might grasp the boundary of truth.

“Moreover, ‘the eastern side: from the middle of Auran, from the middle of Damascus, from the middle of Gilead, and from the middle of the land of Israel, with the Jordan as boundary, you shall measure the eastern side toward the eastern sea.’”

“(Jerome.) In the Book of Numbers I find the following written instead: ‘From there they shall measure the boundaries toward the eastern side, from the village of Enan—that is, Aserenon—as far as Sephania. From Sephania the boundaries shall descend to Rebblah opposite the fountain. From there they shall proceed eastward to the Sea of Chenereth, and extend as far as the Jordan; finally they shall end at the sea.’

“Above it had said: ‘The boundary shall be from the sea as far as Eserenon, the boundary of Damascus.’ From the end, therefore, of the northern side—that is, from the court of Enon—the boundaries extend, according to the Book of Numbers, as far as Sephania, which the Hebrews call Apamia. From Apamia the boundaries descend to Rebblah, which is now called Antioch in Syria.

“And so that you may know that this Rebblah signifies the city that is now most famous in Coele-Syria, what follows says, ‘opposite the fountain.’ It is clear that Daphne is meant, the fountain from which the aforementioned city enjoys a most abundant water supply.

“This place was established by Gnaeus Pompey, who first subjected Judaea to Roman rule by military force. According to the poets’ story, it received from him the name Daphne because of the laurels and cypresses, trees that are especially abundant in that place.

“‘From there,’ it says, ‘the boundaries shall proceed eastward to the Sea of Chenereth,’ as far as the Lake of Tiberias. It is called a sea, although it has fresh water, according to the idiom of Scripture, by which gatherings of waters are called ‘seas.’

“‘And the boundaries shall extend,’ it says, ‘as far as the Jordan, and finally shall end at the sea’: either the Dead Sea, or, as others think, the tongue of the Red Sea, on whose shore Aila is situated, where a Roman legion and garrison are now stationed.

“This is what is said according to the Book of Numbers. According to Ezekiel, however, it is ‘from the middle of Auran,’ which is a town of Damascus in the desert, and ‘from the middle of Gilead.’ Gilead, a mountain joined to the hills of Lebanon, fell by lot to Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh. It lies behind Phoenicia and Arabia. Jacob reached this mountain when he set out from Carrhae and was overtaken by Laban. Jeremiah also speaks of it: ‘Gilead, you are to me the beginning of Lebanon’ (Jer. XXVII).

“Gilead, son of Machir, son of Manasseh, seized it from the territory of the Amorites. The boundary of this side is the Jordan River, which separates it, and the eastern sea, which in this passage they understand as the Dead Sea, not the tongue of the Red Sea.

“Let us speak according to tropology. After the northern boundaries, through a long circuit by way of Ethalon, Sedada, Berotha, Sabarim, Thicon, Auran, Damascus, and the court of Enon, the eastern side reaches as far as Emath: from the middle of the anger of Auran, from the middle of Damascus—that is, through the blood of repentance—and from the middle of Gilead, which is interpreted as ‘revelation’ or ‘the mound of testimony.’

“Thus, after anger and repentance, it shows the hope of salvation; and from the middle of the land of Israel, which contains the vision of peace, it reaches the sweetest streams of the Jordan. These, after being separated by a long distance from the sea, attain the light of the east, so that it ends at the Jordan River, whose name is interpreted as ‘the stream of judgment,’ and at the boundary of the east.

“What is placed in the Septuagint as phoeniconos, that is, ‘of the palm grove,’ is not found in the Hebrew. In its place we translated, ‘you shall measure.’ The error is evident: deceived by the similarity of the letters daleth and resh, they read thamorru instead of thamoddu.”

“But the southern side, toward the south, shall be from Thamar as far as the waters of contradiction, Cades; and the stream as far as the Great Sea. This is the southern side.”

“For this the Book of Numbers says as follows (Num. XXXIV): ‘It shall begin from the wilderness of Sin, which is beside Edom, and its boundaries shall extend eastward to the sea. They shall go around the southern side by the ascent of the Scorpion, pass through Senna, and reach southward as far as Cadesbarne. From there the boundaries shall go out to the village called Addar and extend as far as Asemona. The boundary shall turn from Asemona toward the torrent of Egypt and end at the shore of the Great Sea.’

“In brief, this means that—from the wilderness of Sin, which is beside Edom, and the Red Sea as its boundary—it goes around and passes by the ascent of the Scorpion, through Senna, Cadesbarne, the court of Addar, and Asemona, reaching the torrent of Egypt, which flows into the sea beside the city of Rhinocorura. We should not, on account of Ezekiel, appear to have wandered into an excessively lengthy exposition of Numbers.

“Here, however, the boundary of the southern, that is, meridional side, begins at Thamar, a city in the desert which Solomon also built with remarkable works and which today is called Palmyra. In Hebrew it is called Thamar, a name that in our language means ‘palm.’ It extends as far as the waters of contradiction, Cades, which unquestionably lies in the desert, and the stream that enters the Great Sea, the sea that extends along the shores of Egypt and Palestine. This is the southern side, toward the south.

“After the northern and eastern sides, when the sun of righteousness has risen for us, we receive the southern side, when the whole light from above is poured into us. We enter the banquet with Abraham and are drunk with the wine that gladdens the human heart (Ps. CIII), together with Joseph and his brothers.

“This possession and these boundaries begin at Thamar, that is, at the palm and victory over vices, and extend as far as the waters of contradiction. For virtues are always opposed. Hence the Jews, arguing against Paul, assert that evangelical preaching is opposed throughout the whole world. And in the Gospel we read that Simeon said: ‘This one will be for the fall and rising of many, and for a sign that will be opposed’ (Luke II).

“Every contradiction belongs to holiness, which is interpreted as Cades, as the Psalmist says: ‘The Lord will shake the wilderness of Cades’ (Ps. XXVIII). At first it did not possess the holiness of the Lord, but it was shaken and moved so that it might receive as guest the God who says: ‘Upon whom shall my spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?’ (Isa. LXVI).

“After the wilderness of Cades, as far as the Great Sea in the south, there is the torrent of the southern side. We have spoken above of this torrent: it receives not rains from earth but rains from heaven, gathered from the variety of different virtues.

“‘And the western side: the Great Sea shall be the boundary, in a straight line until you come to Emath. This is the western side.’

“Of this the Book of Numbers writes more clearly and briefly (Num. XXXIV): ‘The western side shall begin from the Great Sea and end at the same boundary.’ That is, from sea to sea—from the torrent of Rhinocorura, which flows into the sea, as far as the place opposite Emath, the city of Syria, about which we spoke above.

“According to the laws of tropology, the west is always in the sea, always amid salt and waves, where shipwrecks are stirred up each day, together with the deaths of wretched people and the loss of riches and merchandise. Yet when we have broken all these things through patience, we come by a straight path to Emath, that is, to the truth of the Lord, who, once persecutions have been overcome, has promised us eternal rewards.

“(Maurus.) To summarize briefly all the foregoing in a single moral sense: whoever desires to possess the inheritance of the Holy Land and to receive with God’s elect and saints the lot of the future homeland must begin from the northern side and proceed toward the east. That is, having abandoned the cold of unbelief, he must move toward the rising of right faith.

“First, as we have said, he must come through Thalon—that is, through repentance for sins—to Sadada, meaning that he must turn away from vices and cease from sins, fearing the indignation of the Lord. In accordance with the Psalmist’s words:

“‘Turn away from evil and do good, and dwell for ever and ever; for the Lord loves judgment and will not abandon his saints. They shall be preserved for ever. But the unjust shall be punished, and the seed of the wicked shall perish,’ and the rest (Ps. XXXVII).

“Thus, moving toward the wells of living water—that is, toward the sacrament of baptism—or toward the teaching of sacred knowledge, he should hasten to go to the spiritual mountains, that is, to holy teachers, so that from them he may receive the light of true knowledge and learn to discipline his body and put to death his earthly members. In this way he may reach the court of the eternal fountain and the boundary of truth itself.

“When the truth itself has shone upon him from the eastern side, and these mysteries have been revealed through the testimonies of the Holy Scriptures, then in the Jordan—that is, in the stream of judgment—he understands the depth of wisdom and recognizes the bath of true purification.

“After he has reached the south, that is, the pure light of knowledge and the ardor of charity, he must endure the battles of contradiction and the heat of persecution. For according to the Apostle: ‘All who desire to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecution’ (II Tim. III).

“When we hasten toward the west and the end of our life draws near, we must be tossed about in the waves of the sea—that is, in the storms of the present age—and thus, through patience, reach the Lord’s truth after overcoming persecutions. In accordance with the Lord’s own judgment, we must possess our souls through patience, receive the rewards of eternal life, possess the land of the living, and dwell in the heavenly Jerusalem [Col. 1070A], that is, in the vision of everlasting peace.

“But who among us is such that he may deserve to pass from this kind of distribution to that lot of the heavenly inheritance? Who will be so blessed that his lot will be Jerusalem, so that he may be there where the temple of God is—or rather, so that he himself may be the temple of God?

“Who will be so blessed that he may celebrate festivals there, where the divine altar burns with perpetual fires? Who will be so blessed that he may place his sacrifice and incense of fragrance upon that fire of which the Savior said: ‘I have come to cast fire’ (Luke XII)?

“Who will be so blessed that he may always celebrate Passover there, in the place that the Lord his God will choose; that he may observe there the day of Pentecost, the festival of propitiation, and the solemnity of Tabernacles—not now through the shadow, but through the very appearance and truth of things?

“Who among us will be considered worthy of the election of the blessed lot when God finally begins to divide the sons, and says to one (Luke XIX): ‘You shall have authority over five cities’; or says to another: ‘You shall have authority over ten cities’; and not only says, ‘Enter into the joy of the Lord your God,’ but also says, ‘You too, sit with me upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel’ (Matt. XIX)?

“And of whom does he say: ‘Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me’ (John XV)? I desire that they too be kings, as I am King of kings; I desire that they too have dominion, as I am Lord of lords.

“Blessed are those who will attain this supreme blessedness. Blessed are those who will ascend to these heights of merit. And blessed is our God, who promised these things to those who love him. These are truly the ones numbered before God by sacred numbers; indeed, they are the ones whose very hairs of the head have also been numbered through Jesus Christ our Lord.

“But since no one can reach the lot of the elect and the possession of the heavenly homeland through pride or envy, whoever desires to attain future goods must strive to go there through true humility and brotherly love. Let him remember what is written: ‘Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted’ (Matt. XXIII).

“Therefore let him despise no one and scorn no one, but rather believe himself inferior to all. Let him know, according to the judgment of the Apostle Peter, that ‘God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears God and practices righteousness is acceptable to him’ (Acts X).

“Consequently, the man who spoke to the prophet showed this by saying:

“‘And you shall divide this land among yourselves, Israel, and measure it out as an inheritance for yourselves and for the resident foreigners who have joined themselves to you, who have fathered children in your midst; and they shall be to you as native-born among the children of Israel. With you they shall divide the possession in the midst of the tribes of Israel. In whatever tribe the resident foreigner resides, there you shall give him his possession: thus says the Lord God.’”

“(Jerome.) Through this chapter we learn—and the arrogance of the Jews is struck down—that nothing is divided between Israel and the people of the nations. For if the land is divided between resident foreigners and strangers together with those who belong to the people of Israel—that is, the native-born—there is no doubt that the inheritance of the gentile people and of the Jewish people is the same, provided that they have turned to the worship of the God of Israel, which Christians possess as their proper name.

“The Jews have the letter of the Law, while we have its spirit; they hold the membranes, while we have the one who is written upon the membranes. Among Moses’ people the land is divided by lot; here, as we have said, it is assigned by the judgment of the Lord. There is one possession for the resident foreigner and the Israelite, and in each tribe an inheritance is given at the command of the Lord God.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

Here the division of the land is described with regard to the inhabitants within it.

“Now these are the names of the tribes: From the northern boundaries, for those traveling by the road of Ethlom: Hamath, the court of Aenon, the boundary of Damascus, to the north beside Hamath; and its eastern side shall be the sea: one portion for Dan. From the boundary of Dan, from the eastern side to the western side: one portion for Asher. Along the boundary of Asher, from the eastern side to the sea-side: one portion for Naphtali. Along the boundary of Naphtali, from the eastern side to the sea-side: one portion for Manasseh. Along the boundary of Manasseh, from the eastern side to the sea-side: one portion for Ephraim. Along the boundary of Ephraim, from the eastern side to the sea-side: one portion for Reuben. Along the boundary of Reuben, from the eastern side to the sea-side: one portion for Judah.” (Jerome.)

Having described the possession of the Holy Land both according to the present prophecy of Ezekiel and according to the Book of Numbers, he now describes the possession of the individual tribes from the eastern side to the western side, that is, to the sea. First, the boundaries begin in the north, for those traveling by the road of Ethlom: Hamath, the court—or, rather, Aser—of Enon, the boundary of Damascus, to the north beside Hamath, about which we have already spoken. The first tribe is Dan, the second Asher, the third Naphtali, the fourth Manasseh, the fifth Ephraim, the sixth Reuben, and the seventh Judah. This is the left-hand side, and the number seven is complete.

Then come the first fruits of the priests and Levites, and the sanctuary of the Lord, with the Holy of Holies in the middle. The city too is described, having on each side, in a square, four thousand five hundred reeds. The suburbs of the priests and Levites are also described in due order, as is the prince’s possession. Again, on the right-hand side, five tribes follow, likewise extending from the eastern side to the western side. The first is Benjamin, the second Simeon, possessing his own allotment separately and by no means mixed with Judah as previously; the third is Issachar, the fourth Zebulun, and the fifth Gad.

There are also three gates on each side, and the name of the city itself—the name inscribed on the golden plate on the forehead of the high priest. We shall discuss all these matters in their proper places.

It should also be noted that the names of the forty-eight cities given in the Book of Numbers to the Levitical tribe for habitation, together with their suburbs, are passed over here. The cities of refuge are also omitted: three beyond the Jordan—namely Bosor, Ramoth, and Gaulon—given to the two and a half tribes, and three within the Jordan—namely Cades, Shechem, and Cariatharbe. For in a mystical description, and in the dwelling of the saints and the perfect way of life, there was no need to describe the aids required by Israel while still placed on earth, hastening through many labors and dangers to reach this city, and saying in each of the saints’ persons: “I am a sojourner and a pilgrim, like all my fathers” (Psalm XXXVIII). And in another place: “I dwelt with those who dwell in Cedar; my soul has long been a pilgrim” (Psalm CXIX).

“Along the boundary of Judah, from the eastern side to the sea-side, shall be the first fruits which you shall set apart: twenty-five thousand in width and length, like the individual portions from the eastern side to the sea-side. And the sanctuary shall be in its midst. The first fruits which you shall set apart for the Lord shall be twenty-five thousand in length and ten thousand in width.”

It is superfluous to discuss matters already discussed, and, where we have labored above, to labor again as though nothing had been said. After the boundaries of the seven tribes have been described from east to west, the first fruits are described. Their width is to be twenty-five thousand reeds, while their length is to be the same as that occupied by each tribe from the east to the sea, whose length is not stated. For no measurement of the tribes’ length was given in their individual descriptions.

But if the width is twenty-five thousand reeds, it may be inferred that the length is much greater, since the length is always greater than the width. In the middle of the first fruits set apart for the Lord is placed the sanctuary, twenty-five thousand reeds in length and ten thousand in width.

When I read this, I can say nothing other than the Apostle’s words: “O depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and inscrutable his ways!” (Romans XI). And elsewhere: “That you may be able to comprehend, with all the saints, what is the breadth and length and height and depth; and to know the love of Christ, which surpasses knowledge, so that you may be filled unto all the fullness of God” (Ephesians III).

The number twenty-five thousand is to be referred to the senses, concerning which it is said: “You shall possess divine understanding”; and the ten thousand to perfect and consummated virtue, which passes from the Decalogue of the Old Instrument to the sacrament of the Gospel, as we briefly touched upon earlier and shall recall here in part. For if, beginning with one and adding numbers, you reach four, you complete the number ten; thus the Old Testament is gathered up in the New, and the New is unfolded in the Old.

“Now these shall be the first fruits of the sanctuary for the priests: to the north, twenty-five thousand in length, and to the sea, ten thousand in width; likewise, to the east, ten thousand in width, and to the south, twenty-five thousand in length.” (Adamantius.)

All the children of Israel received their allotments in the land. For the Levites, God alone is a sufficient inheritance. But since, by God’s command, the Levites received tithes and first fruits of the produce from the children of Israel, they ought also to receive tithes, so to speak, from the land and dwellings—that is, they were to receive tithes from everyone.

Therefore the leading men who were of the sons of Levi approached Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the princes of the tribes of the children of Israel at Shiloh in the land of Canaan and said: “The Lord commanded through Moses’ hand that cities be given us for habitation, together with their suburbs for our animals,” as is found written in the Book of Joshua son of Nun (Joshua XXI).

It was therefore necessary that an allotment also be made of the suburbs and cities, lest the division made among the Levites appear indiscriminate and accidental.

Just as the distribution of the allotment made among the children of Israel had a rationale by which one person was judged worthy of the first allotment and another of the second—concerning which we have discussed above as best we could—and just as those who received land through Moses beyond the Jordan and through Joshua in the land of promise had their order, with the first lot falling to Benjamin and the last among the others to Dan, so there must also be some rationale in the order of the priestly and Levitical allotment: one receives the first lot, another the second, and another the third, through which this or that place is assigned to each.

The sons of Levi are said to be Gershon, Kohath, and Merari, and Kohath is shown to have held primacy in honor—that is, those sons of Kohath who were descended from Amram. For from him came Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. (Nazianzen.)

Thus, from Kohath a certain part became the priestly people, namely Aaron and his sons. Moses, however, must be regarded as belonging to the priestly order—or, if anything greater than the priestly order is possible, to that. The situation concerning his sons is different. The rest of the sons of Kohath held the second rank in the tribe of Levi: those descended from Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel.

After these, the descendants of Gershon received their portion after Kohath, in third place; Merari was last of all. This is the distinction of the first, second, third, and fourth orders, which we first observed in the Book of Numbers.

For after the twelve tribes had been arranged around the ark of the Lord’s covenant according to the four quarters of the world, three tribes were stationed in the east, three in the south, three toward the sea, which is the west, and three toward the north, which is the north (*septentrio*). These groups are likewise assigned here in the same order according to the four quarters of the world.

In the east, where the tribe of Judah was situated—the first among the others—Aaron and his sons are placed. Kohath and the rest, who were appointed to carry the ark of the Lord’s covenant on their shoulders and to sound the trumpets, are stationed as follows: when the first trumpet sounded, those who were in the east moved their camp; when the second sounded, those who were in the south arose; the third summoned those in the west; and the fourth those in the north.

You see how much order, how much distinction, and how much correspondence among events are described in Scripture, and how nothing is done without measure and order. Examine it more carefully, and you will find all these things arranged in this way throughout Scripture.

But who can ascend to all these things and comprehend them? Who can even discover them and observe the order of the mysteries, when the narrative’s text can scarcely be explained according to the letter alone, and when the intermingling of places and persons contained in the history must be disentangled?

What shall we say of those mysteries which are written through these passages, and in which the future distributions of the inheritance are foreshadowed? And by whom will the division of the holy land be carried out, which the meek shall receive as an inheritance? Who can explain the different stations of the camps, and how in the resurrection this distribution is to be made among the individual saints according to priestly or Levitical order?

As the Apostle says, in the resurrection not everything will happen confusedly, but “each in his own order: Christ the first fruits, then those who are Christ’s, who have hoped in his coming, when he has handed over the kingdom to God the Father and subjected every principality and power to him” (1 Corinthians XV). There, without doubt, there will be such observances of the camps, priestly distributions and orders, and meanings of the trumpets.

That the Levites receive forty-two cities apart from the six cities of refuge unmistakably signifies the preaching of the saints. They possess the teaching composed of the Decalogue of the Law and the fourfold number of the Gospel, as though possessing forty cities—ten multiplied by four—to which two are added, because everything they proclaim they announce in both a moral and a mystical sense.

“And the sanctuary of the Lord,” he says, “shall be in its midst. The sanctuary shall belong to the priests, to the sons of Zadok, who kept my ordinances and did not go astray when the children of Israel went astray, as the Levites went astray. And the first fruits from the first fruits of the land shall be holy of holies, beside the boundary of the Levites.” (Jerome.)

Four sides of the priests’ first-fruits are described—not belonging to the people, nor to the common multitude, nor to the Levites, that is, to the lower rank, but properly pertaining to the worship of the priests: the north, west, east, and south. The order of spiritual progress is narrated through these regions, so that, leaving behind the cold of the north, we come to the west, where our vices may set and perish. From there let us pass to the east; when the sun of righteousness has risen for us, let us come to the south, where the light is brightest and perfect.

Thus, both from the north to the sea and from the east to the south, the length is to be twenty-five thousand and the width ten thousand, so that everywhere the same measure of length and width is preserved.

“The sanctuary”—that is, the temple of the Lord—“shall be in the midst” of the priests’ first fruits, and shall be enclosed on every side by equal sides. Since he had said, “These shall be the first fruits of the priests’ sanctuary,” lest all priests claim this place and the observance of its ordinances under the common designation, he adds specifically: “The sanctuary shall belong to the priests, to the sons of Zadok.”

Zadok is interpreted as “just,” concerning whom it is said: “The Lord is just and has loved justice; his face has seen equity” (Psalm X). Instead of Zadok, the Septuagint write Sadduc. This Zadok speaks in the Gospel: “For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V). Concerning him, under Solomon’s name, the Prophet mystically sings: “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your justice to the king’s son.”

Those priests shall possess the Lord’s sanctuary and keep his ordinances who did not go astray when the children of Israel and the Levites went astray. Concerning these we have spoken above: they do not offer victims, but, content with the privilege of their name and the humility arising from their error, they continually say in their heart: “I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Psalm L).

Let the priestly order hear this—even that which was overcome by the heat of the Arian persecution—and afterward, lest it lack the resources of the true faith, submits its neck to that faith’s power. Let it consider it sufficient if it is not expelled from the temple, if it retains some shadow and image of its former name, and does not, lying on its back and belching out luxuries as though immaculate and pure, spew the nausea of its ignorance and barbarous chatter upon us from its lofty throne.

“They shall have,” he says, “first fruits from the first fruits of the land”—that is, the priests, who did not go astray when the children of Israel and the Levites went astray. “First fruits from the first fruits,” like a tithe of tithes; and the Holy of Holies shall be beside the boundary of the Levites, so that the Levites may indeed have the priests’ borders, but may not be able to possess its center—that is, its middle—and the possession itself.

“But for the Levites likewise, beside the boundaries of the priests, twenty-five thousand in length and ten thousand in width. The whole length shall be twenty-five thousand, and the width ten thousand. They shall not sell any of it, nor exchange it, nor transfer the first fruits of the land, because they are consecrated to the Lord. But the five thousand that remain in width, across the twenty-five thousand, shall be profane, for the city’s habitation and its suburbs. And the city shall be in its midst.”

What we translated as “profane,” for which Aquila translated βέβηλον (*bebēlon*), while Symmachus and Theodotion translated λαϊκόν (*laikon*), the Septuagint rendered προτείχισμα (*protei-chisma*), which we may call an outer wall or rampart. That is profane and lay—that is, common—which everyone may inhabit freely.

But what the Septuagint said, “It shall neither be measured nor removed,” in place of our “It shall not be exchanged or transferred,” has no clear meaning.

The Levites’ possession is also described. It is close to the priests’ boundaries and has the same spaces in length and width as the priests’ smaller number has, in view of the greater number of Levites. Nevertheless, it uses its own boundaries and understands itself to be separated from the priestly rank, so as to humble the pride of ministers who, ignorant of the humility proper to their status, swell beyond priests—that is, presbyters—and assess dignity not by merit but by wealth.

Certainly, the first among the ministers, who preaches to the people in every place and never leaves the high priest’s side, considers it an insult if he is ordained a presbyter. He does not remember that, as a minister of tables and widows, he has been assigned to service and ministry not only to priests but also to widows and the poor.

“And they shall not sell any of it,” he says, so that the possession of the Levitical allotment may remain perpetual, merit may not be overcome by price, and we may not transfer it from one person to another, because what has been consecrated to the Lord belongs not to those to whom it has been given, but to the one whose name they bear in possessing it.

The five thousand that remain in width across the twenty-five thousand—length being understood—shall be profane for the city, and all Israelites and everyone from the common people may inhabit them. This does not mean that they are unclean or that anything in the habitation of the holy land is considered contaminated or filthy, but that everyone except the priests is permitted to dwell there.

By these things we understand that everything we refer to the senses—that is, the bodily pleasures which we apprehend through sight, hearing, touch, smell, and taste—is profane, does not possess the sanctity of the temple, and does not belong to the privilege of the priesthood but to lay lowliness.

The city shall be in the middle, concerning which it is written: “The river’s rushing waters gladden the city of God” (Psalm XLV). And: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matthew V). We shall speak of it in what follows.

The term προτείχισμα (*protei-chisma*) means “outer wall” or “rampart,” and διάστημα (*diastēma*) means “space,” which the Septuagint used for “suburbs.” We do not know what meaning they have in this passage.

“And these shall be its measurements: on the northern side, four thousand five hundred; on the southern side, four thousand five hundred; on the eastern side, four thousand five hundred; and on the western side, four thousand five hundred.”

When it says, “And these shall be its measurements,” “of the city” is to be understood. At the end of the preceding chapter it was stated: “And the city shall be in its midst”—that is, in the midst of the land.

It begins with the northern side and places the southern side opposite it. Again, it balances one side with another, placing the western side—that is, the sea—opposite the eastern side. Each side of the city has four thousand five hundred reeds, which, when calculated, make eleven thousand and eighty-five paces. Thus the entire city, as it is written at the end of this volume, has around its circuit eighteen thousand reeds, which make forty-four thousand three hundred and forty paces.

Hence Psalm XLIV, whose title is “For the end, for those who shall be changed,” and which pertains to Idida—that is, “the beloved of the Lord”—or, as Aquila interpreted it, “for the lilies,” and Symmachus, “for the flowers,” contains the mysteries of the Church, which is the city of the Lord. Concerning it the same psalm says: “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in gold and surrounded with variety.” And again: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within,” so that she may not be like whitened tombs, white on the outside, but may wash every part of the dish, both inside and outside.

When we withdraw from the north wind, which is exceedingly cold, we pass to the south. After the light of knowledge has risen within us, we fear the setting of our strength, considering not the past but the future, and not possessing a secure hold on virtue, but saying daily in prayer: “Lead us not into temptation,” which we may be unable to bear.

“The suburbs of the city shall be two hundred and fifty to the north, two hundred and fifty to the south, two hundred and fifty to the east, and two hundred and fifty toward the sea.”

For “suburbs,” which are called *migrash* in Hebrew, the Septuagint again translated διάστημα (*diastēma*), that is, “space.” When two hundred and fifty are stated for each side, reeds are understood—reeds six cubits and one palm in length. Along each side they make just under six hundred and seventeen paces; together, having one thousand reeds, they make two thousand four hundred and sixty-eight paces. These spaces surround the walls of the city, separating the city from everything else.

From this it is shown that no one has permission to use these spaces for carrying out the city’s work or gathering produce. They are to remain free from human use and labor, so that the areas around the city walls may possess the beauty of naturally growing shrubs, grasses, and whatever else the earth produces.

“And whatever remains in length, corresponding to the first fruits of the sanctuary—ten thousand toward the east and ten thousand toward the west—shall be like the first fruits of the sanctuary, and its produce shall be for food, or bread, for those who serve or work for the city. Those serving or working for the city shall serve or work from all the tribes of Israel. All the first fruits, twenty-five thousand by twenty-five thousand, in a square, shall be set apart as the first fruits of the sanctuary and the possession of the city.”

After the description of the holy city and its suburbs, he wishes the remaining portion of the sanctuary’s first fruits—ten thousand reeds extending eastward and another ten thousand extending westward—to be assigned to those who perform the city’s work for various purposes and for whatever the city needs. Thus the laborers may eat from the produce that grows in this area of land, whether they are building the city’s walls or restoring what has been damaged and ruined, so that the city may have its proper cultivation and its structures may be repaired whenever necessity demands.

We find this not only in Israel, or spiritually in the mystery of the Church’s possession, but also occurring in the Roman Empire: certain estates belong to the rights of cities through royal generosity, inheritance, or the gifts of many persons, so that buildings do not gradually collapse and public structures, which are an ornament to the city, are not worn down by prolonged neglect.

The laborers, he says—those who serve in the city’s works—shall come from all the tribes of Israel, so that no one may regard himself as exempt from the city’s work, but all may eagerly build the Church. We read that this also occurred in the tabernacle: according to their varying abilities, some offered gold, silver, scarlet, fine linen, and purple, as well as various and diverse woven materials; others offered skins and goats’ hair.

Although the gifts differed according to the donors’ resources, the reward of all who gave was one—indeed, the reward of those who offered little but gave more in proportion to their means was greater, as in the case of the poor widow who put two small coins into the treasury (Luke XXI). She was praised by the Lord’s judgment, which said: “Truly I say to you, this poor widow has put in more than all the others. For all these gave gifts to God from their abundance; but she, from what she lacked, put in all the living that she had.”

As we have said concerning the city’s works, so this should be briefly noted: all the first fruits of the sanctuary and the city’s possession, calculated together as a square, contain two hundred forty-six thousand and one third. For if twenty-five thousand reeds, each six cubits and one palm long, make, in our measurement—that is, the Roman measurement—sixty-one thousand six hundred sixty-seven paces, there is no doubt that, calculated fourfold, they produce the number given above.

From this we perceive that everything must be understood spiritually: the Church’s possession is much broader than what once existed in Judea. The Jews did not even receive portions of the holy land, but accepted, from the individual tribes, forty-eight cities—not full possession, but habitation and lodging. Thus even those who appear to be laypeople and have not reached the priestly or Levitical rank, if they work in the city of the Lord, may eat from the holy land, the land of the beginning (*initium*, reading uncertain), and the land of believers. One of them said: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm XXVI).

“Whatever remains shall belong to the prince, on every side of the first fruits of the sanctuary and of the city’s possession: opposite the twenty-five thousand of the first fruits, as far as the eastern boundary; and likewise from the sea, opposite the twenty-five thousand, as far as the sea boundary. It shall belong to the prince in the same portions. The first fruits of the sanctuary and the sanctuary of the temple shall be in its midst. The possession of the Levites and the possession of the city shall also be in the midst of the prince’s portions, between the boundary of Judah and within the boundary of Benjamin; it shall belong to the prince.”

We have discussed this prince more fully above, including the fact that he alone would receive as much as one tribe. Now we learn something else: from all the tribes, whatever remains shall be received by him alone, so that there may be no tribe that does not offer gifts to the prince—not from elsewhere, but from the first fruits that serve the temple, the sanctuary, and the portions assigned to the city.

This is what he means by “opposite,” or “facing,” the twenty-five thousand of the first fruits, as far as the eastern boundary—or as far as the boundary of the sea—so that the first fruits lie between the seven and the five tribes, and within those first fruits are the city and its suburbs, with the temple sanctuary in the middle of the city.

Whatever remains of the Levites’ possession and the city’s possession shall likewise be assigned to the prince. The extreme portion of the seven tribes, adjacent to the first fruits, the city, and the temple, shall be in the tribe of Judah; and the extreme portion of the five tribes, under the same arrangement as above, shall be in the tribe of Benjamin. That extreme portion shall belong to the prince.

From this one sees that the mysteries of Holy Scripture are wondrous and are to be pondered more than expressed in words. In the earlier division of the lands beyond the Jordan, the land was divided through Moses among the two tribes of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh. Within the Jordan, it was divided through Joshua son of Nun and Eleazar son of Aaron.

Judah possessed the southern region, while Ephraim and half the tribe of Manasseh possessed the northern region. Later, when explorers were sent from Shiloh through the individual tribes and a description of the land was brought to Joshua and Eleazar, Benjamin received its possession beside Judah to the south and beside Ephraim and the half-tribe to the north.

The second tribe, Simeon, received its inheritance from the tribe of Judah, so that what was written concerning Levi and Simeon might be fulfilled: “I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel” (Genesis XLIX).

Third, Zebulun received Galilee, in which Mount Tabor is located. Fourth, Issachar received the region where Jezreel is, as far as the Jordan. Fifth, Asher received the land as far as Mount Carmel, which overlooks the Great Sea and Tyre and Sidon. Sixth, Naphtali received Galilee as far as the Jordan, where Tiberias is located, formerly called Chinnereth. Seventh, Dan received the territory as far as Joppa, where the towers of Aijalon and Selebi and Emmaus are located, the latter now called Nicopolis.

Although afterward we read that they began, after crossing beyond the other tribes, to claim for themselves the city of Leshem in the tribe of Dan, which today is called Paneas.

Since these things stand thus, and there is such a great difference between the former description of the tribes and the one now given, let us consider how, both in the present description and in the earlier one, the city and temple were placed between the tribes of Judah and Benjamin.

In the earlier description Judah was to the south and Benjamin to the north. Here, on the contrary, Judah is to the north and Benjamin to the south. After Benjamin comes Simeon second, Issachar third, Zebulun fourth, and Gad fifth—five tribes, as is said in what follows. For it is written:

“And for the remaining tribes, from the eastern side to the western side, one portion for Benjamin. Opposite the boundary of Benjamin, from the eastern side to the western side, one portion for Simeon. Along the boundary of Simeon, from the eastern side to the western side, one portion for Issachar. Along the boundary of Issachar, from the eastern side to the western side, one portion for Zebulun. Along the boundary of Zebulun, from the eastern side to the sea-side, one portion for Gad. Along the boundary of Gad, toward the south, to the southeast, the boundary shall be from Tamar as far as the waters of Meribah of Kadesh; its inheritance shall be opposite the Great Sea. This is the land which you shall allot to the tribes of Israel, and these are their portions, says the Lord God.” (Jerome.)

When “one” is always placed at the end of the five and seven tribes, either “portion,” “possession,” or “inheritance” is understood. Aquila and Symmachus, however, translate it with the neuter noun τὸ ὅριον (*to horion*), which means “the boundary.”

This point should be briefly noted concerning the last of the five tribes, the tribe of Gad: although in the earlier description it was beyond the Jordan, here it is placed in the portion previously held by Judah, namely, toward the southern side, to the southeast. Its boundary is from Tamar to the waters of Meribah of Kadesh, its inheritance opposite the Great Sea.

Tamar is the place about which we have already spoken, now called Palmyra and formerly built by Solomon. In Hebrew, *thamar* means “palm,” because there are many palm groves there; some think that the place received its name for this reason.

What follows—“as far as the waters of Meribah of Kadesh, its inheritance opposite the Great Sea”—the Septuagint translated: “From Theman and the water of Maribinoth of Kadesh, the inheritance as far as the Great Sea.”

It should be observed that the Hebrew term *nehela*—whose form is uncertain in the Latin transliteration—is ambiguous, signifying both “inheritance” and “torrent.” Here it ought rather to be understood as “torrent” than as “inheritance.” For this is the torrent that enters the Great Sea at Rhinocorura, as we have already said.

Kadesh, which in the Book of Joshua is called Kadesh-barnea, is in the desert extending as far as the city of Petra. Maribinoth, which is interpreted as “of contradiction,” is not, as many think, the name of a place, but refers to the waters at which the people contradicted the Lord and Moses offended God, as the psalm says: “They tested him at the waters of contradiction, and Moses suffered because of them” (Psalm CV).

The whole inheritance of the Holy Land ends on its southern side, beside the borders of Egypt, at Rhinocorura and the torrent.
