Since Gad is interpreted as “temptation,” in his possession we pass from the palm groves to the waters of contradiction as far as Kadesh, which is interpreted as “holy,” so that we may understand that even after the world’s victory we must remain watchful and always fearful, remembering the verse: “Temptation is the life of human beings upon the earth.”

We must reach holiness while our adversaries oppose us, and thus obtain victory; then, close by, let us contemplate the torrent filled with rain.

“The city’s exits on the northern side shall be measured at four thousand five hundred, and the city shall have gates from all the tribes of Israel. There shall be three gates on the north: one gate of Reuben, one gate of Judah, and one gate of Levi. On the eastern side, four thousand five hundred, and three gates: one gate of Joseph, one gate of Benjamin, and one gate of Dan. On the southern side, you shall measure four thousand five hundred, and there shall be three gates: one gate of Simeon, one gate of Issachar, and one gate of Zebulun. On the western side, four thousand five hundred, and their three gates: one gate of Gad, one gate of Asher, and one gate of Naphtali. The circuit shall be eighteen thousand, and the name of the city from that day shall be, ‘The Lord is there.’”

The preceding discussion explained that the circuit of the city, with each side measuring four thousand five hundred reeds, amounts to eighteen thousand reeds, as is also stated in the present chapter—that is, forty-four thousand three hundred and forty paces.

Now it is written that on each side—that is, along eleven thousand and eighty paces—there were three gates. Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion call these διεξόδους (*diexodous*), while the Septuagint call them διεκβολάς (*diekbolas*). We have translated the term as “exits” or “outlets” of the city.

And this should first be briefly noted: those three tribes were encamped around the Tabernacle in such a way that Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun, the sons of Leah, were to the east; Reuben and Simeon, two sons of Leah, and Gad, the third son of Zilpah, Leah’s maidservant, were to the south; Ephraim, Manasseh, and Benjamin were to the west—namely, the two sons of Rachel, since Joseph was divided into the two tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh in place of the tribe of Levi, which was assigned to the sacrifices; and Dan, Asher, and Naphtali were to the north. Of these, the first and third were sons of Bilhah, Rachel’s maidservant, while the second was the son of Zilpah, Leah’s maidservant—ignoble women—and they were placed in the north because they were born from the stock of quarreling maidservants. This arrangement accords with the Book of Numbers (Num. XXXIV) and with the description of the Tabernacle dictated by God to Moses.

Our city, however, which is “the city of the great King” (Ps. XLVII), whose architect and founder is God, and of which the Psalmist also sings, “Shall a man say, Sion? and a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. LXXXVI), has another description of the tribes in the Holy Land, another measurement of the city, another order of possessions, and another arrangement of the territories of the individual tribes.

First, three gates, or exits, of the city face the northern side: Reuben, the firstborn; Judah, founder of the royal line; and Levi, concerning whose name nothing was said in the Tabernacle or in the description of the sacred rites. Thus, possessing the rights of the firstborn, as a royal and priestly race, we may despise the cold of the north.

Second, to the east are Joseph, Benjamin, and Dan: two sons of Rachel and one of her maidservant Bilhah. To the south are Simeon, Issachar, and Zebulun, the three sons of Leah. To the west, moreover, are Gad, Asher, and Naphtali: the first two of them are sons of Zilpah, Leah’s maidservant, and the third is the son of Bilhah, Rachel’s maidservant.

“Who is wise and understands these things, discerning them and coming to know them?” (Ps. CVI.) For the ways of the Lord are right, and the righteous shall walk in them, “but transgressors shall fall in them” (Hos. XIV).

I think that these twelve gates, or exits, were assigned to the individual tribes according to the quality of their merits and virtues, under the names of the apostles and patriarchs. They are described more clearly in the Apocalypse of John, and many mysteries of the divine Scriptures bear witness to them.

(Bede.) For this is also written in the Apocalypse concerning these gates of the mystical city of God:

“And it had a great and high wall, and it had twelve gates, and at the gates twelve corners, and names written upon them, which are the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel. On the east, three gates; on the north, three gates; on the south, three gates; and on the west, three gates. And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and upon them the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.”

This great and high wall therefore signifies the unconquerable firmness of faith, charity, and hope. The Lord himself, protecting the Church on every side, may also be understood as the great wall, of whom Isaiah says: “A wall and an outer wall shall be placed in it” (Isa. XXVI)—that is, the Lord’s protection and the intercession of the saints, who prepare a way for him by teaching the hearts of believers.

This wall has twelve gates; these gates are the apostles, who, initially, through their writings or their deeds, opened the entrance to the Church for all the nations.

“And at the gates twelve corners”—that is, the teachers who follow in the apostles’ footsteps through the mystery of faith and the word.

“And names written upon them, which are the names of the twelve sons of Israel” (Exod. XXVIII): this signifies the memory of the ancient Fathers implanted in the hearts of preachers. Hence the high priest, upon entering the Tabernacle, is commanded to bear the memorial of the Fathers upon the breastplate of judgment.

“There were three gates on the east, three gates on the north, three gates on the south, and three gates on the west.” By this carefully devised description of the twelvefold number of the gates, I think he wished to indicate its mystery: the total number of the apostles and the perfection of the Church are represented for this reason, because through it the faith of the Holy Trinity was to be proclaimed to the four-square world.

“And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and upon them the twelve names of the twelve apostles and of the Lamb.” What are called gates are also foundations; what is called the city is also the wall. The patriarchs, too, may be designated by the term “foundations,” since they bore within themselves the names of the apostles—that is, their figure. Through them this city was founded, although through the apostles, as through gates, it was opened more widely to the nations who were to believe.

It should also be noted that when the foundations are spoken of in the plural, they signify the teachers or virtues of the Church; but when the term is singular, it signifies the Lord himself, who is the foundation of foundations.

(Hieronymus.) It is necessary that such a city should extend eighteen thousand reeds around its circuit. Under this number, too, in the eighteenth Psalm, the natural and written law and the grace of the Gospel are described—those by which the Church, that is, the city of the Savior, has been built.

Nor will the name of this city be, as before, Jerusalem, which is interpreted as “vision of peace,” but Adonaisan [Adonaisama], which is translated into Latin as “The Lord is there.” He will never depart from it, as he departed from the former people when he said to the disciples, “Rise, let us go from here” (John XIV), and to the Jews, “Your house shall be left to you desolate” (Luke XIII). Rather, he will possess it eternally, and it will itself be his possession. He promised this to the same disciples: “Behold, I am with you always, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII). And speaking to the Father he says: “Father, I will that where I am, they also whom you have given me may be with me, that they may see my glory which you have given me, because you loved me before the foundation of the world” (John XVII).

(Maurus.) The Psalmist explains what this blessedness of the vision of God is like—where the saints will rejoice with the Lord forever and delight in his presence without cessation or end—when he says: “Blessed are they that dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. LXXXIII).

For if the person is considered blessed to whom, for a time, everything goes well and who is shaken by no adversity, what shall we think of that blessedness in which nothing comparable is found, either in quality or in perpetuity?

Yet although this good cannot be explained in human words, its source is not concealed. He says: “They shall praise you.” From this comes that wondrous blessedness; and so that you might understand it as eternal, he added: “For ever and ever.”

But, I ask, what kind of joy is the joy of that age to come, in which it will be granted to rejoice abundantly and never to be able to depart from that joy? All the elect, therefore, will freely sing the praises and mercies of the Lord throughout eternity. There will no longer be uncertainty concerning the forgiveness of sin; the memory of guilt will no longer enslave the secure mind; the soul will not tremble under accusation, but, freed by his forgiveness, will rejoice.

For if in that eternal life a person is touched by no memory of sin, from what will he rejoice that he has been delivered? Or how will he give thanks to the giver for the forgiveness he received, if, through the intervention of forgetfulness concerning his past wickedness, he does not know that he was liable to punishment? And if he does not remember his former misery, from what will he offer praise for the abundance of mercy?

We must therefore ask how the mind of the elect can be perfect in blessedness if the memory of its guilt touches it amid its joys; or how the glory of perfect light can shine when guilt, recalled to the mind, casts a shadow over it.

But it should be understood that, just as we often now remember sad things with joy, so then we shall remember our past wickedness without injury to our blessedness. Often, while we are in good health, we recall past pains without pain; and the more we remember that we were sick, the more we love ourselves as healed.

Thus, in that blessedness too, there will be a memory of sin—not one that defiles the mind, but one that binds it more closely to joy. When the soul remembers its pain without pain, it will thereby more truly acknowledge that it has become indebted to its physician in order to give thanks to him. It will love its received salvation all the more because it remembers the trouble from which it escaped.

Therefore, throughout eternity we shall offer praise to the giver of our mercy, and the consciousness of misery will in no way burden us. For while we behold our evils without any evil of mind, there will never be anything that pollutes the hearts of those who praise him concerning their past iniquities; yet there will always be something that kindles those hearts to praise the one who delivered them.

Hence the Apostle Paul also says to the Philippians: “Our citizenship is in heaven, from where we also await the Savior, Jesus Christ, who will refashion the body of our humiliation, conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. III).

For then the bodies of the elect will be conformed to the glory of the Lord’s body. Although by nature they will not possess equality with his glory, by grace they will possess the likeness of that conformity. Since his likeness is now reproduced in the conduct of the elect, then, in the resurrection, the likeness of eternity will follow in the mind, because “we shall see him as he is” (1 John III), and, according to the Prophet, “we shall be filled with joy in his presence, and our delights shall be at his right hand forever” (Ps. XV).

[Col. 1083]

(842) A LETTER OF BLESSED RABANUS MAURUS, ABBOT OF FULDA AND ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ, TO HUMBERT, ON THE GENERATION IN WHICH MARRIAGE IS PERMITTED

[Col. 1083D] To the truly holy and most blessed Father Humbert, bishop by the grace of God: Rabanus, the most worthless servant of the servants of God, sends greetings in Christ.

Recently a letter came to me addressed from Your Holiness. Among the matters by which your affection decided to test me, it contained a question concerning marriage: you asked me to declare in which degree of relationship it could be lawful. You also mentioned that you had read certain chapters of Pope Gregory to Augustine, bishop of the English nation, as well as the decrees of Zachary concerning the same matter. You likewise wished me to know what Isidore, bishop of Seville, had thought about it in his *Etymologies*, and you asked me to write back to you what I myself thought about all these matters.

When I then saw the magnitude of the undertaking, I replied briefly that so great a matter required both an extended period of time and leisure on the part of the writer; that, being occupied with many things, I could not quickly give a suitable answer to what you asked; but that I first wished to examine the statements of many authorities and the volumes of the sacred books, and then set my hand to writing back.

Afterward, however, when I perceived how eagerly you were pressing for the fulfillment of what had been promised, I anticipated the time and decided to obey your wishes with haste, briefly recalling what I remembered having read and what had suddenly come to mind as I dictated.

Concerning marriage, then, what is permitted and what is forbidden the Lord has made known through the Law and the Gospel. He permitted the proper use of marriage and altogether prohibited incest and fornication.

How kinship is to be respected is shown by the Book of Leviticus:

“The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: I am the Lord your God. You shall not act according to the customs of the land of Egypt, in which you dwelt; nor shall you act according to the practices of the land of Canaan, into which I am going to bring you; nor shall you walk in their ordinances. You shall carry out my judgments and observe my commandments, and you shall walk in them. I am the Lord your God. Keep my laws and judgments, which a person who observes shall live by. I am the Lord.

“No man shall approach his near blood relation to uncover his nakedness. I am the Lord. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father or the nakedness of your mother. She is your mother; you shall not uncover her nakedness. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s wife, for it is the nakedness of your father. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister, whether born of your father or your mother, whether born at home or abroad. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your son’s daughter or your daughter’s granddaughter, for it is your own nakedness. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s wife’s daughter, whom she bore to your father, for she is your sister. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s sister, for she is the flesh of your father. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your mother’s sister, for she is the flesh of your mother. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your paternal uncle, nor approach his wife, who is joined to you by affinity. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your daughter-in-law, for she is the wife of your son; nor shall you uncover her shame. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother’s wife, for it is the nakedness of your brother. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your wife and her daughter; you shall not take her son’s daughter or her daughter’s daughter to uncover her shame, for they are her flesh, and such intercourse is incestuous. You shall not take your wife’s sister as a rival wife during her lifetime, nor shall you uncover her nakedness” (Lev. XVIII).

When the Lord wished to separate his people from the contaminations of the nations, he first prohibited anyone, in a general expression, from approaching a near blood relation, lest he uncover that person’s nakedness. He then subdivided that general prohibition into almost twelve categories. These, however, do not extend beyond the third or fourth degree. For this reason, I think that Pope Gregory responded to Augustine, who was asking about this matter, that marriages in the third or fourth degree were already illicit.

Similarly, in the chapters of Theodore, archbishop of the English nation, which he composed concerning necessary matters, we find that marriage is permitted in the third degree of carnal relationship according to the Greeks, but in the fifth according to the Romans. Nevertheless, they did not dissolve marriages contracted in the third degree if they had previously been joined in ignorance; and they allowed those who were related by blood to marry equally with the blood relations of their wives after the death of the wife.

This Theodore was born at Tarsus in Cilicia. Pope Vitalian ordained him bishop at Rome and sent him to Britain. Consequently, he had been thoroughly instructed in the customs of the Eastern churches, and nothing could escape him concerning the lawful observances that the Greeks or Romans possessed at that time—especially since he was perfectly trained in both languages.

As for the writings of the Roman pontiffs in more recent times, which state that the practice of marriage should be deferred until the sixth or seventh degree, one should believe that they prescribed this more from human custom than from divine law. Blessed Boniface, our patron and martyr, holding this opinion concerning the matter, believed that the bishops of his nation should be consulted, so that they might write back to him what they found explained about it in the judgments of the holy Fathers.

As for Isidore’s assertion in his *Etymologies* that one must abstain from consanguineous unions until the sixth degree and then lawfully enter into marriage, I think he did this because, when he traced the sequence of genealogies, he judged that blood relationship had to be observed as far as he carried the reckoning by counting the order. Thus he decreed that marriage could be resumed for the renewal of the race and the strengthening of friendship once the order of kinship had ceased to be counted.

Above all, however, it must be considered that the discipline of judgment should be tempered in such a way that, through immoderate correction, the accumulation of sin may not be increased. For we know that the one who established the law of kinship in the Law himself commanded in the Gospel that the bond of marriage should not be dissolved, namely, “so that if anyone were to send away his wife, except for the cause of fornication, he would make her commit adultery; and whoever married a woman who had been sent away would commit adultery” (Matt. V).

Following the same reasoning, the Apostle commanded in his Letter (1 Cor. VII) “that a woman should not depart from her husband; but if she did depart, that she should remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband.”

For if, whenever any degree of relationship or consanguinity, however distant, could be found between married persons, the marriage were immediately dissolved, would this not, I think, cause adultery and the crime of fornication to multiply? A married adolescent or young man, denied the companionship of his wife and given no assistance by which he might preserve continence, might, inflamed by lust and instigated by the devil, be defiled by fornication in many ways, and thus his soul might be plunged into the precipice of eternal death.

Therefore, wishing to cut off this kind of vice, the Apostle wrote, saying (ibid.): “It is good for a man not to touch a woman; but because of fornication, let each man have his own wife. Let the husband render the due affection to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband.” A little later: “Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by mutual consent for a time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer.” And again: “Return to the same relationship, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control.”

With all these matters considered, it seems good to me that the constitution of divine law should be preserved inviolable, while scandal, so far as concerns human beings, should be avoided as far as our strength permits. But where scandal can be borne without greater harm, because the greatest thing may already be rashly brought about on account of [Note: [Col. 1086D] Something is missing.] [lacuna].

[Col. 1087A] Since, therefore, you wished me, in my smallness, to write back what I thought about this matter, I judge that, because of the pressure of the present time and my weakness, the decision of Archbishop Theodore should be followed. He stands midway between Gregory and Isidore and defined the matter in his chapters: marriage should be permitted after the fifth degree, since divine law does not contradict this, nor do the statements of the holy Fathers forbid it.

But if intercourse has taken place in the fifth degree in ignorance, it seems better to me that, with the humility of repentance, the man should satisfy God if he does not wish to abstain while married. Nevertheless, he should be taught that it is good for him to abstain from such intercourse, so that perhaps God may grant him repentance and he may recover from the snares of the devil, and afterward offer God, of his own free will, an acceptable offering of continence. Thus, if I am not mistaken, there will be caution in judgment, and justice will be preserved in the deed.

**A TREATISE OF BLESSED RABANUS MAURUS, ABBOT OF FULDA AND ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ, ON THE MARRIAGES OF BLOOD RELATIONS AND ON THE FALSE TRICKS AND DIVINATIONS OF MAGICIANS**

[Col. 1087]

[ON THE MARRIAGES OF BLOOD RELATIONS]

[Col. 1087B] It has always been the custom of great men and illustrious teachers to seek an appropriate answer to matters about which they have been questioned and, relying upon the authority of the holy Scriptures and the judgments of the holy Fathers, to explain briefly and clearly what has been asked of them. Although I am unlearned and inexperienced not only in speech but also in knowledge, I used to imitate this practice according to my limited ability; and when people pressed me with questions on various matters, I tried to answer them from the sacred Scriptures and the judgments of the holy Fathers.

But now, dearest and most diligent guardian of God’s flock, Bonosus, the situation with you has turned out differently. In matters where I had in some way given sufficient answers, I was in no way able to satisfy you; instead, following your custom, you would inquire more shrewdly and investigate more carefully how the things that had been stated could remain unimpaired. Consequently, I have now found it difficult to reach a conclusion on the questions you proposed to me. You objected to the testimonies drawn from the old Law in the letter I wrote in reply to Bishop Humbert concerning the generation at which it was lawful for relatives to marry, as though they were not appropriate to the present age—that is, to the Christian religion. But since I did not find this matter plainly written about in the New Testament, I considered it necessary to offer you examples from the works of the holy Fathers, showing what they thought about the very judgments of God’s Law, so that you, who find it difficult to believe me because of the lowliness of my person, might at least be compelled to believe those who possess great authority.

You proposed two questions to me. One concerned blood relatives: at which generation were they permitted to join themselves to one another in marriage? The other concerned what should be thought about those who are said, by magical illusions or demonic incantations, to deceive people and to be able to overthrow them from their former condition. Therefore, we think that we should write to you first about the marriage mentioned above, [Col. 1087D] and then about the arguments concerning magical art.

But it must first be noted that whenever the precepts of the old Law need to be brought forward as testimony, they must not be despised, because God is the one and the same author of both the Old and the New Testament. For this reason the mediator himself between God and human beings, drawing examples from the Law and the Prophets, confirmed and commended evangelical teaching to his hearers. Thus it is written of him in the Gospel (Luke 4):

> He rose in the synagogue to read, and the book of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. When he had opened the book, he found the place where it was written: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to proclaim good news to the poor; to heal the brokenhearted; to preach release to captives and sight to the blind; [Col. 1088C] to set the oppressed free; to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense.” And when he had folded up the book, he returned it to the attendant and sat down, and the eyes of everyone in the synagogue were fixed upon him. He began to say to them: “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.” And all bore witness to him and marveled at the gracious words that proceeded from his mouth.

After the resurrection, it is likewise read that he said to two disciples who were walking with him on the road and were in doubt (Luke 24):

> “O foolish ones and slow of heart to believe in all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary that Christ should suffer these things and so enter into his glory?” And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.

He is found to have done the same in many other passages, and rightly so. For on the mountain where he was transfigured before three disciples (Matthew 17), “Moses and Elijah appeared with him, speaking, and they were telling of the departure which he was about to accomplish in Jerusalem,” so that it might be understood that he wished to have testimony from the Law and the Prophets.

Hence the Apostle also asserts that the grace of the New Testament is attested by the Law and the Prophets (Romans 7), because “the law is spiritual and holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good.”

From this it must be understood that the Law itself is to be interpreted in some passages only according to history, in others according to allegory, and in still others according to history and allegory at the same time. For, as Blessed Ambrose wrote, the Law is threefold. The first part concerns the mystery of the divinity and belongs to God; the second agrees with the natural law, which forbids sin; the third is the law of practices—that is, the historical observance of the Sabbath, the new moons, and circumcision—which are to be observed spiritually, not carnally, in the age of grace.

The natural law likewise, which agrees in many respects with the Law of Moses, has three parts. The first is that the acknowledged Creator should be honored, and that his splendor and majesty should not be assigned to any created being. The second is the moral part: that one should live well, with moderation governing one’s conduct. For it is fitting that a person who knows the Creator should restrain his life by law, lest his knowledge be rendered fruitless. The third is the instructive part: that knowledge of God the Creator and his example should immediately be passed on to others, so that they may learn how the Creator’s worth is to be honored. This is true Christian prudence, necessary for every Catholic both to learn and to preserve, because through it an honorable life is led in this world and eternal rewards are attained in the future.

[Col. 1089C] Therefore, wherever the subject is the mystery of the divinity, or where precepts are given concerning the avoidance of vices and the attainment of virtues, a historical and moral understanding is good. But wherever the shadow of future things is expressed—as we said concerning the law of practices—a spiritual interpretation must be sought above all.

Moreover, when history recounts the passage of the children of Israel from Egypt through the Red Sea, the construction of the tabernacle in the wilderness, and the miraculous signs performed at the Lord’s command among the earlier people, as well as the battles of the Israelites against the Canaanites and the other nations, these things must indeed be believed to have happened historically; nevertheless, they are to be venerated as mysteries.

Thus the Apostle Paul, understanding mystically the deeds of earlier times, wrote to the Corinthians, saying (1 Corinthians 10):

> I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ.

Likewise, when writing to the Galatians, he compared the two sons of Abraham, one born of a slave woman and the other of a free woman, by way of likeness to two peoples, saying (Galatians 4):

> It is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman. But the one who was born of the slave woman was born according to the flesh, whereas the one born of the free woman was born through the promise.

These things are spoken allegorically:

> For these are the two Testaments: one from Mount Sinai, generating slavery, which is Hagar. Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, joined to the Jerusalem that now exists, and it is in slavery with her children. But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother. For it is written: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband,” and so forth (Isaiah 54).

If Truth itself and his disciples proved and commended their teaching to their hearers from testimonies of the Law, who would dare criticize the assertion of the Law when he sees that it agrees with evangelical teaching?

When salutary precepts concerning charity, chastity, continence, mercy, and the other virtues are brought forward in the Law by divine authority, they must be received with every honor and observed with the greatest diligence. For each person proves himself to be a devoted disciple of Truth itself and a most diligent guardian of God’s commandments when he agrees with God’s Law and believes what is written in it.

For this reason he himself also said to the unbelieving and contentious Jews:

> If you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me also, for he wrote about me. But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words? (John 5)

Likewise, elsewhere in the Gospel (Luke 16), Abraham is read to have answered the rich man, who was crying out to him from the underworld and asking that Lazarus be sent to his father’s house to testify to them, lest they too come to that place of torment:

> “They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them.”

But he said:

> “No, father Abraham; but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent.”

He replied:

> “If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they believe if someone rises from the dead.”

It is as though he were plainly saying: If they do not heed the Law and the Prophets, who teach justice and truth, neither will they rightly obey Christ, who rose from the dead and proclaims evangelical teaching.

Finally, concerning blood relationship, the Lord himself, who gave the Law and afterward added the blessing of the Gospel so that his elect might go from virtue to virtue, spoke to Moses in Leviticus, saying:

> Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: I am the Lord your God. You shall not act according to the customs of the land of Egypt in which you dwelt, nor according to the practices of the land of Canaan, to which I am bringing you. You shall not walk in their statutes. You shall do my judgments and observe my precepts, and you shall walk in them. I am the Lord your God. Keep my laws and judgments; whoever does them shall live by them.  
>   
> No man shall approach his nearest blood relative to uncover her nakedness. I am the Lord. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father or the nakedness of your mother; she is your mother, and you shall not uncover her nakedness. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s wife; for that is the nakedness of your father.  
>   
> You shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister, whether born of your father or of your mother, whether she was born at home or abroad. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your son’s daughter or your granddaughter through your daughter, because that is your own nakedness. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s wife’s daughter, whom she bore to your father; she is your sister.  
>   
> You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s sister, because she is your father’s flesh. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your mother’s sister, because she is your mother’s flesh. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s brother, nor approach his wife, who is joined to you by affinity.  
>   
> You shall not uncover the nakedness of your daughter-in-law, because she is your son’s wife; you shall not uncover her shame. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother’s wife, because that is the nakedness of your brother.  
>   
> You shall not uncover the nakedness of your wife and of her daughter. You shall not take her son’s daughter or her daughter’s daughter to uncover her shame, because they are her flesh; such intercourse is incestuous. You shall not take your wife’s sister as a rival wife during her lifetime, to uncover her nakedness (Leviticus 18).

We have judged that the exposition of this chapter from the sayings of Blessed Father Augustine should be inserted here, so that the sober reader may not hesitate to believe and agree with his understanding, since he is seen to deviate in no way from the path of truth.

“‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father or the nakedness of your mother.’ For that is their nakedness. He forbids intercourse with one’s mother; for in her is the nakedness of both father and mother. For this reason he also forbids intercourse with the stepmother, where he says: ‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s wife; for that is the nakedness of your father.’ Here he explained how, in the case of the mother, the nakedness belongs to both—that is, to the father and the mother—whereas in the case of the stepmother it belongs only to the father.

“‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister, born of your father or of your mother, whether she was born at home or abroad.’ For that is their nakedness. She who was born at home is understood to be born of the father; she who was born abroad is understood to be born of the mother, if perhaps the mother had received her from an earlier husband and had brought her with her into the household when she married her father. Since Scripture warns that one must not uncover the nakedness of one’s sister, it might seem that it did not forbid, and had almost passed over, intercourse with a sister born of both parents. For it does not say, ‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister born of your father and mother,’ but ‘of your father or of your mother.’ Yet who could fail to see that the latter case too is most certainly forbidden? If it is not lawful to uncover the nakedness of a sister born of either parent, how much more is it forbidden in the case of one born of both?

“What, then, is the meaning of the fact that, after inserting the prohibition of intercourse even with one’s own nieces, whether through a son or through a daughter, it continues and says: ‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s wife’s daughter’? If it had stopped there, we would understand that intercourse with the daughter of one’s stepmother was also forbidden, if the stepmother had borne her by an earlier husband, and that she was not the sister of the man in question either through his father or through his mother. But when it added, ‘who is your sister, born of the same father,’ and said, ‘you shall not uncover her nakedness,’ it shows that the prohibition concerns a sister born of the father and the stepmother, of whom it had already spoken above. Or did it wish to prohibit this again more explicitly because the earlier statement was somewhat obscure? Scripture often does this.

“‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s brother, and you shall not go in to his wife.’ It explained what it meant by ‘the nakedness of your father’s brother’: that is, you shall not uncover the nakedness of your uncle; for this means that you shall not go in to his wife. In the wife of one’s uncle it wished the uncle’s nakedness to be understood, just as in the wife of one’s father it means the father’s nakedness.

“‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother’s wife; for that is the nakedness of your brother.’ The question arises whether this is forbidden while the brother is alive or after his death, and it is no small question. If we say that Scripture speaks of the wife of a living brother by a general precept forbidding a man to approach another man’s wife, then this case is certainly included. Why, then, does it distinguish so carefully by specific prohibitions the persons whom it calls members of the household from all others?

“For the prohibition concerning the father’s wife—that is, the stepmother—would not need to be understood as applying only while the father was alive, rather than especially after his death. While the father is alive, who would not see that the prohibition is all the more strict, since the wife of any other man is forbidden to be violated by adultery? It therefore seems to speak of persons who, if they did not have husbands, could enter into marriage unless they were forbidden by law, as is said to be the custom among the Persians.

“But again, if we understand the prohibition as referring to marrying a brother’s wife after the brother’s death, we encounter the passage in which Scripture commands that this be done for the raising up of offspring if he died without children. Accordingly, when this prohibition is compared with that command, so that they do not conflict with one another, an exception must be understood: namely, that no one may marry the wife of a deceased brother if the deceased left descendants. Or perhaps the prohibition means that it was not lawful to marry a brother’s wife even if she had withdrawn from the living brother by divorce. For then, as the Lord says, ‘because of the hardness of the Jews, Moses permitted a certificate of divorce to be given’ (Mark 10); and because she had been dismissed in this way, it might be thought that someone could lawfully take his brother’s wife, since adultery would not be feared once she had departed by divorce.

“‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of a woman and her daughter.’ That is, no one should think that he is permitted to marry his wife’s daughter. For it is not permitted to uncover the nakedness of both the woman and her daughter—that is, to have intercourse with both mother and daughter.

“‘You shall not take the daughter of her son or the daughter of her daughter.’ He also forbade a man to marry his wife’s granddaughter, whether through her son or through her daughter.

“‘You shall not take your wife’s sister as a rival wife.’ Here he did not forbid taking a second wife in addition to the first, which was permitted to the ancients because of the abundance of offspring. But he did not wish one sister to be taken in addition to another, as Jacob appears to have done—either because it had not yet been forbidden by law, or because he was deceived by the fraud of the woman who had been substituted. Yet she came more readily by agreement, whereas he afterward received the other; but it was unjust to dismiss the first, lest he make her commit adultery.

“As for the phrase ‘as a rival wife,’ it is uncertain whether it was inserted to prevent jealousy between sisters, whereas jealousy between women who were not sisters was to be disregarded; or whether it was inserted rather to prevent the act from being done for that reason—that is, to prevent one sister from being taken as a rival to another.”

How marriage law is to be observed among relatives, the same teacher shows when he says:

> What is read afterward—“Whoever sleeps with a blood relative has uncovered the nakedness of his kin; they shall die childless”—raises the question how far this kinship is to be understood, since it is certainly permitted, and has always been permitted, to take a wife from a distant degree. But it must be understood as referring to those degrees whom he prohibited, and according to them the statement was made: “Whoever sleeps with his blood relative.” In this way he left certain cases not mentioned to be understood, such as a sister by both parents, and the wife of one’s mother’s brother—that is, one’s maternal uncle. For he first prohibited the wife of one’s paternal uncle, although this is called not kinship but affinity.

“But what does ‘they shall die childless’ mean, when children have been born from such unions in the past and are born from them today? Is it to be understood that God’s Law established that whatever children are born from such unions are not to be counted as children—that is, that they have no legal right to succeed their parents?”

Some people criticize the reply of Blessed Gregory to the questions of Bishop Augustine of the English nation, who had asked him to what degree the faithful should be joined in marriage with their relatives, and whether marriage with stepmothers and blood relatives was permitted. They do so without due care. For since Gregory is irreproachable in his other doctrines, he cannot rightly be criticized in this answer either. He devoted himself more to agreeing with the Law of God and the judgments of the holy Fathers than to constructing something new from his own opinion. Among other things, he said:

> A certain earthly law in the Roman state permits a brother and sister, or the son and daughter of two full brothers or of two sisters, to unite. But we have learned by experience that offspring cannot grow from such a marriage, and the sacred Law forbids uncovering the nakedness of one’s kin. Therefore it is necessary that the faithful should now be permitted to join themselves in the third or fourth generation. The second degree, as we have said, must abstain from one another in every way.
>
> To have intercourse with one’s stepmother is a grave crime, because it is also written in the Law: “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father” (Leviticus 18). For a son cannot uncover his father’s nakedness. But because it is written: “The two shall become one flesh” (Genesis 2), whoever presumes to uncover the nakedness of his stepmother, who was one flesh with his father, will certainly uncover his father’s nakedness.
>
> Intercourse with a blood relative is also forbidden, because through the earlier union she had become the flesh of one’s brother. It was for this reason that John the Baptist was beheaded and brought to completion through holy martyrdom. He was not told to deny Christ, and he was killed for confessing Christ. But because our Lord Jesus Christ had said, “I am the truth” (John 6), John was killed for the truth and shed his blood for Christ.

In this answer, the careful reader can readily discern whether this bishop of the apostolic see was referring the matter to the precepts of the divine Law mentioned above, or whether he newly established something on his own. His statements do not seem to me to disagree with the judgments of Blessed Augustine cited above; rather, they seem to share his understanding.

I think that what the canons of the Fathers have decreed concerning incestuous marriages should also be inserted, so that it may be seen whether their judgments agree with the writings of the teachers mentioned above.

For in the Council of Agde it is written:

> We decree that incestuous unions are not to be counted as marriages at all. It is even dreadful to name them: for example, if anyone violates carnally the widow of his brother, who had previously been his sister; if a brother takes his full sister as his wife; if anyone marries his stepmother; if anyone joins himself to his cousin. We forbid this in the present time in such a way that we do not dissolve what was established before us. If anyone has intercourse with the widow or daughter of his maternal uncle, or with his father’s daughter, this unlawful union is forbidden. For they will have the freedom to enter into better marriages.

In the Council of Orléans, a decree concerning incestuous unions is likewise read, prescribing that such persons should be admitted to communion:

> No surviving brother is to approach the bed of his deceased brother; nor may anyone dare to join himself to his wife’s sister after losing his wife. If he does so, let him be struck by ecclesiastical discipline.

Likewise, in the Capitularies of the Eastern Fathers, established by Bishop Martin and the other bishops, it is found written:

> If a woman has had two brothers as husbands, or if a man has had two sisters as wives, let them abstain from communion until death. At the point of death, let communion be granted to them through mercy. But if they survive after receiving communion and recover from their illness, let them perform full penance for the prescribed period.

In the decrees of Pope Gregory, who is said among the Romans to be second from the first, it is likewise written:

> If anyone takes his spiritual godmother as his wife, let him be anathema.

And all answered three times:

> Let him be anathema.

> If anyone takes his brother’s wife as his wife, let him be anathema.

And all answered three times:

> Let him be anathema.

> If anyone takes his niece as his wife, let him be anathema.

And all answered three times:

> Let him be anathema.

> If anyone takes his stepmother or his daughter-in-law as his wife, let him be anathema.

And all answered three times:

> Let him be anathema.

> If anyone takes his cousin as his wife, let him be anathema.

And all answered three times:

> Let him be anathema.

For nothing is said or specifically enumerated here about a trinepos or trineptis (a male or female descendant of the third further generation), or about the grandson or granddaughter of a trinepos.

Therefore I think that what divine authority sanctioned in the two Testaments should be followed, as well as what, following its example, the judgment of many Fathers established for observance in common assembly, rather than what any individual, according to his own inclination, decides should be followed on the basis of personal conjecture.

Nevertheless, if anyone wishes to remain continent until the fifth, sixth, or even seventh generation, he should not be prohibited; rather, he should be encouraged. For the farther one is from danger, the safer one will be from destruction. For, as the Apostle testifies, “marriage is honorable, and the marriage bed undefiled” (Hebrews 13).

It is therefore fitting for a Christian to do everything honorably and in proper order.

I too, because I have not dared to put forward anything new of my own, have simply set down the writings and sayings of the elders according to what I found, without prejudicing anyone who may understand the matter better. Let each person think about these things as he wishes, provided that he preserves discernment in judgment and truth in practice.

[Col. 1095]

## On Magical Arts

[Col. 1095A] Concerning magical arts, incantations, and various superstitions, which pagans and false Christians appear to follow in their divinations and perverse observances, it is easy to find what the divine Law decrees in the authority of the Old and New Testaments.

The divine Law detests such persons. In the Book of Exodus it says:

> “You shall not permit sorcerers to live in your land” (Exodus 22).

And again:

> “Whoever sacrifices to gods,” it says, “shall be put to death, except to the Lord alone” (ibid.).

In Leviticus it says:

> “You shall not eat flesh with blood. You shall not practice augury, nor observe dreams. You shall not cut your flesh for the dead, nor make any figures or marks upon yourselves. I am the Lord” (Leviticus 19).

And again:

> “You shall not turn to magicians,” it says, “nor inquire of diviners, lest you be defiled by them” (ibid.).

And again:

> “A man or woman in whom there is a Pythonic spirit or a spirit of divination shall surely be put to death. They shall stone them; their blood shall be upon them” (Leviticus 20).

In Deuteronomy it likewise says:

> When you have entered the land which the Lord your God will give you, beware that you do not wish to imitate the abominations of those nations. Let there not be found among you anyone who makes his son or daughter pass through fire, or who consults diviners, or observes dreams or omens. Let there be no sorcerer or enchanter, no one who consults pythonic spirits or diviners, and no one who seeks the truth from the dead. For the Lord abhors all these things, and because of such crimes he will destroy them as you enter. You shall be perfect and without blemish before the Lord your God. These nations whose land you are to possess listen to augurs and diviners; but you have been instructed differently by the Lord your God (Deuteronomy 18).

What is to be followed or obeyed follows immediately:

> The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your nation and your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him, as you asked of the Lord your God at Horeb, when the assembly was gathered and you said: “I will no longer hear the voice of the Lord my God, and I will no longer see this great fire, lest I die.” And the Lord said to me: “They have spoken well in everything. I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brothers, like you, and I will put my words in his mouth. He will speak to them everything that I command him. Whoever will not listen to his words, which he will speak in my name, I myself will be his avenger. But the prophet who, corrupted by arrogance, wishes to speak in my name what I did not command him to say, or who speaks in the name of other gods, shall be put to death.”

[Col. 1096A] Which prophet this is, whose words they ought to hear and whom they must obey with their whole heart, is clear when it is read in the Gospel that the crowd of believers, seeing the miracles and signs performed by Jesus, cried out:

> “Truly, this is the prophet who is to come into the world” (John 6).

Elsewhere it is written of him:

> “Fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying: ‘A great prophet has arisen among us,’ and ‘God has visited his people’” (Luke 7).

This prophet, therefore, and Lord of all the prophets, who is the way, the truth, and the life, the author of both Testaments, rejects and condemns all errors, divinations, and harmful arts not only in the Old but also in the New Testament. He does not wish truth or healing to be sought from anyone other than himself, because he, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is the one true and almighty God, who alone performs great wonders.

Therefore in the Gospel he invites everyone to himself, saying:

> “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matthew 11).

And again:

> “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (ibid.).

According to Paul’s judgment, he is therefore the Savior of all people, especially of the faithful. Of him Peter also says:

> “There is no other name given to human beings under heaven by which it is necessary for us to be saved” (Acts 4).

In this name also, great signs and healings are performed daily in the Church through the prayers of the faithful, because he says to his disciples in the Gospel:

> “Behold, I give you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy. Go and preach the Gospel; heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons” (Luke 10).

Mark also bears witness concerning him, saying:

> He healed many, so that they pressed upon him in order to touch him. And those who had afflictions and unclean spirits, when they saw him, fell down before him and cried out, saying: “You are the Son of God.” And he sternly warned them not to reveal him. Then he went up into the mountain, called to himself those whom he wished, and they came to him. He made twelve to be with him and to send them out to preach. And he gave them power to heal illnesses and to cast out demons (Mark 3).

Why, then, is it necessary to seek salvation from anyone other than the appropriate physician? Or what reason is there for wishing to learn knowledge or wisdom from anyone other than the source of all wisdom and knowledge?

Of this source it is written (Ecclesiasticus 1):

> All wisdom is from the Lord God, and it has always been with him and exists before all ages. Who has counted the sand of the sea, the drops of rain, and the days of the age? Who has measured the height of heaven, the breadth of the earth, and the depth of the abyss? Who has investigated the wisdom of God that precedes all things? Wisdom was created before all other things, and the understanding of prudence is from eternity. The source of wisdom is the word of God on high, and its ways are eternal commandments.

Whoever wishes to have salvation without the Savior, and thinks that he can become wise without true wisdom, will labor in continual sickness—not saved but ill, not wise but foolish. He will remain foolish and deranged in harmful blindness. Therefore every inquiry and every cure sought from diviners and magicians, or from the demons themselves in the worship of idols, should be called death rather than life. Those who pursue such things, if they do not correct themselves, are heading toward eternal destruction, since the Psalmist says:

> “All the gods of the nations are demons” (Psalm 95).

They continually strive to deceive the people they have ensnared, so as to make them participants in their own destruction.

Thus the vanity of magical arts, transmitted by evil angels, prevailed for many centuries throughout the whole world. Through a certain knowledge of future things and of the underworld, their inventions produced haruspices, auguries, and the things called oracles, as well as necromancy.

Nor is it surprising that magical illusions have produced such things, since the arts of their sorceries advanced so far that they even resisted Moses with signs very similar to his, turning rods into dragons and water into blood.

It is also related in the books of the pagans that a certain very famous witch transformed the companions of Ulysses into beasts. It is also read that the Arcadians made a sacrifice to their god Lycaeus. Whoever partook of it was changed into the form of a beast.

But all these things were fabricated more through magical illusions than accomplished in the reality of events.

Therefore, so that their errors may be made clear to those who are ignorant of them, we think it appropriate first to speak, according to the tradition of our predecessors, about their nature and their inventors.

Magi are those whom the common people call sorcerers because of the magnitude of their crimes. With God’s permission, they shake the elements, disturb the minds of people who have little confidence in God, and kill by the mere violence of the flesh, without anyone swallowing poison.

Hence Lucan:

> A mind, polluted by no foulness of swallowed poison,  
> perishes when bewitched.

For, having summoned demons, they dare to stir them up so that each may destroy his enemies by evil arts. These also use blood and often touch the bodies of the dead with their victims. Necromancers are those whose incantations appear to resuscitate the dead, so that they may divine and answer questions—for νεκρός means “dead” in Greek, while μαντεία is called “divination.” To raise them, blood is added to the corpse. For demons are said to love blood; therefore, whenever necromancy is performed, blood is mixed with water, and they are more easily summoned by the color of blood.

Hydromancy is named from water. Hydromancy consists in summoning the shadows of demons by gazing into water, seeing their deceptive images, and hearing certain things from them there. When blood is added, the dead below are also said to be raised. This kind of divination is said to have been brought from the Persians.

Varro says that there are four kinds of divination: earth, water, air, and fire. Hence, he maintains, the terms geomancy, hydromancy, aeromancy, and pyromancy were coined. Diviners are so called as though they were “full of God.” For they represent themselves as full of divinity and, by a certain crafty fraud, conjecture the future for human beings.

There are two kinds of divination: art and frenzy. Enchanters are so called because they perform their art through words. Arioli are so called because around the altars of idols they utter abominable prayers and offer deadly sacrifices; through these ceremonies they receive responses from demons.

Haruspices are named as though they were “observers of hours.” For they attend to days and hours in conducting affairs and activities, and they consider what a person ought to observe at each particular time. They also inspect the entrails of animals and foretell the future from them.

Augurs are those who attend to the flights and cries of birds, and who report to human beings other signs or unforeseen indications of events that come before them. There are also auspices. For auspices are the signs observed by travelers on a journey. They are called auspices as though from *avium aspicia*, “observations of birds.” Augury is likewise named as though from *avium garria*, that is, “the cries and languages of birds.” Again, augury is as though from *avigerium*, because birds “carry” it.

There are two kinds of auspices: one pertaining to the eyes and the other to the ears. To the eyes belongs the flight of birds; to the ears, their cry.

Pythonesses are named after the Pythian Apollo, because he was regarded as the author of divination. Astrologers are so called because they divine from the stars. Genethliaci are named from their consideration of birth-days. For they describe human births through the twelve signs of heaven and attempt, from the course of the stars, to foretell the dispositions, actions, and events of those being born—that is, under what sign someone was born, or what effect the life of the person being born will have.

These are the people commonly called mathematici. The Latins call this kind of superstition *constellations*, that is, observations of how the stars are positioned when someone is born.

At first, these same interpreters of the stars were called magi, as we read concerning those who announced in the Gospel that Christ had been born. Later, only the mathematici were called by this name. Knowledge of this art was permitted until the Gospel, so that after Christ had been born no one thereafter might interpret anyone’s birth from heaven.

Horoscopes are so called because they observe the hours of human births and their unequal and differing fates. Sortilegi are those who, under their own name, profess the knowledge of divination through a fictitious religion involving what they call “the lots of the saints,” or who promise future events by examining the contents of any writings whatsoever.

Salisatores are so called because whenever any of their limbs leaps or twitches, they foretell that something favorable or grievous will thereby be signified for them.

To all these practices also belong the bindings of accursed remedies, whether in incantations, in characters, or in any objects that are hung up and tied. In all these things there is the art of demons, arising from a pestilential association between human beings and evil angels. Therefore all these practices must be avoided by a Christian and utterly rejected and condemned with every form of execration.

The Phrygians were the first to devise the auguries of birds; Mercury is said to have been the first to devise *praestigium*, “illusion,” which was so called because it dazzles or obstructs the sharpness of the eyes. It is said that an Etruscan was the first to transmit the art of haruspicy; some say it was a Phrygian. This man dictated haruspicy from the hours and afterward disappeared. For, as the fable relates, while a certain peasant was plowing, he suddenly sprang out of the clods, dictated haruspicy, and died on that very day. The Romans translated these books from the Etruscan language into their own.

By such portents, through the deception of demons, human curiosity is mocked when people shamelessly desire to know what they have no right to investigate by any rational means. For this reason power is granted to unclean spirits, so that through vessels suited to them—that is, wicked human beings—they may deceive those who reject the truth and believe a lie. As Paul says (2 Tim. 4; 2 Tim. 3):

> “They will not endure sound doctrine, but, according to their own desires, they will heap up teachers for themselves, itching in their ears. They will indeed turn their hearing away from the truth, but they will turn to fables. Burdened with sins and led by various desires, they are always learning and never able to arrive at knowledge of the truth.”

Just as Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, so these people also resist the truth: people corrupted in mind and disqualified with regard to the faith. But they will make no further progress. For their folly will become manifest to everyone, just as the folly of those men did.

No one should therefore believe that anyone can accomplish anything by magical arts without God’s permission. Whatever is done is either accomplished by a just judgment of God or permitted by him to occur. The magi mentioned above are read to have performed things similar to those performed by Moses:

> “He threw down his staff, and it became a dragon; and they too each threw down their staffs, and they became dragons. But Aaron’s staff devoured their staffs” (Exod. 7).

Thus neither the magi nor the evil angels, through whose agency those things were performed, were creators of dragons. For in corporeal things, throughout all the elements of the world, there are certain hidden, seminal principles. When a temporal opportunity is given to them, they burst forth into their appropriate forms according to their own modes and limits. Thus the angels who perform such things are not called creators of animals, any more than farmers should be called creators of crops, trees, or anything else that grows from the earth, although they know how to provide certain visible opportunities and causes for those things to be born.

What farmers do visibly, the angels do invisibly. God alone, the one Creator, inserted into things the causes themselves and the seminal principles.

Moreover, some people think it necessary to ask how Scripture relates that the pythoness raised Samuel the prophet (1 Kings 18) to converse with Saul, the most impious king, if pythonic divination is to be assigned to the error of magical art.

The following answer may be given to them: it would be utterly unworthy if assent were granted to this according to the words of the historical account. For how could a man who was holy by birth and righteous in the works of his life have been drawn out by magical art? Or, if he was not drawn out, did he consent? Both alternatives are contrary to what ought to be believed of a righteous man. If he was brought there unwillingly, his righteousness gives him no assistance. But if he came willingly, he lost the merit of the spiritual [*—the source is materially uncertain here], which he had sought while placed in the flesh. That is exceedingly absurd, because a person who departs from righteousness in this way remains righteous.

This, however, is a deception of Satan: in order to deceive as many as possible, he pretends that he even has good people in his power. The Apostle demonstrates this, among other things, when he says:

> “Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light” (2 Cor. 11).

To produce an error in which he might glory, he disguised himself in the appearance and under the name of a righteous man, so that the appearance they proclaimed would accomplish nothing, and he might deceive the worshipers of God by pretending that, after departing this life, the righteous were in his power.

Some are deceived by the fact that Satan did not lie concerning the death of Saul and his son, as though it were a great thing for the devil to foresee the bodily death of someone before its arrival, since certain signs commonly appear in those who are about to die—especially when God’s protection appears to have been removed from them. How much more could the devil foresee this, whom the prophetic oracles testify to have been exalted by angelic majesty, and concerning whose greatness the Apostle says: “Do you not know the height of Satan?” (Rev. 2.)

What is surprising, then, if he could foresee a death that was already near, when this is precisely the means by which he deceives and wishes himself to be worshiped as possessing God’s power? For Saul had been made so foolish through his madness that he fled to the pythoness. Corrupted through the cause of his sin, he turned to the very practices he had condemned.

But if someone, on account of the historical account, thinks that what is expressed in its words must not be passed over, lest the account’s historical meaning be empty, he will indeed act rightly—provided that he does not violently drag this matter into the realm of truth, but confines it to Saul’s appearance and understanding. For, having been rejected, Saul could not possess sound understanding.

The historian described Saul’s mind and Samuel’s appearance, expressing what was said and seen while leaving aside whether these things were true or false. For what does he say? Hearing in what appearance the figure had been raised, he understood, it says, that this was Samuel.

Because he understood this, the historian reported it; and because he understood it wrongly, he worshiped someone other than the Lord, contrary to Scripture. Thinking that it was Samuel, he worshiped the devil, so that the devil might obtain the fruit of his deception. For Satan strives to be worshiped as God.

If Samuel had truly appeared to him, surely the righteous man would not have permitted himself to be worshiped, since he had proclaimed that the Lord alone was to be worshiped. And how could a man of God, who was with Abraham in refreshment, say to a man of pestilence, deserving the heat of Gehenna, “Tomorrow you will be with me”?

By these two devices the unwary Satan prepared the subtlety of his deception: he permitted himself to be worshiped under Samuel’s appearance and name, contrary to the law; and he falsely declared that a man oppressed by sins would be with the most righteous Samuel, although there is a great distinction between sinners and the righteous.

This can appear true if Samuel’s name is omitted, because Saul was going to be with the devil: he had passed over to the one whom he worshiped. The devil, always lying hidden beneath a veil, nevertheless betrays himself when he fabricates things that are abhorrent to the persons through whom he attempts to deceive.

But if someone objects to me and says: How do those things come to pass that diviners and false prophets foretell as future? Or how can they provide healing to the sick or inflict illness upon the healthy, if they possess no power or ability of their own?

Let him accept this answer from me: no one should believe them merely because what they foretell sometimes happens, or because they appear to heal the sick or harm the healthy. This occurs by God’s permission, so that those who hear or see such things may be tested, and so that it may become evident what sort of faith or devotion they have toward God.

As we read in Deuteronomy, Moses commanded the people of God by the word of the Lord, saying:

> “If a prophet arises in your midst, or one who claims to have seen a dream, and he foretells a sign or portent, and what he has spoken comes to pass, and he says to you, ‘Let us go and follow other gods, whom you do not know, and let us serve them,’ you shall not listen to the words of that prophet or dreamer. For the Lord your God is testing you, so that it may become clear whether you love him or not with all your heart and with all your soul. Follow the Lord your God and fear him; keep his commandments and hear his voice. You shall serve him and cling to him,” and so forth (Deut. 13).

Here he plainly intended it to be understood that even things spoken by diviners contrary to God are not to be accepted if what they say comes to pass; nor are the things they command to be done, or the things they worship to be worshiped.

God does not show that these events occur apart from his power. Rather, as though someone had asked why he permits them, he explained that they serve as a test, in order to reveal their love—whether they possess love for their God. This is to be known by them rather than by him, who knows everything before it occurs.

It must be understood that the nature of demons is such that, through the perception of an aerial body, they easily surpass the perception of earthly bodies. Because an aerial body is more mobile, their speed also surpasses incomparably not only the running of any human beings or animals but even the flight of birds. Endowed with these two qualities, insofar as an aerial body is concerned—that is, keenness of perception and speed of movement—they announce or report long beforehand things that human beings, because of the slowness of their earthly senses, find astonishing.

The demons have also acquired, through the very long period to which their lives extend, a far greater experience of things than human beings can acquire because of the brevity of life.

Through these abilities belonging to the nature of an aerial body, demons not only foretell many future events but also perform many marvelous things. Because human beings cannot say or do such things, some judge demons worthy of serving them and of receiving divine honors. They are especially driven to this by the vice of curiosity, through their love of false and earthly happiness and of temporal excellence.

Those who cleanse themselves of such desires and do not allow themselves to be carried away and seized by them, but seek and love something that remains always the same and by participation in which they may be blessed, first consider that demons are not thereby to be placed above them because they possess keener bodily perception—namely, the perception of air, the subtler element.

For such people do not think that even among earthly bodies the beasts should be placed above them because beasts perceive many things more keenly. Consider the clever dog: by an exceptionally acute sense of smell it discovers a hidden animal and thus provides a kind of guidance to a human being for capturing it—not through a more prudent understanding of the mind, but through a sharper bodily sense.

Nor do they place above themselves the vulture, because, when a corpse has been thrown down, it flies in from an unexpected distance; nor the eagle, because, flying high, it is said to perceive from a great distance a fish swimming beneath the waves and, plunging heavily into the water, seize it with extended feet and talons.

Nor do they place above themselves the many other kinds of animals that wander among grasses harmful to their health as they feed, yet do not touch any of them in a way that harms them, whereas a human being learns to avoid such things only with difficulty through experience and, because many harmless things are unknown to him, fears them.

From this it is easy to infer how much keener perception may exist in aerial bodies. Yet no prudent person would therefore judge the demons who possess it to be superior to good human beings.

The same may be said concerning the speed of their bodies. This excellence is surpassed not only by birds but also by many four-footed animals, so that in comparison with them human beings must be considered sluggish as lead. Yet people do not therefore think that these kinds of animals should be placed above themselves, since they capture them and bring them into their own use and advantage not by bodily force but by the authority of reason.

As for the third power of demons—the fact that, through their daily experience of things, they have learned how to foresee and foretell many events—those who carefully distinguish such matters from the truth of the truest light rightly hold it in contempt. They do not consider wicked old men, who have experienced more things and therefore seem more learned, to be superior to good young men.

Nor do they think that physicians, sailors, or farmers whom they see to be wicked in will and unjust in character should for that reason be preferred to themselves, merely because the physicians foretell many things about illnesses, the sailors about storms, and the farmers about the kinds of trees and fruits, all so accurately that to someone inexperienced in such matters they seem to be divining.

As for the fact that demons not only foretell certain future events but also perform certain marvelous things, this should not be disregarded by prudent people, given the excellence of their bodies. Many unjust and ruined human beings exercise their bodies in such a way and can accomplish so much through various arts that those who do not know of such things, and have never seen them, scarcely believe them even when they are reported. How many marvels have tightrope walkers and other performers in the theater accomplished! How many have craftsmen, especially mechanics, accomplished!

Are such people for that reason better than human beings who are good and endowed with holy devotion?

I have mentioned these things so that anyone who considers them without obstinacy or the vain contentiousness of resistance may at the same time reflect on this: if human beings can accomplish so much from the underlying coarser material—whether their own bodies or the earth, water, stones, wood, and various metals—that those who cannot do such things often call them divine in amazement at the comparison; and if some of those human beings are more powerful in their arts while others of those who cannot perform them are better in character, how much better and greater things demons can accomplish through the capacity and facility of their exceedingly subtle body, that is, air.

Yet they are unclean and perverse spirits because of the depravity of their will, especially the arrogance of pride and the malice of envy.

How powerful the element of air is—the element in which their bodies excel—for invisibly grinding, moving, changing, and manipulating many visible things would take too long to demonstrate now. I think that this will readily occur to anyone who considers the matter even moderately.

Since this is so, the first thing to understand—because the question concerns the divination of demons—is that they generally foretell the things they themselves are going to do.

For they often receive the power both to inflict diseases and to make the air itself unhealthy by corrupting it, and to persuade the wicked and those who love earthly advantages to commit evil deeds. They know that such people will consent to the things they urge upon them.

They urge these things by marvelous and invisible means, penetrating human bodies imperceptibly through the subtlety of their own bodies and mingling with human thoughts through certain imagined visions, whether the people are awake or asleep.

Sometimes, however, they foretell not things that they themselves do, but things whose future occurrence they foresee through natural signs—signs that cannot enter into human perception—and they announce them beforehand.

A physician, for example, foresees what someone ignorant of this art does not know how to foresee; but he is not for that reason to be considered a diviner. What is surprising, then, if, just as a physician foresees future good or bad health from the disturbed or regulated condition of the human body, so a demon foresees future storms from a condition and arrangement of the air known to him but unknown to us?

Sometimes demons also learn not only human dispositions expressed in words but even those conceived in thought, since they thoroughly perceive certain signs expressed by the mind throughout the body. From these signs they also foretell many future events—marvelous, certainly, to others who do not recognize how such things are arranged.

For just as a more agitated movement of the mind appears on the face, so that even human beings can perceive externally something of what is taking place within, it should not be incredible that even lighter affections give certain signs through the body—signs that cannot be perceived by the duller human sense but can be perceived by the keener sense of demons.

By this and similar abilities demons foretell many future events, although they are far removed from the height of that prophecy which God works through holy angels and prophets. If they foretell anything concerning God’s arrangement of events, they hear it in order to announce it; and when they proclaim what they hear from that source, they do not lie. For angelic and prophetic oracles are utterly truthful.

If anyone is indignant that demons also hear and proclaim certain such things, as though it were unworthy that what is spoken so that it may become known to human beings should be reported not only by the good but also by the evil, let him consider that even among human beings we see the commandments of a good life sung alike by the righteous and the perverse. This does not harm the truth; indeed, it contributes to a greater knowledge and renown of the truth, even when those who contradict it in their conduct speak whatever they know about it.

In their other predictions, however, demons generally both deceive and are deceived. They deceive because, when they foretell their own plans, something is suddenly commanded from above that disrupts all their designs. It is as though certain human beings, subject to various authorities, should arrange something that they suppose their superiors will not prohibit and promise that they will carry it out, while those who possess greater authority, following another and higher plan, suddenly prohibit the entire arrangement and preparation.
