They are also deceived when, like physicians, sailors, and farmers—but far more keenly and with far greater excellence, because of the sharper perception of their aerial body—they foresee events from natural causes. For these events too are suddenly and unexpectedly changed by angels serving the supreme God in devotion, through another arrangement unknown to the demons.

It is like what happens when something external affects a sick person and causes him to die, although a physician, observing the preceding signs of health, had promised that he would live. Or it is like when, having foreseen the condition of the air, certain sailors predict that a particular wind will blow for a long time, but the Lord Christ, sailing with his disciples, commands it to cease, “and there was a great calm” (Mark 4).

Or it is like when a farmer, knowledgeable about the nature of the soil from the number of seeds, promises that a particular vine will bear fruit that year, but in that same year an unexpected condition of the weather dries it up, or a more powerful command uproots it.

Thus many events belonging to the demons’ foreknowledge and predictions, which they foresee as future through lesser and customary causes, are altered when those causes are obstructed by greater and hidden causes.

They also deceive deliberately, out of a desire to deceive and an envious will, because they rejoice in human error. But lest they lose the weight of authority among their worshipers, they arrange for blame to be assigned to their interpreters and to those who conjecture the meaning of their signs whenever the interpreters have been deceived or have lied.

Sometimes, however, the wicked spirits themselves—deceivers of human beings and enemies of their salvation—foretell the decline of their own worship and the ruin of idols, so that they may appear to know in advance what will happen in particular kingdoms or places and what adverse event may befall their faction. Those who read the histories of the pagans are not ignorant of this.

What is surprising, then, if, when the overthrow of temples and images was already imminent—an overthrow that the prophets of the supreme God had foretold long beforehand—it was disclosed to the demonic Serapis by one of his worshipers nearby, so that, as he withdrew or fled, he might commend his supposed divinity?

For the demons themselves are driven out, or, bound by higher commands, are dragged away and removed from their places, so that God’s will may be done concerning the things in which they were worshiped—God who had foretold long beforehand that this would occur throughout all nations and had commanded that it be brought about through his faithful servants.

Why should the demon not have been permitted to foretell this, when he already knew that it was impending? This prediction was attested both in the prophets, by whom such things were written down, and to the prudent it made clear how vigilantly the demons’ deception and their worship must be avoided.

For although, during such a long period, they had remained silent in their temples about these future events—which they could not have failed to know, since they had been foretold through the prophets—once the events began to approach, they wanted to appear to foretell them, lest they be thought ignorant and defeated.

Since this had been foretold and written down so long beforehand—to pass over other matters for the moment—consider what the prophet Zephaniah says:

> “The Lord will prevail against them, and he will destroy all the gods of the nations of the earth; and they will worship him, each one from his own place, all the islands of the nations” (Zeph. 2).

Either the gods worshiped in the temples of the nations did not believe that these things would happen to them, and therefore did not frequently wish to announce them through their seers to the fanatics; or, although they knew with complete certainty that these events would occur, they remained silent in their temples so that people who understood the prophecy would not even then begin to abandon and despise them, since the prophets were testifying to the future overthrow of their temples and images and were prohibiting their worship.

But once the time arrived when the prophecies of the one God—who forbids these false gods and commands with the greatest force that they not be worshiped—were to be fulfilled, why should the demons not also have been permitted to proclaim that this was known to them? From this it would become clearer whether they had previously not believed these things or had feared to announce them to their worshipers.

At the end, as though they had nothing else to do, they even wanted to display their divinity in the very place where they were already exposed as having long pretended to possess divination. Nevertheless, even these things, which they scarcely ever reveal and then only secretly, should not move us if some demon has arisen to disclose to his worshipers what he learned from the prophetic utterances or from the oracles of angels. Why should this not happen, since it is not an assault but a testimony to the truth?

For there is one thing that should be demanded from the fanatics themselves, and which they have never previously produced and will never afterward attempt to produce except perhaps as a fabrication: that their gods, through their seers, dared to foretell anything against the God of Israel; or that they could say anything about this God whom their most learned authors, who were able to read and know all those things, sought more to discover—who this God was—than they were able to deny that he was God.

Moreover, this God—whom none of them dared to deny as the true God, because even if someone did deny him, he would not only suffer the punishments due to him but would also be convicted by clear effects—this God, as I have said, whom none of them dared deny to be the true God, openly foretold through his seers, that is, his prophets, that those others were false gods and had to be entirely abandoned, and that their temples, images, and rites had to be overthrown. By an open exercise of power he commanded it; by manifest truth he fulfilled it.

Who, then, is so foolish that he would not choose to worship the one whom those gods he once worshiped do not forbid him to worship? Once he begins to worship him, he will certainly not worship those whom the one he worships forbids to be worshiped.

I mentioned shortly before, and I repeat now, that the prophets had foretold that the nations themselves would worship him after the false gods they had previously worshiped had been destroyed:

> “The Lord will prevail against them,” he says, “and he will destroy all the gods of the nations of the earth; and they will worship him, each one from his own place, all the islands of the nations.”

The reference here is not to islands alone; rather, all the nations situated in these places worship God.

Nor is this surprising, since elsewhere he names not islands but the whole world, saying:

> “All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations will worship in his presence. For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he will rule the nations” (Ps. 21).

That these things were to be fulfilled through Christ is sufficiently clear from many other testimonies and from that same psalm from which I have quoted. For shortly before, the prophet himself had spoken of his future passion, saying:

> “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones. They themselves looked upon and observed me; they divided my garments among themselves, and upon my clothing they cast lots” (ibid.).

A little later he adds the passage I quoted:

> “All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord,” and so forth.

Moreover, the earlier testimony I cited, where it says, “The Lord will prevail against them, and he will destroy all the gods of the nations of the earth,” clearly shows, in the word “will prevail,” that this too was foretold: namely, that the pagans would first attack the Church and persecute the Christian name as far as they could, so that, if possible, it might be entirely wiped from the earth.

Because the Lord was going to overcome them through the endurance of the martyrs, the greatness of miracles, and the faith that followed among the peoples, it is therefore said, “The Lord will prevail against them.” For it would not be said, “He will prevail against them,” unless he were resisting them in their attack.

Thus it was also prophesied in the psalm:

> “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise futile things? The kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Ps. 2).

A little later it says:

> “The Lord said to me: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession.’”

Through these and similar prophetic testimonies it is shown to have been foretold that what we see fulfilled through Christ would happen: that the God of Israel, whom we understand to be the one true God, would be worshiped not only among that one nation called Israel but among all nations, and that he would remove all the false gods of the nations both from their temples and from the hearts of their worshipers.

Let these people now go on daring to defend their former vanities with noisy clamor against the Christian religion and against the true worship of God, so that they may perish amid the tumult. For this too was foretold concerning them in the psalms, where the prophet says:

> “You sat upon the throne, judging justice. You rebuked the nations, and the wicked perished; you blotted out their name forever and ever. The swords of the enemy have failed utterly, and you destroyed their cities. Their memory perished amid the tumult, but the Lord remains forever” (Ps. 9).

It is therefore necessary that all these things be fulfilled. Nor should the fact that the few who still remain dare to display their empty doctrines and mock Christians as though they were utterly ignorant disturb us, since we see the things that were foretold being fulfilled among them.

From the time when the nations raged and the peoples devised futile things against the Lord and against his Christ, when the blood of the saints was shed and the Church was ravaged, up to the present time—and indeed from then onward—their numbers have been diminishing day by day.

The oracles of God make us exceedingly strong against their insults and arrogant mockery, since we see and rejoice that what was foretold concerning this matter too is being fulfilled. For through the prophet he addresses us as follows:

> “Hear me, you who know judgment, my people, in whose heart is my law. Do not fear the reproaches of human beings, and do not be overcome by their slander; do not consider their contempt of you to be of great importance. For just as clothing, so they will be consumed in time, and as wool by the moth, so they will be eaten. But the righteous remain in it forever.”

We must therefore pay attention and take every precaution lest, in our own times—when we see the Christian religion spread throughout the whole world—because of the negligence of pastors and the inertia of teachers, those few who still remain should confuse the rite of the worship of the true God and, corrupted by demonic illusions, practice false divinations among God’s people.

They deceive the rustic and uneducated, so that, having abandoned the truth itself, which “is the light of the world and enlightens every person coming into this world,” they seek knowledge of the future from these darknesses and seek the salvation either of their souls or even of their bodies from deceivers of human beings.

For by such transgressions God is especially provoked and stirred to vengeance. Therefore, through Ezekiel, he threatens, saying:

> “Woe to the foolish prophets, who follow their own spirit and see nothing. Like foxes in the deserts, so will the prophets of Israel be. Have you not seen a vain vision and spoken lying divinations? And you say, ‘The Lord says,’ when I have not spoken. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because you have spoken vanity and seen a lie, behold, I am against you, says the Lord God. My hand will be against the prophets who see vanity and divine lies. They shall not be in the council of my people; they shall not be written in the record of the house of Israel, nor shall they enter the land of Israel” (Ezek. 13).

To the teachers, rebuking their negligence through the same prophet, he speaks as follows:

> “You did not go up to oppose them, nor did you build a wall for the house of Israel, so that you might stand in battle on the day of the Lord” (ibid.).

And again:

> “Woe,” he says, “to the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves. Are not flocks fed by shepherds? You ate the milk, clothed yourselves with the wool, and killed what was fat, but you did not feed my flock. You did not strengthen what was weak; you did not heal what was sick; you did not bind up what was broken; you did not bring back what was cast away; you did not seek what had perished. But you ruled over them with harshness and with power. And my sheep were scattered because there was no shepherd, and they became food for all the beasts of the field; they were scattered” (Ezek. 34).

For this reason it is also said through Jeremiah:

> “From the least to the greatest, all pursue greed. From prophet to priest, all speak lies. They treated the wound of the daughter of my people with disgrace, saying, ‘Peace, peace,’ when there was no peace. They were confounded because they committed abomination. Therefore thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will feed this people with wormwood, and I will give them gall-water to drink. I will scatter them among nations whom neither they nor their fathers knew, and I will send the sword after them until they are consumed” (Jer. 8).

How displeasing to almighty God is the negligence of pastors and the error of their subjects is shown not only by prophetic testimonies but also by the deeds of the ancients. For in the Book of Kings we read: [how an evil spirit deceived Ahab, king of Israel, through false prophets, so that, believing them, he perished; and how Ahaziah, his son, when he was ill, sent messengers to consult Beelzebub, the god of Ekron, to ask whether he might live and recover from his illness (3 Kings 22; 4 Kings 1); wherefore the prophet Elijah …]
sent by God, rebuked him, saying: “Because you sent messengers to consult Beelzebub, the god of Ekron, as though there were no God in Israel from whom you could inquire of the word, therefore you shall not come down from the bed onto which you have climbed, but shall surely die.” And so he died, according to the word of the Lord that Elijah had spoken; and he did not obtain the recovery that he had sought (ibid.).

Therefore, all of us—namely, prelates and subjects, the great and the small [Col. 1108D], priests and the people—must take the greatest care lest the fraud, deceit, and wickedness of the ancient enemy lead anyone astray through such an illusion, so that we should wish to learn the truth from liars and seek the remedy for our illness from pestilential diseases and the authors of death. Rather, let us hasten in devout hearts to the living Lord and the giver of life to all, beseeching him through sacred prayers, fasts, and almsgiving that, in his goodness, he may take thought for his servants, rescuing us from all our enemies, and may teach us to do his will. For he is the Lord our God; may he grant us his good Spirit, who will lead us along the right path and give us life in his righteousness, so that, under his guidance [Col. 1109A], we may render him pleasing service throughout our lives and, after this life, by his grace [Col. 1110A] may deserve to possess everlasting blessedness. Amen.

[Column 1109]

**(A.D. 842) TREATISE ON THE SOUL BY BLESSED RABANUS MAURUS, ABBOT OF FULDA AND ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ**

**PREFACE TO KING LOTHAR**

[Column 1109B]

To the most excellent lord, Lothar, king—great, peaceful, and crowned—given to us by God’s gift, his final servant, Maurus, sends greetings.

Since I perceive in your nobility an eagerness and desire to know many things and to investigate them abundantly, and since I admire the keenness of your understanding, in which your highness particularly flourishes, I have resolved, in accordance with the smallness of my little intellect, to set aside something for you. It has been gathered, as it were, from the books of certain learned men and can easily be committed to memory, so that the vigor of your ancient intellect might become more abundant and the loyalty of my little intellect might in some manner serve your service.

I have therefore written for you certain things concerning the definition of the soul: why it is called “soul,” and what the soul is; also concerning its origin, and whether it is believed to possess a form. I have written as well about its quantity—whether it is smaller in little children and greater in stronger persons—and about where it is chiefly believed to have its seat. Then I have discussed its moral virtues, and a little also about its dwelling-place, that is, the possession of the body.

All these things I excerpted from the statements of a certain great man, Aurelius Cassiodorus Senator; some, however, from the book of Prosper, a most learned man. I have also taken care to add certain matters from the understanding of my own little intellect.

But because it is fitting that your excellence know many things, I have appended several chapters on the discipline of Roman military service, [Note: [Column 1109D] We have not yet found this little work; otherwise we would have appended it.] describing how recruits in ancient times were accustomed to be trained. I did this because I judged it necessary on account of the very frequent incursions of the barbarians. I excerpted these matters from a little book by Flavius Vegetius Renatus, which he wrote about the most ancient Romans, and compiled them, striving to record them more briefly, carefully avoiding prolixity and also avoiding the appearance of writing things that are not in use in the present age. I also foresaw that, if I became too lengthy, I might serve boredom rather than delight.

**CHAPTER ONE. Concerning the nature, etymology, and definition of the soul**

The term “soul” properly applies to human beings, not to beasts. For the human soul is far different from the life of beasts. The life of beasts consists in blood, so much so that when the blood fails and the body comes to an end, life itself also ends together with the spirit. The soul of a human being, however, does not come to an end with the blood. Thus it is rightly called *anima*, as though from the Greek *ἄναιμα*, that is, “separate from blood,” because even after the death of the body it lives in its own substance.

It may also be defined in this way: the soul is so called because it animates, that is, gives life to, the substance of its own body. Most significantly, the soul is called a spiritual substance, which is not consumed by any shedding of blood and is therefore distinguished far from blood, although through the failure of the blood it appears to leave the dwelling-place of the body. But it is one thing to leave one’s dwelling-place for whatever reason, and another thing to come to an end together with that dwelling-place.

Some define it differently, saying that the soul receives its name from wind, because “wind” is called *ἄνεμος* in Greek. For this reason, they derive its etymology from wind: we appear to live by drawing breath into our mouths. This is enough, very briefly, concerning why it is called “soul.” Now, however, it must be explained what the soul is.

The philosophers say that the soul is a simple, natural substance, differing in species from the matter of its body, an organ of the members, and possessing the power of life. They wished to call it a simple substance because nothing can be found in it apart from spiritual substance. They called it distinct from the matter of the body because it possesses nothing corporeal in itself. They called it an organ of the members because all the members of the body are arranged through its agency. They said that it possesses the power of life because, whenever it has filled the body, it immediately makes it living.

This is the definition of the soul according to the inventions of the teachers of secular literature. The authority of all truthful teachers agrees on this point: the soul is a spiritual substance created by God, proper to itself, giving life to its body, rational and immortal, but capable of turning in either direction, that is, toward good or toward evil.

We say that the soul was created by God in opposition to the opinions of those who, asserting that it possesses some part of divinity, have woven errors rather than truth. No one who thinks rightly doubts that the soul was created. Solomon bears witness to this when he says concerning Wisdom: “I made every breath” (Wisdom 24). And again: “And the dust will return to the earth from which it came, and the spirit will return to God who gave it” (Ecclesiastes, final chapter).

The soul is also affirmed to be spiritual because it retains nothing corporeal within itself. Every body is encompassed by length, breadth, and depth, and all these are absent from the soul. Although it is burdened by the mass of the body, it nevertheless considers many things spiritually, both far away and near at hand; with a certain perceptive insight it searches out invisible things. It thinks about heavenly matters, and it desires to know certain lofty things concerning God himself. If it were corporeal, it would certainly be unable to consider any of these things.

It is a substance proper to itself because no other spirit takes on flesh in such a way as to suffer or rejoice together with the afflictions of its own body. It gives life to its own body because, as soon as it has been placed by God into the body, it ineffably gives life to it and loves it, to such an extent that whatever the body is known to endure is referred to the soul, and that which cannot die fears destruction and death.

It is rational because it deals with divine matters, understands human things, and grasps with a certain subtlety whatever can be taught through arts and disciplines. For this reason it surpasses all animals in teachable understanding: it arranges all fitting things in accordance with reason. Whatever adornment is added to the world has been discovered through its activity. It gives walls to cities, invents defensive weapons, fashions garments in various forms, lays roads through trackless places, and crosses the seas through the ingenuity of art. No one, therefore, should doubt the rationality of the soul, since through the generosity of its authority it is able to investigate and accomplish so many and such great things.

That it is immortal is proved in many ways. The philosophers assert that everything which lives in itself and gives life to another is immortal. That the soul does both is evident: it lives in itself and gives life to the body. They also say that all immortal things are simple. The soul consists of simple substance and is therefore immortal.

There are other philosophical arguments approving the soul’s immortality, but it is unnecessary to enumerate them for the sake of brevity. Our own truthful assertions likewise approve the soul’s immortality. The soul was made in the image of God. Since we know, believe, and confess that God is wholly immortal, it follows that he made immortal that which he fashioned in his own image. For it could not possibly be that what was made in the image and likeness of God should be mortal. In its immortality, therefore, it is like God.

But when it is said that the soul is like God, someone may ask, “How am I like God, when I cannot do things like him?” The answer is that a human being makes a picture bearing the likeness of a human being, but the picture itself cannot imitate what a human being does. Thus a human being, made in the likeness of God, cannot imitate God in creating things.

The soul is said to be capable of turning in either direction, as we prove daily through many experiences. Those whom we now see rejoicing with great exultation, we soon observe to be saddened by excessive grief. Others are now gentle through compassion, now again terrifying through the greatest indignation. They are now raised up toward virtues, now slipping down into vices. In many and innumerable ways the soul is known to be changeable and capable of turning.

For if it were not changeable, the good would never become evil, nor the wicked good; the grasping would never become generous, nor the generous miserly. But, as has been said, it is found in every way to be subject to change and the experience of turning. Now a few things must be said about its origin, concerning which there is much uncertainty.

**CHAPTER TWO. From where the soul derives its origin**

We read that, after the first man had been formed from the clay of the earth, God breathed into his face, as Scripture says: “Then the Lord God formed the man from the clay of the earth and breathed into his face the breath of life; and the man became a living soul” (Genesis 2). From this it is clear that the soul derives its origin from God.

When God is said to have breathed into him, we must not understand that God breathed in the way that we, by breathing out our spirit, extend our lips outward with a certain movement—for God is incorporeal and invisible. Rather, he is said to have breathed because of the dignity of the work, namely, the soul, which he is known to have made in his own likeness.

For this reason some have said that, as soon as human seed has coagulated into a living substance, souls are immediately created and given to bodies. Those who investigated the natures of things, however, assert that on the fortieth day of conception the mortal and human breast [Alternative reading: “animal”] receives a soul. They offer as evidence that at that time it begins to move in the womb.

It is also reported as the opinion of some that, by the command of almighty God, just as the human body is transmitted from human fleshly seed, so too a new origin of souls is generated from the quality of the soul, and that for this reason the soul is subject to original sin, which is remitted through the washing of baptism to infants and to those not yet capable of committing any sins.

We, however, do not dare either to dismiss this or to affirm it, because blessed Augustine, a most approved teacher, is praiseworthily said to have doubted about this matter and not dared to confirm it. Rather, he held most truly that God creates souls, and that by his hidden and most just judgment they are subject to original sin.

In such matters, and in similar matters so hidden, it is better to confess ignorance than to make a perverse and dangerous assertion. Such an assertion could be counted as error, since the prophet says: “For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?” (Isaiah 40). And the Apostle says: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part” (Romans 9).

If the Prophet and the Apostle say that the mind of the Lord cannot be investigated by anyone, and if the Apostle, ascending to the height of the third heaven (1 Corinthians 13), penetrating the secrets of paradise and learning certain mysteries which he says are unlawful for human beings to speak, affirms that he knows only in part, who will dare to say that he can know and declare what none of the holy teachers is found to have explained fully?

But we must proceed to what remains and ask whether the soul is believed to have a form.

**CHAPTER THREE. Whether the soul is believed to have a form**

Anyone who wishes to discuss form more clearly must first grasp the nature of form. For that is called a form which is enclosed by some extent of lines. Whatever is encompassed by spaces and lines is necessarily corporeal. Indeed, space itself cannot exist at all without corporeal outlines. Likewise, outlines cannot in any way be comprehended without corporeal space.

Since this is so, it is clear that the soul, which is incorporeal, does not possess a form at all. Every form is made upon a corporeal surface. Since a body cannot exist except as solid and tangible, whereas the soul is incorporeal and intangible and lacks solidity, it follows that it cannot in any way possess a form.

If anyone is troubled by what the Apostle says concerning Christ the Lord: “Who, being in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God” (Philippians 2), let us understand that the Apostle is speaking there of the substance in which Christ is equal to the Father. For God, being incorporeal, invisible, incomprehensible, and wholly present everywhere, cannot possess any form.

When we read in the Gospel about Abraham, Lazarus, and the rich man (Luke 16)—that Lazarus had Abraham’s bosom and that the rich man asked for his tongue to be cooled by the tip of a finger—we must understand that neither did the rich man’s tongue speak, since it is incorporeal, nor did Lazarus’s soul possess fingers with which to cool the rich man’s burning, nor could Abraham have a bosom in the manner of bodily human beings.

For Scripture contains such things and similar things not only concerning spiritual creatures, but also concerning the supreme and incomprehensible God. Certain passions are attributed to him which plainly cannot happen to the divine unchangeableness—for example, when God is said to repent, to grow angry, to abhor, and to hate. None of these things is fitting to that supreme majesty. But such expressions are referred to God so that certain human realities may be understood more briefly and easily according to our customary way of speaking.

In the same way, although the soul is formless, it is said to have a form.

**CHAPTER FOUR. Whether the soul is believed to be smaller in little children and greater in stronger persons**

A very subtle and scrupulous question may also arise concerning the quantity of the soul: whether it is smaller in little children, since reason is not fully present in them, while it appears to be greater in persons of more mature age. Yet young people are also found to be senseless, and old people less wise.

In the case of little children, we must observe that the soul’s reason is impeded in them by the weakness and smallness of the body. In young and foolish persons, it is depressed either by some inequality among the bodily parts or by a certain thickness of the humors, and by such an impediment is prevented from expressing its power.

To make this clearer by an example, let us consider things that are familiar. If fire is enclosed in a small vessel, although it is accustomed to seek the heights, it is hindered by the narrowness of the place. If you place beneath it some heavy, thick, or viscous material, it is impeded by that thickness from rising upward. But if you place beneath it suitable material, it immediately displays all its power as it seeks the heights.

So the power and reason of the soul are hindered in little children by the smallness of their limbs; in young and mature persons they are depressed, as has been said, by some inequality of the bodily parts or by the thickness of the humors.

For this reason we see those whom we had just perceived to be wise and clever become inept and senseless through some sudden injury to the brain or through heaviness in the region of the heart. For this reason, too, people become deaf and bleary-eyed, and become weak through some diminution of their bodily members.

And what should we say about such afflictions, when we see the minds of wise people very frequently overwhelmed by excessive drinking and distension of the belly, so that someone whom you had just seen as supremely wise can scarcely understand that he is alive?

Reason in little children therefore grows through reflection and exercise, not through an increase in the soul. As all souls are immortal, so they must also be believed to be rational. It remains now to turn our discussion to where the soul is most clearly shown to have its seat.

**CHAPTER FIVE. Where the soul’s seat is chiefly believed to be**

Although the soul is spread throughout all the members of the body, and arranges the limbs through a certain organ and movement and assigns them their proper functions, nevertheless, as is shown by clear indications, it does not preside equally over every member.

Some assert that the soul properly and chiefly retains its seat in the heart, claiming that the purest blood and the vital spirit are contained there, and that varieties of good and evil thoughts arise from it. No one doubts that these increase the soul through their own power.

Many others say that the seat of the soul is in the brain, which can be believed on the basis of clear indications. Since the soul was created in the image of God, it was fitting that it should seek, in a certain manner, the citadel of its body.

To speak reverently of the Divinity: although we believe and confess that God is everywhere, and that by the power of his divinity he penetrates and fills all visible and invisible things, Scripture nevertheless says that he properly has his seat in heaven: “Heaven is my throne.” It was fitting that she who governs her body should hold the principal citadel of her temple, in imitation of her Creator. Just as he is said to sit in the highest places, so she is believed to reside in the elevated part of her body. From there all the members are governed with orderly direction, as though from a citadel.

Thus the rounded shape of the brain appears to have been made in the likeness of the heavenly sphere, where the immortal soul might claim a dwelling worthy of itself. It was fitting that it should seek the higher places, because everything whose nature is subtle seeks what is lofty. Even visible fire is seen to reach upward toward the heights.

There are also other indications showing that the soul has its seat at the crown of the head. It is entirely certain that all bodily sensation is contained in the head. If some joy takes possession of the mind, it is immediately revealed by the cheerfulness of the face. But if distress arrives, we are not weighed down by some disorder of the viscera; rather, we are immediately seized by a certain stupor of the head, so much so that it dulls the sight and numbs the hearing, and the soul leaves certain signs of indignation there.

Since this is so, it is rightly believed that the soul has its seat at the crown of the head.

But since we have said only a little about the soul—why it is called soul, what it is, where it originates, whether it is believed to possess a form, and where its seat is chiefly believed to be—we must now turn to expressing its moral virtues. First, we must investigate what virtue is.

**CHAPTER SIX. Concerning its moral virtues, and first, what virtue is**

There are therefore four moral virtues of the soul: prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance. But since we name these virtues, we must first explain why virtue is called virtue and what virtue is.

Virtue is so called from *vis*, that is, from strength. It is called this because it endures all things that may occur through a certain force and strength of mind and spirit.

Virtue, then, is every holy, invisible, and incorporeal thing: holy, most pure, and entirely without evil. Wherever it remains, it makes all things holy, pure, firm, and stable. No one receives it unwillingly, and no one loses it except one who of his own accord gives himself over to loss and deception.

It is also defined in this way: virtue is a disposition of the mind, the adornment of rational life, an arrangement of character, a desire for piety, and every honor and worship of divinity.

As has been said, it is divided into four moral virtues. They are called moral because through them human behavior is adorned and ennobled. If prudence is absent from human beings, they are immediately disfigured by dullness of mind. If fortitude is absent, they are at once surrendered to weakness. Where justice is absent, who does not know that everything crooked, twisted, and deformed is present? If temperance is also lacking, all things excessive and exceeding proper measure will dishonor the mind through their very excess.

If these four virtues possess a person’s mind, it will be supported like a house by four corners, so that it does not collapse under any force of storms. Rather, whatever it wishes to build, it will place upon an exceedingly firm foundation.

These four virtues are so closely joined to one another that none can in any way attain perfection without the others. Prudence must be supplied with fortitude. Justice adorns fortitude. Temperance restrains justice with a certain moderation, so that it does not burn beyond measure, but does everything according to due proportion.

Now let the names of these virtues be explained individually and more clearly: why they are called what they are called, and what the particular nature of each one is.

**CHAPTER SEVEN. Concerning prudence**

Prudence is so called as though from foresight, because through its insight it perceives what may occur, whether prosperous or adverse, so that it may act cautiously and not at some time be elated by prosperity or cast down by adversity.

It is also called wisdom by another name, because it tastes, on the palate of the heart, what it ought to reject and what it ought to admit into its depths.

Prudence, or wisdom, is therefore knowledge of divine or human matters, insofar as it is granted to human beings. Through it we understand what we ought to avoid and what we ought to do. Through it we grasp the investigation of truth and its discovery.

But since those who pursue the world are also called prudent, we must investigate how greatly they differ from one another. Worldly prudence, insofar as it is able, seeks to corrupt what is sound and whole, and rejoices when its own profits are increased by the losses of others.

Concerning this, the Lord, speaking in the Gospel about the unjust steward, says that he acted prudently because, at the expense of his master, he acquired profit and looked ahead to the future. Concerning this prudence Paul says: “The prudence of the flesh is death”—certainly, the death of the soul (Romans 8).

In contrast, the prudence or wisdom acquired through God’s gift can perish neither through its own sin nor through another’s. It does not wish to inflict loss upon others for the sake of its own gain, but desires to provide for everyone as for itself.

Concerning this prudence Paul, after discussing the prudence of the flesh, adds: “But the prudence of the spirit is life and peace” (ibid.). It is clear that he was speaking of the life of the soul. For spiritual prudence always desires to strive toward what is true and holy, although it sometimes falls into error.

This happens because it is hindered by the weakness of its bodily burden: no one living in the flesh can perfectly foresee and avoid everything. Hence that distinguished teacher, who was carried away to the secrets of the third heaven, contemplated the delights of paradise, and heard certain secrets which human beings are not permitted to speak, says, burdened by this affliction: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma” (1 Corinthians 13).

But since we have said that prudence supplies fortitude, something must now be said about fortitude.

**CHAPTER EIGHT. Concerning fortitude**

Fortitude is endurance and perseverance in good things, and tolerance and victory against all the temptations of vices. It ought to be present in the mind in such a way that it not only conquers adversities, but also overcomes, kills, and extinguishes all seductive and pleasurable things that arouse carnal delight.

When it has done this, it will rightly be called fortitude. For if it overcomes adversities but consents to the allurements of wanton flesh, it will be called not fortitude but dissolution, because it is dissolved toward pleasurable things.

It is briefly but most honorably defined in the saying: “No one conquers better than the one who conquers himself.”

But since the name of this virtue is also turned toward the left, something must be said about that. There is also a diabolical fortitude, concerning which the Lord speaks to blessed Job: “His strength is in his loins, and his fortitude is in the navel of his belly” (Job 38). Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “When a strong armed man guards his courtyard, the things he possesses are at peace” (Luke 11).

We understand the strong man to be the devil and his courtyard to be the world. When one stronger, namely Christ, came upon that courtyard, the devil was defeated and overcome and was cast out.

But the diabolical fortitude that strengthens the wicked in evil, and the fortitude of Christ by which the saints are strengthened to endure adversity, differ not only in their action but also in the variety of their names.

Diabolical fortitude is called obstinacy, stubbornness, or perversity—qualities that do not allow a person to be recalled from evil acts by holy exhortations. The fortitude of Christ, however, is perseverance or endurance, and also patience, which bears all adversities with long-suffering and patience.

Justice must accompany this fortitude. Justice is called rectitude or equity, lest what is strong should in some way become evil through lacking right order.

**CHAPTER NINE. Concerning justice**

Justice is so called as though from the guardianship of law, because it guards whatever the law commands and avoids whatever it forbids.

If justice is joined to fortitude, it adorns it in every way. For whatever is strong, unless it is just, will undoubtedly be directed toward the evil side.

Justice, therefore, is the proper nobility of the mind, which gives each person the recompense owed to him: bestowing worthy praise upon the good, and bringing upon the wicked and malicious the due correction of reproach.

Through justice we offer God the worship and honor owed to his divinity, and also love. We embrace our neighbors with the worthy affection of love.

For what is more just than to love God with one’s whole heart, since we were created by him when we did not exist?

We wrongly call captivity evil, for there is also a good captivity, of which it is said: “Ascending on high, Christ led captivity captive” (Psalm 67).

What can be more righteous than to love our neighbors, who were created like us and redeemed in the same manner as we were? Through this same justice, our faults and those of our neighbors would be restrained by worthy and due correction.

Since unlawful things are restrained and checked by justice, and correction cannot be made without a certain fervor and ardor of zeal, temperance rightly follows justice, lest the fervor of justice exceed due measure and, through excessive correction, we cast down the one whom we ought to win by admonishing and correcting.

**CHAPTER TEN. Concerning temperance**

Temperance is so called because through its moderation it tempers the mind of each person. It is also called temperance because it tempers the mind against heat and cold, lest excessive cold, through its excess, constrict the flourishing branches.

Temperance is therefore a virtue of the mind which, through its moderation, imposes a measure upon the whole of life, so that nothing is rejected through excessive hatred or caressed through excessive love. Considering all variations with careful attention, it tempers and moderates them.

It is also called discernment by another name, because it discerns everything so that it does not exceed the proper measure and does not incline too far either to the right or to the left, but proceeds along a certain royal road and moderates its pace so that it does not go beyond due measure.

Hence that philosophical saying is extremely brief, but highly approved and especially necessary in this life: “Nothing in excess.”

When it says “nothing,” it shows that even a good thing can be excessive. Thus Solomon says: “My son, do not be excessively righteous” (Ecclesiasticus 7).

Jacob also speaks allegorically about this when he says: “I have oxen and sheep with young, and tender little ones; if I make them labor too much in walking, they will die” (Genesis 33).

The oxen and sheep with young signify souls that conceive the word of God in their minds. If they are forced to undertake too long a journey, they lose what they have conceived in their minds.

The tender little ones are those about whom Paul says: “I gave you milk to drink, not food, for you were not yet able; indeed, you are not yet able. For you are still little ones” (1 Corinthians 3).

Such persons must therefore be given light commandments, signified by milk, until they are able to use solid and strong food, that is, stronger commandments.

These virtues are necessary for everyone, but they provide the greatest glory and adornment to royal excellence.

Through prudence, a king looks ahead for everyone, carefully and rationally considering what may occur; with the sharpness of understanding, like the edge of the eyes, he cautiously perceives adversities and prosperities.

Through fortitude, he bears with a brave and unshaken mind everything that he has foreseen, whether adversity or prosperity: the changing events of the world, wars, disturbances and rebellions, and also the various dispositions of human beings. For the more people royal excellence governs, the more events and accidents it perceives; therefore it is fitting that it overcome everything with the strongest spirit.

Who ought to be more just than a king? Although all judges and administrators, led by greed, may strive to arrange unjust things, when they consider the king’s justice they will not dare to inflict anything unjust upon his subjects, because they will fear just retribution.

It is especially fitting that a king be temperate, so that his commands may suit everyone: neither excessively lax nor again exceedingly burdensome, but arranged with such moderation and balance that everything may be done according to the ability of all.

Then lambs will find in the royal edicts a place to which they can go, and elephants will know where they can swim—that is, gentle and simple people will not be crushed by the force of the commands, while the powerful and strong will always see and fear one who is more powerful and stronger than they.

Upon these four virtues, like the most solid columns, the honor and glory of all royal dignity are raised, and everything is happily governed and adorned.

But since these matters concerning the soul and its moral virtues have been arranged briefly and with less elegance, it remains to say something about the position and dignity of its dwelling-place. For it was fitting that she who was created with such great dignity, and who is said to have been made in the image and likeness of God, should be adorned with a suitable dwelling.

I will therefore approach the marvelous work of God in the human body with as much admiration as I can. If I cannot write about it in a manner fully worthy of the subject, I shall nevertheless attempt to do so devoutly, drawing the briefest extracts from the extensive writings of approved teachers.

**CHAPTER ELEVEN. Concerning the condition and arrangement of the body**

The human body, compacted by marvelous workmanship, is distinguished from all living creatures by the upright height of its stature. If it is considered member by member, great mysteries are contained in it by those who strive to investigate them.

The head itself, rising above all the members, at whose crown we chiefly believe the soul to have its seat, was formed in the likeness of the heavenly sphere and is constructed from six bones, so that the number six—which is acknowledged to be perfect—may be understood to be present in the creation of the human being. Much could be said about the perfection of this number, but for the sake of brevity it must be omitted here.

Beneath the rounded concavity of the head appear the two rows of eyes, in the likeness of the two heavenly lights or, to say something more sacred, in the likeness of the two Testaments.

Beneath these, most appropriately, are arranged the other paired members, ordered through the conjunction of duality: the ears, nostrils, lips, arms, hands, sides, legs, and feet. All these are so fittingly joined to one another in affection that they seem to have one and the same understanding and function.

Alongside these paired and twinned members there are other members which, though singular in their own unity, are most appropriately suited to the paired members: the nose, mouth, throat, chest, belly, navel, and the very generative organ, which God in marvelous dispensation granted for renewing the offspring of the human race.

All these members appear to possess great beauty because, placed in the middle, they correspond with the paired members, so that neither side can claim one of them without the other.

God therefore joined all these members, together with the rest, through worthy workmanship into a dwelling-place for the soul, which was created in his image.

**CHAPTER TWELVE. Concerning the functions of the five senses**

It remains now to say a little about the functions of the five senses. Although they also seem to exist in beasts, they nevertheless differ from them by a long interval, because in us they are rational, whereas in beasts they lack reason.

The first of these is sight. Through a certain power of the soul, which we call vision, it emerges through the pupil of the eye and perceives with a certain subtlety things that are not very far away. It recognizes the colors of visible things through the illuminated air. If things are situated very far away, however, sight fails because of the distance itself.

The second is hearing. It has been arranged so that through winding, resonant passages it draws sounds toward itself, distinguishes them, and understands what has been heard. For this reason it does not have straight and open passages, but passages winding in curved, cochlea-like turns, so that the emitted sound, being delayed by them, may produce the power of discernment and understanding.

For if an emitted sound were received along a straight path, it would lose discernment and understanding through its very speed.

The third is smell. Through it we recognize all foul odors and pleasant fragrances; we avoid putrid things as deserving abhorrence, while drawing fragrant things within us through a certain delight of the soul and being refreshed by the sweetness of their smell.

The fourth is taste. Through it we distinguish by the flavor of the palate everything that we put into the mouth, whether sweet or bitter. Although it distinguishes all the qualities of flavors, it is itself shown to possess no flavor.

The fifth is touch. Although it has been assigned to all the members, it is chiefly entrusted to the hands, to which the use of action has also been especially given. Whatever must be done is done with the hands.

But if we wished to examine the Creator’s marvelous work in each individual member and to discuss each one according to the capacity of my little intellect, this little work would become more extensive than I had intended.

Since I wished to make these matters known briefly to your highness—or rather, to recall to memory things already known—I ask that, if your excellence judges anything in this little work to be useful, God’s gift be praised in it: he who makes the tongues of infants eloquent and is accustomed to open the closed mouths of the mute.

But if there are things that rightly make your nose wrinkle, I ask fitting pardon as a human being. For the one who can avoid every false coloring of speech will be called perfect, as the Apostle James asserts: “The man who does not stumble in speech is perfect” (James 3). Yet this belongs to very few, as the prophet says: “Every human being is a liar” (Psalm 11).

**MARTYROLOGY OF BLESSED RABANUS MAURUS, ABBOT OF FULDA AND ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ**

[Canisius, *Lectiones antiquae*, from a manuscript codex of the monastery of St. Gall]

[Column 1121]

[Column 1121A]

# Prologue

> **Editorial note:** This Prologue, absent from the editions published by Canisius, and the verses to Archchaplain Grimold which follow, are given from Mabillon’s *Analecta*. — Editor.

## To Ratleicus, Abbot of Seligenstadt

Rabanus, servant of Christ Jesus and servant of his servants, to the venerable man Ratleicus, priest and abbot: greetings in the Lord.

Because you asked me, dearest brother, to compose for you a martyrology covering the whole year and to insert in it all the feasts of the saints that I could find, I did as much as I could. For each day I inserted the names of the saints that I found written or recorded by earlier generations in little books; and, wherever I read how a particular saint had died or suffered martyrdom, I briefly noted, as best I was able, how the saint had ended life.

But since you have found and read many writings of the ancients, you will examine this little work by means of them and make it useful to readers as far as you can, so that what my ignorance and weakness could not suitably accomplish, your knowledge and diligence may profitably complete. Commend me in your holy prayers to almighty God, so that he himself, the author and giver of our salvation, may by his grace and through the intercession of his saints release wretched me from the bonds of sins and make me a participant in eternal blessedness.

May the eternal God preserve you through all ages,

And grant you eternal life in the citadel of heaven.

## The Dedication Poem Follows: To Grimold, Archchaplain

To the sweetest brother and most reverend abbot Grimold, Rabanus, the least worthy servant of God’s servants, sends greetings in Christ.

Thus from written sources I have properly composed this little book

Of the holy Fathers, beloved brother, for you,

So that you may know the deeds of those whose feasts you celebrate,

And the end of their lives, by which they departed from here to heaven.

Thus, aided by their merits and prayers,

May you too joyfully pass into the kingdom of heaven,

Where the eternal God, the mighty creator of humankind,

May place and bless you together with the saints.

Live on, strength of mine, and anchor of my wearied affairs,

My refuge in shipwreck and my safe shore and land.

You alone are our honor, our ever most faithful city,

Safe rest for my spirit afflicted by cares.

Though mountains and fields with their waves may lie between us,

My mind is with you, confined by no earthly soil.

My mind follows you, and my song of love follows too,

Desiring in my heart all prosperity for you.

May Christ, who made you known to me and granted you as a friend,

Preserve you everywhere in health for me.

Before the earth’s foundation and the heaven’s swift-moving circle

Pass away, may your love for me never cease.

This I have said, Father; I say it again and again:

Remember me, just as I too remember you.

May God unite in the heavenly citadel, rejoicing together,

Those whom here on earth he joined as friends.

# Rabanus’s Martyrology Begins

## January

### 1 January

The octave of the Lord’s Nativity, on which day our same Lord was circumcised in the flesh according to the law of Moses and received the name Jesus, which an angelic oracle had foretold concerning him before his conception in the womb.

On the same day is the nativity of the martyr Almachius.

> **Editorial note:** Baronius affirms that he suffered not under Diocletian but under Honorius or Theodosius. Alypius was indeed prefect of the City at that time; Symmachus’s letters to him prove this. But how could he have been killed by pagans under a Christian emperor? The accounts that Theodoret gives concerning Telemachus differ. Nor do I know whether he could have been enrolled by the emperor “among the choir of martyrs.” Such matters do not belong to emperors. — Basnage.

He was killed by gladiators on the orders of Alypius, prefect of the City, when he said: “Today is the day of the Lord’s octave: cease from the superstitions of idols and from polluted sacrifices.”

On the same day at Rome is the nativity of Martina, virgin and martyr, who suffered under the emperor Alexander. She was tortured for the faith of Christ by many kinds of torment and finally struck with the sword. By her prayers she also destroyed idols and images and converted many to the faith of Christ. After the blessed virgin’s death, Alexander was struck by anguish of heart and, tearing his own flesh like a mad dog, breathed out his wicked life amid great torment.

Likewise, on the same day at Rome, the passion of Concordius, priest and martyr, carried out under the emperor Antoninus by the count Torquatus.

> **Editorial note:** There was no persecution at that time. — Basnage.

Because he refused to sacrifice to idols, he underwent the death sentence.

### 2 January

At Antioch, Macarius the abbot.

At Rome, Telesphorus, pope, who established that a fast should be observed for seven weeks before Easter and that Mass should be celebrated at night on the Lord’s Nativity. For at all times no one was to presume to celebrate Mass before the course of the third hour, the hour at which the Lord ascended the cross; and before the sacrifice a hymn was to be sung, namely, “Glory to God in the highest.”

He too was crowned with martyrdom and was buried beside the body of blessed Peter in the Vatican on 2 January.

### 3 January

At Rome, Anterus, pope and martyr, who governed the Church for twelve years. He diligently sought out the deeds of the martyrs and deposited them in the church, and he too was crowned with martyrdom. He was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way.

At Paris, the burial of Genovefa, virgin, whom Saint Germanus, bishop of that city, consecrated to God as a virgin in infancy.

At the city of Tomi, the nativity of Titus, bishop. Under Licinius, he was seized among the recruits; because he refused military service, he was beaten nearly to death, confined in prison, and placed in a stocks until a reply should come. He was then thrown into the sea, and when his body was carried onto the shore, it was buried by deeply religious men in the estate of Amandus, a religious man, where great cures take place.

### 4 January

The nativity of Theogenes, martyr, who completed his passion in the Hellespont under the emperor Licinius and the tribune Telicentius. First he was stretched between four columns and beaten with clubs; then he was thrown into prison to die there of hunger. But by the Lord’s invisible mercy he was fed there for forty days with heavenly food and continually remained in praise of God. Finally he was thrown into the sea and suffered martyrdom.

> **Editorial note:** Instead of *martyrizavit*, read “he was subjected to martyrdom.” This expression occurs several times below.

Euricus, Eustochius, Zozius, and Germanus lifted him from the sea, placed him in a coffin, and buried him in the forum of the Hellespont.

On the same day, the passion of Peter, also called Balsamus, martyr, under the emperor Maximian, with Severus acting as governor. Because Peter refused to sacrifice to the gods, Severus ordered him to be suspended and torn with hooks; finally he was killed with the sword and buried in the city of Aulon.

On the same day, the passion of Lucian, priest and martyr, who was sent from Rome to preach the word of God. He suffered martyrdom in Gaul under Caesar Julian and was killed by the sword in that region. Through his preaching many were converted to the faith. At his tomb many miracles are displayed and very many cures take place.

### 5 January

At Jerusalem, the burial of Simeon the prophet, who carried the infant Lord Jesus in his arms and blessed him.

At Antioch, the burial of Simeon the monk, who stood upon a column, performed many miracles there, and died in peace. His body was then transferred to Antioch by the bishop of that city and the Christian people, with psalms and hymns and many lamps, and was buried there in the greater church.

Vigil of the Epiphany.

### 6 January

The Epiphany of our Lord Jesus Christ.

### 7 January

The passion of Saint Fausta, virgin, under the emperor Maximian. By the power of her patience she first converted Evilasius, the chief official of the palace and her torturer, to the faith, and also the prefect who had been ordered to torture her. She was suspended and torn with instruments; afterward she was handed over to beasts, but was defiled by none of them. Then her head was pierced with nails; afterward she was thrown into a boiling frying pan filled with pitch, but was not harmed. Thus, while Evilasius and the prefect were subjected to torments, she gave up her spirit. When the Christian people heard this, they buried the bodies of the saints.

### 8 January

At Autun, the burial of Egemo, bishop; and at Metz, the burial of Saint Patience, bishop.

### 9 January

The nativity of Epistici, Jocundus, Secundus, Saturninus, Vitalis, Felix, Rusticus, Quintus, Etartaxis, and Fortunatus.

> **Editorial note:** Read “Epictetus,” who suffered in Africa under Decius. — Basnage.

### 10 January

The nativity of Paul, the first anchorite, whose life blessed Jerome wrote. He remained alone in the desert from the sixteenth year of his age until his one hundred and thirteenth year. Fed by the Lord through a raven, he wore a tunic woven from palm leaves. Antony saw his soul carried by angels into heaven among the choirs of apostles and prophets.

On the same day at Rome, in the cemetery of Callistus, the nativity of Miltiades, bishop and confessor, who established in the Church that the faithful should in no way fast on Sundays.

### 11 January

The bringing of the Lord out of Egypt, and the nativity of Saint Salvius, confessor. On his feast Saint Augustine preached a sermon to the people of Carthage.

### 12 January

In Achaea, the nativity of Saints Cyriacus, Moscentius, and Saturus, citizens of Arabia.

> **Editorial note:** Read “Innocentius.” Yet no Innocentius who suffered martyrdom in January is found in the martyrologies. — Editorial note.

> **Editorial note:** Satyrus is celebrated in the Roman Martyrology as having suffered in Achaea; here he is called a citizen of Arabia. Arabia, however, is a city in Persia, not far from the river of the same name. Did a Persian come to Achaea and die there? — Editorial note.

As he passed before a temple of an idol, he blew upon it and made the sign of the cross over his forehead; the idol fell. Those who seized him and had been watching him led him to the duke, reported what had happened, and he was beheaded.

### 13 January

The octave [*Octabas*; corrected *Octava*] of the Theophany (*Theophamae*).

At Poitiers, the burial of Hilary, distinguished bishop and confessor, who under Constantius Augustus, the heretic, was driven into exile in Phrygia because of the Catholic faith. Among his other miracles, it is reported that he raised a dead man by prayer.

On the same day, Saint Agricus, bishop; and at Antioch in Egypt, the passion of Saints Julian and Basilissa, his wife.

Julian was born of noble lineage in the time of Diocletian and Maximian (*Maximini*; corrected *Maximiani*). Trained in the disciplines of the philosophers, he was a devout lover of the Catholic faith. When his parents tried by strong persuasion to draw him into marriage, he is said to have replied: “It is neither my inclination nor my age that I should do what you urge.”

When they persisted stubbornly in their entreaties, he said: “I have neither the freedom to permit nor the power to refuse what you urge. I commit it and leave it to the power of my God.” Nevertheless, he asked his parents for a delay of one week, so that he might learn the will of the heavenly majesty through clear signs.

When that interval had passed, he was overcome by sleep and, while sunk in slumber, saw Christ in a *horoma* (vision) saying:

> **Editorial note:** That is, “vision.” Thus in the *Passion of Perpetua and Felicity*: “Before we fought, I see this in a vision [*horoma*].” — Basnage.

 “Rise; do not fear, and do not dread either persuasive words or your parents’ wishes. For you will take a wife who will not separate you from me by defiling you, but who through you will remain a virgin.” And later: “Many young men and virgins will, through your teaching and manner of life, be approved as members of the heavenly army,” and so forth.

Thus it came about that, with Christ’s help, they built several monasteries in the district of Antioch, so that ten thousand monks lived under Julian’s direction (*conversarent*; corrected *conversarentur*). Under Basilissa, a thousand virgins were dedicated to the service of God.

Afterward Julian suffered martyrdom with his fellow soldiers for the name of Christ under the ruler Marcian. First he was beaten with clubs, and he restored the eye of the man who struck him after it had been torn out. Moreover, he overturned more than five hundred images of idols at once.

After this he was thrust into a dark prison with the prefect’s son, the young Hircicallus, who had recently been converted to the faith, a place where the bodies of the condemned were rotting. But by the wondrous grace of Christ the foul odor was changed into the sweetness of ambrosia, and clear light gladdened the holy martyrs.

Then, at the prefect’s request, he raised from the dead a corpse that had not yet been buried. But while the torturer’s madness continued, by imperial decree the holy martyrs were enclosed in thirty vats in the circus spectacle. These were packed inside with a mass of black pitch, fuel of bitumen, and the stench of sulfur; burning brushwood was placed beneath them, so that the flame rose thirty cubits into the air. Yet they emerged unharmed.

Then a burning wick, soaked with oily liquid, was fastened to the fingers of their hands and feet. When this attempt too had been frustrated, they were offered to wild beasts for devouring, but the beasts did not dare tear their sacred limbs. Finally they were slaughtered with swords. Soon afterward ten lepers were cured at their tomb, demonstrating the glory possessed by martyrs.

### 15 January

In Campania, the nativity of Felix, priest and confessor. Among other things, Bishop Paulinus writes of him that, when persecutors were sending him to prison and he was lying bound and covered with shells and potsherds, an angel released him and led him out during the night.

On the same day is the nativity of Felix, his brother, whom Dracus, prefect of the City, compelled to sacrifice to idols. Dracus beat him with clubs and ordered him to be deported into exile, where he was also to cut squared stones. Yet through the power of God he converted many there to the faith, namely the tribune Probus and those who were with him.

Then he destroyed an idol of Apollo. Later the faithful built a temple to God on that site. After twelve years, on that same Sunday, having completed the mysteries, he departed to the Lord Jesus Christ.

In the city of Spoleto, the nativity of Pontianus, martyr, who suffered in the time of the emperor Antoninus under the judge Fabianus. Because Pontianus refused to sacrifice to idols, Fabianus ordered him to be beaten most cruelly with rods; then to walk barefoot over burning coals. Afterward two lions were released to devour him, but he was not harmed by them at all. Seeing this, the judge ordered lead to be melted and poured over his back; but when this too did him no harm, he was beheaded.

### 15 January

In Palestine, the burial of the prophet Habakkuk, whose relics, together with those of the prophet Micah, were brought to light by divine revelation in the time of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius.

### 16 January

The nativity of Saint Marcellus, pope, who, on the order of the emperor Maximian—or Maxentius—was first beaten with clubs and expelled from the presence of the man whom he had rebuked.

Afterward, when the emperor heard that Marcellus had made the house of blessed Lucina, whom he had condemned to confiscation because she had given her possessions to Christians, into a church and celebrated Mass there, he ordered boards to be laid in that church, in the middle of the city, for the animals of the public stable, and assigned that same bishop to serve the animals under public guard. After serving there for many years, he died clothed in a hair shirt. John the priest and blessed Lucina embalmed him with spices, and he was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla.

At Arles, the burial of Saint Honoratus, bishop and confessor. Among his other miracles, it is said that by prayer he drove a dragon from the island of Hilarina and founded a monastery there.

In the district of Mandinum, at the monastery of Peronne, the burial of Saint Fursey, confessor. Born and raised in Ireland, he left his homeland and parents and devoted several years to the study of Sacred Scripture. From this he built a monastery in a certain place.

While he was hastening to visit his homeland and parents in order to sow among them the seeds of the sacred word through spiritual discourse, he was one day seized by an illness of the body. Suddenly he was carried away in ecstasy and lay as if lifeless from evening until cockcrow. When he returned to himself, he recognized that it had been an angelic vision. Having received the body and blood of Christ, he lay ill that day and the next.

On the third night he was again lifted up by angels and saw wondrous visions, as his Life records. After he returned to himself, he shone for twelve years through preaching the word of God and through signs of miracles. Finally, after monasteries had been built in Gaul, he departed from there to Christ, enriched by good merits.

His body was honorably buried by the duke Erchanwald and the other faithful in the monastery of Peronne, in the church of Saint Peter the apostle and the other apostles, beside the altar.

Also, at the monastery of Fulda, the dedication of the church of Saint Michael in the brothers’ cemetery.

### 17 January

In the Thebaid of Egypt, the burial of Antony the monk, whose life, full of virtues, and the miracles he performed are proclaimed in writing and by fame throughout almost the whole world.

He died in peace under the emperor Constantine, in the one hundred and fifth year of his age, and was hidden by his disciples in the desert, as he himself had instructed while alive. After many years had passed—that is, in the time of the emperor Justinian, who was the nephew of Justin through his sister—his body was found by divine revelation, brought to Alexandria, and buried in the church of John the Baptist.

At Bourges, the burial of Saint Sulpitius, bishop and confessor.

Among the people of Langres, the nativity of the twins Speusippus, Elasippus, and Melasippus.

> **Editorial note:** Eleusippus and Meleusippus.

When they were twenty-five years old, they were crowned with martyrdom, together with their grandmother Leonilla, Janilla, and Neon, in the time of the emperor Aurelian.

The twins were suspended from a single tree, their hands bound above and their feet below, stretched so tightly that they seemed almost to be torn apart from the very structure of their limbs. Afterward they were thrown into the fire, yet were not harmed by the flames; amid words of prayer they departed together to the Lord.

Seeing this, Janilla confessed that she too was a Christian. She was immediately seized by the crowds, suspended by her hair, and afflicted with many tortures. Because she refused to deny Christ, she was killed with Leonilla by the sword.

Neon, the recorder of the proceedings, also confessed the name of Christ and was crowned with martyrdom.

Benignus the priest taught and baptized these twins. Blessed Polycarp, a hearer of the apostle John, sent Benignus from the East to Gaul, together with Mandochius, his fellow priest, and Tyrso, a deacon.

The twins were buried two miles from the city of Langres.

### 18 January

The dedication of Saint Peter the apostle, who was the first to occupy the Roman see.

After this prince of the apostles had first preached the Gospel in Jerusalem, Caesarea, and the other cities of the Jews, he was afterward sent to preach to the Gentiles. He came to Antioch, where he founded the Church of Christ. From there he proceeded to Rome, arriving in the second year of Caesar Claudius. There he preached the Gospel with the utmost zeal and remained bishop of that city for twenty-five years.

On the same day, the nativity of Saint Prisca, martyr.

### 19 January

At Jerusalem, the nativity of Martha and Mary, the sisters of Lazarus.

### 20 January

At Rome, Fabianus, bishop, who, after presiding over the Church for twenty-five years, suffered martyrdom in the time of Decius and was buried in the cemetery of Callistus.

He divided the regions among the deacons and arranged that seven deacons should be assigned to seven notaries, so that they might collect the deeds of the martyrs in full. He also ordered many structures to be built throughout the cemeteries.

On the same day, the nativity of Saint Sebastian of Milan. He was so dear to the emperors Diocletian and Maximian that they entrusted him with command of the first cohort. When Diocletian learned that he was a Christian and could not be recalled from the faith, he ordered him to be bound in the middle of a field like a target for arrows and shot by soldiers.

When he stood covered with arrows like a hedgehog, the soldiers thought him dead and went away. During the night, however, a certain woman named Irene came to take away the body and found him alive. She brought him into her house and cared for him. When he recovered, he strengthened many in the faith.

Soon he appeared before the emperors themselves and rebuked them as they deserved. Then Diocletian ordered him to be led into the palace hippodrome and beaten until he died. They threw his dead body into the great sewer.

But he appeared in a dream to the holy matron Lucina and said: “Near the circus you will find my body hanging on a hook. It has not been touched by filth. When you have lifted it down, carry it to the Catacombs and bury me in a crypt beside the footprints of the apostles.”

She came during the night and fulfilled everything as he had said.

On the same day, the nativity of the holy Marius and Martha, with their sons Audifax and Ambacum [Abachum], nobles from Persia, who had come to Rome to worship during the reign of Claudius. After enduring clubs, the rack, fires, hooks, and the suspension of their hands, Martha was killed in a pool, while the others were beheaded.

### 21 January

At Rome, the nativity of Saint Agnes, virgin.

> **Editorial note:** Agnes. The prefect wished to prostitute her beneath the theater’s vault, according to custom; for the pagans used to shout: “Christians to the lions, virgins to the pimps!” Hence Tertullian reproached them: “By condemning a Christian woman to a pimp rather than to a lion, you have confessed that among us the stain upon chastity is judged more severe than every punishment and every death.” She was nevertheless that renowned virgin. The time at which she suffered martyrdom is still unknown. It is said that her virginity was preserved undefiled by the help of angels: “Agnes entered the place of disgrace and found an angel of the Lord prepared.” Baronius conjectures that she was crowned under Diocletian. — Basnage.

She was thrown into the fire under the prefect of the City, Symphronius; but when the flames were extinguished through her prayer, she was struck with the sword.

In the Spanish city of Tarragona, the nativity of Saint Fructuosus, bishop and martyr, who wrote a Rule for monks.

The passion of Saint Patroclus, martyr.

### 22 January

In the Spanish city of Valencia, the passion of Saint Valerius, bishop, and Vincent, deacon and martyr, who suffered under the governor Dacianus.

When Vincent publicly professed the name of Christ, Dacianus ordered him to be stretched upon the rack and tortured there for a very long time. From there he was dragged to the gallows—or rather, taken down from the rack—and, going ahead of his torturers himself, reproached the executioner for delaying.

There the holy martyr of God was tortured, beaten, scourged, and burned; with his limbs stretched out, he grew toward punishment. Burning plates were pressed against his chest, and liquid was melted between the glowing edges of the iron; hissing flame was sprinkled with drops. Wounds were inflicted upon wounds, torments raged against torments, and salts scattered into the fires leapt crackling bit by bit [*minutis*; perhaps *minutatim*] over his limbs. Now the weapons of punishment were hurled not merely at his limbs but at his very entrails.

After this he was thrust into a very dark place strewn with fragments of potsherds. There, however, through the ministry of angels, he received the beauty of light and the peace of rest.

Then, at the governor’s order, he was carried away on a little bed and departed to the Lord with the palm of martyrdom. Later it was ordered that his body be thrown into the sea. But once it had been cast in, God willing, it was quickly brought back through the waves to the shore. A religious widow named Jonica first entrusted it to burial, while Christ confirmed his triumph through miracles.

On the same day at the Waters of Salvius, the nativity of Saint Anastasius, monk and martyr from Persia. After enduring many tortures—prison, words, and chains—in Caesarea of Palestine, he was finally subjected to much suffering by the Persians in Persia and ultimately beheaded by their king Chosroes.

### 23 January

At Rome, the nativity of Saint Emerentiana, virgin of Christ and martyr, who was Agnes’s foster-sister.

While she was praying at Agnes’s tomb and defending the worshipers with her from the violence of the pagans, they stoned her.

On the same day is celebrated the passion of the holy martyrs Macarius and Eugenius, who suffered many tortures under the judge Julianus: namely, a burning grating over which pitch and oil had been poured, but the fire did not harm them. Then they were handed over to vipers and serpents, but were not harmed by them in any way. Afterward, by their prayers, they destroyed a huge dragon, and finally were crowned with martyrdom.

### 24 January

The nativity of Saint Timothy the apostle.

At Antioch, Saint Babylas, bishop, and the three little boys Urbanus, Prilidanus, and Eupolinus.

> **Editorial note:** Epolonius.

He suffered for the name of Christ under the emperor Numerianus, and his boys suffered with him. After other tortures, all incurred the death sentence.

### 25 January

At Rome, the translation of the apostle Paul and his conversion at Damascus.

The nativity of Saint Gregory the Theologian.

The nativity of Projectus, martyr.

### 26 January

Saint Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, who, under Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus, while the proconsul was sitting at Smyrna and the whole people were conspiring against him, was handed over to the fire.

At Bethlehem, Saint Paula, at whose prayers blessed Jerome composed several works.

### 27 January
