In Africa, the nativity of Dativus, Vincentius, Julianus, Vincentia, and thirty-two others.

> **Editorial note:** Dativus, Vincentius. Read “twenty-seven” for “thirty-two.” Dativus and Vincentius’s deeds were praised by the Donatists at the Conference of Carthage; they truly were Donatists who were crowned with martyrdom during the persecution, and for that reason the schismatics held them up for praise.

> Baluzius, followed by Ruinartus, argues that the Acts were corrupted by the Donatists, who added a short preface and a longer appendix at the end, containing many accusations against Mensurius and others. Ruinartus is mistaken here. The Acts that we now read were not recognized by the Catholics at the conference as genuine and then corrupted by the Donatists.

> Both points are easily proved. First, the Donatists cited the Acts of those martyrs precisely because Saturninus, Dativus, and the others had belonged to their party. The Catholics, without debating the authenticity of the Acts, drew from them what is called an argument *ad hominem*, intending to prove from the Donatists’ own Acts that a large assembly could have been summoned during the persecution. For the Donatist martyrs confessed that they had “held the gathering and celebrated the Lord’s Day.”

> The second point is proved just as easily. The very conclusion cited by Saint Augustine at the Conference of Carthage is found today in the appendix that Ruinartus conjectures was added by the Donatists. From this one may infer that the appendix, which Baluzius honestly published in full, had already been composed in Augustine’s time and was therefore genuine. Dativus and his companions must accordingly be assigned to the Donatists. — Basnage.

And the nativity of Saint Sulpitius, bishop and confessor.

### 28 January

At Rome, the second [*geminum*; corrected *secundo*] commemoration of Saint Agnes, virgin—that is, her commemoration on account of her nativity.

Charles died.

### 29 January

At Rome, the nativity of Papias and Maurus, soldiers, in the time of Diocletian.

When they saw the steadfastness of the martyrs Saturninus and Sisinnius, they were immediately converted to the faith. Laodicius, prefect of the City, then ordered their mouths, with which they confessed Christ, to be crushed with stones. They were thrown into the prison where they had been baptized by blessed Pope Marcellus.

After eleven days Laodicius ordered them to be laid upon the ground and beaten with clubs until they breathed their last. The priest John gathered their bodies during the night and buried them on the Numentana [Nomentana] Way, at the springs of blessed Peter, where people were baptized.

This is written in the deeds of blessed Pope Marcellus.

At Trier, the burial of blessed Valerius, bishop.

### 30 January

At the monastery of Maubeuge, the nativity of Aldegund, virgin, who was born of noble lineage in the time of Dagobert, king of the Franks, and chose the purpose of virginity.

She persevered in it, and an angelic vision was often revealed to her, exhorting her to remain faithful to her purpose. Finally, amid great brilliance of heavenly light, she departed into eternal life.

### 31 January

In Alexandria, the nativity of Tarsicius [Tharsicius], Zoticus [Cyriacus], and Ammonius.

In Africa, Victor, Publius [Thyrsus], and Saturninus.

# February

### 1 February

In Greece, Polycarp, bishop.

> **Editorial note:** Perhaps Ignatius.

At Ravenna, Saint Severus, bishop.

In Ireland, the nativity of Brigid, virgin, whose birth is proclaimed to have been one of great merit and holiness.

### 2 February

The Purification of Saint Mary, when she was presented in the Temple with the infant Jesus, where the aged Simeon received the Lord Jesus himself into his arms and blessed him.

On the same day, the nativity of Saint Apronianus, registrar, who was baptized by Sisinnius, deacon of Marcellus, pope, and beheaded by the prefect Laodicius in the time of Maximian Augustus.

At Forosimfronium [Forum Sempronii], on the Flaminian Way, 174 miles from Rome, the commemoration of Laurentius and Hippolytus, and the nativity of Saint Fortunatus.

At Orléans, the burial of Sicaria, a virgin consecrated to God.

### 3 February

At Lyons, the burial of blessed Lupicinus, bishop.

In the city of Sebaste in Cappadocia, the passion of Saint Blaise, bishop and martyr of Christ, who was beheaded under the governor Agricolaus together with two little boys, sons of one woman, among those seven who, strengthened by his preaching, suffered martyrdom under the same governor.

### 4 February

At Forum Sempronius, the nativity of Gemini, Gelasius, Mali [Magni], Aquilini [Aquili], and Donatus.

Likewise, Donatus, Themois, and Gelasius.

### 5 February

At the city of Patras, the ordination of Andrew the apostle to the episcopate.

In the Sicilian city of Cathena [Catana], the passion of Saint Agatha, virgin, who suffered martyrdom under the consul Quintianus in the time of Diocletian. After slaps, imprisonment, the rack and tortures, the cutting off of her breasts followed by healing from the Lord, and being rolled over potsherds and coals, she finally completed her martyrdom in prison.

At Vienne, the burial of Avitus, bishop.

### 6 February

At Rome, on the Appian Way in its cemetery, the passion of Saint Soter, virgin.

In Caesarea of Cappadocia, the passion of Saint Dorothea, virgin, and Theophilus, under the prefect Apricius.

Dorothea was entrusted to her two sisters, Christe and Callista, who had recently apostatized from the faith through the sufferings of this life, so that they might turn her away from Christ. But she converted them again to Christ, so that, after the prefect had put them into a vat and burned them, they attained the palm of martyrdom.

Afterward Dorothea was led to the place of punishments, where she also suffered. A certain scholar named Theophilus mocked her because, as she was going to paradise, she said that her bridegroom Christ would send her apples and blooming roses. She obtained these things immediately.

When Theophilus saw this, he at once confessed Christ as the true God and suffered martyrdom under the same prefect, being beheaded.

In the Gallic city of Aderatum [Atrebatum; Arras], the burial of Saint Vedast, bishop and confessor.

At the monastery of Elnone, the burial of Saint Amandus, bishop and confessor.

### 7 February

In Britain, in the city of Augusta, the nativity of Augulus, bishop and martyr.

### 8 February

At Rome, the burial of Saint Paul, bishop, and Julius, pope.

### 9 February

At Soli in Cyprus, the nativity of Alexander and Ammonius, and likewise of another Ammonius and thirty-seven others.

> **Editorial note:** Read “Suevo” or “Soli.”

### 10 February

In Campania, the nativity of Saint Silvanus, bishop and confessor.

In Bethlehem, in the land of Judaea, under King Herod, the passion of Saints Andrew and Apponius.

At the city of Saintes, the burial of Saint Trojan, bishop and confessor, and of Baldegund, abbot.

At Rome, Zoticus, Ireneus, Hyacinthus, and Amantius.

On the same day, the burial of Saint Scholastica, virgin and religious woman. Her brother, Saint Benedict, saw her soul ascending to heaven in the form of a dove. After completing the hymns of matins, he announced this to the brothers and gave thanks to God for it.

### 11 February

At Rome, Calocerius [Calocerus] and Parthenius.

### 12 February

In Africa, the passion of Damian, soldier; of the children Modestus and Ammon [Ammonius]; and of Soticus [Zoticus].

The burial of Simplicius, bishop and confessor.

### 13 February

At Lyons, the burial of blessed Stephen, bishop.

### 14 February

At Rome, the nativity of Saint Valentine, priest, who, after many distinguished works of healing and teaching, was beaten with clubs and then beheaded under Caesar Claudius.

On the same day, the nativity of Saint Valentine, bishop of Terni. He was seized by pagans, beaten with rods, and then, after a prolonged beating, imprisoned because they could not overcome him. In the silence of midnight he was taken from prison and beheaded on the order of the furious prefect of the City, Placidus.

Then Proculus, Ephybus [Ephebus], and Apollonius, his disciples, transferred his body to their church in the city of Terni and buried it during the night. While they kept watch there day after day, they were seized by pagans and handed over to the custody of the consul Leontius. He ordered them to be brought before his tribunal in the middle of the night.

When neither persuasion nor threats could recall them from the faith, he ordered them to be beheaded. They were buried not far from the head of Saint Valentine.

### 15 February

At Antioch, the nativity of Joseph, deacon, and Zeno.

At Terni, the nativity of Saint Agapa [Agapis], virgin, Saturninus, and Castula [Castulus].

XIV KALENDS. Saint Onesimus the apostle; and at Cumae, the nativity of Saint Juliana the virgin, who in the time of the emperor Maximian was first beaten and severely tortured by her own father, Africanus; then, by the prefect Eulesius [Evilasius], whom she had had as her betrothed, she was beaten naked with rods, hung up by her hair, and had molten lead poured over her head. She was again taken back into prison, where she openly contended with the devil. Summoned forth again, she overcame tortures involving wheels, flames, and a boiling cauldron, and completed her martyrdom by decapitation [Col. 1132D]. She indeed suffered at Nicomedia, but after a short time, by God’s arrangement, was transferred to Campania.

XIII KALENDS. At Babylon, the nativity of Polychronius, bishop of that city, who, in the presence of the persecutor Decius, with his mouth beaten by stones, stretched out his hands and raising his eyes to heaven gave up his spirit. Written in the Passion of Saint Laurence.

XII KALENDS. At Nicomedia, the commemoration of Pantaleon the martyr, who completed his martyrdom under the emperor Maximian. Born of his father Eustorgius and instructed in the faith by the presbyter Hermolaus before he was baptized, he freed a boy bound by a serpent and killed the serpent by prayer. After [Col. 1133A] baptism, he gave sight to a blind man, converted his father Eustorgius to the faith, and performed many miracles in the name of Christ. For this reason Maximian ordered him to be hung on the torture-horse and lamps to be hung at his sides; but their flames were suddenly extinguished. Afterwards he was sent into a pan of fire so that he might be burned there by molten lead, but through Christ’s power, when the heat grew cold, he was not harmed at all. Later he was thrown into the sea, but was brought safely from it to the shore. Then he was handed over to wild beasts, but was defiled by none of them. Finally he was beheaded; but his executioners took away the remains of his body and buried them honorably. The presbyter Hermolaus, however, was beheaded together with his two companions, namely Hermippus and Hermocrates, and was buried by Christians [Col. 1133B].

XI KALENDS. The nativity in Africa of Saints Publius, Julian, and Marulus. Likewise, of Julian, Marcellus, Tullus, Lampasius, Majulus, and Julian.

X KALENDS. At Rome, the nativity of Gaius the bishop; and in Cyprus, the nativity of Potamius, Nemesius, and Didymus; and elsewhere, the martyrdom of Victor, Corona, and twenty others.

IX KALENDS. In Africa, the nativity of Saints Verulus, Servulus, Secundinus, Syricius, Felix, Saturninus, Fortunatus, and sixteen others; and the deposition of Eucherius, bishop and confessor.

VIII KALENDS. The Chair of Saint Peter, which he occupied at Antioch, where the disciples were first called Christians [Col. 1133C]; and at Nicomedia, the nativity of Thecla the virgin, disciple of Saint Paul the apostle, who under the emperor Nero was handed over to the fire for the name of Christ, but was not burned. Afterwards she was assigned to wild beasts and serpents, but was harmed by none of them. Finally, at Seleucia, having attained the martyrdom of virginity and the honor of her virtues, she departed in the sleep of peace to the Lord. At Rome, on the Tiburtine Way, at Saint Laurence, the nativity of Saint Concordia, whom the persecution of Decius slaughtered.

VII KALENDS. In Pannonia, the nativity of Saints Senerotus [Sirenus], Antigonus, Rotulus, and Libus; and in Asia, of Polycarp with twelve others.

VI KALENDS. In Palestine, Matthias the apostle, who was chosen to the apostleship from among the seventy disciples in place of Judas the betrayer, and preached the Gospel in Judaea [Col. 1133D].

V KALENDS. In Africa, the nativity of Saints Donatus, Justus, Rotulus, Herena, Pision, and Pamphilus. The nativity of Nestor and Casta.

IV KALENDS. At Alexandria, the nativity of Saints Alexander, Nestor, Theon, Opio, Justus, Donativus, Ampliatus, and Ingenius.

III KALENDS. At Thessalonica, the nativity of Saints Alexander, Antigonus, and Abundius. In Africa, of Dionysius and twenty-four others.

[Col. 1134A] II KALENDS. At Alexandria, of Cereal, Pupulus, Caius, and Serapion.

## March

KALENDS OF MARCH. At Angers, the deposition of Saint Albinus the bishop.

VI NONES. The nativity of Saints Jorgius, Herglius, and Absalon [Lucius, Absalon, and Lorgius]. At Caesarea in Cappadocia, of Luke the bishop and Primitivus; and at the Roman harbor, of Paul, Secundilla, and Januaria.

V NONES. The nativity of Felix, Luciolus, Justus, Fortunatus, Martia, Herotes, Antigonus, Januarius, Tultella, Gabianus, Quiriulus, and Marinus; likewise, of Felix, Florian, and Donatus.

IV NONES. At Rome, the deposition of Julius the bishop; and at Nicomedia [Col. 1134B], the passion of Saints Adrian and thirty-three others.

III NONES. At Rome, of Lucius, pope and martyr. He was driven into exile for the faith of Christ, and afterwards returned safely to the Church by God’s will. He was also beheaded by the emperor Valerian and buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way.

II NONES OF MARCH. The deposition of Saint Quiriacus the presbyter.

NONES. At Carthage, the passion of Perpetua and Felicity, who were assigned to the beasts under the ruler Severus; and when Felicity was giving birth in prison, it was obtained by the prayers of all the soldiers who were suffering together with them that she should give birth in the eighth month.

[Note: [Col. 1133D] The passion of these women is found in Ruinart, *Acta sincera Martyrum*. Valesius, who had seen it, judged it to have been written by a Montanist; and anyone who reads it will readily believe that the women themselves belonged to the sect of the Montanists [Col. 1134D]. BASN.]

It was also granted to Perpetua, among other things, that her mind might somehow be separated from her body, in which she endured the attack of a heifer, so that she still expected something future which she did not know had already happened to her [Col. 1134C].

VIII IDES OF MARCH. At Nicomedia, Quinctilis the bishop and Capitulinus. In Africa, of Rogatus, Felix; likewise, of Rogatus, Beata, Herenia, Urbanus, Cyril the bishop, Silvanus, and Mamilius.

VII IDES. At Sebaste in Lesser Armenia, forty soldiers in the time of King Licinius, under the governor Agricolaus. After frequent bonds and imprisonments, and after their faces had been beaten with stones, they were sent into a lake, where their bodies, bound by ice, were torn apart during the night; and in the morning they completed their martyrdom by the breaking of their legs. Their bodies were then burned and thrown into the river; but by divine providence their remains were found intact and buried with due honor. The more distinguished among them were Cyrion and Candidus.

VI IDES. At Antioch, of Agape the virgin and Mariana. At Smyrna, of Phronis. At Nicomedia, of Palatinus, Firmianus, and Rusticus. At Alexandria, of Heraclius, Zosimus, Alexander, and Candidus and Piperion.

V IDES. At the city of Sebaste, the nativity of the forty martyrs who suffered martyrdom for the name of Christ in the time of the emperor Licinius, under the governor Agricolaus and the commander Lysias [Col. 1135A]. When the governor could not turn them to the worship of the gods, he ordered them to be buried under stones. But those throwing the stones struck one another with them, and could not harm the martyrs. The commander Lysias, burning with anger, took up a stone to strike one of the saints; but, by God’s wondrous will, the stone itself reached the governor’s face.

The governor sent them into a lake frozen with ice, but by God’s will the cold itself was moderated, and the ice dissolved into warm water. One of the forty, terrified by fear of the punishments, fled to the bath; but as soon as he touched its warmth, he was dissolved and gave up his spirit. In his place, the jailer who guarded the holy martyrs, believing in Christ, was substituted, having seen a crown descend from heaven upon each of those who had persevered in confession [Col. 1135B].

The tyrant, filled with anger, ordered them to be led to the shore, their legs broken with clubs, and then thrown into the sea. But, God willing it, the remains of the martyrs were revealed in the depths of the water to devout men, who took them away and honorably placed them in little coffers.

IV IDES. At Rome, the deposition of Saint Gregory the pope, who was a most brilliant teacher in the law of God and converted the English people to the faith through Augustine, Mellitus, and John, servants of God.

III IDES. At Nicomedia, the nativity of Macedonius the presbyter, of Patricia his wife, and of Modesta his daughter. At Nicaea, of Theuseta and Horis, her sons. Of Theodora. All these were burned in the fire. Of Julius the bishop and Alexander.

[Col. 1135C] II IDES. At Carthage, the nativity of Saints Donatus, Ephrosius, and Phronimus; at Nicomedia, the commemoration of Felicissimus and Frontina.

IDES OF MARCH. In Cappadocia, the passion of Saint Longinus the martyr. Concerning him it is narrated in the little book of his martyrdom that, while at one time serving as a soldier under a Roman centurion, he pierced the Lord’s side with a lance on the cross during the Passion; and, seeing the earthquake and the signs that were taking place, he believed in Christ, repenting of his former deeds. Afterwards he became a monk and served Christ for thirty-four years, converting many to the faith of God. Finally he suffered martyrdom in Cappadocia under the governor Octavius; and after his martyrdom he restored the governor to sight, since he had been struck with bodily blindness by divine judgment on account of his unbelief.

[Col. 1135D] XVII KALENDS OF APRIL. The feast of Saint Cyriacus, who, after the long affliction of imprisonment which he endured under Maximian, together with his fellow deacon Sisinnius, Smaragdus, and Largus, performed many miracles. Among these, at the request of Diocletian, he freed Artemia, Diocletian’s daughter, from a demon and baptized her; and, sent there by Diocletian for this purpose, he likewise freed Jobia, the daughter of Sapor, king of the Persians, from a demon and baptized her, together with the king himself and four hundred and thirty others.

Returning to Rome after Diocletian’s death, he was seized with other Christians by his son Maximian [Note: See Baronius in the *Annals* to determine how these things can be reconciled.] and sent into custody because he had made his sister a Christian. Then Maximian ordered that on the day of his procession Cyriacus should be dragged naked and bound in chains before his chariot. After this he was brought out of prison with his companions Largus, Smaragdus, and Crescentianus by the deputy Carpasianus, and his head was covered with liquefied pitch. Four days later he was again brought from prison, stretched out on a rack and dragged, beaten with sinews and clubs; after [Perhaps two or three] days, by Maximian’s order, he was beheaded together with Largus, Smaragdus, and twenty others. Written in the Acts of Marcellus the pope. At that same time God killed Artemia, Maximian’s sister.

XVI KALENDS. In Scotland, the feast of Patrick the bishop, who first preached the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to the Scots on the island of Ireland; and the feast of Mary the martyr. She was also the slave of a certain Tertullus [Col. 1136B], a distinguished man, and, because she did not wish to attend her master’s banquets on the birthday of his son but preferred, in the Christian manner, to devote herself to fasting, she was savagely torn by whips by that same master.

When he could not thereby turn her from her steadfast service of Christ to the worship of idols, she was handed over to the public judge for punishment. While the executioners wished to consign her to the fire, a respite of three days was granted her because of the people’s prayers. When the three days had been completed and she was again to be punished, she was wondrously rescued by the Lord’s mercy.

For when she had poured out a prayer to the Lord, a great rock that had been before her split open through the middle and received her within itself; enclosing her on every side, it resisted the fury of her enemies. When the people rushed toward it and wished, according to the ruler’s order, to destroy the rock itself, lightning and thunder were sent from heaven, and many of them perished, so that two thousand seven hundred of them were destroyed by divine judgment. But the few who remained, converted to the Lord, continued in the Christian religion.

XV KALENDS. At Alexandria, the feast of Colesticus; at Nicomedia, of Aprilis and Servulus; in Lucania, of Quintus, Ingenuus, and Rogata; and in Mauretania, of Timothy.

XIV KALENDS. At the city of Spoleto, the nativity of John the confessor, who came there as a pilgrim from Sicily, built a monastery in its suburb, and lived there for fourteen years, where he also rested in peace.

XIII KALENDS. In Britain, of Saint Cuthbert the bishop [Col. 1136D], who, having led a life full of virtues, finally ended his last day as a hermit. His little body, taken from the grave after eleven years, was found intact, together with the clothing in which he had been dressed, as though it had been placed in the tomb that very day.

XII KALENDS. Of Saint Benedict the abbot, who wrote the Rule for monks with great discernment. On the same day, at Alexandria, the deposition of Serapion the monk.

XI KALENDS. At the city of Narbonne, the feast of Paul the confessor. In Africa, of Saturninus and nine others. At Sebaste, of Decronius and Arion.

X KALENDS. In Africa, the feast of Fidelis and twenty others.

[Col. 1137A] IX KALENDS. In Syria, the commemoration of Seleucus; and in Africa, of Agabus.

VIII KALENDS. The Annunciation of the Lord’s incarnation; and at Jerusalem our Lord Jesus Christ was crucified; and the passion of Saint James, the Lord’s brother, who, while testifying to Christ during the solemnity of Passover, was thrown from the pinnacle of the Temple by the Jews and struck with a fuller’s club.

At Nicomedia, the feast of Dula, a soldier’s slave-girl, who was killed for her chastity. And at Rome, of Quirinus, who was killed by Claudius and thrown into the Tiber, found on the island of Lycaonia, and buried in the cemetery of Pontianus. It is written in the Passion of Saint Valentine.

VII KALENDS. At Sirmium, of Montanus the presbyter and Maxima his wife. At Rome, on the Lavican Way, the feast of Saint Castulus [Col. 1137B], the martyr.

VI KALENDS. At Jerusalem, the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ.

V KALENDS. In Africa, the feast of Rogatus and Successus; at Caesarea of the Sea [Perhaps in Mauretania], the deposition of Saint Dagolaphus; and in Africa, of sixteen others.

IV KALENDS. In the city of Pisa, the feast of Saint Torpes the martyr, whom the emperor Nero ordered to worship the great Diana, mother of the gods. Refusing, filled with the Holy Spirit, he said:

“It is better to worship the one God who made heaven and earth and all that is in them than to honor many gods, that is, demons.”

As Saint Torpes was leaving the palace, thinking deeply within himself, he said: “What shall I do by serving idols and not receiving the baptism of salvation?” Then [Col. 1137C] he climbed a mountain and began to cry out, saying: “Father Antonius, where are you?” The presbyter Antonius answered and said: “And who are you, son?” Saint Torpes said: “I am your servant, Torpes.” Then Antonius baptized him in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

Immediately an angel of the Lord appeared to Saint Torpes and said to him: “Be strong in spirit, for you will be with us in paradise.”

Afterwards Nero went to Rome and ordered his kinsman Satellicus to take Saint Torpes into prison, beat him with blows, and tie him naked to the Column of Habentia. When Saint Torpes had completed his prayer, the column fell and crushed fifty of the impious; Satellicus himself also died beneath it.

Then Satellicus’s son, named Silvinus, while these things were happening, ordered that a lion [Col. 1137D] be released to devour him. It was suddenly released, roaring over him, and died at that very hour. A leopard was released in turn, but it bowed its head and licked his feet.

Then Silvinus ordered his attendants to lead him to the sea and behead him there. But Saint Torpes, placing his hope in the Lord, prayed: “Lord, receive my spirit.” Thus he was beheaded by the executioner. On the same day, the passion of Achacius.

III KALENDS. The feast at Philippopolis of the Lord, and of Jacaicus; and the deposition of Austasius the abbot and Nicaeus the bishop.

II KALENDS. In Africa, the feast of Anesius; the deposition of Ambrose the bishop; and the feast of seven virgins, whose names God knows.

## April

[Col. 1138A]

KALENDS OF APRIL. At Thessalonica, the feast of Agape and Chionia under Diocletian. They were first tormented in prison, then thrown into the fire; but, untouched by the flames, after pouring out a prayer to the Lord, they gave up their souls.

IV NONES OF APRIL. In Africa, of Amphianus, Victor, and fourteen others; and elsewhere, of Marcellinus, Saturninus, Quiriacus, Regina, Procula, and four others.

III NONES OF APRIL. The feast of Theodosia the virgin, who suffered in the time of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, in the city of Caesarea, under the prefect Urbanus. Having left her parents, she had fled to the prison where the confessors of Christ were confined. She was seized by soldiers and led before the tribunal of the judge Urbanus [Col. 1138B]. Standing before him, she was neither deceived by his flatteries nor frightened by his threats; rather, filled with the wisdom of God, she refuted the false gods of the pagans by disputing before the governor.

Therefore the tyrant had her bound with sinews and beaten with whips, but she could not be overcome. Afterwards various tortures were applied to her: fiery pans, lions, and wild beasts; yet she suffered no blemish from any of them. Then she was plunged into the sea, but by God’s aid she was quickly rescued from it. Finally, her head was cut off with a sword; she fell asleep in peace, completed her martyrdom, and was honorably given burial by Christians.

II NONES. At Milan, the deposition of blessed Ambrose the bishop and confessor, whose distinguished life and teaching are proclaimed in the Church.

[Col. 1138C] NONES. At Thessalonica, the nativity of Irene, who, after enduring imprisonment, was struck by an arrow amid her prayers by the count Sisinnius, under whom her sisters Agape and Chionia also suffered martyrdom. Although the aforesaid prefect had them thrown into the fire, they were unharmed by it and, praying to the Lord, gave up their spirits.

VIII IDES. At Sirmium, the feast of Irenaeus, bishop of that place.

VII IDES. At Alexandria, the feast of Peleusius the presbyter; and at Nicomedia, the nativity of Cyriacus with ten others.

VI IDES. In Africa, the feast of Januarius, Macaria, and Maxima; and at Carthage, of Concessa.

V IDES. At Sirmium, the nativity of seven virgins who deserved to be crowned as one.

IV IDES. Of Ezekiel the prophet.

III IDES. At Rome, of Leo the pope, who, forty-seventh after blessed Peter the apostle, occupied the episcopate for twenty-one years. He found [Perhaps overthrew] two heresies. Having sent a delegation to the Catholic emperor Marcian, a synod of two hundred and fifty-six bishops was convened at Chalcedon, in the martyrion of Saint Euphemia the martyr. There they set forth, according to the Catholic faith, two natures in the one Christ the Lord, namely, the divine and the human, and condemned the heretics Eutyches and Nestorius.

II IDES. At Rome, of Julius the pope and confessor, who, under Constantius the Arian, son of Constantine, endured tribulations and exiles for ten months; after Constantius’s death, he returned with great glory to his see. On the same day, in the city of Verona, the passion of Saint Zeno the martyr. Blessed Gregory reports concerning him in the books of the *Dialogues* that, when the river Athesis overflowed, it rose in the church where his body lay buried as high as the upper windows of the roof, but could not enter the church, where a crowd of the faithful had gathered.

IDES OF APRIL. In the city of Chalcedon, the nativity of Euphemia; and at Rome, in the cemetery, the translation of Januarius the martyr.

XVIII KALENDS OF MAY. At Rome, of Tiburtius, Valerian, and Maximus, under Almachius, prefect of the City. The first two were beaten with clubs and struck with the sword; the last was beaten with leaden weights until he gave up his spirit.

On the same day [Col. 1139B], at Nitria, of Fronto the monk, who led seventy monks with him into the desert so that, separated from human beings, they might devote themselves to divine contemplation. But while he was there, the monks themselves, at the devil’s instigation, murmured against their abbot because they could not live in the desert on account of hunger. Their abbot consoled them and promised them aid from the Lord, and so it came to pass.

For the Lord, through an angelic vision, rebuked a certain rich man because, while living in luxury, he did not provide food for his servants living in the desert. Since he did not know where they lived, after receiving advice he loaded seventy camels with provisions and released them to wherever the Lord might lead them. The camels, released by their master, went into the wilderness where the servants of God lived and carried sufficient provisions to them [Col. 1139C].

But Saint Fronto, seeing this and guarding against avarice, did not wish to accept everything; he took half. He placed the other half back on the camels and sent them to their master, and they returned safely to their own lord.

From that year until the end of Fronto’s life, the rich man himself sent food to the brothers at the appointed time, at the same season in which he had sent it [Perhaps earlier]. The Lord commanded other rich men likewise, and, supplied with food from all sources, the servants of God lacked nothing with Saint Fronto. They watched in the works of God, sons with their father. Bringing them to spiritual food, he daily filled them with heavenly speech; exulting, he rejoiced in the Lord, who had given him such understanding that he had sought out the places of the ancient wilderness.

[Col. 1139D] XVII KALENDS. In the city of Cordoba, the feast of Olympias and Maximus, noble persons who, by Decius’s order, were beaten with clubs and then with leaden weights; finally their heads were battered with axes until they gave up their spirits.

XVI KALENDS. In Achaia, in the city of Corinth, of Saints Callistus, Charisius, Leonidas, Christina, Calla, Theodora, and very many other saints.

XV KALENDS. At Antioch, the nativity of Peter the deacon and Hermogenes; and in Africa, of Fortunatus and Marcianus.

XIV KALENDS. The nativity of Eleutherius the bishop and martyr and Antia his mother. Eleutherius was ordained bishop at Aquileia and suffered under the emperor Hadrian. He first converted Felix and Corebus, his companions, to the faith of Christ; on Eleutherius’s account Corebus himself suffered, struck by the sword.

Eleutherius first overcame an iron bed, then a grating with fire beneath it, and afterwards a pan with boiling pitch and fat. Then he subdued wild beasts. Finally, he was beheaded together with Antia his mother, and thus completed his martyrdom.

[Col. 1140B] XIII KALENDS. In Africa, of Calasranus the abbot, Hermogenes, and Expeditius; and in Spain, at Caucoliberis, of Vincent.

XII KALENDS. At Rome, of Anicetus the pope and martyr, who established in the Church that the clergy should not grow their hair long; and he was buried in the cemetery of Callistus.

XI KALENDS. In Asia, the nativity of Maximinus the martyr, who in the time of the emperor Decius was brought before a proconsul named Optimus. When the proconsul compelled him by tortures to sacrifice to idols, and he refused, he was tortured for a long time on the rack and finally crushed with stones.

X KALENDS. At Rome, the deposition of Saint Gaius the pope, who, after ruling the Church for eleven years, four months, and twelve days, was crowned by martyrdom under the ruler Diocletian together with his brother Gabinus.

On the same day [Col. 1140C], in the city of Cordoba, the nativity of Parmenias, Helimena, and Chrysothelus, presbyters, and of Luke and Mucius, deacons, from Babylon. The first of these, even after his tongue had been cut out, continued to speak. All were hung on the rack and bound tightly; then, with burning plates placed around their sides, they were scorched and torn with claws, and finally slaughtered with the sword in the presence of the persecutor Decius. In the Passion of Laurence.

IX KALENDS OF MAY. The nativity of Saint George the martyr [Note: Various accounts are reported concerning Saint George, and they are so uncertain that one can scarcely place faith in them. Henschenius maintains that the commoner who tore up Diocletian’s edict concerning the persecution was Saint George, who suffered martyrdom at Nicomedia in April of the year 303. There you will find more about Alexandra, condemned by Diocletian himself; concerning her, not only Rabanus but also Baluzius speaks here. Those Acts are so full of fables and portentous narratives that it is entirely clear that nothing good or sound can be gathered from them. The single story of Alexandra surpasses all the inventions of the poets [Col. 1140D]; and in fact the man who tore up Diocletian’s edict suffered at the end of February. His passion therefore cannot be assigned to the twenty-third or twenty-fifth day of April. More about George is likewise read in Baronius under 23 April; but if you compare those accounts with the *Life of George, bishop of Alexandria*, you will readily notice that they were drawn from Arian writings. Rabanus and Notker speak of Datianus, not Diocletian; both had read the Acts of the passion. Notker adds that those writings were counted among the apocrypha of his time, a point Rabanus omitted. BASN.]

George, who under Dacianus, the most powerful king of the Persians, who ruled over seventy kings, became renowned through many miracles and converted very many to the faith of Christ; he also strengthened Alexandra, Dacianus’s wife, even unto martyrdom. Finally, he himself was beheaded and completed his martyrdom. I have read his Life and Passion written down [Col. 1140D].

VIII KALENDS. The deposition of Mellitus the bishop in Britain. On this day Ananias, Azarias, and Misael were delivered from the furnace of blazing fire.

VII KALENDS. The nativity of Saint Mark the evangelist at Alexandria [Col. 1141A]. After establishing and organizing churches throughout Libya, Marmarica, Ammoniaca, Pentapolis, Alexandria, and all Egypt, he was finally seized by the pagans who remained at Alexandria. When they saw him celebrating Mass on the holy day of Easter, VIII Kalends of May, they put a rope around his neck and dragged him to the places called Bucoli, which were beside the sea beneath the cliffs, where a church had been built. His flesh fell onto the ground and the rocks were stained with blood.

When evening came, they put him in prison. Around midnight he was first comforted by an angelic visitation; then the Lord himself appeared to him and called him to the heavenly kingdoms. In the morning, as he was being dragged again to the places called Bucoli, giving thanks and saying, “Lord, into your hands I commend [Col. 1141B] my spirit,” he died and was buried with glory by devout men in a place of hewn stone.

He had appointed Annianus as bishop for himself at Alexandria and had likewise provided bishops, presbyters, and deacons for other churches far and wide.

On the same day at Rome, the greater litany at Saint Peter’s.

The feast of Saint Maximus the martyr, who in the time of Decius was arrested in Asia and brought before the proconsul. The proconsul ordered him to be hung on the rack and tortured with various punishments if he would not sacrifice to the great Diana. Because he did not worship her, he ordered him to undergo the death sentence, that is, on VII Kalends of May.

VI KALENDS. The deposition of Saint Marcellinus the pope [Note: There were different opinions concerning Pope Marcellinus in the same century. Rabanus lists him among the saints, whereas Nicholas, Roman pontiff, confessed that he had lapsed into idolatry under Diocletian; the same is also read in the Roman Breviary. It is false that the Donatists did not allege Marcellinus’s lapse into idolatry. They certainly pressed Augustine on this point, since he declared Marcellinus innocent; yet the Donatists themselves acknowledged Melchiades as judge, although he ought to have sacrificed to the gods together with Marcellinus. From this you may conclude only that already in Augustine’s time various rumors concerning Marcellinus had been spread. Whatever the truth about the lapse, the Acts of the Council of Sinuessa, in which the matter is narrated, are spurious. There mention is made of a western pound, to indicate seventy-two witnesses; such an expression had not been in use except in the time of Constantine. BASN.]

After ruling the Church for nine years and four months, and in the time of Diocletian and Maximian, he was beheaded by Diocletian himself for the faith of Christ, together with Claudius, Quirinus, and Antoninus. After thirty-five days he was buried on the Salarian Way in a chamber by the presbyter Marcellus and the deacons, with hymns, on VI Kalends of May.

V KALENDS. The nativity of Anastasius the pope, who was the forty-first to occupy the see after blessed Peter. Finding Manichaeans in the city of Rome, he condemned them; and he established that no foreigner should be received into the clergy unless he presented a written document from five bishops.

IV KALENDS. Of Saint Vitalis, who was the father of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius. He had been a consular soldier and had entered Ravenna with his judge Paulinus. When he saw before his judge a Christian named Ursicinus, a physician by profession and a Ligurian by birth, receive the death sentence after severe tortures, he observed that the place where Christians were beheaded had the name “at the Palm,” because ancient palm trees were there.

Ursicinus, as we have said, was to be beheaded after severe tortures. When he came to the Palm, he was frightened; and, wishing to escape the evil, Vitalis cried out in a loud voice, saying:

“Do not, do not, Ursicinus the physician—you who were accustomed to cure others—wish to wound yourself with the dart of eternal death? You who have come to the contest through such great sufferings, do you wish to lose the crown prepared for you by the Lord?”

Hearing this, Ursicinus fell to his knees and urged the executioner to strike him. Repenting that he had been afraid, he made himself a martyr of Christ.

On the same day, the nativity of Saint Christopher the martyr.

III KALENDS. At Rome, the passion of Cletus the pope [Note: Cletus died in the year 91; but the persecution of Domitian, under whom he ought to have suffered, did not begin until the year 95, or, according to Toinard, the year 94. BASN.]. He was the third after Peter to hold the episcopate of the city of Rome for twelve years, and was crowned there by martyrdom under the emperor Domitian.

[Col. 1142B] II KALENDS. At Alexandria, the nativity of Aphrodisius the presbyter and thirty others. And at Rome, the deposition of Quirinus the bishop.

## May

KALENDS OF MAY. Of Jeremiah the prophet; and at Hierapolis [Note: See Baronius in the *Martyrology*.], of Philip the apostle, who extinguished the heresy of the Ebionites and rested in peace.

The passion of Saint James the apostle at Jerusalem. The scribes and Pharisees placed him upon the pinnacle of the Temple; but when they saw everyone rejoicing in his preaching, they threw him down from the height. He fell unharmed and continued preaching. Then an enraged Pharisee struck him forcefully on the head with a fuller’s club and scattered his brains.

And at Jerusalem, the passion of Saint Judas, also called Quiriacus the bishop, to whom the wood of the Lord’s cross was revealed.

On the same day, at Acaurium, the passion of Saint Sigismund the king.

VI NONES. Of our holy father Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria.

V NONES. At Jerusalem, the discovery of the holy cross by Queen Helena after the Lord’s Passion, in the year 233, while the emperor Constantine, Helena’s son, was reigning.

At Rome, of Alexander the pope, and Eventius and Theodulus, presbyters. The first, after bonds, prisons, the rack, rods, and fires, was killed by extremely numerous punctures throughout all his limbs. The others too, after enduring a long imprisonment, were tested by fire and finally beheaded by the judge Aurelianus in the time of the ruler Trajan.

On the same day [Col. 1142D], the deposition of Saint Philip the confessor.

IV NONES. The passion of Saint Florian the martyr in the time of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, while the most wicked governor Aquilinus was raging at Noricum Ripense. When he saw that he had been overcome by Florian, he ordered him to undergo the death sentence, to be led to the river Anisus, and there thrown from the bridge.

III NONES. At Arles, the deposition of Saint Hilary the bishop, who detected the Pelagian heresy among the collators and worked to correct it. At Auxerre, on the same day, the passion of Saint Juvianus, lector and martyr.

II NONES. The passion of the blessed martyrs Marianus and James and the others who suffered with them for the name of Christ. For by a revelation the Lord had shown them beforehand how they were to end their present life through the glory of martyrdom, as is contained in the account of their martyrdom.

NONES. At Nicomedia, the nativity of Flavius the bishop, Frodisius, Macrobius, and Augustine the bishop; and at Constantinople [Col. 1143B], of Achacius; at Autun, the deposition of blessed Placidus the presbyter.

VIII IDES. The nativity of Saint Victor the martyr in the city of Milan under the emperor Maximian. That emperor ordered blessed Victor, who was of Moorish descent and served as a soldier, to be tortured in many ways because of his faith in Christ and his confession: first, to be confined in prison, where he remained six days without food or drink; then he had him beaten with clubs and repeated blows of the scourge; afterwards his body was covered with molten lead.

But immediately an angel of the Lord appeared and made the lead as cold as water drawn from a spring; his body was not burned in any part. Finally, when he could in no way be turned to the worship of idols, but Victor, persevering in the faith of Christ, had victory everywhere, the aforesaid tyrant ordered his head to be cut off. When Saint Maternus the bishop heard what had happened, he gathered his body and buried it with honor in the aforesaid city.

VII IDES. At Axiopolis, the nativity of Quirillus, Gindeus, and Genonus; at Tarsus in Cilicia, of Aphrodisius; and at Rome, the feast of Saint Beatus the confessor.

### 8 May

**VI Idus.** Of the holy martyrs Falton, Pilion, and the others. At Rome, Calepodius, a priest from Siena, under the emperor Alexander. Alexander had him killed by Laodicius, his body dragged through the city, and thrown into the Tiber on the day [lacuna] of May. Fishermen who found it lifted it out and reported the matter to Bishop Callistus. He took the body, embalmed it with spices [Col. 1143D] and linen cloths, and buried it in his cemetery on the Via Aurelia, at the third milestone from the City, in the crypt of Vildemarus. Then the consul Palmachius was beheaded by Alexander, together with his wife and children and fifty-two other persons of both sexes; among them was the senator Simplicius, who had recently been baptized through the teaching of Pope Callistus and the priest Calepodius. This is written in the Passion of Saint Callistus the Pope.

On the same day, the feast of Gordianus the martyr, who suffered under the most impious emperor Julian. When the aforesaid tyrant had ordered Gordianus, his vicar, while he was still a pagan, to investigate the priest Januarius carefully, to see whether he could somehow turn him away from the faith of Christ, Saint Januarius instead won him for Christ and baptized him together with his wife Marina. When Julian heard what had happened, he ordered the judge Clementianus to punish Gordianus if he refused to sacrifice to idols. In anger he ordered the holy priest Januarius and blessed Gordianus to be condemned by public inscriptions, but commanded that his wife Marina be oppressed in the service of peasants at a certain estate called Aquae Salviae.

When Clementianus saw that Saint Gordianus could in no way be turned from the steadfastness of his faith, he ordered him first to be beaten with leaded scourges and then beheaded. When the Christians learned of this, they came in the silence of night and carried away the venerated body of Saint Gordianus the martyr. Coming to the road called the Latina, a little more or less one mile from the city of Rome [Col. 1144B], they placed him in a crypt on the sixth day before the Ides of May, where they had long before buried Saint Epimachus.

### 9 May

**V Idus.** The Passion of Saint Evellius the martyr. Seeing the passion of Saint Torpes the martyr and the miracles he performed, Evellius believed in Christ. Previously he had been a counsellor of the emperor Nero, observing how Christians were martyred.

### 10 May

**IV Idus.** Of our holy father Epiphanius, bishop of Cyprus; and at Rome, of Saint Pancratius, who, when he was fourteen years old, completed his martyrdom by beheading under Diocletian. On the same day, at Rome, the passion of the holy brothers Nereus and Achilleus.

### 11 May

**III Idus.** The feast of Saint Onesimus the confessor.

On that day the feast of Mary the martyr is also celebrated. She had been the slave-woman of a certain prominent man, Tertullus, but by the kindness of her mind surpassed her master’s nobility and showed herself free in Christ. When her mistress tried by tortures to force her to abandon the faith of Christ, she did not consent in any way. For this reason she was handed over to the governor to be tortured. Yet neither his threats nor his tortures could separate her from Christ. Finally she was brought upon a great rock to be beheaded. When the rock split open, Christ’s servant entered it; immediately the rock closed itself again and did not allow any of her persecutors to pursue Christ’s servant, but keeps her enclosed there until the day of judgment.

On the same day, at the town of Tongeren, the feast of Saint Servatius, bishop and confessor. When he governed the Church of Tongeren, at the time when the Huns were about to come into Gaul, he feared for the people entrusted to him, lest they be devastated by the Huns. He went to Rome to pray that, through the merits and intercession of the holy apostles, he might obtain protection for his people.

While he remained there in such distress for many days, fasting and praying earnestly, he is said to have received this answer from the apostle Peter:

> “Why do you trouble me, most holy man? For it has been entirely decreed in the Lord’s deliberation that the Huns will come into Gaul and devastate it with the greatest violence. Therefore now take my advice: hasten quickly, set your household in order, prepare your burial, and leave clean linen cloths. For you will soon depart from the body, and your eyes will not see the evils that the Huns will inflict in Gaul, as our Lord has said.”

Having received this answer, he returned to the Church entrusted to him and announced Saint Peter’s response to his people. After not many days, he ended his present life and departed for eternal rest. He was also buried at Tongeren. While his tomb stood in the open air, neither snow nor rain fell upon it until his successor, Saint Munulfus the bishop, built a large church in his honour.

### 12 May

**II Idus.** Of the holy father Pachomius, who was distinguished by works of apostolic grace and was the founder of the monasteries of Egypt. He wrote the Rules of the monasteries, which he had learned as an angel dictated them, [Col. 1145B] and also wrote concerning the season of Easter.

On that day, in Syria, the feast of Victor and Corona under the emperor Antoninus, with Sebastian as governor of Alexandria. Victor was a soldier from Cilicia. Sebastian ordered his fingers to be crushed and the skin torn from him. Then he ordered him to be thrown into a fiery furnace, where he remained for three days without being harmed. He was then ordered to drink poison, but he did not die; rather, he converted the poisoner to the faith. Next, it was ordered that the sinews of his body be removed, and then that boiling oil be poured upon his private parts. After this Sebastian ordered burning lamps to be applied to him while he was suspended by his sides. Then he ordered vinegar and lime to be mixed together and put into his mouth. His eyes were torn out; then he was hung head downward for three days, and while he was still breathing Sebastian ordered him to be flayed.

Corona, who was the wife of a certain soldier, then began to bless Saint Victor for the glory of his martyrdom. While she was doing this, she saw two crowns descend from heaven, one sent to Victor and the other to herself. When she declared this before all who were listening, she was seized by the governor. He ordered two palm trees to be bent toward one another and Corona to be tied to each tree with hempen ropes by her hands and feet. When the trees were released, Corona was torn into two parts. She was sixteen years old. Victor too was beheaded and earned the triumph of everlasting victory.

**Ides.** At Sirmium, Timothy and six virgins. In Sardinia, the feast of Simplicius the priest; and in the city of Filasiana, of Rosula.

### 16 May

**XVII Kalends of June.** In the city of Picenum, at Ausimum, the feast of Diocletianus and Florentinus. At Auxerre, the passion of Saint Peregrinus, the first bishop of that city. At Trecas, the burial of Fidolus, priest and confessor.

### 17 May

**XVI Kalends.** At Alexandria, the feast of Adrion, Victor, and Basilla.

### 18 May

**XV Kalends.** Of Hortasius and Serapion, priests, and of Mark the pope and Potamion.

### 19 May

**XIV Kalends.** Of Saint Pudentiana the virgin, who was the daughter of Pudens and the sister of the virgin Praxedis. The sisters Praxedis and Pudentiana divided all their resources between them, began selling all their property, and distributing it to the poor.

In the same place [Col. 1146A] where their father Pudens of blessed memory dedicated a church in my name, this arrangement was agreed upon between me and the consecrated servants of Christ, Praxedis and Potentiana [Pudentiana], his daughters: since they were driven by their desire and their intense fervour of faith, they should strive to construct a baptismal font in that same church for their entire household, which was pagan. Saint Pius consecrated this church with his own hand. There the whole household was baptized and later received its freedom. Saint Pudentiana departed to the Lord in the twelfth year of her life.

On the same day, the feast of the holy eunuchs Calocerius [Calocerus] and Parthenius, servants of the wife of the emperor Decius. One was superintendent of the bedchamber and the other chief secretary. Because they refused to sacrifice to idols, they were killed by Decius.

The burial of Lord Alcuin.

### 20 May

**XIII Kalends.** The passion of the holy martyrs Conon and his son [Note: [Col. 1145D] We have discussed those martyrs at length in the Ecclesiastical History. BASN.], in the city of Leonia in the province of Isauria, while the tyrant Aurelian was reigning under the governor Domitianus.

Saint Conon had a wife, but departed from her and remained chaste. He had a son, took him with him, and lived in solitude. He walked in the ways of Moses, rebuking the waves and performing God’s commandments.

There was a raging river near that place, which no one could cross from the nearby region because of the volume of water. When the people approached, they asked Saint Conon to cross it. Saint Conon rebuked the water, stopped it, and made a road through it. When Saint Conon went down to his monastery, he ordered the waters not to flow for a time. Afterwards, filling themselves with water, they overflowed greatly. When Saint Conon learned what had happened, he went to the river and ordered it to flow as its course had been, according to God’s mercy. Because of this, all who live there to this day rejoice in it; not only the waters but the whole land itself is subject to him.

What is written was fulfilled: “If you have faith like a mustard seed, say to this mountain: Move” (Matthew 17). He commands not only the waters but also the waves.

When the aforesaid Domitianus recognized the holy man’s power, he summoned him and his son and ordered them to be tortured on a grating placed over burning coals, with oil poured into the fire. But he could not overcome them, because God freed them from the fire. Afterwards he ordered a wooden hammer to be brought and commanded that their hands be crushed. But they persevered in the faith they had begun and, making their prayer, surrendered their spirit, departing to the heavenly kingdoms.

### 21 May

**XII Kalends.** In Mauritania, Timothy; at Ravenna, Martyria; and in the city of Auxerre, the burial of blessed Valens [Valentinus], priest and confessor.

### 22 May

**XI Kalends.** In Africa, Castus and Aemilius, who completed their passion by fire. Cyprian writes about them in his book *On the Lapsed*.

### 23 May

**X Kalends.** The passion of Saint Desiderius, bishop and martyr.

### 24 May

**IX Kalends.** In the Gallic city of Mammetum, the feast of the holy brothers and martyrs Rogatianus and Donatianus.

### 25 May

**VIII Kalends.** At Rome, Saint Urbanus, pope and confessor [martyr], whose teaching crowned many with martyrdom.

### 26 May

**VII Kalends.** In Britain, the burial of Augustine, the first bishop of the English.

On the same day, at Rome, the passion of Pope Marcellinus, who suffered during the reign of Diocletian, at a time when there was a great persecution, so that within thirty days seventeen thousand Christians of both sexes were crowned with martyrdom throughout the various provinces.

Because of this persecution, Marcellinus himself was led to sacrifice so that he might offer incense, and he did so. A few days later, moved to repentance, he was beheaded by Diocletian for the faith of Christ, together with Claudius, Cyrinus, and Antonius, and was crowned with martyrdom.

### 27 May

**VI Kalends.** In the city of Paris, the commemoration of Saint Germanus, bishop and confessor. He was born of noble parents. Although his mother, with malicious intent, wished to kill him, he was freed from the danger of death by divine aid. In childhood he was entrusted to holy men to be raised for the service of God and advanced in God’s grace.

Ordained priest by Bishop Nectarius, he was appointed worthy abbot at Saint Symphorianus. In that office he showed, by virtues and also by signs, that he was pleasing to God. Afterwards ordained bishop, he governed the Church of Paris nobly and benefited many, not only through teaching but also through the healing of the sick. Finally, perfected in every good work, he departed to the Lord at the age of eighty.

### 28 May

**V Kalends.** The burial of Pope John. Because he was orthodox and had been gloriously received at Constantinople by the orthodox emperor Justin, the Arian king Theodoric, when John was returning, held him in custody at Ravenna and brought him to death, together with other equally Catholic men, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June.

Saint Gregory mentions him in the book of the *Dialogues*. His body was transferred from Ravenna and buried in the basilica of the holy apostle Peter on the fifth day before the Kalends of June, during the consulship of Olybrius.

### 29 May

**IV Kalends.** At Trier, the burial of Maximinus, bishop and confessor.

On the same day, in the region of Anaunia near the city of Trent, the passion of the holy martyrs Sisinnius the deacon, Martyrius the lector, and Alexander the doorkeeper, who suffered under the consul Stilicho and earned the crown.

Saint Sisinnius was struck on the head with a trumpet and stabbed with axes. Martyrius was beaten with clubs. Alexander was tied by the feet and dragged while still alive, so that along the rocky paths he lost pieces of his quivering limbs until he reached the end of his life.

### 30 May

**III Kalends.** At Antioch, the holy martyrs Sicius [Sycius] and Palatinus, who suffered many tortures for the name of Christ.

### 31 May

**II Kalends.** At Rome, the commemoration of Petronilla the virgin, daughter of the holy apostle Peter. At the request of the faithful, the blessed apostle healed her of paralysis. But as soon as she had risen healed and fulfilled her ministry, he ordered her to return to her bed.

When she began to be perfected in the fear of God, she was not only herself saved but also restored health to many through her prayers. Because she was exceedingly beautiful, the count Flaccus came to her with soldiers to take her as his wife. Petronilla said to him:

> “You have come with armed soldiers to an unarmed girl. If you wish to have me as your wife, have honourable matrons come to me after three days, so that I may come with them to your house.”

The holy virgin therefore spent the allotted three days in fasting and prayer, keeping with her the holy virgin Felicula, her foster-sister, who was perfected in the fear of God.

On the third day Saint Nicomedes the priest came to her and celebrated the mysteries of Christ. As soon as the most holy virgin received the sacrament of Christ, she reclined upon her little bed and gave up her spirit.

On the same day, the most blessed martyrs Cantius, Cantianus, and Cantianilla were martyred under Diocletian, while our Lord Jesus Christ was reigning.

## June

### 1 June

**Kalends of June.** The dedication of the church of Saint Nicomedes the martyr; at Thessalonica, the feast of Octavus; and at Antioch, of Zosimus.

### 2 June

**IV Nones.** At Rome, Marcellinus the priest and Peter the exorcist. They instructed many in the faith while in prison, and after harsh bonds and many tortures were beheaded under the judge Serenus.

The man who beheaded them saw their souls, splendidly adorned, being carried by angels into heaven. He repented and, in his old age, was baptized under Pope Julius under the name Dorotheus.

On that day at Lyon, Saint Blandina with sixty-eight martyrs. From first light until evening, the torturers continually renewed her torments, but finally confessed themselves defeated. Even when struck with tortures a second time, she was not overcome. On the third day she was bound to a post, stretched out in the form of a cross, and prepared as food for wild beasts. When none of the beasts dared touch her, she was taken back to prison.

On the fourth day she was driven on by beatings, burned on grates, and subjected to many other torments. At last she was killed by the sword. Then the fifteen-year-old boy Ponticus was led through every kind of torture with her. Strengthened by her maternal exhortation, he completed his martyrdom before her.

Under the emperor Antoninus. Written in the *Ecclesiastical History*, Book V.

On the same day is the feast of Erasmus the martyr. He sought the desert on Mount Lebanon and remained there for seven years, performing many miracles. He was arrested by the emperor Diocletian because of the faith of Christ and suffered many torments. At the emperor’s command, the most wicked executioners beat him with clubs and leaded scourges; they poured over him boiling lead, pitch, sulphur, wax, and oil. Afterwards he was thrown into prison and weighed down with an iron burden, which by the Lord’s power was turned to ashes and did him no harm. He himself raised the dead and healed many infirm people.

Later, warned by an angel of the Lord, he went to Italy, where he suffered many torments from the emperor Maximian. At last, bearing the palm of martyrdom, he departed into eternal life.

Likewise, on this weekday of June, the feast of Boniface the martyr. He suffered for the name of Christ during the reigns of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian.

His mistress, named Aglaes, sent him from Rome—although he had committed adultery with her—to places where there was a very severe persecution of Christians, so that he might purchase and bring her the body of some saint. Obeying his mistress’s instructions, he went there. He was arrested among the Christians and, by order of the ruler, was first immersed in a boiling cauldron of pitch, but was not harmed at all. He was then struck by the executioner and, after winning the palm of martyrdom, was brought back to his mistress by his companions who had travelled with him.

She received him and buried him at Rome on the Via Latina. There she built a church and served the Lord earnestly.

### 3 June

**III Nones.** In Africa, Quirinus; in Tuscany, Laurentius and forty others. At Orléans, the burial of Saint Leofardus [Liphardus], priest.

### 4 June

**II Nones.** At Nineveh, Dinocus, Attalus, Camara, Fyrina, Julia, Saracia, and Cyprianus.

### 5 June

**Nones of June.** Boniface the archbishop, whose passion was completed by martyrdom among the Frisians [in Frisia], and his fellow bishop Eobanus, together with God’s servants Wintrungus, Walthere, Scirbaldus, Bosan, Hamundus, Aethelhere, Wancarus, Gundacarus, Willehere, and Hadavolfus.

### 6 June

**VIII Idus.** In Africa, Amantius and Lucius. At Alexandria, Andreas, Donatus, and Peregrinus. The burial of blessed Claudius, bishop.

### 7 June

**VII Idus.** In Gaul, at the city of Soissons, the burial of Saint Medardus, bishop and confessor, whose life, full of miracles, has been written. He was generous in almsgiving and distinguished by his virtues; he possessed the spirit of prophecy and governed the bishopric of Vermandois for fifteen years. Finally, departing for heaven, his body was transferred to the city of Soissons, where his tomb became renowned for many titles of virtue.

On the same day, the feast of Saint Nabor the confessor.

### 9 June

**V Idus.** At Rome, Primus and Felicianus, martyrs, who under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian suffered many tortures for the name of Christ.

The most wicked emperors handed them over to the governor Promotus for punishment. When he saw that they could in no way be turned from confessing Christ, he separated them from one another. First he ordered Felicianus, who was eighty years old [Col. 1150A], to be beaten with leaded scourges. Afterwards he sent him to prison and would not allow food or water to be given him. Then he similarly ordered Primus to be beaten with clubs.

After that he ordered the holy martyrs to be given to lions in the amphitheatre. They were not harmed by the lions in any way. When the crowds saw this, more than fifteen hundred believed in Christ. Finally the holy martyrs were beheaded by the aforesaid governor and buried in a suitable place by worshippers of Christ.

On the same day, the commemoration of Getulius the martyr, who suffered under the emperor Hadrian. Since he was a most devoted Christian and had performed many acts of almsgiving and good works, the emperor handed him over to his vicar Cerealis for punishment. Saint Getulius, however, converted him to the faith of Christ by sound preaching, as he also converted Amantius, Cerealis’s brother.

Saint Pope Sixtus baptized Cerealis and confirmed him in the faith. When the aforesaid emperor heard what had happened, he handed Saint Getulius over to his prefect Licinius, ordering him, together with his companions, to be thrown into a burning furnace if he refused to sacrifice to idols. When this was done, they were not harmed by the fire in any way.

### 10 June

**IV Idus.** In Africa, Aresius [Aresius], Rogatus, and twelve others. In Spain, Crispulus [Crispul­lus] and Restitutus. At Nicomedia, the feast of Saint Zacharias. At Auxerre, the burial of Censurius [Censurius], bishop.

### 11 June

**III Idus.** At Rome, of Pope Anacletus [Note: [Col. 1149D] Here Cletus is distinguished from Anacletus; Baronius does the same. Yet if one trusts the ancients, they were one and the same pontiff. Irenaeus, who knew those ancient matters more reliably than modern writers, lists Anacletus and omits Cletus. Indeed, Caius himself, a Roman priest, when listing thirteen successors from Peter to Victor, ought to have omitted either Cletus or Anacletus. There is no mention of Anacletus in the canon of the Mass. Whether he is distinguished from Cletus or made one and the same with him, neither encountered the persecution of Domitian. BASN.]. He was the first to build and arrange a memorial to blessed Peter, having been made a priest by blessed Peter. He was buried beside the body of the blessed apostle Peter and the apostle Barnabas.

### 12 June

**II Idus.** At Rome, on the Via Aurelia at the fifth milestone, the passion of the martyrs Basilides, Cyrinus, Nabor, and Nazarius. Hruocgangus, bishop of Metz, transferred Nabor and Nazarius, together with the martyr Gorgonius [Gorgonius], from Rome to Gaul with the permission of Pope Paul of Rome in the year 765 of the Lord’s Incarnation.

The aforesaid bishop placed Saint Gorgonius [Gorgonius] in the monastery called Gorze, Saint Nabor in the monastery called Novacella, and Saint Nazarius in the monastery called Lorsch, where signs and miracles in the healing of the sick and infirm frequently occur.

### 13 June

**Ides.** In Africa, Lucianus and Fortunatus.

On the same day, the commemoration of Saint Felicula the virgin. After the death of Saint Petronilla, the count Flaccus, who had wished to marry blessed Petronilla, wanted to take Felicula as his wife. When she refused, he handed her over to his vicar for imprisonment in a dark dungeon, where she remained for seven days without food or drink.

Afterwards he raised her onto the rack and ordered her to be tortured there until she gave up her spirit. He then threw her into a sewer. The priest Saint Nicomedes took her out [Col. 1151A] and buried her seven miles from the city of Rome.

When the aforesaid count heard this, he ordered the priest Nicomedes himself to be arrested and brought to sacrifice. When Nicomedes refused, he ordered him to be beaten with leaded scourges until he gave up his spirit. His body was thrown into the Tiber, but a cleric of that priest, Justus in name and deed, gathered his body and buried him beside the walls on the Via Nomentana.

### 14 June

**XVIII Kalends of July.** The prophet Elisha; and at the city of Soissons, the passion of the holy martyrs Valerius and Rufinus.

### 15 June

**XVII Kalends.** The commemoration of Saint Vitus the martyr, who performed many miracles under the emperors Diocletian and Antoninus (the latter is redundant in the source).

His father was named Hylas, a sacrilegious and impious man, who, at the command of the rulers, wished to turn him away from the worship of the true divinity. But the holy boy remained steadfast in confessing the true faith; he was twelve years old.

He suffered many torments for Christ together with his tutor Modestus and his nurse Crescentia. The persecutor sent them to prison and into a burning furnace with lead, resin, and pitch, but the fire did not harm them, nor could the lions harm them in any way. Finally, while resting beneath a tree beside the river called the Siler, they gave their souls back to the Lord.

### 16 June

**XVI Kalends.** Ferreolus the priest and Ferrutio the deacon, at the city of Besançon [Vesontion], who, under the judge Claudius, were stretched out on the torture frame and scourged, then shut up in prison. In the morning, with their tongues cut out, they preached the word of God. After this, thirty awls were driven into the hands, feet, and chest of each. Finally they were struck down with the sword.

At the city of Mainz, the passion of the holy bishop Aureus and his sister Justina, who were killed in a church by the Huns while they were devastating the aforesaid city.

### 17 June

**XV Kalends.** At the city of Orléans, Saint Avitus the priest, whose life shone with miracles. It is written that at his birth a light was sent down from heaven to show that he was holy.

Having become a monk, he sought solitude. There, after performing miracles, he became known to the people as a true servant of God. Afterwards he built a monastery there. He also raised a dead monk in the church by pouring out prayer to the Lord while the other brothers were weighed down by sleep.

Meanwhile, a certain man from the fortress of Tours, acting as an envoy for the salvation of his little people, approached Saint Avitus devoutly and begged him to allow his body to be buried there for the protection of that fortress. He promised in every way to build a fitting structure in his name.

Avitus replied that it was unworthy for a sinful man, entangled in many crimes, to be hidden beneath the roof of a temple; rather, for future judgment, his bones ought to be laid in a grave beneath the humble earth in open fields. He said to him:

> “Nevertheless, so that the desire of your hearts may obtain what it wishes, if you persist, I will not refuse to have a church built in God’s name. For it has been decreed by the Lord that my body be placed near the city of Orléans.”

When this holy man of God ended his temporal life, the people disputed among themselves over the burial of his body. The people of Orléans nevertheless prevailed and carried it away with them. King Hiltiberus of the Franks built a church over his tomb and adorned the sepulchre with precious metals.

### 18 June

**XIV Kalends.** At Rome, Mark and Marcellianus, martyrs, who in the time of Diocletian and Maximian were recalled from the vain enticements of women by Sebastian, the soldier of Christ, strengthened by sound doctrine, and suffered for the name of Christ.

On the same day, at Antioch, the passion of Marina the virgin is celebrated. She suffered many torments for the name of Christ under the prefect Olybrius: bonds, imprisonment, scourging, and the rack. The devil also tried to deceive and overthrow her, first in the form of a dragon and likewise in the form of an Ethiopian; but he was driven away and overcome by the sign of the holy cross. Finally she was beheaded by the aforesaid prefect and ended her life in sacred martyrdom.

### 19 June

**XIII Kalends.** At Milan, the holy Gervasius and Protasius. Ambrose found their tombs after the Lord revealed them, and their bodies were as intact as if they had been killed that very day. When they were being brought into the city, a man who had long been blind received his sight by touching the bier.

The holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius suffered under the governor Astasius [Astacius]. He ordered Gervasius to be struck with leaded scourges until he breathed out his spirit, and Protasius to be beheaded. Their father was Vitalis and their mother Valeria.

Paulinus, a consular official, ordered Saint Vitalis to be suspended on the rack and thrown into a well, and thus God consecrated Vitalis as a martyr. Valeria was seized by pagans and beaten by them for so long that after three days she departed to Christ.

At Rome, the commemoration of Ursicinus the martyr.

### 20 June

**XII Kalends.** The translation of Saint Zeno the martyr.

### 21 June

**XI Kalends.** At Mainz, the feast of Albanus the martyr. Under the emperor Theodosius, he travelled from the island of Namsia with Saint Theonestus and Ursus and came to Milan. From there, with the Lord’s help, he went on to Gaul, remaining in God’s service and ready for martyrdom for the name of the Saviour.

After blessed Ursus received martyrdom in the city of Augusta, Theonestus came to Mainz with Albanus. While Theonestus was preaching the word of God there, Albanus, his disciple, completed his martyrdom and was buried there beside the city.

### 22 June

**X Kalends.** James, son of Alphaeus, the apostle; and in Britain, Saint Albanus the martyr, who in the time of Diocletian was beheaded in the city of Verulamium after scourging and bitter tortures.

When he fell to the ground, the eyes of the man who struck him fell out at the same time. One of the soldiers also suffered with him because he refused to strike him when ordered to do so, terrified by the divine miracle: he had seen the blessed martyr, as he hastened toward the crown of martyrdom, make every intervening stream passable by prayer.

At the city of Nola, the feast of Paulinus, bishop and confessor, concerning whom Gregory relates an account in the book of the *Dialogues*.

### 23 June

**IX Kalends.** Saint Edildrytha [Edildruda], virgin and queen, in Britain. Her body, after being buried for sixteen years, was found incorrupt.

The vigil of Saint John the Baptist.

### 24 June

**VIII Kalends.** The birth of the Lord’s Forerunner; and at Ephesus, the falling-asleep of Saint John the apostle and evangelist.

At Rome, Fuscus and Lucea with twenty-two others. At the city of Autun, the burial of Saint Simplicius.

### 25 June

**VII Kalends.** At Thessalonica, Bigatus and Cantanius. At Rome, Lucia the virgin and Aceius the king.

### 26 June

**VI Kalends.** John and Paul at Rome. The first was superintendent and the second chief secretary of Constantina the virgin, daughter of Constantine. Later, under Julian, they earned martyrdom by beheading at the hands of Terentianus, commander of the camp, who afterwards became a Christian.

### 27 June

**V Kalends.** The discovery of the bodies of the holy martyrs Fuscianus, Victoricus, and Gentianus. They were revealed to Lupicinus, a priest of Amiens, who gathered the relics with Saint Honoratus, bishop of that same city, and placed them in a suitable location.

Although Hilder [Hildericus], king of the Franks, wished to transfer them to himself, he could not do so. Therefore a basilica was built in the same place, and he buried them there with honour.

On the same day, at the city of Ephesus, the feast is celebrated of the seven sleeping brothers: Maximianus, Malchus, Martianus [Martin­ianus], Dionysius, John, Serapion, and Constantine.

Fleeing the persecution of Decius, after many torments they escaped into a great cave on Mount Celeus and remained there in constant prayer. When the emperor Decius heard this, he ordered the mouth of the cave to be blocked so that they would die there.

The emperor Decius and that entire generation died, and other emperors reigned. After 372 years—that is, in the thirty-eighth year of the reign of Theodosius, son of the emperor Arcadius—when a heresy arose that wished to abolish hope in the faith and in the resurrection of the dead, the seven brothers, who had been resting in that cave until then, were raised from their very long sleep.

When they were brought before the people of that age, certain persons seized them because they had brought very ancient coins to the market to purchase food for themselves, as though they were possessors of many treasures. They were forced to hand over what their captors suspected they possessed.

After the truth became known, Bishop Marinus of Ephesus arrived and freed them from the hands of the violent men. They were presented to the emperor Theodosius as a testimony to the future resurrection. Then they returned again to their former place, where they will rest until the day of the universal judgment.

### 28 June

**IV Kalends.** Pope Leo, who was the forty-seventh to sit in the Roman see after the apostle Peter. He sat for twenty-one years, one month, and thirteen days. During his pontificate he established many useful doctrines and expelled harmful errors from the Church of God.

### 29 June

**III Kalends.** At Rome, the passion of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. Under the emperor Nero, they conquered Simon Magus and suffered for the name of Christ on one and the same day. By order of the aforesaid most wicked emperor, Peter was fastened to a cross and Paul was beheaded.

### 30 June

**II Kalends.** At Agrippina, Asclepius and Pamphilus; and at Limoges [Lemovicis], the burial of Saint Martial, bishop and confessor.

## July

### 1 July

**Kalends of July.** On Mount Hor, the burial of Aaron the priest.

On the same day, at Rome, the octave of Lucia the virgin and nun, with Auceius the king, her bridegroom; and the feast of Arelefus the confessor. Dedicated to God from childhood, he sought the monastic life. Saint Maximinus, bishop of Orléans, ordained him priest together with his companion Avitus. Desiring a solitary life, he built monasteries in various places and became renowned for many virtues before and after his death. His holiness benefited many people.

### 2 July

**IV Nones.** At Rome, Processus and Martinianus, who suffered in the time of the emperor Nero.

While the blessed apostles Peter and Paul were being held in custody by the prefect Paulinus, these two men saw the miracles performed by Christ’s apostles and were converted to the faith of Christ. They were baptized by the blessed apostle Peter.

When the aforesaid Paulinus wished to turn them from the true faith and could not, although he inflicted many tortures upon them, he finally ordered their heads to be cut off with the sword.

At Tours, the burial of Saint Monegunda the virgin.

### 3 July

**V Nones.** The translation of the apostle Thomas to Edessa. He had suffered in India.

### 4 July

**IV Nones.** In Gaul, at the city of Tours, the ordination to the episcopate, the translation of the body of Saint Martin, bishop and confessor, and the dedication of his basilica.

### 5 July

**III Nones.** In Sicily, the feast of Agathon and Tryphena [Tryphina]; and at Tomis, of Marinus, Theodotus, and Sodepha [Sedopha].

## Two days before the Nones

The prophet Isaiah, and the octave of the apostles. On the same day is the burial of the blessed confessor Goar, who was born in the province of Aquitaine during the reign of Hildebert, king of the Franks [Col. 1154D], and from infancy was a true worshiper of God. Later ordained priest there, he abandoned his homeland and parents and departed as a pilgrim from the world and a citizen of the heavenly homeland.
