Thus, coming into the province called Trigoria, adjoining the banks of the Rhine and belonging to the diocese of Trier, within the boundaries of Wasaliacum, he chose to serve God there in freedom. He was very hospitable and generous to the poor, and every day he served God diligently in sacred Masses and psalmody. He performed many miracles during his life: for example, by his command he made a hind stand still so that it might provide a certain weary man with a drink of milk. Thereafter he was summoned and came to Rusticus, bishop of Trier. There, unaware that it was a sunbeam shining through the window, he threw down his cloak upon it. When many had attributed this to magic, he was brought before the bishop and, at the bishop’s command, made a small boy—three days old—speak; the boy revealed who his father was, together with his mother. Thus the aforesaid bishop, exposed in his crime, received penance, while the holy man returned to his place and ended his life in peace.

### The Nones of July

In Alexandria, the commemoration of Parmenius, Heraclius [Eraclius], Elias, Apollonius, Anobus, and eighteen others.

### Eight days before the Ides

The commemoration of Procopius in Palestine. He was led from Scythopolis to Caesarea and, at the first confident answer of his reply, was beheaded by the angry judge Flavian [Col. 1155B]. In the district of Austria, at the fortress called Würzburg beside the river Main, the commemoration of the holy martyr Kilian and his two companions. Coming from Ireland, the island of the Scots, they preached the name of Christ in the places mentioned above; there, for confessing the truth, they were slaughtered by an unjust judge named Gozbert, and afterward it became clear through many signs that they were true martyrs of Christ.

### Seven days before the Ides

In the city of Tyre, the commemoration of the holy Anatolia and Audax under the emperor Decius. After Anatolia had healed many sick people, lunatics, and demoniacs in Picenum, she was taken, at the command of Festianus [Faustinianus], to the city of Tyre and afflicted with various kinds of punishments. Then she was shut up for an entire night with a serpent, but was not harmed at all. Indeed, she rescued even the very Marsian who had released the serpent—named Audax—from being devoured by his own serpent in the morning, and converted him to Christ and to martyrdom. After this, he himself was placed in custody for confessing the truth and, without delay, was crowned by a capital sentence.

The virgin herself, pierced through with a sword while standing with her hands extended in prayer—the sword entering through her right side and emerging through her left—suffered on the seventh day before the Ides of July, but was buried in the morning by the citizens of Tyre. Audax, however, because he was from the East, was carried away there by his wife and children.

On the same day, the seventh day before the Ides of July, the burial of our holy Father Ephrem, a most learned and deeply religious man.

On the same day in Egypt, the commemoration of Cyril, bishop. When the commander Lucius compelled him to sacrifice to idols, and he refused to consent, the commander ordered him to be placed amid a blazing fire. When all the wood had burned and only ashes remained, religious men came to collect his bones, but found him sitting upon the pavement with his hands extended toward heaven. Seeing the sign that the Lord had displayed in him, they marveled and were astonished that he had remained unharmed by the fire. Because of this, many believed in Christ. Later the aforesaid commander ordered him struck with a sword, and he, rejoicing, gave up his spirit when struck.

### Six days before the Ides

In Rome, the seven brothers, sons of the holy Felicity: Felix, Philip, Vitalis, Martial, Alexander, Silvanus [Silanus], and Januarius, under Publius, prefect of the City, in the time of the emperor Antoninus. Of these, Januarius, after scourging with rods and the torment of imprisonment, was killed with leaden clubs. Felix and Philip were slaughtered with cudgels. Silvanus was killed by being thrown down. Alexander, Vitalis, and Martial were punished by a capital sentence.

On the same day, the commemoration of Rufina and Secunda, two sisters. During the persecution of the emperors Valerian and Gallienus, because they refused to deny the faith of Christ and to lose their virginity, they were beheaded by the most wicked prefect Archilaus after the various tortures he inflicted upon them.

### Five days before the Ides

In Africa, the commemoration of Marianus, and the burial of Benedict, abbot, and Januarius. In the city of Nicopolis in Armenia, likewise Januarius and Pelagia. Subjected to torture, not only with hooks but also with a potsherd, their bodies endured the same suffering until the fourth day before the Ides [Col. 1156B].

### Four days before the Ides

In Aquileia, the commemoration of the holy Fortunatus and Armiger.

At Lyon in Gaul, the burial of Viventiolus, bishop.

### Three days before the Ides

In Antioch, the passion of Margaret, virgin. When the consul Olybrius wished to violate her and turn her away from the faith of Christ, he afflicted her with many tortures: he ordered her suspended on the rack and her flesh torn with the most severe hooks; afterward he sent her into a dark prison. There she overcame the devil’s temptations, when he appeared to her in the form of a dragon and an Ethiopian, and his deception could do her no harm. Finally she was beheaded by the sword of her persecutor and passed over into eternal life.

### Two days before the Ides [Col. 1156C]

Saint Phocas, bishop of Pontus. Under the emperor Trajan and the prefect Africanus, he overcame imprisonment, chains, iron, and even fire for Christ. His relics are kept in the basilica of the Apostles in the city of Vienne in Gaul.

At Lyon in Gaul, the commemoration of Justus, bishop and confessor.

### The Ides

Saint Cyricus and his mother at the Roman port; Eutropius, Zosima, and Bonosa, sisters; and ten infants. At Sirmium, Agrippinus, Secundus, Maximinus, Martial, and James, bishop.

### Seventeen days before the Kalends of August

At Ostia, the commemoration of Hilarinus. During the persecution of Julian, because he refused to sacrifice, he was beaten with clubs and received martyrdom.

### Sixteen days before the Kalends

At Carthage, the Scillitan martyrs: Speratus, Martial, Cithius, Vesturius [Nartalis, Cythinus, Beturius], Felix, Aquilinus, Lactantius, Januarius, Generosus, Vesta [Aquilus, Letarius, Januaria, Generosa, Bessia], Donata, and Secunda, under the prefect Saturninus [Saturnius]. After their first confession of Christ, they were sent into prison, fastened to a wooden stake, and beheaded with the sword in the morning.

### Fifteen days before the Kalends

At the city of Metz, the burial of the holy confessor Arnulf is celebrated. From childhood he was suited to the service of God. First he was raised among the king’s courtiers, namely by Gundulf, the sub-king and administrator of the palace. Yet his constant meditation was directed toward monasteries and holy places; he was generous in almsgiving and showed the greatest concern for the poor. Later he was ordained bishop of Metz. In that office he performed many miracles in the healing of the sick. When divine inspiration placed in his mind the desire for a solitary life, where he might devote himself continually to divine contemplation, he went into a secluded place and diligently labored in God’s service, until a heavenly calling brought him to eternal rest.

### Fourteen days before the Kalends

Our holy Father Arsenius, of whom it is reported in the Sayings of the Elders that, because of the abundance of his tears, he always kept a handkerchief in his hand or at his bosom.

### Thirteen days before the Kalends

In Africa, the commemoration of Lucianus, Peter, Amabilis, and Nunnina; and of Thebaida and Victor [Victurus]; and at Damascus, Sabinus [Savinius].

### Twelve days before the Kalends

The holy prophet Daniel.

At Rome, the virgin Praxedes, sister of Potentiana. In the time of the emperor Antoninus she supported many Christians from her own resources. When it became known to the emperor Antoninus that an assembly was being held at the title of Praxedes, he sent for and arrested the presbyter Symmetrius together with twenty-two others. He ordered them to be punished with the sword without interrogation at that same title. The blessed Praxedes gathered their bodies and buried them in the cemetery of Priscilla on the seventh day before the Kalends of July.

Then, overcome by grief, the blessed Praxedes groaned and prayed to the Lord that she might depart from this world. Her prayers and tears reached the Lord Jesus Christ. After the martyrdom and crown of those saints mentioned above, the consecrated virgin departed to the Lord on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August.

At the city of Tibur in Italy, the commemoration of Symphorosa with her seven sons: Crescentius, Julian, Nemesius, Primitivus, Justinus, Stacteus, and Eugenius. She suffered together with them under the emperor Hadrian. He ordered Symphorosa to be beaten with clubs and then suspended by her hair. When she could not be overcome in any way, he ordered her bound to a stone and thrown into a river. Her brother Eugenius, a leading member of the Tiburtine municipal council, gathered her body and buried it.

In the morning the emperor ordered seven stakes to be fixed in place and her sons stretched upon pulleys there. Crescentius was pierced through the throat, Lucianus through the chest, Nemesius through the heart, Primitivus through the navel; Justinus was stretched apart and cut through each joint and articulation of his body; Stacteus was fixed to the ground with innumerable spears until he died; and Eugenius was split open from the chest down to the lower parts.

On the following day the emperor Hadrian came to the shrine of Hercules and ordered their bodies all to be removed and thrown into a deep pit. After seven days, on the eighth day after their martyrdom, the devil seized the daughter of the emperor Hadrian. Coming to the place where the saints had been buried, the devil cried out through her mouth: “My lords, seven brother-martyrs of Christ, you are burning me, wretched woman.”

Hadrian himself was likewise seized by a demon and miserably ended his bodily life.

On the same day, in the city of Verona, the translation of Saint Zeno the martyr, whom the blessed Gregory mentions in the books of the *Dialogues*.

On the same day, the passion of Victor, bishop of Marseille. Under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian he was slaughtered by the governor Arterius [Col. 1158A] because of the faith of Christ, together with the soldiers Eleutherius, Felicianus, and Alexander. When the aforesaid bishop had been handed over to prison to be guarded by those soldiers, he was visited there by an angelic vision. The guards, seeing a brilliant light, fell at the knees of blessed Victor and begged him for healing. When the holy bishop had baptized them, and they persevered to the end in confessing the name of Christ, they were crowned with martyrdom. The bishop likewise was beheaded at the emperor’s command.

After the martyrdom of the saints had been completed, the emperor Maximian was severely tormented by demonic affliction. Amid his sufferings he began to cry out to the governor Arterius, saying: “Alas, wretched man that I am, I am struck and tormented by holy men! As I see, they now exclude us also from the light which we took away; the punishment we inflicted torments us; what we have received is greater than what we are proved to have inflicted.” He was tortured until the fourth day; on the fifth day he hanged himself. Already consumed by every foulness of decay and boiling with worms, he ended the evil course of his life by a fitting death.

### Eleven days before the Kalends

The Nativity of Mary Magdalene.

In Antioch, the commemoration of Cyril, bishop, and Andrew; and at Ancyra [Ancyro] in Galatia, the commemoration of Plato, whose deeds are recorded.

### Ten days before the Kalends

The burial of Saint Apollinaris, bishop, at Ravenna. Ordained at Rome by the apostle Peter, he was sent there. He also preached in Emilia, in the regions of Corinth, in Mysia, along the bank of the Danube [Col. 1158C], and in the regions of Thrace. In these places he was sent into exile; wherever he went, he performed innumerable miracles and endured sufferings.

He was beaten with excessive slaughter, then beaten for a long time with clubs, placed barefoot upon burning coals, beaten again, suspended on a rack and tortured, and his mouth was crushed with a stone. Then he was shut in a dreadful prison under a very heavy weight of iron and stretched upon a wooden frame, where, though neglected by human beings, he was publicly fed by an angel. Thereafter he was sent into exile in chains. There he was again beaten for a long time with clubs, and, after being bound again at Ravenna, was beaten and wounded by pagans. Once more he was sent into prison and beaten.

Thus he completed his martyrdom under Caesar Vespasian and the patrician Demosthenes. He governed the Church for twenty-eight years and four days.

### Nine days before the Kalends

In the city of Tyre, the commemoration of Saint Christina, virgin. Believing in the Son of God and serving his worship, she could not in any way be separated from it by her father Urbanus. Instead, she smashed his idols and scattered them, giving them to the poor. Because of this deed her father afflicted her with many tortures: he beat her with leaden clubs, likewise scourged her naked with rods, and had twelve men beat her with cudgels, tearing her flesh from her bones.

Afterward he ordered her burned with fire, but he did not prevail. Then he ordered her sunk into the sea with a stone tied around her neck, but she was delivered from it by the Lord’s help. When her father had been killed because of his crimes, she suffered many tortures under other judges, namely Dione and Julianus. But when her enemies had been killed by God’s judgment, she passed through martyrdom to Christ.

On the same day, the commemoration of Saint Victorinus. Hearing with his brother Severinus the voice of God in the Gospel saying to the rich man, “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything that you have and give to the poor,” and the rest (Matthew 10), both brothers abandoned the riches of the world. Distributing all they possessed to the poor, they chose an eremitical life and lived nobly there. Although Victorinus was for a time deceived by the devil, he nevertheless, by the Lord’s grace, remained victorious over the enemy and triumphed nobly, as is fully related in their *Life*.

### Eight days before the Kalends

The Nativity of the apostle James, son of Zebedee.

On the same day at Rome, the commemoration of Eutychianus [Eutycianus], pope and martyr. He decreed that only beans and grapes should be blessed among the fruits placed upon the altar. In his time he personally buried 341 martyrs in various places. He also decreed that whenever any of the faithful buried a martyr, the burial should in no way take place without a dalmatic and a purple colobium; this decree was then widely publicized.

On the same day, the passion of Saint Christopher the martyr, who was martyred in the city of Samos by King Dagnus. The king ordered him tortured with various punishments. But the holy man obtained from the Lord that many should believe in Christ through him, including the king himself. When the king lost an eye from the strike of an arrow, Christopher healed it after his passion with a drop of his blood, just as he had foretold to him, and converted him to the faith of Christ.

### Seven days before the Kalends [Col. 1159C]

At Laodicea in Phrygia, the commemoration of the holy Jovianus and Julianus.

### Six days before the Kalends

In Syria, Simeon the monk.

In the city of Nola in Campania, the commemoration of Felix; and elsewhere, of Julia and Jocunda.

In the city of Auxerre, the commemoration of Saint Etherius [Etherius], bishop.

### Five days before the Kalends

At Rome, Victor, pope and martyr. He decreed in the Church that, when necessity required it, wherever a person might be found—whether in a river, a spring, or the sea—provided the confession of Christian belief had been declared, any person coming from paganism might be baptized. He was buried beside the body of the blessed apostle Peter in the Vatican.

On the same day at Rome, the burial of Saint Innocent, pope. He issued regulations concerning the whole Church, the rules of monasteries, Jews, and pagans. He found many Cataphrygians, whom he sent into exile to a monastery. He also found the heretics Pelagius and Coelestinus and condemned them. He decreed that those born of a Christian [perhaps an addition: “must”] should be born again through baptism—that is, baptized—which Pelagius condemned.

### Four days before the Kalends

The burial of Saint Lupus, bishop of Troyes. He came with Germanus to Britain and served as a priest there for fifty-two years. In the time of King Attila, who was ravaging Gaul, he fortified Troyes by prayer while all the battles were being lost, as is sung in his hymn.

At Rome on the same day, the passion of Felix, pope and martyr. Felix declared Constantius, son of Constantine, a heretic, when he was rebaptized a second time by Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia [Col. 1160A]. At the command of that same Augustus Constantius, Felix was crowned with martyrdom and beheaded.

At Orléans, the burial of the blessed Prosper, bishop, a most learned and holy man.

On the same day, the passion of Simplicius [Simplicianus] and Faustinus, brothers, who were beheaded in the city of Rome for the faith of Christ under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian. Likewise their sister, named Beatrix, because she buried their bodies together with the presbyters Crispus and John, was strangled by the prefect Lucretius and gave up her spirit, having persevered to the end in confessing Christ. Lucretius, however, was seized by an unclean spirit and died at his own banquet.

### Three days before the Kalends

At Rome, Abdon and Sennen [Abdon and Sennen], sub-kings, who, while suffering imprisonment in Curnula, a city of the Persians, under Decius, were finally brought to Rome in chains, where they were tormented with various punishments. First they were beaten with leaden clubs and afterward killed with the sword.

At Auxerre, the burial of Ursus, bishop.

### Two days before the Kalends

In the African city of Sinnada, the commemoration of the holy Democritus, Secundus, Dionysius, and Thyrsus.

At Auxerre, the burial of Saint Germanus, bishop and confessor, who was renowned for many virtues, learning, and continence. Twice he defended the faith of the Britons against the Pelagian heresy.

At Vercelli, Eusebius, bishop, who suffered martyrdom when the Arians stirred up persecution under the emperor Constantius.

# August

### The Kalends of August

The seven holy Maccabean brothers with their mother, who suffered under King Antiochus.

At Rome, the dedication of the first church built and consecrated by the blessed Peter.

### Four days before the Nones

At Rome, Stephen, pope, who was crowned with martyrdom in the persecution of the emperor Valerian.

On the same day, the commemoration of Saint Theodora with her three sons, in the province of Bithynia, in the city of Nicaea, during the time of Diocletian and under the comes Leucadius. He bound her with iron and sent her with her sons to Nicetius, the governor of Bithynia. First he had her eldest son, Evodius, beaten with clubs because he boldly confessed Christ. Then he had her and all her sons consumed by fire. This is written in the passion of Saint Anastasia [Col. 1160D].

### Three days before the Nones

In Antioch, Saint Stephen the protomartyr. It is said that one of the stones with which he was struck in the arm is kept there, and that many healings are performed through it.

On the same day in Jerusalem, the discovery of the body of the same blessed Stephen the martyr and of the holy Gamaliel and Nicodemus.

### Two days before the Nones

Saint Justin, confessor of Christ. It is related of him in the passion of Xystus and Laurence that he converted many to the faith of Christ and also buried many holy martyrs.

### The Nones

In the city of Augsburg, the passion of Saint Afra the martyr, whose conversion, life, and passion are preserved in writing.

Elsewhere, the commemoration of the holy Florianus [Col. 1161A] and Philistina.

At the city of Châlons, the burial of Memmius [Memmius], bishop and confessor. It is written of him that, ordained bishop in the city of Rome by the blessed apostle Peter, he was sent to Gaul together with Saint Dionysius, Saint Sixtus, and Saint Eucharius to preach the word of God. He also performed many miracles and, finally ending his present life nobly, departed to eternal rest.

### Eight days before the Ides

At Rome, Saint Sixtus, bishop, and Felicissimus and Agapitus [Agapetus], deacons, who were beheaded under Decius. Four other deacons—Januarius, Magnus, Vincentius [Innocentius], and Stephen—were beheaded with him, as is recorded in the *Acts of the Pontiffs*.

### Seven days before the Ides

At Aricia, Donatus, bishop and martyr. As Gregory recalls in the book of the *Dialogues*, he restored by prayer the holy chalice that had been broken by pagans [Col. 1161B] during the Mass.

At Milan, the Nativity of Saint Faustinus.

### Six days before the Ides

Saint Cyriacus the martyr. Ordained deacon by the blessed Pope Marcellus together with his companion Sisinnius, he performed many miracles under the emperor Maximian and drove demons from possessed people. Finally, by order of Maximian, he was beheaded by Carpasianus, the deputy governor, together with twenty-one others.

### Five days before the Ides

At Rome, Saint Romanus, a soldier. Moved by the confession of Saint Laurence, he asked him to baptize him. Soon afterward, at the command of Decius, he was brought out, beaten with clubs, and beheaded.

In the city of Verona, the passion of the holy martyrs Firmus and Rusticus, who suffered during the reign of the emperor Maximian [Maximinian] and Anulinus, his counsellor.

### Four days before the Ides [Col. 1161C]

Saint Laurence under Decius. After numerous tortures—imprisonment, various beatings, and burning metal plates—he finally completed his martyrdom by being roasted upon an iron grating.

### Three days before the Ides

At Rome, the commemoration of Saint Susanna, virgin, daughter of the presbyter Gabinus and niece of Pope Caius [Gaius]. This virgin suffered under the emperor Diocletian because she refused to be joined in marriage to his son Maximus and chose to remain a virgin. Caius [Gaius], bishop, and Serena Augusta urged her to remain steadfast in the faith of Christ and in perpetual chastity.

For this reason Diocletian ordered her, after other tortures, to be struck in her own house, and thus she completed her martyrdom. The aforesaid Serena Augusta gathered the body of the holy virgin and wiped the blood she had shed in that same place with her own veil. She placed it in a silver chest in her palace, where she did not cease praying day and night at secret intervals. Serena herself adorned the body of Saint Susanna with linen cloths and spices and placed it beside the bodies of the saints in the cemetery of Alexander.

**Note:** [Col. 1161D] Bede has the same account; nevertheless Baluzius, in his notes on Lactantius, warns that this history completely collapses: first, it is false that Serena was an Augusta, since Diocletian had only one wife, named Prisca. Second, Rabanus is mistaken in believing that Diocletian had a son to whom he wished to marry Susanna and dedicate her to him; for the Augustus had no sons, but his daughter Valeria married Galerius. Finally, that Valeria outlived her husband and died a miserable death under Licinius. Nevertheless, on this subject see Aringhus, *Roma Subterranea*, book IV, chapter 79, who adds the following from a manuscript: “He placed her beside the bodies of the saints Chrysanthus and Daria on the Salarian Way, in a sand-pit near Saint Alexander, in the city of Teiguna, on the third day before the Ides of August.” Leo III restored the church of Susanna from its foundations. BASN.

On the same day, the passion of Saint Tiburtius the martyr. It is written in the passion of Saint Sebastian the martyr that, having been converted to the faith of Christ and baptized by the presbyter Polycarp, the blessed Sebastian received him from the baptismal font; Tiburtius then bravely resisted pagans and unbelievers. At the command of the governor Fabianus, he walked barefoot over burning coals and was not harmed at all. Thereafter, through the plotting of the apostate Torquatus, he was pierced with a sword by the aforesaid Fabianus and completed his martyrdom.

After this, Torquatus arranged for Castulus, the palace official and host of the saints, to be arrested. He was suspended three times and interrogated three times; persevering in confessing the Lord, he was thrown into a pit, and a mass of sand was poured over him. He too departed to Christ with the palm of martyrdom. When they had endured this bravely and had sung the Lord’s praise, the wicked judge ordered both of them to be struck through the sides with spears where they stood, and they departed through the glory of martyrdom to the starry kingdoms.

On the same day, the burial of the blessed Gaugericus, bishop, who was born in the fortress of Eposium. From his youth he devoted himself to meditation on the law of God and to psalmody. Later he was ordained bishop of the city of Cambrai by the blessed bishop of Reims. He became renowned for many virtues, especially in releasing prisoners who were held in jails. When he was unable to obtain their release from the governors who had sent them to prison, he earned their release from the Lord by pouring out his prayer. He also gave sight to the blind and healed the sick.

After he had happily completed thirty-three years in the episcopate, he departed to the Lord. Many signs of miracles made clear that these things occurred at his tomb [Col. 1162C].

### Two days before the Ides

In the Sicilian city of Catania, the commemoration of Euplius [Euplius], deacon. After being tortured for a very long time, he was beheaded by the consular governor Calvisianus during the reign of Diocletian and Maximian.

### The Ides

At Rome, Saint Hippolytus. During the time of Decius, he was bound by the feet to the necks of untamed horses and dragged through thorns and briars until he gave up his spirit. Also Concordia, his nurse, who was beaten with leaden clubs before him and suffered martyrdom, and nineteen others from his household, who were beheaded together.

On the same day, the commemoration at Rome of Saint Cassianus. When he refused to worship idols, his persecutor asked what profession he practiced. He replied that he taught children their letters. Immediately stripped of his clothing and bound with his hands behind his back, he was placed in the midst of them. The children, whom he had made hostile to himself by teaching, were given permission to kill him. As deeply as they had grieved while learning, so joyfully did they now take revenge: some struck him with writing tablets and boxwood rods [as in the manuscript], while others wounded him with writing-styles. The weaker their hands were, the more prolonged death made his martyrdom more grievous. The poet Prudentius wrote about him [Col. 1163A].

Also on the same day, at the city of Poitiers, the burial of Saint Radegund, queen; and in the province of Germany, of Saint Wigberht [Vuigberht], priest and confessor.

### Nineteen days before the Kalends of September

The commemoration of Saint Eusebius, priest and confessor. Under the Arian emperor Constantius, with the similarly heretical bishop Liberius plotting against him [Note: Col. 1163D], he completed his confession. For the aforesaid Constantius, with Liberius substituted in office, shut the presbyter Eusebius in a certain chamber of his house, which was only four feet wide. There he persevered constantly in prayer. After remaining confined for seven months, he fell asleep on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of September.

The presbyters Gregory and Orosius and his relatives gathered his body and buried it in a crypt beside the body of the blessed Sixtus, martyr and bishop, on the Appian Way in the cemetery of Callistus. There they also placed an inscription in his memory: “To Eusebius, man of God.”

At that time the emperor Constantius heard that the presbyters Gregory and Orosius were gathering the body of the presbyter Eusebius, and ordered Gregory to be shut alive in the same crypt. Then the presbyter Orosius secretly gathered the blessed Gregory, who was half alive, at night because of the Augustus Constantius; after he had breathed his last, Orosius buried him beside the body of the presbyter Saint Eusebius.

**Note:** [Col. 1163D] Who was this bishop Liberius? Was he the Roman pontiff who, under Constantius, forswore the orthodox faith? Baronius had the manuscript *Acts of Eusebius*, but did not clarify the matter. BAS.

### Eighteen days before the Kalends

The Assumption of Saint Mary.

At Nicomedia, the commemoration of the holy Strato, Philip, and Eutychianus, with their companions.

### Seventeen days before the Kalends

In Alexandria, the commemoration of the holy Orion, Aemilius, and Agnatus.

In Persia, the commemoration of Saint Thyrsus with his companions.

### Sixteen days before the Kalends

At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Mammes. During the reign of the tyrant Aurelian, when the persecution of Christians was at its height, he was ten years old. Leaving everything, he fled to a mountain with his flocks, which he pastured there, and lived on their milk. There divine visitation came upon him and foretold how he would suffer for the name of Christ.

When wild beasts came to him and he sat reading the Gospel every day, they moved about him with the greatest gentleness. Through their milk the servant of God helped both himself and other poor people with nourishment. When the governor Alexander heard that he lived communally among the beasts, he attributed it to magic. He summoned him and afflicted him with many tortures: he suspended and tortured him on the rack, sent him into a furnace of blazing fire, but the fire could not harm him at all.

Afterward he ordered him stoned, until, when the stones had been gathered and thrown upon the martyr of Christ, his body was almost completely covered. The persecutor, believing him dead, withdrew. But the Lord preserved his martyr unharmed and afterward, by a divine calling, summoned him to the heavenly kingdoms. Thus he gave up his soul in peace and departed to eternal rest.

### Fifteen days before the Kalends

The commemoration of Saint Agapetus the martyr. When he was a boy of fifteen, he suffered for the faith of Christ under King Antiochus. He was beaten with sinews and most savage scourges; smoke from a fire was applied to him, and boiling water was poured over his belly, but none of these things harmed him. Finally he was beheaded and thus completed his martyrdom.

### Fourteen days before the Kalends

The commemoration of Saint Magnus, or [rather, “also”] Saint Andrew the martyr with his companions, 2,597 in number.

### Thirteen days before the Kalends

The prophet Samuel.

In Alexandria, the commemoration of Dioscorus; elsewhere, the burial of Filibert, abbot.

In Lucania, the holy Valentinian and Leontius.

In the city of Sinnada, the commemoration of the holy Piricius, Arcius, Maximus the confessor, Pamphilus, and Colonus the confessor.

### Twelve days before the Kalends

In Spain, the Nativity of the holy Vincent and Julian.

In Sardinia, the commemoration of the holy Luxorius [Luxurius] and Trajan.

In the Minatian village of Gabalum, the commemoration of Saint Privatus the martyr.

### Eleven days before the Kalends

Saint Timothy. Coming from Antioch, he was received at Rome under Pope Miltiades and given lodging by Sylvester, who later became bishop. After preaching there for a whole year and several months and converting many to Christ, he was arrested by Tarquinius, prefect of the City. Tortured by a long imprisonment, and refusing to sacrifice to idols, he was beaten a third time and subjected to the most severe punishments. Finally he was beheaded and buried beside the blessed apostle Paul. This is written in the history of Saint Sylvester.

On the same day at Autun, the passion of Saint Symphorianus the martyr.

### Ten days before the Kalends

The passion of three brothers under the governor Lysias [Col. 1164C], in the province of Lycia, in the city of Aegeae: Claudius, Asterius, and Neon. The governor ordered them tortured one by one.

First, he ordered Claudius suspended on the rack, flames applied to his partly mutilated feet, and his sides burned with a very sharp potsherd and a burning candle. He likewise ordered his brother Asterius suspended on the rack and burning coals placed beneath his feet. He ordered the third brother, Neon, tortured by the neck, coals placed upon him, and his back beaten with sinews.

He ordered the women—Domnina [Donuina] and Theonilla—to be thrown to the ground, beaten with blows, their heads shaved, and then burned with coals. Finally he ordered their bodies enclosed in a sack and sunk in the sea.

### Nine days before the Kalends

The Nativity of the apostle Bartholomew, whose name is derived from the Syriac language and is interpreted as “son of the one who suspends the waters.” He preached in Lycaonia [“In Lycaonia”]. Finally, in the city of Albanum in Greater Armenia, he was flayed alive by barbarians and beheaded at the command of King Astyages. Thus he was committed to the earth on the ninth day before the Kalends of September.

### Eight days before the Kalends

The passion of Genesius the martyr under the emperor Diocletian. At first, while still a pagan, he practiced the profession of mime; afterward he became a confessor of Christ. He was tortured by his persecutors in many ways: beaten with clubs, suspended on the rack, burned with flames, and finally beheaded.

### Seven days before the Kalends [Col. 1165A]

The commemoration at Rome of Herenaeus [Irenaeus] and Abundius. During the Decian persecution, Valerian ordered them killed in a sewer because they had lifted the body of the blessed Concordia, which had been thrown into the sewer. Justinus the presbyter also lifted their bodies and buried them in a crypt beside the blessed Laurence.

### Six days before the Kalends

In the city of Arles in Gaul, the burial of Saint Caesarius, bishop.

At Autun, the burial of Saint Syagrius, bishop.

### Five days before the Kalends

In Africa, the burial of Saint Augustine, bishop. First transferred from his own city to Sardinia because of the barbarians, he was recently brought from there to Ticinum [Ticinum] by Luitprand, king of the Lombards, and honorably buried.

On the same day, the commemoration of Saint Hermes the martyr.

### Four days before the Kalends [Col. 1165B]

At Venosa, a city of Apulia, the commemoration of Felix, bishop of the city of Tubrozi; Januarius, priest; and Fortunatianus and Septiminus, lectors. During the reign of Diocletian, they were arrested in their own city by the procurator Magnellianus on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July. Thereafter, long tormented in many bonds and prisons, in Asia and in Sicily, they finally completed their course by execution with the sword.

The commemoration of Saint Sabina the martyr.

On the same day the beheading of Saint John the Baptist is celebrated. He was first buried in Samaria, but is now in Alexandria; moreover, his head was brought from Jerusalem to the Phoenician city of Emesa [Edessa].

### Three days before the Kalends

At Rome, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Felix and Audactus, of Gaudentia the virgin with her three companions, and the burial of Agilus, abbot.

### Two days before the Kalends [Col. 1165C]

At Trier, the burial of Saint Paulinus, bishop and confessor. Because of the Catholic faith he had been exiled by the emperor Constantius, son of Constantine, and there he came to rest.

# September
# September

**Kalends of September.** At Cenomanni, a city of Gaul: the feast of Victor [Victorius], bishop. For when Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, went to bury Leporius, the bishop of the aforesaid city, and had come to the town, he looked around and saw a man working in a vineyard. He was a cleric who had attained the office of subdeacon. It was revealed to the holy man of God that this man would succeed to the episcopal office. Saint Martin called him to himself and said to him: “Bless me, Lord Victor.” He replied: “You bless me, my lord, and blessed be your word.” Thus, by order of the holy man, he followed him. After summoning and gathering the people, Martin ordained him bishop; he baptized his son, named Victorinus, and took him with him to be nurtured for the service of God. After the death of his father, he also ordained him bishop of that same city.

**Fourth day before the Nones.** At Lyons in Gaul, the death of Justus, bishop and confessor. When he had been ordained bishop after the diaconate, he ruled for many years with such purity, modesty, piety, and patience, with such care for the poor and such observance of the divine commandments, that he surpassed even those magnificent and distinguished priests of the Lord in every grace of virtue. He presided over the Church of the Lord’s people with such great glory for his flock that, until his expulsion, the raging devil burned with envy. When a popular uprising was persecuting him, he went into exile after many tribulations and reached Egypt, accompanied only by a boy. There, among the anchorites, he led the strictest life and conducted himself nobly. Saint Antiochus, a priest of Lyons, moved by devoted duty, resolved to go to visit his bishop; and Saint Justus the bishop foretold to those who were with him that he would come to him. After some days, the holy man of God departed from this world. By divine providence he merited that his bones be transferred to his own see and honorably buried there.

[Col. 1166B] **Third day before the Nones.** In Alexandria, Aristippus, bishop; and in Syria, Antoninus, a boy of twenty years; and Ariston, bishop; and at Cauda, Vitalian.

**Second day before the Nones.** In the city of Chalon-sur-Saône, the feast of Saint Marcellus the martyr, who suffered under the emperor Antoninus through the governor Priscus. Because he refused to worship idols, he was tortured in many ways. Thus the holy martyr, strengthened in spirit by heavenly power, changed his punishments as he changed the places of the idols: his limbs were stretched on the rack and torn by the shriek of chains; he was burned by balls of fire [so the manuscript]; and, after his limbs had been disjointed by blows, the scorched elements of his body were joined together again. But the strongest athlete, holding within his heart the passion of his author, Jesus Christ, triumphed in a more glorious contest, and the novelty of the torments could not alter his ancient faith. [Col. 1166C] He always answered the questions of the wicked persecutor that it could in no way happen that one who had received the living God through his senses should worship senseless stones or the images of demons. When the most wicked governor perceived, amid the punishments, that he was made stronger by divine favor, he ordered him buried up to the waist—an unheard-of example of cruelty, and one more insane than the persecutor’s fury. But after remaining for three days in praise of Christ, almighty Lord and his God, with mouth and love, meanwhile committing his earthly limbs to the earth, he sent forth his holy spirit to heaven.

**Nones.** At the harbor of Rome, Taurinus and Herculanus; and in Alexandria, Nymphus and Saturninus; and the death of Blessed Ingenui, bishop; and in Campania, Quintus. In Gaul, in the city of Besançon, the feast of the holy martyrs [Col. 1166D] Ferreolus and Ferrutio.

**Eighth day before the Ides.** The prophet Zechariah. At Rome, on the Salarian Way, at the fiftieth milestone from the City, the feast of Saint Eleutherius, bishop. In the territory of Cappadocia, in the city of Ructa, the feast of Saint Cottidius, Eugenius, bishop, and his companions.

**Seventh day before the Ides.** The feast of Saint Chlodoald, confessor. In Campania, Innocentius; and at Benevento, Januarius, Festus, Acutus, and Saints Synotus and Desiderius. At Arles, a city of Gaul, the feast of Saint Augustalis, bishop. At Orléans, Saint Evortius, bishop and confessor, who after Desinianus merited the episcopate of that Church. He was also shown worthy, by divine providence, to receive the episcopate through the election of the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove, as is read in the Life written about him. He completed his days in a noble and holy manner of life and became renowned for miracles. Recognizing the day of his death by revelation, he chose Saint Anianus as his future successor, so that no dissension might arise among the people; and thus he passed to heavenly glory. In the city of Autun in Gaul, at a place called Alise, the feast of Saint Regina the martyr, whose Acts are preserved.

**Sixth day before the Ides.** The feast of the holy Mother of God. At Nicomedia, Saint Adrian the martyr with twenty-three others; and in the suburbs of the Church of Mainz, the feast of Saint Disibod, confessor.

**Fifth day before the Ides.** At Rome, Gorgonius the martyr, and Candidus, Quirinus, Domitianus, Eunoius, Sisinnius, Heraclius, Alexander, [Col. 1167B] John, Claudius, Athanasius, Valens, Elianus, Melicius, Ecdicius, Acacius, Jubianus, Elianus, Theodulus, Cyril, Flavius, Severianus, Valerius, Chudion, Sacerdos, Driscus, Evacius, Juvenalis, Philoctimon, Etius, Micallus, Lysimachus, Theophilus, Eutychius, Xanthius, Aggius, Leontius, Insitius, Gaius, Basilides. All these forty suffered together in the time of the emperor Licinius, the governor Agricolaus, and the general Lysias.

On the same day, in the Sabine territory, the passion of Jacinthus, deacon and martyr, is celebrated. He was handed over by the persecutor Luxurius to the governor Leontius. When Luxurius could not compel him to sacrifice to idols, he sent him into a fire, which was immediately extinguished. Then he sent him into water, but he was brought back unharmed to the shore. When Luxurius was later struck by a serpent, as the holy man had foretold him, he lay swollen on the road. For as the serpent passed near a tree, it fell onto his head between his neck and the collar of his tunic and thus entered into his belly. Nevertheless, that impious man ordered the governor Leontius to inflict the death sentence on the holy martyr. Thus the holy man departed to the Lord with the crown of martyrdom.

**Fourth day before the Ides.** At Rome, the death of Pope Hilary, through whom Victorius wrote the Paschal Order. On the same day, the death of Saint Salvius, bishop. Gregory, bishop of Tours, wrote about his holiness, relating that he had seen in a revelation a sword drawn by the divine voice hanging over the *regulum* [so the manuscript; sense uncertain], which King Chilperic had ordered to be built. The truth of the vision followed immediately. For twenty-two days later, the king’s sons died in that same house.

[Col. 1167D] **Third day before the Ides.** At Rome, Protus and Hyacinthus, who were eunuchs of Saint Eugenia the virgin. They came with her from the city of Rome to Alexandria and were received by Bishop Helenus, to whom their arrival had been revealed in a vision. They lived in a certain monastery among the monks in male clothing. Later, a malicious woman named Melanthia, suspecting that Eugenia, who lived in male clothing, was a man, desired to violate her. But when the secret was disclosed, it was discovered that Eugenia was not a man but a woman. Compelled by imperial order, she returned to Rome with her eunuchs. There, together with the virgin Basilla, the two eunuchs were killed by the sword at the command of Augustus Gallienus. Blessed Eugenia later suffered for the name of Christ, namely on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, and departed to the Lord with the crown of martyrdom.

**Second day before the Ides.** At Antioch, Timotheus; in Pamphylia [perhaps “Pampalia”], Syrus; in the city of Catana in Sicily, Euplus. At Lyons, the death of Blessed Sacerdos, bishop. In Gaul, in the city of Autun, the death of Blessed Evantius, bishop.

**Ides.** In Gaul, in the city of Tours, the death of Lidorus, bishop.

**Eighteenth day before the Kalends of October.** Saint Cornelius, bishop. First his mouth was beaten with lead-weighted clubs, and then he was beheaded together with twenty-one others of both sexes, and with Cerealis, a soldier, and his wife Sallustia, whom Cornelius had healed of an illness. He suffered under Decius. In his own time, Cornelius, at the request of a certain matron named Lucina, secretly removed at night the bodies of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul from the catacombs. Blessed Lucina received the body of Saint Paul first and placed it on her estate on the Ostian Way, beside the place where he had been beheaded. Blessed Cornelius, the bishop, received the body of Saint Peter and placed it near the place where he had been crucified, among the bodies of the saints, in the temple of Apollo on the Golden Mount. In the Vatican, in Nero’s palace, on the third day before the Kalends of July.

On the same day, the feast of Saint Cyprian, bishop, who under the emperor Valerian, after a long exile, completed his martyrdom by decapitation six miles from Carthage beside the sea. Also the death of Saint Maternus, bishop. On the same day is the Exaltation of the holy cross.

**Seventeenth day before the Kalends.** The passion of Nicomedes the martyr. On the same day, the feast of Saint Aper, bishop, and Leobinus, confessor. In Alexandria, the feast of Saint Serapion and Leontius; at Ancyra in Galatia, the feast of Seleucus, Valerius, and Cyrion; at Tomis, Strato and Macrobius; at Nuceria in Campania, Constans; at Ancyra, Paul, bishop; and in the territory of Chalon-sur-Saône, at the fort of Nortium, the feast of Saint Valerian the martyr. At Lyons in Gaul, the death of Albinus, bishop.

**Sixteenth day before the Kalends.** The feast of Saint Euphemia the virgin, who suffered martyrdom under the emperor Diocletian, with Priscus as proconsul, in the city of Chalcedon. She overcame, for Christ, tortures and prisons, beatings and the devices of wheels, fires and the weights of corner-stones, wild beasts and blows of rods, sharp saws and flaming frying pans, and again the bite of a beast. She was buried a thousand paces from the city of Chalcedon by her father, the senator Philosophron.

On the same day the passion of the martyrs Lucia and Geminianus is celebrated. They suffered under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian. Lucia had remained a widow for thirty-six years. All the years of her life were seventy-five, as is found written in the little book of her passion. She was betrayed to the emperors by her son Euprepius because she was a Christian. She was seized and placed in chains, but was delivered from the various punishments inflicted on her by the persecutor. For she turned the prison into a river; when subjected to beatings, she felt nothing; indeed, she turned the man who beat her to stone; she caused a temple of the gods, built of gems and gold, to collapse from its foundations; she overcame fire; and she changed pitch and lead into water. She could not be harmed by these punishments. Rather, she gained Geminianus as a companion in her suffering. With him she bravely preached the truth to the persecutors, and at last they were ordered by the governor Apophrasius to be beheaded. Thus they departed to the heavenly kingdom.

**Fifteenth day before the Kalends.** In Britain, Socrates and Stephen. In Gaul, near the city of Maastricht, in the village of Liudovico, the passion of Lambert, bishop, who had been devoted to God’s service from infancy. He lived among monks for seven years, leading a holy life. After Faramundus had been deposed from the episcopal see and expelled from the territory of Maastricht, the ranks of the clergy and the common people together petitioned the Lord with one loud voice that they might receive Lord Lambert as their pastor. With the consent of Pepin, then prince, they merited to bring him back to his own people. There he lived nobly for many years in the Church of God. But Dodo, a member of the household of the aforesaid prince Pepin, caused him to be killed by a most wicked plot. He himself departed to the Lord through an innocent death.

**Fourteenth day before the Kalends.** At Milan, the death of Eustorgius, bishop, and Satyrus. At Chalcedon, Trophimus; and at Nicomedia, Jocianus.

**Thirteenth day before the Kalends.** At Naples in Campania, the feast of the holy Januarius, bishop of the city of Benevento, with Sosius, deacon of the city of Misenum, and his deacon Festus, and his lector Desiderius. After chains and prisons, they were beheaded in the city of Pozzuoli under the emperor Diocletian and the judge Dracontius. As they were being led to death, Proculus, deacon of Pozzuoli, and two laymen, Eutyches and Acutius, saw them among the others and asked why just men were being ordered to be killed. When the judge saw that they were Christians, he ordered them to be beheaded with the others. Thus all seven were beheaded together. The Christians took their bodies away by night. The Neapolitans placed Januarius beside the city in the basilica of Misenum, and Sosius likewise in the basilica of Pozzuoli; Proculus, Eutyches, and Acutius beside the basilica of Saint Stephen; and the people of Benevento collected Festus and Desiderius.

[Note: [Col. 1169D] Here Rabanus omitted the portentous history of Eustace, and rightly so; Notker likewise. BASN.]

**Twelfth day before the Kalends.** At Cyzicus, the feast of the virgin Fausta and Evilasius under the emperor Maximian. Evilasius, who was chief of the palace, ordered her first to be shaved and handed over to dishonor, and then to be tortured and suspended. At that time a flash of lightning came from heaven and struck many of the attendants. Then he ordered chests to be brought; she was placed inside and fixed there, as though she were a piece of wood, and they tried to saw her in half. But the executioners could not injure her with their saws. Evilasius, astonished by this, began to believe in Christ. When this was reported to the emperor, he sent the prefect, who tortured Evilasius severely while he was suspended. He also ordered Fausta to be brought out of prison naked and without a *maforte* [so the manuscript], and her head to be bored through and nails driven into it. Later not only her head and face, but also her chest and her whole body down to the shins were filled with nails. After this he ordered a frying pan to be heated, but it cooled while she sang psalms. A voice from heaven intervened and called them, and thus they gave up their spirits. Fausta was thirteen years old, and Evilasius eighty.

**Eleventh day before the Kalends.** The feast of Saint Matthew the Evangelist in Ethiopia. While preaching the word of God there and converting many to the faith of Christ, he was finally attacked by a swordsman sent by King Hirtacus, who struck him with a sword and made him a martyr of Christ.

**Tenth day before the Kalends.** The holy martyrs of the Theban Legion: Mauritius, Candidus, Exsuperius; and Saint Emmeram, martyr.

**Ninth day before the Kalends.** The feast of Saint Sosius, deacon of the city of Misenum in Campania. He was thirty years old when, together with Blessed Januarius, bishop of Benevento, he received decapitation as a martyr in the time of the emperor Diocletian. Once, while he was reading in the church of Misenum in the presence of Bishop Januarius—for Januarius frequently visited him because of his holiness and wisdom—the same bishop suddenly saw a flame rising from Sosius’s head, which no one else saw, and declared that he would become a martyr. After not many days, the deacon was seized and sent to prison. When the bishop came to visit him with his own deacon Festus and his lector Desiderius, he too was seized with them, and all were killed together with three others.

On the same day, in the East, in the city of Iconium, the feast of Thecla, who, instructed by the apostle Paul in the confession of Christ, overcame fires and wild beasts. After many struggles and after teaching many people, she came to Seleucia and rested in peace.

Likewise on the same day at Rome, the passion of Pope Linus, who was the first after the apostles to hold the episcopal chair there. He held it for eleven years, seven months, and thirteen days.

**Eighth day before the Kalends.** The Conception of John the Baptist. At Autun, the feast of Andochius, priest, Thyrsus, deacon, and Felix, who, sent from the East by Saint Polycarp the bishop to teach Gaul under the emperor Aurelian, were crowned most gloriously. They were beaten with scourges, suspended all day at the end with their hands reversed, and thrown into a fire, but were not burned. At last their necks were struck with bars, while Symphorianus, then twenty years old and later himself a martyr, was always keeping vigils and prayers.

On the same day, the death of Solemnis, bishop, who had been devoted to God’s service from infancy and also became renowned for miracles. One day, as he was setting out on his journey, he encountered a man blind, deaf, and mute from birth. He embraced him, kissed him on the neck, and quickly restored him to health. When the bishop of the city of Chartres died, Solemnis was chosen for the episcopate; he accepted it unwillingly. When King Clovis, still a pagan, who at that time ruled the Franks, wished to go to war against the Goths, Solemnis armed him with the sign of the cross on his heart and breast. After obtaining victory over his enemies and returning home, Clovis was baptized with joyful grace, through the favor of divine power, together with Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims. With the same bishop, Solemnis brought forth as sons, regenerated in the Holy Spirit of adoption, three hundred and seventy noble lords at the sacred font. Thus this holy man of God, after serving three Olympiads in the episcopate, departed from this light to Christ.

At Rome, the feast of Priscilla and Liberius, bishop and confessor. At Lyons in Gaul, the death of Saint Lupus, bishop.

**Seventh day before the Kalends.** The feast of Saint Firminus the martyr. In Asia, the feast of Bardomianus, Eucarpius, and twenty-six others.

**Sixth day before the Kalends.** The holy martyrs Cyprian, bishop, and Justina. Under Diocletian, Justina suffered much for Christ. She also converted Cyprian himself to Christ, when he was a magician and tried to drive her mad by his magic. With him, now made a bishop and distinguished teacher, she suffered martyrdom under the emperor Claudius.

**Fifth day before the Kalends.** Cosmas and Damian, during the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian, with Lysias as governor, in the city of Aegeae. After enduring many tortures, chains, and prisons, and after divinely overcoming the sea, fires, the cross, stoning, and arrows, they were put to death by decapitation.

**Fourth day before the Kalends.** At Rome, Stacteus; in Africa, Martialis, Laurentius, and twenty others. At Auxerre, the death of Saint Alodius, bishop. In the Gallic city of Genua, the death of Salonius [Salomon], bishop. On the same day in Germany, the death of Leoba, virgin. Born on the island of Britain from the Saxon people, she nobly preserved her resolve of virginity after entering a monastery. Later she was summoned to Germany by Saint Boniface, archbishop [Col. 1171C] of the Church of Mainz, to instruct the servants of God in the German monasteries in the divine Scriptures. There she performed many miracles during her life; indeed, after her death, when she was buried in the Bochonia forest, that is, in the monastery of Fulda, in accordance with Saint Boniface’s decree, she manifested her holiness through no small number of miracles.

**Third day before the Kalends.** The dedication of the church of Saint Michael the Archangel on Mount Garganus. In the Thracian city of Heraclea, the feast of Eutychius Plautus. At Auxerre, the death of Fraternus, bishop.

**Second day before the Kalends.** At Bethlehem in Judea, the death of Jerome, priest, whose life and teaching are everywhere esteemed praiseworthy in the Churches of Christ—how he translated the divine books from Hebrew into Latin and expounded the prophetic books in an allegorical sense. When he had completed eighty-eight years of life, he left the present life and departed to eternal rest.

# October

**Kalends of October.** In Gaul, in the city of Auxerre, the death of Saint Germanus, bishop; in the city of Reims, of Remigius, bishop; in the city of Arras, of Blessed Vedastus, bishop; and at the monastery of Ghent, of Saint Bavo, bishop. The lives and deeds of all these men are preserved in writings full of miracles.

On the same day, the feast of Frontus [Fronton], bishop and confessor. Within the boundaries [variant: *terminis*] of the city of Petrocorica [variant: Petragorica, Périgueux], at a place called Linicasium, he received a blessed [variant: *felix*, “happy”] beginning of light. Thus, devoted to service and living among monks, he became renowned for many virtues and converted many to the faith of Christ. At last, after holy labors made famous by the signs of his virtues, he departed from present tribulation to eternal rest.

**Sixth day before the Nones of October.** In Gaul, the feast of Saint Leudegarius, bishop and confessor. At Nicomedia, Saint Eleutherius.

**Fifth day before the Nones.** Among the ancient Saxons, the feast of two priests named Hewald. They came with Bishop Willibrord and crossed into Germany to the Saxons. When they began preaching Christ there, they were seized by the pagans and killed. At night, much light appeared for a long time around their bodies and revealed where they were and what their merit was.

On the same day, the passion of Saint Leutgar, bishop of Autun, is celebrated. He became a martyr in the time of Christian kings—that is, of King Lothar, his brother Theodoric, and also Hiltricus—through the malicious conspiracy of Ebroin, who was mayor of the palace. He was afflicted with most cruel tortures and tormented by the gouging out of his eyes. At last he was killed by the sword. After his martyrdom, the Lord glorified his relics with many signs of miracles.

**Fourth day before the Nones.** In Egypt, Martius and Mauricianus. At Rome, Marcellus, bishop; and in Africa, Audactus. At Auxerre, the death of Marsus, priest.

**Third day before the Nones.** In Sicily, the feast of Eutychius and thirty others. In Gaul, in the city of Valence, the death of Blessed Apollinaris, bishop. In Gaul, in the city of Auxerre, the feast of the holy siblings Firinatus, deacon, and Flaviana, virgin consecrated to God.

**Second day before the Nones.** The death of Saint Mark, bishop; and in Apulia, Castus and Aemilius. In Gaul, in the city of Agen, the feast of Saint Faith the martyr. In the city of Auxerre, the death of Romanus, bishop.

**Nones of October.** The passion of the holy martyrs Sergius and Bacchus, who suffered for the name of Christ under the emperor Maximian. Sergius was first secretary and chief among the pagans, and a friend of the emperor. Blessed Bacchus was second secretary of the same pagan school. They suffered for the name of Christ under Antiochus the general, by order of the emperor Maximian. Bacchus, while stretched out and beaten with rawhide scourges, gave up his spirit. Sergius, after many tortures, was struck with the sword and thus departed to Christ.

**Eighth day before the Ides of October.** The feast of Reparata, virgin and martyr, who suffered in Caesarea, a city of Palestine, under the governor Decius. Because she refused to sacrifice to idols, a pot filled with boiling lead was first brought for her. Then her breasts were cut off, and burning lamps were applied to her. Afterward she was thrown into a furnace of blazing fire. Since she was harmed by none of these things, she was finally beheaded, and at once a white dove came forth from her neck. Christians took her body, embalmed it with spices, and buried it.

**Seventh day before the Ides.** At Paris, the passion of Dionysius, bishop and martyr, Eleutherius, priest, and Rusticus, deacon. They are reported to have been sent into Gaul by Pope Clement to preach the word of God and to have suffered martyrdom there.

[Note: [Col. 1173D] Rabanus seems to doubt whether Dionysius was sent into Gaul by Clement; the phrase “they are reported” indicates the doubt. In the ninth century this opinion was promoted and defended by Hilduin, Rabanus’s contemporary, but it had not yet prevailed. BASN.]

On the same day, the feast of Domninus the martyr, who was beheaded by order of the emperor Maximian himself because of his faith in Christ. After his martyrdom he performed many miracles in the healing of the sick and weak.

**Sixth day before the Ides.** In Britain, Paulinus, bishop of York.

**Fifth day before the Ides.** In Gaul, in the city of Tours, the death of Venantius, abbot and confessor.

**Fourth day before the Ides.** At Rome, the feast of Edistius; in Syria, of Eustace, priest, and Eucharistus, Burrus, and Bonatus; and in Campania, of Patria and Fortunata [so the manuscript].

**Third day before the Ides.** In Spain, the feast of Faustus, Marcus, and Adria; at Chalcedon, Marcellus; and in Alexandria, [Col. 1173B] Saint Anastasius, bishop.

**Second day before the Ides.** The feast of Saint Callistus, pope. During the persecution of the emperor Alexander, he was tortured for a long time in prison by hunger and beaten daily with clubs. He was strengthened and comforted in a vision by his priest Calepodius, who had previously completed his martyrdom. While Callistus was in the same prison, he healed a certain soldier named Privatus both of the pain and the foulness of his ulcers. When Alexander heard this, he had the soldier killed with lead-weighted clubs. He ordered Blessed Callistus to be thrown from a window of the house, sunk into a well with a stone tied to his neck, and covered with rubble. Fourteen days later, his priest Asterius came at night with clerics, lifted the body, and buried it in the cemetery of Calepodius.

On the second day before the Ides of October, in the city of Córdoba, Saint Lupus and Aurelia. At Lyons in Gaul, the translation of the body of Justus, bishop and confessor.

**Ides.** In Gaul, at Cologne in the Agrippine territory, the feast of the Mauri; at Capua, Libulus; and of Saint Fortunata in her homeland [perhaps “the empress”].

**Seventeenth day before the Kalends of November.** The death of Saint Gallus, confessor. In Asia, the feast of Cereas and two hundred and seventy others.

**Sixteenth day before the Kalends.** At Nicomedia, Alexander. In Mauretania, Ninus, Victurius, Nobilitanus, Maurianus, Lucius, Mittinus, and Crescentianus.

**Fifteenth day before the Kalends.** Saint Luke the Evangelist, who was a Syrian from Antioch, a physician by profession, and a disciple of the apostles. He later followed Paul until his confession, serving the Lord without blame. He never had a wife or children. At the age of seventy-four, he died in Bithynia, full of the Holy Spirit.

At Rome, Saint Tryphonia, wife of Caesar Decius. After her husband had been divinely punished following the killing of the blessed Xystus and Laurence, she asked to be baptized together with Decius’s daughter Cyrilla by the priest Justin. She died the following day and was buried in a crypt beside Saint Hippolytus.

**Fourteenth day before the Kalends.** The feast of Saint Pelagia. At first she had followed the pagan way of life and practiced prostitution, devoted to worldly allurements. Later, through the grace of God and the teaching of Saint Nonnus, bishop, she was converted to the faith of Christ and baptized by that same bishop. She distributed all her property and possessions to the poor. Wearing sackcloth and dressed in a cheap garment, she went into exile and at Jerusalem led a monastic life in male clothing. She had built a small cell for herself on the Mount of Olives, where the Lord ascended into heaven. There she ended her present life and happily departed to eternal life.

**Thirteenth day before the Kalends.** The feast of Simplicius. His chastity and life, confirmed by miracles, became the cause of the salvation of many, so that a multitude of three thousand people was received into the bosom of Mother Church and washed in the font of life.

[Col. 1174B] **Twelfth day before the Kalends.** Saint Hilarion, our father, whose Life Jerome wrote, full of virtues. On the same day, the feast of Saint Asterius, priest of Callistus. After he had raised Callistus’s body from the well and buried it, the emperor Alexander heard of this three days later and ordered him thrown from a bridge. His body was found and buried by certain Christians in the same city. This is written in the passion of Pope Callistus.

**Eleventh day before the Kalends.** In the province of Thrace and in the city of Adrianople, the passion of Philip, bishop, Severus, priest, and Hermes, deacon. When persecution was raging, they opposed the emperor’s order, enforced by wicked governors, to close and plunder the churches of the Christians. For this reason they were subjected by the governor Passus, and also by Justinus, to many tortures: prisons, chains, and scourges, and finally the burning of fire. Strengthened by the Lord’s power, they persevered to the end in confessing his name.

**Tenth day before the Kalends.** Venantius, abbot, who, despising the luxury of the world and carnal marriage, chose the monastic life, by which he might serve God alone. Once, while serving as abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin, he returned on Sunday after completing his prayer. Supported on a staff, he stood motionless in the middle of the confessors’ courtyard, with ears and eyes raised intently toward heaven for a very long time. Then, moved from the spot, he began to utter groans and draw out long sighs. When his companions asked him what this was, or whether he had seen something divine and would tell them about it, he replied:

“Woe to us, idle and sluggish men! Behold, the solemn celebrations of the Mass are already being completed in heaven, while we sluggish men have not even begun the sacrament of this ministry. Truly, I tell you, I heard the voices of angels in heaven proclaiming ‘Holy’ in praise of the Lord.”

No sooner had he said this than he began to celebrate the solemn Mass in the monastery. Nor will I omit the following. Once, as he was returning, as we said above, from the basilicas that he had visited for the sake of prayer, the words of the Lord’s Prayer were being sung in a basilica during Mass. When they said, “Deliver us from evil,” he heard a voice from the tomb of someone saying the same words: “Deliver us from evil.” This is judged not to have been without the merit of perfection, that he had deserved to hear such a thing. Later he performed many miracles, endowed with the grace of great virtues. When the course of his present life had been completed, he departed from this world to receive eternal life.

**Ninth day before the Kalends.** At Nicomedia, the feast of Severus and Dorotheus. At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Longinus.

**Eighth day before the Kalends.** The passion of the martyrs of Christ, Chrysanthus and Daria, who preserved perpetual chastity under the appearance of marriage. Chrysanthus converted Daria from the error of paganism and magical superstition to the faith of Christ. Thus, amid various tortures which the tribune Claudius first inflicted on them under the emperor Numerian [Note: [Col. 1175D] Something seems to be missing], he was converted to the faith of Christ through the power of God and the prayers of the saints. He also merited becoming a martyr of Christ together with his wife and children. Later they were handed over by a certain Celerianus to prison and punishments and finally submerged in a deep pit; thus they sent their holy souls to the heavenly kingdoms.

Likewise on the same day, Crispin and Crispinian became martyrs of Christ in the city of Soissons under the emperors Maximian and Diocletian, through the tyrant Rictiovarus. The same Rictiovarus ordered the glorious martyrs, stretched out on the racks, to be beaten with clubs. Then he ordered stakes to be driven into their nails and individual thongs to be taken from their backs, but by divine assistance they were freed from this punishment. Then Rictiovarus, raging madly, ordered millstones to be hung around each of their necks and them to be submerged in the river Axona during winter, as though beneath the ice. But, protected by the shield of divine power, they joyfully said:

“Beside the water of refreshment you will lead us, O Lord” (Psalm XXII).

But while creation served its God, neither water could drown the martyrs, nor a stone weigh them down, nor cold constrict them. Rather, as though delighted by summer baths, they cast off the millstone burden, swam to the opposite bank of the river, and reached it unharmed.

When Rictiovarus saw this miracle, he was driven by anger at the instigation of the devil. He ordered them to be bound again and lead to be poured into the fire and melted, intending to submerge the holy martyrs in it and destroy them. But because the invincible right hand of Christ protected them, the fire returned them unharmed. As these things were happening, a drop of boiling lead leapt into Rictiovarus’s eye, tormented him with severe pain, and blinded him. Yet, raging and possessed by madness, instead of seeking healing for body and soul, he hastened his own death in his insanity. For he ordered pitch, fat, and oil to be boiled together and the holy martyrs to be thrown into it again, as though they were to be consumed by the punishment.

When the attendants had obeyed and completed everything that the impious man had ordered, the holy martyrs, steadfastly relying on their hope, confidently said to God in prayer:

“You are powerful, O Lord our God, to free us from the tortures inflicted by the wicked one. And just as you willed us to suffer through confessing your holy name, so also, to the confusion of the devil and his servants, you are able to bring us unharmed from this punishment as well.”

As soon as the prayer ended, the angel of the Lord brought them out of the fire without pain. Then, seeing that he had prevailed over nothing against Christ’s martyrs through all the punishments he had inflicted, Rictiovarus, raging furiously, threw himself into the fire and thus ended his unworthy life by a most evil death. When Maximian soon heard of the destruction of his servant Rictiovarus, he ordered both Crispin and Crispinian to be punished by the sword. With the sword already threatening their necks, they gave thanks to the Lord and ended their present life by a blessed death.

On that same day at Rome, on the Salarian Way, forty-six soldiers who were baptized together by Pope Dionysius and immediately afterward beheaded by order of the emperor Claudius. There are also one hundred and twenty-one other martyrs there, among whom were four soldiers of Christ: Theodosius, Lucius, Marcus, and Peter. Written in the passion of Saint Xystus.

**Seventh day before the Kalends.** At Nicomedia, the feast of Lucian, Florius, Heraclides, and Martianus.

**Sixth day before the Kalends.** The vigil of the apostles Simon and Thaddeus. In Sardinia, the feast of Protus and Januarius; and in Phrygia, of Eumenes and Conon, Diodorus and Metrobius.

**Fifth day before the Kalends.** The vigil of the apostles Simon and Thaddeus. At Rome, Saint Cyrilla, daughter of Caesar Decius, who under the emperor Claudius was slaughtered and killed by the sword and buried by the priest Justin together with her mother beside Saint Hippolytus.

**Fourth day before the Kalends.** In Lucania, Saint Hyacinthus, Quintus, Felicianus, and Lucius.

**Third day before the Kalends.** At Rome, the feast of Saint Pontianus, pope and martyr, who was deported by the emperor Alexander, together with the priest Hippolytus, into exile on the island of Sardinia, where he died.

## Two days before the Kalends

In Gaul, Saint Quintinus, who suffered martyrdom under the emperor Maximian; after fifty-two years his body was discovered, as an angel revealed it, and buried on the eighth day before the Kalends of July.

## November

### Kalends of November

At the fortress of Dijon, the feast of Benignus the presbyter, who was sent from the East into Gaul by Saint Polycarp, bishop, in the time of Aurelian, together with Andochius, his fellow presbyter, and Thyrsus, the deacon. When Aurelian learned of his preaching, he ordered him to be bound, beaten, and brought before him. Having heard the steadfastness of his words, he ordered him to be beaten with very hard sinews and handed him over to Terentius the count for punishment. Terentius had him stretched on a rack and beaten, then again committed him to prison. In the morning he destroyed the idols by praying, and was brought back to prison. There they drove ten heated awls into his hands, and fastened his feet with molten lead into a pierced stone. They shut twelve savage dogs in with him for six days. An angel brought him heavenly bread, removed the awls, and freed him from the lead and iron.

After this, it was ordered that his neck be beaten with an iron bar and his body pierced with a spear. When this had been done, a snow-white dove ascended from the prison into heaven before the eyes of the Christians, and an exceedingly sweet fragrance, like that of paradise, followed. When Aurelian had departed from the place, Leonilla arrived and buried his body, embalmed with spices, not far from the prison itself.

On the same day, the feast of Saint Caesarius the deacon and Julian the presbyter. Caesarius, coming from Africa to Terracina, a city of Campania, in the time of the emperor Claudius, was arrested by Firmin the pontiff while publicly denouncing the idolaters, and was confined in custody. After being tormented there for many days, he was handed over to Leontius, the governor of Campania. Since Leontius could not overcome him with words, he ordered him, bound with his hands tied and naked, to be dragged before his own cart as far as the temple of Apollo. When they arrived there, the temple collapsed at his prayer and killed Firmin the pontiff. After this he was confined in prison by Luxorius, the city’s first magistrate, and remained there for one year and one month.

Then, when he was brought out into the forum, he was surrounded by heavenly light from God while he prayed, so that Leontius himself believed, clothed the naked Caesarius in his own military cloak, and was baptized. He received the body and blood of the Lord from the hand of Julian the presbyter. Immediately afterward, when the prayer had been said over him, he gave up his spirit on the third day before the Kalends of November. Then Luxorius ordered Julian and Caesarius to be put into a sack and thrown into the sea. On that same day they were cast back onto the shore and buried by Eusebius, the servant of God, near the city of Terracina. The same Eusebius later suffered martyrdom together with Felix the presbyter.

On the same day, the burial of Severinus, a monk from the city of Tibur.

On this very day the commemoration of all the saints is celebrated. Pope Boniface established it: with the permission of Caesar Phocas, he dedicated the ancient shrine, which the ancients called the Pantheon, in honor of the holy Virgin Mary and all the saints.

Likewise, on this day, in the monastery of Fulda, the dedication of the church of Saint Boniface and the translation of the body of that same holy martyr.

### Four days before the Nones

In Africa, the feast of Publius, Victor, Hermes, Justus, and Papias.

### Three days before the Nones

In Caesarea of Cappadocia, the feast of Germanus, Domninus, Theophilus, Vitalis, Justus, and Eremitis.

On the same day, the burial of Saint Permenius [Firminus], the confessor.

### Two days before the Nones

At Augustodunum, the burial of Blessed Proculus, bishop.

At Ruthenis [Ruthenis], in Gaul, the feast of Saint Amantius, bishop.

In Gaul, at Bourges [near Bourges], the burial of Saint Inlusor, a boy and confessor; and at Nicaea, of Domninus.

In Africa, the feast of Primus, Caesarius, Gregory, Porsirius, Amantius, Saturninus, Victorina, and Perpetua.

### Nones of November

At Terracina, a city of Campania, the feast of the holy Felix the presbyter and Eusebius the monk, in the time of the emperor Claudius. Eusebius had buried the holy martyrs Julian and Caesarius, and by praying and fasting at their tombs had converted many to the faith; Felix the presbyter baptized them. Both were arrested by Leontius, the son of Leontius the governor, chiefly because Caesarius had made his father a Christian. They were brought into the forum, and, since they could not be overcome, were confined in prison. That same night, because they refused to sacrifice, they were beheaded and thrown into the river. Their bodies came as far as the sea and were cast back onto the shore. A certain presbyter from Capua, named Quartus, found them, immediately placed them on a vehicle, and carried them to his house. Searching carefully, he also found their heads, joined them to the bodies, and buried them near Saint Caesarius.

### Eight days before the Ides of November

The burial of Wilbrord, bishop of the people of the English, a most holy man and highly renowned for the grace of miracles. Ordained at Rome by Pope Sergius, he was sent into Germany to preach the word of God, and there rested in peace.

### Seven days before the Ides

In Africa, the feast of Rogatus, Donatus, Julia, and Januarius.

On the same day, the feast of Saint Rufus, bishop and confessor of the city of Metz, who was transferred from that city, with the consent of Bishop Drogo, to the district of Worms, to a village called Oterheim, in the time of the emperor Lothar and King Louis. There, too, his holiness shone forth through many miracles.

[Note: Here two days are missing in the Martyrology.]

### Four days before the Ides

At Rome, the burial of Saint Leo, bishop.

In Antioch, the feast of Demetrius, bishop; Amnesius, Eustachius [Anianus, Eustosius]; and his companions.

At Orléans, the burial of Blessed Minitor [Minitor], bishop.

### Three days before the Ides

The burial of Blessed Martin, archbishop and confessor of Tours. His life and teaching are evident to nearly all the faithful through the miracles that the Lord performed through him, and there is no need for us to recall anything here, since Sulpicius Severus clearly described his life, virtues, and signs in eloquent language; Gregory also, bishop of that same city, discussed them at fullest length in his books of Miracles.

On the same day the passion of Menna the martyr is celebrated.
