He abandoned earthly military service because the emperor Diocletian, in his cruelty, was forcing Christians to worship idols and adore false gods. The holy servant of God first withdrew into the desert and served the Lord there with earnest devotion. Later, when the pagans were celebrating the emperor’s birthday, he came into the city and rebuked the superstitious worshipers of idols for their vanity.

Through the governor Bagasius he was afflicted with many torments. Bagasius wished to turn him away from the faith of Christ and restore him to the error of the pagans and to earthly military service, but Christ’s martyr utterly refused. Then the governor ordered him first to be stretched upon a stake and beaten with bull’s sinews, so that the blood flowing from his body filled the ground all around. Afterward he ordered iron thorns to be made, and commanded that the holy martyr Menna be bound and dragged over them.

Then the governor ordered him to be beaten for a long time across the shoulders. Next he ordered burning lamps to be placed beneath his body. When fire was brought and placed beneath him for nearly two hours, he said no word to the governor, but cried out only to the Lord, saying: “Christ God, help me.” Finally, when the governor could in no way separate him from Christ, he ordered him to be beheaded. Thus the holy man of God, happily leaving the present age, passed into the heavenly kingdom.

### Two days before the Ides

In Africa [Asia], the feast of the holy Inaurulus, Publius [Aurelius and Publius].

In Caesarea of Cappadocia, the feast of the holy Germanus, Theophilus, Caesarius, and Saint Eusebius.

### Ides

At Tours, a city of Gaul, the burial of Saint Briccius [Britius], bishop and confessor, who succeeded Saint Martin in the episcopate.

### Eighteen days before the Kalends of December

At Heraclea, a city of Thrace, the feast of Saint Clentinus and Theodota, Filominus [Clementinus, Theodotus, Philomenus], Heraclius, Martialis, Donatus, and many other saints.

### Seventeen days before the Kalends

In Africa, the feast of the holy Secundus, Fidentianus, Varicus, and Martialis.

### Sixteen days before the Kalends

At Capua, the feast of Augustine; and in Africa, of Vitalis and Januarius.

At Lyon in Gaul, the burial of Saint Eucherius [Eucherius], bishop.

### Fifteen days before the Kalends

Of our holy Father Gregory, worker of miracles.

And at Orléans, a city of Gaul, the burial of Saint Anianus, bishop and confessor.

### Fourteen days before the Kalends

The passion of Saint Romanus the martyr, who under the governor Asclepiades attained the glory of sacred martyrdom. When the aforementioned Asclepiades wished to turn Saint Romanus away from the faith of Christ and lead him back into pagan error, he subjected him to severe tortures; but Romanus remained steadfast in the right faith and true confession.

A little child was also brought forward as a witness, so that through his declaration he might show whether Christ was the Son of God or whether the false gods were to be worshiped. The child answered that Christ, the Son of God, was to be worshiped, not the false deities of the gods. The governor ordered the little child to be harshly treated, but nevertheless could neither overcome him nor lead him into error.

Then Asclepiades ordered Romanus and the child to be thrown into prison together and, on the following day, cast into a great fire. But an excessive rain sent by God extinguished it. Angered by this, the governor ordered the child to be slaughtered, but Romanus’s tongue to be cut out. Yet by God’s grace, after his tongue had been cut out, he continually sang praises to God and persevered in confessing Christ.

When this was reported to Maximinus, Diocletian’s son-in-law, he ordered Romanus to be put into prison and strangled there during the night. Thus the holy martyr of Christ departed to the heavenly realms on the eighteenth day of November.

### Thirteen days before the Kalends

In Caesarea of Cappadocia, the feast of Maximus, Mucianus, Neophytus, and forty others.

### Twelve days before the Kalends

At Heraclea, the feast of Bassus and Dionysius; and in Caesarea of Cappadocia, of Agapetus [Agapius].

### Eleven days before the Kalends

[Note: Who is this Maurus, who was a monk for eighteen years in the time of Numerian, that is, in the third century? At that time there were no monks, nor was their name known. Baronius omitted him, and his passion is not found in the Martyrology; only Maurus, bishop of Verona, is listed on 21 November. BASN.]

Of Maurus the martyr, who had been a Christian from infancy. By prayers and fasts he entreated Christ the Lord, and he did not cease frequently to give alms to widows and the needy. Since he practiced this throughout all the days of his life, by God’s will the Holy Spirit placed in his mind the desire to enter a monastery.

After he had lived there for not very long, he began to be so loved by all the brothers that they all honored him as a father. When he had completed eighteen years of monastic life, a desire arose in his mind to visit the see of the holy apostle Peter. Setting out, he reached Rome with God’s help. After learning all the mysteries and the rule of the Church, he began in the city of Rome to provide even more generously his customary comforts to Christians and the needy.

When he had remained there for three years, at the very time when the most impious Numerian obtained the imperial power and began to send threatening orders throughout his cities and provinces, commanding that if any Christian were found who did not sacrifice to the gods, he should be tortured with various punishments and put to death, Celerinus had obtained the prefecture of Rome. He too, devoted to idols, had long searched through all the cities and places so that wherever Christians were found, they might be destroyed after being subjected to various kinds of torture.

He afflicted Blessed Maurus with many tortures. First, he ordered him to be beaten with knotted clubs; then his jaws to be crushed with lead weights; afterward, while he was suspended on the rack, his flesh to be scraped with claws and burning lamps applied to his sides; finally, he ordered his head to be cut off.

Recognizing that his body came from their own homeland, African sailors secretly carried it away at night. They wrapped it in clean linen cloths with spices and placed it in a sarcophagus. At his head they wrote: “Maurus, servant of God and Christ Jesus, leaving hunc [hoc] saeculum (‘this age’) for the faith of Christ, acquired eternal life.” After several days, all the sailors, united in purpose, secretly lifted the sarcophagus onto their ship.

When this came to the attention of the prefect Celerinus, he became angry and ordered all the sailors to be arrested. When they heard this, they all fled, and none of them was found. Seeing this, the prefect Celerinus, armed with the counsel of the devil, ordered the same ship, in which the martyr’s body was, to be filled with brushwood and burned in the middle of the sea after fire had been set beneath it. But with the Lord as its pilot, it carried his martyr to the harbor of salvation wherever Christ willed.

### Ten days before the Kalends

Saint Cecilia, who instructed her husband Valerian and his brother Tiburtius to believe in Christ and to suffer martyrdom, and who afterward herself suffered martyrdom, overcoming fire but being killed by the sword under Almachius, prefect of the city.

On the same day, Saint Mederasma the virgin.

On that day also, the feast of Longinus the martyr. While serving in the earthly military, at the time when the Lord was fastened to the cross, he stood nearby and, by order of Pontius Pilate the governor, pierced and opened the Lord’s side with a spear. When he saw the signs that occurred because of the Lord—the darkening of the sun and the earthquake—he believed in our Lord Jesus Christ. Striking his breast, he cried out in a loud voice: “Truly this is the Son of God” (Matthew 27).

Afterward, leaving military service, he was instructed in the Lord’s commandments by the holy apostles. Observing Christ’s venerable commands, he received the seal of faith and offered his entire self to the Lord. He gave alms, restrained his body in chastity, preserved a pure conscience, and lived a heavenly life on earth.

When he was in Caesarea of Cappadocia, he lived a quiet monastic life for twenty-eight years. Turning many away from wickedness, he enlightened them by the word of truth, forbidding sacrifices to idols and sowing the Lord’s venerable commandments through his word.

When the governor Octavian heard this, he ordered him to be brought before him, wishing to turn him away from the faith of Christ and true religion. For this reason he afflicted him with many tortures. Finally, he ordered him to undergo the sentence of death. Later, while praying beside the holy martyr’s body, the governor himself recovered the sight and health that he had previously lost because of his crimes.

### Nine days before the Kalends

At Rome, the burial of Saint Clement, bishop, who, by order of Trajan, was sent into exile across the Pontic Sea. After he had called many to the faith through his miracles and teaching, he was thrown into the sea with an anchor tied to his neck. But, while his disciples prayed, the sea withdrew for three miles, and they found his body in a stone coffin in a marble temple, with the anchor beside it.

On the same day, the feast of Saint Felicitas, martyr and mother of seven sons, who was beheaded for Christ by order of Antonius.

At the monastery of Bobbio, the burial of Saint Columbanus, abbot.

The feast of Saint Trudo, confessor.

### Eight days before the Kalends

At Rome, the feast of Saint Chrysogonus, who completed his martyrdom under Diocletian. Recorded in the passion of Saint Anastasia.

On the same day, the feast of Saint Crescentianus, who was imprisoned with the deacon Caesarius, and with Largus and Smaragdus, during the persecution of Maximinus, son of Maximian. Brought out of prison by order of Carpasianus the deputy governor, he was suspended on the rack, beaten with clubs, and scraped for a long time with claws. Then, after flames had been placed around his sides and he had been burned for a long time, he gave up his spirit. He was buried by John the presbyter in the cemetery of Priscilla.

At that time Maximinus killed his sister Artemia. Recorded in the deeds of Pope Marcellus.

### Seven days before the Kalends

The feast of Saint Peter, bishop of Alexandria. Adorned with every virtue and inferior to none of his predecessors in divine Scripture, he was truly both priest and sacrifice of God. He was suddenly seized and, by Maximinus’s command, beheaded. At the same time many other bishops from Egypt were slaughtered with him. Recorded in Book Nine of the Ecclesiastical History.

At Nicomedia, the passion of Blessed Marculus, priest and martyr, who in the time of the tyrannical emperor Constans suffered martyrdom for the name of Christ at the hands of Macharianus and Paulus, the most severe persecutors. Although he was afflicted with various tortures, he could in no way be turned away from the profession of the true faith. Finally, Macharianus brought him to a very high cliff and threw him down from it. Yet, with Christ protecting him, his body remained whole among the roughest rocks and sharpest crags; his soul, however, leaving the prison of the body, passed into eternal life.

### Six days before the Kalends

At Rome, the burial of Siricius, bishop, and Saturninus; at Aquileia, of Valentinus, bishop; and at Capua, of Nicanor, Cassianus, and Felicissimus.

At Augustodunum, the burial of Saint Amator, bishop.

### Five days before the Kalends

At Nicomedia, the feast of Marcellus, Peter, Numerius, Hierena, and Melosa, and the burial of Optatus, bishop.

### Four days before the Kalends

In Syria, the feast of Trophimus, Theodolus, Expicacus, Eucherius, Eusebius, and Julius.

### Three days before the Kalends

At Rome, the feast of Saint Saturninus, Serius [Senis], and Sisinnius, deacon, under Maximian. He first condemned them, with others, to dig sand for the construction of Diocletian’s baths. Then they were tormented for a long time in prison, where they taught many pagans and baptized them.

Brought out again, bound in chains and barefoot, they were ordered before Laodicius, prefect of the city, to be raised on the rack, stretched with sinews and clubs, and beaten with scourges. Afterward he ordered flames to be applied to their sides, and, when they had been taken down from the rack, ordered their heads to be cut off.

The very Christian Thrason, who had provided much for the martyrs from his own resources, gathered their bodies with John the presbyter and buried them on his estate on the Salarian Way.

While these men were engaged in the struggle, two soldiers, Papias and Maurus, believed. They were immediately arrested by Laodicius and, not long afterward, crowned with martyrdom. Recorded in the deeds of Pope Marcellus.

On the same day, at Mannetis [Toulouse] in Gaul, the feast of Saturninus, bishop and martyr. This martyr Saturninus, as the story goes, was ordained by disciples of the apostles and sent to the city of Toulouse. Incited by the pagans, he was bound by the feet to a wild bull and dragged down the steps of the Capitol. Thus he ended his present life, his skull shattered. His relics have shone forth through miracles in many places.

### Two days before the Kalends

The feast of Saint Andrew the apostle, whose name is interpreted as “manly” or “beautiful,” the brother of Peter. He preached in Scythia and Achaia, and there, in the city of Patras, he died suspended on a cross.

At Rome, Castulus and Eucrepitus [Euprepis]; and at Milan, Ambrose, bishop.

## December

### Kalends of December

At Rome, the feast of Candida, Viribon [Lucius, Rogatus, Cassianus], and thirty others, and the dedication of the basilica of Saint Alban the martyr, together with the ordination of Blessed Boniface the martyr.

### Four days before the Nones

At Rome, the feast of Primentius, Pontianus, Piminus, Daphrosa, Dimeter [perhaps Demetrius], and Jubianus.

In Mauretania, of Verus [Severus], Securus, Januarius, and Victorinus.

### Three days before the Nones

In the East, the feast of Metrobius, Claudicus, and Felix.

At Nicomedia, of Ambicus, Victurus [Victor], and Julius.

In Africa, of Crispinus, Magina, John, Stephen, and Victor [Claudius].

In Pannonia, of Saint Agricola; and at Tingis, of Cassianus the presbyter.

### Two days before the Nones

The feast of Barbara the martyr.

[Note: The place where she suffered is not indicated. Some assert that she was crowned in Tuscany, others at Nicomedia. None of the ancients reported an event so extraordinary, although they say it occurred under Maximinus. No writer earlier than John Damascene mentions Barbara or her father. If Damascene is the author of Barbara’s Acts, that is doubtful. BASN.]

She suffered for Christ in the time of the emperor Maximian [Maximinus]. Her father, named Dioscorus, was extremely wealthy but pagan and a worshiper of idols. Because his only daughter refused to marry and refused to worship false gods, he afflicted her with many tortures. Finally, by order of the governor, she was beheaded by her own father, and her martyrdom was completed in a good confession together with Saint Juliana.

As her father was coming down from the mountain, fire descended from heaven and consumed him, so that not even his ashes could be found.

On the same day, the feast of Heraclius, Christianus, and Pudens.

At the monastery of Fleury, the arrival from Rome of the body of Saint Benedict, abbot.

### Nones

The feast of Dalmatius the martyr.

The feast of Saint Crispinus and Felix.

In Africa, in the city of Tagura [Thagura], the feast of Julius, Potamia, and Gratus, and seven others.

### Eight days before the Ides

In Africa, the feast of Zelotus, Fortunatus, and Gathus.

On the same day, the feast of Nicholas, metropolitan bishop of the Church of Myra. In the time of Constantine Augustus, when pagans and heretics were in tumult and harassed the Church of God with their errors, he came there, suppressed the error, and calmed the persecution.

There was a certain governor there named Eustachius, who had injured many Christians out of greed for money. The governor was to receive more than two hundred pounds of silver in order to destroy them.

Later, through the envy of the devil, a considerable persecution arose in the city at the hands of the master of the soldiers and the prefect Ablabius, who persuaded the emperor, on the basis of false accusations, to imprison the holy men of God. When this had been done—that is, when Nepotianus, Ursus, and Eupoleon had been shut inside the prison—the emperor ordered them to spend the night there and then be beheaded with the sword.

When the holy men heard this, they scattered dust on their heads and cried out to the Lord to help them, saying:

“Lord God of Saint Nicholas, have mercy on us. Just as you acted for the three men who in Lycia were unjustly and wrongfully sentenced to death and saved them, so save us also, holy Nicholas, servant of Christ. And if you are far from us, may your prayer and petition become near to us. Intercede for us with your Lord God and our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, that, having been saved from an unjust and deadly storm, we may be made worthy to come and worship the most holy footprints of your sanctity.”

When Nepotianus had said these and similar things, the three men cried out together, as if with one mouth, praying.

That very night Saint Nicholas appeared in person to the emperor and said to him:

“Emperor Constantine, arise and release those three men whom you hold in prison: Nepotianus, Ursus, and Eupoleon, masters of the soldiers, because they have been falsely accused. If you do not obey me, I will stir up war against you in the court, and I will hand your flesh and entrails over to beasts to devour, bringing a petition against you before the heavenly King Christ.”

The emperor said: “Who are you, and how did you enter my palace?”

The holy man said: “I am Nicholas the sinner, bishop, who dwell in the metropolitan city of Myra in Lycia.”

Having said this, he departed. Again, during that same night and hour, he came and appeared to the prefect Ablabius, saying the same things:

“Ablabius, joyful in heart and mind, arise and release those three innocent men, the masters of the soldiers, whom you hold in prison. If you are unwilling to release them and do not listen to me, I will bring petitions against you before the immortal King Christ. You will fall into illness, end your life consumed by worms, and your entire household will perish miserably.”

Ablabius said to him: “But who are you, and from where have you come to speak such things here?”

The holy Nicholas said: “I am Nicholas the sinner, the servant of God, who is in Myra, the metropolis.”

Having said this, he departed in the same manner.

When the emperor awoke, he sent to Ablabius, saying: “Go, summon the prefect Ablabius, and tell him what I saw and heard.” When everything had been reported to him, he dismissed the messenger. Likewise, the prefect sent back the same messenger, reporting the same things to the emperor.

Immediately the emperor ordered the three men, the masters of the soldiers, to be brought before him in the presence of the whole assembly, with the generals and the prefect gathered there. After questioning them about everything and learning the truth of the vision—that they had been kept in custody innocently through the prayers of Saint Nicholas—he said to them:

“Know this: I did not give you this life, but the one whom you invoked, Saint Nicholas, to whom you sent. Cut the hair of your heads, change your clothing, and give thanks to him. Remember me also.”

He gave them various sacred vessels to carry with them: a Gospel book entirely of gold, two small golden censers, and a golden paten ornamented with precious stones. Then the emperor sent them away.

They journeyed to Myra, the metropolis of Lycia, worshiped Saint Nicholas, cut the hair of their heads, and changed their clothing. With many tears they distributed to the poor the things they possessed—gold, silver, and clothing. For many years they continued these practices, glorifying and praising the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, now and forever, throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

### Seven days before the Ides

In Antioch, the feast of Polycarp and Theodore.

On the same day, the feast of Saint Sabinus, bishop and martyr, who suffered for the name of Christ in the time of Maximian Augustus, together with Marcellus and Exsuperantius, his deacons.

A certain Venustianus, a distinguished man in the region of Tuscany, could not turn the holy bishop away from the faith of Christ or lead him to the worship of idols. He therefore ordered his hands to be cut off because, after knocking down and breaking a small shrine of Jupiter, he had thrown it to the ground.

He tortured his deacons with various torments. He had them suspended on the rack, ordered their sides to be torn with claws, and fire to be placed beneath them. When they had breathed out their spirits there, he ordered their bodies to be thrown into the river. Fishermen removed them from the river, and a noble woman named Serena, from the city of Spoleto, buried them. Saint Sabinus had illuminated her nephew while he was in prison by blessing him.

After several days, Venustianus, by divine judgment, suffered great pain in his eyes. His servants brought him to the aforementioned bishop. The holy man of God taught him to renounce the devil, converted him to the faith of Christ, and baptized him with his wife and children.

When Maximian Augustus learned this, he sent his soldier to cut off the heads of Venustianus, his wife, and his children. He ordered Sabinus to be beaten in the city of Spoleto without respite until he failed. After being beaten for a long time, he gave up his spirit.

### Six days before the Ides

In the city of Verona, the feast of Saint Zeno the martyr, on the occasion when the waters of the river Athesis rose as high as the upper windows of his church but could not enter it, displaying the martyr’s power.

And the burial of Saint Eucharius, bishop.

### Five days before the Ides

In Africa, the feast of Peter, Successus [Bassianus, Primitivus], Turnus, Publicianus, and twenty others.

### Four days before the Ides

The feast of Saint Eulalia the virgin in the city of Barcelona in Spain, under the governor Dacianus. When she was thirteen years old, she was beheaded after many tortures; and when her head had been cut off, a dove was seen to come forth from her body.

On the same day, of the holy martyrs Habundus and Carpofolus [Abundius and Carpophorus].

### Three days before the Ides

At Rome, Damasus, pope and confessor. He established that psalms should be sung day and night in the Church of Christ.

On the same day, the holy martyrs Fuscianus, Victoricus, and Gentianus [Victorice and Gratianus].

### Two days before the Ides

In Spain, in the city of Mérida, the feast of Eulalia the virgin, and of Hermogenes, Donatus [Donata], and twenty-two others.

### Ides

The feast of Saint Lucia the virgin of Syracuse, under Paschasius the governor. When Paschasius ordered lions [perhaps “pimps”] to violate her, they could not move her at all, neither with ropes nor with many pairs of oxen. She endured pitch resin and boiling oil without injury. Finally, struck with a sword thrust into her bowels, she nevertheless did not die until priests came and she received communion of the Lord’s body and blood. She suffered in the time of Diocletian and Maximian.

### Nineteen days before the Kalends of January

In Antioch, the feast of Drusus and his companions Zosimus and Theodore.

At Lyon in Gaul, of Saint Viator, bishop.

At Reims, of Nicasius, bishop, and Sacrepis [Eutropia].

At Vienne, of Lupicinus, bishop, Aspedia, and Theodulus.

### Eighteen days before the Kalends

In Africa, the feast of Faustinus, Lucius, Candidus, Caelianus, Marcus, Maximus, Januarius, and Fortunatus.

### Seventeen days before the Kalends

At Ravenna, of Valentinus, Navalis, Agricola, and Concordius.

At Arles, the dedication of the basilica and altar of Saint Genesius the martyr.

### Sixteen days before the Kalends

Of Saint Ignatius, bishop and martyr, who was the third bishop of Antioch after the apostle Peter. In the eleventh year of Trajan he was sent to Rome bound for the beasts. The remains of his body were brought back and lie at Antioch outside the Daphne Gate, in the cemetery of the church.

### Fifteen days before the Kalends

At Laodicea, the feast of Theotimus and Basilianus.

In Africa, of Quintus, Simplicius, Pomponius, and Paul.

### Fourteen days before the Kalends

At Nicomedia, of Zosimus, Cyriacus, Paul, and Secundus.

The feast of the holy bishops Anastasius and Siddimus [Syndimius].

At Auxerre, of Blessed Gregory, bishop.

### Thirteen days before the Kalends

At Gildo, a city in Thrace [commonly Gelduba], of Bajulus.

At Rome, of Zephyrinus, bishop.

In the East, the feast of Saint Thecla the virgin and Saint Liberatus.

### Twelve days before the Kalends

Of Thomas the apostle, whose name is interpreted as “abyss” and “Didymus,” that is, “like Christ.” He preached to the Parthians and Medes. He was pierced with a lance and died there in the city of Calamina in India, where he was buried with honor on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January.

And in Tuscany, of John and Festus.

### Eleven days before the Kalends

In Antioch, the feast of Saint Basil.

At Rome, on the Lavican Way between the two laurel trees, the feast of thirty holy martyrs, all crowned on one day.

At Rome, on the Portuensian Way, the burial of Saint Felix, bishop.

Elsewhere, the passion of Theodosia the virgin and Didymus the monk.

### Ten days before the Kalends

The feast of Gregory the presbyter, who in the time of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian suffered many tortures in the city of Spoleto under the judges Flaccus and Tircanus. First he was beaten with knotted clubs; afterward he was ordered to be burned on a fiery grate. While this was happening, a great earthquake occurred within the city of Spoleto, and more than three hundred pagan souls were crushed.

Then he was sent to prison, and burning lamps were placed against his sides. Finally, in the middle of the amphitheater, he was beheaded by Aqualinus the sword-bearer, and thus passed into eternal glory.

The burial at Rome of Victoria, under Decius. She had been betrothed to the pagan Eugenius, but was unwilling either to marry or to sacrifice. After she had driven a poisonous dragon from the region and performed many other miracles—including gathering many virgins to serve the Lord in the cave where the dragon had previously lived—she was struck in the heart with a sword by the executioner Thaliacus, count, at the request of her betrothed. She was buried on the tenth day before the Kalends of the same month.

At Nicomedia, the feast of thirty-five martyrs.

Elsewhere, of Evaristus, Victor, and five hundred thirty-two others.

### Nine days before the Kalends of January

In the city of Tripoli, Saint Lucian; and the feast of the holy Metrobius, Paulus, Zenotus, Theutinus, and Timistus [Zenobius, Theotimus, and Drusus].

In Antioch of Syria, the feast of forty canonical holy virgins, and of two others together, Drusus and Donatus.

## VIII Kalends

At Bethlehem, the Nativity according to the flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ; and the feast of Saint Anastasia, who during the time of Diocletian first endured harsh and cruel confinement from her husband Publius. In it, however, she was greatly consoled and strengthened by Chrysogonus, the confessor of Christ. Then she was tormented by the prefect of Illyricum in an equally severe and prolonged imprisonment. During this confinement she was nourished for two months with heavenly food by Saint Theodota, who had previously suffered martyrdom. Then she was placed on a ship with two hundred men and two hundred women, to be drowned at sea, and was carried to the Palmaria Islands. There she was stretched out by her hands and feet and bound to fixed stakes; a fire was kindled around her waist, in which she completed her martyrdom. All who had come with her likewise gloriously suffered martyrdom by various forms of execution.

On the same day, the feast of Saint Eugenia the virgin, who was the daughter of Philippus, prefect of Alexandria and of all Egypt, sent there by the emperor. For the sake of faith in Christ and love of chastity, she rejected secular dress and the pleasures of the world. She put on men’s clothing and went to Saint Helenus the bishop, together with her eunuchs Protus and Eugenius. Through him they were washed in baptism and entered a monastery of monks, living monastically in male attire. When the abbot died, Saint Eugenia was appointed in his place; there she became renowned for holy conduct and miracles.

For when she saved a certain woman named Melantia from a fever by the sign of the cross, Melantia herself, instigated by the devil, attempted to draw him into sexual intercourse with her. When he refused to consent, she accused him, as the monk and abbot Eugenius, of having wished to violate her. But all these charges were proved false by Philippus the prefect, because Eugenia revealed that she was a woman, not a man. After Philippus her father had recognized this, together with Claudia her mother and Eugenia’s brothers Auctus and Sergius, they were converted to the faith of Christ and baptized.

Afterward Saint Eugenia went with Protus and Hyacinthus to Rome, where she too suffered martyrdom by order of the emperor Gallienus, through Nicetius, prefect of the City. When he compelled her to offer sacrifices to the goddess Diana and she refused to comply—indeed, after reducing the idol itself to dust—the prefect ordered her to be thrown into the Tiber with a stone tied around her neck. But she was freed from there by God’s grace. Later she was cast into a blazing furnace, but was in no way harmed by the fire. Finally, on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, just as the Savior himself had previously revealed to her, she was placed in confinement and killed by an executioner; thus she departed for the heavenly kingdom.

## VII Kalends

In the town of Cofargamala in the Jerusalem region, the passion of Saint Stephen, the first martyr and deacon.

## VI Kalends

**Note:** Among many people the opinion prevailed concerning John that he did not die; Augustine reports this view while criticizing it. Others believed that he fell asleep but was soon taken up into heaven. Hippolytus asserted this, in the work he wrote on the twelve apostles, as reported by Combefis. Do not, however, suppose that this was Hippolytus of Portus, who lived in the third century; he is a different person, reporting that John’s remains, when sought, were not found. Rabanus also seems to have held the same view, since here he claims that the Assumption of John the Evangelist was celebrated in his own time. **BASN.**

The Assumption of Saint John the Evangelist at Ephesus, and the appointment to the episcopate of Saint James, the Lord’s brother, who was the first of the Jews to be ordained bishop at Jerusalem by the apostles and was crowned with martyrdom at mid-Passover.

## V Kalends

At Bethlehem, the feast of the holy nursing infants who suffered for Christ under Herod.

## IV Kalends

In Africa, the feast of Domici, Victuri [Dominici, Victoris], Crescentius, Primianus, and Bishop Lybosus. And at Rome, in the cemetery of Callistus, that of Felix and Bishop Boniface, concerning an ordination [Note: Something appears to be missing.].

## III Kalends

At Tours, the burial of blessed Perpetuus the bishop, who built the church of Saint Martin.

## II Kalends

The burial of Saint Sylvester, bishop and confessor; and the passion of Saint Columba the virgin at Sens under the emperor Aurelian. After overcoming the fire, she was beheaded.

[Col. 1187]

# Two Short Works of Blessed Rabanus Maurus, Abbot of Fulda and Archbishop of Mainz

[In Labbe, *Councils*, appendix to volume VIII.]

## I. Canonical Responses to Certain Questions of Reginbald the Chorepiscopus

[Col. 1187D] To the most reverend and beloved brother Reginbald, Rabanus, the least of the servants of God, sends greetings in the Lord.

After your Holiness wished to present yourself to our lowliness, you strongly impressed upon us your desire to see us again. Thus, recognizing the gravity of your character, the propriety of your speech, the humility of your bearing, and the cheerfulness of your countenance, which your affection displayed to us, we would not wish to be deprived of your presence if in any way we could have it continually. But because true charity has this nature: that what it cannot possess bodily with itself, it never ceases to possess spiritually, although you are absent in body, you do not cease to be present in spirit. This will continue until, by God’s grace, having been stripped of the body, we shall be present with God. Yet that we can attain this is more a gift of God than a human capability. But we have already been saved in hope; and blessed is the one who hopes in the Lord.

Furthermore, since your Reverence then showed me certain chapters written on a little sheet, in which you urged me to answer you concerning the matters contained there, I reread, as far as was possible, the books of the divine Testaments and the judgments of the holy Fathers. As time allowed, I gathered together the points necessary for answering these questions. For the arrival of King Louis—which I do not doubt you know—was imminent and pressing, so that we were occupied with receiving him. Nor was it now possible to devote ourselves to calm reading, since our mind itself felt divided among many concerns. But because the fervor of your affection compels me to obey you, after moderating our worldly anxieties, we resolved to comply as far as the frailty of the human mind permitted, and especially to follow your will. The sequence of those chapters was as follows.

### I

First you asked what should be done with a person who, by enticement, had stolen a Christian man and handed him over to a pagan people for sale, from whom the man sold could no longer free himself. I then replied to you that it seemed to me that the offender had incurred the guilt of murder against that man. Later, when reading the divine ordinance in Deuteronomy, I found this judgment confirmed, since it imposed an equal measure of punishment upon a murderer and upon one who sold a person after stealing him.

For just as it is written there (Deut. XIX) that a murderer must give “life for life,” “eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot,” so it also commands that anyone who is caught enticing his brother from among the children of Israel and selling him for a price be put to death, and that the evil be removed from the midst of God’s people (Deut. XXIV). Hence it seems to me that, just as the divine law establishes an equal sentence for a murderer and for one who sells a stolen person, so canonical authority should punish in the same manner the person who, by stealing and enticing his brother, has sold him, and the person who has unjustly killed his Christian neighbor—and all the more severely when he has handed him over to a pagan people and has shown no compassion for the ruin of his soul.

In the Council of Ancyra it is written as follows (Canons 21, 22):

> Those who have committed voluntary murder shall indeed submit themselves continually to penance, but shall attain completion only toward the end of life. Concerning involuntary homicides, the earlier ruling prescribed that completion should be attained after seven years of penance, whereas the second prescribed that a period of five years be completed.

But in all judgments the sentence must be moderated according to the intention and devotion of the penitent. If someone has truly performed penance, paying it with tears, fasts, and prayers and giving generous alms, the priest has the authority to mitigate the judgment in his case. But for one who is hard of heart and negligent in performing penance, the prescribed period must be observed in full.

### II

Concerning infants who are found dead with their father and mother, when it is not apparent whether the infant was crushed or suffocated by them, or died a natural death: the parents ought not therefore to consider themselves secure or to remain without penance. Nevertheless, consideration should be given to compassion in their case, when not intention but the outcome was the cause of death.

If, however, they know that they themselves were the killers, they must realize that they have sinned grievously. This is confirmed in the Council of Ancyra in the following manner (Canon 20):

> Concerning women who commit fornication and kill their children, or who take measures to expel what has been conceived in the womb: the ancient ruling excludes them from the Church until the end of life. But now we define more humanely that they should be granted a period of ten years according to the established stages of penance.

Others, however, declare that such a person should perform three years of penance—namely, one who has inadvertently crushed an infant—and that one of these years should be observed on bread and water, with abstinence from all luxury during the period of penance.

### III

Concerning the man who took his neighbor’s widow in marriage, it must be considered in which degree of generation marriage between relatives may take place, and an equal judgment must be applied to both sexes. For some judged that this could be done in the third or fourth generation, others in the fifth, and others in the sixth.

But the chief point to be considered there is what the divine law prescribes concerning this matter, about which we have already replied to Bishop Humbert when he inquired. We have now sent you the form of that response as well. For it is clear that the sacred canons pronounce anathema upon anyone who marries from his own kindred, or a woman whom his kinsman had possessed. Therefore the greatest caution must be exercised, lest eternal condemnation follow the offense of incest.

### IV

You also asked what should be done if a father and son, or two brothers, or an uncle and nephew, committed fornication with one woman. It is clear that this must be punished with severe vengeance, since it is found to be a grave crime. All adultery is forbidden where it is written: “You shall not commit adultery.” How much more so when the woman is a kinswoman, or the wife or concubine of a kinsman?

The Book of Leviticus shows what the Lord commanded in the law as punishment for such acts. It is written there (Lev. XX):

> If anyone commits adultery with another man’s wife and commits adultery with his neighbor’s spouse, both the adulterer and the adulteress shall surely be put to death. If anyone lies with his stepmother and uncovers his father’s nakedness, both shall surely be put to death; their blood shall be upon them. If anyone lies with his daughter-in-law, both shall surely be put to death, because they have committed an abomination; their blood shall be upon them. If a man takes a woman and her mother, he has committed an abomination; he shall be burned alive together with them, and such wickedness shall not remain among you. If anyone takes his sister, the daughter of his father or the daughter of his mother, and sees her nakedness, and she sees her brother’s shame, they have committed a monstrous act; both shall be killed in the sight of the people, because they have mutually uncovered their nakedness, and they shall bear their iniquity. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your maternal aunt or your paternal aunt; anyone who does this shall expose the shame of his flesh, and both shall bear their iniquity. If anyone lies with the wife of his paternal uncle or maternal uncle and uncovers the nakedness of his kinsman, both shall bear their iniquity; they shall die childless. If anyone takes his brother’s wife, he has done an unlawful thing; he has uncovered his brother’s nakedness, and they shall be childless.

These judgments make clear how greatly every incest and pollution of illicit intercourse displeases the Lord, since he judged that such a crime should be punished by the sentence of death. For it is not permitted for a son to lie with his father’s wife, nor for a father to lie with his son’s wife, since he forbade lying with a stepmother or with a daughter-in-law. Nor is it proper to take one’s brother’s wife, since such a union is judged to result in childlessness—that is, to make the offender liable to death.

If, then, the Lord commanded in the law that the shame of incest be avenged by the sentence of death, how will an incestuous person escape the punishment of sin in the Gospel, where perfect justice is found? Especially since there a temporal punishment is decreed, whereas here the fire of everlasting Gehenna is proclaimed.

Perceiving this distinction, the Apostle writes to the Hebrews (Heb. X):

> Anyone who violates the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you suppose, will be deserved by the one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, regarded as profane the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace?

Therefore it is most necessary that the sinner strive to mitigate the harsh sentence of judgment through worthy penance, lest uncorrected wickedness be punished by everlasting vengeance. Thus John the Baptist in the Gospel exhorted the crowds who were going out to be baptized by him, saying:

> Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath? Therefore produce worthy fruits of repentance, for already the ax is placed at the root of the trees. Every tree, therefore, that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire (Luke III).

It is easy to recognize what the sacred canons prescribe concerning incestuous persons. For in the Council of Caesarea it is written (Canon 2):

> If a woman marries two brothers, she shall be cast out until death. Nevertheless, at the end, because of mercy, if she promises that, once restored to health, she will dissolve the bonds of this union, she may attain the fruit of penance. But if the woman or the man in such a marriage should die, penance will be difficult for the one who remains alive.

Hence it is clear that it is equally evil for a woman to marry two men, for a man to take two wives, for a father and son to commit fornication with one woman, for an uncle and nephew to lie with one woman, or for anything similar to occur. Therefore it is just that those who sin in this manner should perform penance until the end of their lives.

Unless, perhaps, because of excessive weeping, deep contrition, and devoted penance, a priest should decide that something more humane ought to be done in the penitent’s case. For when the Lord visits someone’s heart with the compunction of tears and the bitterness of weeping, the priest has authority to shorten the period of penance, as it is written in the Council of Laodicea (Canon 2):

> Concerning those who have sinned through various crimes and, persevering in prayer, confession, and penance, have undergone a complete conversion: according to the nature of the offense, after the period of penance has been completed, communion should be granted to such persons because of clemency and goodness.

In the Council of Ancyra it is likewise written concerning adultery (Canon 19):

> If anyone’s wife has committed adultery, or if he himself has committed adultery, he ought to attain completion through seven years of penance, according to the former stages.

Accordingly, Theodorus judged that one who has committed incest ought to do penance for twelve years.

What the other teachers think about this you will be able to find in the little books they composed on penance. Some judged that fifteen years, others twelve, others ten, and others seven, should be completed for such crimes. But you, following the footsteps of the ancient Fathers, should shorten the period only for those who have performed penance devoutly and with tears. The others should complete the prescribed period, because it is written in Solomon:

> Whoever hides his crimes will not prosper; but whoever confesses and abandons them will obtain mercy (Prov. XXVIII).

For God is gracious and merciful, but:

> His mercy is from generation to generation toward those who fear him. He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts (Luke I).

And:

> Whoever is hard of mind will fall into evil. Whoever keeps the commandment keeps his soul, but whoever neglects his ways will die (Prov. XXVIII; Prov. XIX).

### V

You asked about a slave who has fled from his master: if he should die while fleeing, is it permitted to sing Masses or psalms for him? We do not find this forbidden in the divine books. Nevertheless, we know that the apostles most strongly commanded that “slaves be subject to their masters with all fear, not only to the good and gentle but also to the harsh” (1 Pet. II), and that they obey them in all things.

In the canon of the Council of Gangra it is written as follows (Canon 3):

> If anyone, under the pretext of divine worship, teaches a slave to despise his own master, to withdraw from his service, and not to serve him with goodwill and all honor, let him be anathema.

From this it is understood that if the person who teaches a slave to despise his own master and withdraw from his service has merited anathema, how much more the one who despises his master and refuses to submit to his service.

Nevertheless, there is a distinction between one who flees through pride and one who flees out of necessity, compelled by the cruelty of his master. Hagar, Sarah’s maidservant, fled because her mistress afflicted her; but when the angel instructed her to return and submit herself to her mistress, she returned to her.

Likewise, Onesimus, the slave of Philemon, fled from his master. But through the teaching of the Apostle Paul he believed in Christ and was baptized, and through the Apostle’s intervention he was restored to his own master. Every fugitive slave must be admonished by faithful teachers, wherever he may be, to return to his master and submit himself to him, lest, by despising the Lord’s commandment, he be struck with perpetual anathema.

Nevertheless, if he dies while fleeing, prayer should be offered for him, unless perhaps he is entangled in some greater crime or has fallen into treachery, so that prayer cannot benefit him. Yet Augustine, writing to Laurence, says among other things:

> When sacrifices, whether of the altar or of any kind of almsgiving, are offered for all the baptized, they are thanksgivings for the very good, propitiations for those who are not very evil, and, for the very evil—even if there is no assistance for the dead—consolations of whatever kind for the living. For those whom they benefit, they either bring about complete remission, or at least make their condemnation more tolerable.

### VI

Concerning the man who pretended to be a priest although he had not been ordained and who performed the office of baptism, it must be investigated whether the person baptizing had himself been baptized and whether he baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity with triple immersion.

If this was so, he is not to be baptized again. Rather, what was done must be confirmed through the imposition of the bishop’s hand and the anointing of sacred chrism. For what has once been accomplished in the sacrament of baptism may not be repeated, since there is one Lord, one faith, and one baptism.

Nevertheless, the man who acted presumptuously, and not from some necessity, must be restrained by canonical discipline.

Therefore, as blessed Ambrose testifies, after churches had been established in all places and offices had been ordered, the arrangement became different from what it had been at the beginning. At first everyone taught and everyone baptized, on whatever days or at whatever times the opportunity arose. Philip did not seek a particular time or day on which to baptize the eunuch, nor did he impose a fast. Nor did Paul and [lacuna] delay the time when they baptized the jailer together with all his household. Nor did Peter have clergy or seek a day when he baptized Cornelius with his entire household; he did not baptize them himself, but ordered the brothers who were with him at Joppa to do so. For at that time no one had yet been ordained except the seven deacons.

Thus, so that the people might grow and multiply, everyone was permitted to evangelize, baptize, and explain Scripture in the church. But once the Church had encompassed all places, meeting places had been established, and rulers and the other offices had been ordered for the churches, no one from the clergy who had not been ordained dared presume to perform an office that he knew had not been entrusted or granted to him. The Church then began to be governed by a different order and foresight.

If everyone could perform the same functions, this would be irrational, and the matter would appear common and utterly worthless. For this reason deacons now do not preach among the people, nor do other clerics or laymen baptize, nor are believers immersed on any day except when they are ill.

Therefore the writings of the Apostle do not entirely correspond to the ordination now existing in the Church, because they were written during the Church’s earliest beginnings. For he himself calls Timothy, whom he had made a presbyter, a bishop, because the first presbyters were called bishops, so that when one departed, another might succeed him.

Finally, in Egypt presbyters confirm, if a bishop is not present. But because later presbyters who were unworthy began to seek the primacy, the arrangement was changed. The council took care that not rank but merit should create a bishop, who would be appointed by the judgment of many priests, lest an unworthy person rashly usurp the office and become a scandal to many.

That the baptism of Christ is one, and that although it is administered by different ministers it should neither be repeated nor changed, the Holy Gospel shows, where the words of John the Baptist are recorded as follows:

> I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove and remaining upon him, and I did not know him. But the one who sent me to baptize in water said to me: “Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, this is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.” And I saw and bore witness that this is the Son of God (John I).

Blessed Augustine explained this passage as follows:

> What, then, did John learn through the dove, except that a certain property would belong to Christ? Although many ministers would baptize, whether just or unjust, the holiness of baptism would be attributed only to him upon whom the dove descended. Concerning him it was said: “This is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.” Let Peter baptize: this is the one who baptizes. Let Paul baptize: this is the one who baptizes. Let Judas baptize: this is the one who baptizes. For if baptism existed according to the diversity of merits, since merits are diverse, baptisms would also be diverse. But there is one baptism, and there is one Christ, who through his various ministers baptizes with baptism for the remission of all sins.

Therefore the sacred canons command that those baptized by heretics should not be baptized again, but should receive security within the Catholic Church through the imposition of hands and the sole invocation of the Holy Spirit, whom no one receives from heretics.

### VII

Concerning those who eat meat during Lent before Easter, or who make an oath at the altar or upon the relics of the saints, it is clear that they act unjustly, because they oppose the divine commandments.

Thus through Isaiah the Lord rejects the fasting of the wicked, saying:

> Behold, on the day of your fast you pursue your own will, and you exact payment from all your debtors. Behold, you fast for lawsuits and quarrels, and strike with a wicked fist. Do not fast as you have done until this day, so that your cry may be heard on high. Is this the kind of fast that I have chosen, for a person to afflict his soul for a day? Is it to twist his head like a circle, to spread sackcloth and ashes beneath him? Do you call this a fast and a day acceptable to the Lord? Is not this rather the fast that I have chosen: to loosen the bonds of wickedness, to undo the oppressive bundles, to set free those who are crushed, and to break every burden? Share your bread with the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house. When you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh. Then your light will break forth like the dawn, and your healing will arise quickly; your righteousness will go before you, and the glory of the Lord will gather you. Then you will call, and the Lord will answer; you will cry out, and he will say, “Here I am,” because I am the merciful Lord your God (Isa. LVIII).

Hence it is written in the canon of the holy Fathers (Council of Laodicea, Canons 50 and 52) that:

> It is not proper to celebrate weddings or birthdays during Lent, or to break the fast and pass through the whole of Lent without reverence;

rather, it is more fitting to venerate the whole of Lent with strict judgment.

For it is not right that one who divides the unity of the Church and dissolves the traditions of the holy Fathers should go unpunished, but he must pay a fitting penalty for this. The punishment, however, must be moderated according to the judgment of the priest and the measure of the penitent. For, as was said above, one who truly repents and manifests the contrition of his heart through signs of tears should be treated with lighter discipline, because God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart. Whenever a sinner is converted and performs penance, doing judgment and righteousness, he shall live and not die.

It is not the length of time but the disposition of the soul that must be weighed, because the Lord accepted the three-day penance of the Ninevites and forgave Peter’s denial, washed away by the bitterest tears, when, rising on the third day, he commanded him, by an angelic summons, to come among the other disciples into his presence and reconciliation.

These things, holy brother, I have dictated to you hastily, as the opportunity of time allowed, prepared, if anything is lacking in the answers, to explain it to you more clearly at a suitable time. But diligently instruct the flock entrusted to you, and assist us with your prayers, so that we may write something worthy for you and daily rejoice with you in your good work. May Almighty God increase you in good works in this life and reward you with everlasting recompense in the future.

## II. Whether Chorepiscopi May Ordain Priests and Deacons with the Consent of Their Bishop

[Col. 1195]

[Col. 1195C] After you had departed from us, I considered what you had reported in person: how certain Western bishops had understood the order of chorepiscopi, and how some of them were reordaining as priests and deacons those who had previously been ordained by chorepiscopi in the time of their predecessors, as well as re-consecrating churches consecrated by them, profaning all the former sanctification as though it had not been legitimate, although those chorepiscopi had performed these acts with the consent and command of their bishops.

Thus schisms also arise in the Church of God when the rulers of God’s people disagree with one another in their teaching: some saying that chorepiscopi may, with the consent and command of their superiors—that is, the bishops of the cities under whose jurisdiction they live—lay hands on the baptized so that they may receive the Holy Spirit, and ordain priests and deacons, as well as the other degrees of the Church; while others insist that this ministry belongs to them in no way, but only to those bishops who preside over cities.

From this, plainly, arise sects, envy, anger, quarrels, rivalries, dissensions, and contentions. Through these things many of the people, seeing disagreement among their teachers, are greatly scandalized.

For such litigants do not follow that apostolic harmony about which Paul entreats the Philippians, saying (Phil. II):

> If there is therefore any consolation in Christ, any comfort from love, any fellowship of the Spirit, any compassion and mercy, complete my joy by being of the same mind, having the same love, united in soul and thinking the same thing; doing nothing through rivalry or empty glory, but in humility regarding one another as superior, each looking not to his own interests but to those of others.

Likewise, wishing to commend his younger associates to his hearers and make them not despised but acceptable, he admonishes the Corinthians, saying (1 Cor. IV):

> I ask you, therefore, brothers, be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ. For this reason I sent Timothy to you, who is my beloved and faithful son in the Lord; he will remind you of my ways, which are in Christ Jesus, just as I teach everywhere in every church.

And again (1 Cor. XVI):

> If Timothy comes, see that he is without fear among you, for he is doing the work of the Lord, as I am also. Therefore let no one despise him. Escort him in peace, so that he may come to me, for I am waiting for him with the brothers.

He clearly received this commandment of humility from Truth itself, which in the Gospel instructed the disciples who were contending about primacy, saying (Matt. XX):

> The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who exercise authority over them are called benefactors. But you are not to be so; rather, let the greater among you become as the younger, and the leader as the servant.

And, teaching them by his own example, he continues (Luke XXII; Matt. XX):

> I am among you as one who serves; for the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many.

The apostles had assistants in preaching the Gospel of Christ, who also performed ordinations at their command. Thus it is read in the book that Pope Damasus wrote about the bishops of the Roman Church at the request of the presbyter Jerome: Linus and Cletus performed ordinations of presbyters at the command of blessed Peter. Yet after Peter’s passion, it was not one of them but Clement who succeeded to the honor of the chair, since the prince of the apostles himself handed it over to him, as the letter of Clement himself, written by Peter’s command to James, the Lord’s brother, testifies.

From this I believe that the custom of chorepiscopi first originated and has been retained in the Church to the present day: namely, that chorepiscopi, ordained by their own bishops, should, according to their command, ordain deacons and priests and the other degrees, and perform the remaining priestly offices.

I therefore wonder how those who provoke this controversy can despise the order of chorepiscopi so greatly that they attribute to them scarcely anything more than the dignity of priests. This agrees neither with new nor ancient practice, nor with the doctrines and customs of the apostles themselves; indeed, in its meaning it also disagrees with the doctrine.

For it is clear that not reason and humility but envy and pride dominate these men, so that, despising their fellow workers, they alone desire to appear powerful and endowed with sanctifying authority. What the holy Fathers wrote for concord and union among the individual dignities, they regard rather as a harmful condemnation than as an ordered arrangement.

The sacred canons prescribe how each order should preserve its measure, from the least to the greatest, and how the lower degree should always be subject to the higher. Thus deacons must not presume to baptize without a bishop or priest, unless perhaps extreme necessity compels them to undertake these offices when the persons mentioned above are far away. They are also to receive the grace of holy communion after priests, whether a bishop or priest gives it to them. Nor is it permitted for deacons to sit among priests, nor may they dare to sit in the presence of a priest; they should sit only at the priest’s command.

Likewise, they command that honor be shown to deacons by those who serve them, namely subdeacons and all clerics.

Concerning priests, it is written in the decrees of Pope Gelasius as follows (Gelas. I, letter 9, chapter 6):

> We forbid priests no less to extend themselves beyond their proper measure and boldly to assume for themselves what belongs to the episcopal dignity. They must not seize the power of making chrism or of administering episcopal confirmation; nor, in the presence of any bishop, must they presume to undertake either prayer or sacred action unless they are ordered to do so. In his presence they must not presume to sit unless commanded, nor to handle the venerable mysteries. They must remember that they are in no way permitted, without the supreme pontiff, to have the right to make a subdeacon or acolyte. Nor should they doubt that, if they think to carry out on their own authority anything specifically belonging to the episcopal ministry, they are immediately to be deprived of the dignity of the presbyterate and of holy communion.

Concerning chorepiscopi, it is written in the Council of Ancyra as follows (Canon 12):

> Chorepiscopi are not permitted to ordain priests or deacons; nor are the priests of a city permitted to do so in any parish without the command or letters of the bishop.

I note that it does not say that chorepiscopi are entirely forbidden to ordain deacons or priests, but that they may not do so except by the command or letters of their own bishop in each parish.

Also in the Council of Antioch it is read as follows (Canon 10):

> “Those who are appointed chorepiscopi in villages or estates, although they have received the laying on of hands from bishops, and although they have been consecrated as bishops, nevertheless the holy synod has decreed that they should recognize their proper rank, govern the churches subject to them, and be content with the administration and care of those churches. They may also ordain lectors, subdeacons, and exorcists. These promotions shall suffice for them; but they shall not dare to ordain either a presbyter [Col. 1198C] or a deacon apart from the bishop of the city (that is, without the knowledge of the city’s bishop [Note: [Col. 1197D] The parenthesis is Rabanus’s]), to whom he himself, together with the estate, is subject.”

But since he says that chorepiscopi receive the laying on of hands from bishops, and indeed that they are consecrated as bishops, why are they not permitted, with the consent of the bishops to whom they are subject, to perform consecrations to the sacred orders and to sign the faithful with holy chrism? For it is pointless for anyone to possess episcopal consecration if he is not permitted to exercise the ministry of a bishop.

Why, then, does the ordaining bishop invoke the Holy Spirit, that he may sanctify the person being ordained and bestow it [Possibly: “that he may bestow the sanctification of the person being ordained”], if he himself, the one who invokes and ordains, afterward reproaches that person, after he has properly completed the consecration [Col. 1198D]? Does he not mock the Lord, whose gift he asks for, when afterward he despises that gift? Does not the slander by which he derides the Lord’s signification [Possibly: “sanctification”] reach the very author of sanctification?

It is therefore clear that, through the word of God, every sanctification is accomplished in the Holy Spirit. Why, then, does he not fear to blaspheme and diminish the power of the Holy Spirit, when it is written (Luke 12):

> “Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come.”

Thus the apostle Peter, in the Acts of the Apostles, [Col. 1199A] when he saw that the centurion Cornelius and those who were with him had received the grace of the Holy Spirit, refuted the Jews who disputed with him because he had entered among the Gentiles and eaten with them, answering in these words:

> “If therefore God gave them the same grace as he gave us, who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could hinder God?”

When they had heard this, they fell silent and glorified God, saying:

> “Then God has given repentance unto life also to the Gentiles” (Acts 11).

Therefore, whoever God honors with the gift of his Spirit ought not rightly to be dishonored by human beings. Nor should anyone count as slanderous what is evidently ordained by divine disposition, for “the things that are, have been ordained by God.”

Accordingly, the dignity of the lower-ranking bishops [Col. 1199B] is not taken away when responsibility for the whole province is entrusted to the metropolitan. For without him it is not permitted to ordain a bishop in the province, to convene a general council, or to undertake any other act in the province, except those matters that clearly belong to the individual parishes and bishoprics.

For if it were not permissible to have chorepiscopi within the order of bishops, they would in no way have been counted among the three hundred and eighteen Fathers who were present at the Council of Nicaea. In their catalogue, more than twelve chorepiscopi are included; yet among the number of Fathers fixed for that council, no presbyters or deacons are found named, but only metropolitans, bishops, and chorepiscopi are listed individually.

Why, then, does a bishop of any city wish [Col. 1199C] and decide to ordain a chorepiscopus for himself, if he considers that ordination itself to have no efficacy? The Apostle says (Romans 14):

> “Blessed is the one who does not judge himself in what he approves. But whoever makes a distinction, if he eats, is condemned, because it is not from faith. Whatever is not from faith is sin.”

We understand that this judgment was pronounced not merely to distinguish the kinds and differences of foods, but to remove every ambiguity and duplicity, so that we may not be children, tossed about by every wind of doctrine, but sound and steadfast in faith and firm in apostolic teaching.

> “For a double-minded man is unstable in all his ways, and the one who hesitates is like a wave of the sea, driven and tossed by the wind” (James 1).

[Col. 1199D] Therefore let that man not think that he receives anything from the Lord, for Truth itself says in the Gospel:

> “Amen, I say to you: whatever you ask for when you pray, believe that you will receive it, and it will be done for you. For all things are possible to the one who believes” (Mark 11; Mark 9),

because true faith saves the one who rightly believes; and the righteous person lives by his faith—namely, the faith that works through love.

The wisdom of the holy Fathers provided this for their successors, and the sacred authority of the canons established it: that dissension and schisms should not arise in the Church of Christ, but rather that unity and the harmony of peace should prevail there. Therefore it assigned to each order its office according to its measure, so that, through the practice of humility and love, Christian peace and concord might endure among the people of God.

[Col. 1200A] Concerning this, Truth itself, urging the disciples to imitate him, says:

> “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matthew 11).

This yoke joins the faithful together through charity; it does not scatter them through contention. This burden does not oppress the one who bears it through the heaviness of its weight; rather, through the comfort of consolation, it lifts and supports him.

It is therefore of no benefit to these reprovers and empty-talking teachers that, in defending their error, they try to take their argument from the Acts of the Apostles: that Peter and John were sent by the apostles from Jerusalem into Samaria to lay hands on those who were being baptized by Philip [Col. 1200B], so that they might receive the Holy Spirit, since this could not otherwise be done than by the apostles’ completing and perfecting what their minister had rightly begun.

For this Philip was not one of the Twelve, but one of the seven deacons who had shortly before been ordained by the apostles. He is also counted first after Stephen in the catalogue of the seven Levites. Hence, after Stephen’s death, the historian seems immediately to turn to describing Philip’s activities, saying:

> “Now on that day a great persecution arose against the church that was at Jerusalem, and all were scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles” (Acts 8).

And shortly afterward:

> “Those therefore who had been scattered went about preaching the word of God. Philip [Col. 1200C], going down to the city of Samaria, proclaimed Christ to them. The crowds paid close attention to what Philip said, hearing and seeing with one accord the signs that he performed. For many of those who had unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, came out; and many paralytics and lame people were healed. And there was great joy in that city” (ibid.).

And not long afterward:

> “When the apostles who were in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. When they had come, they prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit. For he had not yet come upon any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Then they laid [Col. 1200D] hands upon them, and they received the Holy Spirit” (ibid.).

The same Philip also baptized the eunuch of “Candace, queen of the Ethiopians,” as the narrative goes on to relate. After his departure, Philip “went through all the cities, preaching the gospel, until he came to Caesarea” (Acts 8).

Luke also mentions him elsewhere, after recounting Paul’s journey to Jerusalem, saying:

> “The next day we departed and came to Caesarea. Entering the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, we stayed with him. He had four unmarried daughters who prophesied” (Acts 21).

From this it is evident that this Philip was neither a bishop [Col. 1201A] nor a chorepiscopus, but only a deacon and evangelist. If he had been a chorepiscopus, the historian would certainly not have passed over this in silence.

The apostles had not yet separated from one another in order to ordain bishops or chorepiscopi in the individual provinces or cities. They remained only in Jerusalem, preaching the word of God, until, through the direction of the Holy Spirit, they were sent throughout the world to preach to the Gentiles.

Thus the entire ecclesiastical order, distributed in each place according to their arrangement, has been preserved in the Catholic Church to this day. Just as one faith, one baptism, and one religion are held by Christians throughout the whole world, so, by the distribution of the one and same Holy Spirit, peace and concord are everywhere firmly strengthened among God’s elect, and every form of discord is driven far away.

For, according to the Apostle (Romans 2):

> “All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God; but whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him.”

Therefore the same teacher of the Gentiles admonishes us, saying (Ephesians 4):

> “I, a prisoner in the Lord, therefore beseech you to walk worthily of the calling to which you have been called, with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling.”

It is fitting for all the faithful [Col. 1201C] and members of Christ’s body to anticipate one another in honor and to bear with one another, lest, contrary to the Apostle, they “become desirous of empty glory, provoking one another and envying one another” (Galatians 5). Rather, let them all be of one mind in prayer, “sympathetic, loving the brotherhood, compassionate, humble” (1 Peter 3), doing nothing through contention, because God is not a God of dissension but of peace.

This alone is granted to us as the rule of belief by the Lord’s command: that we strive to enter through the narrow gate and attend to the narrow way that leads to life, not the broad and spacious way that leads to death.

For if we display signs of good devotion and gentleness through the duties of humility and obedience, becoming true imitators of God, we shall follow the example of Christ the Lord. While we were still sinners, he “died for us, ungodly servants: the righteous for the unrighteous, so that he might offer us to God, put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit” (1 Peter 3). He “destroyed death and brought [Col. 1201D] life and incorruption to light through the Gospel” (2 Timothy 1).

Exalted among the angels and humble among human beings, he wished to serve, not to be served. Therefore, at the mystical supper, he washed the feet of his disciples and wiped them with the linen cloth with which he was girded. He ate with tax collectors and sinners; he allowed a sinful woman to approach him and consented that she wash his feet with her tears and wipe them with her hair, fearing nothing of the Pharisees’ superstitious reproach. For this reason he answered their unjust complaints in these words:

> “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7).

And again:

> “I have not come,” he says, “to call the righteous, but sinners” (Mark 2).

And elsewhere:

> “The Son of Man has come to save what was lost” (Matthew 18).

And again:

> “The Son of Man did not come to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him” (John 3).

But if, despising our other brothers [Col. 1202A] and fellow servants, we wish to be raised on high and desire to appear to human beings as the only powerful and glorious ones, we unquestionably imitate the boasting of him who, despising the other saints, wished to be exalted like God over the ranks of the angels—not through humility but through arrogance—when he said:

> “I will ascend into heaven; above the heights of the clouds I will set my throne toward the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14).

Therefore the treacherous dragon, deservedly cast down from angelic exaltation into the Tartarus of hell, dragged with him a third of the stars. There, if we follow his folly, we too, expelled from the fellowship of the saints because of our proud minds, shall suffer eternal punishments in Gehenna with him.

How both prelates and subjects ought to conduct themselves, [Col. 1202B] Peter, the pastor of the Church, admonishes in his Epistle:

> “Therefore I exhort the elders among you, as a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, and as one who shares in the glory that is to be revealed: shepherd the flock of God that is among you, overseeing it not under compulsion but willingly, according to God; not for the sake of shameful gain but eagerly; not as domineering over the clergy, but becoming an example to the flock from the heart. And when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory. Likewise, young men, be subject to the elders. And all of you inculcate humility toward one another [Col. 1202C], because God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (1 Peter 5).

Therefore it seems necessary to me that we all humble ourselves under the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt us at the time of visitation. Whoever recognizes that he has been placed in a higher dignity by divine election should regard his fellow soldiers and ministers as worthy of all honor and, out of mutual love, give them the opportunity to accomplish and perform good works. For the days will come when not honors and dignities but the actions of good works will be required.

The Son of God will come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will repay each according to his works.

> “We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may render an account of the things done in the body, whether good or evil” (Romans 14; 2 Corinthians 5).

But the one who is of a lower rank [Col. 1202D] should not, in arrogance, attempt to desire greater things that do not belong to him. Rather, he should be content with the office that divine ordering has chosen to confer upon him. By believing rightly, teaching correctly, and acting well, he should advance daily toward God, so that he may obtain the good reward of his ministry.

For “the one who ministers well acquires for himself a good standing.” Hence Truth itself says:

> “Whoever ministers to me, let him follow me; and where I am, there my minister will be also. If anyone ministers to me, my Father will honor him” (John 12).

And elsewhere he says:

> “I will,” says the Father, “that where I am, there my minister also may be.”

[Col. 1203A] It is a great honor to be Christ’s minister. Therefore a great reward follows those who minister well, so that they may rejoice without end with Christ and his holy angels in heavenly blessedness. For this reason it is not fitting for Christ’s servants to contend over the superiority of honor, but rather to compete in the usefulness of sound preaching and the constancy of good works, so that Christ’s people may hear from their mouths the word of right faith and see in their actions a good example through the mark of humility.

For, according to the sentence of Truth:

> “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Matthew 11).

Those who have received a rank of honor in Christ’s Church [Col. 1203B] should hear the Lord himself showing and commanding how they ought to live and what they ought to do:

> “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands, and be like people waiting for their lord when he returns from the wedding, so that when he comes and knocks they may immediately open to him” (Luke 12).

And he immediately adds what reward will follow those who act in this way:

> “Blessed are those servants whom, when the Lord comes, he finds watching. Amen, I say to you: he will gird himself, make them recline at table, and, passing by, minister to them” (ibid.).

And shortly afterward:

> “Who, do you think, is the faithful and wise steward whom the lord appoints over his household, to give them their measure of grain at the proper time? Blessed is that servant whom, when his lord comes, he finds doing so. Truly I say to you: he will set him over all [Col. 1203C] that he possesses” (ibid.).

Such a reward is not promised to sluggish and dull teachers who contend for primacy in this world and for riches, but to those who labor well and serve God worthily.
